docs.title: A
docs.text:
• Act - is the execution phase of a challenge-based or inquiry cycle, where learners move from investigation and planning into producing, testing, sharing, or implementing a response in the real world.
  • Activation - Learners are encouraged to recall and activate prior knowledge to prepare for new learning.
  • Adaptive Difficulty - Adaptive difficulty adjusts task challenge in response to learner performance so work remains demanding enough to promote growth without becoming discouraging or trivial.
  • Adaptive Learning - Adaptive learning tailors content, pacing, support, or task sequence in response to evidence about a learner's current performance, needs, or prior knowledge.
  • Adaptive Mastery Learning - Learners progress through levels of difficulty with personalized challenges and just-in-time feedback.
  • Advance Organizers - Concept maps, outlines, or visual guides that help learners structure new information before instruction.
  • Analogies - Analogies connect a new idea to a more familiar situation, structure, or experience so learners can reason about the unfamiliar in terms they already understand.
  • Analogies and prior knowledge activation - Uses comparisons to familiar concepts to support understanding.
  • Anchored Instruction - Anchored instruction situates learning around a shared, meaningful scenario or \"anchor\" that gives learners a concrete context for inquiry, analysis, and problem solving.
  • Application - Learners actively apply knowledge in meaningful tasks.
  • Application of Knowledge - Learners apply concepts to real-world problems or case studies.
  • Argument Construction - Learners develop structured arguments with supporting evidence.
  • Argumentation - Learners construct logical, evidence-based arguments to support their claims.
  • Articulation - Learners verbalize their thought processes and reasoning.
  • Assess performance - Measures learner progress and determines mastery of content.
  • Assessment - Assessment is the structured collection of evidence about learner understanding, performance, or progress for the purposes of feedback, decision making, grading, or revision.
  • Assigned Positions - Learners are assigned a specific stance on an issue and must argue from that perspective.
  • Assigned Readings - Learners engage with pre-selected texts, articles, or book chapters to build foundational knowledge.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
• Case Studies - Case studies are the element in which learners analyze a concrete scenario, incident, or example in order to reason about concepts, decisions, or consequences.
  • Case Study - Learners analyze a real or hypothetical scenario to apply concepts.
  • Case-Based Learning - Learners analyze real-world scenarios to apply theoretical concepts.
  • Challenge Identification - Challenge identification is the element in which learners or instructors surface the central obstacle, tension, or problem to be addressed.
  • Class Discussion - Structured conversations where learners analyze and reflect on content.
  • Coaching - Instructors provide individualized support and guidance.
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship - Cognitive apprenticeship is the element in which learners observe expert thinking, practice with coaching, and gradually assume more responsibility.
  • Cognitive Conflict - Deliberately introduces contradictions or challenges to a learner’s existing knowledge to provoke deeper reasoning.
  • Cognitive Load Management - Cognitive load management is the element in which instruction is designed to reduce unnecessary processing and preserve effort for learning-relevant work.
  • Collaboration - Collaboration is the short-form canonical target for learners working together toward a shared product, understanding, or decision.
  • Collaborative Decision-Making - Collaborative decision-making is the element in which learners evaluate options together and negotiate a shared choice or recommendation.
  • Collaborative Discussion - Collaborative discussion is the element in which learners build understanding together through shared talk, comparison of ideas, and negotiated meaning.
  • Collaborative Inquiry - Collaborative inquiry is the element in which learners investigate a question together through shared sensemaking and evidence use.
  • Collaborative Learning - Learners work in structured teams to solve problems and complete tasks.
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving - Learners work together to analyze and solve problems.
  • Communication Channels - Communication channels are the element in which learners use designated tools or spaces to coordinate, discuss, ask questions, and share updates during a learning activity.
  • Comparing Cases - Comparing cases is the element in which learners inspect two or more examples, solutions, texts, or scenarios side by side in order to notice meaningful similarities, differences, and governing principles.
  • Competency-Based Learning - Competency-based learning is the element in which progression is organized around demonstrated competence rather than seat time.
  • Concept Mapping - Concept mapping is the element in which learners represent concepts and their relationships visually, typically as nodes and labeled links.
  • Conceptual Overviews - Conceptual overviews are elements that present the broad structure, central idea, or organizing logic of a topic before moving into details.
  • Conceptual Questioning - Learners answer thought-provoking questions designed to challenge assumptions and deepen understanding.
  • Conceptual Scaffolding - Conceptual scaffolding is the element in which learners are given temporary structures, prompts, or representations that help them understand the underlying ideas of a domain before handling them independently.
  • Concrete Modeling - Concrete modeling is the element in which physical or tangible representations are used to make abstract relationships visible.
  • Consensus Building - Learners work collaboratively to synthesize differing viewpoints into a shared understanding.
  • Consensus Discussion - Learners work collaboratively to agree on a shared perspective or decision.
  • Contextualization - Contextualization is the element in which new ideas, texts, or tasks are framed within a meaningful situation, purpose, domain, or prior experience.
  • Continuous Review - Learning materials and concepts are revisited systematically to reinforce retention and prevent forgetting.
  • Create a Low-Stress Environment - Create a low-stress environment is the element of designing routines, norms, and spaces that reduce unnecessary anxiety during learning.
  • Create a Relaxed Learning Environment - Create a relaxed learning environment is the element of arranging social and physical conditions that support safety, calm, and participation.
  • Creating Visual Representations - Creating visual representations is the element in which learners externalize understanding through diagrams, sketches, models, or other visuals.
  • Criteria Development - Learners create rubrics or evaluation frameworks for assessment.

docs.title: D
docs.text:
• Data Analysis - Data analysis is the element in which learners inspect, interpret, organize, or transform data in order to answer questions, identify patterns, or justify conclusions.
  • Debate - Debate is the element in which learners take positions, justify them with evidence, and respond to alternatives in a structured exchange.
  • Debriefing - Debriefing is the element in which learners reflect on an activity, simulation, or performance to consolidate what happened and why.
  • Decision-Making - Learners evaluate options and make informed choices within a structured learning activity.
  • Demonstration - A demonstration presents a complete or partial model of a skill, process, or solution so learners can observe expert performance before attempting it themselves.
  • Differentiated Team Roles - Learners take on distinct roles in collaborative learning to enhance accountability and engagement.
  • Digital Learning - Digital learning is the element in which instruction, resources, or interaction are mediated through digital tools, platforms, or networks.
  • Digital Tools - Digital tools are the element in which learners use software, platforms, or digital applications to create, collaborate, practice, or receive feedback.
  • Direct instruction - Presents new content through explicit explanations, lectures, or demonstrations.
  • Discrepant Events - Discrepant events are demonstrations, observations, or scenarios that violate learner expectations in a noticeable way.
  • Discussion Prompt - A structured question or statement initiates meaningful conversation.
  • Discussion Sections - Smaller, instructor- or TA-led sessions where learners analyze and discuss course material in depth.
  • Discussion-Based Learning - Discussion-based learning is the element in which talk, interpretation, and response are central vehicles for learning.
  • Drill & Practice - Drill and practice is the element in which learners repeatedly perform a focused skill or response pattern until it becomes more fluent or automatic.
  • Dual Coding - Dual coding is the element in which verbal and visual representations are used together to support understanding and memory.

docs.title: E
docs.text:
• Eliciting Student Thinking - Encourages learners to express their ideas, reasoning, and problem-solving approaches verbally.
  • Engage - Engage is the element in which instruction opens with an activity or prompt that draws attention and establishes interest.
  • Enhance retention and transfer - Helps learners apply knowledge to new contexts through reflection and extension activities.
  • Epitome (Elaboration Theory) - A simplified version of the full concept is introduced first before elaborating on details.
  • Erroneous Examples - Erroneous examples are worked examples that intentionally contain a mistake for learners to identify, explain, and correct.
  • Evidence-Based Reasoning - Learners evaluate competing models based on real-world evidence and refine their understanding.
  • Expert Groups - Learners become subject-matter experts on a topic and teach their peers.
  • Expert Modeling - Expert modeling is the element in which a skilled performer demonstrates not only what to do, but how an expert notices cues, makes decisions, and checks quality during performance.
  • Explicit Teaching - Explicit teaching is the element in which instructors directly explain, model, and sequence key knowledge or procedures rather than leaving them to be inferred.

docs.title: F
docs.text:
• Fading - Fading is the element in which instructional support is deliberately reduced as learner competence grows.
  • Fading Scaffolding - Fading scaffolding is the element in which supports such as hints, prompts, or models are progressively reduced so that learners take on more of the task independently.
  • Feedback - Learners receive input from instructors or peers to refine their work.
  • Final Exam - A cumulative assessment evaluating learners' mastery of the entire course material.
  • Flipped Classroom - Flipped classroom is the element in which initial content exposure happens before class so in-class time can focus on application and feedback.
  • Formative Assessment - Ongoing, low-stakes assessment to provide feedback and adjust instruction.

docs.title: G
docs.text:
• Gain attention - Engages learners with an unexpected event, question, or real-world scenario to capture focus.
  • Gamification - Gamification is the element in which points, progress indicators, challenges, or other game-like structures are used to shape participation and persistence.
  • Goal Setting - Goal setting is the element in which learners or instructors establish clear targets for performance, progress, or improvement.
  • Gradual Release - Gradual release is the element in which responsibility for performance shifts from teacher or system to learner across stages of modeling, guided practice, and independent work.
  • Graphic Organizers - Graphic organizers are visual structures that help learners sort, compare, and connect ideas.
  • Group Work - Group work is the element in which learners work together on a shared task, product, or problem.
  • Guided Discovery - Guided discovery is the element in which learners investigate, infer, or notice patterns for themselves, but with prompts, constraints, examples, or feedback that keep the exploration productive.
  • Guided Inquiry - Guided inquiry is the element in which learners investigate questions or problems with structured prompts, facilitator support, or staged resources that keep the inquiry productive.
  • Guided Practice - Guided practice is the element in which learners attempt a task with active support before moving to independent work.

docs.title: H
docs.text:
• Hands-on Learning - Hands-on learning is the element in which learners manipulate materials, tools, or environments directly while applying ideas in practice.
  • Hints - Hints are partial prompts or cues that help learners continue a task without fully giving away the answer.
  • Hypertext Navigation - Learners explore interconnected digital content at their own pace.

docs.title: I
docs.text:
• Immediate Feedback - Immediate feedback is the element in which response information is delivered close to the learner's action so it can still shape the next step.
  • In-Class Activities - Learners engage in active, structured tasks during class to apply knowledge.
  • Individual Reflection - Learners independently analyze their experiences, thoughts, or learning progress.
  • Individual Response - Learners answer a question or solve a problem independently before group discussion.
  • Information Literacy - Information literacy is the element in which learners identify information needs, locate sources, evaluate credibility, and use information responsibly.
  • Inquiry and Research - Learners investigate a topic through questioning and data gathering.
  • Inquiry-Based Exploration - Learners investigate open-ended problems and generate solutions.
  • Inquiry-Based Learning - Inquiry-based learning is the element in which learners investigate questions, evidence, or problems in order to build understanding through guided exploration.
  • Integration - Learners reflect on and connect learning to their own experiences and future applications.
  • Investigate - Investigate is the element in which learners collect information, examine evidence, or test ideas to answer a question.
  • Iterative Learning - Iterative learning is the element in which learners improve through repeated cycles of attempt, feedback, revision, and retry.

docs.title: J
docs.text:
• Jigsaw - Jigsaw is the element in which parts of a topic are distributed across learners who then teach one another to assemble the whole.
  • Jigsaw Learning - Jigsaw learning is the short-form canonical target for the jigsaw-style distribution of expertise and peer teaching.
  • Journaling - Journaling is the element in which learners record reflections, observations, questions, or progress over time in written form.
  • Just-in-Time Information - Instruction is provided at the point of need rather than upfront.
  • Just-in-Time Learning - Just-in-time learning is the element in which information, guidance, or resources are provided at the moment they are needed for the task at hand rather than front-loaded in advance.
  • Justification - Justification is the element in which learners explain why a claim, choice, or solution is warranted using reasons, criteria, or evidence.
  • Justification & Argumentation - Learners defend their conclusions with evidence, fostering critical reasoning.

docs.title: K
docs.text:
• Knowledge Synthesis - Learners integrate multiple perspectives and sources to develop a cohesive understanding.
  • Knowledge-Building - Knowledge-building is the element in which learners collectively construct, refine, and extend ideas rather than only consume or repeat them.
  • Knowledge-Building Discourse - Learners engage in structured discussions to deepen understanding.

docs.title: L
docs.text:
• Learner Choice - Learner choice is the element in which learners are given meaningful options about task, process, product, or pathway.
  • Learning Management Systems - Learning management systems are the element in which course organization, materials, communication, and tracking are coordinated through an LMS.
  • Learning Outcomes - Learning outcomes are explicit statements of what learners should know, understand, or be able to do by the end of an instructional experience.
  • Lectures - Instructor-led presentations that deliver structured content to learners.
  • Literature Review - Literature review is the element in which learners gather, evaluate, and synthesize existing sources on a topic in order to understand the current state of knowledge or argument.

docs.title: M
docs.text:
• Mastery Learning - Mastery learning is the element in which progression depends on demonstrated understanding rather than time alone.
  • Mastery Progression - Learners cannot advance until they demonstrate mastery of foundational content.
  • Metacognition - Metacognition is the element in which learners monitor, explain, and regulate their own thinking.
  • Metacognitive Reflection - Metacognitive reflection is the element in which learners examine how they thought, what strategies they used, where they were confused, and what they should do next.
  • Metacognitive Strategies - Metacognitive strategies are deliberate learner moves for planning, monitoring, checking, and revising thinking during learning.
  • Metaphors - Metaphors are explanatory comparisons that map a less familiar concept onto a more familiar image or experience.
  • Midterm Exam - A structured, formal assessment given at the midpoint of a course.
  • Mission-Based Learning - Learners engage in a structured, goal-oriented challenge.
  • Model Revision - Learners refine their conceptual models based on evidence and feedback.
  • Modeling - Instructors or advanced learners demonstrate expert thinking and behavior.
  • Moderation - An instructor or facilitator guides discussions to ensure productive engagement.
  • Multimedia Instruction - Multimedia instruction is the element in which teaching combines spoken or written language with visuals, diagrams, animation, or other media in a coordinated instructional sequence.
  • Multimedia Learning - Multimedia learning is the element in which learners engage with coordinated combinations of words, visuals, audio, animation, or interactive media.
  • Multimedia Projects - Multimedia projects are the element in which learners create artifacts that combine text, visuals, audio, video, or interaction.

docs.title: N
docs.text:
• Negotiation - Negotiation is the element in which learners work through competing interests, priorities, or interpretations in order to reach a decision, compromise, or shared position.
  • Non-Examples - Non-examples are intentionally chosen instances that do not meet the target concept, criterion, or quality standard.
  • Note-Taking - Note-taking is the element in which learners record, organize, and condense information in ways that support later understanding and retrieval.

docs.title: O
docs.text:
• Observation - Observation is the short-form canonical target for instructional activities in which learners watch people, processes, or contexts carefully in order to notice patterns, behaviors, or constraints.
  • Observation/Shadowing - Observation/shadowing is the element in which learners watch practice in context in order to notice decisions, routines, and tacit moves before attempting similar work themselves.
  • Open-Ended Discussion - Facilitated dialogue where learners explore topics without predetermined answers.
  • Optional Quizzes or Discussion Sections - Supplementary activities designed to reinforce learning and provide formative feedback.

docs.title: P
docs.text:
• Part-task practice - Isolated, repeated practice of elements that require automation for efficient task performance.
  • Peer Assessment - Peer assessment is the element in which learners evaluate the work or reasoning of peers against shared criteria.
  • Peer Collaboration - Learners work together to complete tasks or solve problems.
  • Peer Discussion - Learners engage in structured conversations with classmates to explore and refine ideas.
  • Peer Explanation - Learners verbalize their thinking to peers, strengthening their own understanding.
  • Peer Feedback - Peer feedback is the element in which learners respond to one another's work with comments intended to improve revision or performance.
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review - Peer feedback/peer review is the element in which learners evaluate one another's work against criteria and provide revision-oriented feedback.
  • Peer Instruction - Peer instruction is the element in which learners explain, compare, and revise answers with one another around conceptual questions.
  • Peer Interaction - Learners engage with one another through discussions, debates, or collaborative tasks.
  • Peer Review - Peer review is the element in which learners examine and respond to one another's work using shared criteria, prompts, or examples.
  • Peer Teaching - Learners explain concepts to peers, reinforcing their own understanding.
  • Performance-Based Assessment - Performance-based assessment is the element in which learners demonstrate knowledge or skill by performing, producing, or solving something observable rather than only selecting answers.
  • Personalized Pacing - Personalized pacing is the element in which learners move through content or practice at different rates based on need and progress.
  • Perspective-Taking - Learners consider multiple viewpoints to develop empathy and deeper understanding.
  • Persuasion - Learners develop techniques to convince others using logic and evidence.
  • Position Development - Learners construct and refine their stance on an issue through evidence-based reasoning.
  • Practice - Encourages learners to apply new knowledge or skills through structured activities.
  • Pre-Class Preparation - Pre-class preparation is the element in which learners engage with readings, videos, prompts, or other materials before a live class session so that class time can focus on discussion, application, or problem solving.
  • Pre-Class Video/Lecture - Instructional content is delivered via video or recorded lecture before in-class activities.
  • Pre-Reading Activities - Pre-reading activities are tasks completed before reading in order to activate prior knowledge, establish purpose, surface key vocabulary, or prepare attention for important ideas.
  • Pre-Reading Questioning - Pre-reading questioning is the element in which learners preview a text through guiding questions before or during initial reading.
  • Pre-Seminar Preparation - Learners review content before engaging in discussion-based activities.
  • Prior Knowledge Activation - Prior knowledge activation is the element in which learners recall, surface, or organize what they already know before engaging with new material.
  • Problem Presentation - Learners are introduced to a real-world problem to analyze and solve.
  • Problem Scenario - Learners engage with a structured real-world scenario that requires problem-solving.
  • Problem Scenarios - Problem scenarios are concrete situations presented to learners as the context for inquiry, analysis, or solution development.
  • Problem Solving - Problem solving is the element in which learners identify, analyze, and respond to a challenge by generating and evaluating possible solutions.
  • Problem-Based Learning - Problem-based learning, as an element, refers to the use of an authentic or ill-structured problem as the immediate driver of inquiry, information seeking, and solution development inside a larger design.
  • Problem-Solving Tasks - Learners complete structured activities that require critical thinking and application.
  • Procedural information - Step-by-step instructions and just-in-time guidance to assist learners in acquiring procedural fluency.
  • Procedural Learning - Procedural learning is the element in which learners acquire stepwise routines, methods, or operations through guided performance.
  • Progress Tracking - Progress tracking is the element in which learners or instructors monitor advancement through goals, tasks, competencies, or milestones over time.
  • Promote a Sense of Home - Promote a sense of home is the element of creating belonging, familiarity, and social warmth within a learning environment.
  • Provide feedback - Gives learners corrective or reinforcing feedback to improve performance.
  • Provide guidance - Offers scaffolding, modeling, or examples to support learning.
  • Public Display - Public display is the element in which learner work is made visible to a wider audience in the classroom or beyond.
  • Public Product - Public product is the element in which learners create work intended for real audiences beyond the teacher alone.
  • Public Speaking - Public speaking is the element in which learners present ideas aloud to an audience with attention to clarity, organization, evidence, and delivery.

docs.title: Q
docs.text:
• Question Formulation - Learners generate their own questions to guide inquiry.
  • Quizzes - Short, low-stakes assessments that reinforce learning and provide feedback.

docs.title: R
docs.text:
• Real-World Math - Real-world math is the element in which mathematical reasoning is embedded in practical or authentic contexts.
  • Real-World Problems - Real-world problems are tasks framed around authentic issues, needs, or dilemmas outside purely academic abstraction.
  • Reassessment - Learners revisit and revise their responses after discussion or additional learning.
  • Rebuttals - Learners counter opposing viewpoints with evidence-based arguments.
  • Recall prior knowledge - Activates learners' existing mental models to connect new information.
  • Reciprocal Teaching - Learners take turns guiding discussion and questioning content.
  • Reflection - Learners analyze their experiences, actions, or decisions to deepen learning.
  • Reflection Activities - Reflection activities are structured tasks that ask learners to examine what they did, understood, or would change next.
  • Representational Drawing - Representational drawing is the element in which learners sketch, diagram, or draw structures and relationships to support understanding.
  • Research - Learners conduct investigations to explore topics, gather evidence, and develop conclusions.
  • Resource Evaluation - Learners assess the credibility and relevance of sources.
  • Resource Hubs - Resource hubs are centralized collections of materials, links, tools, or references that learners can return to during a course or project.
  • Retrieval Practice - Retrieval practice is the element in which learners recall information from memory rather than only re-exposing themselves to it.
  • Review - Learners reflect on their own or peers’ work before finalizing.
  • Revision - Learners improve their work based on feedback and self-reflection.
  • Rhetorical Strategies - Rhetorical strategies are deliberate moves learners use to persuade, frame, emphasize, appeal to an audience, or strengthen the force of an argument.
  • Role Reversal - Learners switch sides in a debate or discussion to argue from the opposite perspective.
  • Role-Playing - Role-playing is the element in which learners adopt roles and act through a scenario, interaction, or decision process from that perspective.
  • Rubric Design - Rubric design is the element in which criteria and performance levels are made explicit through a structured evaluative framework.
  • Rubrics - Rubrics are the element in which criteria and performance levels are made explicit to guide quality work and evaluation.

docs.title: S
docs.text:
• Scaffolded Inquiry - Gradually shifts learners from guided exploration to independent inquiry.
  • Scaffolding - Scaffolding is the element in which support is added temporarily so learners can perform tasks they could not yet complete independently.
  • Scenario-Based Learning - Scenario-based learning is the element in which instruction is organized around a realistic situation, case, or mission that requires learners to interpret information and make decisions in context.
  • Scientific Reasoning - Scientific reasoning is the element in which learners generate explanations, evaluate evidence, test claims, and revise models using disciplinary norms of inquiry.
  • Self-Assessment - Self-assessment is the element in which learners judge their own work, understanding, or progress against explicit criteria.
  • Self-Explanation - Self-explanation is the element in which learners explain to themselves why something is true, why a step works, or how a solution fits the problem.
  • Self-Monitoring - Self-monitoring is the element in which learners track their own attention, behavior, progress, or accuracy during learning.
  • Self-Paced Learning - Self-paced learning is the element in which learners control the rate or sequence of progress through material within a designed structure.
  • Self-Testing - Self-testing is the element in which learners quiz themselves or otherwise attempt to retrieve knowledge without immediate external prompting.
  • Seminar Format - Seminar format is the element in which learning is organized around sustained discussion of a shared text, question, or issue with facilitator support but strong learner participation.
  • Shared Documents - Shared documents are the element in which multiple learners contribute to a common editable artifact.
  • Simple-to-complex sequencing - Learning progresses from basic concepts to more detailed, complex ideas.
  • Simulations - Simulations are the element in which learners engage with realistic, model-based scenarios that approximate authentic systems or environments.
  • Small-Group Instruction - Small-group instruction is the element in which learners work with an instructor or facilitator in a reduced-size group for targeted teaching, discussion, or support.
  • SMARTER Goals - SMARTER goals are a structured goal-setting element that asks learners to define goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, evaluated, and revised or rewarded, depending on the local formulation.
  • Social Learning - Social learning is the element in which interaction with peers, models, or communities is treated as a direct source of learning.
  • Socratic Questioning - Socratic questioning is the element in which prompts are used to probe assumptions, clarify reasoning, test evidence, and extend implications.
  • Socratic Seminar - Socratic seminar is the element in which learners build understanding through text-centered questioning and discussion.
  • Solution Development - Learners synthesize information to propose and test solutions.
  • Spaced Learning - Spaced learning is the element in which practice or review is distributed over time rather than massed together.
  • Spaced Repetition - Spaced repetition is the element in which key material is revisited at strategically increasing intervals rather than massed into a single session.
  • Spiral Curriculum - Spiral curriculum is the element in which important ideas are revisited repeatedly over time, with each return expanding complexity or depth.
  • State objectives - Clearly communicates the learning goals to set expectations and focus attention.
  • Structured Academic Controversy - Structured academic controversy is the element in which learners argue multiple sides of an issue before synthesizing a shared conclusion.
  • Structured Debate - Structured debate is the element in which learners examine opposing claims using explicit roles, turn structures, evidence requirements, and response rules.
  • Structured Discussion - Structured discussion is the element in which talk is guided by prompts, roles, turns, protocols, or evidence requirements rather than left entirely open.
  • Structured Questioning - Instructors guide learners with sequenced, purposeful questions to scaffold deeper inquiry.
  • Submission - Learners submit work for assessment, feedback, or peer review.
  • Summarization and Synthesis - Learners distill key concepts from a discussion, reading, or experience.
  • Summative Assessment - Summative assessment is the element in which a learner's performance is judged at the end of a unit, course, or other instructional sequence.
  • Supportive information - Supportive information provides the cognitive strategies, mental models, and conceptual frameworks necessary for tackling complex tasks.

docs.title: T
docs.text:
• Task Management - Task management is the element in which learners organize, track, assign, or sequence work across a project or collaborative activity.
  • Team-Based Inquiry - Students work in structured groups to analyze problems, construct solutions, and reflect together.
  • Technology Integration - Technology integration is the element in which digital tools are used in direct service of learning goals, feedback, access, or collaboration.
  • Think-Aloud - Think-aloud is the element in which an instructor, peer, or learner verbalizes reasoning while performing a task.

docs.title: V
docs.text:
• Video Prompts - Video prompts are short video clips used to launch attention, curiosity, discussion, or analysis.
  • Video-Based Reflection - Video-based reflection is the element in which learners review recorded performance to analyze choices, patterns, and next steps.
  • Virtual Whiteboards - Virtual whiteboards are the element in which learners sketch, annotate, and collaborate in a shared digital visual workspace.

docs.title: W
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing - The entire class participates in discussion or presentation of ideas, often following small-group activities.
  • Whole-task performance - Whole-task performance engages learners in authentic, complex tasks that integrate multiple skills and knowledge areas simultaneously, mirroring the conditions of real-world practice.
  • Worked Examples - Worked examples are the element in which learners study complete or partial solutions before attempting similar problems independently.

docs.title: Draft
docs.text:
• Addressing Student Misconceptions - Students of all ages carry misleading or outright wrong prior beliefs into a lesson, some well-documented and predictable, others idiosyncratic — anticipating them in advance and treating them with respect even while correcting them is more effective than assuming a blank slate.
  • Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence (ABC) Model - The ABC model analyzes behavior as an environmental trigger (antecedent) producing an observable action (behavior) followed by an outcome that strengthens or weakens its recurrence (consequence) — the applied-behavior-analysis framework for identifying what is actually maintaining a classroom behavior before intervening.
  • Child-Directed Speech - Child-directed speech — exaggerated pitch, careful articulation, and simplified structure used when speaking with infants and toddlers — increases infant attention and supports early phoneme discrimination.
  • Constructed-Response Assessment Items - Completion, short-answer, and extended-response (essay) items ask students to recall and produce an answer rather than recognize one, reducing guessing but introducing a genuine scoring-reliability problem that model answers, sample-reading, and rubrics are all meant to address.
  • Digital Open Badges - Digital Open Badges are portable, metadata-rich micro-credentials that recognize discrete competencies, including informal learning that traditional grades and degrees do not capture or make transparent.
  • Learning Analytics-Driven Feedback - Learning Analytics-Driven Feedback uses models built from learner interaction data to predict at-risk learners and surface targeted feedback to learners or instructors, compensating for the reduced visibility distance and online instructors have into struggling learners.
  • Makerspace - A Makerspace is a physical or mobile space, formal or informal, where learners use digital and physical tools to design, build, and iterate on self-directed projects.
  • Open Educational Resources (The 5Rs) - Open Educational Resources are teaching materials licensed to grant free, perpetual permission to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute them — the "5Rs" test that distinguishes genuine open licensing from merely free-to-enroll access.
  • Research Data Collection Methods - Observation, surveys, and archival/content analysis are the main methods researchers use to gather data, each with a distinct tradeoff between ecological validity, depth, and cost that mirrors — but is methodologically distinct from — their use as classroom-assessment techniques.
  • Selected-Response Assessment Items - Multiple-choice, true-false, and matching items ask students to select rather than construct a response — easy to score objectively, but hard to write well, and appropriate mainly for recognition-level rather than complex learning goals.
  • Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ) - The Self-Regulation Questionnaire is a 63-item self-report instrument, built on the Miller and Brown seven-step model of self-regulation, that scores a person's overall self-regulation capacity as high, moderate, or low.
  • Specific Learning Disabilities - A learning disability is a significant, specific gap between a student's ability and one narrow area of academic achievement (reading, writing, or math) that persists despite ordinary teaching effort and isn't explained by broader intellectual, sensory, or language-acquisition factors — with dyslexia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia as the three most commonly diagnosed forms.
  • Text underlining and annotating - A study aid involving marking text to indicate importance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Act is the execution phase of a challenge-based or inquiry cycle, where learners move from investigation and planning into producing, testing, sharing, or implementing a response in the real world.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A defined challenge or problem to respond to
  • Enough prior investigation for learners to justify their action
  • A concrete product, intervention, or decision that can be observed and discussed

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Action can become performative if learners are rushed into output before they understand the problem
  • Real-world implementation may require time, permissions, materials, or external partners
  • The more public the action, the more carefully success criteria and support need to be structured

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working on authentic problems
  • Learners who benefit from applying knowledge in visible ways
  • Groups developing collaboration, decision-making, and follow-through

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Applying learning to a real or realistic context
  • Producing a justified solution, artifact, or intervention
  • Learning from implementation, feedback, and revision

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Turns planning into observable performance
  • Increases authenticity and accountability
  • Creates conditions for reflection, debrief, and iteration

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

  • A project team prototypes and tests a proposed solution with users
  • Students present and defend an action plan to stakeholders

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Adaptive difficulty adjusts task challenge in response to learner performance so work remains demanding enough to promote growth without becoming discouraging or trivial.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A way to detect current performance or readiness
  • Rules or instructor judgment for increasing, decreasing, or stabilizing challenge
  • Feedback that helps learners understand why the task changed

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Poor calibration can frustrate learners or create false ease
  • Opaque adaptation can make the system feel arbitrary or unfair
  • Difficulty should change the learning challenge, not only the speed or quantity of work

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with wide variation in prior knowledge
  • Learners practicing skills that benefit from repeated attempts
  • Learners in digital environments where task sequencing can update quickly

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Sustaining productive challenge
  • Preventing boredom from under-challenging tasks
  • Reducing disengagement from overwhelming tasks

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Keeps learners closer to a productive difficulty range
  • Supports persistence by making progress visible
  • Can help systems respond to readiness without forcing a uniform pace

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:

  • Mastery Progression

  • Quizzes

docs.text:
• Game-Based Mastery Learning (e.g., Duolingo Pattern)
  • Cognitive Load Reduction (CLT + Scaffolding Approach)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A math platform raises problem complexity after consistent accuracy and lowers it after repeated errors
  • A language app adjusts item difficulty based on recent response patterns
  • An instructor offers increasingly open-ended prompts as learners demonstrate competence

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Corbalan, G., Kester, L., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2008). Selecting learning tasks: Effects of adaptation and shared control on learning efficiency and task involvement. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 33(4), 733-756. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cedpsych.2008.02.003

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Adaptive learning tailors content, pacing, support, or task sequence in response to evidence about a learner's current performance, needs, or prior knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Evidence about learner performance, progress, or misconceptions
  • A mechanism for changing sequence, support, or difficulty
  • Instructional logic that connects adaptation to actual learning goals

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Adaptation logic can be shallow if it only tracks correctness and not the kind of error or misunderstanding
  • Highly adaptive systems can be hard for instructors and learners to interpret
  • Personalization should not isolate learners from shared discussion, collaboration, or common goals

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with heterogeneous readiness levels
  • Learners needing more practice or support in specific subskills
  • Learners in digital or blended environments where progress data is available continuously

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Matching instruction more closely to current readiness
  • Supporting mastery while reducing unnecessary repetition
  • Making it easier to differentiate without fully separating learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Supports personalized pacing
  • Can route learners to more practice, feedback, or challenge
  • Helps instructors manage variation when used transparently

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Activating students' prior knowledge is usually beneficial, but it is a mixed blessing when that prior knowledge is itself misleading or wrong — a common situation at any grade level, not just among young children. A kindergartner may think the sun literally "rises" (echoing adult speech) or that the earth is flat because it looks flat from the ground; a high school student may believe a boulder falls faster than a pebble, or that an object dropped from a moving car falls straight down rather than continuing to travel alongside the car as it falls.

Because misconceptions are so common, effective teaching involves anticipating them wherever possible, which is a two-part task. First, know or guess likely preconceptions in advance so learning activities can be designed to counteract and revise them — many are well-documented by educational research and can be anticipated systematically (Tanner & Allen, 2005; Chiu & Lin, 2005), even though a busy lesson can still surprise a teacher with an unexpected one. Common documented science misconceptions include: stars/constellations appearing in the same sky position every night (counter: have students track a bright star's position weekly over several weeks); the world being flat like a pancake (counter: use a globe or software like Google Earth to show how a round Earth looks locally flat); dinosaurs and early humans coexisting (counter: construct an actual evolutionary timeline); rivers always flowing north-to-south (counter: identify real rivers flowing south-to-north, e.g. the Red River, and discuss that "south" isn't inherently "lower"); force being required to keep an object moving, not just start it (counter: explain inertia directly and demonstrate it with low-friction motion, e.g. a hovercraft or dry-ice puck); volume, weight, and size being identical concepts (counter: have students weigh objects of different sizes/volumes and compare); and seasons being caused by Earth's changing distance from the sun rather than its axial tilt (counter: model the tilt with a globe and light source, and demonstrate reduced heating at oblique angles) (Chi, 2005; D. Clark, 2006; Slotta & Chi, 2006; Owens, 2003). Some misconceptions extend beyond content facts into beliefs about people — for instance, that girls are less talented than boys at math or science, a belief some students resist giving up even though research generally does not support it (Hyde & Linn, 2006).

Second, and just as important: treat students' existing beliefs with respect, even when they include misconceptions or errors, especially when a student persists with a misconception despite instruction. Most people, students included, hold their beliefs for reasons, and appreciate having those beliefs acknowledged rather than dismissed — even a religiously-motivated disagreement with a scientific theory taught in class (e.g., objections to evolution rooted in a more interventionist view of life's origins) needs respectful acknowledgment of the disagreement, however awkward that may feel, rather than simple correction-by-authority.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Advance knowledge (from research or prior teaching experience) of the misconceptions most likely to arise for a given topic, so counteracting activities can be planned rather than improvised
  • A stance of respectful acknowledgment for a student's existing belief even while working to revise it, particularly when the belief is tied to identity, culture, or personal conviction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Some misconceptions are so deeply tied to other beliefs that students may resist revising them consciously or unconsciously — correction alone, without addressing why the belief is held, may not be sufficient
  • Idiosyncratic, student-specific misconceptions cannot be anticipated from research alone and can only be caught by attentively listening to and watching individual students

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Any learner population, since misconceptions occur at every grade level, not only among young children
  • Learners whose misconceptions are tied to identity or personal conviction, who need acknowledgment of disagreement handled with particular care

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Accurate conceptual understanding that replaces, rather than merely sits alongside, a prior misconception
  • Preservation of student trust and willingness to engage, even when a strongly held belief is being challenged

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Constructivism — misconceptions are a direct consequence of learners actively constructing understanding from incomplete or misleading everyday experience, rather than passively absorbing correct information

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:

  • Concept Mapping

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Just-In-Time Teaching's WarmUps are one concrete mechanism for surfacing misconceptions before they interfere with new instruction — see Just-In-Time Teaching (JiTT).

  • Chiu, M. H., & Lin, J. W. (2005). Promoting fourth graders' conceptual change of their understanding of electric current via multiple analogies. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 42(4), 429-464.
  • Chi, M. T. H. (2005). Commonsense conceptions of emergent processes: Why some misconceptions are robust. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(2), 161-199.
  • Clark, D. (2006). Longitudinal conceptual change in students' understanding of thermal equilibrium: An examination of the process of conceptual restructuring. Cognition and Instruction, 24(4), 467-563.
  • Slotta, J. D., & Chi, M. T. H. (2006). Helping students understand challenging topics in science through ontology training. Cognition and Instruction, 24(2), 261-289.
  • Owens, K. D. (2003). Common misconceptions in science.
  • Hyde, J. S., & Linn, M. C. (2006). Gender similarities in mathematics and science. Science, 314(5799), 599-600.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Concept maps, outlines, or visual guides that help learners structure new information before instruction. Advance organizers (Ausubel, 1968) give learners an overview of what is to come, helping them store, label, and package the content for later retention — for example, "Listen to this story and think of the three things the duckling did" primes a listener to organize what follows around a specific retrieval structure before hearing it.

Advance organizers typically appear within a broader anticipatory set — Hunter's (1982) term for the lesson-opening phase that comes right after gaining students' initial attention. Before this phase can work at all, a teacher must first secure learners' actual attention, since it's difficult to communicate a lesson's purpose while students are still settling in, talking, or distracted. Research on attention (Solso, 1988) identifies four appeals that reliably draw an attending response: psychophysical appeal (varying the color, size, intensity, or pitch of stimuli — most efficiently a teacher's own voice inflection, gesture, posture, and movement); emotional appeal (using stimuli learners already have emotional associations with — calling students by name, referencing something personal like an article of clothing, or using words from a student's native language); discrepancy appeal (novelty or surprise — a history teacher dressing in period costume, a science teacher producing an unusual smell before an experiment, a math teacher opening with an unsolvable problem); and commanding stimuli appeal (an assertively delivered instruction or agreed-upon code word that reliably gets compliance, e.g. "Now listen closely").

Once attention is secured, the anticipatory set's job is to build a genuine learning set: making the lesson's goal feel relevant, placing it in a context learners can relate to, and clearing other distracting stimuli from mind — often by having learners recall past learning through drawing, summarizing, reading a short passage, or writing, explicitly linking past and present learning. Advance organizers are one common way to fill this anticipatory-set role, though the anticipatory set is the broader concept and can also work through other retrieval-priming activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Learner attention already secured (via a psychophysical, emotional, discrepancy, or commanding-stimuli appeal) before the advance organizer is introduced, since an organizer delivered to a distracted class accomplishes little
  • An overview structure genuinely tied to the lesson's actual content, not a generic preamble

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • An advance organizer only helps if it is actually used to store and retrieve the coming content — presenting one and then failing to reference it during the lesson wastes its organizing function

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Best for conceptual and content-heavy subjects like history, STEM, and law.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Analogies connect a new idea to a more familiar situation, structure, or experience so learners can reason about the unfamiliar in terms they already understand.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A source example learners actually know well enough to use
  • Explicit explanation of which features map across the analogy
  • Follow-up clarification about where the analogy stops being accurate

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak analogies can create misconceptions if surface similarities hide important structural differences
  • Learners may overextend an analogy unless limits are named directly
  • Analogies work best as a bridge into understanding, not as a substitute for formal explanation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners encountering abstract or technical ideas
  • Learners who need support connecting prior knowledge to new concepts
  • Learners who benefit from concrete representations before formal terminology

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:

  • Building an initial mental model of a new concept
  • Improving explanation, recall, and transfer

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Makes abstraction more approachable
  • Supports comprehension and retention through meaningful comparison
  • Helps instructors expose structure, not just vocabulary

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Anchored instruction situates learning around a shared, meaningful scenario or "anchor" that gives learners a concrete context for inquiry, analysis, and problem solving.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A rich anchor such as a story, case, video, event, or scenario
  • Tasks that require learners to revisit the anchor from multiple angles
  • Enough information in the anchor to support inquiry without fully resolving the problem

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak or artificial anchors can feel decorative rather than instructionally central
  • If the anchor carries too much irrelevant detail, it can distract from the intended concept
  • Learners may need scaffolds to extract salient details from a complex anchor

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing applied reasoning
  • Learners who benefit from contextualized rather than decontextualized tasks
  • Groups working on collaborative interpretation and decision making

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Connecting concepts to realistic situations
  • Supporting transfer and problem framing
  • Encouraging inquiry, evidence use, and discussion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Makes learning goals feel purposeful and coherent
  • Supports repeated return to a common reference point
  • Creates a natural bridge between explanation and application

docs.text:
• A video case anchors a unit on environmental decision making
  • A workplace incident report anchors a safety-training investigation
  • A civic planning scenario anchors data analysis, argumentation, and presentation

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Applied behavior analysis — using behaviorist techniques to change socially important behavior (Lovitt, 1994) — begins by analyzing a behavior into three components: antecedents (the environmental events or stimuli that trigger a behavior), behaviors (what the person actually does, says, or observably does), and consequences (the outcome that either encourages or discourages the behavior's recurrence). If a behavior reliably occurs when a specific antecedent is present, that pattern implies a favorable outcome has been reinforcing it, making the antecedent a genuine "trigger" for the next occurrence.

Only observable actions qualify as "behaviors" in this sense — attitudes, values, beliefs, feelings, and self-images are not behaviors, however important they are to a student's school life. The "Hey, Dad! Watch me…" test distinguishes the two: "Watch me ride a bike" (or "do a handstand," or "solve this problem") passes, since it names something observable; "Watch me feel good about myself" (or "have a positive attitude," "be motivated," "have an interest in science") fails, since none of these describe anything a bystander could actually see.

Antecedents acquire their power to trigger behavior through repeated association with what has followed that behavior in the past. Common classroom antecedents include: seating arrangement (sitting near a particular peer is an antecedent to talking and not completing work; sitting near a window or door predicts inattention; sitting near the teacher predicts on-task work); teacher proximity (students are more likely to go off-task the farther the teacher is from them, and to work better during independent seatwork when the teacher circulates); style of asking questions (attention is higher when a teacher asks a question, pauses, scans the whole class, then calls on someone); activity transitions (disruptive behavior is more likely during transitions between activities); the nature of the activity (some students attend during whole-group discussion but disrupt during individual seatwork, or vice versa); who is leading the lesson (students may attend for the regular teacher but misbehave for a substitute or student teacher); and the teacher's manner toward students (harsh criticism, mockery, or an unjust accusation predicts talking back). Antecedents matter practically because they point toward low-profile, non-intrusive prevention: rather than interrupting a lesson to stop two students talking, a teacher can simply change their seats beforehand; rather than repeatedly calling out names from a desk, a teacher can walk the room to prevent misbehavior before it starts.

Consequences can be positive (a pleasant outcome that increases the likelihood of recurrence) or negative reinforcement (removing an aversive condition after a desired behavior, which also increases its likelihood — as when Thorndike's puzzle-box cats learned to pull a cord that opened an escape door more quickly on each trial). Teachers rarely deliberately arrange negative reinforcement, since it requires first putting a student in an unpleasant situation, which runs counter to a general preference for positive, nonaversive techniques (Donnellan & LaVigna, 1990) — but teachers frequently trigger it inadvertently. A student who wants to escape difficult work, a dull exercise, or a teacher perceived as unfair may complain, refuse work, or disrupt class to delay or avoid it; if the teacher responds by changing the assignment or removing the student to the hallway, that response has just negatively reinforced the avoidance behavior, making it more likely next time. This "negative reinforcement trap" is one applied behavior analysts (e.g. Iwata, 1987) suspect accounts for more learned inappropriate behavior than positive reinforcement does — students more often learn to escape or avoid something undesirable than to be rewarded for something appropriate.

A five-step procedure for changing classroom behavior, drawn from applied behavior analysis: (1) identify precisely both the inappropriate behavior and the appropriate behavior meant to replace it, stated positively rather than as a prohibition — "Complete your assignments," not "No talking or staring out the window" (the negatively-stated version fails the so-called Dead Person's Rule: if a dead person could satisfy the stated goal by definition, it isn't a properly stated behavioral goal); (2) identify the antecedents to both behaviors and change them — new seating, an overhead projector so the teacher's back never faces the class, reviewing rules before an activity, warm-up tasks to eliminate dead time; (3) identify what is reinforcing the inappropriate behavior and stop supplying it — ignoring attention-seeking misbehavior (extinction), ensuring peers don't attend to it, holding students accountable for incomplete work rather than shortening assignments in response to complaints; (4) set up procedures to reinforce the replacement behavior, preferring reinforcers natural to the school setting — extra homework time, lunch with a favorite teacher, extra recess, an educational game, library time, computer access — since these are available at nearly no cost and so get used more consistently than purchased rewards (see Conditioning Natural Reinforcers); and (5) use punishment only as a last resort, after the above have been tried, and under appropriate professional guidance — options in roughly increasing severity include brief time-out (10-30 minutes, appropriate only when the behavior's goal is attention rather than escape), loss of privileges, restitution (repairing, cleaning, or paying for damage), and positive practice (writing about why the misbehavior was a poor choice, or practicing the correct behavior instead).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Ability to state both the problem behavior and its intended replacement in strictly observable terms
  • Systematic observation of what precedes and follows a target behavior, rather than assuming its cause from a student's presumed personality or attitude

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Only applies cleanly to behaviors that pass the observability test — the model has nothing directly to say about attitudes, feelings, or internal states
  • A teacher can easily create or sustain a negative-reinforcement trap without realizing it, simply by responding in the way that provides the most immediate relief from a disruption
  • Negative reinforcement (removing an unpleasant condition to strengthen a behavior) is rarely deliberately arranged by teachers, since it requires first placing a student in an aversive situation

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Reinforcement Theory — the ABC model is the diagnostic front end that identifies what a reinforcement or punishment plan should actually target
  • Functional Behavior Assessment — shares the antecedent-identification logic, organizing triggers into physiological, environmental, and instructional categories

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Fading Scaffolding — the ABA five-step procedure's step 5 (fading punishment/reinforcement once behavior change is established) parallels general fading logic elsewhere in instructional design

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Kounin's Classroom Management Research — an independently developed, prevention-oriented tradition that converges on similar antecedent-management advice (arranging space and routines to prevent disruption before it starts)
  • Low-Profile Classroom Control — Rinne's anticipation phase is essentially antecedent-monitoring in practice

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Child-directed speech (sometimes called "parentese" or, informally, "baby talk") is a near-universal pattern adults adopt when addressing infants and toddlers: exaggerated vowel and consonant sounds, higher pitch, slower pace, and heightened facial expression relative to adult-directed speech. It increases infant attention and engagement, and helps infants more clearly perceive the phonemic boundaries of the language(s) around them. It also establishes an early reciprocal turn-taking rhythm between speaker and listener that anticipates conversational structure well before the infant can speak.

Infants begin life able to discriminate the phonemes of any human language, but by around 10 months this discrimination narrows to the phonemes actually present in their ambient language(s); contrasts not used in the ambient language(s) come to be treated as equivalent. Because this narrowing happens early and is influenced by the speech infants actually hear, child-directed speech during this window plausibly supports the phoneme discrimination that later underlies clear speech perception and production.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A responsive adult actually interacting with the infant — child-directed speech from a live, attentive speaker, not passive media exposure, is what the evidence supports
  • An infant who is awake, alert, and available to attend to the interaction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Prolonged, overly simplified speech beyond the toddler years can delay exposure to more complex, age-appropriate vocabulary and syntax if it isn't gradually withdrawn as the child's own language develops
  • Recorded media using exaggerated, child-directed-style speech (children's television, videos) does not substitute for responsive live interaction — the research support is specifically for reciprocal, adult-attentive speech

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Infants (birth–12 months) during early phoneme discrimination and babbling
  • Toddlers (12–36 months) during early receptive and productive vocabulary growth
  • Infants and toddlers in multilingual homes, to support phoneme discrimination across more than one ambient language

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Phoneme discrimination within the ambient language(s)
  • Early attention to and engagement with a speaking partner
  • Foundational turn-taking patterns that later support conversational exchange

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Support Early Language Development — child-directed speech is one concrete practice within this broader principle

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Constructed-response items ask students to recall information and produce their own answer rather than recognize a provided one, which reduces guessing compared with selected-response items. Two major kinds are used: completion/short-answer items (answerable in a word, phrase, number, or symbol — the same underlying format whether phrased as a statement to complete or a question to answer) and extended-response items (answers ranging from a paragraph to several pages, often called essay questions when they run long).

Completion and short-answer items are easy to construct and are sometimes called "objective" on the assumption that only one answer is correct — but unless a question is phrased very precisely, multiple genuinely correct answers often exist ("Where was President Lincoln born?" can correctly be answered "in a log cabin," "on Sinking Spring Farm," "in Hardin County," or "in Kentucky"), which undercuts that objectivity in practice. Common errors: more than one defensibly correct answer; too many blanks in one item, making it confusing rather than difficult in the intended way; and blank-length or spacing that inadvertently cues the expected answer.

Extended-response items are the most adaptable format for measuring complex learning outcomes — particularly integration and application — and, because they require writing, double as a way to assess writing skill directly. They have a reputation for being easy to write, but a genuinely well-constructed item (one clearly worded, tied to the actual learning outcome, and capable of assessing complex thinking) is hard to devise. Common errors: an ambiguous question that gives students no real guidance on what's being asked (leaving them free to answer "yes" or "no," or to address only one of several plausible dimensions of the topic); scoring without a rubric, so the same teacher scores the same response differently depending on unrelated factors (unexpected responses, irrelevant information, grammatical errors); a "halo" effect from grading one student's whole test at once rather than one question across all students at once, so accumulated impressions of a given student bleed into how later answers on the same paper are scored; and offering students a choice of prompts, which undermines score comparability since students are no longer really taking the same test.

The central disadvantage of extended-response items is unreliable scoring: different teachers can score an identical response differently, and the same teacher can score the same response differently on different occasions (Linn & Miller, 2005). Several concrete steps improve scoring reliability and validity: (1) write an outline of a model answer before scoring begins, to make explicit what students are actually expected to include; (2) read a sample of student answers first, to calibrate expectations and notice common misconceptions before scoring in earnest; (3) decide in advance how irrelevant information and mechanical errors (grammar, spelling) will be handled, rather than deciding ad hoc per paper; and (4) score using either point-scoring or a scoring rubric, rather than an unstructured overall impression. In point-scoring, specific components of an answer are each assigned a point value — useful for consistency, but prone to pulling attention toward easily-counted facts (e.g., naming risk factors) at the expense of the higher-level thinking the item may actually have been designed to assess. A scoring rubric that describes the quality of an answer at each performance level is generally the stronger alternative when higher-order thinking is the real target — see Rubrics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A genuinely clear prompt: well-constructed extended-response items make the actual task explicit through wording and, often, planning notes or hints, not through length or elaborateness alone
  • A model answer and a scoring plan (rubric or point-scoring) prepared before scoring begins, not improvised paper by paper

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Completion and short-answer items outside mathematics are poorly suited to complex learning outcomes and are frequently harder to score reliably than they first appear, since genuinely unambiguous phrasing is difficult to achieve
  • Extended-response scoring reliability degrades specifically when there is no rubric, when papers are graded question-by-question-per-student rather than one question across all students, and when choice among prompts is offered
  • Point-scoring's ease of use comes at a real cost to validity when the actual goal is higher-order thinking rather than fact enumeration

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students in a K-12 or classroom-assessment context; extended-response items are the natural choice when the learning goal itself requires integration, application, or written expression that selected-response items structurally cannot assess

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Recall and production of specific factual content (completion/short-answer); integration, application, and writing skill (extended-response)

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Rubrics — the recommended scoring structure for extended-response items when higher-order thinking, not just factual coverage, is the target
  • Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment — the scoring-reliability problem this page describes is a direct instance of that principle's reliability concerns

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A third-grade mathematics extended-response item asking students to divide books among classrooms and explain their reasoning in words (Illinois Standards Achievement Test, 2006)
  • A fifth-grade science item asking students to plan a full investigation (prediction, materials, controlled/manipulated variables, procedure) rather than just answer a single question (Washington State Assessment of Student Learning, 2004)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A demonstration presents a complete or partial model of a skill, process, or solution so learners can observe expert performance before attempting it themselves. The instructor or system makes thinking visible — articulating what is being done and why — rather than simply showing the end result.

docs.title: Design Implications
docs.text: Demonstrations reduce the cognitive burden of initial skill acquisition by giving learners a reference model to study and imitate Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]. Their value depends heavily on how thinking is made visible: narrated or annotated demonstrations that explain reasoning produce better learning than silent ones. Demonstrations should be followed by practice opportunities, since passive observation without application leads to shallow encoding Pairing worked examples with practice or fading supports transfer better than examples alone. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear, accurate model of the target performance
  • Narration or annotation that makes reasoning explicit, not just actions (Think-Aloud or written commentary)
  • A follow-on activity that requires learners to apply what they observed (Practice)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Passive observation without prompts or practice creates illusions of understanding Pairing worked examples with practice or fading supports transfer better than examples alone. [-S] — learners often overestimate how much they have learned from watching alone
  • Less effective for open-ended or creative tasks where there is no single correct approach
  • Can anchor learners to a single solution method; pairing with Non-Examples or Comparing Cases reduces this risk

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices encountering a skill or process for the first time Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]
  • Learners with limited prior knowledge who would otherwise spend effort on unguided search
  • Less beneficial for learners with strong prior knowledge, who may find explicit modeling redundant Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M]

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Procedural skill acquisition: understanding the steps of a process
  • Schema formation: building a mental model of task structure
  • Metacognitive modeling: learning what expert monitoring and decision-making looks like

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Worked Examples — a demonstration applied to a problem-solving context enacts this principle by giving learners a complete solution to study before attempting their own; the worked example is the demonstration with added reasoning annotation
  • Explicit Instruction — demonstration enacts this principle by having the expert narrate decisions aloud ("I'm choosing this approach because…"), converting tacit knowledge into observable, learnable steps rather than leaving learners to infer intent from outcomes
  • Cognitive Load Management — by externalizing each step of a task, demonstration lets learners attend to understanding the structure rather than holding intermediate states in working memory while simultaneously figuring out what to do next
  • Scaffolding — a demonstration functions as temporary external structure; the key design decision is when and how to fade it — moving from full worked examples to partial examples to problem-only as competence grows

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Practice — the necessary follow-on; demonstration without practice rarely transfers
  • Think-Aloud — the narration method that makes demonstration effective
  • Fading — progressively reduces the completeness of demonstrations as expertise grows
  • Non-Examples — contrasting a correct demonstration with a flawed one sharpens discrimination
  • Procedural Information — text or diagram form of the same function

docs.title: Patterns That Use This Element
docs.text:
• Cognitive Apprenticeship — modeling phase
  • Four-Component Instructional Design — worked examples as the demonstration component of learning tasks
  • Gagné's 9 Events — "present the content" event

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Use Worked Examples — Presents a fully solved problem with step-by-step reasoning, then asks learners to solve a similar problem. The worked example is the demonstration component.

Think-Aloud Modeling — Instructor verbalizes their reasoning while solving a problem or reading a text, making metacognitive moves visible (monitoring confusion, checking work, revising approach).

Khan Academy — Video demonstrations with narrated step-by-step problem solving, followed by practice exercises with hints. The hint system itself delivers sub-demonstrations on demand.

Codecademy — Annotated code demonstrations inline with coding exercises; learners see a working example before writing their own version.
