docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Digital badges are small digital images representing a learner's achievement within a specific domain, embedded with metadata (issuer, date, criteria/rubric, and evidence of learning) that makes what was actually learned far more transparent than a traditional grade or degree (Farmer & West, 2016). Open badges add a specific technical affordance on top of this: they can be exported to portable "backpacks" and displayed across institutions and platforms, rather than being locked into one issuing system — this portability is what separates them from closed badge systems like Khan Academy's or Duolingo's.

Farmer and West (2016) identify open badges as solving two persistent credentialing problems: they recognize competencies developed in informal settings (after-school programs, workplace training, self-directed online learning) that traditional grading structures cannot capture at all, and they make formal credentials more transparent by breaking a single opaque grade into discrete, evidenced micro-competencies. Badges have been used to serve several distinct functions beyond simple certification: as a map of learning pathways (badges sequenced to guide a learner through a domain), as a motivational and self-regulation tool (a visible, choosable goal that increases learner autonomy), and as a competency-based assessment mechanism that lets learners redo and rework a task until they meet the badge's criteria — a direct alternative to time-based, norm-referenced grading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A well-specified, evidenced set of criteria for each badge (rubric, required evidence) — this is what makes badges more transparent than a grade, and what critics argue too many "lightweight" badges lack
  • A backpack or portfolio system that supports import/export if portability across institutions is a design goal (this is what distinguishes an open badge from a closed one)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Badge proliferation ("lightweight" badges issued without rigor) can clutter the badging landscape and undermine end users' (employers', other institutions') ability to judge a badge's value — the badging community's central open problem is establishing norms for rigor (West & Randall, 2016)
  • Ecosystem recognition is difficult: a badge earns real value only when institutions or organizations outside the issuer recognize and accept it, which requires alignment of standards, requirements, and objectives that often do not naturally align across institutions
  • General awareness of badges among decision-makers (employers, admissions, HR) remains low, limiting badges' practical signaling value regardless of design quality

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in informal or blended settings whose competencies would otherwise go uncredentialed (after-school programs, vocational/work-based training, self-directed online learners)
  • Learners who benefit from increased autonomy and choice in what to pursue and demonstrate, since badge systems often let learners select which badges to work toward

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Recognition and credentialing of discrete, evidenced competencies rather than an aggregate grade
  • Increased self-direction, self-regulation, and intrinsic motivation through choice and visible incremental progress
  • Support for competency-based (mastery) assessment, where learners rework a task until badge criteria are met, rather than time-based grading

  • Self-Determination Theory

  • Teacher Learning Journeys (Penn State, NASA, and NSTA partnership) — 63 professional-development activities offered as badges and stamps, letting teachers self-regulate their own PD pathway
  • The MOUSE Squad program — badges recognizing technology skills developed by disadvantaged students in after-school settings, used as evidence on college applications

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Erroneous examples are worked examples that intentionally contain a mistake for learners to identify, explain, and correct. They are useful when the design goal is to make misconceptions visible and strengthen conceptual discrimination, not just demonstrate a correct procedure.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A correct comparison standard: Learners need criteria, prior knowledge, or a correct model to evaluate the error.
  • Explanation prompts: The activity should ask what is wrong, why it is wrong, and how to repair it.
  • Instructional safety: Learners need to treat errors as analyzable, not shameful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Absolute novices may be confused: Without a baseline model, learners may encode the wrong procedure.
  • Trivial mistakes do little: The error should illuminate a real misconception, not a typo.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with enough prior knowledge to critique a partially wrong solution.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Strengthen conceptual understanding, misconception detection, and self-monitoring.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Expert modeling is the element in which a skilled performer demonstrates not only what to do, but how an expert notices cues, makes decisions, and checks quality during performance. It is useful when learners need access to expert judgment that would otherwise remain tacit.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task with meaningful expert judgment
  • Narration or annotation that reveals expert decision points

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Experts may omit tacit moves unless prompted to make them explicit

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make expert reasoning visible and support transfer to learner performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit teaching is the element in which instructors directly explain, model, and sequence key knowledge or procedures rather than leaving them to be inferred. It is useful when learners need clarity about what to attend to and how to proceed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear target concept or procedure
  • Explanation or modeling that highlights the critical moves

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Explicit teaching without practice or feedback remains incomplete

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fading scaffolding is the element in which supports such as hints, prompts, or models are progressively reduced so that learners take on more of the task independently. It is useful when learners need a designed bridge from guided performance to independence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A scaffold that can be reduced across attempts
  • Evidence of learner readiness for less support

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reducing support too quickly can destabilize performance

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase independence while preserving successful performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fading is the element in which instructional support is deliberately reduced as learner competence grows. It is useful when the design goal is to transition from supported performance to independence without either over-supporting or abandoning learners too early.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An initial scaffold or model to reduce
  • Evidence that the learner is ready for less support
  • A planned progression from more support to less

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Premature fading can trigger failure or overload
  • Late fading can create dependence and redundancy

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support transfer of responsibility and increasingly independent performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Group work is the element in which learners work together on a shared task, product, or problem. It is useful when the task benefits from distributed reasoning, division of labor, or collaborative sensemaking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task worth doing together
  • Clear expectations for roles, contribution, or output
  • Structures for accountability and coordination

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Unequal participation is common without structure
  • Poor task design can reduce collaboration to parallel solo work

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided discovery is the element in which learners investigate, infer, or notice patterns for themselves, but with prompts, constraints, examples, or feedback that keep the exploration productive. It is useful when the goal is active sensemaking without leaving learners entirely unguided.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A discoverable pattern, concept, or relationship
  • Prompts or constraints that focus attention
  • Feedback or debrief to consolidate what was discovered

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too little structure can overwhelm novices
  • Too much structure collapses discovery into direct telling

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who can benefit from active inference when support is available.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build conceptual understanding, noticing, and transfer through supported exploration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided inquiry is the element in which learners investigate questions or problems with structured prompts, facilitator support, or staged resources that keep the inquiry productive. It is useful when the goal is inquiry with support rather than direct telling or unguided discovery.

• A question or problem worth investigating
  • Prompts, scaffolds, or resources that shape the inquiry path

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too much support can collapse inquiry into direct instruction
  • Too little support can leave learners lost

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.text: Hands-on learning is the element in which learners manipulate materials, tools, or environments directly while applying ideas in practice. It is useful when understanding depends on doing, making, testing, or experiencing rather than only discussing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:

  • Clear connection between the action and the concept or skill
  • Time for debrief or reflection after the activity

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:

  • Resource and space demands may limit implementation

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Hints are partial prompts or cues that help learners continue a task without fully giving away the answer. They are useful when the design goal is to preserve productive struggle while reducing the chance of stuckness, confusion, or abandonment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task learners can still attempt: Hints are most useful when learners retain meaningful work to do.
  • Graduated support: Strong implementations move from light cueing to more explicit help only as needed.
  • Alignment to the misconception or step: Hints need to target the actual obstacle.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Over-helping: Hints that reveal too much can bypass learning.
  • Weak targeting: Generic hints frustrate learners if they do not address the real issue.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who are engaged but temporarily stuck on a problem, procedure, or draft move.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Maintain momentum while supporting independence and strategy use.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Immediate feedback is the element in which response information is delivered close to the learner's action so it can still shape the next step. This page captures the element-level implementation of the broader immediate-feedback principle.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
In face-to-face instruction, a teacher can visually notice disengagement or confusion; a distance instructor cannot, and many learners fail to recognize their own need for help or fail to seek it even when it is available (Baker & Inventado, 2016). Educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics (LA) address this by mining the large amounts of interaction data online and distance courses generate — content-management, discussion-forum, gradebook, and clickstream data — to build models that predict which learners are at risk and to surface feedback that would otherwise depend on an instructor noticing in person.

Baker and Siemens' (2014) framework groups the relevant methods into three families most useful for distance education: prediction modeling (inferring a target variable — e.g., likelihood of dropping a course — from other data, as in Purdue's Course Signals project); structure discovery, most often social network analysis of learners' interaction patterns, used to understand collaboration quality or sense of community; and relationship mining (association rule mining, sequential pattern mining, correlation mining), which surfaces unexpected if-then patterns, such as which behavior sequences characterize successful vs. unsuccessful collaborative groups.

These models feed three uses that benefit learners directly: automated feedback to students (progress visualizations, skill-mastery indicators, misconception flags); feedback to instructors (dashboards flagging which students are at risk and why, as in Purdue's Course Signals, which paired predictions with suggested instructor interventions and measurably improved retention when instructors acted on them); and automated intervention, where the system itself adapts — selecting practice problems based on a student's inferred mastery, as in intelligent tutoring systems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Sufficient volume and quality of interaction data (content-management, gradebook, discussion, clickstream) to train and validate a model
  • A validated model — tested on data representative of the population and context where it will actually be used, since a model built on one course's population can fail on a different course even within the same institution (Baker & Inventado, 2016)
  • A low-risk ("fail-soft") intervention paired with the prediction, since no predictive model is perfect and the cost of an incorrect intervention needs to stay low

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Privacy: the same longitudinal data that enables useful long-term analysis also creates privacy exposure; there is no simple solution that fully protects privacy without discarding data that could reveal long-term harms or benefits
  • Feature engineering (turning raw logs into meaningful predictive variables) is typically the most time-consuming and theory-dependent step — a purely data-driven approach without domain theory tends to underperform one that integrates educational theory
  • Prediction models can generalize poorly across contexts (different courses, institutions, populations) if not explicitly validated for the target context

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in fully or partially online/distance courses, where instructors have fewer natural opportunities to observe disengagement or confusion directly
  • At-risk learners specifically — the primary value of prediction modeling is identifying who needs support, not universal feedback to all learners equally

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Early identification and remediation of disengagement or course-failure risk
  • Skill-level mastery tracking (e.g., "skill bars" in Cognitive Tutors) that helps learners target their own study effort
  • Improved retention and completion in distance/online programs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Immediate Feedback
  • Mastery Learning

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:

  • Immediate Feedback

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Purdue's Course Signals project — mined LMS, student-information-system, and gradebook data to give instructors near-real-time, color-coded risk indicators and suggested interventions, improving student help-seeking and retention when instructors acted on the signals
  • Cognitive Tutors' "skill bars" — visual indicators of a student's inferred mastery of specific skills, later extended to communicate suspected misconceptions
  • Social network analysis of discussion-forum interaction patterns to identify learners at risk of feeling isolated from the learning community

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Baker, R. S., & Inventado, P. S. (2016). Educational data mining and learning analytics: Potentials and possibilities for online education. In G. Veletsianos (Ed.), Emergence and Innovation in Digital Learning (pp. 83–98). AU Press. Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/educational_data_mining_and_learning_analytics

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A makerspace is "an informal site for creative production in art, science, and engineering where people of all ages blend digital and physical technologies to explore ideas, learn technical skills, and create new products" (Sheridan et al., 2014, as cited in Dousay, 2017). Makerspaces sit at the intersection of Constructivism (learning through social interaction, at the learner's own pace) and constructionism (Papert & Harel) — the idea that learning is strengthened specifically by making a tangible artifact.

Makerspaces vary along several independent dimensions (Dousay, 2017): location (permanent facility vs. mobile/pop-up), tools and technology (industrial-arts tools like woodworking and electronics vs. digital tools like 3D printers and design software, or a mix), staffing (paid personnel, volunteers, or blended), and access (open to the public, membership-based, or closed to a specific enrolled group, as most K-12 school makerspaces are). A given makerspace's profile across these four dimensions can also shift over time as it evolves.

Learning in a makerspace is driven by a learner-centered, self-regulated dynamic: the learner chooses what to make, and the responsibility for acquiring the knowledge and skill needed falls to them, supported by on-site expertise, tutorials, and materials. This structure maps closely onto problem-based learning — a makerspace project is typically an ill-structured problem (build or fix something the learner has never attempted, with many valid approaches), making the makerspace a natural, informal-learning-friendly way to bring PBL's benefits into formal curricula without needing a fully scripted PBL unit.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to relevant tools and materials (ranging from basic craft supplies to 3D printers and design software) appropriate to the projects learners want to pursue
  • On-site or accessible expertise (staff, volunteers, or peer mentors) to support learners when they get stuck, since informal making relies on help-seeking rather than a scripted curriculum
  • Tolerance for failure, experimentation, and unintentional damage to equipment or materials as a normal part of the process (Kurti, Kurti, & Fleming, 2014)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• "Learning may occur, but it is not the primary objective" (Kurti, Kurti, & Fleming, 2014, p. 8) — a makerspace's informal emphasis means formal learning outcomes are not guaranteed unless deliberately integrated with curriculum, as in the JHHS FabLab and WyoMakers examples
  • Formal integration requires school and administrative willingness to accept risk and cede some control (interdisciplinary team teaching, non-traditional assessment), which can conflict with standardized curriculum structures
  • Access-model decisions (open, membership, or closed) carry real budget, staffing-credential, and equity tradeoffs that must be resolved before a space can be sustainable

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Self-directed learners with sufficient intrinsic motivation to define and pursue their own project goals
  • Learners across the full age range, from PK-12 through adult community members, though access policy often restricts who may use a given space

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• 21st-century skills: critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and creativity (the "4Cs")
  • Discipline-specific competencies acquired incidentally through project work (e.g., ecology through urban-planning-style projects, geometry through 3D design)
  • Self-regulated learning and self-directed problem-solving

docs.title: Examples

  • The Jackson Hole High School FabLab — a closed-access, curriculum-integrated space combining industrial-arts and digital tools, used across English and other subject-area courses
  • Public library makerspaces (e.g., the Chicago Public Library's Maker Lab)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Observation is the short-form canonical target for instructional activities in which learners watch people, processes, or contexts carefully in order to notice patterns, behaviors, or constraints.

Observation also functions as a teacher's primary informal assessment tool — continuously monitoring students' learning and motivation during instruction in order to decide whether to adjust teaching in the moment (Airasian, 2005). This is demanding in practice: beginning teachers find it harder than experienced ones, since it requires improvising responsively to student needs while simultaneously tracking the lesson's own goals and plan (Borko & Livingston, 1989). Observation-as-assessment covers both non-verbal behavior (who's looking out the window during a demonstration) and what students say (comments in a group indicating confusion), and feeds a range of in-the-moment decisions: who to call on next, whether to speed up or slow the pace, when more examples are needed, and whether a behavior problem is emerging. Moving around the room helps teachers observe more effectively from more vantage points, but the sheer pace and complexity of a real classroom limits how much any teacher can actually take in this way — a real constraint on how much can be inferred from observation alone, not a failure of technique.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear purpose for what to notice
  • Prompts or criteria that focus attention

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Unguided observation may stay impressionistic

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve noticing, evidence gathering, and situated understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Wiley (2014) argues that "open" in education should be defined by open licensing, not open entry — a distinction he draws to correct what he saw as damage MOOCs did to the term. The Open University's original 1971 sense of "open" meant anyone could enroll regardless of prior achievement; MIT's 2001 OpenCourseWare initiative added a different meaning — course materials released under a license anyone could freely use. Wiley proposes a concrete test, the 5Rs, for whether a copyrightable work is genuinely open: it must grant free, perpetual permission to Retain (make and keep copies), Reuse (use the work as-is in varied contexts), Revise (adapt or modify it, e.g. translate it), Remix (combine it with other open works), and Redistribute (share the original, revisions, or remixes with others). Creative Commons licenses are the most common mechanism for granting all five permissions at once — a Khan Academy video, MIT OpenCourseWare notes, an OpenStax textbook, or a Wikipedia article under CC licensing all pass the 5R test; a MOOC that is free to enroll in but forbids copying, requires registration deadlines, and charges for a credential does not, no matter how many people can access it.

Wiley frames the value of true 5R openness as "permissionless innovation" (Thierer, 2014): when materials can be freely forked, translated, and recombined without seeking permission or paying a fee, the cost of instructional experimentation drops sharply — designers do not need to negotiate rights before trying something new. He extends the same logic beyond content alone into a proposed four-part open education infrastructure: open resources (the historically dominant case — OER itself), open credentials (advanced by Mozilla's Open Badges work), and two areas Wiley identifies as still underdeveloped — open competencies (institutions tend to treat their competency frameworks as proprietary even while promoting OER to students, which stalls collaborative development of competency-based education) and open assessments. Weller (2018) offers a complementary practical observation: OER succeeded where the earlier "learning objects" movement largely failed because it mapped onto an existing practice teachers already did (adapting a text) rather than requiring new technical packaging standards and metadata schemes — the lesson being that content-reuse innovations succeed when they need minimal new infrastructure, not when they depend on an unfamiliar standard.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A license that explicitly grants all five permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute) — anything less (e.g., "free to view but not to copy or modify") does not meet the 5R bar even if access itself is free
  • For adoption at scale: content reuse succeeds fastest when it maps onto a practice instructors already engage in (adapting an existing text) rather than requiring new infrastructure or metadata standards to be learned first

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Free enrollment (open access) is a different property from open licensing (the 5Rs) — conflating the two, as Wiley argues MOOCs did, can actually set back the broader cause of genuinely open, remixable materials
  • Competencies and assessments remain far less commonly openly licensed than content itself, even at institutions that promote OER use among their own students — this asymmetry limits collaborative innovation in competency-based education specifically

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Any learner or instructor wanting to adapt, translate, remix, or redistribute existing materials rather than only consume them as originally packaged

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Not learner-facing directly — a resource property that enables instructional designers and instructors to adapt, combine, and iterate on materials at low cost

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Digital Open Badges

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Khan Academy videos, MIT OpenCourseWare, and OpenStax textbooks under Creative Commons licenses, all passing the 5R test
  • Mozilla's Open Badges as an early instance of open credentialing infrastructure (see Digital Open Badges)

docs.text:
• Wiley, D. (2014). The MOOC misstep and the open education infrastructure. Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/open_educational_resources
  • Weller, M. (2018). Twenty years of EdTech. EDUCAUSE Review, 53(4). Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/twenty_years_of_edtech

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performance-based assessment is the element in which learners demonstrate knowledge or skill by performing, producing, or solving something observable rather than only selecting answers. It is useful when the learning target involves application, integration, or authentic performance. Typically the teacher observes both the process (e.g., data collection during an experiment) and the product (e.g., the completed report), though for some tasks (a paper drafted partly outside class) only the product may actually be visible, and for others (group interaction skills) there may be no discrete product at all.

Two related terms are often used loosely as synonyms but mean something distinct (Linn & Miller, 2005): alternative assessment describes tasks that aren't pencil-and-paper, while authentic assessment describes tasks resembling those actually done in the "real world" — and authenticity is a matter of degree, not a binary. Conversing in Japanese with native speakers while actually in Japan is highly authentic; conversing in Japanese with native speakers in a U.S. classroom is still highly authentic; conversing with the teacher in Japanese during a lesson is moderately authentic; a matching test pairing Japanese and English vocabulary is much less authentic. A five-paragraph essay is a complex performance assessment, but not a highly authentic one, since that specific format is rarely used outside school; a letter to an editor or a memo to a principal is comparatively more authentic, since those formats are genuinely used in work contexts.

Performance assessments carry real, specific tradeoffs (Linn & Miller, 2005). Their advantages: they can measure complex learning outcomes other methods can't reach; they assess process as well as product, not product alone; and well-designed ones communicate the actual instructional goal to students clearly, which tends to give them strong content validity. Their central disadvantage is that they are typically very time-consuming for both students and teachers to complete and score — which means fewer of them can be given, so if they aren't carefully planned against the full range of intended learning goals, content validity actually suffers from under-coverage even though the individual assessment task itself has strong validity. State curriculum standards can help here by specifying concretely what a performance task in a given domain (e.g., a specific level of technical skill in a dance curriculum) should actually require.

docs.text:

  • Clear performance criteria or rubric
  • Observation or artifact review

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Scoring can be labor-intensive
  • Poor rubric design can reduce reliability

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
People tend to change their behavior when they know they're being watched — the Hawthorne effect. Observational research can be done naturalistically, in the participants' natural environment where they are usually unaware they're being observed (reducing the likelihood of the Hawthorne effect), or in a laboratory setting, where the researcher can control confounding factors and distractions at the cost of ecological validity and the expense of maintaining the controlled setting. A naturalistic classroom observation loses control — a substitute teacher on the observation day, for instance, could change student behavior and skew the data — that a laboratory setting would avoid, but at the price of studying behavior somewhat removed from its natural context.

Surveys trade off in a similar way depending on question format. Highly structured, forced-choice surveys (a fixed response set like "strongly disagree" through "strongly agree," or a numeric scale) let responses be coded and analyzed quickly with statistical software, but typically yield only surface information across many variables rather than deep understanding of any one. Open-ended surveys let each participant devise their own response, which can surface deeper insight but makes comparing answers across participants much harder. Because surveys rely on self-report, they are vulnerable to social desirability bias and related inaccuracies: participants may want to project a particular image, feel uncomfortable answering honestly, misjudge their own behavior, or simply lack awareness of the behavior being asked about.

Content analysis examines existing media — old texts, images, commercials, song lyrics — to explore patterns or themes in a culture (a classic example is Ariès's 1962 history of childhood, Centuries of Childhood, and content analyses of television commercials for sexual, violent, or ageist content are a similar case). This spares a researcher the time and expense of recruiting respondents, but limits conclusions to how accurately the analyzed media actually reflects the population's real actions and sentiments. Secondary analysis (archival research) goes further and analyzes data that has already been collected for some other purpose. It similarly avoids recruiting new subjects, but the researcher must assess the quality of the original data collection and is limited to whatever questions and data the original study happened to collect — a secondary analysis cannot ask a question the original data was never positioned to answer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A method chosen to match what the research question actually needs — naturalistic observation and open-ended surveys for depth and ecological validity, laboratory observation and forced-choice surveys for control and comparability

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Any self-report method carries the risk that a participant's stated answer diverges from their actual belief or behavior, for reasons ranging from deliberate impression management to genuine lack of self-awareness
  • Content analysis and secondary/archival analysis are both limited to the population and questions the original material or dataset can actually speak to, regardless of how interesting a new question might be

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Choosing a data-collection method whose tradeoffs match the research question, rather than defaulting to whichever method is most familiar or convenient

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Research Design Taxonomy — Quantitative/Qualitative and Descriptive/Correlational/Experimental

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Observation — the classroom-assessment use of observation is a related but distinct application from the research-methodology use described here

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A researcher choosing naturalistic classroom observation over a lab setting specifically to avoid altering the behavior they want to study
  • A study using archival school-district records instead of newly collected survey data, accepting the tradeoff of being limited to whatever the district happened to record

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
In selected-response items — multiple-choice, true-false, and matching — students select a response the teacher or test developer provides rather than constructing one in their own words, so the item measures recognition rather than recall. Because results don't depend on a scorer's judgment (and so are often machine-scored), these items are called "objective," and their elimination of scoring error increases reliability. But teachers who rely on objective items exclusively risk reducing the validity of their overall assessment, since objective items aren't appropriate for every learning goal — effective assessment depends on aligning the technique to the actual goal (if the goal is for students to conduct an experiment, they should be asked to conduct one, not asked about conducting one).

True-false items suit factual knowledge — vocabulary, formulae, dates, proper names, technical terms. They're efficient (simple structure, quick to complete) and easier to construct than multiple-choice or matching items, but carry a 50 percent guessing probability, which makes it hard to interpret how much a given score actually reflects knowledge. Matching items present two parallel columns (terms, phrases, symbols, or numbers) for the student to pair up, typically with more items in the second column than the first (so a single error doesn't force a second one); they mostly measure lower-level knowledge — people and achievements, dates and events, terms and definitions — and depend on genuinely homogeneous columns, which are harder to construct than they look. Multiple-choice items are the most widely used selected-response format because, unlike true-false and matching, they can be adapted to assess higher-order thinking (application) as well as factual recall; students must recognize the correct answer rather than merely reject the incorrect one, and four or five alternatives reduce guessing well below the true-false item's 50 percent.

Common item-writing errors, by format:

Format Error Why it fails True-false Broad generalization stated as absolutely true or false A statement that's "usually" true (e.g., "The president is elected to office") ignores real exceptions (succession), making the item ambiguous True-false Opinion presented as fact A statement some people believe and others don't has no defensible true-false answer True-false Two ideas combined in one item If one half is true and the other false, students can't tell which to mark True-false / multiple-choice Irrelevant cues Absolute qualifiers ("always," "never," "all") tend to signal false items; qualified language ("usually," "generally") tends to signal true ones — students learn to exploit the pattern rather than the content Matching Non-homogeneous columns Mixing categories (e.g., a mix of dates and names) in one column lets students eliminate options by category rather than by knowing the answer Matching More than ~10 items per list Long lists (recommended range: 4-7) make the search itself the difficulty, not the content Matching Non-logical order An alphabetized or otherwise unordered second column forces time-consuming searching unrelated to the content being tested Multiple-choice Unclear stem A stem that doesn't clearly state the problem (e.g., a list of true/false facts about a country followed by "which statement is true") forces students to evaluate every alternative as its own true-false item Multiple-choice Implausible distractors An alternative anyone could rule out on background knowledge alone effectively turns a four-option item into a much easier two- or three-option one Multiple-choice Irrelevant cues A correct alternative that's noticeably longer, or grammatically mismatched incorrect alternatives, or an uneven distribution of the correct answer across positions, all let test-savvy students guess without knowing the content Multiple-choice "All of the above" Lets a student who confirms the first two alternatives as true skip evaluating the rest, and lets one confirmed-false alternative rule out the option entirely — neither behavior tests the intended knowledge

Other common item-writing mistakes cut across formats: unclear wording (leaving students unsure what's actually being asked), lifting sentences directly from the textbook or lecture notes (removing them from their original context can quietly change or obscure their meaning), and testing trivial facts (the exact year of a theorist's birth) rather than what's actually important to know.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Careful, deliberate item construction — selected-response items are easy to score but hard to write well, and most common problems stem from teachers not investing enough time in construction
  • A learning goal genuinely suited to recognition-level assessment, since aligning item type to the actual instructional goal is what makes the assessment valid in the first place

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• True-false items carry a 50 percent guessing floor that limits how confidently a score can be interpreted
  • Selected-response formats as a whole are poorly suited to complex learning outcomes like integration, application-in-context, or written expression — see Constructed-Response Assessment Items for formats built for those goals
  • Deliberately including some negative-phrased items to give students practice with a format standardized tests use is a defensible tradeoff, but should be a deliberate choice, not an accident

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students in a K-12 or classroom-assessment context; true-false's guessing floor makes it a weaker choice specifically when a precise estimate of individual knowledge matters

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Recognition-level factual, definitional, and lower-order conceptual knowledge (true-false, matching); recognition-level knowledge extending to application (multiple-choice)

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment — selected-response items trade some validity (format constrains what can be assessed) for reliability (no scorer judgment involved)

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Constructed-Response Assessment Items — the complementary item family for goals selected-response can't reach

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A true-false item testing whether "the U.S. Civil War Battle of Fort Sumter" occurred before or after a listed date, versus a poorly-worded version bundling two separate historical claims into one statement
  • A multiple-choice item testing application of the "law of diminishing returns" concept via a novel scenario, versus one merely testing recall of the definition

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ; Brown, Miller, & Lawendowski, 1999) is a self-report assessment built directly on Miller and Brown's seven-step model of self-regulation (Miller & Brown, 1991; Brown, 1998), itself built on Kanfer's foundational work (Kanfer, 1970a, 1970b). Respondents rate each item on a five-point scale (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree), covering behaviors such as goal-tracking, distractibility, follow-through, learning from mistakes, and resistance to peer conformity. Scores above 239 indicate high (intact) self-regulation capacity (top quartile); scores from 214-238 indicate moderate self-regulation capacity; scores below 213 indicate low (impaired) self-regulation capacity (bottom quartile).

Because the instrument's items map onto the seven-step model's stages (receiving information, evaluating it against norms, triggering change, searching for options, formulating a plan, implementing it, and assessing effectiveness), a low overall score can be paired with item-level review to identify which step in the self-regulation cycle is faltering for a given learner, rather than treating self-regulation as a single undifferentiated trait.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Administered as a self-report instrument; requires a respondent capable of introspecting on and honestly reporting their own habitual behavior

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Self-report format means results reflect the respondent's self-perception, which may not fully match observed behavior
  • Best used as a reflective or diagnostic starting point, not a definitive clinical or high-stakes measure

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners capable of introspective self-report, from adolescence through adulthood

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Self-diagnosis of where in the self-regulation cycle (per the Self-Regulated Learning Miller & Brown model) a learner's habitual difficulty lies, to target support accordingly

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Self-Regulated Learning — the SRQ operationalizes the Miller & Brown seven-step self-regulation model into a scorable instrument

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A learner scoring in the low range overall, but whose individual item responses cluster around "searching for options" and "formulating a plan," may benefit specifically from structured goal-planning support rather than generic motivational encouragement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: SMARTER goals are a structured goal-setting element that asks learners to define goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, evaluated, and revised or rewarded, depending on the local formulation. In this wiki, the main instructional value of SMARTER goals is not the acronym itself but the discipline it brings to making goals concrete enough to monitor and adjust.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful learning target that can be broken into observable progress markers
  • Time to define the goal clearly and revisit it later
  • Some mechanism for evaluation, feedback, or revision

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Overly rigid templates can produce compliant wording without genuine commitment
  • Not every worthwhile learning goal is equally easy to quantify
  • Goals need monitoring and feedback to matter instructionally

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners building self-regulation and planning habits
  • Novices who benefit from proximal, concrete targets
  • Adults or adolescents managing longer learning sequences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Making goals interpretable and trackable
  • Supporting progress monitoring and revision
  • Turning vague aspiration into a usable plan

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Clarifies what success looks like
  • Supports monitoring, feedback, and persistence
  • Helps instructors and learners align on the next step

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A learning disability (LD) is a specific impairment of academic learning that interferes significantly with one particular aspect of schoolwork — reading, writing, listening, speaking, or math — without necessarily affecting the others. By definition, an LD is diagnosed only after other explanations are ruled out: it is not an LD if the difficulty stems from a physical, sensory, or motor impairment, from a general intellectual impairment, or from the ordinary challenges of learning English as a second language. A genuine LD is also one that ordinary teaching effort hasn't resolved, though what counts as "ordinary effort" varies across teachers, schools, and students. LDs are by far the most common special-education category, accounting for roughly half of all students receiving special-education services and an estimated 5-20% of all students overall (U.S. Department of Education, 2005; Ysseldyke & Bielinski, 2002) — common enough that most teachers encounter at least one affected student every year regardless of grade level.

The three most commonly diagnosed specific learning disabilities are:

  • Dyslexia — difficulty in the area of reading, most often rooted in phonological processing difficulty (manipulating the sounds within words), along with rapid visual/verbal processing problems, letter reversal, difficulty reading left-to-right, and trouble associating letters with sounds. It appears to be rooted in neurological differences in the brain regions active in letter recognition, verbal response, and sound manipulation, and a number of genes have been linked to its development (National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, 2016). Treatment typically means adapting teaching methods to the student's specific problem area rather than a single universal remedy.
  • Dysgraphia — a writing disability often co-occurring with dyslexia (Carlson, 2013). It has distinct subtypes: phonological dysgraphia (inability to sound out words and write them phonetically) and orthographic dysgraphia (able to spell regularly-spelled words but not irregularly-spelled ones). Some students with dysgraphia additionally have motor-control difficulty that makes forming letters by hand hard, independent of the spelling-related subtypes.
  • Dyscalculia — difficulty specifically in mathematics, in students of otherwise average intelligence (terms in the literature include dyscalculia, mathematical learning disability, and mathematics disorder). Evaluating third-graders with dyscalculia, Cowan and Powell (2014) found difficulties concentrated in domain-general factors — working memory, reasoning, processing speed, and oral language — as well as in multi-digit skills specifically, including number-system knowledge.

Because a specific learning disability affects one narrow academic area rather than general capability, it is identified mainly during the school years, when a person's academic abilities are actively being tested and compared — once a person's job or daily life no longer requires that specific skill under testing conditions, the disability may become far less noticeable or relevant.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Ruling out physical, sensory, intellectual, or English-language-acquisition explanations before treating a persistent academic gap as a specific learning disability
  • Teaching methods tailored to the specific affected area (e.g., altered reading instruction for dyslexia) rather than a generic remediation approach

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Because LDs are narrowly scoped by definition, a student's strong performance in other academic areas doesn't rule out a genuine, significant disability in one specific one — the profile is uneven by definition, not a sign the diagnosis is wrong

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students showing a persistent, significant gap in one specific academic skill area despite otherwise-typical general ability and ordinary teaching support

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Functional reading, writing, or mathematics skill in the specific affected area, achieved through methods adapted to the disability's particular mechanism rather than generic extra practice alone

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supporting Students with Intellectual Disabilities — a useful contrast: intellectual disability affects general cognitive/adaptive functioning broadly, while a specific learning disability by definition does not

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A single struggling student can often be understood through more than one theoretical lens, each suggesting a different intervention. Consider a tenth-grader who adds two-digit numbers without carrying (42 + 59 = "911" rather than 101), correctly on some problems and not others: a Behaviorism lens suggests the incorrect strategy has simply been intermittently reinforced by occasional correct answers, so instructional credit should shift toward showing correct carrying work, not just the final answer; a Metacognition lens suggests the student is responding too impulsively and not reflectively enough (see Cognitive Styles), so having the student "think aloud" through each problem may help; and a Self-Regulated Learning/sociocultural lens suggests the student has learned the correct procedure but not consolidated it without support, calling for mentored practice within the student's zone of proximal development rather than more independent repetition.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Clearly communicates the learning goals to set expectations and focus attention. Goal statements, though written for the teacher's own planning, are properly expressed from the learner's point of view: "learners will acquire the ability to construct a convincing argument" is a goal statement, while "the teacher will show students examples of logical arguments" is not, since it describes teacher action rather than what students will learn.

There are two distinct approaches to turning a general goal into concrete objectives, and each fits different kinds of learning. The cognitive approach (Gronlund, 2004) starts with a general, long-term goal (e.g., "the student will understand the nature and purpose of photosynthesis") and adds a handful of specific indicators — example behaviors by which a student might display that understanding (e.g., explaining the process, diagramming its steps, describing its ecological effects). Critically, these indicators are meant only to be representative, not exhaustive — "it is neither desirable nor possible for a list of indicators to be complete—only for it to be representative" (Gronlund, 2004) — since the goal is genuinely broader than any fixed checklist of behaviors could capture, and different students may legitimately demonstrate the same understanding in different ways. This approach suits long-term, multi-lesson goals where specifying every possible correct behavior in advance isn't practical, but critics note the risk that a small sample of indicators may fail to actually clarify the intended goal, leaving both teacher and student uncertain what "understanding photosynthesis" really requires.

The behavioral approach (Mager, 2005) reverses the sequence: instead of starting from a general goal and sampling indicators, it starts directly from the specific, concrete behaviors students should perform, and treats that set of behaviors as the complete, not merely representative, definition of success. For a genuinely short-cycle, well-defined skill (e.g., a beginner learning to inline-skate: tying boots correctly, wearing safety gear correctly, skating 15 meters without falling, stopping within 3 meters on demand), there is no other legitimate way to demonstrate the goal — scoring 100% on a written quiz about skating would not itself count as meeting this objective, though it might satisfy a different, verbal-knowledge goal. This approach fits well-defined, short-term skills precisely because "success" can genuinely be enumerated in full, unlike a long-term understanding goal.

Neither approach is universally superior: teachers often combine or alternate between them to capture each one's advantages, using the cognitive approach for broad, long-term understandings and the behavioral approach for narrowly-defined, short-cycle skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• For the cognitive approach: a genuinely long-term, multi-lesson goal paired with a representative (not exhaustive) sample of indicator behaviors
  • For the behavioral approach: a narrowly-defined, short-cycle skill where the complete set of success behaviors can actually be enumerated

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A small, poorly-chosen set of cognitive-approach indicators may fail to clarify the general goal, leaving students unclear on what mastery actually requires
  • Applying the behavioral approach's "complete enumeration" logic to a genuinely broad, long-term understanding goal will either produce an unmanageably long list or falsely narrow the goal to whatever behaviors happen to be listed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

  • Long-term conceptual understanding (cognitive approach) versus short-cycle, well-defined skill mastery (behavioral approach)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Supportive information provides the cognitive strategies, mental models, and conceptual frameworks necessary for tackling complex tasks. It makes explicit the domain knowledge and reasoning patterns required to navigate ill-defined problems, functioning as a bridge between prior knowledge and the demands of authentic application.

docs.title: Design Implications
docs.text: Supportive information reduces extraneous cognitive load by externalizing the "why" and "how" of domain expertise Cognitive Load Theory [+S]. By providing learners with organized mental models before they engage in high-stakes problem solving, it allows them to dedicate mental resources to schema construction rather than inefficient search strategies Cognitive Load Theory [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Accurate analysis of prerequisite concepts, heuristics, and strategic reasoning patterns specific to the target task.
  • Delivery sequenced to coincide with the learner's point-of-need, ensuring information is contextually grounded.
  • Integration with concrete examples or cases to ensure abstract concepts are successfully encoded.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Decoupling information from application opportunities leads to shallow encoding; learners often fail to transfer knowledge that is not practiced in situ [-S].
  • Experts often suffer from "expert blind spot," failing to articulate foundational mental models that novices require to begin.
  • Over-provision of supportive information to advanced learners can cause redundancy effects, hindering engagement and efficiency [~S].

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice to intermediate learners entering domains defined by high cognitive complexity (e.g., sciences, systems engineering, clinical diagnostics).
  • Learners transitioning from rule-based execution to adaptive, principled decision-making.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Schema formation: building accurate mental models of system behavior and causal relationships.
  • Metacognitive growth: developing strategic awareness of how to approach multi-step tasks.
  • Facilitating transfer: providing generalizable principles that can be applied to novel, authentic problem contexts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Scaffolding — acts as an external cognitive structure that can be gradually faded as internal mental models strengthen.
  • Worked Examples — provides the theoretical framework that helps learners decode the steps within a worked example.
  • Clear Structure and Presentation — organizes complex domain knowledge into hierarchical schemas that facilitate long-term retention.
  • Explicit Instruction of Strategies — makes tacit expert heuristics and reasoning paths visible for novice imitation.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Demonstration — provides the concrete instance for the abstract principles found in supportive information.
  • Advance Organizers — primes the learner's cognitive architecture to receive incoming supportive information.
  • Case Study — serves as the primary context for applying the mental models delivered via supportive information.
  • Demonstration — visualizes the expert reasoning described in supportive information.
  • Direct Instruction — the common delivery method for ensuring foundational knowledge is complete and unambiguous.

docs.title: Patterns That Use This Element
docs.text:
• Four-Component Instructional Design — defines "supportive information" as one of four component types; it is delivered non-recurrently, before or alongside the whole learning task
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship — the modeling and coaching phases provide the conceptual scaffolding that functions as supportive information

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• 4C/ID Model (Software Training) — Sequences supportive information about logic (e.g., cell reference types in Excel) before requiring learners to build complex formulas.
  • Harvard Business School Case Method — Introduces analytical frameworks like Porter’s Five Forces as supportive information prior to the messy, open-ended case discussion.
  • Medical PBL — Provides diagnostic frameworks and decision-trees as supportive information before students are presented with undifferentiated clinical cases.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Think-aloud is the element in which an instructor, peer, or learner verbalizes reasoning while performing a task. It makes otherwise hidden judgment, strategy, and error-checking processes visible so learners can observe not just what to do, but how to decide.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful task: There needs to be a visible decision process worth narrating.

  • Connection to later learner use: Learners should apply, imitate, or critique the reasoning afterward.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Expert blind spots: Skilled performers may omit tacit decisions unless prompted.
  • Cognitive overload: Dense narration can overwhelm novices if too many ideas are packed together.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Whole-task performance engages learners in authentic, complex tasks that integrate multiple skills and knowledge areas simultaneously, mirroring the conditions of real-world practice. Rather than decomposing learning into isolated components, this element requires learners to coordinate knowledge across domains while solving meaningful, non-trivial problems.

docs.title: Design Implications
docs.text: Whole-task performance accelerates skill acquisition and transfer by embedding learning within realistic contexts, allowing learners to understand how component skills operate interdependently Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. By grounding instruction in the authentic cognitive and social demands of a discipline, this approach helps learners overcome the "transfer problem"—the difficulty of applying decontextualized knowledge to novel, complex situations. Effective whole-task design often follows a simple-to-complex sequence, where learners perform a "whole" task from the start but with high levels of support that gradually fade Scaffolding and Fading [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• High-fidelity environments or simulations that permit genuine decision-making and reflect the complexity of professional practice.
  • Instructional scaffolds, such as coaching or worked examples, to manage cognitive load during initial phases.
  • Explicit performance criteria that align with professional standards rather than arbitrary classroom benchmarks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Less effective for absolute novices who lack the prerequisite procedural fluency or vocabulary to engage with the task; initial part-task practice may be required to prevent cognitive overload Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M].
  • High implementation cost, often requiring specialized equipment, expert mentors, or longitudinal time commitments.
  • Risk of learner disorientation if task complexity is not carefully modulated or if scaffolding is removed prematurely.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Professional practitioners-in-training (e.g., medicine, law, engineering) who must navigate multidimensional roles.
  • Advanced learners who possess sufficient domain background to synthesize multiple knowledge types.
  • Learners developing "adaptive expertise," characterized by the ability to manage complexity under real-world constraints.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Complex skill integration and procedural fluency within holistic workflows.
  • Transfer of learning to ill-defined or novel professional scenarios.
  • Development of metacognitive judgment and situational awareness through repeated, integrated practice.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Situated Learning — grounds knowledge construction in authentic contexts, ensuring that skills are encoded with the environmental cues necessary for successful future application.
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship — provides the social structure for learners to observe and gradually adopt the tacit reasoning and decision-making processes of experts during complex tasks.
  • Scaffolding — manages the inherent complexity of whole tasks by providing temporary, fading supports that allow learners to experience the "whole" before they have mastered every "part."
  • Authentic Audiences and Purposes — increases learner investment by anchoring performance in real-world consequences and professional standards.
  • Explaining Their Thinking — requires learners to articulate the rationale behind their integrative decisions, fostering metacognitive monitoring and deeper schema formation.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Problem-Based Learning — drives inquiry through the structure of an authentic, ill-structured problem.
  • Simulations — provides the high-fidelity environment necessary for safe, repeated whole-task performance.
  • Coaching — offers the targeted guidance required as learners navigate integrated challenges.
  • Debriefing — essential for reflecting on the integrated decision-making process after the task is complete.
  • Part-task practice — often a necessary precursor or supplement for routine skills that must be automated to free up working memory.

docs.title: Patterns That Use This Element
docs.text:
• Four-Component Instructional Design — makes "Learning Tasks" (whole tasks) the backbone of the entire instructional sequence.
  • Merrill's First Principles — centers all instruction around a series of real-world problems (whole tasks).
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship — sequences learning from global (whole-task) to local (part-task) and back to global.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Harvard Medical School: Principal Clinical Experience (PCE) — Trainees manage patient care in real-time, integrating diagnostic reasoning, communication, and procedural skills under supervised conditions.
  • Georgia Tech Capstone Design — Students execute a complete design cycle where thermal, structural, and financial constraints must be balanced through iterative, interdependent decision-making.
  • Stanford Law School Mills Legal Clinic — Students handle real client matters, requiring the synthesis of legal research, negotiation, drafting, and ethical judgment in a single workflow.
