docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Debate format is a structured discussion pattern in which learners prepare positions, present arguments, respond to opposing claims, and justify conclusions within a defined sequence. Its instructional value comes from forcing learners to clarify claims, weigh evidence, anticipate counterarguments, and communicate under constraint. Debate is most useful when the goal is disciplined argumentation rather than simply "having opinions."

The pattern can take many forms, but the core features are role clarity, timed turns, rebuttal, and some method for judging argument quality. Well-designed debate encourages perspective-taking and evidence use; poorly designed debate can reward speed, dominance, or rhetorical performance over reasoning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A debatable question: The topic should support competing claims that can be reasoned about with evidence.
  • Preparation time: Learners need time to gather evidence and build arguments.
  • Explicit structure: Opening statements, rebuttals, and closing moves should be clearly sequenced.
  • Evaluation criteria: Learners need to know how reasoning, evidence, responsiveness, and communication will be judged.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Dominance effects: Confident speakers can overwhelm quieter learners without strong moderation.
  • Performance pressure: Public speaking demands may distort participation if supports are absent.
  • False binaries: Some topics can be oversimplified if the format forces a rigid pro/con split.
  • Argument without reflection: Learners may defend positions mechanically unless debriefing reconnects the debate to learning goals.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Argumentation: Building and defending claims with evidence.
  • Perspective-taking: Understanding and responding to opposing positions.
  • Oral communication under structure: Practicing concise, audience-aware speaking.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in humanities, civics, law, policy, and ethics contexts: Strong fit for contested questions and interpretive reasoning.
  • Groups developing discussion discipline: Debate gives discussion a more explicit argumentative frame.
  • Learners ready for evidence-based disagreement: Best when participants can tolerate challenge productively.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Dialogic learning perspectives — understanding can deepen through structured contestation of ideas.
  • Social constructivist perspectives — knowledge is sharpened when claims are publicly examined and revised.
  • Rhetorical traditions — communication improves when argument structure and audience response matter.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Debate should not be the default for every topic; some learning goals call for collaborative synthesis instead of adversarial framing.
  • Learners often need debriefing to move from winning moves to substantive understanding.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Introduce the resolution and clarify evaluation criteria.
  2. Assign positions or let teams prepare opposing interpretations.
  3. Have teams research, organize evidence, and rehearse arguments.
  4. Run the structured debate with openings, rebuttals, and closings.
  5. Debrief the quality of reasoning, evidence use, and what learners now think.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Class Discussion
  • Feedback
  • Assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Debate
  • Perspective-Seeking/Multiple Perspectives
  • Peer Discussion
  • Positive Self-Talk

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Learners can debate individually, in pairs, or in teams depending on confidence and skill.
  • Supports can include evidence organizers, speaking frames, and role rotation.
  • Some debates can culminate in position revision rather than fixed winner/loser outcomes.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Socratic Seminar
  • Structured Academic Controversy (SAC)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Civics learners debating policy approaches using evidence from assigned sources.
  • Ethics students defending competing interpretations of a professional dilemma.
  • Professional training cohorts debating tradeoffs among organizational decisions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Useful for sharpening claim-evidence reasoning and public argument structure.
  • Strongest when paired with reflection that allows learners to reconsider their initial positions.

docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Develop Understanding is a lesson-scale pattern that moves learners from initial exposure to meaningful conceptual grasp by activating prior knowledge, introducing new ideas clearly, giving guided opportunities to use them, and then connecting them to broader contexts or prior learning. The pattern is intentionally transitional: it does not stop at presentation, but it also does not assume that understanding will emerge from exploration alone.

This is a useful default pattern when the goal is conceptual understanding rather than pure recall or open-ended inquiry. It works best when instructors want a structured path from introduction through clarification and application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A concept or relationship worth understanding: Best for ideas that need more than memorization.
  • Activation of prior knowledge: Learners need a bridge from what they already know to what is new.
  • Guided use of the concept: Learners should practice applying or explaining the idea before being asked to use it independently.
  • Connection-making: The pattern should end by linking the new concept to other knowledge, contexts, or uses.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Shallow presentation risk: If the lesson stops at explanation, understanding remains fragile.
  • Weak activation: New learning is harder to integrate when prior knowledge or misconceptions are never surfaced.
  • Limited transfer: Learners may understand in one narrow form unless the pattern includes varied examples or contexts.
  • Not sufficient for highly complex skills alone: More elaborate patterns are needed when coordinated performance is the real goal.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding: Learners grasp relationships, reasons, and meaning.
  • Connection-making: New ideas are tied to prior knowledge and relevant contexts.
  • Preparedness for later practice: Learners build a foundation that supports more independent application.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners new to a concept: Good fit for first-pass understanding that still needs active processing.
  • Learners who benefit from explicit bridges: Particularly useful when misconceptions or fragmented knowledge are likely.
  • Mixed-experience groups: Activation and connection routines help different learners enter the lesson productively.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist perspectives — understanding develops by connecting new ideas to prior knowledge.
  • Generative learning perspectives — explanation, connection, and use strengthen conceptual processing.
  • Guided instruction traditions — learners often need support before independent application.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• The pattern should not become lecture plus token practice; the central work is in sense-making and connection.
  • Some topics require more iterative revisit than a single understanding-building lesson can provide.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Activate prior knowledge, intuition, or relevant experience.
  2. Introduce the new concept with a clear explanation or representation.
  3. Guide learners through examples, questions, or short applications.
  4. Check understanding and address misunderstandings.
  5. Connect the concept to broader contexts, related ideas, or future use.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Problem Presentation
  • Practice
  • Formative Assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Guided Practice
  • Creating Visual Representations
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Explicit Instruction: Vocabulary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Prior-knowledge activation can be adapted to learner experience and background.
  • Examples can vary in complexity and representation.
  • Instructors can adjust the amount of modeling or guided practice based on learner response.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Gagne's 9 Events of Instruction
  • Merrill's First Principles of Instruction

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A concept lesson that starts with a familiar example, introduces a new model, and checks understanding through short application tasks.
  • A literacy lesson that connects prior experience to a new comprehension strategy and then practices it on a brief text.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Provides a practical bridge between direct introduction and deeper later application.
  • Works well as a reusable lesson structure when conceptual clarity is the immediate priority.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:

  • Pearson, P. D., & Gallagher, M. C. (1983). The instruction of reading comprehension. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 8(3), 317-344. https://doi.org/10.1016/0361-476X(83)90019-X

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Discussion-Based Learning is a pattern in which understanding is built through structured conversation rather than one-way presentation alone. Learners make claims, test interpretations, compare perspectives, and refine ideas through dialogue guided by prompts, norms, and facilitation moves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A question or problem worth discussing
  • Norms for participation and disagreement
  • Facilitation that keeps the discussion evidence-based

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Dominance and silence problems
  • Weak prompts lead to shallow talk
  • Discussion without synthesis can feel inconclusive

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Deepen understanding through explanation and comparison.
  • Build argumentation, listening, and interpretive judgment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from articulation, critique, and collaborative reasoning.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social Learning
  • Constructivism

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Discussion needs structure; open talk alone does not ensure conceptual progress.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Pose a discussable question or text.
  2. Give learners time to prepare an initial position.
  3. Use prompts to compare, probe, and challenge ideas.
  4. Synthesize what changed or what remains contested.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Discussion Prompt
  • Peer Discussion
  • Socratic Questioning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Perspective-Taking
  • Social Learning

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Socratic Seminar
  • Structured Academic Controversy (SAC)
  • Discussion Group

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Seminar-style text discussion with facilitator prompts and synthesis.
  • Structured peer discussion after a pre-reading question.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Mercer, N., & Howe, C. (2012). Explaining the dialogic processes of teaching and learning. Learning, Culture and Social Interaction, 1(1), 12-21. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lcsi.2012.03.001
  • Resnick, L. B., Asterhan, C. S. C., & Clarke, S. N. (Eds.). (2015). Socializing intelligence through academic talk and dialogue. AERA.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Discussion Group is a structured pattern for using small-group or whole-group talk to deepen understanding, surface interpretation, and test ideas in relation to a prompt or problem. It is more than "talk in groups"; the pattern works by giving discussion a clear purpose, enough preparation, and enough moderation that the conversation stays intellectually productive.

The pattern is useful across in-person, online, synchronous, and asynchronous settings. Its main strength is that it lets learners build understanding socially while making thinking visible. Its main risk is drift: without structure, discussion often becomes uneven, shallow, or dominated by a few voices.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A worthwhile prompt or problem: Discussion needs a question that invites interpretation, reasoning, or comparison.
  • Participation structure: Learners need norms, roles, or routines that support broad contribution.
  • Facilitation: The instructor or moderator needs to steer toward evidence, clarification, and synthesis.
  • Closure or synthesis: Discussion should end with some form of consolidation, not just stop when time runs out.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Dominance and silence: Some learners may over-contribute while others withdraw without structure.
  • Off-topic drift: Discussions easily lose focus when prompts are weak or facilitation is absent.
  • Uneven preparation: Poor preparation reduces depth quickly.
  • Not every task needs discussion: Sometimes explanation or practice is more efficient than talk.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Interpretation and explanation: Learners articulate and refine understanding.
  • Collaborative meaning-making: Ideas are strengthened through response and comparison.
  • Academic discussion habits: Learners practice listening, responding, and building on others' contributions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in online, blended, or discussion-rich environments: Strong fit where shared interpretation matters.
  • Adult learners drawing on experience: Discussion lets learners connect content to existing knowledge and contexts.
  • Groups working with texts, cases, or problems: Useful when there is a common object to discuss.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — knowledge is shaped through dialogue and shared interpretation.
  • Dialogic learning perspectives — structured discussion helps learners articulate and revise thinking.
  • Collaborative learning perspectives — peers can co-construct understanding through guided exchange.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Discussion alone does not guarantee learning; prompt quality and facilitation determine depth.
  • Some learners need preparation scaffolds or alternative participation routes to engage equitably.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present a discussion prompt, text, case, or problem.
  2. Give learners brief preparation time individually or in pairs.
  3. Run the discussion with moderation, turn structure, or roles.
  4. Press for clarification, evidence, and comparison of ideas.
  5. End with synthesis, reflection, or a written takeaway.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Discussion Prompt
  • Peer Interaction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Inquiry-based Learning
  • Perspective-Seeking/Multiple Perspectives
  • Purposeful Reflection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Discussion can be synchronous or asynchronous, oral or text-based.
  • Roles such as summarizer, challenger, or evidence-checker can support different learner needs.
  • Prompts can be more scaffolded for novice groups and more open for experienced groups.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Collaborative Inquiry
  • Socratic Seminar

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Online forum discussions tied to a case, reading, or weekly question.
  • Small-group problem discussion before whole-class synthesis.
  • Professional learning groups discussing a shared scenario or decision point.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Often increases engagement and makes thinking more visible.
  • Strongest when learners are accountable for building on one another's ideas rather than posting isolated comments.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• McAndrew, P., Goodyear, P., & Dalziel, J. (2006). Patterns, designs and activities: Unifying descriptions of learning structures. International Journal of Learning Technology, 2(2-3), 216-242. https://doi.org/10.1504/IJLT.2006.010632
  • Mercer, N., & Howe, C. (2012). Explaining the dialogic processes of teaching and learning: The value and potential of sociocultural theory. Learning, Culture and Social Interaction, 1(1), 12-21. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lcsi.2012.03.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Instructional planning is normally described as if goals and objectives are chosen by educators rather than students — but this places a real burden on everyone involved: curriculum writers must be confident their specified goals genuinely matter, teachers must motivate students toward goals the students didn't choose, and students must master objectives regardless of personal interest. Critics argue this can be a serious impediment to learning (Kohn, 2004), especially for the youngest students, who may have little patience for an agenda set entirely by others (Kohn, 1999; Seitz, 2006), and in culturally diverse classrooms, where students and families may hold legitimate but unconventional expectations about what matters to learn (Banks & Banks, 2005).

Emergent curriculum responds by building instruction explicitly on interests students themselves express, rather than on goals set by curriculum documents or teachers in advance. Because it unfolds spontaneously, planning for it doesn't mean specifying objectives ahead of time — student interests are somewhat predictable in kind but not usually foreseeable far in advance (Peterson, 2002). A canonical example: a first-grade teacher plans a Halloween unit and reads a Halloween book aloud, but students turn out far more interested in one illustration — a full moon partly hidden by clouds — and begin asking why the moon is sometimes full, why it rises in different places each month, and whether the moon or the clouds are the ones actually moving. Rather than redirecting back to the planned unit, the teacher sets the Halloween plans aside, finds books on the moon and solar system, invites a local amateur astronomer to visit, and lets the class build paper-mâché moon models and a moonscape mural — the original goals aren't rejected so much as set aside in favor of something the children found more immediately compelling.

The defining feature is not that these activities could happen (a curriculum document could specify moon astronomy too) but why they happen: because the children wanted them, not because a predetermined plan called for them. This reframes the teacher's core challenge from planning activities that match preset goals to responding flexibly and sensitively as student interest becomes visible. Two practices support this responsiveness: continuous observation — watching, listening, and often keeping informal written records of student comments and activities, which doubles as an ongoing, authentic assessment of what students are actually learning; and curriculum webbing — brainstorming connections among student-suggested and teacher-suggested initiatives, done jointly with students, independently by the teacher, or jointly with co-teachers/assistants (a structure that works especially well in preschool, kindergarten, or special-education classrooms with more than one adult present; Vartuli & Rohs, 2006).

Emergent curriculum can seem, to skeptics, like a formula for curricular and management chaos, but it has proven successful particularly in early childhood and the earliest elementary grades (Seitz, 2006; Wurm, 2005). A structurally similar approach is possible even with older students: a documented high school program had students begin with personally relevant problems and experiences, discuss them with classmates, and formulate their own research questions to study more formally and systematically (Hawkins, 2006; see Socratic Seminar) — an emergent curriculum in substance, since what students studied emerged from their own expressed interest rather than being predetermined.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Continuous, attentive observation of students' expressed interests, informal enough to happen alongside ordinary classroom activity rather than as a separate assessment event
  • Genuine willingness to set aside a planned unit when student interest points somewhere else, rather than redirecting students back to the original plan
  • Curriculum webbing or an equivalent process for connecting emerging student interest to genuine learning content and activities

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Because goals are not specified in advance, the approach offers none of the accountability guarantees of a predetermined curriculum (e.g. ensuring specific standards are covered) — a real tradeoff, not a flaw to be engineered away
  • Best-documented success is concentrated in early childhood and early elementary settings; applying the same degree of open-endedness with older students in standards-driven contexts requires more structure (as in the Hawkins 2006 example, where student-generated interests were still channeled into formal, systematic study)

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: [lesson] (though a single emergent thread, as in the moon example, can extend across days or weeks)

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Motivation and depth of engagement that a predetermined curriculum's topic selection cannot reliably produce, since the topic is by construction one students already care about

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Young children (early childhood through early elementary), where the approach has its strongest track record
  • Older students in contexts flexible enough to formalize student-generated interests into structured inquiry (e.g., research projects, seminar discussion)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Constructivism [+M] — building instruction from students' own developing interests and questions is a direct application of constructivist, learner-centered planning

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Begin with a planned activity or topic as an entry point, without treating it as fixed.
  2. Continuously observe student engagement, interest, and questions during the activity, keeping informal notes where useful.
  3. When genuine, sustained student interest emerges (even in an unplanned direction), use curriculum webbing to connect that interest to viable learning content and activities.
  4. Set aside the original plan as needed and follow the emergent thread with new materials, experts, or projects.
  5. Continue observing and webbing as the topic evolves, treating the process itself as ongoing assessment of student learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The pattern is inherently responsive to whichever specific interests a given group of students expresses, rather than needing separate personalization for individual students

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Socratic Seminar — the Hawkins (2006) high-school example channels emergent, student-generated interest into the kind of structured discussion this pattern describes

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Kohn, A. (2004). What does it mean to be well educated? And more essays on standards, grading, and other follies. Beacon Press.
  • Kohn, A. (1999). The schools our children deserve: Moving beyond traditional classrooms and "tougher standards". Houghton Mifflin.
  • Seitz, H. (2006). The plan: Building on children's interests. Young Children, 61(2), 36-41.
  • Banks, J. A., & Banks, C. A. M. (Eds.). (2005). Multicultural education: Issues and perspectives (5th ed.). Wiley.
  • Peterson, R. (2002). Teaching how to read the world and change it: Critical pedagogy in the intermediate grades. In Rethinking our classrooms (Vol. 2). Rethinking Schools.
  • Vartuli, S., & Rohs, J. (2006). Selecting curriculum content that stays in children's hearts and minds. Early Childhood Education Journal, 34(1), 5-9.
  • Wurm, J. P. (2005). Working in the Reggio way: A beginner's guide for American teachers. Redleaf Press.
  • Hawkins, D. (2006). Cited in Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020), Instructional strategies for complex thinking. In Educational psychology.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Differentiating instruction. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Most educational games teach isolated facts or drill discrete skills. Epistemic games instead immerse a learner in the epistemic frame of a professional community of practice — the situated understandings, effective social practices, powerful identities, and shared values that make someone, for example, an urban planner or a soldier — so that facts arrive as a byproduct of doing the community's actual work rather than as content to memorize (Shaffer, Halverson, Squire, & Gee, 2005). In Madison 2200, players don't study urban ecology facts; they act as city planners given a budget, citizen letters, and a site to redesign, and ecological facts "come for free" because they are needed to make planning decisions. In Full Spectrum Warrior, players don't memorize military doctrine; they must think and act like a professional soldier to keep their squad alive.

Building an epistemic game requires an epistemography of the target practice — detailed study of how practitioners develop their community's characteristic ways of thinking, deciding what is worth knowing, and judging when an answer is good enough — so the game can preserve the linkages between knowing and doing that are central to that frame, while leaving out what is safe to omit. Games can target initiation (introducing novices to an unfamiliar epistemic frame, as in Madison 2200) or transformation (surfacing "expectation failures" that push already-expert practitioners to reorganize their thinking around atypical, breakdown-inducing cases).

The mechanism connects to serious play (Rieber, Smith, & Noah, 1998): learners voluntarily commit enormous time and effort to activities they find intrinsically engrossing, sometimes losing track of time entirely (Csikszentmihalyi's "flow"), and this state is most reliably produced by challenge calibrated to the learner's skill, personal choice/control, curiosity, and fantasy/identity (Malone, 1981) — exactly the ingredients an epistemic game supplies through role, narrative stakes, and a complex system to master. This distinguishes epistemic games from drill-and-practice game mechanics: the motivation here comes from inhabiting a valued identity and navigating a meaningful, complex system, not from streaks, points, or level-gates (contrast with Game-Based Mastery Learning, which uses game mechanics to sustain repetitive skill practice rather than to simulate a professional practice).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A target community of practice whose values, decisions, and characteristic reasoning can be studied in enough depth (an "epistemography") to be preserved in simplified but authentic form
  • A simulated world complex enough to require the same kind of situated decision-making the real practice demands, rather than a thin narrative wrapper around drill questions
  • Guided immersion, not unguided exploration — novices left to explore a rich environment with no support tend to form spurious patterns; the game world (non-player characters, embedded knowledge, structured feedback) must supply the guidance an expert mentor would

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• High design cost: building a genuine epistemic game requires ethnographic-depth study of the target profession's practices, far more investment than a typical educational game or gamified quiz
  • Best suited to complex, ill-structured domains with real professional stakes and judgment calls; overkill for simple factual or procedural learning better served by more direct practice
  • As of the source article's writing, few complete epistemic games existed in wide circulation — this is more a design aspiration/pattern to build toward than an off-the-shelf product category

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Unit
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Deep, transferable understanding of a complex domain via situated decision-making, rather than isolated fact recall
  • Development of professional identity, values, and judgment — not just declarative or procedural knowledge

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners for whom the target domain is complex and ill-structured enough that direct instruction on isolated facts would strip out the judgment and context that make the domain meaningful
  • Both novices (initiation into an unfamiliar epistemic frame) and experienced practitioners (transformation, via games built around atypical cases that expose gaps in current understanding)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated Learning [+S] — the mechanism by which players in Full Spectrum Warrior or Madison 2200 transfer understanding to new contexts is explicitly framed as situated learning
  • Flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi) — sustained engagement in serious play depends on calibrating challenge to skill, producing the absorbed state epistemic games aim for
  • Self-Determination Theory [+M] — self-determination (reconciling extrinsic goals with personal choice) affects the quality of learning within serious play

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Conduct an epistemography of the target community of practice: study how practitioners reason, decide what's worth knowing, and judge good answers.
  2. Design a simulated world and role that requires the same category of decisions the real practice demands, embedding necessary facts/knowledge in non-player characters, tools, or environment rather than as separate exposition.
  3. Give the learner a concrete goal or directive from within the fiction (e.g., a mayor's request, a mission briefing) that frames the whole unit of play.
  4. Let the learner act within the world, receiving in-fiction consequences and guidance (not a external quiz) as feedback.
  5. For transformation-focused games, center the scenario on an atypical case that exposes a gap or "expectation failure" in the learner's current framing of the practice.
  6. Debrief explicitly on the epistemic frame the learner practiced, connecting it back to the real-world practice and other contexts.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Simulations
  • Role-Playing
  • Feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Situated Learning
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• The complexity and specific scenario instances can scale to a learner's current expertise (initiation for novices vs. transformation scenarios built around atypical cases for experienced practitioners)
  • Learners can be given different roles within the same simulated world (e.g., different departments in an urban-planning scenario), personalizing which facet of the practice they inhabit most deeply

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Game-Based Mastery Learning — both use game structures to sustain engagement, but mastery learning targets repeatable skill drills with progression gates, while epistemic games target situated professional judgment through role and narrative stakes

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Madison 2200 — players act as urban planners redesigning a downtown pedestrian mall, learning urban ecology as a byproduct of planning decisions
  • Full Spectrum Warrior — players think and act as a professional soldier, with military doctrine distributed between the player and AI-controlled squad members
  • SimCity integrated into a high-school economics unit, where students build and defend a functioning city and encounter economic principles through the consequences of their design choices

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Shaffer, D. W., Squire, K. R., Halverson, R., & Gee, J. P. (2005). Video games and the future of learning. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/video_games_and_the_future_of_learning
  • Rieber, L. P., Smith, L., & Noah, D. (1998). The value of serious play. Educational Technology, 38(6), 29–37. Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/the_value_of_serious_play
  • Malone, T. (1981). Toward a theory of intrinsically motivating instruction. Cognitive Science, 5(4), 333–369.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit teaching is the short-form canonical pattern for clearly stating goals, demonstrating performance, and guiding practice.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Explicit Teaching
  • Modeling
  • Guided Practice

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Direct Instruction

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Rosenshine, B. (2012). Principles of instruction. American Educator, 36(1), 12-19.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Five "E" Model is a popular pattern for implementing constructivism in the classroom, defined by the Biological Science Curriculum Study (BSCS). It sequences a constructivist lesson through five stages: students Engage with the topic, Explore it directly, Explain their experience, Elaborate on the concept, and undergo Evaluateion — with evaluation feeding back into the next cycle of lessons rather than only closing the current one.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Time for genuine student-led exploration before formal vocabulary or explanation is introduced
  • A teacher willing to act primarily as facilitator during Explore, providing materials and guidance rather than direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Direct instruction should be minimal during Explore — introducing formal explanation too early undercuts the model's premise that terminology is more meaningful once a learner already has a concrete experience to attach it to

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Inquiry-driven concept formation, where formal terms and explanations are introduced after (not before) direct experience with the phenomenon

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners for whom hands-on exploration and peer discussion, rather than lecture-first instruction, is the intended path to understanding

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivism — the model operationalizes both psychological constructivism (individual discovery during Explore) and social constructivism (peer/teacher dialogue during Explain and Elaborate)
  • Sociocultural Theory — the Explain stage's introduction of formal terminology by the teacher-as-expert, after the student already has an experiential referent, mirrors scaffolded vocabulary acquisition within a zone of proximal development

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Engage — Students have their first encounter with the topic through questions, discussion, or a problem, connecting it to prior knowledge. This assesses current understanding, establishes the lesson's organizational groundwork, and stimulates anticipation.
  2. Explore — Students directly explore the topic and materials, individually or (preferably) in groups, building a common understanding and practicing communication about it. The teacher facilitates and provides materials but keeps direct instruction minimal, letting students guide their own inquiry.
  3. Explain — Students put their experience into communicable form: articulating process, sequence, and results to themselves, peers, or the teacher. The teacher introduces formal terminology only now — replacing a student's informal description (e.g., magnets "stick" to metal) with the correct term (e.g., "an attracting force") — because the student now has an experiential context to attach the term to, and because establishing common language aids both communication and the teacher's diagnosis of misconceptions.
  4. Elaborate — Students expand on the concept, make connections to related concepts, and apply their understanding to new contexts or real-world examples (e.g., extending an observation about a lamppost's changing shadow to questions about where to plant flowers for sunlight). These extensions often prompt further inquiry and new understandings.
  5. Evaluate — An ongoing process of assessing understanding throughout all four prior stages, plus a more formal assessment (test, report, presentation, rubric, or checklist) to determine whether learning objectives were met. Evaluation is not necessarily the lesson's endpoint: its results can reveal gaps needing further enrichment and can directly shape the design of future lessons, giving the whole model a cyclical structure in which questions lead to answers that lead to further questions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Constructivism — sequences discovery before formal explanation, consistent with a constructivist view of concept formation
  • Bloom's Taxonomy — the stages naturally progress from lower to higher cognitive levels, from initial engagement (Remembering/Understanding) through Elaborate and Evaluate (Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating)

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Explore-stage group size and scaffolding can be adjusted for learners needing more structure, without changing the overall five-stage sequence

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Guided Discovery Learning — shares the emphasis on direct student exploration before formal explanation
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship — both stage expert explanation and vocabulary after, not before, the learner's own attempt

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Constructivism in the classroom. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Flipped Classroom is a pattern that shifts some direct instruction or initial content acquisition outside class so that class time can be used for application, discussion, problem solving, and feedback. The key design move is not simply assigning video before class; it is reallocating synchronous time toward higher-value interaction and practice.

The pattern works best when pre-class work is tightly tied to in-class activity. If learners can skip the preparation with little consequence, or if class time still defaults to lecture, the flip becomes superficial.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Accessible pre-class materials: Learners need reliable access to videos, readings, or other preparation resources.
  • Clear accountability: Pre-class work must connect directly to what happens in class.
  • Active in-class design: Class time should focus on application, discussion, guided practice, or feedback.
  • Instructor responsiveness: Teachers need to diagnose what learners understood before or during class and adapt accordingly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Preparation compliance: The pattern weakens quickly when many learners arrive unprepared.
  • Access inequities: Device, bandwidth, time, and home-study constraints can undermine pre-class learning.
  • Weak classroom redesign: Simply moving lecture to video without improving in-class work does not realize the pattern's value.
  • Not every topic benefits equally: Some topics need more in-class modeling or explanation than the pattern assumes.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Better use of synchronous time: Reserving class for interaction, application, and support.
  • Prepared initial exposure: Letting learners encounter explanations at their own pace before class.
  • Higher-order in-class work: Using class for problem solving, discussion, and feedback rather than first exposure alone.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who benefit from replayable input: Pre-class videos or readings can support pacing and review.
  • Learners in content-heavy courses: Useful when lecture would otherwise consume most class time.
  • Groups ready for active in-class participation: The pattern assumes class time will be used productively once content exposure is moved out.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Blended and active-learning perspectives — class time is more valuable when used for interaction and guided application.
  • Self-regulated learning perspectives — learners manage part of the initial exposure outside class.
  • Formative assessment perspectives — instructors can use class time to respond to learner needs rather than broadcast content uniformly.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Flipping is a scheduling pattern, not a pedagogy by itself; the quality of pre-class and in-class design matters more than the label.
  • Some learners need stronger preparation scaffolds or alternative access routes for pre-class materials.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Assign short pre-class materials that introduce or reactivate key ideas.
  2. Use a check, prompt, or quick task to make preparation visible.
  3. Spend class time on guided application, discussion, or problem solving.
  4. Provide targeted feedback and clarification during in-class work.
  5. Close with synthesis or a follow-up task that consolidates learning.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Pre-Class Video/Lecture
  • In-Class Activities
  • Formative Assessment
  • Peer Collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Guided Practice
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Inquiry-based Learning
  • Multimodal Instruction

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Learners can pause, replay, or revisit pre-class materials at their own pace.
  • In-class tasks can be adjusted based on preparation data or quick checks.
  • Pre-class input can be offered in multiple formats when needed.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Discussion Group
  • Traditional Lecture / Reading / Midterm / Final Assessment

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Physics courses with short pre-class explanations followed by in-class problem solving.
  • Biology classes where learners watch or read background content before labs or discussions.
  • Professional training modules that move explanation into pre-work and reserve workshops for coached application.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Can improve the value of class time when the redesign is genuine.
  • Most effective when pre-class work is concise and class time is visibly more interactive than a lecture-first alternative.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bergmann, J., & Sams, A. (2012). Flip your classroom: Reach every student in every class every day. International Society for Technology in Education.
  • Bishop, J. L., & Verleger, M. A. (2013). The flipped classroom: A survey of the research. In 2013 ASEE Annual Conference & Exposition Proceedings. https://doi.org/10.18260/1-2--22585
  • Lo, C. K., & Hew, K. F. (2017). A critical review of flipped classroom challenges in K-12 education: Possible solutions and recommendations for future research. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 12(1), 4. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-016-0044-2

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Flipped Learning is a pattern that moves some initial content exposure outside class so synchronous time can be used for application, discussion, and feedback. This page serves as the canonical short-form target for links that refer to the flipped model under the broader "flipped learning" label.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Accessible pre-class materials
  • Clear connection between preparation and class activity
  • Active in-class design

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Preparation compliance is variable
  • Access inequities can weaken the model
  • Moving lecture out of class is not enough by itself

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Better use of synchronous time.
  • Replayable initial exposure before class.
  • More guided application during class.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from replayable inputs and interactive class time.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Active-learning and blended-learning perspectives.
  • Self-regulated learning perspectives.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Assign pre-class exposure to key content.
  2. Check preparation briefly.
  3. Use class for problem solving, discussion, and feedback.

docs.title: Elements Used

docs.text: • Short pre-class videos followed by in-class coached application.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bergmann, J., & Sams, A. (2012). Flip your classroom: Reach every student in every class every day. International Society for Technology in Education.
  • Lage, M. J., Platt, G. J., & Treglia, M. (2000). Inverting the classroom: A gateway to creating an inclusive learning environment. The Journal of Economic Education, 31(1), 30-43. An earlier "inverted classroom" paper credited with popularizing the model in higher education, using pre-class preparation and in-class economics experiments — a direct precursor to the model Bergmann and Sams later branded "flipped."
  • Walvoord, B. E., & Anderson, V. J. (1998). Effective grading: A tool for learning and assessment. Jossey-Bass.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Formative Assessment is a pattern in which instruction repeatedly cycles through eliciting evidence, interpreting it, and adjusting teaching or learning before final evaluation. It is a practical pattern for embedding low-stakes checkpoints into a lesson or unit.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear success criteria
  • Low-stakes evidence collection
  • Actionable follow-up for learners or instructors

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Can become compliance-oriented if nothing changes
  • Weak evidence yields weak instructional decisions

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Diagnose understanding during instruction.
  • Support timely adjustment and revision.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from frequent feedback and revision opportunities.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-Regulated Learning
  • Information Processing Theory

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Frequent checks do not help if they interrupt meaningful task flow without improving the next step.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Elicit evidence of current understanding.
  2. Interpret the evidence against criteria.
  3. Give feedback or re-teaching.
  4. Let learners revise or retry.

docs.title: Elements Used

docs.title: Key Sources

  • Clark, I. (2012). Formative assessment: Assessment is for self-regulated learning. Educational Psychology Review, 24(2), 205-249. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9191-6

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Fostering Communities of Learning is a pattern for organizing a class as a knowledge-building community rather than a collection of isolated learners. Learners investigate topics, share expertise, teach one another, and reflect on how the community's understanding is evolving. The pattern treats learning as distributed across people, roles, and artifacts, with the instructor shaping the norms and supports that let the community function productively.

FCL is strongest when the curriculum can be organized around sustained inquiry and reciprocal teaching rather than tightly scripted delivery. Its value comes from combining individual accountability with collective responsibility for improving shared understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Sustained community structure: The pattern needs enough time for learners to build trust, distribute expertise, and revisit ideas.
  • Shared inquiry topics: Learners need common problems or themes that support investigation and exchange.
  • Instructor orchestration: Teachers need to structure roles, dialogue, and synthesis so the community remains productive.
  • Opportunities for learners to teach and learn from peers: Knowledge should circulate through the group rather than only through the instructor.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Implementation complexity: FCL requires stronger classroom culture and facilitation than simple group work.
  • Participation inequities: Community language can mask uneven labor unless roles and accountability are explicit.
  • Weak fit for narrow short-term objectives: The pattern works better for sustained understanding than one-off coverage.
  • Inquiry drift: The community still needs coherent goals, prompts, and checkpoints.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Unit
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Knowledge building: Improving ideas collectively over time.
  • Distributed expertise: Learners become responsible for different parts of the inquiry and teach others.
  • Deep conceptual understanding: Topics are revisited through research, sharing, and reflection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in inquiry-rich courses: Strong fit for science, humanities, social sciences, and interdisciplinary study.
  • Groups developing collaborative responsibility: Useful when the class should function as a learning community rather than only a sequence of individuals.
  • Learners who can contribute experience and interpretation: Works especially well when learner knowledge is treated as a resource.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — understanding grows through participation in a knowledge-building community.
  • Communities-of-practice traditions — learners deepen participation through shared work, roles, and discourse.
  • Reciprocal teaching and distributed cognition perspectives — teaching others and sharing responsibility strengthen learning.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Community alone does not guarantee rigor; inquiry and contribution norms must still be explicit.
  • Some learners need more direct scaffolds before they can contribute productively to a shared knowledge community.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Launch a shared inquiry theme or problem.
  2. Organize learners into roles, teams, or areas of distributed expertise.
  3. Have learners investigate, create artifacts, and share interim findings.
  4. Use peer teaching, discussion, and reflection to improve collective understanding.
  5. Revisit the community's evolving knowledge and identify next questions.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Reflection
  • Formative Assessment
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Communities of Practice
  • Inquiry-based Learning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Mentoring/Coaching

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Learners can contribute different strengths, backgrounds, and inquiry responsibilities.
  • Roles can rotate so expertise is distributed rather than fixed.
  • Teachers can vary the degree of structure depending on how mature the learning community is.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Collaborative Inquiry
  • Jigsaw Method

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Science communities where learners investigate subtopics and teach findings back to the class.
  • Humanities courses where groups develop domain expertise and contribute to shared interpretive discussions.
  • Professional learning cohorts that collectively build a shared evidence base around practice problems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Supports deeper communal ownership of learning than simple group work.
  • Particularly valuable when knowledge building and distributed expertise are explicit goals.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Brown, A. L., & Campione, J. C. (1996). Psychological theory and the design of innovative learning environments: On procedures, principles, and systems. In L. Schauble & R. Glaser (Eds.), Innovations in learning (pp. 289-325). Erlbaum.
  • Scardamalia, M., & Bereiter, C. (2006). Knowledge building: Theory, pedagogy, and technology. In R. K. Sawyer (Ed.), The Cambridge handbook of the learning sciences (pp. 97-115). Cambridge University Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Gagne's 9 Events of Instruction is a structured lesson pattern that sequences attention, objectives, recall, presentation, guidance, practice, feedback, assessment, and transfer. It is a classic design for lessons where the instructor wants to move learners through a complete learning cycle with explicit support at each stage. The pattern is especially useful when content needs to be introduced clearly and practiced systematically within a bounded instructional sequence.

Its strength is coherence: each event sets up the next. Its limitation is rigidity. Not every domain or lesson benefits from a fully linear sequence, especially when inquiry, design, or open-ended exploration are the primary aims.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear learning objectives: The pattern assumes the lesson has defined outcomes.
  • Time for the full cycle: Attention, practice, feedback, and transfer all need deliberate space.
  • Instructional materials for each stage: Designers need prompts, examples, practice, and assessment aligned to the lesson goal.
  • A teacher or system that can provide feedback: The pattern loses force if performance and feedback are weak.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Prescriptive feel: The sequence can become mechanical if applied without judgment.
  • Weak fit for open inquiry: Highly exploratory learning may need more flexible sequencing.
  • Front-loading risk: Too much explanation before performance can reduce active processing.
  • Transfer stage often gets dropped: Many implementations stop at assessment instead of helping learners generalize.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Structured concept and skill learning: Useful for lessons that need clear sequencing.
  • Retention and transfer: The full pattern aims to move beyond exposure into later use.
  • Aligned practice and feedback: Keeping performance and correction central to instruction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in formal instructional settings: Strong fit for classroom, online module, and corporate lesson design.
  • Novices needing clear structure: Helpful when learners benefit from explicit sequencing and guidance.
  • Designers building reusable lesson templates: The pattern provides a stable instructional scaffold.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information-processing traditions — different phases of instruction support different learning processes.
  • Guided instruction traditions — learners often benefit from explicit sequencing, practice, and feedback.
  • Transfer-oriented design — retention is stronger when instruction includes recall and application stages.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• The pattern should be adapted, not followed ritualistically.
  • More complex or inquiry-heavy learning may need nonlinear returns across the events rather than one pass through them.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Gain attention.
  2. State objectives.
  3. Stimulate recall of prior knowledge.
  4. Present new content.
  5. Provide learning guidance.
  6. Elicit performance.
  7. Provide feedback.
  8. Assess performance.
  9. Enhance retention and transfer.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Guided Practice
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Formative Assessment
  • Multiple Methods of Assessment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Individual events can be emphasized differently depending on learner readiness.
  • Digital modules can adapt pacing or feedback inside the overall sequence.
  • Instructors can shorten or merge events when the lesson does not require full elaboration.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Develop Understanding
  • Merrill's First Principles of Instruction

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A short online lesson that activates prior knowledge, teaches a new concept, and checks application with feedback.
  • Instructor-led technical training that sequences demonstration, practice, feedback, and transfer tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This page is the short-form canonical target for Duolingo-style game-based mastery learning, where frequent practice, progression gates, feedback, and motivational signals are combined in a mastery sequence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Short feedback-rich practice cycles
  • Visible progression and challenge calibration

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Gamification signals must stay aligned with learning goals

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Build incremental skill mastery with persistent return to practice.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Mastery Learning
  • Game-Based Learning

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Game-Based Mastery Learning
  • Game-Based Mastery Learning (e.g., Duolingo Pattern)

docs.title: Key Sources

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Game-Based Mastery Learning combines mastery progression with game-like mechanics such as levels, streaks, rewards, adaptive challenge, and immediate feedback. The pattern works by requiring learners to demonstrate competence before moving forward while using feedback and progression signals to sustain engagement. Its value is not the game layer alone; it is the pairing of repeated practice, visible progress, and retry loops.

This pattern can be highly effective for incremental skill development, especially when tasks can be broken into frequent attempts with fast feedback. It becomes weaker when reward mechanics overshadow learning goals or when mastery thresholds are poorly calibrated.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Frequent checkable tasks: The pattern needs short cycles of attempt, feedback, and retry.
  • Visible progression: Learners need to see what they have mastered and what comes next.
  • Clear mastery thresholds: Advancement rules should reflect meaningful competence rather than arbitrary completion.
  • Adaptive or sequenced challenge: Difficulty should rise in response to growing skill.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Motivational distortion: Rewards can crowd out intrinsic interest if they become the main reason for participation.
  • Mastery frustration: Thresholds that are too strict can demotivate struggling learners.
  • Shallow gamification: Points and badges alone do not create strong learning.
  • Weak fit for complex open-ended performance: The pattern works best for modular skill progression rather than ambiguous whole-task judgment.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Incremental skill mastery: Building competence through repeated successful performance.
  • Persistence and return: Encouraging ongoing engagement across many short practice cycles.
  • Retention through revisit: Bringing earlier material back into later practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working on cumulative skills: Strong fit for language, math, notation, and other practice-heavy domains.
  • Learners benefiting from visible progress markers: Especially useful when momentum and habit matter.
  • Digital learning participants: Many implementations depend on platform-based tracking and adaptation.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Mastery learning perspectives — progression should depend on competence rather than simple seat time.
  • Feedback and self-regulation perspectives — visible progress and frequent correction support monitoring and persistence.
  • Game-based motivation perspectives — challenge, progression, and reward can sustain engagement when aligned well.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Extrinsic mechanics should support learning goals, not replace them.
  • Some domains require richer forms of assessment than rapid mastery loops can provide.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Worked examples can become redundant or counterproductive for advanced learners. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present a short challenge at an appropriate difficulty level.
  2. Give immediate feedback and allow retry or correction.
  3. Require a defined mastery threshold before progression.
  4. Reintroduce prior content through review or spaced challenge.
  5. Increase difficulty or reduce support as competence grows.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Difficulty can adapt to learner performance.
  • Different learners can move at different speeds through the same progression map.
  • Feedback and hints can be faded as mastery grows.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:

  • Traditional Lecture / Reading / Midterm / Final Assessment

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Duolingo-style language progression with retries, streaks, and review loops.
  • Mastery-based digital math practice with adaptive item difficulty.
  • Technical skill trainers that unlock later levels only after demonstrated competence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Often increases persistence and visibility of progress in modular skill domains.
  • Works best when mastery definitions are instructionally meaningful and not merely gamified gating.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Goal-Based Scenarios organize learning around a mission or role-based objective that learners pursue inside a realistic scenario. Instead of learning content first and applying it later, learners confront a goal, make decisions, access information as needed, and experience the consequences of their choices. The scenario gives purpose and coherence to the learning sequence.

GBS is especially useful when the instructional target involves judgment, procedure, and context-sensitive decision making. It combines authenticity, problem solving, and feedback in a form that can be more motivating than decontextualized instruction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful mission: Learners need a clear goal that makes the scenario worth engaging.
  • A realistic scenario with consequences: The context should preserve enough of the real task structure to support transfer.
  • Just-in-time supports: Learners should be able to access information, hints, or resources when needed.
  • Feedback and debriefing: The scenario needs consequences, reflection, or coaching to turn action into learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• High design burden: Strong scenarios require careful writing, sequencing, and support design.
  • Weak authenticity undermines engagement: A thin or artificial mission makes the pattern feel contrived.
  • Novice overload: Learners may need more scaffolding if the scenario assumes too much prior knowledge.
  • Not ideal for purely factual coverage: The pattern is strongest when learners must do something with knowledge.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Unit
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Contextualized decision making: Using knowledge in realistic situations.
  • Procedural and strategic application: Coordinating choices, information gathering, and action.
  • Transfer to authentic performance: Learning in conditions closer to eventual use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Professional and adult learners: Strong fit for workforce, corporate, clinical, and technical training.
  • Learners motivated by purposeful roles or missions: Useful when context helps sustain engagement.
  • Learners preparing for scenario-based performance: Best where judgment under conditions matters.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated learning perspectives — knowledge is more usable when learned in context.
  • Experiential learning perspectives — action, consequence, and reflection support deeper learning.
  • Goal-oriented motivation perspectives — clear missions can organize attention and persistence.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Scenarios need instructional discipline; immersion alone does not guarantee learning.
  • Some learners need more direct explanation or guided practice before complex scenarios become productive.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present a mission, role, or goal inside a realistic scenario.
  2. Have learners identify what they need to know or do to succeed.
  3. Let learners act, gather information, and make decisions within the scenario.
  4. Provide feedback, consequences, or coaching tied to those decisions.
  5. Debrief the reasoning and connect it to target concepts or future situations.

docs.text:
• Problem Scenario
  • Problem Presentation
  • Feedback
  • Reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Problem-based Learning
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes
  • Experiential Learning
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Different learners can pursue different paths within the same scenario.
  • Supports can be adjusted from heavily guided to more open mission execution.
  • Roles, stakes, and domain framing can be adapted for different audiences.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Anchored Instruction
  • Problem-Based Learning (PBL)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Clinical training scenarios where learners manage a patient case through evolving decisions.
  • Business simulations built around a crisis or client objective.
  • Public-sector or military training built around mission execution with constrained information.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Supports engagement and transfer when learning needs to feel purposeful and situated.
  • Strongest when scenarios are paired with explicit debrief rather than left as pure experience.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Guided Discovery Learning is a pattern in which learners investigate examples, data, or problems and are led by prompts, questions, and scaffolds toward important concepts or principles. The key word is guided. Learners are not left to discover ideas entirely on their own; the instructor shapes the sequence, materials, and questions so that exploration becomes productive rather than random.

The pattern is useful when the goal is to build conceptual understanding through active sense-making. It becomes weaker when the task is too open, the domain is too unfamiliar, or the guidance is too thin for novice learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A discoverable concept or structure: The task should make patterns or principles accessible through investigation.
  • Strong scaffolding: Questions, examples, prompts, or constraints must channel attention to relevant features.
  • Instructor monitoring: Learner interpretations need to be checked and refined during the process.
  • A consolidation step: Learners need help articulating what was discovered and why it matters.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Misconception risk: Weak guidance can allow incorrect patterns to harden.
  • Novice overload: Learners without enough prior knowledge may need more explicit support.
  • Time demands: Discovery sequences often take longer than direct explanation.
  • False discovery: Overly constrained tasks can pretend to be discovery while actually hiding the answer in a script.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding: Learners infer principles from evidence or examples.
  • Hypothesis testing and reasoning: Learners compare possibilities and refine interpretations.
  • Ownership of understanding: Learners experience the concept as something they worked out, not only received.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners exploring relationships or patterns: Strong fit for science, math, and concept-rich domains.
  • Groups that benefit from active sense-making: Useful when engagement rises through investigation.
  • Learners with enough foundation to interpret evidence: Best when some background or support is already in place.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through active reorganization of experience.
  • Inquiry-oriented perspectives — questions and evidence can drive conceptual learning.
  • Scaffolding perspectives — guidance helps learners notice the right patterns without doing all the thinking for them.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Discovery without guidance is not the same pattern and is often much weaker for novices.
  • Some concepts are better introduced explicitly before or alongside guided discovery.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present a problem, set of examples, or phenomenon worth investigating.
  2. Ask learners to observe, compare, or test hypotheses.
  3. Use prompts and questions to guide attention toward important features.
  4. Have learners articulate patterns, rules, or explanations.
  5. Consolidate the discovered principle and connect it to later use.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Scaffolded Inquiry
  • Reflection
  • Feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Inquiry-based Learning
  • Guided Practice
  • Pre-reading Questioning
  • Purposeful Reflection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Learners can work with different examples or contexts while pursuing the same conceptual target.
  • Guidance can be more explicit for novices and lighter for learners with stronger prior knowledge.
  • Discovery products can be oral, visual, or written depending on learner needs.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Collaborative Inquiry
  • Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning (POGIL)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Science learners inferring relationships from data patterns.
  • Math learners identifying a rule or structure by comparing worked instances.
  • Professional learners examining examples of practice and deriving principles from guided prompts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Can produce strong conceptual engagement when learners are guided to notice meaningful structure.
  • Most effective when discovery is followed by explicit consolidation and feedback.
