docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Johann Herbart (1776–1841) held that learning is influenced by a learner's interest in the subject and in the teacher, and that teachers should consider a student's existing mental sets — what they already know — before presenting new information. From this premise he proposed what became known as the formal steps: (1) review material that has already been learned by the student; (2) prepare the student for new material by giving them an overview of what they are learning next; (3) present the new material; (4) relate the new material to the old material that has already been learned; and (5) show how the student can apply the new material and show the material they will learn next (Hergenhahn, 2009).

The pattern is historically significant as one of the earliest attempts to systematize lesson sequencing around a psychological premise (that new learning must be anchored to prior knowledge) rather than around the content's own logical structure alone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A lesson with clearly separable "old" and "new" content, so review and relation steps have real material to work with
  • Enough time within the lesson to move through all five steps rather than jumping straight to presentation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Can feel mechanical or padded for content with no natural connection to prior learning
  • Assumes a single linear path through prior knowledge to new knowledge, which fits well-sequenced curricula better than open-ended exploration

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Durable connection of new content to a learner's existing knowledge base, rather than isolated presentation of new material.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners for whom prior-knowledge activation and explicit relating are not automatic — the pattern makes both steps deliberate rather than assumed.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Advance Organizers — the "prepare" step is functionally an advance organizer, giving learners a frame for what's coming before it arrives

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Review material already learned
  2. Prepare the student for new material with an overview of what's coming
  3. Present the new material
  4. Relate the new material explicitly to the old
  5. Show how the student can apply the new material, and preview what comes next

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes prior-knowledge activation and explicit relation-building a required step rather than an optional add-on to presentation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The review and relate steps can be adapted in depth depending on how much the class's prior learning actually varies learner to learner

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Gagné's 9 Events — a later, more granular lesson-sequencing pattern covering similar ground (recall of prior learning, presentation, relating content, application) with additional steps for attention, guidance, and feedback

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A lesson opening with a short review of the prior day's content, an overview of the new topic, direct instruction, an explicit comparison ("this is like what we just did, except..."), and a closing application task

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hergenhahn, B. R. (2009). An introduction to the history of psychology. Wadsworth.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). History of educational psychology. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Madeline Hunter combined a number of direct-instruction techniques into a single, comprehensive approach she called mastery teaching (distinct from the separate term "mastery learning") or the effective teaching model (M. Hunter, 1982; R. Hunter, 2004). Its features span before, during, and after a lesson.

Before the lesson, the curriculum is analyzed into its basic elements and how they relate to each other, expressed at a level appropriate to the students (e.g., teaching photosynthesis to advanced students as chemical reactions involving chlorophyll and carbon dioxide, versus to first-graders as a process akin to breathing).

Preparing students to learn makes the most of the moment when attention is highest: creating an anticipatory set — an activity that focuses students' attention on the upcoming content, often a question drawing on everyday knowledge or a prior lesson (e.g., "If you are making a salad strictly of fruit, which of these would be OK to use: apple, tomato, cucumber, or orange?") — directing attention to what lies ahead (e.g., via advance organizers), and explicitly stating lesson objectives.

Presenting information clearly and explicitly means setting a basic lesson structure and staying with it, using familiar language, staying concise, and offering plentiful, varied examples — models and analogies can help (e.g., "think of a fruit as a decoration on the plant, since picking it doesn't kill the plant"), but can also mislead if used carelessly, since an analogy's features may diverge from the real concept in ways students overgeneralize.

Checking for understanding and guided practice asks questions that require active thinking from everyone, not just volunteers: a full-class choral response, a non-verbal signal (raising hands), or brief individual written or verbal responses, supplemented by individually-addressed questions. This gives the teacher a rough read on overall understanding even though some students may let more knowledgeable peers carry the response.

Independent practice consolidates rather than introduces new material: the teacher works through the first few problems together with students before turning practice over to them, but keeps independent-practice stretches brief and interspersed with feedback rather than assigning one long, unsupervised block.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Curricula and learning goals that are tightly organized and divisible into small, clearly related parts

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Consolidated mastery of clearly defined content and skills, verified through frequent, whole-class checks for understanding

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in subjects or topics well-suited to teacher-directed, tightly sequenced instruction (see Direct Instruction for where this fit is and is not appropriate)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Direct Instruction — Hunter's model is an integration of several direct-instruction techniques into one lesson-length sequence

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Analyze the curriculum into its basic elements and their relationships, at a level appropriate to the learners.
  2. Open with an anticipatory set that orients attention to the upcoming content, plus explicit lesson objectives.
  3. Present information in short, logical pieces, using familiar language and plentiful varied examples.
  4. Check for understanding throughout via whole-class response (choral or non-verbal signal) supplemented by individual questioning.
  5. Transition to brief, interspersed independent practice with frequent feedback, rather than one long unsupervised block.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers — used to build the anticipatory set and orient attention before new content
  • Guided Practice — the "work through the first few together" step before independent practice

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The level at which curriculum elements are expressed (e.g., photosynthesis as chemistry vs. as breathing) can be adjusted to student age and prior knowledge

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Direct Instruction — the broader teacher-directed tradition this model draws its component techniques from
  • Mastery Learning — a related but distinct term Hunter explicitly distinguishes her model from

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teaching fruits vs. vegetables: an anticipatory-set question about a fruit salad, examples presented one feature at a time, whole-class raise-hands or choral checks ("say 'fruit' or 'vegetable' as I point"), then brief practice sorting additional examples with feedback.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hunter, M. (1982). Mastery teaching. TIP Publications.
  • Hunter, R. (2004). Madeline Hunter's mastery teaching: Increasing instructional effectiveness in elementary and secondary schools (Rev. ed.). Corwin Press.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Instructional strategies that stimulate complex thinking. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Jigsaw Learning is the short-form canonical target for the jigsaw pattern in which learners develop expertise on one part of the material and then teach it to peers so the group can assemble a fuller understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Distributed expertise across group members
  • Interdependence so each role matters

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners need support to explain accurately to one another

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text: • Build peer learning, accountability, and distributed expertise.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Jigsaw Method

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Aronson, E., & Patnoe, S. (2011). Cooperation in the classroom (3rd ed.). Pinter & Martin.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Jigsaw Method is a cooperative learning pattern in which learners become responsible for one part of a larger topic, develop expertise in that part, and then teach it to peers who depend on them for the whole picture. The pattern is designed to create positive interdependence: no learner can complete the full task alone without contributions from others.

Its value comes from combining preparation, peer teaching, and synthesis. Jigsaw can improve engagement and accountability when each role matters, but it can fail if expert preparation is weak or if the final synthesis never checks what peers actually learned from one another.

Two documented variants differ in when specialization happens. In the original version (Aronson et al., 2001), 5-6-student groups are each assigned one aspect of a complex problem from the start; expert groups then disband and re-form so each new group contains one student from each former expert group. In a second version (Slavin, 1994), 4-5-student groups first work together on the entire problem before disbanding into expert groups focused on one aspect, and finally reform into the original groups to add each member's new expertise back into the group's shared understanding — giving every learner a whole-problem orientation before specialization narrows their focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A topic divisible into meaningful parts: The content should break into components that can later be recombined.
  • Expert preparation time: Learners need time and support to understand their assigned piece well enough to teach it.
  • Interdependence by design: The final task should require contributions from all parts.
  • Synthesis and correction: The instructor needs to consolidate and address misconceptions after peer teaching.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak expert preparation weakens the whole pattern: If learners do not become real experts, peer teaching is shallow.
  • Participation imbalance: Some learners may carry more than others unless accountability is explicit.
  • Fragmentation risk: Learners may miss the whole unless the final synthesis is strong.
  • Not ideal when content cannot be partitioned cleanly: Some tasks resist meaningful jigsaw structure.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Distributed expertise: Learners develop and share responsibility for different content segments.
  • Peer teaching: Teaching becomes part of learning.
  • Knowledge synthesis: Learners reassemble parts into a coherent whole.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in collaborative classrooms: Strong fit where peer learning is a central norm.
  • Mixed-ability groups: Jigsaw can give many learners meaningful contribution roles when designed well.
  • Learners working with broad topics or multi-part content: Best when the whole benefits from division and recombination.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cooperative learning perspectives — positive interdependence can improve participation and shared responsibility.
  • Social constructivist perspectives — teaching and discussion deepen understanding.
  • Generative learning perspectives — preparing to explain to others strengthens processing.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Peer teaching needs support; the pattern does not guarantee accuracy or depth on its own.
  • A jigsaw is only as strong as its synthesis and accountability mechanisms.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Divide the topic into meaningful subtopics and assign expert roles.
  2. Have expert groups study and prepare their subtopic.
  3. Re-form mixed groups where each learner teaches their portion.
  4. Synthesize the full topic through discussion or a shared task.
  5. Assess whole-group or individual understanding of the complete content.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Communities of Practice
  • Perspective-Seeking/Multiple Perspectives
  • Mentoring/Coaching

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Different learners can take roles aligned with interest or readiness.
  • Expert materials can vary in complexity depending on learner support needs.
  • Accountability can be individual, group-based, or mixed.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Fostering Communities of Learning (FCL)
  • Discussion Group
  • Student-Teams Achievement Divisions (STAD) — another small-team cooperative structure, organized around shared whole-class content and individual testing rather than subtopic specialization

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• History learners examining different primary sources and teaching their significance to peers.
  • Science groups becoming experts on different parts of a system before building a shared explanation.
  • Professional learning cohorts dividing complex policy or process documents for peer teaching.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Can improve engagement and responsibility when every learner's part matters.
  • Strongest when expert preparation, peer teaching, and final synthesis are all treated as essential.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Just-in-time learning is the short-form canonical pattern for providing support, information, or practice at the moment it is needed for performance.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Just-in-Time Learning
  • Just-in-Time Information

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Merrill's First Principles Application

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Merrill, M. D. (2002). First principles of instruction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 50(3), 43-59.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Just-In-Time Teaching (JiTT), developed by Gregor Novak and colleagues (Novak et al., 1999), relies on a feedback loop between web-based pre-class materials and the classroom. Students prepare by reading assigned material and completing short web-based assignments; their responses reach the instructor a few hours before class, letting the instructor adapt that day's lesson to exactly what students are struggling with. This shifts class time from content transfer toward active learning and cooperative problem-solving.

Three types of JiTT activities serve different moments in the learning cycle: WarmUps are short, pre-instruction assignments that prompt initial thinking about upcoming content, surfacing where cooperative in-class work should focus and revealing misconceptions and prior knowledge before class even starts; Puzzles are post-instruction wrap-up assignments that provide closure and integrate concepts already covered; GoodFors are enrichment essays connecting class content to the real world, doubling as discussion starters and helping keep material fresh in memory.

Marrs and Novak (2004) identify three theoretical elements JiTT combines: (1) it operationalizes active learning, since moving content transfer to pre-class preparation frees class time for cooperative problem-solving, consistent with evidence that active-learning approaches promote learning (NRC, 2000; Hake, 1998; Paulson, 1999; Udovic et al., 2002); (2) it operationalizes constructivism (Piaget; Kujawa & Huske, 1995) by structuring opportunities for students to build new understanding on existing knowledge — since pre-existing misconceptions can block accurate new mental models, WarmUps specifically function to surface those misconceptions so class time can address them directly, rather than assuming a blank slate; and (3) it provides prompt feedback, occurring essentially every class meeting through the instructor's response to submitted WarmUps — consistent with How People Learn's finding that the best learning environments are assessment-centered, and that formative assessment lets learners adjust their thinking before any summative, graded assessment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A web-based (or equivalent) submission channel that gets student responses to the instructor with enough lead time (a few hours) to actually adapt the day's plan
  • Genuine willingness to restructure the planned lesson based on submitted responses, rather than treating WarmUps as a compliance check disconnected from what actually happens in class

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The adaptive benefit disappears if the instructor doesn't have (or doesn't take) enough time between submission and class to actually revise the lesson plan
  • WarmUp/Puzzle questions need genuinely complex, thought-provoking answers — a question with an obvious, single correct answer won't surface the misconceptions the pattern depends on

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: [lesson]

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Class time shifted from passive content transfer to active, cooperative problem-solving
  • Misconceptions and prior-knowledge gaps surfaced and addressed before they interfere with new learning

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in courses meeting regularly enough (e.g., multiple times per week) for the pre-class/adapt/in-class cycle to function as a genuine feedback loop

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivism [+M] — WarmUps structure opportunities for students to build new understanding on existing knowledge, and specifically surface misconceptions that would otherwise block that construction
  • Active Learning [+M] — moving content transfer outside class is precisely what frees class time for active, cooperative work

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Assign pre-class reading/materials along with a WarmUp: a short, web-based assignment with genuinely complex questions, due a few hours before class.
  2. Review submitted WarmUp responses before class to identify where students are struggling or holding misconceptions.
  3. Adapt the day's in-class activities to focus specifically on those struggling points, using cooperative problem-solving.
  4. After the topic is covered, assign a Puzzle to provide closure and integrate the concepts.
  5. Periodically assign a GoodFor enrichment essay to connect the material to the real world and seed discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Because each class session's plan is adapted to that specific cohort's actual submitted responses, the pattern personalizes at the level of the whole class's current understanding rather than requiring individual-student customization

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Flipped Learning — shares the move of relocating initial content exposure outside class, but JiTT adds the explicit instructor feedback loop that adapts the specific day's activities
  • Team-Based Learning — a related model that also begins each unit with an out-of-class preparation phase followed by an in-class readiness check

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Novak, G. M., Patterson, E. T., Gavrin, A. D., & Christian, W. (1999). Just-in-time teaching: Blending active learning with web technology. Prentice Hall.
  • Marrs, K. A., & Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-time teaching in biology: Creating an active learner classroom using the internet. Cell Biology Education, 3(1), 49-61.
  • Brame, C. (n.d.). Just-in-time teaching (JiTT). Vanderbilt University Center for Teaching. https://cft.vanderbilt.edu/guides-sub-pages/just-in-time-teaching-jitt/
  • National Research Council. (2000). How people learn: Brain, mind, experience, and school (Expanded ed.). National Academy Press.
  • Hake, R. R. (1998). Interactive-engagement versus traditional methods: A six-thousand-student survey of mechanics test data for introductory physics courses. American Journal of Physics, 66(1), 64-74.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Just-in-time teaching (JiTT). In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
LDA Reflection is a lightweight reflection pattern used to help learners pause after an activity, analyze what happened, and identify what to carry forward. In this wiki, the pattern functions as a practical debrief routine rather than a named external theory model. Its value is in turning experience, discussion, or performance into something learners can interpret and reuse.

The pattern is especially useful at the end of a lesson, discussion, simulation, sprint, or practice cycle. It gives instructors a compact structure for surfacing what learners noticed, what they still need, and how they will apply or revise their understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A completed learning episode: Reflection needs a concrete experience, task, or artifact to look back on.
  • Focused prompts: Learners need questions that direct attention to evidence, strategy, and next steps.
  • Psychological safety: Reflection is stronger when learners can identify struggle without penalty.
  • A path forward: The pattern should connect reflection to revision, planning, or future application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Vagueness risk: General prompts often produce shallow recap instead of useful reflection.
  • Time compression: Reflection gets cut easily unless it is treated as part of the learning design.
  • Compliance writing: If nothing is done with the reflection, the pattern loses value quickly.
  • Not a substitute for feedback: Reflection supports learning best when paired with discussion, evidence, or coaching.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Metacognitive awareness: Helping learners notice what they understood and where they struggled.
  • Transfer of learning: Identifying what should be used again in a future context.
  • Revision planning: Turning reflection into a next step rather than a summary only.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in practice-heavy or discussion-heavy settings: Strong fit after activities that generate rich experience.
  • Adult learners connecting learning to context: Useful when learners need to link content to work, life, or prior experience.
  • Learners building reflective habits: A compact routine can normalize reflection without requiring long journaling tasks.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Reflective practice traditions — learning deepens when action is examined after the fact.
  • Self-regulated learning perspectives — reflection supports monitoring, evaluation, and next-step planning.
  • Experiential learning perspectives — experience becomes more educative when it is interpreted and connected to later action.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Reflection should be specific and actionable; generic feelings checks alone rarely produce much instructional value.
  • Some learners need examples or sentence stems before short reflection routines become substantive.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Prompt learners to recall the task, decision, or key moment they are reflecting on.
  2. Ask them to identify what worked, what was difficult, and why.
  3. Have learners connect the experience to a concept, strategy, or future situation.
  4. End with a concrete next step, revision target, or transfer commitment.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Reflection
  • Individual Reflection
  • Feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Purposeful Reflection
  • Self-monitoring
  • Experiential Learning
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Reflection can be written, spoken, paired, or shared with the whole group.
  • Prompts can emphasize strategy, emotion, evidence, or transfer depending on the lesson.
  • The pattern can be very brief or expanded into longer journaling or conferencing.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Discussion Group
  • Structured Peer Review

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• End-of-lesson exit reflection focused on one success, one challenge, and one next step.
  • Post-simulation debrief where learners identify a key decision and what they would change.
  • Brief reflection after a peer discussion or collaborative task before the class synthesizes learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Converts experience into interpretable evidence for learners.
  • Particularly useful as a low-overhead routine that keeps reflection embedded in instruction.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Boud, D., Keogh, R., & Walker, D. (1985). Reflection: Turning experience into learning. Kogan Page.
  • Schön, D. A. (1983). The reflective practitioner. Basic Books.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Learning-for-Use is a pattern for designing inquiry so that knowledge is learned in response to a meaningful need and then refined through application. The model typically moves through three broad phases: motivate the need for new knowledge, support knowledge construction, and then refine that knowledge through use in a consequential task. The central idea is that knowledge becomes more retrievable and transferable when learners acquire it for a purpose rather than as isolated content.

LfU is especially useful when designers want inquiry to remain conceptually grounded instead of becoming a loose research activity. It provides a way to connect motivation, construction, and application inside one coherent sequence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful knowledge need: Learners should encounter a problem or task that creates demand for understanding.
  • Inquiry with conceptual purpose: Exploration should be tied to building usable knowledge, not just information collection.
  • An application phase: Learners need to use what they built in a consequential context.
  • Instructional guidance: Teachers need to help learners connect experience, concept formation, and later application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Artificial motivation weakens the pattern: If the initial problem does not genuinely create a need to know, the sequence feels staged.
  • Inquiry drift: Exploration can become diffuse without conceptual checkpoints.
  • Novice support needs: Some learners need more structure before inquiry becomes productive.
  • Time intensity: The full motivate-construct-refine cycle takes more time than straightforward exposition.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Usable conceptual knowledge: Learning ideas in ways that support later retrieval and application.
  • Transfer: Connecting understanding to meaningful action beyond the first lesson.
  • Problem-centered inquiry: Organizing learning around a reason to know.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in science, engineering, and applied domains: Strong fit where concepts are tightly tied to real tasks.
  • Learners who need relevance to sustain inquiry: Useful when motivation grows from meaningful problems.
  • Groups working through inquiry with application: Best when exploration leads into use, not only discussion.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated learning perspectives — knowledge is more usable when learned in meaningful contexts.
  • Constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through active inquiry and application.
  • Transfer-oriented perspectives — application after construction helps stabilize and retrieve knowledge later.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Motivation should create a need for knowledge, not distract from the concept itself.
  • Some learners need more explicit instruction within the inquiry sequence than the model may initially suggest.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Motivate learning by presenting a meaningful problem, challenge, or need to know.
  2. Support knowledge construction through inquiry, exploration, and sense-making.
  3. Refine knowledge through application in a consequential task or context.
  4. Revisit what was learned to strengthen transfer and future use.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Scaffolded Inquiry
  • Practice
  • Reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Problem-based Learning
  • Inquiry-based Learning
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes
  • Real-world Math

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Problems can be varied to fit learner interests, roles, or community relevance.
  • Guidance can be more explicit for novices and lighter for experienced learners.
  • Application tasks can take multiple forms as long as they require use of the constructed knowledge.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Problem-Based Learning (PBL)
  • Anchored Instruction

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Science learners exploring environmental data because they need it to explain a local problem.
  • Engineering learners investigating a principle so they can apply it in a design challenge.
  • Business learners constructing concepts through inquiry and then using them in a decision scenario.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Helps connect motivation, concept building, and transfer inside one inquiry model.
  • Particularly useful when designers want learners to need the knowledge before formally learning it.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Edelson, D. C. (2001). Learning-for-use: A framework for the design of technology-supported inquiry activities. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 38(3), 355-385. https://doi.org/10.1002/1098-2736(200103)38:3<355::AID-TEA1010>3.0.CO;2-M

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The MOOC combines several earlier innovations — open enrollment, video-based instruction, discussion-forum interaction, and open-content licensing — into a single, free, large-scale online course (Weller, 2018). The earliest MOOCs (Downes and Siemens's open courses in 2008–2009) were built around Connectivism: learning was meant to happen through learners forming and navigating their own network of connections across distributed content and peers, not through a fixed instructor-delivered sequence.

That original design was largely abandoned once the pattern scaled commercially. After Stanford's 2011 course (Sebastian Thrun) drew over 100,000 learners and attracted venture-capital investment, "xMOOC" platforms (Coursera, Udacity, edX) adopted a broadcast, video-lecture-plus-quiz model — closer to a traditional course delivered at scale than to the connectivist, learner-networked design the format is named for. Weller (2018) notes this is a recurring edtech pattern: the pedagogical model a technology is originally named for and the model it is actually implemented with can diverge sharply once it scales for a commercial audience. Wiley (2014) makes a sharper version of the same critique from a licensing angle: because xMOOC content is typically not openly licensed (no free copying, translation, or redistribution), imposes registration deadlines and start/end dates, and charges for credentials, it fails the Open Educational Resources (5Rs) test for genuine openness — in his words, once you strip away the "open entry" framing, a typical xMOOC is "nothing more than" a traditional online class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Infrastructure capable of serving very large, unbounded enrollment with minimal marginal cost per additional learner — which pushes toward pre-recorded video and automated or peer assessment rather than instructor-graded feedback
  • A content licensing decision (open vs. closed) that determines whether the course is "open" only in the open-entry sense or also in the 5R licensing sense

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• At scale, individualized instructor feedback becomes impractical, so assessment shifts to automated quizzes or peer grading — a real reduction in feedback quality and immediacy relative to smaller-enrollment courses
  • The connectivist pedagogy the pattern was originally built around does not survive contact with a broadcast, video-lecture delivery model — a "MOOC" today is more reliably described by its scale and open enrollment than by any specific pedagogy
  • Completion rates for MOOCs are notoriously low relative to traditional courses, a direct consequence of minimal enrollment commitment and light-touch support structures

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Reaching very large, geographically dispersed audiences with a single course offering
  • Reducing per-learner marginal cost for widely-demanded introductory content

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Self-directed learners able to persist through a course with minimal individualized instructor support or accountability structure
  • Learners for whom free, open enrollment (regardless of prior credentials) is the primary access barrier being removed

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Connectivism [~M] — the pattern's original design rationale, though largely abandoned in mainstream commercial implementations

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Open Educational Resources (5Rs) — most commercial xMOOC content fails the 5R openness test (no free copying, translation, or redistribution), which Wiley (2014) argues undermines the "open" framing of the pattern's own name

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Produce pre-recorded video lectures and other content, since live, individualized delivery does not scale to the intended enrollment.
  2. Open enrollment broadly, with minimal or no prerequisite screening.
  3. Deliver content asynchronously, typically week-by-week, with embedded low-stakes quizzes.
  4. Support peer interaction through discussion forums (with variable, self-organized engagement).
  5. Assess primarily through automated quizzes or peer/rubric-based grading rather than instructor feedback.
  6. Optionally charge a fee for a verified certificate or credential, separate from free access to the content itself.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text: • Open Educational Resources (5Rs) (when the content is genuinely openly licensed)

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Online Course Design (Community of Inquiry) — the same interaction-design concerns (learner-learner, learner-instructor, learner-content) apply at MOOC scale, though instructor interaction is necessarily far thinner

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Some platforms allow self-paced progression through pre-recorded content rather than a fixed weekly schedule
  • Discussion forums allow learners to self-select which topics or peer discussions to engage with

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Online Course Design (Community of Inquiry) — shares concern for interaction design, but MOOC scale makes deep learner-instructor interaction impractical in a way a smaller online course does not face

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Coursera, edX, and Udacity's commercial xMOOC platforms, built around video lectures and automated quizzes
  • The original Downes/Siemens connectivist MOOCs (2008–2009), built around distributed, learner-networked content rather than centralized video lectures

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Weller, M. (2018). Twenty years of EdTech. EDUCAUSE Review, 53(4). Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/twenty_years_of_edtech
  • Wiley, D. (2014). The MOOC misstep and the open education infrastructure. Republished in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/open_educational_resources

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mastery Learning is a pattern in which instruction is organized around clear criteria, formative checks, corrective support, and reassessment before progression. Unlike one-pass instruction, the pattern assumes some learners will need additional explanation, feedback, or time before moving on.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear mastery thresholds
  • Frequent formative checks
  • Corrective instruction and reassessment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Scheduling and workload pressures
  • Risk of reducing mastery to narrow test performance

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Reliable competence before advancement.
  • Reduced accumulation of unresolved misunderstandings.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners building cumulative skills and prerequisite knowledge.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Bloom's mastery learning tradition.
  • Self-Regulated Learning

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Not all complex performances can be reduced to a single mastery threshold.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Define mastery criteria.
  2. Teach and model the target performance.
  3. Check understanding formatively.
  4. Provide corrective support for non-mastery.
  5. Reassess before advancing.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment
  • Feedback
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Mastery Learning
  • Formative Assessment

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Merrill's First Principles of Instruction is a task-centered pattern that organizes learning around five recurring moves: problem-centered work, activation of prior knowledge, demonstration, application, and integration. Rather than prescribing a rigid lesson script, it identifies a set of instructional conditions that tend to support effective learning across many settings. The pattern is strongest when learners are working toward meaningful performance, not just isolated recall.

Its practical strength is that it balances authenticity with structured support. Learners encounter real or realistic tasks, but instruction still includes activation, modeling, guided application, and integration into personal or professional use.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Meaningful whole tasks: Learning should be organized around authentic or realistic problems rather than decontextualized fragments alone.
  • Activation of prior knowledge: Learners need help connecting new instruction to what they already know.
  • Demonstration and guided application: Learners should see examples and then apply knowledge with support.
  • Integration: Instruction should help learners bring new learning back into their own contexts and practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Design effort: Strong task-centered instruction requires more intentional design than content-first sequencing.
  • Weak fit for pure fact coverage: The pattern is most useful when understanding and application matter.
  • Support needs vary by expertise: Some learners need more modeling and guidance than others.
  • Authenticity can be faked: Poorly designed "real-world tasks" weaken the pattern quickly.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Applied understanding: Learners use knowledge in meaningful tasks.
  • Transfer: Instruction is designed from the start for later use.
  • Integrated performance: Concepts, procedures, and strategy come together around a task.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult and professional learners: Strong fit where real-world performance matters.
  • Learners in concept-and-skill domains: Useful when both understanding and application are required.
  • Designers building task-centered instruction: Provides a reusable high-level structure across domains.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Task-centered instruction traditions — authentic problems organize learning more effectively than isolated content alone.
  • Constructivist and generative perspectives — activation, demonstration, and application support meaningful learning.
  • Transfer-oriented design — integration improves the chances that learning will be used later.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Not every lesson needs all five principles equally, and designers still need to adapt to domain and learner expertise.
  • Task-centered instruction may need supplemental explicit teaching for foundational subskills.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]
  • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+M]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Worked examples can become redundant or counterproductive for advanced learners. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Organize instruction around a real or realistic problem or task.
  2. Activate relevant prior knowledge or experience.
  3. Demonstrate what successful performance or reasoning looks like.
  4. Have learners apply the knowledge with support and feedback.
  5. Integrate learning by reflecting, teaching, or using it in a new context.

docs.title: Elements Used

  • Practice
  • Reflection

docs.title: Affordances

  • Guided Practice

  • Purposeful Reflection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Learners can work on tasks relevant to their own contexts while following the same instructional arc.
  • Demonstration and guidance can be adjusted based on expertise.
  • Integration can take many forms, including teaching others, reflection, or workplace application.

docs.title: Related Patterns

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Clinical training where learners analyze a case, study demonstrations, practice decisions, and reflect on use in real settings.
  • Technical lessons that begin with a real task, activate prior knowledge, model performance, and then move into coached application.
  • Adult education modules that connect existing experience to a new strategy and then ask learners to apply it in work or life.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Provides a practical high-level design frame for instruction that aims at use, not just exposure.
  • Works well across domains when designers keep the task at the center rather than treating the principles as a checklist.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Model-Evidence Link pattern structures reasoning by having learners compare competing models or explanations against available evidence, judge which links are strong or weak, and revise their conclusions accordingly. Rather than asking learners to memorize one correct explanation, the pattern gives them practice weighing evidence, examining fit, and making scientific or disciplinary reasoning visible.

It is particularly useful when learners need to evaluate explanations in the face of uncertainty, conflicting claims, or conceptual change. The pattern works best when the competing models are coherent enough to compare and the evidence is rich enough to discriminate among them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Competing models or explanations: Learners need at least two meaningful explanatory options to compare.
  • A usable evidence set: The evidence should support analysis rather than simply reveal the answer immediately.
  • Reasoning scaffolds: Learners need prompts or structures that help them articulate how evidence supports or challenges each model.
  • Revision opportunities: The pattern is strongest when learners can update their explanations after discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak evidence design: If the evidence is misleading or too sparse, the reasoning exercise becomes arbitrary.
  • Overload risk: Too many models or too much data can swamp novices.
  • False balance: Not all competing models are equally plausible, so the task needs careful framing.
  • Requires explicit debrief: Learners may compare models superficially without teacher-supported synthesis.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Scientific or disciplinary reasoning: Using evidence to evaluate explanatory claims.
  • Conceptual change: Revising understanding when evidence better fits an alternative model.
  • Argumentation with evidence: Justifying interpretations explicitly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in science and evidence-rich disciplines: Strong fit where model comparison is part of expert reasoning.
  • Learners confronting misconceptions: Useful when contrasting explanations can surface weak reasoning.
  • Secondary, higher education, and adult learners: Best when learners can work with claims and evidence explicitly.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Inquiry-oriented perspectives — learners deepen understanding by evaluating evidence against explanations.
  • Epistemic cognition perspectives — knowledge improves when learners examine how claims are warranted.
  • Conceptual change traditions — comparing competing explanations can destabilize misconceptions and support revision.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Learners often need substantial scaffolding to reason well with competing models.
  • The pattern supports explanation and evidence use but is less suited to rote foundational coverage.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present the focal phenomenon and two or more competing models.
  2. Introduce the relevant evidence set.
  3. Have learners judge how strongly each piece of evidence supports or weakens each model.
  4. Ask learners to justify which model best fits the evidence and why.
  5. Debrief the reasoning and revise explanations.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Peer Discussion
  • Formative Assessment
  • Reflection

docs.title: Affordances

• Inquiry-based Learning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Purposeful Reflection
  • Creating Visual Representations

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• The number of models and complexity of the evidence can be adjusted by learner readiness.
  • Learners can work individually first and then compare reasoning in pairs or groups.
  • Supports can include comparison charts, sentence stems, or partially completed evidence tables.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Collaborative Inquiry
  • Discussion Group

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Earth science learners comparing climate explanations against observational data.
  • Physics learners weighing competing motion models using a shared evidence set.
  • Biology learners comparing causal explanations for a phenomenon and revising their reasoning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Supports evidence-based reasoning and helps learners make model comparison explicit.
  • Especially useful where misconceptions persist because learners have not been asked to weigh alternatives carefully.

  • Lombardi, D., Sinatra, G. M., & Nussbaum, E. M. (2013). Plausibility reappraisals and shifts in middle school students' climate change conceptions. Learning and Instruction, 27, 50-62. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2013.03.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Online learners routinely report a sense of psychological distance or isolation that face-to-face learners do not — Moore (1989) called this transactional distance and argued it is reduced by deliberately designing for three types of interaction: learner-to-learner, learner-to-instructor, and learner-to-content. A meta-analysis of 74 distance-education studies confirmed all three types matter for achievement (Bernard et al., 2009).

The Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 1999) operationalizes this at the course level by defining a quality online learning experience as the overlap of three "presences": cognitive presence (learners constructing meaning through sustained discourse and reflection), social presence (learners feeling able to project themselves as real people and connect with the group), and teaching presence (design, facilitation, and direct instruction that organizes and guides the other two). This pattern is the course-design counterpart to Community of Inquiry as a general collaborative-learning principle — here it is applied specifically to structuring an entire online course, not just a single discussion.

Course-design literature converges on a recurring set of moves that build these presences across a semester: a consistent course structure maintained throughout (Swan, 2001); frequent, low-latency instructor feedback — studies of instructor immediacy found learners in high-immediacy conditions showed greater learning gains and retention (Bodie & Michel, 2014); well-designed collaborative assignments that create real interdependence rather than parallel individual work; and explicit, deliberate interaction design, since transactional distance does not close on its own just because a discussion board exists.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A course structure maintained consistently across weeks/units so learners are not relearning navigation each module
  • Assignment and communication design that deliberately builds each of the three interaction types (learner-learner, learner-instructor, learner-content), not just whichever is easiest to set up (e.g., posting content is easy; instructor feedback loops require ongoing effort)
  • Institutional and faculty support — quality standards reviews consistently find institutional commitment, planning, and leadership among the strongest predictors of online course quality (Shelton, 2011)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Higher faculty time cost: online teaching has been found to demand meaningfully more instructor time than face-to-face teaching, especially during advising and assessment periods (Tomei, 2006)
  • The CoI framework's empirical base leans on self-report, achievement, and perception measures, which has drawn methodological criticism (Rourke & Kanuka, 2009)
  • Interface and technology quality matters independently of pedagogy — a course can be well-designed for CoI presences and still underperform if the platform is confusing (see User-Centered Design for Learning)

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Course
  • Program

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Reducing transactional distance and learner isolation in fully online or blended courses
  • Building sustained, cognitively substantive discourse rather than surface-level "post and reply" participation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in asynchronous or synchronous online courses, where the absence of physical co-presence otherwise leaves learner-to-learner and learner-to-instructor interaction to chance
  • Learners who report needing a stronger sense of community and belonging to persist in online programs

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Community of Inquiry [+S] — the underlying principle this pattern operationalizes at course scale
  • Moore's transactional distance theory — names the problem (psychological distance) this pattern's interaction design is meant to solve

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Establish a consistent course structure (navigation, weekly rhythm, assignment format) and hold it constant across the term.
  2. Design at least one recurring activity for each of Moore's three interaction types: learner-to-content (structured materials/activities), learner-to-instructor (feedback loops, office hours, announcements), and learner-to-learner (discussion, peer review, group work).
  3. Build cognitive presence deliberately — discussion prompts and tasks should require synthesis and application, not just response-and-reply.
  4. Establish social presence early (introductions, low-stakes interaction) before demanding higher-stakes collaboration.
  5. Maintain teaching presence throughout via timely, specific feedback — immediacy affects learning gains, not just satisfaction.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Feedback
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Communication Channels

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Community of Inquiry
  • Collaborative Learning
  • User-Centered Design for Learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Synchronous vs. asynchronous communication channels can be offered in combination so learners can choose the mode that fits their schedule and preferred feedback immediacy
  • Group composition and interaction structures can be adjusted for learners who report feeling isolated versus those already well-connected to peers

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Flipped Classroom — shares the concern with using synchronous/interactive time well, though flipped classroom assumes a physical class session this pattern does not

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A weekly-rhythm asynchronous course with structured discussion prompts, peer response requirements, and a 48-hour instructor feedback commitment on assignments
  • A blended synchronous course using video conferencing for real-time discussion alongside an asynchronous discussion board for reflection

  • Moore, M. G. (1989). Editorial: Three types of interaction. American Journal of Distance Education, 3(2), 1–7.
  • Garrison, D. R., Anderson, T., & Archer, W. (1999). Critical inquiry in a text-based environment: Computer conferencing in higher education. The Internet and Higher Education, 2(2–3), 87–105.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Peer Instruction is a pattern in which learners first answer a conceptual question individually, then discuss their reasoning with peers, and then answer again before instructor debrief. The key mechanism is not the poll itself. It is the combination of commitment, peer explanation, reconsideration, and feedback that helps learners confront misconceptions and refine understanding.

The pattern is especially effective for conceptual questions that require reasoning rather than recall. It works well in large classes because it creates active processing without needing the instructor to hear every learner individually.

In practice, students typically answer individually via clickers or a handheld response system (anonymously, with results visible immediately to the instructor); if a large fraction of the class (usually 30-65%) answers incorrectly, students discuss in small groups while the instructor circulates, then answer again, with the instructor closing the cycle by explaining the correct answer and following up with related questions — each full cycle typically taking 13-15 minutes. The evidence for its effectiveness is unusually well quantified: Hake's (1998) large survey compared 2,084 students in 14 traditionally-taught introductory physics courses against 4,458 students in 48 courses using "interactive engagement" methods (broadly, active, feedback-rich approaches including peer instruction), finding pre/post-test learning gains almost two standard deviations higher for the interactive-engagement group (0.48 ± 0.14 vs. 0.23 ± 0.04). Assessing peer instruction specifically across eight years at Harvard, Crouch and Mazur (2001) found even larger gains (0.49 to 0.74), compared to just 0.25-0.40 for traditionally-taught sections at the same institution during the same period. Deslauriers, Schelew, and Wieman (2011) found a similar effect in a more tightly controlled comparison: two sections of the same large-enrollment physics course, showing no prior differences, were taught identically until one section was "flipped" for a single week (pre-class reading and quizzes, in-class small-group discussion of clicker and written-response questions, no lecture) while the other continued as before — the flipped section still showed a substantial learning-gain advantage over the matched control from that single week's change alone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Conceptually rich questions: The prompt needs to provoke reasoning and disagreement, not simple memory.
  • Initial individual commitment: Learners should answer before discussion so they have something to compare and defend.
  • Peer explanation time: The discussion phase must give enough time for reasoning exchange.
  • Instructor debrief: Learners need closure on why the stronger reasoning is stronger.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak questions flatten the pattern: Fact recall items do not generate much conceptual change.
  • Noisy consensus risk: Learners can converge on an answer socially without improving reasoning if facilitation is weak.
  • Technology is optional but not sufficient: Clickers or polling help, but the real work happens in the discussion.
  • Not ideal for first exposure to very unfamiliar material: Some initial orientation may be needed before conceptual polling works.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text: • Lesson

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding: Surfacing and revising misconceptions.
  • Reasoning articulation: Learners explain why an answer makes sense.
  • Formative diagnosis: Instructors see where understanding is strong or weak.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in STEM and concept-heavy courses: Strong fit for questions where common misconceptions are predictable.
  • Large-group settings: Useful where whole-class interactivity is otherwise difficult.
  • Learners who benefit from peer explanation: The pattern leverages students as reasoning partners.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — learners refine ideas by explaining and comparing reasoning with peers.
  • Conceptual change traditions — confronting conflicting explanations can trigger revision of prior understanding.
  • Formative assessment perspectives — repeated questioning provides immediate evidence about current understanding.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Peer instruction is not just polling; without discussion and debrief it loses much of its value.
  • The pattern is stronger for conceptual reasoning than for pure procedural fluency.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Pose a conceptual question and have learners answer individually.
  2. Reveal the distribution or ask learners to compare responses without announcing the answer.
  3. Have learners discuss reasoning with peers.
  4. Re-poll or reassess after discussion.
  5. Debrief the reasoning and clarify the concept.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Reassessment
  • Feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Formative Assessment
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Purposeful Reflection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Questions can be delivered through clickers, cards, hand signals, or digital polls.
  • Pairs or small groups can be mixed intentionally depending on confidence and prior knowledge.
  • The amount of instructor explanation after the repoll can vary depending on the quality of peer reasoning.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share
  • Discussion Group

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Physics learners debating force or motion concept questions before repolling.
  • Medical learners comparing diagnostic reasoning on a conceptual clinical prompt.
  • Math or engineering classes using concept checks before moving into longer problem work.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Often improves engagement and conceptual understanding in large classes.
  • Most effective when misconceptions are surfaced through strong questions and resolved through debrief.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Problem-Based Learning is a pattern that organizes a course, unit, or module around a complex problem that learners must investigate and respond to. Instead of teaching all required content first, the pattern uses the problem to generate the need for inquiry, evidence gathering, collaboration, and explanation. Learners identify what they need to know, research relevant information, test ideas, and refine proposed responses.

The pattern is strongest when the problem is authentic enough to matter and the facilitation is strong enough to keep the inquiry rigorous. It is not equivalent to minimal guidance. Good PBL is structured, coached, and accountable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful ill-structured problem: The problem should require interpretation, inquiry, and judgment.
  • Access to evidence and resources: Learners need materials, data, cases, or sources they can investigate.
  • Facilitated inquiry: Instructors need to scaffold process and evidence use without taking over the problem.
  • A decision, proposal, or product: Learners should arrive at some defended response to the problem.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Novice overload: Learners with limited background may need more direct support or preteaching.
  • Busy-work risk: Inquiry can become shallow if evidence use and synthesis expectations are weak.
  • Time intensity: PBL usually takes longer than direct explanation-first instruction.
  • Coordination demands: Group work can mask uneven understanding unless roles and accountability are designed clearly.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Unit
  • Course

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Problem solving and reasoning: Applying knowledge to ambiguous situations.
  • Evidence-based inquiry: Identifying what must be learned and using sources purposefully.
  • Transfer: Learning in ways that resemble authentic future use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Higher education, adult, and professional learners: Strong fit where authenticity and application matter.
  • Learners developing self-directed inquiry habits: PBL builds planning, monitoring, and revision.
  • Collaborative groups: The pattern benefits from distributed reasoning and shared investigation.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through engagement with a meaningful problem.
  • Situated and experiential learning traditions — realistic contexts improve relevance and application.
  • Self-regulated learning perspectives — extended problem work requires planning, monitoring, and adaptation.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Some foundational objectives are learned more efficiently through explicit instruction before or during PBL.
  • The pattern depends on facilitation; unguided open-ended work is not the same thing.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Introduce a complex authentic problem.
  2. Have learners identify what they know, what they need to know, and how they will investigate.
  3. Support inquiry, evidence gathering, and collaborative reasoning.
  4. Ask learners to propose and justify a response, solution, or recommendation.
  5. Debrief what was learned about both the problem and the inquiry process.

docs.title: Elements Used
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Problem-Solving Tasks
  • Reflection

  • Guided Practice

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Problems can be selected or adapted for learner context and domain.
  • Inquiry supports can be heavier for novices and lighter for more experienced learners.
  • Products can vary, including presentations, proposals, designs, or cases.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Anchored Instruction
  • Case-Based Learning (Harvard Method)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Medical learners diagnosing and responding to a patient scenario.
  • Business learners working through a complex organizational case.
  • Engineering or civic learners designing responses to a local real-world problem.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Strong pattern for integrating inquiry, collaboration, and authentic transfer.
  • Most effective when the problem is real enough to matter and the facilitation is strong enough to prevent drift.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
POGIL is a team-based inquiry pattern in which learners work through carefully designed activities that move from exploration to concept invention to application. Rather than receiving a finished explanation first, learners examine a model, dataset, or representation, answer sequenced questions, infer the underlying concept, and then apply it in new situations. The "process-oriented" part emphasizes not only content learning but also process skills such as communication, teamwork, and self-management.

The pattern is useful when instructors want inquiry without abandoning structure. It provides more guidance than open discovery and more learner reasoning than direct explanation-first teaching.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Carefully designed guided materials: POGIL depends on activities that sequence attention and inference well.
  • Team roles or norms: Learners need structures that support collaborative responsibility.
  • Facilitation rather than constant telling: The instructor monitors, questions, and clarifies instead of front-loading all explanations.
  • A model-to-concept-to-application flow: Learners need to move beyond observation into generalization and use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Design quality is critical: Poor prompts or weak models can make the inquiry confusing.
  • Some learners need more explicit support: Even guided inquiry can overload novices if too much is implicit.
  • Time demands: POGIL often takes longer than lecture-based coverage.
  • Role compliance can become superficial: Team roles only help if they actually structure interaction.

docs.title: Grain Size
docs.text:
• Lesson
  • Unit

docs.title: Target Goals
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding through inquiry: Learners infer principles from structured evidence.
  • Process skill development: Teamwork, communication, and self-management are built into the pattern.
  • Application after invention: Learners use the concept after constructing it.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in STEM and inquiry-rich courses: Strong fit where models, data, or representations can anchor concept building.
  • Groups ready for structured collaboration: POGIL assumes learners can work interdependently with guidance.
  • Learners who benefit from scaffolded inquiry: Best when exploration is supported rather than fully open.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist perspectives — learners build concepts actively from structured exploration.
  • Inquiry-oriented perspectives — understanding deepens through guided questioning and evidence use.
  • Cooperative learning perspectives — group roles and shared reasoning support content and process development.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• POGIL still needs enough guidance for novices; it is not a defense of minimal instruction.
  • Some straightforward procedural content may be more efficiently taught with direct demonstration first.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Contradicting
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M]

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
1. Present a model, representation, or dataset for learners to explore.
  2. Use sequenced questions to guide pattern noticing and interpretation.
  3. Have learners articulate the concept or principle they infer.
  4. Move into application tasks that test and extend the concept.
  5. Debrief both the content and the group's inquiry process.

docs.title: Elements Used

• Scaffolded Inquiry
  • Structured Questioning
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Practice

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
• Teams can have differentiated roles that support participation and accountability.
  • Instructors can vary the amount of structure in the prompts depending on learner readiness.
  • Application tasks can be tuned for different pacing or complexity levels.

docs.title: Related Patterns

  • Collaborative Inquiry

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Chemistry learners using data and representations to infer a concept before solving related problems.
  • STEM lessons where model analysis leads into concept naming and then application.
  • Online inquiry activities with guided prompts and team roles.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Offers a middle path between lecture-first instruction and open inquiry.
  • Particularly useful when instructors want both conceptual reasoning and process-skill development.
