  • Multimedia Learning - Multimedia learning is the principle of combining words, visuals, and other media in ways that support understanding without overloading attention.
  • Multimedia Projects - Multimedia projects ask learners to create meaning through more than one medium, such as text, image, audio, video, interaction, or digital composition.
  • Multimodal Instruction - Multimodal instruction presents and develops learning through more than one representational mode, such as text, speech, image, gesture, diagram, demonstration, or interactive media.
  • Multiple Methods of Assessment - Using multiple methods of assessment means gathering evidence of learning through more than one type of task, representation, or performance.

docs.title: N
docs.text: • Note-taking - Note-taking is the instructional principle of helping learners externalize important information, structure, and interpretation while reading, listening, observing, or solving problems.

docs.title: O
docs.text: • Observation/Shadowing - Observation and shadowing are learning designs in which learners watch peers, experts, or practitioners perform authentic work in order to notice strategies, decisions, routines, and contextual demands that are difficult to infer from…

docs.title: P
docs.text:
• Pairing Non-examples with Examples - Pairing non-examples with examples helps learners understand a concept, procedure, or category by seeing both what fits and what does not.
  • Peer Discussion - Peer discussion is the instructional principle of using structured talk among learners to deepen interpretation, explanation, and understanding.
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review - Peer feedback and peer review are instructional structures in which learners evaluate one another's work against shared criteria in order to improve the work and deepen their own understanding.
  • Peer Learning - Peer learning is the principle that learners can deepen understanding by explaining, questioning, modeling, and responding to one another.
  • Perspective Seeking/Multiple Perspectives - Perspective seeking is the instructional principle of actively engaging with multiple viewpoints in order to better understand a topic, event, text, or problem.
  • Perspective-Taking - Perspective-taking is the principle of intentionally examining a situation, text, problem, or decision from viewpoints other than one's own.
  • Physical Activity - Physical activity in learning contexts means intentionally incorporating movement, exercise, or embodied breaks to support attention, energy, regulation, and readiness to learn.
  • Positive Self-talk - Positive self-talk is the deliberate use of supportive, instructional, or regulating internal language to influence how a learner interprets difficulty, effort, and performance.
  • Pre-reading Questioning - Pre-reading questioning is the instructional principle of using questions before a text, source, or reading task to activate prior knowledge, orient attention, and establish a purpose for reading.
  • Problem-based Learning - Problem-based learning organizes learning around complex, meaningful problems that do not have a single obvious answer.
  • Procedural Learning - Procedural learning is the principle of helping learners acquire and refine sequences of action, routines, or task procedures until performance becomes more accurate, fluent, and reliable.
  • Process-based Writing - Process-based writing treats writing as a sequence of intentional moves such as generating ideas, planning, drafting, revising, editing, and reflecting rather than as a one-shot product.
  • Purposeful Reflection - Purposeful reflection is structured time for learners to examine what they did, what they understood, where they struggled, and what they should do next.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: • Quiet Learning Spaces - Quiet learning spaces reduce competing demands on attention so learners can focus on reading, listening, problem solving, and reflection.

docs.title: R
docs.text:
• Real-world Math - Real-world math connects mathematical ideas to situations learners recognize as meaningful in work, home, community, finance, health, civic life, or further study.
  • Reflection - Reflection is the principle of deliberately examining one's experience, reasoning, performance, or progress in order to extract lessons and guide future action.
  • Reflective Practice - Reflective practice is the principle of examining actions, decisions, and outcomes in order to improve later performance.
  • Reinforcement Theory - Reinforcement theory is the principle of shaping behavior by making desired responses more likely through contingent consequences such as feedback, reward, or progression.
  • Retrieval Practice - Retrieval practice is the principle of strengthening learning by having learners actively recall information, ideas, or procedures from memory rather than only restudy them.
  • Rhetorical Skill Development - Rhetorical skill development is the principle of helping learners craft arguments, communicate persuasively, respond to audiences, and use language strategically for effect.

docs.title: S
docs.text:
• Scaffolding - Scaffolding is the principle of providing temporary support that helps learners perform beyond what they could do independently.
  • Scaffolding & Fading - Scaffolding & Fading is the short-form canonical target for designs that provide temporary support and then reduce it as learner independence grows.
  • Scaffolding and Fading - Scaffolding provides temporary, contingent support to learners as they develop new skills or knowledge.
  • Self-Determination Theory - Self-determination theory is used here as a principle emphasizing autonomy, competence, and relatedness as conditions that support motivation.
  • Self-Directed Learning - Self-directed learning is the principle of helping learners plan, monitor, and manage important parts of their own learning process.
  • Self-monitoring - Self-monitoring is the practice of checking one's current understanding, performance, strategy use, or progress against a goal, model, or success criterion.
  • Self-Regulated Learning - Self-regulated learning is the principle of designing instruction so learners can plan, monitor, adjust, and reflect on their own learning processes.
  • Self-Regulation - Self-regulation is the short-form canonical target for instructional designs that help learners plan, monitor, and adjust behavior, effort, and strategy over time.
  • Sequencing - Sequencing is the principle of arranging instructional content, tasks, or supports in an order that helps learners build understanding progressively.
  • Simulations & Immersive Virtual Environments - Simulations and immersive virtual environments let learners practice decisions, procedures, and interpretations inside a designed representation of reality.
  • Situated Learning - Situated learning is the principle that learning is shaped by the contexts, practices, and communities in which knowledge is used.
  • Skills Sprint - Skills sprints are short, intensive learning cycles organized around producing something meaningful under time constraints.
  • Social Constructivism - Social constructivism is the principle that learners build understanding through interaction with other people, language, and shared activity.
  • Social Interdependence - Social interdependence is the principle that the structure of relationships among learners shapes the quality of collaboration, motivation, and learning.
  • Social Learning - Social learning is the principle that understanding and performance often develop through interaction with other people, not just individual study.
  • Spaced Learning - Spaced learning distributes study or practice across multiple sessions separated by intervals of time, rather than concentrating the same total effort into a single block.
  • Speech-to-text - Speech-to-text converts spoken language into written text, giving learners another route for composing, capturing ideas, and participating in text-based environments.
  • Strengths-based Approach - A strengths-based approach starts from the assumption that learners bring assets, knowledge, strategies, identities, and capabilities that instruction should recognize and build on.
  • Summative Assessment - Summative assessment is the principle of evaluating learner performance at the end of an instructional sequence in order to judge the level of competence, understanding, or achievement reached.

docs.title: T
docs.text:
• Text Chats - Text chats use live or near-live written exchange as a learning space for discussion, coordination, questioning, and low-stakes composition.
  • Text-to-Speech - Text-to-speech (TTS) converts written text into spoken audio, giving learners an additional way to access reading materials, instructions, and feedback.
  • Transfer of Learning - Transfer of learning is the principle of helping learners apply what they have learned in one context to new tasks, situations, or problems.

docs.title: V
docs.text: • Video Replay Analysis - Video replay analysis uses recorded performance, instruction, or interaction as an object for review.

docs.title: W
docs.text: • Worked Examples - Worked examples present a partially or fully solved problem so learners can study task structure, decision points, and reasoning before attempting similar problems independently.

docs.title: Draft
docs.text:
• Access-Use-Effectiveness Framework - A three-stage framework for evaluating school or district technology integration — having devices (access) does not imply using them for instruction (use), and using them does not imply doing so in pedagogically sound, student-centered ways (effectiveness).
  • Bullying Prevention and Intervention - Effective bullying response requires recognizing the full set of participant roles (not just bully and victim), addressing the power imbalance and repetition that define bullying, and treating cyberbullying as a distinct problem requiring its own detection and response strategies.
  • Character Education - Character education integrates ethical understanding, emotional/caring responses, and concrete moral action, typically operating schoolwide through democratic practice, relationship-building, and service rather than through rule recitation alone.
  • Classroom Space and Procedural Design - Preventing management problems before they start depends on how classroom space is arranged, whether procedures (conventional, efficiency-focused) are distinguished from rules (moral, responsibility-focused), how difficulty is sequenced, how much structure is given, and how transitions are handled.
  • Cognitive Styles - Cognitive styles are relatively stable individual differences in how people typically perceive, remember, and solve problems — distinct from the broader, less reliable notion of "learning styles" — and knowledge of a student's style can be used either to play to their existing strengths or to deliberately build the balance they lack.
  • Communities of Innovation - A Community of Innovation is a group focused on producing innovative output together, distinguished by named characteristics at the individual, group, and organizational level — hacker motivation, dynamic expertise and autonomy; group flow, idea prototyping, cognitive diversity, and productive critique; flexible structure and psychological safety.
  • Cone of Experience (Concrete-to-Abstract Media Selection) - Dale's Cone of Experience arranges learning experiences along a continuum from concrete, direct experience to abstract, symbolic (verbal) experience, as guidance for balancing — not ranking — media and instructional method choices.
  • Criterion- and Norm-Referenced Testing - Criterion-referenced tests report what a student can and cannot do against a fixed standard; norm-referenced tests report how a student compares to others who took the same test — genuinely different information, suited to different decisions, and not interchangeable.
  • Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms - Many taken-for-granted classroom norms — eye contact, wait time, the purpose of a question, competition versus cooperation, punctuality — reflect specific cultural assumptions (often an independent, individualist view of the self) that can mismatch a student's own cultural norms and produce misunderstanding on both sides, independent of the student's actual ability or motivation.
  • Designing a Valid Experiment - A scientific experiment isolates one manipulated variable between an experimental and control group, guards against experimenter and participant-expectancy bias through blinding, and uses random sampling for generalizability and random assignment for causal inference — two distinct uses of randomness that are often conflated.
  • Educational Psychology as Both Art and Science - Educational psychology bridges the scientific study of learning with the art of teaching practice — research findings inform practice, and practice raises new questions for systematic study, in a continuing loop.
  • Educational Readiness - Educational readiness has two complementary meanings — a student's preparedness for the activities and expectations of school, and a teacher's or school's responsibility to adjust instruction to meet students where they actually are.
  • Effective Classroom Management Plan Criteria - A comprehensive classroom management plan establishes positive relationships, prevents attention-seeking and work-avoidance behavior, redirects misbehavior quickly and unobtrusively, stops chronic misbehavior with consistent simple strategies, teaches self-control, and respects cultural differences — a synthesis of the humanist, applied-behavior-analysis, and prevention-oriented traditions.
  • Evidence-Based Teaching and Scientific Reasoning - Teaching should be grounded in evidence rather than personal impression or ideology, because personal inquiry is systematically vulnerable to confirmation bias; the scientific method guards against this through systematic empiricism, empirically answerable questions, and public, self-correcting knowledge.
  • Fostering Creative Thinking - Creative thinking — generating ideas that are new, useful, and appropriate — can be deliberately stimulated through divergent-thinking prompts, protecting intrinsic motivation from constant evaluation, and finding room for experimentation alongside necessary assessment.
  • Four Boundaries of Learning Community (Access, Relationships, Vision, Function) - Because "learning community" is used inconsistently across research and practice, West and Williams propose defining any community by which of four boundaries actually bind it — access, relationships, vision, and function — so designers can diagnose what a given design will and won't produce.
  • Free-Choice Learning Environment Design - Free-choice learning environments (museums, hobbies, self-directed exploration) give visitors real control over what and how deeply they engage, with no externally imposed curriculum or sequence, so the design must be intrinsically compelling on its own terms rather than backed by grades or tests.
  • Functional Behavior Assessment - Disruptive behavior is more effectively addressed by identifying the specific triggering circumstance — physiological, environmental, or instructional — than by focusing on a student's personality, and fair, well-documented responses build the collaborative trust that makes long-term support possible.
  • Gender-Equitable Classroom Interaction - Even teachers who intend to interact with boys and girls equally tend, on average and without realizing it, to give boys more attention, more "public" visibility, and more credit for correct knowledge — patterns that are trends with many individual exceptions, and that a teacher who consciously attends to them can change.
  • Grading Policy Decisions - Composing a grade requires teachers to make several separable, often-unexamined decisions — how to weight components, whether to fold in social skills or effort, and whether to grade absolutely or relatively — each with real tradeoffs that a single "best" answer doesn't resolve.
  • High-Stakes Testing and Accountability Effects - Accountability systems like NCLB depend on content standards being neither too broad nor too narrow, on tests actually aligning with those standards, and on measuring growth as well as absolute proficiency — and when any of these break down, the predictable results are curriculum narrowing, teaching to the test, and unreliable comparisons across schools and states.
  • Informal Learning - Informal learning is self-directed, unofficial learning "pulled" by the learner's own perceived need rather than "pushed" by a predetermined curriculum, and accounts for the large majority of adult and workplace learning even though organizations still spend most training budgets on formal instruction.
  • Intelligence Testing: Uses and Limits - Standardized intelligence tests are among the most reliable instruments in psychology and predict a range of academic and occupational outcomes, but they must be periodically re-normed against the population, and they have long been criticized as culturally biased and blind to non-academic forms of ability.
  • Learner-Centered Paradigm of Education - The learner-centered paradigm replaces a time-fixed, group-based, sorting-oriented school system with one that holds attainment constant and lets pace and path vary to fit each learner.
  • Least Restrictive Environment - Students with disabilities should be educated alongside non-disabled peers in regular classrooms and school programs as much as the specific student and setting allow, with the precise combination of settings determined case by case rather than fixed by disability category alone.
  • Natural and Logical Consequences - Natural consequences arise on their own from an action, and logical consequences are imposed by others but have an obvious connection to it; both work better than punishment at reducing misbehavior because they focus on repairing the future rather than blaming the past, though they fail when the misbehavior is too serious, or when the student's motive is power rather than attention.
  • NBPTS Five Core Propositions for Accomplished Teaching - The National Board for Professional Teaching Standards defines accomplished teaching across five propositions — commitment to students, subject and pedagogical mastery, managing and monitoring learning, systematic reflection, and membership in learning communities.
  • Performance Technology - Performance Technology treats instruction as one of several possible interventions for closing a performance gap, and requires analyzing the organizational system around a learner before assuming training is the right solution.
  • Preserve Heritage Language While Acquiring an Additional Language - Maintaining and developing a bilingual student's heritage language supports, rather than competes with, the acquisition of a new majority or school language, while heritage-language loss is associated with slower additional-language development.
  • Standardized Test Fairness and Bias - Standardized tests can distort measured performance for specific groups through three distinct, documented mechanisms — biased item content and format, differential predictive accuracy, and stereotype threat — each requiring a different fix, and none reducible to "the test is simply biased or not."
  • Support Early Language Development - Early language development is fastest in environments with responsive, reciprocal adult-child interaction — conversational turn-taking, varied input, and immediate feedback — rather than passive exposure to language alone.
  • Supporting Gifted and Talented Students - Students with unusually high IQ or exceptional talent (traditionally an IQ of 130 or higher) are not the socially maladjusted stereotype often assumed, but they do languish without accommodation, and support usually means blending acceleration with enrichment rather than choosing one.
  • Supporting Students with ADHD - ADHD is a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactive-impulsive behavior with a documented neurobiological basis, distinct from ordinary high activity — classrooms can inadvertently aggravate it, but structure, predictability, and explicit self-monitoring instruction (not medication decisions, which are outside a teacher's control) are the levers a teacher actually has.
  • Supporting Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder - Autism spectrum disorder is defined by disturbances in social interaction, communication, and repetitive behavior or interests that vary widely in severity across the "spectrum" — distinct from intellectual disability — and is not caused by vaccination despite persistent popular belief.
  • Supporting Students with Intellectual Disabilities - Intellectual disability is defined by both cognitive capacity and adaptive functioning, and effective classroom support boils down to three general strategies — extra time and practice, embedding activities in daily-life context, and full inclusion in both social and academic activities.
  • Technology Integration Levels (SAMR / RAT / PIC-RAT) - A family of frameworks (RAT, SAMR, PIC-RAT) for judging whether a specific use of technology in instruction merely replaces a prior practice or meaningfully improves or transforms it.
  • TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) - TPACK holds that effective teaching with technology requires an integrated understanding of content, pedagogy, and technology together, not mastery of the three in isolation.
  • Twelve Characteristics of Effective Teachers - Walker (2008) asked in-service and preservice teachers to identify what made their own most effective teachers effective; twelve characteristics emerged, spanning preparation, disposition, fairness, and personal connection rather than any single instructional technique.
  • Universal Design for Learning (UDL) - Universal Design for Learning holds that accessibility features should be built into learning materials and environments by default, following three principles — multiple means of representation, expression, and engagement — rather than retrofitted for individual learners after the fact.
  • User-Centered Design for Learning - User-centered design applies human-computer-interaction methods — personas, prototyping, and usability evaluation — to reduce the extraneous cognitive load a learning interface imposes, alongside pedagogical design.
  • Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment - A high-quality classroom assessment needs validity (the interpretations and uses made of its results are justified), reliability (its results are consistent across occasions, raters, and items), and freedom from bias (it doesn't distort performance based on a student's group membership) — three genuinely distinct properties, each with its own failure modes.
  • Well-Structured vs. Ill-Structured Problems - Problems vary in how much information and how clear a solution procedure they provide; well-structured problems support algorithms with guaranteed correct solutions, while ill-structured problems require heuristics that work often but not always.
  • Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference - When a teacher and student are from different racial or ethnic backgrounds, critical feedback needs a third component beyond ordinary praise-plus-criticism — an explicit assurance that the teacher believes the student can reach a higher standard — because students of color have historically-grounded reasons to distrust negative feedback from a white teacher.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Davies and West (2014) argue that technology-integration efforts should be evaluated as progressive stages rather than as a single access/no-access binary. Their three stages: (1) access — do teachers and students have working, adequate technology available; (2) use — do they actually use it for instructional purposes, as opposed to administrative tasks or passive consumption; and (3) effectiveness — is the technology used in pedagogically sound, student-centered ways that measurably facilitate learning.

The framework was developed as a corrective to access-only indicators (such as the earlier LoTi Framework) that treat widespread device availability, or even pervasive use, as itself sufficient evidence of quality integration. Davies and West's review of national survey data shows most schools plateau at stage 1 or 2: 97% of teachers report daily computer access, yet 29% of those with daily access rarely or never use it instructionally, and even when technology is used, it more often serves record-keeping or information-gathering than pedagogically-driven redesign of instruction. This is the crux of the framework's diagnostic value: a school reporting high device saturation and high classroom use can still be evaluated as failing at stage 3 if the use amounts to digitized worksheets rather than a pedagogical change technology specifically enables.

The framework operates at the institutional or programmatic level — evaluating a school's or district's overall technology-integration effort — which distinguishes it from Technology Integration Levels (SAMR / RAT / PIC-RAT), which judge the effect of a single lesson's or task's specific technology choice, and from TPACK, which assesses an individual teacher's knowledge rather than an institution's implementation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Data collection at all three stages — device/access counts alone are insufficient; usage logs or observation are needed to distinguish use from non-use, and pedagogical review is needed to distinguish effective from merely administrative use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Access is a necessary but nowhere near sufficient condition for effective integration — treating 1:1 device rollout as the endpoint of a technology-integration initiative, rather than its starting condition, is the framework's central warning
  • Moving from stage 2 to stage 3 (use to effectiveness) typically requires professional development in pedagogy, not additional technology — throwing more devices or software at a use-without-effectiveness problem does not resolve it

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Not learner-facing directly — an evaluative framework for school/district technology leaders and instructional designers assessing an institution's technology-integration program, in the same category as Performance Technology

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not a learning objective — an institutional diagnostic for whether a technology investment is translating into pedagogically meaningful classroom practice

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Technology Integration Levels (SAMR / RAT / PIC-RAT) — judges a single lesson or tool choice's effect, complementary to this framework's institutional/programmatic scope
  • TPACK — assesses an individual teacher's integrated knowledge, distinct from this framework's institutional-level access/use/effectiveness diagnosis

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A district reporting 97% daily device access, where survey data still show large shares of teachers rarely using the devices instructionally — stalled at stage 1–2
  • A classroom using tablets daily only for digitized worksheets and drill exercises — stage 2 (use) without stage 3 (pedagogically transformative effectiveness)

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Davies, R. S., & West, R. E. (2014). Technology integration in schools. In Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology (4th ed., pp. 841–853). Springer. Prepublication version in R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/technology_integration

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use language that preserves disciplinary rigor while reducing unnecessary linguistic difficulty. Accessible vocabulary and syntax do not mean "watering down" content; they mean introducing essential terms intentionally, explaining them clearly, modeling sentence structures that learners will encounter in authentic texts, and removing avoidable wording barriers that would otherwise block participation and comprehension.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Accessible vocabulary and syntax matter because learners can fail a task for language reasons even when the underlying idea is within reach. Limiting and organizing unfamiliar language can reduce unnecessary processing demands Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S], while asking learners to explain and reuse key terms in their own words makes vocabulary more durable than definition exposure alone Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The key design tension is that supports should open the door to authentic disciplinary language, not replace it permanently, so explanations, glossaries, and sentence frames should gradually give way to more independent use Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Identify the small set of essential terms learners must understand and use, rather than introducing large numbers of unfamiliar words at once
  • Provide plain-language explanations, examples, and non-examples before expecting independent use
  • Model sentence structures learners will need in discussion, reading, and writing, with supports such as sentence frames, glossaries, or worked examples
  • Recycle key vocabulary across speaking, reading, and writing so terms become usable tools rather than one-time definitions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Oversimplification can hide the actual language of the discipline; supports should bridge into authentic terminology, not replace it permanently
  • Too many new terms or overly dense syntax can overwhelm working memory and suppress content understanding Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]
  • Accessibility depends on learner background knowledge, language proficiency, and context; the same wording may be clear for one group and opaque for another
  • If instructors simplify language without explicitly teaching target terms, learners may understand the lesson but still fail when faced with authentic texts or assessments

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners new to a discipline's vocabulary, genres, or sentence structures
  • Multilingual learners and learners re-entering formal education who need explicit bridges into academic language
  • Learners with lower reading fluency or working-memory limits who benefit from reduced linguistic load while acquiring new content
  • Learners who avoid participation because they do not yet control the language needed to explain their thinking

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build access to disciplinary texts, instructions, and discussions
  • Improve comprehension of new concepts without separating language from content
  • Increase participation in discussion and writing by giving learners usable language structures
  • Support transfer from simplified explanation to authentic academic or workplace language

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist accounts (Vygotsky, Bruner) support language scaffolds as tools that let learners participate in meaning-making before they can do so fluently on their own
  • Cognitive Load Theory supports reducing unnecessary linguistic complexity so working memory can focus on the target concept rather than decoding the wording
  • Information-processing perspectives support repeated, structured exposure to key terms and sentence forms so they can be encoded, retrieved, and reused
  • Adult-learning perspectives qualify the need for transparent, relevant language that respects learners while making expectations legible

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Learners still need contact with authentic domain language; permanent simplification can underprepare them for real texts, conversations, and assessments
  • Vocabulary support is strongest when paired with active use and explanation, not definition lists alone Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Language supports should fade as learner control grows, or they risk becoming a crutch Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — limiting and organizing new terms reduces the linguistic load learners must carry at once
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — vocabulary becomes durable when learners explain and apply it in their own words
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — language support is most effective when instructors respond to the learner's actual confusion rather than pre-scripted simplification
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — syntax frames and glossaries should be withdrawn gradually as learners internalize disciplinary language

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Explicit Instruction: Vocabulary — focuses on the direct teaching of word meanings and usage
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — accessible wording works best when paired with coherent organization
  • Multimodal Instruction — visuals, audio, and examples can reinforce unfamiliar vocabulary and syntax
  • Scaffolding and Fading — language supports should be deliberately reduced over time

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Accessible Syntax — revises sentence complexity while preserving the core concept
  • Relevant Vocabulary Instruction — explicitly selects and revisits high-value terms
  • Simplify and Clarify Instructions — removes avoidable ambiguity from task directions
  • Assigned Readings paired with glossaries, margin notes, or sentence frames can make complex texts usable without replacing them

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Binder, K. S., Tremblay, K. A., & Joseph, A. (2020). Vocabulary accessibility and acquisition: Do you get more from a financestor or a sociophite? Journal of Research in Reading, 43(4), 395-416. doi:10.1111/1467-9817.12319
  • Alloway, T. P. (2006). How does working memory work in the classroom? Educational Research and Reviews, 1(4), 134-139.
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (2009). Simply put: A guide for creating easy-to-understand materials.
  • Devlin, M., Kift, S., Nelson, K., Smith, L., & McKay, J. (2012). Effective teaching and support of students from low socioeconomic status backgrounds. Office for Learning and Teaching.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activation is the principle of prompting learners to surface prior knowledge, experiences, or related schemas before new instruction.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Activation is most useful when new content will make more sense if learners first retrieve what they already know, what they assume, or what experiences they can connect to the topic. In strong instruction, activation is not just a warm-up: it can support meaningful chunking and prior organization before new material arrives Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S], and it becomes more powerful when learners explain their predictions or prior ideas rather than merely listing them Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The same mechanism can also backfire if incorrect prior knowledge is activated and then left unexamined, which is why confidently expressed errors need prompt correction if they are going to become productive learning moments High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A prompt that draws out what learners already know — effective activation requires some visible retrieval, comparison, prediction, or preview rather than a vague reminder to “think about it”
  • A clear bridge from prior knowledge to new content — the instruction that follows has to explicitly connect prior ideas to the new material

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Activated misconceptions may also need correction — prior knowledge can help comprehension, but inaccurate prior knowledge can distort it unless the lesson addresses the mismatch
  • Activation without follow-through becomes ritual — quick openers do little if later instruction never uses what learners surfaced

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners entering a new topic with some relevant background knowledge, experience, or analogies to draw on
  • Learners who benefit from explicit schema preparation before dense reading, explanation, or problem solving
  • Learners prone to shallow initial engagement, where retrieval and prediction can increase attention at the start of a lesson

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve comprehension, readiness, and knowledge integration
  • Increase the likelihood that new ideas are interpreted through usable prior schemas rather than treated as isolated facts
  • Surface preconceptions early enough to revise them during instruction

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information Processing Theory — retrieval of relevant prior knowledge helps organize incoming information and reduces the burden of interpreting content from scratch
  • Cognitive Activation — activation increases the chance that learners will engage conceptually rather than passively receive content
  • Analogical Reasoning — analogies and prior examples can provide the bridge that makes new ideas interpretable

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — supports the role of prior knowledge, but qualifies that learners may construct flawed understandings if activation is not followed by feedback, contradiction, or refinement

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — activation helps when it supports meaningful chunking and prior organization, but weak prior knowledge limits the benefit
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — prompts that ask learners to explain predictions or prior ideas can deepen the value of activation
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M] — surfacing confidently held misconceptions can be instructionally productive if corrected promptly, but risky if left unresolved

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Pre-Reading Questioning — one of the most direct operationalizations of activation before reading or explanation
  • Explicit Instruction — activation strengthens explicit teaching when prior knowledge is deliberately tied to new content rather than assumed
  • Knowledge Organization — activation helps learners fit new information into a meaningful structure

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Pre-Reading Activities — Before a dense article or textbook section, learners generate predictions, define likely key terms, or answer a short anticipatory question set. The value comes from making prior ideas visible so the reading can confirm, refine, or contradict them.

Prior Knowledge Activation — In a science lesson, learners first explain what they think causes seasons or why objects float, then compare those ideas to a demonstration or text. This turns activation into a diagnostic starting point rather than a ritual opener.

Background Knowledge Activation — A routine in which an instructor uses a quick write, brainstorm, or concept map to surface what learners already know before introducing new material. Strongest when the teacher refers back to the activation during the lesson rather than abandoning it after the opener.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ausubel, D. P. (1968). Educational psychology: A cognitive view. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
  • Bransford, J. D., Brown, A. L., & Cocking, R. R. (Eds.). (2000). How people learn. National Academy Press. https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/9853/how-people-learn-brain-mind-experience-and-school-expanded-edition

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Active learning is the principle that learners should do meaningful cognitive work with content rather than only receive it. The core move is not activity for its own sake, but requiring learners to explain, apply, compare, predict, generate, or revise so that understanding is constructed through use.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
Active learning improves learning when the activity requires learners to think with the content rather than merely touch it. Explanation, prediction, retrieval, and comparison are especially valuable because they force learners to surface assumptions, test understanding, and revise mental models Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. That is why active learning typically works best when tasks are focused, accountable, and supported with feedback: poorly structured activity can still become busywork, while well-designed activity can even turn confidently expressed mistakes into opportunities for stronger retention when those errors are corrected and discussed High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S].

The effect size for active learning in STEM is unusually large and consistent for an education intervention: Freeman et al.'s (2014) meta-analysis of 225 studies comparing constructivist/active class designs against traditional lecturing found students in straight lecture courses were 1.5 times more likely to fail (odds ratio 1.95) than students in courses with some active learning, and that assessment performance (exams, concept inventories) improved by about half a standard deviation on average (d = 0.47) — with no significant difference in this effect across biology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, geology, math, physics, or psychology. A publication-bias check found the result would require a large number of unpublished null-result studies (114 for exam/concept-inventory performance, 438 for failure rate) to overturn — leading the authors to compare the strength of evidence to a medical trial that would ethically need to be stopped early for benefit. Beyond raising performance broadly, active learning has also been shown to disproportionately help already-disadvantaged students specifically Active learning narrows achievement gaps for disadvantaged and underrepresented students [+S], functioning as an equity intervention in gateway STEM courses, not merely an average-performance one.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task that requires thinking: Learners need something to decide, produce, explain, or test.
  • Alignment to the objective: The activity needs to exercise the target understanding or skill.
  • Processing time: Learners need enough time to articulate and revise ideas.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Busywork risk: Activity without cognitive demand does little.
  • Weak guidance: Novices can flounder if active tasks are under-supported.
  • Time tradeoff: Active learning often covers fewer topics but with better processing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from explanation, application, and retrieval rather than passive exposure alone.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve conceptual understanding, transfer, and durable retention through use.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivism
  • Information Processing Theory

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Active learning still needs structure, modeling, and feedback to be instructionally effective.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — active tasks are strongest when learners explain, compare, or justify rather than only complete an action
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S] — prediction and discussion tasks can make errors instructionally valuable when they are surfaced and corrected
  • Active learning narrows achievement gaps for disadvantaged and underrepresented students [+S] — in STEM gateway courses, a uniformly applied active-learning redesign has been shown to disproportionately benefit already-disadvantaged students, narrowing rather than just shifting the overall achievement distribution
  • Discussion promotes more active thinking than lecture, though lecture is no worse for transmitting information [+M] — direct observational evidence for why moving from passive lecture toward active formats changes the kind of thinking students actually do in class

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Guided Practice
  • Explaining Their Thinking
  • Social Learning

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Learners solve, discuss, and compare approaches instead of only hearing a lecture.
  • A lesson pauses for prediction, retrieval, or explanation before moving on.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Freeman, S., Eddy, S. L., McDonough, M., Smith, M. K., Okoroafor, N., Jordt, H., & Wenderoth, M. P. (2014). Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(23), 8410-8415. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1319030111
  • Chi, M. T. H., & Wylie, R. (2014). The ICAP framework: Linking cognitive engagement to active learning outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Analogical reasoning is the principle of using relational similarity between a familiar case and a new case to support understanding, inference, and transfer. It is useful when the surface details differ but the underlying structure is similar enough to guide thinking.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Analogical reasoning is most valuable when learners need help seeing a new concept through the structure of something they already understand. The principle works best when the analogy highlights deep relational similarity rather than superficial resemblance alone, because a coherent mapping can reduce interpretive burden and help learners organize new information Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]. In instruction, that means the teacher or task must help learners map the source and target explicitly, notice where the analogy is helpful, and identify where it breaks down; analogies become even stronger when learners explain why the mapping works Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Poor analogies do not merely fail to help; they can actively mislead by inviting false transfer from surface features, though even confident misreadings can become productive if the mismatch is made explicit and corrected High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A familiar source domain and a target domain with meaningful structural overlap — the analogy has to preserve a genuine relation, not just a catchy comparison
  • Prompts that make the shared relation explicit — learners often need help seeing how the source maps onto the target
  • Discussion of where the analogy breaks down — instructional analogies are strongest when their limits are named

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Surface-feature matches can mislead learners if the deep structure differs
  • Overextended analogies can create misconceptions
  • Weak prior knowledge limits the benefit — if learners do not understand the source domain, the analogy cannot do much explanatory work

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners encountering abstract, invisible, or complex concepts for the first time
  • Learners who benefit from conceptual bridges between familiar and unfamiliar domains
  • Novices who need support recognizing structural similarity across contexts

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve conceptual understanding, transfer, and relational reasoning
  • Help learners recognize underlying structure rather than relying only on surface cues
  • Support explanation and prediction in new domains through structured comparison

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Structure-mapping perspectives on analogy — analogical reasoning works when relational correspondences are preserved across domains
  • Metaphors & Analogies — provides the broader family of instructional moves that analogical reasoning belongs to
  • Information Processing Theory — analogies can reduce interpretive burden by linking new content to existing schema

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — analogies support construction of meaning, but only if learners actively interpret and test the mapping rather than accept it uncritically

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — analogies can support chunking and organization when the relational mapping is coherent
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — analogies become stronger when learners explain why the mapping works
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M] — analogies that trigger confident but incorrect predictions can still be instructionally useful if the mismatch is corrected explicitly

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Metaphors & Analogies — analogical reasoning is one of the strongest structured forms of analogy use in teaching
  • Activation — analogies often work by activating prior knowledge before introducing a new concept
  • Constructivist Learning — analogies help learners build new understanding out of familiar structures

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Analogies — A teacher explains electric current through a water-flow analogy, then explicitly identifies where the analogy helps and where it breaks down.

Metaphors — Learners compare the structure of an atom to a solar system model, then critique the limits of the comparison so the metaphor does not harden into misconception.

Comparing parallel cases — In math or science, learners study two situations with different surface details but the same underlying relationship, then explain the shared structure before solving a new transfer problem.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog0702_3
  • Richland, L. E., Zur, O., & Holyoak, K. J. (2007). Cognitive supports for analogies in the mathematics classroom. Science, 316(5828), 1128-1129. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1142103

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Annotating is the practice of marking a text with notes, questions, summaries, definitions, or visual cues while reading. Done well, it turns reading from passive exposure into active sense-making: learners identify what matters, track confusion, connect ideas to prior knowledge, and leave behind an external record of their thinking that can support discussion, writing, and review.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Annotating improves reading when it makes thinking visible rather than just making the page colorful. Notes that paraphrase, question, summarize, or justify why a passage matters tend to support comprehension more than simple highlighting because they force learners to explain and organize ideas while reading Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Section summaries, margin codes, and lightweight note structures can also reduce the burden of holding a complex text together in working memory by turning it into manageable units Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. That is why annotation works best with a clear purpose, light structure, and a follow-up use such as discussion or writing; otherwise it easily becomes a ritual of marking without understanding, especially for learners who have not yet been shown what useful annotation looks like Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A text or media artifact worth interrogating, not just skimming
  • Clear annotation purposes such as tracking claims, defining terms, noting evidence, marking confusion, or summarizing sections
  • Visible structures for annotation such as margin space, shared codes, prompts, or digital tools
  • A follow-up task like discussion, synthesis, or writing so annotations become part of learning rather than busywork

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Highlighting without explanation often creates the appearance of study without improving understanding
  • Over-annotation can split attention and disrupt overall comprehension, especially in dense or unfamiliar texts
  • Learners need modeling; many do not naturally know what useful annotations look like
  • Annotation is less effective when texts are far beyond the learner's reading level or when the task lacks a clear purpose

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners reading dense informational, disciplinary, or argumentative texts
  • Learners who need support monitoring comprehension and distinguishing main ideas from detail
  • Learners preparing for seminar discussion, evidence-based writing, or source evaluation
  • Learners who benefit from externalizing thought processes to reduce memory burden during reading

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve comprehension of complex texts through active engagement
  • Strengthen metacognitive monitoring by noticing confusion, assumptions, and gaps
  • Support evidence gathering for writing, discussion, and analysis
  • Build habits of purposeful rereading, summarizing, and question generation

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist and sociocultural perspectives support annotation as a way for learners to actively construct meaning rather than merely receive it
  • Metacognitive accounts support annotation as an external trace of comprehension monitoring, question generation, and repair
  • Self-regulated learning frameworks support annotation when learners use it intentionally to set purposes, track understanding, and prepare next steps
  • Cognitive Load Theory qualifies annotation as helpful when it organizes attention, but potentially harmful if it adds unnecessary task demands

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Annotation quality matters more than annotation quantity
  • Prompted annotation is usually stronger for novices than open-ended "mark whatever seems important"
  • The strategy is most useful when learners explain why something matters, not when they only mark it Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — annotations that paraphrase, justify, or question the text improve learning more than passive marking
  • Liu (2006) found that students taught to annotate readings with questions and comments — rather than simply underlining passages — later wrote essays judged better-reasoned and more critically astute than students who annotated less actively, connecting annotation directly to Critical Thinking.
  • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — section summaries, headings, and coded notes help learners manage complex text by organizing it into meaningful units
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — guided prompts and teacher modeling improve annotation quality for learners who do not yet know what to notice
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — teaching a reading process ("define, question, summarize, connect") works better for novices than only asking for an end product

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Note-taking — annotation is note-taking anchored directly to a source text
  • Evaluating Sources — annotation can focus attention on evidence, credibility, and bias
  • Inquiry-based Learning — annotations help learners generate and refine questions from reading
  • Purposeful Reflection — reviewing one's own annotations supports metacognitive reflection after reading

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Social Annotation — learners annotate together inside a shared digital text and respond to one another's questions and interpretations
  • Assigned Readings with instructor-provided annotation prompts before seminar or discussion
  • Pre-Seminar Preparation — annotations can serve as evidence banks for later dialogue
  • Margin codes such as ?, !, claim, evidence, and connection can provide lightweight structure for novices

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Pressley, M., & Afflerbach, P. (1995). Verbal protocols of reading: The nature of constructively responsive reading. Routledge.
  • Kintsch, W. (1998). Comprehension: A paradigm for cognition. Cambridge University Press.
  • Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2014). Close reading and writing from sources. International Reading Association.
  • Liu, J. (2006). Assessing student critical thinking through annotation. [Cited via secondary source without full publication details]
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Critical thinking. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
  • Oster, L. (2001). Using the think-aloud for reading instruction. The Reading Teacher, 55(1), 64-69.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Give learners structured access to people with deeper domain expertise so they can ask questions, hear expert reasoning, receive targeted feedback, and compare their own thinking to more mature practice. Expert access is most valuable when it is interactive rather than performative: learners bring a real task, problem, or uncertainty, and the expert responds with explanation, modeling, questioning, and calibrated support.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Asking experts works best when the interaction helps learners move from vague confusion to more precise reasoning. The expert's role is not only to provide answers, but to make disciplinary judgment visible, surface key vocabulary and distinctions, and redirect learners toward productive next steps. This is strongest when support is contingent on what the learner actually understands Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M], when the expert prompts learners to explain their own reasoning instead of merely listening to answers Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], and when the expert gradually hands responsibility back to the learner rather than remaining the permanent problem-solver Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]. In practice this often overlaps with Coaching, Feedback, Demonstration, and Conceptual Questioning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to a relevant expert, mentor, instructor, practitioner, or more knowledgeable peer who can explain decisions, not just outcomes
  • A concrete learner question, artifact, case, or task; unguided "ask me anything" formats are usually less productive than interaction around real work
  • Psychological safety so learners can reveal uncertainty, partial understanding, or misconceptions without social penalty
  • A mechanism for follow-through such as revision, practice, or reflection; expert advice that is not applied quickly is easily forgotten

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Hard to scale with fidelity in large-group settings; responsive expert interaction is time-intensive and depends on scarce human attention
  • Quality varies with the expert's instructional skill; deep content knowledge alone does not guarantee clear explanation or effective questioning
  • Can produce dependency if experts solve problems for learners instead of diagnosing understanding and fading support Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]
  • Less effective when learners lack enough background knowledge to ask meaningful questions or interpret expert answers without additional scaffolding
  • Can intimidate learners with low confidence, low status, or limited language proficiency unless the interaction is deliberately structured and supportive

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices or near-novices who need access to expert vocabulary, heuristics, and standards of quality
  • Learners entering a profession, discipline, or authentic practice community where tacit knowledge matters
  • Learners developing confidence in help-seeking, discussion, and disciplinary communication
  • Learners working on complex or ambiguous tasks where feedback on judgment is more useful than answer keys alone
  • Less necessary for advanced learners who can already self-diagnose many errors and may benefit more from independent performance or peer critique

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Clarify concepts, terminology, and decision criteria in a domain
  • Improve problem formulation by helping learners ask better, more specific questions
  • Develop metacognitive awareness by comparing novice reasoning to expert reasoning
  • Support transfer on complex tasks through contingent hints, questioning, and feedback rather than answer-giving
  • Build professional or disciplinary identity through contact with authentic practice and standards

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist accounts (Vygotsky, Bruner) support expert interaction as a way to extend learner performance through guided dialogue and shared meaning-making
  • Social learning theory (Bandura) supports learning through observation, modeling, and guided imitation of more capable others
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship operationalizes the principle by making expert thinking visible and combining modeling, coaching, scaffolding, and fading
  • Cognitive Load Theory qualifies expert support as most useful when it reduces unproductive search and clarifies decisions for novices

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Overly directive expert help can suppress generative processing if learners are positioned as passive recipients rather than active explainers
  • The value of expert access depends on contingency; interactive questioning and hints outperform simple explanation for transfer in tutoring studies Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]
  • Support should fade as competence grows; keeping experts as constant problem-solvers can interfere with independence Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — expert interaction is more effective when support is responsive to learner understanding, especially through hints and questioning rather than explanation alone
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — expert questioning is especially valuable when it prompts learners to explain their own reasoning instead of only listening to answers
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — expert involvement should decrease as competence increases so learners assume more responsibility for performance
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — experts can improve novice learning by redirecting attention from "getting the right answer" to strategies, criteria, and process

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Mentoring/Coaching — a broader relationship structure in which expert guidance is sustained over time rather than episodic
  • Communities of Practice — extends expert access into sustained participation in a practice community
  • Guided Practice — turns expert explanation into coached performance on real tasks
  • Explaining Their Thinking — experts are most useful when they elicit learner reasoning rather than replacing it
  • Purposeful Reflection — follow-up reflection helps consolidate what was learned from the interaction and what remains uncertain

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Cognitive Apprenticeship — learners observe expert reasoning, attempt similar work, and receive coaching with gradually fading support
  • Leveraging Instructor Office Hours — scheduled access to disciplinary experts for question-driven clarification, feedback, and advice
  • Coaching — one-to-one or small-group expert guidance during performance
  • Demonstration — experts make tacit processes visible before learners attempt the task themselves
  • Clinical rounds, design critiques, code reviews, and studio conferences are common real-world forms of this principle when experts respond directly to learner work

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Daley, B. J. (1999). Novice to expert: An exploration of how professionals learn. Adult Education Quarterly, 49(4), 133-147. ERIC
  • Du, J., & Ling, C. X. (2010). Asking generalized queries to domain experts to improve learning. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 22(6), 812-825. summary
  • van de Pol, J., Volman, M., & Beishuizen, J. (2010). Scaffolding in teacher-student interaction: A decade of research. Educational Psychology Review, 22(3), 271-296. doi:10.1007/s10648-010-9127-6
  • Chi, M. T. H., Siler, S. A., Jeong, H., Yamauchi, T., & Hausmann, R. G. (2001). Learning from human tutoring. Cognitive Science, 25(4), 471-533. doi:10.1207/s15516709cog2504_1
  • Collins, A., Brown, J. S., & Newman, S. E. (1989). Cognitive apprenticeship: Teaching the crafts of reading, writing, and mathematics. In L. B. Resnick (Ed.), Knowing, learning, and instruction: Essays in honor of Robert Glaser (pp. 453-494). Lawrence Erlbaum.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Assessment for learning is the principle that assessment should be used during instruction to support learning, not only after instruction to certify it. The central question is not "What grade does this produce?" but "What does this evidence suggest we should do next?" It overlaps strongly with formative assessment, but highlights the instructional purpose of assessment evidence: clarifying goals, surfacing current understanding, and guiding revision.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
A teacher's own beliefs about the purpose of assessment shape whether assessment for learning actually happens in practice, not just whether it's nominally intended. Teachers holding an incremental view of ability (Dweck, 2000) — that ability grows with learning — communicate that the goal is mastering material and figuring things out, and use assessment results to decide whether to move on, re-teach, or provide targeted remediation ("We are going to practice over and over again. That's how you get good. And you're going to make mistakes. That's how you learn." — Patrick, Anderman, Ryan, Edelin, & Midgley, 2001, p. 45). Teachers holding a fixed view of ability instead communicate that the goal is doing well on tests, especially outperforming others, which pushes assessment toward ranking rather than diagnosis (Harlen, 2006) — see Goal-Orientation Theory for the fuller mastery/performance-orientation framework this maps onto. This matters directly for self- and peer-assessment specifically: those practices only function as intended in a classroom genuinely built around incremental, learning-goal-oriented norms — in a classroom emphasizing interpersonal competition instead, students have a real incentive to inflate their own (and their friends') self-assessments, since accurate reporting costs them relative standing.

Assessment for learning works when evidence changes what happens next for the learner or the instructor. Midstream checks are most useful when they clarify the target, expose current misunderstandings, and create an immediate next move such as regrouping, reteaching, revising, or choosing a new strategy Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]. This is also why low-stakes design matters: learners are more likely to reveal uncertainty when the checkpoint is framed as information for improvement rather than judgment, and that makes the evidence more instructionally useful for both self-monitoring Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] and process-focused revision rather than mere answer chasing Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Transparent goals and criteria: Learners need to know what the evidence is about.
  • Evidence that informs a next step: Assessment prompts should reveal something instructionally useful.
  • Revision pathways: Learners need a chance to act on the result.
  • Instructional responsiveness: Teachers or systems must be able to adapt based on what the evidence shows.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Summative contamination: Heavy grading pressure can make learners hide uncertainty instead of exposing it.
  • Weak task alignment: Poorly designed prompts create misleading signals.
  • Performative checking: Frequent assessment without instructional change turns the practice into compliance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners building foundational competence: Benefit when misunderstandings are identified before they harden.
  • Learners who need more confidence to reveal uncertainty: Low-stakes assessment can normalize partial understanding.
  • Instructors serving mixed-readiness groups: Assessment evidence supports grouping, pacing, and differentiation.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Clarifying the goal state: Helping learners understand what quality looks like.
  • Guiding improvement: Turning evidence into revision, re-teaching, or support.
  • Developing self-assessment: Helping learners judge progress against criteria.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Formative assessment theory emphasizes using evidence to adapt teaching and learning.
  • Self-regulated learning supports using criteria and feedback for learner monitoring.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Assessment does not automatically become "for learning" just because it happens midstream.
  • High-stakes accountability systems can distort the learning function of assessment.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — assessment evidence matters when it leads to a responsive next instructional move
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — low-stakes checks help learners notice what they understand and what still needs work
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — assessment for learning is stronger when it directs attention toward revision strategy and criteria, not only correctness

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Multiple Methods of Assessment
  • Competency-Based Learning & Assessment
  • Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference — an added requirement for feedback quality specifically when teacher and student differ in racial or ethnic background
  • High-Stakes Testing and Accountability Effects — the accountability pressure that can distort assessment for learning's low-stakes design

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Using exit tickets to decide whether the next lesson should reteach, extend, or regroup.
  • Giving draft feedback before a final submission so learners revise against criteria.
  • Asking learners to self-rate confidence before checking answers and then discussing mismatches.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education, 5(1), 7-74. https://doi.org/10.1080/0969595980050102
  • Hawe, E., & Dixon, H. (2017). Assessment for learning: A catalyst for student self-regulation. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 42(8), 1181-1192. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2016.1236360
  • Dweck, C. S. (2000). Self-theories: Their role in motivation, personality, and development. Psychology Press.
  • Harlen, W. (2006). On the relationship between assessment for formative and summative purposes. In J. Gardner (Ed.), Assessment and learning (pp. 103-117). Sage.
  • Patrick, H., Anderman, L. H., Ryan, A. M., Edelin, K. C., & Midgley, C. (2001). Teachers' communication of goal orientations in four fifth-grade classrooms. The Elementary School Journal, 102(1), 35-58.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Audiobooks provide spoken access to written texts, allowing learners to listen to fluent reading while focusing attention on meaning rather than decoding every word independently. They are especially useful when the goal is comprehension, vocabulary exposure, access to complex content, or sustained engagement with texts that would otherwise be inaccessible or exhausting in print alone.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Audiobooks are most powerful when decoding demands would otherwise block access to meaning. By shifting some of the processing burden from word recognition to listening, they can help learners engage with richer ideas, vocabulary, and discussion-ready content that print alone might make unreachable Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]. But the instructional value depends on what happens around the listening: pause-and-summarize prompts, print follow-along, discussion, or note-taking keep audio from becoming passive exposure and make comprehension more generative Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. If independent print reading is also a goal, audio support should eventually be reduced or strategically paired with print so responsibility transfers rather than remaining permanently outsourced Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Reliable access to audio versions of target texts, plus devices and headphones or speakers
  • A clear instructional purpose: comprehension, access, vocabulary exposure, text discussion, or paired reading support
  • Guidance on how to listen actively, such as pausing, replaying, taking notes, or following along in print
  • Follow-up tasks that require sense-making rather than passive consumption

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Listening alone does not automatically build decoding skill; if word recognition is a goal, audiobooks should be paired with print or other reading instruction
  • Fixed narration pace can create overload or disengagement unless learners can pause, replay, or change speed
  • Learners may drift into passive listening if there is no annotation, discussion, or accountability
  • Audio quality, accent, and speech synthesis quality matter; poor narration can increase cognitive effort rather than reduce it

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with decoding difficulties, visual impairments, fatigue, or print-access barriers
  • Multilingual learners who benefit from hearing phrasing, pronunciation, and prosody while building comprehension
  • Learners tackling texts whose ideas are within reach but whose print demands would otherwise block access
  • Learners who are more likely to persist with complex reading when audio support lowers the entry barrier

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Increase access to complex texts and ideas
  • Support listening comprehension, vocabulary growth, and background knowledge building
  • Improve persistence and volume of reading for learners who avoid print-only assignments
  • Bridge toward more independent reading when paired deliberately with print, highlighting, or note-taking

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory supports audio access when decoding demands would otherwise consume working-memory resources needed for comprehension
  • Dual-coding and multimedia perspectives support pairing spoken language with visible text or highlights to strengthen mapping between print, sound, and meaning
  • Universal-design and access-oriented reasoning supports offering equivalent routes into the same content for learners with different barriers

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Audiobooks are strongest for access and comprehension; they are not a complete replacement for direct reading instruction when decoding itself is the target
  • Audio support should be faded or strategically combined with print when the long-term goal is independent reading Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]
  • Learners understand more when listening is paired with prompts, notes, or explanation rather than treated as background exposure Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — audiobooks can reduce the processing burden of print decoding, especially when paired with visible chunking or text highlighting
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — comprehension gains are stronger when learners pause to summarize, annotate, or explain what they heard
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — guided read-alouds and audio-supported reading work best when instructors respond to confusion with prompts, clarifications, and replay
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — if independent print reading is the goal, audio support should be reduced strategically over time rather than remain the only access route

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Text-to-speech — one implementation path for providing audio access to digital text
  • Multimodal Instruction — audiobooks are strongest when combined with text, visuals, or guided discussion
  • Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax — hearing fluent phrasing can make unfamiliar language more accessible
  • Note-taking — listening notes and pause summaries prevent passive consumption

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Read Aloud with Highlighting — pairs audio with synchronized visual attention cues
  • Read-Alouds — an instructor-mediated version that adds pausing, questioning, and discussion
