  • Audiobook plus print follow-along during Assigned Readings for learners who need access to complex course texts
  • Speed-adjustable audiobook listening with pause-and-summarize prompts before seminar or writing tasks

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Best, E. (2020). Audiobooks and literacy: A rapid review of the literature. National Literacy Trust.
  • Milani, A., Lorusso, M. L., & Molteni, M. (2010). The effects of audiobooks on the psychosocial adjustment of pre-adolescents and adolescents with dyslexia. Dyslexia, 16(1), 87-97. doi:10.1002/dys.419
  • Kartal, G., & Simsek, H. (2017). The effects of audiobooks on EFL students' listening comprehension. The Reading Matrix, 17(1), 112-123.
  • Wood, S. G., Moxley, J. H., Tighe, E. L., & Wagner, R. K. (2018). Does use of text-to-speech and related read-aloud tools improve reading comprehension for students with reading disabilities? A meta-analysis. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 51(1), 73-84. doi:10.1177/0022219416688170

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Design learning tasks for real or realistically consequential audiences beyond the teacher-as-grader. When learners write, present, build, or investigate for an authentic purpose, the work becomes more than an academic exercise: it carries audience expectations, real constraints, and a reason to revise. This tends to increase relevance, accountability, and transfer, but only when the audience and task are genuinely aligned rather than superficially "real-world" in name only.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Authentic audiences and purposes improve learning when they change the quality of the task rather than just the packaging around it. Work for a real stakeholder or believable public reader usually increases relevance, revision effort, and whole-task integration because learners have to coordinate multiple decisions in something closer to full performance Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. At the same time, authenticity raises complexity, so novices often need models, checkpoints, and explicit criteria to keep the audience from becoming a source of anxiety or performance theater instead of meaningful learning Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M]. Clear success criteria still matter even in authentic work, because realistic stakes do not by themselves tell learners what strong performance looks like Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A product, performance, or communication task that resembles real disciplinary or workplace use
  • A credible audience or stakeholder, such as peers, community partners, clients, families, or public readers
  • Clear quality criteria grounded in that audience's needs and conventions
  • Time for feedback and revision; authenticity without iteration often becomes exhibition rather than learning

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Fake authenticity undermines the principle; learners notice when an audience is nominal or the task has no real consequence
  • Publicness can increase anxiety, especially for novices or learners with low confidence, so privacy, consent, and audience sizing matter
  • Authentic tasks are often more complex and therefore need scaffolding, examples, and structured checkpoints
  • Audience demands can eclipse the learning goal unless criteria keep attention on the intended knowledge or skill

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who disengage from decontextualized school tasks and need a clearer reason for doing the work
  • Adult and adolescent learners preparing for workplace, civic, or community communication
  • Learners developing professional identity, audience awareness, and revision habits
  • Learners ready to integrate multiple skills in a meaningful performance rather than isolated drills

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve transfer by practicing knowledge and skills in realistic contexts
  • Strengthen communication decisions around audience, purpose, tone, and evidence
  • Increase motivation and persistence through meaningful outcomes
  • Build revision habits by exposing work to readers, users, or stakeholders beyond the instructor

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated-learning perspectives support authentic audiences because learning becomes tied to real communicative situations and norms of practice
  • Constructivist perspectives support learner meaning-making through consequential tasks rather than decontextualized exercises
  • Self-determination theory helps explain motivational gains when learners experience autonomy, competence, and relatedness through real purposes
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] supports integrated performance tasks as stronger preparation for transfer than isolated subskills alone

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Authenticity increases complexity; novices may need more scaffolds, models, and checkpoints than advocates sometimes assume
  • Public audience alone does not guarantee quality learning; learners still need explicit goals and criteria Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S]
  • The strongest designs balance authenticity with instructional support rather than choosing one over the other

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — authentic audience tasks often require integrated performance closer to real use than isolated drills
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — public or stakeholder-facing work benefits from explicit quality targets and success criteria
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices need process supports for revision, research, and audience analysis, not only the expectation of a polished final product
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — authentic tasks work best when instructors coach learners responsively as complexity rises

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Inquiry-based Learning — authentic audiences often emerge from real questions and investigations
  • Competency-based Learning & Assessment — authentic products can serve as demonstrations of competence
  • Learner Choice — choice over topic, format, or audience can amplify authenticity when still aligned to goals
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — real-world work still needs explicit expectations and supports

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Digital Publishing — student work is shared with real readers beyond the classroom
  • Student Blogging — learners document process and communicate to peers or wider audiences
  • Project-Based Learning (PBL) — projects framed around real community or workplace problems
  • Reports for community partners, public explainers, policy briefs, exhibitions, or client-facing presentations are all viable forms when the audience actually matters

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Wiggins, G. (2009). Real-world writing: Making purpose and audience matter. English Journal, 98(5), 29-37.
  • Rule, A. C. (2006). The components of authentic learning. Journal of Authentic Learning, 3(1), 1-10.
  • Jacobson, E., Degener, S., & Purcell-Gates, V. (2003). Creating authentic materials and activities for the adult literacy classroom: A handbook for practitioners.
  • Mirra, N., Honoroff, B., Elgendy, S., & Pietrzak, G. (2016). Reading and writing with a public purpose. Journal of Language and Literacy Education, 12(1), 1-22.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Behaviorism, as an instructional principle, emphasizes observable performance, repeated practice, feedback, and reinforcement in shaping learning. It is useful when the target is consistent performance on clearly defined behaviors or skills.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Behaviorism is strongest when instruction is aimed at reliably producing or strengthening clearly observable performance. It treats learning less as hidden conceptual change and more as a change in what learners can do under given conditions. In instructional design, this often shows up in repetition, immediate feedback, reinforcement schedules, and tightly specified success criteria Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]. The principle is highly effective for some forms of skill automation and habit formation, and it becomes stronger when learners can also track progress against visible criteria Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. It is weaker when deeper interpretation, explanation, or generative understanding is the main goal, and even novice performance shaping often benefits from attention to process rather than outcomes alone Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear target behaviors or performances — the learner needs to know exactly what action, response, or routine is being shaped
  • Frequent feedback and consequences — reinforcement depends on a short loop between behavior and response
  • Opportunities for repeated performance — behaviorist learning designs rely on practice density

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Behaviorist designs can underrepresent deeper meaning-making if used alone
  • Observable performance is not the whole of learning — learners may perform correctly without flexible understanding
  • Extrinsic reinforcement can narrow attention — reward structures may crowd out broader inquiry if overused

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners acquiring foundational routines, habits, or well-defined procedural skills
  • Learners who benefit from explicit expectations, repetition, and immediate feedback
  • Learners in mastery-oriented environments where accuracy and consistency matter

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Support skill acquisition through feedback, repetition, and performance shaping
  • Increase accuracy, fluency, and consistency on well-defined tasks
  • Build reliable routines before or alongside more generative forms of learning

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Reinforcement and practice traditions — behavior changes when consequences and repetition shape responding over time
  • Reinforcement Theory — provides the clearest adjacent principle in the wiki for consequence-based shaping
  • Deliberate Practice — overlaps behaviorism where repeated performance and feedback are tightly coupled

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — qualifies that observable performance alone does not capture the internal meaning-making many domains require

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — behaviorist routines are stronger when performance targets are specific and demanding
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — visible criteria and progress tracking can strengthen performance shaping
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — novice skill acquisition may benefit when repeated performance is coupled with attention to process, not only outcomes

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Deliberate Practice — shares the emphasis on repeated performance with feedback, though often with a stronger role for strategy and reflection
  • Mastery Learning — often uses performance criteria and repeated practice before progression
  • Reinforcement Theory — behaviorism’s clearest principle-level neighbor in the current wiki

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Drill Practice — Repeated performance with rapid corrective feedback is a classic behaviorist instructional move.

Mastery Learning — Learners continue practice and assessment cycles until they meet a defined performance threshold.

Fluency-building routines — In reading, math facts, or procedural training, short repeated trials with immediate correctness feedback can shape accurate and automatic responding.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Skinner, B. F. (1954). The science of learning and the art of teaching. Harvard Educational Review, 24(2), 86-97.
  • Schunk, D. H. (2012). Learning theories: An educational perspective (6th ed.). Pearson.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Building empathy is the instructional principle of helping learners understand how other people perceive, feel, and interpret a situation. In learning environments, empathy matters because it improves listening, collaboration, conflict navigation, and the ability to respond thoughtfully across differences in experience or identity. It is usually cultivated through structured perspective-taking, dialogue, narrative exposure, reflection, and authentic interaction rather than through abstract exhortation alone.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Building empathy requires more than telling learners to care about other people. Perspective-taking strengthens when learners encounter concrete accounts, listen carefully, reflect on what they assumed, and compare their interpretation with what another person actually says or experiences; that reflective explanation work is one reason these activities often depend on learners making sense of perspectives in language Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~M]. Empathy-building is also more likely to transfer when it is tied to authentic interaction, dialogue, or community participation rather than abstract exhortation alone Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~M]. That means empathy-building tasks have to be structured and carefully facilitated: without safety, specificity, and reflection, they can collapse into stereotype performance, shallow agreement, or defensive conflict rather than deeper understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Structured perspective-taking: Learners need prompts, scenarios, or narratives that make another person's point of view concrete.
  • Psychological safety: Empathy-building work requires norms that reduce ridicule, defensiveness, and performative disclosure.
  • Skilled facilitation: Instructors need to help learners distinguish understanding another perspective from simply agreeing with it.
  • Reflection opportunities: Learners need time to compare their assumptions with what they heard or observed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Forced disclosure: Activities that pressure learners to expose trauma, identity, or private experience can backfire.
  • Superficial role play: Empathy does not grow from caricature or thin simulations that flatten other people's lived reality.
  • Identity threat: Poorly facilitated dialogue can heighten defensiveness rather than perspective-taking.
  • Indirect evidence base in this repo: Current linked claims here mainly support reflection, explanation, and transfer mechanisms rather than empathy-specific outcomes directly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working in groups or communities: Particularly relevant when collaboration, discussion, or service is central to the learning design.
  • Learners navigating difference: Useful in multicultural, interdisciplinary, and civic learning contexts where understanding other perspectives matters.
  • Learners developing communication and relationship skills: Strong fit for oral communication, leadership, mentoring, and conflict resolution goals.
  • Learners with rigid initial assumptions: Structured empathy work can help unsettle oversimplified views and expand interpretation.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Perspective-taking: Recognizing how a situation can look different from another position or experience.
  • Improved listening and discussion: Responding to others with greater care, curiosity, and specificity.
  • Inclusive collaboration: Working more productively across different backgrounds, roles, and priorities.
  • Reflective judgment: Noticing one's own assumptions and revising them after dialogue or observation.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social learning theory — learners pick up empathic discourse and listening practices by observing modeled interaction.
  • Transformative learning theory — empathy can deepen when learners critically examine assumptions and encounter disorienting alternative perspectives.
  • Social constructivist views of learning — understanding is built through dialogue with other people, not in isolation.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Empathy-building is not value-neutral; facilitation choices shape whose experiences are centered and whose are simplified.
  • Perspective-taking activities can increase confidence in misunderstanding if learners infer too much from too little evidence.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~M] — empathy work is stronger when learners articulate what another perspective means and how it differs from their assumptions
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~M] — authentic interaction and perspective-taking tasks are more likely to transfer than decontextualized discussion about empathy

These are indirect anchors: in this repo, the strongest nearby evidence supports explanation, authentic participation, and transfer mechanisms that empathy-building activities often rely on, rather than empathy as a standalone outcome.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Perspective Seeking/Multiple Perspectives — empathy often grows when learners examine the same issue from more than one position.
  • Peer Discussion — dialogue is one of the most common vehicles for empathy-building.
  • Communities of Practice — recurring participation in a community can deepen understanding of others' roles and constraints.
  • Debriefing — reflection after interaction helps convert experience into changed interpretation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Empathy interviews: Learners interview a peer, client, or community member using prompts focused on needs, frustrations, and lived experience.
  • Perspective journaling: After discussion or field observation, learners write from another stakeholder's viewpoint and then reflect on what they still do not know.
  • Narrative comparison: Learners compare multiple first-person or community narratives about the same issue before discussion.
  • Structured listening rounds: Small groups take turns summarizing another person's view before offering their own response.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Nelsestuen, K., & Smith, J. (2020). Empathy interviews. The Learning Professional, 41(5), 59-59.
  • Sachs, M. E., Kaplan, J., & Habibi, A. (2019). Echoing the emotions of others: Empathy is related to how adults and children map emotion onto the body. Cognition & Emotion, 33(8), 1639-1654. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699931.2019.1577226
  • Setlhodi, I. I. (2018). Mentoring in the web-class for adult learners. In Handbook of research on student-centered strategies in online adult learning environments (pp. 206-220). IGI Global. https://doi.org/10.4018/978-1-5225-5084-4.ch010

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Bullying is defined by two features together, not either alone: a power imbalance between the parties (physical, social, or otherwise) and repetition over time — a single conflict between peers of roughly equal standing is not bullying in this technical sense, even if it is a serious behavior problem in its own right. Bullying takes several forms: verbal (name-calling, threats), social/relational (exclusion, rumor-spreading, damaging relationships), and physical.

Bullying involves more participant roles than the common "bully and victim" framing suggests. Beyond the direct roles of bullying and being bullied, there are several indirect roles: assistants (who join in once bullying starts), reinforcers (who encourage it, e.g., by laughing), outsiders (who neither intervene nor participate, but whose inaction functions as tacit permission), and defenders (who intervene on behalf of the student being bullied). A given student can occupy more than one role, including both bullying others and being bullied, at different times or in different settings.

Reporting rates are low: national survey data (2012 Indicators) find roughly 40% of students who experience bullying do not disclose it to an adult, which means visible incident counts substantially undercount the actual scope of the problem. Effects extend to more than the student directly targeted: students who are bullied show elevated rates of depression, anxiety, academic decline, and school avoidance; students who bully others show elevated risk of violence and substance abuse into adulthood; and bystanders themselves show elevated risk of mental health and substance-use problems, even when not directly involved. Bullying is a risk factor for suicide, particularly in combination with other risk factors (e.g., existing depression), but is not by itself a sufficient or direct cause — treating it as the single explanation for a suicide oversimplifies a multi-causal outcome and can obscure other risk factors that also need addressing.

Cyberbullying is a distinct phenomenon, not simply bullying that happens to occur online, and requires different detection and response strategies: it is persistent (can occur at any hour, following a student outside school), often more permanent (screenshots, shares) and harder to fully remove than in-person incidents, frequently anonymous (raising the difficulty of identifying a responsible party), and can occur in contexts (gaming platforms, group chats) less visible to adults than a school hallway.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit adult attention to the indirect roles (assistants, reinforcers, outsiders, defenders), since intervention aimed only at the direct bully-victim pair misses most of the social dynamic that sustains bullying
  • Reporting channels that account for the low base rate of disclosure — passive reporting alone will substantially undercount the problem
  • Awareness that cyberbullying requires monitoring and response approaches distinct from in-person bullying (documentation of digital evidence, awareness of platforms outside school's typical visibility)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A student can simultaneously be a bully in one context and a target in another; rigid categorization can miss this and misdirect intervention
  • Anti-bullying messaging that treats it as a single, simple cause of suicide risks both overstating causality and understating the importance of addressing co-occurring risk factors (e.g., depression)
  • Grouping students identified as bullies together for intervention risks peer contagion effects (see Adolescent Peer Group Structure) that can worsen rather than improve behavior

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students broadly, with roles and dynamics shifting somewhat by developmental stage (social/relational bullying becomes more salient with the rise of crowd and clique structures in early adolescence)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Recognizing and interrupting the indirect roles (reinforcement, tacit permission via bystanding) that sustain bullying, not just responding after the fact to direct incidents
  • Building a classroom/school culture where defending is a recognized, supported role rather than a personally risky one

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Adolescent Peer Group Structure [+M] — sociometric status (particularly rejected and neglected status) is both a risk factor for being targeted and a consideration in designing intervention
  • Social Learning Theory [+M] — the reinforcer role operates through direct observational reinforcement of the behavior being modeled

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Character Education — schoolwide relationship-focused, non-punitive climate is a preventive foundation bullying-specific intervention builds on

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. StopBullying.gov.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Peer relationships. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Case studies use realistic scenarios, dilemmas, or incidents as the object of analysis so learners must interpret evidence, weigh alternatives, and justify action. Rather than receiving rules first and applying them later, learners grapple with ambiguity closer to professional practice: what matters here, what information is missing, what options are plausible, and how should a decision be defended?

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Case-based learning is powerful because it places concepts inside realistic uncertainty instead of leaving them as detached rules. When learners have to interpret evidence, justify a decision, and compare alternatives, they are more likely to build transferable judgment than when they only rehearse isolated subskills Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. That transfer is stronger when learners explain why their response fits the case rather than simply picking an answer Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The tradeoff is that ambiguity can overload novices, so the strongest case designs combine realism with structure: prompts, expert modeling, staged information release, and responsive questioning that helps learners move through complexity without simply being told the answer Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A well-chosen case with enough complexity to require interpretation, not just recall
  • Time for analysis, discussion, and revision of judgment rather than a single quick answer
  • Facilitation that pushes learners to justify claims with evidence from the case
  • Clear connection between case analysis and underlying concepts, frameworks, or procedures

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Poorly written or overly contrived cases reduce authenticity and invite superficial discussion
  • Novices can become overwhelmed by ambiguity if cases are introduced without enough framing, vocabulary, or modeling
  • Discussion can collapse into opinion-sharing unless learners are held to evidence, criteria, and reasoning
  • Case learning is weaker when learners never compare their judgment to expert reasoning or later outcomes

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners preparing for professions where judgment under uncertainty matters
  • Learners developing analytical reasoning, decision-making, and argumentation
  • Learners who benefit from concrete scenarios instead of abstract exposition alone
  • More effective once learners have at least minimal background knowledge about the domain and its core concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Apply concepts to realistic, messy, and incomplete situations
  • Strengthen evidence-based reasoning and decision justification
  • Compare multiple interpretations or solution paths without assuming one obvious answer
  • Build transfer from classroom knowledge to practice-oriented situations

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated and experiential perspectives support case work because learners engage with realistic situations that approximate use contexts
  • Constructivist perspectives support case analysis as an active process of interpretation, comparison, and meaning-making
  • Social constructivist perspectives support discussion-based case teaching where reasoning is sharpened through challenge and perspective-taking
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] aligns with case-based learning when the case requires integrating multiple concepts into a coherent response

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Cases are not automatically effective for novices; some learners need models, prompts, or worked analyses before open discussion
  • Transfer is stronger when learners articulate why a response fits the case rather than merely selecting an option Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Facilitation matters: questioning and hints often outperform simply telling learners what the right answer was Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — cases can approximate whole-task professional reasoning better than isolated subskill drills
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — discussion and written justification improve learning when learners explain why their interpretation fits the evidence
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — instructor probing and responsive hints improve transfer more than answer-giving alone
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M] — some novices need component instruction or worked examples before cases become productive

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Authentic Audiences & Purposes — cases become stronger when decisions are framed for realistic stakeholders
  • Inquiry-based Learning — case work often begins with uncertainty, question generation, and evidence seeking
  • Explaining Their Thinking — case analysis depends on visible reasoning, not just chosen conclusions
  • Ask Experts — expert commentary can make tacit judgment visible after learners attempt a case themselves

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Case-Based Learning (Harvard Method) — structured whole-class analysis of a complex case
  • Case Studies — localized use of real or simulated scenarios for application and discussion
  • Medical diagnosis cases, business decision memos, legal briefs, and engineering incident reviews are all common implementations
  • Interrupted cases, where new information is released in stages, can preserve uncertainty while creating natural decision points

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Kaddoura, M. A. (2011). Critical thinking skills of nursing students in lecture-based teaching and case-based learning. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 5(2).
  • Hoffer, E. R. (2020). Case-based teaching: Using stories for engagement and inclusion. International Journal on Social and Educational Sciences, 2(2), 75-80.
  • Vinney, L., Friberg, J. C., & Smyers, M. (2019). Case-based perspective-taking as a mechanism to improve metacognition and higher-level thinking. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 19(3), 91-104.
  • Ellet, W. (2007). The case study handbook: How to read, discuss, and write persuasively about cases.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Character education goes beyond teaching a list of rules ("always tell the truth," "obey the teacher"). Effective programs integrate three components: cognitive understanding of ethical concepts, emotional/caring responsiveness to others, and concrete moral action — recognizing that mature moral behavior requires both conscious reasoning and embodied, intuitive response in the moment a choice actually arises. Programs that work well tend to operate at the schoolwide level, not just within individual classrooms: all staff — teachers, administrators, and support staff alike — orient around positive relationships, with cooperation and mutual care as the explicit theme rather than competition. Discipline in these settings is framed around conflict resolution rather than obedience or punishment, and democratic practices (class meetings where students help set rules and resolve disagreements) are a significant, recurring mechanism rather than an occasional activity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Sustained, schoolwide commitment rather than a standalone unit or lesson — the approach depends on consistency across settings and staff, not just within one classroom
  • Structures for democratic participation (regular class meetings, student input into rules) and for service or collaborative projects that give students real practice acting on ethical commitments, not just discussing them

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Time-intensive: relationship-building and democratic process compete directly with pressure to maximize time on academic content
  • Works best with buy-in across a diverse staff and student population; a single enthusiastic teacher within an otherwise punitive or competitive school culture will have limited reach
  • Emphasizing responsiveness to others' needs (a care orientation) without also supporting students' own goals and autonomy risks producing compliance rather than genuine ethical development — see the tension between Positions 2 and 3 in Gilligan's Ethic of Care

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 learners broadly; the schoolwide framing makes this most coherent as a whole-school or whole-grade design rather than an individual classroom intervention

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Integration of ethical reasoning, empathetic response, and moral action — not just the ability to state the "right answer" to a hypothetical dilemma
  • Internalized responsibility and care for others, developed through practice (service, collaborative decision-making) rather than instruction alone
  • Conflict-resolution skills as an alternative to compliance-based discipline

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development — provides the reasoning-development backdrop character education programs aim to move students through
  • Gilligan's Ethic of Care — the emphasis on relationships, responsiveness, and reconciling self/other needs is a direct application of the care orientation
  • Turiel's Social Domain Theory — effective programs distinguish genuinely moral concerns (fairness, harm) from conventional classroom norms, rather than treating every rule with equal moral weight

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Class meetings used to set rules and resolve classroom disagreements collaboratively
  • Cross-grade "buddy" programs (e.g., older students as reading buddies for younger ones)
  • Service-learning projects (soup kitchens, tutoring, community repair projects) that connect classroom ethics to visible social consequences
  • Ethical discussion woven directly into existing subject content (literature, history, science) rather than taught only in a dedicated block

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Elkind, D., & Sweet, F. (2004). How to do character education. Retrieved from http://www.goodcharacter.com/Article_4.html
  • Berkowitz, M., & Bier, M. (2006). What works in character education: A research-driven guide for educators. Center for Character and Citizenship.
  • Narvaez, D. (2009). Moral complexity: The fatal attraction of truthiness and the importance of mature moral functioning. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 5(2), 162-181.
  • Nucci, L. P. (2009). Nice is not enough: Facilitating moral development. Merrill/Prentice Hall.
  • Minow, M., Shweder, R., & Markus, H. (Eds.). (2008). Just schools: Pursuing equality in societies of difference. Russell Sage Foundation.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Moral development. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Check-ins are brief, recurring opportunities for learners to signal how they are doing, what they understand, and what kind of support they need. They can be social, emotional, or task-focused, but their instructional value comes from turning invisible learner state into something that can guide the next move. Used well, check-ins help establish belonging, normalize support-seeking, and give instructors a low-cost way to detect confusion, overload, or disengagement early.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Check-ins work when they convert private uncertainty into usable instructional information. A short confidence rating, confusion prompt, or support request can improve self-monitoring for learners Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] and create openings for responsive scaffolding by the instructor Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M], but only if something actually changes as a result. That is why the core design requirement is not the prompt itself but the follow-through: regrouping, clarifying, slowing down, or offering support in response to what learners report. In some settings, check-ins can also surface confident misunderstanding early enough to correct it before it hardens High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Predictable routine: Check-ins work best when they are expected and lightweight rather than unusual high-pressure events.
  • Actionable follow-through: Learners need to see that their responses influence support, pacing, regrouping, or discussion.
  • Appropriate scope: Prompts should match the context, ranging from quick confidence checks to brief social connection questions.
  • Low-friction participation: Multiple response modes help, especially in online or mixed-comfort settings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• No follow-up: Check-ins become hollow if learners disclose need and nothing changes.
  • Oversharing pressure: Social-emotional prompts can feel intrusive if they ask for more than the setting can hold safely.
  • Routine drift: Check-ins lose value when they become formulaic and disconnected from instruction.
  • Time creep: Extended check-ins can crowd out the lesson if they are not bounded clearly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in online or distributed settings: Check-ins can reduce isolation and provide a regular signal channel that would otherwise be absent.
  • Learners with variable readiness or stress: Brief check-ins help surface barriers before they compound into disengagement.
  • Groups building trust and belonging: Especially useful early in a course, team, or collaborative project.
  • Instructors managing dynamic groups: Check-ins provide fast formative evidence about confidence, understanding, and support needs.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Belonging and connection: Helping learners feel seen and included in the learning environment.
  • Self-monitoring: Prompting learners to notice and report confidence, confusion, or progress.
  • Instructional adjustment: Giving instructors usable evidence to regroup, reteach, or change pace.
  • Support-seeking habits: Normalizing asking for help before frustration or non-participation escalates.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist views of learning — social participation and interaction shape readiness to engage.
  • Humanistic learning perspectives — learners are more likely to engage when safety and belonging are addressed.
  • Self-regulated learning — even very brief prompts can help learners monitor their current state and signal when they need support.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Check-ins do not create belonging by themselves; they only help if the surrounding environment is responsive.
  • Some learners prefer lower-visibility response modes and may disengage if all check-ins require public disclosure.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — brief confidence and confusion prompts help learners notice and report their own current state
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — check-ins matter instructionally when responses lead to tailored clarification, regrouping, or support
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S] — early disclosure of confident confusion can make later correction more memorable

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment — check-ins are one lightweight way to gather evidence during learning rather than after it.
  • Flexible Grouping — check-in results can inform regrouping by need, confidence, or pacing.
  • Immediate Feedback — the value of a check-in rises when it leads to prompt response.
  • Building Empathy — some check-ins help learners understand peers' current experiences and constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Confidence meters: Learners rate readiness or understanding on a 1-5 scale before or after a task.
  • Opening prompts: A meeting begins with a quick response to "What is one thing you need today to be successful?"
  • Exit check-ins: Learners note one point of confusion, one success, and whether they want follow-up.
  • Private digital pulse checks: In online environments, short forms or chat reactions let learners signal status without speaking publicly.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Champion, T. D. (2015). Scheduled check-ins increase student completion of assignments in an online non-majors science course at an HBCU. SoTL Conference.
  • Fischer, J., & Alpert, A. (2019). Promoting intern resilience: Individual chief wellness check-ins. The Journal of Teaching and Learning Resources.
  • Kluch, S. (2020). Leading remotely: What managers need to keep teams engaged. Gallup.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Chunking is the instructional design strategy of breaking complex information or tasks into smaller, more manageable units (chunks) to align with the limited capacity of human working memory. By organizing discrete items into familiar, meaningful groups, chunking reduces intrinsic cognitive load and enhances learning retention.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Chunking matters because learners cannot process unlimited novelty at once. When information is grouped into meaningful units, working memory can handle it more efficiently and learners are more likely to retain the underlying structure rather than just the surface details Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. The design challenge is that chunks are not universal: novices usually need smaller, more explicit units, while more experienced learners can handle larger integrated structures Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~M]. Good chunking therefore reduces overload without hiding how the parts connect into a coherent whole.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Logical Grouping: Information must be organized into units that share a conceptual, functional, or structural relationship.
  • Hierarchical Structure: Effective chunking often requires clear headings, bulleted lists, and a visual hierarchy to signal the boundaries of each chunk.
  • Fading Support: For complex procedures, chunks should gradually be integrated into larger holistic units as learner expertise grows.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Prior Knowledge Dependence: What constitutes a "chunk" depends on the learner's existing schemas; an expert can process larger, more complex chunks than a novice Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~M].
  • Over-segmentation: Breaking information into too many tiny pieces can disrupt the learner's understanding of the global task structure or the relationships between parts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice Learners: Benefit most from smaller, more frequent chunks to prevent cognitive overload Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S].
  • Learners with Low Working Memory Capacity: Essential for managing the processing burden during acquisition of new concepts.
  • Learners with Attention Deficits: Helps maintain focus by providing natural stopping points and "bite-sized" goals.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Knowledge Retention: Storing complex conceptual information in long-term memory.
  • Procedural Fluency: Learning step-by-step processes by mastering individual stages before integration.
  • Reading Comprehension: Improving the processing of dense or technical texts by segmenting them into thematic blocks.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information Processing Theory — identifies chunking as a key mechanism for transferring info from working memory to long-term memory.
  • Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller) — chunking is the primary method for reducing intrinsic cognitive load Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S].
  • Miller's Law (Miller 1956) — establishes the average working memory limit of 7 (±2) units.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — organizing information into meaningful units lowers working-memory burden and improves manageability

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding and Fading — chunking is often the first step in a scaffolded instructional sequence.
  • Worked Examples — can be chunked to show the sub-steps of a problem solution.
  • Graphic Organizers — provide a visual framework for how chunks relate to each other.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A chemistry lesson breaks stoichiometry into interpreting formulas, balancing equations, and converting quantities before asking learners to coordinate the full procedure.
  • A professional training module presents one decision rule per screen with a recap diagram after every three steps so learners can integrate the parts into the larger workflow.
  • A coding tutorial introduces one new construct at a time, then combines earlier chunks into a small working program once each part is stable.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0043158
  • Thalmann, M., Souza, A. S., & Oberauer, K. (2019). How does chunking help working memory? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 45(1), 37–55. https://doi.org/10.1037/xlm0000578
  • Juanengsih, N., et al. (2024). The Use of Chunking Technique Combined with the Writing Is Thinking Technique to Control Students' Cognitive Load When Learning About the Human Reproductive System. KnE Social Sciences, 83–90. https://doi.org/10.18502/kss.v9i8.15489
  • Lin, H., & Dwyer, F. M. (2010). The effect of different chunking strategies in complementing animated instruction. Journal of Instructional Psychology, 37(2).

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The easiest management problems to solve are the ones that never happen. Before the school year begins, arranging classroom furniture and materials to focus attention on learning already reduces behavior problems; once school begins, procedures, rules, and paced instruction extend that prevention further.

Arranging classroom space. The best arrangement depends on grade level, subject, the teacher's philosophy, and the room and furniture available, but should always help students focus on learning tasks and minimize distraction (Boyner, 2003; Nations & Boyett, 2002). Displays and bulletin boards make a room interesting and can publicly recognize student work, but too many can make a room feel busy, distracting, and physically smaller — a good strategy is to decorate some wall space at the start of the year but leave room to add more as curriculum needs emerge, especially for high-maintenance displays like aquariums or plants that don't need to be ready on day one. Computer placement, often constrained by power and cable outlets, should be decided early since it constrains where desks and shelves can sensibly go afterward. The main, central part of the room should stay as open as possible so the teacher can see and reach every student. Seating itself matters: instructional communication theory suggests seating arrangement shapes how the teacher communicates with students and how students interact with each other, affecting engagement, motivation, and focus (McCorskey & McVetta, 1978), and students report a general preference for flexible over fixed seating (mobile chairs, trapezoidal tables on casters, over rectangular tables and immobile chairs) (Harvey & Kenyon, 2013) — see Classroom Seating Arrangements for the specific configuration options and how to match them to instructional goals. Some teachers manage without a permanent room of their own ("floating" between other teachers' rooms, common for specialist subjects like elementary music) — a portable cart of supplies, an overhead projector available in every room used, and a dedicated shelf or corner in each room can offset this constraint.

Procedures vs. rules. Procedures (or routines) are specific ways of doing common, repeated tasks — taking attendance, turning in homework, gaining the teacher's attention during seatwork. Because they mainly serve the practical purpose of coordinating many people's actions in limited time and space, procedures are more like social conventions than moral expectations, and are only indirectly about what is ethically right or desirable (Turiel, 2006) — see Turiel's Social Domain Theory for the underlying distinction between conventional and moral social knowledge. Most procedures can be accomplished in more than one equally valid way, so the specific choice matters less than the fact that the whole class coordinates around some choice. Rules, by contrast, express standards of behavior for which individual students need to take responsibility — they are really about encouraging responsibility for learning and respect for others, not mere coordination. Effective rule sets tend to be few in number (most experts recommend keeping rules minimal for memorability — Thorson, 2003; Brophy, 2004), stated positively ("Do X" rather than "Do not do Y"), and general enough to cover a range of specific behaviors without becoming so vague ("Show respect") that they're effectively unenforceable. Because rules carry more personal-responsibility weight than procedures, there is a stronger case for involving students in setting them (Brookfield, 2006; Kohn, 2006) than for procedures, though some blend of teacher-set and student-input rules is typical in practice, and any classroom or school district's own imposed rules and procedures always take precedence.

Pacing and structuring lessons. Preventing management problems through pacing depends on three linked strategies. First, selecting tasks at an appropriate level of difficulty — students engage most when tasks are of moderate difficulty, neither too easy nor too hard (Britt, 2005); a common approach is to begin units with relatively easy, familiar tasks and introduce harder material gradually as students show they can handle more (Van Merrionboer, 2003), which also gives the teacher a chance to diagnose learning needs before adjusting content — though sequencing alone doesn't solve the deeper challenge of enduring individual differences among students, which requires actual differentiation. Second, providing a moderate amount of structure and clarity — students, especially those with certain learning difficulties, benefit from explicit guidelines on open-ended assignments (Marks et al., 2003), but excessive specificity (dictating exact wording, sources, and structure) eliminates the assignment's educational value by leaving no room for the student's own thinking; the ideal amount is an application of Vygotsky's zone of proximal development — enough support that students accomplish more than they would unaided, calibrated to the specific assignment and student, and ideally decreasing over time (Chesebro, 2003) — see Scaffolding & Fading. Third, managing transitions, which are disproportionately prone to distraction and lost time because students may have to wait while the teacher prepares the next activity, and can start to feel like unsupervised time. The easier fix is simply organizing materials well ahead of time to minimize the gap; the harder, more durable fix is teaching students to manage their own behavior during transitions — discussing appropriate talk levels, practicing waiting for an ending signal, or giving advance warning before an activity ends — which reduces how much monitoring the teacher needs to do at exactly the moment attention is divided (Marzano & Marzano, 2004).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A room arrangement decided with instructional goals and visibility in mind before the year begins, not improvised after problems appear
  • A working distinction, in the teacher's own planning, between procedures set mainly for coordination and rules that carry genuine moral weight
  • Task sequencing planned from easy to hard within a unit, and structure calibrated to the specific assignment and student rather than fixed at one level all year

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Overspecifying structure to reduce ambiguity can eliminate the very thinking an assignment was designed to develop
  • Task-difficulty sequencing addresses within-unit pacing but does not by itself solve enduring, class-wide individual differences in readiness — those require differentiation, not just sequencing
  • A rule so general it becomes vague ("Show respect") risks being ignored and becoming unenforceable, defeating the purpose of having it

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All K-12 students; task-difficulty sequencing and structure calibration are especially relevant for students with learning difficulties who benefit from more explicit guidance (Marks et al., 2003)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Smooth-flowing activities and minimized transition-related disruption, freeing management attention for genuine instructional needs rather than routine coordination problems

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Turiel's Social Domain Theory [+M] — the theoretical basis for treating procedures (conventional domain) and rules (moral domain) as genuinely different kinds of expectation, not merely different in degree
  • Kounin's Classroom Management Research [+M] — the broader evidence base that these early-planning, procedure-teaching practices distinguish effective from less effective managers

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — supports calibrating structure to the zone of proximal development rather than applying one fixed level

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding & Fading — the general principle behind moderate, calibrated structure that fades over time
  • Effective Classroom Management Plan Criteria — this page implements that principle's "prevent attention-seeking and work-avoidance behaviors" criterion
  • Immediate Feedback — timely feedback on behavior, alongside space and procedural design, is part of communicating that learning and positive behavior are classroom priorities

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Classroom Seating Arrangements — the specific seating configurations (traditional, roundtable, horseshoe, pods) this principle's space-arrangement guidance applies to
  • Establish Consistent Routines — a concrete procedure-teaching strategy

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Turiel, E. (2006). Thought, emotions, and social interactional processes in moral development. In M. Killen & J. G. Smetana (Eds.), Handbook of moral development (pp. 7-35). Erlbaum.
  • Marzano, R. J., & Marzano, J. S. (2004). The key to classroom management. Educational Leadership, 61(1), 6-13.
  • Van Merrienboer, J. J. G. (2003). Fostering integrated learning and transfer of complex cognitive skills. Educational Technology Research and Development, 51(3), 5-19.
  • McCorskey, J. C., & McVetta, R. W. (1978). Classroom seating arrangements: Instructional communication theory versus student preferences. Communication Education, 27(2), 99-111.
  • Harvey, E. J., & Kenyon, M. C. (2013). Classroom seating considerations for 21st century students and faculty. Journal of Learning Spaces, 2(1).
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Preventing management problems. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instruction should make its structure visible. Learners need to know what they are learning, why it matters, how the content is organized, and what successful performance looks like. Clear structure and presentation reduce avoidable confusion, support attention, and let learners spend effort on the idea or task itself rather than on guessing the lesson's logic.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Clear structure and presentation matter because learners often waste effort trying to infer what the task is, where the lesson is going, and what counts as success. Visible organization, signaling, and consistent formats reduce that avoidable load and make it easier for learners to focus on the substance of the work Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. The practical implication is not just “make materials neat,” but make sequence, goals, and emphasis legible enough that novices can orient themselves without having to decode the design first. Clear goals and criteria also improve focus and task commitment Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S], especially when presentations make the process and sequence of success visible rather than only naming the final destination Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit learning goals, sequence, and transitions so learners can orient themselves within the lesson or resource
  • Coherent organization of information into meaningful sections, steps, or chunks
  • Clear signaling of what is essential versus supplementary
  • Consistent visual, verbal, or interface conventions across materials so learners are not forced to relearn the format each time

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Over-structuring can turn learning into compliance if it leaves no room for exploration or learner agency
  • Clarity of presentation cannot compensate for unclear content goals or weak task design
  • Dense slides, verbose directions, and inconsistent formats create unnecessary load even when the underlying content is sound
  • Learners with stronger prior knowledge may need less explicit structuring than novices

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices entering an unfamiliar topic, tool, or routine
  • Learners with attention, working-memory, or processing-speed constraints who benefit from predictable organization
  • Learners returning to formal education who need explicit orientation to expectations and workflow
  • Learners engaging in online or blended environments where structure must be embedded in the material rather than improvised live

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve comprehension of new content by making conceptual organization visible
  • Reduce avoidable confusion about instructions, expectations, and task sequence
  • Support retention through clear signaling, repetition, and connection to prior knowledge
  • Make success criteria legible so learners can self-monitor more effectively

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information-processing perspectives support clear sequencing and signaling because learners remember better when information is organized and cued
  • Cognitive Load Theory supports reducing extraneous load through coherent presentation and visible structure
  • Multimedia and signaling principles support combining words, visuals, and layout in ways that direct attention to important relationships
  • Adult-learning perspectives support transparent expectations and relevance cues, especially for learners balancing multiple responsibilities

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Clear presentation improves access, but it does not substitute for meaningful practice, feedback, or authentic application
  • Different learners need different levels of structure; what is clarifying for one learner may feel redundant to another
  • Presentation clarity is strongest when paired with explicit goals and calibrated support rather than generic neatness

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — structured presentation helps learners process fewer, more meaningful units at once
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — clear goals and criteria improve focus and task commitment
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — structure is strongest when instructors also respond to actual learner confusion during delivery
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices benefit when presentations make the process and sequence of success visible, not only the final objective

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax — wording clarity and structural clarity are mutually reinforcing
  • Chunking — one of the main mechanisms for clear presentation
  • Scaffolding and Fading — early structure should support learners until they can navigate more independently
  • Multimodal Instruction — multiple modes can clarify structure when they are coherent rather than cluttered

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Module overviews, lesson roadmaps, worked agendas, and slide decks with consistent signaling
  • Flipped Classroom — especially dependent on clear structure because pre-class and in-class phases must align visibly
  • State Objectives and Advance Organizers are concrete ways to implement this principle
  • Numbered procedures, exemplars, and checklists help make task structure inspectable for novices

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Diep, A. N., Zhu, C., Cocquyt, C., De Greef, M., Vo, M. H., & Vanwing, T. (2019). Adult learners' needs in online and blended learning. Australian Journal of Adult Learning, 59(2), 223-253.
  • Palis, A. G., & Quiros, P. A. (2014). Adult learning principles and presentation pearls. Middle East African Journal of Ophthalmology, 21(2), 114-122. doi:10.4103/0974-9233.129748
  • Miraldi, L. B., & Miraldi, P. N. (2018). Best practices in slide design. In The handbook of communication training.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Clear structure is the short-form canonical target for designs that make the organization, sequence, and expectations of learning visible and easy to follow.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Clear structure matters when learners need to orient themselves quickly, understand what comes next, and preserve attention for the content rather than for decoding the course or lesson architecture. The principle is not about rigidity for its own sake. It is about reducing avoidable confusion so learners can invest effort in understanding, practice, and transfer, and well-structured organization does that partly by grouping information into meaningful units rather than leaving learners to search for the pattern themselves Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. Structure is also stronger when goals and progress markers are visible enough for learners to monitor where they are and what remains to be done Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The most effective structures make goals, sequence, expectations, and transitions legible without becoming so rigid that they block adaptation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A visible organization of tasks, sections, or expectations — learners should be able to tell where they are, what matters now, and what comes next
  • Signals that help learners orient to what comes next — headings, agendas, transitions, and consistent routines all reduce navigational effort

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Structure that is too rigid may limit adaptive use
  • Structure is not the same as over-specification — too many rules, labels, or steps can itself become noise

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners navigating unfamiliar content, platforms, or routines
  • Novices who benefit from visible sequence and expectations
  • Learners with executive-function, organization, or attention challenges who need stronger orientation supports

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Reduce confusion and help learners navigate instruction more effectively
  • Preserve cognitive effort for the content rather than course logistics
  • Improve readiness for transitions between explanation, practice, and reflection

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory — clear structure can reduce extraneous load created by confusing organization and weak signaling
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — the broader design principle that this short-form page points to
  • Information Processing Theory — organization and signaling help learners select and organize information more effectively

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — qualifies that learner exploration still matters and that structure should support inquiry rather than pre-empt it entirely

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — well-structured organization can reduce working-memory demands by grouping information into meaningful units
  • Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [~M] — novices benefit when instructional structure reduces unnecessary search
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — structure is stronger when goals and progress markers are visible enough for learners to monitor against

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Clear Structure & Presentation — the fuller, more detailed page on the same design family
  • Cognitive Load Management — clear structure is often one mechanism for managing extraneous load
  • Sequencing — structure and sequencing usually work together to make instruction legible

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Clear Structure & Presentation — A lesson or course makes goals, agenda, transitions, and expectations explicit so learners know how to move through it.

Consistent lesson architecture — Each session follows a stable pattern such as preview, model, guided practice, independent application, and reflection, reducing orientation overhead.

Visible unit maps and checklists — Learners can see how tasks connect and what completion looks like, which improves navigation and self-monitoring.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ambrose, S. A., et al. (2010). How learning works. Jossey-Bass.
  • Clark, R. C., Nguyen, F., & Sweller, J. (2006). Efficiency in learning. Pfeiffer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive activation is the principle of prompting learners to think deeply, make connections, explain reasoning, and grapple with ideas rather than merely recall or comply. It is useful when the goal is conceptual understanding and transfer rather than superficial completion.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive activation is strongest when instruction asks learners to interpret, compare, justify, predict, or reconcile ideas instead of only producing answers. The principle assumes that conceptual understanding depends on mentally effortful processing, and explanation prompts are one of the clearest ways to produce that kind of deep processing Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Not all difficulty is activating, though. Productive activation requires challenge that is cognitively meaningful and accompanied by enough support that learners stay engaged rather than overwhelmed Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]. In practice, activation often comes from good questions, discrepant cases, comparison tasks, and requests for explanation, including tasks that surface misconceptions strongly enough to correct them memorably High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Tasks that demand explanation, interpretation, or comparison — activation depends on work that requires thought, not just task completion
  • Prompts that surface reasoning rather than just answers — learners need to explain why, not merely what

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Overchallenge without support can overwhelm rather than activate
  • Busywork can look active while remaining cognitively shallow
  • Activation is easier to claim than to design — many tasks require effort but not meaningful reasoning

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working toward conceptual understanding rather than only recall
  • Learners in discussion, inquiry, or problem-solving environments
  • Learners who need help moving from passive reception to active sensemaking

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Increase depth of processing and conceptual engagement
  • Improve the ability to justify, connect, and revise ideas
  • Support transfer by strengthening relational understanding rather than isolated recall

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist Learning — learners build stronger understanding when they actively process and connect ideas
  • Metacognition — cognitively activating tasks often require learners to notice and explain their own reasoning
  • Information Processing Theory — deeper processing and organization improve learning quality

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — activation is only productive when challenge stays within a range learners can actually process

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explanation prompts are one of the clearest mechanisms for cognitive activation
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M] — cognitively activating tasks can be especially productive when they expose misconceptions and then correct them
  • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — activation is stronger when reasoning tasks are organized well enough that effort goes into meaning-making rather than disorientation

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Active Learning — active learning becomes more valuable when the activity is cognitively demanding rather than merely participatory
  • Explaining Their Thinking — one of the strongest practical realizations of cognitive activation
  • Activation — activation of prior knowledge often serves as the entry point into deeper cognitive work

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Compare-and-contrast tasks — Learners examine two cases, representations, or solutions and explain the deeper relation or distinction between them.

Discrepant Events — Learners encounter evidence that conflicts with their expectations and must explain the mismatch.

Justification — Instead of giving an answer only, learners must explain why a claim, method, or interpretation is warranted.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Kunter, M., & Baumert, J. (2006). Who is the expert? Teaching and Teacher Education, 22(4), 429-440.
  • Lipowsky, F., Rakoczy, K., Pauli, C., Reusser, K., & Klieme, E. (2009). Quality of geometry instruction and its short-term impact on students’ understanding. Learning and Instruction, 19(6), 527-537. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2008.11.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive apprenticeship is the principle of making expert thinking visible through modeling, coaching, scaffolding, and gradual participation in authentic tasks.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive apprenticeship is most valuable where the important knowledge is embedded in judgment, interpretation, and process rather than in declarative rules alone. It treats learning as guided entry into expert practice, and visible models are especially valuable early because they reduce unproductive search for novices Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]. The instructor does not merely explain content; they model thinking, coach performance, calibrate support, and then fade assistance as learners become more capable Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M]. The principle is especially strong for writing, diagnosis, inquiry, design, and other domains where expertise is partly tacit and situated.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to modeled expert performance — learners need to observe how experts think through authentic or realistic work, not just inspect finished outputs
  • Coaching and scaffolded participation — the principle depends on guided learner performance after observation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Tacit reasoning stays hidden unless experts externalize it — experts often omit the very moves novices most need to see
  • The full sequence is resource-intensive — modeling, coaching, and fading require more sustained interaction than content transmission alone
  • Poorly timed fading can destabilize learning — supports need to be withdrawn in response to performance, not on an arbitrary timetable

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices entering a disciplinary, professional, or craft-like practice
  • Learners developing complex cognitive skills such as diagnosis, writing, design, inquiry, or problem solving
  • Learners who need access to expert judgment rather than only explicit rules

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build strategic thinking, situated performance, and increasing independence
  • Make tacit expert heuristics visible and learnable
  • Support transfer from coached performance to more independent work

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated Learning — learning is shaped by participation in authentic practices and communities
  • Scaffolding — calibrated support is one of the core mechanisms that lets learners do work they cannot yet do alone
  • Cognitive Load Theory — modeling and fading can reduce the burden of unguided search during early acquisition

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — generally compatible, but qualifies that apprenticeship should still preserve learner sensemaking rather than collapse into imitation alone

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M] — visible models reduce unproductive search for novices during early learning
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — support is strongest when it adapts to learner performance rather than staying fixed
  • Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M] — expert guidance should be faded as learners develop stronger schemas and greater independence

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing — observation often provides the first exposure to expert practice before coached participation
  • Modeling — cognitive apprenticeship extends modeling into a fuller cycle of coached performance
  • Scaffolding — explains how support is calibrated and gradually removed

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Cognitive Apprenticeship

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Cognitive Apprenticeship — A full instructional pattern in which expert modeling, coaching, articulation, and fading are sequenced over time.

Clinical rounds and supervised diagnosis — Learners observe diagnostic reasoning, attempt their own interpretations, receive targeted coaching, and gradually assume more of the reasoning burden.

Studio critique and guided design practice — In design education, instructors model tradeoffs, coach works-in-progress, and reduce direct guidance as learners gain fluency with critique and revision.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Collins, A., Brown, J. S., & Newman, S. E. (1989). Cognitive apprenticeship. In Knowing, learning, and instruction.
  • Collins, A., Brown, J. S., & Holum, A. (1991). Cognitive apprenticeship: Making thinking visible. American Educator, 15(3), 6–11, 38–46.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive disequilibrium is the principle of using mismatch, surprise, or contradiction to unsettle an existing mental model and create readiness for revision. It is useful when conceptual change requires learners to notice that their current explanation no longer fits the evidence.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive disequilibrium is most useful when learners hold a stable but inaccurate or oversimplified model that ordinary explanation is unlikely to dislodge. The principle works by creating a productive mismatch between expectation and evidence, and that mismatch is especially potent when it exposes a confidently held but wrong expectation that can then be corrected clearly High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S]. The contradiction can trigger attention and rethinking, but only if learners are also given enough support to interpret what happened and revise the model Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. Without that support, disequilibrium can produce confusion, defensiveness, or superficial surprise instead of learning, which is why learners often need to explain the mismatch explicitly to turn surprise into conceptual revision Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A salient contradiction between expectation and evidence — the learner has to experience the mismatch clearly enough to notice that their current model is inadequate
  • Support for explaining and resolving the conflict — learners need prompts, dialogue, or modeling that help them reconstruct understanding rather than just sit with the surprise

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too much contradiction without support can produce confusion instead of learning
  • Not every surprising event causes conceptual change — the contradiction has to be meaningfully tied to the target concept
