  • Learners may defend prior beliefs — disequilibrium is strongest when the classroom norm supports revision rather than face-saving

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with stable misconceptions or overgeneralized explanations
  • Learners in conceptual domains such as science, math, history, or argumentation where conflict between expectation and evidence can be made visible
  • Learners ready to revise an explanation rather than only memorize a correction

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Support conceptual change and deeper reasoning through productive surprise
  • Help learners recognize when an existing explanation no longer fits the evidence
  • Move learners from contradiction toward a more adequate explanatory model

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Conceptual change traditions — conceptual revision often requires dissatisfaction with an existing explanation
  • Constructivist Learning — learners must actively reorganize meaning after the contradiction is noticed
  • Error Analysis — examining wrong predictions or models can make revision possible

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — too much unresolved contradiction or complexity can overload learners rather than productively activate them

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S] — confidently held but corrected errors can produce especially strong learning when feedback is clear
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — learners often need to explain the mismatch to get beyond surprise and into conceptual revision
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — contradiction is more productive when support adapts to learner confusion and response

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Error Analysis — cognitive disequilibrium often begins by surfacing and examining an incorrect but plausible model
  • Cognitive Flexibility — once the original model is destabilized, learners may need to represent the concept in more than one way
  • Cognitive Activation — disequilibrium is one route to deeper cognitive engagement

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Discrepant Events — A demonstration produces a result opposite to what learners predicted, forcing them to reconcile expectation and evidence.

Prediction-then-observation routines — Learners commit to an explanation before seeing data or a result, then must account for the mismatch when their prediction fails.

Historical or scientific misconception challenges — Students compare a common but flawed explanation against a stronger one using concrete evidence that the initial account cannot explain.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Posner, G. J., Strike, K. A., Hewson, P. W., & Gertzog, W. A. (1982). Accommodation of a scientific conception. Science Education, 66(2), 211-227. https://doi.org/10.1002/sce.3730660207
  • Limon, M. (2001). On the cognitive conflict as an instructional strategy for conceptual change. Learning and Instruction, 11(4-5), 357-380. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0959-4752(00)00037-2

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive flexibility is the principle of helping learners represent, interpret, and apply knowledge in more than one way rather than locking it into a single rigid schema. It is useful when domains are complex, case-based, or open to multiple valid perspectives.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive flexibility matters most in ill-structured domains where oversimplified rules break down and learners must adapt understanding across contexts. The principle does not reject structure; it resists premature rigidity. Learners need repeated exposure to varied cases, perspectives, and representations so they can reorganize knowledge instead of merely retrieving one memorized version, which is one reason contextualized whole-task experience can support flexible transfer better than isolated drills Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]. The challenge is pacing. Too much variability too early can overwhelm novices Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M], while too little variability can leave learners with brittle knowledge that fails outside the original example. Explanation across cases and perspectives is one of the strongest ways to make flexibility visible and learnable Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Multiple representations, cases, or viewpoints — flexibility develops when learners see a concept behaving differently across contexts
  • Tasks that require adapting understanding across contexts — learners need to compare, reframe, and transfer rather than reproduce one routine response

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too much variability can overwhelm novices without support
  • Learners still need a coherent throughline — flexibility is not fragmentation or randomness
  • Complex domains are a better fit than tightly procedural ones

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in medicine, law, design, policy, writing, and other ill-structured or case-based domains
  • Learners who must interpret ambiguity rather than apply a single fixed rule
  • Learners moving from foundational understanding toward adaptive transfer

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve transfer, adaptive reasoning, and the ability to reframe knowledge
  • Help learners avoid overgeneralizing from one case or representation
  • Build the capacity to reorganize knowledge under shifting conditions

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Flexibility Theory — the most direct pattern-level expression of this principle
  • Perspective-Taking — shifting viewpoint is one of the mechanisms by which flexibility develops
  • Constructivism — knowledge is reorganized through active interpretation across contexts

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — variability and nonlinearity need to be calibrated to learner readiness

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S] — flexible transfer is stronger when learners encounter knowledge in integrated, contextualized use
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explanation across cases and perspectives can deepen flexible understanding
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M] — novices may still need staged simplification before they can benefit from high variability

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Perspective-Taking — multiple viewpoints often drive the need for flexible interpretation
  • Constructivist Learning — cognitive flexibility assumes knowledge is actively reorganized, not merely stored
  • Cognitive Disequilibrium — contradiction and instability can sometimes trigger the need for more flexible models

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Cognitive Flexibility Theory — Learners revisit concepts across multiple cases, perspectives, and representations instead of mastering one linear explanation.

Cross-case comparison in medicine or law — Students compare superficially similar cases with different underlying structures, then explain why the same rule cannot be applied mechanically.

Multiple-solution-method analysis — Learners study several valid approaches to the same problem and articulate what each method reveals or obscures.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Spiro, R. J., Feltovich, P. J., Jacobson, M. J., & Coulson, R. L. (1991). Cognitive flexibility, constructivism, and hypertext. Educational Technology, 31(5), 24-33.
  • Jacobson, M. J., & Spiro, R. J. (1995). Hypertext learning environments, cognitive flexibility, and the transfer of complex knowledge. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 12(4), 301-333. https://doi.org/10.2190/4T1B-6E7P-7J9M-3X4M

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive load management is the short-form canonical target for instructional choices that reduce extraneous processing, sequence support, and calibrate task demands to learner expertise.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive load management matters when instruction risks overwhelming working memory before learners have formed stable schemas. In practice, this means chunking information and removing unnecessary complexity so learners can devote more attention to the underlying idea or procedure Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. These moves usually make early learning more manageable, but the same supports can become inefficient once learners are more knowledgeable, so guidance should fade or simplify as expertise grows Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Attention to what consumes working memory
  • Support matched to task complexity and learner expertise

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Over-management can remove productive challenge

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Preserve capacity for understanding and schema construction.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — reducing unnecessary processing and organizing material into coherent units preserves capacity for schema formation
  • Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M] — supports that help novices can become inefficient or redundant as learner expertise increases

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A math lesson introduces multi-step equation solving in short worked chunks, with each step visually separated and narrated before learners attempt a full problem.
  • A science simulation hides advanced controls for novices, then gradually reveals more variables once learners can explain the core system.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (1998). Cognitive architecture and instructional design. Educational Psychology Review, 10(3), 251-296. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive load reduction is the short-form canonical target for instructional moves that simplify presentation, reduce extraneous processing, and make initial learning more manageable.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive load reduction is most useful at the point where presentation format, task setup, or competing demands would otherwise consume the attention learners need for understanding. The practical implication is not to make learning easy in the abstract, but to remove avoidable processing so learners can focus on the structure of the idea or task Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. Chunking, signaling, and simplification often help novices learn faster at first, but oversimplifying can also weaken later transfer if learners never reconnect the simplified version to authentic complexity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Attention to sources of unnecessary processing
  • Design choices that simplify without removing the core learning

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Too much simplification can weaken later transfer

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Preserve working-memory capacity for understanding and schema formation.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Management
  • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — reducing extraneous processing helps working memory stay available for understanding and schema formation

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Scaffolding

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A history text is reorganized into short sections with headings, key dates, and a timeline so learners can process causal relationships without hunting for structure.
  • A coding tutorial removes unnecessary UI options and provides starter files so novices can focus on the target concept before handling full project complexity.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (1998). Cognitive architecture and instructional design. Educational Psychology Review, 10(3), 251-296. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive Load Theory, as a design principle, emphasizes managing the demands placed on working memory so learners can devote more capacity to schema construction rather than avoidable confusion. In practice this means simplifying presentation, sequencing support, and reducing unnecessary processing costs.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Cognitive Load Theory implies that performance problems are often design problems, not just learner problems. When instructional materials split attention, add unnecessary complexity, or demand too much search too early, working memory is consumed by coordination rather than learning. Reducing that avoidable load usually helps novices form schemas faster Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S], but the same supports can become redundant for more advanced learners, so the practical goal is calibrated load, not permanent simplification Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Instructional choices that reduce extraneous load
  • Sequencing or support aligned to learner expertise
  • Attention to how information is presented, not just what is presented

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Over-simplification can underprepare learners for real complexity
  • Supports that help novices may burden experts

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Especially important for novices and for content with high intrinsic complexity.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve comprehension and early schema formation by reducing avoidable overload.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Load management should support meaningful learning, not strip away all challenge.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — design choices that organize information and reduce unnecessary search help preserve working-memory capacity
  • Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M] — guidance calibrated for novices can lose value or become burdensome as expertise increases

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding
  • Worked Examples
  • Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A novice algebra lesson uses a single integrated visual instead of separate text and diagram panels that learners must constantly coordinate.
  • A software onboarding flow replaces open-ended exploration with worked examples and progressively harder tasks until users can perform the workflow independently.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (1998). Cognitive architecture and instructional design. Educational Psychology Review, 10(3), 251-296. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Teachers commonly speak of students' learning styles — preferred ways of engaging with material — but the term can misleadingly imply more cross-situational consistency than actually exists: a student who prefers diagrams to outlines can typically still learn well from either, given the chance (Loo, 2004; Stahl, 2002). Cognitive styles are a more specific and better-evidenced construct: relatively stable (though not perfectly so) individual differences in how a person typically perceives, remembers, and solves problems, rather than a mere preference (Zhang & Sternberg, 2006).

Two well-studied cognitive styles are field dependence/independence and impulsivity/reflectivity. Field-dependent individuals perceive patterns holistically, as a whole; field-independent individuals are more inclined to analyze a pattern's parts separately (Witkin, Moore, Goodenough, & Cox, 1977; Zhang & Sternberg, 2005). The distinction correlates with school preferences: field-dependent students tend to work better in groups and prefer open-ended fields like literature and history, while field-independent students tend to work better alone and prefer highly analytic fields like math and science — though these are only tendencies, with plenty of individual exceptions. An impulsive cognitive style reacts quickly but makes comparatively more errors; a reflective style reacts more slowly but makes fewer errors (Evans, 2004). Reflectivity suits many academic demands better — mathematical problem-solving and certain reading tasks specifically benefit from it — but some classroom-relevant skills actually develop better with some impulsivity: being a good cooperative-learning partner may depend on responding spontaneously to others' suggestions, and effective teamwork in sports may depend on not stopping to reflect on every move.

There are two distinct ways to use knowledge of a student's cognitive style (Pritchard, 2005). The more obvious approach is to build on existing style strengths: a field-independent, reflective student can be encouraged toward relatively analytic, independent tasks; a field-dependent, impulsive student toward more social or spontaneous ones. The less obvious, and often more valuable, approach is to deliberately build balance where a student lacks it: a student low in field independence may need explicit help organizing and analyzing academic tasks (e.g., structuring a lab report); an already highly reflective student may need encouragement to try ideas more spontaneously, as in a creative-writing exercise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Enough observation of a student across multiple contexts to distinguish a genuine, relatively stable cognitive style from a momentary preference or a single task's demands

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Field dependence/independence and impulsivity/reflectivity are tendencies, not fixed categories — a meaningful fraction of students will contradict the general trend for their style, so styles should never be used to "lock" a student into one mode of learning or to substitute for the student's own expressed preferences and choices
  • The reflective/field-independent profile is not simply "better" — it fits some academic tasks well and others (spontaneous cooperative work, quick teamwork) poorly

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Students whose task performance seems to depend more on how they characteristically process information than on effort or general ability
  • Students who could benefit from deliberately practicing the style they currently lack, not only tasks that flatter their existing style

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Task and activity design that matches a student's current cognitive-style strengths where efficient
  • Deliberately built cognitive flexibility, for students whose style creates a real limitation in specific academic domains (e.g., an impulsive style undermining multi-step math problem-solving)

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Multiple Intelligences Theory [~M] — critics (Morgan, 1996, cited on that page) argue MI theory's proposed "intelligences" may in part simply relabel existing cognitive-style research rather than identify genuinely separate abilities, suggesting real conceptual overlap between the two frameworks

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Witkin, H. A., Moore, C. A., Goodenough, D. R., & Cox, P. W. (1977). Field-dependent and field-independent cognitive styles and their educational implications. Review of Educational Research, 47(1), 1-64.
  • Zhang, L. F., & Sternberg, R. J. (2005). A threefold model of intellectual styles. Educational Psychology Review, 17(1), 1-53.
  • Zhang, L. F., & Sternberg, R. J. (2006). The nature of intellectual styles. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
  • Evans, J. St. B. T. (2004). Rationality and reasoning. Psychology Press.
  • Pritchard, A. (2005). Ways of learning: Learning theories and learning styles in the classroom. David Fulton Publishers.
  • Loo, R. (2004). Kolb's learning styles and learning preferences: Is there a linkage? Educational Psychology, 24(1), 99-108.
  • Stahl, S. A. (2002). Different strokes for different folks? A critique of learning styles. American Educator, 26(3), 29-49.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Learning differences. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Collaborative learning is the principle of designing tasks so learners build understanding through shared work, dialogue, and interdependence rather than isolated effort alone.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Collaborative learning is strongest when the task genuinely benefits from multiple perspectives, shared reasoning, or distributed effort. It is not synonymous with placing learners in groups. The principle works when collaboration changes the intellectual work itself: learners explain, challenge, compare, synthesize, and co-construct understanding in ways that would be less likely in isolation Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The main design problem is quality control. Without structure, group work often becomes uneven participation, social loafing, or parallel solo work under a collective label, which is why collaboration improves when facilitation and support respond to actual learner needs rather than assuming groups will self-organize productively Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. Collaborative work is also stronger when groups monitor progress against visible goals and criteria instead of relying on vague goodwill Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task that benefits from joint work — learners need a reason to rely on one another’s thinking, not just to divide labor
  • Structures for contribution, accountability, and synthesis — roles, prompts, checkpoints, or shared products help make participation visible and meaningful

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Group work without design can become uneven or superficial — collaboration needs norms, facilitation, and task architecture
  • Interdependence is easy to claim and hard to create — many “group tasks” are really parallel individual tasks with minimal integration

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working on interpretive, design, problem-solving, or discussion-rich tasks
  • Learners who benefit from exposure to alternative reasoning and explanation
  • Learners in classrooms where social participation is part of the learning goal as well as the method

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve collective reasoning, explanation, and participation
  • Strengthen the ability to justify ideas, respond to alternatives, and build shared understanding
  • Develop collaborative habits such as listening, coordination, and shared accountability

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social Learning — learners often acquire concepts, strategies, and dispositions through interaction with others
  • Community of Inquiry — collaboration can improve meaning-making when cognitive, social, and teaching presence are aligned
  • Social Interdependence — positive interdependence helps explain when collaboration improves outcomes rather than merely redistributing work

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — collaboration can increase processing demands if tasks, roles, or communication structures are poorly designed

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explaining ideas to peers can deepen understanding and reveal gaps
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — collaboration improves when support and facilitation respond to learner needs rather than assuming groups will self-organize productively
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — collaborative work is stronger when learners and groups monitor progress against visible goals and criteria

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion — structured talk is one of the main mechanisms through which collaborative learning produces understanding
  • Perspective-Seeking/Multiple Perspectives — collaboration is especially valuable when disagreement and comparison sharpen thinking
  • Social Learning — provides the broader explanation for why interaction can itself be instructional

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Collaborative Learning — A shared-work pattern in which learners are jointly responsible for meaning-making rather than simply co-located.

Jigsaw Method — Learners build distributed expertise and then teach one another, making interdependence explicit.

Collaborative Inquiry — Groups investigate a question together and synthesize evidence, requiring reasoning to be externalized and coordinated.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Johnson, D. W., Johnson, R. T., & Smith, K. A. (2014). Cooperative learning. Journal on Excellence in College Teaching, 25(3-4), 85-118.
  • Webb, N. M. (2009). The teacher’s role in promoting collaborative dialogue in the classroom. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 79(1), 1-28. https://doi.org/10.1348/000709908X380772

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
West's (2014) Communities of Innovation (COI) framework identifies characteristics at three levels that predict a group's capacity for collaborative creativity, positioned as an evolution of Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998) specifically for groups whose purpose is producing innovative output.

Individual (but socially influenced) characteristics: - Hacker motivation — Himanen's "hacker ethic": work motivated by intrinsic value to others (not primarily money), a playful and passionate approach, and open sharing of tools and information. Companies that grant employees time for self-directed, intrinsically motivating projects (e.g., Google's "20% time") have produced some of their most creative output this way. - Dynamic expertise (Hakkarainen et al.) — treating expertise as the ongoing ability to surpass one's current competence, rather than a fixed accumulation of skill. Groups whose members show more dynamic expertise are measurably more innovative. - Entrepreneurial autonomy — autonomy over the means of accomplishing a task (not necessarily the ends) sustains intrinsic motivation and creativity (Amabile); perceived organizational control over members impedes it.

Group-level characteristics: - Group flow (Sawyer, extending Csikszentmihalyi) — ten elements (shared goal, close listening, complete concentration, sense of control, blended egos, equal participation, familiarity, communication, moving ideas forward through improvisation, and productive risk) that correlate with peak innovative output, though it is fragile and hard to sustain, especially online. - Idea prototyping — rapidly making ideas tangible (as IDEO does with products, spaces, and even organizational structures) so the group can learn from and discuss a concrete artifact rather than an abstraction. - Cognitive and skill diversity ("innoversity") — diverse perspectives, including "weak ties" to people outside the group, generate more creative syntheses; conventional brainstorming underperforms because groupthink suppresses this diversity, whereas techniques like the nominal group technique (individual idea development before group sharing) protect it. - Culture of critique and reflection — the ability to give and receive criticism productively, contingent on an organizational culture where failure is recoverable and treated as a source of learning ("productive failure"). - Common vision — a group's shared understanding of what it hopes to accomplish (not necessarily how), which is most effective when clear, widely shared, and attainable.

Organizational-level characteristics: a flexible, organic structure (rather than rigid hierarchy) that can quickly reorganize teams and approve ideas for prototyping; a climate of mastery, purpose, and autonomy (Pink; Amabile) rather than reliance on extrinsic rewards, which tend to diminish creativity; and psychological safety (Rogers, 1954) — unconditional acceptance of the individual, an absence of external evaluation of the person (as opposed to the work), and empathic understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A culture where failure is recoverable and treated as a source of learning, so members are willing to critique and be critiqued
  • Structures that protect individual idea generation before group evaluation, to avoid groupthink and preserve cognitive diversity
  • Flexibility to reorganize teams and reduce approval friction for prototyping new ideas

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Group flow is fragile, difficult to predict or engineer in advance, and some research suggests it may not transfer to fully online, asynchronous collaboration at all
  • Autonomy over means (not ends) is the specific mechanism that sustains creativity; unconstrained autonomy over goals is not what the research supports, and appropriate constraints can actually improve creativity
  • Extrinsic rewards for creative work tend to diminish intrinsic motivation and creativity rather than enhance it

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners and teams engaged in collaborative, open-ended creative or design work (studio-based courses, capstone projects, design challenges), rather than individual skill practice

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Collaborative creativity and innovation specifically, as distinct from individual creative ability
  • Skills in giving and receiving critique productively as part of an iterative design process

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-Determination Theory [+M] — autonomy (over means), a core SDT need, is repeatedly identified as central to sustaining the intrinsic motivation that drives innovative work
  • Builds explicitly on Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998) as a specifically innovation-focused evolution of that framework

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Four Boundaries of Learning Community (Access, Relationships, Vision, Function) — a Community of Innovation is one kind of bounded community; this framework describes what makes such a community specifically productive of innovation once it exists
  • Community of Inquiry — shares an interest in productive group discourse, though COI targets creative/innovative output specifically rather than inquiry and sensemaking generally

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Google's "20% time" policy, credited with producing AdSense, Gmail, and Google News through hacker-motivated, self-directed projects
  • IDEO's studio structure — flat organization, rapid prototyping of products, spaces, and team structures themselves
  • BYU's Center for Animation studio, where biweekly student-run critique sessions over a year and a half drove collaborative innovation on an animated short

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• West, R. E. (2018). Communities of innovation: Individual, group, and organizational characteristics leading to greater potential for innovation. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/communities_of_innovation (originally published in TechTrends, 58(5), 53–61.)
  • Sawyer, R. K. (2008). Group genius: The creative power of collaboration. Basic Books.
  • Amabile, T. M. (1998). How to kill creativity. Harvard Business Review, 76(5), 77–87.
  • Rogers, C. R. (1954). Toward a theory of creativity. A Review of General Semantics, 11(4), 249–259.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Communities of practice are groups that deepen learning through sustained participation around a shared domain, problem space, or profession. Members do not just exchange information; they build shared language, norms, tools, and standards of practice over time. Learning happens through contribution, observation, feedback, and increasingly central participation in the work of the community.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Communities of practice support learning because people often learn complex work by participating with others who are already doing it, not by studying rules in isolation. Newcomers gain access to tacit knowledge, language, tools, and standards through recurring contribution, explanation, and feedback, and communities become more educative when members articulate and compare reasoning rather than only exchange resources Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. They also become more capable as responsibility gradually shifts toward fuller participation Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S], ideally through authentic shared work that stays tied to integrated performance rather than isolated drills Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. The design challenge is that communities can easily become exclusionary or vague, so entry points, contribution norms, and authentic shared work have to be deliberately structured, with responsive guidance for newcomers as they enter the practice Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A shared domain of interest or practice that gives the group a real reason to convene
  • Recurring interaction over time, not one-off discussion
  • Norms and structures that support contribution, feedback, and knowledge sharing
  • Opportunities for newcomers to participate at manageable levels before taking on more central roles

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Communities can become exclusionary or dominated by experts unless participation norms are intentionally designed
  • Without a shared purpose or recurring activity, the group becomes a discussion forum rather than a practice community
  • Informal knowledge sharing alone is insufficient if there is no mechanism for applying, testing, or revising ideas in practice
  • Healthy communities take time to build; they are difficult to force through short-term assignments alone

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult and professional learners building identity in a field, trade, or role
  • Learners who benefit from ongoing peer and expert interaction rather than isolated coursework
  • Newcomers to a practice who need access to tacit norms, vocabulary, tools, and examples
  • Learners whose motivation and persistence increase when they feel they belong to a meaningful community

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Develop participation in authentic disciplinary or workplace practices
  • Build shared language, standards, and repertoires for solving recurring problems
  • Increase help-seeking, peer teaching, and collaborative problem-solving
  • Support professional identity formation and long-term learning beyond a single course

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated-learning theory strongly supports communities of practice: learning occurs through participation in authentic social practice, including legitimate peripheral participation
  • Social constructivist perspectives support knowledge development through dialogue, shared tools, and co-construction of meaning
  • Apprenticeship-oriented perspectives support the movement from novice observation to guided participation to fuller contribution
  • Networked-learning and connectivist perspectives qualify the idea for online and distributed communities where expertise is spread across people and tools

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Communities do not automatically teach well; newcomers often need explicit scaffolds, role clarity, and protected entry points
  • Peer exchange is strongest when members explain and externalize their reasoning, not when they merely trade answers Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Support should gradually shift from expert-heavy guidance to broader member participation as people gain competence Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]
  • Coaching and feedback inside communities are most effective when responsive to actual learner need rather than generic advice Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — communities become more educative when members articulate and compare reasoning, not just exchange resources
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — newcomers benefit when experienced members provide responsive prompts, hints, and mediation
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — strong communities shift responsibility from experts to broader member participation over time
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — communities of practice are especially useful when learning remains tied to authentic, integrated work rather than isolated drills

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Ask Experts — communities widen access to expertise beyond isolated expert encounters
  • Mentoring/Coaching — mentoring relationships often serve as entry points into a broader practice community
  • Peer Discussion — discussion is one mechanism communities use, but not the whole structure
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes — communities provide real audiences, norms, and feedback loops for learner work

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Fostering Communities of Learning (FCL) — a structured pattern for collaborative inquiry and shared knowledge building
  • Community Involvement — invites learning relationships that extend beyond the classroom
  • Professional learning networks, code review communities, nurse book clubs, teacher inquiry groups, and apprenticeship cohorts are common real-world forms
  • Online communities can function well when they include recurring tasks, visible artifacts, and norms for contribution rather than only informal chat

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Abedini, A., Abedin, B., & Zowghi, D. (2021). Adult learning in online communities of practice: A systematic review. British Journal of Educational Technology, 52(4), 1663-1694. doi:10.1111/bjet.13120
  • Boud, D., & Middleton, H. (2003). Learning from others at work: Communities of practice and informal learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 194-202.
  • Lave, J., & Wenger, E. (1991). Situated learning: Legitimate peripheral participation. Cambridge University Press.
  • Office of Educational Technology. (2014). Designing online communities of practice for educators to create value. U.S. Department of Education.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Community-based learning is the principle of connecting learning to shared participation, responsibility, and contribution within a classroom, local community, or broader social context. It matters when learning is strengthened by belonging, collective meaning-making, and contribution beyond the individual.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Community-based learning is strongest when learners are not only consuming content but participating in a setting where their work affects or serves others. The principle works by linking knowledge to belonging, contribution, and real social context. It can deepen meaning, motivation, and transfer because learning is tied to actual people, settings, and responsibilities rather than remaining purely school-internal Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. But community participation only becomes educative when learners receive enough responsive support to navigate the social and practical complexity of real settings Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] and when reflection helps them monitor what they are learning from the experience rather than merely completing service hours Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The central risk is tokenism: “community” language without authentic participation, reciprocity, or reflection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A genuine social or community context — the task should connect to a real group, audience, issue, or shared responsibility
  • Shared responsibility or participation — learners need to contribute in ways that matter beyond individual completion
  • Structures for contribution and reflection — experience alone is not enough; learners need to interpret what the community context means for the learning

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Token community references weaken authenticity
  • Participation needs equitable norms and access
  • Community work can drift toward service without learning unless goals are explicit

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who benefit from authentic contribution, civic connection, or shared social purpose
  • Learners in project-based, service-learning, internship, or community-partnered settings
  • Learners whose motivation and transfer improve when knowledge is embedded in real responsibility

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build belonging, civic or social awareness, and knowledge through participation
  • Improve transfer by tying concepts to meaningful contexts and relationships
  • Develop responsibility, perspective taking, and contribution beyond the self

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated Learning — learning is strengthened when it is embedded in authentic social practice
  • Social Learning — interaction and participation can be direct sources of learning
  • Community of Inquiry — collaborative spaces need social and cognitive structures, not just participation

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — community-based tasks can become overwhelming if they add social complexity without enough instructional structure

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — authentic, integrated activity can improve transfer beyond fragmented practice
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — learners often need responsive support to participate productively in complex real-world settings
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — reflection and progress tracking strengthen the learning value of community participation

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Communities of Practice — emphasizes learning through increasing participation in a practice community
  • Situated Learning — explains why community context can improve transfer and meaning
  • Collaborative Learning — community-based learning often depends on well-structured shared work

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Service-learning projects — Learners apply course concepts through work tied to an actual community need, then reflect on both the content and the social context.

Community partner briefs or deliverables — Students create analyses, resources, or recommendations for an external partner, making quality and clarity matter beyond grading.

Local inquiry with public-facing outcomes — Learners investigate a neighborhood, organization, or social issue and present findings to a real audience rather than only to the instructor.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Eyler, J., & Giles, D. E. (1999). Where's the learning in service-learning? Jossey-Bass.
  • Bringle, R. G., & Hatcher, J. A. (1995). A service-learning curriculum for faculty. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning, 2(1), 112-122.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Community of inquiry is the principle that meaningful learning in collaborative settings depends on the interaction of social presence, cognitive presence, and teaching presence. It is useful when instruction relies on discussion, collaboration, and shared sensemaking rather than only individual study.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Community of inquiry is most useful when learning depends on sustained discourse rather than isolated content delivery. The principle holds that collaborative meaning-making becomes stronger when three conditions are present together: learners feel socially present enough to participate, the instructional design drives cognitively substantive inquiry, and teaching presence organizes and guides the process. Discussion is strongest when learners articulate and refine their own reasoning in public Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], when facilitation responds to confusion and keeps inquiry moving productively Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M], and when the group monitors the quality and direction of its inquiry rather than drifting socially Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. If any one of the three is weak, the experience tends to degrade: discussion becomes socially pleasant but shallow, intellectually demanding but socially fragile, or well-intentioned but poorly guided.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A shared space for dialogue and inquiry — learners need a common setting, prompt, or object of inquiry to work around
  • Facilitation that guides learners toward substantive meaning-making — teaching presence matters because discourse rarely becomes deep on its own
  • Norms that support participation and intellectual risk-taking — social presence helps learners contribute, disagree, and revise ideas publicly

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak facilitation can leave interaction socially active but cognitively thin
  • Low trust or weak social presence can suppress contribution
  • Cognitive presence takes design, not just discussion time — prompts, tasks, and synthesis structures matter

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in online, blended, seminar, and discussion-rich environments
  • Learners expected to build understanding through dialogue, interpretation, and response
  • Groups whose learning depends on both participation and collective sensemaking

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Support collaborative meaning-making, sustained discourse, and reflective inquiry
  • Improve the quality of discussion by balancing participation, facilitation, and conceptual work
  • Build learning communities in which ideas can be explored publicly and productively

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social Learning — interaction with others is treated as a direct source of learning
  • Social Constructivism — shared dialogue and interpretation can shape understanding
  • Collaborative Learning — inquiry communities depend on well-designed collaborative structures

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — discussion-rich environments can overload learners if the discourse is poorly structured or insufficiently scaffolded

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — discussion is stronger when learners articulate and refine their own reasoning
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — teaching presence matters because inquiry often needs responsive support and facilitation
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — communities are more effective when learners and groups monitor the quality and direction of their inquiry

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Collaborative Learning — community of inquiry explains one strong form of collaborative meaning-making
  • Peer Discussion — discourse is the main medium through which inquiry communities operate
  • Social Learning — provides the broader rationale for why group interaction can be educational

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Online Course Design (Community of Inquiry) — Applies this principle at the scale of a full online course, structured around Moore's three types of interaction.

Discussion Group — A structured discussion environment where facilitation, prompts, and synthesis shape the quality of inquiry.

Online seminar forums with active facilitation — Learners respond to a shared problem or text, build on peers’ ideas, and receive guidance that keeps the discourse substantive rather than merely social.

Problem-centered cohort discussions — Groups investigate a shared case or challenge over time, with instructor prompts that sustain both participation and conceptual depth.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Garrison, D. R., Anderson, T., & Archer, W. (2000). Critical inquiry in a text-based environment. The Internet and Higher Education, 2(2-3), 87-105. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1096-7516(00)00016-6
  • Garrison, D. R., & Arbaugh, J. B. (2007). Researching the community of inquiry framework. The Internet and Higher Education, 10(3), 157-172. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iheduc.2007.04.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Competency-based assessment is the short-form canonical target for designs that evaluate learners against explicit competencies or standards rather than normed averages or seat-time expectations.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Competency-based assessment shifts the design question from how long learners spent in instruction to what they can actually do with acceptable quality. That usually improves transfer and decision quality when assessment tasks mirror meaningful performance Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S], but it also raises the bar for clarity: competencies, evidence, and mastery thresholds all have to be specified well enough that different assessors can judge the same work consistently.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear competencies
  • Evidence aligned to those competencies
  • Standards for judging mastery

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Complex competencies are harder to assess well

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Judge learning by demonstrated performance against clear criteria.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Competency-Based Learning & Assessment

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S] — competency judgments are stronger when they rest on integrated performances that resemble actual use

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Mastery Learning

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A teacher preparation program assesses classroom facilitation through observed teaching, annotated lesson plans, and a rubric tied to explicit competencies instead of a single written final.
  • A cybersecurity course certifies learners on incident response only after they can complete a live scenario within defined quality criteria, not just explain the steps on paper.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Le, C., Wolfe, R. E., & Steinberg, A. (2014). The past and the promise: Today's competency education movement. Jobs for the Future.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Competency-based learning and assessment organize progress around demonstrated mastery rather than seat time, pacing norms, or one-shot averages. Learners advance by showing they can perform clearly defined competencies, often through applied tasks, performance assessments, or repeated attempts. The design promise is tighter alignment between what matters and what is assessed, but that promise depends on the quality of the competencies, evidence, and supports.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Competency-based learning and assessment are strongest when mastery is defined as credible performance rather than completion or time spent. Clear competencies, repeated attempts, and authentic evidence usually make progress more legible and improve transfer because learners are judged on what they can actually do Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. But the system only works if competencies are well specified Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] and learners receive enough process support to reach them Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M]; otherwise “mastery” becomes either a vague slogan or a fragmented checklist.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit competencies that describe observable performance, not vague aspirations
  • Assessments that actually elicit the target competence in credible ways
  • Opportunities for practice, feedback, revision, and reassessment before high-stakes judgments
  • Tracking systems and instructional routines that let learners know where they are and what remains to be demonstrated

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Competencies can become atomized checklists if they are defined too narrowly
  • Flexible pacing sounds equitable but can become isolating or unmanageable without strong advising and feedback loops
  • Reliable assessment of complex competencies is labor-intensive and requires shared rubrics or calibration
  • Mastery claims are only as trustworthy as the evidence used to infer them

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult, professional, and nontraditional learners who need transparent progress markers and flexible routes to mastery
  • Learners whose prior experience should count only when it can be demonstrated through evidence
  • Learners in workforce, technical, health, and performance-oriented domains where competencies can be observed in practice
  • Learners who benefit from multiple attempts and feedback cycles rather than single averaged scores

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Demonstrate usable competence on clearly defined skills or performances
  • Support transfer by linking assessment to authentic or application-rich tasks
  • Make learner progress inspectable so feedback and next steps are concrete
  • Separate "not yet" from failure by allowing revision and reassessment

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated-learning perspectives support competency systems when progress markers, feedback, and revision make self-monitoring actionable
  • Adult-learning perspectives support flexible pathways and recognition of prior experience, provided competence is still demonstrated
  • Experiential and apprenticeship perspectives support performance-based demonstrations over purely declarative testing
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] supports competency assessment when evidence comes from integrated performances instead of isolated fragments

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Competency systems fail when competencies are underspecified, overfragmented, or detached from authentic performance
  • Learners still need explicit goals and calibrated challenge; mastery alone is not motivational without clear standards Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S]
  • Novices often need process coaching and scaffolds before they can demonstrate mastery independently Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — competency claims are stronger when based on integrated performances that resemble real use
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — well-specified mastery criteria focus effort and clarify expectations
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — learners often need process-level guidance before they can demonstrate mastery
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — supports and reassessment opportunities should gradually lead toward independent demonstration, not permanent dependence on scaffolds

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Authentic Audiences & Purposes — credible demonstrations often involve products or performances for real stakeholders
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring — competency systems need visible progress and next-step clarity
  • Guided Practice — repeated coached attempts are often necessary before a valid mastery judgment
  • Formative Assessment — feedback cycles are part of making mastery achievable rather than merely sortable

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Performance checklists and rubric-based demonstrations in technical training, clinical education, and workplace certification
  • Standards-/Mastery-Based Grading — classroom grading organized around demonstrated standards
  • Grade Students Based on Demonstrated Learning — evaluation based on evidence rather than averages or behavior proxies
  • Applied projects, simulations, and observed performances are stronger competency evidence than multiple-choice recall alone

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Henri, M., Johnson, M. D., & Nepal, B. (2017). A review of competency-based learning: Tools, assessments, and recommendations. Journal of Engineering Education, 106(4), 607-638. doi:10.1002/jee.20180
  • Collins, J. B., Harsy, A., Hart, J., Haymaker, K. A., Hoofnagle, A. M., Kuyper Janssen, M., & O'Shaughnessy, J. (2019). Mastery-based testing in undergraduate mathematics courses. PRIMUS, 29(5), 441-460.
  • Shearer, R. L. (2017). Adaptive learning, competency-based education, and personalization: Implications for distance education and adult learners. Journal of Lifelong Learning Society, 13(1), 49-71.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Edgar Dale's Cone of Experience (1946, revised 1969) organizes instructional media and methods along a continuum of concreteness: direct, purposeful experience ("seen, handled, tasted, touched, felt, and smelled") at the broad base, moving up through observed and mediated experience (demonstrations, dramatized experience, exhibits, field trips, motion pictures), to highly abstract verbal and visual symbols at the narrow top (Lee & Reeves, 2018). Dale later mapped Bruner's three modes of representation onto the Cone: enactive (learning by doing), iconic (learning through observation), and symbolic (learning through abstraction). Dale explicitly called the Cone a "visual analogy" for the progression of experience, not a prescription that concrete media are always superior or that instruction should be sequenced strictly bottom-to-top.

The Cone is one of the most widely misapplied models in instructional design. It is frequently confused with the "Remembering Cone" or "Bogus Cone" — the claim that learners retain 10% of what they read, 20% of what they hear, 30% of what they see, and so on up to 90% of what they say and do. Dale never made this claim, never attached retention percentages to any level of the Cone, and the "evidence" for the Remembering Cone appears to have been fabricated by petroleum-industry trainers in the 1960s (Molenda, 2003; Subramony, 2003). Any citation of specific retention percentages attributed to Dale should be treated as evidence of the myth, not the actual model.

Dale's own guidance was for balance, not maximization of concreteness: "Too much reliance on concrete experience may actually obstruct the process of meaningful generalization" (Dale, 1969, p. 130), and providing fully realistic experience is not always efficient in terms of cost, time, and effort. The Cone's real contribution was linking media selection to a psychological theory of abstraction (Seels, 1997), influencing later, more rigorous media-selection frameworks (e.g., Briggs, 1972) that account for learner age, learner type, and task type.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A genuine need to choose among media/methods of varying concreteness for a given content and audience, rather than a single fixed medium mandated in advance

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Do not cite specific retention percentages ("people remember 10% of what they read...") as coming from Dale — this is the debunked "Bogus Cone," not his actual model, and its use as decision-support is not evidence-based
  • The Cone is descriptive/organizing, not prescriptive: it does not tell a designer which specific level is correct for a given objective, only that concreteness and abstraction trade off
  • For young children especially, real and concrete experience provides a necessary foundation, but even here, over-reliance on concrete experience can obstruct meaningful generalization to the abstract concept being taught

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Younger or novice learners typically benefit more from concrete, direct, or iconic (observed) experience as a foundation before abstraction
  • All learners benefit from balanced combinations rather than experience concentrated at one extreme of the continuum

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Concept and generalization formation, which requires eventual movement toward abstraction even when direct experience provides the initial foundation
  • Vicarious experience of things learners cannot directly encounter (Dale argued audiovisual materials extend the range of vicarious experience "regardless of the limitations of time and space")

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • The "Remembering Cone" / "Bogus Cone" retention-percentage claim is not part of Dale's actual model and has no credible evidentiary basis (Molenda, 2003; Subramony, 2003) — a claim frequently, incorrectly attributed to this principle

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • User-Centered Design for Learning — both concern deliberate choice of instructional medium, though this principle addresses concreteness/abstraction rather than interface usability

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Combining a hands-on lab (direct experience) with a follow-up abstract discussion of the underlying principle, rather than relying on either alone
  • Using video or simulation (iconic/mediated experience) to bring inaccessible phenomena (historical events, microscopic processes) into a classroom as vicarious experience

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Lee, S. J., & Reeves, T. C. (2018). Edgar Dale and the cone of experience. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/edgar_dale
  • Dale, E. (1969). Audiovisual methods in teaching (3rd ed.). Dryden Press.
  • Subramony, D. P. (2003). Dale's cone revisited: Critically examining the misapplication of a nebulous theory to guide practice. Educational Technology, 43(4), 25–30.
  • Molenda, M. (2003). Cone of experience. In A. Kovalchick & K. Dawson (Eds.), Education and Technology: An Encyclopedia. ABC-CLIO.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Constructivism, as an instructional principle, emphasizes that learners build understanding by connecting new information to prior knowledge through active interpretation, explanation, and application. In practice, the principle pushes design toward tasks that make thinking visible, surface misconceptions, and require learners to organize meaning rather than passively receive it.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Constructivism implies that learning strengthens when learners have to make sense of ideas for themselves rather than only receive finished explanations. Explaining, testing, revising, and comparing interpretations help learners connect new information to what they already know and expose misconceptions that would otherwise remain hidden Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Those same meaning-making opportunities can be especially powerful when they surface confident but inaccurate models that are then revised explicitly High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S]. The practical consequence is that instruction should create active meaning-making opportunities, but with enough modeling, feedback, and structure that learners do not simply construct stable misunderstandings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Active meaning-making tasks
  • Connections to prior knowledge
  • Opportunities to explain, test, and revise ideas

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Under-guidance risk: Active learning does not mean unsupported discovery for novices.
  • Misconceptions can stabilize: Learners need feedback and comparison with stronger models.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from explanation, inquiry, application, and concept building.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Build conceptual understanding and transferable mental models.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivism as a theory base for active meaning-making.
  • Information Processing Theory supports connecting and organizing new information into existing schema.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivist activity still benefits from guidance, modeling, and scaffolded inquiry.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — constructivist tasks work best when learners explain and connect ideas rather than only encounter them
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S] — conceptual change can deepen when learners revise confidently held misconceptions after evidence or feedback

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Explaining Their Thinking
  • Creating Visual Representations
  • Error Analysis

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Learners explain and revise a model after seeing conflicting evidence.
  • Students compare multiple solutions and defend which one best fits the criteria.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bransford, J. D., Brown, A. L., & Cocking, R. R. (Eds.). (2000). How people learn. National Academies Press.
  • Fosnot, C. T. (2013). Constructivism: Theory, perspectives, and practice (2nd ed.). Teachers College Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Constructivist learning is the short-form canonical target for instructional links that emphasize learners actively building meaning through explanation, comparison, inquiry, and revision.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Constructivist learning implies that understanding strengthens when learners do more than receive information: they explain, compare, test, and revise their ideas against evidence or feedback. Self-explanation in particular often improves conceptual understanding because it forces learners to make relationships and assumptions explicit Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The practical design consequence is that activity alone is not enough; tasks need comparison, feedback, or social checking so misconceptions are surfaced rather than simply rehearsed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Active meaning-making tasks
  • Opportunities to connect to prior knowledge
  • Feedback or comparison that supports revision

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Unguided activity can leave misconceptions untouched

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Build conceptual understanding and transferable mental models.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Constructivism

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — active meaning-making is strongest when learners explain the relationships and assumptions inside their own understanding

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Constructivism

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• After a physics demonstration, learners explain why two objects accelerated differently, compare explanations with peers, and revise them after seeing force diagrams.
  • In literature, students generate an interpretation of a passage, test it against textual evidence, and then refine it in response to alternative readings.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Fosnot, C. T. (2013). Constructivism: Theory, perspectives, and practice (2nd ed.). Teachers College Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating visual representations is the instructional principle of having learners organize, explain, or generate knowledge in visual form, such as diagrams, sketches, concept maps, timelines, models, graphs, or annotated layouts. Externalizing thinking visually can reduce the burden of holding complex relations entirely in working memory while also making structure, comparison, and gaps in understanding easier to inspect. It is especially useful when the learning goal involves systems, patterns, relationships, sequences, or multi-step reasoning.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Creating visual representations helps when the structure of an idea is hard to hold or communicate in linear language alone. Diagrams, maps, timelines, and sketches can reduce working-memory burden by making relationships visible Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S], and they often deepen understanding when learners also explain what the representation means Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The important distinction is that the visual should encode reasoning, not just decoration: the strongest tasks require learners to choose a representation that fits the content and then use it to inspect, discuss, or revise their thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful mapping task: Learners need a clear reason to represent something visually, such as showing sequence, causality, hierarchy, comparison, or spatial arrangement.
  • Modeling or exemplars: Many learners need examples of how a visual representation should encode information, not just blank space.
  • Interpretation support: Instructors should prompt learners to explain what the visual means, not only produce it Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].
  • Fit to content: The representation type should match the structure of the knowledge being learned.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Decorative visuals: Visual production can become superficial if aesthetics replace reasoning or explanation.
  • Unclear conventions: Learners may struggle if symbol systems, labels, or expectations are not made explicit.
  • Accessibility limits: Visual tasks need alternatives or supports for learners with visual-processing, motor, or technology constraints.
  • Cognitive overload: Highly complex diagrams can overwhelm novices unless structure is chunked or scaffolded Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S].

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners grappling with complex relationships: Useful when understanding depends on seeing connections, sequence, or structure.
  • Learners who benefit from externalizing thought: Visuals can make tacit reasoning discussable and revisable.
  • Learners in numeracy and data contexts: Graphs, charts, and models can support both interpretation and communication of quantitative ideas.
  • Learners with multimodal strengths: Visual representation can provide additional access routes beyond text-only explanation.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Organizing knowledge: Making categories, relationships, and patterns visible.
  • Explaining reasoning: Showing how ideas connect rather than listing them linearly.
  • Supporting retention and transfer: Creating an artifact that can be revisited, discussed, or adapted in new contexts.
  • Improving problem solving: Representing the structure of a problem before or during solution.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Dual coding and multimedia learning perspectives — combining verbal and visual processing can strengthen comprehension when the modes are aligned.
  • Information processing views of learning — visual externalization can reduce memory burden and support comparison across parts of a task.
  • Generative learning perspectives — drawing, mapping, and diagramming can deepen understanding when learners actively organize meaning.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Visual production does not guarantee understanding; learners can create polished representations that mask weak reasoning.
  • Some content is better clarified through direct verbal explanation before learners are asked to visualize it independently.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — external visual structure helps learners manage complex relationships without holding every connection in working memory
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — visual representations become more instructive when learners explain how the representation encodes the underlying idea

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Graphic Organizers — one common implementation of visual representation for organizing and comparing ideas.
  • Metaphors & Analogies — visual representations often help concretize analogical relationships.
  • Multimodal Instruction — creating visuals complements learning across multiple modes.
  • Explaining Their Thinking — the strongest visual tasks usually require verbal or written explanation alongside the artifact.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Concept maps: Learners diagram how ideas, causes, or terms connect, then explain the map to a peer.
  • Annotated diagrams: Learners label a process, system, or text structure and add notes about why the parts matter.
  • Data visualizations: Learners convert raw data into graphs or charts and interpret what the visual shows.
  • Sketch-to-explain routines: Before solving a complex problem, learners draw the situation, sequence, or relationship structure first.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Cromley, J. G., Du, Y., & Dane, A. P. (2020). Drawing-to-learn: Does meta-analysis show differences between technology-based drawing and paper-and-pencil drawing? Journal of Science Education and Technology, 29(2), 216-229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-020-09836-y
  • Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight ways to promote generative learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28(4), 717-741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9
  • Ainsworth, S. (2006). DeFT: A conceptual framework for learning with multiple representations. Learning and Instruction, 16(3), 183-198. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.03.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Criterion-referenced standardized tests measure performance against a specific standard or criterion, independent of how anyone else performed — a report might state that a student mastered 65 percent of the grade-level problems, or classify a student as basic, proficient, or advanced based on a pre-set mastery threshold. Norm-referenced standardized tests instead report performance relative to a norm group — a representative sample of students who took the test while it was being developed (drawn from the state, for state tests, or from the nation, for national tests) — so a student scoring in the 85th percentile scored better than 85 percent of that norm group. The two report genuinely different information from the same underlying test content: a criterion-referenced report describes what a student can or cannot do; a norm-referenced report describes how a student compares to others. Because classroom teachers planning instruction need to know what students can and cannot do, criterion-referenced tests are typically more instructionally useful (Popham, 2004), and current standards-based accountability (including NCLB) relies predominantly on criterion-based tests — norm-referenced tests have consequently become concentrated in more specialized uses like diagnosis and placement of students with disabilities or exceptional abilities (Haertel & Herman, 2005). Some newer tests blend both: reporting a student's mastery level on a content standard and the percentage of students who reached that level.

Standardized tests serve several distinct classroom purposes. They assess progress in a wider context than any one teacher's classroom can provide — since teachers vary in grading criteria and content coverage, two students who both earn an A in a math class can score very differently on an externally-referenced test (one at the 50th percentile, one at the 90th), and that gap is genuinely informative to the student, parents, and school, not necessarily a sign either teacher graded wrongly. They help diagnose strengths and weaknesses — often through individually-administered diagnostic tests, which give detailed component-level information (for reading: word recognition, comprehension, fluency) beyond what a single achievement score reveals, typically combined with classroom observation, school/medical records, and interviews to build a fuller profile, sometimes toward a learning-disability diagnosis (usually requiring both an aptitude test of general cognitive functioning and an achievement test of specific content knowledge). They select students for programs (the SAT/ACT for college admission; other norm- or criterion-referenced tests for special education, gifted programs, or ability-group placement) — a use that is high-stakes for students whenever it functions as a real gate. And they support accountability, holding schools and teachers publicly responsible for student learning.
