The relationship is not one-directional: with expertise comes innovation, and with innovation comes more questions for systematic study. Teaching decisions — how to sequence a lesson, which technique fits a particular class — draw on craft knowledge that isn't fully reducible to a research finding, even where research constrains and informs the choice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Willingness to treat research findings as informing, rather than replacing, professional judgment about a specific class or student
  • A practice of turning classroom observations and innovations back into questions that could be studied systematically

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Treating teaching as pure craft (ignoring research evidence) risks repeating known ineffective practices
  • Treating teaching as pure applied science (ignoring situated judgment) risks over-standardizing decisions that depend on a specific class, student, or moment

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preservice and practicing teachers forming a professional identity that has to hold both scientific evidence and situated craft judgment at once

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Recognizing when a teaching decision is well-settled by research evidence versus when it depends on artful, situated judgment the evidence doesn't resolve

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Reflective Practice — the practitioner side of this loop: using reflection on one's own experience (not only external research) to refine practice

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Reflective Practice

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher whose classroom-management approach draws on both a study of effective techniques and their own accumulated read of a specific group of students

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Merriam-Webster Dictionary. (2020a). Art. Retrieved from https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/art
  • Merriam-Webster Dictionary. (2020b). Science. Retrieved from https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/science
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Educational psychology: Art or science? In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Readiness traditionally refers to a student's preparedness to cope with or profit from the activities and expectations of school — for example, whether a kindergartner is in good health, has moderately good social skills, can manage personal physical needs unsupervised, and can use a pencil to draw simple shapes. At older ages, this same idea is often called prerequisites instead of readiness (e.g., a student needs advanced algebra before taking physics).

This traditional framing focuses attention entirely on the student's adjustment to school, and away from the reverse possibility: that schools and teachers also bear responsibility for adjusting to students. A five-year-old's need to play and stay active is a reason a kindergarten teacher must be "ready" to build a program with substantial play and physical activity — if the teacher cannot or will not do this, the resulting mismatch is not the child's failure to be ready. The same logic extends to older students: a teacher with a visually impaired student must adjust their approach, not expect the student to "sink or swim." This teacher-facing sense of readiness is central to special education, and matters broadly whenever a classroom's students are diverse — which is most of the time (Arduini-Van Hoose, 2020).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear, concrete readiness indicators appropriate to the specific skill or content being introduced (e.g., a working productive vocabulary and use of complete sentences, as precursors to formal reading instruction)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Readiness assessed only against the student risks blaming students (or their families) for a mismatch that is equally a failure of the teacher or school to adjust
  • Readiness criteria calibrated to one population (e.g., typically-developing children) can misclassify students with disabilities or different developmental trajectories as "not ready" when the actual need is instructional adjustment

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Students entering a new stage of schooling (e.g., kindergarten, a new subject with prerequisites)
  • Students with disabilities or atypical developmental trajectories, for whom the teacher-adjustment sense of readiness is especially load-bearing

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not itself a content objective — readiness is a precondition-diagnosis concept that determines which objectives are currently reachable

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding — once a mismatch between student readiness and task demand is identified, scaffolding is one primary response
  • Transfer of Learning — prerequisite mastery (a form of readiness) is itself a factor affecting transfer

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A reading-readiness table can list parallel expectations for the child (e.g., a productive vocabulary of 5,000-8,000 words, using complete sentences, matching some letters to sounds) and for the teacher (e.g., answering children's questions, highlighting letters and sounds in the classroom, providing paper and marking tools) side by side (Copple & Bredekamp, 2006).

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Copple, C., & Bredekamp, S. (Eds.). (2006). Basics of developmentally appropriate practice: An introduction for teachers of children 3 to 6. National Association for the Education of Young Children.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher's perspectives on learning. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Approaches to classroom management have historically grouped into three traditions: a humanist tradition emphasizing communication and problem-solving between teacher and student (Ginott's Congruent Communication; Glasser's Choice Theory); an applied behavior analysis tradition applying behaviorist principles to the classroom (see Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model and Reinforcement Theory); and a newer classroom-management/prevention tradition emphasizing the teaching skills involved in organizing instruction and preventing misbehavior before it starts (Kounin's Classroom Management Research). Each tradition has genuine strengths and limitations, and effective managers in practice blend elements of all three rather than relying on just one.

A comprehensive classroom management plan should incorporate strategies that accomplish six things:

  1. Establish positive relationships between all classroom participants. A positive, supportive environment meeting students' needs for belonging and acceptance is a necessary foundation for an orderly classroom.
  2. Prevent attention-seeking and work-avoidance behaviors. Management time is best spent engaging students in learning and preventing behaviors that interfere with it — through both physical-space arrangements and taught rules and routines for working in that space.
  3. Redirect misbehavior quickly and unobtrusively once it occurs. Most classroom problems are minor off-task or attention-seeking events; techniques for handling them should not themselves cause more disruption than the original behavior.
  4. Stop persistent and chronic misbehavior with strategies simple enough to use consistently. Management systems requiring a response to every single act of positive or negative behavior are rarely practical in a busy classroom.
  5. Teach self-control. Students should have the opportunity to exercise internal control before external control is imposed, and any external controls that are imposed should come with an explicit plan for fading them out.
  6. Respect cultural differences. Verbal and nonverbal techniques for redirecting disruptive behavior do not mean the same thing to every cultural group, and reward/consequence systems can unintentionally violate cultural norms (see Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A plan that draws on more than one tradition — purely reactive approaches (humanist, behavior-analytic) address misbehavior once it has occurred, but neither is inherently prevention-oriented the way the Kounin tradition is
  • Explicit attention to cultural variation in how management techniques are received, not just to whether a technique "works" on average

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Systems requiring a response to every instance of behavior are not practical at classroom scale and tend to break down under the ordinary busyness of a school day
  • A plan built entirely around external control, without any fading toward student self-control, works against criterion 5 even if it succeeds at criteria 2-4 in the short term

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students in a K-12 classroom setting; the "respect cultural differences" criterion specifically foregrounds students whose cultural background diverges from mainstream classroom-management assumptions

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Sustained engagement in learning tasks and minimized disruption, achieved through a durable management structure rather than moment-to-moment improvisation

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Kounin's Classroom Management Research [+M] — evidence that these criteria, especially prevention and consistent consequences, distinguish more effective from less effective managers
  • Ginott's Congruent Communication [+M] — a concrete technique set for criterion 1 (positive relationships) and criterion 5 (teaching self-control through elicited rather than imposed cooperation)
  • Glasser's Choice Theory and Cooperative Learning [+M] — cooperative learning as a specific strategy for criterion 1 and criterion 2

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Teaching Styles as Warmth and Control [~M] — these six criteria describe what an authoritative (warm-and-controlled) style aims to achieve, but the same criteria can be pursued through authoritarian methods that satisfy criteria 2-4 while badly violating criterion 5

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Rewarding an already-intrinsically-motivating activity can reduce future engagement with it [-M] — relevant to designing criterion-5 self-control fading plans that don't over-rely on external reward

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Functional Behavior Assessment — a complementary, more individualized approach for the subset of students whose disruptive behavior does not respond to a general classroom-wide plan
  • Classroom Space and Procedural Design — the concrete prevention-oriented practices (space, rules, procedures, transitions) that implement criterion 2
  • Natural and Logical Consequences — implements criteria 3 and 4 with consequences distinct from punishment
  • Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms — directly implements criterion 6

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model — the applied-behavior-analysis tradition's specific technique for criteria 2-4
  • Low-Profile Classroom Control — a technique set aimed squarely at criterion 3

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ginott, H. G. (1972). Teacher and child: A book for parents and teachers. Macmillan.
  • Glasser, W. (1990). The quality school: Managing students without coercion. Harper & Row.
  • Kounin, J. S. (1970). Discipline and group management in classrooms. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.
  • Emmer, E. T., Evertson, C. M., Clements, B. S., & Worsham, M. E. (1994). Classroom management for secondary teachers (4th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Doyle, W. (1986). Classroom organization and management. In M. C. Wittrock (Ed.), Handbook of research on teaching (3rd ed., pp. 392-431). Macmillan.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Systems of classroom management. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Empathy interviews are structured, open-ended conversations designed to help educators or designers understand how learners experience school, work, systems, and support. Unlike a survey or diagnostic checklist, the goal is not only to collect facts but to hear how learners interpret challenges, strengths, motivations, and belonging in their own words. Used well, empathy interviews improve the instructor's model of the learner and can lead to more responsive supports, stronger relationships, and better alignment between instruction and lived reality.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Empathy interviews are valuable because they replace assumption with direct evidence about how learners experience the system. Open-ended listening can reveal barriers, strengths, and motivations that standard diagnostics miss, and that usually leads to better instructional fit when the information is actually used to change supports or communication. These conversations depend heavily on learners explaining their experience in their own words Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~M], and they are most useful when what is learned feeds into more authentic, context-sensitive design rather than abstract learner profiles Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~M]. The design risk is extractive listening: if interviews gather stories without altering practice, they produce the appearance of care without the instructional value.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear listening purpose: Interviewers need to know what they are trying to understand, such as barriers, motivations, strengths, or belonging.
  • Open-ended prompts: Questions should invite story, explanation, and concrete examples rather than short confirmatory answers.
  • Trust and confidentiality: Learners need clear boundaries around what will be recorded, shared, or acted on.
  • Instructional follow-through: Interviews matter most when what is learned shapes support, curriculum, communication, or design decisions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Extractive use: Interviews can become performative if learner stories are collected but never used to improve the experience.
  • Power dynamics: Learners may censor themselves if they fear consequences from honesty.
  • Boundary risk: Not every challenge disclosed in an empathy interview can or should be handled by the instructor alone.
  • Indirect evidence base in this repo: Current linked claims support explanation, transfer, and reflection mechanisms more directly than empathy interviews as an independent intervention.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners whose needs are not well captured by standard diagnostics: Especially useful when context, identity, or history strongly shape engagement.
  • Learners in redesign or improvement efforts: Empathy interviews are strong for courses, services, or supports that need to be adapted around learner experience.
  • Educators building relationships early: Useful at the beginning of a course, mentoring relationship, or intervention.
  • Programs serving heterogeneous populations: Interviews can surface variation in barriers and strengths that one-size-fits-all design misses.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improved instructional fit: Helping educators tailor examples, supports, expectations, and communication.
  • Belonging and trust: Giving learners a structured opportunity to feel heard and taken seriously.
  • Context-aware support: Identifying what barriers or assets shape participation, persistence, and performance.
  • Reflective interpretation by educators: Moving from assumptions about learners to evidence-informed decisions.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Humanistic and belonging-oriented views of learning — learners engage differently when they feel recognized, safe, and respected.
  • Self-determination theory — understanding learner experience can help instructors better support autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
  • Transformative and reflective practice traditions — hearing learner narratives can unsettle instructor assumptions and shift design choices.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Interviews do not automatically produce empathy or better design; interpretation quality matters.
  • Listening to learners is not the same as agreeing with every preference or turning every interview into an individualized curriculum.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~M] — empathy interviews depend on learners narrating and interpreting their own experience in ways that reveal real barriers and strengths
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~M] — interviews are most instructionally valuable when they reshape authentic tasks, supports, and contexts rather than staying as detached listening exercises

These are indirect anchors: empathy interviews rely on explanation, authentic context, and reflective interpretation, but the current claim inventory does not yet include a dedicated empathy-interview claim.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Building Empathy — empathy interviews are one concrete way to build grounded understanding of learner experience.
  • Cultural & Life Experiences Connections — interviews help instructors connect instruction to real learner contexts.
  • Instructor Accessibility — these conversations are more useful when learners see the instructor as approachable and responsive.
  • Debriefing — post-interview reflection helps convert what was heard into changed instructional choices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Beginning-of-course learner interviews: Short structured conversations about goals, barriers, prior experience, and support needs.
  • Design interviews before program revision: Staff interview learners about friction points before changing curriculum or services.
  • Mentoring check-in interviews: A mentor periodically revisits learner priorities, constraints, and sense of progress.
  • Affinity-informed listening rounds: Learners choose whether to share in individual, paired, or small-group interview formats.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Anaissie, T., Cary, V., Clifford, D., Malarkey, T., & Wise, S. (2020). Liberatory design: Your toolkit to design for equity, version 1.0.
  • Ishimaru, A. M. (2019). Just schools: Building equitable collaborations with families and communities. Teachers College Press.
  • Meyers, S., Rowell, K., Wells, M., & Smith, B. C. (2019). Teacher empathy: A model of empathy for teaching for student success. College Teaching, 67(3), 160-168. https://doi.org/10.1080/87567555.2019.1579699
  • Nelsestuen, K., & Smith, J. (2020). Empathy interviews. The Learning Professional, 41(5), 59-59.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engagement is the principle of designing learning so that learners attend, participate, and sustain effort in cognitively meaningful ways. It matters when attention, persistence, and active involvement affect whether instruction actually results in learning.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Engagement matters because even strong content design has little effect if learners do not attend, participate, or persist long enough to benefit from it. The principle is broader than “interest.” It includes behavioral participation, cognitive investment, and emotional willingness to stay with the work. Engagement can be supported through relevance, challenge, autonomy, interaction, and visible progress, and learners are often more likely to persist when goals are challenging but intelligible Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S], when progress is visible enough to monitor Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M], and when novices can focus on actionable process rather than distant outcomes Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. It is still easy to mistake surface activity for meaningful involvement. The core design question is not whether learners are busy; it is whether they are invested in thinking and continuing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear reason for learners to invest attention — relevance, curiosity, challenge, or social purpose usually needs to be visible
  • Tasks that require participation rather than passive exposure alone — engagement grows when learners must respond, decide, explain, or create

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Surface attention-grabbers do not guarantee deep engagement
  • Engagement is fragile when success feels unattainable — learners who see no path to competence often withdraw
  • Novelty fades — designs that rely only on surprise or entertainment often lose power over time

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners at risk of withdrawal, passivity, or low persistence
  • Learners whose effort depends strongly on relevance, autonomy, or visible success
  • Learners in discussion, project, or technology-rich environments where participation is a key mediator of learning

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Increase participation, persistence, and active involvement in learning
  • Improve willingness to attend to difficult tasks and sustain effort
  • Strengthen cognitive and emotional investment in meaningful learning work

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Motivation — engagement is often the visible behavioral and cognitive expression of motivated learning
  • Active Learning — participation can increase engagement when the activity requires meaningful thought
  • Self-Determination Theory — autonomy, competence, and relatedness help explain when engagement rises or falls

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — tasks can appear engaging yet still fail if they overload learners or split attention

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — appropriately challenging goals can increase effort and persistence when learners are committed and supported
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — visible progress can help sustain engagement by showing learners that effort is going somewhere
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — engagement may be easier to sustain when novices can focus on actionable process rather than distant outcomes

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Learner Choice — meaningful choice is one common route to stronger engagement
  • Game-Based Learning — can increase participation and persistence when challenge, progress, and feedback are well designed
  • Motivation — engagement is often the most visible outcome of motivational conditions

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Learner Choice — Giving learners meaningful options can increase ownership and persistence when choices remain aligned to goals.

Video Prompts — A short, concrete stimulus can focus attention and launch interpretation, especially when followed by explanation or discussion.

Project launches with visible purpose — Learners are more likely to stay engaged when they know what the work is for, who it matters to, and what success looks like.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Fredricks, J. A., Blumenfeld, P. C., & Paris, A. H. (2004). School engagement. Review of Educational Research, 74(1), 59-109. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543074001059
  • Sinatra, G. M., Heddy, B. C., & Lombardi, D. (2015). The challenges of defining and measuring student engagement in science. Educational Psychologist, 50(1), 1-13. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.1002924

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Epistemic cognition is the principle of helping learners reason about knowledge itself: what counts as evidence, how claims are justified, how certainty should be calibrated, and how knowledge is constructed or revised. It is useful when the goal is not only to know content, but to judge the quality of arguments and evidence.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Epistemic cognition matters when learners need to move beyond “what do I think?” toward “how do I know?” The principle is especially important in argument-rich, research-rich, and uncertainty-rich contexts where the quality of evidence, the strength of justification, and the limits of certainty all matter. Strong epistemic instruction helps learners evaluate claims, compare standards of evidence, and calibrate confidence, especially when they have to explain why a claim is justified rather than merely endorse it Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. It also becomes more powerful when learners monitor the strength of their evidence and the calibration of their certainty Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. Weak epistemic instruction often collapses into opinion sharing or vague skepticism because the norms for evidence and justification are never made explicit, though overconfident mistakes can become useful if they are followed by strong evidence-based correction High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Tasks that require judging claims, evidence, or justification — epistemic cognition develops when learners must evaluate rather than only recall
  • Prompts that surface standards for good reasoning — learners need explicit norms for what counts as warranted or weak
  • Opportunities to compare stronger and weaker justifications — contrast sharpens epistemic judgment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Learners may default to opinion-sharing unless evidence norms are explicit
  • Abstract discussion about knowledge can stay detached from practice if not anchored in real claims
  • Certainty calibration is hard — learners may swing between overconfidence and blanket relativism

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners evaluating sources, arguments, interpretations, or competing explanations
  • Learners in humanities, sciences, civics, research, and inquiry-heavy settings
  • Learners who need stronger standards for evidence and justification in discussion or writing

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve evaluation of evidence, reasoning quality, and certainty
  • Help learners distinguish stronger from weaker justifications
  • Build the habit of asking what warrants a claim and how confidence should be calibrated

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Argumentation and disciplinary-literacy traditions — knowing includes knowing what counts as evidence and justification
  • Evaluating Sources — one of the clearest practical applications of epistemic cognition
  • Perspective-Taking — evaluating claims often requires comparing viewpoints and standards

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Behaviorism — purely performance-focused instruction may underrepresent epistemic judgment because observable correctness does not capture warrant quality

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — requiring learners to explain why a claim is justified can deepen epistemic understanding
  • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M] — overconfident error can be instructionally useful when it is followed by evidence-based correction
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — epistemic judgment improves when learners monitor the quality of their evidence and certainty

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Evaluating Sources — directly operationalizes epistemic judgment around credibility and evidence
  • Perspective-Taking — learners often need to compare competing interpretations and standards
  • Debate — argument-focused settings often require explicit epistemic norms to stay productive

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Justification — Learners are asked not only for an answer or claim, but for the evidence and reasoning that warrant it.

Source comparison routines — Students evaluate multiple sources making related claims and determine which is better supported and why.

Argument critique in discussion or writing — Learners compare strong and weak uses of evidence, confidence, and counterargument rather than only choosing a side.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hofer, B. K., & Pintrich, P. R. (1997). The development of epistemological theories. Review of Educational Research, 67(1), 88-140. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543067001088
  • Greene, J. A., Sandoval, W. A., & Bråten, I. (Eds.). (2016). Handbook of epistemic cognition. Routledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Error analysis is an instructional principle that treats learner errors as valuable opportunities for deepening conceptual understanding and improving long-term retention. By actively analyzing their own mistakes or studying erroneous examples, learners develop metacognitive monitoring and critical reasoning skills High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S].

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Error analysis works when mistakes are treated as information rather than only as failure. Comparing incorrect and correct solutions, explaining why an error happened, and receiving timely corrective feedback can deepen conceptual understanding and improve retention Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models. [+M], especially when the error was made with high confidence High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S]. The practical limit is that learners need enough knowledge and support to analyze the mistake productively; for complete novices, poorly timed error work can add confusion instead of insight.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Corrective Feedback: Errors only lead to learning if they are followed by clear, immediate, and non-punitive corrective feedback High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S].
  • Comparison Opportunities: Comparing a correct model with an incorrect one is more effective than studying errors in isolation Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models. [+M].
  • Explanation Prompts: Learners should be prompted to explain why an error occurred and how to correct it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Low Confidence Errors: Mistakes made due to a pure lack of knowledge are less likely to lead to long-term learning than high-confidence errors High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~M].
  • Novice Overload: For absolute novices, seeing errors before mastering the correct procedure can be confusing and increase extraneous cognitive load Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models. [-M].
  • Cultural Barriers: In some instructional contexts, errors are seen as failures to be avoided rather than learning opportunities, requiring a shift toward a growth mindset.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Intermediate Learners: Most capable of benefiting from erroneous examples after they have a basic grasp of a topic.
  • Learners with Deep-Seated Misconceptions: Essential for surfacing and correcting intuitive but incorrect beliefs Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models. [+M].
  • All Learners (for Hypercorrection): Any learner who makes a high-confidence mistake is primed for deep learning upon correction.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Conceptual Understanding: Developing a deep grasp of the underlying "why" of a domain.
  • Metacognitive Monitoring: Learning to recognize and correct one's own errors in real-time.
  • Long-term Retention: Strengthening memory for facts and principles through the "hypercorrection effect."

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivism — knowledge is actively built through the correction of mental models.
  • Information Processing Theory — surprise from a high-confidence error triggers deeper attention and memory reconsolidation High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S].
  • Generative Learning — guessing an answer (even incorrectly) before being told is more effective than passive reading.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S] — confidently held mistakes can become especially memorable learning opportunities when corrected clearly
  • Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models. [+M] — comparing incorrect and correct examples can deepen conceptual understanding when learners can interpret the contrast

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Explaining Their Thinking — self-explanation is the mechanism by which error analysis works.
  • Worked Examples — can be modified into erroneous examples.
  • Foster Growth Mindset — error analysis requires a safe environment where mistakes are valued.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Erroneous Examples in Math: Showing a student a hypothetical peer's calculation error and asking them to find and fix it.
  • Khan Academy Hints — Uses error-driven feedback where hints are tailored to specific common mistakes the learner makes.
  • "Surprise" Quizzes: Asking students to predict an outcome before a demonstration; the surprise of a wrong prediction triggers the hypercorrection effect.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Metcalfe, J. (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology, 68, 465–489. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010416-044022
  • Durkin, K., & Rittle-Johnson, B. (2012). The effectiveness of using erroneous examples to support learning of decimal magnitude. Learning and Instruction, 22(3), 206–214. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2011.11.001
  • Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2009). Surprising feedback improves later memory. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 16(1), 88–92. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.16.1.88

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teaching adult learners how to systematically evaluate sources prepares them to navigate information in an increasingly complex, digital world. It is important to help adult learners understand why they need to evaluate the trustworthiness of a source, equip them with strategies to do so, and give them ample opportunities to practice these essential information and Digital Literacy skills. As learners develop skills and strategies for evaluating sources for authenticity and relevance, they are further developing their Reasoning and Metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Evaluating sources improves learning when learners move beyond surface cues and justify why a source is trustworthy, useful, or suspect Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Explicit routines for checking evidence, expertise, corroboration, and relevance are especially important for novices Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] because polished design or familiar domain labels can easily masquerade as credibility. The implication for instruction is to use real source comparison tasks where quality changes the outcome of an argument, decision, or inquiry, so learners practice judgment rather than memorizing a checklist. That judgment improves further when credibility criteria and evidence expectations are explicit Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] and when instructor prompts respond to the actual weakness in a learner’s source reasoning Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Repeated opportunities to evaluate real sources rather than isolated checklist exercises
  • Explicit criteria for credibility, evidence, expertise, bias, currency, and relevance
  • Access to comparison sources and open-web verification methods such as lateral reading
  • Tasks where source quality materially affects conclusions, arguments, or decisions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Learners may over-rely on superficial heuristics such as domain type, design polish, or professional tone
  • Checklist-only instruction can become mechanical if learners are not asked to justify their judgments
  • Source evaluation changes across domains; standards for news, research, policy, and advocacy texts are not identical
  • Learners need enough background knowledge to notice implausible claims or missing evidence

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners working with web sources, media, research, or civic information
  • Adult learners re-entering study or workplace contexts where digital information quality varies sharply
  • Learners developing academic research habits, media literacy, and evidence-based decision-making
  • Learners who need explicit routines for checking claims before using them in writing, discussion, or action

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Judge credibility, expertise, bias, and evidentiary support across source types
  • Compare sources rather than accept single-source claims at face value
  • Build metacognitive habits for slowing down and verifying before sharing or citing
  • Use higher-quality sources in inquiry, argumentation, and problem solving

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information-processing perspectives support explicit routines for checking sources before integrating information into understanding
  • Self-regulated-learning and metacognitive perspectives support monitoring one’s own trust judgments and revising them when evidence changes
  • Inquiry and disciplinary-literacy perspectives support evaluating sources in relation to task, audience, and domain norms rather than through generic trust labels alone

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Surface features are not enough; learners must be taught to check external reputation, evidence trails, and corroboration
  • Domain heuristics such as .gov or .edu can help but are insufficient on their own
  • Learners need active comparison and justification, not only exposure to misinformation examples

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — source evaluation improves when learners explain why a source is or is not trustworthy
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices need explicit evaluation routines rather than only being told to “use credible sources”
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — instructor coaching improves learners’ source judgments when prompts respond to the actual weakness in their reasoning
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — evaluation improves when credibility criteria and evidence expectations are explicit

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Inquiry-based Learning — inquiry quality depends on source quality
  • Annotating — annotation can focus attention on credibility signals, claims, and evidence
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — learners need explicit frameworks for evaluation, not just warnings about misinformation
  • Debate — debates become more rigorous when learners are accountable for source quality, not just rhetorical performance

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Reading Laterally — learners verify claims by consulting external sources before trusting a page
  • Website Domain Analysis — teaches basic domain heuristics as an entry point, though not a complete method
  • Resource Evaluation and Research are direct implementation elements
  • Comparing a polished but unreliable site against corroborated sources can make the need for evaluation visible

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Wineburg, S., & McGrew, S. (2017). Lateral reading: Reading less and learning more when evaluating digital information.
  • Breakstone, J., McGrew, S., Smith, M., Ortega, T., & Wineburg, S. (2018). Why we need a new approach to teaching digital literacy. Phi Delta Kappan, 99(6), 27-32.
  • Rapchak, M. E., Lewis, L. A., Motyka, J. K., & Balmert, M. (2015). Information literacy and adult learners. Adult Learning, 26(4), 135-142. doi:10.1177/1045159515594150
  • Afflerbach, P. A., & Cho, B. Y. (2010). Determining and describing reading strategies: Internet and traditional forms of reading. In Metacognition, strategy use, and instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Ben Goldacre (2013) argues that teaching should be an evidence-based profession, which would require a cultural shift: recognizing that we don't necessarily "know" what works best and need evidence that something works; giving teachers better access to research outcomes; helping teachers understand how research works so they can become critical consumers of it; and giving teachers access to networks of others interested in research. This isn't only research done by academics — research by teachers on their own practice is itself part of the same evidence base, and is increasingly embedded in schools as a contributor to school improvement.

Personal inquiry — drawing conclusions from one's own experience — is a weaker basis for this than it feels like from the inside. Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for evidence that we're right while ignoring evidence that we're not; because our assumptions guide our perceptions, "believing is seeing" at least as much as "seeing is believing." This can be an unconscious cognitive blind spot or a more deliberate defense of an existing view, and much of what passes for personal inquiry consists of validating what we already believe by discussing it with others who already agree.

Philosopher Karl Popper proposed the criterion that separates scientific from unscientific claims: falsifiability. Scientific inquiry involves genuine attempts to reject or refute a theory or assumption; a theory that cannot be falsified is not scientific (Thornton, 2005). The scientific method itself rests on three fundamental features (Stanovich, 2010): systematic empiricism — learning through carefully planned, recorded, and analyzed observation rather than casual impression; empirical questions — questions about how the world actually is, which can therefore be answered by systematic observation, as opposed to questions no observation could settle; and public knowledge — publication that lets other researchers detect and correct errors in method or conclusion, so that scientific knowledge is self-correcting over time in a way one researcher's private conviction is not.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Structures that give teachers real access to research findings and to networks of other research-engaged practitioners, not just an individual expectation to "read more"
  • A habit of treating a striking personal classroom observation as a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion already reached

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A belief or practice that cannot in principle be shown wrong by any classroom evidence isn't a testable claim about what works, however confidently it's held
  • Discussing a teaching approach only with colleagues who already agree reinforces confirmation bias rather than correcting it — some form of outside challenge or published, peer-reviewed evidence is needed to catch what a like-minded group will not

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preservice and practicing teachers evaluating a new technique, a colleague's confident recommendation, or their own striking classroom experience

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • The ability to distinguish evidence that could in principle have come out otherwise (and so genuinely tests a claim) from evidence that would look the same regardless of whether the claim was true

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Educational Psychology as Both Art and Science — this principle is the epistemic half of that same art/science relationship: what makes the "science" side trustworthy in the first place

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Educational Psychology as Both Art and Science

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A teacher who notices a technique "worked great" for one class and, before adopting it broadly, checks whether a controlled study backs the impression or looks for a colleague who tried it and got a different result
  • A department that shares research findings and invites outside speakers, rather than relying solely on internal consensus about what works

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Goldacre, B. (2013). Building evidence into education. UK Department for Education.
  • Thornton, S. (2005). Karl Popper. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Retrieved from https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/popper/
  • Stanovich, K. E. (2010). How to think straight about psychology (9th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). The science of educational psychology; The scientific method. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Networking and supporting adult learners in expanding their social networks provide access to additional resources and Social Supports, which can impact their trajectory and Motivation. Knowledge and utilization of existing informal and formal social networks to raise awareness of local learning opportunities can improve persistence and feelings of Safety. This can have a significant impact on vulnerable populations, especially adults who have been negatively impacted by Adverse Experiences, Socioeconomic Status, language barriers, and physical or cognitive limitations. When it comes to getting a job, networks are especially important to low-skilled workers and immigrants.​

Proactive networking behaviors have been associated with increased productivity, hope, and a more positive view of one's future work self. Access to peers, expertise, and learning networks are strong predictors of opportunities to engage in workplace learning. Across the adult work lifespan, the informal learning that takes place in personal and social networks is important across many contexts such as hearing about job opportunities, gaining initial entry, connecting with potential employers, and gaining access to choices about different ways of updating skills, knowledge and experience.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Expanding social networks matters because access to opportunity is often mediated through people, not just through formal curriculum. New ties to peers, mentors, community organizations, and professional groups can increase belonging, information flow, and practical access to learning or work opportunities, especially for learners who start with limited institutional access. But networks do not become educative automatically: learners usually need explicit support for outreach, help-seeking, and follow-through Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M], they benefit when they can explain their goals and problems clearly to others Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], and strong networks should gradually support greater independence rather than permanent reliance on a single gatekeeper Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]. Programs also have to design against the tendency for networking to simply reproduce existing privilege, which is easier when learners have clear goals for what kinds of ties and opportunities they are trying to build Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Deliberate structures for introductions, connection-making, and follow-up rather than assuming networks grow automatically
  • Access to peers, mentors, community organizations, affinity groups, or professional communities that can widen opportunity
  • Support for networking behaviors such as outreach, reciprocal exchange, and asking for help
  • Attention to inclusion so learners with fewer existing connections are not left behind by a “networking” norm that rewards the already connected

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Network-building can reproduce inequity if programs simply leverage existing privilege rather than intentionally broadening access
  • Learners with adverse experiences, language barriers, or low confidence may need explicit support to participate in networking spaces
  • Large or loosely structured networking events often produce weak ties without durable follow-through
  • Social-network expansion is valuable only if connections are relevant, trusted, and usable for learning or opportunity

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult learners entering new educational, workplace, or community environments
  • Learners with limited professional or institutional access who need bridges to opportunity
  • Learners in transition: immigrants, re-entry populations, career changers, and first-generation participants in formal learning systems
  • Learners whose persistence and belonging improve when they can locate trusted peers and mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Increase access to information, guidance, and opportunity through new ties
  • Strengthen help-seeking, peer support, and professional communication
  • Build belonging and identity within a learning or professional community
  • Support persistence by reducing isolation and increasing access to practical resources

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social learning theory supports learning through observation, modeling, and interaction with peers and mentors
  • Connectivist perspectives support the idea that knowing where to access people and knowledge is itself a crucial capability
  • Situated-learning perspectives support network expansion because access to communities is part of participating in authentic practice
  • Communities-of-practice thinking explains why network growth often changes not just opportunity but also identity and belonging

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Not all network growth is helpful; ties must be trustworthy and relevant enough to support learning or opportunity
  • Learners often need explicit scaffolds for outreach, communication, and follow-up rather than vague encouragement to “network”
  • Network effects can be slow and indirect, so programs should not assume immediate measurable outcomes from a single intervention

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — mentoring and networked support are most useful when people respond to learners’ actual needs rather than offering generic advice
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — networks become more educative when learners explain problems, reasoning, and goals clearly to others
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — strong networks support independence over time rather than permanent dependency on a single gatekeeper
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — networking support is stronger when learners have clear goals for who they need to meet and why

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Communities of Practice — networks deepen when they become recurring communities around shared work
  • Ask Experts — expert access is often a key reason to expand networks
  • Check-ins — regular low-stakes contact can help relationships form before higher-stakes support is needed
  • Cultural & Life Experiences Connections — network-building should respect and build from learners’ existing communities and identities

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Mentor matching, alumni panels, affinity-based peer groups, and professional learning communities
  • Community Involvement — builds bridges between learners and broader support systems
  • Online professional networks or cohort channels can widen access when paired with structured participation norms
  • Networking routines tied to concrete goals, such as informational interviews or resource-mapping exercises, are stronger than generic mixers

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Department for Education. (2018). Decisions of adult learners. Kantar Public and Learning and Work Institute.
  • Hellerstein, J. K., & Neumark, D. (2020). Social capital, networks, and economic wellbeing. The Future of Children, 30(1).
  • Dorner, H. (2012). Effects of online mentoring in computer-supported collaborative learning environments. American Journal of Distance Education, 26(3), 157-171. doi:10.1080/08923647.2012.697697
  • Ngcoza, K., & Southwood, S. (2019). Webs of development: Professional networks as spaces for learning. Pythagoras, 40(1).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Experiential learning is learning by doing, which may include self-directed learning activities. Helping learners make sense of experiences is foundational to adult learning. There are four key elements of experiential learning: concrete experience, reflection and observation, development of new ideas, and experimenting with new ideas. Active participation in experiential learning benefits both learners and the community. Adult learners gain concrete experiences and reflect on them by comparing the new experiences with Background Knowledge. It fosters the upgrading of life skills, such as a respect for diversity, exposure to multiple perspectives, and offers opportunities for critical reflection and Cognitive Flexibility. Experiential learning can also foster personal autonomy, self-fulfillment, interpersonal effectiveness and Social Awareness and Relationship Skills.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Experiential learning works because it puts learners in situations where concepts have consequences. Integrated tasks, realistic roles, and repeated cycles of action and reflection tend to improve transfer more than isolated practice alone Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S], but only when experience is interpreted rather than merely lived through. That is the central design point: reflection and explanation are what turn experience into learning Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], and coaching is often necessary so learners can revise decisions in real time rather than simply repeat them Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]. Without those supports, learners may simply reinforce ineffective habits or mistake activity for progress, especially if novices are immersed without guidance on what to notice or how to act Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful task, role, or situation that learners can actively engage in rather than only hear about
  • Structured reflection so experience becomes interpretable and transferable
  • Opportunities to test revised understanding in a new action cycle
  • Facilitation that connects experience back to concepts, models, or criteria

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Experience alone is not enough; without reflection and feedback, learners may simply repeat ineffective habits
  • High-complexity experiences can overwhelm novices unless tasks are scaffolded
  • Experiential tasks can become performative or logistically heavy if not clearly tied to the learning goal
  • Reflection must go beyond narration (“what happened”) toward interpretation and next steps

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing applied, professional, or interpersonal competence
  • Adult learners who benefit from relevance, realism, and visible use-value
  • Learners who need to integrate concepts, judgment, and action rather than memorize isolated facts
  • Learners who may disengage from abstract instruction unless they can test ideas in practice

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Strengthen transfer from theory to practice
  • Develop reflective judgment by comparing action, outcome, and alternative choices
  • Build autonomy and confidence through repeated cycles of doing, reflecting, and retrying
  • Deepen understanding by linking concepts to consequences in realistic contexts

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Experiential Learning Theory [+S] — Kolb's experiential cycle directly supports the move from concrete experience to reflection, abstraction, and experimentation
  • Deweyan and constructivist perspectives support learning through doing and meaning-making from consequences
  • Sociocultural perspectives qualify experiential learning by emphasizing the role of guided participation, context, and tools
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] supports integrated performance tasks as especially useful for transfer

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Unguided experiential learning can impose too much cognitive load on novices
  • Reflection quality matters; learners need prompts, models, and sometimes expert feedback to interpret experience well
  • Some foundational knowledge may need explicit instruction before an authentic experience becomes productive

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — integrated experiences support transfer better than fragmented subskill drills
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — reflection and explanation are what convert experience into insight
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — experiential tasks are stronger when coaching responds to learner decisions in real time
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices in experiential settings benefit from guidance on what to attend to and how to act, not only from immersion

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Debriefing — a core mechanism for making experience educative
  • Problem-Based Learning — one form of experiential design centered on complex problems
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes — real stakes and users strengthen the relevance of experience
  • Communities of Practice — experiential learning deepens when learners participate in real social practices over time

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Simulations, internships, clinical rounds, labs, community projects, and field-based inquiry
  • Project-Based Learning (PBL) — learners build knowledge through extended authentic work
  • Anchored Instruction — realistic scenarios anchor inquiry and applied reasoning
  • Reflection journals, post-task debriefs, and iteration cycles are typical implementation supports

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Dernova, M. (2015). Experiential learning theory as one of the foundations of adult learning practice worldwide. Comparative Professional Pedagogy, 5(2).
  • Hansman, C. A. (2001). Context-based adult learning. New Directions for Adult and Continuing Education, 89, 43-52.
  • Zeivots, S. (2016). Emotional highs in adult experiential learning. Australian Journal of Adult Learning, 56(3), 353-373.
  • Knowles, M. S., Holton, E. F., & Swanson, R. A. (2015). The adult learner (8th ed.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explaining their thinking, also known as self-explanation, is an instructional principle where learners generate explanations for themselves as they solve problems or study worked examples. This process requires learners to make their internal reasoning explicit, helping them to bridge gaps in understanding, integrate new information with prior knowledge, and monitor their own comprehension Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Explaining their thinking improves learning because it forces learners to make relationships, assumptions, and decision points explicit instead of leaving them tacit Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. That usually deepens conceptual understanding, supports transfer, and exposes gaps in reasoning that would remain hidden if learners only produced answers. The design constraint is that self-explanation is not spontaneous for many learners: prompts, comparisons, and worked examples are often necessary at first so explanation becomes a disciplined habit rather than an empty request to “show your work.”

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Conceptual Prompts: Prompts should focus on "why" a particular step or principle was applied, rather than just "what" was done Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+M].
  • Comparison Opportunities: Encouraging learners to compare different solution methods and explain their relative advantages can deepen understanding.
  • Scaffolded Practice: For novices, self-explanation should be supported with hints or menus of possible explanations to prevent cognitive overload.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Prior Knowledge Dependence: Learners must have sufficient background knowledge to generate correct and meaningful explanations; otherwise, they may reinforce misconceptions Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~M].
  • Implementation Difficulty: Spontaneous self-explanation is rare; learners often require explicit training or structured prompts to engage in the process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Intermediate to Advanced Learners: Most effective for those with enough domain background to bridge conceptual gaps.
  • Learners in Mathematics and Science: Particularly effective for domains with highly structured procedural and conceptual relationships Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].
  • Self-Directed Learners: Helps develop metacognitive monitoring and independent study habits.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Conceptual Understanding: Developing a deep grasp of the underlying principles of a domain.
  • Procedural Transfer: Applying a learned method to a new, unfamiliar type of problem.
  • Metacognitive Monitoring: Recognizing and correcting errors in one's own thinking.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-Regulated Learning (Zimmerman) — self-explanation is a key strategy for metacognitive monitoring and regulation.
  • Information Processing Theory — identifies self-explanation as a method for deep processing and schema formation.
  • Constructivism — emphasizes that knowledge is actively built by the learner through meaningful interaction with the content.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — making reasoning explicit helps learners connect steps, principles, and assumptions instead of leaving them implicit

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Worked Examples — self-explanation is most effective when applied to the study of worked solutions.
  • Modeling — instructors can model self-explanation through think-aloud protocols.
  • Scaffolding and Fading — prompts for self-explanation should fade as learner expertise grows.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Khan Academy Think-Alouds — Instructors model the self-explanation process by verbalizing their reasoning while solving problems.
  • Codecademy Debugging Exercises — Requires learners to explain why a piece of code is incorrect and how to fix it, promoting conceptual understanding of programming principles.
  • Prompted Self-Explanation in Math: Asking a student, "Why can we divide both sides of this equation by 3?" after they perform the step.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Chi, M. T. H., Bassok, M., Lewis, M., Reimann, P., & Glaser, R. (1989). Self-explanations: How students study and use examples in learning to solve problems. Cognitive Science, 13(2), 145–182. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1302_1
  • Rittle-Johnson, B. (2017). Promoting self-explanation to improve mathematics learning: A meta-analysis and instructional design principles. ZDM Mathematics Education, 49(4), 599–611. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-017-0834-z
  • McNamara, D. S. (2004). SERT: Self-explanation reading training. Discourse Processes, 38(1), 1–30. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326977dp3801_1

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In an increasingly digital world, adults who struggle with using technology can benefit from direct instruction for an array of digital tools. This type of instruction, which supports Digital Literacy, includes understanding the basic functions of computer hardware (trackpads, monitors, and USB components) and navigating basic digital functions (setting up email accounts, using search engines, starting files). Adults who are explicitly taught how to use digital technology often show improvements in Composition skills and Disciplinary Literacy, specifically when using technology for health purposes. One-on-one direct instruction tailored to the learner is most effective.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Explicit instruction in computer basics is often necessary because many foundational digital routines are invisible to experienced users but cognitively demanding for novices. Modeling steps, naming interface conventions, and providing guided hands-on practice reduce the unproductive search and anxiety that can otherwise block participation in digital tasks altogether Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. The key is to tie instruction to real learner goals and provide responsive support during hands-on use Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M], then fade support toward independent use so “computer basics” does not remain abstract training that never transfers beyond the lesson Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to the actual devices, interfaces, and accounts learners need to use in real life
  • Direct modeling of concrete operations such as logging in, opening applications, saving files, switching windows, and troubleshooting simple errors
  • Guided practice with immediate support while learners perform the steps themselves
  • Plain-language explanations of digital vocabulary and interface conventions that experienced users often take for granted

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Learners can become overloaded if too many new device concepts, interface cues, and procedures are introduced at once
  • Shame, fear of failure, and stereotype threat often suppress help-seeking in basic digital-skills instruction
  • Demonstration alone is insufficient; learners need hands-on repetition on the actual tools they will later use independently
  • Generic “computer basics” lessons are weak when they are not tied to real learner goals such as job search, communication, health portals, or coursework

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult learners with limited prior access to computers or low confidence using them
  • Older adults and re-entry learners who need explicit orientation to current interfaces and conventions
  • Learners whose goals depend on basic digital participation, including email, search, file handling, and online forms
  • Learners who benefit from low-stakes guided practice before moving into independent digital tasks

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build fluency with foundational device and interface operations
  • Reduce anxiety and increase willingness to explore digital tools
  • Support access to higher-order digital tasks by stabilizing the basics first
  • Enable participation in online learning, communication, and information-seeking tasks

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information-processing perspectives support highly explicit, sequenced demonstration for basic digital routines
  • Adult-learning perspectives support instruction that is goal-relevant, respectful, and immediately useful to real tasks
  • Cognitive Load Theory supports reducing interface complexity and introducing procedures in manageable chunks
  • Gagne-style sequencing fits well because learners often need demonstration, guided practice, and immediate feedback for foundational technical skills

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Learners still need opportunities to explore and adapt once basic procedures are secure; permanent over-direction can block transfer
  • One-to-one or small-group support is often more effective than mass instruction because breakdown points vary widely across learners
  • Support should gradually shift from full demonstration toward independent use on real tasks Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S]

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novice technology users benefit from explicit “how to do it” routines before being asked to complete independent outcomes
  • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — basic computer procedures should be broken into manageable steps to reduce overload
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — responsive support during hands-on practice is more effective than generic explanation alone
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [~S] — support should be withdrawn gradually as learners begin to navigate devices independently

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Clear Structure & Presentation — digital-skills instruction benefits from visible step structure and stable conventions
  • Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax — interface language and technology jargon often need explicit unpacking
  • Explicit Instruction: Internet Search — search instruction depends on a foundation of basic device and browser competence
  • Scaffolding and Fading — support should narrow as competence develops

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Address Digital Literacy — introduces basic digital tools and terminology explicitly
  • Browser and email onboarding with modeled steps, guided repetition, and immediate troubleshooting
  • File-management mini-lessons tied to real tasks such as uploading assignments or attaching documents
  • Small-group digital-skills labs where learners practice the same routine repeatedly with support nearby

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Chaffin, A. J., & Harlow, S. D. (2005). Cognitive learning applied to older adult learners and technology. Educational Gerontology, 31(4), 301-329. doi:10.1080/03601270590916803
  • Dickinson, A., Eisma, R., & Gregor, P. (2011). The barriers that older novices encounter to computer use. Universal Access in the Information Society, 10(3), 261-266. doi:10.1007/s10209-010-0208-6
  • Seo, H., Erba, J., Altschwager, D., & Geana, M. (2019). Evidence-based digital literacy class for older, low-income African-American adults. Journal of Applied Communication Research, 47(2), 130-152. doi:10.1080/00909882.2019.1587176
  • Tsai, H. Y. S., Shillair, R., & Cotten, S. R. (2017). Social support and “playing around.” Journal of Applied Gerontology, 36(1), 29-55. doi:10.1177/0733464815609440

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teaching learners how to effectively search the internet is critical for helping them learn how to find accurate and relevant information and aids in developing information literacy. Learners need to learn to draw upon their Background Knowledge to frame a good research question, generate associated vocabulary, and create a search string that will bring up relevant information. Since an internet search requires sorting through extensive pieces of information, this task can be heavy on learners' Working Memory. Teaching adult learners search skills such as utilizing quotation marks, asterisks, and connecting words can help alleviate that load, as well as build a Learner Mindset for research. This skill is especially important to teach explicitly since just letting the learners explore does not help them make the mental connections necessary to search effectively, and this can be frustrating for them.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Explicit instruction in internet search is valuable because searching is a compound process, not a single skill. Learners have to translate a question into terms, judge results, revise queries, and manage credibility signals all at once, which is why novice searchers benefit from visible routines for query design and revision Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] and chunked decision-making rather than one opaque “search better” demand Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. The design goal is not to teach search tricks in isolation, but to help learners search more deliberately and reflect on why a search succeeded or failed Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] so the skill transfers across tools and interfaces. Search instruction also improves when feedback responds to where the learner’s search logic actually broke down Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit modeling of how to turn questions into search terms, refine queries, and interpret results
  • Practice tasks where learners actually search, compare results, and revise strategies
  • Search goals tied to real inquiry tasks so learners can judge relevance, not just mechanics
  • Guidance on both search construction and result evaluation; the two are inseparable in practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Search instruction can become tool-fragmented if it focuses on operator trivia without linking to question quality and source evaluation
  • Interfaces change over time, so durable principles matter more than memorizing one platform layout
  • Learners may overtrust the first result or sponsored results unless this is explicitly addressed
  • Searching itself imposes cognitive load because learners must juggle terms, intent, and credibility at once

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with limited search experience or weak digital-literacy foundations
  • Adult learners returning to formal study, online work, or information-heavy environments
  • Learners who can state a need in everyday language but struggle to translate it into effective search behavior
  • Learners doing research, problem solving, or civic information tasks online

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Formulate better search queries from information needs
  • Refine searches iteratively when initial results are weak or off-target
  • Distinguish relevant from irrelevant or low-quality results
  • Reduce frustration and search abandonment by giving learners concrete routines for improvement

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information-processing perspectives support breaking search into manageable sub-processes: question framing, term selection, result scanning, and refinement
  • Cognitive Load Theory supports explicit routines and chunked instruction because search requires juggling many competing signals
  • Self-regulated-learning perspectives support planning, monitoring, and revising search behavior rather than treating search as a one-shot act
  • Instructional models that emphasize guided demonstration and practice fit well because search expertise is often tacit unless modeled

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Learners do need exploratory searching, but exploration is more productive after explicit modeling of useful search moves
  • Search skill without source evaluation is incomplete; good queries can still return misleading sources
  • Operators and tricks matter less than question quality, vocabulary choice, and iterative revision

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novice searchers benefit from process-level routines for query design and revision
  • Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — search instruction should break the task into smaller decisions rather than treating it as one opaque skill
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — search feedback works best when instructors respond to where the learner’s search logic failed
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — learners improve when they explain why they chose terms, why results were poor, and how they will revise

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Evaluating Sources — search and source evaluation are interdependent
  • Inquiry-based Learning — effective searching supports independent investigation
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — search routines should be taught in a visible, sequenced way
  • Explicit Instruction: Online Reading Strategies — search is one part of broader online reading competence

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Query expansion exercises, keyword extraction from a problem statement, and guided result comparison
  • Web Search Scavenger Hunt — constrained practice on query generation and retrieval
  • Boolean Operators — a narrower strategy inside the broader principle
  • Instructors modeling a failed search and then revising it can normalize iteration and reduce frustration

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Afflerbach, P. A., & Cho, B. Y. (2010). Determining and describing reading strategies: Internet and traditional forms of reading. In Metacognition, strategy use, and instruction.
  • Gross, M., & Latham, D. (2013). Addressing below proficient information literacy skills. Library & Information Science Research, 35(3), 181-190. doi:10.1016/j.lisr.2013.03.001
  • Kingsley, T., & Tancock, S. (2014). Internet inquiry. The Reading Teacher, 67(5), 389-399.
  • Roberts, L. (2017). Research in the real world. College & Research Libraries, 78(4), 527.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction in math strategies may support some adult learners once conceptual understanding is in place.
