  • Escalating punishment intensity in response to a student's continued disruption is a less effective strategy than better-targeted trigger identification and documented, collaborative adjustment

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Students exhibiting recurring disruptive behavior where the underlying trigger has not yet been clearly identified
  • Students under a formal behavior plan, where documentation and due process directly affect how support can be adjusted

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Reduction in disruptive behavior through trigger avoidance or explicit alternative-response instruction, rather than through increased punishment alone
  • Sustained collaborative support built on documented, defensible teacher judgment

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Reinforcement Theory [+M] — once a trigger and desired alternative response are identified, reinforcing that alternative response follows directly from established reinforcement practice

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Explicit Interpersonal Skills Instruction — a complementary strategy for students whose disruptive behavior stems from an actual social-skills gap rather than a specific environmental trigger

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Heineman, M., Dunlap, G., & Kincaid, D. (2005). Positive support strategies for students with behavioral disorders in general education settings. Psychology in the Schools, 42(8), 779-794.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behavior disorders. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Game-based learning is the instructional principle of using a game itself as the learning environment, with goals, rules, feedback, and progression aligned to specific learning outcomes. Unlike light gamification layered onto ordinary tasks, game-based learning makes the core learning activity intrinsically game-like: learners make decisions, test strategies, receive immediate consequences, and improve through repeated attempts. When designed well, it can increase time on task, support mastery through iteration, and make complex systems or decisions easier to experience directly.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Game-based learning is strongest when the game mechanics require the same thinking the learning goal requires. Repeated attempts, immediate consequences, and visible progression can support mastery and persistence, especially when learners are allowed to fail safely and try again High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S]. But engagement alone is not evidence of learning: if the reward structure can be optimized without understanding the target concept or strategy, the game teaches the wrong thing. Reflection and debriefing are therefore essential for turning in-game success into transferable understanding Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+M], and some goals are still better served by giving novices worked models before asking them to learn through play alone Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S]. Game-based learning is strongest when the game also approximates whole-task decision making closely enough to support later transfer Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Aligned learning goals: The win conditions and mechanics need to reflect the target skill, not merely add entertainment.
  • Tight feedback loops: Learners need immediate in-game consequences, hints, or progress signals so they can adjust strategy during play.
  • Repeatable challenge: The design should support multiple attempts, safe failure, and a visible path toward improvement High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S].
  • Debrief or reflection: Without explanation and transfer prompts, learners may improve at the game without extracting the intended concept or strategy Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+M].

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Reward distraction: Points, badges, or competition can crowd out the learning goal if they are easier to optimize than the target skill.
  • Misaligned mechanics: A game can be engaging while still teaching the wrong habits if the mechanics reward shortcuts unrelated to the intended outcome.
  • Accessibility barriers: Reading load, pace, device demands, or sensory complexity can exclude learners if not deliberately designed for.
  • Transfer gap: Success in a simulated or fictional environment does not guarantee transfer unless the task structure and debrief connect clearly to real use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who benefit from active experimentation: Particularly useful when understanding improves through trying, observing consequences, and iterating.
  • Learners with low engagement in traditional formats: Game structure can increase participation when it clarifies goals and makes progress visible.
  • Learners practicing decision-making in systems: Strong fit for content involving strategy, tradeoffs, sequencing, and dynamic feedback.
  • Groups learning social or collaborative skills: Multiplayer or team-based formats can surface communication, coordination, and role-taking.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Procedural fluency through repetition: Repeated attempts can support mastery when each round gives useful feedback.
  • Strategic decision-making: Learners practice selecting, testing, and revising plans under constraints.
  • Complex problem solving: Simulated systems let learners observe interactions, consequences, and tradeoffs.
  • Motivation and persistence: Progression systems can sustain effort when challenge and feedback are well calibrated.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi) — game-based environments can sustain attention when challenge and skill are well matched.
  • Constructivist learning theory — learners build understanding by acting in an environment, seeing consequences, and revising mental models.
  • Self-Regulated Learning (Zimmerman) — games with clear goals and feedback support monitoring, persistence, and strategy adjustment.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• The motivational benefits of games are not automatic; novelty can mask weak instructional design.
  • Some learning goals are better served by direct explanation or worked examples before game-based practice, especially for novices Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S].

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S] — safe failure and rapid retry can make corrections inside games especially memorable
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+M] — debrief and reflection are what convert in-game experience into explicit understanding
  • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S] — novices often need modeled play or strategy examples before game-based practice becomes productive
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+M] — games support transfer best when their decisions and constraints resemble the real target performance

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Simulations & Immersive Virtual Environments — simulations overlap with game-based learning when the experience models a system learners must navigate.
  • Immediate Feedback — games depend on fast consequence signals to support adaptation and persistence.
  • Error Analysis — game loops often create repeated opportunities to learn from mistakes.
  • Guided Practice — many instructional games work best after some initial modeling or guided rehearsal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Scenario-based digital games: Learners manage resources, make choices, and see consequences unfold across rounds or levels.
  • Board or card games for concept practice: Structured turn-taking and rules create repetition with feedback while keeping attention high.
  • Quiz-show style review games: Fast cycles of attempt and feedback can increase practice volume when questions still align to real objectives.
  • Collaborative mission games: Teams solve a shared problem, requiring explanation, coordination, and iterative strategy updates.

docs.text:

  • Liu, Z. Y., Shaikh, Z., & Gazizova, F. (2020). Using the concept of game-based learning in education. International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning, 15(14), 53-64. https://doi.org/10.3991/ijet.v15i14.14675
  • Boghian, I., Cojocariu, V. M., Popescu, C. V., & Mâţă, L. (2019). Game-based learning - Using board games in adult education. Journal of Educational Sciences and Psychology, 9(1).
  • An, Y. (2020). Designing effective gamified learning experiences. International Journal of Technology in Education, 3(2), 62-69. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijte.v3i2.27

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Cognitive-ability differences between boys and girls are, collectively, close to non-findings: many studies find none at all, a few find small differences (boys slightly stronger in math, girls slightly stronger in reading/literature), and these small differences have been shrinking over time — differences within each gender group are consistently far larger than differences between the groups (Hyde, 2005). What does differ, on average, is classroom interaction style rather than ability: boys are more likely to speak up during discussion, sometimes without being called on and even when less informed than classmates (Sadker, 2002), and in mixed-sex small-group work, group members (echoing a broader societal pattern — Tannen, 2001) tend to give less weight to girls' comments and contributions.

Teachers, even when genuinely intending equal treatment, show three documented interaction asymmetries, seemingly without realizing it. Attention paid: teachers interact with boys 10-30% more often than girls, varying by grade level and teacher (Measor & Sykes, 1992) — plausibly because boys' greater assertiveness draws more responses, or because teachers redirect boys more often to manage mischief (Erden & Wolfgang, 2004). Public versus private talk: teachers tend to talk to boys from a greater physical distance than to girls (Wilkinson & Marrett, 1985), plausibly reflecting a broader expectation of businesslike task orientation for boys/men versus expressive nurturing for girls/women (Basow & Rubenfeld, 2003; Myaskovsky, Unikel, & Dew, 2005); conversing across a room is inherently more "public" (many classmates can overhear) than conversing at close range, so this asymmetry alone gives boys' interactions more classroom visibility. Distribution of praise and criticism: teachers tend to praise boys more for displaying correct knowledge but criticize girls more for displaying incorrect knowledge — equivalently, they tend to overlook boys' wrong answers and overlook girls' right answers (Golombok & Fivush, 1994; Delamont, 1996). The (almost certainly unintended) net effect is to make boys' knowledge seem more important and boys themselves seem more competent, while making girls' knowledge less visible and girls seem less competent. A mirrored pattern appears for behavior rather than knowledge: teachers tend to praise girls for "good"/compliant behavior regardless of its relevance to the lesson, and criticize boys for "bad" behavior — overlooking girls' inappropriate behavior and boys' appropriate behavior — which makes girls seem better-behaved than they may really be (and their goodness more salient than their academic competence) while making boys seem more troublesome than they may really be.

These are genuine average trends, not universal rules — there is wide individual variation in both directions, and a teacher who becomes consciously aware of these patterns has real, exercisable choice to counteract them even in a busy classroom.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Conscious attention to one's own patterns of attention, physical proximity, and praise/criticism across gender, since these asymmetries operate largely below a well-intentioned teacher's own awareness

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• These are group-level trends that hide substantial individual variation — a specific boy or girl may fully contradict the general pattern, so the guidance should inform self-monitoring, not assumptions about any individual student
  • Attention and praise/criticism asymmetries are typically unintended side effects of other dynamics (assertiveness differences, mischief management, societal role expectations), not deliberate favoritism — addressing them requires noticing the pattern, not assuming bad intent

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• All students in a mixed-gender classroom, since the relevant intervention is a change in teacher behavior rather than a targeted student intervention
  • Girls specifically with respect to knowledge-visibility (correct answers overlooked, incorrect answers over-criticized) and boys specifically with respect to behavior-visibility (appropriate behavior overlooked, inappropriate behavior over-criticized)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Equitable perceived competence across genders, undistorted by asymmetric praise/criticism patterns unrelated to actual knowledge or ability
  • Equitable classroom participation and voice, particularly in mixed-sex small-group work where girls' contributions are more likely to be overlooked

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive sex differences are close to non-findings once studied carefully (Hyde, 2005) — any instructional design assuming a substantive gender-based ability gap is working from an empirically unsupported premise

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Social Interdependence — genuine interdependence in group work (per Johnson & Johnson's requirements) is undermined if some members' contributions are systematically discounted, as this principle documents happening along gender lines

  • Sadker, D. (2002). An educator's primer on the gender war. Phi Delta Kappan, 84(3), 235-244.
  • Tannen, D. (2001). You just don't understand: Women and men in conversation. Quill.
  • Measor, L., & Sykes, P. (1992). Gender and schools. Cassell.
  • Erden, F. T., & Wolfgang, C. H. (2004). An exploration of the differences in prekindergarten, kindergarten, and first grade teachers' beliefs related to discipline when dealing with male and female students. Early Child Development and Care, 174(1), 3-11.
  • Wilkinson, L. C., & Marrett, C. B. (Eds.). (1985). Gender influences in classroom interaction. Academic Press.
  • Basow, S. A., & Rubenfeld, K. (2003). "Troubles talk": Effects of gender and gender-typing. Sex Roles, 48(3-4), 183-187.
  • Myaskovsky, L., Unikel, E., & Dew, M. A. (2005). Effects of gender diversity on performance and interpersonal behavior in small work groups. Sex Roles, 52(9-10), 645-657.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Goal setting and monitoring is the instructional principle of helping learners define specific, challenging targets and systematically tracking their progress toward those targets. This process is central to self-regulated learning (SRL), as it directs attention, mobilizes effort, and provides a framework for metacognitive evaluation Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S].

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Goal setting and monitoring improve learning because they give effort a target and feedback a reference point. Specific, challenging goals usually focus attention and sustain performance better than vague intentions Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S], while regular monitoring helps learners notice whether their current strategy is working. The key instructional nuance is that novices often need process goals before outcome goals Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M]: they need to know what to do next, not just what success should eventually look like. Without that distinction, goal setting can produce pressure without guidance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Goal Specificity: Goals must be clear, measurable, and time-bound (e.g., SMARTER goals) to reduce ambiguity Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+M].
  • Process Goals for Novices: For complex tasks, novices should focus on "how-to" (process) goals before transitioning to achievement (outcome) goals Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M].
  • Feedback Loops: Monitoring is ineffective without regular feedback that allows learners to compare their current state to their target goal Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S].

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Goal Conflict: Having too many competing goals can lead to fragmented attention and reduced performance.
  • Low Self-Efficacy: Learners who do not believe they can achieve a goal are unlikely to commit to it, regardless of its specificity or difficulty.
  • Expertise Reversal: While specific, difficult goals benefit novices, experts sometimes perform better with broader or more autonomous goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice Learners: Benefit from proximal, process-oriented goals to manage the complexity of new tasks Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M].
  • Self-Regulated Learners: Essential for anyone seeking to take proactive control of their own skill acquisition.
  • Professional Practitioners: Goal setting is a key driver of performance and professional growth in complex, real-world environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Skill Acquisition: Learning new procedures or techniques through structured, incremental targets.
  • Task Persistence: Maintaining effort during long or difficult instructional sequences.
  • Metacognitive Monitoring: Developing the habit of checking one's own progress and adjusting strategies as needed.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Goal-Setting Theory (Locke & Latham) — established the link between goal difficulty, specificity, and performance Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S].
  • Self-Regulated Learning (SRL, Zimmerman) — goal setting and monitoring are core components of the "Forethought" and "Performance" phases of the cyclical model.
  • Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan) — autonomous goal setting supports the need for competence and autonomy.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S] — clear, challenging goals focus effort and make progress interpretable
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices often learn more effectively when goals specify the next process to execute rather than only the final outcome to reach

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding and Fading — goals provide the structure that can be scaffolded and then faded.
  • Error Analysis — monitoring leads to the detection of errors, which can then be analyzed for deeper learning.
  • Learner Choice — allowing learners to set their own goals increases commitment and autonomy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Khan Academy Progress Tracking — Uses specific "Mastery Goals" and progress bars to help learners set targets and monitor their progress in real-time.
  • Duolingo Streaks — Employs daily goals and visual feedback (streaks) to encourage persistence and self-monitoring.
  • SMARTER Goal Templates: Worksheets that guide students in defining Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound, Evaluated, and Rewarded targets.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Locke, E. A., & Latham, G. P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705–717. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.57.9.705
  • Zimmerman, B. J. (2000). Attaining self-regulation: A social cognitive perspective. In M. Boekaerts, P. R. Pintrich, & M. Zeidner (Eds.), Handbook of self-regulation (pp. 13–39). Academic Press. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-012109890-2/50031-7
  • Zimmerman, B. J., & Kitsantas, A. (1999). Acquiring writing revision skill: Shifting from process to outcome self-regulatory goals. Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(2), 241–252. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.91.2.241

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Assigning a grade is rarely a single, self-evident calculation — it bundles several genuinely separable policy decisions, each carrying real tradeoffs.

Weighting assignments. Teachers must decide, ideally before a grading period begins, how much each component (weekly quizzes, homework, performance assessments, class participation) contributes to the final grade. This decision itself communicates values to students and parents and shapes effort allocation — a homework component worth only 5 percent signals, accurately, that homework isn't worth much individual effort.

Whether to include social skills or effort. Elementary teachers are more likely than middle or high school teachers to fold some social-skills assessment (group cooperation, self-regulation) into a subject grade or report separately (Popham, 2005). Whether to weight effort or improvement is similarly contested: one approach lets students submit drafts and earn credit partly for the degree of improvement shown, but this systematically shortchanges already-high-performing students who have little room left to visibly improve, unless the teacher deliberately designs additional challenge for them. In practice, many teachers use "hodgepodge grading" — blending achievement, effort, growth, attitude, homework, and participation into one number — and a survey of over 8,500 middle and high school students in Virginia found this blended approach broadly supported by both teachers and students in practice (Cross & Frary, 1999), even though it makes any single grade harder to interpret as a pure measure of subject mastery.

Absolute vs. relative grading. In absolute grading, a grade reflects a fixed standard the teacher set in advance, independent of how the rest of the class performed — if every student meets the criterion for an A, every student gets an A; if none do, none do (Popham, 2005). In relative grading ("grading on the curve"), students are ranked against each other, and grades are assigned by rank regardless of the absolute level of performance — useful for compensating when an assessment turns out much easier or harder than intended, but carrying two real costs: an A in one class doesn't necessarily represent the same performance level as an A in another class (since the comparison is only ever within one class), and — more corrosively — Bishop (1999) argues that relative grading gives students a direct personal incentive to discourage their classmates from studying hard, since a serious classmate directly makes it harder for everyone else to earn a good relative grade.

How grades are described. Traditional letter grades (A-F) are convenient, simple, and easy to average, but reveal nothing about which specific objectives a student has or hasn't met (Linn & Miller, 2005). Pass-fail (or satisfactory/unsatisfactory) systems are simpler still and give students room to explore unfamiliar subjects without risking their overall record, but at the cost of even less information about actual performance — and function especially cleanly under a mastery-learning approach, where "pass" already means demonstrated mastery of every objective by definition. A third option — an explicit checklist of objectives, with each rated (e.g., Proficient/Partially Proficient/Needs Improvement) — communicates strengths and weaknesses far more precisely to students and parents, at the cost of becoming unwieldy if the objective list grows too long to take in at a glance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Weighting decisions made and communicated before a grading period begins, not improvised as work comes in
  • Clarity, stated to students, about which of these decisions (weighting, effort inclusion, absolute-vs-relative, description format) the class's grading actually reflects

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Relative grading creates a structural incentive for students to want their peers to do worse, not better — a direct conflict with any classroom goal of peer support or collaboration
  • Effort/improvement-based grading components can inadvertently penalize the students who most need continued challenge (those already performing well) unless the teacher deliberately designs harder follow-on work for them
  • Coarser grade descriptions (letter grades, pass/fail) trade away diagnostic information for simplicity — a trade that is not free even when convenient

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• All students; relative grading's peer-discouragement effect is specifically a concern in classes intended to foster collaboration or peer support
  • Already-high-performing students are specifically disadvantaged by grading schemes that weight improvement heavily without a plan for their continued challenge

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • A grade that accurately and legibly communicates the intended thing (mastery, relative standing, growth, or some deliberate blend) rather than an unexamined default that happens to be convenient to compute

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Social Interdependence [-M] — relative grading's built-in incentive against helping classmates runs directly counter to cooperative-learning goals; a class using both should recognize the tension rather than assume they coexist without friction

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment — grading decisions inherit the underlying assessment's validity and reliability properties, but add a further, separable layer of composition choices

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Equitable Grading — addresses bias and inconsistency in how grading criteria are applied, a related but distinct concern from the compositional choices this page describes
  • Standards-Based Grading — one specific resolution to the letter-grade-vs-objective-checklist tradeoff described here, favoring mastery-of-standards over points

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Popham, W. J. (2005). Classroom assessment: What teachers need to know (4th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Cross, L. H., & Frary, R. B. (1999). Hodgepodge grading: Endorsed by students and teachers alike. Applied Measurement in Education, 12(1), 53-72.
  • Bishop, J. H. (1999). Are national exit examinations important for educational efficiency? Swedish Economic Policy Review, 6(2), 349-401.
  • Linn, R. L., & Miller, M. D. (2005). Measurement and assessment in teaching (9th ed.). Pearson.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Grading and reporting. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Graphic organizers are visual structures that help learners sort, connect, sequence, compare, or hierarchize information. Their instructional value comes from making the structure of knowledge visible: instead of holding relationships only in working memory, learners can externalize categories, links, and patterns in a shared visual form. This makes graphic organizers especially useful for reading, writing, planning, problem solving, and any task where the arrangement of ideas matters as much as the ideas themselves.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Graphic organizers help when the structure of a task matters as much as its content. By externalizing categories, sequences, and relationships, they can reduce working-memory demands and make it easier for learners to inspect how ideas fit together Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. Their value depends on fit: a well-chosen organizer clarifies reasoning, while a mismatched template can flatten or distort it. That is why organizers work best when instructors explain why this representation fits this task and when learners use the organizer to discuss, write, or solve rather than merely fill blanks Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear representational purpose: The organizer should match the task, such as sequencing, comparison, cause-and-effect, hierarchy, or concept mapping.
  • Modeling and explanation: Learners often need to see how to use the organizer before they can use it well independently.
  • Relevant content to organize: Organizers are most helpful when learners are working with information that has an interpretable structure.
  • Discussion or follow-up use: The organizer should support explanation, planning, revision, or analysis rather than being a one-off worksheet.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Template misuse: A mismatched organizer can confuse learners or flatten the structure of the task.
  • Over-scaffolding: Highly prefilled organizers can reduce thinking if learners only complete labels mechanically.
  • Visual overload: Dense layouts with too many branches or symbols can add rather than reduce cognitive burden Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S].
  • Weak transfer: Learners may not generalize organizer use unless they understand why the representation fits the task.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners managing high information load: Useful when texts, lectures, or tasks contain many connected ideas.
  • Learners planning writing or explanation: Organizers can support drafting, argument structure, and synthesis.
  • Learners building disciplinary literacy: Strong fit for history, science, mathematics, and other domains where relationship structure matters.
  • Learners who benefit from externalizing thought: Organizers make intermediate thinking steps easier to inspect and revise.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Organizing information: Identifying categories, relationships, and sequence.
  • Improving comprehension: Helping learners see how parts of a text, problem, or concept fit together.
  • Supporting planning and revision: Using visual structure to prepare writing, discussion, or solution paths.
  • Strengthening recall and transfer: Giving learners a reusable schema they can apply to new material.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Dual coding and multimedia learning perspectives — aligned verbal and visual representation can support comprehension.
  • Information processing views — organizers reduce the need to hold all relationships in mind at once.
  • Schema-oriented learning perspectives — organizers help learners build and inspect knowledge structure.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Organizers do not automatically improve learning; they help most when they are explained, discussed, and matched to the task.
  • Advanced learners may need less structured organizers or may prefer building their own representations.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — organizers reduce working-memory burden by making categories, sequence, and relationships externally visible
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — organizers teach more when learners explain how the visual structure represents the idea or task

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Creating Visual Representations — graphic organizers are one concrete form of visual externalization.
  • Metaphors & Analogies — organizers can help make analogical or conceptual relationships visible.
  • Process-Based Writing — organizers often support planning, sequencing, and revision in writing.
  • Pre-Reading Questioning — organizers can structure anticipation and comprehension before or during reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Cause-and-effect maps: Learners trace how events, policies, or variables influence one another.
  • Compare-contrast charts: Learners organize similarities and differences before discussion or writing.
  • Story or argument maps: Learners outline structure before drafting or summarizing.
  • Partially completed organizers: Instructors prefill key nodes and ask learners to supply connections or examples.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hall, T., & Strangman, N. (2002). Graphic organizers. National Center on Accessing the General Curriculum.
  • Robinson, D. H., Katayama, A. D., Beth, A., Odom, S., Hsieh, Y. P., & Vanderveen, A. (2006). Increasing text comprehension and graphic note taking using a partial graphic organizer. The Journal of Educational Research, 100(2), 103-111. https://doi.org/10.3200/JOER.100.2.103-111
  • Singleton, S. M., & Filce, H. G. (2015). Graphic organizers for secondary students with learning disabilities. Teaching Exceptional Children, 48(2), 110-117. https://doi.org/10.1177/0040059915603129
  • MacArthur, C. A., & Lembo, L. (2009). Strategy instruction in writing for adult literacy learners. Reading and Writing, 22(9), 1021-1039. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9133-5

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided practice is the instructional principle of giving learners repeated opportunities to apply a skill or concept while support is still available. It sits between initial explanation or modeling and independent performance. The purpose is not mere repetition: guided practice lets learners attempt the task, receive targeted feedback, and gradually assume more of the work as scaffolds are faded. It is especially important when a skill has multiple steps, hidden decision points, or a high likelihood of early error.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Guided practice matters because early application is where misunderstanding becomes visible, but also where novices are most likely to rehearse errors if left alone too soon. Multiple supported attempts, contingent feedback, and gradual fading help learners stabilize a new routine without turning support into dependency Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S] Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S]. The design challenge is calibration: too little guidance leaves learners floundering, while too much held for too long creates redundancy and weak transfer Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M]. Strong guided practice therefore stays close to the learner’s current need and points clearly toward independence, often by moving from modeled examples into near-transfer attempts rather than into independent performance immediately Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear model or explanation first: Guided practice works best after learners have seen or heard what good performance looks like.
  • Contingent support: Instructors need to observe learner attempts closely enough to give help where it is actually needed Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S].
  • Multiple attempts: Learners need enough practice rounds to adjust based on feedback rather than only try once.
  • A path toward independence: Support should reduce as competence grows Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S].

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Premature independence: If support is removed too early, learners may rehearse errors or disengage.
  • Permanent support: If guidance never fades, learners may complete tasks successfully without building independence Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M].
  • Practice without diagnosis: Repetition alone is weak when misconceptions are not noticed and corrected.
  • Over-fragmentation: Excessive chunking can obscure the whole-task purpose if practice never reconnects to authentic performance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice learners: Benefit most when a new skill still requires support to perform successfully.
  • Learners practicing multistep procedures: Strong fit for literacy, numeracy, writing, digital tasks, and applied routines.
  • Learners needing confidence through success with support: Guided practice can make difficulty manageable without hiding the challenge.
  • Learners transitioning from model to performance: It bridges explanation and independent application.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Procedural fluency: Rehearsing a skill accurately enough that it becomes more stable and efficient.
  • Error correction during learning: Catching misconceptions before they harden through repeated unguided practice.
  • Transfer of responsibility: Moving learners toward independent performance as support fades.
  • Retention through structured practice: Strengthening learning by applying ideas soon after they are introduced.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory — guided practice reduces unnecessary search and helps novices focus on meaningful steps rather than floundering.
  • Self-regulated learning — learners develop monitoring and adjustment by attempting tasks with support still available.
  • Instructional scaffolding traditions — guidance is calibrated to current performance and withdrawn as competence develops.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Some advanced learners may need less guided practice and more independent or whole-task challenge.
  • Guided practice should not replace authentic performance; it should prepare learners for it.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S] — guided practice works best when support responds to the learner’s actual error pattern and current need
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S] — guidance should narrow as competence grows so practice leads toward independent performance
  • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S] — guided practice is especially effective when learners move from modeled examples into closely related attempts
  • Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows. [~M] — prolonged high guidance can become redundant once learners no longer need the same level of support

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Worked Examples — guided practice often follows worked examples so learners can apply a model immediately.
  • Scaffolding and Fading — guided practice is one of the main places where contingent support and fading are enacted.
  • Immediate Feedback — the quality of guided practice depends heavily on quick correction and coaching.
  • Chunking — breaking complex tasks into manageable parts often makes guided practice more workable for novices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Teacher-led problem solving: Learners solve a near-transfer item while the instructor prompts, checks, and intervenes only where needed.
  • Supported writing conferences: Learners draft or revise with short targeted coaching on one or two moves at a time.
  • Guided reading or decoding practice: Learners rehearse a specific reading move with immediate cueing and correction.
  • Software practice with hints: A digital system provides step-level prompts that fade as accuracy improves.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• National Research Council. (2012). Improving adult literacy instruction: Supporting learning and motivation. National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/13468
  • Numrich, C., & Kennedy, A. S. (2017). Providing guided practice in discourse synthesis. TESOL Journal, 8(1), 28-43. https://doi.org/10.1002/tesj.254
  • Massengill, D. (2004). The impact of using guided reading to teach low-literate adults. Journal of Adolescent & Adult Literacy, 47(7), 588-602. https://doi.org/10.1598/JAAL.47.7.5
  • Hua, Y., Morgan, B. S., Kaldenberg, E. R., & Goo, M. (2012). Cognitive strategy instruction for functional mathematical skill: Effects for young adults with intellectual disability. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 47(3), 345-358.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Handouts, online guides, and visual reading aids support learning by externalizing structure, highlighting key information, and reducing the amount learners must infer or hold in working memory while reading. They can take the form of annotated handouts, reading guides, visual cues, glosses, diagrams, highlighted sections, or structured digital supports. Their main value is not decoration but orientation: they help learners see what matters, where to look, and how parts of a text or task fit together.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Handouts, online guides, and visual reading aids are most useful when learners would otherwise spend too much effort figuring out where to focus and how a text or task is organized. Well-designed cues, chunking, and readable formatting can reduce extraneous processing and make important relationships visible, especially in dense or unfamiliar materials Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. The instructional risk is over-support: if guides do all the interpretive work, learners may never develop independent reading strategies. These aids should therefore orient attention and model structure without permanently replacing the learner’s own sense-making, which is why they work better when learners are prompted to explain and use the guide actively rather than simply receive it Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear visual hierarchy: Learners need cues that distinguish headings, key terms, examples, steps, and supporting details.
  • Alignment to the reading task: The aid should support what learners are being asked to do, such as preview, annotate, compare, or synthesize.
  • Accessible formatting: Legibility, spacing, contrast, and device compatibility matter as much as content.
  • Explanatory support: Visual aids work better when learners are prompted to interpret or use them actively rather than just receive them.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Decorative clutter: Extra visual features can increase distraction instead of reducing it.
  • Over-support: Highly guided aids can reduce independence if learners never transition to reading without them.
  • Mismatch to learner needs: A single guide format may not suit all readers, devices, or contexts.
  • Static support: Reading aids are less useful if they do not adapt to the actual comprehension demands of the task.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners facing dense or unfamiliar texts: Especially useful when readings contain complex structure, technical vocabulary, or multiple representations.
  • Learners with working-memory or attention constraints: External structure can lower orientation demands while reading.
  • Multilingual learners and developing readers: Guides can support navigation, vocabulary focus, and text interpretation.
  • Learners in digital or blended settings: Online guides can reduce confusion about where to focus in asynchronous materials.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improved reading navigation: Helping learners locate central ideas, sequence, and key evidence.
  • Comprehension support: Making difficult texts or multimodal materials more manageable.
  • Strategic reading habits: Supporting previewing, note-taking, annotation, and synthesis.
  • Retention and transfer: Providing a structured artifact learners can revisit during practice or review.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Multimedia and dual-coding perspectives — aligned visual and verbal supports can improve comprehension when they clarify rather than duplicate aimlessly.
  • Cognitive Load Theory — reading aids can reduce extraneous processing by making task structure and key cues visible.
  • Information processing views — guides help learners orient attention and encode important information more deliberately.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Reading aids should be faded or varied when the long-term goal is independent reading without heavy support.
  • Not all visual supports help; poorly designed cues can fragment attention or oversimplify meaning.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — reading aids can lower extraneous processing by making structure and emphasis visible
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S] — guides are more effective when learners use them to interpret, annotate, or explain rather than only follow them passively

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Clear Structure & Presentation — reading aids are one way to make instructional structure visible.
  • Creating Visual Representations — learners can also build their own guides and representations, not just receive them.
  • Graphic Organizers — many reading aids are organizer-like supports for sequencing and comparison.
  • Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax — readable wording and readable formatting reinforce one another.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Annotated handouts: Headings, callouts, examples, and margin notes help learners identify what matters during reading.
  • Digital reading guides: A course page breaks a text into sections with preview questions and interpretation prompts.
  • Visual glosses and cueing: Key vocabulary, symbols, or process markers are visually highlighted to support comprehension.
  • Structured note guides: Learners receive a partial outline or concept frame to complete while reading or listening.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Carlson, R., Padron, K., & Andrews, C. (2018). Evidence-based instructional strategies for adult learners: A review of the literature. Codex, 4(4), 29-47.
  • Osborne, H. (2006). Health literacy: How visuals can help tell the healthcare story. Journal of Visual Communication in Medicine, 29(1), 28-32. https://doi.org/10.1080/17453050600572889
  • Mellar, H., Kambouri, M., Sanderson, M., & Pavlou, V. (2004). ICT and adult literacy, numeracy and ESOL. NRDC.

docs.title: Preserve Heritage Language While Acquiring an Additional Language
Description
docs.text: Most children worldwide grow up bilingual or multilingual; the United States is unusual in its relative monolingualism and in schooling practices that sometimes implicitly treat a student's home language as an obstacle to English acquisition rather than an asset. Bilingual proficiency ranges from balanced fluency in both languages to more uneven competence across domains, and many bilingual students in U.S. schools are in the process of losing proficiency in a heritage language while still developing English — a pattern of language attrition that research links to slower, not faster, English development: a strong vocabulary base in a first language facilitates rather than competes with acquiring a second (Hansen, Umeda, & McKinney, 2002). Fully proficient bilingual learners also show cognitive advantages in metalinguistic awareness — the ability to reflect on language as an object, not just use it — and in flexibility of concept expression (Jimenez, Garcia, & Pearson, 1995; Francis, 2006).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Meaningful, ongoing opportunities to actually use the heritage language, not just passive exposure at home
  • Adult and peer models fluent in the heritage language
  • Family and school support for heritage-language maintenance rather than pressure toward English-only use
  • Assessment conducted in both languages where possible, so that language loss (attrition) is not mistaken for a language disorder

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Negative attitudes toward a heritage language, or pressure to assimilate, can accelerate language loss and its downstream costs to English development
  • Unbalanced bilingualism (strong in one language, weak in the other) limits the cognitive and academic advantages associated with full bilingual proficiency
  • Speech-language intervention conducted only in English is less effective for multilingual children with language impairments than intervention that uses both of the child's languages (Kohnert, Yim, Nett, Kan, & Duran, 2005)

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Students from multilingual homes, which represents a global majority of children
  • English Language Learners in U.S. and other Anglophone school settings
  • Children of immigrant or refugee families, where heritage-language loss risk is often highest

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Continued development of heritage-language proficiency alongside the school/majority language, not instead of it
  • Metalinguistic awareness and the cognitive flexibility associated with full bilingual competence
  • Accurate identification of language-development needs (distinguishing typical attrition from an actual disorder)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Language Acquisition Theory [+M] — the social-interactionist account's emphasis on responsive interaction applies to whichever language(s) a child is developing
  • Constructivism [+M] — bilingual learners construct meaning across, and connect concepts between, multiple language systems

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Support Early Language Development — the same responsive-interaction principle, applied specifically to maintaining a heritage language alongside a new one

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Primary Language Support with Bilingual Texts
  • Connecting ELLs' Background Knowledge to Content

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hansen, L., Umeda, Y., & McKinney, M. (2002). Ragged interlanguage morphology and orders of acquisition issues. Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development, 23(1-2), 6-20.
  • Jimenez, R. T., Garcia, G. E., & Pearson, P. D. (1995). Three children, two languages, and strategic reading: Case studies in bilingual/monolingual reading. American Educational Research Journal, 32(1), 67-97.
  • Francis, N. (2006). Bilingual competence and bilingual proficiency in children. In J. Kroll & A. De Groot (Eds.), Handbook of bilingualism (pp. 137-163). Oxford University Press.
  • Kohnert, K., Yim, D., Nett, K., Kan, P. F., & Duran, L. (2005). Intervention with linguistically diverse preschool children: A focus on developing home language(s). Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools, 36, 251-263.
  • Meyers-Sutton, C. (2005). Multilingualism. In J. L. Berko Gleason (Ed.), The development of language (pp. 407-444). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Language development. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Standardized testing is "high-stakes" when performance carries real consequences — for students (a graduation test required for a diploma, a licensure exam required for a career), or for schools (under the No Child Left Behind Act, or NCLB, failing to reach targeted proficiency levels can trigger reduced funding or restructuring). Accountability, standardized testing, academic content standards, and teacher quality are the four components of the broader Standards-Based Reform movement in U.S. education, dating to the 1980s.

Content standards must be neither too broad nor too narrow. A standard as broad as "students should be able to construct meaning through experiences with literature, cultural events and philosophical discussion" (with no grade level indicated) gives teachers nothing to prepare students for; a standard as narrow as "students can define, compare, and contrast synonyms and antonyms" produces a restricted curriculum. A 2005-06 American Federation of Teachers study found standards in several states weak, particularly in reading, with one-fifth of reading standards redundant across grade levels — the same standard repeated word-for-word at least half the time across different grades. Compounding the difficulty, even a handful of broad standards typically expands into dozens of specific goals, benchmarks, and objectives underneath — one state's first-grade math standard, judged high quality, contained 5 broad standards, 10 goals, and 29 total objectives — leaving more content than any single school year can realistically cover.

Tests must actually align with the standards they're meant to assess, or the whole premise of accountability collapses: a mismatch between what's tested and what the standards specify means test results simply cannot speak to students' standards-based proficiency, undermining the "theory of action" NCLB depends on. The 2006 American Federation of Teachers study found only 11 states had all their tests aligned with their own state standards.

When there are too many standards to test them all, tests must sample, which creates genuine unpredictability. Reliably assessing any one content standard requires more than one or two items, so testing all standards every year is not feasible — and when a significant fraction of standards go untested in a given year, teachers are put in the position of guessing which ones will actually appear, with real instructional cost when the guess is wrong (studying content that isn't tested, and not studying content that is). One prominent testing expert, Popham (2004), called this "a muddleheaded way to run a testing program" (p. 79).

Absolute proficiency and student growth are not the same thing, and rewarding only the former creates a real distortion. NCLB's Adequate Yearly Progress (AYP) framework is based on the absolute level of performance reached at one point in time, not on how much a student improved to get there — which means a school whose students improve substantially but still fall short of the proficiency line gets no credit for that improvement, while a school whose already-proficient students stagnate can still meet AYP. Because AYP timetables require every school to reach the same proficiency target by a fixed date, schools starting from a lower baseline must show much larger year-over-year gains than schools starting closer to the target already. Growth (or value-added) models correct for this by tracking how much an individual student's score changed year to year rather than only where it landed — and the evidence for why this matters is substantial: in one study, low-achieving fourth-grade students in Dallas, Texas were followed for three years, and 90 percent of those with effective teachers passed the seventh-grade math test, versus only 42 percent of those with ineffective teachers (cited in Bracey, 2004) — see Effective Teachers Compound Their Advantage Over Consecutive Years. The same study found low-achieving students were more likely than high-achieving students to be assigned an ineffective teacher three years running, compounding the disadvantage rather than correcting for it.

States define "proficient" very differently from each other, which undermines any comparison across state lines. Because NCLB lets each state set its own content standards, assessments, and proficiency thresholds, apparent proficiency rates can diverge sharply from a common external yardstick: in 2003, Colorado and Missouri reported 67 percent and 21 percent of fourth-graders proficient in reading on their own state tests respectively, but the same students scored 34 percent and 28 percent proficient on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) — a well-regarded, nationally-standardized test (Linn, 2005). The gap shows there is no common meaning behind "proficient achievement" as states currently define it.

The predictable downstream effect of high-stakes testing is curriculum narrowing and teaching to the test. Surveys of elementary teachers found more instructional time devoted to math and reading, and less to social studies and science, in 2004 than in 1990 (Jerald, 2006); principals in high-minority-enrollment schools in several states reported reduced arts instruction. This has a real cost beyond the narrowing itself: reading comprehension in a subject like science or social studies depends on prior vocabulary and background knowledge in that subject (Recht & Leslie, 1988), so students can develop strong general reading skills yet still struggle with subjects they were given little instructional time to build background knowledge in. Teachers surveyed nationally (over 4,000 respondents) largely reported adapting instruction to the tests — elementary teachers reported the heaviest influence (56 percent said the tests shaped their daily or near-daily teaching, versus 46 percent of middle school and 28 percent of high school teachers) — while also expressing real skepticism about the tests themselves: 40 percent reported teachers had found ways to raise scores without improving actual learning, and over 70 percent said the scores didn't accurately reflect what minority students know and can do (Pedulla, Abrams, Madaus, Russell, Ramos, & Miao, 2003).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Content standards specific enough to guide instruction but few enough to actually be taught and assessed within a school year
  • Genuine, verifiable alignment between published standards and the content actually tested — not merely asserted alignment
  • A growth or value-added component in accountability calculations, not absolute-proficiency measurement alone, if the system is meant to fairly credit schools serving initially lower-performing students

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Standards too broad give teachers nothing concrete to teach toward; standards too narrow restrict the curriculum to trivial specifics — neither failure mode is safer than the other
  • When only a sample of many standards can be tested each year, some amount of teacher guessing about what will appear is structurally unavoidable, not merely a matter of insufficient effort
  • Comparing "proficiency rates" across states (or even across a state's own tests from different years) without a common external reference like NAEP risks comparing numbers that don't mean the same thing
  • Heavy accountability pressure predictably narrows instructional time away from untested subjects, with a genuine downstream cost to comprehension in exactly those subjects once they are addressed

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• All students in accountability-tested grades and subjects; students in initially lower-performing schools bear a disproportionate share of the pressure created by absolute (non-growth) proficiency targets
  • Students in untested subjects (art, and often social studies/science at some grade bands) are indirectly affected by instructional-time reallocation even though they are not themselves being tested

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Accurate, comparable information about whether students are meeting content standards, without the curriculum-narrowing and teaching-to-the-test side effects that undermine the deeper goal of actual learning

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Assessment for Learning [-M] — high-stakes accountability testing is explicitly assessment of learning for external certification, and the pressure it creates can actively distort assessment for learning's low-stakes, revision-friendly design goals

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Effective teachers compound their advantage over consecutive years [+M] — direct evidence for why growth-based accountability measures matter, and why teacher assignment patterns can compound rather than correct disadvantage

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Criterion- and Norm-Referenced Testing — high-stakes accountability testing under NCLB is predominantly criterion-referenced
  • Standardized Test Fairness and Bias — a separate but related set of concerns about whether high-stakes tests measure the same thing equally well across student groups

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Tennessee's practice of reporting both AYP status and a growth category (below-average, average, above-average) on school report cards, so a school with high proficiency but low growth, or low proficiency but high growth, is visible either way rather than collapsed into a single pass/fail label

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• American Federation of Teachers. (2006). Smart testing: Let's get it right. AFT.
  • Popham, W. J. (2004). America's "failing" schools: How parents and teachers can cope with No Child Left Behind. RoutledgeFalmer.
  • Bracey, G. W. (2004). Setting the record straight: Responses to misconceptions about public education in the U.S. (2nd ed.). Heinemann.
  • Linn, R. L. (2005). Fixing the NCLB accountability system. CRESST Policy Brief, National Center for Research on Evaluation, Standards, and Student Testing.
  • Jerald, C. D. (2006). The hidden costs of curriculum narrowing. Center for Comprehensive School Reform and Improvement.
  • Recht, D. R., & Leslie, L. (1988). Effect of prior knowledge on good and poor readers' memory of text. Journal of Educational Psychology, 80(1), 16-20.
  • Pedulla, J. J., Abrams, L. M., Madaus, G. F., Russell, M. K., Ramos, M. A., & Miao, J. (2003). Perceived effects of state-mandated testing programs on teaching and learning: Findings from a national survey of teachers. National Board on Educational Testing and Public Policy, Boston College.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). High-stakes testing. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Holistic learning is the principle of helping learners grasp the overall structure, purpose, or whole of a domain before becoming lost in isolated details. It is useful when understanding depends on seeing how parts relate within a larger conceptual system.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Holistic learning matters when learners are likely to lose meaning by encountering details before they have a coherent sense of the larger structure. The principle does not reject detail or analysis. It argues that details are more learnable when learners can place them inside a meaningful whole, because organizing parts into a larger structure can reduce memory burden and improve coherence Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]. In practice, holistic designs often start with an overview, model, framework, or authentic whole task and then elaborate parts without severing them from the larger purpose Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. The main design risk is vagueness: a “big picture” that is too abstract to guide later understanding does not help much, and some novices still need staged simplification before the whole becomes usable Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A coherent whole or organizing framework to present — learners need a visible structure, process, or conceptual map that shows how details will fit together
  • Connections between the overview and later detail — the whole must continue to matter as instruction elaborates parts

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too much abstraction too early can feel empty without later grounding
  • Not all learners benefit from the same level of overview first — some may still need local examples or concrete anchors before the whole becomes meaningful
  • Holistic design can become rhetorical rather than instructional — saying “here is the big picture” is weaker than giving learners a structure they can actually use

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners studying conceptually dense or highly interconnected material
  • Novices who need help orienting to the logic of a domain before working on parts
  • Learners at risk of fragmenting knowledge into disconnected facts or procedures

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build big-picture understanding and integrative mental models
  • Help learners connect parts, purposes, and relationships across a domain
  • Improve transfer by preserving the coherence of the whole while learning the parts

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Sequencing and schema-building traditions — learners often understand details better when they can place them into a larger structure
  • Cognitive Load Management — a useful overview can reduce disorientation and help learners organize incoming detail
  • Information Processing Theory — organized, meaningful structures improve encoding and later retrieval

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M] — very complex wholes may still need simplification or staged entry for absolute novices

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — holistic structures can reduce memory burden when they help learners organize parts into meaningful units
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — seeing and practicing the whole can improve transfer in complex domains
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M] — wholes still need calibration when the initial complexity is too high

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Creating Visual Representations — diagrams and maps often make the whole visible
  • Scaffolding — holistic designs still need supports so learners can move from overview to workable understanding
  • Knowledge Organization — holistic learning depends on preserving meaningful conceptual structure

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Reigeluth's Elaboration Theory — Learners begin with an epitome or simple whole, then elaborate progressively while keeping the larger structure in view.

Whole-task previews before subskill focus — In writing, programming, or design, learners first see the complete workflow or product before analyzing individual components.

Concept maps that return throughout a unit — The same framework is revisited as new detail is introduced, helping learners keep parts integrated into the whole.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Reigeluth, C. M. (1979). In search of a better way to organize instruction. Journal of Instructional Development, 2(3), 8-15.
  • van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Kirschner, P. A. (2018). Ten steps to complex learning (3rd ed.). Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315113210

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Immediate feedback is feedback delivered close enough to a learner's action that it can still shape interpretation, correction, and the next attempt. Its value is not just speed, but timeliness relative to the learner's current thinking: when feedback arrives while the reasoning path, misconception, or uncertainty is still active, it is easier to adjust strategy and avoid rehearsing errors. Immediate feedback is especially useful during skill acquisition, guided practice, and high-frequency retrieval or problem-solving tasks.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Immediate feedback works because correction is most usable while the learner’s reasoning path is still active. Timely explanation can interrupt repeated error High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S], improve self-monitoring Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M], and make the next attempt meaningfully different from the last one when the support is actually responsive to the learner’s move Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. But immediacy is not a universal good: some tasks benefit from sustained effort before review, and fast feedback that is vague or misaligned can misdirect learning just as efficiently as it helps. The design question is not “How fast can feedback be?” but “When will feedback most improve the next action?”

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A visible learner action: The system or instructor must be able to observe a step, response, draft move, or decision worth responding to.
  • Actionable information: Feedback should tell learners what to correct, reconsider, or try next, not just whether they were right.
  • Opportunity for another attempt: Immediate feedback matters most when learners can use it right away.
  • Alignment to the target skill: Fast feedback on the wrong thing can misdirect effort just as efficiently as it corrects.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Overcorrection: Excessive intervention can interrupt productive struggle and reduce learner agency.
  • Thin feedback: Instant correctness signals without explanation can leave misconceptions intact.
  • Public risk: Immediate feedback in front of peers may heighten embarrassment or threat for some learners.
  • Timing tradeoff: Some higher-order tasks benefit from delayed, synthesized feedback rather than rapid interruption at every step.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice learners: Benefit strongly when errors are corrected before they become entrenched.
  • Learners practicing high-frequency skills: Strong fit for reading, numeracy, language learning, and digital procedures.
  • Learners building self-monitoring: Timely feedback helps them connect outcome to strategy while the attempt is still fresh.
  • Learners vulnerable to repeated error cycles: Immediate correction can reduce unproductive rehearsal and confusion.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Correcting misconceptions during learning: Preventing errors from being repeated without revision.
  • Strengthening strategy adjustment: Helping learners alter what they do on the very next attempt.
  • Supporting confidence through clarity: Replacing uncertainty with specific, usable next steps.
  • Increasing retention of corrections: Leveraging timely surprise and explanation to improve later recall.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated learning — feedback helps learners compare current performance with goals and adjust strategy.
  • Gagne's instructional sequence — feedback is a core event that helps learners verify and refine performance.
  • Error-based learning perspectives — well-timed correction can create durable learning when it interrupts confident misunderstanding.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Immediate is not always best; complex writing, projects, and discussion sometimes benefit from more synthesized feedback after a fuller performance.
  • The effect depends on feedback quality. Fast but vague feedback often adds little.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [+S] — feedback is especially powerful when it interrupts and corrects an active misconception before it is rehearsed again
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — timely feedback helps learners connect outcome to strategy while the attempt is still fresh
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — immediate feedback helps most when it addresses the actual decision or misconception that just occurred

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment — immediate feedback is one of the most actionable forms of formative assessment.
  • Guided Practice — guided practice depends on feedback that arrives while practice is still underway.
  • Error Analysis — timely correction helps learners understand and revise errors before they harden.
  • Check-ins — quick check-ins can trigger immediate feedback and support adjustments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Step-level tutoring feedback: A digital system flags an incorrect move and gives a hint before the learner proceeds.
  • Live coaching during practice: An instructor responds to a reading, writing, or math step while the learner is still working.
  • Immediate corrective feedback on retrieval: Learners answer a prompt, see the correct answer, and try again quickly.
  • Inline draft comments during conferences: Feedback is given during revision rather than after the writing task is fully over.
