  • Emotional risk: Peer discussion around high-stakes topics needs stronger facilitation and norms.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing disciplinary language: Peer discussion helps learners rehearse vocabulary, explanation, and reasoning talk.
  • Learners benefiting from social meaning-making: Strong fit when understanding improves through comparison and dialogue.
  • Learners in collaborative or inquiry settings: Discussion supports group interpretation and shared problem solving.
  • Learners needing belonging and participation: Structured talk can reduce isolation and increase engagement when norms are strong.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding through explanation: Learners clarify their own understanding by speaking it aloud.
  • Critical reasoning: Learners examine alternative interpretations and defend claims.
  • Language development: Learners practice disciplinary vocabulary, syntax, and verbal reasoning.
  • Perspective-taking: Learners notice that a problem or text can be interpreted in more than one way.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — knowledge is built through interaction and co-construction.
  • Social learning theory — learners observe, model, and revise reasoning through others' talk.
  • Self-regulated learning — discussion can support monitoring and revision when learners compare their own thinking to peers' explanations.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Discussion is not inherently deep; the cognitive demand depends on the prompt and the structure of interaction.
  • Some learners may need sentence stems, wait time, or alternate participation modes to benefit fully.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — peer talk improves learning when learners must articulate and justify reasoning rather than only trade answers
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — discussion helps learners notice the strengths and gaps in their own reasoning by comparing it with peers

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Peer Feedback/Peer Review — feedback is one specific form of peer discussion centered on improvement of work.
  • Communities of Practice — recurring peer discussion helps sustain shared practice and meaning-making.
  • Perspective Seeking/Multiple Perspectives — discussion is a core mechanism for surfacing alternative views.
  • Building Empathy — structured peer talk can deepen understanding of others' experience and reasoning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Think-pair-share: Learners explain an initial idea to a partner before whole-group discussion.
  • Small-group text talk: Learners compare interpretations of a passage using evidence from the text.
  • Peer problem discussion: Learners explain how they approached a problem and where their reasoning diverged.
  • Online discussion prompts: Learners post and respond to one another with evidence and clarification questions.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• King, A. (2002). Structuring peer interaction to promote high-level cognitive processing. Theory Into Practice, 41(1), 33-39. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15430421tip4101_6
  • Cross, T., & Palese, K. (2015). Increasing learning: Classroom assessment techniques in the online classroom. American Journal of Distance Education, 29(2), 98-108. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2015.1023594

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer feedback and peer review are instructional structures in which learners evaluate one another's work against shared criteria in order to improve the work and deepen their own understanding. The learning benefit is reciprocal: reviewers practice noticing quality, naming evidence, and proposing revisions, while recipients receive more perspectives and revision cues than instructor-only feedback can usually provide. Peer review is not automatically effective, however; learners need preparation, clear criteria, and protocols that keep the feedback specific, respectful, and usable.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Peer feedback improves learning when it teaches learners to recognize quality and act on revision cues, not just receive more comments. Reviewing a peer’s work can sharpen evaluative judgment because learners must explain what is working, what is weak, and why Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], while recipients gain additional information they can use to monitor and revise their own work Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]. The design challenge is credibility and specificity: peer review collapses quickly into vague praise, surface correction, or distrust unless learners share criteria, practice giving feedback, and have time to revise in response. In practice, peer review often needs modeled prompts and structured protocols before it becomes reliably useful Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Shared criteria or rubric: Learners need a common standard for what to look for and comment on.
  • Preparation for giving feedback: Strong peer review usually requires modeling, examples, and sentence frames or protocols.
  • Time for revision: Feedback matters most when the recipient can act on it.
  • A psychologically safe climate: Learners need norms that make critique about the work rather than the person.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Vague praise or vague criticism: Feedback that is non-specific is rarely useful.
  • Reviewer inexperience: Learners may miss important issues or focus only on surface errors unless coached.
  • Trust and status issues: Learners may discount peer comments if the process lacks credibility or safety.
  • Misalignment with the task: Peer review is weaker when learners do not understand the genre, content, or criteria well enough to respond meaningfully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners engaged in drafting and revision: Especially useful for writing, design, presentations, and project work.
  • Learners building evaluative judgment: Reviewing peer work helps learners notice quality and criteria more explicitly.
  • Learners who benefit from multiple perspectives: Peer review can diversify the feedback a learner receives.
  • Learners developing communication and critique skills: The process builds both giving and receiving feedback productively.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improved revision quality: Using external feedback to strengthen a draft, product, or performance.
  • Metacognitive monitoring: Learning to recognize quality, gaps, and next steps in one's own work.
  • Constructive critique skills: Practicing evidence-based, actionable feedback.
  • Agency and participation in assessment: Involving learners more actively in the improvement process.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through interaction and shared criteria.
  • Self-regulated learning — peer feedback supports monitoring, revision, and strategic adjustment.
  • Reflective and evaluative learning traditions — reviewing others' work sharpens one's own sense of quality.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Peer review should complement, not automatically replace, expert feedback where technical accuracy or domain nuance matters.
  • Anonymous peer review can reduce some social friction, but it can also reduce accountability or relational learning depending on the context.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — reviewing peer work deepens learning when learners explain what is strong, weak, and why
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — peer review helps recipients and reviewers monitor quality and identify concrete next steps
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — peer feedback improves when the process includes modeled prompts, protocols, and responsive support

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion — peer review is a more criteria-driven form of peer discussion centered on improvement.
  • Formative Assessment — peer feedback is often a low-stakes formative mechanism before final evaluation.
  • Process-Based Writing — drafting and revision make peer review especially useful.
  • Building Empathy — constructive peer review depends on understanding audience, tone, and the impact of feedback.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Structured draft review: Learners use a rubric and sentence stems to comment on a peer's draft before revision.
  • Gallery walk critique: Learners review several products and leave targeted feedback linked to criteria.
  • Real-time digital peer response: Learners respond to classmates' work in a shared platform while the task is still revisable.
  • Two-stage review: Learners first identify strengths and evidence, then suggest one or two specific next moves.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Leijen, D. A. J. (2017). A novel approach to examine the impact of web-based peer review on the revisions of L2 writers. Computers and Composition, 43, 35-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2016.11.005
  • Lin, G. Y. (2018). Anonymous versus identified peer assessment via a Facebook-based learning application: Effects on quality of peer feedback, perceived learning, perceived fairness, and attitude toward the system. Computers & Education, 116, 81-92. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.08.010
  • Wu, Y., & Schunn, C. D. (2020). When peers agree, do students listen? The central role of feedback quality and feedback frequency in determining uptake of feedback. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 62, 101897. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cedpsych.2020.101897

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer learning is the principle that learners can deepen understanding by explaining, questioning, modeling, and responding to one another. It is useful when learners can benefit from articulating ideas and encountering alternate explanations at a similar level of expertise.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Peer learning is strongest when learners are asked to do real intellectual work with and for one another rather than merely sit in groups. Its value comes from explanation, comparison, and mutual response. Learners often make their own thinking clearer when they have to explain it to someone else Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S], and peer settings are stronger when learners monitor contribution, progress, and understanding rather than assuming interaction alone is enough Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The main instructional challenge is quality control: peers can also amplify misconceptions or normalize shallow reasoning if tasks and facilitation are weak, which is why peer learning often benefits from structures and prompts that respond to learner needs rather than leaving interaction fully unshaped Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Tasks that require learners to explain or respond to each other — peer learning depends on articulation, not just co-presence
  • Norms for respectful and accountable interaction — learners need expectations for listening, challenge, and evidence use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Peers can reinforce misconceptions if explanation quality is not monitored
  • Not all peer interaction is instructional — the task has to require intellectual exchange, not only coordination
  • Uneven confidence can distort participation — strong structures may be needed so some learners do not dominate while others hide

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who benefit from explanation, comparison, and rehearsal of ideas in dialogue
  • Learners in large classes, discussion-heavy courses, or collaborative environments where peer response can multiply opportunities to think aloud
  • Learners who may respond well to near-peer language, examples, and models

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve understanding through explanation, comparison, and collaborative reasoning
  • Strengthen learners’ ability to justify ideas and respond to alternatives
  • Increase participation and responsibility for learning beyond teacher-only interaction

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social Learning — peers can act as models, interpreters, and feedback sources
  • Social Constructivism — understanding is often co-constructed in interaction
  • Community of Inquiry — peer learning is stronger when discourse is both socially and cognitively supported

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — peer interaction can add coordination demands that need to be managed through structure and task design

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explaining to peers can deepen conceptual understanding
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — peer contexts are stronger when learners monitor contribution, progress, and understanding
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — peer learning often benefits from instructor or peer structures that respond to learner needs

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion — one of the clearest vehicles for peer learning
  • Community of Inquiry — explains how peer interaction can become substantive inquiry rather than social activity alone
  • Collaborative Learning — peer learning is a narrower principle focused on learner-to-learner explanation and response

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Peer Instruction — Learners answer a conceptual question individually, discuss reasoning with peers, then revise their answer.

Jigsaw Method — Each learner becomes a temporary expert and teaches part of the whole to peers.

Peer revision or peer explanation routines — Learners respond to drafts, interpretations, or solutions and improve their own understanding through explaining what works and why.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Topping, K. J. (2005). Trends in peer learning. Educational Psychology, 25(6), 631-645. https://doi.org/10.1080/01443410500345172
  • Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2013). The relative benefits of learning by teaching and teaching expectancy. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 38(4), 281-288. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cedpsych.2013.06.001

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performance Technology (also called Human Performance Technology, HPT) holds that instructional designers should not assume training is the answer to a performance problem until they have analyzed the gap between desired and actual performance and identified its cause. HPT emerged in the 1960s–70s out of behaviorism — its "father," Thomas Gilbert, was a student of B.F. Skinner — and is grounded in general systems theory: any solution must be understood as operating inside a larger system of people, processes, and organizational culture, not in isolation (Stefaniak, 2018).

Where instructional design assumes instruction is the answer and designs it well, HPT starts a step earlier by asking whether instruction is the right answer at all. A performance analysis compares the desired and actual states of performance to locate the gap; a cause analysis then identifies why the gap exists — is it a skills/knowledge deficit (which instruction can fix), or a deficit in environment, incentives, tools, or feedback (which it cannot)? Gilbert's (1978) Behavioral Engineering Model is the classic tool for this diagnosis, separating causes into environmental supports (information, resources, incentives) and the individual's own repertoire (knowledge/skill, capacity, motives).

When the cause is not a knowledge/skill gap, the appropriate intervention is non-instructional: job aids, workplace redesign, electronic performance support systems, feedback systems, communities of practice, or process re-engineering, rather than a training course.

Rossett and Schafer (2007) offer a concrete taxonomy for one of these non-instructional interventions, Performance Support Tools (PSTs), which they distinguish sharply from instruction: "Instruction is not performance support. It is planned experience that enables an individual to acquire skills and knowledge to advance the capability to perform" (p. 5). PSTs split into sidekicks (real-time, in-the-moment job aids used concurrently with a task, like GPS turn-by-turn navigation) and planners (used in advance to access community-curated knowledge before starting a task, like planning a driving route before a trip). Effective PSTs are characterized by four factors: convergence (proximity — the support is situated where the task and performer actually are), simplicity (focused on the here-and-now task, not a broader curriculum), relevance (the right tool for the performer's specific goal), and personalization (the learner can adjust the level of support to their own experience, and may contribute back user-generated content that improves the tool for others).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to organizational data (or the ability to gather it) sufficient to compare desired vs. actual performance and identify root cause
  • Willingness to recommend a non-instructional intervention when that is what the cause analysis indicates, even if the client requested "training"

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Most directly evidenced and practiced in workplace/organizational settings; the systems-level analysis is harder to apply where the designer has no authority over surrounding organizational conditions (e.g., a single K-12 classroom)
  • Does not replace instructional design where the cause genuinely is a knowledge or skill deficit — HPT is a broader diagnostic frame, not a substitute for good instructional design once training is the right call

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Employees or performers embedded in an organizational system where environmental factors (resources, incentives, feedback, tools) may be limiting performance as much as or more than skill

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not learning objectives per se — performance objectives: closing a measurable gap between desired and actual organizational or individual performance, by whatever intervention (instructional or not) actually closes it

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Rooted in behaviorism and general systems theory (Stefaniak, 2018); a systems view is "holistic," focuses on interactions among elements rather than the elements themselves, and treats systems as nested within larger systems (Foshay, Villachica, & Stepich, 2014)

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Scaffolding and Fading — an instructional intervention that HPT would only recommend once cause analysis rules out non-instructional causes

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Gilbert's (1978) Behavioral Engineering Model as a feedback/cause-analysis tool
  • Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSS) and job aids as non-instructional interventions
  • Communities of practice and knowledge management systems as infrastructural, non-instructional supports

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Gilbert, T. F. (1978). Human competence: Engineering worthy performance. McGraw-Hill.
  • Stefaniak, J. E. (2018). Performance technology. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/performance_technology
  • Foshay, W. R., Villachica, S. W., & Stepich, D. A. (2014). Cousins but not twins: Instructional design and human performance technology in the workplace. In J. M. Spector, M. D. Merrill, J. Elen, & M. J. Bishop (Eds.), Handbook of research on educational communications and technology (4th ed., pp. 39–49). Springer.
  • Rossett, A., & Schafer, L. (2007). Job aids and performance support: Moving from knowledge in the classroom to knowledge everywhere. Pfeiffer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Perspective seeking is the instructional principle of actively engaging with multiple viewpoints in order to better understand a topic, event, text, or problem. It differs from simple exposure because learners are asked to investigate how and why different people interpret the same issue differently. In educational settings, this can strengthen reasoning, critical reading, dialogue, and humility by showing that understanding often improves when learners compare interpretations instead of remaining inside a single frame.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Perspective seeking improves reasoning when learners compare how different people frame the same issue and explain why those differences exist. That comparison can weaken premature certainty and deepen interpretation because explanation and comparison push learners to reorganize their own understanding Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. It can also support reflective revision as learners notice where their first interpretation was partial or overconfident Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The important design constraint is ethical and epistemic judgment: multiple perspectives are not the same as false balance, and the goal is not to flatten differences in evidence or harm. Strong perspective work helps learners analyze contrast more carefully, not treat every position as equally valid.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to genuinely different viewpoints: Learners need texts, cases, voices, or participants that represent meaningful variation in perspective.
  • A comparison task: Learners should analyze how viewpoints differ, not just list that difference exists.
  • Discussion and reflection structure: Prompts, norms, and synthesis routines help learners compare perspectives productively.
  • A topic worth interpreting: Perspective seeking is strongest when the issue involves judgment, values, identity, or competing explanations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Tokenized difference: Superficial inclusion of one contrasting view can flatten complexity instead of expanding it.
  • False balance: Not every issue requires treating all positions as equally supported or equally ethical.
  • Identity strain: Some learners may experience perspective work as invalidating if harmful or dehumanizing viewpoints are mishandled.
  • Cognitive overload: Too many perspectives at once can confuse learners if they lack structure for comparison.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing critical reading and reasoning: Strong fit when the goal is to interpret texts, cases, or claims more deeply.
  • Learners in civic, historical, ethical, or social inquiry contexts: Perspective seeking is especially useful where interpretation and disagreement matter.
  • Learners building social understanding across difference: Useful for dialogue, collaboration, and empathy-building.
  • Multilingual and diverse learning groups: Comparing perspectives can widen access to meaning when multiple voices and experiences are present.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Comparative interpretation: Understanding how different people frame the same issue.
  • Critical reasoning: Weighing evidence, assumptions, and implications across perspectives.
  • Intellectual humility: Reducing certainty that one's initial interpretation is the only reasonable one.
  • Dialogue across difference: Building capacity to engage with disagreement without collapsing into avoidance or defensiveness.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist views of learning — understanding deepens as learners actively interpret and reorganize meaning.
  • Social learning and social constructivist perspectives — interaction with others' reasoning supports new learning.
  • Transformative learning traditions — encountering other perspectives can challenge assumptions and reframe interpretation.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Perspective seeking is not the same as requiring learners to validate harmful views.
  • More perspectives are not automatically better; quality, relevance, and ethical framing matter.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — perspective comparison deepens reasoning when learners explain how and why interpretations differ
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — multiple perspectives can prompt learners to notice limits in their first interpretation and revise it

The current claim inventory supports explanation and reflective revision mechanisms more directly than perspective-seeking as a standalone intervention.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Building Empathy — perspective seeking can deepen empathy when learners actively investigate how others understand a situation.
  • Peer Discussion — structured discussion is one common vehicle for comparing perspectives.
  • Discussing Race — race-conscious dialogue often depends on careful perspective comparison and interpretation.
  • Evaluating Sources — comparing perspectives is stronger when learners also assess evidence quality and credibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Multiple-text comparison: Learners read contrasting accounts of the same event and identify differences in framing, evidence, and implication.
  • Stakeholder analysis: Learners compare how different stakeholders would interpret or be affected by a decision.
  • Perspective interview synthesis: Learners interview others about an issue and compare their own assumptions to what they heard.
  • Structured debate preparation: Learners prepare to argue a position they do not initially hold in order to understand it more precisely.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Brookfield, S. D. (1997). Assessing critical thinking. New Directions for Adult and Continuing Education, 1997(75), 17-29. https://doi.org/10.1002/ace.7503
  • Eyal, T., Steffel, M., & Epley, N. (2018). Perspective mistaking: Accurately understanding the mind of another requires getting perspective, not taking perspective. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(4), 547-571. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspa0000115
  • LaRusso, M., Kim, H. Y., Selman, R., Uccelli, P., Dawson, T., Jones, S., Donovan, S., & Snow, C. (2016). Contributions of academic language, perspective taking, and complex reasoning to deep reading comprehension. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 9(2), 201-222. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1116035

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Perspective-taking is the principle of intentionally examining a situation, text, problem, or decision from viewpoints other than one's own. It supports empathy, argument quality, and more flexible reasoning by forcing learners to compare assumptions, evidence, and consequences across positions.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Perspective-taking helps learners move beyond their default frame by requiring them to reason through how another person or stakeholder might interpret the same situation. That can improve empathy and argument quality because learners must compare assumptions, evidence, and likely consequences rather than treating their first reading as complete, and the explanatory work itself can deepen understanding Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]. For novices, this often works best when the perspective-taking task is structured with prompts, roles, or comparison routines rather than left open-ended Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. The design caution is that perspective-taking should deepen analysis, not perform shallow role-play or imply that all perspectives are equally well supported or ethically acceptable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Contrastive viewpoints: Learners need access to distinct interpretations, roles, or stakeholder positions.
  • Structured comparison: Prompts should ask how and why perspectives differ, not just list them.
  • Norms for respectful disagreement: Productive perspective-taking depends on intellectual safety.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• False equivalence risk: Not all perspectives are equally evidence-based or ethically valid.
  • Superficial role-play: Perspective-taking can become performative if learners do not engage with actual reasoning or evidence.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners developing empathy, argumentation, historical understanding, or collaborative reasoning.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Compare interpretations, understand stakeholder positions, and reason beyond a single viewpoint.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Social-constructivist and dialogic learning traditions support understanding through exposure to alternative perspectives.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Perspective-taking should deepen analysis, not flatten real differences in power, evidence, or consequence.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S] — perspective-taking improves analysis when learners explain another viewpoint rather than merely naming it
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — novices often need structured roles or prompts before perspective-taking becomes analytically useful

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Perspective-Seeking/Multiple Perspectives
  • Social Learning
  • Building Empathy

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Debates that require learners to articulate the strongest case for an opposing position.
  • Historical inquiry that compares how different groups experienced the same event.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Kuhn, D. (1991). The skills of argument. Cambridge University Press.
  • Nussbaum, E. M., & Schraw, G. (2007). Promoting argument-counterargument integration in students' writing. The Journal of Experimental Education, 76(1), 59-92. https://doi.org/10.3200/JEXE.76.1.59-92

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Physical activity in learning contexts means intentionally incorporating movement, exercise, or embodied breaks to support attention, energy, regulation, and readiness to learn. This can range from short movement breaks to physically active tasks or longer routines that help learners recover from fatigue and re-engage. The instructional value is usually indirect: physical activity does not teach content by itself, but it can improve the conditions under which focus, mood, and persistence are more available.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Physical activity is most useful as a readiness and regulation support rather than as content instruction by itself. Brief movement can help some learners reset attention, notice internal state, and return to demanding work with more control Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The instructional implication is not that movement is always better, but that it should be timed and framed to improve the next learning action. When movement is disconnected from task demands, inaccessible, or overly generalized, it becomes disruption rather than support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear purpose: Movement should support transition, energy regulation, alertness, or embodied learning rather than feeling random.
  • Feasible participation: Activities need to be physically, socially, and spatially workable for the group.
  • Respect for variation: Learners need options or modifications so participation is not exclusionary.
  • Connection to the learning flow: The activity should support readiness for the next task or deepen the task itself.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• One-size-fits-all movement: Learners differ in comfort, mobility, health, and cultural expectations around movement.
  • Lost instructional coherence: Breaks can feel disruptive if they are not integrated intentionally.
  • Overclaiming: Physical activity can support readiness and attention, but it is not a universal cognitive solution.
  • Accessibility and safety: Activities require attention to environment, health needs, and opt-out paths.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners dealing with fatigue or long sedentary sessions: Strong fit when sustained sitting reduces alertness and engagement.
  • Learners who benefit from regulation support: Movement can help some learners reset emotionally or cognitively.
  • Adult learners balancing stress and attentional fragmentation: Brief movement can improve readiness for the next task.
  • Groups in embodied or applied learning contexts: Physical activity can directly support tasks that involve gesture, movement, or spatial reasoning.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improved task readiness: Increasing alertness and willingness to re-engage after prolonged sitting or cognitive fatigue.
  • Attention and mood regulation: Supporting conditions for focus and persistence.
  • Embodied learning support: Using movement when bodily action clarifies or reinforces meaning.
  • Well-being during learning: Making the learning environment more sustainable physically and mentally.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated learning and attentional control perspectives — movement can support regulation of state before demanding work.
  • Self-determination theory — activity choices and energizing routines can support motivation and readiness.
  • Cognitive load-related perspectives — brief breaks may reduce fatigue and help restore attention for complex tasks.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Benefits depend on duration, intensity, timing, and learner fit; more movement is not always better for every task.
  • Physical activity should support learning rather than function as a mandatory performance unrelated to instructional goals.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — routines that help learners notice and regulate their state can improve later strategy adjustment and persistence

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Mindfulness Activities — both can function as readiness and regulation supports before or during learning.
  • Check-ins — movement-based check-ins can help surface energy, readiness, and attention.
  • Quiet Learning Spaces — environment design affects whether movement and rest can coexist productively.
  • Skills Sprint — brief movement breaks can support focus across intensive practice sessions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Short movement breaks: Learners stand, stretch, walk, or reset between dense instructional segments.
  • Walk-and-talk discussion: Pairs discuss a prompt while moving, then return to record insights.
  • Optional movement stations: Learners choose a physically active way to reset before resuming work.
  • Embodied concept routines: Learners use gesture or movement to represent a process, sequence, or relation.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Opprezzo, M., & Schwartz, D. L. (2014). Give your ideas some legs: The positive effect of walking on creative thinking. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 40(4), 1142-1152. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036577
  • Pontifex, M. B., Hillman, C. H., Fernhall, B., Thompson, K. M., & Valentini, T. A. (2009). The effect of acute aerobic and resistance exercise on working memory. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, 41(4), 927-934. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181907d69
  • Ratey, J. J., & Loehr, J. E. (2011). The positive impact of physical activity on cognition during adulthood: A review of underlying mechanisms, evidence and recommendations. Reviews in the Neurosciences, 22(2), 171-185. https://doi.org/10.1515/RNS.2011.017

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Positive self-talk is the deliberate use of supportive, instructional, or regulating internal language to influence how a learner interprets difficulty, effort, and performance. In learning settings, its value lies less in generic optimism than in how learners talk themselves through challenge: naming what to do next, reducing catastrophic interpretation, and maintaining effort when a task is uncomfortable. Positive self-talk can support regulation and persistence, but it works best when it is specific, credible, and tied to action.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Positive self-talk helps when internal language changes what the learner does next, not just how the learner feels for a moment. Self-talk that points toward a concrete process or coping move can support monitoring and regulation under stress Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M], and novice learners often benefit more from process-focused cues than from outcome-only encouragement Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. The design constraint is credibility: vague positivity or denial of real difficulty often backfires. Effective self-talk sounds plausible, action-oriented, and connected to the task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear function for the self-talk: It may be motivational, instructional, calming, or interpretive, but it should match the moment.
  • Credible phrasing: Self-talk should feel believable and actionable rather than hollow affirmation.
  • Practice and modeling: Learners often need examples of how to rephrase unhelpful internal language.
  • Connection to strategy: Positive self-talk is stronger when it points toward a next step or coping move.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Forced positivity: Overly upbeat language can feel false and may increase resistance or shame.
  • No strategy link: Encouragement without action guidance often has limited effect.
  • Context blindness: Self-talk cannot solve structural barriers, unclear instruction, or lack of support by itself.
  • Individual variability: Some learners may respond better to instructional or distanced self-talk than to affirmational language.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners facing anxiety or self-doubt: Especially relevant when internal dialogue amplifies stress or avoidance.
  • Learners building self-regulation: Self-talk can support pause, reframing, and strategic next steps.
  • Learners encountering difficult or evaluative tasks: Strong fit for presentations, tests, revision, and sustained problem solving.
  • Learners developing growth-oriented interpretations of challenge: Useful when effort and error are easily misread as inability.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Regulating response to difficulty: Reducing unhelpful internal escalation during challenge.
  • Sustaining persistence: Supporting continued effort when a task becomes uncomfortable.
  • Improving strategic action: Using self-instruction to guide attention and next steps.
  • Strengthening learner identity: Shifting from fixed or defeatist interpretations toward more workable ones.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated learning — self-talk can function as an internal regulation tool for attention, interpretation, and action.
  • Expectancy-value perspectives — internal dialogue shapes whether learners believe effort is worthwhile and possible.
  • Self-determination theory — self-talk may support competence and persistence when it reinforces effective action.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Positive self-talk should not be used to deny real difficulty or suppress appropriate emotion.
  • Learners often benefit more from specific instructional or distanced self-talk than from vague encouragement.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — learners improve when they can notice their current state and choose a more effective next move
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — beginners often perform better when inner language points to a concrete process instead of only a hoped-for result

The current claim inventory supports regulation and process-focused guidance mechanisms more directly than self-talk as a standalone intervention.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Foster Growth Mindset — self-talk often shapes whether challenge is interpreted as growth or failure.
  • Mindfulness Activities — both principles can support more deliberate response to stress and difficulty.
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring — self-talk becomes more effective when it refers to concrete goals and next steps.
  • Check-ins — brief self-check prompts can help learners notice and redirect internal dialogue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Instructional self-talk prompts: Learners practice phrases like "First I identify the goal, then I choose a strategy."
  • Reframing routines: Learners replace defeatist statements with credible next-step language.
  • Distanced self-talk: Learners speak to themselves in second or third person to increase perspective during stress.
  • Pre-performance cue cards: Learners prepare short self-talk scripts for presentations, tests, or difficult problem sets.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Kross, E., Bruehlman-Senecal, E., Park, J., Burson, A., Dougherty, A., Shablack, H., Bremner, R., Moser, J., & Ayduk, O. (2014). Self-talk as a regulatory mechanism: How you do it matters. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 106(2), 304-324. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0035173
  • Gainsburg, I., & Kross, E. (2020). Distanced self-talk changes how people conceptualize the self. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 88, 103971. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2019.103971
  • Hatzigeorgiadis, A., Zourbanos, N., Galanis, E., & Theodorakis, Y. (2011). Self-talk and sports performance: A meta-analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6(4), 348-356. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691611413136

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-reading questioning is the instructional principle of using questions before a text, source, or reading task to activate prior knowledge, orient attention, and establish a purpose for reading. The value lies less in predicting the "right" answer than in helping learners notice what they already know, what they wonder, and what they should look for. When used well, pre-reading questions can improve comprehension by reducing aimless reading and by surfacing misconceptions early enough to address them.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Pre-reading questioning improves comprehension when it gives learners a reason to read and a frame for what to notice. Orienting questions can reduce aimless attention by narrowing what must be held and tracked during reading Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S], and they can support more deliberate monitoring as learners compare early predictions to what the text actually shows Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The key design risk is over-directing interpretation: questions should focus attention without predetermining every conclusion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful reading purpose: Questions should help learners know what to watch for in the text or task.
  • Connection to prior knowledge: Prompts should invite learners to activate existing knowledge, assumptions, or curiosity.
  • Alignment to the actual text demand: Questions need to prepare learners for the kind of comprehension or analysis the reading requires.
  • Return to the questions after reading: The questions should inform later discussion, annotation, or revision of understanding.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Leading prompts: Questions can narrow interpretation too much if they predetermine what learners are supposed to notice.
  • Shallow activation: Generic warm-up questions may fail to connect meaningfully to the text.
  • Premature certainty: Learners may become attached to initial predictions unless the post-reading phase invites revision.
  • Overload from too many questions: Excessive prompting before reading can become distracting rather than orienting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners approaching unfamiliar texts: Strong fit when the topic, vocabulary, or genre may otherwise feel opaque.
  • Learners developing strategic reading habits: Pre-reading questions help shift reading from passive decoding to active inquiry.
  • Multilingual learners and developing readers: Advance orientation can make comprehension demands clearer and more manageable.
  • Learners in content-heavy courses: Questions can focus attention on the most important concepts, patterns, or claims.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Activate background knowledge: Bringing relevant prior understanding into the reading task.
  • Improve reading purpose and attention: Helping learners know what they are reading for.
  • Surface misconceptions: Revealing assumptions that need to be tested or revised.
  • Support later comprehension and discussion: Creating a frame for note-taking, annotation, and post-reading synthesis.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Information processing views — orienting questions can direct attention and improve what gets encoded during reading.
  • Constructivist perspectives — learners interpret new text through the lens of what they already know and believe.
  • Expectancy-value and motivational views — questions can increase relevance and curiosity before the reading begins.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Pre-reading questions can constrain interpretation if they are too narrow or overly teacher-directed.
  • Some texts are better entered first with open noticing before specific questions are introduced.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — orienting prompts can reduce the amount of undirected information learners try to manage at once
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — pre-reading questions help learners check what they already think and revise it as they read

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Graphic Organizers — graphic organizers can make pre-reading questions more visible and usable.
  • Note-taking — pre-reading questions help determine what learners should attend to and record.
  • Inquiry-based Learning — question generation before reading can frame the text as evidence for inquiry.
  • Handouts/Online Guides/Visual Reading Aids — reading guides often embed pre-reading questions as orientation tools.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Prediction and purpose prompts: Learners answer a small set of questions before reading and revisit them afterward.
  • Question-generation warm-up: Learners create their own questions from a title, heading set, or opening image.
  • KWL-style framing: Learners identify what they know, want to know, and later what they learned.
  • Source anticipation: Before reading a document, learners predict what perspective, evidence, or problem the text might contain.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ajideh, P. (2003). Schema theory-based pre-reading tasks: A neglected essential in the ESL reading class. The Reading Matrix, 3(1).
  • Clinton, V., & van den Broek, P. (2012). Interest, inferences, and learning from texts. Learning and Individual Differences, 22(6), 650-663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2012.07.004
  • Rasheed, H. (2014). Examining the effectiveness of pre-reading strategies on Saudi EFL college students' reading comprehension. English Language Teaching, 7(11), 79-91. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p79

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Problem-based learning organizes learning around complex, meaningful problems that do not have a single obvious answer. Learners investigate the problem, identify what they need to know, gather evidence, propose solutions, and revise their thinking as they work. The strength of PBL is that it ties knowledge to use and makes learning purposeful, but it is not equivalent to leaving learners on their own. Strong PBL depends on careful facilitation, scaffolds for inquiry and collaboration, and enough domain grounding that the problem is challenging without becoming chaotic.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Problem-based learning is strongest when the problem requires learners to integrate knowledge in ways that resemble real use, which is why whole-task work often supports transfer better than fragmented drill alone Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S]. At the same time, open problems can impose too much search on novices without enough prior structure Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [~M], so facilitation and scaffolding matter Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]. Novice learners often need process guidance for how to investigate, compare evidence, and decide what to do next Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M], not just exposure to a challenging problem.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful, complex problem: The problem should require investigation, judgment, and integration of knowledge rather than simple recall.
  • Access to evidence and resources: Learners need materials, data, cases, or sources they can use to investigate the problem.
  • Facilitative support: Instructors need to guide process, questioning, and evidence use without taking over the problem.
  • A product or decision point: PBL is strongest when learners must articulate, defend, or test a proposed response.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Novice overload: Learners without sufficient background knowledge can flounder if the problem is too open too soon.
  • Process without rigor: PBL can become busy but shallow if evidence use and synthesis are weak.
  • Time intensity: Good PBL typically requires more time than direct instruction for setup, inquiry, and reflection.
  • Group coordination burden: Collaboration can obscure individual learning unless roles and accountability are clear.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners tackling authentic or interdisciplinary problems: Strong fit when knowledge has to be integrated rather than applied one fact at a time.
  • Adult learners seeking relevance: PBL works well when learners need to see why the content matters.
  • Learners developing self-directed inquiry habits: The model builds planning, monitoring, evidence use, and revision.
  • Collaborative groups: PBL often benefits from distributed roles and shared reasoning.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Problem solving and reasoning: Applying knowledge to ambiguous, open-ended situations.
  • Evidence-based inquiry: Identifying what must be learned and using sources to inform a response.
  • Self-directed learning: Planning, monitoring, and revising a learning path through the problem.
  • Transfer to authentic situations: Using knowledge in contexts closer to real practice or decision making.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through active problem engagement.
  • Situated and experiential learning traditions — problems grounded in realistic contexts strengthen relevance and application.
  • Self-regulated learning — PBL demands planning, monitoring, and adaptation across an extended task.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• PBL is weaker when learners lack enough conceptual grounding to investigate productively; some direct teaching is often needed first or during the task.
  • Not every objective requires full PBL; some foundational skills are acquired more efficiently through explicit instruction and guided practice.
  • Savery (2019) himself notes that meta-analyses (Newman, 2003; Sanson-Fisher & Lynagh, 2005) found the evidence base for PBL's superiority over traditional instruction "methodologically flawed" and inconclusive — a caution against treating PBL's effectiveness as more settled than the literature actually supports.
  • Reigeluth (2011), in Learner-Centered Paradigm of Education, identifies four specific weaknesses of problem-based instruction — team assessment can hide an individual "loafer," insufficient repeated practice for transfer, no automaticity training, and inefficient unguided search — addressed by the Project Space and Instructional Space pattern.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — integrated, authentic problem solving is often better preparation for later transfer than isolated subskill practice
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — learners benefit when facilitation responds to where their inquiry or reasoning is actually breaking down
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — novices often need explicit investigation and decision routines before open-ended success criteria become productive
  • Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [~M] — beginners can waste effort on unguided search unless the problem space is structured well enough to support learning

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Inquiry-based Learning — PBL is one inquiry form centered on authentic problems.
  • Experiential Learning — problem-centered work often provides the concrete experience that later reflection builds on.
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes — real stakeholders or consequences often strengthen PBL design.
  • Guided Practice — novices often need coached practice with inquiry and problem-solving moves inside PBL.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Community issue investigation: Learners analyze a local problem, gather evidence, and propose responses.
  • Case-based team problem solving: Small groups work through a realistic professional dilemma with incomplete information.
  • Design challenge: Learners create and defend a solution to a practical constraint-based problem.
  • Cross-disciplinary PBL module: Learners integrate literacy, numeracy, and research skills to address a shared problem.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Marra, R. M., Jonassen, D. H., Palmer, B., & Luft, S. (2014). Why problem-based learning works: Theoretical foundations. Journal on Excellence in College Teaching, 25(3-4), 221-238.
  • Thorndahl, K., & Stentoft, D. (2020). Thinking critically about critical thinking and problem-based learning in higher education: A scoping review. The Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 14(1). https://doi.org/10.14434/ijpbl.v14i1.28773
  • Lin, L. F. (2017). Impacts of the problem-based learning pedagogy on English learners' reading comprehension, strategy use, and active learning attitudes. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(6), 109-125. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i6.2320
  • Savery, J. R. (2019). Overview of problem-based learning: Definitions and distinctions. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/overview_of_problem_based_learning

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Procedural learning is the principle of helping learners acquire and refine sequences of action, routines, or task procedures until performance becomes more accurate, fluent, and reliable. It is useful when knowing how to do something matters as much as, or more than, declarative understanding alone.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Procedural learning is most important when the learning target is a repeatable performance: solving an equation type, revising a sentence, carrying out a lab technique, debugging a workflow, or following a diagnostic sequence. The principle assumes that declarative explanation alone is not enough. Learners need models that reduce blind search at the start Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M], repeated performance guided by process-focused attention Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M], timely feedback, and support that adapts as performance improves Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. Its main limitation is transfer: if the procedure is learned only as rote sequence without conceptual grounding, learners may struggle when conditions change.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A target procedure or routine — the instructor needs to know what sequence, method, or workflow learners are acquiring
  • Clear modeling, feedback, and repeated use — procedural knowledge is strengthened through visible demonstration and repeated performance with correction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Procedural fluency without conceptual understanding can limit transfer
  • Over-explaining can interfere with early performance if the learner cannot yet coordinate the whole sequence
  • Some procedures need staging — complex routines may require partial support or simplified entry points before full independent performance

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners acquiring new routines, methods, or repeatable performance patterns
  • Novices in technical, mathematical, clinical, craft, or workplace procedures
  • Learners who need to move from explanation to reliable execution

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build accurate, increasingly fluent performance of procedures and routines
  • Reduce error through repeated, feedback-rich execution
  • Support the transition from supported procedure use to independent performance

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Deliberate Practice — focused repetition and feedback refine procedural performance
  • Behaviorism — repeated response plus feedback can shape reliable routines
  • Information Processing Theory — repeated performance helps move procedures from effortful processing toward greater fluency

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — qualifies that procedures are more transferable when learners also understand why the procedure works

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M] — explicit models can reduce blind search for novices as they acquire new procedures
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — novices often improve more when attention is directed to execution and process than to end-state outcomes alone
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — procedural learning is stronger when support adapts to learner performance rather than staying fixed

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Explicit Instruction — often supplies the visible model and sequence that procedural learning needs
  • Scaffolding — helps learners perform procedures they cannot yet execute independently
  • Deliberate Practice — explains how procedures improve through focused repetition with feedback

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Procedural Information — Stepwise guidance is provided just in time as learners perform a routine or method.

Fading Scaffolding — Hints, prompts, or partial steps are gradually removed as learners become more capable of independent execution.

Modeled routine followed by coached repetition — The teacher demonstrates a procedure, learners practice with immediate correction, and then support is reduced over successive attempts.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Anderson, J. R. (1982). Acquisition of cognitive skill. Psychological Review, 89(4), 369-406. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.89.4.369
  • Anderson, J. R. (1993). Rules of the mind. Lawrence Erlbaum.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Process-based writing treats writing as a sequence of intentional moves such as generating ideas, planning, drafting, revising, editing, and reflecting rather than as a one-shot product. Its core premise is that writers improve when the process itself is taught, supported, and made visible. This is especially useful for learners developing complex writing skills, because it breaks writing into revisable stages while still keeping the final communicative purpose in view.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Process-based writing helps because strong writing rarely emerges from a single unsupported attempt. Staging planning, drafting, revising, and editing can make the task more manageable and regulate cognitive load Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M], while reflection across drafts can improve monitoring and self-correction Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]. Novice writers often benefit from process goals for what to do in the next stage Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M], and explaining revision choices can deepen understanding of what stronger writing requires Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. The main caution is over-fragmentation: the process should support the communicative whole, not replace it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Visible stages of the writing process: Learners need explicit support for planning, drafting, revising, and editing.
  • Feedback during the process: Process-based writing is strongest when writers receive response before the final submission.
  • Time for revision: Learners need enough cycles to actually act on feedback and rethink ideas.
  • A meaningful writing purpose: Process work should still connect to audience, genre, and communicative goal.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Stage over-fragmentation: Breaking writing into steps can become mechanical if learners lose sight of the whole text and its purpose.
  • Revision avoidance: Learners may treat early drafts as final unless revision expectations are explicit and supported.
  • Feedback overload: Too much commentary too early can stall writing rather than improve it.
  • Process without quality criteria: Writers still need models of strong writing, not only encouragement to keep drafting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing writing fluency and control: Strong fit for novice and developing writers who benefit from staged support.
  • Multilingual learners: Process routines can make revision and language experimentation more manageable.
  • Learners who experience writing as high-stakes or fixed: A process focus can normalize drafting and improvement.
  • Writers tackling more complex genres: Planning and revision become more important as task complexity grows.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Stronger draft development: Improving how ideas are generated, organized, and expanded over time.
  • Revision skill: Helping learners rethink content, structure, and clarity rather than only proofreading.
  • Metacognitive awareness in writing: Noticing what a text is trying to do and where it still needs work.
  • More sustainable writing habits: Building repeatable routines that transfer across assignments and genres.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated learning — writing improves when learners plan, monitor, revise, and reflect deliberately.
  • Metacognitive perspectives — process-based writing helps learners notice what good writing requires at each stage.
  • Information processing views — staged writing can reduce overload by separating generation, organization, and revision work.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Not every writing task needs a full multistage cycle; short forms may be better served by lighter process support.
  • Process instruction should not make writing feel like a rigid formula that ignores audience, voice, or purpose.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — writers improve when they can track what is working across drafts and choose better next steps
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explaining revision decisions strengthens understanding of genre, clarity, and purpose
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M] — developing writers often need concrete stage-by-stage goals rather than only a final performance target
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — coaching and feedback are most useful when they target the learner’s current bottleneck in the writing process

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Journaling — journaling can provide low-stakes writing practice and reflection that feeds larger writing tasks.
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review — revision is stronger when learners get and use feedback before final submission.
  • Guided Practice — early writing stages often benefit from teacher modeling and coached rehearsal.
  • Graphic Organizers — organizers can support planning and structural revision.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Draft-revise cycles: Learners submit early drafts, receive feedback, and revise before final evaluation.
  • Stage-specific mini-lessons: An instructor teaches planning, paragraphing, revision, or editing at the point of need.
  • Writers' workshop routines: Learners alternate between independent drafting, conferences, peer review, and revision.
  • Process reflections: Writers briefly explain what changed between drafts and why.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hayes, J. R., & Flower, L. S. (1980). Identifying the organization of writing processes. In Cognitive processes in writing (pp. 3-30). Lawrence Erlbaum.
  • Wei, Z., Shang, H., & Briody, P. (2012). The relationship between English writing ability levels and EFL learners' metacognitive behaviour in the writing process. International Journal of Academic Research in Progressive Education and Development, 1(4), 154-180.
  • Fernandez, R., Peyton, J. K., & Schaetzel, K. (2017). A survey of writing instruction in adult ESL programs: Are teaching practices meeting adult learner needs? COABE Journal, 6(2), 5.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Purposeful reflection is structured time for learners to examine what they did, what they understood, where they struggled, and what they should do next. The key distinction is intention: reflection is tied to a learning goal, experience, product, or decision rather than being a generic request to "think about it." Well-designed reflection helps learners consolidate meaning, monitor progress, and connect present learning to future action.

Purposeful reflection can happen before, during, or after a task. It is especially useful after complex work, feedback, discussion, or practice because it helps learners interpret experience instead of merely having it. Reflection is strongest when prompts are specific, evidence-based, and revisited over time so learners can compare earlier and later thinking.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Purposeful reflection works when learners revisit a specific performance, decision, or experience closely enough to interpret it rather than merely remember it. Reflection can strengthen monitoring and strategic adjustment Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M], and explanatory reflection often deepens conceptual understanding by making reasoning and misconceptions explicit Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]. For novices, reflection is most useful when prompts direct attention toward evidence, process, and next steps rather than asking for vague introspection Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. Reflection without action, however, quickly becomes compliance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A defined reflection target: Learners should reflect on a specific task, goal, misconception, experience, or product.
  • Structured prompts or protocols: Questions should direct attention toward evidence, strategy, and next steps rather than invite vague summary.
  • Time close to the learning event: Reflection is most useful when learners can still recall the reasoning, difficulty, or feedback they are analyzing.
  • Some follow-through: Reflection should feed later revision, discussion, goal-setting, or planning so it affects future learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Unstructured reflection drifts: Broad prompts often produce superficial recap instead of analysis.
  • Reflection without action stalls: If learners never use reflection to revise work or strategy, it becomes compliance writing.
  • Emotional overreach: Reflection should not require personal disclosure beyond what is instructionally relevant and psychologically safe.
  • Novice ambiguity: Learners new to reflection may need examples, sentence stems, or modeling to reflect productively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing metacognition: Reflection helps learners name strategies, obstacles, and patterns in their own learning.
  • Adult learners connecting learning to experience: Reflection is well suited to integrating coursework with prior work, family, or community contexts.
  • Learners engaged in complex tasks: Strong fit after inquiry, projects, performances, fieldwork, or revision cycles.
  • Learners rebuilding academic confidence: Structured reflection can make growth visible and counter all-or-nothing interpretations of success and failure.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Metacognitive awareness: Monitoring understanding, effort, and strategy use.
  • Transfer and application: Connecting what was learned in one context to future tasks or settings.
  • Revision and improvement: Using reflection to plan concrete changes in approach or product quality.
  • Identity and agency development: Helping learners see themselves as capable participants in learning.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Reflective practice traditions — reflection supports sense-making from action and experience.
  • Self-regulated learning — learners use reflection to evaluate progress and choose next strategies.
  • Constructivist perspectives — meaning deepens when learners reinterpret experience and connect ideas across contexts.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Reflection is not inherently effective; it becomes useful when prompts are disciplined enough to focus attention on evidence, strategy, and change.
  • Reflection should complement, not replace, direct practice, feedback, and explicit instruction.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — reflection is strongest when it helps learners evaluate progress and choose a better next move
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S] — putting reasoning into words can deepen understanding of what happened and why
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — beginners usually reflect better when prompts focus on process, cues, and next actions

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Journaling — journaling is one common routine for structured reflection over time.
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring — reflection helps learners interpret progress and set next steps.
  • Formative Assessment — reflection helps learners make use of feedback and evidence about current performance.
  • Experiential Learning — experience becomes more educative when learners analyze and reinterpret it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Reflection
  • Individual Reflection
  • LDA Reflection

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Barrett, H. (2005). Researching electronic portfolios and learner engagement. Retrieved from http://google.electronicportfolios.com/reflect/whitepaper.pdf
  • Brown, J. O. (2002). Know thyself: The impact of portfolio development on adult learning. Adult Education Quarterly, 52(3), 228-245. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741713602052003005
  • Sage, M., & Sele, P. (2015). Reflective journaling as a flipped classroom technique to increase reading and participation with social work students. Journal of Social Work Education, 51(4), 668-681. https://doi.org/10.1080/10437797.2015.1076264
  • Tailab, M., & Marsh, N. (2020). Use of self-assessment of video recording to raise students' awareness of development of their oral presentation skills. Higher Education Studies, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v10n1p16

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Quiet learning spaces reduce competing demands on attention so learners can focus on reading, listening, problem solving, and reflection. "Quiet" here does not only mean low sound; it also includes lower interruption, fewer notifications, clearer routines, and an environment that helps learners sustain concentration. For some adult learners, especially those managing stress, fatigue, shared living spaces, or prior chaotic learning experiences, environmental stability is itself an instructional support.

This principle matters most when the task requires concentration, comprehension, memory, or self-regulation. Quiet spaces are not the only effective learning environments, and total silence is not always necessary, but instructors should deliberately reduce avoidable distractions when the cognitive demands of the task are high.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Quiet learning spaces matter when the task places heavy demands on concentration, comprehension, or self-regulation. Reducing interruptions and noise can lower extraneous processing demands Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] and make it easier for learners to monitor and protect their own attention Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The design implication is not universal silence. It is better alignment between environment and task: some work requires calm and low interruption, while other work depends on purposeful interaction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Reduced interruptions: Learners need a setting with minimal conversational, technological, or environmental disruptions.
  • Task-environment alignment: Quiet matters most for reading, writing, planning, test preparation, and other attention-heavy work.
  • Usable routines for focus: Learners benefit from norms such as device management, notification control, headphones, or dedicated focus intervals.
  • Psychological safety: The space should feel predictable and non-threatening, not merely silent.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Not one-size-fits-all: Some learners focus better with low-level background sound, movement breaks, or collaborative talk depending on the task.
  • Access inequities: Many adult learners do not control their home, workplace, or caregiving environments.
  • Silence without structure: A quiet room alone will not solve weak task design or low clarity.
  • Overcorrection: Excessively rigid silence can undermine collaboration, belonging, or oral language practice when discussion is actually the goal.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with attention regulation challenges: Fewer distractions can support sustained focus and task completion.
  • Learners affected by stress, fatigue, or adverse experiences: Predictable environments can reduce cognitive and emotional load.
  • Learners doing language-heavy tasks: Reading and writing often suffer when background speech or frequent interruption competes for processing.
  • Learners studying in unstable environments: Adults balancing work, housing, or family demands may need explicit support in creating temporary focus conditions.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained attention: Maintaining focus across reading, writing, planning, or practice intervals.
  • Comprehension and memory: Supporting deeper processing during demanding tasks.
  • Self-regulation: Helping learners notice and manage distractions.
  • Task persistence: Reducing the friction that leads to procrastination or abandoning work.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive load perspectives — reducing extraneous distraction leaves more capacity for the task itself.
  • Attention and self-regulation perspectives — focus improves when the environment reduces interruption and supports inhibition.
  • Human needs and safety perspectives — some learners need calm, predictable environments before sustained learning is possible.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Quiet is not the instructional goal by itself; it is a support condition whose value depends on the task.
  • Collaborative discussion, oral rehearsal, and socially interactive work may require intentionally non-quiet settings.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — reducing distraction can leave more working-memory capacity available for the actual learning task
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — focus-friendly routines can help learners notice and manage distraction more deliberately

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Instructor Accessibility — accessible learning conditions include environmental supports, not just interpersonal support.
  • Check-ins — regular check-ins can surface environmental barriers that undermine focus.
  • Physical Activity — learners may need a mix of calm focus conditions and intentional movement breaks.
  • Clear Structure & Presentation — environmental clarity and instructional clarity often work together.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Dedicated reading zone: A library corner, side room, or protected class interval used for uninterrupted reading or writing.
  • Device-down protocol: Learners silence notifications and set brief focus intervals during cognitively demanding tasks.
  • Noise-managed test prep: Headphones, seating adjustments, or quiet blocks used during assessment preparation.
  • Home-study planning routine: Learners identify when and where they can create the most stable study conditions outside class.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Cunningham, H. V., & Tabur, S. (2012). Learning space attributes: Reflections on academic library design and its use. Journal of Learning Spaces, 1(2). https://libjournal.uncg.edu/jls/article/view/280
