  • Dietz, S., & Henrich, C. (2014). Texting as a distraction to learning in college students. Computers in Human Behavior, 36, 163-167. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2014.03.045
  • Vasilev, M. R., Liversedge, S. P., Rowan, D., Kirkby, J. A., & Angele, B. (2019). Reading is disrupted by intelligible background speech: Evidence from eye-tracking. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 45(11), 1484-1512. https://doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000680
  • Rozental, A., & Carlbring, P. (2014). Understanding and treating procrastination: A review of a common self-regulatory failure. Psychology, 5, 1488-1502. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2014.513160

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Real-world math connects mathematical ideas to situations learners recognize as meaningful in work, home, community, finance, health, civic life, or further study. The point is not merely to decorate abstract content with a story problem; it is to show how mathematical reasoning helps make sense of actual decisions, quantities, tradeoffs, and patterns. For adult learners especially, relevance can improve persistence and reduce the sense that math is disconnected from everyday competence.

This principle also broadens what counts as mathematical experience. When instructors draw on learners' cultural practices, workplace tasks, and informal problem-solving, math becomes something learners already use and can extend, not just something delivered by school. The quality of the context matters: examples should be authentic enough to support transfer without adding unnecessary complexity or stereotyping learner experience.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Real-world math improves engagement and transfer when the mathematical structure is tied to situations learners actually care about. Authentic contexts can make the purpose of a concept clearer and support whole-task application Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S], but relevance alone is not enough. Learners still need help seeing the underlying structure, explaining why the math fits the situation Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S], and navigating the extra complexity that context can introduce Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. The best real-world math tasks respect learner experience without letting the context overshadow the mathematics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Authentic contexts learners recognize: Problems should connect to real uses of quantity, data, measurement, comparison, or modeling.
  • Faithful mathematical structure: The context must illuminate the concept instead of distracting from it.
  • Instructor knowledge of learner context: Relevance depends on understanding learners' goals, work, community, and prior math experiences.
  • Opportunities to explain reasoning: Real-world math is strongest when learners justify how the math fits the situation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Fake relevance: Thin word problems or contrived contexts can feel manipulative and reduce trust.
  • Context overload: Rich situations can introduce literacy or background-knowledge demands that obscure the math.
  • Cultural mismatch: A context that feels authentic to one group may be confusing or alienating to another.
  • Transfer is not automatic: Learners still need help abstracting the underlying structure so they can use the math elsewhere.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adult learners rebuilding confidence in math: Relevance can reduce resistance and increase willingness to engage.
  • Learners preparing for work or everyday problem solving: Strong fit when goals include budgeting, measurement, data interpretation, or quantitative decision making.
  • Learners whose experiences are often excluded from school math: Real-world framing can increase belonging when it respects cultural and community knowledge.
  • Learners integrating math with other domains: Useful when numeracy is embedded in science, civics, health, trades, or technical study.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Applied numeracy: Using math to analyze and act in everyday or workplace situations.
  • Conceptual understanding: Seeing how mathematical structure explains real situations.
  • Transfer: Recognizing when previously learned math applies in a new context.
  • Motivation and persistence: Increasing willingness to engage with math because it feels worthwhile.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Situated learning perspectives — understanding strengthens when knowledge is tied to meaningful activity and context.
  • Andragogical perspectives — adults are more likely to engage when content is clearly relevant to immediate goals and problems.
  • Constructivist and sociocultural perspectives — learners interpret math through prior knowledge, tools, language, and social practice.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Real-world framing does not remove the need for explicit explanation, worked examples, and focused practice.
  • Context should support abstraction, not trap learning inside a single familiar example.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S] — math tied to meaningful situations can support later application better than decontextualized drill alone
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — contextual math tasks often need responsive support so the situation clarifies rather than obscures the concept
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S] — learners understand applied math more deeply when they justify why a model or method fits the real situation

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Explicit Instruction: Math Strategies — real-world tasks still benefit from direct teaching of methods and representations.
  • Creating Visual Representations — diagrams, tables, and models help learners connect context to mathematical structure.
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes — relevance grows when math supports meaningful tasks and decisions.
  • Problem-based Learning — real-world math often works through applied, open-ended problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Budget comparison task: Learners compare phone plans, wages, or household expenses using proportional reasoning and estimation.
  • Workplace measurement problem: Learners calculate materials, time, or error tolerance for a job-related task.
  • Community data inquiry: Learners interpret local charts, rates, or survey results to make an argument.
  • Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI) for Math

docs.text:
• Brooks, C. (2015). Making maths useful: How two teachers prepare adult learners to apply their numeracy skills in their lives outside the classroom. Adults Learning Mathematics, 10(1), 24-39.
  • Civil, M., Stoehr, K. J., & Salazar, F. (2020). Learning with and from immigrant mothers: Implications for adult numeracy. ZDM Mathematics Education, 52(3), 489-500. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-019-01087-6
  • Garrett, L., Huang, L., & Calhoun, M. (2016). A framework for authenticity in the mathematics and statistics classroom. The Mathematics Educator, 25(1), 32-55.
  • Piesch, H., Gaspard, H., Parrisius, C., Wille, E., & Nagengast, B. (2020). How can a relevance intervention in math support students' career choices? Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology, 71, 101185. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2020.101185

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection is the principle of deliberately examining one's experience, reasoning, performance, or progress in order to extract lessons and guide future action. It is most valuable when it is tied to decisions, evidence, or revision rather than open-ended rumination.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Reflection improves learning when it turns a past action or judgment into evidence for a better next move. Learners are more likely to regulate effectively when they examine what happened against a visible standard and decide what to change Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]. The key design constraint is specificity: vague reflection prompts often produce generic recap, while focused prompts tied to evidence, strategy, or revision are more likely to shape future performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A recent experience, performance, or decision to examine
  • Prompts that focus attention on evidence, strategy, or next steps
  • A way to use the reflection in future action

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Vague prompts produce superficial answers
  • Reflection without follow-through can become performative

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners building self-awareness, judgment, and adaptive strategy use.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve transfer, self-monitoring, and future performance.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Metacognition
  • Self-Regulated Learning

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — reflection is most useful when it helps learners evaluate current performance and choose a stronger next action

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Purposeful Reflection
  • Metacognition

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Post-task reflection that identifies one strong move, one weak move, and one next adjustment.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Schon, D. A. (1983). The reflective practitioner. Basic Books.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflective practice is the principle of examining actions, decisions, and outcomes in order to improve later performance.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Reflective practice matters most in domains where improvement depends on interpreting experience rather than merely repeating procedures. The principle assumes that performance alone does not automatically generate learning. Learners and practitioners need a structured way to revisit what happened, name why it happened, and decide what to change next, and reflective practice is strongest when learners compare performance to explicit goals or criteria Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]. Reflection also benefits from focusing on process changes rather than only end results Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M], and from explaining reasoning in enough detail that future action can actually improve Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]. Reflection becomes powerful when it is tied to future action; it becomes weak when it remains generic, purely expressive, or disconnected from the next attempt.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A meaningful action, performance, or experience to examine — reflection needs an actual event, artifact, or decision sequence as its object
  • Prompts or structures for analysis — without guidance, reflection often stays descriptive rather than analytic
  • A path from reflection to revision — the goal is not only insight but a changed next move

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Reflection without action can stall — learners may become better at describing experiences without improving future performance
  • Unstructured reflection often stays superficial — vague prompts invite generic self-report rather than evidence-based analysis
  • The timing matters — some reflection is strongest immediately after performance, while some benefits from later distance and comparison

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in practicum, project, writing, studio, professional, or performance-based settings
  • Learners developing judgment and adaptive expertise rather than only discrete procedures
  • Practitioners expected to improve through cycles of action and review

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve judgment, adaptation, and future performance
  • Increase metacognitive awareness about decisions and outcomes
  • Build habits of evidence-based self-review rather than impressionistic self-report

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Reflection — reflective practice is one of the most direct applications of the broader reflection principle
  • Self-Regulated Learning — reflection supports self-monitoring, evaluation, and tactical adjustment
  • Metacognition — reflective practice makes internal reasoning, criteria, and blind spots more visible

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Deliberate Practice — qualifies that reflection alone is not enough unless it is paired with repetition, feedback, and another attempt

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — reflective practice is stronger when learners compare performance to explicit goals or criteria
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — reflection often benefits from focusing on process changes rather than only end results
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — explaining one’s reasoning can deepen the learning value of reflection beyond simple description

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Reflection — reflective practice is a performance-anchored form of reflection
  • Purposeful Reflection — emphasizes that reflection should be directed toward usable insight and next steps
  • Self-Regulated Learning — supplies the mechanism by which reflection informs future action

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Reflective Practice
  • LDA Reflection

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Reflective Practice — A structured cycle of action, analysis, adjustment, and re-application.

Video-Based Reflection — Learners review a recording of their own performance, identify decision points, and name one concrete change for the next attempt.

Post-practicum or post-clinical debriefs — Learners examine what happened in a professional situation, identify the reasoning behind their actions, and plan a better response for the next similar case.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Schon, D. A. (1983). The reflective practitioner. Basic Books.
  • Boud, D., Keogh, R., & Walker, D. (Eds.). (1985). Reflection: Turning experience into learning. Kogan Page.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reinforcement theory is the principle of shaping behavior by making desired responses more likely through contingent consequences such as feedback, reward, or progression. It is useful when the design goal is to stabilize specific performance patterns.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
Reinforcement theory is strongest when the instructional goal is to increase the frequency, reliability, or stability of a clearly observable behavior. It assumes that consequences matter: responses followed by useful reward, recognition, progression, or other positive consequences become more likely, while unsupported or unrecognized responses tend not to stabilize. In learning design, reinforcement often appears in immediate correctness feedback, progress signals, badges, mastery gates, or explicit acknowledgment of successful performance. It tends to work better when success criteria are explicit Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S], when progress is visible enough to sustain productive behavior Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M], and when novice learners are reinforced around process and execution rather than distant outcomes alone Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. Its main limitation is that it explains persistence of behavior more easily than depth of understanding.

Behavioral scientists draw a sharp distinction between a positive consequence (something pleasant delivered to encourage a behavior — smiles, praise, prizes) and a genuine positive reinforcer (a consequence demonstrably shown to increase the frequency of the target behavior). Praising a student's punctuation is a positive consequence; it only qualifies as a positive reinforcer once records actually show the student's correct punctuation increasing as a result. The same distinction applies on the punishment side: a negative consequence (something unpleasant delivered after misbehavior — scolding, response cost, exclusion) is only a genuine punisher if it demonstrably reduces the target behavior's frequency; scolding that produces short-term remorse but no lasting behavior change is a negative consequence, not a punisher, and its continued use should be reassessed rather than repeated on the assumption that it "should" be working.

The expert practice of positive reinforcement is a demanding, multi-step commitment, not simply praising good behavior when noticed: (1) baseline measurement of the specific target behavior, (2) assessment of what actually functions as a reinforcer for this learner, (3) immediate, continuous delivery of the reinforcer contingent on the target behavior, and (4) a planned, gradual fading of the reinforcer — ideally toward a natural reinforcer rather than indefinite extrinsic delivery. Most informal classroom reward systems (snack time, weekly awards, popcorn parties) skip most of these steps and so do not constitute reinforcement in this technical sense, even though they may still have other beneficial effects.

Negative reinforcement — removing an aversive condition after a desired behavior, which increases that behavior's likelihood — is illustrated by Thorndike's puzzle-box cats, who learned to pull an escape cord more quickly on each trial because doing so ended their confinement. Teachers rarely deliberately arrange negative reinforcement (doing so requires first placing a student in an unpleasant situation, which runs against a general preference for positive, nonaversive techniques — Donnellan & LaVigna, 1990), but they frequently trigger it inadvertently: a student wanting to escape difficult work, a dull exercise, or a teacher perceived as unfair may complain, refuse work, or disrupt class to delay or avoid it, and a teacher who responds by changing the assignment or removing the student to the hallway has just negatively reinforced that avoidance behavior. This "negative reinforcement trap" is suspected by some applied behavior analysts (Iwata, 1987) to account for more learned inappropriate classroom behavior than positive reinforcement does — see the Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model for the fuller antecedent/behavior/consequence framework this trap sits within.

When punishment is used, research identifies similar conditions for it to function as an effective punisher rather than an ineffective negative consequence: (1) precise identification and baseline measurement of the target behavior, (2) precise identification of an alternative, positive behavior to reinforce in its place, (3) assessment of the most effective potential punisher before using it, (4) consistent, immediate reinforcement and punishment on a continuous schedule until both the target and alternative behaviors change, and (5) fading of both the reinforcer and the punisher once the behavior change is established (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 1987; Sulzer-Azaroff & Mayer, 1986). Punishment paired with reinforcement of an alternative behavior produces fewer emotional side effects (fear, avoidance, anxiety) than punishment used alone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Observable responses — reinforcement works best when the desired behavior can be identified and responded to
  • Consistent contingent consequences — the consequence needs to follow the target behavior closely enough that the connection is legible

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• External rewards can crowd out intrinsic reasons for engagement if overused — see the overjustification effect [-M], strongest when reward is tied piecemeal to output rather than delivered at a flat rate, and on tasks that are not already well-defined with a clear performance standard
  • Reinforcement is weaker for complex conceptual change than for routine behavior shaping
  • Inconsistent consequences can train the wrong thing — learners may respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the teacher intended

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners building habits, routines, and reliable response patterns
  • Learners in environments where visible progress, immediate feedback, or performance cues shape participation
  • Learners acquiring foundational fluencies before deeper strategic flexibility is expected

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Strengthen desired performance patterns and routines
  • Increase reliable responding, persistence, and accuracy on defined tasks
  • Make successful learning behaviors more likely to recur

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Behaviorist learning theory — consequences shape the likelihood of future responding
  • Behaviorism — reinforcement theory is one of the clearest consequence-based learning principles
  • Game-Based Learning — many game-like environments operationalize reinforcement through progression and reward systems

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Self-Determination Theory — external consequences can support behavior, but may weaken autonomy and intrinsic motivation if poorly designed

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Rewarding an already-intrinsically-motivating activity can reduce future engagement with it [-M] — the clearest documented case where adding reinforcement backfires
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — reinforcement is often more effective when success criteria are explicit and challenging
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — visible progress and consequences can help learners notice and sustain productive behaviors
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — novice learners may respond better when reinforcement is tied to process and execution rather than distant outcomes only

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Behaviorism — the broader performance-shaping orientation that reinforcement theory helps explain
  • Game-Based Learning — often operationalizes reinforcement through progress systems, rewards, and challenge
  • Mastery Learning — can use contingent progression as a consequence structure
  • Token Economies — a structured classroom-scale application of secondary (token) reinforcers
  • Conditioning Natural Reinforcers — the fading step in the expert practice of positive reinforcement, transferring control to intrinsic reinforcers
  • Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model — the applied-behavior-analysis framework for identifying what a reinforcement plan should actually target, including the negative-reinforcement trap

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Immediate correctness feedback — Learners receive rapid confirmation or correction after a response, making successful patterns easier to repeat.

Mastery gating and progression systems — Learners unlock later tasks only after demonstrating successful performance on earlier ones.

Recognition of productive routines — A classroom explicitly reinforces completion of planning, checking, and revision behaviors that support later performance.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Skinner, B. F. (1953). Science and human behavior. Macmillan.
  • Schunk, D. H. (2012). Learning theories: An educational perspective (6th ed.). Pearson.
  • Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (1987). Applied behavior analysis. Merrill.
  • Sulzer-Azaroff, B., & Mayer, G. R. (1986). Achieving educational excellence: Using behavioral strategies. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
  • Iwata, B. A. (1987). Negative reinforcement in applied behavior analysis: An emerging technology. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 20(4), 361-378.
  • Donnellan, A. M., & LaVigna, G. W. (1990). Alternatives to punishment: Solving behavior problems with non-aversive strategies. Irvington.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behaviorism in the classroom. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Retrieval practice is the principle of strengthening learning by having learners actively recall information, ideas, or procedures from memory rather than only restudy them. It is useful when the goal is durable retention and easier future access.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Retrieval practice works because the act of remembering strengthens future access better than passive review alone. The design implication is to build in frequent recall opportunities, preferably spaced over time and followed by feedback when correctness matters. Difficult retrieval can be productive, and even high-confidence errors can improve retention once corrected High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S], but retrieval demands need to stay calibrated so learners are challenged without getting lost or simply rehearsing mistakes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Questions or prompts that require recall
  • Sufficient spacing or repetition for retrieval to matter
  • Feedback when accuracy is important

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Retrieval without feedback can reinforce errors
  • Very difficult retrieval can become discouraging if learners lack enough support

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve retention, fluency of recall, and transfer through repeated remembering.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Testing-effect research.
  • Metacognition

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors. [~S] — retrieval becomes especially memorable when confident mistakes are corrected clearly after recall

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Spaced Learning
  • Immediate Feedback

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A biology course opens each lesson with short no-notes prompts that ask learners to explain last week’s concepts before new content begins.
  • A language app revisits previously learned vocabulary with delayed recall items and immediate corrective feedback rather than only offering rereading.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249-255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rhetorical skill development is the principle of helping learners craft arguments, communicate persuasively, respond to audiences, and use language strategically for effect. It is useful when learning goals include persuasion, rebuttal, explanation, or public argument.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Rhetorical skill development matters when learning requires more than having ideas; learners also need to shape those ideas for an audience, purpose, and context. The principle treats communication as strategic rather than neutral. Strong rhetorical instruction helps learners consider evidence, audience expectation, stance, organization, and delivery together, and Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. suggests that learners improve when they are asked to articulate why a rhetorical move works rather than merely imitate it. For novices, Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. also supports teaching concrete drafting and revision moves before judging only the final persuasive impact. Its central risk is superficial polish: persuasive style can be mistaken for strong argument if learners are not also held to standards of evidence and reasoning, and Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. supports routines that ask learners to check audience fit, evidence quality, and structure while revising.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A communicative purpose and audience — rhetorical skill grows when learners must write or speak for someone and for some purpose
  • Criteria for effective argument or persuasion — learners need explicit standards for credibility, organization, evidence, and response to opposition

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Rhetorical performance without evidence can become style without substance
  • Audience awareness is hard to teach abstractly — learners need real or realistic communicative situations
  • Performance pressure can narrow experimentation — learners may need low-stakes rehearsal before public or graded rhetorical tasks

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners writing arguments, making presentations, debating, or explaining to audiences
  • Learners in humanities, civics, writing, communication, and disciplinary argument settings
  • Learners who need to strengthen not only what they say, but how they frame and support it

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Improve persuasive communication, argument quality, and audience awareness
  • Help learners connect evidence, structure, and rhetorical strategy
  • Build the ability to respond to counterargument, purpose, and audience expectation

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Epistemic Cognition — rhetorical quality depends on how claims are warranted and justified
  • Perspective-Taking — effective rhetoric requires anticipating audience positions and responses
  • Peer Learning — rhetorical skill often develops through critique, rehearsal, and response from others

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Behaviorism — repeated performance can improve delivery routines, but rhetorical quality depends on judgment and audience adaptation, not habit alone

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S] — learners often strengthen rhetorical quality by explaining and justifying their reasoning explicitly
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — rhetorical novices often improve more when instruction targets process moves than when it focuses only on final persuasive impact
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — rhetorical performance improves when learners monitor audience, structure, and evidence quality against criteria

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Epistemic Cognition — strong rhetoric depends on how claims are justified, not just how they sound
  • Perspective-Taking — audience adaptation is one of the main rhetorical demands
  • Debate — debate often provides a high-pressure environment for developing rhetorical strategy and rebuttal

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Argument writing with audience revision — Learners revise a claim or essay after considering what a skeptical reader would question or need clarified.

Debate and rebuttal routines — Students practice using evidence strategically, anticipating counterargument, and adjusting language for persuasive effect.

Presentation critique with rhetorical criteria — Peers or instructors give feedback on clarity, organization, evidence use, and audience adaptation rather than on style alone.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Toulmin, S. (2003). The uses of argument (Updated ed.). Cambridge University Press.
  • Graff, G., & Birkenstein, C. (2021). They say / I say (5th ed.). W. W. Norton.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding provides temporary, contingent support to learners as they develop new skills or knowledge. Fading is the systematic and gradual removal of those supports as the learner gains competence, leading to independent performance and the transfer of responsibility.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Scaffolding and fading work because novices often need temporary support to perform productively, but that support only remains helpful when it responds to actual learner need Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S]. The long-term aim is transfer of responsibility, so support has to be reduced as competence grows Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S]. If scaffolds remain too long they can create redundant load or dependency, and if they disappear too early they can trigger overload or failure. The design problem is calibration, not just support provision.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Contingency (Diagnosis): The instructor or system must constantly assess the learner's current performance to provide support only when and where it is needed Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S].
  • Transfer of Responsibility: The goal is always the internalization of the skill, not just the completion of the task Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S].
  • Variety of Scaffolds: Supports can include think-aloud modeling, worked examples, hints, or coaching.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Expertise Reversal: Scaffolding that remains in place for an expert can cause redundant cognitive load and hinder performance Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows..
  • Over-Scaffolding: Support that is too high or not faded quickly enough can lead to learner dependence.
  • Premature Fading: Withdrawing support before the learner has developed the necessary internal schemas can lead to cognitive overload and failure.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice Learners: Benefit from high-fidelity scaffolding during initial skill acquisition to manage intrinsic load Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S].
  • Learners in the "Zone of Proximal Development": Scaffolding is specifically designed to support learners as they tackle tasks just beyond their independent capability.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Complex Skill Acquisition: Learning to perform integrated, multi-step tasks.
  • Problem-Solving: Developing the ability to navigate ill-structured or novel challenges.
  • Self-Regulation: Learning to monitor and adjust one's own performance as external scaffolds fade.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky) — the distance between what a learner can do unassisted and what they can do with guidance.
  • Cognitive Load Theory — scaffolding manages extraneous load for novices; fading prevents redundant load for experts Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+M].
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship — utilizes modeling, coaching, and scaffolding/fading as core instructional methods.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+S] — support is most effective when it adapts to the learner’s current difficulty instead of staying fixed
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S] — the purpose of scaffolding is growing independence, so support should be withdrawn deliberately as competence develops

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Worked Examples — often the first stage in a scaffolded sequence.
  • Chunking — breaking the task into units that can be individually scaffolded.
  • Modeling — a type of scaffold where expert performance is demonstrated.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Khan Academy Hints — Provides on-demand, progressive hints that scaffold a problem-solving task; the learner is encouraged to use fewer hints as they progress.
  • Codecademy Completion Problems — Initially provides full code examples, then transitions to "fill-in-the-blank" code, and finally to independent coding challenges.
  • Faded Worked Examples — A sequence where the first problem is fully worked, the second is half-worked, and the third is a full problem to solve.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89–100. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.1976.tb00381.x
  • van de Pol, J., Volman, M., & Beishuizen, J. (2010). Scaffolding in teacher–student interaction: A decade of research. Educational Psychology Review, 22(3), 271–296. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9127-6
  • Renkl, A., Atkinson, R. K., Maier, U. H., & Staley, R. (2002). From example study to problem solving: Smooth transitions help learning. Instructional Science, 30(4), 293–308. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016027302995

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding & Fading is the short-form canonical target for designs that provide temporary support and then reduce it as learner independence grows.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Scaffolding and fading matter when learners are expected to perform work they cannot yet do independently but can accomplish with the right support. The principle is not simply “help, then stop helping.” Support has to be calibrated to need, and Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. supports adapting help to learner performance rather than fixing it in advance. The reduction of support also has to respond to evidence of growing capability. Too much support held too long creates dependency and redundancy, which is consistent with Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases.. Too little support or premature fading destabilizes performance before the learner has a workable schema or routine, while Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. supports heavier early guidance for novices.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Temporary support tied to learner need — hints, prompts, models, partial solutions, or structure must actually help the learner perform beyond current independent capacity
  • A plan to reduce that support over time — the design needs a path from guided performance to increasing independence

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Too much or too little support at the wrong time undermines learning
  • Support cannot stay generic forever — fading depends on evidence about learner progress
  • Not all supports fade the same way — some are reduced in amount, some in specificity, and some by shifting responsibility to the learner

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices learning new procedures, concepts, or complex performances
  • Learners who can succeed with support but are not yet ready for full independence
  • Learners in environments where guided practice is a bridge to later autonomous work

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Support transition from guided to independent performance
  • Reduce unproductive search while preserving learner responsibility
  • Build confidence and competence through calibrated release of support

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Scaffolding and Fading — the fuller principle page that this short-form canonical page points to
  • Scaffolding — explains why support is needed during early learning
  • Cognitive Load Theory — support and fading can reduce overload early and avoid redundancy later

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Self-Determination Theory — support should still preserve autonomy and growing ownership rather than feel controlling

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — support is stronger when it adapts to learner performance rather than staying fixed
  • Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M] — guidance becomes redundant as expertise grows, so fading is essential
  • Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M] — early support can reduce blind search for novices before independence develops

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding — the broader principle of temporary support during learning
  • Guided Practice — often provides the instructional context in which fading happens
  • Procedural Learning — many procedural tasks depend on fading from modeled or prompted performance to independence

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Fading Scaffolding — Hints, prompts, or partial steps become shorter, less specific, or less frequent as competence grows.

Merrill's First Principles — Learners move from activation and demonstration toward application with progressively less support.

Worked example to independent problem sequence — Learners first study or complete a heavily supported version, then solve increasingly less scaffolded problems on their own.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Renkl, A., Atkinson, R. K., Maier, U. H., & Staley, R. (2002). From example study to problem solving: Smooth transitions help learning. Instructional Science, 30(4), 293-308. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016027302995
  • van de Pol, J., Volman, M., & Beishuizen, J. (2010). Scaffolding in teacher-student interaction: A decade of research. Educational Psychology Review, 22(3), 271-296. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9127-6

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding is the principle of providing temporary support that helps learners perform beyond what they could do independently. This page serves as the canonical short-form target for links that refer to scaffolding without explicitly naming fading or transfer of responsibility.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Scaffolding is useful when learners can succeed with support but not yet on their own. Well-calibrated prompts, hints, models, or partial structures can improve learning when they respond to the learner’s actual bottleneck Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M]. The design consequence is that scaffolding should be temporary: support that never fades can reduce independence, while support withdrawn too early can overload the learner Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task slightly beyond independent reach
  • Support calibrated to the learner's current need
  • A plan to reduce support over time

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Over-scaffolding can create dependence
  • Premature withdrawal can trigger overload

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners building new concepts, procedures, or complex performances.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Support successful performance while developing independence.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Sociocultural and apprenticeship traditions.
  • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [+M] — support helps most when it is matched to the learner’s current difficulty
  • Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner. [+S] — effective scaffolds are designed to hand more of the task back to the learner over time

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Scaffolding and Fading

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Hints, worked examples, modeling, and coaching that are reduced as competence grows.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89-100. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.1976.tb00381.x

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-determination theory is used here as a principle emphasizing autonomy, competence, and relatedness as conditions that support motivation.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Self-determination theory is most useful in learning design when motivation, persistence, and ownership matter as much as immediate task completion. The core idea is not simply “give learners freedom.” It is that learners are more likely to engage deeply when instruction supports three needs at once: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Competence support is especially important because Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. suggests that clear, appropriately challenging goals can strengthen effort when learners believe progress is possible. Poorly designed autonomy can feel like abandonment, and Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. supports giving learners visible ways to track whether their choices are working. Relatedness without challenge can become pleasant but low-demand, while Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. suggests that early competence is often built best through manageable process goals rather than pressure to prove mastery immediately. The principle is strongest when autonomy, competence, and relatedness are treated as interdependent.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Some meaningful learner agency — autonomy support requires real choices, voice, or rationale, not just cosmetic options
  • A path to felt competence — learners need feedback, support, and task design that makes progress visible and attainable
  • Relational support and belonging — the environment must communicate that the learner is known, respected, and part of a meaningful social setting

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Choice without support can weaken competence — too much freedom too early can create anxiety or avoidance
  • Controlling structures can reduce ownership — excessive compliance pressure may produce short-term task completion while undermining deeper engagement
  • Motivation is not solved by relevance language alone — learners also need success experiences and relational trust

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners whose engagement depends on a strong sense of agency, progress, and belonging
  • Learners recovering from repeated failure, compliance-only schooling, or disengagement
  • Adolescents and adults balancing external demands with internal goals

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Increase sustained engagement and persistence
  • Strengthen learner ownership of goals and effort
  • Improve motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness together

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-Determination Theory — provides the clearest conceptual basis for the autonomy–competence–relatedness triad
  • Learner Choice — one practical route to autonomy support
  • Engagement — SDT helps explain why some learners invest effort and others withdraw or comply minimally

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Explicit Instruction — qualifies that structure is not the opposite of autonomy; clear guidance can support competence when it is not controlling

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — competence grows when goals are clear and challenging, but the motivational effect depends on learner commitment and support
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — visible progress strengthens competence and helps learners act on goals
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — process goals can support competence for novices more effectively than pressure to hit outcomes immediately

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Motivation — SDT is one of the strongest explanatory frameworks for why motivation rises or falls
  • Engagement — autonomy, competence, and relatedness often determine whether learners actually participate and persist
  • Learner Choice — one of the most visible ways to operationalize autonomy support

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Learner Choice — Learners select among meaningful tasks or products while still working toward shared goals, increasing ownership without removing structure.

Strengths-Based Approach — Instruction emphasizes existing capabilities and growth, which can reinforce felt competence and willingness to engage.

Game-Based Learning — Well-designed game systems can support competence through visible progress, autonomy through branching choices, and relatedness through social play or shared challenges.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The "what" and "why" of goal pursuits. Psychological Inquiry, 11(4), 227-268.
  • Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2020). Self-determination theory: Basic psychological needs in motivation, development, and wellness. Guilford Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-directed learning is the principle of helping learners plan, monitor, and manage important parts of their own learning process.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Self-directed learning is most valuable when learners are expected to take meaningful responsibility for goals, resources, pacing, or evaluation rather than simply comply with a fixed sequence. The principle does not mean abandoning structure. It means designing supports that let learners make consequential decisions while still receiving enough guidance to avoid drift, confusion, or false confidence. Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. supports making progress visible through check-ins, trackers, or reflection prompts rather than assuming learners will monitor themselves reliably. For many learners, the challenge is not willingness but capability: planning, monitoring, and revising are themselves learned behaviors, and Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. suggests that novices often need process-level guidance before autonomy becomes productive. Self-direction also works better when goals are concrete and demanding enough to organize effort, which is consistent with Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals..

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Learner agency over some part of the learning process — learners need real decisions to make about goals, resources, strategies, sequencing, or products
  • Structures for planning and monitoring — self-directed learning depends on visible goals, progress indicators, reflection prompts, or check-ins rather than freedom alone
  • Support for evaluation and adjustment — learners need ways to judge whether their chosen path is working and what to change next

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Many learners need scaffolds before they can direct learning effectively — weak planning, monitoring, or help-seeking can turn freedom into frustration
  • Choice without criteria can create drift — learners may select easy, familiar, or low-value paths unless quality expectations are explicit
  • Uneven prior knowledge changes what autonomy is productive — some learners can self-direct immediately; others need a gradual release

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Adolescents, adults, and advanced learners expected to manage parts of their own learning process
  • Learners in project-based, inquiry-based, or asynchronous environments where planning and persistence matter
  • Learners building autonomy after a period of heavier instructional support

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Build learner ownership, planning, and strategic control
  • Improve the ability to set goals, choose resources, and monitor progress
  • Support transfer from externally structured learning to increasingly independent learning

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-Regulated Learning — self-directed learning depends on the learner’s ability to plan, monitor, and revise actions over time
  • Learner Choice — meaningful choice is one of the practical mechanisms that makes self-direction possible
  • Self-Determination Theory — autonomy can increase motivation when paired with competence support and relatedness

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory — too much open responsibility too early can overload novices who do not yet have stable schemas or routines for self-management

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — self-directed learning is stronger when learners can compare progress against visible goals or criteria
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — novice learners often need process-level guidance before they can self-direct effectively toward outcomes
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — self-direction is more productive when learners set clear and appropriately challenging goals rather than vague intentions

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Self-Regulated Learning — provides the mechanism-level account of how learners plan, monitor, and revise
  • Learner Choice — one of the most visible design levers for enabling self-direction
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring — helps operationalize self-direction through explicit plans and progress checks

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text: • Self-Directed Learning

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Self-Directed Learning — A course pattern in which learners set goals, select resources, monitor progress, and review outcomes within a structured environment.

Choice Boards — Learners choose among aligned tasks or products, but the board still anchors those choices to learning goals and expectations.

Independent inquiry with scheduled checkpoints — Learners pursue a question or project of their choice, but must submit plans, progress updates, and self-assessments at defined intervals so autonomy is paired with accountability.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Knowles, M. S. (1975). Self-directed learning. Association Press.
  • Garrison, D. R. (1997). Self-directed learning: Toward a comprehensive model. Adult Education Quarterly, 48(1), 18-33. https://doi.org/10.1177/074171369704800103

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Self-monitoring is the practice of checking one's current understanding, performance, strategy use, or progress against a goal, model, or success criterion. It turns learning from something that merely happens to the learner into something the learner actively observes and adjusts. In instruction, self-monitoring matters because learners rarely improve from effort alone; they improve when they notice what is working, what is not, and what to change next.

Self-monitoring can be applied to reading comprehension, writing, math problem solving, behavior, pacing, attention, or persistence. It is strongest when learners have explicit criteria and some realistic action they can take in response to what they notice. Without that structure, requests to "monitor yourself" often collapse into vague self-report rather than useful regulation.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Self-monitoring improves learning because effort becomes more useful when learners can compare current performance to a target and respond while the task is still in progress Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]. Clear goals also matter: learners monitor more accurately when they know what success looks like and what counts as progress Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]. For novices, self-monitoring often needs process cues and structured checkpoints before it becomes accurate or efficient Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M]. Without those supports, “monitor yourself” often collapses into vague self-report.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear criteria or goals: Learners need a target, rubric, checklist, model, or success condition to compare against.
  • Visible checkpoints: Monitoring works better when learners pause at defined moments rather than wait until the end.
  • A strategy menu: Learners need concrete next moves they can use if they detect a problem.
  • Feedback compatibility: Self-monitoring is stronger when external feedback confirms, challenges, or sharpens learner judgment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Weak criteria produce weak monitoring: If expectations are fuzzy, learners cannot evaluate accurately.
  • Monitoring overload: Too many checklists or interruptions can break flow and increase task burden.
  • Inaccurate self-judgment: Novices may overestimate or underestimate performance without modeling and calibration.
  • No action path: Monitoring does little if learners cannot revise, seek help, or change strategy afterward.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners building self-regulation: Strong fit when the goal is more independent, strategic learning.
  • Learners prone to rushing or disengaging: Monitoring can slow impulsive responding and increase persistence.
  • Learners in reading, writing, and math tasks: These domains benefit from regular comprehension and strategy checks.
  • Adult learners managing complex demands: Monitoring helps learners balance effort, time, and confidence across competing responsibilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Metacognitive control: Noticing comprehension, confusion, and strategy effectiveness during learning.
  • Performance improvement: Catching errors earlier and revising before the task is complete.
  • Goal progress tracking: Comparing current work to a desired standard over time.
  • Independent learning habits: Reducing reliance on constant instructor correction.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Self-regulated learning — self-monitoring is one of the central performance-phase processes in regulated learning.
  • Metacognitive perspectives — learners improve when they evaluate understanding and strategy use during a task, not only afterward.
  • Feedback theory — external feedback becomes more useful when learners are already comparing current performance to a target.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring is not the same as introspection; it works best when tied to observable criteria and actionable decisions.
  • Learners often need modeling, calibration, and prompts before self-monitoring becomes accurate or efficient.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — learners regulate better when they regularly check their understanding or performance against a target
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S] — monitoring works better when the learner has a clear, challenging standard to compare against
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [~M] — beginners often need concrete monitoring routines tied to process, not only end-state outcomes

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Goal Setting & Monitoring — monitoring depends on having a target worth tracking.
  • Formative Assessment — monitoring improves when learners receive evidence about current performance.
  • Purposeful Reflection — reflection often uses self-monitoring data to plan next steps.
  • Guided Practice — learners often need coached monitoring before doing it independently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Reading check stops: Learners pause after a section to summarize, note confusion, and choose a repair strategy.
  • Writing revision checklist: Learners compare a draft against criteria before submitting it for feedback.
  • Math accuracy monitoring: Learners check whether units, operations, and solution reasonableness match the problem.
  • Attention or pacing tracker: Learners log focus intervals, interruptions, or work completion during independent study.

docs.text:
• Bol, L., Campbell, K. D. Y., Perez, T., & Yen, C. J. (2016). The effects of self-regulated learning training on community college students' metacognition and achievement in developmental math courses. Community College Journal of Research and Practice, 40(6), 480-495. https://doi.org/10.1080/10668926.2015.1068718
  • Cho, K., Cho, M. H., & Hacker, D. J. (2010). Self-monitoring support for learning to write. Interactive Learning Environments, 18(2), 101-113. https://doi.org/10.1080/10494820802602670
  • Farrell, A., & McDougall, D. (2008). Self-monitoring of pace to improve math fluency of high school students with disabilities. Behavior Analysis in Practice, 1(2), 26-35. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03391729
  • Ghanizadeh, A. (2017). The interplay between reflective thinking, critical thinking, self-monitoring, and academic achievement in higher education. Higher Education, 74(1), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-016-0031-y

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-regulated learning is the principle of designing instruction so learners can plan, monitor, adjust, and reflect on their own learning processes. This page serves as the principle-level target for references that emphasize learner control and strategic regulation.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Self-regulated learning improves when instruction makes planning, monitoring, and adjustment visible and actionable rather than assuming learners will do these things on their own. Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. supports building routines in which learners compare current performance with criteria, interpret feedback, and decide what to change next. Learners who regularly monitor progress and interpret feedback are more likely to adapt strategies effectively, but most learners need explicit prompts, models, and structures before these habits become reliable. The design move is to externalize regulation first, then gradually hand more of it to the learner.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear goals or standards
  • Feedback or evidence learners can interpret
  • Opportunities to adjust strategy

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners often need explicit support to regulate well

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve planning, persistence, monitoring, and revision.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Self-Regulated Learning

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — Explicit progress checks and comparison to criteria improve learners’ ability to adjust strategy, effort, and help-seeking.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Metacognition
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A writing course uses planning checklists, mid-draft self-ratings, and revision memos so learners can monitor progress against clear criteria.
  • An online math platform asks learners to predict difficulty, check performance after practice, and choose the next support option based on that reflection.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Zimmerman, B. J. (2002). Becoming a self-regulated learner. Theory Into Practice, 41(2), 64-70. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15430421tip4102_2

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-regulation is the short-form canonical target for instructional designs that help learners plan, monitor, and adjust behavior, effort, and strategy over time.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Self-regulation becomes more likely when learners have clear goals, usable feedback, and explicit opportunities to interpret what is or is not working. Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. makes the core design implication unusually direct: learners need visible checkpoints and criteria so they can decide whether to persist, revise, or seek support instead of repeating the same approach. In practice, this means designing reflection prompts and decision moments rather than treating regulation as an invisible personal trait.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clear goals or standards
  • Feedback or signals learners can use
  • Opportunities to adjust strategy or effort

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners often need explicit supports before self-regulation becomes reliable

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Strengthen planning, persistence, monitoring, and adaptive adjustment.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Self-Regulated Learning

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — Prompting learners to monitor progress against goals improves adaptive adjustment and strategic control.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Metacognition
  • Goal Setting & Monitoring

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A project-based course requires weekly progress checks in which learners compare current work to rubric criteria and select one concrete adjustment for the next week.
  • A reading intervention asks learners to pause after each section, rate comprehension, and decide whether to reread, annotate, or ask for clarification.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Zimmerman, B. J. (2002). Becoming a self-regulated learner. Theory Into Practice, 41(2), 64-70. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15430421tip4102_2

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sequencing is the principle of arranging instructional content, tasks, or supports in an order that helps learners build understanding progressively. It is useful when learning depends on the order in which complexity, support, and ideas are introduced.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Sequencing matters because the same content can feel coherent or overwhelming depending on the order in which learners meet it. Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. supports breaking material into meaningful units so early encounters do not overload working memory, and Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. suggests that staged complexity can help novices before full-task integration. The implication for design is to order instruction around dependency and readiness rather than convenience, then revisit or reorder supports as learners become more capable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A rationale for order based on dependency, complexity, or learner readiness
  • Transitions that connect one stage to the next

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Poor sequencing can overload learners or leave key prerequisites unstated

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Support cumulative understanding and reduce avoidable confusion.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Scaffolding
  • Cognitive Load Management

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S] — Grouping information into meaningful units reduces working-memory strain and makes progressive ordering more manageable.
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~S] — Practicing components before full-task performance can reduce overload for novices when tasks are highly complex.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Holistic Learning
  • Mastery Learning

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A statistics unit starts with interpreting distributions, then moves to sampling, and only later introduces inference once learners can reason about variation.
  • A carpentry course teaches tool setup and key subskills before asking learners to complete a full cabinet build, then integrates the pieces into a whole-task performance.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Reigeluth, C. M. (1979). In search of a better way to organize instruction. Journal of Instructional Development, 2(3), 8-15.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Simulations and immersive virtual environments let learners practice decisions, procedures, and interpretations inside a designed representation of reality. Their value is not novelty by itself. They are useful when they make otherwise inaccessible experiences visible, repeatable, safer, or more manipulable than the real setting would allow. Good simulations help learners coordinate knowledge, perception, and action under conditions that resemble authentic performance.

These environments can support motivation and transfer because learners are doing something closer to the eventual task, not merely hearing about it. At the same time, simulation quality varies widely. If the interface is confusing, the scenario is unrealistic, or the task lacks debriefing and feedback, the medium can add distraction without improving learning.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Simulations and immersive environments work when they let learners rehearse meaningful whole performances under conditions that are safer, cheaper, or more repeatable than real life Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]. They are especially useful for novices when complexity is staged and support is available Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M], and when coaching or debriefing responds to how the learner actually performed Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. High fidelity alone is not enough: if the interface is confusing or the scenario misrepresents the real task, the medium adds distraction rather than transfer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task worth simulating: The simulation should represent decisions, dynamics, or constraints that matter in real performance.
  • Guidance and debriefing: Learners need framing before the experience and reflection or feedback after it.
  • Usable interface and access: Technical barriers should not consume the cognitive resources needed for learning.
  • Alignment with real practice: The environment should preserve the important structure of the task, not only its surface features.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Technology overload: Rich media can increase extraneous load if navigation, controls, or visuals are poorly designed.
  • False authenticity: Simulations that oversimplify key variables can mislead learners about real practice.
  • Equity and access barriers: Devices, bandwidth, motion sensitivity, and disability access all shape usefulness.
  • No transfer bridge: Learners may enjoy a simulation without generalizing from it unless instructors make the connections explicit.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners preparing for complex applied performance: Useful when practice in the full real setting is costly, risky, or unavailable.
  • Novices who need safe rehearsal: Simulations can provide repeatable attempts before real-world consequences are introduced.
  • Learners benefiting from multimodal representation: Spatial, procedural, and interactive tasks may become easier to perceive and test.
  • Adult and professional learners: Strong fit for workforce, technical, clinical, and community-based scenarios.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Applied decision making: Practicing judgments under realistic constraints.
  • Procedural fluency in context: Coordinating multiple steps or cues inside a meaningful scenario.
  • Transfer to performance settings: Moving from training conditions to authentic application.
  • Reflection and revision: Using debriefing to improve later decisions or strategies.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Experiential learning perspectives — learning strengthens when learners act, observe consequences, and reflect.
  • Situated learning perspectives — performance is easier to transfer when it is learned in context-rich conditions.
  • Multimedia and cognitive load perspectives — simulations can support learning when information is integrated clearly and unnecessary complexity is controlled.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• More immersion is not automatically better; fidelity only helps when it supports the learning objective.
  • Simulations should often be sequenced from simpler to more complex cases, especially for novices.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S] — realistic, integrated task rehearsal can prepare learners for later application better than abstract explanation alone
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — simulations are stronger when facilitation targets the learner’s actual decision or performance breakdowns
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [~M] — novices often need simplified or staged practice before full simulation complexity becomes productive

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Experiential Learning — simulations provide structured experiences that later reflection can interpret.
  • Problem-based Learning — many simulations organize learning around decisions in realistic scenarios.
  • Immediate Feedback — simulations are more effective when consequences and coaching are visible.
  • Guided Practice — novice learners often need supported runs before independent performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Clinical decision simulator: Learners diagnose, prioritize, and respond to a changing patient scenario.
  • Virtual workplace rehearsal: Learners practice safety, customer interaction, or troubleshooting in a modeled environment.
  • Civic or historical simulation: Learners make decisions within a constrained system and analyze outcomes.
  • Goal-Based Scenarios (GBS)
