docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Several closely related models help teachers and designers judge the effect a specific use of technology is having on instruction, rather than whether technology is used at all (Kimmons, 2018):

  • RAT (Hughes, Thomas, & Scharber, 2006) — technology use either Replaces a prior practice with no discernible change in outcomes, Amplifies learning that was already occurring, or Transforms learning in ways that were not previously possible.
  • SAMR (Puentedura, 2003) — Substitution (a direct tool swap, no functional change), Augmentation (a small functional improvement), Modification (a significant redesign of the task), or Redefinition (the task becomes possible only because of the technology). SAMR splits RAT's single "amplify" level into two (augmentation vs. modification), giving finer-grained distinction between small and large functional improvements.
  • PIC-RAT (Kimmons, 2018) — crosses RAT's teacher-facing question (is the technology used to Replace, Amplify, or Transform prior practice?) with a second, learner-facing question: what is the student's relationship to the technology — Passive, Interactive, or Creative? Plotting both questions on a grid distinguishes, for example, a teacher merely projecting notes instead of writing on a chalkboard (Passive-Replace) from students creating and publishing a collaborative writing blog (Creative-Transform).

The shared claim across all three models is that low-value technology integration substitutes for a prior practice with no functional change, while high-value integration uses the technology to do something that was previously impossible — and that most classroom technology use starts, and often stays, in the low-value quadrant unless teachers are deliberately pushed to reconsider it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An existing (or imaginable) non-technology version of the task, so that "replace" vs. "amplify/transform" has a clear point of comparison
  • Willingness to redesign the task itself, not just swap tools, to reach the higher (transform/redefine) levels

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• These are heuristic, self-assessment frameworks, not empirically validated learning-outcome predictors — a "transformative" use of technology is not guaranteed to produce better learning outcomes than a well-designed "substitution" use; the framework describes the kind of change, not its educational value in a given context
  • Provides no guidance on which content/pedagogy/technology combination to choose in the first place — see TPACK for that prior decision

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Not learner-facing; a self-assessment tool for teachers and designers reflecting on their own technology choices

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not a learning objective — a design heuristic for evaluating whether a planned or existing use of technology is worth the investment relative to a non-technology alternative

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • TPACK — TPACK informs which technology, pedagogy, and content combination to choose; SAMR/RAT/PIC-RAT then evaluates the effect of that choice

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A history teacher moving class notes from a chalkboard to a PowerPoint slide — Passive-Replace on the PIC-RAT grid
  • Students producing and publishing a collaborative creative-writing blog that solicits peer, parent, and public feedback — Creative-Transform on the PIC-RAT grid

docs.text:

(Eds.), Proceedings of Society for Information Technology & Teacher Education International Conference 2006 (pp. 1616–1620).
  • Puentedura, R. R. (2003). A matrix model for designing and assessing network-enhanced courses [Unpublished].

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Text chats use live or near-live written exchange as a learning space for discussion, coordination, questioning, and low-stakes composition. They are useful because they blend social interaction with writing practice: learners have to formulate ideas for an audience, respond to others, and keep pace with an unfolding conversation. In some contexts, chats also lower the participation threshold for learners who are less ready to speak aloud in front of a group.

Text chats are not just casual add-ons. They can serve instructional purposes such as brainstorming, peer response, vocabulary practice, clarification during presentations, and collaborative sense-making. Their value depends on prompt quality, facilitation, and whether the pace of the chat matches the linguistic and cognitive demands placed on learners.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Text chats are useful when they create a lower-stakes written channel for learners to ask questions, respond to peers, and make thinking visible in real time. They can support monitoring and clarification because learners are able to check others’ responses against their own understanding as the exchange unfolds Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. The design challenge is pace: when too many threads move at once, chats can overload attention and require more facilitation, prompting, and responsive support to stay productive Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]. Chats help most when the prompt is focused and the moderator keeps participation legible.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear communicative purpose: Chats should be tied to discussion, questioning, synthesis, or coordination, not just activity for its own sake.
  • Prompting and moderation: Learners need structures that keep the exchange focused and inclusive.
  • A manageable pace: Fast chats can overwhelm learners if too many threads compete at once.
  • Norms for participation: Instructors should make expectations visible for turn-taking, respect, and response quality.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Cognitive overload: Real-time text can strain attention, working memory, and language processing.
  • Surface participation: Without good prompts, chats can stay reactive and shallow.
  • Access and typing barriers: Device access, keyboarding speed, and digital familiarity affect participation.
  • Miscommunication risk: Tone, brevity, and lag can create misunderstanding without facilitation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who benefit from low-stakes written interaction: Chats can support participation before or alongside formal writing.
  • Multilingual learners: Text chat can create more processing time than oral discussion while still supporting interaction.
  • Learners in online or blended settings: Strong fit for synchronous and asynchronous remote participation.
  • Learners developing discussion habits: Chats help practice response, questioning, and audience awareness.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Informal written communication: Building fluency in short-form audience-aware writing.
  • Collaborative meaning-making: Using peers' ideas to refine one's own thinking.
  • Questioning and clarification: Surfacing confusion and requesting explanation in real time.
  • Participation and belonging: Expanding who gets to contribute in discussion-centered learning.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Social constructivist perspectives — learners build understanding through interaction, dialogue, and shared sense-making.
  • Collaborative learning perspectives — knowledge can be strengthened through peer exchange and negotiated meaning.
  • Connectivist perspectives — networked communication tools can support learning through connection and distributed interaction.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Text chat is not automatically inclusive; pace, access, and language demands can still exclude learners.
  • Chat works best for focused exchange, not for every deep discussion or extended explanation.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — live written exchange can help learners compare their understanding with others and adjust quickly
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — chat discussions often need active prompting and moderation to remain focused and useful

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion — text chat is one medium for structured peer exchange.
  • Authentic Audiences & Purposes — chats give learners immediate audiences for communication.
  • Multimodal Instruction — text chat adds a written interaction mode alongside oral or visual channels.
  • Speech-to-text — dictation tools can help some learners participate in chat-based environments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Discussion Prompt
  • Discussion Group
  • Backchannel during presentation: Learners post questions, examples, and clarifications while a lesson is in progress.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Heafner, T., & Plaisance, M. (2014). Exploring synchronous text chat in remotely delivered early field experiences. Journal of Interactive Learning Research, 25(3), 327-352.
  • Lin, H. (2015). A meta-synthesis of empirical research on the effectiveness of computer-mediated communication in SLA. Language Learning & Technology, 19(2), 85-117.
  • Payne, J. S., & Whitney, P. J. (2002). Developing L2 oral proficiency through synchronous CMC: Output, working memory, and interlanguage development. CALICO Journal, 20(1), 7-32. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v20i1.7-32
  • Tare, M., Golonka, E. M., Vatz, K., Bonilla, C. L., Crooks, C., & Strong, R. (2014). Effects of interactive chat versus independent writing on L2 learning. Language Learning & Technology, 18(3), 208-227.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Text-to-speech (TTS) converts written text into spoken audio, giving learners an additional way to access reading materials, instructions, and feedback. It is useful when decoding, visual fatigue, pace, or attention barriers make print alone harder to process. TTS can widen access to content, support rereading, and help learners coordinate listening with visual text.

TTS is most effective when it is treated as an access and support tool, not as a substitute for all reading instruction. Learners still need support in comprehension, vocabulary, annotation, and independent meaning-making. The tool helps when it removes unnecessary access barriers so that the learner's effort can shift toward understanding and using the content.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Text-to-speech is most useful when reading access, not conceptual ability, is the main barrier to engagement. By shifting part of the processing burden from print decoding to coordinated listening and reading, TTS can make dense text more manageable Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S]. But its value depends on active use: learners still need to pause, replay, annotate, and monitor comprehension rather than letting audio wash over them Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]. TTS works best as an access support inside a broader reading routine, not as a substitute for strategy instruction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A genuine access need or comprehension benefit: TTS is most useful when audio support reduces barriers to engaging with text.
  • Learner control over pacing: Playback speed, pausing, replay, and chunking are important for usefulness.
  • Appropriate text selection: Dense, technical, or lengthy text often benefits most from supported listening.
  • Integration with comprehension routines: TTS should be paired with note-taking, annotation, questioning, or discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Passive listening risk: Audio alone does not guarantee active comprehension.
  • Voice quality and pronunciation issues: Synthetic voices may distort meaning, especially with domain-specific vocabulary.
  • Not equally helpful for every learner or task: Some learners comprehend better through print, and some tasks require close visual attention.
  • Access without strategy: TTS can remove one barrier while leaving comprehension problems untouched if instruction does not adapt.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with reading-access barriers: Strong fit for learners with decoding difficulty, visual impairment, or reading fatigue.
  • Learners processing dense academic text: Audio support can help learners sustain engagement with long or complex materials.
  • Multilingual learners: TTS can support pronunciation, listening, and vocabulary access when paired with text.
  • Adult learners balancing speed and stamina: Listening while following print can help learners manage effort and persistence.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Access to print-based content: Making written materials more usable.
  • Reading comprehension support: Helping learners stay with text long enough to make meaning.
  • Independent study habits: Enabling learners to use audio support strategically outside class.
  • Engagement with feedback and instructions: Making written guidance easier to revisit and process.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Dual-channel and multimedia perspectives — coordinated visual and auditory presentation can support processing when designed carefully.
  • Cognitive load perspectives — audio support can reduce some access burdens and free attention for comprehension.
  • Accessibility and universal design perspectives — multiple representations increase the likelihood that learners can engage with the material.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• TTS is not automatically beneficial; poor pacing, low-quality synthesis, or passive use can limit comprehension.
  • The tool supports access, but it does not replace explicit reading strategy instruction.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [~S] — audio support can reduce some of the access burden that print alone places on working memory
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M] — TTS is strongest when learners actively check and regulate comprehension while listening

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax — simpler language and audio support often work together.
  • Instructor Accessibility — TTS is one route for improving access to written materials.
  • Annotating — learners can combine audio playback with highlighting, notes, and questions.
  • Speech-to-text — reading and writing access tools often complement one another.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Read-aloud support for assigned text: Learners listen while following along in the print version.
  • Audio review of instructor feedback: Written comments are revisited through TTS so learners can process them more carefully.
  • Chunked listening routine: Learners pause after each paragraph or section to summarize and annotate.
  • Pronunciation-supported vocabulary review: Learners use TTS to hear unfamiliar academic language while reading it.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Hillaire, G., Iniesto, F., & Rienties, B. (2019). Humanising text-to-speech through emotional expression in online courses. Journal of Interactive Media in Education, 2019(1), 12. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.510
  • Podsiadlo, M., & Chahar, S. (2016). Text-to-speech for individuals with vision loss: A user study. In Interspeech 2016 (pp. 347-351). https://doi.org/10.21437/Interspeech.2016-1289
  • Stodden, R. A., Roberts, K. D., Takahashi, K., Park, H. J., & Stodden, N. J. (2012). Use of text-to-speech software to improve reading skills of high school struggling readers. Procedia Computer Science, 14, 359-362. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2012.10.041
  • Wood, S. G., Moxley, J. H., Tighe, E. L., & Wagner, R. K. (2018). Does use of text-to-speech and related read-aloud tools improve reading comprehension for students with reading disabilities? A meta-analysis. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 51(1), 73-84. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416688170

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
TPACK (Koehler & Mishra, 2009) extends Shulman's concept of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) — the specialized knowledge of how to teach a particular subject — by adding technology as a third interacting knowledge domain. Teaching with technology is treated as an ill-structured problem: there is no single best way to integrate a given technology into a curriculum, because content, pedagogy, and technology constrain and reshape one another differently in every classroom context.

The framework names three core knowledge domains — Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), and Technology Knowledge (TK) — and the knowledge that emerges at their intersections: Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) (how to teach a specific subject), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK) (how technology and content shape and constrain each other — e.g., how carbon-14 dating changed archaeology), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) (how teaching and learning change when a given technology is used in a given way, independent of subject matter), and TPACK itself — the emergent understanding of how to teach a specific subject, using specific pedagogical approaches, with specific technologies, in a specific classroom context. Digital technologies complicate this more than older tools because they are "protean" (usable in many ways), unstable (rapidly changing), and opaque (their inner workings are hidden), unlike a pencil or a chalkboard (Koehler & Mishra, 2009).

TPACK is not additive — a teacher cannot be TPACK-competent by separately mastering content, pedagogy, and technology. What matters is the ability to flexibly navigate the interactions between all three as they play out in a specific, dynamic classroom context; a change in any one factor has to be compensated for by changes in the other two.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A specific content area, pedagogical approach, and technology considered together, rather than technology adopted as a generic "add-on"
  • Designer or teacher fluency in reasoning about the interactions among the three domains, not just competence in each domain separately

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Technology Knowledge is inherently unstable and dates quickly, so TPACK is not a one-time competency but requires ongoing re-integration as tools change
  • Provides a diagnostic lens for why technology integration succeeds or fails, but does not by itself prescribe which technology to choose — see Technology Integration Levels (SAMR / RAT / PIC-RAT) for frameworks that evaluate the effect of a specific choice

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and instructional designers making decisions about which technology to use for a specific content area and pedagogical goal

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not a learner-facing objective — a designer/teacher competency: producing technology-integrated instruction that is well-matched to both the content and the pedagogical goal, rather than technology used for its own sake

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Builds directly on Shulman's (1986, 1987) construct of Pedagogical Content Knowledge, extending it to include technology as a third interacting domain

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • Technology Integration Levels (SAMR / RAT / PIC-RAT) — a complementary framework for judging the effect a specific technology choice is having, once a TPACK-informed choice has been made

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing simulation software over a static diagram because it lets students manipulate variables a way the content and the pedagogical goal (inquiry-based understanding of a process) both call for
  • A whiteboard used differently in a teacher-led lecture (front of room, teacher-controlled) versus a brainstorming session (open to all, focal point for negotiation) — same technology, different TPK depending on pedagogical intent

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Koehler, M. J., & Mishra, P. (2009). What is technological pedagogical content knowledge? Contemporary Issues in Technology and Teacher Education, 9(1), 60–70. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/tpack
  • Mishra, P., & Koehler, M. J. (2006). Technological pedagogical content knowledge: A framework for integrating technology in teacher knowledge. Teachers College Record, 108(6), 1017–1054.
  • Shulman, L. S. (1986). Those who understand: Knowledge growth in teaching. Educational Researcher, 15(2), 4–14.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Transfer of learning is the principle of helping learners apply what they have learned in one context to new tasks, situations, or problems. It is useful when instruction aims beyond immediate performance toward later use and adaptation.

Mechanistically, learners store propositions (basic units of knowledge) in long-term memory; when new information enters working memory, long-term memory is searched for associations that combine with it, reinforcing the new information and helping assign it meaning. Learning that occurs across varying contexts creates more of these associative links and encourages generalization of the skill or knowledge (Schunk, 2004), building an associative network learners can draw on for future problem-solving (Souza, 2016). Information in memory is, in this sense, "flexible, interpretive, generically altered, and its recall and transfer are largely context-dependent" (Helfenstein, 2005).

docs.title: Transfer Taxonomy
docs.text:
Transfer takes several distinct forms (Schunk, 2004):

Type Characteristics Positive Prior learning assists new learning Negative Prior learning hinders or interferes with new learning Zero Prior learning has no influence on new learning Near Many elements overlap between the original learning conditions and the new situation Far The new situation is very different from the one in which learning occurred Literal The skill is performed exactly as learned, in a new situation Figural General knowledge is applied to a new situation, often via analogy or metaphor Low-road Well-established skills transfer spontaneously, even automatically High-road The learner consciously and deliberately ("mindfully") evaluates the new situation and applies prior learning to it Forward-reaching High-road transfer in which learners think about possible other uses while learning Backward-reaching High-road transfer in which learners, in a new situation, think back to previous situations that might apply

docs.title: Factors Affecting Transfer
docs.text:
Souza (2016) identifies four factors that shape how well transfer occurs: context and degree of original learning (how well the learner acquired the knowledge in the first place), similarity (commonalities between the original learning and the new situation, including environmental and memory cues), critical attributes (the characteristics that make something unique and thus recognizable across contexts), and association (connections among multiple events, actions, and pieces of information, including the conditions and emotions the learner attaches to them). Learners increase transfer through effective practice and by mindfully abstracting knowledge — examining experience for similarities via methods such as seeking underlying principles, building models, and identifying analogies and metaphors.

Transfer is less a deliberate act by the learner than a product of the learning environment; teachers, as part of that environment, are themselves an instrument of transfer, for better or worse (Souza, 2016). See Hugging and Bridging for Transfer for two concrete teacher techniques (building situational similarity, and building abstraction/connection) aimed directly at promoting positive transfer.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Transfer of learning improves when learners encounter underlying structure across varied contexts rather than mastering only one narrow version of a task. Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. supports keeping the integrated logic of performance visible when the goal is later adaptation rather than isolated success. Whole-task performance, comparison across examples, and prompts that make general principles explicit are especially useful because they help learners see what should carry over when surface details change. The practical implication is to design for variation and abstraction, not just successful completion in the original setting.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Tasks that vary context while preserving underlying structure
  • Prompts that make generalizable principles visible

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Transfer is weak when learning stays tied to one narrow context

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Improve flexible use of knowledge beyond the original learning setting.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Analogical Reasoning
  • Cognitive Flexibility

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [+S] — Learners transfer more effectively when they practice integrated tasks that preserve the structure of later performance.

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Experiential Learning
  • Problem-based Learning
  • Educational Readiness — mastery of prerequisite skills (a form of readiness) is itself one of the factors that determines how well new learning transfers

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• After learning a proportional reasoning strategy in recipes, learners apply the same structure to map scales, probability tables, and budgeting scenarios.
  • A nursing program asks learners to practice the same clinical reasoning routine across different patient cases so they generalize decision patterns rather than memorize one script.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Perkins, D. N., & Salomon, G. (1992). Transfer of learning. International Encyclopedia of Education.
  • Schunk, D. H. (2004). Learning theories: An educational perspective (4th ed.). Pearson.
  • Souza, D. A. (2016). How the brain learns (5th ed.). Corwin Press.
  • Helfenstein, S. (2005). Transfer: Review, reconstruction, and resolution. University of Jyväskylä.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher's perspectives on learning. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Walker (2008) asked in-service and preservice teachers to identify characteristics of their most effective teachers — "effective" meaning teachers who made the most significant and positive impact on their lives. Twelve characteristics emerged from those responses:

  1. Prepared. Ready for each class, prioritizing time on task; students report that learning feels easy because time passes quickly while they're engaged.
  2. Positive. Optimistic about teaching and about students, available to students, communicating about progress, giving praise, and supporting students to respond positively to one another.
  3. Hold High Expectations. Hold the highest standards and believe all students can be successful, challenging students to do their best and building their confidence.
  4. Creative. Resourceful and inventive, doing things outside the norm to keep students engaged and motivated.
  5. Fair. Fair in handling students and grading, giving equal opportunity and clear, consistent expectations — while recognizing that not all students learn the same way, so "fair" does not necessarily mean treating everyone identically.
  6. Display a Personal Touch. Approachable and personally connected with students, sharing experiences and taking a genuine interest in them.
  7. Cultivate a Sense of Belonging. Project that the classroom is where they want to be, and make students feel welcome and comfortable there too.
  8. Compassionate. Concerned about students' academics as well as their personal issues, showing sensitivity and compassion.
  9. Have a Sense of Humor. Make learning fun and don't take everything seriously, using humor while teaching and in difficult situations.
  10. Respect Students. Give and earn the highest respect, avoid deliberately embarrassing students, and address sensitive issues privately.
  11. Forgiving. Forgive students for inappropriate behavior, don't hold grudges, and refuse to give up on difficult students.
  12. Admit Mistakes. Admit when wrong and apologize for mistakes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Willingness to treat "effectiveness" partly as a matter of disposition and relationship, not only instructional technique — these characteristics are largely about how a teacher relates to students rather than which method they use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The framework is derived from retrospective student and teacher accounts of who was memorable and impactful, not from a controlled study linking these traits to measured learning outcomes — treat it as a bottom-up description of what students value, not as validated causal evidence

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teacher preparation programs and individual teachers reflecting on which of these characteristics they already display and which need deliberate development

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • A teacher-student relationship durable enough to support learning even where a specific instructional technique is imperfect

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• NBPTS Five Core Propositions for Accomplished Teaching — a complementary, standards-body framework covering overlapping ground (commitment to students, equitable treatment) from a top-down direction
  • Set a High Bar for Each Student — operationalizes characteristic 3 (Hold High Expectations)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A teacher who privately, rather than publicly, addresses a student's behavior or grade concerns (characteristic 10)
  • A teacher who is transparent with a class after making a grading or instructional error (characteristic 12)

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Walker, J. (2008). Twelve characteristics of an effective teacher: A longitudinal, qualitative, quasi-research study of in-service and pre-service teachers' opinions. Educational Horizons. Retrieved from https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ815372.pdf
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). The nature of teaching. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Universal Design for Learning borrows its core idea from architecture: just as modern public buildings build in ramps, automatic doors, and braille signage from the start rather than adding them only when a specific need arises, UDL holds that accessibility features (text-to-speech, speech-to-text, adjustable font size and color contrast, dictionaries and glossaries) should be built into educational hardware and software by default (U.S. Office of Educational Technology, 2016). The framework specifies three principles:

  1. Multiple means of representation — content should be accessible in more than one way (digital books, screen readers with text-to-speech, adjustable color contrast and text size, selectable reading levels).
  2. Multiple means of expression — learners should have more than one way to demonstrate and express what they know (writing, online concept mapping, speech-to-text).
  3. Multiple means of engagement — multiple activity or content options for a given competency, plus opportunities for increased collaboration or scaffolding, to sustain interest and motivation.

In practice, Rose and Meyer's (2002) own recommended classroom tactics span several concrete moves: using varied methods to present content (case studies, music, role-play, cooperative learning, hands-on activities, field trips, guest speakers) alongside varied materials (online resources, video, podcasts, manipulatives, e-books); giving explicit cognitive support — organizing cues ("I've explained the four main points; now I'll summarize them"), non-lecture background material (images, artifacts, video), and scaffolds like syllabi, outlines, and study guides; addressing multiple learning styles by pairing oral and written instructions and building movement into lessons; and offering flexible assessment formats (visual or oral presentation, not only written response). Assessment flexibility matters beyond UDL's own framing, too: conventional assessment methods can seriously underestimate what a student with a disability actually knows, since a fixed format may test an unrelated barrier (holding a pencil, hearing a question clearly, marking an answer within a time limit) rather than the target competency (Koretz & Barton, 2003/2004; Pullin, 2005) — reminding a visually impaired student to "look closely at the board" doesn't help them see it, and only adds anxiety. Portfolios (a collection of student work demonstrating development over time, with reflective commentary), regular informal observation notes, and recruiting a teaching assistant to administer brief individual assessments are all documented ways to supplement conventional testing without redesigning it from scratch (Carothers & Taylor, 2003; Wesson & King, 1996) — though using a different assessment format for some students than others does raise real fairness questions about whether the resulting grades are genuinely comparable.

Because these features are built in for everyone rather than retrofitted for a labeled subgroup, UDL avoids segregating learners with disabilities into visibly separate materials, and in practice benefits far more learners than the specific accessibility need that originally motivated a given feature (e.g., captions help learners in noisy environments or those still acquiring the language of instruction, not only learners who are deaf or hard of hearing). Districts that have adopted UDL as an organizing framework report substantial outcomes: Bartholomew Consolidated School Corporation (Columbus, Indiana) reported an 8-percentage-point graduation-rate increase for general-education students and a 22-point increase for special-education students after adopting a universal design approach district-wide, alongside increases in Advanced Placement participation and pass rates.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Content and assessment formats designed with built-in flexibility (alternate representations, alternate response modes, activity choice) from the start of development, not added afterward for specific learners
  • Institutional commitment to select or build tools around UDL's three principles rather than single-format defaults

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• UDL asks for flexibility to be designed in upfront, which is more design effort at the outset than a single-format default, even though it reduces later retrofit cost per learner
  • Multiple means of engagement/expression still need to converge on the same underlying competency — offering many formats is not itself a guarantee that each format assesses the same construct fairly

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• All learners by design, though the framework was developed with learners who have disabilities in mind — the "curb-cut effect" (a feature built for one group benefiting many others) is central to its rationale
  • Learners for whom a single representation or response format would otherwise be a barrier unrelated to the actual competency being assessed (e.g., a learner who understands content but struggles with a specific reading level or motor-input method)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Any objective where the specific format of representation or response is not itself the target competency — i.e., most academic and skill objectives, where the goal is understanding or performance, not "ability to use this particular interface"

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text: • User-Centered Design for Learning — both concern building interface/format flexibility into learning technology by default; UCD focuses on usability and cognitive load broadly, UDL specifically on representation/expression/engagement options for accessibility

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Nimble Tools — delivers standard assessments with embedded accommodations (custom keyboard overlays, text-to-speech, sign-language avatar, image magnification) built into the same underlying instrument
  • Bartholomew Consolidated School Corporation's district-wide UDL adoption, associated with substantial graduation-rate gains for both general- and special-education students

  • Rose, D. H., & Meyer, A. (2002). Teaching every student in the digital age: Universal design for learning. Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development.
  • Gray, T., & Silver-Pacuilla, H. (2011). Breakthrough teaching and learning: How educational and assistive technologies are driving innovation. Springer.
  • Koretz, D., & Barton, K. (2003/2004). Assessing students with disabilities: Issues and evidence. Educational Assessment, 9(1-2), 29-60.
  • Pullin, D. (2005). Accommodations for students with disabilities in large scale testing: An evidentiary approach. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 31(4), 21-33.
  • Carothers, D., & Taylor, R. (2003). How teachers and administrators rank the effectiveness of selected inclusive practices. Journal of Instructional Psychology, 30(2), 168-175.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Learning technologies fail not only when the pedagogy is wrong, but when the interface itself creates barriers — a learner who cannot find an assignment or navigate a confusing menu is paying a cognitive cost that has nothing to do with the content being taught (Earnshaw, Tawfik, & Schmidt, 2018). Usability describes how easily an interface can be used as intended; user experience (UX) is the broader "person's perceptions and responses that result from the use... of a product, system, or service" (ISO, 2010). User-centered design (UCD) is the practice of centering users' needs and mental models throughout the design process rather than treating the interface as an afterthought to the pedagogy.

The connection to instructional design runs directly through Cognitive Load Theory: a poorly designed interface — confusing navigation, unfamiliar terminology, inconsistent layout — increases extraneous cognitive load, which competes with the working-memory resources a learner needs for germane, schema-building processing. Distributed cognition and activity theory extend the picture to collaborative and tool-mediated settings, treating knowledge as distributed across people and artifacts rather than held only in an individual mind.

UCD proceeds iteratively: identifying user needs (often via personas — detailed fictional users built from real interview/observation data), gathering requirements, and building prototypes of increasing fidelity — from paper prototypes (fast, cheap, focused on navigation and workflow, not visuals) to wireframes (layout, no visual polish) to functional prototypes (interactive, close to final). At each stage, evaluation methods appropriate to that fidelity level are used: ethnography and focus groups early (front-end analysis), card sorting to align navigation with users' mental models, heuristic evaluation (e.g., against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics) and cognitive walkthroughs during prototyping, and think-aloud studies, A/B testing, or eye-tracking once a functional prototype exists.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Access to real (or representative) users for needs identification, persona-building, and evaluation — UCD's evidence base comes from data about actual users, not designer assumptions
  • An iterative process budget: UCD assumes multiple rounds of prototyping and revision rather than a single build-then-ship cycle

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Adds design and evaluation overhead relative to skipping usability work entirely; the investment pays off mainly when the interface is complex, novel, or used repeatedly by many learners
  • Usability improvements reduce extraneous load but do not by themselves improve the pedagogical design of the content — the two are complementary, not substitutes

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Any learner using a digital interface to access instruction, but the payoff is largest for novices unfamiliar with the interface's conventions, and for accessibility-dependent learners (e.g., users with autism, as in eye-tracking studies of facial-expression-identification interfaces)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not a content objective — a precondition for reliably measuring content learning at all: if learners cannot navigate the interface, learning-outcome data is confounded by usability failures

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory [+M] — extraneous cognitive load from a poorly designed interface directly competes with the working-memory resources needed for germane processing
  • Distributed cognition and activity theory — extend the picture from an individual user's cognitive load to knowledge distributed across people, tools, and artifacts in collaborative or workplace learning contexts

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Scaffolding and Fading — both concern how much support structure a learner needs and when it should be reduced, though scaffolding targets content mastery while UCD targets interface usability
  • Cone of Experience (Concrete-to-Abstract Media Selection) — both concern deliberate media/interface choice, though UCD addresses usability rather than concreteness/abstraction

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Building a persona from user interviews before designing a course's navigation structure
  • Paper prototyping a course's menu structure and running an open card sort to check it against learners' own mental categories
  • A heuristic evaluation of an LMS course page against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics before launch

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Earnshaw, Y., Tawfik, A. A., & Schmidt, M. (2018). User experience design. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/user_experience_design
  • Nielsen, J. (1994). Heuristic evaluation. In J. Nielsen & R. L. Mack (Eds.), Usability inspection methods (pp. 25–62). Wiley.
  • International Organization for Standardization. (2010). Ergonomics of human-system interaction — Part 210: Human-centred design for interactive systems (ISO 9241).

docs.title: Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment
Description
docs.text:
Validity is "the evaluation of the adequacy and appropriateness of the interpretations and uses of assessment results" for a given group (Linn & Miller, 2005, p. 68) — crucially, validity describes the interpretation and use of a result, not the assessment procedure itself. A mathematics test on fractions given to recent immigrants might validly assess a fluent-English student's understanding of fractions while invalidly assessing a limited-English student's (whose low score may just as easily reflect English proficiency as math skill). Validity is a matter of degree, not an all-or-nothing property, and rests on three kinds of evidence: content validity (does the assessment actually cover the content and tasks it's supposed to, in the right proportions?) — a Table of Specifications, cross-tabulating content areas against instructional objectives with a planned item count in each cell, is the standard tool for checking this before writing a test, since it makes over-sampled and under-sampled content visible in advance; construct validity (is performance actually explained by the intended underlying construct — e.g., mathematical reasoning or reading comprehension — rather than by an irrelevant factor like test anxiety, English proficiency, or reading speed that happens to be entangled with it?); and criterion-related (predictive) validity (does the assessment actually predict the outcome it's meant to predict — e.g., do fall-semester reading scores actually predict which students will need help passing the spring state test?). Effective assessment design in general depends on aligning the assessment technique to the actual learning goal: if the goal is for students to conduct an experiment, the assessment should have them conduct one, not answer questions about conducting one.

Validity and reliability apply beyond classroom assessment to measurement generally, including research instruments measuring constructs — personality traits, emotional states, attitudes, and abilities that can't be observed directly, either because they're tendencies rather than constant states (being "highly extroverted" doesn't mean acting extroverted at this exact moment) or because they involve internal processes like thoughts or feelings. Reliability itself breaks down into three distinct kinds of consistency: over time (test-retest reliability), across items measuring the same thing (internal consistency), and across different raters or researchers (interrater reliability). Crucially, reliability does not entail validity: a kitchen scale that is miscalibrated will consistently under- or overestimate a weight — highly reliable, since the same amount poured on produces the same reading each time, but not valid, since the reading is wrong. Any valid measure is, by necessity, reliable; the reverse does not hold.

Reliability is the consistency of a measurement (Linn & Miller, 2005) — would a student's score be similar if the test were given on a different day, with different items from the same content domain, or graded by a different rater? Perfect consistency is never realistic, since memory, attention, fatigue, and anxiety all fluctuate, and even trained raters vary somewhat scoring the same essay or performance. But reliability is not fixed — three concrete levers raise it: more tasks or items (a single confusing item drags down a 5-item test's score by 20 percent, but only 2 percent on a 50-item test, so more items dilute the effect of any one chance factor); clearer directions and item wording (ambiguity forces guessing about what's actually being asked, which is noise, not signal); and clearer scoring criteria (the less a score depends on which rater happened to grade it, the more reliable it is).

Freedom from bias means the assessment method or its administration doesn't distort a student's measured performance because of personal characteristics like gender, ethnicity, or social class (Popham, 2005). Two distinct forms matter for classroom assessment specifically: offensiveness (negative stereotypes embedded in the assessment itself — e.g., a health-class item where all the doctors are men and all the nurses are women — can distract or disengage the students the stereotype targets, degrading their measured performance for reasons unrelated to the content); and unfair penalization (an item disadvantages a group not through offense but through differential background experience — e.g., a math item assuming familiarity with American football disadvantages recent immigrants unfamiliar with the sport, or a teamwork item using a symphony orchestra as its reference point is easier for students from families who attend concerts). Unfair penalization is a real, specific failure mode, distinct from simply "some students doing worse" — asking about a sport actually covered in a physical-education class isn't unfair penalization, since the relevant knowledge was taught in class rather than assumed from outside background.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit awareness that validity is a property of an interpretation, not of the test itself — the same test can support a valid conclusion for one group of students and an invalid one for another
  • A Table of Specifications or equivalent planning tool used before writing test items, not as an after-the-fact check
  • Enough items or tasks, in a content domain, to dilute the effect of any single confusing or unrepresentative item

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A test can be highly reliable (very consistent) while still being invalid for a given interpretation — reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity
  • Reducing extraneous factors that inflate or deflate a score (anxiety, unfamiliar language, reading speed) improves construct validity specifically, and is a design responsibility, not just a scoring one
  • Bias review by developers from varied backgrounds and statistical item analysis both help, but do not fully eliminate content or format bias — see Standardized Test Fairness and Bias for documented cases that survive this kind of review

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students; unfair penalization and offensiveness specifically affect students whose background, culture, or social class differs from the assumptions embedded in an assessment's content or framing

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Assessment results that support the specific instructional or accountability conclusion being drawn from them, rather than results that are merely consistent or merely convenient to score

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Criterion- and Norm-Referenced Testing — validity and reliability apply to standardized as well as teacher-made assessments, with additional considerations
  • Research Data Collection Methods — the same reliability/validity distinction, applied to research instruments and constructs rather than classroom assessments specifically
  • Standardized Test Fairness and Bias — documented, large-scale cases of the bias and validity failures this principle describes in general form
  • Assessment for Learning — validity and reliability are prerequisites for assessment evidence to be trustworthy enough to act on

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Selected-Response Assessment Items — trades some validity for high reliability, since objective scoring removes rater variation but constrains what can be assessed
  • Constructed-Response Assessment Items — the reverse tradeoff: broader validity for complex goals, at real risk to reliability without a rubric or model answer

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Linn, R. L., & Miller, M. D. (2005). Measurement and assessment in teaching (9th ed.). Pearson.
  • Popham, W. J. (2005). Classroom assessment: What teachers need to know (4th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Selecting high-quality assessments; Methods of data collection. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Video replay analysis uses recorded performance, instruction, or interaction as an object for review. Learners or instructors pause, revisit, and analyze moments that would otherwise pass too quickly to examine. This makes it possible to notice decisions, patterns, cues, and missed opportunities with much more precision than relying on memory alone.

The principle is especially valuable for performance domains where timing, communication, physical execution, or situational judgment matter. Replay creates distance from the original event, which can support more accurate reflection and discussion. Its usefulness depends on focus: simply watching video again is less powerful than analyzing it against a question, standard, or goal.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Video replay analysis is powerful because it gives learners a stable record of performance instead of relying on memory alone. Replay can strengthen self-monitoring by making discrepancies between intention and action more visible Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M], and it becomes especially useful when learners have to explain what happened and why Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S]. Replay rarely teaches on its own, though; insight depends on analytic focus, pause-and-discuss structure, and responsive coaching that helps learners interpret what they are seeing Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear analytic focus: Learners need to know what they are looking for in the replay.
  • Pause-and-discuss opportunities: Video is most useful when learners can stop, annotate, compare, or explain key moments.
  • Feedback or debrief structure: Replay analysis works best when paired with coaching, self-explanation, or guided reflection.
  • Psychological safety: Reviewing one's own performance requires norms that keep critique specific and constructive.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Replay without criteria: Watching video repeatedly without a lens often produces shallow commentary.
  • Overemphasis on surface features: Learners may focus on visible details and miss underlying reasoning.
  • Performance anxiety: Self-video can feel exposing or threatening without careful framing.
  • Technical and privacy barriers: Recording, storage, and access need to be handled responsibly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners in performance-heavy domains: Strong fit for teaching, speaking, clinical, technical, athletic, and workplace practice.
  • Learners developing metacognitive awareness: Replay can help learners notice habits they miss in the moment.
  • Learners benefiting from concrete evidence: Video gives a shared object for discussion instead of relying on vague recall.
  • Adult and professional learners: Useful when improvement depends on analyzing authentic practice.

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Self-assessment and reflection: Noticing strengths, errors, and alternatives in one's own performance.
  • Performance improvement: Identifying specific moments to revise in later attempts.
  • Reasoning about practice: Connecting visible action to intention, decision making, and outcomes.
  • Feedback literacy: Learning to interpret evidence and use critique productively.

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Metacognitive and self-regulated learning perspectives — replay supports monitoring, evaluation, and revision.
  • Multimedia learning perspectives — video can preserve multiple cues that learners can revisit and integrate.
  • Reflective practice traditions — practitioners improve when they examine concrete records of action.

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Replay analysis needs focus and facilitation; video by itself does not guarantee insight.
  • Learners may need to analyze others before analyzing themselves if self-review is too cognitively or emotionally demanding at first.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M] — replay makes it easier for learners to compare actual performance to intended performance
  • Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [~S] — explaining specific replay moments can deepen understanding of what went right or wrong
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M] — guided questioning and feedback help learners extract more from replay than unguided rewatching

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Purposeful Reflection — replay provides concrete evidence for reflection instead of relying on memory alone.
  • Immediate Feedback — replay can make feedback more specific and discussable.
  • Self-monitoring — video helps learners compare what they intended with what they actually did.
  • Multimodal Instruction — replay adds a visual and auditory record that learners can revisit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Reflection
  • Feedback
  • Teaching practicum replay: Candidates pause classroom footage to analyze questioning, pacing, or responses to learners.
  • Presentation review: Learners examine a recorded talk to identify clarity, structure, and delivery choices.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Baecher, L., & McCormack, B. (2015). The impact of video review on supervisory conferencing. Language and Education, 29(2), 153-167. https://doi.org/10.1080/09500782.2014.994528
  • Dovigo, F. (2020). Through the eyes of inclusion: An evaluation of video analysis as a reflective tool for student teachers within special education. European Journal of Teacher Education, 43(1), 110-126. https://doi.org/10.1080/02619768.2019.1693993
  • Nagro, S. A. (2020). Reflecting on others before reflecting on self: Using video evidence to guide teacher candidates' reflective practices. Journal of Teacher Education, 71(4), 420-433. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022487119872700
  • Tripp, T. R., & Rich, P. J. (2012). The influence of video analysis on the process of teacher change. Teaching and Teacher Education, 28(5), 728-739. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tate.2012.01.011

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Problems vary along two related dimensions: how much of the information needed for a solution is actually given, and how many (and how clear) the rules or procedures for reaching a solution are. A well-structured problem provides most of the needed information and can, in principle, be solved with relatively few clearly understood rules — the word problems common in math classes are a classic example, since everything needed is contained in the stated problem and the solution procedure is relatively clear and precise. An ill-structured problem has the opposite qualities: the needed information is not necessarily contained in the problem itself, many different procedures are potentially applicable, and multiple different solutions are plausible (Voss, 2006) — extreme examples include "How can the world achieve lasting peace?" or "How can teachers ensure that students learn?"

A well-defined, guaranteed-correct procedure for a well-structured problem is called an algorithm (e.g., the procedure for long division, or the instructions for a computer routine) (Leiserson et al., 2001). Algorithms only work when a problem is genuinely well-structured and there is no ambiguity about whether the algorithm even applies; carried to an ill-structured problem, where there is real ambiguity about how to proceed or even what the problem is actually asking, algorithms fail. For ill-structured problems, a heuristic — a general strategy or "rule of thumb" that often works but is not guaranteed to — is more appropriate (e.g., scanning a library catalog for relevant-looking titles when starting research for a term paper offers no guarantee of finding the best sources, but succeeds often enough to be worth trying).

Many real problems are not purely one or the other. A nine-dot puzzle ("connect all nine dots using only four straight lines") looks well-structured — nine dots, four lines, a seemingly precise task — but is not completely so, since the puzzle's real solution requires information (that lines may extend beyond the dots) that was never explicitly stated. Learners applying the simple algorithm "draw one line, then another, then another" fail; solving it requires recognizing that a heuristic-like reframing (questioning what "draw a line" was actually taken to mean) is needed instead.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Accurate diagnosis of whether a task is genuinely well-structured (an algorithm will work) or actually ill-structured behind a well-structured-looking surface (a heuristic or reframing is needed)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Applying an algorithm to an ill-structured problem, or expecting a single guaranteed procedure where none exists, produces persistent failure that looks like a reasoning deficit but is really a mismatched strategy
  • Functional fixedness [-M] is especially likely to trap solvers on problems that look well-structured but actually depend on an unstated assumption

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Correctly classifying a problem as well- or ill-structured before choosing a solution approach, rather than defaulting to algorithmic procedure regardless of fit

docs.title: Strategies for Solving Ill-Structured Problems
docs.text: Beyond recognizing structure, several general strategies help regardless of a problem's specific content (Thagard, 2005): problem analysis — identifying a problem's component parts and working on each separately, especially useful for ill-structured problems (e.g., "devise a plan to improve bicycle transportation in the city" decomposes into installing bike lanes, educating cyclists and motorists, fixing potholes, and revising relevant traffic laws); working backward — starting from the target solution and reasoning back to the given problem, useful when a well-structured problem contains distracting or misleading elements; and analogical thinking — using a structurally similar prior problem or experience to guide a new one (e.g., applying lessons from improving conditions for cars to the bicycle-transportation problem, since both involve roadway and driver-education measures).

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Analogical Reasoning — one of the general strategies useful across both well- and ill-structured problems
  • Problem-based Learning — deliberately poses ill-structured problems as a design choice

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A "word lily" problem ("lilies double their lake coverage every day; it takes 100 days to cover the whole lake — how many days to cover half?") is well-structured and solvable by working backward from Day 100, but a solver who treats the stated lily size as relevant has misrepresented the problem and will be misled by irrelevant information.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Voss, J. F. (2006). Toulmin's model and the solving of ill-structured problems. In D. Hitchcock & B. Verheij (Eds.), Arguing on the Toulmin model (pp. 303-311). Springer.
  • Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., Stein, C., & Cormen, T. H. (2001). Introduction to algorithms (2nd ed.). MIT Press.
  • Thagard, P. (2005). Mind: Introduction to cognitive science (2nd ed.). MIT Press.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Problem-solving. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference
Description
docs.text:
Feedback that both encourages and includes genuine criticism is already a delicate balance to strike, and it becomes measurably harder across a racial or ethnic difference between teacher and student: students of color have historically grounded reasons to distrust critical comments from a white teacher, since such comments can be (and too often have been) a vehicle for lower expectations rather than genuine developmental feedback. Cohen, Steele, and Ross (1999) found that effective — "wise" — feedback across this kind of difference needs three components together, not just the usual two: positive comments, criticism, and — the addition that makes it "wise" — an explicit assurance that the teacher believes the student is capable of reaching a higher standard. Without that third component, criticism risks being read (not unreasonably, given the historical pattern) as confirmation of a lower expectation rather than as an investment in the student's actual growth.

This same three-part structure extends directly to conversations with parents and guardians: the same trust dynamic that makes wise feedback necessary with a student of a different racial or ethnic background applies when discussing that student's performance with their parents, and the same three components — positive framing, honest criticism, and an explicit statement of belief in the student's capability — apply there too.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Genuine, specific criticism — wise feedback is not a way to avoid giving critical feedback, it is a way to give it so it lands as intended
  • An explicit, stated assurance of belief in the student's capability, not merely an implied or assumed one — the whole mechanism depends on this being made visible, not left for the student to infer

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Feedback that only ever offers uncritical praise across this kind of difference avoids the trust problem by avoiding the substance of feedback altogether, which serves the student's actual learning far worse than doing the fuller, harder work of wise feedback properly
  • This principle does not imply that critical feedback should be softened or diluted — the criticism itself should be just as honest and specific as it would be otherwise; only the framing around it changes

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students whose racial or ethnic background differs from their teacher's, particularly students of color receiving feedback from a white teacher

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Critical feedback that is actually received and acted on as intended, rather than filtered through a reasonable, historically-grounded suspicion that it reflects lowered expectations rather than genuine developmental investment

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Immediate Feedback — wise feedback is a specific structural requirement for feedback quality that sits alongside, not instead of, timeliness and specificity

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Worked examples present a partially or fully solved problem so learners can study task structure, decision points, and reasoning before attempting similar problems independently.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Worked examples are most effective when learners are new to a task or domain. By externalizing problem structure, they reduce the unproductive search that novices would otherwise spend on unguided problem solving Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]. A meta-analysis of mathematics outcomes confirms medium performance benefits across grade levels Worked examples improve mathematics performance, especially for novices. [+S]. These benefits are not automatic: examples must be paired with practice, fading, or reflection to support transfer Pairing worked examples with practice or fading supports transfer better than examples alone. [+S], and prompting learners to explain a solution to themselves amplifies learning beyond passive study. As expertise grows, explicit guidance becomes redundant and can impede performance Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M], shifting the design challenge from providing structure to progressively removing it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An explicit demonstration element (Demonstration or Procedural Information) — learners need a complete model to study before attempting problems on their own
  • Prompts that surface reasoning (Eliciting Student Thinking or Articulation) — passive reading of examples produces weaker learning than active explanation
  • A way to follow examples with application (Practice) — without subsequent problem-solving, knowledge stays inert

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Less effective when the main goal is open-ended generation or creative exploration
  • Can create illusions of understanding if used without prompts or practice
  • Benefits drop when examples are not aligned with later transfer tasks
  • Effectiveness diminishes as learner expertise grows; continued use with advanced learners may become counterproductive

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novice learners encountering a domain or representation for the first time
  • Learners at risk of cognitive overload during unguided problem solving
  • Learners acquiring procedural skills that have clear correct steps
  • Effects diminish as expertise increases Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M] — reduce or fade examples as competence develops

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Early schema formation: building a mental model of task structure
  • Procedural fluency with explanation, not just rote execution
  • Recognizing structural similarity across problem types
  • Transitioning from guided to independent performance

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller) — worked examples reduce extraneous cognitive load by making problem structure explicit, freeing working memory for schema formation
  • Information Processing Theory — examples externalize solution steps, reducing the working-memory demand of holding intermediate states in mind
  • Self-Regulated Learning — prompts and example fading support monitoring and adaptive control of learning

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism — emphasizes that learners build understanding through active generation and exploration; over-reliance on worked examples may reduce generative processing and limit transfer to novel problems

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M] — worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices
  • Pairing worked examples with practice or fading supports transfer better than examples alone. [+S] — pairing examples with practice or fading supports transfer
  • Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M] — guidance becomes redundant as expertise grows (expertise reversal)
  • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S] — example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve outcomes vs. problem-only practice
  • Worked examples improve mathematics performance, especially for novices. [+S] — worked examples improve math performance across grades (meta-analysis)

docs.title: Related Principles
docs.text:
• Purposeful Reflection — worked examples gain power when paired with structured prompts to reflect on why each step was taken
  • Guided Practice — provides the scaffolded practice phase that converts example study into transferable performance
  • Explaining Their Thinking — self-explanation of worked examples is one of the strongest amplifiers of example-based learning
  • Pairing Non-Examples With Examples — extends worked examples by contrasting correct solutions with common errors, sharpening discrimination

docs.title: Validated
docs.text: • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S] — Van Gog, Kester & Paas (2011) showed that sequences of worked examples and practice problems reduced cognitive load and improved transfer scores compared to problem-only practice in secondary circuits troubleshooting (n=48).

docs.title: Illustrative
docs.text:
Worked Example Routine — A classroom instructional routine in which the teacher presents a fully solved problem, thinks aloud through each step using explicit modeling, then immediately asks learners to solve a near-transfer problem. The routine builds in self-explanation prompts before the independent attempt.

Comparing Multiple Solution Methods — Learners study two or more worked examples of the same problem solved differently, then compare and explain which method is more efficient or generalizable. Particularly effective for building flexible procedural knowledge in mathematics.

ASSISTments — A free web-based math platform (grades 6–12) that delivers practice problems with on-demand worked example hints that walk through solution steps. Learners can request a hint at any step, receiving targeted procedural guidance rather than the full solution. Heffernan & Heffernan (2014) report learning gains relative to homework-only conditions across several randomized school studies.

Carnegie Learning MATHia — An adaptive intelligent tutoring system for middle and high school math that combines worked examples, mastery-based problem sets, and step-level hints that prompt learners to explain their reasoning before providing guidance. Mastery gating ensures learners do not advance until they demonstrate independent performance.

Code walkthroughs with commentary — A common pattern in programming instruction: an instructor or tutorial presents annotated worked code explaining why each line exists, then immediately assigns a coding exercise that requires adapting or extending the example. Widely used in MOOCs (e.g., Codecademy, CS50) and textbooks.

Annotated reading comprehension walkthroughs — A teacher reads a complex text aloud, using think-aloud to make comprehension strategies visible (identifying main idea, inferencing, monitoring confusion), then asks learners to apply the same strategies to a new passage with structured annotation prompts.

  • Activities for Student Self-Reflection - This strategy involves creating activities that allow students to reflect on their own learning.

  • Address Stereotypical Beliefs About Parents and Poverty - Teachers and educators should challenge and avoid stereotypical beliefs about parents and families living in poverty.
  • Address Technology-Related Fears - Recognize and address adult learners' fears related to technology, such as data loss, privacy concerns, or damaging equipment.

  • Addressing Implicit Bias - Recognizing and addressing implicit biases involves moving away from the idea that being biased is inherently negative and acknowledging that everyone possesses biases.
  • Addressing Stereotype Threat - Teachers use strategies to support students who experience stereotype threat, helping them thrive academically and socially.

  • Aggregating Information - Aggregating involves finding and displaying patterns in discussions and other communications.
  • AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity - Utilizing an AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity involves taking a more in-depth look into the data used to build algorithms and the way products are used by and for Black and Brown students in schools.
  • Air Writing - Air writing involves writing letters or words in the air while simultaneously visualizing the shape of the letters and saying their names.
  • Allow Think-Time and Re-reading (Processing Speed) - Allowing plenty of think-time and time for re-reading for students who might need more time to process.
  • Allowing Think-Time and Re-Reading - Allowing plenty of think-time and time for re-reading provides students who need more time to process information the space they need to fully understand the material.
  • Alphabet Books - Alphabet books involve students creating entries for each letter of the alphabet related to a specific topic, such as mathematics vocabulary.
  • Alphaboxes - Alphaboxes is a strategy that encourages collaborative interaction with text by using a grid with boxes labeled with letters of the alphabet.
  • Alternative Math Assessments - Alternative assessments to timed tests in math focus on accurately measuring a learner's fact fluency through a variety of methods that mitigate the concerns and limitations of traditional timed tests.
  • Always Be Positive - Maintaining a positive attitude in all interactions, from classrooms to playgrounds, during school and after.
  • Ample Space - Classrooms with ample space are more conducive to providing appropriate learning environments for students and associated with increased student engagement and learning.
  • Amplifying Key Ideas - Amplifying involves drawing attention to important ideas and concepts, both in the course materials and in student comments or other work.
  • Analogies - Analogies are comparisons of two things that are alike in some way, used as advance organizers to help students realize that a new topic relates to something familiar.
  • Analysis of Classroom Dynamics Through Shadowing - This strategy involves a teacher or coach shadowing students to analyze classroom dynamics and student experiences.
