  • Analyzing Errors (with Taboo game) - Learners play Taboo to practice choosing keywords, and the instructor identifies the strategies of finding synonyms and giving precise descriptions.
  • Analyzing Projects for ELL Support - Analyzing project-based learning (PBL) projects through the lens of English Language Learners (ELLs) involves identifying the language skills, vocabulary instruction, speaking and listening scaffolds, and language functions needed for…
  • Analyzing Self-Talk - Students identify patterns or themes in their self-talk, such as recurring thoughts or feelings related to specific situations or times of day.
  • Analyzing Video Replays - Video replay analysis involves reviewing short video clips, replays of key segments, or recordings of one's performance to enhance metacognition, improve long-term memory, and cultivate a learner mindset.
  • Anglo-Saxon Phoneme-Grapheme Mapping - Spelling by explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping requires the learner to match the letters/letter combinations in a word to the speech sounds they represent using a grid; each box of the grid represents a phoneme.
  • Applicable Reflection - Applicable reflection involves guiding students to consider how their past performance will influence their future work.
  • Applied Science Testing - Applied science testing involves using scientific principles to evaluate real-world materials and products.
  • Apply Student-Centered Strategies to Support Learning Differences - This strategy involves using a data-driven, student-centered plan to implement specific instructional strategies that address a selected student's learning differences (including strengths and challenges).
  • Applying Student-Centered Strategies to Support Learning Differences - Educators use data-driven, student-centered plans to implement strategies that support individual learning differences, including both strengths and challenges.
  • Art and Writing Skill Development Stages - Drawing and writing skills in young children develop through distinct stages, progressing from random scribbling to letter and word practice.
  • Arts and Crafts - Creative activities such as arts and crafts can help learners explore their creativity and learn something new.
  • Arts Integration - Integrate arts activities like fiction writing, dance, drama, graphic design, music, drawing, painting, or ceramics into all subjects to enhance learning and engagement.
  • Ask Open-Ended Questions - Don’t assume you know how a student is feeling.
  • Ask Parents for Their Ideas - Schools can include parents by regularly asking for feedback regarding issues of concern.
  • Ask the 4 Questions - This approach involves asking and answering four key questions to provide quality feedback: What can the student do?
  • Ask the Right Questions - Before you hit “share,” what questions should you ask?
  • Assess and Differentiate - It is important to assess not only the content but also the language as you scaffold and teach vocabulary, structure, and function of the language.
  • Assess Fluency Components - Assessing must attend to fluency components and the learner.
  • Assessing and Differentiating Language Skills in PBL - Assessing and differentiating language skills in project-based learning (PBL) involves evaluating not only content knowledge but also language proficiency.
  • Assessing Needs and Wants with Likert Scales - Using a five-point Likert scale to quantitatively measure student interest and understanding.
  • Asset-Based Teaching - A pedagogical approach that focuses on planning with learners’ strengths at the forefront, recognizing that every learner has something to learn, share, and contribute.
  • Association - Association is a mnemonic device that links new information to something already known to make it easier to remember.
  • Assume Support - Be aware that families’ attitudes and beliefs about education may vary, and it’s a mistake to assume that all students have parents who promote school engagement.
  • Asynchronous Voice - One of the limitations of discussion is that rich, face-to-face conversations can only happen when all parties are available, so we’re limited to the time we have in class.
  • Attention Breaks - Practice attentive behavior during non-crucial times during the school day.
  • Attention Check - An attention check is a practice where a teacher announces a short pause, and students reflect on where their attention is.
  • Attention Signals - Attention signals are techniques used by instructors to regain focus and quiet a noisy learning environment.
  • Audio + Structured Activity - Students engage with audio resources (music, podcasts, voice-recorded lectures) accompanied by a structured activity.
  • Audio Books - Audio books provide an auditory learning experience where the text of a book is read aloud, allowing learners to listen instead of or in conjunction with reading.
  • Audio Commentary - Audio commentary involves instructors and learners using audio recordings to provide personalized feedback on work.
  • Audiobooks - Allowing learners to listen to audiobooks supports learners with auditory processing strengths.
  • Audiobooks & E-books - Audiobooks and e-books can be used to enhance literacy skills, comprehension, and engagement, especially for emerging readers, English language learners, and students with reading challenges.
  • Audiobooks for Literacy Reinforcement - Audiobooks can reinforce and inspire literacy skills and enjoyment for all students, including emerging readers and ESL/ELL learners.
  • Augmented Reality (AR) for Manufacturing Training - AR provides step-by-step instructions while a trainee is practicing, using AR headsets to provide step-by-step instructions while a trainee is practicing.
  • Augmented Reality (AR) for Medical Education and Training - AR is used to create models of the human body that let medical students learn anatomy in depth; provide more training opportunities for medical students with the help of simulations; and allow students to practice surgeries on virtual…
  • Augmented Reality (AR) for Military Training - AR creates training environments required for soldiers to train more often, save travel costs, and reduce the need for special equipment.
  • Augmented Reality (AR) for Space Industry Training - Augmented reality can assist astronauts with tasks such as maintaining a space station by providing visual work instructions without turning to manuals.
  • Augmented Reality (AR) in Classroom - Augmented reality can be used to turn an ordinary class into an engaging experience.
  • Awareness of Implicit Biases - This involves recognizing and addressing unconscious attitudes, stereotypes, and categories that affect behavior and understanding, particularly in the context of education.
  • Awareness of Self-Talk - Creating awareness of self-talk involves understanding what self-talk is, how it impacts confidence and self-esteem, and identifying it in real-life situations.

docs.title: B
docs.text:
• Backchannel Discussions - A backchannel is a conversation that happens right alongside another activity.
  • Background Knowledge Activation - Before engaging in text-based discussions, instructors activate learners' background knowledge related to the text's setting and themes.
  • Badges - Badges are a digital way to acknowledge learner work.
  • Balanced Assessment System - The system should inform core instruction as well as intervention needs in your school.
  • Balanced Classroom Decorations - Display student work.
  • Balancing Homework with Physical Activity - Encourage children to balance homework with physical activity by talking to teachers, setting up standing desks, and breaking up long periods of sitting with short bursts of physical activity.
  • Balancing Screen Time with Physical Activity - Promote a balance between screen time and physical activity by encouraging children to use screens for active purposes, such as making nature documentaries, videoing sports skills, or playing video dance games.
  • Ball Toss Game - A simple game involving tossing a ball, often used with preschoolers to develop counting skills.
  • Barometer: Taking a Stand on Controversial Issues - In this activity, learners express opinions by standing along a continuum labeled with 'Strongly Agree' and 'Strongly Disagree.' After taking a stand, learners explain their positions, referring to evidence and examples.
  • Be Present for Students - When students talk openly about race, they can feel some anxiety.
  • Before or After-School Physical Activity Programs - Offer structured physical activity programs before or after school, such as morning exercises, intramural sports, or opening school facilities for recreational use.
  • Behavioral Shadowing - An adult shadows a child closely (within arm's reach) to prevent specific harmful behaviors (e.g., biting, hitting) before they occur.
  • Big 10 Student Motivators - Ten research-backed strategies that encourage playful learning, innovative thinking, and problem-solving skills while engaging students in core subjects.
  • Big Ten Student Motivators - These strategies encourage playful learning, boost students’ innovative thinking and problem-solving skills, and at the same time engage students in reading, writing, researching, discussing, and analyzing materials in all subjects.
  • Bigger/Smaller/Equal - If the teacher says a number greater than 10, students expand their bodies to take up as much space as they can (while keeping their feet firmly planted on the ground—no running around).
  • Black Genius Profile - This strategy involves capturing Black learners’ genius using specific elements such as Interest Awareness, Racial Identity, Social Justice, Multi-cultural Navigation, Selective Trust, and Can-do Attitude.
  • Blackout Conversation - Students transform conversational text selections into poetry by blacking out sections to reveal only key terms and phrases, focusing on the meaning, nuances, and silences of each character's dialogue.
  • Blended Learning - Blended learning combines face-to-face instruction with online learning through an LMS, offering the advantages of direct interaction and the convenience of eLearning.
  • Block Play - Block play involves using blocks to create structures and designs, either independently or collaboratively.
  • Blocks and Legos: Maker Spaces and Fab Labs - Maker spaces and fab labs provide learners with opportunities to invent, design, and build things.
  • Body Scan Meditation - Incorporate a body scan meditation to bring calmness and awareness to the classroom, maximizing students’ potential.
  • Body Scan Meditation Check-In - Students participate in a guided body scan meditation to bring calmness and awareness into the classroom.
  • Bolster Credibility - Did the writer engage with anyone who disagrees?
  • Book Clubs - Book clubs are small groups of learners who choose, read, and discuss a shared text.
  • Book Clubs / Literature Circles - Book clubs, also known as literature circles, are a grouping system to organize active learning events based on student-selected areas of interest.
  • BOOKMATCH: Scaffolding Independent Book Selection - BOOKMATCH is a tool for helping students select just-right books for independent reading.
  • Boolean Operators - For older students, teach them Boolean Operators (and, or, not, near, ( ), *) to better refine their searches.
  • Bounce Cards - Bounce cards provide a structured way for students to engage in cooperative learning by promoting active listening, turn-taking, and perspective sharing.
  • Braille Texts for Literacy Development - Braille texts are used to build literacy skills such as decoding and syntax.
  • Brain Breaks - Brain breaks are short periods of time when learners change up the routine of incoming information.
  • Brain Dumps - Brain dumps involve learners writing down everything they can recall about a specific topic within a set time.
  • Brain-Based Classroom Redesign - Redesigning the classroom environment based on brain-based methods involves creating a space that supports reflective thinking, movement, choice, and collaboration.
  • Brain-Based Learning - Activating the different parts of the brain involved with the various senses during the learning process to engage learners with content, help them learn and retain more.
  • Brain-Based Learning Activities - Activities that engage multiple senses (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, tactile) to activate different parts of the brain, enhancing learning and retention.
  • Brain-Based Learning Through Movement - Brain-based learning strategies involve engaging multiple senses and encouraging movement to improve learning and retention.
  • Brain-Based Learning with Movement Breaks - Incorporating movement, social interaction, and distributed learning to enhance brain function and retention.
  • Brainstorming 'Stuff We Want to Know About' - Learners and instructors co-create an ongoing list of topics of interest and questions related to course content.
  • Brainstorming (Pre-Reading) - Learners are given a limited time (e.g., five minutes) to brainstorm ideas related to the reading topic.
  • Brainstorming Topics of Interest - Brainstorming an ongoing class list of stuff learners want to know about and are interested in—a phenomenon, an event, or a law, for example.
  • Break Tasks into Pieces - Divide tasks into smaller chunks.
  • Break Time Consequence - Writing instructions in bold letters on the chalkboard stating that students who continue talking during the lesson will have time taken off their break.
  • Breathing Exercises - Breathing exercises can help learners to focus and settle their feelings and thoughts.
  • Breathing Techniques and Mindfulness Strategies - Teaching breathing techniques and mindfulness strategies equips students with tools to manage challenging situations.
  • Bridging Cultures - The Bridging Cultures Project helps teachers understand assumptions underlying individualism and collectivism, highlighting cultural differences that may diverge from school-based practices and values.
  • Bridging Individualism and Collectivism - This strategy focuses on understanding and addressing the differences between individualistic and collectivistic value systems in the classroom.
  • Brief Instruction Steps - Breaking up instructions into short, concrete steps allows learners to pay attention to and remember one instruction at a time.
  • Bright Spaces with Plenty of Light and Air - Creating spaces that are colorful, special vents controlled air flow, and having an accessible fan can replicate this if vents aren't available.
  • Bring Something From Home - Ask students to bring something from home that makes their classroom feel more like home, such as a photograph, a stuffed animal, or a musical instrument.
  • Bring the Outdoors In - Allowing an indoor/outdoor space that becomes an extension of classroom learning.
  • Broaden Your Palate - Make a point to check sites that do not agree with your politics.
  • Build a Community on Student Voice - Building a community on student voice involves creating a classroom environment where students feel safe and empowered to share their thoughts, ideas, and needs.
  • Build Community Through Peer Feedback - Offering students frequent opportunities to share feedback and revise their work fosters a supportive classroom culture and builds relationships.
  • Build in Thinking Time - Providing dedicated, silent thinking time before pair talk allows students to generate their own ideas and rehearse explanations before being influenced by their partner.
  • Build Relationships with Each Student - Create positive learning environments and engaging instruction to help all students achieve success.

  • Building a Community on Student Voice - Building a community on student voice involves creating opportunities for students to share and discuss their thoughts, ensuring that they feel safe to do so.
  • Building a Sound Wall - A sound wall is a classroom tool that helps educators reinforce the importance of explicitly teaching letter-sound correspondence and supports key aspects of learning to read that are backed by the science of reading.
  • Building a Supportive Classroom Environment for Mistakes - This strategy focuses on specific actions to foster a learning environment where mistakes are seen as opportunities.
  • Building a Trusting Community - The key step is building a trusting community by giving students time to reflect and write about elements of their lives and to share these reflections.
  • Building Community Through Peer Feedback in PBL - Building community through peer feedback involves giving students opportunities to frequently share feedback and revise their work.
  • Building Cultural Competency Skills for School Staff - Training staff in behaviors, attitudes, and policies that enable effective cross-cultural relationships.
  • Building Trusting Relationships - Prioritizing building relationships with learners can create a supportive and safe learning environment.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
• Call-and-Response - Call-and-response involves the instructor initiating a phrase or word, and the students responding with a pre-determined phrase or word.
  • Calm and Honest Reflection - After feeling and expressing emotions related to a mistake, engaging in calm and honest reflection involves asking oneself what happened and what triggered those feelings.
  • Calm-Down Corner - Dedicated, positive space where learners practice emotional regulation skills.

  • Calming Combinations - Combining two or more calming sensory strategies can create a more effective and personalized approach to self-regulation.
  • Calming Movement - Using calming movement involves engaging in repetitive and rhythmic vestibular input to promote relaxation and self-regulation.

  • Calming Oral Sensory Input - Employing oral sensory input as a calming strategy involves engaging the mouth to provide sensory experiences that promote self-regulation.
  • Calming Proprioceptive Input - Using proprioceptive input, also known as \"heavy work,\" involves engaging muscles and joints to provide a calming and organizing sensory experience.
  • Calming Sensory Input - Providing access to calming sensory input through various means, such as tactile bins filled with sand, rice, or beans for tactile stimulation; weighted blankets or stuffed animals for deep pressure; and chewy pendants or snacks for oral…

  • Chalkboard Math App - App for students to practice basic math.
  • Challenge Based Learning - Challenge Based Learning (CBL) provides an efficient and effective framework for learning while solving real-world challenges.
  • Challenge Based Learning (CBL) - Challenge Based Learning (CBL) is a customizable framework that provides an efficient and effective way for learners to solve real-world challenges.
  • Challenge the Text - Challenge the Text is a strategy that encourages students to critically examine texts by asking and answering their own text-dependent questions.
  • Changing Spaces with Mood Lighting - Using lights with different colors to create a fresh perspective.
  • Character Emotion Analysis - This strategy involves having students analyze characters' feelings in literature to improve their self-awareness and emotional recognition.
  • Character Profile Creation - Students create character profiles to help them form a deeper understanding of a book’s characters.
  • Character Scrapbooking - Students select four key events from a novel and create scrapbook entries representing a character's inner thoughts, feelings, and experiences during each event.
  • Chart-Based Retrieval and Spaced Practice - A simple classroom exercise to demonstrate the effectiveness of spaced practice using a chart.
  • Check for Understanding - After giving instructions, check for understanding by asking related questions and observing compliance.
  • Checking Your Blind Spot - Recognizing and addressing unconscious bias involves acknowledging its existence, understanding how it impacts decision-making, and implementing strategies to mitigate its effects.
  • Checklists - Checklists can be used to measure and document student learning by tracking whether learners are accomplishing specific tasks or expectations.
  • Checklists & Rubrics - Checklists and rubrics provide clear criteria for self- and peer-assessments.
  • Children's Literature for Math Instruction - Children's literature for math instruction is a strategy in which stories, picture books, or narrative texts are used to introduce mathematical ideas, contexts, or discussion.
  • Children's Literature Integration - Integrating children's literature, especially multicultural literature, into math instruction to enhance engagement and comprehension.
  • Choice Boards - Choice boards offer learners options for how they demonstrate their learning, increasing engagement and ownership.
  • Choice-Based Quiet Time Activities - Choice-based activities during quiet time give students the power to select their preferred independent tasks, enhancing engagement and promoting a sense of control.
  • Chunk Directions - Giving learners more manageable chunks of information can help ensure they’re able to continue to engage in a meaningful way when dealing with sustained attention.
  • Chunking Directions - Breaking down directions into smaller, more manageable sections to support sustained attention.
  • Circle Count - Stand in a circle and try to count off as quickly as possible all the way around the circle.
  • Circle Time Emotions - End each week with a group circle where students discuss different topics and share their feelings.
  • Circulate and Listen During Pair Talk - Actively circulating and listening to pair discussions allows teachers to monitor student engagement, reinforce expectations, offer support, and gauge the success of the thinking process.
  • Clarification of Vocabulary, Symbols, and Language Structures - Supporting learners to construct meaning from words, symbols, and numbers using different representations.
  • Clarify Vocabulary, Symbols, and Language Structures - Constructing meaning from words, symbols, and numbers using different representations ensures that learners understand the language of the content.
  • Clarifying - Clarifying involves identifying and resolving areas of uncertainty in a text or problem.
  • Class Anchor Charts or Plus/Delta Chart - After a formative assessment or test the class may have a discussion about what problems on the assignment caused concerns.
  • Class Book - Class books involve students creating individual pages that are compiled into a single book.
  • Classical Music - Playing classical music (Bach, not Mahler) at a low volume when learners enter the room to set a professional tone.
  • Classical Music for Ambiance - Playing classical music (e.g., Bach) at a low volume when students enter the room sets a professional and calming tone.
  • Classification Tasks - Classification tasks involve sorting objects or concepts into categories based on shared properties.
  • Classroom Checklists - Classroom checklists are visual aids used to help students, teachers, and parents stay on track with various tasks and assignments.
  • Classroom Design Optimization - Optimizing classroom design (noise levels, temperature, seating arrangement) can minimize distractions and improve learning.
  • Classroom Games - Classroom games transform review time into engaging, collaborative activities that motivate learners and reinforce learning.
  • Classroom Library - A classroom library is a dedicated space within the classroom stocked with a variety of books to promote reading engagement and literacy skills.
  • Classroom Management with Graphic Organizers - Teachers put the most important policies, procedures, and expectations into graphic form to increase the likelihood that students will follow them.
  • Classroom Physical Activity Breaks - Integrating movement-based activities into the classroom to energize learners, relax and calm a class, or redirect attention.
  • Classroom Seating Arrangements - This strategy involves strategically organizing the physical space of a classroom to maximize student engagement, motivation, participation, and positive relationships.
  • Classwide Peer Editing - Classwide peer editing involves having students review and critique examples of student writing.
  • Clear Online Communication - Establishing clear channels and rules of online communication with your students ensures that you are getting back to students reasonably quickly when they have questions and is an important component of establishing strong connections…
  • Cloud Text-to-Speech API - Cloud Text-to-Speech allows developers to create natural-sounding, synthetic human speech as playable audio.
  • Co-constructing Knowledge - Co-constructing knowledge involves teachers and students dialoguing and creating knowledge together, rather than teachers simply filling students with content.
  • Co-Teaching and Collaboration - ELL teachers and math teachers collaborate to identify target content, key vocabulary, academic language, and language-focused tasks for lessons.
  • Cognitively Demanding Tasks - Cognitively demanding tasks require a high level of cognitive engagement to complete.
  • Cold Call to Sample Pair Responses - Using cold call to select students to share their pair's responses reinforces expectations around engagement and attention.
  • Collaborative Creation of Exemplars - After completing collaborative problem-solving tasks, learners examine leveled exemplars of responses and identify the characteristics of each level.
  • Collaborative Group Work - Teachers should emphasize collaborative learning within a project.
  • Collaborative Group Work in PBL - In project-based learning (PBL), collaborative group work involves intentionally structuring activities to ensure students work together to achieve common goals.
  • Collaborative Learning Space Design - Creating collaborative learning spaces involves intentionally designing classrooms to facilitate group work and interaction.
  • Collaborative Margin Comments - Collaborative margin comments involve using collaborative document platforms like Google Docs or Microsoft Word Online to provide direct feedback within the document.
  • Collaborative Peer Review - Learners connect with others to provide and receive feedback for improvement on writing tasks.
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving with Sticky Notes - Learners individually solve a problem on sticky notes, then share and discuss their responses in small groups.
  • Collaborative Storytelling - Learners work in pairs to create a story by responding to guiding questions.
  • Collaborative Storytelling with Guiding Questions - Collaborative storytelling involves students working in pairs to co-create a narrative by responding to a series of guiding questions.
  • Collaborative Writing - Making arrangements for learners to work together through the entire process of writing—planning, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing—results in higher quality writing products.
  • Collaborative Writing with Online Platforms - Collaborative writing using online platforms involves students jointly composing texts through digital tools like Google Docs.
  • Collect My Data - Learners choose a category of items to collect data on, creating tally charts to record observations, and then graph the data to visualize findings.
  • Collective Data Analysis - Collective data analysis involves a systematic and iterative process of making sense of data through collaboration, especially in participatory action research.
  • Color-Coded Supplies - Color-coding school supplies can make organization easier and more streamlined for kids and the adults in charge.
  • Combination of Strategies - Combining two or more calming sensory strategies to create a more comprehensive and effective approach to self-regulation.
  • Comfortable Learning Spaces - Creating classrooms as comfortable spaces where students feel at home.
  • Common Ground Group Assignments - Providing group assignments where learners can find common ground and/or interests involves designing collaborative tasks that encourage learners to identify shared interests, values, or goals.
  • Common Language for Multimodal Composition - Creating a shared vocabulary or metalanguage empowers learners to analyze and discuss their multimodal composition process.
  • Communicate High Expectations and Provide Appropriate Support - Expect more and you will get it.
  • Communicate Quickly and Easily Through Mobile Apps - Mobile apps like Remind can provide a quick and easy way for parents, teachers, and students to communicate about student progress, assignments, and other school-related activities.
  • Communicating Positive Expectations - Teacher expectations have a dramatic impact on learner performance and behavior.
  • Communication Boards - Communication boards are visual aids that display symbols, pictures, words, or phrases to help individuals with limited or no verbal communication express their thoughts, needs, and ideas.
  • Community Building on Student Voice - Creating a classroom community where student voices are valued involves providing time and opportunities for students to share and discuss their thoughts.
  • Community Involvement - Encouraging community involvement by using online communities to support learning and fostering a sense of collaboration through social media.
  • Compare and Contrast Sources - Present learners with multiple sources on the same topic and have them compare and contrast the information presented.
  • Comparing Multiple Solution Methods - Learners compare and contrast multiple solution methods for the same problem, as opposed to studying one method at a time.
  • Compassionate Curiosity - Act as a non-judgmental investigator to better understand students and respond with empathy.
  • Complete Scripts of Academic Routines - Provide scaffolding, like speech examples, for discourse routines that may not be obvious to learners.
  • Complex Instruction - A pedagogy that redefines who is 'smart' by utilizing multi-ability access points, norms and roles that support interdependency between learners, and attention to status and accountability for learning.
  • Composition Projects: Multimodal - For adolescent learners, the Composition process can become more robust, as learners begin to express ideas through multiple media, which includes visual, audio, and digital production.
  • Compound Word Study - Begin teaching how to spell multisyllable words by beginning with compounds.
  • Comprehension Checks - During reading activities, instructors periodically check for understanding by asking questions.
  • Comprehension Monitoring - This strategy involves the ability of readers to know when they understand what they read and to use strategies to improve their understanding when it is blocked.
  • Concentric Circles - Learners form two circles, one inside circle and one outside circle.
  • Concept Discovery Through Examples and Non-examples - Expose learners to a wide range of examples and nonexamples and allow them to discover the concept.
  • Concept Mapping - Concept maps are visual tools that help learners organize and articulate what they know about a given concept or topic.
  • Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) - CRA is an instructional approach that uses concrete materials, visual representations, and abstract symbols to teach math concepts.
  • Confront Fears - This strategy involves actively identifying and addressing fears that hold individuals back from achieving success.
  • Connect content to student lives - This strategy involves showing students how a topic connects to their lives, giving an example of a particular idea as they would experience it in their native country, or asking them to bring music or art from their culture and describe…
  • Connect Math to Student Strengths - Help learners understand how math is used in ways that relate to their personal strengths by relating math to student interests.
  • Connect Prior Knowledge to New Learning - Building connections to prior understandings and experiences helps learners integrate new information into their existing knowledge base.
  • Connect with Parents Early in the School Year - Connecting with parents as soon as possible in the school year through personalized phone calls, emails, in-person conversations, or letters home.
  • Connect Writing to Real-World Applications - Instructors connect the importance and usefulness of writing to learners' lives and future careers.
  • Connecting - Connecting involves relating a current problem or text to prior knowledge and experiences.
  • Connecting Background Knowledge to Content - A method for making instruction more culturally relevant by connecting content to learners’ experiences.
  • Connecting Concepts to Procedures - Conceptual understanding must precede and coincide with instruction on procedures.
  • Connecting ELLs' Background Knowledge to Content - This strategy involves making instruction more culturally relevant by connecting content to ELLs' experiences.
  • Connecting Emotions to Actions - Learners begin to reflect on how emotions connect with actions.
  • Connecting Languages - Encourage students to see connections between their languages to better understand how languages are structured and organized.
  • Connecting Math to ESOL - This strategy brings a little bit of math could make for some interesting discussions in English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) contexts.
  • Connecting New Vocabulary to Texts - This approach involves integrating vocabulary instruction directly with texts to enhance understanding and retention.
  • Connecting Struggles to Strategies - Connecting struggles to strategies involves explicitly teaching students various problem-solving strategies and helping them understand when and why to use each strategy effectively.
  • Connection of Prior Knowledge to New Learning - Building connections to prior understandings and experiences to facilitate new learning.
  • Consider Socio-Cultural Factors - Acknowledge that access to technology and digital literacy can vary based on socio-economic background, social environment, and cultural factors.
  • Consider the News Source - Who is the news source, anyway?
  • Consider Your Own Identity - Educators need to reflect on their own biases and privileges to effectively lead discussions about race.
  • Consistent Classroom Routines and Schedules - Maintaining predictable classroom routines and schedules provides students with a sense of security and predictability, which supports emotional regulation.
  • Consolidate Key Points - Summarizing and consolidating key points after pair talk helps to solidify understanding and ensure that all students have a clear takeaway.
  • Constructive Decision-Making Process - Brainstorming and displaying a constructive decision-making process as a visual reminder in the classroom helps students make good choices.
  • Consult Fact-Checking Sites - Get used to regularly consulting fact-checking sites.
  • Content Word Signal - Using a content \"word of the week\" to signal that it's time for silence involves selecting a term related to the current curriculum (e.g., integer, renaissance, circuit) and using it as a cue for students to become quiet.
  • Content-Focused Questioning - Asking students questions that focus on the main points of the text and how the author supports those points with evidence and examples.
  • Content-Related Signal Word - Using a content \"word of the week\" to signal that it’s time for silence.
  • Context-Specific Journaling - Context-specific journaling requires individuals to reflect on specific experiences such as team assignments, internships, or professional practices.
  • Contextual Vocabulary Introduction - Introducing vocabulary words within the context of a story or reading passage allows learners to understand their meanings in relation to the surrounding text.
  • Conver-Stations - A small-group discussion strategy that gives learners exposure to more of their peers’ ideas and prevents the stagnation that can happen when a group doesn’t happen to have the right chemistry.
  • Conversations about Emotions and Social Issues - Have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice.
  • Cooperative Classroom Activities - Design classroom activities that involve cooperative work rather than competitive or individualistic work.
  • Cooperative Learning - Designing classroom activities that involve cooperative work encourages a growth mindset.
  • Cooperative Learning Activities - Designing classroom activities that involve cooperative—rather than competitive or individualistic—work environments boosts motivation and success.
  • Cooperative Learning Strategies - Using structured group activities to enhance learning and social interaction.
  • Cooperative Teaching - Cooperative teaching involves structuring learning activities so that students work together, teaching each other concepts and skills.
  • Correcting Students in a Constructive Way - Correcting and disciplining learners for inappropriate behaviors is a necessary part of the job.
  • Countdown Clock / Visual Analog Timer - A countdown clock or visual analog timer can help kids get a better sense of how time can be broken into chunks and visualize the passage of time.
  • Countdown Technique - The countdown technique involves the teacher counting down from a number, such as \"I need two people...
  • CRAAP Test - Teach kids how to confirm the credibility of a website with a scoring guide like the CRAAP test worksheet (Yup, this is a real evaluation tool!).
  • Create a Calm-Down Corner - Set aside a dedicated, positive reflection space in the classroom where kids can go to practice their emotional regulation skills.
  • Create a Character Profile - Creating a character profile helps students form a deeper understanding of a book’s characters.
  • Create a Classroom Code of Conduct - Teachers and students collaborate to establish a classroom code of conduct based on respectful, fair, kind, and empathetic behaviors.
  • Create a List of Positive Self-Talk Statements - Generating a collection of affirmative statements for learners to read and internalize.
  • Create a Word Wall for Emotions - Build your students’ emotion vocabulary by giving them direct access to those words and feelings.
  • Create Beautiful Spaces - Transforming schools into beautiful spaces by displaying high-quality student work from projects can have a transformative impact, especially for students whose communities and homes are not always beautiful places.
  • Create culture kits - Creating culture kits involves students creating their own collections of items that represent their culture to bring their culture alive as a way of sharing and discussing what can be learned from different multicultural traditions.
  • Create Space for Students to Reflect - Providing structured opportunities for students to pause, reflect, and think about themselves, their ideas, and their feelings about projects can transform a classroom culture.
  • Creating a Classroom Library - Setting up a classroom library involves acquiring books and materials, organizing the shelves, creating labels, and making the space cozy.
  • Creating a Common Language for Multimodal Composition - Empowering students with a shared vocabulary to analyze and discuss the multimodal composition process.
  • Creating a Culture of Error - Creating a culture of error involves fostering a classroom or learning environment where mistakes are viewed as valuable learning opportunities rather than failures.
  • Creating a Digital Library Section for SEL Topics - A digital library includes a dedicated section of books focused on social and emotional learning (SEL) topics.
  • Creating A Sense of Belonging - Learners who feel like they belong in school are more motivated, engaged, and ultimately show higher performance.
  • Creating a Strengths-Based Culture - A method for empowering learners by focusing on their strengths rather than their weaknesses, creating authentic learning experiences that enable them to develop skills and talents.
  • Creating an Action Plan - Creating an action plan involves outlining the specific steps needed to achieve a goal.
  • Creating Beautiful Spaces in PBL - Creating beautiful spaces in PBL involves displaying student work from projects in the school building to honor and celebrate high-quality student work.
  • Creating Collaborative Spaces - Creating collaborative spaces involves designing the learning environment to facilitate group work and interaction among learners.
  • Creating Questions - Creating Questions is a strategy where learners generate questions about what they are listening to.
  • Creating Quiet Spaces - Creating quiet spaces involves designating areas in the learning environment where learners can retreat for individual reflection, focused work, or relaxation.
  • Creating Space for New Ideas - Schools should provide opportunities for teachers to try new things and make mistakes.
  • Creating Space for Student Reflection in PBL - Creating space for student reflection involves integrating moments for students to pause and think about themselves, their ideas, and how they feel about the project.
  • Creating Strategy Charts - Developing visual aids and lists of problem-solving strategies in collaboration with learners.
  • Creating Visuals - When students express information visually, they are activating more cognitive processes while problem solving and increasing their experience with alternate texts.
  • Creative Analogies and Comparisons - Simplify complex ideas by linking them to familiar situations, making them easier to understand and remember.
  • Creative Check-In Questions - Instructors ask thought-provoking questions to encourage reflection and emotional awareness.
  • Creative Handwriting Activities - Engaging and enjoyable writing activities that move away from traditional pencil and paper tasks.
  • Creative Presentations - Creative presentations are visual aids designed to engage learners and keep their attention through the use of bright colors, creative fonts, and a combination of photos, charts, and icons.
  • Creative Writing - Former teachers Ed Kang and Amy Schwartzbach-Kang incorporated storytelling and creative writing into their after-school program’s science lessons.
  • Critical Lens Development - Developing a critical lens involves analyzing the affordances and constraints of different modes of communication to understand how they enhance or inhibit meaning.
  • Critical Response Process - The Critical Response Process is a structured method for giving feedback that puts the learner in control.
  • Cross-Age Peer Tutoring - Cross-age peer tutoring involves pairing students from different grade levels, with older students acting as tutors for younger students.
  • Cross-Curricular Art Integration - Integrating art with other subjects like science and history to enhance learning experiences.
  • Cross-Grade-Level Tutoring - Form cross-grade-level alliances where older learners tutor those in lower grades.
  • Cultivate Multiple Ways of Knowing and Making Meaning - Honoring multiple and diverse ways of developing understandings of the world ensures that learners have opportunities to connect with the material in ways that resonate with their individual strengths and backgrounds.
  • Cultivate Understanding and Respect Across Languages and Dialects - Using translations, descriptions, movement, and images to support learning in unfamiliar or complex languages promotes understanding and respect for diverse linguistic backgrounds.
  • Cultivating Belonging Through Environmental Cues - This strategy involves using simple yet powerful cues in the classroom environment to promote a sense of belonging among students.
  • Cultivation of Multiple Ways of Knowing and Making Meaning - Honoring multiple and diverse ways of developing understandings of the world.
  • Cultivation of Understanding and Respect Across Languages and Dialects - Using translations, descriptions, movement, and images to support learning in unfamiliar or complex languages.
  • Cultural Exchange Kits - Students create 'Culture Kits' with special items that bring their culture alive.
  • Cultural Responsive Practice - Culturally responsive practice involves engaging students in the learning process through an understanding of how their identity and perspective is shaped by their culture and community experiences.
  • Culturally and Historically Responsive Literacy - Culturally and historically responsive literacy is an equity framework to help educators teach literacy learning goals such as identity development, literacy skill development, intellectual development, and criticality.
  • Culturally Competent Family Engagement - Culturally competent family engagement involves training school staff in behaviors, attitudes, and policies that enable effective cross-cultural relationships.
  • Culturally Responsive Curriculum Scorecards - Tools developed collaboratively by educators, parents, students and researchers as a method of evaluating the degree to which learning goals, assignments, books, materials and other elements of curricula are responsive to diverse cultural…
  • Culturally Responsive Instruction (CREATE Model) - This strategy entails providing instruction that empowers students intellectually, socially, emotionally, and politically by using cultural referents to impart knowledge, skills, and attitudes.
  • Culturally Responsive Practice - Engaging learners cognitively and emotionally by understanding how their identity and perspective are shaped by culture and community experiences.
  • Culturally Responsive Teaching - Culturally responsive teaching involves engaging students in the learning process, both cognitively and emotionally, through an understanding of how their identity and perspective is shaped by their culture and community experiences.
  • Culture Responsive Instruction - Creating culture responsive instruction asks teachers to provide culturally responsive instruction for their students by making standards-based content and curricula accessible to students and teaching in a way that students can understand.
  • Cumulative Review - Cumulative review involves systematically revisiting previously learned concepts and skills throughout a course or learning period.
  • Curated Material Selection - Regularly assessing materials for relevance and discarding broken, old, or useless items frees up space and guides purchasing decisions.
  • Curating Resources - Curating involves selecting and arranging readings, videos, and other resources to scaffold concepts.
  • Cursive Handwriting Activities - Activities designed to teach and practice cursive handwriting, which can be beneficial for students who struggle with pencil control and letter formation.
  • Customizable Display of Information - Providing adjustable settings and accessible formats to accommodate individual needs and preferences.
  • Customizing Display of Information - Customizing the display of information involves modifying the appearance of digital content to reduce reading effort and improve comprehension.

docs.text:
• Daily Class Schedules - Structuring the school day with specific time allocations for various subjects and activities.
  • Daily Math Facts Practice - Beginning each math lesson with spaced practice to review arithmetic facts.
  • Daily Review - Daily review is a strategy where instructors begin lessons with a short (5-10 minute) review of previously studied material.
  • Data-Based Decision-Making for Core Instruction - Teachers can use data to guide instructional decisions in Tier 1 settings.
  • Daytime Blue Light Exposure - Exposure to blue light (sunlight, full-spectrum LEDs, digital screens) during the day can increase alertness and improve cognitive performance by influencing hormonal secretion, particularly in adolescents whose sleep-wake cycles are…
  • De-emphasize Answers, Emphasize Reasoning - Spend more time on reasoning than on finding the correct answer.
  • De-emphasize Behavioral Factors - Remove non-academic criteria, like behavior or participation, from grades, focusing instead on academic mastery to provide a more accurate representation of a student's knowledge.
  • Dealing with Feelings - Adults can learn to deal with the emotions that arise when they make mistakes, even if they were not sufficiently guided as children.
  • Debate for the Opposite Team - Learners are assigned to argue a position that is opposite to their own, requiring them to see things from a different perspective.
  • Debriefing Emotional Experiences - Debriefing emotional experiences involves a structured discussion at the end of the day where each child expresses an emotion they experienced and shares the context.
  • Define and Apply Ethical Responsibility - Define responsibility and ethical responsibility.
  • Deliberate Practice - Deliberate practice involves focused, strategic efforts to improve specific skills or knowledge areas.
  • Demonstrating Caring - Demonstrating caring is a powerful way to build positive relationships with learners.
  • Demonstration-Based Flipped Classroom - Subjects like Maths, Chemistry, Physics, etc.
  • Demystification of Learning Challenges - Demystification involves explaining to learners how memory and learning work, especially when they are struggling.
  • Descriptive Feature Chart - A descriptive feature chart is a graphic organizer with horizontal and vertical axes used to develop a descriptive model of an organism.
  • Design at the Margins - This principle involves designing with the students at the edges of a community in mind, particularly those disempowered due to identity or poverty.
  • Designated Calm-Down Spot - Creating a designated calm-down spot is providing a safe and structured space within the classroom where students can go to regain control over their emotions.
  • Designing Personalized Learning for Engagement - Ensuring that personalized learning opportunities are designed to maximize the engagement of all students, regardless of disability status, involves making learning choices flexible and accessible for all, with a recognition that…
  • Develop a Reliability Checklist - Bring learners together and explain that different sources online present different information, even about the same topics.
  • Develop Cultural Awareness - Developing cultural awareness as an educator includes building empathy for diverse learners, intentionally recognizing how one's own identity intersects with learners' identities, and creating an awareness of how the environment can…
  • Develop Educator Understanding - Educators develop their own understanding of self-awareness and how it affects learning by reading up on the resources and research available.
  • Develop Observable Criteria - Using Bloom's Taxonomy, Webb's Depth of Knowledge, and Marzano's Dimensions of Learning to develop measurable course objectives that are concise, student-friendly, and clearly communicated.
  • Developing a Critical Lens for Multimodal Analysis - Increasing students' awareness of effective and ineffective multimodal combinations by analyzing a mode's affordances and constraints.
  • Developing Cultural Awareness - Developing cultural awareness as an educator is an ongoing process that includes building empathy for diverse learners, intentionally recognizing how one's own identity intersects with learners' identities, and creating an awareness of…
  • Developing Positive Classroom Pride - Instilling pride is a powerful way to develop positive teacher-learner relationships.
  • Diagram Similarities and Differences - Learners generate a list of similarities and differences between words and complete a Venn diagram.
  • Dialogic Reading - Dialogic reading is an interactive reading technique where the adult helps the child become the teller of the story instead of passively listening.
  • Dictation Software - Dictation software allows learners to speak their ideas and have them transcribed into text.
  • Dictation/Speech-to-text - Dictation, also known as speech-to-text or voice recognition, involves using technology to convert spoken words into written text.
  • Dictionary & Thesaurus - Incorporating web dictionaries and thesauruses into vocabulary lessons allows learners to quickly search and understand unfamiliar words.
  • Differentiated Teaching - Differentiated teaching methods are used to extend the knowledge and skills of every student in every class, regardless of their starting point.
  • Digital Literacy Instruction - Digital literacy instruction involves teaching learners how to effectively use digital technology, communication tools, and networks to locate, evaluate, use, and create information.
  • Digital Noise Monitoring - Digital noise monitoring involves using apps or devices like Super Sound Box, Class Dojo, or Too Noisy to detect and signal excessive noise levels in the classroom.
  • Digital Publishing - Digital publishing involves using online platforms and tools to share student writing and creations with a wider audience, fostering engagement and providing valuable feedback.
  • Digital Storytelling - Digital stories are multimedia narratives that combine various elements such as photographs, video, animation, sound, music, text, and a narrative voice.
  • Digital Tips for Quick and Thoughtful Peer Feedback - Using digital tools to facilitate peer feedback can make the process easier and more efficient.
  • Digital Word Detectives - Students read e-books and use digital tools (dictionaries and notes) to support their development of vocabulary.
  • Digital Word Detectives: Building Vocabulary With e-Book Readers - Students read e-books and use digital tools (dictionaries and notes) to support their vocabulary development.
  • Dim or Natural Lighting - Using dim or natural lighting in classrooms or learning spaces to promote a calm and focused environment.
  • Dimensions of Critical Evaluation - Talk with learners about the multiple dimensions of critical evaluation, including: Relevance (importance to a reading purpose), Accuracy (factual and updated details that can be verified), Bias/Perspective (author's position or slant),…
  • Direct Instruction (Online) - Direct instruction in online learning involves pre-developed presentations, assessing student work and providing instructive feedback, diagnosing misconceptions, clarifying concepts, and referring students to additional resources or…
  • Direct Instruction: Genre-specific Writing Strategies - Direct instruction of genre-specific writing strategies involves explicitly teaching the characteristics and conventions of different writing genres to enhance students' understanding and skills in both reading and writing.
  • Direct Instruction: Keyword Search - Explicit instruction in keyword search strategies involves teaching learners how to effectively select and combine keywords to refine search queries and retrieve relevant information from the internet.
  • Direct Instruction: Patterning - Direct instruction of patterning skills involves teaching learners to identify and create patterns using various mediums such as colors, sizes, shapes, sounds, and numbers.
  • Direct Instruction: Phonics - Direct Phonics instruction connects letters to sounds to decode and comprehend text.
  • Direct Instruction: Problem-solving Strategies - Instructors teach and model various strategies for tackling problems, then give learners the opportunity to choose which strategies they use and reflect on the outcomes of their choices.
  • Direct Instruction: Spelling - Direct instruction in spelling involves explicitly teaching spelling patterns, high-frequency words, and strategies for addressing frequently misspelled words.
  • Direct Instruction: Web-based Reading Strategies - Research shows that, along with traditional reading comprehension strategies, students use unique strategies to read the non-linear, hyperlinked structure of online texts.
  • Discipline-Specific Literacy - Discipline-specific literacy involves teaching reading, writing, speaking, and thinking skills unique to each subject area.
  • Discipline-Specific Reading - Have students read articles from subject-specific columns and publications.
  • Discuss the Benefits of Positive Self-Talk - Openly communicating what self-talk is and how it can help.
  • Discussing Emotions - This strategy involves incorporating discussions about emotions into the learning environment through whole-class discussions and individual reflections.
  • Discussing Potential Emotions in Advance - Learners think about emotions in advance by discussing their thoughts.
  • Discussing Race with Students - This strategy involves creating a classroom environment conducive to complex conversations about race through activities that help students notice and celebrate similarities and differences.
  • Discussion (Pre-Reading) - In this pre-reading activity, the instructor prepares several sentences expressing different opinions about the reading topic and places them around the room.
  • Discussion Web - A discussion web is a graphic organizer that enables students to examine both sides of an issue before agreeing on a conclusion, promoting deeper processing of texts through meaningful conversational discussion.
  • Discussion-Oriented Flipped Classroom - Homework is assigned in the form of video lectures and external video resources.
  • Discussions - Engage learners in text-based discussions where they discuss what they read with each other, and teachers set expectations and routines for productive discussions.
  • Discussions to Guide Reflection - Invite students to think about their thinking.
  • Distributed Practice - Distributed practice involves practicing content in short sessions spaced out over time, contrasting with massed practice (cramming) where content is practiced in one long session.
  • Distributed Practice (Spaced Learning) - Distributed practice, also known as spaced learning, involves reviewing information or practicing skills across multiple sessions spread out over time, rather than in one continuous session (massed practice).
  • Distributed Practice (Spacing Effect) - Distributed practice, also known as the spacing effect, is a learning technique where reviews of information or practice of a task are spaced out over time rather than massed together.
  • Diversity of Perspectives and Identities - Learning from multiple and varying perspectives involves incorporating diverse voices, experiences, and viewpoints into the curriculum.
  • Document Outline - The \"Document outline\" tool in Google Docs can be an easy and effective way to ask students to pick out evidence that supports the main ideas they’ve found.
  • Document Outline Strategy - Using the “Document outline” tool in Google Docs, students pick out evidence that supports the main ideas they've found.
  • Dolch Sight Word List - Cloze Passage Worksheets - Grade-level cloze passage worksheets using Dolch sight words.
  • Dolch Sight Word List - Flash Cards - Sets of printable flash cards for Dolch sight words, organized by grade level.
  • Dolch Sight Word List - Word Shape Worksheets - Word shape worksheets for Dolch sight words.
  • Dolch Sight Word Lists - The Dolch Sight word list includes the most common 220 words and 95 nouns encountered in children’s books.
  • Dolch Word List - Word Search Puzzles - Word search puzzles using Dolch sight words.
  • Domain Check - One simple search tip you can give students is to check the domain on search results.
  • Don’t Jump Into \"Fix It\" Mode - Resist the urge to immediately find solutions.
  • Don’t Say My Number - A counting game where a chosen number is forbidden, and learners must skip it while counting aloud in sequence.
  • Dot Card Flash - One learner flashes a dot card to another for 3 seconds, then hides it.
  • Dot Card Matching Games - Learners match dot cards with equal quantities but different arrangements, or match dot cards to corresponding numeral cards.
  • Double-Entry Journals - This strategy encourages learners to record their responses to a text as they read.
  • DragonBox Algebra 5+ App - Help kids develop their problem-solving and algebra skills with different levels of difficulties.
  • Dramatic Play - Dramatic play, also known as pretend play, is a learning strategy where learners actively experiment with social and emotional roles through imagination.
  • Draw Time When Felt Emotion - Learners draw pictures of a time when they felt specific emotions and share with classmates.
  • Drawing and Memory Enhancement - Drawing is a powerful technique to enhance memory and recall by engaging learners in multiple cognitive processes.
  • Drawing and Writing Developmental Stages - Understanding the developmental stages of drawing and writing can help educators tailor activities to match a child's current abilities.
  • Drawing for Early Writing and Reading Development - Drawing is a strategy to foster creativity, planning, and the development of foundational literacy skills in young learners.
  • Drawing for Emergent Writing - Drawing activities support emergent writing by allowing unstructured drawing time and using drawings in literacy activities.
  • Drawing for Formative Assessment - Inviting learners to express their understanding through drawings provides insights into their comprehension and any misconceptions.
  • Drawing for Memory and Comprehension - Drawing involves visually, kinesthetically, and semantically processing information, which forces learners to grapple with what they’re learning and reconstruct it in a way that makes sense to them.
  • Drawing for Memory and Learning - Drawing is used as a learning and memory tool.
  • Dual Color Highlighting - Dual color highlighting is a feature within text-to-speech software that highlights words being read aloud in one color (e.g., yellow) while highlighting the sentence in another color.
  • Dynamically Introduce Academic Vocabulary - Use repeated encounters with a word in various authentic contexts to help learners internalize the definition.

docs.title: E
docs.text:
• E.S.C.A.P.E. Junk News - A handy acronym to help students remember six key concepts for evaluating information.
  • Easy-Access Educational Tools - Making educational tools readily available to students supports self-advocacy by fostering independence and choice.
  • Education Calendars - Education calendars are visual aids designed to keep students, parents, and teachers informed about important dates, events, and activities.
  • Educational Charts - Educational charts are visual aids that present data in an accessible and understandable format, revealing patterns and stories behind the numbers.
  • Educational Infographics - Educational infographics are visual aids that simplify complex information into easily digestible formats using a combination of charts, icons, and text.
  • Educational Posters - Educational posters are visual aids that add color and helpful resources to a classroom environment.
  • Educational Research Map Visualization - This strategy involves using a research map visualization tool to explore education and learning sciences research.
  • Effective Feedback - Feedback is any response from a teacher regarding a student's performance or behavior.
  • Effective Materials Management - Using an 'in' and 'out' basket system for papers, labeling cubbies, bookshelves, bins, and folders, and providing easily accessible supplies cuts down on student time locating materials and supports organization.
  • Effort-Based Praise - Praising learners' efforts and strategies—as opposed to their intelligence—cultivates a growth mindset and enhances motivation and performance.
  • Electricity and Circuit Tasks - Electricity and circuit tasks involve investigating how electricity flows in simple circuits using tools like electric testers and puzzle boards.
  • Eliminate Extra Credit - Avoid extra credit opportunities as they depend on resources and time, and should not be necessary to demonstrate curriculum understanding.
  • Eliminate Homework and Extra Credit - Eliminate the inclusion of homework and extra credit in final grades.
  • Eliminate Internal Negative Chatter - Becoming aware of your negative thoughts and actively working to eliminate them.
  • Embrace Errors as Learning Opportunities - Creating a classroom culture where errors become learning opportunities involves changing the assumption that math ability is binary—either you're good at it or not.
  • Embracing Errors as Learning - This strategy involves creating a classroom culture where errors are seen as opportunities for learning rather than indicators of failure.
  • Emotion Charades - Emotion Charades involves a student acting out a scenario that makes them feel a certain way, while the rest of the group guesses the emotion being portrayed.
  • Emotion Cue Cards - Emotion cue cards are portable visual or auditory prompts designed to remind students of strategies for managing emotions, such as using a fidget or taking a mindfulness break.
  • Emotion Emojis - Students express how they are feeling by drawing or sharing an emoji.
  • Emotion Emojis Check-In - Students express their current feelings by drawing or sharing an emoji that represents their emotional state.
  • Emotion Guessing Game - An emotion guessing game involves an instructor or student making an emotion face, and the others guess the emotion being expressed.
  • Emotion Hello Song - The Emotion Hello Song involves singing a greeting song with different emotional expressions.
  • Emotion Identification Activities - These activities focus on helping learners identify and express emotions through various means, enhancing their emotional literacy and self-awareness.
  • Emotion Identification and Labeling - Learners identify, label, and match facial expressions and feelings.
  • Emotion Identification Games - These activities involve various games and exercises to help children recognize and understand different emotions.
  • Emotion Identification through Literature - This strategy involves using emotion posters as a tool during read-alouds to help students infer and name a character's emotions through language and pictures.
  • Emotion Password - Learners are required to make a particular face to enter the classroom.
  • Emotion Reflection Through Journaling - Learners reflect on experiences, tracking patterns in their emotions and behaviors to enhance self-understanding and goal-setting.
  • Emotion Songs - Emotion songs involve creating or adapting songs to explore different emotions.
  • Emotion Word Inclusion in Instruction - Educators frequently use emotion words when talking to learners, helping the learners understand how the educator is responding to their emotions and supporting the development of their emotional vocabulary.
  • Emotion-Based Story Discussions - Emotion-based story discussions involve reading stories and having learners identify and discuss the characters' feelings.
  • Emotion-Focused Pretend Play - Incorporate play by joining in play in the pretend area and starting conversations about how the imaginary characters they are acting out feel.
  • Emotional Check-ins - Beginning the day by asking students how they are feeling helps to identify potential emotional triggers.
  • Emotional Regulation Strategies - Educators identify students' strengths and challenges in emotional regulation—the ability to control responses to emotional stimuli.
  • Emotional Thermometer - An emotional thermometer is a visual tool used to help children recognize and gauge the intensity of their emotions.
  • Emotional Vocabulary Building - Learners are provided direct access to emotion words, using a word wall or chart to expand their emotional vocabulary.
  • Emotional Walking Game - The Emotional Walking Game involves learners walking around while embodying different emotions upon hearing a signal.
  • Empathy for Educators - Engage in actions to build an empathic mindset.
  • Emphasis on Reasoning over Answers - De-emphasizing answers and spending more time on reasoning can build confidence.
  • Emphasis on the Learning Process - Helping learners focus on and value the process of learning, rather than just the grades they receive, promotes a growth mindset.
  • Emphasize Reasoning over Answers - De-emphasizing correct answers and spending more time on reasoning involves shifting the focus from finding the right solution to understanding the problem-solving process.
  • Emphasize the Value of Learning - Help learners focus on and value the process of learning rather than solely on grades.
  • Emphasize Time on Task - Time plus energy equals learning.
  • Employ Common Language and Strategies Across Disciplines - Employing common language and strategies across disciplines involves aligning writing expectations and terminology across different subject areas.
  • Empowering Students as Leaders - Identify students with challenging behaviors who exhibit leadership qualities.
  • Empowering Students Through Self-Advocacy - Empowering students to advocate for themselves involves teaching them about their rights and needs, and providing them with opportunities to communicate and act on that understanding.
  • Empowering Teachers with EQUIP - EQUIP is a customizable observation tool designed to track patterns in student participation, empowering teachers to build more equitable classrooms.
  • Encourage Active Learning - Learning is not a spectator sport.
  • Encourage Cooperation - Learning is enhanced when it is more like a team effort than a solo race.
  • Encourage Feedback and Sharing - Encouraging learners to share their work with peers and online fosters a collaborative writing environment and broadens the audience for their work.
  • Encourage Reading Diverse Texts - Learners read diverse texts and then think and talk about different genres to acquire academic language.
  • Encourage Student Self-Advocacy - Empowering students to become self-advocates involves helping them understand their strengths and challenges, and providing them with a voice in their learning.
  • Encouraging Help-Seeking Behavior - Creating a classroom environment where students feel comfortable asking for help.
  • Encouraging Self-Advocacy - Self-advocacy involves understanding one's needs, knowing what support might help, and communicating those needs to others to promote independence and problem-solving.
  • Encouraging Student Self-Advocacy - Empowering learners to communicate their needs, understand their rights, and actively seek support.
  • Encouraging Students to Ask for Help - This strategy focuses on creating a classroom environment where students feel comfortable asking for help when they are struggling.
  • Engage Positive Role Models - Involving families and community members in classroom and school activities.
  • Engage with Empathy - Engage in effective online communication with empathy by taking the time to read and understand the original post, exchanging ideas with one or more users, tagging and mentioning community members, carefully crafting your message,…
  • Enhanced Acoustics and Noise Control - Creating schools that buffer external noise from classrooms can improve student outcomes.
  • Enriched Learning Environment - Creating a brain-friendly and enriched classroom environment involves optimizing the learning space by considering layout, furniture choices, color selections, lighting, nature, environmental print, and organization of materials.
  • Enrichment Through Art and Music - Teachers integrate art and music from diverse cultures into their lessons to enrich learning, engage students, and promote cultural understanding.
  • Environmental Interaction Analysis - These activities explore the relationships between people and their environments by examining environments, inhabitants, and the tracks they leave behind.
  • EQ Feeling Chart - Pair students and check-in with each other using an EQ Feeling Chart.
  • EQ Feeling Chart Check-In - Students use a provided EQ Feeling Chart to identify and communicate their current emotions.
  • EQ Feeling Chart Exploration - Learners use the EQ Feeling Chart to identify and communicate their feelings with a partner.
  • Equitable Assessment Rubrics - Rubrics aligned to learning standards, objectives, and activities that illuminate student learning and mastery, with meaningful comments for formative assessment.
  • Equitable Calling on Students - Ensure all learners get response opportunities, not just high achievers.
  • Equitable Classroom Observations - EQUIP is a customizable observation tool for tracking patterns in student participation, aiming to empower teachers in building more equitable classrooms.
  • Equitable Grading - Equitable grading focuses on fair and consistent grading practices to address biases.
  • Errors as Learning Opportunities - Creating a classroom culture where errors become learning opportunities shifts the perception of mistakes as failures to opportunities for growth and understanding.
  • Establish Consistent Routines - Use consistent routines and methods of giving instructions to help students know what is expected of them.
  • Establish Ground Rules for Peer Critique - Establishing ground rules for peer critique ensures that the process is productive, respectful, and beneficial for all learners.
  • Establish Guidelines for Discussing Race - Establish guidelines or agreements for group members to make when having discussions of race to ensure respectful and productive dialogue.
  • Establish Guidelines for Discussions - Establish clear guidelines for group discussions, emphasizing engagement, comfort with discomfort, speaking one's truth, and accepting non-closure.
  • Establish Talk Partners - Establishing pre-arranged talk partners helps to streamline pair talk activities.
  • Estimate and Predict - Learners use estimation and prediction skills by asking how they might do on an upcoming project or how long it might take them to complete a task or assignment.
  • Estimation and Prediction - Asking students to use estimation and prediction skills.
  • Estimation and Prediction Activities - Estimation and prediction activities help learners to develop an understanding of self-awareness as they learn to understand how they do work.
  • Estimation and Prediction for Self-Awareness - Learners use estimation and prediction skills to reflect on their abilities.
  • Ethical Responsibility Tools - Defining responsibility and ethical responsibility, providing specific tools such as graphic organizers or visual representations to help students consider the ethical and moral responsibilities of their decisions.
  • Exercise Contests - Organize contests to incentivize students to be more physically active, such as a month-long or year-long challenge.
  • Exercise for Cognitive Enhancement - Regular physical exercise boosts cognitive function by increasing neurotransmitter levels, promoting neurogenesis in the hippocampus, and improving focus and attention.
  • Exit Tickets - Exit tickets are short prompts given at the end of a lesson to encourage self-assessment, reflection, and growth mindset.
  • Expect Excellence - Demonstrating a belief in excellence and setting high expectations is essential for creating a successful PBL culture.
  • Expecting Excellence in PBL - Expecting excellence in PBL involves setting high expectations for all students and actively dispelling the myth that PBL does not work for \"those kids.\" By ensuring proper scaffolding and understanding students' current realities,…
  • Explicate, Validate, and Address Negative Emotions - When learners come into a course with negative emotions and expectations, it can affect not only their learning but also their capacity to learn.
  • Explicit and Systematic Writing Instruction - Explicit and systematic teaching of strategies, skills, and knowledge needed to be a proficient writer.
  • Explicit Conversations about Emotions and Social Issues - Engaging learners in explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice, helps them develop a deeper understanding of social awareness and empathy.
  • Explicit Discussion of Perspectives - Explicitly discuss different perspectives, encouraging students to consider viewpoints other than their own.
  • Explicit Discussions About Perspectives - Have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice.
  • Explicit Discussions of Perspectives - Facilitating structured conversations where learners explore multiple viewpoints and consider how different individuals might experience the same event.
  • Explicit Instruction in Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination - Providing explicit instruction for students to develop the skills associated with self-advocacy and self-determination involves teaching and encouraging them to empower themselves by understanding their needs and rights, communicating…
  • Explicit Instruction on Book Selection and Care - Teach learners how to select appropriate independent reading books, care for them, understand expectations for their reading work, and follow library maintenance procedures.
  • Explicit Instruction: Argumentation with Evidence - This instructional strategy involves directly teaching learners how to construct arguments and support claims with evidence, particularly in online settings.
  • Explicit Instruction: Decoding - Explicit instruction in decoding involves providing direct and systematic teaching of phonics and word recognition skills.
  • Explicit Instruction: Handwriting - Direct teaching approach to handwriting, breaking down essential components like letter formation, size, and spacing.
  • Explicit Instruction: Spelling - Explicit spelling instruction involves directly teaching spelling rules, patterns, and strategies rather than relying solely on incidental learning or discovery.
  • Explicit Instruction: Writing Strategies - Explicit instruction in writing strategies involves directly teaching students specific methods for planning, drafting, revising, and editing their work.
  • Explicit or Direct Instruction - Explicit instruction is a structured teaching approach where instructors make goals, objectives, expectations, and instructional content explicit.
  • Explicit Strategy Instruction - Explicitly teaching strategies involves providing learners with specific tools and techniques to solve problems and improve their learning.
  • Explicit Teacher Modeling - Explicit teacher modeling involves the teacher both describing and modeling a skill or concept.
  • Explicit Teaching - When teachers adopt explicit teaching practices they clearly show students what to do and how to do it.
  • Explicitly Addressing Social Awareness - The approach involves specifically identifying student strengths and challenges related to social awareness and then employing aligned strategies to leverage those strengths to support learning.
  • Explicitly Discuss Different Perspectives - Engage learners in structured discussions that explore diverse viewpoints and consider the experiences of others.
