  • Exploration Station - Establishing a dedicated computer as a station for exploration allows learners to discover their preferred composition pathway.
  • Exploration Station for Multimodal Pathways - Creating a designated computer station where students can explore their preferred composition pathway.
  • Expository Advance Organizers - Expository advance organizers give students a broad idea of the lesson’s purpose before it begins by clearly stating the goals of the lesson.
  • Express Confidence in Learners - Another way to communicate positive expectations is by directly telling the learners that they have the ability to do well.
  • Expressing Interest in Ethnic Background - Teachers demonstrate genuine care for students' cultural needs by encouraging them to research and share their ethnic backgrounds, fostering a trusting classroom environment.
  • Expressing Interest in Students' Ethnic Backgrounds - Teachers can actively demonstrate genuine care for students' cultural, emotional, and intellectual needs by encouraging students to research and share information about their ethnic backgrounds.
  • Expressive Outlets - This strategy encourages learners to express their emotions through journaling, drawing, or talking out loud.
  • Expressive Writing - Expressive writing involves putting thoughts and feelings into words, often focusing on emotionally charged or stressful experiences.
  • Extended Writing Opportunities - Extended writing opportunities involve providing learners with regular practice in writing to enhance their skills.
  • Extension Projects for Advanced Students - Challenge advanced learners with real-world extension projects that apply their knowledge in meaningful ways.

docs.title: F
docs.text:
• Facilitating Discourse (Online) - Facilitating discourse in online learning involves more than simply requiring students to post in a discussion forum.
  • Facilitating Learning - Teachers should redirect their role in the classroom from instructor to facilitator to reduce the power differential between the instructor and students.
  • Fair Communication Anchor Charts - Displaying anchor charts outlining fair communication protocols for class discussions and/or projects requiring teamwork involves creating visual aids that articulate the rules and expectations for respectful and inclusive communication.
  • Familiar, Quiet, and Repetitive Tasks - Using familiar, quiet, and repetitive fine motor and visual tasks can be a calming experience for many children.
  • Familiar, Repetitive Tasks - Providing learners with familiar, quiet, and repetitive fine motor and visual tasks to complete at the beginning of the day or during transition times to promote calmness and focus.
  • Family Book Club - Choose a book that is representative of your students and in their home language if possible.
  • Family Engagement - Family engagement is a practice in which families and school personnel collaborate to support and improve the learning and development of children.
  • Family Engagement: Supporting Children with Disabilities - Family engagement is a practice in which families and school personnel collaborate to support and improve the learning and development of children, including those with disabilities.
  • Faux-Flipped Classroom - This is a specific model targeting young learners.
  • Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward Model - The Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward Model is a structured approach to providing effective feedback.
  • Feedback Format - Feedback can be delivered in various formats, including written, verbal, or video.
  • Feedback Sandwich - The feedback sandwich technique involves delivering feedback in three parts: compliment, correct, compliment.
  • Feedback Through Different Media - Delivering feedback through various media, such as video, allows for a more encouraging tone of voice and relaxed body language compared to impersonal email feedback.
  • Feeling Face Snack Time - Learners pull a 'feeling face' card and eat their snack while showing the matching emotion.
  • Feelings Ring Around the Rosie - During recess, learners play 'Ring Around the Rosie' while acting out different emotions.
  • Fictional Characters to Teach Social Awareness - Use current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness.
  • Fidget Contracts - Fidget contracts are agreements between a learner and an educator or caregiver that outline specific rules and guidelines for using fidget tools.
  • Fidget Utilization Protocol - Fidgets are tools to aid focus and self-regulation, not toys.
  • Field Trips - Field trips are educational excursions that take learners outside of the classroom to experience real-world environments and engage with content in a multisensory, interactive manner.
  • Find the Difference - Similar to 'Find the Total', but learners subtract to find the difference between two dot cards.
  • Find the Total - Learners are shown two dot cards and asked to find the total number of dots.
  • Finger Speed-Differences - Same as speed-sums, except whoever find the difference between the two numbers first wins.
  • Finger Speed-Sums - Students meet in pairs with one hand behind their back.
  • Finger-Painting: Arts Integration - Integrating arts like fiction writing, dance, drama, graphic design, music, drawing, painting, or ceramics into all subjects helps learners learn and find their talents and interests.
  • Fishbowl - Two learners sit facing each other in the center of the room; the remaining learners sit in a circle around them.
  • Fishbowl Discussion - Fishbowl is a strategy for facilitating group discussions.
  • Fist Tapping & Arm Tapping - Fist tapping and arm tapping are multisensory spelling strategies that involve tapping out the syllables and sounds of words.
  • Five High Fives - Students try to give a high-five to five different classmates.
  • Five-Stage Problem-Solving Model - A five-stage model to help learners understand, identify, and resolve issues.
  • Flashcards - Flashcards are a study tool used for memorization and reinforcement of knowledge.
  • Flexible Seating - Flexible seating involves providing learners with a variety of seating options and allowing them to choose where they sit based on their individual needs and preferences.
  • Flexible Seating Patterns and Configurations - Providing a variety of different furniture that allows students to work in different areas, depending on the project or time of day.
  • Flipped Learning - Flipped learning is a pedagogical approach that reverses the traditional learning environment by delivering instructional content, often via pre-recorded videos or other materials, outside of class, and using class time for active…
  • Focus on Enjoyable Moments - This strategy entails consciously choosing to fill one's mind with positive images and thoughts, making it a habit to bring the mind back every time it goes astray.
  • Focus on Issues of Justice - Authentic projects that focus on issues of justice engage students by having them work on something that matters, impacting their lives, their community, and the lives of those they care about.
  • Focus on the Question They Answered Correctly - Instead of focusing on a student’s mistake, instructors identify the question a student answered correctly, even if it’s different than the one asked.
  • Focus Projects on Issues of Justice - Projects center on authentic issues that matter to students and their communities, impacting their lives and the lives of those they care about.
  • Focused-Attention Practices - Focused-attention practice is a brain exercise for quieting the thousands of thoughts that distract and frustrate us each day.
  • Focusing Projects on Issues of Justice - Focusing project-based learning (PBL) projects on issues of justice involves designing projects that allow students to work on topics that matter to their community, their lives, and the lives of those they care about.
  • Follow the Platinum Rule - Treat others the way they want and need to be treated.
  • Follow Up After Discussions About Race - This strategy involves taking actions that might change inequities revealed during a discussion and giving learners time to do something that will change the learning environment.
  • Follow-Up After Disciplining a Student - After disciplining a learner, the instructor should do the following: touch base with the learner, acknowledge post-disciplinary successes, and don't give up too quickly.
  • Follow-up After Discussions - Teachers encourage students to take actions to address inequities revealed during the discussion, such as writing letters to the editor or meeting with the principal.
  • Formative Assessment to Gauge Student Progress and Guide Instruction - Assessing student work on a regular basis provides both the teacher and the student with a sense of the student’s progress, indicates strengths and areas for improvement, and helps the teacher plan appropriately to meet the student’s needs.
  • Formative Feedback - Teacher performance management processes can be viewed as part of a growth mindset by making it formative, rather than summative, and inviting participation of the teacher in the process.
  • Fossil Analysis - Fossil analysis tasks involve examining and describing fossils to develop a 'Fossil Guide.' Learners create drawings and written descriptions for each fossil, enhancing understanding of fossil identification and paleontological concepts.
  • Foster Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination - This strategy emphasizes the importance of developing self-advocacy and self-determination skills in students, particularly those with disabilities.
  • Foster Self-Awareness - Self-awareness is the ability to correctly identify your own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they impact behavior.
  • Fostering Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination - This involves prioritizing self-advocacy and self-determination skills in education systems to improve educational and life outcomes for students with disabilities.
  • Fostering Student Self-Knowledge - Fostering student self-knowledge involves implementing measures that help students understand themselves as learners.
  • Four Moves - If you have time to scroll Facebook or watch the news, you probably have a moment to decide if a news story seems credible.
  • Four Moves and a Habit - A framework for fact-checking that includes four key moves: Check for previous work, go upstream to find the source, read laterally, and circle back.
  • Free Choice Time - Provide learners with the autonomy to select their learning activities, mirroring the self-directed learning seen in preschool environments.
  • Free Choice Time: Student-Directed Learning - Providing learners with choice in activities promotes engagement, responsibility, and independence.
  • Free Graphing Calculator App - An awesome app with an intuitive, user-friendly interface that works more as a tool to do complex calculations.
  • Free Math Worksheets - Free math worksheets provide accessible and structured practice materials to support math learning.
  • Free Play - Free play is a child-led activity where learners explore and develop skills through self-directed interactions with their environment and peers.
  • Frequent Student Reflections - This strategy involves prompting learners to reflect on their learning more often, allowing them to better understand their strengths and weaknesses, make connections between topics and disciplines, and grow as they self-assess their…
  • Frequent, Low-Stakes Quizzes - Administering frequent quizzes with minimal impact on grades to reinforce learning and identify gaps in understanding.
  • Frustration and Stress Prevention/Reduction Techniques - Educators should practice techniques to prevent/reduce their stress and frustration.
  • Fry Word Lists - The Fry word list contains 1,000 high-frequency words divided into ten levels, further split into groups of twenty-five words based on frequency and difficulty.
  • Functional Wall Displays - Using walls for bulletin boards displaying student work and curricular supports, such as a word wall or math posters, makes resources easily accessible during instruction.

docs.title: G
docs.text:
• Gain Attention Before Giving Instructions - Use techniques such as clapping or knocking to signal students to stop, look, and listen before giving instructions.
  • Gallery Quote Walk - Students pick a quote that expresses how they feel in the moment.
  • Gallery Quote Walk Check-In - Students read displayed quotes and choose one that reflects their current feelings.
  • Gallery Walk - Stations or posters are set up around the classroom, on the walls, or on tables.
  • Game-Based Incentives for Quiet - Implementing a game-based incentive, such as \"Silent 20,\" where students are given 20 seconds to return to their seats and be completely quiet.
  • Game-Based Learning (GBL) - Game-based learning involves designing learning activities so that game characteristics and game principles inhere within the learning activities themselves.
  • Games - Gaming involves using games as a way to help learners learn by doing.
  • Games + Structured Activity - Students engage with educational games designed to introduce or reinforce specific concepts.
  • Gamification - Gamification is the integration of game elements like point systems, leaderboards, badges, or other elements related to games into “conventional” learning activities in order to increase engagement and motivation.
  • Generating and Asking Questions - This strategy involves readers asking themselves questions throughout the reading process.
  • Genre Study - Genre study is an approach to teaching literature that involves exploring the characteristics and conventions of different literary genres.
  • Gestures - Gestures are physical movements, typically of the hands or arms, used to communicate meaning or support learning.
  • Give Hints and Clues to Help Students Answer Questions - Teachers should do more delving and rephrasing for learners for whom they have high expectations.
  • Give Prompt Feedback - Knowing what you know and don’t know focuses learning.
  • Goal Setting for Writing - Setting clear goals for writing, encouraging peer support, self-assessment, and providing feedback on progress.
  • GoNoodle Activities - GoNoodle provides interactive videos that encourage learners to engage in movement and play, supporting attention and learning.
  • GoNoodle: Physical Activity & Movement Breaks - GoNoodle offers videos and activities to encourage physical activity and movement breaks through gestures and movement.
  • Good Tutee-Tutor Contact - Regular contact between tutees and tutors is part of the tutoring process, increasing tutee motivation and involvement.
  • Grade Students Based on Demonstrated Learning - Instead of averaging scores over time, emphasize grading students on their ultimate level of mastery at the end of a unit.
  • Gradual Increase of Independent Reading Time - Start with short independent reading sessions and gradually increase the amount of time as students build reading stamina.
  • Gradual Release of Responsibility in Multimodal Composition - Using the gradual release of responsibility model to support students in multimodal composition.
  • Graphic Notes - Use visual cues in note-taking to help learners organize the information you are sharing with them orally.
  • Graphic Organizers (Math) - Graphic organizers break down math problems into steps, which helps students figure out what’s being asked in a word problem or which operation to use.
  • Graphic Organizers / Guided Notes (for Processing Speed) - During lecture, learners are provided with graphic organizers or guided notes to help pull out the important points.
  • Graphic Organizers and Guided Notes (Processing Speed) - Providing students with graphic organizers or guided notes during lectures to help them pull out the important points.
  • Graphic Organizers and Visual Aids - Tools that help students identify and focus on the most important information by presenting it in a structured and visual format.
  • Graphic Organizers and Visual Aids (Attention) - Using graphic organizers and visual aids to help students identify the most important information and focus on it.
  • Graphic Organizers and Visual Aids (for Attention) - These tools help learners identify the most important information and focus on it.
  • Graphic Organizers as Text Illustrations - Students add a graphic organizer to a finished expository or argumentative writing piece to illustrate a key concept or process.
  • Graphic Organizers as Thinking Tools - Students interact with content by organizing chunks of it into graphic organizers in groups, pairs, or individually, then comparing their results.
  • Graphic Organizers for Assessment - Students complete a graphic organizer that shows relationships between terms or concepts instead of taking a quiz, or as part of a quiz, to evaluate understanding of a body of content.
  • Graphic Organizers for Classroom Management - Put the most important classroom policies, procedures, and expectations into graphic form to increase the likelihood that students will follow them.
  • Graphic Organizers for Lecture Support - Instructors deliver lectures using a graphic organizer to visually connect concepts, rather than using PowerPoint or a standard outline.
  • Graphic Organizers for Math - Graphic organizers help learners break down math problems into steps to understand what’s being asked or which operation to use.
  • Graphic Organizers for Note-Taking - Learners use graphic organizers to structure notes from readings, research, films, or podcasts.
  • Graphic Organizers for Pre-Reading - Students identify the text structure (compare/contrast, cause/effect, etc.) before reading and complete a graphic organizer that supports that structure as they read.
  • Graphic Organizers for Pre-Writing - Students use graphic organizers to plan and structure their ideas before drafting a written piece, jotting down notes rather than writing complete sentences.
  • Graphic Organizers for Retrieval Practice - Students recall as much as they can about a topic (Brain Dump) and then sort their dumped information into a graphic organizer.
  • Graphic Organizers for Unit Planning - Present students with a graphic organizer to show how the parts of a unit fit together, providing a sense of where they are in the unit and why they are learning the individual parts.
  • Graphic Organizers/Guided Notes - During lecture provide students with graphic organizers or guided notes to help pull out the important points.
  • Greek Combining Forms - Because scholars have drawn from the Greek language to name scientific concepts and discoveries since the Renaissance, middle school students will encounter hundreds of words derived from Greek in math, science, and philosophy texts.
  • Group-Based Flipped Classroom - The group-based model focuses on group learning.
  • Groups - The teacher calls out a number (e.g., 3), and the students have 10 seconds to get themselves into groups of that size.
  • Growth Mindset Development - Growth mindset development involves cultivating the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through dedication, effort, and learning from mistakes.
  • Growth Mindset Feedback - Growth mindset feedback focuses on praising effort, strategies, and persistence rather than innate abilities.
  • Guide Student Reflection - Teachers use many strategies to guide students through a period of reflection.
  • Guided Discovery with Word Sorting - Use guided discovery with word sorting and teacher questioning to help students understand spellings that depend on the position of a sound in a word or established conventions (like –ve).
  • Guided Inquiry - Guided inquiry is an educational approach that blends inquiry activities with direct instruction.
  • Guided Peer Response using PeerMark™ - Guided peer response using Turnitin PeerMark™ involves instructors pre-setting specific questions for learners to answer when providing feedback to their peers.
  • Guided Play - Guided play combines the child-directed aspects of free play with intentional learning goals through light adult scaffolding.

docs.title: H
docs.text:
• Have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice - Integrate direct instruction on understanding and managing emotions, as well as discussing relevant social issues, including social justice, to promote social awareness and emotional intelligence.
  • Headings and Highlight Strategy - Students read an excerpt of a difficult article in Google Docs.
  • Health and Dietary Planning - Tasks involve studying the food pyramid, learning about daily requirements, and planning food for one day.
  • Heat Transfer Investigations - Heat transfer investigations involve exploring how different materials and environments affect the transfer of heat.
  • Hexagonal Thinking - Hexagonal thinking is a mixed retrieval and elaboration strategy that uses hexagonal cards, paper, or programs to investigate how ideas and concepts are connected.
  • High Frequency Word Lists - High-frequency word lists (e.g., Dolch and Fry) are collections of the most commonly used words in reading and writing.
  • Highlight and Explore Patterns, Critical Features, Big Ideas, and Relationships - Accentuating important information and how it relates to the learning goal helps learners focus their attention and understand the key concepts.
  • Highlight Math Vocabulary - Model how to highlight or circle mathematical words in word problems that prompt multiplication or division.
  • Highlighting and Exploration of Patterns, Critical Features, Big Ideas, and Relationships - Accentuation of important information and its relationship to the learning goal.
  • Highlighting Strategy - The highlighting strategy is a digital approach to enhance text engagement, using tools to create individualized highlighters with different colors in digital documents.
  • Highlighting Strategy with Add-on Tool - Students use a Google Doc add-on tool to create individualized highlighters in different colors.
  • Historically Responsive Literacy - Historically Responsive Literacy (HRL) is a framework that seeks to cultivate literacy, intellect, and self-efficacy by connecting learning deeply to who we are and what agency we have in the world.
  • Hoax Website Analysis - Learners examine famous website hoaxes to identify clues that suggest the site is not genuine.
  • Home Language Reading Demonstrations - When new students come to the classroom, ask them to read books in their home language to show you what they know about reading.
  • Home Literacy Environment Checklist - This checklist is a tool designed to help parents assess and enhance the literacy-richness of their home environment.
  • Home Living Center Role Play - Learners visit the home living center to role play different characters and relate these characters to different emotions.
  • Home Surveys - Sending weekly, biweekly, or monthly surveys home can provide ongoing data and insight into students and their families.
  • Home-Based Literacy Support - Home-based literacy support involves schools providing families with resources and guidance to support students’ learning at home.
  • Hot Seat - One learner assumes the role of a book character, significant figure in history, or concept (such as a tornado, an animal, or the Titanic).
  • How Close to 100? - A game played in partners where children roll two dice to determine the dimensions of an array to draw on a 100 grid, aiming to fill the grid as much as possible.
  • How Many Are Hiding? - An activity where children have cubes and a cup.
  • How Spelling Supports Reading - Instruction on the relationship between spelling and reading.
  • Hyperlinked Teaching - Hyperlinked teaching provides students with direct avenues for further inquiry and exploration.

docs.title: I
docs.text:
• I Wonder Journals - At Crellin Elementary School in Oakland, Maryland, teachers encouraged students to ask “I wonder” questions to push their learning beyond the classroom.
  • Identify Feelings - Students identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings.
  • Identify Key Background Knowledge in Math Problems - Identify what kinds of background knowledge learners need to understand a math problem.
  • Identify Self-Talk - Have students record messages from their inner voice over a week in a journal or notebook.
  • Identifying and Addressing Self-Regulation Strengths and Challenges - This strategy involves educators identifying students' strengths and challenges related to self-regulation, and then using strategies to leverage strengths to support learning.
  • Identifying and Supporting Learners with Relationship Skills - Identifying and supporting learners who have learning strengths or challenges related to relationship skills helps them improve and succeed.
  • Identifying Feelings - Learners identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings.
  • Identifying Obstacles - Identifying obstacles involves recognizing potential challenges that could impede progress toward a goal.
  • Identifying Self-Talk - Students record the messages from their inner voice over the course of a week in a journal or notebook.
  • If It Happened to You... - This activity enhances empathy and emotional regulation by presenting students with scenarios from YA novels or short stories, stripped of character names and page numbers, and asking them to discuss how they would approach the situation…
  • IKEA VR Kitchen Visualizer - The IKEA VR kitchen visualizer uses VR technology to give customers a better understanding of what to think about when planning and designing their kitchens and reassure them in their decisions by allowing them to walk around in a virtual…
  • Illustrate Through Multiple Media - Making learning come alive with simulations, graphics, activities, and videos engages learners in a variety of ways and enhances comprehension.
  • Illustration Through Multiple Media - Making learning come alive with simulations, graphics, activities, and videos.
  • Implement Measures for Student Self-Knowledge - Implementing measures for student self-knowledge involves using various tools and strategies to help students understand their strengths, interests, and areas for growth.
  • Implicit Instruction: Vocabulary - Implicit vocabulary instruction involves teaching vocabulary “in the moment” by providing quick explanations and leveraging heavy context, usually with Tier III words.
  • Implicit Vocabulary Instruction - Implicit vocabulary instruction involves teaching words 'in the moment' using heavy context, often with Tier III words.
  • Impressions First - Before diving into specifics, encourage students to share their initial impressions of the mentor text.
  • Improve Classroom Air Quality - Poor indoor air quality is a major contributor to absenteeism.
  • Improve Indoor Air Quality - Poor indoor air quality in schools is a major contributor to absenteeism, especially for students with asthma.
  • Improved Air Quality - Indoor air quality is also a concern because poor air quality is a major contributor to absenteeism for students with asthma.
  • Improvisation in Mathematics - This strategy involves using improvisation and acting exercises to enhance mathematical understanding and creativity.
  • In a Hot Seat - Using a stimulus like a photo or item, learners create a character different from themselves, developing details about the character’s life.
  • Include Physical Activity - Brief breaks for active play can help children who struggle with attention.
  • Inclusive Cultural Response - Inclusive Cultural Response involves addressing gaps in cultural learning and representation by adding and including texts and making changes in units of study.
  • Inclusive Innovation Process - The Inclusive Innovation Process is a framework that facilitates growth with equity through a student, community, and educator-led research and design process.
  • Incorporate Crafts to Remember Positive Self-Talk - Using creative activities to reinforce positive self-talk, such as making crafts with positive affirmations written on them.
  • Incorporate Mindfulness Techniques - Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.
  • Incorporate Students' Cultural Practices - This strategy involves integrating students' cultural backgrounds and experiences into lesson design and classroom activities.
  • Incorporate Technology into Reflection - This strategy involves leveraging students' familiarity with technology to create more engaging and interactive reflection opportunities.
  • Incorporating Methods for Self-Testing - A potent method for helping students become active participants in learning is to reframe the concept of testing.
  • Incorporating Physical Activity Into Classroom Learning - Incorporate movement into classroom instruction by having science classes explore natural settings, using physical movements to teach math, or acting out stories in language arts.
  • Incorporating Self-Testing - Reframing the concept of testing involves using frequent, non-graded tests as progress checks to ensure students don’t fall behind.
  • Increase Classroom Space and Reduce Overcrowding - Provide ample classroom space to support student engagement and learning.
  • Increase Latency Periods When Questioning Students - Increasing latency (wait time) for low-achieving learners will help them improve.
  • Increase Student Language Production - Increase student-to-student interaction with academic language.
  • Increase Synchronous Teacher Presence - Teacher presence in synchronous sessions helps to reduce feelings of isolation in students enrolled in online courses and increase student engagement and agency, and ways to reduce distractions and cognitive overload.
  • Independent Practice - Independent practice is when learners practice skills and concepts on their own, after guided practice.
  • Independent Reading - Independent reading involves students selecting and reading books on their own, within their reading level and interests.
  • Individual Deliberate Practice - Deliberate practice is a structured approach to skill development that focuses on intentional, effective, and consistent effort to improve performance.
  • Individual Spaces - Creating designated areas within the classroom to serve specific functions, such as independent work, collaborative projects, or mini-lessons, can promote student engagement.
  • Individualized \"Highlighter Tool\" - Students use an individualized \"highlighter tool\" (e.g., a Google Doc add-on) to create custom highlighters in different colors.
  • Indoor Air Quality Improvement - Improving indoor air quality reduces absenteeism, particularly for students with asthma, and addresses “sick building syndrome.” Proper ventilation systems and pollutant reduction create a healthier learning environment.
  • Inflectional Endings Instruction - Inflectional endings instruction focuses on teaching the rules for adding suffixes (e.g., -ed, -s, -es, -ing, -er, -est) to base words.
  • Informal Games and Jam Sessions - Encourage participation in informal games and jam sessions to foster creativity, collaboration, and enjoyment without the pressure of competition.
  • Inhibition Support Strategies - These are strategies used to leverage student strengths in order to address challenges with inhibition, such as the ability to suppress attention to irrelevant input and to focus on pertinent stimuli or information.
  • Initiating a Conversation with Learners to Correct Name Pronunciation - The instructor initiates a conversation with the learner by following the steps outlined below.
  • Inquiry-Based Writing - Engage in focused investigation with “immediate and concrete data” that learners gather and analyze, as a springboard to higher quality writing.
  • Instill Intrinsic Motivation - Helping students understand that positive actions lead to positive feelings about themselves.
  • Instructor and Peer Feedback - Combining instructor feedback with peer feedback enhances the learning process.
  • Instructor as Facilitator - Reducing the power differential between instructor and students by acting more as a facilitator than an instructor fosters a nurturing environment.
  • Integrate Emotions into Daily Schedule and Routine - Integrate the teaching of emotions into daily schedules and routines.
  • Integrating Art and Science - This strategy combines art activities with science concepts to teach specific scientific principles through artistic expression.
  • Integrating Math with Music and Dance - Integrating math with music and dance is a strategy in which rhythm, pattern, movement, and structure are used to explore mathematical relationships.
  • Integrating Movement into Daily Activities - Integrating movement into daily activities involves incorporating physical activity into routines and tasks that are typically sedentary.
  • Intensive Instruction/Active Engagement - Intensive instruction involves active learner engagement and plenty of time on task.
  • Interaction with Natural Environment - Incorporating natural elements (views of nature, plants) into the learning environment can improve focus, well-being, and academic performance.
  • Interactive Delivery with Questioning - Engage students through interactive discussions driven by questions and answers.
  • Interactive Modeling - Interactive Modeling is an instructional practice where the educator provides instruction for self-checking and provides an example.
  • Interactive Read-Alouds - Interactive read-alouds involve stopping during the reading process to engage learners in discussions and activities that promote deeper understanding of the text.
  • Interactive Scenarios - Use simulated environments or situations that mirror real-world challenges.
  • Interactive Storytelling - Interactive storytelling involves creating narratives where the reader or user can make choices that affect the story's direction and outcome.
  • Interdisciplinary Activities - Interdisciplinary activities present issues, themes, and problems that require skills and knowledge from more than one subject to address or answer.
  • Interest Inventories - Interest inventories are surveys used to assess students' areas of interest.
  • Interest-Based Negotiation - Interest-Based Negotiation involves establishing different perspectives, backgrounds, interests, and options for resolution, creating a single team out of the interested parties.
  • Interpreting the News - Learners pick a current news item and explore it from different points of view, examining whether the news is reported objectively and what other interpretations might exist.
  • Intervene in Abusive Language - Teachers must step in when abusive language occurs.
  • Interviews to Guide Reflection - Set aside time at the end of a learning sequence—a lesson, a unit, a school day, or a school year—to question each other about what has been learned.
  • Introduce Evaluation Concepts - Introduce concepts like “relevance, accuracy, bias, and reliability” and using these terms regularly as a part of classroom discourse can help students get used to questioning sources and the motivations authors may have.
  • Introduce Summary Frames - Learners read a section of text to themselves before verbally summarizing the passage to a partner or completing sentence frames.
  • Introducing Yourself Via Video - Providing a personal video introduction at the start of the course allows students to see you as a human being which can mitigate the anonymity of text-based conversation and encourage human connections.
  • Involving Learners in Classroom Design - Involving learners in classroom design means actively soliciting their input and ideas when creating or modifying the physical learning environment.
  • Involving Students in Classroom Redesign - Involving learners in the process of designing and transforming their learning environment can create a space that better meets their needs and preferences.
  • Irregular Anglo-Saxon Word Instruction - Teaching methods for irregular words include: grouping words with some memorable similarity, calling attention to the odd part of the word that must be learned by heart, using a multisensory memory strategy that gives the students many…
  • Islamic Geometry Exploration - Exploring Islamic geometry with students centers on exploration, joy, and solidarity.

docs.title: J
docs.text:
• Jigsaw - In the Jigsaw method, learners are divided into 'expert groups' to master a specific portion of the material and then regroup to teach that material to their peers.
  • Journal Reflections - Students think back on their experiences and outcomes to gain a greater understanding of themselves.
  • Journal Reflections for Self-Awareness - This strategy involves having students think back on their experiences and outcomes and then record them in a journal.
  • Journaling for Metacognitive Awareness - Journaling involves writing or recording thoughts and feelings to develop metacognitive awareness and build self-regulation skills.
  • Journaling for Self-Reflection - Journaling strategies include instructional practices that promote self-reflection along with tips for teachers in providing productive feedback.

docs.title: K
docs.text:
• Kagan Cooperative Learning Strategies - Implement Kagan Cooperative Learning Strategies to encourage active participation and engagement in learning.
  • Keep Instructions Concise - Avoid lengthy instructions, especially for learners with low English proficiency.
  • Keep Your Love of Teaching - Continue creating engaging projects and lessons and keep enjoying the students.
  • Key Word Flash Cards - Create flash cards for the four mathematical operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division).
  • Keyword Strategy - The keyword strategy is a mnemonic technique that enhances memory by linking new information to keywords already encoded in memory.
  • Kids React - Perform an online image search for the words “school lunch,” and project the results or create handouts with the images from the search results.
  • Know Your Own Perspectives - Reflect deeply on your own attitudes and beliefs and how they may impact your opinions and actions.
  • KWL Chart - A KWL chart is a graphic organizer used to structure a lesson by tapping into what students already Know (K), what they Want to know (W), and what they have Learned (L) about a topic.
  • KWL Charts - KWL (Know, Want to know, Learned) charts are advance organizers that help students activate prior knowledge, identify learning goals, and reflect on what they have learned.

docs.title: L
docs.text:
• Labeling Emotions Throughout the Day - Labeling emotions involves intentionally naming and describing one's own emotions and helping others label theirs throughout the day.
  • Ladder of Feedback - The Ladder of Feedback is a structured protocol to guide peer feedback that includes a sequential framework with specific questions, sentence stems, and success criteria.
  • Language Experience Approach - The language experience approach is a whole language method that integrates the development of reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through the use of learners' experiences.
  • Language Songs - Using songs to teach language involves engaging learners through music and rhythm to enhance vocabulary development, phonological awareness, and overall literacy skills.
  • Last Lesson, Last Week, Last Month - This activity involves looking back to the most important information presented yesterday, last week, and last month.
  • Lateral Reading - Lateral reading is a digital literacy strategy that involves evaluating the trustworthiness of online information by leaving the original site and consulting other digital sources to see what they say about it.
  • Latin Prefixes, Suffixes, and Roots - Direct teaching about the meaningful parts of words begins with the most common inflections, but then extends to prefixes, suffixes, and roots of Latin origin.
  • Leaderboards - Leaderboards showcase the distribution of point totals that learners have accumulated through various learning activities.
  • Learn About Students' Math Backgrounds - Understanding learners' math backgrounds is important.
  • Learner Choice as a Continuum - Learner choice involves transitioning from teacher-led content delivery to learner-driven purpose discovery.
  • Learner-Centric Approach - A learning approach where the problem is presented as an open-ended one, so there are several ways to solve it, with each solution leading to a different set of outcomes.
  • Learner-Generated Examples - Provide opportunities for learners to generate their own examples of a concept.
  • Learner-to-Learner (Peer) Feedback - Learner-to-learner (peer) feedback involves having learners provide constructive feedback on each other's work.
  • Learning Clubs - Learning clubs are a grouping system used to organize active learning events based on student-selected areas of interest.
  • Learning Goal Setting - This strategy involves defining clear objectives prior to engaging in a learning experience, such as shadowing.
  • Learning Interest Inventories - Learning interest inventories help instructors and learners identify areas of interest and ways of finding joy in learning and demonstrating that learning.
  • Learning Logs - Learning logs are short, reflective writing activities completed at the beginning or end of a class to review previously learned material or focus on new concepts.
  • Learning Strategy & Tool \"Fair\" - A 'Learning Strategy & Tool Fair' allows learners to explore a variety of learning strategies and tools in a hands-on, exploratory environment.
  • Learning Through Reflection - Link and construct meaning from experiences.
  • Lecture Support with Graphic Organizers - Instructors present lecture content using graphic organizers rather than standard PowerPoints or outlines, visualizing how concepts are related to each other.
  • Lesson Plans - Lesson plans are visual aids used by educators to stay organized and inspire their creativity.
  • Let students know what order they will be called on - This strategy allows students who are prone to challenges with inhibition to plan their response and wait until their turn.
  • Letter Formation Activities - Activities focused on teaching and practicing correct letter formation, including directionality, sequencing, and motor planning.
  • Letter Names and Letter Sounds Instruction - Explicit and direct instruction of letter names and letter sounds, which is critical for early literacy development.
  • Letter Strategy - The letter strategy is a mnemonic technique that involves using acronyms and acrostics to aid memory.
  • Letting students know what order they will be called on - Informing students of the order in which they will be called upon to respond can help reduce challenges related to inhibition.
  • Leverage Strengths to Address Self-Awareness Challenges - Educator identifies specific student strengths and/or challenges related to self- awareness, and uses/justifies aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning.
  • Leverage the Native Language - Integrate students' native languages into project work.
  • Leveraging Family Knowledge - Teachers can enhance curriculum and instructional practices by finding ways for students to contribute their own cultural experience, funds of knowledge, talents, and interests in the classroom.
  • Leveraging Instructor Office Hours - Instructors can share a great deal of insights and academic advice by opening up their regular office hours weekly to allow for help with a variety of questions, including those that concern a particular course.
  • Leveraging Native Language in PBL - Leveraging the native language in project-based learning (PBL) involves using students' multilingual abilities as an asset.
  • Leveraging Strengths for Attention - Identifying students' strengths related to attention and using those strengths to support and further develop their attention skills.
  • Leveraging Strengths for Emotional Regulation - Identifying students' strengths related to emotional regulation and using those strengths to support their learning and development.
  • Leveraging Strengths in Relationship Skills - This method involves an educator identifying specific learner strengths and/or challenges related to relationship skills and uses or justifies aligned strategies to leverage learner strengths to support learning.
  • Leveraging Strengths Thinking - Shifting from deficit to strengths thinking, which views families as having significant expertise and resources that can inform and improve student learning.
  • Leveraging Strengths to Address Attention Challenges - Identify specific student strengths and/or challenges related to attention then use strategies to leverage student strengths to support a student’s attention during learning.
  • Leveraging Strengths to Address Learning Differences - This strategy involves educators identifying specific student strengths and/or challenges and using aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning, including self-awareness and self-regulation.
  • Leveraging Strengths to Improve Relationship Skills - This strategy focuses on identifying and supporting students' relationship skills by leveraging their existing strengths.
  • Leveraging Strengths to Support Attention - This strategy focuses on identifying a learner's strengths and using those strengths to support their attention during learning.
  • Leveraging Strengths to Support Processing Speed - This strategy involves identifying a student’s strengths and using them to address challenges related to processing speed.
  • Liberation Literature and Counter-Narratives - Liberation literature involves exposing learners to literature that places out-group identities at the center of the curriculum to counter common negative stereotypes or omissions.
  • Life Back Then - Learners pick a time in history and a character who lived then, researching and presenting this to the class.
  • Limit Background Noise - Minimizing background noise, such as television, conversations, or lyrical music, enhances concentration and learning.
  • Line Awareness Activities - Activities focused on improving line awareness, which is crucial for writing legibly within a given space.
  • Listen to the Voices of Students - Providing students authorship and allowing them to share their stories empowers them, fostering agency and leadership.
  • Listening and reading for specific information - This strategy involves actively seeking particular details or information within a text or audio material to understand the overall message.
  • Listening to the Voices of Students in PBL - Listening to the voices of students involves giving them authorship in sharing and telling their own stories, creating agency and leadership.
  • Literacy Centers - Literacy centers are designated areas in the classroom where students work independently or collaboratively on meaningful literacy tasks to explore and expand their learning.
  • Literature Circles - Literature circles involve small groups of students who choose a book, meet to discuss it, and complete projects to demonstrate understanding.
  • Literature/Social Stories - Using literature or social stories to explicitly teach relationship skills involves selecting or creating narratives that model positive social interactions, communication strategies, and conflict resolution techniques.
  • Live Writing Demonstrations - Instructors demonstrate the writing process in real-time, in front of learners, to make the thinking and decision-making involved in writing visible.
  • Logic Puzzles - Logic puzzles are challenges designed to exercise the brain and improve memory, hand-eye coordination, and spatial and cognitive skills.
  • Logs and Journals to Guide Reflection - Periodically ask students to reread their journals, comparing what they knew at the beginning of a learning sequence with what they know now.
  • Low-Stakes Quizzes - Low-stakes quizzes are brief assessments designed to help learners gauge their understanding without the pressure of high grades.
  • Low-Stakes Writing - Teachers at University Park Campus School used daily low-stakes writing activities to foster student voice, self-confidence, and critical thinking skills—a school-wide strategy used in every subject.

docs.title: M
docs.text:
• Magnetism Investigations - Magnetism investigations involve exploring how magnets interact with different objects and mapping the effects of magnets on compasses.
  • Maintain Optimal Classroom Temperature - The temperature in a workspace affects engagement levels and overall productivity.
  • Maintain Presence for Students - Teachers should make themselves available for short talks with students before and after school or between classes.
  • Maintaining an Inclusive Curriculum - A culturally responsive curriculum is both inclusive in that it ensures that all students are included within all aspects of the school, and it acknowledges the unique differences students may possess.
  • Maintaining High Expectations - In culturally responsive instruction, achievement expectations are determined individually.
  • Maintaining High Expectations for Student Performance - Given that culturally responsive instruction is a student-centered philosophy, it should come as no surprise that expectations for achievement are determined and assigned individually for each student.
  • Maintaining Sensitivity to Language Concerns - In traditional classrooms, students who are not native English speakers often feel marginalized, lost, and pressured into discarding their original language in favor of English.
  • Make Learning Relevant - Teachers can boost student engagement and knowledge retention by connecting learning to students' interests, talents, learning styles, and sense of ownership in the education process.
  • Make the Invisible Visible (Power Dynamics) - This principle focuses on bringing power dynamics to the forefront and acknowledging their presence in the design process.
  • Make-Believe: Problem-Based Learning - Providing learners with real-world experiences and problems, and allowing them to work alongside experts, fosters engagement and prepares them for real-world challenges.
  • Maker Spaces and Fab Labs - Establish physical spaces where learners can invent, design, and build things using a variety of materials and tools, from wood scraps to technology.
  • Making and confirming predictions - This strategy involves forming educated guesses or anticipations about the content or outcome of a text or audio material and then verifying these predictions as one engages with the material.
  • Making Connections - Making connections involves linking new information to existing knowledge and experiences to enhance understanding and retention.
  • Making Connections (Text-to-Self, Text-to-Text, Text-to-World) - Making Connections is a comprehension strategy that helps learners relate a text to their own lives (text-to-self), to other texts they have read (text-to-text), or to events in the real world (text-to-world).
  • Making Inferences - This strategy requires readers to evaluate or draw conclusions from information in a text, even when the author does not explicitly state it.
  • Making Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination Critical Priorities - Integrating self-advocacy and self-determination into education systems to empower students with disabilities.
  • Manipulatives - Provide manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete.
  • Manipulatives: Sentence Combining - Using physical or digital manipulatives to combine simple sentences, thereby reducing working memory load and improving syntax knowledge.
  • Manipulatives: Sentence Construction - Using physical objects to represent parts of speech in sentences.
  • Map It Out! - Before a trip, children map the route, calculate mileage, estimate travel time, and track progress along the way.
  • Mapping Online Reading Behavior - Learners create visual maps to track the links and sites they visit while reading online texts.
  • Mass, Density, and Buoyancy Experiments - Mass, density, and buoyancy experiments involve exploring how the mass and density of objects affect their buoyancy in different liquids.
  • Matched Examples and Non-examples - Present matched examples and nonexamples for concepts with related attributes.
  • Math Art - Math Art involves creating drawings and designs that explore mathematical concepts and patterns.
  • Math Cards - An activity that uses cards with different representations of the same numerical answer (area model, dominoes, number sentence) to encourage number sense and understanding of multiplication, as opposed to memorization and time pressure.
  • Math Centers - Math centers involve setting up various stations in the classroom where learners can practice and apply mathematical concepts through activities like games and tablets.
  • Math Coach Role-Playing - Organize students into small groups where they take turns acting as \"math coaches.\" One student reads a word problem aloud, and the other students (the math coaches) advise the reader on which mathematical operation to use in solving the…
  • Math Coaching - Small groups of learners work together to solve word problems.
  • Math Games - Math games are structured activities designed to stimulate enthusiasm for math learning by providing opportunities to explore fundamental number concepts, engage in strategic mathematical thinking, and deepen understanding of numbers.
  • Math Games and Movement Breaks - Incorporating quick, fun, physical math games for when learners get antsy.
  • Math Journaling - In their math journals, students can write about things they are having trouble with or things that they've figured out.
  • Math Journals - Math journals are a way to gauge a student’s understanding of particular math concepts.
  • Math Key Word Flashcards - Learners create flashcards for each of the four mathematical operations.
  • Math Songs - Math songs are musical compositions designed to teach and reinforce math concepts and skills.
  • Math Talks - Math talks are structured conversations focused on mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies.
  • Math Talks / Number Talks - Math Talks, also known as Number Talks, are short, daily classroom routines where students solve math problems mentally and share their strategies.
  • Math Vocabulary Word Walls - Create a class word wall displaying mathematical terms and vocabulary to support working memory and develop language skills.
  • Mathematical Dance - Mathematical dance involves using movement to illustrate mathematical concepts.
  • Maximization of Transfer and Generalization - Supporting the application of learning to new contexts.
  • Maximize Transfer and Generalization - Applying learning to new contexts helps learners develop the ability to use what they have learned in real-world situations.
  • Meaningful Grading Through Feedback - Grades should represent multiple opportunities for students to demonstrate learning based on descriptive, concrete, and actionable feedback.
  • Measurement Tasks - Measurement tasks involve using measurement tools and techniques to quantify physical properties such as length, volume, and temperature.
  • Memory Game (Matching) - A memory game where learners match pairs of word cards to reinforce vocabulary and memory skills.
  • Mentor Texts - Mentor texts are examples of high-quality writing used to teach students how to improve their own writing skills.
  • Metacognitive Accountable Talk Stems - Accountable talk stems are phrases and sentence starters that facilitate structured, text-based discussions and promote higher-order thinking and metacognition.
  • Metacognitive Awareness for Self-Regulation - Journaling (or recording in an alternative form) can help students develop their metacognitive awareness to build self-regulation skills.
  • Metacognitive Journaling - Metacognitive journaling involves writing about one's own thinking, including tendencies, changes in thinking over time, biases, or blind spots.
  • Metacognitive Reflection - This strategy focuses on learners' awareness of their thought processes as they complete tasks, emphasizing self-improvement rather than assessment.
  • Metacognitive Strategies - Metacognitive strategies teach students to think about their thinking.
  • Method of Loci (Memory Palace) - The method of loci involves creating a mental 'memory palace' by associating items to be remembered with specific locations in a familiar place.
  • Micro Flipped Classroom - Short video lectures are distributed as study material along with short assignments.
  • Micro-Goal Setting - Setting achievable micro-goals encourages consistent, incremental learner progress.
  • Mind Mapping - Mind mapping is a visual thinking tool used to capture information and ideas.
  • Mindful Break - A mindful break involves students ringing a bell when they feel the class needs a break, stopping the lesson, standing up and stretching in silence, and then sitting down for mindful breathing.
  • Mindful Listening - Mindful listening is a practice of focusing on sound to introduce mindfulness.
  • Mindful Moment - A mindful moment involves pausing, settling the nervous system, and refocusing attention and energy on a new task.
  • Mindfulness and Movement Integration - Integrating mindfulness with movement involves combining physical activity with practices that promote awareness, focus, and presence.
  • Mindfulness Breaks - Mindfulness breaks are short, structured activities designed to create internal balance and a sense of being present in the moment.
  • Mindfulness Practices - Incorporating mindfulness practices such as yoga, breathing exercises, and meditation into the learning environment to calm the nervous system and promote self-regulation.
  • Mindfulness Techniques - Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.
  • Mindfulness Techniques for Emotional Regulation - Incorporating mindfulness techniques helps students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.
  • Mindfulness Techniques for Managing Emotional Impulses - Incorporating mindfulness techniques helps students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity, resulting in improved self-regulation skills.
  • Mindfulness Techniques for Self-Regulation - This approach incorporates mindfulness techniques to help students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.
  • Mini Classroom Exercise Breaks - Implement short exercise sessions throughout the school day, such as encouraging jumping jacks in the morning or scheduling five-minute movement breaks between classes where students can do activities like push-ups, dancing, or running in…
  • Mini-Lessons on Features - Create mini-lessons for each writing feature you want students to emulate (organization, title, sentence variety, imagery, evidence, introduction).
  • Minimally Invasive Hand Gesture - Using a minimally invasive hand gesture to secure student attention.
  • Mirror Faces - Learners pair up, and one makes an emotional face while the other mirrors it, promoting recognition and understanding of facial expressions associated with different emotions.
  • Mirrors, Windows, and Sliding Glass Doors - Using the concept of mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors helps students engage with diverse stories and experiences.
  • Mistake-Friendly Classroom - Creating a mistake-friendly classroom involves fostering an environment where mistakes are seen as a fundamental part of learning, rather than a source of embarrassment or failure.
  • Mitigating Racial Bias in Edtech Products - The AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity provides guidance on how to mitigate racial bias in the design and development of edtech products.
  • Mix It Up - The \"Mix It Up\" strategy involves intentionally creating opportunities for individuals to interact with people outside of their normal social circles to foster understanding and break down social barriers.
  • Mnemonic Devices - Mnemonic devices are memory aids that use patterns, rhymes, acronyms, or other techniques to help learners recall information.
  • Mobile Communication for Family Engagement - Utilizing text messages to inform families about their student’s progress, as well as general tips for supporting children’s learning.
  • Model and Example Feedback - This approach involves communicating with learners the purpose for an assessment and/or student feedback.
  • Model Assignment or Skill - Modeling a skill or assignment by verbalizing thought processes while working through it.
  • Model Drawing Strategy - Teaching fraction and percentage word problems using a model-drawing strategy.
  • Model Empathy and Explain - Explicitly model empathy by demonstrating understanding and sharing in the feelings of others, then explain the thought process behind showing empathy.
  • Model Positive Connections to Literacy - Teachers share their own positive experiences with reading and writing to foster a positive literacy environment.
  • Model Positive Connections to Math - Model positive connections to math is a strategy in which educators explicitly demonstrate curiosity, usefulness, and positive affect toward mathematical thinking.
  • Model Reflection - Students need to encounter reflective role models.
  • Model the Assignment or Skill - Teachers demonstrate how to perform a task or skill by verbalizing their thought processes while completing it.
  • Model-Eliciting Activities (MEAs) - Model-eliciting activities (MEAs) are activities that encourage learners to invent and test models.
  • Modeling a Growth Mindset - Teachers, like the students they teach, can learn to develop a growth mindset, but this requires careful planning by school management.
  • Modeling and Practice (Source Evaluation) - Explicitly model how to evaluate each dimension of source evaluation, and provide repeated opportunities for learners to practice and apply these strategies to information they encounter during the research process.
  • Modeling Empathy - Teachers' behaviors and actions create the culture in the classroom.
  • Modeling Positive Self-Talk - Demonstrating positive thinking skills aloud when talking about oneself and others.
  • Modeling Reflection - Share parts of the reflection brought them to another level of understanding as they worked together in a learning community.
  • Modeling Skills and Interaction - Modeling involves demonstrating the skills you expect from your students, both in terms of interaction and analysis.
  • Modified Grading Scale - Shift away from the 0-100 scale, which punishes students severely for missing work, and use a more compressed scale like 0-4 to diminish the impact of a single missed assignment.
  • Modified Jigsaw Activities - The jigsaw strategy involves dividing a task into subtopics, assigning one to each group member.
  • Monitor and Adjust Classroom Temperature - Maintaining an optimal temperature range (68º and 74º Fahrenheit) in classrooms can significantly affect student engagement and productivity.
  • Monitoring Progress - Monitoring progress involves regularly assessing advancement towards goals.
  • Moose Math App - A game app made of funny characters, referred to as the Dust Funnies.
  • Morphological Analysis of Latin and Greek Roots - Morphological analysis of Latin and Greek roots involves teaching learners about the meaningful parts of words, including prefixes, suffixes, and roots of Latin and Greek origin.
  • Morphological Instruction - Instruction that makes students aware of inflections (–ed, –s, –es, –ing, –er, –est, which are also called grammatical suffixes), morphemes that change the number, person, or tense of the word to which they are added, but they do not…
  • Motion and Forces Experiments - Motion and forces experiments involve exploring how forces affect the motion of objects.
  • Motor Images - Motor images, also known as muscle memory, involve using physical movements and actions to enhance learning and recall.
  • Movement Breaks - Movement breaks are brief, structured activities incorporated into classroom settings to energize learners, improve focus, and enhance learning.
  • Multimodal Assignments - Multimodal assignments involve a variety of assessment methods that challenge learners to create video or audio projects, write personal essays, or complete quizzes.
  • Multimodal Composition - Multimodal composition involves creating texts using various modes of communication such as images, words, sound, and movement.
  • Multimodal Composition Projects - Multimodal composition involves learners combining different modes of communication (linguistic, visual, audio, gestural, spatial) to enhance the message they want to convey.
  • Multimodal Learning Logs/Blogs - Learning logs or blogs are used for groups to reflect on their learning, document the content of each session, and share what supported or interfered with their learning.
  • Multiple Display Boards/Screens - Using multiple surfaces or screens for instruction and collaboration.
  • Multiple Examples - When teaching a new technique, providing multiple examples helps students understand and apply the technique in their own writing.
  • Multiple Exposures - Multiple exposures provide students with multiple opportunities to encounter, engage with, and elaborate on new knowledge and skills.
  • Multiple Modalities for Perceiving Information - Sharing information through various modalities beyond text and images, such as audio, video, simulations, or interactive models.
  • Multiple Representations: Number Line - The number line is used as a visual representation of numerical relationships.
  • Multiple Representations: Visual Representations - Using visual representations can lead to clearer delivery of content and greater retention of key concepts in long-term memory.
  • Multiple Texts - Reading multiple texts on the same topic expands learners' understanding, encourages critical thinking, and fosters synthesis skills.
  • Multiple Ways to Perceive Information - Presenting information in more ways than images and text alone enhances comprehension and caters to diverse learning preferences.
  • Multiple Writing Surfaces - Multiple writing surfaces involve providing learners with a variety of spaces where they can write and express their ideas, such as walls, tables, or portable whiteboards.
  • Multiplicative Double Counting - Multiplicative double counting involves tracking all three units (groups, unit rate, and total) to solve a multiplication problem.
  • Multipurpose Spaces - Designing spaces that lend themselves to a variety of learning styles and activities are best.
  • Multisensory Instruction - Multisensory instruction uses a combination of visual, auditory, and tactile-kinesthetic techniques to enhance memory and learning.
  • Multisensory Memory Strategies for Irregular Words - Multisensory memory strategies for irregular words involve using multiple senses (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, and tactile) to enhance memory and retention of irregularly spelled words.
  • Multisyllable Word Instruction - Multisyllable word instruction focuses on teaching learners how to break words into syllables to improve spelling and reading skills.
  • Music & Dance - Incorporate music and dance into the learning environment to engage verbal, visual, and kinesthetic senses.
  • Music and Dance Integration - This strategy uses movement, rhythm, and music to enhance learning and understanding of various concepts, particularly in mathematics.
  • Music and Emotions - Learners listen to different types of music and discuss how it makes them feel, fostering emotional awareness and providing a creative outlet for emotional expression.
  • Mystery Emotion - Learners are challenged to guess the emotion the instructor is acting out in order to solve the mystery of what it is.

docs.title: N
docs.text:
• Name Pronunciation - Pronouncing learners' names correctly can help develop trust and rapport.
  • Name the Negative Voice - Have students name their negative inner voice (e.g., Adverse Antoine, Ruthless Ralph, Cranky Kirsten).
  • Naming the Negative Voice - Students give their negative inner voice a name to externalize it, allowing them to treat it as a separate entity.
  • Narrative Advance Organizers - Narrative advance organizers involve storytelling at the beginning of a lesson to engage students and relate to important concepts.
  • Natural Lighting - Before the advent of cheap electricity, schools often relied on natural lighting.
  • Navigator-Tourist Peer Learning - Pair struggling learners ('tourists') with learners who have mastered the content ('navigators').
  • Needs and Wants Assessment with Likert Scales - Using Likert scales and fill-in questions to gauge student interest and understanding allows educators to inform their planning based on student needs.
  • Negotiated Grades - Grades should be negotiated between students and teachers according to agreed upon learning goals and evidence of learning in one or more languages.
  • Nighttime Blue Light Reduction - Reducing exposure to blue light from digital screens before bed can improve sleep quality and quantity, which enhances learning by preventing disruptions to sleep patterns and storage processes.
  • No-Zero Grading Policy - Setting the lowest possible grade for any assignment or test at 50 percent, even when students turn in no work at all, to give all students a chance to succeed.
  • Noise Level Monitoring Tools - Using electronic tools to monitor classroom noise levels and provide auditory or visual signals when the noise becomes too loud.
  • Noise Monitoring Tools - Noise monitoring tools are technological aids used to visually or audibly signal when noise levels in the classroom exceed an acceptable threshold.
  • Non-Competitive Physical Activities - Encourage pre-teens and teenagers who dislike organized sports to explore non-competitive physical activities.
  • Non-Confrontational Check-ins - Non-confrontational check-ins involve engaging students in informal, positive interactions before they enter the classroom to socialize them into productive behaviors.
  • Non-intensive Home Numeracy Environment (HNE) Intervention Program - Teachers can provide families information and suggestions for providing students more math exploration and play in their homes.
  • Nonconfrontational Statements and Informal Chitchat - Catching students at the door before they enter the classroom and using “nonconfrontational statements” and “informal chitchat” to socialize them into productive behaviors.
  • Normalizing Struggle - Normalizing struggle involves creating a classroom culture where challenges and failures are viewed as opportunities for growth.
  • Normalizing Trouble - Normalizing struggle involves acknowledging that challenges and failures are a natural part of the learning process and a sign of growth.
  • Normalizing Trouble and Struggle - Creating a classroom culture where challenges and failures are seen as opportunities for growth and learning.
  • Note-Taking Using Graphic Organizers - Learners use graphic organizers to take notes on their reading, research, films, or podcasts, visually structuring information and relationships between concepts to enhance comprehension and retention.
  • Note-Taking/Note-Making - Note-taking/note-making involves students taking notes on key points from a lesson and then making notes by writing their own reflections, reactions, and personal connections to the material.
  • Novelty Attention-Getters - Novelty attention-getters use unique and unexpected stimuli to capture young students' attention and quiet the classroom.
  • Novelty Sounds - Using novel sounds such as wind chimes or rain sticks captures young students’ attention.
  • Number Rack App - Helps kids learn to use numbers and master them in a visual way, offering moveable, colored beads.
  • Number Relationships and Reasoning Strategies - Basic facts should be taught using number relationships and reasoning strategies, not memorization.
  • Number Talks - Number Talks are short, daily classroom routines that provide students with opportunities to mentally solve and discuss numerical problems.
  • Numbers to 100 - A game where learners find numbers in sequential order on road signs, license plates, and maps to reinforce number recognition and ordering skills.

docs.title: O
docs.text:
• Observations and Conversations - Monitoring student learning through observations and conversations helps determine understanding of concepts and problem-solving abilities.
  • Offer Services and Events to Bring Parents into the School - Offer free classes and workshops that focus on topics of interest to parents, such as family nutrition, child development, or homework help.
  • Offering Multiple Options for Family Engagement - Providing a variety of options will improve overall participation, particularly for families with significant barriers to engagement.
  • On-the-Job Training (OJT) - On-the-job training (OJT) involves designing experiential activities for groups of trainees, based at the actual location where they will be working.
  • One-on-One Conference - One-on-one conferences involve providing individualized feedback to a learner in a private setting.
  • One-Sentence Response - When instructors ask a question, rather than having students raise hands, every learner writes a sentence to answer the question.
  • Ongoing Feedback - Ongoing feedback involves providing feedback at various stages of the writing process rather than only on final products.
  • Ongoing Feedback and Reflection - Learning management systems (LMS) such as Google Classroom, Canvas, and Schoology allow teachers to conduct formative and summative assessments during PBL.
  • Online Videos for Family Learning - Using online videos to make it easier for families with different language needs to explore and learn together.
  • Open Classroom Climate - An open classroom climate is a learning environment where students feel safe to discuss social and political issues and express their opinions freely without judgment.
  • Open Communication and Trust - Friendly message from teacher to foster open, comfortable communication systems and mutual respect, and when helping students succeed becomes a group effort, academics and attitudes improve.
  • Operation Math App - Provides a very easy way to learn and practice math with a very easy-to-understand user interface, with everything clearly explained and accessible.
  • Optimal Student Flow - Organizing the classroom layout to match the flow of the day, such as moving from reading to math centers, can enhance efficiency.
  • Optimize Classroom Acoustics - Reducing noise levels in classrooms can greatly affect teacher and student performance.
  • Optimize Classroom Acoustics and Noise Levels - Classroom noise levels significantly impact teacher and student performance.
  • Optimize Classroom Lighting - Maximize the use of natural lighting in classrooms.
  • Optimize Classroom Size and Space - Overcrowded classrooms are linked to increased aggression and decreased engagement and learning in students.
  • Optimize Classroom Temperature - Maintaining an ideal temperature range (68-74°F) in classrooms can significantly impact student engagement and achievement.
  • Optimize Natural Lighting - Artificial lighting has negative impacts on those in schools, while natural lighting has positive impacts.
  • Optimizing Classroom Space - Overcrowded classrooms are linked to increased aggression and decreased engagement.
  • Optimizing Natural Lighting - Incorporating natural lighting in classrooms boosts morale, reduces off-task behavior, and improves test scores.
  • Optimizing School Facilities - Improving the learning environment by addressing factors like acoustics/noise, air quality, lighting, temperature, and space.
  • Organized Online Resources - Storing lesson plan ideas, instructional websites, and electronic copies of worksheets using organizational sites such as Livebinders.com, or desktop applications such as Evernote can streamline the organizational process and increase…
  • Organizing Information and Taking Notes - This strategy involves effectively structuring and recording information to enhance understanding and retention.
  • Outdoor Book Walk - Find a public park or walkable street where you can post pages of a book to create a walkable reading experience that families can do together.

docs.title: P
docs.text:
• Pairing with Positive Role Models - Pairing learners with peers who demonstrate strong relationship skills involves intentionally matching learners who may face challenges in social interactions with those who exhibit positive behaviors such as effective communication,…
  • Paragraph Shrinking - A PALS activity focused on identifying main ideas and summarizing paragraphs.
  • Parental Involvement in Physical Activity - Engage parents by providing details about the benefits of physical activity and encouraging their participation.
  • Parental Modeling of Reading - Parents demonstrate the value of reading by being reading role models themselves, reading books, magazines, or newspapers regularly at home.
  • Partner Reading - Partner reading is a cooperative learning strategy in which two learners work together to read an assigned text.
  • Partner Reading with Retell - A PALS activity aimed at improving reading fluency and summarization skills.
  • Patience - Teaching higher-level thinking skills and analyzing mentor texts can be a new experience for struggling learners, and it doesn't come easily.
  • Pattern Recognition in Learning - Pattern recognition is a cognitive process where the brain identifies recurring structures, relationships, or sequences to assign meaning and enhance memory.
  • Pay Attention, Pause, Paraphrase - Pay Attention, Pause, Paraphrase is a structured conversation strategy for small groups or pairs to promote active listening.
  • Peer and Self-Assessment - Peer and self-assessment give students the opportunity to review their work against a set of criteria.
  • Peer Coaching - Peer coaching is a reciprocal helping relationship between equals who support each other's learning through mutual trust and open discussion.
  • Peer Observation - Peer observation is a collaborative process where teachers observe each other's classroom practices to improve teaching and learning.
  • Peer Review/Peer Editing - Peer review involves students providing feedback on each other's work to foster a collaborative learning environment, increase motivation, and develop a growth mindset.
  • Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS) - PALS is a structured peer tutoring approach that involves pairing learners to work together on academic activities.
  • Peergrade - Peergrade is a platform that allows learners to give and receive feedback effectively.
  • Pegword Strategy - The pegword strategy is a mnemonic technique that uses rhyming words to represent numbers or order.
