  • Pencil Grasp Activities - Activities aimed at promoting a functional pencil grasp, which is essential for comfortable and efficient handwriting.
  • Pepperoni Pizza - A game where children roll a dice twice.
  • Personalized Math with Cultural Connections - Effective math instruction connects to real-life and culturally relevant contexts, engaging students and making concepts more accessible.
  • Perspective-taking and Empathy - Take the time to consider each student’s perspective and the challenges they may be facing.
  • Philosophical Chairs - A statement that has two possible responses—agree or disagree—is read out loud.
  • Phoneme Awareness Training - Direct instruction in phoneme awareness helps children in the early stages of learning to spell and helps remediate the problems of poor spellers at any age.
  • Phoneme-Grapheme Mapping - Phoneme-grapheme mapping is a strategy used to match the letters or letter combinations (graphemes) in a word to the speech sounds (phonemes) they represent.
  • Phonics-Based Spelling Instruction - Encourages learners to apply their phonics skills to spell new words by segmenting phonemes (sound units) and connecting them with corresponding letters.
  • Phonological and Metalinguistic Awareness Exercises - Facilitate reading acquisition by asking students to say words that start with the same sound(s) in English or the L1.
  • Phonological Awareness Development through Rhyming - Using rhyming as a literacy tool to develop phonological awareness.
  • Physical Activity & Recess - Integrating physical activity, such as games, walking, or jogging, with learning activities can improve students' health, focus, and social skills.
  • Physical Activity Breaks - Physical activity breaks are short periods of movement integrated into daily routines to improve focus, energy levels, and physical well-being.
  • Physical Activity-Encouraging Environment - Design school environments that encourage physical activity by including playground equipment, walking trails, and bike racks.
  • Pictionary (Pre-Reading) - Key words from the text are selected, and the class is divided into two or three groups.
  • Picture Dictionaries - Picture dictionaries are reference tools that use illustrations to define words and concepts, making them accessible to language learners of all ages.
  • Picture Schedules and Visual Planners - Picture schedules or visual planners use images to lay out the steps to do a task.
  • Picture Writing - Picture writing unlocks the imagination, builds confidence, and develops foundational early literacy skills.
  • Pictures & Visuals - This strategy involves the use of images, videos, and other visual aids to enhance learning and memory.
  • Pictures (Pre-Reading) - The instructor selects three or four pictures related to the reading topic and provides them to small groups of learners.
  • Pinwheel Discussion - Learners are divided into 4 groups.
  • Pizza Box Portfolios - Pizza box portfolios are a great space-saving solution.
  • Planned Physical Activity - Planning for physical activity is essential for pre-teens and teenagers to ensure they meet daily requirements.
  • PLaNS (Play Learning and Narrative Skills) - The PLaNS approach supports writing skills through guided play and includes practical resources to help with lesson planning.
  • Platform Agnostic Design - Instructional designers create tools that work across any platform, avoiding bias towards specific operating systems or web browsers.
  • Play Memory Games - Memory games help hone focus for learners in a fun way, enabling them to concentrate when something challenging is presented.
  • Playful Spaces - Bringing fun back into learning by creating playful spaces.
  • Playground: Pickup Sports and Jam Sessions - Encouraging informal games and activities without emphasizing competition provides opportunities for play and creativity.
  • Playing with Techniques - Provide low-pressure exercises for students to experiment with the writing techniques they have analyzed.
  • Playworks TeamUp Recess Program - The Playworks TeamUp program aims to make recess more organized, safe, and healthy by fostering improvements in recess organization, enhancing students’ familiarity with a variety of games, and increasing their access to playground…
  • Poetry Exploration through Digital Libraries - Using digital libraries with audio and visual components to engage learners with a variety of poems.
  • Points or Experience (XP) Systems - Point systems or experience (XP) systems reward learners for completing various tasks, assignments, or assessments.
  • Political Education - Political education involves developing a comprehensive understanding of the historical, social, and political contexts that shape a problem.
  • Portfolio Development - Learners regularly select work samples, reflect on their choices, and organize their work into a portfolio.
  • Positive Affirmations - Using positive affirmations involves creating and repeating positive statements about oneself to build inroads into the subconscious mind, opening up the possibility of a new state of thoughts.
  • Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) - PBIS is a proactive approach schools use to improve school safety and promote positive behavior.
  • Positive Intention & Generosity in Networking - The \"Positive Intention & Generosity in Networking\" strategy emphasizes focusing on how one's interests and goals align with those of the people they meet and offering valuable resources beyond the obvious.
  • Positive Scripts - Creating positive scripts involves regularly constructing and narrating uplifting stories with a positive outline, visualizing goals as already achieved to internalize them.
  • Post-Reading Discussions - After reading, instructors facilitate discussions to explore learners' favorite parts of a narrative text or to confirm information learned in an informational text.
  • PQP (Praise-Question-Polish) - The PQP (Praise-Question-Polish) technique guides learners to provide specific and constructive feedback on each other's work.
  • Practice Changing Negative Thoughts into Positive Ones - Challenging learners to reframe negative thoughts into positive affirmations.
  • Practice Responsible Decision-Making - Give students opportunities to practice responsible decision-making by using pairs or small groups to analyze problem scenarios (e.g., cheating, bullying) that connect to their everyday lives at school, in order to make decisions about,…
  • Practice Time - Give students time to practice what they just learned in a low-stakes environment, without grading or evaluation.
  • Praise Effort and Strategies - When learners succeed, praise their efforts and strategies rather than their intelligence.
  • Praising Effort and Strategies - Praising effort and strategies focuses on acknowledging the process and hard work learners invest in their tasks, rather than praising innate intelligence.
  • Pre-Entry Socialization - Pre-entry socialization involves engaging students in brief, positive interactions before they enter the classroom to set a productive tone.
  • Pre-Reading Graphic Organizers - Students identify the text structure prior to reading (e.g., compare and contrast, description, problem-solution, cause and effect, sequence of events) and complete a supporting graphic organizer while reading to fill in the components.
  • Pre-reading: 4 Ps (Preview, Predict, Prior Knowledge, Purpose) - The 4 Ps of pre-reading include previewing the text, predicting the content, activating prior knowledge, and defining the purpose for reading.
  • Pre-reading: Generating Questions - Generating a list of pre-reading questions that will help learners achieve their purpose for reading.
  • Pre-reading: Skim a Book Systematically - Skimming or pre-reading a book involves a systematic approach to discover whether the book requires a more careful reading.
  • Pre-reading: Skimming Text - Pre-reading involves skimming a text to identify key ideas before reading from start to finish.
  • Pre-reading: Understand the Purpose of the Reading - Understanding the purpose of pre-reading is to increase the capacity to comprehend material before starting to read.
  • Pre-recorded Instructional Video - Pre-recording instructional videos in advance is a versatile teaching strategy.
  • Pre-recording Instructional Videos - Pre-recording instructional videos in advance is a versatile teaching strategy.
  • Pre-Shadowing Preparation Activities - Pre-shadowing preparation involves several activities to set up a meaningful shadowing experience.
  • Pre-Teaching Vocabulary - Pre-teaching vocabulary involves introducing new words before encountering them in a text or lesson.
  • Pre-Writing Skills Activities - Activities focused on building foundational skills necessary before formal handwriting instruction begins, such as line awareness, spatial awareness, and pencil grasp.
  • Pre-Writing with Graphic Organizers - Students use graphic organizers to plan and structure their ideas before writing drafts, aiding in idea generation and organization.
  • Predictability: Environment & Structure - Creating consistent interfaces and repetitive structures or frameworks in learning environments to facilitate predictability.
  • Predicting - Predicting involves anticipating what will happen next in a text or problem.
  • Prediction Relay - A PALS activity that emphasizes making predictions while reading.
  • Predictive Emotion Planning - Learners anticipate emotions linked to upcoming activities.
  • Preferential Seating - Place students who have trouble hearing, seeing, focusing on, or paying attention to instruction happening in seats where they will be best able to focus.
  • Preliminary Data Collection - Preliminary data collection involves gathering contextual data to gain a deeper understanding of the local settings where a problem exists.
  • Prep Activities for Shadowing - This involves creating learning goals for the shadowing day, choosing a student to shadow, and coordinating with the student, their parents, and school staff to ensure a smooth and meaningful experience.
  • Prepare for Parental Reactions - To do this work, a teacher must be confident in her belief that such discussions are essential for students' development, that they are part of her curriculum, that they're important for helping students understand their world and giving…
  • Prepare Instructions Carefully - Plan and organize instructions beforehand, grouping similar tasks together to streamline the instruction-giving process.
  • Prepare the Ground - Building a trusting community is crucial for honest talks about race.
  • Present Tense Messages - This strategy involves shifting the focus of internal dialogue from future anxieties to actionable steps in the present to manage overwhelming feelings.
  • Pretend Play - Pretend play, also known as dramatic play or make-believe, involves learners exploring imagined situations and roles.
  • Previewing - Prepare learners for upcoming tasks or materials.
  • Prewriting Activities - Engage in brainstorming before beginning to draft a composition.
  • Primary Language Support with Bilingual Texts - Using bilingual picture books and resources in a learner's primary language to support their comprehension and engagement with new content.
  • Prioritizing Agency for Students With Disabilities - Prioritizing agency for students with disabilities involves fostering self-advocacy and self-determination skills to enable them to engage more effectively in their education.
  • Prioritizing Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination - Making self-advocacy and self-determination critical priorities in education systems involves prioritizing them throughout, such as by incorporating them into teacher preparation and assessments of learning and through associated measures…
  • Probing Questions - Probing questions are used to encourage deeper reflection and critical thinking by challenging assumptions, exploring reasons and evidence, considering different viewpoints, examining implications, and questioning the basis of the inquiry…
  • Problem Scenario Analysis - Providing students with real-life problem scenarios (e.g., cheating, bullying) and having them analyze the situation, consider possible consequences, share their decisions, and reflect on their reasoning.
  • Problem Solving - Problem solving involves designing activities that require learners to come up with solutions - ways of dealing with issues or challenges that they can then use back on-the-job.
  • Problem Solving: Draw a Picture - The 'draw a picture' strategy is a problem-solving technique in which learners make a visual representation of the problem.
  • Process for Constructive Decision-Making - Brainstorm with students a process for constructive decision-making and display it in the classroom as a visual reminder of how to make good choices.
  • Process Writing (Journals) - Process writing uses journals to encourage writing skills from the beginning levels of English proficiency.
  • Process Writing Approach - Includes many related activities, including a greatly increased quantity of writing (only some of which is completed to publication) and a focus on writing throughout the course, along with mini-lessons on embedded skills.
  • Process-Focused Learning - Emphasizing and valuing the process of learning, rather than solely focusing on grades, promotes a growth mindset and encourages learners to embrace challenges.
  • Proctor Intervention for Rapid Guessing - When learners are flagged for rapid guessing during assessments, proctors should approach them, pause their test, and engage them in a low-pressure conversation about what’s going on.
  • Producing Counter-texts - Producing counter-texts involves crafting alternative versions of existing texts to highlight missing perspectives, challenge stereotypes, and address biases.
  • Progress Monitoring - Progress monitoring involves identifying skills that students have mastered and concepts that need additional attention.
  • Project Management Tools for Group Work - Using project management tools such as Project Pals, Headrush, and Student Corner can help teachers drive student engagement and improve communication.
  • Project Options and Self-Grading - Offer up plenty of options in types of projects and also collaborate with students in creating a criteria chart for each project.
  • Project-based Learning - Project-based learning (PBL) is an instructional approach that engages learners in real-world, complex problems or challenges.
  • Project-Based Learning (PBL) - Project Based Learning is a teaching method in which learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to investigate and respond to an engaging and complex question, problem, or challenge.
  • Project-Based Learning (PBL) in Math - Project-Based Learning (PBL) is a teaching method where learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period to investigate and respond to an engaging and complex question, problem, or challenge.
  • Project-Based Transformation of Society - This instructional strategy involves students working in small groups to identify and propose solutions to crucial problems in their society.
  • Promote a Growth Mindset - Promoting a growth mindset involves giving feedback that values effort and encourages persistence.
  • Promote a Growth Mindset in Math - Promote a growth mindset by giving feedback that values effort and encourages persistence, showing learners that there is always room to improve their skills.
  • Promoting a Growth Mindset - Promoting a growth mindset, particularly in mathematics, encourages learners to believe that intelligence is not fixed.
  • Promoting Belonging Through Cues and Representations - Promoting belonging involves using small, but powerful cues in the environment to foster a sense of connection and recognition.
  • Promoting Belonging Through Instruction - Teachers promote belonging in the math classroom through instructional choices and practices that address equity and opportunity.
  • Promoting Self-Determination and Self-Advocacy in Students with Disabilities - Fostering self-determination and self-advocacy involves empowering students with disabilities to understand their needs, rights, and goals, and to actively participate in decisions about their education and lives.
  • Promoting Self-Directed Learning Strategies - Promoting self-directed learning involves explicitly teaching students strategies for problem-solving, metacognition, and self-reflection to become independent learners.
  • Prompt Cards for Emotional Regulation - Prompt cards, particularly emotion cue cards, offer accessible reminders of self-regulation strategies.
  • Prompted Source Evaluation - Pair strategy instruction with written prompts to guide students toward independence.
  • Prompts & Questions - Providing guiding prompts and questions for students to use when reading or participating in discussions deepens their understanding of texts and gives them space to question and grapple with issues of power, justice, and equity.
  • Propaganda Technique Identification - Learners are taught about propaganda techniques and then asked to identify the use of these techniques in online advertising.
  • Provide Easy-Access Educational Tools - Providing easy-access educational tools involves making a variety of resources readily available to students to support their learning.
  • Provide Instructions Before Starting Work - Ensure instructions are given before learners begin their tasks to avoid confusion and errors.
  • Provide Manipulatives - Learners are provided with manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete.
  • Provide Manipulatives (Processing Speed) - Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete and support processing speed.
  • Provide Opportunities for Success - Setting reasonable and realistic expectations, changing modifications for every student, and insisting on high-quality and excellent work.
  • Provide Writing Models - Providing writing models involves sharing exemplary pieces of writing with learners to illustrate effective writing techniques and structures.
  • Providing Accessible Educational Tools - Providing easy access to a variety of educational tools empowers students to take control of their learning.
  • Providing Choices About Content - Mature learners decide what to learn when they discover there’s something they need to know or something about which they need to know more.
  • Providing Easy-Access Educational Tools - Making educational tools readily available to learners promotes independence and self-directed learning.
  • Providing Graphic Organizers or Guided Notes - During lectures, providing students with graphic organizers or guided notes helps them pull out the important points and follow the structure of the lecture.
  • Providing Manipulatives - Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete supports understanding and processing, particularly in subjects like math or science.
  • Publicize Volunteer Opportunities and Student Involvement - Schools outline specific ways for parents to help in the classroom and at school, from inviting parents to watch group presentations to asking them to chaperone field trips.
  • Pupil-Generated Word Problems - Learners create their own word problems to enhance awareness and sharpen basic math skills, fostering comfort in solving a variety of math problems.
  • Puppet Shows to Explore Emotions - Puppet shows can be used to act out different scenarios and explore the emotions of the characters involved.
  • Purpose (Pre-Reading) - Learners are given a specific purpose for reading, typically in the form of discussion questions about the content prepared by the teacher.
  • Purposeful Scheduling for Learner Connections - Instructors can allocate class time specifically for getting to know learners through various activities.
  • Push for Deeper Analysis - Encourage students to go beyond surface-level analysis and consider how sentence structure and other elements create meaning.
  • Putting Empathy in the Curriculum - Explicitly discuss empathy with students and integrate it into existing lessons.

docs.title: Q
docs.text:
• Quality Homework Assignments - Assigning homework that reinforces learning, encourages real-world application, and offers enriching experiences.
  • Question Formulation Technique (QFT) - The Question Formulation Technique (QFT) is a structured method for generating and improving questions to develop critical thinking skills, increase self-efficacy, and encourage participation in civic life.
  • Question-based eLearning Design - Question-based eLearning design is an instructional approach that replaces the traditional expository method with a more inquiry-based one.
  • Questioning - Questioning is a powerful tool and effective teachers regularly use it for a range of purposes.
  • Questioning Techniques to Address Errors - Strategic questioning is used to guide students to recognize their errors and correct their thinking, emphasizing conceptual understanding over rote memorization.
  • Quick Reflection Prompts - This strategy involves using short, focused prompts at the end of a class period or learning experience to encourage learners to articulate their ideas and deepen their understanding.
  • Quick Writes - Quick Writes are short, focused informational writing tasks completed in under ten minutes, aimed at helping students process, organize, and remember information and ideas.
  • Quiet Classroom/Pockets of Quiet - Creating a quiet classroom by reducing background noise to support increased Attention towards learning.
  • Quiet Environment/Pockets of Quiet - Reducing background noise in classrooms supports increased learner attention.
  • Quiet Signals - Quiet signals are predetermined cues or actions used by teachers to quickly and effectively quiet a noisy classroom.
  • Quiet Space - Creating a designated quiet space in the classroom allows children to self-regulate and reduce sensory overload by limiting auditory, visual, and other sensory input.
  • Quiet Space for Self-Regulation - Designating a quiet space in the learning environment where learners can take breaks to regroup and calm themselves.
  • Quiet Time - Quiet time is a structured period of 10–15 minutes where students engage in calming activities like reading, writing, drawing, puzzles, or meditation to transition back into the classroom in a purposeful and relaxed manner.

docs.title: R
docs.text:
• Racial Equity in PBL - Build Community Through Peer Feedback - When students are given the opportunity during projects to frequently share feedback and revise their work, it creates moments to witness growth and progress.
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Create Beautiful Spaces - For so many of our students, their communities and homes are not always beautiful places...
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Create Space for Students to Reflect - Reflection is rare in traditional classrooms, where the emphasis is on urgency and doing assignments quickly.
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Expect Excellence - A belief in excellence, demonstrated by setting high expectations, is the fuel that runs a successful PBL culture.
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Focus Projects on Issues of Justice - Authentic projects that address issues of justice lead to higher student engagement because students are doing work that matters, work that impacts their community, their lives, the lives of those they love and deeply care about.
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Listen to the Voices of Students - Give students authorship in sharing and telling their own stories, which a good project allows them to do.
  • Racial Equity in PBL - Spark Engagement with Student-Generated Questions - Projects driven by student-generated questions result in increased engagement and investment.
  • Racial Identity Work - Racial identity work involves examining one's own racial identity, confronting personal biases, and understanding how privilege and misinformation can affect work as an educator.
  • Racial Identity Work for Educators - Racial identity work for educators involves understanding one's own racial identity, privilege, and biases to create a more inclusive and equitable learning environment.
  • Raise Awareness of Self-Talk - Raise awareness by helping students understand the concept of self-talk: what it is, how it affects self-esteem and confidence.
  • Rapid Sequencing of Examples - Present instances of a concept in rapid sequence or allow all instances to be viewed simultaneously.
  • Rate (and Change) Tasks - Ask learners to rate the level of challenge in an activity on a scale of 1 to 10.
  • Reaction Observations - Reaction observations involve observing and describing the properties of liquids and their mixtures.
  • Reactive Cultural Response - Reactive Cultural Response is the ability to change the structure, activities, and focus of a class within the school year as you see the personality of a given group of kids emerge.
  • Read Aloud - Encouraging learners to read questions and their own writing aloud helps leverage auditory processing strengths.
  • Read Aloud with Highlighting - Read aloud features, often combined with word and sentence highlighting, provide auditory support while reading digital text.
  • Read and Reflect - Read and reflect involves students engaging in discussions or summarizing activities after reading independently.
  • Read-Alouds - Read-alouds involve an educator reading a text aloud to learners, often pausing to model effective reading and thinking strategies such as questioning, inferencing, and using context cues.
  • Read-Alouds with Deliberate Topics - Teachers strategically select and read aloud stories that incorporate social-emotional learning (SEL) themes to foster self-reflection, promote social awareness, and strengthen relationship skills among students.
  • Read-Alouds with Discussion - Teachers read aloud stories about social and emotional learning and facilitate discussions that prompt student self-reflection.
  • Reader's Theater - Reader's Theater is a strategy that combines reading practice and performing by having learners read scripts created from books or stories aloud.
  • Reading Aloud - Encouraging students to read questions and their own writing aloud leverages strengths in auditory processing.
  • Reading and Understanding Written Math Problems - Word problems can be challenging.
  • Reading and Writing for Real-World Math Applications - Learners select and summarize published articles that highlight the ways math is present in different facets of the real world.
  • Reading Conferences - Reading conferences involve one-on-one interactions between an instructor and a learner during independent reading time.
  • Reading Documentation and Reflection - Have students record details about their reading such as book titles, number of pages read, and new vocabulary.
  • Reading in Math Class - Have students read articles from sources such as Math Horizons or Martin Gardner's Scientific American columns.
  • Reading Laterally - Reading Laterally is the practice of verifying information by consulting multiple external sources to evaluate the credibility of a source before engaging deeply with it.
  • Reading Online Strategy: Evaluating Online Information - Students learn to analyze and evaluate the information they encounter online by assessing the reliability of websites.
  • Reading Online Strategy: Formulating Effective Search Queries - This strategy focuses on teaching students how to formulate effective search queries to locate reliable information online.
  • Real-world Math Applications - Connecting math concepts to real-world applications is a strategy that can be used to enhance understanding, relevance, and engagement.
  • Real-World Reframes - When a student expresses frustration or negativity (e.g., 'I can’t do this stuff!'), reflect their feelings and then prompt them to take action.
  • Reasonable Feedback - Reasonable feedback involves providing feedback that is manageable and not overwhelming for the student.
  • Reasoning-Focused Instruction - De-emphasizing correct answers and focusing on the reasoning process can build student confidence and provide insight into problem-solving strategies.
  • Recess - Offer daily recess to allow students to be active, which can improve memory, conflict resolution skills, and creativity.
  • Reciprocal Peer Tutoring - Reciprocal peer tutoring (RPT) involves pairing students of similar abilities to work together, alternating the roles of tutor and tutee.
  • Reciprocal Teaching: Peer Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS) - PALS is a peer tutoring strategy designed to improve reading comprehension and fluency among students, primarily in grades 2–6.
  • Recognizing the Value of Learning from Mistakes - This strategy changes perceptions about mistakes, viewing them as learning opportunities.
  • Recording Devices - Allowing students to record lessons so they can play them back and go over anything that might be confusing.
  • Redirecting Language - Redirecting language is a classroom management tool that uses clear, non-negotiable instructions to redirect student behavior.
  • Reducing Visual Clutter - Reducing visual clutter involves minimizing the amount of unnecessary or distracting visual stimuli in the learning environment.
  • Reflect on Learning - Student reflection on learning, particularly when done collaboratively, is critical for moving knowledge of content and strategies into Long-term Memory.
  • Reflecting on Student Strengths and Challenges - Educators identify specific student strengths and/or challenges related to learning, social-emotional learning or other domains, and uses aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning and address challenges.
  • Reflection After Writing - Reflection involves pausing after completing a writing assignment to consider how the assignment went.
  • Reflection Exercises - Reflection exercises are activities designed to promote emotional self-awareness and regulation by encouraging learners to think about their feelings and behaviors.
  • Reflection on Learning - Reflection on learning involves linking a current experience to previous learnings (called scaffolding).
  • Reflection on Lessons - This strategy involves teachers reflecting on each lesson before and after teaching.
  • Reflection on Student Learning - This strategy involves teachers assessing and reflecting on each student's comprehension and engagement by using critical thinking questions that encourage deep thinking about math concepts.
  • Reflection Prompts - Reflection prompts are specific questions or statements used to guide learners in thinking deeply about their learning process, content understanding, and personal growth.
  • Reflection with Others - This strategy involves teachers reflecting on their teaching practice by engaging in peer collaboration and seeking feedback from colleagues who teach similar math concepts.
  • Reflective Assessment - Grades should reflect learning over time rather than be an end in and of itself.
  • Reflective Journaling - Reflective journaling is a technique used to encourage reflective learning by highlighting students’ thoughts and perceptions about course content.
  • Reflective Prompts - Reflection prompts encourage learners to think deeply about their learning experiences.
  • Reflex Math App - Among all the math fluency apps listed here, Reflex stands out with a research-based system of learning math for students ages 2-8.
  • Reframe Anxiety as Excitement - This technique involves changing one’s mindset from anxiety to excitement, leveraging the similar physiological responses (faster heartbeats and cortisol surges) associated with both emotions.
  • Reframe Negative Self-Talk - Practice reframing negative thoughts, statements, or situations into more positive alternatives.
  • Reframing Negative Self-Talk - Reframing involves rephrasing negative thoughts, statements, or situations into more positive alternatives.
  • Regular Physical Education (PE) Classes - Implement consistent PE classes to help students burn off energy and be active, improving their ability to focus in class.
  • Regular Text Referencing - Regularly referring back to mentor texts in teacher conferences, whole-class lessons, or discussions reinforces learning and helps students internalize new techniques.
  • Reinforce Positive Behaviors - Recognizing and positively reinforcing positive actions when they are observed.
  • Relate Math to Learner Strengths - Help learners understand how math gets used in the world in ways that relate to their personal strengths.
  • Relate Math to Student Strengths - Connecting math to students' personal strengths involves helping students understand how math is used in the real world in ways that align with their interests and expertise.
  • Relating Math to Student Strengths - This strategy leverages learners’ existing strengths and interests to make math more relatable and engaging.
  • Relationship Skills Identification and Support - This strategy involves educators identifying students with strengths or challenges in relationship skills and implementing targeted supports.
  • Relevant Vocabulary Instruction - Instructors should present vocabulary that is useful and/or necessary for learners, based on their learning goals.
  • Remote Support with Augmented Reality (AR) - AR apps allow technicians and users to communicate with experts in real time.
  • Remove Visual Distractions - When learners are struggling with a difficult task, clutter in the classroom or on the desk can make it impossible to keep the brain focused.
  • Repairing Harm - Repairing harm is a restorative practice where, instead of simply being sent off to a punishment, a student who has misbehaved is tasked with figuring out how to repair whatever damage was caused by their behavior, and then to actually…
  • Repeat Key Points - Repeat the key points for students several times and in several different ways.
  • Repeat Key Points (Processing Speed) - Repeating key points for students several times and in several different ways to support processing speed.
  • Repeating Key Points in Different Ways - Repeating the key points for students several times and in several different ways helps reinforce understanding and supports learners who need more time to process information.
  • Repertoire of Strategies - Procedural fluency requires having a repertoire of strategies.
  • Repetition - Repeat key points multiple times in simple language.
  • Replace Negative Influences with Positive Ones - This strategy focuses on intentionally minimizing exposure to negative external factors and actively seeking out positive influences to support a more constructive mindset.
  • Representation of Diverse Perspectives and Identities - Incorporating multiple and varying perspectives within learning content to honor and value diverse approaches to learning.
  • Require Retakes - Allowing or requiring retakes emphasizes a growth mindset and reinforces perseverance.
  • Rereading - Rereading is a literacy strategy where a reader revisits a sentence, paragraph, or entire text to improve accuracy, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension.
  • Research Map - A research map is a visual representation of research topics and their interconnections, allowing users to explore academic literature in a structured and intuitive way.
  • Research Map Visualization - This is a visual representation of education and learning sciences research published in peer-reviewed journals from 2009-2018.
  • Research Reports - Research reports are visual aids designed to present data and insights in an engaging and accessible format.
  • Resistance Reading and Counter-Narratives - Resistance reading and writing counter-narratives are strategies to develop learners' abilities to critique a text (or an image or other media) and to respond in writing, sharing their concerns and critiques.
  • Respect Diverse Talents and Ways of Learning - There are many roads to learning.
  • Respectful Redirection - Respectful redirection is a quick, in-the-moment strategy to give corrective feedback to students using a calm tone, neutral body language, and clear, concise wording.
  • Responding with \"Yet\" introduces the idea of a growth mindset, fostering the belief that abilities can improve over time.
  • Response Devices - Response devices allow learners to anonymously share answers with the whole class.
  • Responsible Decision-Making Practice - Learners engage in problem-solving scenarios in pairs or small groups, connecting to their everyday lives (e.g., cheating, bullying), to make decisions, analyze situations, and consider possible consequences.
  • Restate The Question - Restating the question encourages critical reading skills and provides clarity around instructions.
  • Rethinking Accountability - Recognize that students did not choose the current situation and should not be unjustly penalized for its challenges.
  • Retrieval Practice - Retrieval practice involves actively recalling information from memory without having it in front of you.
  • Retrieval Practice with Graphic Organizers - After students do a Brain Dump, where they try to recall as much as they can about a given topic, without the aid of any supporting texts, they sort their dumped information into some kind of graphic organizer, and possibly working in…
  • Rhyming Games - Rhyming games involve activities that focus on identifying and creating rhyming words to enhance phonological awareness.
  • Rhythmic Clapping/Counting - The teacher claps/counts out a rhythm.
  • Rice Tables and Sandboxes: Science Through Inquiry - Engaging learners in hands-on exploration and inquiry-based science education allows them to discover and test new understandings.
  • Rich Library: Audio & Braille - Using audiobooks and Braille texts to reinforce and inspire literacy skills.
  • Rich Library: Complexity - Providing access to a diverse collection of reading materials that vary in academic vocabulary and syntax complexity supports literacy and reading fluency.
  • Rich Library: Multimodal - Providing learners with a variety of resources in multiple formats, such as blogs, lyrics, videos, web pages, online discussions, and fanfiction, to enhance disciplinary literacy and engagement.
  • Rich Library: Multimodal Resources - Providing learners with access to multiple resources, including blogs, videos, audiobooks, and digital books, exposes them to diverse genres and can increase interest and motivation.
  • Rich Library: Poetry - Provides access to a collection of poems and poetry-related resources to enhance literacy and engagement with poetry.
  • Rich Resources: Diversity - Providing diverse materials in the classroom helps learners deepen their self-understanding and understanding of others, positively impacting their perceptions of themselves and each other.
  • RIP Toolbox (Repetition, Imagery, Patterns) - The RIP Toolbox is a memory-enhancing strategy that utilizes three key elements: Repetition, Imagery, and Patterns.
  • Role Play - Role playing involves acting out different scenarios in a safe environment, allowing learners to make mistakes and learn from them.
  • Role-Playing Emotional Scenarios - Learners act out how to manage emotions in different scenarios.
  • Role-Reversal 2.0 (Flipping the Teacher) - Students are asked to create videos demonstrating their understanding.
  • RSOWV/TRAP Mnemonics - RSOWV (Relax, Slowdown, Organize, Write, Visualize) and TRAP (Translate, Repeat, A Picture, Practice) are mnemonic strategies designed to enhance memory and learning.
  • Rubrics - Rubrics are evaluation tools consisting of a set of criteria, a fixed scale, and descriptors that distinguish the differences in the levels of the scale.

docs.title: S
docs.text:
• Safe and Healthy Elementary School Recess - Implementing a safe and healthy recess with programs like Playworks TeamUp aims to build a positive school climate by promoting social, emotional, physical, and academic development.
  • Sail through Math App - A fun math fluency iOS app that uses storytelling to help young learners develop math skills over time.
  • Say it Once - Repeating instructions can lead to lazy listening habits in learners.
  • Scaffold Structure and Function - Provide students with the language tools, such as sentence starters and stems, necessary for project success.
  • Scaffolded Instruction - Scaffolded instruction involves supporting learners in various ways as they learn and gradually withdrawing supports as they become capable of independent performance of a task or skill.
  • Scaffolded Peer Review - Scaffolded peer review involves providing learners with structured support and guidance to improve the quality and effectiveness of their feedback.
  • Scaffolding - Scaffolding is a support technique to help learners manage their responses in an emotionally safe context.
  • Scaffolding for Self-Regulation - Scaffolding involves providing temporary support to learners to help them manage their emotional and behavioral responses in new or challenging situations.
  • Scaffolding Self-Regulation - Scaffolding can help students learn how to manage their responses in an emotionally safe context.
  • Scaffolding Structure and Function in PBL - Scaffolding structure and function in project-based learning (PBL) involves providing students with the necessary tools to demonstrate their understanding of content by giving them specific functions and structures of the language.
  • Schema-Based Instruction - Schema-based instruction involves teaching learners to recognize and understand the underlying structure (schema) of problems, particularly word problems in mathematics.
  • School Newsletters - School newsletters are visual aids designed to keep staff, students, and parents informed and engaged with school events and activities.
  • Schwa Instruction - Teach children about schwa (/ ə/), the unaccented vowel sound that has been emptied of its identity and can be described as a lazy vowel.
  • Science Through Inquiry - Engage learners in hands-on, exploratory science activities that encourage questioning, discovery, and testing to develop new understandings.
  • Screen Readers - Screen readers convert text into spoken audio, enabling learners to listen to written material.
  • Secret Student - A classroom management system where a student's name is secretly selected each day, and the teacher observes whether the \"Secret Student\" exhibits good listening and learning behaviors.
  • See, Think, Wonder - A thinking routine developed by Project Zero to stimulate curiosity, normalize error, increase critical thinking skills, and ensure that every learner starts from a place of success.
  • SEL Discussions on Ethical Dilemmas - This strategy involves using age-appropriate, real-life ethical dilemmas as discussion starters to help students practice responsible decision-making.
  • SEL Discussions through Literary Characters - Students read and discuss social and emotional learning (SEL) topics through the lens of characters in literature.
  • SEL Integration through Literature - Integrating social and emotional learning (SEL) into language arts curricula involves using literature to explore emotions, build community, handle conflict, and counter bias.
  • SEL Questioning - Teachers can implement simple SEL questions focused on kindess, metaphors, challenges, and support to grow students’ emotional intelligence skills.
  • SEL Videos with Discussion - This strategy involves showing short video clips on Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) topics, followed by discussions or related activities.
  • SEL-Focused Digital Libraries - This strategy involves curating digital libraries to include a section of books dedicated to Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) topics.
  • Selecting Culturally Responsive Texts - This strategy involves selecting and incorporating culturally responsive texts into the curriculum and classroom libraries.
  • Selecting Tiered Vocabulary Words - Categorize vocabulary words into three tiers to prioritize instruction: Tier 1 (basic words, rarely require instruction), Tier 2 (high-frequency academic words, crucial for mature language), and Tier 3 (low-frequency, content-specific…
  • Self- and Peer-Editing - Self- and peer-editing are collaborative processes where learners evaluate their own writing and provide feedback to peers.
  • Self-Awareness - Identify Feelings - This strategy involves having learners identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings.
  • Self-Awareness - Journal Reflections - This activity involves having learners think back on their experiences and outcomes, which helps provide them with a greater understanding of themselves.
  • Self-Evaluation in Writing - Self-evaluation involves teaching students how to review their writing to decide if changes are needed.
  • Self-Instruction - Self-instruction, also known as self-talk or self-statements, is a strategy where learners talk themselves through a task or activity to self-regulate their behavior.
  • Self-instructions - Teachers model articulating how they solve a problem and prompt students to explain their own thinking.
  • Self-Monitoring of Attention (SMA) - Self-monitoring of attention is a strategy where learners self-assess their behavior and record the results.
  • Self-Monitoring of Behavior - Self-monitoring is a strategy where learners self-assess their behavior and record the results, increasing or decreasing the frequency, intensity, or duration of existing behavior.
  • Self-Monitoring of Performance (SMP) - Self-monitoring of performance is a strategy where learners monitor an aspect of their academic performance, such as the rate at which they correctly complete class work or the overall accuracy of their performance.
  • Self-Organized Learning Groups - Learning cohorts can be formed for employees to learn from each other on topics like improving Scrum processes or new skills such as technical tools or programming languages.
  • Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) - SRSD is an instructional approach designed to enhance students' writing skills by addressing their affective, behavioral, and cognitive characteristics.
  • Self-Regulation - Mindfulness Techniques - Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help learners manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.
  • Self-Regulation - Scaffolding - Scaffolding can help learners learn how to manage their responses in an emotionally safe context.
  • Self-Regulation Scaffolding - Scaffolding provides learners with a safe and emotionally supportive context to learn how to manage their responses to challenging or stimulating situations.
  • Self-Reinforcement - Self-reinforcement involves individuals selecting a reinforcer and rewarding themselves for reaching or exceeding a set criterion.
  • Self-Reinforcement in Writing - Self-reinforcement involves using effort-based and behavior-specific praise to encourage students during the writing process.
  • Self-Talk Brainstorm - Provide learners with scenarios of challenging situations and have them brainstorm possible neutral or positive self-talk responses.
  • Sensitivity to Language Concerns - Celebrating diversity of language and tailoring instructional materials to non-native English speakers are essential for a culturally responsive classroom.
  • Sensory Processing and Handwriting - Activities that incorporate sensory experiences to enhance handwriting skills.
  • Sensory Stimulation - Sensory stimulation involves providing experiences that engage a person's senses to improve regulation, attention, and focus.
  • Sentence Combining - Practice how to combine two simple sentences into a compound or complex sentence.
  • Sentence Frames - Use sentence frames to help structure respectful responses in debate or disagreement situations online.
  • Sentence Starters - When you ask a question, rather than just having students raise hands and you picking one volunteer, have every student in the class write a sentence.
  • Sentence Stems for Reflection - Teachers can use sentence stems to stimulate reflection and make it more accessible to learners.
  • Separate Product, Process, and Progress Criteria - Instead of eliminating grades for behavior and participation, differentiate between grades for product, process, and progress criteria.
  • Set a High Bar for Each Student - Hold high expectations for all students.
  • Set Aside Your Own Reaction - Responding with empathy means letting students’ reactions come first.
  • Set Clear Objectives - Objectives aligned with standards, activities, and assessments, providing students with a clear understanding of the knowledge and skills they will demonstrate.
  • Setting Achievable Micro-Goals - Micro-goals involve breaking down larger objectives into smaller, manageable steps.
  • Setting Goals - Lessons have clear learning intentions with goals that clarify what success looks like.
  • Seven Blind Mice - Learners hear the story 'Seven Blind Mice,' stopping after each mouse’s perspective to take notes or engage in jigsaw reading.
  • Shadow a Student - Shadowing involves following a student throughout their school day to gain insights into their experiences, challenges, and needs.
  • Shadowing (Behavior Adjustment) - An adult follows a child closely, within arm's reach, to provide constant direct supervision and prevent unwanted behaviors (e.g., biting) before they occur.
  • Shadowing (for behavior adjustment) - An adult follows a child everywhere they go, staying within arm's reach to prevent unwanted behavior before it happens.
  • Shadowing a Student - Shadowing is a direct observation technique where an adult follows a student throughout their school day to gain real-time qualitative evidence of the student's experiences.
  • Shadowing for Behavior Adjustment - Shadowing is a strategy used to address harmful behaviors in children, such as biting or hitting.
  • Shadowing to Address Behavior Problems - Shadowing can be used as a direct intervention to address behavior problems in the classroom.
  • Shadowing to Adjust Behavior Problems - This is a behavior management technique where an adult closely follows a child, acting as their \"shadow,\" to prevent harmful behaviors like biting or hitting.
  • Shape Search - Learners identify two- and three-dimensional shapes in their surroundings, promoting geometric awareness and real-world application of geometric concepts.
  • Share Teacher's Written Work - Instructors share their written work with learners, soliciting feedback and criticism to model the value of continuous improvement.
  • Shared Reading - Shared reading is an interactive reading experience where an adult reads aloud while children follow along.
  • Shared Reflection - Shared reflection involves creating a classroom culture where each student is recognized as being on an individual path of improvement—and, no student has reached the end of the path, because there is no end.
  • Shared Writing - Shared writing involves a teacher and students collaboratively composing a text, with the teacher acting as a scribe.
  • Sharing and Discussion of Independent Reading - After independent reading, gather students to talk about their books through various activities such as book clubs or creating commercials to interest others.
  • Shoeless Learning Spaces - Creating shoeless learning spaces where children often learn with shoes off, perhaps because it reminds them of home and creates a relaxed learning environment.
  • Short Conversations (Pre-Reading) - Learners are given a sentence from the reading and engage in a conversation with a partner about the sentence.
  • Show and Tell for Multimodal Composition - Devoting a few minutes each week for learners to show the effects of different multimodal combinations or tell about their multimodal composition process creates a space akin to an author’s chair in writing workshops.
  • Show and Tell for Multimodal Design - Devoting time each week for students to show the effects of different multimodal combinations or tell about their multimodal composition process.
  • Show Me - Use slides or the board to provide another way for learners to get the information or directions.
  • Signage and Displays - Small details, such as wall displays are important.
  • Silent Countdown - The Silent Countdown is a technique where the teacher uses a visual countdown (e.g., with fingers) to signal the students to become quiet and attentive.
  • Silent Game Incentive - A silent game incentive uses a gamified approach to encourage students to quiet down after an activity.
  • Simple-to-Difficult Examples - Start with simple examples when introducing a concept, then progress to more complex ones later.
  • Simplify and Clarify Instructions - Ensure formulations are short, easy to understand, and precise.
  • Simplify Grading Scales - Eliminate the 0 to 100 scale as it disproportionately punishes missed assignments.
  • Simulation Learning - Simulation learning engages learners in active learning experiences where they learn from each other, not just from the instructor.
  • Simulations - Simulations use electronic or software-based activities to simulate a real-world situation to which a learner must react.
  • Simulations + Structured Activity - Students engage with simulations designed to provide hands-on experience with real-world scenarios or abstract concepts.
  • Six Consumer Questions - A set of six questions designed to help evaluate the trustworthiness of a news story.
  • Six Thinking Hats - The Six Thinking Hats technique is a parallel thinking process that separates thinking into six clear functions and roles, each identified with a colored symbolic 'thinking hat.' By mentally wearing and switching 'hats,' participants can…
  • Skimming - Skimming involves reviewing a text quickly, focusing on headings, captions, and highlighted information, to gain familiarity with the material before reading it thoroughly.
  • Skip Counting with Movement - Make up a movement that comes in 2, 3, or more parts.
  • Small Group Instruction - Small group instruction involves a teacher working with a small number of students on a specific skill or concept.
  • SMART Goal Setting - SMART goal setting ensures goals are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-Specific.
  • Snap It - A game where children make a train of connecting cubes, snap the train into two parts, hide one part behind their back, and show the remaining cubes.
  • Snowball Discussion - Learners begin in pairs, responding to a discussion question only with a single partner.
  • SOAP (Specific, Observable, Appropriate, Personal) - SOAP is an acronym that serves as a guide for teachers when selecting behaviors for students to self-monitor.
  • SOAR Feedback Method - The SOAR method helps maximize the impact of feedback on student writing by ensuring it is Specific, Ongoing, Action-Oriented, and Reasonable.
  • Social Annotation - Social annotation is a collaborative method where learners add notes, comments, and multimedia to texts, images, and other digital content, fostering conversation and deeper understanding.
  • Social Awareness - Model Empathy and Explain - Model empathy and explain explicitly discuss different perspectives have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice.
  • Social Awareness Instruction with Current Events - This strategy involves using current events and fictional characters to explicitly teach social awareness.
  • Socratic Seminars - Socratic seminars are formal discussions based on a text, where the leader asks open-ended questions.
  • Soliciting Feedback on Instruction - Instructors should encourage learners to provide feedback on their teaching.
  • Songs and Rhymes - Using songs and rhymes to memorize information is a mnemonic technique that leverages rhythm and melody to enhance recall.
  • Songwriting - Songwriting involves students creating their own verses or entire songs to enhance language development, phonemic awareness, and vocabulary.
  • Sound Walls - Sound walls help educators reinforce the importance of explicitly teaching the skills of letter-sound correspondence and support key aspects of learning to read that are backed by the science of reading, including phonemic awareness (the…
  • Sound-blocking Devices - Sound-blocking devices, such as noise-reducing headphones or earmuffs, can help children with auditory sensitivities manage sensory input by reducing background noise.
  • Spaced Learning Through Activity Breaks - Breaking up learning or work into short chunks of time interspersed with activity breaks leverages the 'spacing effect,' a well-replicated phenomenon in psychology.
  • Spaced Practice - Spaced practice involves distributing learning sessions over time, contrasting with massed practice (cramming).
  • Spaces that Foster Creativity - Traditional spaces designed in the industrial revolution were designed to maximize efficiency.
  • Spacing Activities in Handwriting - Activities designed to improve spacing between letters and words, which is crucial for overall legibility.
  • Spark Engagement with Student-Generated Questions - Students formulate questions and investigate topics they are curious about or consider important.
  • Speak the Future, Design the Future (Changing the Discourse) - This principle emphasizes that the language used to discuss education shapes the limits of our imagination.
  • Specific Feedback - This strategy involves providing targeted feedback on student writing that is directly tied to specific words, phrases, sentences, or paragraphs.
  • Specific Goal Questioning - Design questions with a specific goal in mind, such as identifying grabbers or understanding essay structure.
  • Specific Technique Identification - Providing specific guidance on what to look for in a text, naming sentences or words whenever possible, helps students learn from the text.
  • Speech-to-Text Technology - Speech-to-text technology converts spoken language into written text, benefiting individuals with dyslexia, dysgraphia, or physical disabilities by enabling them to express themselves in writing without the barriers of spelling,…
  • Speed Chatting (Pre-Reading) - Speed chatting is a pre-reading activity where learners form two rows facing each other and ask simple questions related to the reading topic.
  • Squeeze Ball or Theraputty - Providing a squeeze ball or Theraputty offers a tactile outlet for students to manage frustration and agitation.
  • Stages of Drawing and Writing Development - Children progress through stages of drawing and writing development, from random scribbling to controlled scribbling, lines and patterns, pictures of objects or people, and letter and word practice.
  • Stand Up/Sit Down - The rules are simple: if the teacher gives the number 10, students stand up.
  • Standard Inverted Classroom - Learners are asked to go through lecture videos and other study material that are prerequisites for the next class.
  • Standard-Based Regrouping - Form homogeneous groups based on learners' mastery of specific standards.
  • Standards-/Mastery-Based Grading - Standards-/Mastery-Based Grading emphasizes grading based on the level of mastery of learning objectives.
  • Standards-Based Grading - Shift from arbitrary points and percentages to evaluating students on mastery of specific learning standards, making expectations clear and grades meaningful.
  • Start with Yourself (Identity Mapping) - This principle encourages educators to reflect on their own intersectional identities and how these identities shape their perceptions and relationships with others.
  • Stations: Interacting with Multiple Texts - The Stations strategy involves small groups of learners rotating through different stations to interact with a variety of resources (informational texts, poetry, art, photography, maps, videos, audio clips) related to a specific event,…
  • Step In When Abusive Language Occurs - Addressing offensive language promptly and consistently is crucial for creating a safe and respectful classroom environment.
  • Stick-It Together (Collaborative Problem-Solving) - Students work in small groups to collaboratively solve math problems.
  • Stop and Jot - Stop and Jot is a processing activity that provides structured opportunities for learners to pause and respond in writing to key questions during a lesson.
  • Storage Areas - Organization is a key component of successful learning environments.
  • Story and Concept Maps - Story and concept maps are visual representations used to organize information and enhance comprehension, particularly of narratives and complex relationships.
  • Story Map - Story maps are graphic organizers that help learners visually represent and understand the key elements of a narrative, such as characters, setting, plot, conflict, and resolution.
  • Story Telling (Pre-Reading) - The instructor prepares a short, personalized narrative related to the reading topic.
  • Storybook Emotion Analysis - This strategy involves using storybooks to explore and discuss the emotions of characters.
  • Storytelling in Explainer Animations and Videos - Combining visual elements with engaging narratives to capture the learners' attention and facilitate long-term information retention.
  • Strategic Desk Arrangement - Arranging desks strategically can support different learning activities.
  • Strategies to Develop Positive Classroom Pride - Use these strategies to develop positive classroom pride: display learner work, positively reinforce learners verbally on a regular basis, publicly ask other staff members to enter the classroom so that they can see a specific…
  • Strategies to Remember Name Pronunciation - Use time-honored tricks to remember name pronunciation, like word association, writing down each syllable in English phonetics, and rhyming, as well as new-fangled ones like name pronunciation websites.
  • Strategy Identification & Reflection - This strategy involves having students actively identify and reflect on the strategies they use to overcome challenges.
  • Strategy Identification and Application - This strategy involves explicitly teaching problem-solving strategies and providing opportunities for students to practice using them when they feel 'stuck.' Students are encouraged to be mindful of how they are getting themselves unstuck…
  • Strategy Instruction - Strategy instruction teaches learners how to learn effectively by applying principles, rules, or multi-step processes to solve problems or accomplish learning tasks.
  • Strategy Instruction (Self-Regulated Strategy Development - SRSD) - Explicit teaching of writing strategies, especially self-regulated strategy development (SRSD).
  • Strength-Based Approach to Responsible Decision-Making - This approach involves identifying and leveraging a student’s strengths to address challenges in responsible decision-making.
  • Strength-Based Approach to Self-Awareness - This method involves identifying a student's strengths related to self-awareness and using those strengths to address their challenges.
  • Strength-Based Approach to Social Awareness - This method involves identifying a student's strengths related to social awareness and using those strengths to address their challenges.
  • Strength-Based Strategies for Responsible Decision-Making - Educators identify students' strengths related to responsible decision-making and leverage these strengths to address challenges.
  • Strength-Based Strategies for Self-Awareness - Educators identify and support students by recognizing their strengths related to self-awareness and using these strengths to address challenges.
  • Strength-Based Strategies for Social Awareness - Educators identify students' strengths related to social awareness and leverage these strengths to address challenges.
  • Strengths-Based IEPs - A shift in mindset where the Individualized Education Program (IEP) focuses as much on the learner’s strengths as it does on their weaknesses, leveraging abilities to help address needs.
  • Strengths-Based Teaching - A teaching approach that focuses on identifying and leveraging learners’ strengths to improve overall learning and engagement.
  • Structured and Sustained Family Engagement Programs - Creating engagement programs that are embedded throughout a school’s structure and are sustainable.
  • Structured Discussion Techniques - Facilitating productive discussions requires clear expectations, modeling, sentence starters (particularly for English language learners), and routines.
  • Structured Music and Dance Activities - Structured music and dance activities involve incorporating movement and rhythm into educational content, particularly for preschoolers.
  • Structured Observation Protocol - A structured observation protocol involves using a template or guide to record factual details about a student's experiences without interpretation, opinion, or judgment.
  • Structured Questioning for Pair Talk - Using structured questions with clear goals and timeframes provides focus and scaffolding for pair talk activities.
  • Structured/Segmented Instruction - Structured instruction involves systematically teaching information that has been chunked into manageable pieces.
  • Structuring Lessons - A lesson structure maps the teaching and learning that occurs in class.
  • Student Assessment Reports - Student assessment reports are visual aids used to track and communicate student progress in an engaging and approachable manner.
  • Student Blogging - Student blogs allow time to reflect on their mathematical process.
  • Student Choice - Incorporating student choice involves allowing learners to make decisions about their learning experiences, such as selecting which strategy to use in problem-solving, choosing how to demonstrate their knowledge, or deciding the sequence…
  • Student Demonstrations - Student demonstrations involve learners showcasing their understanding of a topic or skill through a performance, presentation, or hands-on activity.
  • Student Feedback on the Class - This strategy involves asking for student feedback to inform your teaching practice and improve engagement.
  • Student Game Design - In this approach, learners build their own game around a specific course topic or principle.
  • Student Hand Signals - Student Hand Signals is a strategy where learners use non-verbal cues to indicate their understanding or opinion after listening to a statement.
  • Student Led Math Conferences - Throughout the year, teachers can have personal math conferences with the students.
  • Student Models - Student models are examples of writing produced by other students, typically curated by instructors and made available for learners to reference.
  • Student Portfolio Creation - Student portfolio creation involves students selecting and organizing their best work samples to demonstrate their progress, reflect on their learning, and set goals.
  • Student Presentation of Collaborative Work - After completing a collaborative problem-solving task, groups project their work and present their final responses to the class.
  • Student Presentations: All About Me - Instructors begin the year having the learners do an 'All About Me' presentation, which involves sharing facts about themselves and including pictures or video.
  • Student Reflection (Responsible Decision-Making) - This strategy focuses on using student reflection to leverage strengths and address challenges related to responsible decision-making, which is the ability to make constructive choices about one’s behavior and social interactions in an…
  • Student Self-Knowledge - Student self-knowledge involves helping learners understand their strengths, interests, and areas for growth as learners.
  • Student Shadowing - An adult (educator, administrator, or school leader) follows a student throughout their school day to observe their experiences, interactions, and environment firsthand.
  • Student Shadowing (for educator insights) - Educators spend the majority of a school day shadowing a student to gain real-time qualitative data about their experiences.
  • Student Shadowing (for high school instructors) - A veteran teacher or coach shadows one or two students for a couple of days to gain insights into their experiences.
  • Student Shadowing (Qualitative Data Collection) - A school leader spends time shadowing a student to gather qualitative data about their lived experiences in the school.
  • Student Shadowing (Teacher/Coach Observation) - A teacher or coach shadows a student to gain insights into their experiences and identify areas for improvement in teaching practices.
  • Student-Created Magazines - In Alessandra King’s algebra class, students created a magazine with dozens of articles about real world applications of math.
  • Student-Driven Classroom Transformation - Involving students in the design and transformation of their learning environment to promote ownership, engagement, and a sense of community.
  • Student-generated Problems - Learners create their own problems based on concepts they're learning, share them with peers, and solve each other's problems.
  • Student-Generated Questions - Projects driven by student-generated questions allow learners to investigate topics they are curious about or think are important.
  • Student-Generated Questions in PBL - Sparking engagement with student-generated questions involves encouraging students to investigate topics they care about and identify questions they want to answer.
  • Student-Led Conferences - Student-led conferences (SLCs) are meetings where students take the lead in discussions with parents about their progress and learning, supported by the teacher.
  • Student-Pair Math Games - Pair-based games facilitate active learning through friendly competition, requiring students to recall and apply math skills in a dynamic setting.
  • Study of Written Models - Direct, guided practice was found to be an effective instructional strategy, especially for students with low skills.
  • Summaries and Recaps - Reinforce and clarify concepts, making sure information is both understood and remembered.
  • Summarization - Explicit teaching of the elements of a summary of a text leads to improved ability and increased confidence in writing summaries.
  • Summarizing - Summarizing involves integrating important information from a text or problem to create a concise overview.
  • Summative Assessment to Measure Learning Over Time - Interim and summative assessments both measure learning over time.
  • Supply Caddy - Instead of having supplies scattered all over the place, keep them all in a shower caddy or cleaning supply caddy.
  • Support Decoding of Text, Mathematical Notation, and Symbols - Ensuring that text and symbols do not impede the learning goal involves providing strategies and tools to help learners decode and understand written and symbolic information.
  • Support for Decoding Text, Mathematical Notation, and Symbols - Ensuring that text and symbols do not impede the learning goal by providing necessary support for decoding.
  • Supported Independent Reading - Independent reading involves students selecting and reading texts at their independent reading level or texts easy enough to decode and understand without much effort.
  • Supporting Self-Regulation - Identifying and supporting students who have learning strengths or challenges related to self-regulation.
  • Sushi Monster App - A free math app with a playful interface and characters to help kids expand their math skills and knowledge.
  • Syllabication Instruction - Teach children the six basic syllable types and how they affect spelling.

docs.title: T
docs.text:
• T-Chart - A T-chart is a graphic organizer shaped like the letter T, with a horizontal line at the top to signify a broad category and a vertical line that allows learners to compare attributes of a concept, organism, or phenomenon.
  • Tactile Toys / Fidgets - Tactile toys and fidgets are self-regulation tools that promote movement and tactile input to help with attention, focus, and sensory processing.
  • Tactile Toys for Sensory Integration - Providing tactile toys can help awaken sensory receptors, which may decrease fidgeting, attention issues, and behavior problems.
  • Take A Break Station - A designated space in the classroom where children can take a moment to decompress, reset, and self-regulate their emotions and behaviors.
  • Take Action, Be Intentional - Create an atmosphere that enables teachers to meet the needs of all students.
  • Talk About Real-Life Challenges and Situations - Facilitating discussions about the challenges learners are facing and how they feel about those situations.
  • Talk Moves - Talk moves are sentence frames we supply to our learners that help them express ideas and interact with one another in respectful, academically appropriate ways.
  • Talking to Young Children About Race and Racism - This strategy involves parents and caregivers initiating conversations with young children about race, racism, and anti-racism.
  • Targeted and Specific Communication with Families - Tailoring message content for different populations, such as non-native English speakers, families with different cultural backgrounds, and those with students in special education.
  • Targeted Networking - The \"Targeted Networking\" strategy involves focusing on specific activities, groups, or individuals who align with one's interests and goals in order to build meaningful relationships and connections.
  • Task Analysis - Task analysis involves breaking down a writing assignment into smaller, manageable tasks.
  • Task Force Teams of Inquiry - Forming task force teams of inquiry by letting teams form (or helping with this) and asking each team to select a topic from the brainstorm list.
  • Task Management for Writing - Task management focuses on helping students plan and manage their time and distractions while working on writing assignments.
  • Teach Academic Vocabulary - Provide explicit instruction on academic vocabulary that will be encountered during the project.
  • Teach Key Words for Standardized Test Prompts - Instructors teach terms that help learners understand prompts and perform well on standardized tests.
  • Teach Kids to Choose Their Self-Talk - 1) Share a definition of self-talk.
  • Teach Mindfulness Strategies - Teach students various mindfulness strategies, from meditation and deep breathing to journaling and drawing.
  • Teach Positive Actions - Education on positive actions for a healthy body (nutrition, exercise, and sleep), intellect (thinking, decision-making, problem-solving), self-management (managing time, energy, emotions), getting along with others (treating others…
  • Teach Self-Regulation Skills - Self-regulation is the ability to alter and regulate our emotional and behavioral responses.
  • Teach-OK - A peer teaching strategy that begins with the teacher spending a few minutes introducing a concept to the class.
  • Teacher as Writer - To understand the writing process, teachers have to write also.
  • Teacher Modeling - Demonstrating writing strategies and techniques by showing students how you use them yourself.
  • Teacher Racial Identity Work - Teacher racial identity work involves educators examining their own racial identity, biases, and privilege to create a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment.
  • Teacher Read-Aloud That Models Reading for Deep Understanding - A teacher read-aloud involves a teacher fluently reading a text aloud to learners, intentionally modeling strategies of understanding that can be reinforced in shared, guided, and independent reading.
  • Teacher-Led Physical Math Games - Teacher-led physical activities integrate movement and mathematical practice in an abbreviated time frame, suitable for station breaks and transitions, and are adaptable to different grade levels.
  • Teacher-Student Reading Conferences - Schedule regular conferences with students to get a sense of their independent reading and provide instructional support.
  • Teaching Academic Vocabulary - Explicitly teach mathematical academic vocabulary, including math-specific terms and the difference between mathematical and common definitions of words.
  • Teaching Academic Vocabulary in PBL - In project-based learning (PBL), teaching academic vocabulary involves identifying specialized or technical words that students will encounter during a project and planning instruction to teach these words.
  • Teaching Social Awareness Through Current Events and Fictional Characters - Model empathy and explain different perspectives in current events and fictional characters.
  • Team-Building Through Problem-Based Learning - Using problem-based learning in multi-cultural groups helps learners get used to working in a multi-cultural environment.
  • Technology Accessibility - Classrooms that have a variety of media allow for different learning activities and might include a projector, a white board, digital cameras, laptops, satellite TV, video production, and even Ipad accessibility.
  • Technology Breaks - Taking short, scheduled breaks from technology during study periods reduces the negative effects of media multitasking.
  • Teen Exercise as Stress Management - Encourage teens to engage in regular exercise as a way to manage stress, improve focus, and enhance overall well-being.
  • Temperature Control - Maintaining an optimal temperature range in classrooms affects student engagement and productivity.
  • Temperature Monitoring & Adjustment - Monitoring the temperature of a learning environment and making adjustments to maintain an optimal temperature range can improve learner focus and reduce distractions.
  • Temperature Monitoring for Learning Environments - This strategy involves monitoring the temperature of a learning environment and making adjustments to maintain optimal conditions for learners.
  • Temperature Regulation - Temperature regulation is an important finding across individuals of all ages is that the temperature in which a person works affects engagement levels and overall productivity—including student achievement.
  • Test-Study-Test Technique - The test-study-test technique is a spelling instruction strategy where students take a pretest, correct their errors under teacher guidance, and then study the corrected words before taking a final test.
  • Text + Social Annotation + Structured Activity - Students engage with text resources, typically online versions, that are equipped with social annotation tools.
  • Text + Structured Activity - Students engage with text resources (physical or digital) accompanied by a structured activity designed to ensure active learning and engagement with the material.
  • Text Chats in Instruction - Integrating text chats into instruction involves using real-time messaging platforms to facilitate communication and collaboration among learners.
  • Text Illustrations with Graphic Organizers - Learners add graphic organizers to finished expository or argumentative writing to illustrate a concept, providing a supportive diagram that aids reader comprehension.
