  • Text-Based Discussions - Text-based discussions involve engaging learners in discussions about what they read, with a focus on using evidence from the text to support their responses.
  • Text-to-Speech (TTS) - Text-to-speech (TTS) technology converts written text into spoken words, enhancing accessibility and comprehension for individuals with dyslexia, visual impairments, or other learning differences.
  • Text-to-Speech (TTS) Software - Text-to-speech (TTS) software allows written text to be read aloud.
  • Text-to-Speech Software - Text-to-speech (TTS) software converts written text into spoken words, aiding individuals who benefit from auditory learning or have reading difficulties.
  • Text-to-Text, Text-to-Self, Text-to-World - Text-to-Text, Text-to-Self, Text-to-World is a strategy that helps learners connect ideas in a text to their own experiences and beliefs (text-to-self), events happening in the world (text-to-world), and other texts they have encountered…
  • The Best Part of Me Book - Have the class create a book in which each student tells one thing they like about themselves.
  • The Disciplinary Steps - Follow these steps when disciplining learners: review what happened, identify and accept the learner's feelings, review alternative actions, explain the building policy as it applies to the situation, let the learner know that all…
  • The Frayer Model - A tool for teaching a concept, not isolated facts.
  • The Pencil Pledge - The Pencil Pledge is a classroom management technique that helps create a positive learning environment by promoting respect for materials and self-regulation.
  • The Role of Background Knowledge - When it comes to background knowledge, learners may have relevant experiences that just need to be drawn out.
  • The Title (Pre-Reading) - Learners are given the title of the reading and asked to form small groups to pool their knowledge about the topic.
  • Things to Consider as a Healthy Skeptic - Provide adolescents with opportunities to see the value of a healthy skepticism toward information they encounter in both online and offline contexts.
  • Think Time - Allow plenty of think-time and time for re-reading for students who might need more time to process.
  • Think-Aloud Modeling - Think-aloud modeling is a strategy in which an instructor performs a task while verbalizing the reasoning, checks, and decisions normally kept internal.
  • Think-Alouds - Model learning by reading aloud an article on a current event or topic of study, pausing to ask questions and make comments and connections to prior knowledge.
  • Think-Alouds for Online Reading Strategies - Teachers model their online reading strategies through think-alouds.
  • Think-Pair-Share (Turn & Talk) - Think-Pair-Share is a cooperative learning strategy designed to encourage individual participation and articulate communication.
  • Think-Time and Re-Reading - Sufficient time is allowed for learners to process information and re-read materials if needed.
  • Think-Write-Pair-Share - Think-Write-Pair-Share is a collaborative learning strategy where students first think individually about a topic or question, then write down their thoughts, pair with a partner to discuss their responses, and finally share their ideas…
  • Think-Write-Share - Think-Write-Share is a strategy that involves learners thinking about a question, writing down their responses, and then sharing their thoughts with the class.
  • Thinking About Emotions in Advance - Begin the school day by asking your students a question to find out how they are feeling or what might be bothering them.
  • Thinking Critically - This strategy encompasses questioning, reflection, and evaluation to understand, solve problems, and make informed decisions.
  • Thinking Tools with Graphic Organizers - When teachers deliver content through lectures, readings, or video, they can have students interact with the content by completing a graphic organizer in groups, pairs, or even on their own.
  • Three-Tiered Writing Conferences - The Three-Tiered Writing Conference approach provides a structured format for brief, effective writing conferences between teachers and students.
  • Through the Eyes of the People in a Story - Learners pick a character from a short story or book and relive the main events from that character’s point of view.
  • Tier Two Vocabulary Instruction - Focuses on teaching high-frequency words used by mature language users that can add significantly to language ability.
  • Tiered Seating Areas - Tiered areas allow for groups to convene to discuss ideas and communicate procedures.
  • Tiered Vocabulary Instruction - Tiered vocabulary instruction categorizes words into three tiers based on their frequency and utility.
  • Timely Feedback - Timely feedback involves providing feedback as soon as possible after the learner demonstrates proof of learning.
  • Timely Peer Review - This strategy involves conducting peer reviews at multiple points in the writing process, including before the assignment is due, on the day it is due, and after it has been graded.
  • Timers - Timers, both visual and auditory, are used to help learners gauge how much time remains during an activity, supporting greater attention and task completion.
  • Tossing Activity - A hands-on activity that integrates movement with learning, often involving the physical act of tossing objects.
  • TPRI Diagnostic Assessment - The TPRI (Texas Primary Reading Inventory) is a diagnostic instrument designed to identify the reading development of students in kindergarten through third grade.
  • Training Handouts - Training handouts are supplementary materials distributed during training sessions to enhance learner engagement, structure interactions, and provide a reference for key content.
  • Trait Identification and Construction - These tasks involve the study of traits, requiring learners to identify animal body parts from puzzle pieces and construct either real or mythical animals.
  • Trampoline Review - Trampoline Review is a kinesthetic learning strategy that involves learners jumping on a small trampoline or performing other motor activities while reviewing information.
  • Translanguaging - Translanguaging recognizes that multilingual speakers have a single linguistic repertoire that they use to understand the world.
  • Translate Academic to Social Language - Model how to say something in a more academic way or how to paraphrase academic texts into more conversational language.
  • Translate Report Cards Into Multiple Languages - Using communication apps to translate report cards into multiple languages (e.g., Spanish, Arabic, Vietnamese, and Mandarin Chinese) makes it easier for parents to understand their child's progress, particularly in districts with diverse…
  • Travel Journals - Every student at Normal Park Museum Magnet, a K–8 school in Chattanooga, Tennessee, created a travel journal to chart their learning.
  • Turn and Talk - Turn and Talk involves learners engaging in short discussions with a partner to explain what they heard.
  • Turn-and-Talk - Turn-and-talk involves having learners engage in short, structured discussions with a partner to review and reinforce what they have learned.
  • Turn-around Time - Providing timely feedback is crucial for learners to reflect, correct, and extend their performance.

docs.title: U
docs.text:
• Uncluttered Environment - A learning environment with minimal visual distractions is created by storing supplies and materials off of tables and desks and limiting decorations and other things hanging on the walls.
  • Uncluttered Learning Environment - A clean, organized, and uncluttered learning environment is free from distractions and allows the focus to be on learning.
  • Understand Your Bias - This activity increases awareness of personal stereotypes and prejudices, helping learners recognize how their viewpoint influences their perception of others.
  • Unit Planning with Graphic Organizers - When introducing a unit to students, show them how the parts of the unit fit together with a graphic organizer, providing a sense of where they are in the unit at any given time and helping them understand why they are learning the…
  • Untimed Tests - Untimed tests remove the pressure of completing assessments within a set time limit, allowing learners to focus on problem-solving without time-related anxiety.
  • Use \"I\" Statements to Avoid Blame - Avoid using “you” statements, which can make students defensive.
  • Use Body Language and Demonstrations - Reinforce verbal instructions with body language, gestures, and demonstrations to aid comprehension.
  • Use Books to Teach Emotions - Stories are used as examples of handling emotions in a responsible way.
  • Use Current Events & Fictional Characters - Using current events and fictional characters as tools to teach social awareness.
  • Use current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness - Utilize real-world events and fictional narratives to explore social dynamics, ethical dilemmas, and diverse perspectives.
  • Use Estimation and Prediction - Students use estimation and prediction skills.
  • Use Positive Affirmations - Replace negative messages from the inner voice with positive affirmations.
  • Use Quotations to Cite Textual Evidence - Using quotations to cite textual evidence involves teaching students to select and incorporate direct quotes from texts to support their claims.
  • Use Templates and Tools That Allow for Scaffolding - Using templates and tools that allow for scaffolding involves providing students with structured supports to guide their writing process.
  • Use this Toolkit: Mitigating Racial Bias in Edtech - This toolkit is designed to guide educational technology (edtech) companies in identifying and mitigating racial bias in the design and development of their products.
  • Use Visual Aids - Supplement verbal instructions with visual aids to support learners' understanding, especially for low-level students.
  • Use Worked Examples - The instructor presents a fully solved problem — showing each step and explaining the reasoning behind it — and then asks learners to solve a similar problem independently or in pairs.
  • User-Friendly Library Website Practices - This strategy focuses on making library websites more accessible and user-friendly to encourage greater utilization of library resources by students.
  • Using a Culturally Responsive Curriculum Scorecard - The Culturally Responsive Curriculum Scorecard is a tool designed to evaluate the extent to which curricula are culturally responsive.
  • Using Colors for Different Feelings - Learners use different colors to represent different emotions in art, which creates associations between emotions and visual cues, enhancing emotional expression and awareness.
  • Using Empathy Interviews for Family Engagement - Empathy interviews involve targeted, one-on-one conversations with a small sample of people to learn from their lived experiences, such as used by organizations like Stanford d.School and The Learning Accelerator.
  • Using Manipulatives - Manipulatives are physical objects used as teaching tools to engage students in hands-on learning, especially in mathematics.
  • Using Positive Affirmations - Replacing negative messages from the inner voice with positive affirmations.
  • Using Reflection for Habit Formation - This strategy promotes reflective classrooms to ensure learners are fully engaged in making meaning.
  • Using Technology - Technology is a powerful tool in math instruction for ELLs.
  • Utilize Text Messaging for Parent Engagement - Text messaging is used as a primary means of communication for educators and community leaders to engage parents.
  • Utilizing Mobile Communication Apps for Parent Engagement - Mobile communication apps (e.g., ClassDojo, Spotlight, Remind, and Seesaw) offer simple ways for educators to send texts, video summaries, and alerts to parents about school activities or their child’s progress.

docs.title: V
docs.text:
• Validate Feelings - Tell students they have the right to feel the way they feel.
  • Valuing the Learning Process - Valuing the learning process involves emphasizing the importance of understanding, exploration, and growth over achieving high grades.
  • Varying Irrelevant Attributes in Examples - When teaching concepts, use examples in which the irrelevant attributes vary widely.
  • Varying Levels of Choice in Assessments - Give students a choice about the areas of focus in a paper or project.
  • Venn Diagrams - Venn diagrams are visual organizers that emphasize comparisons and contrasts between two or more items or concepts.
  • Verbal Feedback on Writing - Verbal feedback uses voice recording technology to provide balanced feedback and promote a growth mindset.
  • Verbal Repetition - Verbal repetition is a strategy where learners repeat information verbally to reinforce understanding and retention.
  • Video Report Cards - Sending parents a link to a personalized video that provides context about their child’s report card, such as a history of the child’s performance in core subjects, areas for growth, and recommendations to further support the child’s…
  • Videoconferencing for Collaboration - Videoconferencing platforms with built-in collaboration features such as Microsoft Teams and Google Meet can help teachers replicate teamwork experiences online.
  • Videos - Videos are dynamic resources for supporting curricula, engaging students through sight and sound.
  • Videos (Pre-Reading) - A short video relating to the topic of the reading is shown.
  • Videos: SEL Topics - Using short video clips on SEL topics followed by discussions and/or related activities promotes relevance and meaningful connection of these topics to learners' background knowledge and personal lives.
  • Virtual Embodiment - Virtual embodiment is used to give people the experience of the golden rule in operation.
  • Virtual Flipped Classroom - Classroom time for tutoring is completely eliminated in this model.
  • Virtual Reality (VR) for Empathy Training - VR is used to guide new workers through a virtual phone call with a Fidelity “customer” going through a financial crisis, training them about empathy.
  • Virtual Reality (VR) Skills Management Assessments - Virtual reality is used to prepare employees for the commotion when customers swarm stores on Black Friday and evaluating how workers respond to angry shoppers.
  • Virtual Reality (VR) Training - Virtual Reality (VR) training is a method of using VR technology to create simulated environments where learners can engage in interactive training scenarios.
  • Visual Cues - Using graphics or gestures can help learners who face auditory processing challenges.
  • Visual Mnemonics - Visual mnemonics involve creating visual images to cue a strategy or represent a concept.
  • Visual Organizers - Visual organizers are tools that visually represent ideas and concepts, helping learners construct meaning and strengthen recall.
  • Visual Prompts for Essay Writing - Using artwork along with life lesson statements can help adolescents write essays.
  • Visual Reading Aids - Visual reading aids, such as reading guides, colored overlays, and tracking rulers, are tools designed to make text more accessible and readable.
  • Visual Representations in Mathematics - This evidence-based strategy involves using visual representations, such as schematic diagrams, to help learners understand abstract mathematics concepts and solve problems.
  • Visual Timers - Visual timers help teach the concept of time to children with special needs.
  • Visualizations and Mind Maps - Use visuals such as infographics and mind maps to help transform abstract concepts into clear and engaging formats.
  • Visualizing - Visualizing involves creating a mental image or representation of a problem or text to aid in understanding.
  • Vocabulary Instruction - Explicitly teaching vocabulary words and their definitions, along with providing context, to help students understand and use new words effectively.
  • Vocabulary Meaning Through Context - Instructors should present vocabulary in context so that learners can deduce the meaning for themselves, aiding understanding and retention.

docs.title: W
docs.text:
• Wait Time - Wait time is the period of silence between the time a question is asked and the time when one or more learners respond to that question.
  • Wall Calendar - A large calendar for family appointments and events can help kids see that organization is a lifelong skill.
  • Warning and Consequence - This technique involves giving high school students a clear warning that talking during the lesson will result in a consequence, such as taking time off their break.
  • Waste Reduction Solutions - These tasks involve examining and sorting waste items in a garbage can, categorizing and charting the items, and proposing solutions to reduce the amount of solid waste.
  • Watch Emotion Videos - Share helpful videos that explains big emotions to kids.
  • Web Annotation Tools - Learners use free web-based tools to annotate online documents, including slideshows, blog posts, or PDFs.
  • Web-based Dictionary & Thesaurus - Incorporating web dictionaries and thesauruses into vocabulary lessons allows learners to quickly search for and understand unfamiliar words.
  • Web-Search Scavenger Hunt - A web-search scavenger hunt is a fun way to help students learn how to effectively use search engines to find accurate information.
  • Website Domain Analysis - Learners are taught the differences between .com, .gov, .org, and .edu domains to assess the reliability of websites.
  • Website Evaluation Checklist - Learners examine websites (both reliable and unreliable) using a checklist to assess various elements such as the corroboration of information, writer reliability, information currency, documentation, advocacy, and conflict of interest.
  • Weekly Student Reflection - Students spend 10-15 minutes every week reflecting on their learning experiences by responding to prompts, enhancing dialogue, inspiring openness, and diversity.
  • What Would Their Day Look Like? - Learners select a photo of a person or animal in an unfamiliar situation and imagine what their daily life might be like.
  • What's My Emotion? Game - Using an EQ Feeling Chart, students identify how they are feeling individually.
  • What’s Below the Surface? (Iceberg Analysis) - This strategy involves using the metaphor of an iceberg to encourage students to extend their knowledge and further develop their ideas beyond the surface level.
  • What’s My Emotion? Game - One learner demonstrates an emotion through body language and facial expressions, while the rest of the class guesses the emotion.
  • What’s My Number? - A guessing game where one person thinks of a number and provides clues, and others use logical reasoning and deduction to determine the number.
  • Where Are the People Like Me? - Learners examine media examples to consider who is represented and who is not, then explore the impact of this lack of diversity and how it might affect those who are misrepresented or not represented.
  • Which One Doesn’t Belong? - The instructor or learners place 3-4 dot cards on the table.
  • Whole Class Self-Monitoring - Whole class self-monitoring involves the entire class participating in self-monitoring techniques, adapted from individual self-monitoring methods.
  • Windows, Mirrors, and Sliding Glass Doors - This strategy involves using stories and materials that act as mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors to help students identify their place in the world.
  • Word Building - Word building is a literacy strategy used to reinforce vocabulary and spelling skills by having learners manipulate letter tiles or squares to construct words.
  • Word Detective (Word Identification in Context) - Learners identify target vocabulary within varied contexts.
  • Word Maps - A word map is a visual organizer that promotes vocabulary development.
  • Word Problem Creation - Learners select math operations and create multistep word problems for peers to solve, integrating math and literacy skills.
  • Word Processing and Technology Tools - Use word processing and other technology tools to support writing.
  • Word Processing for Composition - Word processing involves using computer software to write, edit, and format text.
  • Word Processing for Writing Skills - Using word processing software like Google Docs allows learners to write, share, review, and revise their work.
  • Word Sort - Students work in small groups, with each group given an envelope containing key terms on separate slips of paper.
  • Word Sorts - Word sorts are a hands-on activity where learners categorize words based on shared features to build phonological processing, morphological knowledge, vocabulary, and spelling skills.
  • Word Study - Word study is an approach to spelling instruction that emphasizes the investigation and understanding of patterns in words rather than rote memorization.
  • Word Walls - Word walls are a strategy for supporting vocabulary development and retention by providing learners with constant access to important content vocabulary.
  • Worked Example Routine - This routine provides a structured approach to using worked examples in teaching to prevent passive or superficial engagement.
  • Worked Examples Types - Modelling examples provide maximum guidance by paying explicit attention to the process needed to reach an acceptable solution, such as a librarian internship where the librarian explains what (s)he’s doing and why it’s done in that…
  • Write Alouds - Write-aloud lessons, also known as modeled writing, involve an experienced writer (typically the teacher) verbalizing their thought process while writing.
  • Write with a Transition Handout - Before learners write, provide a handout of transitions.
  • Write Your Own Word Problem - For homework, assign learners the task of writing some of their own word problems containing some of the key words discussed in class.
  • Writing Conferences - Writing conferences are brief, individualized meetings between a teacher and a student focused on the student's writing.
  • Writing Down Goals - Writing down goals makes them tangible and helps prioritize them.
  • Writing Process Approach - A process-oriented approach to writing instruction that places the learner at the center of interactive learning among teachers and students.
  • Writing Workshops - Writing workshops create environments with multiple stations focusing on different aspects of writing, such as transitions, topic sentences, or source integration.
  • WWYD Critical Incidents - Learners are presented with mini case studies that feature a conflict or misunderstanding and are asked, 'What would you do if you were person X/person Y?' This activity encourages learners to consider different perspectives and offer…

docs.title: Y
docs.text:
• Yoga, Breathing, and Meditation - Using yoga, breathing, and meditation techniques in educational settings involves incorporating these practices to provide calming stimulation and regulate the nervous system.
  • Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) - Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an approach where young people collaborate with adults to conduct research and implement actions to address issues in their communities.

docs.title: Z
docs.text: • Zoom Family Hours - Hold evening office or family hours on Zoom for parents and family members to pop in and ask questions or otherwise engage with you about their children.

  • 3-Source Rule - When students are doing online research in her class, Je Hen enforces the three-source rule.
  • 5-Minute Writing Conferences - This strategy involves conducting brief, targeted conferences with each student to provide personalized feedback on their writing.
  • \"Document Outline\" Tool - Students use the \"Document outline\" tool in Google Docs to extract evidence supporting the main ideas they've found in a text.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use the "Document outline" tool in Google Docs to extract evidence supporting the main ideas they've found in a text. They write headings for paragraphs or groups of paragraphs and select "Heading 1" from the drop-down menu. Sentences or phrases representing supporting evidence are summarized and labeled "Heading 2." The tool automatically populates an outline that can be exported to the top of the document for easy review and writing initiation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to Google Docs and relevant documents.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires familiarity with Google Docs, may be time-consuming, and relies on the accuracy of the extracted evidence.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Organize information, identify supporting evidence, facilitate writing initiation, and enhance reading comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simplifies the process of extracting evidence and creating an outline, promotes critical analysis, and supports writing initiation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The complexity of the text and the specificity of the headings can be adjusted based on students' skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Argument Construction
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of the outline, accuracy of the extracted evidence, and depth of analysis.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Streamlining the organization of information and facilitating writing initiation can enhance comprehension and analytical skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school and high school students, particularly in social studies or other content-heavy subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, promote collaborative discussion, develop critical thinking skills, encourage justification with text evidence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Slows down the reading process, promoting deeper engagement. Encourages dialogue and discussion about the text. Reinforces the skill of identifying main ideas and supporting evidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can modify text complexity or group sizes. Can be adapted for individual or whole-class activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Practice

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use the EQ Feeling Chart to identify their feelings. One student acts out their feeling through body language and facial expressions, while the rest of the class guesses the emotion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart, space for students to act out emotions, and a willingness to participate in a game.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may feel uncomfortable acting out their emotions. The effectiveness of the activity depends on creating a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for pre-K through college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify and express feelings, develop non-verbal communication skills, increase emotional awareness, foster empathy and understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a fun and engaging way to explore emotions. Encourages students to develop their non-verbal communication skills. Promotes empathy and understanding through guessing and observation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose from a range of emotions or focus on specific emotional categories. The level of participation can be adjusted based on individual comfort levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in acting out and guessing emotions. Assess the accuracy of students' guesses and the expressiveness of their actions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Acknowledging emotions calms the amygdala and reduces the intensity of felt emotions, helping individuals feel more in control. Promotes emotional literacy and awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary school teachers use the 'What's My Emotion?' game as a regular check-in activity to help students develop their emotional literacy and non-verbal communication skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When students are doing online research in her class, Je Hen enforces the three-source rule. Students must confirm information they find on three different websites to make sure it’s valid. Try doing that with the tree octopus!

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Need to confirm information found on three different websites.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To confirm information is valid.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps confirm the validity of information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Ability to find 3 valid sources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves conducting brief, targeted conferences with each student to provide personalized feedback on their writing. Prior to the conferences, teachers read student essays, record a score from the rubric, and note one strength and one area for improvement. Students reflect on their papers and choose a growth area to discuss. During the five-minute conference, the student shares their self-assessment, and the teacher provides targeted feedback. This approach allows for more effective communication and relationship-building compared to written comments alone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires significant class time (three 55-minute periods for a class of 30). Teachers must prepare notes on each student's essay in advance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time-intensive, requiring careful management and preparation. May not be suitable for all class sizes or schedules.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students, particularly in English Language Arts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student writing through targeted instruction, enhance understanding of rubrics, and build stronger relationships between teachers and students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides individually targeted instruction, allows students to ask questions, and fosters a stronger teacher-student relationship. Improves student understanding of rubrics.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students choose a specific growth area to focus on during the conference, tailoring the feedback to their individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvement in scores between original and revised essay drafts. Monitor student participation in outside-of-class conferences. Assess changes in class culture and teacher-student relationships.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students learn more from discussing their writing in a five-minute conference than from written comments. Improves relationships and fosters a more supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A set of questions to determine the credibility of a news story. These include asking whether the story is outrageous, whether the headline matches the article, whether quotes are in context, whether the story attacks a generic enemy, and who the news source is.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to news stories

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires critical thinking skills and attention to detail

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate news stories for credibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to evaluating news stories

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different age groups and levels of expertise

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Ability to answer questions about the credibility of a news story

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps readers identify false narratives and avoid being conned by propagandists.

docs.title: Examples
