docs.title: Description
docs.text: Academic Choice empowers learners by providing them with options in their learning and involves a three-phase process: planning, working, and reflecting. Teachers decide on the goal of the lesson or activity, then give learners a list of options for what to learn and/or how to go about their learning in order to reach the defined goal.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to pre-plan the learning activities, the different choices offered, and the methods of planning and reflecting for the learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • It may be difficult for teachers to fit Academic Choice into an already full schedule. If not implemented correctly, learners may struggle to make effective choices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, but can be adapted for older learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase engagement, promote self-directed learning, foster deeper thinking, enhance productivity, reduce behavior problems

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports intrinsic motivation by meeting the needs for competence, belonging, and autonomy. Allows learners to work from their areas of strength and interest. Mirrors the natural learning cycle by allowing learners to generate goals, interact with materials, and make sense of their experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Having choices allows learners to work from their areas of strength and personal interest. They're then more likely to feel invested in their work and to draw personal meaning from it.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and motivation levels. Assess the quality of learner work. Collect learner feedback on their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When learners have choices in their learning, they become highly engaged and productive. They’re excited about learning and sharing their knowledge. They’re likely to think more deeply and creatively, work with more persistence, and use a range of academic skills and strategies. In addition, research has generally found that children have fewer behavior problems when they have regular opportunities to make choices in their learning, a finding supported by anecdotal evidence from teachers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A third grade class is studying insects, and the teacher wants the children to get some basic information about these animals. The teacher gives children choices in how to get such information, including by reading a book about insects, listening to a recording about insects, interviewing someone who studies insects, or observing and recording insects’ appearance and behavior.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves accepting what happened after processing emotions, taking responsibility for any wrong actions, and sharing feelings and experiences with others involved. If the relationship with the other person is important, it requires having the courage to talk to them without accusation or excuses, simply sharing how one feels and what one experienced. This includes being open to receiving the other person's sadness and anger, understanding that their feelings matter too. If resolution isn't possible, accepting that outcome while still learning from the situation is crucial.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Courage to be vulnerable, willingness to take responsibility, and the ability to communicate openly and respectfully.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires willingness from both parties to engage. Resolution may not always be possible.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adults seeking to resolve interpersonal conflicts and learn from their mistakes.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote acceptance, encourage taking responsibility, and foster open communication to resolve conflicts and strengthen relationships.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates conflict resolution, builds stronger relationships, and promotes personal accountability. Encourages vulnerability and open communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different relationship dynamics and communication styles. Emphasis on personal feelings and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evidence of improved communication, reduced conflict, and increased mutual understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Stronger relationships, improved conflict resolution skills, and enhanced personal growth.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Practicing active listening, using 'I' statements to express feelings, and seeking mediation if direct communication is too challenging.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves adjusting the complexity of sentence structures to suit the learner's cognitive capacity. In practice, instructors can provide sentence starters for learners to build more complex sentences, or they can simplify their syntax to reduce cognitive load on Working Memory.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of learners' language abilities, ability to provide clear sentence structures and modifications.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful assessment of learners' needs, and instructors must be mindful of not oversimplifying to avoid undermining learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, including those with learning disabilities and multilingual learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce cognitive load, improve comprehension, facilitate effective communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive strain, promotes understanding, and supports language development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentence starters can be tailored to the individual's level, and syntax complexity can be adjusted based on learner feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation, evaluate sentence construction skills, and gather feedback on the clarity of instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and confidence in sentence construction; reduced cognitive burden; enhanced language skills; and development of increased syntactic fluency.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using non-fiction texts at adaptive reading levels or providing sentence starters.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves intentionally activating and building upon learners' existing knowledge and experiences to enhance comprehension and engagement. Teachers can research students’ native countries, cultures, and educational systems and draw on students’ experiences to connect what they are reading to their own lives. Approaches include: asking students to speak with peers in their home language about a topic, using a graphic organizer, finding materials that will engage students and involve them in the learning process so that they find elements they can connect to and learn from, inviting students to share special traditions, holidays, and foods from their cultures throughout the year and across the curriculum, or asking students to interview their family members in order to learn more about their memories and experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to research students' backgrounds and create opportunities for sharing. Requires sensitivity to students' comfort levels with sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Risk of making assumptions or putting students on the spot. Requires time and effort to gather information and prepare culturally relevant materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • English language learners and students from diverse backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, increase engagement, validate student experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes content more accessible and relevant, fosters a sense of belonging, promotes deeper understanding and retention

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt activities to different language proficiency levels and cultural backgrounds. Provide multiple ways for students to share their knowledge and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe increased student participation and engagement. Analyze student work for connections to their backgrounds. Gather student feedback on relevance and accessibility of content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that connecting content to students' background knowledge enhances comprehension and retention (e.g., Steffensen, Joag-Deve, & Anderson, 1979).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Having students share music or art from their culture, interviewing family members about their memories and experiences, using "mirror books" where students can see themselves

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognize that adults have diverse levels of technology exposure and experience. Do not assume familiarity with current tools or platforms. Incorporate introductory resources and guidance for learners with limited experience to ensure they can successfully engage with the course materials.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of diverse skill levels, flexibility in instruction, supportive learning resources

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources to accommodate diverse needs

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners with varying degrees of technological experience and exposure.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable all learners to participate, regardless of previous experience. Provide foundational knowledge for those with limited exposure to technology.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces barriers to entry, provides a supportive learning environment, promotes confidence and engagement

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer optional introductory modules on technology basics, provide step-by-step instructions for using online tools, assign peer mentors to support learners with limited experience

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement, solicit feedback on support resources, track usage of optional introductory modules

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased participation and engagement, reduced frustration among learners with limited experience, improved learning outcomes

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on identifying and addressing the learning needs of students with varying processing speeds. Processing speed refers to the pace at which individuals take in information, make sense of it, and respond, affecting learning in various areas such as lectures, note-taking, mental math, and conversations. The strategy involves identifying student strengths and challenges related to processing speed and using targeted interventions. This includes providing graphic organizers or guided notes, repeating key points in multiple ways, using manipulatives to make concepts concrete, and allowing ample think-time and time for re-reading. These strategies aim to leverage student strengths to support their learning process, especially in areas where processing speed presents a challenge. By recognizing and accommodating these differences, educators can create a more inclusive and effective learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of processing speed and its impact on learning, assessment tools to identify student strengths and challenges, targeted interventions (e.g., graphic organizers, guided notes, manipulatives), time for observation and reflection

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation and assessment to identify student needs, interventions may need to be adjusted over time, may be time-consuming to implement effectively, requires ongoing professional development and support

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with varying processing speeds, students who take longer to process information, students who struggle with note-taking, mental math, or keeping up with rapid conversations, educators looking to create a more inclusive and supportive learning environment

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify student strengths and challenges related to processing speed, leverage student strengths to support learning, provide targeted interventions to address processing speed challenges, create a more inclusive and effective learning environment, enhance student understanding and retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses individual learning needs, leverages student strengths to support learning, provides targeted interventions, creates a more inclusive learning environment, enhances understanding and retention

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and grade levels, can be used with individual students or small groups, interventions can be tailored to specific student strengths and challenges

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Gain attention
  • State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student performance on tests and assignments, student engagement and participation in class, student self-reflection on their learning process, teacher observations of student behavior and learning patterns

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that accommodating processing speed challenges can lead to improved student performance, increased engagement, and a more positive learning experience. Targeted interventions can help students overcome learning barriers and reach their full potential.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing graphic organizers or guided notes during lectures to help students pull out important points. Repeating key points for students several times and in several different ways. Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete. Allowing plenty of think-time and time for re-reading for students who might need more time to process.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Setting achievable micro-goals encourages consistent, incremental progress, leading to a growth mindset and increased confidence. These small wins, repeated over time, help learners see that progress is attainable and that their efforts are paying off. This approach breaks down larger, more daunting tasks into manageable steps, making the overall goal seem less overwhelming and more approachable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to break down tasks into manageable steps. Instructors need to provide clear guidance and support to help learners achieve their micro-goals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If micro-goals are too easy, they may not provide enough of a challenge to promote growth. If they are too difficult, they may lead to frustration and discouragement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who are easily discouraged or overwhelmed by large tasks

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase confidence, promote a growth mindset, foster incremental progress, and improve motivation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners see tangible progress, reduces feelings of being overwhelmed, and builds confidence through repeated success. Instructors can use micro-goals to scaffold learning and provide targeted support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Micro-goals can be tailored to individual learner needs and skill levels. Instructors can provide different sets of micro-goals for learners with varying levels of proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner progress towards micro-goals, monitor their confidence levels, and observe their persistence in the face of challenges. Compare performance between learners who are using micro-goals and those who are not.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that small wins repeated over time can lead to a growth mindset and increased confidence. Setting achievable goals can support self-regulation and increase motivation as learners begin to successfully tackle difficult challenges in smaller steps.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Managing classroom acoustics and noise levels greatly impacts teacher and student performance. Excessive noise can cause dissatisfaction and stress, reducing engagement and achievement. Building schools or modifying classrooms to buffer external noise improves student outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Acoustic materials, quiet spaces, noise-canceling headphones, or facility modifications.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly and may require significant changes to the learning environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners and educators in K-12 or higher education settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student engagement and achievement, reduce teacher and student stress, create a more conducive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, enhances focus, improves auditory processing

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer noise-canceling headphones or designated quiet areas for learners sensitive to noise.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure noise levels in classrooms, assess student engagement and achievement, survey teacher and student satisfaction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that reduced noise levels improve student engagement and academic achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using acoustic panels, soundproofing classrooms, providing noise-canceling headphones.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Acronyms use the first letter of each word in a list or phrase to create a new, memorable word or abbreviation. Acrostics use the first letter of each item to form a sentence or phrase. These devices can aid in recall by providing a simple, easily remembered cue.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of items to be remembered. Ability to create words or phrases from the first letters of those items.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not work well for complex or abstract concepts. The acronym or acrostic must be easily remembered itself.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially useful for those who need to memorize lists or sequences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve recall of lists, names, or sequences; simplify complex information into easily remembered cues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by condensing information into a single, easily remembered word or phrase. Activates pattern recognition to facilitate recall.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create their own acronyms or acrostics tailored to their learning style and the specific information they need to remember.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the number of items recalled correctly after using an acronym or acrostic. Monitor the ease with which learners can generate and use these devices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of mnemonic devices in improving memory recall (Radovic et al., 2019).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • HOMES for the Great Lakes (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior); My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles for the planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Role-play how to handle different situations, especially those that students struggle with. Write each scenario on a note card. For example: You get invited to a birthday party. You slip and fall while walking home from school. You open a birthday present you don’t like. Then, have students talk them through or act them out. How would they feel? What would they do? How does their feeling connect with their behavior?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Note cards with scenario descriptions, time for role-playing and discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may feel uncomfortable acting or sharing personal experiences, requiring thoughtful facilitation and adaptation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly those who struggle with handling difficult emotions and social situations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice responsible handling of emotions, develop emotional literacy, improve conflict resolution skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides vicarious learning experiences in a safe environment, enhances emotional literacy through active participation, promotes empathy and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Selection of scenarios to match student interests and experiences, flexible role assignment to different student emotional levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student participation in discussions, reflective writing, and other activities that demonstrate understanding of emotional concepts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased emotional literacy, better conflict resolution skills, and improved emotional regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students role-play a scenario where they receive a gift they don't like and practice expressing gratitude and finding something positive about the gift.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Acting and role-playing are active learning strategies in which learners physically enact scenarios to deepen understanding, explore different perspectives, and practice social skills. This approach involves simulating real-world situations, allowing learners to apply their knowledge in a dynamic and engaging way. For younger learners, this can involve dramatizing narratives to build Background Knowledge and enhance comprehension. For older learners, small groups can act out stories for others to guess. Educators can create environments and activities that promote problem-solving, decision-making, and social-emotional learning through drama.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires space for movement, props (optional), and prepared scenarios or scripts. Instructor should facilitate discussion and reflection after each activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel uncomfortable performing. Requires careful facilitation to ensure inclusivity and prevent reinforcement of stereotypes. Effectiveness depends on the quality of the scenario and the level of engagement from participants.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for K–12 and adult learners in professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Strengthen comprehension, explore different perspectives, build empathy, develop social skills, enhance problem-solving abilities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners actively, promotes kinesthetic learning, supports social-emotional development, enhances comprehension through embodiment, allows for exploration of complex social situations in a safe environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios can be adapted to different skill levels, with varying degrees of complexity. Roles and scenarios can be customized to reflect learners' interests and cultural backgrounds. Learners can choose their own roles and adapt scripts to match their style.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Case Study
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Role Reversal

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation. Assess the depth of understanding demonstrated in their portrayals. Evaluate their ability to apply learning to new scenarios. Measure improvement in social skills and empathy through role-playing activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that acting out texts improves comprehension and retention (Education Week). Research demonstrates that embodiment enhances understanding and reduces distraction in math problems (Scientific Studies of Reading). Reader's Theater has been shown to improve fluency, comprehension, and motivation (Reading Rockets).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Action-oriented feedback focuses on providing students with specific steps they can take to improve their writing. Rather than just marking grammar mistakes, this approach aims to help students see how the actions they take can benefit their future writing. Conferring with students can facilitate this process, allowing teachers to suggest specific actions, such as varying sentence structure. Peer editing with specific suggestions can also move writers forward.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to engage in conferencing and provide actionable suggestions. Peer editing can supplement teacher feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and effort compared to simply marking errors. Students must be receptive to feedback and willing to take action.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students at all levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build a growth mindset in writing by helping students understand and implement specific steps to improve their writing skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to see writing as a process of continuous improvement. Helps them develop specific skills and strategies that can be applied to future writing assignments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor feedback to the individual needs of the student, suggesting actions that are relevant to their specific writing challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the specificity and actionability of feedback provided. Monitor student's ability to implement feedback and improve their writing skills over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Action-oriented feedback is key in building a growth mindset by showing students that specific actions can lead to tangible improvements in their writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Action planning involves developing explicit plans to consciously modify behaviors and improve future performance based on self-reflection. It includes comparing prior knowledge with new knowledge, selecting significant learnings, envisioning how to apply these learnings to future situations, and committing to specific, actionable steps to change behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, tools for documenting insights (journals, logs), and a commitment to enacting change.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the learner's willingness to follow through with the action plan. May require support to develop realistic and achievable goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those looking to improve specific skills or behaviors.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote behavioral change, support self-improvement, encourage application of learning in future contexts, and foster self-regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to self-improvement, connects reflection to actionable steps, and encourages learners to take ownership of their learning and development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Action plans can be tailored to individual goals, learning styles, and areas for improvement. Specificity in plans allows for personal agency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evidence of behavioral change, self-reported progress toward goals, and application of learning in new situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that action planning can lead to improved self-regulation, academic performance, and personal development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student reflects on a project and commits to improving their time management skills for the next assignment. A learner identifies a specific communication behavior to change based on feedback from peers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activating students’ background knowledge about a topic before reading involves asking questions or discussing related experiences to help students think about what they already know. This process connects new information to prior knowledge, increasing comprehension and interest in the new material. It also helps teachers understand any misconceptions or gaps in learner Background Knowledge, particularly when introducing new concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Preparation of relevant questions; time for discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if students lack sufficient background knowledge; requires careful planning

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly when introducing a new topic

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Connect new information to prior knowledge, increase comprehension, boost interest, and identify misconceptions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves comprehension; increases engagement; provides a foundation for new learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions and activities can be tailored to students' experiences and interests

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased participation in discussions, improved comprehension of new material

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Activating background knowledge helps students make connections to what they already know and understand the purpose for reading a text, ultimately leading to increased comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a text about a new place, the teacher asks, “Have you ever traveled to a new place? How did it compare to where you lived or what you thought it would be like?”

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves readers activating their existing knowledge and using it to comprehend what they are reading. Background knowledge consists of a person’s experiences with the world, including prior reading, and concepts for how written text works, such as word identification, print concepts, word meaning, and text organization. Cognitive scientists' schema theory supports this, stating that as people learn, they develop knowledge structures (schemas) connected to others. Good readers connect their background knowledge to new information in a text, activating relevant schemas as they read, which affects their understanding and reaction to the text. Schemas related to text organization are particularly important for comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires learners to reflect on their existing knowledge related to the text. Instructors need to facilitate discussions and provide prompts to help learners make connections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to activate relevant background knowledge if they lack experience with the topic. Misconceptions or inaccurate background knowledge can hinder comprehension if not addressed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with reading comprehension, including K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension by connecting existing knowledge to new information, activate relevant schemas, and understand text organization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comprehension by leveraging existing knowledge, facilitates understanding of text organization, and supports the activation of relevant schemas for better understanding and recall.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can focus on activating and using background knowledge relevant to their own experiences and interests. Instructors can provide prompts to help learners make connections between their existing knowledge and the text.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Analogies and prior knowledge activation
  • Demonstration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to make connections between their existing knowledge and the text. Assess comprehension through discussions, summaries, or written responses that demonstrate the use of background knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that connecting background knowledge to new information significantly improves reading comprehension. Schema theory supports the idea that activating relevant schemas enhances understanding and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a text about the American Revolution, learners discuss what they already know about the historical period, including key figures, events, and causes. As they read, they make connections between their existing knowledge and the new information in the text, enhancing their comprehension.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activating background knowledge involves prompting learners to recall and connect prior experiences, information, and understandings before engaging with new content. This can be achieved through questions, discussions, or brief activities that encourage learners to think about what they already know about the topic. Activating prior knowledge helps learners make connections between new information and their existing mental models, enhancing comprehension and retention. This strategy is particularly effective before reading a text or starting a new unit of study.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Well-crafted questions or activities that prompt learners to recall and connect to their prior knowledge. Teachers need to be prepared to facilitate discussions and validate learners' contributions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful planning to ensure that prompts are relevant and accessible to all learners. Some learners may feel uncomfortable sharing personal experiences or may have limited prior knowledge on the topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially beneficial for learners with diverse backgrounds and experiences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, foster connections between new and existing knowledge, increase engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes new content more accessible, supports deeper understanding, increases learner motivation and engagement, and supports long-term retention of information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can differentiate prompts and activities based on learners' individual backgrounds and experiences. Learners can also choose to share personal stories or examples related to the topic.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Analogies and prior knowledge activation
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of learner engagement in discussions, the depth of connections they make between new and existing knowledge, and their ability to apply prior knowledge to solve problems or answer questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that activating background knowledge improves comprehension, retention, and engagement. By connecting new content to what learners already know, educators can create more meaningful and effective learning experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a narrative text, a teacher might ask, "Have you ever felt like you were afraid to do something new?" or "Have you ever traveled to a new place? How did it compare to where you lived or what you thought it would be like?"

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activating students' prior knowledge involves prompting learners to recall and share what they already know about a topic before introducing new information. This process helps learners make connections between existing knowledge and new concepts, increasing engagement and comprehension. Strategies include brainstorming, listing everything they know about a topic, and creating concept maps.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured prompts, such as open-ended questions or graphic organizers. Instructor must facilitate discussion and address any misconceptions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time to uncover and address misconceptions. Effectiveness depends on learners' ability to connect new information to their prior knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for adult learners with diverse backgrounds.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Connect new information to existing knowledge, increase engagement, and identify misconceptions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation by connecting learning to real-world experiences, supports culturally responsive teaching, and ensures representation of all learners in the curriculum.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with prompts tailored to learners' backgrounds. Flexible formats allow for verbal, written, or visual responses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student responses to identify gaps in knowledge. Compare initial understanding with post-instruction understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows connecting new content with prior knowledge improves comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Actively Listen to What Students Say
Description
docs.text: Give your full attention and listen to both a student’s words and tone of voice. State in your own words what you think you’ve heard and then confirm by asking, “Is that what you’re telling me?” That simple question gives students an opening to correct any misunderstanding and shows respect for their feelings and perspective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Active listening skills, a willingness to understand student perspectives

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort, may be challenging with students who struggle to express themselves

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, counselors, mentors, parents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, build trust, enhance understanding, show respect for student perspectives

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters better dialogue, reduces misunderstandings, creates a more supportive environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use active listening in one-on-one conversations, small group discussions, and whole-class settings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor communication patterns, observe interactions, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances student-teacher relationships, promotes a more inclusive and understanding environment, improves conflict resolution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After a student shares their thoughts, summarize what you heard and ask if you understood correctly: 'So, what you're saying is... Is that right?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves creating activities that allow students to reflect on their own learning. Encourage students to reflect on their learning by engaging in activities that promote metacognition. This could involve writing summaries using prompts, creating concept maps or videos, or writing a math autobiography.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Activities that promote metacognition, a way for students to record their reflections, and a willingness to allow students to choose the activities that they find most engaging.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to create and facilitate activities that promote metacognition.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote metacognition, foster self-awareness, encourage ownership of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to reflect on their own learning and take ownership of their learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can create a variety of activities that promote metacognition. Students can choose the activities that they find most engaging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Practice
  • Creating Visual Representations

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student self-awareness, increased student ownership of learning, and deeper understanding of math concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of activities for student self-reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher asks students to write a summary of a math concept in their own words. The teacher provides prompts to guide the students' thinking.

docs.title: Address Biases in the Use of Language and Symbols
Description
docs.text: Honoring a wide variety of forms of language ensures that learning materials and discussions are free from bias and stereotypes. This includes avoiding language that reinforces harmful stereotypes. It also involves using inclusive language that respects diverse identities and backgrounds. This strategy promotes equity and creates a welcoming learning environment for all learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful analysis of the language used in learning materials. Instructors need to be trained in culturally responsive teaching strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources. Some learners may be resistant to challenging their own biases and stereotypes. It's essential to create a safe and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those from marginalized groups or those studying social justice issues; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote equity, reduce bias, foster cultural awareness, support inclusive learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports equity by reducing bias and stereotypes, fosters cultural awareness by exposing learners to diverse perspectives, and supports inclusive learning by creating a welcoming environment for all learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use inclusive language that respects diverse identities and backgrounds. Avoid language that reinforces harmful stereotypes. Encourage learners to challenge bias and stereotypes in learning materials and discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of bias and stereotypes through discussions or written assignments. Track improvements in cultural awareness and sensitivity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that addressing bias and stereotypes can promote equity, foster cultural awareness, and support inclusive learning. Studies show that inclusive learning environments can improve academic outcomes for all learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using inclusive language that respects diverse identities and backgrounds. Avoiding language that reinforces harmful stereotypes. Encouraging learners to challenge bias and stereotypes in learning materials and discussions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators should avoid assumptions about learners' digital literacy and provide explicit instruction on fundamental digital skills. This includes conducting internet searches, using different search engines, refining search terms, and understanding common technology jargon. Address misconceptions by providing basic training and clarifying terminology.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Knowledge of common digital tools and terminology, instructional materials tailored to varying skill levels

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and resources for instruction. Some learners may be resistant to admitting lack of digital skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners with limited digital experience, those unfamiliar with current technology or jargon

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' basic digital skills, address misconceptions, enhance confidence in using technology

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and frustration related to technology, improves ability to navigate online resources, enhances learning outcomes

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer introductory workshops on digital basics, provide one-on-one support for learners struggling with technology, create resources that explain common technology jargon

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Administer pre- and post-tests to measure digital literacy. Observe learners' ability to use digital tools in class.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased confidence in using technology, improved ability to access and use online resources, enhanced learning outcomes

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognize that students may not share the ability to automatically read, interpret, and reply to textual information at the same level as educators. Avoid assuming that all students can fluently read, process, and respond to written communications. Remote instruction may force students to read and process text at an unprecedented level, which can overwhelm them. Keep written communication as clear and concise as possible, provide video directions to accompany text, offer face-to-face meetings, limit email communication, decrease quantity and increase quality, and proofread all written information to remove teacher jargon and ensure student-friendly language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of student literacy levels, commitment to clear and accessible communication, access to multimedia tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires extra effort and planning, may be challenging with limited resources or time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student comprehension, reduce frustration and overwhelm, improve communication effectiveness, promote equitable access to information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports diverse literacy levels, reduces cognitive load, improves student engagement, promotes clear and effective communication

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by using varied formats (written, verbal, visual), simplified language, and tailored support for individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student comprehension through feedback, quizzes, and class participation; assess clarity of communication through student feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes better understanding and engagement, reduces communication barriers, and enhances student success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Provide short, clear instructions, use visual aids, offer verbal explanations, and check for understanding regularly.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Be aware of potential mother tongue interference. Position yourself close to students who have difficulty following instructions and use their names to increase engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of learners' language backgrounds.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Multilingual learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide targeted support to learners facing language-related challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides personalized support and increases engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use different scaffolding techniques based on learners' language proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow instructions with targeted support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and engagement for multilingual learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher provides additional explanations and examples to a learner whose first language has a different sentence structure.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Addressing speed of processing involves identifying students' strengths and challenges related to processing speed (the pace at which one takes in information, makes sense of it, and begins to respond) and using aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning. This can include providing graphic organizers or guided notes during lectures, repeating key points multiple times and in different ways, providing manipulatives to make complex concepts concrete, and allowing ample think-time and time for re-reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to be aware of students' strengths and challenges related to processing speed, willingness to implement aligned strategies, and provide appropriate scaffolds and supports.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Identifying students' strengths and challenges related to processing speed can be time-consuming. Some students may be resistant to using strategies designed to support processing speed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who have challenges with processing speed, students who may be ahead of their peers in processing information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support students who struggle with processing speed, leverage students' strengths, improve learning outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students who struggle with processing speed to access information more easily, provides opportunities for students to leverage their strengths in other contexts, supports learning in all aspects of school, including processing lectures, formulating responses, and reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be tailored to individual student needs and strengths. For example, some students may benefit more from graphic organizers, while others may prefer manipulatives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student work samples demonstrating the use of aligned strategies, student reflections on the effectiveness of the strategies used, educator reflections on the impact of the strategies on student learning

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that addressing speed of processing can improve learning outcomes for students who struggle with processing speed. Sheppard & Vernon (2008) conducted a review of 50 years of research of processing speed showing the relation to intelligence. Fry & Hale (1996) showed evidence that processing speed, working memory, and fluid intelligence develop over time. Kail & Salthouse (1994) stated that processing speed is a mental capacity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing a student with a graphic organizer during a lecture to help them pull out the important points. Repeating the key points for students several times and in several different ways. Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete. Allowing plenty of think-time and time for re-reading.

docs.title: Address Stereotypical Beliefs About Parents and Poverty
Description
docs.text: Teachers and educators should challenge and avoid stereotypical beliefs about parents and families living in poverty. Recognizing that all parents want to be involved in their children's education, regardless of socioeconomic status, is critical. Empathy and kindness should be at the forefront of communication to connect with parents at their level and engage them in supporting their children’s education.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment to self-reflection and ongoing learning. Willingness to challenge personal beliefs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to confront personal biases. Requires sustained effort and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, educators, and school staff

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote positive relationships, increase parent involvement, reduce bias

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improved understanding of diverse family circumstances, enhanced communication, more equitable practices

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailored training and reflection activities to address individual biases and promote empathy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor changes in attitudes and behaviors. Gather feedback from parents and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Challenging stereotypes can lead to more equitable and supportive relationships between schools and families.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognize and address adult learners' fears related to technology, such as data loss, privacy concerns, or damaging equipment. Offer clear, reassuring guidance and support. Design user-friendly interfaces and provide explicit instructions to reduce anxiety and promote a positive user experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Empathy, clear communication, user-friendly design, robust technical support

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and resources for individual support, addressing deep-seated fears can be challenging

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners with anxiety or fear related to technology.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce technology-related anxiety, promote confidence in using technology, foster a positive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces barriers to participation, fosters a supportive learning environment, increases engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide clear and simple instructions, offer one-on-one technical support, provide a safe and non-judgmental environment for asking questions

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Solicit feedback on anxiety levels and support resources, observe learner participation and engagement, track usage of technical support

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced anxiety related to technology, increased confidence in using technology, improved learning outcomes

docs.title: Addressing Biases in the Use of Language and Symbols
Description
docs.text: Actively working to identify and eliminate biases in language and symbols to promote inclusivity. This involves using neutral language, avoiding stereotypes, and representing diverse perspectives. This approach creates a welcoming and respectful learning environment for all learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Neutral language, diverse perspectives, resources for addressing bias, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing vigilance and reflection to identify and address biases. Some learners may be resistant to challenging their own biases.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those from marginalized or underrepresented groups

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote inclusivity, reduce bias, foster respect, create a welcoming learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces bias and stereotypes. Fosters respect and inclusivity. Creates a welcoming learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use neutral language, avoid stereotypes, and represent diverse perspectives. Encourage learners to challenge and question biased content. Provide resources and support for addressing bias.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognizing and addressing implicit biases involves moving away from the idea that being biased is inherently negative and acknowledging that everyone possesses biases. This process necessitates bringing biases into the open for examination in a non-judgmental manner. Key strategies include personal self-awareness through techniques like substitution (considering if feelings or responses would be the same if the person were different) and analyzing informal networks to identify potential homogeneity. Additional measures encompass leadership trials, building blended teams to increase awareness of diverse perspectives, and utilizing panel interviews to reduce bias in recruitment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Teachers use strategies to support students who experience stereotype threat, helping them thrive academically and socially. This involves understanding the research behind stereotype threat and implementing evidence-based strategies to overcome it.

Stereotype threat is the concern that one will be seen through a negative, stereotyped lens for a group one belongs to (Aronson & Steele, 2005) — for example, women regarding mathematics performance. Its measurable effect on test performance is triggered by two specific conditions occurring together: the test is explicitly framed as high-stakes and as measuring intelligence or ability, and test-takers are reminded of their stereotyped identity beforehand (even something as minor as a demographic question before the test). The underlying mechanism is not a lack of genuine competence or effort — even individuals who believe themselves competent show the effect, because actively suppressing the negative stereotype consumes working memory capacity that would otherwise support the task itself. The effect is strongest, counterintuitively, for those who most want to do well, and its practical consequence is that a stereotyped group's standardized test scores can substantially underestimate their real competence specifically under high-stakes conditions — the same individuals often perform much closer to their actual ability on a low-stakes version of the same task. This mechanism is why strategies here should target the two triggering conditions directly (unnecessary high-stakes framing, unnecessary identity-reminder cues) rather than only offering general encouragement.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: Break content into smaller time intervals if learners cannot stay on task. Children can concentrate on one task for two to five minutes per year old. Using timers, have learners show their work after a short period. Consider calling the child to the desk for checks. This provides physical movement and monitors progress.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher sets a timer for 15-minute work intervals followed by brief breaks for students who struggle to stay focused. A parent uses a timer during homework sessions, checking in with the child every 10 minutes to monitor progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Give learners a broad question or problem that is likely to result in lots of different ideas, such as “What were the impacts of the Great Depression?” or “What literary works should every person read?” Have learners generate responses by writing ideas on post-it notes (one idea per note) and placing them in no particular arrangement on a wall, whiteboard, or chart paper. Once lots of ideas have been generated, have learners begin grouping them into similar categories, then label the categories and discuss why the ideas fit within them, how the categories relate to one another, and so on. Some teachers have learners do much of this exercise—recording their ideas and arranging them into categories—without talking at first. In other variations, participants are asked to re-combine the ideas into new, different categories after the first round of organization occurs. Often, this activity serves as a good pre-writing exercise, after which learners will write some kind of analysis or position paper.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires post-it notes, markers, a wall, whiteboard, or chart paper, and clear instructions for learners. A broad question or problem to be addressed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires careful facilitation to ensure all learners are engaged and on task, may be challenging for learners who struggle with generating ideas or categorizing information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for brainstorming and problem-solving activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Generate ideas, identify patterns and relationships, promote collaboration and discussion, enhance critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes collaboration and discussion, enhances critical thinking skills, provides a visual representation of ideas, supports diverse learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions and problems can be tailored to learners' interests and backgrounds. Learners can choose the categories they want to create.

docs.text: This strategy involves repeating empowering statements to oneself during times of stress. Examples include 'I can only do my best' or 'I know I can do this.' Repeating affirmations helps build self-confidence and resilience, promoting a positive mindset during challenges.

docs.title: AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity
Description
docs.text: Utilizing an AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity involves taking a more in-depth look into the data used to build algorithms and the way products are used by and for Black and Brown students in schools. The toolkit provides actions that can be taken at every stage of product design and development to mitigate racial bias in the design and development of products.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity, a commitment to racial equity, and the ability to implement the recommended actions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing commitment and effort to address racial bias. May be challenging to implement all of the recommended actions. May not be effective if users are not committed to racial equity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Edtech companies, product developers, and educational institutions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Mitigate racial bias in AI-powered edtech products, ensure equitable outcomes for Black and Brown students, and promote culturally responsive design and development

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical guidance for identifying and addressing racial bias in AI-powered edtech products, promotes culturally responsive design and development, and helps ensure equitable outcomes for Black and Brown students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The toolkit can be adapted to the specific needs and context of different edtech products and organizations. Users can select the actions that are most relevant to their work.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Scenario
  • Question Formulation
  • Just-in-Time Information

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Air writing involves writing letters or words in the air while simultaneously visualizing the shape of the letters and saying their names. This multisensory technique creates a motor image and enhances memory encoding through visual and auditory reinforcement. Air writing can be used to practice letter forms, spelling words, and other written content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for physical movement, learning material to be practiced, and understanding of the connection between movement and recall

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners with physical limitations, requires careful coordination of visual, auditory, and kinesthetic senses, may be disruptive in some classroom settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, particularly those who struggle with handwriting or spelling

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve letter formation, enhance spelling skills, strengthen memory encoding, cater to visual and kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines visual, auditory, and kinesthetic senses, enhances memory encoding, improves letter formation and spelling skills, caters to visual and kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adapt the size and speed of their air writing to suit their individual needs. They can also use different colors or visualize the letters in different fonts to enhance memorability.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to form letters and spell words correctly after practicing air writing, assess their engagement and participation, evaluate performance on spelling tests and handwriting assessments

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Air writing has been shown to improve letter formation, enhance spelling skills, and strengthen memory encoding. It engages multiple senses and caters to visual and kinesthetic learning styles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student practices writing the letter "o" in the air while visualizing its shape and saying its name aloud. A student practices spelling the word "cat" by writing each letter in the air while visualizing the word and saying each letter aloud.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Allowing plenty of think-time and time for re-reading for students who might need more time to process. This strategy involves providing extended pauses for reflection and multiple opportunities to review content.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: • Support processing speed, improve comprehension, and promote thoughtful reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces time pressure, allows for deeper processing, promotes self-regulation, and supports individual learning pace

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: Alphabet books involve students creating entries for each letter of the alphabet related to a specific topic, such as mathematics vocabulary. This strategy introduces students to a delightful genre while helping them develop essential vocabulary for mathematical thinking. The format invites the use of words, graphic representations, and symbols to communicate mathematical ideas.

docs.text: • Materials for creating pages (paper, art supplies), access to textbooks, thesauruses, and math dictionaries, and a way to compile the book.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to resources and time for students to research and create their entries. May be challenging for learners with limited vocabulary.

docs.text: • Suitable for upper elementary and middle school levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop vocabulary, introduce a genre, provide experience in the writing process, and promote mathematical communication.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Introduces a genre, develops vocabulary, allows for experience in the writing process, and invites meaningful communication.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fifth-grade teacher assigned students letters of the alphabet and sent them on a search for new and complex words in their math textbook, notes, thesaurus, and mathematics dictionary. Students used each word in a sentence, drew a representation, or wrote a real-world connection.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Alphaboxes is a strategy that encourages collaborative interaction with text by using a grid with boxes labeled with letters of the alphabet. Students generate words, questions, concepts, or ideas related to the text and write them under the corresponding letter in each box. It can be used as a pre-reading or post-reading activity to stimulate thinking and discussion about key ideas in the text. This strategy moves students beyond simple recall of factual information to higher-level cognitive processes such as generating questions, making connections, providing explanations, identifying unfamiliar words, and presenting different points of view. Students work in pairs or small groups, sharing cognitive responsibility and externalizing their thoughts as they work through the task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to texts, Alphaboxes grid (paper or digital), and structured activity guidelines. Requires facilitation to model the process and guide initial interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Requires explicit instruction and modeling. May not be suitable for students who struggle with collaboration or have limited vocabulary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners, especially useful for encouraging collaborative interaction with text and facilitating higher-level cognitive processes.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate critical thinking, collaborative interaction with text, enhance recall, facilitate higher-level cognitive processes, and distribute cognitive responsibility among group members.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active engagement with text, enhances comprehension through collaborative discussion, promotes higher-level cognitive processes, and distributes cognitive load among group members.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various text types and content areas. Can be modified to require different numbers of boxes to be filled in. Can be used with different groupings (pairs, small groups, whole class).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the quality and depth of student responses in the Alphaboxes grid. Evaluate the level of cognitive processing demonstrated in the responses. Assess the effectiveness of group collaboration through observation and participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies indicate that generating questions, making connections, providing explanations, identifying and discussing unfamiliar vocabulary words, and presenting alternative perspectives are all higher-level cognitive processes that increase learning (Block & Johnson, 2002; Duke & Pearson, 2002; Pressley, 2006).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Analogies are comparisons of two things that are alike in some way, used as advance organizers to help students realize that a new topic relates to something familiar. By linking new information to prior knowledge, analogies facilitate understanding and retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear understanding of the target concept and a relevant, familiar analogy.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Analogies must be carefully chosen to ensure they accurately represent the target concept and do not introduce misconceptions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for introducing complex or abstract topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Connect new information to existing knowledge, facilitate understanding of complex concepts, and improve retention.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding by relating new information to familiar concepts, making abstract ideas more concrete, and improving engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Analogies can be tailored to the specific prior knowledge of students and the complexity of the topic.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Analysis of Classroom Dynamics Through Shadowing
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves a teacher or coach shadowing students to analyze classroom dynamics and student experiences. Key aspects include observing how long students sit passively, noting opportunities for active participation, and assessing the balance between lecture and collaborative activities. The goal is to identify areas where instruction can be improved to increase student engagement and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for shadowing, a structured observation protocol, and a willingness to reflect on and adapt teaching practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for observer bias, may not capture the full complexity of the classroom environment, and requires a commitment to change.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, coaches, and administrators looking to improve classroom dynamics and student engagement.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify areas where instruction can be improved, increase student engagement, and improve the overall classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides direct insights into student experiences, helps identify areas for improvement, and promotes reflective teaching practices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Shadowing can focus on specific students or classroom activities, allowing for tailored observations and feedback.
