docs.text: • Improved classroom dynamics, increased student engagement, and enhanced learning experiences for all students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ask students to identify patterns or themes in their self-talk. For example, at 10:00 each day, right before we dive into science, Juanita might notice that she begins to feel lousy. She dreads coming back from PE because she knows it will be time to start the science lab that she doesn’t understand. Her voice says things like, “Hopefully my partner, Berta, understands this stuff because I guess I can just copy from her.” Identifying these patterns will be the first step towards combatting negative self-talk.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Recorded self-talk messages, analytical skills, time for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be honest and open about their thoughts and feelings. May be challenging to identify subtle patterns.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify patterns and themes in self-talk.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners recognize recurring thoughts and feelings related to specific situations or activities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing structured questions or prompts to guide the analysis.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review analysis of self-talk messages for identified patterns and themes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Greater understanding of the triggers and contexts for negative self-talk (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before launching a project, teachers should analyze it through the lens of English Language Learners (ELLs) by considering: What language skills will students need? What vocabulary instruction might they need? What speaking and listening skills should we scaffold? What functions of the language must be considered? This type of analysis should occur before the project launches.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of language acquisition and the needs of ELLs, along with detailed project planning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires extra time and effort in project design and may require additional resources for language support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers designing PBL projects for ELL students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify language-related challenges and plan supportive instruction for ELL students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to proactively address the language needs of ELLs, promoting greater equity and access to learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailoring the analysis to specific project tasks and considering the individual language levels of learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduced language-related barriers, increased participation of ELLs, and improved language skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps plan supportive instruction for ELL students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners play Taboo to practice choosing keywords, and the instructor identifies the strategies of finding synonyms and giving precise descriptions. The instructor guides reflection on the keyword search strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Taboo game, sample keyword lists for commonly searched topics

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The game may not transfer well to other contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Any grade level

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice choosing effective keywords

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Opportunity to practice and analyze keyword effectiveness. Provides instructor feedback on strategies. Supports metacognitive reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to any discipline or subject matter.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Students' keyword choices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • By studying their own errors learners can see when they have used incorrect strategies or procedures, which is particularly important in strengthening numeracy and supporting English language learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Analyzing project-based learning (PBL) projects through the lens of English Language Learners (ELLs) involves identifying the language skills, vocabulary instruction, speaking and listening scaffolds, and language functions needed for students to succeed. This includes determining the skills students will need in terms of language, planning vocabulary instruction, scaffolding speaking and listening skills, and considering the functions of the language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Thorough analysis of project tasks, understanding of ELL students' language levels, and planning for targeted language support strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires additional time and effort in project design, and might necessitate ongoing adjustments based on student progress and feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and curriculum designers aiming to support English Language Learners (ELLs) in project-based learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To identify and address the specific language needs of English Language Learners within the context of project-based learning activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to ensure that PBL activities are accessible and supportive for ELLs, enhancing their language acquisition and content understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different project types and language proficiency levels, allowing educators to tailor support based on individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Pre-Class Video/Lecture
  • In-Class Activities
  • Formative Assessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved ELL student participation, enhanced language skills demonstrated in project outputs, and positive feedback from students and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that supporting ELLs through PBL can enhance their language skills, content knowledge, and overall engagement in learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Analyzing a genetics and traits project to identify the need for students to justify answers and providing sentence starters for justification.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students identify patterns or themes in their self-talk, such as recurring thoughts or feelings related to specific situations or times of day. This analysis helps students understand the triggers and underlying beliefs that drive their negative self-talk.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Students' self-talk logs or journals. Time for reflection and analysis. A supportive environment for sharing insights and discoveries.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may find it challenging to identify patterns and themes on their own. Some students may be resistant to analyzing their thoughts and feelings. The accuracy of the analysis depends on students' honesty and self-awareness.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students who are developing self-awareness and emotional intelligence.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To help students recognize recurring patterns and themes in their self-talk.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-awareness by identifying triggers and underlying beliefs. Supports emotional regulation by understanding the roots of negative thoughts. Promotes critical thinking by analyzing patterns and themes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and learning styles. Students can focus on specific situations or emotions that are relevant to their lives. Educators can provide different types of prompts and questions to guide the analysis.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' analyses for accuracy and depth of insight. Assess students' ability to articulate patterns and themes in their self-talk. Observe students' engagement and participation in discussions about self-talk.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that self-analysis can improve self-regulation and self-efficacy. By analyzing their self-talk, students can gain insights into the drivers of their behavior and develop strategies to manage it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Juanita notices that she begins to feel lousy right before science class because she dreads the science lab. Students identify patterns in their self-talk related to academic performance, social interactions, or extracurricular activities. Students discuss the triggers and underlying beliefs that drive their negative self-talk in a supportive group setting.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Video replay analysis involves reviewing short video clips, replays of key segments, or recordings of one's performance to enhance metacognition, improve long-term memory, and cultivate a learner mindset. By pausing, reviewing, interacting with, and discussing videos showing learning in action, learners can engage in deeper reflection, reasoning, and cognitive flexibility.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to video recording equipment, playback devices, and video analysis software. Facilitators who can guide the analysis and provide constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and resources for recording and reviewing videos. Learners may feel self-conscious about being recorded. Effective facilitation is needed to ensure productive analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in various educational levels, particularly those in professional training, skills development, or academic programs where performance can be recorded and reviewed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance metacognition, improve long-term memory, foster a learner mindset, deepen reflection, reasoning, and cognitive flexibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports deeper reflection, enhances reasoning and cognitive flexibility, and improves long-term memory. Learners can identify areas for improvement and adjust their strategies based on visual evidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to individual learning goals and performance areas. Learners can focus on specific aspects of their performance or key segments of a lesson.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Demonstration
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved self-awareness and ability to identify areas for improvement, enhanced performance based on video analysis, increased metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances skill development, improves self-reflection, and fosters a growth mindset. Effective for professional training, sports coaching, and academic learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Analyzing video replays of surgical procedures to improve technique, reviewing recorded classroom discussions to enhance teaching strategies, and examining personal performance in athletic training to refine skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Spelling by explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping requires the learner to match the letters/letter combinations in a word to the speech sounds they represent using a grid; each box of the grid represents a phoneme. This helps fix phoneme-grapheme correspondences in children’s minds and supports spelling, reading, and writing development.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Phoneme-grapheme grids, word lists, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction, may not be effective for learners with severe phonological deficits

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • First-grade students, second- and third-grade students who missed the fundamentals in the earlier grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling skills, enhance reading fluency, develop phoneme-grapheme awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens the connection between sounds and letters, helps learners visualize the sound structure of words, supports reading and writing development

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction. Focus on specific phonemes or graphemes that the learner is struggling with.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in mapping phonemes to graphemes. Monitor progress in spelling and reading skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping supports spelling, reading, and writing development by helping fix phoneme-grapheme correspondences in children’s minds.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Applicable reflection involves guiding students to consider how their past performance will influence their future work. It reminds students that they’re going to have to use at least some of these skills again, so there’s no sense in making the same mistakes. Reflection has a real and immediate purpose: You know where this course is going, so how are you going to improve the quality of your own journey?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Transparency about future tasks and assignments, documentation of reflections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a clear understanding of how the curriculum builds on itself.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who struggle to see the relevance of their learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve future performance, connect past learning to future tasks, promote skill development

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for assessing how past performance will influence future work, encourages continuous improvement. Digital tools can make reflections easy to access for individuals.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can be transparent about future tasks and assignments, and make reflections accessible. Students can store their reflections wherever that work is happening.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in student work over time, ability to articulate connections between past and future tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that connecting learning to future tasks improves student motivation and performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher asks students to reflect on their writing process by answering questions such as, 'What did you learn from your last writing assignment?' and 'How will you apply that knowledge to your next assignment?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Applied science testing involves using scientific principles to evaluate real-world materials and products. Learners test the solubility of different packing materials and compare the quality and price of different kinds of plastic kitchen wrap. These activities improve evaluative skills and understanding of the application of science in daily life.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to various materials and products. Evaluation criteria need to be well-defined.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying science and technology

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply scientific principles to real-world scenarios, test the solubility of materials, compare product quality and price

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Demonstrates relevance of science in daily life. Enhances evaluative and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.text: • Accuracy in testing solubility, correct comparison of product quality and price, logical justifications of evaluations

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved evaluative skills, enhanced understanding of the application of science.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Packing Materials (NYSED): Learners test the solubility of different items used in packing. Plastic Wrapped (KDE): Learners compare the quality and price of different kinds of plastic kitchen wrap.

docs.title: Apply Student-Centered Strategies to Support Learning Differences
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using a data-driven, student-centered plan to implement specific instructional strategies that address a selected student's learning differences (including strengths and challenges).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Data on student learning differences (strengths and challenges), a student-centered plan, and specific instructional strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful data collection, analysis, and the development of a tailored instructional plan.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with identified learning differences, including strengths and challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support students with learning differences by leveraging their strengths and addressing their challenges through targeted instructional strategies.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators personalize instruction to meet the specific needs of students, leveraging their strengths to support their learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to the individual student's data, including strengths, challenges, and learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• individual reflection
  • practice
  • provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Use pre- and post-assessments to measure student progress and compare results. Observe students' active engagement in learning tasks and note improvements in academic skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research validates the effectiveness of student-centered strategies for improving learning outcomes for students with diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Applying Student-Centered Strategies to Support Learning Differences
Description
docs.text: Educators use data-driven, student-centered plans to implement strategies that support individual learning differences, including both strengths and challenges. This involves understanding a student’s specific needs based on various data points, such as performance on different types of assessments (e.g., free-response vs. multiple-choice), reading comprehension in different contexts (e.g., guided reading vs. independent reading), and engagement in interest-based programs. Strategies are then tailored to leverage strengths and address challenges, such as providing accommodations for working memory limitations or teaching self-monitoring techniques for independent reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Student data (assessment results, work samples, observations). Collaborative planning with educators, specialists, and parents. Access to resources and materials to implement targeted strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time and effort to collect and analyze student data. May require additional training for educators to effectively implement student-centered strategies. Success depends on accurate identification of student strengths and challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, special education teachers, instructional coaches, and other educational professionals working to support students with diverse learning needs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Implement targeted strategies to support individual learning differences, leverage student strengths, address academic challenges, foster student-centered learning environments

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Personalizes learning by addressing individual student needs. Leverages student strengths to foster motivation and engagement. Provides targeted support to address specific challenges. Promotes data-driven decision-making in instructional planning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to each student's unique strengths and challenges. Accommodations and modifications are adjusted based on ongoing data collection and student feedback. Learning activities are designed to align with student interests and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student work samples showing improved performance after strategy implementation. Observations of student engagement and motivation. Data from formative and summative assessments demonstrating progress toward learning goals. Student self-reflections on their learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Implementing data-driven, student-centered strategies has been shown to improve academic outcomes and increase student engagement. Research supports the effectiveness of leveraging student strengths and providing targeted support to address learning differences.

docs.title: Art and Writing Skill Development Stages
Description
docs.text: Drawing and writing skills in young children develop through distinct stages, progressing from random scribbling to letter and word practice. These stages include: 1) Random Scribbling (15 months to 2½ years), where children discover the lines and scribbles they create through movement; 2) Controlled Scribbling (2 years to 3 years), where scribbles become more controlled with repeated marks; 3) Lines and Patterns (2½ years to 3½ years), where children understand that writing is made up of lines, curves, and patterns; 4) Pictures of Objects or People (3 years to 5 years), where children begin to draw recognizable images with increasing detail; and 5) Letter and Word Practice (3 to 5 years), where children begin to experiment with letters, particularly those in their own names, and understand that text and print have meaning. Encouraging art and writing skills involves providing a variety of art materials, noticing the process rather than just the product, helping children express strong feelings through art, and displaying their work to show its value.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of art materials (crayons, markers, paint, play-dough, etc.), paper, and a supportive environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires parents/educators to focus on the process rather than the product, which may be challenging for some. Timetables are approximate, and children may master skills faster or slower than indicated.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Very young children (15 months to 5 years)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the developmental stages of drawing and writing, encourage creativity and self-expression, develop problem-solving skills, and learn the power and meaning of words.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for understanding the developmental progression of drawing and writing skills. Offers practical strategies for encouraging creativity and self-expression. Helps children develop problem-solving skills and understand the power and meaning of words.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to individual developmental pace. Activities and materials can be adjusted to suit the child's interests and sensory preferences. Emphasis is placed on the process of creating, rather than the product, allowing for individual expression and exploration.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's drawings and writing to identify the stage of development. Assess the child's creativity, self-expression, and problem-solving skills. Track the child's understanding of the power and meaning of words.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creative activities help children learn how to solve problems, come up with their own answers, discover the cause-and-effect of their actions, and feel confident about the choices they make. Art experiences help children develop independence within limits, and gives them the opportunity to represent their ideas on paper or in other formats. Most important, creative expression lets children tap into the magic of their own imaginations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creative activities such as arts and crafts can help learners explore their creativity and learn something new. Engaging in these activities can support emotional expression, enhance fine motor skills, and provide a break from traditional academic tasks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for arts and crafts

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources and preparation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for younger learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore creativity, enhance fine motor skills, promote emotional expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports creativity and emotional expression, enhances fine motor skills, provides a break from traditional academic tasks

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted to suit individual interests and skill levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of learner engagement and creativity

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Arts and crafts activities can enhance creativity, fine motor skills, and emotional expression.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrate arts activities like fiction writing, dance, drama, graphic design, music, drawing, painting, or ceramics into all subjects to enhance learning and engagement. This approach helps learners find their talents and interests, providing creative outlets for expression and deeper understanding. Arts integration makes learning more engaging and relevant, fostering creativity and critical thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be knowledgeable about different art forms and techniques. Need space and materials for arts activities. Curriculum integration is necessary to connect arts activities to learning objectives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional training for instructors. May be challenging to assess learning outcomes in some art forms. Some learners may be hesitant to participate if they do not consider themselves artistic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for elementary and high school students, as well as adult learners in arts-based programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner engagement and understanding, foster creativity and critical thinking, help learners discover their talents and interests, provide creative outlets for expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides creative outlets for expression, enhances learner engagement and understanding, and fosters creativity and critical thinking. Arts integration helps learners find their talents and interests and make learning more relevant.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of arts activities to cater to different interests and skill levels. Provide support and guidance to help learners develop their artistic skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate learner creativity and self-expression in their art projects. Assess their ability to apply concepts learned in other subjects through arts activities. Gather feedback from learners about their experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that arts integration enhances learner engagement, creativity, and critical thinking. Arts activities provide creative outlets for expression and make learning more relevant.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students write a play based on a historical event, create a dance to explain a scientific concept, or design a graphic to illustrate a mathematical equation. A group of adult learners creates ceramic pieces to represent their cultural heritage, enhancing their understanding of history and identity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Don’t assume you know how a student is feeling. Be attentive to nonverbal cues and ask them directly. When you ask open-ended questions, students can share what’s on their minds without feeling like you’ve already sized up the situation. Offer options by saying, “I noticed you had your head down in class today. Are you frustrated, angry, or nervous about something?”

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Effective communication skills, a safe and supportive environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort, may be challenging with students who are hesitant to share

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, counselors, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student-teacher communication, foster trust, provide opportunities for self-expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to share their thoughts and feelings, builds rapport, provides valuable insights into student experiences

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust questions based on individual student needs and circumstances

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Response

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student responses, monitor changes in communication patterns, gather student feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances student-teacher relationships, promotes emotional well-being, and improves classroom climate.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Schools can include parents by regularly asking for feedback regarding issues of concern. Teachers can elicit questions from parents about potential discussion topics before Back-to-School Night, making them feel valued and increasing interest. This helps create a culture of common understanding and empowers parents to be directly involved with their child’s specific academic journey.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Communication channels to solicit feedback, willingness to listen and respond to parent concerns

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to analyze and respond to feedback, may be difficult to address all concerns

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, educators, and parents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, increase parent involvement, build trust

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters a sense of partnership, provides valuable feedback, empowers parents

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to address specific concerns and interests of individual parents.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency of feedback, gather data on parent satisfaction

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Soliciting and responding to parent feedback can build trust and increase parent involvement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This approach involves asking and answering four key questions to provide quality feedback: What can the student do? What can't the student do? How does the student's work compare with that of others? How can the student do better? Providing answers to these questions helps the learner understand where they stand in regards to their work and guides them towards improvement. These four questions are also helpful when providing feedback to parents.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful observation and assessment of learner performance

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming, requires thorough knowledge of the learner's strengths and weaknesses

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a comprehensive assessment of learner performance, guide improvement, inform instruction, communicate progress to parents

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear framework for feedback, promotes self-reflection, facilitates communication

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The questions can be tailored to the individual learner and their specific learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance. Track learner progress. Analyze the effectiveness of the feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective teaching and learning occurs when teachers have answers for these questions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses the four questions during a parent-teacher conference to discuss a student's progress in reading. A coach uses the four questions to provide feedback to an athlete on their performance during a game.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before you hit “share,” what questions should you ask? You might share On the Media’s 11 guidelines. Listen to the whole show for more detail, and find additional chapters in the group’s clear and helpful “Breaking News Consumer’s Handbook”. Or consult the Newseum’s popular Believe It Or Not? lesson plan that walks teachers and learners through basic news literacy. Students learn to ask these six “consumer questions” when vetting a story: Who made this? How was this made? Why was this made? When was this made? What is this missing? Where do I go from here?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of questions and examples of online sources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires critical thinking skills and attention to detail.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Equip learners with questions to evaluate the credibility of online information.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for evaluating online information and identifying reliable sources.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adapt the questions to fit their needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Resource Evaluation
  • Question Formulation
  • Consensus Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to apply the questions to evaluate online information and identify reliable sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners become more discerning consumers of online information. Enhanced media literacy: Learners are better equipped to assess the credibility of online sources.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: It is important to assess not only the content but also the language as you scaffold and teach vocabulary, structure, and function of the language. Through assessment of these students' language skills, you can decide how you will differentiate, whether through products or process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Assessment tools that measure both content and language and a flexible approach to teaching.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to assess and differentiate effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly ELL students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Inform instruction, provide targeted support, and promote student growth.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to adjust instruction based on student needs and ensures that all students are supported.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of assessment methods and provide differentiated instruction based on student performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student performance, increased engagement, and a more supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Ensure what further scaffolds and instruction you should be providing

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Assessing must attend to fluency components and the learner. Assessments often assess accuracy, neglecting efficiency and flexibility. Timed tests do not assess fluency and can negatively affect learners, and thus should be avoided. Alternatives include interviews, observations, and written prompts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires skilled educators, diverse assessment tools, and a commitment to learner-centered evaluation. Demands time, resources, and thoughtful planning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be resource-intensive, may introduce subjective bias, and may require reevaluation of assessment policies and grading structures.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provides thorough evaluation, reduces anxiety, promotes comprehensive insights, improves assessment validity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a more holistic understanding, reduces stress, enhances feedback quality, and supports personalized learning pathways.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize assessment using varied tools, accommodate individual needs, and offer options for demonstrating proficiency in multiple formats.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluates learner skill through performance tasks, oral examinations, and portfolio reviews, examining accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability. Collects learner perceptions via surveys and assesses conceptual understanding with open-ended problems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides thorough evaluation, reduces anxiety, promotes comprehensive insights, improves assessment validity

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Alternatives include interviews, observations, and written prompts.

docs.title: Assessing and Differentiating Language Skills in PBL
Description
docs.text: Assessing and differentiating language skills in project-based learning (PBL) involves evaluating not only content knowledge but also language proficiency. As educators scaffold and teach vocabulary, structure, and function of the language, they should assess these skills to determine further support needed. Through assessment, teachers can decide how to differentiate instruction, whether through products or processes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ongoing assessment of language skills, flexible instructional strategies, and a commitment to meeting diverse student needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing assessment and adjustment, and may necessitate additional resources or support to effectively differentiate instruction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with a particular focus on English Language Learners (ELLs) in project-based learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To provide targeted support to students, especially English Language Learners (ELLs), by assessing and differentiating language skills within project-based learning activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides individualized support based on student needs, enhances language skills, and promotes student progress and engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different project types and proficiency levels, allowing educators to tailor assessment and differentiation strategies to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student performance, enhanced language skills observed in project work, and positive feedback from students and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that assessing and differentiating language skills enhances student achievement and promotes equitable learning outcomes, particularly for ELLs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using formative assessments to evaluate vocabulary use and language structures, and adjusting instruction based on assessment results to provide additional support or extension activities.

docs.title: Assessing Needs and Wants with Likert Scales
Description
docs.text: Using a five-point Likert scale to quantitatively measure student interest and understanding. Create statements for a unit of study to gauge student interest first, and then their understanding and experience with the content, materials, activities after. Include a couple fill-ins and evaluate responses for patterns and repetition. Use both the tally of numbers from the Likert and the fill-ins to inform planning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to create clear and concise survey statements. Analysis of Likert scale and fill-in responses to inform instructional planning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Likert scales may not capture the full complexity of student interests and needs. Fill-in responses may be difficult to interpret or may not provide useful information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable across all learner levels, including K-12, higher education, and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gauge student interest, assess understanding of content, inform instructional planning, and personalize learning experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a quick and efficient way to gather data on student interests and needs. Allows for personalized instruction based on student feedback. Supports a learner-centered approach to teaching.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the number and type of statements used in the survey. Fill-in responses can be tailored to specific learning objectives or content areas.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Data collected from Likert scales and fill-in responses. Analysis of trends and patterns in student feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that using formative assessment to inform instruction increases student engagement and learning outcomes. Studies indicate that personalized learning experiences lead to improved student motivation and achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a Likert scale to assess student interest in different topics. Using fill-in responses to identify areas where students need additional support.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A pedagogical approach that focuses on planning with learners’ strengths at the forefront, recognizing that every learner has something to learn, share, and contribute. It involves proactively planning for instructional opportunities, providing multiple access points for success, presenting a variety of modality choices, and promoting a positive climate for learners to learn from each other. Key strategies include bounce cards (cooperative learning activities), See, Think, Wonder (thinking-made-visible routine to stimulate curiosity and critical thinking), and Which One Doesn’t Belong? (analytic thinking exercise to compare similarities and differences).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Conversation topics, three-column organizer, group of three or four images connected with a math standard

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires intentional planning and a willingness to get to know learners as learners. May be challenging to implement in a classroom with diverse abilities and needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in elementary school

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create initiative-taking and lifelong learners, cultivate high expectations, promote active listening, increase critical thinking skills, encourage perspective sharing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active listening, turn-taking, and perspective sharing. Normalizes error and stimulates curiosity. Provides multiple access points for success and promotes a positive learning climate.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose topics for classroom conversation and plan how to discuss them. Provide a three-column organizer for learners to record their observations, thoughts, and wonders.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner participation in discussions, quality of connections made between learners, ability to share different perspectives

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports learners in becoming curious analytical problem solvers who are conversant in divergent ideas and embrace discussing different perspectives. Promotes active listening, turn-taking, and perspective sharing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners choose topics for classroom conversation and plan how to discuss them in a variety of ways. Learners are shown a stimulating image and use a three-column organizer to record their observations, thoughts, and wonders. Resource: Edutopia - 3 Activities That Guide Every Student to Contribute in Class

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Association is a mnemonic device that links new information to something already known to make it easier to remember. This can involve creating mental images, stories, or connections that tie the new information to familiar concepts or people. The more unique or silly the association, the better.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ability to create mental images and connections. A clear understanding of the new information to be remembered.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective for abstract or complex information without a strong personal connection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for visual and creative learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory by creating connections between new and existing knowledge.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages existing knowledge to facilitate learning. Turns abstract concepts into concrete, memorable images or stories.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create personalized associations that are meaningful to them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the ability to recall information by using the created associations. Track the use of associations in explaining concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Linking new information to existing knowledge enhances memory and understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Remembering the name of a new co-worker by associating them with a familiar person with the same name. Associating Isaac Newton with eating a Fig Newton while discovering gravity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Be aware that families’ attitudes and beliefs about education may vary, and it’s a mistake to assume that all students have parents who promote school engagement. Logistics related to online learning (consistent internet access, reliable devices, quiet spaces) are also highly variable. An empathetic practitioner should assume that all families and students are doing the best they can with what they have in the current situation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Open communication with families, flexibility in expectations, access to resources and support services.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset and potentially additional resources or training.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, school administrators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate empathy for families' circumstances, reduce judgment, provide equitable support, improve student outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters a more understanding and supportive environment, reduces stress and anxiety for both educators and families, and promotes better collaboration

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor support to the specific needs and circumstances of individual families, recognizing their unique challenges and strengths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvements in family engagement, student well-being, and academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more supportive and equitable learning environment for all students, regardless of their home situation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Offer flexible deadlines, provide resources for families facing financial or logistical challenges, and communicate with parents to understand their perspectives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One of the limitations of discussion is that rich, face-to-face conversations can only happen when all parties are available, so we’re limited to the time we have in class. With a tool like Voxer, those limitations disappear. Like a private voice mailbox that you set up with just one person or a group (but SOOOO much easier), Voxer allows users to have conversations at whatever time is most convenient for each participant. So a group of four learners can “discuss” a topic from 3pm until bedtime—asynchronously—each member contributing whenever they have a moment, and if the teacher makes herself part of the group, she can listen in, offer feedback, or contribute her own discussion points. Voxer is also invaluable for collaborating on projects and for having one-on-one discussions with learners, parents, and your own colleagues.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to a voice messaging platform such as Voxer, a topic of discussion, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who lack access to technology or who struggle with digital literacy skills, requires careful monitoring to ensure respectful communication and avoid off-topic discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for online and blended learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote flexible and accessible communication, encourage peer learning and collaboration, provide opportunities for ongoing feedback and support, enhance digital literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages flexible and accessible communication, promotes peer learning and collaboration, provides opportunities for ongoing feedback and support, enhances digital literacy skills, supports self-paced learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the topics they want to discuss and the format of their contributions. Teachers can provide personalized feedback and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review learner contributions to the voice messaging platform, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances communication skills, promotes collaboration and peer learning, improves digital literacy skills

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Practice attentive behavior during non-crucial times during the school day. At periodic intervals, have practice attention breaks using a timer or an app on the phone. Signal when the work period begins, and have the child mark whether he/she was paying attention. This can help train a student's brain to understand what attention looks like, and how often he/she is tempted to disengage.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Timer or attention tracking app, designated work periods, a method for marking attention (e.g., checklist, digital tool).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be disruptive if not managed effectively. Some learners may not accurately self-assess their attention.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with attention, especially children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Train attention, increase self-awareness of attention lapses, improve focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases self-awareness of attention, provides structured practice, helps develop attentive behavior, can be easily integrated into the school day

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Frequency and duration of breaks can be adjusted. The method of self-marking (e.g., apps, timers) can be adapted to individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency of self-marked attention lapses. Monitor the improvement of attentive behavior over time. Collect feedback from learners on their self-awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Attention breaks can significantly improve self-awareness and attentive behavior, especially for learners who need structured practice. They provide a method for understanding and reducing attention lapses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses a timer to signal attention breaks during independent reading time, having students note whether they were focused. A parent incorporates attention breaks during homework sessions, using a tracking app to monitor attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An attention check is a practice where a teacher announces a short pause, and students reflect on where their attention is. Learners are encouraged to notice what their mind is doing and to understand they have a choice about where to direct their attention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space and brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use guided audio, videos, or instructor-led exercises.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, reduce stress, enhance self-regulation, improve cognitive function

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, supports emotional regulation, improves attention, enhances self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various durations and settings. Can be integrated into existing lessons or used as standalone activities. Use different mindfulness techniques to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In the middle of a lesson, or during the middle of independent or group work time, ask students to pause and “check in with their attention.” Is their attention here, in class? Was their mind wandering? If so, where had their attention gone? Emphasize that mind-wandering is completely normal and to be expected — it’s what minds do! The important thing is to notice what the mind is doing, and then to understand you now have a choice about where to direct your attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Attention signals are techniques used by instructors to regain focus and quiet a noisy learning environment. These signals can range from simple auditory cues like flicking the lights or ringing a bell to more elaborate call-and-response routines. Effective attention signals are taught and rehearsed to ensure 100% compliance. The goal is to quickly and efficiently regain learners' attention so that instruction can continue.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent implementation, clear expectations, and rehearsal to ensure 100% compliance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become ineffective if overused or if learners do not understand the signal. Some learners may find certain signals disruptive or annoying.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Regain learners' attention, establish a quiet environment, prepare learners for instruction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Quickly and efficiently regain learners' attention, minimize disruption, and establish clear expectations for behavior. Provides a structured way to transition between activities and maintain a productive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Attention signals can be tailored to the specific age group and learning environment. Simple auditory cues may be more effective for younger learners, while call-and-response routines may be more engaging for older learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly and effectively learners respond to the attention signal. Track the number of times the signal needs to be used during a lesson.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved classroom management: Research suggests that consistent use of attention signals can reduce disruptive behavior and increase instructional time. Enhanced focus: By quickly regaining learners' attention, attention signals can help learners stay focused and engaged in the lesson.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include flicking the lights, ringing a bell, raising a hand, or using a call-and-response routine. Harry Wong's Give Me 5 is a well-known example of an attention signal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students engage with audio resources (music, podcasts, voice-recorded lectures) accompanied by a structured activity. This combines the advantages of audio learning with the benefits of active engagement and application of concepts. Audio resources are typically smaller in file size and easier to host, making them accessible to learners with limited bandwidth.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creation or selection of audio resources and design of structured activities. Instructor must provide clear instructions and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of content or learners. Requires careful planning to ensure active engagement and understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who prefer audio-based learning and those with limited access to technology or bandwidth.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide accessible and flexible content, promote active learning, facilitate understanding and application of concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a low-bandwidth alternative to video, provides flexibility and accessibility, promotes active engagement with the material. The sound of a human voice can play an important role in learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Structured activities can be tailored to different learning styles and needs. Audio resources can be selected based on learner interests and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completion and quality of structured activities, learner feedback, performance on related assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective when paired with well-designed structured activities that promote active engagement and application of the audio material. Can improve learner outcomes and engagement in the absence of video technology.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Audio books provide an auditory learning experience where the text of a book is read aloud, allowing learners to listen instead of or in conjunction with reading. This strategy can improve comprehension, vocabulary, and fluency, especially for learners with reading difficulties or those learning a new language. Audio books are accessible via physical media (CDs) or digital platforms, and can be used independently or as part of a structured literacy program. The use of audiobooks also helps learners practice active listening and improve their focus and attention skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to audio books (physical or digital), playback devices (e.g., CD players, smartphones, computers), and headphones. Teachers may need to curate a collection that aligns with curriculum goals and learner needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners who prefer visual learning or those with auditory processing difficulties. Requires access to technology and reliable internet connectivity for digital formats.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beneficial for all learners, particularly effective for struggling readers, English language learners, and students with visual impairments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve listening comprehension, increase vocabulary, enhance reading fluency, support diverse learning styles, and foster a love of literature.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports auditory learners, provides access to complex texts for those with lower reading levels, and allows for multitasking (e.g., listening while commuting). Helps build phonemic awareness and pronunciation skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adjust playback speed, choose books based on interest, and listen repeatedly to reinforce understanding. Digital platforms often offer transcripts for simultaneous reading.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess listening comprehension through quizzes, discussions, and written summaries. Track vocabulary growth and fluency improvements. Monitor student engagement and preferences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that audio books can significantly improve reading comprehension and vocabulary acquisition, particularly for struggling readers and English language learners. Studies show that listening to audio books can also increase reading motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses audio books to provide access to grade-level texts for students with dyslexia. An ESL instructor uses audio books to improve pronunciation and listening skills. Resource: Learning Ally, Audible.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Audio commentary involves instructors and learners using audio recordings to provide personalized feedback on work. This approach can be more personal and nuanced compared to written feedback, allowing for tone and inflection to enhance communication. It typically involves recording verbal feedback and sharing it with the learner for review.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to audio recording tools (e.g., smartphone, computer with microphone), a platform for sharing audio files, and clear guidelines for providing effective audio feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time to provide feedback compared to written comments. Accessibility concerns may arise for learners with hearing impairments unless transcripts are provided.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where personalized feedback is beneficial.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide personalized feedback, enhance communication through tone and inflection, and improve learner engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for more nuanced and personal communication compared to written feedback. Can enhance engagement by adding a human element to online feedback. Facilitates detailed explanations and guidance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can tailor their feedback to the individual learner, addressing specific strengths and weaknesses in their work.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Technology Integration
  • Individual Response

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of audio feedback. Observe learner engagement and participation in feedback activities. Measure improvements in the quality of revised work based on audio feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This approach can enhance learner engagement and understanding of feedback, leading to improved learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Tools like Camtasia Studio, voice memos on smartphones, WimbaCLASSROOM, and Zoom (using recording and screen sharing) can be used for audio commentary.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Allowing learners to listen to audiobooks supports learners with auditory processing strengths. This format lets them absorb information through their preferred modality, enhancing comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to audiobooks

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners who prefer visual or kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with strengths in auditory processing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, engage learners with auditory strengths, support reading skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages auditory strengths, provides an alternative to traditional reading, enhances comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of audiobooks that match learners' interests and reading levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess comprehension through quizzes, discussions, or written assignments, compare performance with traditional reading tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that audiobooks can improve reading comprehension and engagement for learners with auditory processing strengths. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of audiobooks in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Allowing students to listen to novels during independent reading time, using audiobooks for assigned readings. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Audiobooks and e-books can be used to enhance literacy skills, comprehension, and engagement, especially for emerging readers, English language learners, and students with reading challenges. Audiobooks bridge the decoding gap, allowing learners to access age-appropriate stories and complex content. E-books offer customizable features like adjustable fonts and text size, catering to individual learning preferences. Following along visually while listening can enhance word-recognition ability, while listening alone can expand vocabulary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to audiobooks and/or e-books, devices (e.g., computers, tablets, smartphones), reading apps (e.g., Sora, Libby), and library cards (for some platforms).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some may argue that listening to audiobooks is not equivalent to traditional reading. The selection of free titles may be limited to older classics. Requires reliable access to technology and digital resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Emerging readers, K-12 students, English language learners, students with reading difficulties (e.g., dyslexia), and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance literacy skills, improve comprehension, expand vocabulary, increase engagement with reading, and support learners with reading challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides access to complex texts, supports decoding skills, strengthens comprehension, offers a stigma-free reading experience, and accommodates different learning preferences through customizable features. For educators, it offers a tool to engage reluctant readers and provide differentiated instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adjust the playback speed, font size, and background color. Digital platforms enable text-to-speech capabilities, and learners can choose between listening alone or following along with the text.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Demonstration
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learners' reading progress, comprehension levels, and engagement in class discussions. Observe their ability to follow along with the text while listening and track their recommendations to peers. Collect data on learners' attitudes toward reading and their self-perception as readers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show audiobooks can improve reading skills, vocabulary, and comprehension. They also provide access to books above learners' reading levels and can spark interest in reading. Can also create feelings of relaxation and stress reduction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Audiobooks can reinforce and inspire literacy skills and enjoyment for all students, including emerging readers and ESL/ELL learners. They offer a way to experience literature and other reading selections in audio form. Some selections are audio only, while others include text to follow or interactive features. They can improve English skills or study literature in new ways.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to audiobooks (either physical or digital), devices for listening (e.g., computers, tablets, smartphones), and a quiet environment for focused listening.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Audiobooks may not fully replace the benefits of traditional reading. Learners need to be actively engaged and not just passively listening to benefit from the strategy. Digital access may be a barrier for some learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, including emerging readers and ESL/ELL learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce literacy skills, improve English skills, increase reading enjoyment, and accommodate diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides auditory support for reading comprehension, supports vocabulary development, enhances engagement with literature, and accommodates different learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offers multiple categories of books and different download or listening formats. Some selections are audio only, others include text to follow on the site as you listen, while others include options to interact with the book by clicking, responding, and watching animations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation in discussions about the audiobooks. Assess comprehension through quizzes, summaries, or creative projects.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that audiobooks can improve reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, and motivation to read, especially for struggling readers and English language learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A backchannel is a conversation that happens right alongside another activity. While those of us in the audience listened to presenters and watched a few short video clips, a separate screen was up beside the main screen, projecting something called TodaysMeet (update: TodaysMeet has shut down. Use YoTeach! instead.) It looked a lot like those chat rooms from back in the day, basically a blank screen where people would contribute a few lines of text, the lines stacking up one after the other, no other bells or whistles. Anyone in the room could participate in this conversation on their phone, laptop, or tablet, asking questions, offering commentary, and sharing links to related resources without ever interrupting the flow of the presentations. This kind of tool allows for a completely silent discussion, one that doesn’t have to move at a super-fast pace, and it gives learners who may be reluctant to speak up or who process their thoughts more slowly a chance to fully contribute.

docs.title: Behavioral Feedback for Correct and Incorrect Responses
Description
docs.text:
Behavioral science distinguishes how to respond to a learner's correct versus incorrect responses, based on research into what actually changes behavior rather than what feels intuitively corrective.

Correct responses. When a learner responds correctly, the teacher should do two things immediately: (1) tell the learner the answer is correct, and (2) briefly describe what they did to obtain the correct answer (e.g., "That's right. You listed the five major events." rather than just "Correct."). Better learning results from telling learners not only what they got right, but why (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 1987).

Incorrect responses. Scolding or verbally punishing careless mistakes is strongly discouraged. Instead, regardless of why the learner erred (carelessness, lack of knowledge, or lack of understanding), the recommended response is: (1) if the problem is purely factual, simply give the correct answer; (2) if it involves a more complex skill, point out the relevant rule, procedure, or steps; (3) ask the learner to correct the answer; or (4) assign extra practice. These responses deliberately omit preaching, scolding, or dwelling on the error itself, since such responses tend to produce anxiety and distaste for the work, encouraging disengagement rather than correction (Rodgers & Iwata, 1991).

Cautions for two groups. These recommendations improve learning for most students, but not universally. Low-achieving learners given material that is too difficult make many errors and experience mostly negative consequences; research shows that when error rates are high, little is learned from informational feedback at all (Kulik & Kulik, 1988; McKeachie, 1990) — the deeper fix is designing instruction to produce fewer errors in the first place, not delivering feedback differently. Separately, learners who are highly dependent on adult attention may persist in mistakes because of the attention the mistake itself draws; when a teacher's response focuses on the error (e.g., circling a reversed letter) rather than the correct answer, this can inadvertently reinforce the incorrect response. Experiments in which teachers circled only correct responses, and drew no attention at all to errors, produced dramatic improvements in learners' correct letter and digit formation (Hasazi & Hasazi, 1972; Stromer, 1975).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Enough diagnostic clarity to tell whether an error is factual, procedural, or conceptual, so the right corrective response (answer, rule, or extra practice) can be chosen

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Not effective as feedback alone for learners already experiencing high error rates — for that population, the priority is redesigning instruction to reduce errors (see Effective Presentation for Errorless Learning), not adjusting the feedback wording
  • Risks reinforcing the wrong behavior in learners whose mistakes are attention-seeking, if the teacher's response draws more attention to the error than to correct performance

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Most classroom learners receiving routine correctness feedback
  • Learners prone to attention-seeking through errors, for whom feedback should deliberately highlight correct responses over incorrect ones
  • Low-achieving learners with high error rates, for whom the underlying instructional design (not the feedback style) is the priority to fix

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforcing correct performance patterns while correcting errors without provoking anxiety, avoidance, or inadvertent reinforcement of the mistake itself

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. On a correct response, state that it is correct and briefly name what the learner did to get there.
  2. On an incorrect response, avoid scolding or dwelling on the mistake; instead give the correct answer (factual errors), name the relevant rule or steps (procedural/conceptual errors), have the learner redo it, or assign extra practice.
  3. For learners with persistently high error rates, treat this as a signal to simplify or resequence instruction rather than only adjusting feedback delivery.
  4. For learners who seem to seek attention through mistakes, deliberately shift attention toward correct responses and minimize visible attention to errors.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Effective Presentation for Errorless Learning — reduces the error rate this feedback approach is designed to respond to
  • Least-to-Most Prompting Hierarchy — prompts prevent errors before the response; this strategy addresses what to do once a response has been made

docs.text:

  • Rodgers, T. A., & Iwata, B. A. (1991). An analysis of error-correction procedures during discrimination training. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 24(4), 775-781.
  • Kulik, J. A., & Kulik, C. C. (1988). Timing of feedback and verbal learning. Review of Educational Research, 58(1), 79-97.
  • McKeachie, W. J. (1990). Research on college teaching: The historical background. Journal of Educational Psychology, 82(2), 189-200.
  • Hasazi, J. E., & Hasazi, S. E. (1972). Effects of teacher attention on digit-reversal behavior in an elementary school child. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 5(2), 157-162.
