docs.title: Description
docs.text: An adult shadows a child closely (within arm's reach) to prevent specific harmful behaviors (e.g., biting, hitting) before they occur. The adult remains unobtrusive, avoiding special attention or punishment, while ensuring the safety of the child and classmates. The goal is to break the cycle of harmful behavior and teach alternative strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A dedicated adult (teacher, aide, or trained volunteer), a clear understanding of the target behaviors, a shadowing protocol, and a commitment to consistent and unobtrusive observation. Requires close proximity and constant supervision.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be labor-intensive and may require additional staffing, may be perceived as intrusive if not implemented carefully, and may not address the underlying causes of the behavior without additional support and intervention.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Young children (e.g., preschool or early elementary) exhibiting behaviors that can harm themselves or others, such as biting or hitting. Useful for children with limited verbal skills who may be using aggression as a form of communication.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent harmful behaviors, ensure the safety of all children in a classroom, identify triggers for aggressive behaviors, teach alternative strategies for communication and interaction, and break the cycle of negative behavior patterns.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate intervention to prevent harm, allows for close observation of triggers and patterns, protects other children in the classroom, and creates opportunities to teach and reinforce positive behaviors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The shadowing protocol can be adjusted based on the specific behaviors and needs of the child. Alternative communication strategies can be introduced and reinforced during shadowing to help the child express themselves more effectively.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduction in the frequency of target behaviors, increased use of alternative communication strategies, improved social interactions, and a safer classroom environment. Data can be collected through direct observation and incident reports.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a safe and supportive environment while addressing harmful behaviors. Breaking negative cycles allows the child to develop more appropriate strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A preschool teacher shadows a child who has bitten classmates on two occasions, preventing further incidents and teaching the child to use words to express frustration. The shadowing continues until the child is incident-free for two weeks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ten research-backed strategies that encourage playful learning, innovative thinking, and problem-solving skills while engaging students in core subjects. These motivators include providing choice, fostering collaboration, integrating meaningful talk, encouraging problem solving, inquiry learning, risk-taking, unlocking creativity, developing empathy, teacher-student negotiation, and ensuring adequate recess and brain breaks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Supportive classroom environment, flexible curriculum, resources for various activities and projects, trained educators who can facilitate student-led discussions and collaborations

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift from traditional teaching methods, may need additional training for educators, some students may struggle with the open-ended nature of certain activities

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students; adaptable for various educational settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote playful learning, enhance innovative thinking and problem-solving skills, increase student engagement in core subjects, foster collaboration and communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances student engagement and motivation, fosters collaboration and communication, develops problem-solving and creative thinking skills, promotes a positive and supportive learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt activities and tasks to suit different student interests and skill levels. Provide diverse options for projects and assessments to cater to different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Peer Teaching
  • Collaboration
  • Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation in activities. Evaluate the quality of student projects and presentations. Gather feedback from students on their learning experiences. Assess improvements in problem-solving and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • These strategies prepare students for college, career, and life by developing skills valued by employers and educational institutions. They also promote a positive and supportive learning environment where students feel empowered to take risks and express their creativity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students select their own reading materials, collaborate on research projects, engage in student-led discussions, propose solutions to community problems, take risks in expressing their ideas, develop empathy through social interactions, and negotiate deadlines and assessment formats with their teachers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These strategies encourage playful learning, boost students’ innovative thinking and problem-solving skills, and at the same time engage students in reading, writing, researching, discussing, and analyzing materials in all subjects. They include choice in independent reading, writing topics, and projects, collaboration, meaningful talk, problem solving, inquiry learning, encouraging risk taking, unlocking creativity, developing empathy, teacher-student negotiating, and going out for recess/enjoying time to play outside/five-minute brain breaks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of learning materials and resources. Collaborative learning environment. Instructor facilitation and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant planning and preparation. Some learners may need more guidance and structure.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Engage students in learning, boost innovative thinking, develop problem-solving skills, enhance critical thinking, foster collaboration, encourage creativity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement and motivation. Develops innovative thinking and problem-solving skills. Fosters collaboration and creativity. Encourages critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted to suit diverse learning needs and interests. Learners can choose topics and projects based on their preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner engagement and participation. Quality of collaborative projects. Problem-solving and critical-thinking skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that these motivators enhance engagement, achievement, and 21st-century skills. Studies also show that play-based learning promotes creativity and innovation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing learners with choices in reading materials. Encouraging collaboration through group projects. Incorporating problem-solving activities in math class. Facilitating inquiry-based learning in science.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: If the teacher says a number greater than 10, students expand their bodies to take up as much space as they can (while keeping their feet firmly planted on the ground—no running around). If the teacher says a number less than 10, students shrink their bodies to take up the least space they can. If the teacher gives the number 10 exactly, students hold their body neutrally and make an equals sign with their arms. As before, the teacher moves to sums and differences once students get the rules.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An open space where students can move freely. Teacher needs to be able to call out numbers, sums, or differences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for students with physical limitations. Students may get confused if they don't grasp the math concepts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce the concepts of greater than, less than, and equal to. Promote kinesthetic learning, enhance active recall, provide an opportunity for movement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging way to understand math concepts. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust complexity of numbers based on skill levels of the students. Students may come up with different physical expressions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' physical expressions in response to the given numbers. Assess their math comprehension through their physical responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • May help students grasp the concept of inequalities and equality in a kinesthetic and engaging way. Supports active participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When the teacher says '15', students expand their bodies; when the teacher says '7', students shrink their bodies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves capturing Black learners’ genius using specific elements such as Interest Awareness, Racial Identity, Social Justice, Multi-cultural Navigation, Selective Trust, and Can-do Attitude. Parents complete a Black Genius profile for their child as an advocacy tool, cultural tool, and personal learning tool to learn more about the child’s interests, skills, expectations, strengths, and growth areas to support their healthy development. The profile is completed with the input of the child and involves reflecting on questions to capture their thoughts and ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Black Genius Profile workbook, trained facilitators, time for reflection and discussion, and a commitment to cultural responsiveness.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional support for families and educators to understand and implement the framework effectively. Could be perceived as a deficit-based approach if not implemented with sensitivity and care.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Black learners, parents, educators, and caregivers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Capture Black learners’ genius, promote positive racial identity formation, support advocacy, enhance cultural responsiveness, facilitate personal learning, and support healthy development.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for understanding and celebrating Black learners' unique strengths and perspectives. Enhances communication and collaboration between parents, educators, and learners. Promotes a strengths-based approach to learning and development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Profiles can be tailored to individual learners' experiences, interests, and cultural backgrounds. Flexible completion methods allow for varying levels of input from children and parents.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Eliciting Student Thinking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the completion and use of Black Genius Profiles. Gather feedback from learners, parents, and educators on the effectiveness of the framework. Observe changes in learners' self-esteem, academic performance, and social-emotional development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Empowers Black learners by affirming their identities and strengths. Facilitates culturally responsive teaching practices. Enhances parent-educator collaboration to support learners' holistic development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Parents complete the Black Genius profile with their child to advocate for their needs at school and support their cultural identity and academic performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students transform conversational text selections into poetry by blacking out sections to reveal only key terms and phrases, focusing on the meaning, nuances, and silences of each character's dialogue. Working in pairs, students read aloud the text, then independently examine their character's subtext—what they're really saying, hiding, feeling, expressing, or withholding. After blacking out the 'background noise,' they reread the remaining words and phrases with their partner, highlighting the essence of the conversation. This exercise aims to foster social awareness, empathy, and relationship skills by encouraging active listening, reflection, and deeper understanding of others' experiences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Text selections featuring dominant character dialogue. Blackout markers or pens. Facilitation of paired and independent reading activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of texts and sensitivity in interpreting character emotions. Success depends on students' willingness to engage deeply with the text and their partners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social awareness, improve relationship skills, enhance empathy, and promote active listening.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to take time to truly listen and reflect on the experiences of others. Helps students understand unspoken words and identify strengths, habits, and needs in interactions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Text selections can be tailored to address specific social or emotional themes relevant to the students. Focus can be shifted to different characters or aspects of the conversation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student interpretations of character motivations, quality of blackout poetry, and participation in partner discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances social awareness and relationship skills by emphasizing active listening and reflection. Improves understanding of nuances and unspoken words in conversations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using chapters from Sharon Draper’s 'Tears of a Tiger' written explicitly in the form of character dialogue.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Blended learning combines face-to-face instruction with online learning through an LMS, offering the advantages of direct interaction and the convenience of eLearning. It involves live training sessions, additional online resources, and assignments to ensure complete understanding. This approach allows for documenting and reporting on training effectiveness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • LMS that supports a wide range of content formats (Word, PowerPoint, PDF, video, audio). Face-to-face training facilities. Instructors skilled in both in-person and online instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and coordination. May be challenging to implement in resource-constrained environments. Relies on the quality of both in-person and online components.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for corporate training, higher education, and adult education settings where both in-person and online resources are available.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Combine the benefits of face-to-face and online learning, enhance learner engagement, provide flexibility, document and report on training effectiveness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines the advantages of direct interaction with the convenience of eLearning. Allows for documenting and reporting on who has taken the training session and how effective it was. Provides flexibility for learners to access resources at their own pace.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize online resources to match individual learner needs. Offer a variety of in-person and online activities to cater to diverse learning preferences. Provide personalized feedback through the LMS.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Supportive information
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Lectures
  • Discussion Sections
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Response

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner participation in both in-person and online activities. Assess performance on assignments and exams. Gather feedback from learners on their experiences with blended learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective training technique that combines the benefits of face-to-face and online learning. Enhances learner engagement and provides flexibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Holding a live training session with a group of learners, posting extra resources to an LMS, and assigning a task or exam. Offering a course with weekly in-person meetings and online modules to complete at the learner's own pace.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Block play involves using blocks to create structures and designs, either independently or collaboratively. It supports problem-solving, imagination, self-expression, mathematical concepts, continuity and permanence, creativity, scientific reasoning, self-esteem, and social and emotional growth.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a full set of unit blocks, assorted props, open storage shelves, and sufficient space and time for building and rebuilding.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require guidance for children to fully realize the learning potential. Requires adequate space and organization to avoid chaos. Requires time and space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood learners through primary grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, foster imagination, encourage self-expression, strengthen mathematical understanding, promote creativity, build scientific reasoning, enhance self-esteem, and support social and emotional growth.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances problem-solving abilities, fine and gross motor skills, mathematical skills, and language and literacy abilities. Fosters creativity, self-esteem, and social-emotional development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to suit individual interests and developmental levels by providing assorted props tied to children’s current interests and experiences. Open-ended nature allows for solo or group play.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's problem-solving strategies, creativity in design, application of mathematical concepts, and social interactions during play. Assess the complexity and stability of structures built.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies and educator experiences show block play enhances cognitive, social, emotional, and physical development in young children. Provides opportunities for testing hypotheses and building scientific reasoning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A pre-K teacher leads a block building activity that promotes early math reasoning and Spatial Skills by asking questions throughout the building process to challenge students to think critically to solve the problems they encounter.

docs.title: Blocks and Legos: Maker Spaces and Fab Labs
Description
docs.text: Maker spaces and fab labs provide learners with opportunities to invent, design, and build things. These spaces encourage exploration, imagination, and collaboration, mirroring the principles of play. Learners can create jewelry, build guitars, design robots, or sew their own clothes. Maker spaces can integrate technology or use simple materials like wood scraps and soda bottles. This hands-on approach allows learners to apply theories in practical ways and solve real-world problems, fostering deeper engagement and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated maker space or fab lab with necessary tools and materials. Instructor guidance and support. Collaboration opportunities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant resources to set up and maintain. Some learners may need more guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, higher education, adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster creativity, encourage exploration, promote collaboration, apply theoretical knowledge, solve real-world problems

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances creativity and innovation. Provides hands-on learning experiences. Encourages collaboration and teamwork. Applies theoretical knowledge to practical situations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose projects based on their interests and skill levels. Instructors can provide different materials and tools to accommodate various needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner projects and creations. Participation in collaborative activities. Problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that maker spaces promote creativity, innovation, and problem-solving skills. Studies also show that hands-on learning experiences improve knowledge retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school physics class uses the fab lab to build prototypes of energy-efficient devices. A community college offers a maker space for adult learners to design and create their own inventions. A university engineering program integrates maker space activities into its curriculum.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporate a body scan meditation to bring calmness and awareness to the classroom, maximizing students’ potential. This practice helps students become more aware of their physical sensations and emotional states, which can lead to improved self-regulation and focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Meditation script or recording, quiet space, time for meditation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may find it difficult to sit still and focus during meditation. It is important to create a comfortable and supportive environment where students feel safe and relaxed. Meditation may not be suitable for all students, especially those with certain mental health conditions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote calmness and awareness, enhance self-regulation and focus, improve emotional awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a calming and centering activity that can help students manage stress and improve their focus. Can be adapted to different age groups and developmental levels. Promotes self-awareness and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose different meditation scripts and durations to suit the needs of their students. Students can also be encouraged to modify the meditation to fit their own preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in the activity. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness. Monitor student behavior and academic performance to assess the impact of meditation on their self-regulation and focus.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Incorporating meditation or mindfulness into the classroom can help bring calmness and awareness, and even maximize students’ potential.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students participate in a guided body scan meditation to bring calmness and awareness into the classroom. This involves focusing attention on different parts of the body to notice sensations and promote relaxation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A quiet space, a guided meditation script or recording, and time for the meditation (5-10 minutes).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to focus during the meditation. The effectiveness of the activity depends on creating a calm and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for pre-K through college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote calmness, increase body awareness, reduce stress, improve focus and concentration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way to practice mindfulness and relaxation. Can be easily integrated into the classroom routine. Promotes self-awareness and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The length and complexity of the meditation can be adjusted based on the age and experience of the students. Can be adapted to focus on specific areas of the body or specific emotional states.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement in the meditation. Gather feedback from students on their experience with the meditation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mindfulness activities enhance academic performance, support mental health, and improve focus.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers integrate body scan meditations into their classrooms to help students manage stress and improve their ability to focus on learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Did the writer engage with anyone who disagrees? Did they call a senator whose legislation bugs them? Did they try to grasp what the president-elect was doing, or merely repeat one of his more outrageous statements? If it's a broadcast interview, was the guest presented with genuine opposing views and challenged to answer? Those who wrestle with opposing arguments do you a service and often improve their own arguments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to news sources that engage with opposing viewpoints.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort to find and evaluate diverse perspectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage learners to seek news sources that engage with opposing viewpoints and challenge their own arguments.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking and open-mindedness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can seek out diverse perspectives on topics of interest.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Discussion Prompt
  • Moderation
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and engage with opposing viewpoints in news sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners are more likely to consider diverse perspectives and challenge their own assumptions. Enhanced media literacy: Learners become more discerning consumers of news.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Analyze news sources to determine if they engage with opposing viewpoints and challenge their own arguments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Book clubs, also known as literature circles, are a grouping system to organize active learning events based on student-selected areas of interest. Learners investigate content area topics by drawing on multiple texts, including websites, printed material, video, and music. They then share their learning using similar media, such as learning logs or blogs, discussing questions and observations about books they are reading. Group members share background knowledge and make inferences and predictions that strengthen verbal reasoning. Book clubs can be created within a classroom, grade level, or across different classes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of texts (books, magazines, websites, videos), computers with internet access, learning logs or blogs, and class time for discussions and activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful structuring and organization to ensure effective group investigations. Students may need guidance in selecting appropriate materials and staying on track. Success depends on learners' ability to collaborate and engage in meaningful discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school students (Grades 6-8), but adaptable for other grade levels and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Motivate reading and writing, enhance comprehension, strengthen verbal reasoning, expand social networks, promote knowledge sharing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for collaboration, discussion, and reflection. Students engage with multiple types of texts and genres to gather and synthesize information. Learners take ownership of their learning by selecting topics of interest and sharing their discoveries with peers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners choose topics of interest, types of texts, and methods of sharing learning. Flexible grouping allows for diverse perspectives. Can be adapted to fit various content areas and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Assigned Readings
  • Case Study
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, track knowledge sharing, analyze depth of discussions and blog posts, review student reflections and projects.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Motivates reading and writing, enhances comprehension, strengthens verbal reasoning, expands social networks, promotes knowledge sharing. Research shows literature circles support learning across topics and encourages students to select materials of interest.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Book clubs are small groups of learners who choose, read, and discuss a shared text. Learners take ownership of their reading experience by selecting books, establishing group rules, pacing their reading, and guiding their conversations. Instructors provide choice in books, group membership, rules, conversation topics, and final products. The emphasis is on fostering a shared reading experience where learners share thoughts, analyze texts, and critically think together. Structures may vary, including discussions, projects, and written reflections, to suit diverse learner needs and objectives. This approach promotes engagement, critical thinking, and social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of books. Class time for reading and discussion. Facilitation by the instructor to guide discussions and provide support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure meaningful discussions and prevent off-topic conversations. Some students may be unprepared or dominate discussions, requiring instructor intervention. Assessment can be challenging due to varied reading materials and group dynamics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school to high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, develop critical thinking skills, foster collaborative discussions, increase student engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages student ownership and motivation through choice. Provides a social context for learning and discussing texts. Promotes deeper engagement with reading material and critical thinking skills. Enhances vocabulary and communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer diverse book choices catering to different interests and reading levels. Allow learners to set their reading pace and discussion topics. Provide options for final projects to accommodate different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Description
docs.text: BOOKMATCH is a tool for helping students select just-right books for independent reading. It introduces various criteria that influence book selection, such as book length, ordinary language, organization, prior knowledge, manageable text, appeal to genre, topic appropriateness, connection, and high interest. Students use these criteria to select books, discuss and evaluate their choices, and become more aware of their personal preferences as readers. This approach helps students become independent and responsible for their book selections during independent reading time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Bounce cards provide a structured way for students to engage in cooperative learning by promoting active listening, turn-taking, and perspective sharing. Students choose topics for classroom conversation and plan how to discuss them in a variety of ways. In this strategy, teachers model conversation techniques and then explicitly teach the following three approaches that students can use to respond to one another’s comments during a conversation: Bounce: Bounce an idea off what a peer said or elaborate on it. Sum it up: Rephrase what a peer said and comment on certain parts. Inquire: Ask a question.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Brain breaks are short periods of time when learners change up the routine of incoming information. These breaks refresh thinking and help learners discover another solution to a problem or see a situation through a different lens. During these minutes, the brain moves away from learning, memorizing, and problem solving. The brain break helps to incubate and process new information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use movement, games, or creative activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to transition back to learning. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Junk Bag: Pick any object out of the junk bag and ask students to come up with two ways this object could be reinvented for other uses. Squiggle Story: Draw one squiggly line. Give students one minute to stand and draw with their nondominant hand, turning the line into a picture or design of their choice. Opposite Sides: Have students stand and blink with the right eye while snapping the fingers of their left hand. Symbolic Alphabet: Sing the alphabet with names of objects rather than the letters. Other Languages: Teach sign language or make up a spoken language. Mental Math: Give a set of three instructions, counting the sequence to a partner for 30 seconds. Invisible Pictures: Have a student draw a picture in the air while their partner guesses what it is. Story Starters: Begin a story for one minute, either individually or with a partner. The students then complete or continue it with a silly ending. Rock Scissors Paper Math: With that call, students lay out one, two, three, or four fingers in the palm of their hand. The first player to say the correct sum of both players’ fingers wins.

docs.text: • A high school teacher leads a daily mindfulness exercise at the beginning of class to help students focus and manage stress before starting their academic work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Bridging Cultures Project helps teachers understand assumptions underlying individualism and collectivism, highlighting cultural differences that may diverge from school-based practices and values.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing commitment and self-reflection. May require significant adjustments to established teaching practices.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand cultural values, adapt classroom practices, enhance communication, create inclusive learning environments

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides insights into cultural values, facilitates communication, creates inclusive classroom environments, enhances understanding of student behaviors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows teachers to reflect on their own cultural biases and assumptions. Encourages adaptable teaching practices to meet diverse student needs.

docs.text: • Improved classroom management, enhanced academic achievement, increased student engagement, culturally responsive teaching.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on understanding and addressing the differences between individualistic and collectivistic value systems in the classroom. Individualism emphasizes independence and individual achievement, while collectivism emphasizes interdependence, helpfulness, and group success. By recognizing these differing values, teachers can adapt their practices to honor both home and school cultures. For example, teachers can encourage collaborative work and group celebrations in addition to individual assignments. A kindergarten teacher bridged these values by allowing a student to discuss how she cooked eggs with her grandmother, thus validating the social context of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to understand the principles of individualism and collectivism. Requires flexibility in classroom management and curriculum design.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Risk of stereotyping if not implemented carefully. May require significant changes in traditional teaching methods.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to higher education learners, particularly those from collectivistic backgrounds in individualistic school settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster understanding and respect for diverse cultural values, reduce cultural conflicts, enhance classroom harmony

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cultural misunderstandings and conflicts, promotes inclusivity, enhances student engagement by valuing their cultural background

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust teaching strategies to balance individual and group activities. Provide opportunities for students to share their cultural values and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe reduced conflicts and increased collaboration among students. Gather student feedback on their sense of cultural validation and belonging.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies have shown that understanding and respecting collectivistic values can improve classroom efficiency, task completion, and harmony (e.g., Bridging Cultures Project).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Assigning two children to each classroom task instead of one, increasing choral reading to practice English skills without spotlighting individual students, incorporating group celebrations for individual academic achievements

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Breaking up instructions into short, concrete steps allows learners to pay attention to and remember one instruction at a time. When there are multiple steps, providing written or visual instructions for learners to refer back to is helpful in supporting their Working Memory and Speed of Processing. Combining audio and picture instructions can facilitate the use of both the visual and auditory channels of Working Memory to increase the likelihood of learners carrying out all the instructions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to break down instructions into small, manageable steps. Visual or written aids may be needed. Audio recording equipment may be used.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to prepare instructions in very small steps. Learners may become overly reliant on step-by-step guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with attention challenges or lower English proficiency

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learner attention, reduce working memory load, increase comprehension

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive overload, supports working memory, and improves comprehension by providing manageable, step-by-step guidance. Uses multiple modalities to engage visual and auditory learning channels.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use varied formats (written, audio, visual) to cater to different learning preferences. Adjust step complexity based on individual learner needs. Provide additional scaffolds such as demonstrations or examples.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow multi-step instructions. Track error rates in task completion. Gather feedback on clarity and effectiveness of instructions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive overload, supports working memory, and improves comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher breaks down a complex math problem into smaller, manageable steps, providing both written and verbal instructions for each step.

docs.title: Bright Spaces with Plenty of Light and Air
Description
docs.text: Creating spaces that are colorful, special vents controlled air flow, and having an accessible fan can replicate this if vents aren't available.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of lighting options such as lamps and colored lights. A designated space for reading and relaxation. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing lights.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve engagement, improve productivity, reduce stress

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes relaxation and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred lighting arrangement. Provide a variety of lighting options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that access to natural light and fresh air can increase engagement, improve productivity, and reduce stress. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ask students to bring something from home that makes their classroom feel more like home, such as a photograph, a stuffed animal, or a musical instrument. This provides students with something familiar if they’re feeling down or homesick and represents all families within the classroom.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom space to display items, clear guidelines for items brought from home

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult for students without access to meaningful items, requires sensitivity to diverse family situations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early grade students, students feeling homesick or anxious

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student comfort, build community, represent diverse families

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a sense of belonging, provides comfort, promotes sharing

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students choose items that are meaningful to them.

docs.text: • Observe student behavior and engagement, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that access to nature can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Make a point to check sites that do not agree with your politics. You may discover stories that are wrong — but you'll know what other people are consuming, which will sharpen your own thinking. Be open to the idea that some falsehoods are sincerely held. In spite of all the warnings here, some inaccurate news stories grow out of haste or misinformation rather than pure cynicism. If a news source consistently passes the tests in this guide, support it. Gathering reliable information isn't free. Helping to pay for it aligns the news source's interests with yours.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to diverse news sources and financial resources to support reliable sources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort to find and evaluate diverse perspectives and financial resources to support reliable sources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage learners to seek out diverse perspectives and support reliable news sources.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking and open-mindedness.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and engage with diverse perspectives in news sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners are more likely to consider diverse perspectives and challenge their own assumptions. Enhanced media literacy: Learners become more discerning consumers of news.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Seek out news sources that do not agree with your politics and support reliable news sources financially.

docs.title: Build a Community on Student Voice
Description
docs.text: Building a community on student voice involves creating a classroom environment where students feel safe and empowered to share their thoughts, ideas, and needs. This includes daily check-ins, reflection sheets, sentence stems, and student-led discussions. By amplifying student voices, educators can better understand their needs and build their confidence to speak up and advocate for their learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to create a safe and supportive classroom culture, provide opportunities for student sharing and discussion, and offer support tools for students who struggle to articulate their thoughts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant time investment and careful facilitation to ensure that all voices are heard and respected.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those who may feel marginalized or hesitant to speak up.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, promote self-advocacy, and create a more inclusive and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, promotes self-advocacy, and creates a more inclusive and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various communication styles and needs through different discussion formats and support tools.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Moderation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in discussions, monitor their ability to articulate their needs, and observe their confidence in speaking up.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that amplifying student voices can lead to increased engagement, improved self-advocacy, and a more positive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing daily check-ins where students share their feelings and goals. Using reflection sheets to process learning and behavioral decisions. Providing sentence stems to assist students in expressing their thoughts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Offering students frequent opportunities to share feedback and revise their work fosters a supportive classroom culture and builds relationships. Meaningful feedback contributes to growth, progress, and a sense of connection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires establishing clear guidelines for providing constructive feedback. Demands a classroom environment that values collaboration and mutual respect.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time to facilitate peer feedback sessions. Can be challenging to ensure that feedback is always constructive and supportive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly beneficial for building a strong sense of community within the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a supportive classroom culture, foster relationships among students, promote growth and progress, improve student work through meaningful feedback.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances collaboration and communication skills. Provides opportunities for students to learn from each other. Builds a sense of community and mutual support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual student needs and learning styles. Allows students to provide feedback on topics that resonate with them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Feedback
  • Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and effectiveness of student feedback. Assess student revisions and improvements to their work. Review student reflections on the peer feedback process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Frequent peer feedback builds a strong, supportive classroom culture, fostering collaboration, growth, and a sense of community.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students providing feedback on each other's project proposals. Learners offering suggestions for improving each other's presentations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing dedicated, silent thinking time before pair talk allows students to generate their own ideas and rehearse explanations before being influenced by their partner. This ensures that all students engage in generative thinking processes and are prepared to contribute to the discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires allocating dedicated time for silent thinking and explicitly instructing students to use this time productively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to stay focused during silent thinking time. Requires creating a classroom culture that values and respects silence.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly important for students who are less confident or need more time to process information.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure that all students engage in generative thinking, allow students to formulate their own ideas before being influenced by others, promote deeper processing of information, and encourage active participation in discussions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Gives students time to explore their schema, rehearse explanations, and generate ideas. Prevents them from being overwhelmed by their partner's ideas. Models thoughtful reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The amount of thinking time can be adjusted based on the complexity of the topic and students' needs. Students can be given prompts to guide their thinking.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether students are using the thinking time productively. Listen to the quality of their contributions during pair talk. Ask students to reflect on how the thinking time helped them prepare for the discussion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Dedicated thinking time can improve the quality and depth of student contributions during pair talk, leading to better understanding and retention of information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Create positive learning environments and engaging instruction to help all students achieve success. Implement caring and emotionally supportive classrooms for students with challenging life or school experiences. This involves showing interest in students’ welfare, respecting their perspectives, telling them they can succeed, knowing their academic and social needs, and recognizing their achievements.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time to get to know each student, a commitment to creating a caring and respectful classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires genuine effort and consistency, may not be effective if students are resistant or distrustful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors, and anyone working with learners in a teaching capacity

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster student engagement, improve academic outcomes, create supportive and inclusive classroom environments

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student motivation, improves classroom dynamics, enhances student-teacher relationships, supports social and emotional learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt interactions and support to meet the unique needs and backgrounds of each student.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement in class, track improvements in academic performance, and gather feedback on classroom climate.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases student cooperation and engagement, fosters a welcoming and inclusive school climate, and promotes equity and improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Attend student events, provide personalized feedback, and create opportunities for informal check-ins.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing a chance for teachers to reflect upon their new ideas and consider what they learned from the process is vitally important. Ideally, this reflection should focus less on whether the idea was a success or a failure, but rather on what the teacher learned from the process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for reflection, as well as a supportive and non-judgmental environment. Teachers need to feel safe sharing their thoughts and feelings without fear of criticism.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some teachers may resist self-reflection or find it challenging to be honest with themselves. Requires a long-term commitment to fostering a culture of reflection and continuous improvement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators at all levels, particularly those seeking to improve their teaching practices or reflect on their professional development experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking and self-awareness among teachers, encourage continuous improvement and professional growth, and foster a deeper understanding of teaching practices and their impact on student learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps teachers identify their strengths and weaknesses, learn from their mistakes, and develop strategies for improving their teaching practices. Promotes a more reflective and intentional approach to teaching.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide teachers with a variety of reflection prompts and frameworks to guide their thinking. Allow teachers to choose the reflection methods that work best for them, such as journaling, peer discussions, or video analysis.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track teacher participation in reflection activities. Collect teacher reflections on their teaching practices and professional growth. Evaluate the impact of reflection on student learning outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that teachers who engage in regular self-reflection are more effective and more satisfied with their jobs. Building time for self-reflection fosters a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school provides teachers with release time to participate in peer observation and reflection activities, where they observe each other's teaching practices and provide feedback. Resource: Gerstein, Jackie. "The Educator with a Growth Mindset: A Staff Workshop."

docs.title: Building a Community on Student Voice
Description
docs.text: Building a community on student voice involves creating opportunities for students to share and discuss their thoughts, ensuring that they feel safe to do so. This approach allows teachers to understand students' needs and wants while building their confidence to speak up and advocate for their learning. Strategies include daily check-ins, reflection sheets, sentence stems, starters, and word banks, and student-led discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A supportive classroom environment, structured opportunities for student voice, and strategies to help students articulate their thoughts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to create a supportive classroom environment and facilitate meaningful discussions. Students may initially resist sharing their thoughts or feel uncomfortable speaking up in a group setting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and learning levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote self-advocacy, foster a sense of belonging, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances students' ability to recognize their strengths and needs, encourages them to take responsibility for their learning, and prepares them for success in various environments by promoting independence and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can provide sentence stems, starters, and word banks for students who struggle to articulate their thoughts. They can also provide one-on-one support to students who may be reluctant to share their thoughts in a group setting.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, their willingness to share their thoughts, and their ability to advocate for their learning. Measure students' sense of belonging and their perceptions of safety in the classroom.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that student voice leads to improved academic outcomes, increased engagement, and a more supportive learning environment. Students become more confident, capable, and successful in their learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Daily check-ins can get students engaged in discussions about how they feel, what they want to learn, and what they learned. Reflection sheets can be incorporated into projects, classroom management, or after activities. Sentence stems, starters, and word banks can assist students in expressing their thoughts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A sound wall is a classroom tool that helps educators reinforce the importance of explicitly teaching letter-sound correspondence and supports key aspects of learning to read that are backed by the science of reading. It can include phonemic awareness (the ability to isolate and manipulate the smallest units of sounds within spoken language) and phonics (the ability to make the connection between the sounds of spoken language and the printed letters and words on a page).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom display area, materials for creating the sound wall (e.g., letter cards, picture cards), and explicit instruction on letter-sound correspondences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing maintenance and updates as students learn new letter-sound correspondences. May not be effective if students do not receive explicit instruction on how to use the sound wall.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-5 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce letter-sound correspondence, improve phonemic awareness, and support phonics skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports the development of foundational reading skills by explicitly teaching letter-sound relationships. Enhances phonemic awareness and phonics skills, which are crucial for reading development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sound walls can be adapted to meet the needs of individual students by focusing on specific letter-sound correspondences that they struggle with.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved phonemic awareness, phonics skills, and reading fluency. Increased student engagement and motivation in reading activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Backed by the science of reading, which emphasizes the importance of explicit instruction in letter-sound correspondence for reading development.

docs.title: Building a Supportive Classroom Environment for Mistakes
Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on specific actions to foster a learning environment where mistakes are seen as opportunities. Teachers should avoid simply marking errors without explaining why they're wrong, give students a chance to correct their mistakes and redo their work, and make improvement a significant factor in the evaluation process. In class discussions, respond to mistakes by asking students to explain their reasoning, starting with what is right, and allowing them to seek help from classmates. Additional approaches include showcasing mistakes and lessons learned, holding biweekly class meetings to share mistakes, and teachers sharing their own mistakes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher commitment to changing their approach to mistakes, a classroom culture that values learning over perfection, and structured activities that encourage reflection and sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant shift in mindset and may face resistance from those accustomed to traditional evaluation methods. May take time to establish trust and openness in the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and students of all ages, especially in environments that prioritize perfection and avoid risk-taking.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a classroom culture where mistakes are valued as part of the learning process, fostering risk-taking, self-reflection, and collaborative learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes a growth mindset, reduces anxiety around mistakes, encourages self-reflection and improvement, and builds a supportive learning community.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subject areas and grade levels. Can be tailored to specific learning needs and classroom dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Assess performance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, willingness to take risks, improved problem-solving skills, and positive attitudes toward mistakes. Observable changes in teacher feedback and evaluation practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced learning outcomes, greater creativity, and a more resilient learner mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a 'Mistake of the Week' bulletin board, implementing a 'No-Shame Revision' policy, holding regular class meetings to discuss mistakes and lessons learned, and teachers sharing their own mistakes to model vulnerability and learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The key step is building a trusting community by giving students time to reflect and write about elements of their lives and to share these reflections. Highlighting student voices is essential in making the connections that lay the ground for fruitful discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a commitment to creating inclusive and equitable learning environments. Access to multimedia tools, diverse stories, and expert-developed discussion guides. A willingness to address and mitigate personal biases.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure respectful and productive conversations. May require additional training and support for educators and facilitators. Potential for discomfort or resistance from individuals with differing perspectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels, particularly those working with diverse student populations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create environments conducive to complex conversations about race, foster understanding of diverse perspectives, promote positive racial identity formation, address inequities, and center learners of color in design.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tools and resources for meaningful conversations about race, promotes empathy and understanding, addresses inequities, and centers learners of color in design and development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Content and activities can be adapted to different age groups and cultural contexts. Discussion guides can be tailored to specific topics and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Case Study
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and quality of student discussions, assess changes in attitudes and behaviors related to race and equity, and evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to promote positive racial identity formation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of discussing race in educational settings to promote understanding, empathy, and positive racial identity formation. Culturally responsive teaching practices have been shown to improve student engagement and academic outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school math teacher has students write in journals so he can connect with them and how they're feeling about his class. A literature teacher asks a different student each day to bring in lyrics to a favorite song. Each morning, she plays the selected song and devotes 10 minutes to discussing its lyrics—and ties what students observe about the characters or mood of that song into a class text. Another way to set a trusting atmosphere is to bring people of color who are experts in their field (engineers, poets, or biologists) to speak to the class.

docs.title: Building Community Through Peer Feedback in PBL
Description
docs.text: Building community through peer feedback involves giving students opportunities to frequently share feedback and revise their work. This creates moments to witness growth and progress and allows students to contribute to a strong, supportive classroom culture, building the relationships and connection they need.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured opportunities for peer feedback, clear guidelines for providing constructive feedback, and a classroom environment that values collaboration and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure that feedback is constructive and respectful, and may necessitate additional training or support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, as peer feedback benefits all learners by providing opportunities for reflection, revision, and community building.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To foster a supportive classroom culture, enhance student learning, and promote growth and progress through meaningful peer feedback.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages a supportive and collaborative classroom environment, enhances critical thinking skills, and promotes student ownership of their learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to provide and receive personalized feedback, making the learning experience more relevant and meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Interaction
  • Submission
  • Review
  • Feedback
  • Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, improved quality of work, and a stronger sense of community in the classroom.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that peer feedback enhances student learning, promotes a sense of community, and fosters a more collaborative and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing regular peer review sessions where students provide feedback on each other's drafts, and providing clear guidelines for giving constructive and specific feedback.

docs.title: Building Cultural Competency Skills for School Staff
Description
docs.text: Training staff in behaviors, attitudes, and policies that enable effective cross-cultural relationships. This includes shifting from deficit to strengths thinking, which views families as having significant expertise and resources. Staff should get to know families, local community resources, and create a welcoming school culture.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training resources, cultural competency experts, and a supportive school administration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and commitment from school staff. May be challenging to change ingrained attitudes and biases.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • School staff (teachers, administrators, counselors)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance cross-cultural relationships, improve family-school partnerships, and support student learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters better communication and understanding between school staff and families, leading to more effective partnerships. Encourages a strengths-based approach, valuing the expertise and resources of families.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Training can be tailored to the specific demographics and cultural contexts of the school community.

docs.text:
