  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess staff's cultural competency skills through surveys, observations, and feedback from families. Monitor improvements in family-school partnerships and student outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that culturally competent school staff can build stronger relationships with families, leading to improved student achievement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Prioritizing building relationships with learners can create a supportive and safe learning environment. Instructors greet each learner, and show vulnerability and care. When learners feel valued and supported, they may experience positive emotions that lead to more learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for interaction and check-ins. Intention to build genuine connections with each learner.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time constraints, large class sizes, and reluctance to share personal information can be challenges. May come across as insincere if not genuinely executed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster positive relationships, create a sense of safety and support, increase learner motivation and engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a positive emotional climate, increases motivation, reduces behavioral issues, and improves learner achievement. Fosters feelings of safety, support, and value.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Personalized greetings, individual check-ins, and sharing personal stories can be tailored to the specific needs and interests of learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner participation, positive feedback, reduced behavioral issues, and improved attendance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that strong learner-teacher relationships increase motivation, reduce behavioral issues, and improve learner achievement and classroom climate. This can increase Motivation in adult learners as it incorporates relevant real-world application and enhances learner autonomy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Call-and-response involves the instructor initiating a phrase or word, and the students responding with a pre-determined phrase or word. This technique serves as a cue for students to quiet down and refocus their attention. Examples include: Teacher: "Holy"; Students: "Macaroni"; Teacher: "1, 2, 3, eyes on me"; Students: "1, 2, eyes on you"; Teacher: "The only easy day"; Students: "Was yesterday."

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pre-planning and explicit teaching of the call-and-response phrases. Consistency in using the technique is essential for effectiveness.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lose its effectiveness if overused or if students become disengaged with the chosen phrases. Requires the teacher to be proactive in initiating the call-and-response.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gain student attention, transition between activities, foster engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a fun and engaging way to regain student attention. Helps create a predictable routine that students can easily follow.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The call and response can be customized to fit the grade level, content, or interests of the students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly and consistently students respond to the call-and-response. Monitor the noise level in the classroom before and after using the technique.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Classroom management: Provides a quick and effective way to quiet a noisy class and regain student attention without resorting to negative reinforcement or disciplinary action.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary teacher uses "Hocus Pocus" as the call and the students respond with "Everybody Focus". A high school teacher says, "To infinity," and the students respond with "and beyond."

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dedicated, positive space where learners practice emotional regulation skills. Stocked with tools like emotion charts, fidget toys, and social-emotional books to provide a safe place to recenter and refocus. It supports the ability to self-regulate and return to learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a dedicated space and a variety of emotional regulation tools. Facilitator guidance is needed to help learners use the space effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be stigmatizing if not implemented carefully. Requires clear expectations and guidelines for use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to middle school students, learners with emotional or behavioral difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, reduce reactivity, enhance focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a safe and structured space for managing emotions, reduces reactivity, and enhances focus. Provides tools for self-regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to personalize the space and choose tools that work for them. Flexible options can include different sensory items, books, or activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency and effectiveness of using the calm-down corner. Monitor changes in behavior and emotional regulation over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-regulation: Research indicates that calm-down corners enhance the ability to manage emotions effectively. Enhanced focus: Better emotional management supports improved attention and learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Create a quiet space with soft seating, calming colors, and sensory tools. Teach learners how to use the tools effectively. Source: The Responsive Counselor.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After feeling and expressing emotions related to a mistake, engaging in calm and honest reflection involves asking oneself what happened and what triggered those feelings. This includes examining the facts, identifying potential information gaps, considering impulsive decisions, and exploring whether unresolved emotions from the past were triggered. Evaluating fairness, examining expectations, and attempting to view the situation from another's perspective are crucial. Honesty, however difficult, is essential for growth.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, a willingness to be honest with oneself, and the ability to consider multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for individuals who struggle with self-awareness or have difficulty seeing beyond their own perspective. Could be emotionally taxing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adults who have made a mistake and are looking to learn from it.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Analyze events objectively, identify triggers, and consider different perspectives to gain deeper understanding and promote personal growth.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages critical thinking, promotes empathy, and helps individuals understand their own triggers and biases. Facilitates a more balanced and informed perspective.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustable questions to suit different situations. Can be combined with journaling or discussions with trusted individuals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Perspective-Taking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evidence of increased self-awareness, ability to recognize triggers, and consideration of alternative viewpoints.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved decision-making, stronger relationships, and greater personal growth.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a structured reflection worksheet to guide the process, discussing the situation with a trusted friend or mentor, or practicing active listening to understand other perspectives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using calming auditory input involves managing and altering sounds in the environment to reduce overstimulation and promote relaxation. Strategies include using a quiet voice, monitoring classroom noise with a noise meter, playing white noise (e.g., rain sounds, ocean sounds, a fan), playing quiet, calming music, and using noise-reducing headphones. Reducing or altering auditory input can help children who are easily overwhelmed by sound.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Noise meter, white noise machine or recording, calming music, noise-reducing headphones.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may find certain sounds irritating or distracting. Headphones should be used safely and appropriately.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with auditory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce overstimulation, promote relaxation, manage auditory input

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way to manage auditory input, helping to reduce overstimulation and promote emotional regulation. Offers a means to create a more calming and predictable auditory environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of auditory input can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may prefer white noise, while others may prefer calming music.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after auditory input. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage auditory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that reducing or altering auditory input can decrease overstimulation and promote relaxation in children with auditory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Combining two or more calming sensory strategies can create a more effective and personalized approach to self-regulation. Examples include playing in a tactile bin while listening to white noise on headphones, sitting or lying with a weighted blanket while looking at sensory bottles, chewing gum while working on a fine motor task, and rhythmic rocking with calming breathing techniques. Experimentation and trial and error are key to finding the best combinations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Combination of materials and tools from other calming strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation and experimentation to identify the most effective combinations. May require additional resources and preparation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-regulation, promote relaxation, create personalized sensory experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a more comprehensive and personalized approach to managing sensory input and promoting emotional regulation. Offers flexibility in addressing individual needs and preferences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The combinations of strategies can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Experimentation is encouraged to find the most effective combinations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after using the combination of strategies. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Anecdotal evidence suggests that combining sensory strategies can be more effective than using individual strategies alone.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using calming movement involves engaging in repetitive and rhythmic vestibular input to promote relaxation and self-regulation. Activities include rocking, swaying, gentle swinging, Row, Row, Row Your Boat activities, and gentle back and forth movement on a scooter or therapy ball. These movements can help a child reset when they are overstimulated, overwhelmed, or dealing with tantrums.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Rocking chair, exercise ball, scooter board, therapy ball.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Activities should be safe and appropriate for the child's age and abilities. Supervision may be necessary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote relaxation, provide vestibular input, support self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way to engage the vestibular system, helping to reduce anxiety and promote emotional regulation. Offers a movement-based way to manage sensory experiences and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of movement can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may prefer rocking, while others may prefer swinging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after calming movement. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that repetitive and rhythmic vestibular input can promote relaxation and self-regulation in children with sensory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating repetitive and rhythmic vestibular input, such as rocking, swaying, or gentle swinging, into the learning environment to help learners reset when they are overstimulated, overwhelmed, or dealing with tantrums. This can be achieved by adding rocking chairs or exercise balls to the room.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated space for movement activities. Rocking chairs, exercise balls, or other equipment for vestibular input. Clear guidelines for appropriate movement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some movement activities may be disruptive to other learners. May require additional supervision to ensure safety. Requires careful planning to integrate movement breaks into the learning schedule.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who experience sensory overload, anxiety, or difficulty managing their emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce overstimulation, promote self-regulation, provide vestibular input

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way for learners to regulate their emotions and attention through movement. Can be integrated into various learning activities and settings. Is a low-cost and easily accessible strategy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of movement activities to meet the diverse needs and preferences of learners. Allow learners to choose the type and intensity of movement that works best for them. Provide options for individual or group movement activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in movement activities. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of different movement activities. Track changes in learners' behavior, attention, and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that repetitive and rhythmic movement can reduce anxiety and promote self-regulation. Studies have shown that vestibular input can improve attention and cognitive function.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Employing oral sensory input as a calming strategy involves engaging the mouth to provide sensory experiences that promote self-regulation. Activities include chewing snacks like bagels and fruit leather, using chewy pendants or bracelets, sucking thick smoothies through a straw, and blowing activities like blowing a feather across a table. Chewing provides proprioceptive input, while sucking and blowing can be calming.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Oral sensory snacks (e.g., bagels, fruit leather), chewy pendants or bracelets, straws, feathers or pompoms.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may have allergies or dietary restrictions. Chewing items should be safe and appropriate for the child's age and abilities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-regulation, reduce anxiety, provide proprioceptive input

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides proprioceptive and sensory input that can help to reduce anxiety and promote emotional regulation. Offers an oral way to manage sensory experiences and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of oral sensory input can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may prefer chewing, while others may prefer sucking or blowing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after oral sensory input. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that oral sensory input, such as chewing, can reduce anxiety and promote self-regulation in children with sensory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using proprioceptive input, also known as "heavy work," involves engaging muscles and joints to provide a calming and organizing sensory experience. Activities include squishing play dough or a stress ball, pulling against resistance bands, pushing or moving chairs or desks, climbing, holding a heavy door open, carrying books, and chewing against resistance. These activities stimulate muscles and joints, which can be calming.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Play dough or stress ball, resistance bands, chairs or desks, climbing equipment, heavy books, chewy items.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Activities should be safe and appropriate for the child's age and abilities. Supervision may be necessary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-regulation, provide calming and organizing sensory input

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way to engage the proprioceptive system, helping to reduce anxiety and promote emotional regulation. Offers a physical way to manage sensory experiences and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of heavy work can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may prefer pushing, while others may prefer pulling.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after proprioceptive input. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that proprioceptive input can reduce anxiety and promote self-regulation in children with sensory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing access to calming sensory input through various means, such as tactile bins filled with sand, rice, or beans for tactile stimulation; weighted blankets or stuffed animals for deep pressure; and chewy pendants or snacks for oral sensory input. Other calming auditory input includes playing white noise or calming music.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A collection of sensory tools and activities (e.g., tactile bins, weighted blankets, chewy pendants, noise-reducing headphones). A designated space for sensory activities. Clear guidelines for appropriate use of sensory tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some sensory tools may be expensive or require special maintenance. Some learners may be sensitive or allergic to certain sensory materials. Requires careful monitoring to ensure safety and prevent misuse of sensory tools.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who experience sensory sensitivities, anxiety, or difficulty focusing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce anxiety, promote self-regulation, provide sensory stimulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a variety of sensory experiences that can help learners regulate their emotions and attention. Allows learners to choose the type of sensory input that works best for them. Can be integrated into various learning activities and settings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of sensory tools and activities to meet the diverse needs and preferences of learners. Allow learners to choose the type and intensity of sensory input that works best for them. Provide options for individual or group sensory activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in sensory activities. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of different sensory tools and activities. Track changes in learners' behavior, attention, and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that sensory integration activities can improve attention, reduce anxiety, and promote self-regulation. Studies have shown that weighted blankets can reduce anxiety and improve sleep quality. Chewing can provide calming proprioceptive input and improve focus.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Calming strategies are techniques and methods used to help children manage and reduce feelings of anger and other intense emotions. These strategies are taught and practiced during calm periods, allowing children to build a repertoire of coping mechanisms they can use when needed. The effectiveness of a strategy may vary depending on the child and the intensity of the emotion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A list of calming strategies, time to teach and practice the strategies, support from educators and caregivers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of a strategy may vary depending on the child and the intensity of the emotion. Requires consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children, especially those learning to manage anger and other intense emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional regulation skills, provide coping mechanisms, reduce the intensity of anger, promote self-soothing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a range of practical methods for managing emotions, supports self-regulation, enhances emotional awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different strategies can be tried to find the most effective ones for each child. Strategies can be adapted to suit individual preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's use of calming strategies during periods of emotional distress. Monitor improvements in their ability to manage and reduce feelings of anger.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional literacy and self-regulation. Provides children with tools to manage their emotions more effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples of calming strategies include taking a cool drink, finding a quiet space, talking to a favorite teddy, taking deep breaths, squeezing a fidget, or taking a mindfulness break.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Calming strategy cards provide learners with reminders of emotional regulation strategies, such as squeezing a fidget or taking a mindfulness break, to use when feelings escalate or when they are losing control. These strategies can become part of students' long-term memory and support their emotional self-regulation through repeated use. When learners are calm, instructors should discuss feelings of anger and different options that are available for cooling down. Learners choose what strategies might suit them best, and practice these strategies during periods of mild to acute anger.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A set of pre-made or custom-made calming strategy cards. Requires discussion and practice to effectively implement strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness may vary depending on the learner's emotional state and the appropriateness of the chosen strategy. Requires consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily designed for children but adaptable for all ages who struggle with emotional regulation, including learners with emotional and behavioral disorders

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-regulation, manage emotions, build awareness of calming strategies, support emotional well-being

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers visual and tangible prompts for self-regulation. Allows learners to identify personalized calming strategies. Supports emotional awareness and coping skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select and customize cards with strategies that work best for them. Blank cards can be added for personalized strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and effectiveness of learners using the cards to manage their emotions. Track the strategies that learners find most helpful.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes self-regulation and emotional awareness, which can reduce outbursts and improve overall well-being. Fosters independence in managing emotions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A learner uses a card to remind themselves to take deep breaths when feeling anxious during a test. A child uses a card to find a quiet space when feeling overwhelmed in a crowded environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using tactile input to provide calming sensory experiences involves engaging the sense of touch to reduce anxiety and promote relaxation. Activities include running hands through a tactile bin filled with materials like sand, rice, or beans, and applying deep pressure through hugs, weighted blankets, or weighted stuffed animals. Squishing with a pillow or beanbag chair can also provide full-body calming sensory input.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tactile materials (e.g., sand, rice, beans), weighted blankets or stuffed animals, pillows or beanbag chairs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may have sensitivities or aversions to certain textures. The effectiveness may vary based on individual preferences and needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce anxiety, promote relaxation, provide sensory input for self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides calming and grounding sensory input, which can help to reduce anxiety and promote emotional regulation. Offers a tactile way to manage sensory experiences and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of tactile input can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may prefer the texture of sand, while others may prefer deep pressure.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after tactile input. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that tactile input, such as deep pressure, can reduce anxiety and promote relaxation in children with sensory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Managing visual input involves altering the visual environment to reduce overstimulation and promote relaxation. Strategies include dimming lights, limiting visual distractions by creating a clear, clutter-free workspace, using visual dividers or study carrels, providing repetitive visual input like fish tanks or sensory bottles, and using a visual picture schedule. Decreasing visual stimulation can help children who are easily overwhelmed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dimmer switches, storage containers, visual dividers or study carrels, fish tank, sensory bottles, visual picture schedule.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may have specific visual needs that must be accommodated. Visual schedules must be clear and easy to understand.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with visual sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce overstimulation, promote relaxation, manage visual input

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way to manage visual input, helping to reduce overstimulation and promote emotional regulation. Offers a means to create a more calming and predictable visual environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The type of visual input can be tailored to individual preferences and needs. Some children may benefit from sensory bottles, while others may prefer visual dividers.

docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after changes in visual input. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage visual input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that reducing visual stimulation can decrease overstimulation and promote relaxation in children with visual sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners draw a dot card and recreate the arrangement on a large, blank dot card using counters. This helps them count and recognize various arrangements of quantities. Start with small numbers like 1-3 for beginners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dot cards, large blank dot card, counters.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require one-on-one instruction or facilitation for learners who struggle with counting. The game's effectiveness relies on having physical materials readily available.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-K to 1st Grade learners who are beginning to learn subitizing.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop number sense, recognize quantity arrangements, improve counting skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a hands-on approach to understanding number arrangements. Enhances number sense by associating physical representation with numerical value. Allows learners to work at their own pace and build confidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable by adjusting the range of numbers used. The large, blank dot card can be modified to different sizes to suit individual learner needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Case studies involve the use of real-life situations that have occurred. Cases come in many forms, from a simple 'what would you do in this situation?' question to a detailed description of a situation with accompanying data to analyze. Most case-based assignments ask learners to answer open-ended questions or develop a solution to an open-ended problem.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Real-life cases that reflect actual situations, facilitator to guide the learning process

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Cases may not be fully representative of all situations, and success depends on the facilitator's ability to guide the learning process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All employee levels in corporate training settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply knowledge to real-life situations, develop problem-solving skills, foster critical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to learn from examples, develop problem-solving skills, and foster critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Case studies can be tailored to reflect the learner's own working environment.

docs.text: • Assess the learner's answers to open-ended questions and solutions to open-ended problems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learning is more effective as many people learn better from examples than from basic principles.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This principle emphasizes sharing power with students and families in the design of learning experiences. It involves activities like spectrum activities, where students express their agreement or disagreement with statements about their school experience by physically moving to different parts of the room. It also includes fishbowl experiences, where students discuss their experiences in school while teachers and school leaders listen. This approach aims to center students as co-designers of their learning, empowering them and giving them a greater voice in their education. The focus is on breaking precedent and allowing students to shape their own learning experiences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to relinquish control and trust students' perspectives, as well as resources for facilitating student-led activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to implement if students are not accustomed to having a voice in their education. Requires careful facilitation to ensure that all students have the opportunity to participate and that their voices are heard.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and school teams seeking to create more student-centered learning environments and involve students in decision-making processes.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, increase student voice, foster co-design of learning experiences, and promote student engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, promotes a sense of ownership over learning, and fosters a more collaborative and equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific activities and prompts can be tailored to the age and interests of the students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure student perceptions of their voice and influence in school decisions, track student engagement in co-design activities, and assess the impact of student-led initiatives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, a greater sense of ownership over learning, and a more collaborative and equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • CityBridge has used a “spectrum activity,” in which students vote with their feet when describing their experience of school. During the Breakthrough Design Fellowship, they designed and facilitated a fishbowl conversation for a group of older students who attended “opportunity schools” (also known as alternative schools). Students became the center of focus, while the adults who teach them had to just listen.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: App for students to practice basic math. The app, as the name suggests, comes with an interface offering a chalkboard to go with the math practice. It helps kids to learn all the basic math facts corresponding to addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in a quickly-engaging manner. It generates math practice in two different modes: answer mode and flashcard mode. While the first one allows entering answers and getting feedback, the second one allows verbal answering.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Chalkboard Math app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for advanced math topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice and develop skills in basic math facts (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division).

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback, allows for verbal answering, and engages students through a chalkboard interface.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Generates math practice in two different modes: answer mode and flashcard mode.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track scores and completion rates in the app.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Offers math practice with immediate feedback, improving basic math skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students using the app to practice math facts in flashcard mode or answer mode, receiving immediate feedback.

docs.text: Challenge Based Learning (CBL) provides an efficient and effective framework for learning while solving real-world challenges. docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Solve real-world problems, foster collaboration and communication, promote lifelong learning skills, develop sustainable solutions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Real-world relevance, collaborative environment, hands-on learning, fosters lifelong learning skills, promotes sustainable solutions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Challenges can be adapted to learner interests and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Engage

  • Act

  • Solution development

docs.text: • Provides an efficient and effective framework for learning while solving real-world challenges (The Challenge Institute).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Challenge Based Learning (CBL) is a customizable framework that provides an efficient and effective way for learners to solve real-world challenges. It fuels collaboration to identify big ideas, ask thoughtful questions, and identify, investigate, and act on challenges. CBL aims to help learners gain deep subject area knowledge and develop the skills necessary to thrive in an ever-changing world. The CBL framework includes three interrelated phases: Engage, Investigate, and Act.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to real-world challenges, collaborative tools and resources, and a supportive learning environment that encourages inquiry and problem-solving.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant time commitment and may necessitate a shift in traditional teaching practices to fully integrate the framework.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and educational levels, especially those seeking to apply knowledge to solve real-world problems.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop deep subject area knowledge, enhance problem-solving skills, foster collaboration, and encourage lifelong learning through real-world challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to problem-solving, fosters collaboration and critical thinking, and enhances engagement by connecting learning to real-world issues.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The framework is customizable and adaptable to different subjects and learning environments, allowing learners to tailor their experiences to specific interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Team-Based Inquiry
  • Evidence-Based Reasoning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of solutions developed, depth of subject area knowledge demonstrated, and effectiveness of collaboration and communication skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that CBL enhances learning outcomes, promotes critical thinking, and prepares learners for success in an ever-changing world.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Addressing health challenges by developing sustainable solutions, focusing on local and global challenges to engage learners in creating solutions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Challenge the Text is a strategy that encourages students to critically examine texts by asking and answering their own text-dependent questions. This process involves taking multiple perspectives and uncovering assumptions and biases within the text. By challenging what is said, students develop agency and enter their voices into the textual discourse. The strategy can be used during or after reading, and it helps students understand what is not included in the text, make inferences, and support their analysis with textual evidence. Students should be given prompts and scaffolding to generate questions. The strategy places an anti-bias lens on the literacy experience by raising issues related to power within social contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Central text (literary or informational), prompts and scaffolding for generating critical questions, time for students to generate and respond to questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may need significant support generating critical questions. May require careful facilitation to ensure a safe space for discussing sensitive topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage critical thinking, examine the validity of a text, develop agency, improve text comprehension, uncover biases, support marginalized perspectives

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking, gives voice to marginalized perspectives, improves comprehension, and encourages engagement with the text.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentence starters for English language learners to structure effective questions. Flexible implementation during shared or independent reading.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality and depth of student-generated questions. Ability to provide evidence-based responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports critical literacy practices and empowers students to question and analyze texts from multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using lights with different colors to create a fresh perspective. Change allows for a mental break, and lighting can do a great deal to alter a space depending on the activity. Bringing in lamps from home to create softer lighting during reading times can be an adaptation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of lighting options such as lamps and colored lights. A designated space for reading and relaxation. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing lights.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Alter mood, reduce stress, promote relaxation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes relaxation and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred lighting arrangement. Provide a variety of lighting options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that lighting can affect mood, behavior, and learning outcomes. Studies have shown that natural light is linked to more productive performance, as well as greater health and well-being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves having students analyze characters' feelings in literature to improve their self-awareness and emotional recognition. Students identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings of characters to connect literary analysis with emotional intelligence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a book with strong emotional content, visual aids (optional), and a teacher to facilitate discussion. Can be integrated into regular reading sessions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the selected literature and the teacher's ability to guide discussion. Some students may struggle with emotional inference or expressing their feelings.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotion recognition, develop empathy, improve inferential skills, connect emotions to characters' actions and motivations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops social-emotional skills, encourages critical thinking, connects literature to emotional understanding, promotes empathy by understanding characters' perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and reading levels by selecting appropriate texts and adjusting the complexity of questions. Can be modified to focus on specific emotions or social situations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Class Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, analyze their responses to questions about characters' emotions, and assess their ability to connect emotions to characters' actions and motivations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of social-emotional intelligence and enhances reading comprehension. Literature provides a safe context to explore complex emotions and social situations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students create character profiles to help them form a deeper understanding of a book’s characters. This can involve creating lists of adjectives, illustrating characters, reflecting on character motivations, and describing how characters make them feel.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for creating character profiles, such as paper, pencils, and art supplies, and a list of profiling prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires structured activities to be effective. Some students may struggle with character analysis. Requires careful planning and management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-5 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop a deeper understanding of characters, enhance critical thinking, and promote reflection on character motivations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for students to analyze characters, reflect on their motivations, and develop empathy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose the characters they want to profile. Provide a variety of profiling activities to cater to different learning styles and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Demonstration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student-created character profiles to assess their understanding of characters. Monitor the depth and quality of student reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Develops a deeper understanding of characters, enhances critical thinking, and promotes reflection on character motivations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students select four key events from a novel and create scrapbook entries representing a character's inner thoughts, feelings, and experiences during each event. They use drawings, images, magazine cutouts, and quotes to share insights. Entries can be shared and discussed with peers, or transposed to social media platforms. This activity promotes relationship skills by encouraging students to unpack relationships within the text, examine how these relationships interact, and consider how people handle similar situations in different ways. This analysis celebrates creativity and visual literacy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Completed reading of a novel. Materials for scrapbooking (e.g., paper, markers, images, quotes). Option to use social media platforms.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires creativity and visual literacy skills. Success depends on students' willingness to share and discuss their personal insights.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build relationship skills, enhance understanding of character relationships, promote creativity, and encourage visual literacy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers an interactive way to engage students in understanding characters and relationships. Celebrates creativity and visual literacy. Builds social media skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Events and characters can be selected by students. Format of scrapbook entries (e.g., drawings, images, quotes) can be chosen to match individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess scrapbook entries, quality of discussions, and depth of analysis of character relationships.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances relationship skills and understanding of character interactions. Celebrates creativity and promotes a deeper understanding of how people handle situations differently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Selecting scenes featuring fights, romantic connections, or turning points from a novel. Creating Instagram posts from the perspective of a character.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A simple classroom exercise to demonstrate the effectiveness of spaced practice using a chart. Learners copy a chart from memory, highlight what they recall, and then complete the chart using notes or textbooks, highlighting the new additions. This process is repeated over several days, demonstrating increased recall and retention. The key is to have a discussion with students about why they should use this sort of learning strategy over cramming the night before the test. Also, like most of the learning strategies, pointing out to students that these steps can easily be applied to a wide range of topics across most classes. This isn’t a strategy that is specific to psychology class.  It works with math, English, history, science, etc.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creating a chart with relevant information. Minimal class time spread over several days. Student commitment to repeating the exercise.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial preparation of the chart. Effectiveness relies on student participation and reflection. May not be suitable for all learners or subjects.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school and college students across various subjects, particularly effective for demonstrating spaced practice benefits.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Demonstrate effectiveness of spaced practice, improve recall, enhance retention, promote self-assessment, encourage application across subjects

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a tangible demonstration of spaced practice effectiveness. Enhances self-assessment and metacognitive skills. Promotes application across different subjects.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The chart can be adapted to various topics and subjects. Learners can adjust the timing and frequency of practice sessions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the amount of information recalled over successive practice sessions. Compare the amount of yellow highlighting in the charts from day to day.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Demonstrates the benefits of spaced practice over cramming. Encourages students to adopt effective learning strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a chart to outline Jean Piaget’s theory of cognitive development in AP Psychology classes.

docs.text: After giving instructions, check for understanding by asking related questions and observing compliance.
