docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognizing and addressing unconscious bias involves acknowledging its existence, understanding how it impacts decision-making, and implementing strategies to mitigate its effects. This includes personal self-awareness, leadership trials, creating blended teams, measuring change, watching triggers, ongoing training, managing cultural change, and leveraging technology.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training, self-reflection, data collection, and analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and commitment, may be difficult to measure its impact.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals and organizations aiming to promote diversity, equity, and inclusion

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase awareness of unconscious bias, mitigate its effects on decision-making, promote fair and equitable practices

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps to reduce discrimination, promotes fair and equitable treatment, increases diversity and inclusion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Individuals can focus on identifying and addressing their specific biases. Organizations can tailor strategies to their unique contexts and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased diversity in hiring and promotion, reduced incidents of discrimination, improved employee satisfaction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that addressing unconscious bias can lead to more diverse and inclusive workplaces. This can result in improved innovation, creativity, and overall organizational performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Checklists can be used to measure and document student learning by tracking whether learners are accomplishing specific tasks or expectations. A checklist is the least complex type of scoring rubric: it lets a rater indicate whether an expected component is present, but not the quality of that component — essentially a pass/fail judgment per item rather than a graded one. This makes checklists quick and easy to administer, but limited in the feedback they can give — useful mainly for minor assignments or drafts, where a simple presence/absence check is enough. When feedback about the quality of work matters, a rating scale or rubric (which adds a quality judgment to the same basic structure) is the more appropriate tool — see Rubrics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear learning objectives, well-defined criteria aligned to standards, and a rating scale with detailed descriptors.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not constructed carefully, checklists may be too generic and not provide specific enough feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners. Can be adapted for use in various subjects and skill-based areas.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Track task completion, document learning progress, provide a structured assessment tool

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear expectations, supports self-assessment, offers specific feedback, and aids in monitoring progress. Supports a shared understanding of learning targets between educators and students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Checklists can be customized with different scales (e.g., 4-point, 7-point), criteria, and descriptors to align with specific learning objectives and standards.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track alignment between self-assessments and teacher evaluations. Monitor improvements in performance over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates checklists enhance assessment and self-regulation skills.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Rubrics — the more informative next step when quality, not just presence, needs to be assessed

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Linn, R. L., & Miller, M. D. (2005). Measurement and assessment in teaching (9th ed.). Pearson.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher-made assessments. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Checklists and rubrics provide clear criteria for self- and peer-assessments. They help learners understand expectations, monitor their progress, and take charge of revisions, which increases motivation and fosters a growth mindset. Checklists are distilled and simplified versions of rubrics, making them more accessible. Learners evaluate specific features of their work, increasing self-awareness of conventions, and peers work collaboratively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires well-defined criteria and a structured format for checklists or rubrics. Implementation may involve modeling, pair work, and whole-class discussions. Digital tools like Goobric can facilitate self- and peer-assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If criteria are too complex or vague, learners may struggle to apply them effectively. Some students may view checklists as a compliance task rather than a meaningful opportunity for reflection. Requires consistent guided practice for learners to effectively use the checklist to annotate their writing for revision.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 learners, particularly useful in writing workshops

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Set clear criteria for self-assessment, encourage self-regulation, increase motivation, foster a growth mindset, improve writing conventions, enhance peer collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes metacognition, self-regulation, and a growth mindset. Enhances self-awareness of writing conventions and peer collaboration. Checklists simplify rubrics, making them more accessible and usable.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Checklists can be adapted with visuals and simplified language for younger learners. Criteria can be tailored to specific learning objectives and individual student needs. Flexible formats allow for individual, peer, or group assessments.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner-identified areas for improvement to gauge self-awareness. Compare self-assessments with instructor assessments to evaluate accuracy. Analyze depth and specificity of learner feedback to assess comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-assessment: Providing simplified checklists helps learners monitor their progress toward a bigger goal. Enhanced peer feedback: Clear rubrics for students to assess their own and their peers' work promotes metacognition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a middle school classroom, students use a personal narrative checklist with graphics to evaluate their writing pieces and identify areas for improvement. A Google Chrome extension, Goobric, allows for rubrics to be set for students' self- and peer- assessment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Children's literature for math instruction is a strategy in which stories, picture books, or narrative texts are used to introduce mathematical ideas, contexts, or discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A text with a meaningful connection to the mathematical idea.
  • Follow-up discussion, modeling, or problem solving that makes the math explicit.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Story context alone does not guarantee mathematical clarity.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase engagement and make mathematical ideas more concrete and discussable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Read or revisit a text that contains a relevant quantitative or spatial situation.
  • Identify the mathematical structure in the story.
  • Extend into representation, explanation, or problem solving.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Real-World Math
  • Contextualization

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Whitin, D. J., & Whitin, P. (2004). New visions for linking literature and mathematics. NCTM.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating children's literature, especially multicultural literature, into math instruction to enhance engagement and comprehension. By using storybooks that cover math topics, instructors can supplement in-class learning, create connections to real-world contexts, and motivate learners. This approach can be extended through digital libraries or home lending systems to support reading with families.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a collection of children's literature that covers math topics. Digital versions can supplement a physical library. Requires time to integrate these books into lesson plans.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the literature. Requires careful selection to ensure alignment with learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Introduce math concepts, reinforce ideas, improve engagement, apply skills in real-world contexts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation through relatable stories, connects abstract concepts to real-world situations, and allows for cultural exploration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various math topics and cultural contexts. Digital libraries can provide a range of books catering to different learner interests and reading levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Demonstration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement, assess comprehension through discussions and activities related to the literature, and measure improvements in math skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Motivates learners by connecting math to stories and culture. Enhances understanding of abstract concepts through real-world connections.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using multicultural literature to teach math, where students practice counting and interpreting data while motivated by curiosity about other cultures. See the books listed in the provided text for inspiration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Choice-based activities during quiet time give students the power to select their preferred independent tasks, enhancing engagement and promoting a sense of control. Options can range from academic tasks like reading, writing, or unfinished classwork to relaxing activities such as doodling, playing solitary games, or meditating. The teacher’s role is to provide the options, model the routines, and ensure a quiet environment, while refraining from direct interaction with students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of quiet activities, clear explanation of rules and expectations, consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires planning and preparation, may be challenging to manage student choices, requires consistent reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote student engagement, encourage self-regulation, provide a sense of control, enhance focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, promotes self-regulation, provides a sense of control, enhances focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activity choices can be tailored to student interests and needs. The number of choices can be adjusted based on student capabilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and engagement during quiet time. Track the types of activities students choose.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Offering choice-based activities during quiet time can improve student engagement, promote self-regulation, and enhance focus, leading to a more positive and productive learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Choice boards offer learners options for how they demonstrate their learning, increasing engagement and ownership. They present an alternative to standard assessments, empowering learners to choose how they show mastery of a topic and providing instructors with a variety of ways to check for understanding. Choice boards can be structured as a grid or table with various tasks or activities aligned to specific learning objectives. Learners select which tasks to complete, often with a requirement to complete a certain number or type of tasks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and alignment of tasks to learning objectives. Clear instructions and expectations must be provided. Access to necessary resources and materials for completing tasks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel overwhelmed by too many choices. May require more instructor time to prepare and assess. Requires clear communication to ensure learners understand expectations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12, higher education, and professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, provide autonomy in learning, assess understanding in multiple ways, differentiate instruction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation by giving learners a sense of control over their learning. Accommodates different learning styles and preferences. Provides instructors with diverse assessment data. Encourages self-directed learning and responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual learner needs and interests. Difficulty levels can be adjusted. Different modalities (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) can be incorporated into the tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe engagement levels and task completion rates. Analyze the quality and depth of learner work on chosen tasks. Gather feedback from learners about their experiences with the choice board.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that choice boards increase learner motivation, engagement, and ownership of learning (references to research not provided in text). They allow for differentiated instruction and provide multiple pathways to demonstrate understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a middle school English class, students can choose to develop a movie trailer, draft diary entries, or create podcast episodes to demonstrate their analysis of characters in a novel. In a third-grade class, a homework choice board might include options such as finding examples of syllable types in books, reading high-frequency words to a family member, or practicing words on an online app.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Giving learners more manageable chunks of information can help ensure they’re able to continue to engage in a meaningful way when dealing with sustained attention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of formats to present directions and instructions. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources and prep. Some learners may not have a problem with long strings of directions and instructions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who experience anxiety, sensory overload, or difficulty transitioning between activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve sustained attention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Breaks down tasks in more manageable steps.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred direction format. Provide a variety of presentation options. Allow learners to ask questions along the way.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Breaks long strings of directions to maintain attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Breaking down directions into smaller, more manageable sections to support sustained attention. This strategy involves providing information in bite-sized pieces to prevent overwhelm and improve engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of student's attentional capacity, careful planning of instruction, and clear communication

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure logical flow, might not address underlying attentional challenges, and some students may prefer the full set of directions upfront

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who struggle with sustained attention and following lengthy directions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve sustained attention, reduce cognitive overload, and increase comprehension of multi-step instructions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces the amount of information processed at once, provides clear stopping points, supports memory, and enhances engagement

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The size of the chunks can be adjusted based on individual student needs and attention spans. Use of visual cues and reminders can be incorporated.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student's ability to follow directions when presented in smaller chunks. Assess comprehension through task completion and verbal feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that chunking information supports working memory and improves task completion for students with attentional challenges.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Stand in a circle and try to count off as quickly as possible all the way around the circle. Start with 1, then the student on your right says '2,' and the student on their right says '3,' and so on until the count comes back to you. Challenge the kids to go as quickly and seamlessly as possible. When everyone can do this proficiently, count by twos, fives, tens, or threes. You can also start at numbers greater than 1, or try counting backward.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Open space where students can form a circle.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students who are shy or have difficulty counting quickly may feel pressured.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce counting skills, promote teamwork, improve sequencing skills, enhance quick thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simple and engaging activity that fosters teamwork. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the starting number or the skip counting pattern based on student skill level. Count backwards to challenge students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students' accuracy and speed in counting. Observe their ability to work seamlessly as a team.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can reinforce counting skills and promote teamwork through a fun and engaging activity. Supports active participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The class counts off in a circle. Once proficient, they count by threes, starting from 5.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: End each week with a group circle where students discuss different topics and share their feelings. Students can use Circle Time to discuss conflict, repair fractured relationships, and connect with their emotions. Start with "What makes you happy?" and add other emotions as students become familiar with the format.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for circle time, facilitation skills to guide discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be uncomfortable for some students to share, requires careful facilitation to avoid conflict escalation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve emotional literacy, build community, promote conflict resolution

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe space for sharing, promotes emotional awareness, fosters empathy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students share their own feelings and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and emotional expression, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Circle time can improve emotional literacy and build community.

docs.title: Circulate and Listen During Pair Talk
Description
docs.text: Actively circulating and listening to pair discussions allows teachers to monitor student engagement, reinforce expectations, offer support, and gauge the success of the thinking process. This provides valuable information for informing future instruction and addressing misconceptions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be actively present and engaged during pair talk activities, moving around the classroom and listening to conversations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires balancing monitoring with allowing students to have private conversations. Teachers must avoid being intrusive or disruptive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, essential for effective implementation of pair talk activities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement and understanding, provide targeted support, reinforce expectations, and gather information for informing future instruction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to check for understanding, address misconceptions, provide encouragement, and highlight good ideas. Ensures that students stay on task and engage fully in the discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can focus their attention on students who need the most support or who have specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of student engagement and participation. Listen for evidence of understanding or misconceptions. Note the types of questions students are asking and the connections they are making.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Active circulation and listening can improve the effectiveness of pair talk activities, leading to better student understanding and engagement.

docs.title: Clarification of Vocabulary, Symbols, and Language Structures
Description
docs.text: Supporting learners to construct meaning from words, symbols, and numbers using different representations. This involves providing clear definitions, explanations, and examples of complex terms and concepts. Clarifying language structures helps learners understand the relationships between ideas and improve comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear and concise explanations, visual aids, glossaries, and translations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of vocabulary and concepts to ensure relevance and appropriateness. Some learners may find simplified language to be condescending.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with language disabilities, English language learners, and learners encountering new or complex material

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, enhance vocabulary acquisition, support understanding of complex concepts, clarify language structures

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding of complex terms and concepts. Supports vocabulary acquisition. Improves comprehension of language structures.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide definitions, examples, and visual aids to clarify vocabulary and concepts. Use simplified language and sentence structures. Offer translations and glossaries for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner understanding of vocabulary and concepts through quizzes, tests, and discussions. Monitor learner use of clarified language structures in their own writing and speaking. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of clarification techniques.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension: Research indicates that clarifying vocabulary and language structures can significantly improve comprehension, particularly for learners with language disabilities and English language learners.

docs.title: Clarify Vocabulary, Symbols, and Language Structures
Description
docs.text: Constructing meaning from words, symbols, and numbers using different representations ensures that learners understand the language of the content. This includes providing definitions, examples, and visual aids to clarify vocabulary. It also involves breaking down complex sentences and mathematical notation into simpler, more accessible formats. This strategy helps make learning materials more accessible to a wider range of learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful analysis of the language used in learning materials. Instructors need to be prepared to provide additional support and clarification as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more preparation time and resources. Some learners may find too much simplification patronizing. It's essential to strike a balance between clarity and challenge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly English language learners, learners with learning disabilities, or those new to a subject; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, reduce cognitive load, support vocabulary development, promote accessible learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports comprehension by ensuring that learners understand the language of the content, reduces cognitive load by breaking down complex information, supports vocabulary development by providing definitions and examples, and promotes accessible learning by catering to diverse linguistic needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide vocabulary lists and glossaries tailored to learners' needs. Use visual aids and graphic organizers to clarify complex concepts. Offer translations and simplified explanations for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of vocabulary and concepts through quizzes or discussions. Track improvements in comprehension and application of knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that clear and accessible language can enhance comprehension and reduce cognitive load for all learners. Studies show that vocabulary instruction can improve reading comprehension and academic achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing a glossary of key terms at the beginning of a chapter. Using visual aids to explain mathematical concepts. Breaking down complex sentences into simpler phrases.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Clarifying involves identifying and resolving areas of uncertainty in a text or problem. This includes unfamiliar vocabulary, complex sentence structures, and difficult concepts. In math, this entails identifying facts that are known and determining what information is still needed to solve the problem.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to resources for clarifying vocabulary and concepts, such as dictionaries or online tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources and support for learners with significant gaps in knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially English Language Learners (ELLs) and those who struggle with complex texts or problems.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, resolve uncertainties, and support vocabulary development.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners identify and resolve uncertainties, improving comprehension and vocabulary development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different levels of support based on learners' needs, such as glossaries or simplified explanations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, increased vocabulary knowledge, and better problem-solving accuracy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners overcome barriers to understanding, leading to increased comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing a glossary of terms or simplifying complex sentence structures in a text.

docs.title: Class Anchor Charts or Plus/Delta Chart
Description
docs.text: After a formative assessment or test the class may have a discussion about what problems on the assignment caused concerns. The class then reflects on the processes used to find the answer and have a thorough discussion about the mathematical process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Formative assessments, time for class discussion, and a way for students to share their thinking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to facilitate the class discussion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reflect on problems, discuss mathematical processes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to reflect on problems, provides a way for students to discuss the mathematical process, and encourages students to share their thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can have the class discuss what problems on the assignment caused concerns. They can also have the class reflect on the processes used to find the answer.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding, increased student communication, and deeper reflection on learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of class anchor charts and plus/delta charts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher has the class discuss what problems on a formative assessment caused concerns. The class reflects on the processes used to find the answer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Class books involve students creating individual pages that are compiled into a single book. This process combines shared writing with individual contributions, offering an audience for student work and encouraging revision and editing. The format invites students to create representations of their ideas, promoting mathematical communication.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Shared writing activity, materials for creating individual pages (paper, art supplies), and a way to compile the pages into a book.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time to create and compile the pages. The quality of the book depends on the engagement and effort of each student.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for elementary and middle school levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide an authentic audience, encourage revision and editing, promote mathematical communication, and foster individual creativity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a sense of audience, encourages revision and editing, invites creative representations, and promotes mathematical communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students create individual pages based on their understanding and interpretations, allowing for diverse representations of the material.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and accuracy of individual pages, looking for clear explanations and effective representations of concepts. Evaluate the overall coherence and completeness of the class book.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances engagement, promotes revision and editing, and provides an authentic audience for student work.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher prompted students to create and illustrate a word problem using fractional parts of a set of 24. Each student's work became a page in the class book.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Playing classical music (Bach, not Mahler) at a low volume when learners enter the room to set a professional tone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to a music player and classical music selections. Teachers should monitor student reactions and adjust the volume as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may dislike classical music or find it distracting. May not be effective for all classroom environments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a calm and professional atmosphere in the classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Sets a positive tone, reduces anxiety, and promotes a focused environment. Can be easily implemented with minimal effort.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific music genre can be adjusted based on student preferences, but classical music is recommended for its calming effects.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior upon entering the classroom. Monitor the overall atmosphere and noise levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a calm and professional classroom environment. Reduces anxiety and promotes a focused atmosphere.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Playing classical music (e.g., Bach) at a low volume when students enter the room sets a professional and calming tone. The music helps create a focused atmosphere and can reduce disruptive behavior. However, it's essential to monitor student reactions to ensure they are comfortable with the music.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to music and playback equipment, selection of appropriate music, monitoring of student reactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all students, some students may find it distracting, requires careful monitoring and adjustment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a calm and focused classroom environment, reduce disruptive behavior, set a professional tone

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a calming and focused environment, sets a professional tone, reduces the need for verbal commands.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Music selection can be adjusted based on student preferences and cultural backgrounds. Volume can be adjusted to ensure comfort.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and mood upon entering the classroom. Monitor classroom noise levels before and after playing music.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Playing classical music can improve classroom management by creating a calming and focused environment, reducing disruptive behavior and promoting a professional tone.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classification tasks involve sorting objects or concepts into categories based on shared properties. Learners develop and justify their classification schemes, demonstrating their understanding of the properties and relationships between objects or concepts. These tasks can be adapted for various subjects, from classifying rocks based on observable properties to classifying candies based on their attributes. Tasks may include binary classification systems or classification trees, depending on the complexity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Objects to be classified, classification criteria, tools for observation (e.g., magnifying glass), recording sheets

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a variety of materials. Success depends on the clarity of the classification criteria.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners across various subject areas, particularly science and mathematics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop observation skills, enhance analytical thinking, improve understanding of properties, promote justification of reasoning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops analytical and reasoning skills. Encourages observation and critical thinking. Adapts to different content areas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various objects and concepts. Supports different classification schemes. Can be simplified or made more complex based on the learner's level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of the classification scheme, justification of the scheme, accuracy of observations

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced observation and analytical skills. Better understanding of properties and relationships.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Classifying Rocks (KDE): Learners develop classification schemes based on observable properties in rocks. Classifying Candy (NYSED): Learners develop binary classification systems using a selection of candies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classroom checklists are visual aids used to help students, teachers, and parents stay on track with various tasks and assignments. By adding visual aids such as icons and different colors for each point, the checklist can become more memorable and easier to follow. Whether it's for classroom duties or semester assignments, these checklists help keep everyone organized and ensure that nothing is missed. Checklists can also support staff members by providing tips and best practices in a clear, visual format.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to design tools and information. Implementation involves regular updates and use. May require training in organization and planning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overly complex checklists can be confusing. Ineffective use of visuals can hinder understanding. Requires attention to detail and accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, teachers, students, parents, and staff members in various educational settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Keep students on track, help teachers manage tasks, improve organization, enhance memory, provide clear instructions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances organization and memory. Provides clear instructions. Makes tasks easier to remember and follow.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different subjects, tasks, and grade levels. Design elements can be adjusted based on the content and audience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the clarity and effectiveness of the checklist. Assess student compliance and completion rates. Track improvements in organization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-designed classroom checklists have been shown to improve organization and compliance. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include checklists with icons and different colors for each point, and checklists for staff members with tips and best practices. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating classroom checklists.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Optimizing classroom design (noise levels, temperature, seating arrangement) can minimize distractions and improve learning. Strategies include building schools that buffer external noise, maintaining a comfortable temperature range (68–74°F), and using flexible seating arrangements matched to the task at hand. Factors that can interfere with learning are noise, temperature, and seating arrangement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Noise-buffering materials, thermostat control, and flexible seating options. Requires awareness of noise levels, temperature, and seating arrangement effects on learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Difficulty in controlling noise levels in some environments. Requires investment in materials and equipment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners in structured classroom environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Minimize distractions, improve focus, and enhance learning outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces noise interference, improving reading, writing, and comprehension skill learning. Minimizes distractions caused by thermal discomfort. Allows for flexible seating arrangements that match the task at hand.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting seating arrangements to individual needs and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure noise levels, temperature, and seating arrangement types. Track instances of distraction and academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Optimizing classroom design can influence a significant portion of variance in academic outcomes (Uncapher, 2016). Noisy interference makes it difficult for kids to stay on task, impacting reading, writing, and comprehension skill learning (Uncapher, 2016).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classroom games transform review time into engaging, collaborative activities that motivate learners and reinforce learning. These games can take many forms, from board game adaptations to interactive question-and-answer formats. Key elements include clear rules, defined objectives, and opportunities for learners to actively participate and compete in a supportive environment. The goal is to make review fun, reduce anxiety, and promote deeper understanding through active recall and peer interaction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires planning and preparation to design or select appropriate games. Materials may include board games, cards, whiteboards, or digital platforms. Clear rules and objectives must be communicated.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to manage large classes or diverse skill levels. Some learners may be more focused on winning than on learning. Requires careful monitoring to ensure fairness and inclusivity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beneficial for all grade levels and subjects, particularly when reviewing for exams or consolidating knowledge after a unit of study.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, reinforce learning, reduce anxiety, promote deeper understanding, foster collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation through gamification. Reduces test anxiety by creating a low-stakes environment. Encourages collaboration and peer teaching. Provides immediate feedback on understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Games can be adapted to different learning styles and content areas. Rules can be modified to accommodate diverse learner needs and promote inclusivity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Assess performance
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Provide feedback
  • Team-Based Inquiry

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation levels. Collect data on team performance and individual contributions. Assess learner understanding through game outcomes and feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that classroom games can significantly improve student motivation, engagement, and learning outcomes. Games promote active recall, peer interaction, and a positive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Jeopardy, Family Feud, Bingo, Monopoly, Pass the Chicken, Ping Pong, Headbands, Spin the Wheel

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A classroom library is a dedicated space within the classroom stocked with a variety of books to promote reading engagement and literacy skills. Effective classroom libraries are well-organized, inviting, and accessible to all students. They typically include a diverse collection of books catering to different reading levels, interests, and cultural backgrounds. They often feature comfortable seating arrangements, clear signage, and organizational systems that allow students to easily find and return books. Teachers explicitly model how to care for books and use the library respectfully. The goal is to create a space where learners can independently explore and develop a love for reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a dedicated space in the classroom, a collection of books, shelving or bins for organization, and clear guidelines for library use. Ongoing maintenance to curate and update the collection is also necessary.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant initial investment to build a diverse book collection. Requires ongoing effort to maintain organization and promote responsible book handling. Limited space may restrict the size and variety of the library.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels, particularly effective in early childhood and elementary classrooms to establish strong reading habits.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a love of reading, increase reading frequency, improve comprehension skills, foster independent learning, and expand vocabulary.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides easy access to a wide range of reading materials, encourages independent reading choices, and supports personalized learning experiences. Facilitates the development of positive attitudes toward reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to meet diverse learner needs by including books at varying reading levels, in multiple languages, and on topics of interest to individual students. Flexible organization allows for customization based on curriculum themes and student preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement with books, track reading frequency and completion rates, monitor book check-out patterns, and assess comprehension through discussions and written reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that access to a well-stocked classroom library can significantly improve reading achievement and foster a lifelong love of reading. Studies show that students who have access to classroom libraries read more frequently and perform better on standardized reading tests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary teachers set up themed book bins, create cozy reading nooks, and host regular book talks to promote their classroom libraries. A high school English teacher curates a collection of young adult literature aligned to course themes. Resource: Jim Trelease, The Read-Aloud Handbook.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers put the most important policies, procedures, and expectations into graphic form to increase the likelihood that students will follow them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers must determine their class policies, procedures, and expectations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Making policies, procedures, and expectations clear.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases the likelihood that students will follow classroom policies, procedures, and expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can customize policies, procedures, and expectations to their class.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Classroom follows expectations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased likelihood that students will follow classroom policies, procedures, and expectations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating movement-based activities into the classroom to energize learners, relax and calm a class, or redirect attention. These breaks are short (1-5 minutes) and should be implemented 2-3 times per day. Encourages teachers to get out of their seats and participate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires 1–5 minutes of class time, incorporation of school health team, school wellness policy knowledge and administrator approval. Minimal equipment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some activities may not be suitable for all learners. Requires teacher participation and enthusiasm.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, general education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Energize students, improve focus, manage stress, increase motivation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves students' physical well-being, manages emotions, and energizes the brain.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for all abilities by modifying activities, equipment, or rules. Students can suggest and choose activities they find enjoyable and accessible.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement. Monitor changes in student behavior and focus after implementing breaks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps students organize thoughts to better manage stress and control impulses, improve student engagement, increase focus and reduce antsy behavior

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This strategy involves strategically organizing the physical space of a classroom to maximize student engagement, motivation, participation, and positive relationships. Different arrangements, such as traditional rows, roundtables, horseshoes, or pods, can impact communication patterns, pedagogy, and on-task behavior. In virtual spaces, features like gallery view, breakout rooms, and screen sharing can enhance interaction. The goal is to align the seating arrangement with the instructional goals and activities to support student learning effectively.

Instructional communication theory holds that seating arrangement shapes how the instructor communicates with students and how students interact with each other, with consequences for engagement, motivation, and focus (McCorskey & McVetta, 1978); more recent research finds students generally prefer flexible over fixed seating — mobile chairs and trapezoidal tables on casters over rectangular tables with immobile chairs (Harvey & Kenyon, 2013). Student-centered spatial design, oriented around learners actively constructing knowledge, can support learning outcomes (Rands & Gansemer-Topf, 2017), though most classrooms in practice are still built around more conventional seating models.

Common configurations, each with different tradeoffs: - Traditional (rows) — students face the teacher, backs to one another; minimizes student-student communication and supports a "sage on the stage" model. Teacher-student interaction concentrates on students in the front row or middle of the room; back-row students tend to be less engaged. - Roundtable — teacher and students all face one another around a single large table (or desks arranged to the same effect); supports both whole-class and pairwise dialogue. - Horseshoe / semicircle — a modified roundtable that lets the teacher move around the room while all participants still face each other; encourages discussion, though engagement concentrates on students directly opposite the teacher, with somewhat less for students immediately adjacent. Works well when the teacher wants to project and discuss material at the front of the room. - Double horseshoe — an inner and outer horseshoe; invites even more discussion than a single horseshoe, though inner-circle students have their backs to the outer circle, limiting some interaction (offset somewhat by turning around for group work). - Pods (groups/pairs) — rectangular, circular, or trapezoidal tables (or clustered desks) forming groups of 3-4 or pairs; well suited when students will spend a large portion of class time working together, and communicates that the room is a learning community built around peer work.

Recommendations for using these options: align arrangement with activity (group pods for group work, a horseshoe for whole-class discussion, changing arrangement mid-class as goals shift); bolster arrangement with engagement when changing the physical setup isn't practical (e.g., deliberately directing more attention to horseshoe-side students who'd otherwise get less, or using Think-Pair-Share in a fixed traditional layout to get peer interaction anyway); and set up early, designating time (or enlisting students) to arrange and later reset the room rather than losing instructional time to it.

Seating arrangement also functions as a behavioral antecedent, independent of its communication effects: sitting near a particular peer can be an antecedent to talking and not completing work, sitting near a window or door an antecedent to inattention, and sitting near the teacher an antecedent to staying on task — see Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Adaptable furniture (desks, tables, chairs), planning for space allocation, clear communication with students, and familiarity with virtual platform features

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires physical or virtual space adjustments, may need modifications based on specific classroom constraints, and success depends on clear expectations and routines

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels and subjects, adaptable for in-person and virtual learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, optimize communication patterns, foster positive relationships, and support different types of learning activities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured environments for different tasks, maximizes interaction, supports diverse learning activities, and fosters a sense of community

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize configurations to suit different learning needs, provide visual and auditory cues to define each space, and allow for flexible seating options where possible

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement levels in different arrangements, collect feedback through surveys or discussions, and monitor task completion rates in each configuration

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that flexible seating arrangements can enhance student engagement and learning outcomes. Studies show that different classroom setups impact student-student and instructor-student interactions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A class using group work utilizes group pods, while a class focused on whole-class discussion uses a horseshoe arrangement. Instructors strategically change arrangements to suit shifting learning goals.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Think-Pair-Share (Turn & Talk) — a way to get peer interaction even in a traditional row-based layout that can't easily be reconfigured

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model — seating placement as a behavioral antecedent
