docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classwide peer editing involves having students review and critique examples of student writing. The focus is on reviewing and critiquing examples of student writing, which can be real or mock examples displayed or distributed to the entire class. Students compliment the piece, from word choice to sentence structure and tone to organization, make specific suggestions about the piece, and point out objective grammar, spelling and continuity errors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear expectations for feedback, structured activities, and teacher guidance. Students need to be trained on how to give effective feedback and provide constructive criticism.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and monitoring to ensure both students are actively engaged and benefiting from the activity. Also, some students may struggle with giving or receiving feedback, requiring additional support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach students how to give praise and feedback - essential peer teaching skills - reinforce writing skills, and enhance understanding of effective writing techniques.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe and supportive environment for students to practice giving and receiving feedback, enhances writing skills, and reinforces understanding of effective writing techniques.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various subjects and topics, allowing students to focus on areas where they need the most support. Flexible structure accommodates different learning styles and paces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student interactions and collaboration skills, assess individual understanding of the material through quizzes or assignments, and gather feedback from students about their experience with classwide peer editing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that classwide peer editing can lead to improved academic outcomes, enhanced social skills, and increased student engagement. Students reinforce their learning by teaching, while also benefiting from personalized support.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using the Complimenting, Suggesting, and Correcting model during writing workshops

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establishing clear channels and rules of online communication with your students ensures that you are getting back to students reasonably quickly when they have questions and is an important component of establishing strong connections with students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors should be ready to answer questions reasonably quickly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to manage when instructors are busy

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Online learners of all levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Establish strong connections with students and improve student satisfaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Clarifies communication channels and expectations, facilitates timely responses, and provides feedback for improved communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can establish a 'hotline' to reach out with questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduced amount of confused emails and questions from learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Having a strong teaching presence online can mean spending time setting up your LMS so that there's a central hub where the resources are gathered.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cloud Text-to-Speech allows developers to create natural-sounding, synthetic human speech as playable audio. It can convert text or Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) input into audio data like MP3 or LINEAR16 (the encoding used in WAV files). Developers can use the audio data files to power applications or augment media like videos or audio recordings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A Google Cloud Platform account. Access to the Cloud Text-to-Speech API. Programming skills to integrate the API into applications.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires familiarity with cloud computing and API integration. Costs may be associated with usage of the API. Not all SSML elements are supported for all languages.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Developers and content creators who want to integrate text-to-speech capabilities into their applications and media.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable speech synthesis in applications, enhance accessibility of digital content, create audio files from text, augment media with synthetic speech

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for dynamic generation of speech from text. Provides a wide selection of custom voices differing by language, gender, and accent. Supports configuration of speaking rate, pitch, volume, and sample rate hertz. Enhances synthetic speech through Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML).

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Developers can choose from various voices, configure audio output settings, and use SSML to fine-tune the speech synthesis process.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and naturalness of the synthesized speech. Measure the effectiveness of the API in different applications. Collect user feedback on the accessibility and usability of the resulting audio content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Cloud Text-to-Speech enables developers to create more accessible and engaging applications and media by providing high-quality synthetic speech.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Cloud Text-to-Speech in a voice assistant app to provide natural language feedback, creating audio files for e-learning content, augmenting videos with synthesized narration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Co-constructing knowledge involves teachers and students dialoguing and creating knowledge together, rather than teachers simply filling students with content. It means giving up the 'myself and them' role of teacher and students and fully embracing the wonder and journey of 'us'.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be open to student input and willing to relinquish some control over content. It needs a classroom environment that supports dialogue and collaboration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are not comfortable working in groups or who prefer more structured instruction. Requires careful facilitation to ensure all voices are heard and that the discussion stays focused and productive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all levels, K-12, higher education, and adult learners, especially in subjects where collaborative learning and critical thinking are emphasized.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a collaborative learning environment, build student agency, promote critical thinking, and connect learning to real-world experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages social interaction and dialogue, increasing engagement and motivation. Enhances understanding through diverse perspectives and shared inquiry. Develops critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the level of structure and guidance provided. Scaffolded prompts and questions can support learners who are new to collaborative learning. Project options can be tailored to learner interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assessments can include group projects, presentations, and discussions. Student reflections and self-evaluations can provide insights into their learning and participation. Observations of group dynamics and collaborative skills can also be assessed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that co-construction of knowledge increases student engagement, motivation, and learning outcomes. Studies indicate that collaborative learning fosters critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students working in groups to research and present on a topic. Teachers facilitating class discussions where students share their perspectives and insights.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: ELL teachers and math teachers collaborate to identify target content, key vocabulary, academic language, and language-focused tasks for lessons. These tasks may include writing a proof, reading a math problem, explaining problem-solving, or writing numbers as words. The ELL specialist guides the math teacher through this process, which becomes integrated into the math teacher's planning. After the lesson, teachers identify areas needing clarification and share insights with colleagues. Content teachers can use language objectives to target language demands.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Collaborative planning time for ELL and math teachers, tools for identifying language demands in math lessons

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires coordination and time for collaborative planning, may be challenging to implement in settings with limited resources

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Integrate language and math instruction, enhance collaboration between ELL and math teachers, improve learner understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines expertise of ELL and math teachers, enhances learner outcomes

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailoring instruction to meet the specific language needs of ELLs in math

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's performance on language-focused tasks in math, assess learner understanding of mathematical concepts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learner outcomes in both language and math, increased collaboration between educators

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When planning a lesson, a math teacher and an ELL teacher could collaborate to identify both the target content, such as key standards, concepts, or specific topics, as well as key vocabulary, academic language, and the language-focused tasks learners will need to complete the lesson.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitively demanding tasks require a high level of cognitive engagement to complete. These tasks require students to make connections between and among mathematical ideas in new ways. Research has shown that using high cognitive demand tasks in ways that support that rigor will lead to increases in student learning. These tasks require students to read them, determine what the question is, and determine how to use the information provided in the task. High cognitive demand tasks often have multiple ways of finding an answer or multiple correct answers. When this is true, you and your students have much more to talk about. And many more student ideas come out in the conversation. All of this offers an opportunity to make sense of one another’s thinking and for each student to learn how to communicate about her or his own thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tasks that require cognitive engagement, questions that maintain high cognitive demand, focus on the Standards for Mathematical Practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful planning and preparation by the instructor to ensure tasks are appropriately challenging. Requires a classroom culture that supports discussion and the exchange of ideas.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 teachers, school and district leaders, and math coaches

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical thinking, make connections between mathematical ideas, enhance problem-solving skills, promote mathematical discourse

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages deep engagement with mathematical concepts. Facilitates discussions and the exchange of ideas. Supports the development of communication skills and mathematical precision.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks can be adjusted to meet different levels of prior understanding. Encourages multiple approaches to problem-solving. Provides opportunities for various student ideas to emerge and be discussed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Cognitive Conflict
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the level of cognitive demand in tasks by observing student engagement and depth of discussion. Evaluate the types of questions that are asked and whether they raise or lower the cognitive demand. Assess student communication and use of mathematical terms and representations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research has shown that using high cognitive demand tasks in ways that support that rigor will lead to increases in student learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In the "Buying Lunch" task, students are required to determine different combinations of lunch items to purchase within a budget, promoting problem-solving and decision-making skills. (See original document for example.)

docs.title: Cold Call to Sample Pair Responses
Description
docs.text: Using cold call to select students to share their pair's responses reinforces expectations around engagement and attention. It ensures that all students are prepared to participate and provides a sampling of responses for the class to consider. This also allows the teacher to create a shared understanding of high-quality responses and identify areas for re-teaching.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires establishing a routine for cold calling and ensuring that students understand that they may be called on to share their thoughts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may feel anxious about being cold called. Teachers must be sensitive to students' needs and provide support as needed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for promoting accountability and participation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce engagement and attention, provide a sampling of responses, create a shared understanding of high-quality responses, and identify areas for re-teaching.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to stay engaged, promotes active listening, and provides opportunities for students to learn from each other's ideas. Reduces the reliance on volunteers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can support less confident students by letting them know in advance that their ideas are good and that they will be called on to share.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of student engagement and participation. Assess the quality and depth of student responses. Monitor whether students are listening to and building on each other's ideas.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Cold call can improve student engagement, promote active listening, and lead to a deeper understanding of the material.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After completing collaborative problem-solving tasks, learners examine leveled exemplars of responses and identify the characteristics of each level. They then create posters or anchor charts using their own work to illustrate the differences between the levels. This activity promotes metacognition, self-assessment, and a shared understanding of quality work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Exemplars of varying quality, materials for creating posters or anchor charts, student work samples, time for discussion and creation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of exemplars to ensure clear differentiation between levels. Some learners may struggle with self-assessment and providing constructive feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-6, adaptable for other grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-assessment skills, enhance metacognition, foster a shared understanding of quality work, provide peer feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops critical thinking skills, promotes self-reflection and peer assessment, strengthens understanding of assessment criteria, encourages collaborative learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Exemplars can be leveled to match the learners' current skill level. Learners can also choose which pieces of their work to use as examples, allowing for individual expression and reflection.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student discussions, review the content and clarity of posters/anchor charts, assess student self-assessments and peer feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners develop a deeper understanding of assessment criteria and improve their ability to self-assess and provide constructive feedback. The collaborative creation of exemplars fosters a shared understanding of quality work.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A 5th-grade class completes a collaborative math problem and then examines exemplars that are rated level 1 through level 4. They discuss what makes each level distinct and create a poster using their own work to show the differences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers should emphasize collaborative learning within a project. It allows ELL students to be supported by their peers. It gives them opportunities to orally use and practice the academic vocabulary and other language structures and functions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom culture that values collaboration and well-designed collaborative tasks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to manage groups effectively and ensure equal participation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELL students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote peer support, encourage language practice, and enhance social skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a supportive environment for language practice and enhances communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategically pair ELLs with supportive peers and provide structured activities for collaboration.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Team-Based Inquiry

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased language use, improved communication skills, and positive peer interactions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Gives opportunities to orally use and practice the academic vocabulary and other language structures and functions

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In project-based learning (PBL), collaborative group work involves intentionally structuring activities to ensure students work together to achieve common goals. This can be done through critique and revision processes, collaborative products, labs, and team-building activities. Collaborative work provides English Language Learners (ELLs) with opportunities to practice academic vocabulary and language structures orally, supported by their peers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful planning of collaborative activities, clear communication of expectations, and facilitation of positive group dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure equitable participation and avoid dominant group members, and may necessitate additional support for ELLs to fully participate.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with a particular focus on English Language Learners (ELLs) in project-based learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To enhance language acquisition and collaborative skills among all students, especially English Language Learners (ELLs), by providing structured opportunities for peer interaction and support within PBL activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a supportive environment for ELLs to practice language skills, enhances teamwork and communication skills, and builds a collaborative classroom culture.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different project types and proficiency levels, allowing educators to tailor group tasks and roles to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Peer Teaching
  • Consensus-Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student communication, enhanced collaboration skills observed in group activities, and positive feedback from students and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that collaborative learning enhances language skills, content knowledge, and social-emotional development for all students, particularly ELLs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing critique and revision sessions where students provide feedback on each other's work, creating collaborative products that require teamwork and communication.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating collaborative learning spaces involves intentionally designing classrooms to facilitate group work and interaction. This includes incorporating elements such as large, round or rectangular tables instead of individual desks, flexible bookshelves that can be moved to create nooks and crannies, and at least three different kinds of seating options. The goal is to foster a sense of community where everyone can see each other and participate actively. This design approach recognizes that learning is enhanced through social interaction and that physical spaces can either support or hinder collaboration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Large tables (round or rectangular), flexible bookshelves, diverse seating options, classroom space that allows for reconfiguration, teacher willingness to relinquish traditional classroom setup

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant investment in new furniture and materials, potential for noise and distraction if not managed effectively, requires clear guidelines and expectations for group work, may require training for teachers to effectively facilitate collaborative activities

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, higher education, adult learners in various educational and training settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster collaboration, improve communication skills, enhance community participation, create flexible learning environments, support diverse learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages teamwork, improves communication and social skills, fosters a sense of community, allows for flexible grouping and activities, supports diverse learning styles, enhances engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Furniture arrangements can be adapted to support different group sizes and activities. Seating options can be chosen to accommodate individual preferences and needs. The space can be reconfigured to support various instructional methods and learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Class Discussion
  • Reflection
  • Team-Based Inquiry

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe group dynamics and interactions during collaborative activities, assess the quality of collaborative work products, survey students about their experiences with group work, track student engagement and participation in class discussions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that collaborative learning spaces can improve communication skills, foster a sense of community, and enhance student engagement. These environments support active learning and promote deeper understanding of concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Albemarle County Public Schools implementing flexible bookshelves and large tables to support collaborative work (as cited in the provided text). Classrooms designed with mobile furniture that can be easily reconfigured to support various group activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Collaborative margin comments involve using collaborative document platforms like Google Docs or Microsoft Word Online to provide direct feedback within the document. Learners and instructors can add comments, suggestions, and questions directly in the margins of the document, fostering real-time interaction and iterative improvement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to collaborative document platforms like Google Docs or Microsoft Word Online and clear guidelines for providing constructive margin comments.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on learners' familiarity with the platforms and their ability to provide thoughtful, relevant feedback. May require initial training on platform usage.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where collaborative writing and feedback are essential.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate direct feedback within documents, enhance real-time collaboration, and improve the iterative writing process.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a direct and contextual way for learners and instructors to give and receive feedback within the document. Enhances real-time collaboration and iterative improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors and learners can tailor their feedback to specific parts of the document, addressing individual needs and concerns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Peer Interaction
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Digital Tools

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of margin comments. Observe engagement and participation in collaborative feedback activities. Measure improvements in the quality of revised documents based on margin comments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This approach can enhance collaboration and feedback in writing processes, leading to improved learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Google Docs and Microsoft Word Online are examples of platforms that support collaborative margin comments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners connect with others to provide and receive feedback for improvement on writing tasks. Students do their own thinking and writing first and then connect with others to provide and receive feedback for improvement. This type of collaborative learning contrasts with cooperative writing where students in a group complete individual parts of a writing task without peer feedback and then put the pieces together to present as a final product.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Writing tasks, peer review checklists or guides, digital platforms for collaboration and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires structuring and modeling, especially for emergent writing. May need teacher supervision to ensure maximum benefit.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly beneficial for English language learners. Can be adapted for various grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop writing skills, enhance critical thinking, foster collaboration and communication, improve revision skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and increases self-confidence and motivation, especially for English language learners. Enhances writing quality through peer feedback and collaboration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use checklists or guides to have learners review each other's writing and make comments. Products can also have sentences or word banks that allow learners to collaboratively arrange them to create a story.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student participation and engagement during peer review, assess the quality of feedback provided by students, review the improvements made in writing based on peer feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports collaborative peer review as a method for improving student writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implement collaborative peer review activities by providing students with checklists or guides to review each other's writing and provide constructive feedback.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners individually solve a problem on sticky notes, then share and discuss their responses in small groups. The groups then synthesize the best parts of each individual response to create a 'best possible answer' on a common page. This strategy encourages accountability, participation, and the defense of one's thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sticky notes, problem-solving pages, common space for group answers, time for individual work and group discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure equal participation and prevent dominant students from overshadowing others. Students may need guidance in providing constructive feedback and resolving disagreements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-6, adaptable for other grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, enhance problem-solving skills, encourage accountability and participation, review concepts, support teamwork

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases accountability by requiring individual contributions, promotes teamwork and collaboration, facilitates peer learning and support, encourages critical thinking through discussion and defense of answers

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying group sizes, adjusting the difficulty of the problems, or modifying the roles within the groups. Teachers can also strategically group students based on their individual needs and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student interactions and discussions, review individual and group responses, assess the quality and depth of collaborative answers

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students improve their collaborative abilities and mathematical reasoning. The structured process helps students engage with the material more deeply and learn from their peers, leading to a more thorough understanding of the concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A 4th-grade math class uses sticky notes to solve a word problem individually. They then come together in groups to discuss their approaches and create a combined solution. The teacher observes how they share ideas and justify their reasoning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners work in pairs to create a story by responding to guiding questions. First, individuals think silently about their response to a question. Then, they share their answers with their partner and decide together which one to write down. The process repeats through a series of questions, and the pairs then write a simple version of their story with illustrations, practice telling it, and present it to another small group.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Guiding questions, large easel paper, writing utensils, time for thinking, sharing, and writing. Can be adapted for digital platforms.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require modeling and scaffolding, especially for introductory activities. Some students may dominate the collaborative process if not monitored effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary through high school students, particularly beneficial for English language learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop narrative writing skills, encourage active participation, enhance collaboration, foster creativity and imagination

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases engagement and active participation by decreasing group size, provides structured support for narrative writing, and allows for individual thinking time before collaboration. Reduces anxiety and increases self-confidence and motivation, especially for English language learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adjust the guiding questions to suit the grade level and learning objectives. The number of questions can be modified based on the time available and the learners' needs. Modeling responses to each question can be provided for introductory activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation during discussions, review the quality and creativity of the stories produced, assess students' ability to incorporate narrative elements effectively.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that English language learners working in pairs produce better texts in terms of task fulfillment, grammatical accuracy, and complexity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implement the activity as an introduction to a unit on stories or as a reinforcement/review activity. Use free online sites designed for collaborative writing as follow-up homework, where partners work together to write segments answering similar questions and then post the link to their creation in a class blog.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Collaborative storytelling involves students working in pairs to co-create a narrative by responding to a series of guiding questions. Each student first spends a minute thinking silently about their individual response to a question. Then, the pair shares their answers and decides together which one to write down. After answering all questions, students write a simple version of their story with illustrations, practice telling it, and present it to another small group. This method enhances collaboration by ensuring individual thought precedes group discussion, leading to a final product superior to what a student might create alone. The questions prompt students to consider setting, characters (protagonist and antagonist), the main problem, character histories, internal thoughts, dialogue, a positive event, a negative event, and the story's ending.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Guiding questions, large easel paper for each pair, writing and drawing materials, time for individual thinking, pair sharing, story writing, practice, and presentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The number of questions should be limited to avoid overwhelming students. Requires careful facilitation to ensure all students participate actively. Effectiveness depends on the quality of guiding questions and the structure of the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to high school students, particularly beneficial for English language learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop narrative writing skills, enhance collaboration, improve task fulfillment, grammatical accuracy, and complexity in writing, foster critical thinking and communication skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and increases self-confidence and motivation among students, especially ELLs. Promotes active participation, enhances collaborative opportunities, and improves the quality of written texts. Structured questioning promotes deeper thinking and better story elements.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The teacher can modify the number and type of guiding questions used based on the learners' needs and abilities. They can also adjust the amount of thinking and sharing time provided.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Demonstration
  • Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and complexity of the written stories, observe student participation and collaboration during pair work, assess the clarity and creativity of story presentations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that ELLs working in pairs produce shorter but better texts in terms of task fulfillment, grammatical accuracy, and complexity. Collaborative writing lowers anxiety and increases self-confidence and motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary school teacher introduces a unit on stories by having students work in pairs to answer guiding questions about setting, characters, and plot, then create and present their collaborative stories. Adapted from Navigating the Common Core With English-Language Learners by Larry Ferlazzo and Katie Hull Sypnieski.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making arrangements for learners to work together through the entire process of writing—planning, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing—results in higher quality writing products. Technology is used to support and share writing, especially for classes that do not meet daily, or assign writing as an out-of-class activity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured group activities, technology for sharing, clear roles and responsibilities

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effective group management, may not suit all learners, unequal participation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing quality, promote teamwork, enhance collaboration skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides peer support, enhances learning through collaboration, improves writing quality

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Collaborative tasks can be tailored to different group sizes and writing tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased collaboration, greater teamwork

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Collaboration through the entire writing process results in higher quality writing products

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Collaborative writing using online platforms involves students jointly composing texts through digital tools like Google Docs. These platforms enable features such as commenting on each other's writing, tracking changes in suggestion mode, and simultaneous co-authoring. Students can work together to write segments answering similar questions and then post the link to their creation in a class blog. This approach leverages technology to enhance collaboration and provides opportunities for peer feedback and revision.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to online platforms such as Google Docs, internet connectivity, and familiarity with collaborative writing tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires reliable internet access and digital literacy skills. May be challenging for students with limited technology experience. Relies on constructive peer feedback, which requires training and facilitation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students, as well as adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance collaborative writing skills, improve peer feedback and revision processes, develop digital literacy, and promote effective online communication.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates real-time collaboration, provides clear records of changes and suggestions, allows for asynchronous contributions, and enhances peer interaction. Improves writing quality through constructive feedback and iterative revision.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose their partners, select topics of interest, and use the platform's features to adapt the writing process to their needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality of collaborative writing products, assess the depth and specificity of peer feedback, and track student participation and engagement in online discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Utilizing online platforms for collaborative writing can lead to improved writing quality, enhanced peer interaction, and increased student engagement. It supports the development of essential digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school English class uses Google Docs to write a collaborative research paper, with students commenting on each other's drafts, tracking changes, and co-authoring sections simultaneously. Students then share the work with class via a class blog.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners choose a category of items to collect data on, creating tally charts to record observations, and then graph the data to visualize findings. This reinforces data collection, organization, and representation skills, while also creating a tangible keepsake of the trip.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, pencil, and materials for creating tally charts and graphs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the availability of items in the chosen category. May require assistance with graphing for younger learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce data collection, improve data organization and representation skills, and enhance understanding of graphing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces data collection and organization. Enhances understanding of graphing and data representation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their own data categories. Vary the complexity of the data representation method (e.g., bar graph, pie chart).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to collect and organize data accurately. Evaluate the completeness and accuracy of the resulting graphs.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Playing games and activities will help your children become more engaged in your family adventures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Collective data analysis involves a systematic and iterative process of making sense of data through collaboration, especially in participatory action research. Techniques such as data dives, grounded analysis, and gallery walks are used to unpack data, identify themes, outliers, and interesting data points. This process requires careful examination and discussion to draw meaningful conclusions from the data.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Data, tools for data analysis, and skilled facilitators to guide the process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and requires careful attention to detail. Ensuring that all voices are heard and that the analysis is not dominated by a few individuals is crucial.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Researchers, students, and community members involved in participatory action research

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify themes, draw conclusions, develop insights, foster collaboration, validate experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Brings multiple perspectives to the analysis, increases the rigor of the findings, empowers participants to make sense of their own data, and fosters a sense of ownership.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The methods used can be tailored to the specific type of data and the skills of the participants.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Data Analysis
  • Summarization and Synthesis
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the rigor of the analysis, the validity of the conclusions, and the extent to which the findings are used to inform action.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Develops key academic skills, affirms student experiences, and gives credibility to student voice. Facilitates a transformative process where students can articulate what they already know based on research.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using data dive worksheets and activities to pick apart surveys. Applying grounded theory to group emerging themes and generate theory.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Color-coding school supplies can make organization easier and more streamlined for kids and the adults in charge. Assigning different colors to various supplies can help kids quickly identify what they need for each subject or task. Assign different colors to various supplies to help quickly identify them. Use the first color for papers that need to come home but that don’t need to go back to school. Use the second color for papers that need a caregiver’s attention and have to be returned to school. And use the third color for homework, labeling one pocket “To Do” and the other “Completed.”

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • School supplies (folders, notebooks, etc.), colored labels or markers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires initial setup and consistent use. May not be effective for learners with color blindness. Dependent on the learner maintaining the color-coding system.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with organization, visual learners, learners of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve organization of learning materials, enhance visual identification of supplies, reduce time spent searching for materials

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual system for organizing supplies, reduces cognitive load in identifying materials, promotes efficiency and independence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Colors can be assigned based on the learner's preferences and needs. Color-coding system can be adapted to different subjects or tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to quickly identify and retrieve supplies. Track the organization of learning materials. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the color-coding system.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual cues, such as color-coding, have been shown to improve organization and memory. Color-coded systems can reduce cognitive overload and promote efficiency.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use different colored folders for different subjects. Assign a specific color to papers that need to be signed by a parent.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Combining two or more calming sensory strategies to create a more comprehensive and effective approach to self-regulation. Examples include digging in a tactile bin while listening to white noise, sitting with a weighted blanket while looking at sensory bottles, or chewing gum while working on a fine motor task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A collection of sensory tools and activities. A designated space for implementing these strategies. Clear guidelines for participation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and coordination to implement effectively. May require additional resources and support. Some learners may require individualized guidance to find the right combination of strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who require a more comprehensive approach to self-regulation

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-regulation, promote calmness, address multiple sensory needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses multiple sensory needs simultaneously. Allows learners to customize their self-regulation strategies. Can be adapted to various learning activities and settings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to experiment with different combinations of strategies to find what works best for them. Provide a variety of sensory tools and activities to choose from. Offer guidance and support in developing personalized self-regulation plans.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in these strategies. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of different combinations of strategies. Track changes in learners' behavior, attention, and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that combining sensory strategies can be more effective than using single strategies alone. Studies have shown that multi-sensory approaches can improve learning and behavior in learners with diverse needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating classrooms as comfortable spaces where students feel at home. This includes providing cozy spaces where students can relax and read, such as allowing them to sit or lie down while reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Comfortable seating options such as bean bag chairs, cushions, and rugs. A designated space for reading and relaxation. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional space and resources. Some learners may find it difficult to focus in a relaxed environment. Requires clear expectations and guidelines for appropriate behavior.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase comfort, reduce stress, promote relaxation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes relaxation and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred seating arrangement. Provide a variety of comfortable seating options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in reading activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that creating comfortable learning environments can reduce stress and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing group assignments where learners can find common ground and/or interests involves designing collaborative tasks that encourage learners to identify shared interests, values, or goals. This strategy fosters a sense of connection and belonging, promoting positive relationships and teamwork. Common ground can be found through shared academic interests, hobbies, cultural backgrounds, or personal experiences. When learners work together on assignments that align with their shared interests, they are more likely to engage in meaningful discussions, support each other's learning, and develop stronger relationships.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful planning and design of group assignments that align with the learners' interests and learning objectives. Facilitation and guidance to ensure that all learners have the opportunity to participate and contribute. Assessment methods that recognize and value both individual and group contributions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of this strategy depends on the learners' willingness to engage with their peers and the presence of genuine common ground. There is a risk that some learners may dominate the group or that conflicts may arise due to differences in opinions or working styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and backgrounds, particularly those who may feel isolated or disconnected from their peers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a sense of connection and belonging, promote positive relationships and teamwork, encourage meaningful discussions and support among learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates opportunities for learners to discover shared interests and values, fosters a sense of community and belonging, and promotes positive social interactions and teamwork. This can lead to increased engagement, motivation, and academic achievement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Group assignments can be tailored to the specific interests and backgrounds of the learners, ensuring that they have the opportunity to connect with peers who share their passions. Learners can also be given choices in terms of the topics, tasks, or roles within the group, allowing them to express their individuality and contribute in meaningful ways.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learners' interactions, participation, and teamwork during group assignments. Gather feedback from the learners about their experiences and perceptions of the group dynamic. Assess the quality of the group's work, including the depth of their discussions, the level of support they provide to each other, and the overall outcomes of the assignment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that collaborative learning experiences, particularly those that focus on shared interests and goals, can effectively promote positive relationships, increase engagement, and improve academic outcomes. When learners feel connected to their peers and have the opportunity to contribute to a shared goal, they are more likely to invest in their learning and achieve success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A group of learners who share an interest in environmental sustainability are assigned a project to research and propose solutions to a local environmental problem. They work together to gather data, analyze information, and develop a presentation to share their findings with the community. Through this process, they connect over their shared passion for the environment and build strong relationships based on mutual respect and collaboration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a shared vocabulary or metalanguage empowers learners to analyze and discuss their multimodal composition process. This involves selecting one mode (linguistic, visual, audio, gestural, or spatial), analyzing examples, and creating a class definition. Pointing out how each mode is used in different subjects and contexts helps learners understand its versatility and application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires time for discussion and analysis. Needs anchor charts or digital platforms for recording terms and definitions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time investment to build a comprehensive glossary. Learners may struggle with abstract concepts if not grounded in concrete examples.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners involved in multimodal composition, especially those new to the concept or needing support in articulating their design choices.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower learners with the language to analyze and discuss multimodal compositions. Develop understanding of different modes of communication and their applications.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a foundation for analyzing and discussing multimodal works. Enhances understanding of how different modes function and interact.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to choose the modes they want to analyze. Scaffolding can be provided by pre-selecting examples and guiding discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and specificity of learner discussions about multimodal works. Analyze the extent to which learners use the common language in their own compositions and analyses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that having a common language improves learners' ability to analyze and discuss multimodal compositions, leading to more effective design choices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a multimodal glossary with terms and definitions, referencing MODE's 2012 multimodal glossary as a resource.

docs.title: Communicate High Expectations and Provide Appropriate Support
Description
docs.text: Expect more and you will get it. High expectations are important for everyone – for the poorly prepared, for those unwilling to exert themselves, and for the bright and well-motivated. Expecting tutees to perform well becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy when everyone holds high expectations for themselves and make extra efforts. In challenging tutees and developing in them a sense of independence and responsibility for their learning, the appropriate amount of support must also be provided, one step at a time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Positive attitude, tutor enthusiasm and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a positive and supportive environment, high expectations must be balanced with appropriate support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Boost confidence and motivation, enhance independence and responsibility, promote a growth mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts confidence, enhances independence, promotes a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Make positive expectations clear at the beginning of the session. Periodically discuss how well the tutee is doing. Encourage tutees to write more; ask for drafts of work, and give opportunities for revision. Be energized and enthusiastic in your interaction with tutees.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased tutee confidence, improved performance, positive feedback about tutor support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that high expectations and appropriate support enhance learning outcomes. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor makes positive expectations clear at the beginning of the session. The tutor is energized and enthusiastic in their interactions with tutees.

docs.title: Communicate Quickly and Easily Through Mobile Apps
Description
docs.text: Mobile apps like Remind can provide a quick and easy way for parents, teachers, and students to communicate about student progress, assignments, and other school-related activities. This supports increased information flow and collaboration between home and school.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Smartphone or device with internet access. App installation and account setup.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Relies on parents having access to technology and being comfortable using it. May not be suitable for families who prefer face-to-face communication.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for parents with limited time or access to traditional communication methods

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, enhance parent engagement, support student progress

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides instant updates, facilitates two-way communication, breaks down language barriers (with translation features), increases parent awareness of student activities and performance

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Translation features cater to multilingual families. Teachers can tailor updates to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency of communication between teachers and parents. Monitor student attendance and academic performance. Gather feedback from parents on the usefulness of the app.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies of text messaging efforts have shown high rates of parent engagement and positive outcomes for middle school students as well as for preschoolers. Mobile communication can bridge gaps in understanding and involvement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teacher expectations have a dramatic impact on learner performance and behavior. Educators should monitor interactions to communicate high expectations to all learners. Techniques include calling on all learners equitably, increasing wait time, giving hints, and expressing belief in their abilities. This strategy bolsters student self-confidence and encourages them to remain on task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Monitor interactions to call on all learners equitably, increase wait time, give hints, and express belief in their abilities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires conscious effort to ensure equitable participation and appropriate support for all learners. It can be challenging to maintain high expectations for all learners, especially those with a history of underperformance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner performance and behavior through positive expectations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts learner self-confidence, encourages engagement, and reduces off-task behavior. Helps learners believe in their own abilities and strive for success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The instructor can tailor support and feedback according to the learners' needs, providing personalized encouragement and assistance to achieve high expectations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increase in learner participation, improved academic performance, and reduced behavioral issues. Observation of equitable participation and the effectiveness of supportive feedback and encouragement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on teacher expectations and learner achievement demonstrates that expectations have a dramatic impact on learner academic performance and behavior. This bolsters student self-confidence and encourages them to remain on task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Communication boards are visual aids that display symbols, pictures, words, or phrases to help individuals with limited or no verbal communication express their thoughts, needs, and ideas. These boards can be physical or electronic and are designed to provide a means of alternative communication. They are often used in educational, therapeutic, and everyday settings to support communication for individuals with speech and language impairments, autism, or other conditions that affect verbal expression.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Communication board (physical or electronic), symbols/pictures/words/phrases, training for users and communication partners, and ongoing support for implementation and customization.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the user's ability to understand and use symbols/pictures/words/phrases, may require training for communication partners, and can be limited by the user's physical or cognitive abilities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with speech and language impairments, autism, or other conditions affecting verbal expression, including children and adults.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable non-verbal or limited verbal individuals to express thoughts, needs, and ideas; support communication in educational, therapeutic, and everyday settings; facilitate language development and comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual and tangible means of communication, reduces frustration for individuals who cannot express themselves verbally, supports language development and comprehension, and facilitates social interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Communication boards can be customized with personally relevant symbols, pictures, words, or phrases. They can be adapted to different skill levels and communication needs, offering a flexible communication solution.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and effectiveness of communication board use, assess the user's ability to express thoughts and needs using the board, and gather feedback from users and communication partners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research and practice show that communication boards can improve communication, reduce frustration, and enhance social interaction for individuals with limited or no verbal communication. Improves language development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include physical picture boards, electronic speech-generating devices, and apps with customizable symbol sets. Various websites and organizations provide free or low-cost communication board templates and resources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a classroom community where student voices are valued involves providing time and opportunities for students to share and discuss their thoughts. Strategies such as daily check-ins, reflection sheets, sentence stems, and student-led discussions can amplify student voices and build their confidence to speak up and advocate for their learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for discussions, supportive classroom environment, sentence stems and word banks

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort. Some students may be hesitant to share their thoughts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly in elementary and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Amplify student voices, build confidence, foster a safe space for sharing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances communication skills, promotes empathy, fosters a sense of belonging

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and age groups. Strategies can be tailored to specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, improved communication skills, positive classroom environment

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students feel valued and confident to speak up and advocate for their learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing daily check-ins at the beginning or end of the day. Incorporating reflection sheets into projects and activities. Using sentence stems to support student articulation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encouraging community involvement by using online communities to support learning and fostering a sense of collaboration through social media. The physical space of the school should also allow for other adults to participate in classrooms.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to technology and social media. Designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the presence of additional adults.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase collaboration, improve social skills, promote community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes collaboration and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred activities. Provide a variety of activities that involve the community. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more fun.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Collaboration
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that community involvement can increase engagement, improve social skills, and enhance academic achievement. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel connected to their community.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Present learners with multiple sources on the same topic and have them compare and contrast the information presented. Encourage them to consider the information conveyed through photographs and other images as well as text. To aid their work, ask questions such as: When was each page created or updated? What is similar or different about the images on each page? What is the main idea or reason behind each page? What seems to be the author’s purpose on each page?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Multiple sources on the same topic, guiding questions, and worksheets.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort. Some students may need additional support to analyze and compare sources effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable learners to compare and contrast multiple sources on the same topic and think about what makes one source more reliable than another.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners develop critical thinking skills and learn to evaluate the reliability of sources.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different topics and types of sources.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students' ability to identify similarities and differences between sources. Evaluate their ability to determine which sources are more reliable.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Students develop the ability to compare and contrast sources and evaluate their reliability. Enhanced information literacy: Students become more discerning consumers of information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use Venn diagrams to compare and contrast the sources they have reviewed. Encourage students to think about the information conveyed through photographs and other images as well as text.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners compare and contrast multiple solution methods for the same problem, as opposed to studying one method at a time. This approach involves presenting learners with worked examples of different solution methods side by side and encouraging them to identify similarities and differences between the methods.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors need to provide worked examples of different solution methods and encourage learners to discuss and reflect on the similarities and differences between the methods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of worked examples and structured questions to guide learners' comparisons. May not be suitable for learners who struggle with abstract concepts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school students, high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote procedural knowledge, procedural flexibility, and conceptual knowledge. Enhance the ability to generate, recognize, and evaluate multiple solution methods for the same problem.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leads to greater gains in procedural knowledge and flexibility compared to studying multiple methods sequentially. Helps learners become better at solving problems and more likely to use shortcuts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can compare and contrast solution methods at their own pace and focus on the methods that best suit their learning style.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to solve problems using multiple methods. Evaluate their understanding of the concepts underlying the solution methods.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to greater gains in procedural knowledge and flexibility compared to studying multiple methods sequentially. Helps learners become better at solving problems and more likely to use shortcuts. Research shows comparison helps students become better at solving linear equations. This effect was found on problems similar to those in the study packets, and on transfer problems which differed from those the students had already seen.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting learners with two equations, each solved in two different ways, with the solutions side by side on the same page.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Act as a non-judgmental investigator to better understand students and respond with empathy. Acknowledge there’s a lot you don’t know, ask caring questions, listen and observe, imagine the student’s experience, believe that every student wants to be known, and be patient.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training in compassionate communication, willingness to be vulnerable and patient, a commitment to active listening

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel uncomfortable or unnatural at first, can be time-consuming, requires a willingness to question assumptions

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 teachers, counselors, and mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote understanding, empathy, and supportive relationships; reduce judgmental reactions; improve student-teacher connections

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a method to connect with students, improves classroom community, supports students with different backgrounds and needs

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor questions and responses to suit individual students and situations; adapt based on student responses and needs

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior, gather student feedback, assess changes in teacher-student interactions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more supportive classroom environment, improves student engagement, and enhances teacher-student relationships

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask “Is something bothering you?” and listen with intent; provide extended time for homework completion; acknowledge and validate student feelings

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide scaffolding, like speech examples, for discourse routines that may not be obvious to learners. Examples: “The topic of my presentation is __.” “In the first part, I give a few basic definitions. In the next section, I will explain _. In part three, I am going to show ___.”

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Prepare scripts for common academic routines.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may rely too heavily on the scripts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication skills, increase confidence in academic settings, increase Disciplinary Literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds communication skills, reduces anxiety, provides structure

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can provide scripts at different levels of difficulty.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
