docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner presentations for clarity and organization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides scaffolding for discourse routines that may not be obvious to learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A pedagogy that redefines who is 'smart' by utilizing multi-ability access points, norms and roles that support interdependency between learners, and attention to status and accountability for learning. Learning should have multi-ability access points, norms and roles that support interdependency between learners, and attention to status and accountability for learning. Involves learners working in groups of four on a rich task that has multiple entry points and ways it could be solved. Each learner in the group has a role: team captain, resource manager, recorder-reporter and facilitator. The teacher observes group dynamics and assigns status when they notice a valuable contribution, skill, or perspective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Well-designed rich tasks with multiple entry points, pre-assigned group roles, and teachers trained in assigning status.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant training for teachers. Success requires implementing all three core tenets of Complex Instruction simultaneously.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school learners, particularly those from diverse backgrounds and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a strengths-based approach, facilitate social construction of learning, and develop a deep understanding of mathematics

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Changes perceptions of math, encourages bringing entire selves to the pursuit of mathematics, and helps learners view themselves as capable learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks can be designed with multiple entry points to allow for diverse approaches. Individual roles within the groups are assigned to foster collaboration.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Peer Discussion
  • Coaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner engagement, peer feedback, the quality of developed reasoning, and changes in learners’ dispositions towards math.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners developed a stronger sense of belonging, greater participation, and a belief that their peers viewed them as smarter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The teacher observed a learner using a smart technique to organize numbers and publicly acknowledged it, naming it the 'Alexis Method.' High school learners expressed interest in continuing to Algebra II after experiencing a year of Complex Instruction. Resource: MindShift - How A Strengths-Based Approach to Math Redefines Who Is 'Smart'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: For adolescent learners, the Composition process can become more robust, as learners begin to express ideas through multiple media, which includes visual, audio, and digital production.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to technology, diverse media resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more resources, potential for technical issues.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance composition skills, promote creativity, improve digital literacy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances composition, promotes creativity, improves digital literacy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose media, tailor projects.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Composition quality, creativity, digital literacy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced composition skills, improved creativity, digital literacy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a video essay, designing a website, producing a podcast.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Begin teaching how to spell multisyllable words by beginning with compounds. These offer two big advantages: Children more easily detect their syllables, and the spelling of each base word stays the same.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grade 3 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling skills, enhance vocabulary, develop understanding of word structure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete way to understand multisyllabic words, reinforces recognition of base words, builds vocabulary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific compounds that the learner is familiar with. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in spelling compound words. Monitor progress in spelling and vocabulary skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • For multisyllable words, compounds are a great entry-point to improve spelling skills and enhance vocabulary.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: During reading activities, instructors periodically check for understanding by asking questions. These questions encourage learners to revisit their initial thoughts and predict outcomes based on textual evidence. Learners ground their responses in the text, ensuring comprehension and reinforcing critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful development of targeted questions and active monitoring of learner responses.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not properly scaffolded, questions may confuse learners. Over-reliance on comprehension checks can interrupt flow.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly useful during reading activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess understanding, encourage prediction, reinforce critical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time insights into learner understanding. Reinforces the importance of textual evidence in supporting comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust questions based on learner levels. Provide sentence stems for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Formative Assessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner responses for accuracy and depth of understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves comprehension and promotes critical thinking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves the ability of readers to know when they understand what they read and to use strategies to improve their understanding when it is blocked. It involves metacognition. Good readers are aware of and monitor their thought processes as they read, while poor readers do not. Strategies employed to improve understanding are called 'repair' or 'fix-up' strategies, such as rereading, reading ahead, clarifying words in a dictionary, or asking for help.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learners need to be aware of their comprehension levels and be willing to employ fix-up strategies. Instructors should model comprehension monitoring and provide opportunities for practice and reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to accurately assess their comprehension levels. If learners are not familiar with effective fix-up strategies, they may not be able to improve their understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those in upper elementary, middle, and high school, as well as adult learners looking to improve reading comprehension, metacognitive skills, and self-regulation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension by developing awareness of understanding, monitoring thought processes, and employing strategies to improve comprehension when it is blocked.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves self-regulation by enabling readers to monitor their understanding, enhances metacognition by increasing awareness of thought processes, and provides strategies for addressing comprehension difficulties.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can identify and practice fix-up strategies that work best for their individual learning styles and needs. Instructors can provide a range of fix-up strategies and support learners in selecting appropriate ones.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Question Formulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to monitor comprehension through self-assessments, think-aloud protocols, and the use of fix-up strategies. Look for increased awareness of comprehension levels and the ability to address difficulties.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research confirms that comprehension monitoring enhances reading comprehension by promoting self-awareness and the use of effective strategies for addressing comprehension challenges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • While reading a complex text, a learner pauses to ask, 'Do I understand what I just read?' If the answer is no, the learner rereads the section, looks up unfamiliar words, or summarizes the content to improve understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners form two circles, one inside circle and one outside circle. Each learner on the inside is paired with a learner on the outside; they face each other. The teacher poses a question to the whole group and pairs discuss their responses with each other. Then the teacher signals learners to rotate: Learners on the outside circle move one space to the right so they are standing in front of a new person (or sitting, as they are in the video). Now the teacher poses a new question, and the process is repeated. Instead of two circles, learners could also form two straight lines facing one another. Instead of “rotating” to switch partners, one line just slides over one spot, and the leftover person on the end comes around to the beginning of the line. Some teachers use this strategy to have learners teach one piece of content to their fellow learners, making it less of a discussion strategy and more of a peer teaching format.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where learners can form circles or lines, prepared discussion questions, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging in small or crowded classrooms, requires careful facilitation to ensure all learners are engaged and on task, may be difficult for learners who struggle with social interaction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for review activities and quick discussions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active participation, encourage peer teaching and learning, provide opportunities for quick and focused discussions, enhance communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes peer teaching and learning, provides opportunities for quick and focused discussions, enhances communication skills, supports kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussion questions can be tailored to learners' interests and backgrounds. Learners can choose the partners they want to work with.

• Peer Discussion
  • Peer Teaching
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the activity, review the quality of their responses to the discussion questions, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances active learning, promotes peer teaching and learning, improves communication skills

docs.title: Concept Discovery Through Examples and Non-examples
Description
docs.text: Expose learners to a wide range of examples and nonexamples and allow them to discover the concept. Present multiple examples to the learner and inquire about shared characteristics of the examples. Through exploration and discovery (interactive activities), learners can acquire the concept. Then use questions and context-sensitive feedback, to correct any misconceptions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a rich set of examples and non-examples. Needs interactive activities that promote exploration and discovery.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective for learners with limited prior knowledge. Requires careful design to guide exploration and prevent confusion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with a developed knowledge base, suitable for complex or abstract concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-directed learning, foster deeper understanding through exploration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning and critical thinking. Develops problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to explore examples and non-examples at their own pace and in their own way.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Scenario
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to articulate the key attributes of the concept and classify new instances accurately.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • An effective way to learn concepts is to discover them from interacting with a set of examples and nonexamples.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting multiple examples of Impressionist paintings and asking learners to identify common characteristics to discover the concept of Impressionism.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Concept maps are visual tools that help learners organize and articulate what they know about a given concept or topic. Important concepts are enclosed in a circle or box and connected to other concepts by lines that include explanatory phrases to define the relationship (e.g., “begins with”, “includes”, or “aids”). This strategy promotes meaningful connections within a topic, facilitates deeper understanding, and enhances retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured prompts and guidelines for creating concept maps. Instructor must facilitate the activity and provide feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure concepts are well-defined. Effectiveness depends on learners' ability to make meaningful connections.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Organize information, enhance comprehension, and facilitate deeper understanding.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners identify relationships between concepts, encourages meaningful connections, and promotes creativity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with different prompts tailored to learners' needs. Flexible formats allow for individual or group creation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the clarity and accuracy of the concept maps to assess comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows concept mapping is superior to rote memorization, encouraging students to make rich, meaningful connections within a topic.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: CRA is an instructional approach that uses concrete materials, visual representations, and abstract symbols to teach math concepts. Learners first manipulate concrete objects to understand a concept, then draw pictures representing the objects, and finally use abstract numbers and symbols. It aims to ensure a thorough understanding of math concepts/skills. As instructors move through the sequence of instruction, the abstract numbers and/or symbols should be used in conjunction with the concrete materials and representational drawings to promote association of abstract symbols with concrete and representational understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires concrete materials (e.g., chips, unifix cubes, base ten blocks), drawing materials, and explicit teaching methods. Instructors need to describe, model, and provide ample practice opportunities at each level of understanding.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may face barriers to abstract understanding if they do not understand the concept behind the skill, have difficulty with basic facts/memory problems, or repeat procedural mistakes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with math learning problems, but applicable to all learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop conceptual understanding, facilitate problem-solving skills, and promote meaningful connections between concrete experiences and abstract mathematical concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a graduated framework for learners to make meaningful connections, linking learning experiences from concrete-to-representational-to-abstract levels of understanding. By linking learning experiences from concrete-to-representational-to-abstract levels of understanding, the teacher provides a graduated framework for learners to make meaningful connections. Blends conceptual and procedural understanding in a structured way.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to different math concepts and skills. The type of concrete objects, drawing techniques, and strategies for moving to the abstract level can be adapted to suit individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Procedural information
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Simple-to-complex sequencing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner mastery at each level (concrete, representational, and abstract) can be assessed through observation, performance-based tasks, and formal assessments. Ability to explain solutions and problem-solving processes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps passive learners to make meaningful connections and teaches conceptual understanding by connecting concrete understanding to abstract math processes. Supports a graduated framework for students to make meaningful connections. Blends conceptual and procedural understanding in structured way.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using base ten blocks to understand place value, drawing pictures to represent fractions, solving algebraic equations with manipulatives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A natural reinforcer is a reinforcer naturally present in the setting where a behavior occurs — grades in classrooms, the applause of fans on a ballfield, money in the workplace, story hour or parental attention at home. Skinner's own definition is more specific: a natural reinforcer is a change in stimulation that results from the behavior itself, rather than from another person's delivered consequence. The pleasurable sound of hitting the correct piano keys, or a first-grader's satisfaction at seeing correctly formed letters appear on the page, are natural reinforcers in this stricter sense — the behavior's own product is what reinforces it, with no external praise or reward required. Children who enjoy solving puzzles, writing poetry, or reading novels are being naturally reinforced in this way.

Behaviorism is often criticized for producing learners hooked on artificial, extrinsic consequences (de Charms, 1968, 1976), but behavioral scientists (Skinner, 1953, 1974; Lindsley, 1991, 1992a, 1992b; Baer, Wolf, & Risley, 1968) have long advocated the deliberate use of natural reinforcers as an alternative — and, further, a documented process for transferring control from extrinsic to natural reinforcers over time, called conditioning a natural reinforcer (Horcones, 1985, 1987, 1991, 1992). Many learners are not naturally reinforced by classroom activities they nonetheless need to perform (writing, reading, answering questions); for these learners, external reinforcers serve two purposes: they let a teacher shape and strengthen the desired behavior through positive reinforcement, and — if deliberately faded — they let control over the behavior transfer to the learner's own natural, intrinsic reinforcers.

In classroom-management terms, natural reinforcers are specifically ones already available in the school setting at almost no cost — extra time to do homework, lunch with the principal or a favorite teacher, extra recess, an educational game, library time for pleasure reading, or computer access. Because these cost nothing to supply, a teacher can use them far more consistently than reinforcers that must be purchased and brought in, which is itself one reason to prefer natural reinforcers when setting up a procedure to reinforce a replacement behavior (see step 4 of the Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model's five-step behavior-change procedure).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An initial extrinsic reinforcer strong enough to get the target behavior started and reliably performed
  • A deliberate plan to fade the extrinsic reinforcer over time, rather than sustaining it indefinitely

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Extrinsic reinforcers that are never faded remain dependent on someone consistently delivering them — impractical at the scale of a full classroom, and absent whenever the deliverer isn't present — whereas natural reinforcers are available to the learner at all times
  • Some learners stop the target behavior entirely once an unfaded extrinsic reinforcer is removed, since the behavior was never transferred to natural reinforcement
  • Ethical use requires awareness of concerns about paying students for behaviors (e.g., reading, staying off drugs) that ideally should come to be intrinsically motivated

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who do not yet find a required activity naturally reinforcing and need extrinsic support to begin engaging with it at all

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Building genuine, self-sustaining engagement with an activity (reading, practicing an instrument, solving problems) that persists once external reinforcement is withdrawn

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify a behavior the learner does not yet find naturally reinforcing but needs to perform.
  2. Use consistent, immediate extrinsic reinforcement (praise, tokens, points) to get the behavior started and strengthened.
  3. As the behavior becomes established, gradually reduce the frequency and salience of the extrinsic reinforcer.
  4. Pair the fading extrinsic reinforcer with the activity's own natural consequence (the satisfaction of correct performance, the pleasure of the activity itself) so the learner's attention shifts toward it.
  5. Monitor whether the behavior persists as extrinsic reinforcement is withdrawn; if it does not, the fading was likely too fast, or the natural reinforcer is not yet salient enough to the learner.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Token Economies — a token economy is a common starting point for this fading process; conditioning a natural reinforcer describes how to transition away from it
  • Effective Presentation for Errorless Learning — reducing errors during the extrinsic-reinforcement phase makes the eventual natural reinforcer (successful performance) more reliably available to notice

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text: • Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model — natural reinforcers as the preferred choice in that model's replacement-behavior-reinforcement step

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves actively identifying and addressing fears that hold individuals back from achieving success. It encourages a step-by-step approach to breaking down fears, assessing the worst-case scenarios, and exploring ways to view situations more positively. By confronting fears directly, individuals can often realize that the worst-case scenario is not as bad as they think, and the benefits of change are worth the risk. This process helps to change inner dialogue and promote a more positive and courageous mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness and a willingness to confront uncomfortable feelings. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying anxieties. Access to resources such as fear hierarchies, exposure therapy techniques, or support groups can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement for individuals with severe anxiety disorders without professional support. Requires consistent effort to maintain a courageous mindset and avoid avoidance behaviors. May not be effective if not accompanied by a supportive environment and a willingness to take calculated risks.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals held back by fears, anxieties, or a reluctance to take risks.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify and address fears, assess worst-case scenarios, promote positive mindset, encourage risk-taking, reduce anxiety, foster courage.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety by confronting fears directly. Increases motivation by realizing the potential benefits of change. Fosters a growth mindset by encouraging learners to see challenges as opportunities for growth. Enhances self-esteem by promoting a sense of courage and resilience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized strategies for breaking down individual fears and assessing worst-case scenarios. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through journaling, mindfulness exercises, or exposure therapy techniques. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as fear hierarchies or guided prompts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Coaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported anxiety levels using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in risk-taking, proactive behavior, and goal-achievement. Analyze ability to identify and confront fears in real-time situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that confronting fears can reduce anxiety and improve overall well-being (e.g., American Psychological Association). Studies show that exposure therapy techniques can be effective in treating anxiety disorders. Regularly engaging in courageous behaviors can foster a sense of self-efficacy and resilience.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual afraid of public speaking joins a Toastmasters club to practice speaking in a supportive environment. A student afraid of failure in an exam takes steps to prepare thoroughly, seeks help from tutors, and reframes their mindset to focus on learning rather than achieving a perfect score. Resource: American Psychological Association – What is Exposure Therapy?

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves showing students how a topic connects to their lives, giving an example of a particular idea as they would experience it in their native country, or asking them to bring music or art from their culture and describe its significance and meaning to their classmates.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for research, flexible curriculum, willingness to incorporate student input, sensitivity to cultural differences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and sensitivity to avoid putting students on the spot or making assumptions. May require additional resources to support diverse cultural expressions.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Connect Prior Knowledge to New Learning
Description
docs.text: Building connections to prior understandings and experiences helps learners integrate new information into their existing knowledge base. This includes activating prior knowledge before introducing new concepts. It also involves relating new information to learners' personal experiences and real-world contexts. The goal is to make learning more meaningful and relevant for learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be aware of learners' prior knowledge and experiences. Instructors need to be trained in effective strategies for activating prior knowledge and making connections to new learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and effort. Some learners may have gaps in their prior knowledge. It's essential to provide additional support and scaffolding as needed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, promote meaningful learning, support transfer of knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports comprehension by connecting new information to prior knowledge, improves retention by making learning more meaningful and relevant, promotes meaningful learning by relating new information to learners' personal experiences, and supports transfer of knowledge by helping learners apply what they have learned in new contexts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor instruction to learners' prior knowledge and experiences. Provide opportunities for learners to share their own experiences and perspectives. Use analogies and metaphors to connect new concepts to familiar ones.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Analogies and prior knowledge activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of key concepts through discussions or written assignments. Track improvements in comprehension and application of knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that connecting prior knowledge to new learning can enhance comprehension, improve retention, promote meaningful learning, and support transfer of knowledge. Studies show that activating prior knowledge can improve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Activating prior knowledge before introducing a new topic. Relating new information to learners' personal experiences. Using analogies and metaphors to connect new concepts to familiar ones.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A method for making instruction more culturally relevant by connecting content to learners’ experiences. Teachers can enhance their curriculum using a variety of resources in order to make the material more culturally relevant and accessible, helping learners make important connections to content. Steps include:

  1. Assess Existing Knowledge: Find out what background knowledge learners have on a particular topic related to the lesson. This can be done through discussions in their home language, drawing, writing, or using a graphic organizer such as a K-W-L chart.
  2. Connect to Familiar Experiences: Look for ways to connect the content to things that are familiar and learners' experiences. Open up the thinking of the rest of the class to the different cultures of their peers.
  3. Enrich Instruction: Use resources that go beyond the textbook, such as artwork, music, dance, culture kits, special traditions, celebrations, recipes, and realia (concrete objects).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Resources that go beyond the textbook, such as artwork, music, dance, culture kits, realia, etc. Understanding of learners' cultural backgrounds and experiences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to research and prepare culturally relevant materials. Risk of making assumptions about learners' experiences or putting them on the spot. May be challenging if the teacher has limited knowledge of learners' cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly English Language Learners (ELLs)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner engagement, improve content retention, foster cultural understanding, make content more accessible

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Draws on learners' existing knowledge and cultural backgrounds to facilitate deeper understanding. Promotes inclusivity by valuing diverse experiences. Enhances engagement by making content more relevant to learners' lives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the content and resources used based on the specific backgrounds and experiences of learners. Allow learners to contribute their own cultural artifacts and stories to the lesson.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A middle school math teacher taught points on a grid by connecting it to a Vietnamese student's experience navigating a raft using the stars. An Albuquerque teacher used realia to introduce Burro's Tortillas, bringing items into the classroom for the lesson. Resource: Colorín Colorado - How to Connect ELLs' Background Knowledge to Content

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Conceptual understanding must precede and coincide with instruction on procedures. Learning is supported when instruction on procedures and concepts is explicitly connected in ways that make sense to learners and are iterative. Conceptual foundations lead to opportunities to develop reasoning strategies, which in turn deepens conceptual understanding; memorizing an algorithm does not. Examples of explicitly connecting procedures and concepts can be found in the Additional Resources section.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Connecting ELLs' Background Knowledge to Content
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves making instruction more culturally relevant by connecting content to ELLs' experiences. Teachers enhance their curriculum using various resources to make the material more culturally relevant and accessible. They can start by finding out what background knowledge students have on a particular topic and then looking for ways to connect the content to things that are familiar and students' experiences. This also opens up the thinking of the rest of the class to the different cultures of their peers. Teachers can learn about students' native countries, cultures, or educational systems, historical figures, musical and artistic traditions, geography, or biodiversity from students' countries so that they can connect their lessons to something that the students already know. Students can also contribute their own cultural experience, funds of knowledge, talents, and interests in the classroom.

docs.text: This approach involves integrating vocabulary instruction directly with texts to enhance understanding and retention. docs.title: Description
docs.text: Connecting struggles to strategies involves explicitly teaching students various problem-solving strategies and helping them understand when and why to use each strategy effectively. Educators provide opportunities for students to practice getting 'stuck' on problems and then working through them, while being mindful of their process. This helps students become self-directed learners who can independently apply and adapt their thinking.

docs.text:
Acknowledge that access to technology and digital literacy can vary based on socio-economic background, social environment, and cultural factors. Consider the digital divide and provide resources to bridge the gap. Offer affordable technology options, ensure access to internet and devices, and provide culturally relevant training materials.

The scale of this gap is concrete, not just anecdotal: among U.S. students ages 5–17 living in remote rural areas, 41% of Black students and 26% of Hispanic students had either no home internet access or only dial-up, compared with 13% of White students and 11% of Asian students; students below the poverty threshold were far more likely to lack home internet access (26%) than those between 100–185% of the threshold (15%) or above 185% of it (4%) (Musu, NCES). The two most common reasons families cited for lacking home internet access were cost and lack of perceived need (38% each), followed by lacking an adequate computer (8%), unavailability of service in the area (5%), and privacy/security concerns (2%) — a reminder that "bridging the gap" needs to address more than one barrier at once.

docs.text: • Awareness of social and cultural factors, partnerships with community organizations, funding for technology and resources

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Addressing systemic inequalities can be challenging, requires ongoing effort and commitment

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Who is the news source, anyway? Traditional news brands may occasionally get it wrong — sometimes hugely wrong — but at least you know where to find them and hold them accountable. Less prominent news sites might carry compelling stories — but expect them to show you who they are and where they gathered information. Does the news source appear to employ editors? Many news organizations produce stories that are checked before publication. Others don't. It's a big deal. Hiring an editorial staff shows the publication's respect for you, and matters more than "political bias." Are you told, "Trust me"? Don't. Expect everyone to show where their facts come from, link to underlying articles, and demonstrate that they've argued honestly.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators need to reflect on their own biases and privileges to effectively lead discussions about race. Tools like Glen Singleton and Curtis Linton's 'Courageous Conversations About Race' and Peggy McIntosh's work on white privilege can help. The Intercultural Development Inventory can assess cultural acceptance and understanding. Constructing and sharing a racial autobiography can provide insights into one's own identity. This self-reflection ensures educators are aware of their own assumptions, privileges, and biases, which is essential for fostering an inclusive and equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A commitment to self-reflection. Access to tools and resources. Time for personal reflection and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some educators may find it challenging to confront their own biases. Requires ongoing effort and self-assessment. May require additional support or training.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators who aim to lead discussions about race, emphasizing the importance of self-reflection and understanding one's own biases and privileges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-awareness and understanding of one's own biases and privileges. Foster an inclusive and equitable learning environment. Prepare educators to lead discussions about race effectively.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-awareness. Fosters inclusivity and equity. Improves the ability to lead discussions about race effectively.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows educators to explore their own identities and biases at their own pace. Offers a variety of tools and resources for self-reflection. Encourages open and honest self-assessment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Assessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased self-awareness and understanding of biases. Improved ability to lead discussions about race effectively. Enhanced classroom climate and sense of inclusivity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced self-awareness: Reflecting on one's own biases and privileges promotes self-awareness and understanding. Improved discussions: By understanding their own biases, educators can lead discussions about race more effectively, fostering a more inclusive and equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using tools like 'Courageous Conversations About Race' and Peggy McIntosh's work on white privilege. Constructing and sharing a racial autobiography. Completing the Intercultural Development Inventory.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Maintaining predictable classroom routines and schedules provides students with a sense of security and predictability, which supports emotional regulation. Knowing what to expect next can reduce anxiety and enhance students' ability to manage their emotions effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear and consistent routines and schedules, visual aids to communicate the schedule, proactive communication about changes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and consistent implementation. Changes to routines may be disruptive and require additional support for students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students with anxiety or those who thrive on structure and routine.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce anxiety and uncertainty, enhance predictability, and support emotional regulation by creating a stable classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances predictability, reduces anxiety, promotes a sense of security, and supports emotional regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to participate in creating and adjusting routines and schedules, incorporating their preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior for signs of reduced anxiety and improved emotional regulation. Solicit student feedback on the helpfulness of the routines and schedules.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional regulation, reduces anxiety, enhances predictability, and promotes a sense of security in the classroom.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A kindergarten classroom uses a visual schedule to show the daily activities, which helps students anticipate what will happen next and reduces anxiety during transitions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Summarizing and consolidating key points after pair talk helps to solidify understanding and ensure that all students have a clear takeaway. This can be done verbally or, better yet, by writing a list of key points on the board or via a visualiser. Organizing the ideas visually reinforces the meaning and provides a static reference for students to check against their own understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires allocating time for summarizing key points and providing a visual reference for students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The summary must be clear, concise, and accurate. It should not simply repeat what was said during the discussion but should synthesize the key ideas.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, essential for ensuring that all students benefit from pair talk activities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Solidify understanding, provide a clear takeaway, reinforce the meaning of key points, and ensure that all students have a reference for checking their understanding.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students organize and remember key ideas, provides a visual reference for checking understanding, and ensures that all students leave the activity with a clear takeaway. Supports Long-term Memory.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The summary can be tailored to address specific misconceptions or areas of confusion that were identified during pair talk.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Summarization and Synthesis
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether students are using the summary to check their understanding. Ask students to explain the key points in their own words. Assess whether the summary addresses any misconceptions or areas of confusion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Consolidating key points can improve student understanding and retention of information, ensuring that all students benefit from pair talk activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Brainstorming and displaying a constructive decision-making process as a visual reminder in the classroom helps students make good choices. The process involves stages such as staying calm, analyzing the situation, considering choices and consequences, making a choice, and evaluating the outcome.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for creating a visual display (poster, whiteboard, etc.), class time for brainstorming the process, and opportunities for students to refer to the visual reminder during decision-making.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may not always refer to the visual reminder when making decisions. The process may not be applicable to all types of decisions. Some learners may find the structure too rigid.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' ability to make constructive and ethical decisions, analyze situations, evaluate consequences, and reflect on outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured process for decision-making, enhances problem-solving skills, promotes ethical and moral reasoning, encourages self-reflection, and improves responsible behavior.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The visual reminder can be customized with different prompts, visuals, or wording. Steps can be adapted to fit various age groups or specific situations. Learners can be given options for how to display the process.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students’ decision-making processes in the classroom. Review student reflections on their decisions and outcomes. Collect feedback on the usefulness of the visual reminder.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that explicit instruction in decision-making skills can improve students' ethical development and responsible behavior. Visual aids and structured processes can help learners internalize and apply these skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Display a poster with the steps: 1) Stay calm, observe, and identify the problem. 2) Stop, think, and analyze the situation. 3) Capture your thoughts as you consider the choices and their consequences. 4) Make a choice to solve the problem. 5) Evaluate and reflect on the outcome.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Get used to regularly consulting fact-checking sites. These three nonpartisan sites below investigate the truth of various claims: FactCheck.org, Snopes.com, and Politifact.com. And to check the authenticity of images, teach your learners to reverse-Google them to find their origins.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to fact-checking sites and reverse image search tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires critical thinking skills and attention to detail.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach learners to use fact-checking sites to verify the truth of claims and check the authenticity of images.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tools to verify information and avoid spreading misinformation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose topics of interest to fact-check.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Resource Evaluation
  • Research
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to use fact-checking sites to verify claims and check the authenticity of images.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners become more discerning consumers of information. Enhanced media literacy: Learners are better equipped to assess the credibility of online sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use FactCheck.org to verify the truth of a political claim and use Google Reverse Image Search to check the authenticity of a photo.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Asking students questions that focus on the main points of the text and how the author supports those points with evidence and examples. Ensure understanding before discussing techniques. Can start with what they know.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material. Preparation of thoughtful and engaging questions. Time for discussion in class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Students may struggle to answer questions if they lack background knowledge or reading skills. Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure meaningful discussion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for struggling readers and those with limited background knowledge

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, ensure understanding of main ideas, develop critical thinking skills, enhance ability to identify evidence and examples in text

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to reading comprehension. Supports critical thinking by requiring students to analyze and evaluate evidence. Increases engagement by making reading an active and interactive process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to specific texts and student needs. Students can be given opportunities to generate their own questions. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student responses to questions. Participation in discussions. Reading comprehension quizzes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that content-focused questioning improves reading comprehension and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher asks students to identify the main argument of a text and provide evidence from the text to support their claim. Students work in groups to answer questions about a reading passage. Students generate their own questions about a text and share them with the class.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using a content "word of the week" to signal that it’s time for silence. Examples include: integer, renaissance, or circuit. This integrates vocabulary review with classroom management.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to introduce and consistently use the signal word. Students must understand the meaning of the word and its association with silence.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if students do not understand the meaning of the signal word. The novelty may wear off over time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce vocabulary while efficiently signaling the need for silence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines vocabulary review with classroom management, making learning more efficient. Provides a clear signal for students to quiet down and focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The chosen word can be tailored to current topics being studied in class, making it relevant and engaging for students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly and effectively students respond to the signal word. Monitor student recall and understanding of the vocabulary word.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reinforces vocabulary while efficiently signaling the need for silence. Integrates learning and classroom management.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using a content "word of the week" to signal that it's time for silence involves selecting a term related to the current curriculum (e.g., integer, renaissance, circuit) and using it as a cue for students to become quiet. This technique reinforces vocabulary and provides a clear signal for transitioning to quiet activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of relevant vocabulary words, clear explanation of the signal to students, consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the vocabulary is too difficult or unfamiliar, requires consistent reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Regain student attention, reinforce vocabulary, signal a transition to quiet activities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces content vocabulary, provides a clear and consistent signal, integrates learning and classroom management.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The word can be tailored to the current curriculum and student interests. Visual aids or hand motions can be added for additional support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly students respond to the word signal. Monitor classroom noise levels before and after the signal.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using a content word signal can improve classroom management by providing a clear signal for attention while reinforcing vocabulary, leading to a quieter and more focused learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Context-specific journaling requires individuals to reflect on specific experiences such as team assignments, internships, or professional practices. This involves writing down observations about their actions, expressing their thinking about those actions, and describing the significance of the actions. This reflective process is driven by experiential learning, catering to the preferences of adult learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a journal (physical or digital), writing utensils, and dedicated time for journaling. Instructors or facilitators need to provide prompts and feedback to guide reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a specific experience or context for effective implementation. Requires learners to be willing to engage in honest self-reflection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in professional development programs, internships, or team assignments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote experiential learning, enhance self-awareness, improve reflection on actions, develop critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects observations, thoughts, and significance of actions. Aligns with the experiential learning preferences of adult learners. Provides a structured way to reflect on specific experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to focus on experiences that are most relevant to their personal and professional goals. Provide different prompts for reflection based on the type of experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze journal entries to assess the depth of reflection, the quality of observations, and the understanding of the significance of actions. Evaluate changes in thinking and behavior over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports experiential learning and helps learners make meaning of their experiences. Develops self-awareness and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student participating in a team project can use a context-specific journal to record observations about group dynamics, analyze decision-making processes, and reflect on their own behavior within the group.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Introducing vocabulary words within the context of a story or reading passage allows learners to understand their meanings in relation to the surrounding text. This approach involves selecting words that are important for understanding the text or that can add depth to the learners' insight about the situation. By discussing the author's choice of words and their impact, learners can develop a richer understanding of both the vocabulary and the text itself.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection of texts and vocabulary words. Facilitation of discussions that encourage learners to analyze the author's use of language and its impact on the story.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be skilled at facilitating discussions and guiding learners to make meaningful connections between vocabulary and text. May be challenging to find texts that offer a wide range of vocabulary opportunities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those in upper elementary through high school, who need to develop a deeper understanding of how vocabulary contributes to the meaning and impact of texts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary acquisition, improve reading comprehension, and foster appreciation for author's craft by introducing words in meaningful contexts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand the nuances of word meanings and how they contribute to the overall message of a text. Promotes critical thinking and analysis of authorial choices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can select words based on their relevance to the text and the specific needs of their learners. Discussion questions can be tailored to encourage learners to make connections between the vocabulary and their own experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner participation in discussions, analysis of vocabulary in written responses, and demonstration of understanding of the author's use of language. Monitor improvement in reading comprehension and vocabulary acquisition.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners demonstrate a deeper understanding of vocabulary and texts, improved critical thinking skills, and a greater appreciation for the power of language. By understanding the context in which words are used, learners can retain and apply new vocabulary more effectively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A small-group discussion strategy that gives learners exposure to more of their peers’ ideas and prevents the stagnation that can happen when a group doesn’t happen to have the right chemistry. Learners are placed into a few groups of 4-6 learners each and are given a discussion question to talk about. After sufficient time has passed for the discussion to develop, one or two learners from each group rotate to a different group, while the other group members remain where they are. Once in their new group, they will discuss a different, but related question, and they may also share some of the key points from their last group’s conversation. For the next rotation, learners who have not rotated before may be chosen to move, resulting in groups that are continually evolving.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where learners can form small groups, prepared discussion questions, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging in small or crowded classrooms, requires careful facilitation to ensure all learners are engaged and on task, may be difficult for learners who struggle with social interaction or adapting to new groups.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for secondary and higher education learners, particularly effective for discussing complex issues and synthesizing information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active participation, expose learners to diverse perspectives, encourage deeper understanding of complex topics, enhance communication and collaboration skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes exposure to diverse perspectives, provides opportunities for deeper understanding of complex topics, enhances communication and collaboration skills, supports flexible grouping

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussion questions can be tailored to learners' interests and backgrounds. Learners can choose which group they want to rotate to.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the activity, review the quality of their responses to the discussion questions, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking, promotes exposure to diverse perspectives, improves communication and collaboration skills

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student sharing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Raise social awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Discuss social justice events.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Design classroom activities that involve cooperative work rather than competitive or individualistic work. Research suggests that learners are more motivated and successful when working in groups. Learners feel a sense of responsibility to the group to try their best, and this leads to a positive feedback loop of effort and success, encouraging the development of a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to design cooperative activities that are engaging and meaningful. Instructors need to provide clear guidelines and support to help learners work effectively in groups.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may prefer to work individually or may struggle to work effectively in groups. Instructors need to address these challenges and provide appropriate support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially those who are competitive or tend to work in isolation

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, increase motivation, improve success rates, and foster a sense of responsibility and teamwork

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to work together and support each other, creating a positive learning environment. Helps learners develop a sense of responsibility to the group and experience the positive feedback loop of effort and success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Groups can be formed based on learner interests, skill levels, or learning styles. Tasks can be assigned based on individual strengths and areas for improvement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Application
  • Consensus Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement in cooperative activities, monitor their success rates, and assess their sense of responsibility and teamwork. Compare the effectiveness of cooperative activities versus competitive or individualistic activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that learners are more motivated and successful when working in groups. Students feel a sense of responsibility to the group to try their best, and thus will experience the positive feedback loop of effort and success, encouraging the development of a growth mindset.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Designing classroom activities that involve cooperative work encourages a growth mindset. Learners feel a sense of responsibility to the group to try their best, which creates a positive feedback loop of effort and success.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Well-structured group activities, clear roles and responsibilities, facilitation skills to manage group dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure equal participation and avoid social loafing. May be challenging for learners who prefer individual work.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for learners who lack motivation or have a fixed mindset

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, foster a sense of responsibility, encourage effort and success, develop a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters collaboration, encourages mutual support, creates a sense of responsibility, and promotes a growth mindset through shared effort and success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Group assignments can be tailored to individual learner's strengths and interests, ensuring that everyone can contribute meaningfully.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Team-Based Inquiry

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor group dynamics, assess individual contributions, and observe changes in learner attitudes towards collaboration and effort.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that cooperative learning increases motivation, promotes a sense of responsibility, and fosters a growth mindset, leading to greater academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Assign group projects where each member has a specific role and responsibility, and provide feedback on both individual and group contributions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Designing classroom activities that involve cooperative—rather than competitive or individualistic—work environments boosts motivation and success. Learners feel a sense of responsibility to the group to try their best, and thus will experience the positive feedback loop of effort and success, encouraging the development of a growth mindset. Cooperative learning involves structured group activities where learners work together to achieve a common goal. This approach promotes collaboration, communication, and mutual support. Learners share their knowledge, skills, and perspectives, creating a richer learning experience. Working in groups allows learners to feel a sense of responsibility to their peers, motivating them to put in their best effort. The positive feedback loop of effort and success encourages the development of a growth mindset. Instructors should structure cooperative learning activities to ensure that each learner has a meaningful role and that the group's success depends on the contributions of all members.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured group activities with clear goals. Meaningful roles for each learner. A focus on collaboration and communication. Supportive feedback that emphasizes effort and progress.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may prefer to work independently. Group dynamics can be challenging to manage. Requires careful planning to ensure that each learner contributes and benefits from the experience.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who may feel isolated or competitive

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance motivation, promote collaboration, develop communication skills, and foster a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a supportive learning environment. Encourages collaboration and communication. Promotes a sense of responsibility and accountability. Provides opportunities for peer feedback and support. Fosters a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Groups can be formed based on learner interests, skills, or learning styles. Activities can be tailored to the specific needs of each group. Instructors can provide individualized support and feedback to help groups succeed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Team-Based Inquiry

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in learner motivation and engagement. Measure the quality of group work. Assess individual contributions to group projects. Observe changes in learner attitudes towards collaboration.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that cooperative learning enhances motivation, achievement, and social skills (reference Johnson & Johnson's research on cooperative learning). Working in groups promotes a growth mindset and reduces fear of failure (reference research on social support).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Jigsaw activities where each learner is responsible for learning and teaching a specific piece of information. Group projects where learners collaborate to solve a real-world problem. Peer tutoring where learners provide support and guidance to one another.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using structured group activities to enhance learning and social interaction. These activities involve movement, collaboration, and discussion, such as gallery walks, two stray one stay, round robin, and simultaneous round table. These strategies provide opportunities for students to engage with content in a dynamic and interactive way.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Prepared activities with clear instructions and roles. Time for group work and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful management to ensure that all students participate and contribute. Some students may dominate discussions or rely on others to do the work.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students and adult learners in various subjects. Adaptable for different age groups and learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote collaboration, enhance understanding of content, and foster social skills. These strategies provide opportunities for students to interact with each other and learn from different perspectives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation and collaboration. Enhances understanding through peer teaching and discussion. Promotes social skills and communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to different skill levels and learning preferences. Groups can be formed based on student needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and collaboration. Assess understanding through group presentations and discussions. Evaluate individual contributions to group tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that cooperative learning enhances understanding and retention by engaging students in active and collaborative learning experiences. Group activities promote social skills and communication, which are essential for success in academic and professional settings.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cooperative teaching involves structuring learning activities so that students work together, teaching each other concepts and skills. This can include verbally or visually explaining problems, sharing knowledge, and assisting peers. The goal is to deepen understanding through active participation, social interaction, and peer support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured tasks or problems for students to explain. Time allocated for peer interaction and teaching. Instructor guidance and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires clear instructions and guidelines. Some students may dominate the teaching process. Requires monitoring and facilitation to ensure effective peer interaction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of concepts, improve verbal and visual explanation skills, foster social interaction, increase knowledge retention, build peer support networks, and encourage active learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances learning by engaging students in active teaching roles. Promotes deeper understanding through verbal and visual explanations. Improves retention by requiring students to articulate concepts. Strengthens social-emotional memories and fosters cooperative learning environments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks can be tailored to different student abilities and learning styles. Roles and responsibilities can be assigned based on individual strengths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and interaction during teaching activities. Assess comprehension through explanations, problem-solving, and peer evaluations. Gather feedback from students on the effectiveness of cooperative teaching methods.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students doing the teaching are often the ones doing more of the learning. Cooperative learning is a powerful memory-enhancer because learning experiences become more memorable when social-emotional memories are part of the learning event.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students verbally and/or visually explain how to do a math problem. Teachers create opportunities for students to 'teach' the content in partnerships, small groups, or to the whole class.

docs.title: Correcting Students in a Constructive Way
Description
docs.text: Correcting and disciplining learners for inappropriate behaviors is a necessary part of the job. When you correct them, allow them to keep their dignity so that they can reflect on their behavior and choose their behaviors more wisely in the future. The correction process will be counterproductive if it's carried out in a manner that communicates sarcasm, bitterness, or low expectations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must be professional and respectful when correcting learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If the instructor invokes a consequence when angry or upset, it could lead to regrettable actions. This can be avoided by giving yourself a cooling-off period.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' behavior with constructive criticism.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Learners reflect on their behavior rather than resenting the instructor. Creates a more positive classroom.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Follow the disciplinary steps outlined in the document, ensuring that you know all the facts before disciplining the learner.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners will show improved behavior and demonstrate respect for the instructor.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students who go away thinking, 'I hate my instructor' are not as likely to change their behavior as learners who respect the instructor.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A countdown clock or visual analog timer can help kids get a better sense of how time can be broken into chunks and visualize the passage of time. These special clocks use color to show how much time has passed or how much is left, making it easier for children to understand time. They visualize time in chunks using color, making it easier to understand how much time is passing or is left.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Countdown clock or visual analog timer (physical or digital), a task to time

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for all learners. Requires initial setup and explanation. Can be distracting if not used appropriately.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with time management, visual learners, learners with ADHD

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve time management skills, enhance understanding of time duration, reduce time-related anxiety

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of time, reduces reliance on abstract time concepts, promotes awareness of time passing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Time intervals can be adjusted to suit different tasks. The visual design of the clock can be customized. Students can track their time to see how much time a specific task may take, which can help build time awareness.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to manage time during tasks. Track the frequency of on-time task completion. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the timer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual timers have been shown to improve time management skills, especially for learners with attention difficulties. Visual cues for time can reduce anxiety related to time-sensitive tasks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Visual timers are available online and in stores. You can make your own by dividing a clock face into quarters and covering each section with a different color of cellophane wrapping paper.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The countdown technique involves the teacher counting down from a number, such as "I need two people... You know who you are. I need one person...," to prompt students to quiet down and focus. This method, modeled by Teach Like a Champion author Doug Lemov, is a minimally invasive way to regain attention and establish quiet.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent use of the technique, clear explanation of expected behavior, calm and authoritative tone.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lose effectiveness if overused, some students may ignore the countdown, requires consistent reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Regain student attention, reduce classroom noise, establish a sense of urgency

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Minimally invasive, provides a clear signal for expected behavior, creates a sense of urgency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The starting number and pace of the countdown can be adjusted to fit different age groups and classroom dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly students respond to the countdown. Monitor classroom noise levels during and after the countdown.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The countdown technique can improve classroom management by providing a clear and minimally invasive signal for regaining student attention and establishing quiet.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teach kids how to confirm the credibility of a website with a scoring guide like the CRAAP test worksheet (Yup, this is a real evaluation tool!). CRAAP stands for “currency,” “relevance,” “authority,” “accuracy” and “purpose.” Students score websites on things like domain, spelling and grammar, authors listed, and dates updated.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • CRAAP test worksheet.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Confirm the credibility of a website.

docs.title: Affordances
