docs.text: • Confirms the credibility of a website.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Worksheet scores.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved credibility of sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • CRAAP worksheet

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Set aside a dedicated, positive reflection space in the classroom where kids can go to practice their emotional regulation skills. A calm-down corner, sometimes known as a peace corner, gives kids a positive, safe place to recenter and refocus so they can join the learning again. You can stock it with helpful tools like emotion charts, fidget toys, social-emotional books, and more.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated space, calming tools, emotional resources

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires clear expectations and routines, ongoing maintenance and support

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a safe space for emotional regulation, support self-soothing skills, enhance emotional awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Dedicated safe space for emotional regulation, provides tools for self-soothing and emotional expression, promotes self-awareness and emotional regulation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to select preferred coping mechanisms

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' use of the corner and ability to apply skills in classroom activities

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students regulate emotions, learn self-soothing skills, and become self-aware.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Calm down corner with comfortable seating, emotion charts, fidget toys, and social-emotional books.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a character profile helps students form a deeper understanding of a book’s characters. Activities include creating a list of adjectives that describe a character, illustrating a character based on the description in the book, reflecting on a character's future occupation (for child characters), or describing how a character makes them feel in a particular chapter.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for character analysis, creative materials for illustration, and prompts for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require scaffolding for students who struggle with character analysis or creative activities. Success depends on students engaging thoughtfully and creatively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop deeper understanding of characters, improve analytical skills, and encourage empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances character understanding through creative and analytical activities. Encourages empathy by prompting students to reflect on characters' feelings and motivations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose characters that resonate with them. Activities can be adapted to suit different learning styles and creative abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Creating Visual Representations

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved character understanding, analytical skills, and empathy. Increased student engagement and creativity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Deeper character understanding can improve overall comprehension and engagement with literature.

docs.title: Create a Classroom Code of Conduct
Description
docs.text: Teachers and students collaborate to establish a classroom code of conduct based on respectful, fair, kind, and empathetic behaviors. The code is dictated by treating others the way you want to be treated and ensures a positive and productive learning environment. This involves asking students how they want to be treated, leading to a discussion of behaviors that are respectful, fair, kind, and empathetic. The class then agrees that treating others the way you want to be treated is the best code of conduct.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom discussion, collaborative decision-making, willingness to involve students in establishing classroom rules

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time to reach consensus, students may need guidance in identifying appropriate behaviors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators looking to establish a positive classroom climate

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Establish a common understanding of positive and negative behaviors, promote respect and empathy, create a positive and productive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes respect and empathy, establishes clear expectations for behavior, enhances the learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to contribute their ideas and perspectives to the code of conduct.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe classroom behavior and interactions, gather student feedback through surveys or discussions, track disciplinary incidents.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Classrooms with established codes of conduct tend to have better student behavior and a more positive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher facilitates a discussion with students to create a list of agreed-upon behaviors for the classroom.

docs.title: Create a List of Positive Self-Talk Statements
Description
docs.text: Generating a collection of affirmative statements for learners to read and internalize. This list serves as a resource to counter negative thoughts and promote a positive mindset. Learners can choose from pre-made lists or create their own personalized affirmations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a list of positive affirmations or the ability to create one. Time for reflection and personalization.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel superficial if not accompanied by genuine reflection and effort. Some statements may not resonate with all individuals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals of all ages who want to develop a more positive mindset.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide learners with concrete examples of positive self-talk and encourage personal reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a tangible tool for combating negative thoughts. Allows learners to personalize their self-talk, making it more meaningful and effective. Promotes self-awareness and reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select statements that resonate with them or create their own based on their needs and experiences. Lists can be tailored to specific challenges or goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to recall and use affirmations in challenging situations. Self-reported changes in mindset and behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that affirmations can positively impact self-esteem and reduce stress. Having a personalized list can empower learners to actively manage their thoughts and emotions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use a free list of 101 Positive Thinking Affirmations to help learners read through and select their favorite statements. Encourage learners to come up with their own affirmations based on their personal experiences and goals.

docs.title: Create a Word Wall for Emotions
Description
docs.text: Build your students’ emotion vocabulary by giving them direct access to those words and feelings. Try creating a word wall filled with feelings words. Then, when kids are demonstrating certain behaviors, ask them to look at the wall and choose the words to describe how they’re feeling. This helps them connect those actions and emotions and consider what coping strategies they can try.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emotion words, large display area, markers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing maintenance, can become cluttered, may not be accessible to all learners

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expand emotional vocabulary, improve ability to identify and label emotions, connect emotions to behaviors and coping strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual reminder and reference for emotional vocabulary, helps connect emotions with behaviors, promotes self-awareness and emotional regulation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Incorporate student suggestions for feelings words, visually represent emotions with images

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students’ ability to use emotional vocabulary in discussions, writing, and self-reflection activities

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced emotional literacy, better self-awareness, improved ability to manage emotions and behaviors

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A classroom has a word wall labeled "Feelings" with words like happy, sad, angry, frustrated, and excited. When a student is upset, the teacher asks them to identify how they are feeling using the word wall.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Transforming schools into beautiful spaces by displaying high-quality student work from projects can have a transformative impact, especially for students whose communities and homes are not always beautiful places. A school building that honors and celebrates student work brings life, energy, and a sense of pride.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a commitment to creating a visually appealing and welcoming school environment. Demands resources for displaying student work.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to transform the school building. Can be challenging to create beautiful spaces within budget constraints.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly beneficial for students from marginalized communities who may not have access to beautiful spaces in their homes and neighborhoods.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a welcoming and inspiring learning environment, honor and celebrate student work, foster a sense of pride and ownership, transform the school building into a beautiful space.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a sense of pride and ownership in the school building. Provides a welcoming and inspiring learning environment. Honors and celebrates student work.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Student work can be displayed in a way that reflects their unique cultural backgrounds and experiences. Allows students to create and display work that is personally meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Public Product
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the impact of the school environment on student engagement and motivation. Assess student pride and ownership of their school building. Review student reflections on the impact of the school environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creating beautiful spaces in schools transforms the learning environment, fostering a sense of pride, ownership, and inspiration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Displaying high-quality student projects throughout the school building. Transforming classrooms into welcoming and visually appealing spaces.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating culture kits involves students creating their own collections of items that represent their culture to bring their culture alive as a way of sharing and discussing what can be learned from different multicultural traditions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for students to create and share their kits, access to relevant materials, and teacher facilitation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure respect and inclusivity. May require additional resources to support diverse cultural expressions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly in multicultural classrooms.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote cultural sharing, enhance understanding of traditions, create engaging learning experiences, and connect cultures in the classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters cultural exchange, engages students, and promotes understanding of diverse backgrounds and traditions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students create their own kits with items that are meaningful to them, allowing for diverse cultural expressions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of student presentations, depth of cultural understanding, engagement during discussions, and positive feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased cultural awareness, stronger classroom community, enhanced learning engagement, and a celebration of diversity.

docs.title: Create Space for Students to Reflect
Description
docs.text: Providing structured opportunities for students to pause, reflect, and think about themselves, their ideas, and their feelings about projects can transform a classroom culture. Reflection promotes socio-emotional learning and provides a counterbalance to the fast pace of traditional classrooms, which can activate trauma and drain student energy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in classroom culture from urgency to reflection. Demands a commitment to socio-emotional learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time for reflection activities. Can be challenging to integrate reflection into a curriculum that is already packed with content.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly beneficial for students who may experience trauma or anxiety in traditional settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote socio-emotional learning, reduce stress and anxiety, enhance self-awareness, foster a culture of reflection, provide a safe and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a counterbalance to the fast pace of traditional classrooms. Promotes self-awareness and emotional regulation. Creates a more mindful and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Reflection activities can be tailored to individual student needs and preferences. Allows students to reflect on topics that are personally meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate student reflections for depth of insight and self-awareness. Assess changes in student behavior and emotional regulation. Review student journals and other reflective work.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Integrating reflection into PBL creates a safer, more supportive learning environment, fostering socio-emotional learning and reducing stress.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students journaling about their project experiences and feelings. Learners participating in mindfulness exercises before starting project work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Setting up a classroom library involves acquiring books and materials, organizing the shelves, creating labels, and making the space cozy. This approach encourages learners to find joy in selecting and reading books they will love. Organization can be based on genres, topics, themes, Accelerated Reader (AR) levels, or guided reading levels. Book bins can be used to display books by their covers, increasing the likelihood of learners selecting them. Involving learners in deciding categories can enhance engagement and ownership.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A collection of books, shelving or bins, labels, and space to create the library. Requires initial setup and ongoing maintenance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant initial investment to build a diverse library. Requires ongoing maintenance to ensure the library remains organized and engaging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly elementary and middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, promote independent reading, enhance book selection skills, improve organization and accessibility of reading materials

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation through learner choice, promotes independence in reading, fosters a sense of ownership and responsibility

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can help decide the categories and organization of the library, aligning with their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased reading engagement, improved book selection skills, positive feedback from learners regarding the library.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that access to a well-organized and engaging classroom library improves reading habits and fosters a love of reading. Involving learners in the setup and maintenance of the library enhances their sense of ownership and responsibility.

docs.title: Creating a Common Language for Multimodal Composition
Description
docs.text: Empowering students with a shared vocabulary to analyze and discuss the multimodal composition process. This involves selecting one mode (linguistic, visual, audio, gestural, or spatial), analyzing examples, identifying its uses across different subjects and outside of school, and creating a class definition. The goal is to enrich discussions with common definitions and concrete examples.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Anchor chart, examples of different modes, time for discussion and analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming if not managed effectively. Requires careful selection of examples to illustrate each mode. Relies on active participation and collaboration from all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students learning multimodal composition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop a shared understanding of multimodal composition, enhance analytical skills, improve communication about design choices

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to understanding multimodal composition, fosters collaboration, and enhances communication skills. Creates a foundation for analyzing and discussing multimodal texts effectively.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different grade levels and subject areas. The mode of focus can be chosen based on student needs and interests. Examples can be tailored to specific learning contexts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and specificity of student contributions during discussions. Analyze the quality of student definitions and examples. Assess students' ability to apply the common language in their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced student understanding of multimodal composition and improved communication skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a culture of error involves fostering a classroom or learning environment where mistakes are viewed as valuable learning opportunities rather than failures. This approach encourages learners to ask questions, experiment, and explore without fear of negative consequences, promoting a growth mindset and deeper engagement with the material. Technology can be leveraged to support this culture through interactive tools, educational games, and platforms that provide immediate, encouraging feedback, reinforcing that errors are part of the learning process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from both instructors and learners to value mistakes as learning opportunities. Technology platforms should be designed with supportive and encouraging feedback mechanisms. Activities should be structured to allow for exploration and experimentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may initially resist the idea of embracing mistakes due to prior experiences or ingrained beliefs. Requires consistent reinforcement and modeling from instructors to maintain a positive culture of error. May be challenging to implement in high-stakes testing environments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage experimentation, reduce fear of failure, foster deeper learning, improve self-correction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages a growth mindset by reframing mistakes as learning opportunities. Reduces anxiety associated with making errors, promoting greater engagement and willingness to take risks. Provides a supportive environment for asking questions and seeking clarification. Reinforces learning through immediate and encouraging feedback.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning contexts, including classrooms and digital platforms. Feedback can be tailored to individual learner needs and learning styles. Activities can be designed to accommodate different levels of experience and prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Gain attention
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner behavior, such as increased willingness to ask questions and participate in activities. Track the types of questions learners ask to assess their understanding of concepts. Analyze the quality and depth of learner reflections on their mistakes. Measure the impact of the culture of error on learner performance and growth over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that embracing mistakes can lead to deeper learning, increased engagement, and a more positive attitude toward challenges. A growth mindset can improve learner resilience and persistence, as well as foster innovation and creativity. Creates more effective learning. (USC Rossier Brain Study)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers create a safe environment for students to ask questions and make mistakes, reminding them that mistakes can be important learning opportunities. Technology provides interactive learning tools and educational games that allow students to explore and experiment without fear of failure. Digital platforms offer immediate feedback in a supportive and encouraging tone, helping students understand and correct their mistakes.

docs.title: Creating a Digital Library Section for SEL Topics
Description
docs.text: A digital library includes a dedicated section of books focused on social and emotional learning (SEL) topics. This allows teachers and students to easily search for and find titles relevant to specific SEL skills, such as empathy, positive relationships, managing emotions, problem-solving, grit, perseverance, and perspective-taking. The library can be organized by topic, skill, or grade level, making it easier for educators to integrate SEL into their curriculum and for students to find resources that address their specific needs. This approach emphasizes the importance of SEL and provides a convenient way to access relevant literature.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a digital library platform, a collection of SEL-focused books, and a system for organizing and categorizing titles. Staff training may be needed to effectively curate and promote the collection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing maintenance to ensure the collection remains current and relevant. Access to technology and digital literacy skills are necessary. May not address all aspects of SEL without complementary activities and discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and students in elementary and secondary schools who are looking to integrate SEL into their curriculum.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote SEL, improve access to relevant literature, support curriculum integration, and enhance student awareness of SEL topics and skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides easy access to a wide range of SEL resources, supports curriculum integration, and enhances student awareness of SEL skills and topics. Facilitates a more comprehensive approach to SEL by integrating literature into various subject areas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The digital library can be tailored to the specific needs and interests of the school community by selecting titles that reflect diverse perspectives and address relevant social issues. Teachers can create curated lists based on grade level, reading ability, and SEL focus.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance
  • Application
  • Integration
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track usage of the SEL section, survey teachers and students about the usefulness of the resources, and analyze student work for evidence of improved SEL skills. Monitor the diversity and relevance of titles to ensure the collection meets the needs of the school community.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that integrating SEL into the curriculum enhances academic performance, improves student behavior, and promotes positive relationships. A well-curated digital library section can support these outcomes by providing easy access to relevant literature.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Booksource has created a section dedicated to SEL topics, allowing teachers and students to easily search and find titles relevant to them and/or focused on specific SEL skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners who feel like they belong in school are more motivated, engaged, and ultimately show higher performance. Cues of belonging can have a powerful impact on learners. Cues such as including representations of all learners are simple to implement and will improve your classroom environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • This requires intentionality on the part of the instructor to create an inclusive and welcoming environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and require constant upkeep to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support the creation of a community through promoting an inclusive classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • When learners feel like they belong, they will have higher academic performance and overall well-being.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The instructor should be responsive to the needs of all learners and try to make them feel included.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Positive learner feedback, improved classroom culture, increased enthusiasm to participate in class, etc.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When learners feel that they belong to a community, they are more motivated and engaged, and they have higher academic performance and overall well-being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A method for empowering learners by focusing on their strengths rather than their weaknesses, creating authentic learning experiences that enable them to develop skills and talents. This approach maximizes motivation, contribution, and impact by building on assets rather than focusing on deficits. To create a strengths-based culture, instructors can have learners identify and discuss strengths with peers, celebrate strengths in action, identify goals and determine how strengths will be used to achieve them, allow learners to work on passion projects, have experts of the week share talents, create a wall celebrating strengths, model strengths, vary assessment, and reflect on how strengths are used.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for learners to share and discuss their strengths, materials for passion projects, varied assessment options

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset and a willingness to focus on learners’ strengths rather than deficits. May be challenging to implement in a classroom with diverse abilities and needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower learners to manage themselves, build on their assets, and recognize their unique gifts. Build confidence, foster collaboration, and create a positive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases confidence, passion, and engagement. Allows learners to build on their unique gifts and work on areas that are challenging without feeling inadequate. Fosters collaboration and a positive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose passion projects to build and draw on strengths. Provide varied assessment options to allow for strengths to be demonstrated.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Learner Choice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner confidence, engagement, and motivation. Positive feedback from learners and peers. Improved collaboration and communication.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners are more confident, passionate, and do better work when you focus on what’s right with them instead of what’s wrong with them. Creating authentic learning experiences that empower learners to develop the skills and talents to manage themselves and build on their assets, rather than focus on their deficits, maximizes the motivation, contribution, and impact of all learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners identify and discuss strengths with peers. An expert of the week shares unique talents and strengths. Learners create a wall celebrating unique strengths. Resource: Dr. Katie Martin - 10 Ideas for Creating a Strengths-Based Culture

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating an action plan involves outlining the specific steps needed to achieve a goal. This includes breaking down the goal into smaller, manageable tasks, setting milestones, and allocating resources. An action plan provides a clear roadmap for progress.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires time for planning and organization. Access to tools for creating and tracking tasks, such as project management software or simple checklists.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Action plans can become rigid and may need adjustment as circumstances change. Overplanning can lead to analysis paralysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beneficial for anyone with complex goals or projects, including students, professionals, and teams.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a clear roadmap for achieving goals, improve organization, and enhance motivation by showing tangible progress.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simplifies complex goals into manageable steps, enhancing focus and reducing overwhelm. Milestones provide opportunities for celebrating progress and maintaining motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can tailor action plans to their individual preferences and work styles. Visual aids, digital tools, or written plans can be used.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Success is measured by the completion of tasks and milestones outlined in the action plan, leading to the achievement of the overall goal.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Action plans have been shown to increase productivity and goal achievement by providing a clear framework for action and accountability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Breaking down a writing project into tasks such as outlining, drafting, editing, and revising. Developing a marketing campaign with tasks such as market research, content creation, and promotion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating beautiful spaces in PBL involves displaying student work from projects in the school building to honor and celebrate high-quality student work. This can transform the school building into a beautiful, colorful, warm space that brings back life and energy. For students whose communities and homes may not always be beautiful places, this can have a transformative effect.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A commitment to creating a beautiful and welcoming school environment, and resources to display student work in a meaningful way.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in priorities for some schools and may necessitate additional resources or support to transform the school building into a beautiful space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those who may not have access to beautiful or inspiring environments outside of school.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To create a positive and uplifting learning environment, promote student pride in their work, and transform the school building into a beautiful and inspiring space.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances student well-being, promotes a sense of pride in their work, and transforms the school building into a more positive and welcoming space.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to showcase their unique talents and perspectives, making the learning environment more personalized and meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Teaching
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, a stronger sense of pride in their work, and a more positive and welcoming school environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that creating beautiful and inspiring learning environments enhances student well-being and promotes a more positive school culture.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Displaying student work from projects in hallways, classrooms, and restrooms to create a beautiful and inspiring school environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating collaborative spaces involves designing the learning environment to facilitate group work and interaction among learners. This can include arranging desks or tables in clusters, providing comfortable seating areas for small group discussions, and creating writable surfaces for brainstorming and problem-solving. The goal is to encourage learners to work together, share ideas, and learn from one another. Collaborative spaces can support the development of communication, teamwork, and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to rearrange the learning environment to facilitate group work. May require adjustments to classroom management strategies to address learner interaction and collaboration. Instructors must be mindful of the impact of the learning environment on learner interaction and collaboration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may prefer to work independently. It may be challenging to manage group dynamics and ensure that all learners are actively participating. Creating collaborative spaces may not be sufficient to address learner communication and teamwork problems.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, enhance communication skills, foster teamwork, encourage peer learning, create a sense of community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases opportunities for learners to interact and collaborate. Supports the development of communication, teamwork, and problem-solving skills. Promotes peer learning and a sense of community. Can improve learner engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can create collaborative spaces that are tailored to the needs of different learners. Learners can choose to work in groups that suit their learning style and preferences. Creating collaborative spaces can be combined with other personalization strategies, such as flexible grouping and flexible pacing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner interaction and collaboration in group activities. Collect learner feedback on the impact of collaborative spaces on their learning. Measure learner achievement and compare outcomes in collaborative learning environments versus traditional learning environments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced collaboration: Research suggests that creating collaborative spaces can enhance learner collaboration and teamwork skills. Improved communication: Collaborative learning environments can promote communication and peer learning. Increased engagement: Some studies have shown that collaborative learning can lead to improved learner engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher arranges desks in clusters to encourage group work and discussions. A professor provides comfortable seating areas in the classroom for small group projects. A trainer creates writable surfaces on tables and walls for brainstorming and problem-solving activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating Questions is a strategy where learners generate questions about what they are listening to. The instructor stops at intervals during a speech, documentary, or story, and learners write down one or two questions about what they just heard. This encourages learners to actively listen for points of confusion or curiosity. Modeling is important, as learners are typically trained to seek answers rather than identify gaps in understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured intervals during instruction, modeling of effective question formulation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a shift in mindset for learners accustomed to seeking answers rather than asking questions, some learners may struggle with question formulation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance active listening, promote metacognitive thinking, identify areas of confusion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to actively listen for points of confusion or curiosity, promotes metacognitive awareness of what they don't understand

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide sentence stems for learners who struggle with question formulation

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze the quality and relevance of learners' questions, track their ability to identify areas of confusion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that self-questioning strategies can improve comprehension and retention. Practitioner experience indicates that Creating Questions enhances active listening and encourages learners to think critically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Stopping at intervals during a speech and having learners write questions. Resource: Rebecca Alber, Edutopia

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating quiet spaces involves designating areas in the learning environment where learners can retreat for individual reflection, focused work, or relaxation. These spaces can be as simple as a corner with a comfortable chair or as elaborate as a dedicated room with soundproofing and calming decor. The goal is to provide learners with a respite from the noise and stimulation of the classroom, allowing them to recharge and refocus. Quiet spaces can support learner well-being, self-regulation, and concentration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to designate space for quiet activities. May require adjustments to classroom management strategies to address learner use of quiet spaces. Instructors must be mindful of the impact of the learning environment on learner well-being and self-regulation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may not feel comfortable using quiet spaces. It may be challenging to create quiet spaces in small or overcrowded classrooms. Creating quiet spaces may not be sufficient to address learner stress or anxiety.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-regulation, support learner well-being, enhance concentration, reduce stress, create a calming environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a place to retreat for individual reflection and relaxation. Supports self-regulation by allowing learners to manage their own energy levels. Enhances concentration by reducing distractions. Can improve learner well-being by creating a calming and supportive environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can create quiet spaces that are tailored to the needs of different learners. Learners can choose to use quiet spaces when they feel overwhelmed or need to refocus. Creating quiet spaces can be combined with other personalization strategies, such as flexible seating and flexible pacing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner use of quiet spaces and their impact on behavior. Collect learner feedback on the effectiveness of quiet spaces in promoting well-being and concentration. Measure learner stress levels and compare outcomes in environments with quiet spaces versus those without quiet spaces.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-regulation: Research suggests that creating quiet spaces can support learner self-regulation by allowing them to manage their own energy levels. Reduced stress: A calming environment can reduce stress and improve learner well-being. Enhanced concentration: Some studies have shown that quiet spaces can lead to improved learner concentration and focus.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher designates a corner of the classroom as a quiet reading area with comfortable chairs and soft lighting. A professor creates a relaxation room in the library with beanbag chairs and calming music. A trainer provides a meditation space in the training center for learners to use during breaks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Schools should provide opportunities for teachers to try new things and make mistakes. One of the key principles of a growth mindset is the willingness to try new approaches. Begin with the learning in mind; that is, what will teachers and the school learn as part of the process, rather than whether the new idea is going to be a success or a failure.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires administrative support and resources to facilitate experimentation. A culture of trust and open communication is essential for creating a safe space for teachers to take risks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some new ideas may not be successful, and it may be challenging to measure the impact of experimentation on student outcomes. Requires a long-term commitment to fostering a culture of innovation and continuous improvement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators at all levels, particularly those seeking to improve their teaching practices or implement new educational strategies

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage innovation and experimentation among teachers, create a culture of risk-taking and continuous improvement, and promote professional growth through the implementation of new ideas and approaches.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a supportive environment where teachers feel comfortable trying new methods without fear of failure, fosters creativity and innovation in the classroom, and encourages a collaborative approach to problem-solving.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow teachers to choose the new ideas or approaches they want to implement based on their interests and needs. Provide personalized support and resources to help teachers implement and evaluate their chosen strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the number of new ideas implemented by teachers. Collect data on teacher satisfaction and engagement. Evaluate the impact of new approaches on student learning outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that schools that encourage innovation and experimentation among teachers are more likely to see improvements in student achievement and teacher satisfaction. Creating space for new ideas fosters a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school provides funding for teachers to attend workshops or conferences on innovative teaching strategies, then supports them in implementing these strategies in their classrooms. Resource: Gerstein, Jackie. "The Educator with a Growth Mindset: A Staff Workshop."

docs.title: Creating Space for Student Reflection in PBL
Description
docs.text: Creating space for student reflection involves integrating moments for students to pause and think about themselves, their ideas, and how they feel about the project. This practice flips the script on traditional classrooms where the emphasis is on urgency, making schools safer places that can mitigate trauma and energize students. Reflection can be facilitated through mindfulness practices like journaling, meditating, yoga, or connecting to nature.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time dedicated to reflection, a classroom environment that values mindfulness and self-awareness, and access to reflection tools such as journals or meditation guides.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in traditional teaching practices and may necessitate additional training or support to implement mindfulness practices effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those who may experience trauma or anxiety in traditional classroom settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To enhance student well-being, reduce stress, and promote deeper understanding through purposeful reflection in PBL activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes mindfulness, reduces stress, and enhances self-awareness and reflection, leading to deeper understanding and more meaningful learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to engage in reflection activities that are personally relevant and meaningful, making the learning experience more personalized and engaging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Journaling
  • Self-monitoring

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student well-being, improved self-awareness, and more meaningful and reflective project outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that incorporating mindfulness and reflection into the classroom enhances student well-being, reduces stress, and promotes deeper learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing regular journaling sessions, practicing mindfulness exercises, or connecting to nature through outdoor learning activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Developing visual aids and lists of problem-solving strategies in collaboration with learners. These charts serve as resources for students when they encounter challenges, helping them to identify and articulate their problem-solving processes. Language prompts are included to help students talk about their thinking and reflection, promoting both self-directed learning and a connection between struggles and strategic solutions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for collaboration, chart-making materials, and a classroom environment that values reflection and problem-solving.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing maintenance and updates. Students may need explicit instruction in how to use the charts effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, K-12 and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-directed learning, improve problem-solving skills, and promote metacognitive reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual resource for problem-solving, helps students articulate their thinking, and connects struggles with strategic solutions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Co-authoring the charts with students ensures relevance and personalization. Language prompts can be tailored to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student use of problem-solving strategies, improved articulation of thinking processes, and enhanced self-reflection skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Tying struggles to strategies helps students see value in working harder and smarter, leading to more successful outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating charts listing 'how to get unstuck' strategies, providing language prompts for self-talk or partner discussions, and referring to the charts when students are stuck or struggling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When students express information visually, they are activating more cognitive processes while problem solving and increasing their experience with alternate texts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to art supplies or digital tools, supportive environment for creative expression.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with visual expression, may require additional support.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activate cognitive processes, improve problem solving, increase experience with alternate texts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances cognitive processing, improves problem-solving skills, increases exposure to diverse forms of media.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose visual mediums like drawings, infographics, or videos.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of visual representations, clarity of communication, creativity in expression.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced cognitive engagement, improved problem-solving abilities, increased exposure to diverse media.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a diagram to explain a scientific concept, designing an infographic to present research findings, or producing a video to showcase a historical event.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Simplify complex ideas by linking them to familiar situations, making them easier to understand and remember. Help highlight the importance of concepts. Learners can see how theoretical ideas apply in real-world settings, which can enhance their understanding and motivate them to apply these concepts to their own work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection of analogies that accurately represent the concept. Tools for creating visuals to support the analogies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Analogies can be misleading if not carefully chosen. Overuse of analogies can become distracting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with abstract concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Simplify complex concepts, connect learning to real-world applications, improve learner engagement and retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes it easier to grasp complex ideas by comparing them to familiar scenarios. Simplifies the abstract concept.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use analogies and comparisons that are relevant to learners' backgrounds and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Analogies and prior knowledge activation
  • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to explain the concept using the analogy. Evaluate their ability to apply the concept in new situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using analogies and comparisons in eLearning courses is a powerful way to simplify complex ideas by linking them to familiar situations, making them easier to understand and remember.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Explaining 'scalability' in business by likening it to a restaurant increasing the number of tables during peak hours, visualizing data encryption like a secure lockbox, considering photosynthesis similar to cooking, and picturing the scenario of buying tickets for a popular concert to understand economic supply and demand.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors ask thought-provoking questions to encourage reflection and emotional awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A list of thought-provoking questions and time for reflection and discussion (5-10 minutes).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of the activity depends on the quality of the questions and the willingness of students to participate.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for elementary through college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage reflection, promote emotional awareness, foster creativity, build a positive classroom environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a quick and easy way to check-in with students. Encourages reflection and emotional awareness. Promotes creativity and imagination.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The questions can be adapted to focus on specific emotional categories or to address specific classroom needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in answering the questions. Assess the thoughtfulness and specificity of students' responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Acknowledging emotions calms the amygdala and reduces the intensity of felt emotions, helping individuals feel more in control. Promotes emotional literacy and awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers use creative check-in questions as a regular part of their classroom routine to help students connect with their emotions and build a positive learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engaging and enjoyable writing activities that move away from traditional pencil and paper tasks. Instead, these activities incorporate elements like sensory materials, movement, and play to encourage handwriting skill development. They focus on skills like spacing, letter sizing, and paper orientation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Creative materials (e.g., playdough, shaving cream, stickers), varied writing tools, and a supportive environment. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not directly translate to formal handwriting tasks without explicit connections. Relies on transferring skills from creative to traditional writing contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grades, particularly useful for students who are reluctant writers or struggle with traditional handwriting methods.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop various handwriting skills (e.g., spacing, letter size) through creative and engaging activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation and engagement by making handwriting practice fun. Addresses skills in a less formal, more relaxed environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual interests and needs, focusing on specific skill deficits or preferred sensory experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in skills during creative activities, such as consistent letter sizing or spacing. Track progress when transitioning to formal writing tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced handwriting skills through creative engagement and varied practice. Increased motivation and positive attitudes towards writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creative presentations are visual aids designed to engage learners and keep their attention through the use of bright colors, creative fonts, and a combination of photos, charts, and icons. These presentations go beyond traditional slide formats to present information in a visually stimulating and memorable way. By mixing and matching styles, such as combining script fonts with modern fonts, and using image frames to seamlessly incorporate pictures, presenters can create presentations that capture and maintain learners' interest.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to presentation software and design tools. Implementation involves careful planning and integration of visuals. May require training in presentation design.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overly complex or distracting visuals can detract from the content. Ineffective use of design can confuse learners. Requires time and effort to create high-quality presentations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, trainers, and presenters in academic, corporate, and professional development settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Engage learners, maintain attention, stimulate interest, enhance memory, present information visually

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Keeps learners engaged and attentive during presentations. Enhances visual memory and recall of information. Provides a creative and stimulating learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different topics, learning levels, and presentation styles. Design elements can be adjusted to suit the audience and subject matter.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation during presentations. Collect feedback on the effectiveness of visuals. Assess learner comprehension and recall of key points.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creative presentations have been shown to improve learner engagement, motivation, and retention of information. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include presentations using bold color palettes, script fonts, image frames, and a mix of charts and icons to illustrate concepts. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating creative presentations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Former teachers Ed Kang and Amy Schwartzbach-Kang incorporated storytelling and creative writing into their after-school program’s science lessons.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires prompts or activities that encourage storytelling. Requires time for students to write.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with creative writing. Teachers need to provide guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for elementary and middle school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Engage students in science through storytelling. Foster creativity and imagination. Integrate science concepts with writing skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes science more engaging and accessible. Fosters creativity and imagination. Integrates science concepts with writing skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose the topics and characters they want to write about.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student stories to assess creativity, understanding of science concepts, and writing skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engages students in science through storytelling. Fosters creativity and imagination. Integrates science concepts with writing skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask students to imagine a creature that could survive in a local habitat. What color would it be? What features would help it to survive and defend itself? How would it hunt its prey? Students then wrote a story about their creature that combined science concepts with creative storytelling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Developing a critical lens involves analyzing the affordances and constraints of different modes of communication to understand how they enhance or inhibit meaning. This can be done by analyzing a single mode in various media, such as picture books, informational texts, poetry, magazines, blogs, and websites, to identify how images and words work together or against each other. By talking about how modes can enhance or inhibit meaning, learners develop a critical lens and collect exemplar structures to guide their own composition decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to various media for analysis. Needs structured discussion prompts to guide learners' thinking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners to identify subtle affordances and constraints. Learners may need support in connecting their analyses to their own compositions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners involved in multimodal composition, particularly those needing to improve the clarity and effectiveness of their designs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Heighten learners' awareness of effective and ineffective multimodal combinations. Develop a critical lens for analyzing the affordances and constraints of different modes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking skills. Provides concrete examples for analyzing multimodal works. Improves learners' ability to make informed design choices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to choose the media they want to analyze. Scaffolding can be provided by pre-selecting examples and guiding discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the depth and specificity of learners' analyses of multimodal works. Assess the extent to which learners apply their critical lens in their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that analyzing the affordances and constraints of different modes improves learners' ability to make informed design choices and create more effective multimodal compositions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Analyzing picture books to discuss how images and words convey different meanings. Expanding the analysis to other genres and media such as informational texts, poetry, magazines, blogs, and websites.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Critical Response Process is a structured method for giving feedback that puts the learner in control. It involves four steps: Statements of Meaning (Responders state what was meaningful, evocative, interesting, exciting, or striking in the work); Artist as Questioner (The artist asks questions about the work); Neutral Questions (Responders ask neutral questions about the work, and the artist responds); and Opinion Time (Responders state opinions, given permission from the artist; the artist has the option to say no). This method aims to subvert the typical power dynamic between instructor and pupil.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear guidelines for each step, a facilitator (optional), a supportive environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires commitment from both instructor and learner, may be challenging for learners to decline feedback

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, graduate students, professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower learners, shift control of feedback process, promote thoughtful reflection, create a safe environment for feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to take ownership of their learning, provides targeted feedback, fosters a safe environment for sharing, promotes instructor-student collaboration

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The process can be adapted to different disciplines and learning contexts. The learner has the option to decline feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner engagement and ownership of learning. Analyze the quality of feedback and reflection. Monitor the effectiveness of the process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Instructor and student on equal footing with the student deciding what they want to hear feedback on.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A graduate student uses the method during a peer review of research proposals. The student asks for specific feedback on the research design, and the peers provide feedback on the chosen topic.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cross-age peer tutoring involves pairing students from different grade levels, with older students acting as tutors for younger students. The older students reinforce their understanding of the material by teaching it, while the younger students benefit from personalized attention and guidance. This approach fosters a sense of responsibility and leadership in the older students and provides a supportive learning environment for the younger students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful pairing of students, clear learning objectives, and structured activities. Teachers need to provide training and support for tutors to ensure effective instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional planning and coordination to schedule tutoring sessions. Tutors need to be adequately prepared and supported to provide effective instruction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students, particularly effective for reinforcing foundational skills and promoting positive social interactions.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning for older students, provide personalized support for younger students, develop leadership skills, and foster positive relationships between different age groups.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances learning for both tutors and tutees, builds confidence and leadership skills in older students, and provides personalized support for younger students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various subjects and topics, allowing tutors to focus on areas where tutees need the most support. Flexible structure accommodates different learning styles and paces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Provide Guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence

docs.title: Cultivate Multiple Ways of Knowing and Making Meaning
Description
docs.text: Honoring multiple and diverse ways of developing understandings of the world ensures that learners have opportunities to connect with the material in ways that resonate with their individual strengths and backgrounds. This includes valuing different cultural perspectives and learning styles. It also involves providing opportunities for learners to express their understanding in a variety of ways, such as through writing, art, music, or performance. The goal is to create a learning environment that is inclusive and supportive of all learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be aware of learners' diverse backgrounds and learning styles. Instructors need to be trained in culturally responsive teaching strategies and creative assessment techniques.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a variety of learning activities and assessment options to suit different learning styles. Encourage learners to share their cultural perspectives and experiences. Allow learners to express their understanding in creative ways.

Description
docs.text: Using translations, descriptions, movement, and images to support learning in unfamiliar or complex languages promotes understanding and respect for diverse linguistic backgrounds. This includes providing translations of key terms and concepts. It also involves using visual aids, gestures, and real-world examples to clarify meaning. The goal is to create a learning environment where all languages and dialects are valued and respected.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to translation resources and multilingual materials. Instructors need to be trained in culturally responsive teaching strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources. Some learners may be resistant to using translations or visual aids. It's essential to be sensitive to learners' cultural and linguistic needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide translations of key terms and concepts in learners' native languages. Use visual aids, gestures, and real-world examples to clarify meaning. Encourage learners to share their own linguistic and cultural experiences.

This includes ensuring representations of all students, providing cues that signal safety and recognition, and creating inclusive classroom scenarios. The strategies promote belonging through simple cues and by including representations of all students in your classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Culturally responsive practice involves engaging students in the learning process through an understanding of how their identity and perspective is shaped by their culture and community experiences. It encompasses many different aspects of a person’s identities including native language, gender, and able bodiedness as well as aspects that may be less visible such as mental health and learning disabilities. Understanding different cultural frameworks can provide insight into how and where implicit bias shows up in classrooms and curricula and help teachers push back on dominant narratives that have historically and systematically excluded students. Culturally responsive practice taps into students’ funds of knowledge and builds cognitive and emotional capacity for productive struggle, supporting them in becoming independent learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of different cultural frameworks, awareness of implicit bias, a commitment to equity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant amount of work to develop cultural awareness and to understand student identities.

docs.text: Culturally and historically responsive literacy is an equity framework to help educators teach literacy learning goals such as identity development, literacy skill development, intellectual development, and criticality. It involves integrating racial and cultural responsiveness into learning goals, lesson plans, and texts.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires educators to be knowledgeable about different cultures and histories. May be challenging to implement in schools that lack resources or support for culturally responsive teaching.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners make sense of who they are, develop proficiencies in reading and writing, gain knowledge through literacy practices, and develop the ability to understand power, equity, and anti-oppression.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Culturally competent family engagement involves training school staff in behaviors, attitudes, and policies that enable effective cross-cultural relationships. Staff shifts from deficit thinking to strengths thinking, viewing families as having significant expertise and resources that can inform and improve student learning. This includes getting to know families, local community resources, and partners, and creating a welcoming school culture that emphasizes equality, acceptance, and shared values and goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires professional development for school staff on cultural competency, time for staff to get to know families and community resources, and a commitment to creating a welcoming school culture.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and commitment from school staff. Success depends on genuine empathy and a willingness to challenge existing biases and assumptions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools seeking to improve engagement with diverse families, particularly those serving low-income families and families of color.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve cross-cultural relationships, shift from deficit thinking to strengths thinking, and create a welcoming school culture that emphasizes equality, acceptance, and shared values and goals.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creating a welcoming school culture improves engagement, supports student success, and empowers families to actively participate in their child’s education.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Training can be customized to address the specific cultural and linguistic diversity of the school community. Staff can engage in ongoing professional development to deepen their understanding of different cultural norms and practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When school staff are culturally competent, family engagement improves, leading to better student outcomes and a more inclusive school environment (Wood, L, and Bauman, E. 2017).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • School staff receive training on cultural competency and implicit bias. Teachers make home visits to get to know families and their cultural backgrounds. Families and staff work together to identify and address school and community needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tools developed collaboratively by educators, parents, students and researchers as a method of evaluating the degree to which learning goals, assignments, books, materials and other elements of curricula are responsive to diverse cultural backgrounds and inclusive of multiple perspectives. These scorecards can be customized to fit various contexts. Completing the scorecard guides teams through evaluation and scoring, revealing strengths and weaknesses in representation, social justice, and teacher materials.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the curriculum materials. Evaluation team with diverse identities and roles. Familiarity with culturally responsive education principles. Time and capacity to conduct the evaluation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Requires a team of individuals with diverse perspectives. Results are subjective and dependent on the evaluation team's knowledge and biases.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Systematic evaluation process. Customization for different contexts. Multi-stakeholder engagement (educators, parents, students, researchers). Highlights areas for improvement in representation, social justice, and teacher materials.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scorecards can be adapted to different subject areas (ELA, STEAM) and grade levels (K-12). Keywords can be identified to help tailor evaluation efforts.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the curriculum scores in representation, social justice, and teacher materials to gauge its cultural responsiveness and identify gaps for improvement.

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Culturally Responsive ELA Curriculum Scorecard and the Culturally Responsive STEAM Curriculum Scorecard are two such tools. The NYU Metro Center and the NYC Coalition for Educational Justice found that in NYC white authors and characters were widely over-represented in English language arts curriculum in comparison to the student body.

docs.text: This strategy entails providing instruction that empowers students intellectually, socially, emotionally, and politically by using cultural referents to impart knowledge, skills, and attitudes. It involves making standards-based content accessible by incorporating relatable aspects of students' daily lives, such as language, prior knowledge, and extracurricular interests. Teachers use student-centered stories, vocabulary, and language while infusing hip hop, sports, and other student interests without seeming fake.

docs.text: Culturally responsive teaching involves engaging students in the learning process, both cognitively and emotionally, through an understanding of how their identity and perspective is shaped by their culture and community experiences. It encompasses different aspects of a person's identities, including race, language, gender, and ability, and uses this knowledge to promote equity and foster a sense of belonging for each student.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cumulative review involves systematically revisiting previously learned concepts and skills throughout a course or learning period. This strategy aims to reinforce understanding, improve retention, and ensure that learners maintain mastery of essential material over time. Effective cumulative review incorporates various methods, such as revisiting key concepts through discussions, quick quizzes, or activities that integrate past and present learning. The goal is to combat the forgetting curve and enhance long-term memory by consistently activating and applying prior knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires systematic planning to integrate review sessions into the learning schedule. Instructors need to track learner progress and tailor review activities to address specific needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not structured effectively, cumulative review can become repetitive and disengaging. May require significant time allocation, potentially reducing time for new content.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable to all learner levels, including K-12, higher education, and professional development. Especially beneficial for subjects requiring retention of foundational knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce understanding, improve retention, maintain mastery of essential material, combat the forgetting curve, enhance long-term memory

docs.title: Affordances
