docs.text: • Strengthens long-term memory through repeated exposure. Helps learners connect new information to prior knowledge. Provides opportunities for instructors to identify and address gaps in understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by focusing on areas where learners struggle, using varied review methods (quizzes, discussions, activities), and allowing learners to self-select review topics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Continuous Review
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance on review quizzes and activities. Monitor learner engagement during review sessions. Compare pre- and post-review assessment scores to measure improvement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of spaced repetition and cumulative review in enhancing long-term retention and mastery of content. Consistent review helps learners build a strong foundation of knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A math teacher incorporates a 5-minute review of previous topics at the beginning of each class. A language arts instructor revisits key grammar concepts through writing exercises throughout the semester.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Regularly assessing materials for relevance and discarding broken, old, or useless items frees up space and guides purchasing decisions. Online teacher suppliers can support this process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time dedicated to assessing current resources, a system for discarding or repurposing items, and access to information on new materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require difficult decisions about what to discard. Requires educators to stay updated on relevant and useful materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All educators aiming to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of their learning environment.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Declutter classroom space, streamline resources, improve decision-making on material selection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Frees up valuable space, streamlines resource accessibility, improves decision-making on material selection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • This is primarily a task for the educator, but involving students in the process of evaluating and curating classroom materials can increase their sense of ownership and investment in the learning space.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the level of clutter and organization in the classroom. Observe how easily students and teachers can access necessary materials.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances the functionality of the learning environment, making it easier for both educators and students to focus on teaching and learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Curating involves selecting and arranging readings, videos, and other resources to scaffold concepts. This helps students build their understanding step by step, with carefully chosen materials that support each stage of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful selection and organization of resources, and clear communication of the learning path.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May limit student autonomy if not done carefully. Requires instructors to invest time in resource selection and organization.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from structured and organized content

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Scaffold learning, provide relevant resources, facilitate deeper understanding of concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear learning path, ensures access to relevant and high-quality resources, and supports progressive understanding of concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by allowing students to choose resources, providing varied formats, and offering resources at different levels of difficulty.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide guidance
  • Advance Organizers

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student comprehension, increased use of curated resources, and positive feedback on the organization of the course.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Selecting and arranging resources helps students build their understanding of complex concepts in a structured way (Cormier & Siemans, 2010).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities designed to teach and practice cursive handwriting, which can be beneficial for students who struggle with pencil control and letter formation. These activities focus on smooth letter connections, loops, and retracing to improve fluency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Cursive handwriting guides, lined paper, smooth writing tools, and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all students, especially those with significant fine motor difficulties. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Upper elementary grades and above, particularly useful for students who struggle with printed handwriting.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach and practice cursive handwriting, improving pencil control and letter formation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Can improve fluency and legibility by promoting smooth letter connections. Engages different motor skills than printed handwriting.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual skill levels and learning styles. Visual and tactile cues support letter formation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in letter formation, fluency, and legibility. Assess comfort and speed in cursive handwriting.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved cursive handwriting skills, providing an alternative writing style for students who struggle with printed handwriting. Enhanced motor control and letter fluency.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing adjustable settings and accessible formats to accommodate individual needs and preferences. This involves using materials that learners can modify based on their requirements, such as font size, contrast, or text-to-speech options. Customization enhances accessibility and supports diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Accessible digital materials, software with adjustable settings, and awareness of learner preferences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful design of materials and ongoing feedback to ensure customization options meet learner needs. Some learners may require guidance in selecting appropriate settings.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with sensory disabilities (e.g., blindness or deafness), learning disabilities (e.g., dyslexia), and those representing diverse or non-dominant cultures and/or languages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance accessibility, support diverse learning styles, accommodate individual needs and preferences, improve comprehension

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement by allowing learners to tailor content to their specific needs. Supports self-regulation by giving learners control over their learning environment. Promotes inclusivity by accommodating diverse learning styles and abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer options for text size, font, color contrast, audio descriptions, captions, and alternative formats (e.g., braille, large print)

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner use of customization features. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of customization options in supporting learning. Monitor learner performance and engagement with customized materials.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved accessibility and engagement: Research shows that customizable learning environments can enhance motivation and improve learning outcomes for diverse learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Customizing the display of information involves modifying the appearance of digital content to reduce reading effort and improve comprehension. This includes adjusting text size, font, colors, spacing, margins, and justification. Web browsers and e-reading apps often provide options to remove distractions and personalize the reading experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A digital device (computer, smartphone, tablet) with web browser or e-reading app. Digital text content in a customizable format (e.g., EPUB, HTML).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Customization options may vary depending on the software or app used. Some file formats (e.g., PDF) may not allow for text resizing or reflowing. Over-customization can sometimes create new distractions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with visual impairments, dyslexia, attention deficits, or reading difficulties. Useful across all age groups and educational levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce visual distractions, improve readability, accommodate visual impairments, enhance focus, support personalized learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by optimizing visual presentation. Improves reading comfort and reduces eye strain. Supports diverse learning preferences and needs. Allows for a more engaging and accessible reading experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can select font styles, text sizes, color themes, spacing, margins, and justification settings that best suit their individual needs. Reading views can be used to remove distractions and simplify the layout of web pages.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in reading speed, accuracy, and comprehension. Collect user feedback on the effectiveness of different customization settings. Measure the time spent on reading tasks with and without customized display settings.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that customizing the display of information can improve reading fluency, comprehension, and motivation, particularly for students with dyslexia and visual impairments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Safari Reader, Microsoft Edge Immersive Reader, Read and Write for Google extension, Simplified View in Chrome for Android, Center for Inclusive Software for Learning (CISL) at CAST's Clusive.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Structuring the school day with specific time allocations for various subjects and activities. This strategy involves creating a consistent, workable schedule that maximizes instructional time and caters to students' energy levels and needs throughout the day. Schedules may include morning work, language arts, reading groups, specials, math, science/social studies, and recess, strategically arranged to optimize learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of subject mandates, knowledge of student needs and energy levels, and ability to allocate time effectively for each subject.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require adjustments based on unforeseen events or student progress. Can become rigid and less adaptable if not regularly reviewed and revised.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary grade students, particularly in classrooms where effective time management is crucial

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Maximize instructional time, optimize student engagement, cater to student energy levels, provide structure and predictability

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students anticipate the day's activities, reduces time wasted on transitions, and allows for focused instruction in each subject. Enables teachers to plan effectively and address all curriculum areas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Schedules can be adapted to accommodate varying subject priorities and student needs, such as incorporating breaks or activities to address attentional challenges. Flexible pacing within subjects can further tailor the experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, monitor time on task, and collect feedback from students and teachers on schedule effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-structured schedules can lead to improved student focus, better time management skills, and a more efficient learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include structuring the day with reading in the morning, math after lunch, and science/social studies at the end of the day, incorporating recess and specials at optimal times.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Beginning each math lesson with spaced practice to review arithmetic facts. Sessions can be individual, small groups, or whole class, using songs, dry erase boards/pockets, and flashcards. Supports Arithmetic Fact Retrieval, Operations, and Place Value skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Routine practice at the start of each math lesson, using flashcards, dry erase boards, or songs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become monotonous if not varied; requires regular implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop arithmetic fact fluency and apply foundational facts to operations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances arithmetic skills, provides routine practice, and reinforces foundational facts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for individual, small groups, or whole class, using various mediums.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Part-task practice
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvement in arithmetic fact retrieval speed and accuracy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of arithmetic fact retrieval and strengthens understanding of operations and place value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing short arithmetic fact reviews at the start of math lessons using flashcards or songs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Daily review is a strategy where instructors begin lessons with a short (5-10 minute) review of previously studied material. This regular practice strengthens neural connections and helps learners retain information. Reviews focus on key concepts, important vocabulary, math or science formulas, homework, and problem areas identified by learners. Creative approaches like flashcards, pop quizzes, games, and mnemonics can make daily review engaging.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • 5–10 minutes of class time at the beginning of each lesson. Requires preparation of review materials and creative activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If too much time is spent on review or if every point is reiterated, it can become ineffective. The key is understanding what to review and using time efficiently.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, K-12 through adult learners. Particularly effective for vocabulary and math concepts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, improve retention, strengthen neural connections, prepare learners for new content by reviewing previously learned topics

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens memory through repetition, reinforces key concepts, and creates a concrete base for further learning. When combined with creative techniques, it can enhance learner engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to focus on specific problem areas identified by learners. Activities can be modified to suit different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved performance on quizzes and tests, increased retention of key concepts, and better understanding of current material due to a stronger foundation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Neurophysiological studies show repetition strengthens brain connections, improving retention. Research supports its effectiveness in vocabulary and math concept learning. Rosenshine, B. (2012). Principles of instruction: Research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, Spring 2012.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher begins each math class with a quick review of the previous day’s concepts through flashcards and a short quiz, reinforcing key formulas and problem-solving techniques.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers can use data to guide instructional decisions in Tier 1 settings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Collection of data

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires expertise to interpret data.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in Tier 1 settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Guide instructional decisions in Tier 1 settings

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides insight into learner progress.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Supports individualized instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student performance data

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved instructional decisions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Exposure to blue light (sunlight, full-spectrum LEDs, digital screens) during the day can increase alertness and improve cognitive performance by influencing hormonal secretion, particularly in adolescents whose sleep-wake cycles are often delayed. Strategies include maximizing natural sunlight exposure in classrooms or using blue-enriched bulbs. Biological changes during puberty delay the sleep-wake cycle, leading to sleep debt and decreased alertness. Daytime blue-light exposure can help reset the body’s circadian rhythm.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to sunlight or blue-enriched bulbs. Awareness of the timing and duration of exposure.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for eye strain or discomfort with excessive exposure. May interfere with sleep if used too close to bedtime.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily adolescents and learners in environments with limited natural light.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner alertness, improve sleep-wake cycles, and enhance cognitive performance.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances alertness and ability to pay attention. Resets the body’s circadian rhythm, improving sleep-wake cycles. Maximizes cognitive performance during the school day.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjusting the intensity and duration of blue light exposure based on individual needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure alertness levels and cognitive performance during the day. Track sleep patterns and academic outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that students exposed to more sunlight during the school day display higher reading and math outcomes. Replacing artificial lighting with blue-enriched bulbs can improve students’ cognitive performance (Uncapher, 2016).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Spend more time on reasoning than on finding the correct answer. Teachers can present worked examples with wrong answers and have learners find the error, or they can rethink the way they use class participation, focusing on the thought process rather than the answer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A shift in classroom culture from answer-focused to reasoning-focused, teachers who are skilled in facilitating discussions about problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in traditional, answer-focused classrooms. Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure that discussions remain productive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with math or lack confidence in their problem-solving abilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase confidence, encourage multiple approaches, promote discursive learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to explore different problem-solving strategies, promotes deeper understanding, and reduces anxiety by de-emphasizing the importance of a single correct answer.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor activities to the individual learner's reasoning process, providing support and guidance where needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Articulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner participation, monitor increased exploration of different strategies, and assess improvements in reasoning skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing reasoning increases confidence, promotes deeper understanding, and improves problem-solving skills, leading to greater academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask learners to explain their thinking process before sharing the answer, present worked examples with errors and have learners find the mistake, or use think-pair-share activities to discuss different problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Remove non-academic criteria, like behavior or participation, from grades, focusing instead on academic mastery to provide a more accurate representation of a student's knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Defined academic criteria

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May elicit emotion from teachers

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All Levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Focus on academic mastery, eliminate bias, provide accurate grades

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Removes subjectivity, promotes equity

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Focuses on content mastery

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Focus on content mastery

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Grading practices must counteract institutional biases that have historically rewarded students with privilege and punished those without

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Separating grades from behavior

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Adults can learn to deal with the emotions that arise when they make mistakes, even if they were not sufficiently guided as children. This involves creating a safe environment to express feelings without judgment, allowing one's 'inner child' to be seen and heard. This includes feeling emotions like sadness, anger, and shame, expressing what happened and why these feelings arise, listening without judgment, and comforting oneself. Writing can help express these feelings. By releasing tension, one can look at the situation more peacefully and honestly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A safe, private environment. Time for self-reflection and expression. Writing materials, if needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for individuals with deep-seated emotional issues or trauma, potentially requiring professional support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adults who struggle with dealing with their mistakes and associated emotions due to insufficient guidance in childhood.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Learn to cope with negative emotions, release tension, and create a safe emotional environment for self-expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for emotional self-regulation, builds resilience, and promotes self-compassion. Helps individuals understand and process their feelings, leading to a more peaceful and honest perspective.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual emotional needs and preferences. Writing or other forms of self-expression can be used as alternatives to verbal expression.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduced emotional tension, increased ability to self-comfort, and improved self-awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved emotional regulation, enhanced self-compassion, and greater resilience in the face of mistakes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Personal journaling, mindfulness exercises focusing on emotional awareness, or role-playing scenarios to practice expressing feelings in a safe setting.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are assigned to argue a position that is opposite to their own, requiring them to see things from a different perspective. This activity promotes critical thinking, perspective-taking, and the ability to understand and argue opposing viewpoints.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A controversial topic, resources for research, and time for debate and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may resist arguing a position they disagree with, or they may not take the activity seriously. It requires a skilled facilitator to manage the debate and ensure respectful communication.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who tend to be rigid in their thinking and resistant to alternative viewpoints

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking, develop perspective-taking skills, encourage argumentation, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Forces learners to consider opposing viewpoints, promoting critical thinking and perspective-taking. Enhances argumentation skills by requiring learners to defend a position they may not personally agree with. Improves communication skills through debate and discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The topics chosen for debate can be tailored to the learners' interests and the curriculum content. The level of research and argumentation can be adjusted to their abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Positions
  • Argument Construction
  • Rebuttals
  • Role Reversal
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality of arguments, the ability to understand and articulate opposing viewpoints, and the level of critical thinking demonstrated in the debate. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards different perspectives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that debate can improve critical thinking, perspective-taking, and communication skills. Engaging with diverse viewpoints also promotes tolerance and understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students who support stricter gun control laws are assigned to argue against them. Students who believe in climate change are assigned to argue that it is not a serious threat.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Debriefing emotional experiences involves a structured discussion at the end of the day where each child expresses an emotion they experienced and shares the context. This helps children process their feelings and develop emotional self-awareness. Sentence prompts can be used to guide the expression.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a set time at the end of the day (e.g., 5-10 minutes). A facilitator to guide the discussion and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may be reluctant to share their emotions in a group setting. Requires a supportive and inclusive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and early childhood students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote emotional self-awareness, provide a safe space for emotional expression, encourage empathetic listening

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured opportunity for emotional processing, promotes self-awareness, and encourages empathetic communication among peers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentence prompts can be adapted to suit different age groups and emotional literacy levels. Children can choose to express emotions privately or share with the group.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and depth of emotional expression. Track the use of emotion words and the ability to connect emotions with experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that regular emotional check-ins and discussions can improve children's emotional regulation and social competence. (Source: The Impact of Check-ins on Social Emotional Learning Outcomes - https://www.panoramaed.com/blog/check-ins-social-emotional-learning-outcomes)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Define responsibility and ethical responsibility. Give students specific tools such as graphic organizers or methods for creating visual representations to use as they consider the ethical and moral responsibilities of their decisions. For example, depending on age level you could have students create if/then decision trees on the board or use sticky notes to create an option wall. Read current events, discuss if the decisions made are ethical, and evaluate those decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A definition of responsibility, a variety of graphic organizers or methods for creating visual representations, and current events.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to define responsibility and create graphic organizers or visual representations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Define responsibility, apply ethical responsibility, improve decision-making skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with a definition of responsibility, improves the application of ethical responsibility, and improves decision-making skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of graphic organizers or methods for creating visual representations. They can also read current events and discuss if the decisions made are ethical.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Creating Visual Representations
  • Class Discussion
  • Graphic Organizers

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding of responsibility, increased application of ethical responsibility, and improved decision-making skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of defining and applying ethical responsibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher defines responsibility and has students create if/then decision trees on the board. The teacher reads current events and discusses if the decisions made are ethical.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Deliberate practice involves focused, strategic efforts to improve specific skills or knowledge areas. It emphasizes setting clear goals, actively monitoring progress, and seeking immediate feedback to refine performance. Learners actively engage in tasks that push them slightly beyond their current abilities, analyze their performance, and adjust their approach to improve continuously.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear goals, structured practice activities, mechanisms for monitoring progress, and opportunities for feedback. Access to experts or mentors can enhance the effectiveness of deliberate practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and require significant effort to achieve meaningful improvement. May be difficult to implement without clear goals or access to appropriate feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Useful for all learner levels, particularly those seeking to master complex skills or knowledge in areas such as music, sports, or professional fields.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve specific skills, enhance performance, refine strategies, promote continuous learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Accelerates skill development by focusing on targeted improvement areas, fosters self-awareness through active monitoring, and builds resilience by encouraging learners to embrace challenges and seek feedback.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to individual learning goals, skill levels, and preferred learning styles. Learners can choose specific skills to work on and customize practice activities based on their needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track progress toward specific goals, monitor performance on practice activities, and collect feedback from instructors, mentors, or peers. Use self-reflection and goal-setting activities to assess learner engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that deliberate practice is a key factor in achieving expertise and high levels of performance in various domains. Studies have shown that it enhances skill acquisition, improves problem-solving abilities, and promotes continuous learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Musicians practice scales and passages repeatedly to improve technique. Athletes engage in drills and simulations to refine specific skills. Professionals seek feedback from mentors to improve their performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Demonstrating caring is a powerful way to build positive relationships with learners. When your actions and words communicate that you sincerely care for your learners, they are more likely to want to perform well for you and enjoy coming to school. Demonstrate you care by inquiring about aspects of their personal lives, standing by the door and welcoming learners as they enter the classroom, empathizing with learners, listening intently to learners, and expressing gratitude for their accomplishments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must care about and be sincere when interacting with their learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Must make sure to be equitable with all learners and avoid the appearance of having favorites.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve instructor-learner relationships by showing that you care.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Positive instructor-learner relationships can improve learners' attitudes about coming to school and increase their performance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can inquire about different learners' lives, hobbies, trips, and/or sports activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners respond positively to the instructor. They are motivated and work hard.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When learners feel cared for, they are more likely to comply with the instructor's policies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Subjects like Maths, Chemistry, Physics, etc. require careful instructions to deliver content. For example, precision is key in a subject like geometry. In demonstration-based classrooms, screen recording tools are used to create instructional videos assigned as homework. Instead of doing this in the classroom, students can go back and forth in the video to understand concepts fully and come back to the classroom for doubt removal.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires screen recording tools and expertise in creating clear, concise demonstrations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time to create demonstrations, dependent on learners' ability to follow instructions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for subjects requiring precise instruction and visual demonstrations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide precise, repeatable demonstrations, allow learners to review at their own pace, address individual difficulties in class.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to pause, rewind, and rewatch demonstrations as needed.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • In-class time can be used to address individual questions and difficulties.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to replicate demonstrations, performance on related tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can improve learners' procedural knowledge and ability to execute precise tasks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Engineering courses using screencasts to demonstrate CAD software techniques.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Demystification involves explaining to learners how memory and learning work, especially when they are struggling. By validating their experiences and providing insights into the cognitive processes behind learning challenges, learners can develop a better understanding of their strengths and weaknesses. This approach fosters a growth mindset and encourages learners to seek effective strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the learner's specific learning challenges, knowledge of effective learning strategies, and ability to communicate complex concepts in a clear and accessible way

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time and effort to understand the learner's specific needs, effectiveness depends on the learner's willingness to engage with the explanation, may not be sufficient on its own to overcome significant learning challenges

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with learning or have learning disabilities, parents and educators who want to support learners effectively

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness, promote a growth mindset, reduce frustration and anxiety related to learning challenges, encourage the use of effective strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides validation and support, fosters a growth mindset, increases self-awareness, reduces frustration and anxiety, encourages the use of effective strategies

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The explanation can be tailored to the specific learning challenges and cognitive processes of the individual learner. The strategies recommended can be adapted to suit their individual needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' attitudes and behaviors related to learning, assess their self-awareness and understanding of their learning challenges, evaluate their use of effective strategies

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Demystification has been shown to increase self-awareness, promote a growth mindset, and reduce frustration and anxiety related to learning challenges. It empowers learners to take control of their learning and seek effective strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Explaining to a student that their memory is like a closet with a sticking door, and that the goal is to find ways to open the door more easily. Sharing stories of successful individuals who have overcome learning challenges.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A descriptive feature chart is a graphic organizer with horizontal and vertical axes used to develop a descriptive model of an organism. It displays the features of the organism in a structured way, such as body parts, number, color and shape, position, and appearance. It is commonly used in science instruction to help students organize and analyze observations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A pre-designed chart with appropriate categories (e.g., Body Parts, Number, Color and Shape, Position, Appearance); materials for observation (e.g., specimens, books, images); pens and paper or digital tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant initial teacher guidance to ensure students understand how to use the chart effectively; can be time-consuming to fill out all details

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–2nd grade students, but can be adapted for higher grades; useful for visually-oriented learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop a descriptive model of an organism, organize observations, classify features, analyze appearance, and interpret data

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way to organize and display information; supports visual learning and understanding; helps in summarizing and analyzing observations

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be used in whole class, pairs, small groups, or individually; adaptable for different types of organisms and details

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy of the chart in representing the organism's features; completeness of information; ability to use the chart to write a description of the organism; presentation of findings to the class

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports visual learning and helps students systematically organize their observations. Enhances descriptive and analytical skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a chart to describe a butterfly's body parts, number, color and shape, position, and appearance to help K–2 students build a descriptive model of the organism. Resource: WETA - Using Graphic Organizers in Literature-Based Science Instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This principle involves designing with the students at the edges of a community in mind, particularly those disempowered due to identity or poverty. It emphasizes centering race in the work and operates under the belief that what works for those at the margins will be beneficial for all learners. It involves identifying marginalized students (e.g., students of color, those receiving interventions, experiencing family trauma, living far from school, or English Language Learners) and using methods like empathy interviews and student shadowing to understand their experiences. This approach favors process over urgency, ensuring that solutions are deliberate and equity-centered.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a commitment to equity, a willingness to listen to and prioritize the voices of marginalized students, and resources for conducting empathy interviews and student shadowing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and require significant effort to implement effectively. May face resistance from stakeholders who are not committed to equity. Relies heavily on the accuracy and depth of information gathered through empathy interviews and student shadowing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and school teams seeking to create more equitable and inclusive learning environments, particularly in racially diverse schools with achievement gaps.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address achievement gaps, build inclusive school cultures, and ensure that solutions benefit all learners, especially those who are marginalized.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leads to more inclusive and equitable solutions, promotes a deeper understanding of marginalized students' experiences, and fosters a sense of belonging for all learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific methods (e.g., empathy interviews, student shadowing) can be tailored to the context and needs of the school and students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track achievement gaps between different student groups, measure student perceptions of inclusion and belonging, and assess the impact of interventions on marginalized students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved academic outcomes for marginalized students, a more inclusive school culture, and a greater sense of belonging for all learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Yu Ying Public Charter School in Washington, D.C., used this principle to address achievement gaps between Black and Latinx learners and students who were Asian or white. They conducted empathy interviews and student shadowing to understand the experiences of marginalized students and developed interventions to support them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a designated calm-down spot is providing a safe and structured space within the classroom where students can go to regain control over their emotions. The spot should be equipped with tools and resources that support self-regulation, such as stress balls, Theraputty, or visual aids with calming techniques.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated space in the classroom, tools and resources for self-regulation, explicit teaching and modeling of how to use the space.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be ineffective if not introduced and implemented properly. Relies on students recognizing and utilizing the space independently.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students with emotional or behavioral challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students safely manage their emotions, reduce stress and anxiety, and regain focus for learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured and safe environment for students to practice self-regulation skills, promoting independence and emotional awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize the spot with tools and resources that align with individual student needs and preferences, such as sensory items or personalized coping strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency of use and the impact on student behavior and emotional state. Solicit student feedback on the helpfulness of the calm-down spot and its resources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional regulation, reduces classroom disruptions, and empowers students to take control of their emotional responses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A middle school classroom includes a corner with soft lighting, comfortable seating, stress balls, and visual prompts for breathing exercises. Students can use this space to calm down before rejoining class activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ensuring that personalized learning opportunities are designed to maximize the engagement of all students, regardless of disability status, involves making learning choices flexible and accessible for all, with a recognition that individuals’ strengths and needs differ widely. Pairing personalized learning with Universal Design for Learning (UDL) allows educators to design learning opportunities in ways that provide multiple means of engagement, representations of content, and ways to express knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Personalized learning tools, UDL framework, training for educators

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant resources and expertise. May be challenging to implement and sustain.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly students with disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Maximize student engagement, promote personalized learning, enhance accessibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances learning experiences, promotes inclusivity, supports diverse learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and age groups. Learning opportunities can be tailored to specific needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, improved learning outcomes, enhanced accessibility

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students are more engaged in learning and have access to personalized opportunities that meet their unique needs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing flexible learning choices. Offering multiple means of representation and expression.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Bring learners together and explain that different sources online present different information, even about the same topics. As learners work with online information, they should think about which sources are the most reliable. Provide learners with a definition of the term reliable. Have learners offer ideas for questions they might ask themselves when evaluating the reliability of a source. If your learners have trouble getting started, you can model questions for them: Who wrote this source? What was the purpose of the author who wrote this source? What other sources does this source reference? Does this source say the same things as other sources? Does this source echo what I know from personal experience?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Definition of reliable, questions to guide brainstorming, and class discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation. Some students may need additional support to generate questions and apply the checklist effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable learners to develop a checklist of questions for evaluating the reliability of sources.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners develop a systematic approach to evaluating sources and promotes critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can personalize the checklist based on their experiences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to generate relevant questions and apply the checklist to evaluate sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners develop a systematic approach to evaluating sources. Enhanced information literacy: Learners become more discerning consumers of information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students answer the questions for websites they reviewed and choose which of the two or three sources is most reliable.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Developing cultural awareness as an educator includes building empathy for diverse learners, intentionally recognizing how one's own identity intersects with learners' identities, and creating an awareness of how the environment can impact learners' sense of belonging. This involves self-reflection, training, coaching support, and peer collaboration to identify explicit and implicit bias in oneself, in the curriculum, and in broader systems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment to self-reflection and ongoing learning. Access to training, coaching, and peer support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to confront personal biases. Requires sustained effort and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, administrators, and other school staff

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase empathy, reduce bias, promote inclusivity, improve relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improved understanding of diverse learner needs, enhanced communication, more equitable practices

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailored training and coaching to address individual biases and cultural competence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in attitudes and behaviors. Monitor implementation of inclusive practices. Gather feedback from learners and families.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced cultural awareness can lead to more equitable and supportive learning environments for all students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators develop their own understanding of self-awareness and how it affects learning by reading up on the resources and research available. Use the Learner Variability Navigator to support your learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to research articles, books, and online resources, as well as time for reading, reflection, and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a commitment to ongoing learning and professional development. Educators may need support in applying the research to their practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators seeking to improve their ability to support students' self-awareness

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Educators understand the science of emotional regulation and other learning domains and apply them to instruction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides educators with a deeper understanding of self-awareness and its impact on learning. Equips them with the knowledge and tools to better support their students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Educators can focus on the resources and research that are most relevant to their students' needs and learning context.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Educators' ability to articulate their understanding of self-awareness and its impact on learning. Their use of evidence-based strategies to support their students' self-awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved educator knowledge and skills, leading to better support for students' self-awareness and academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Educators participate in professional development workshops, read research articles, and collaborate with colleagues to deepen their understanding of self-awareness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using Bloom's Taxonomy, Webb's Depth of Knowledge, and Marzano's Dimensions of Learning to develop measurable course objectives that are concise, student-friendly, and clearly communicated.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear criteria, well-defined scales, rubrics

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant effort to develop measurable criteria

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create measurable objectives, ensure student-friendly criteria, promote clear communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Measurable criteria, clear expectations, easy understanding for students

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and grade levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Classify each objective by level using Bloom's Taxonomy
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of criteria, effectiveness of communication

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Criteria should be concise, student-friendly, easily understood, and clearly communicated so that students understand expectations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Developing clear criteria for 3rd graders mastering classification

docs.title: Developing a Critical Lens for Multimodal Analysis
Description
docs.text: Increasing students' awareness of effective and ineffective multimodal combinations by analyzing a mode's affordances and constraints. This involves starting with simple media (e.g., a picture book) and discussing how images and words convey different meanings, work together, or contradict each other. Students expand their critical lens by analyzing images in various genres and media. The goal is to collect exemplar structures to guide their own composition decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Examples of multimodal texts (e.g., picture books, informational texts, websites), discussion prompts, time for analysis and reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for students with limited prior knowledge of multimodal composition. Requires careful selection of examples to illustrate different effects. Relies on active engagement in critical analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students learning multimodal composition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking skills, develop awareness of multimodal combinations, collect exemplar structures for composition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical analysis of multimodal texts, fosters deeper understanding of how different modes interact, and guides students in making informed composition decisions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different media types and genres. The complexity of the analysis can be adjusted based on student skill levels. Examples can be chosen to align with student interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality and depth of student analysis during discussions. Analyze students' ability to identify effective and ineffective multimodal combinations. Assess the extent to which students apply their critical lens in their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking skills, enhanced awareness of multimodal combinations, and better composition decisions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Developing cultural awareness as an educator is an ongoing process that includes building empathy for diverse learners, intentionally recognizing how one's own identity intersects with learners' identities, and creating an awareness of how the environment can impact learners' Sense of Belonging. This active process often requires self-reflection, training, coaching support, and peer collaboration to identify how explicit and implicit bias shows up in oneself, in the curriculum, and in broader systems. When educators work towards developing critical awareness of different cultures and perspectives, they can actively work to mitigate Stereotype Threat and build authentic relationships with learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for self-reflection, access to training and coaching resources, collaboration with peers, and a willingness to challenge one's own beliefs and assumptions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a sustained effort and commitment to ongoing learning. Can be challenging to confront one's own biases.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, edtech developers, and instructional designers across all levels (K-12, higher education, adult learning)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of diverse cultures, mitigate implicit biases, foster empathy for diverse learners, create inclusive learning environments

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators recognize their own biases and assumptions. Fosters empathy and understanding of diverse learner experiences. Supports culturally responsive teaching practices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to specific cultural contexts or learner demographics. Reflection prompts can be adapted to focus on particular aspects of cultural awareness.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased self-awareness of biases, improved relationships with diverse learners, and more inclusive curriculum and instructional practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates more equitable and inclusive learning environments for all students, particularly those from historically marginalized groups. Supports culturally responsive teaching practices.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instilling pride is a powerful way to develop positive teacher-learner relationships. Classroom pride shapes identities that in turn drive behavior. Recognizing learner successes decreases the likelihood of negative pride and increases the likelihood of positive pride. As a classroom instructor, you should help learners take pride in their accomplishments and positive behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must be sincere in their proclamations of pride in learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Must be modified for different age ranges. Children are intuitive regarding sincerity, and insincere comments will quickly backfire.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve classroom dynamics by creating a positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • A positive classroom culture can improve learners' pride in their accomplishments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can personalize their approach with elementary and middle school learners, and calm, quiet statements with secondary students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of positive classroom environment, respectful students, and increased participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Positive classroom pride helps learners build positive behaviors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners generate a list of similarities and differences between words and complete a Venn diagram. This activity is an example of a high-yield instructional strategy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Provide Venn diagrams or other graphic organizers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with limited background knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve analytical skills, increase vocabulary, increase Disciplinary Literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds analytical skills, reinforces vocabulary, promotes active learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose words based on their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student diagrams for accuracy and completeness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When students generate a list of similarities and differences between words and complete a Venn diagram, they are working with one of Robert Marzano’s high-yield instructional strategies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dialogic reading is an interactive reading technique where the adult helps the child become the teller of the story instead of passively listening. The adult prompts the child to say something about the book, evaluates the response, expands the response by rephrasing and adding information, and repeats the prompt to ensure learning. This is known as the PEER sequence (Prompt, Evaluate, Expand, Repeat). The adult uses prompts from the CROWD mnemonic: Completion prompts (fill-in-the-blank), Recall prompts (questions about past events in the book), Open-ended prompts (focus on pictures), Wh- prompts (what, where, when, why, how questions), and Distancing prompts (relating the book to outside experiences). Dialogic reading is suitable for children's books with rich, detailed pictures, and the process should be enjoyable and child-led.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A picture book, an adult facilitator, and a willingness to engage in interactive conversation. The adult needs to be familiar with the PEER sequence and CROWD prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require training for adults unfamiliar with the technique. Distancing and recall prompts may be challenging for younger children. Success depends on keeping the interaction enjoyable and avoiding pressure.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preschool-aged children, particularly those with limited experience with books and vocabulary.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance language development, improve vocabulary, develop story comprehension, increase expressive fluency, foster narrative skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases active engagement with books, supports language and literacy development, enhances verbal fluency, builds connections between books and the real world.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be adjusted based on the child's age and language abilities. The technique is adaptable to various book types and can be tailored to the child's interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's language development, vocabulary acquisition, story comprehension, and expressive fluency. Track the child's responses to different types of prompts and their ability to relate the book to real-world experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that children who are read to dialogically demonstrate significant gains in language development compared to those read to traditionally. This approach has shown positive effects across diverse geographic locations and socioeconomic backgrounds.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • During a book reading with a picture of a fire engine, the adult points to the fire truck and asks, "What is this?" (Prompt). The child says, "Truck." The adult responds, "That’s right (Evaluation); it’s a red fire truck (Expansion); can you say fire truck?" (Repetition).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dictation, also known as speech-to-text or voice recognition, involves using technology to convert spoken words into written text. This enables users to focus on expressing their thoughts verbally, rather than struggling with the physical act of writing. It can be integrated into various devices like computers, tablets, and smartphones, often utilizing built-in speech recognition software. Users speak into a microphone, and the software recognizes their speech, converting it into written text. The accuracy can vary depending on the user's speech patterns and the software's capabilities, with more advanced programs offering improved recognition and error correction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a device with a microphone and speech recognition software (e.g., Dragon NaturallySpeaking, Microsoft Speech Recognition). A quiet environment is beneficial for accuracy. Training and practice are needed to become proficient in using the software.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Accuracy can be affected by background noise, speech impediments, and variations in pronunciation. Younger children may find it challenging to use due to inconsistent speech patterns. Requires error correction and monitoring to ensure accuracy. Dependence on technology may hinder development of handwriting skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with dysgraphia, ADHD, executive functioning deficits, learning disabilities, physical disabilities, vision impairments, limited motor skills, or those learning a second language. Particularly beneficial for middle school, high school, and college students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate writing for individuals with dysgraphia, ADHD, or executive functioning deficits, improve writing production, reduce anxiety around writing, and enhance core reading and writing abilities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables individuals to bypass handwriting difficulties and focus on content creation, improves writing mechanics and legibility, promotes independence by reducing reliance on human transcribers, decreases anxiety related to writing, and enhances phonemic awareness by visually connecting spoken words to their written form.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can adjust settings for language, accent, and speaking style to improve accuracy. Software can be trained to recognize individual voices and speech patterns. Integrates with various applications like word processors and email programs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvements in writing length, complexity, and mechanics. Observe student confidence and engagement in writing tasks. Compare dictated text to handwritten work for legibility and accuracy. Monitor the frequency and types of errors made during dictation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates improved writing quality and quantity for students with learning disabilities. Studies show enhanced phonemic awareness and error correction skills. Assistive technology can significantly improve academic performance and reduce anxiety related to writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A middle school student with dysgraphia uses Dragon NaturallySpeaking to dictate essays, resulting in longer, more detailed assignments and improved grades. A college student with ADHD uses speech-to-text to take notes during lectures, helping them capture information more effectively and stay focused. Case studies available from assistive technology vendors and educational research publications.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dictation software allows learners to speak their ideas and have them transcribed into text. This supports learners with strengths in auditory processing by allowing them to bypass visual cues involved with writing and focus on expressing their thoughts orally.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to dictation software, training on its use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all writing tasks, some learners may struggle with speaking their thoughts clearly

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with strengths in auditory processing who struggle with writing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate idea generation, improve writing fluency, support learners with auditory strengths

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages auditory strengths, reduces cognitive load associated with writing, facilitates idea generation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide training on dictation software, offer prompts and scaffolds to support idea generation

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess writing quality, track improvements in writing fluency, gather learner feedback on the effectiveness of the software.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that dictation software can improve writing outcomes for learners with certain learning differences. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of dictation software in enhancing writing fluency.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using dictation software for brainstorming, drafting essays, or completing written assignments. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating web dictionaries and thesauruses into vocabulary lessons allows learners to quickly search and understand unfamiliar words. When learners look up challenging words while reading, they monitor their comprehension and activate cognitive processes that support increased recall and consolidation to long-term memory. Features such as voice search, audio pronunciation, and embedded quizzes can further support vocabulary building and practice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to web dictionaries and thesauruses, such as Merriam-Webster Dictionary app, Oxford Dictionaries or Dictionary.com.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to actively search for and look up words, which may be time-consuming. Reliance on dictionary definitions may not always provide sufficient context for understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in vocabulary lessons or those who encounter unfamiliar words while reading

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve vocabulary acquisition, enhance reading comprehension, promote active learning, support self-directed learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides quick access to definitions and synonyms, supports auditory learners with voice search and audio pronunciation, promotes active reading and comprehension monitoring.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose between text-based and audio-based definitions, and can use quizzes for self-assessment and practice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' use of dictionaries and thesauruses while reading. Review digital notes (vocabulary definitions or explanations). Score each definition according to a Vocabulary Rubric. Identify common misconceptions, misunderstandings, or lack of knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced vocabulary acquisition: Quick access to definitions and synonyms helps learners understand and retain new words. Improved reading comprehension: Looking up unfamiliar words promotes active reading and comprehension monitoring.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Differentiated teaching methods are used to extend the knowledge and skills of every student in every class, regardless of their starting point. The objective is to lift the performance of all students, including those who are falling behind and those ahead of year level expectations. To ensure all students master objectives, effective teachers plan lessons that incorporate adjustments for content, process, and product.

Carol Ann Tomlinson, a leading authority on differentiation, stresses one clarification that heads off much confusion about the approach: "Differentiated instruction is not the 'Individualized Instruction' of the 1970s." Differentiation means varying instructional technique to teach as many students as possible effectively — it does not mean writing a distinct course of study for every individual student, and treating the two as synonymous (as they often are informally) has fueled much of the debate over whether differentiation is practically feasible at scale.

In a differentiated classroom, teachers start from their existing curriculum and instruction, then ask what would need to change so every learner leaves with the knowledge, understanding, and skill to take on the next phase of learning — adapting instruction based on students' readiness, interest, and learning profile across four elements: content (the facts, concepts, principles, attitudes, and skills students access — kept conceptually consistent across students, with complexity adjusted rather than the underlying concept changed), process (how students make sense of content), product (how students demonstrate learning), and affect/environment. Tomlinson organizes the supporting guidance into three "pillars": a philosophy (diversity is normal and valuable; every student can learn; the teacher is responsible for structuring student success; every student deserves equitable access), a set of principles (a learning-conducive environment; a quality foundational curriculum; assessment-informed teaching; instruction actually designed from that assessment data; a flexible classroom), and concrete practices (proactive planning around student profiles; modifying approaches to student need; "teaching up" — pitching work just above a student's current comfort level rather than at or below it; assigning tasks that stay challenging, engaging, and purposeful for every student; and flexible grouping such as stations, interest groups, or orbital studies).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Requires teachers to assess and plan for diverse learning needs.
  • Genuine assessment data informing instructional design, not just informal impressions of student ability

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Can be time-consuming to plan and implement effectively.
  • Often mistakenly conflated with individualized instruction (writing a separate course of study per student), which fuels unnecessary skepticism about its feasibility in large, mixed-ability classes

docs.title: Implementation Variability
docs.text: • Which of the four elements (content, process, product, affect/environment) is adjusted, and how much, varies by classroom, subject, and student profile — there is no single fixed recipe

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Extend the knowledge and skills of all students, regardless of their starting point, by adjusting content, process, and product.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Accommodates diverse learning needs and ensures all students can master objectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustments can be made to content, process, and product based on individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Start from the existing curriculum and instruction rather than a blank slate.
  2. Assess students' current readiness, interests, and learning profiles.
  3. Identify what would need to change — in content, process, product, or affect/environment — for every learner to reach the next phase of learning.
  4. Design tasks that stay challenging, engaging, and purposeful for each student ("teaching up" rather than down).
  5. Use flexible grouping (stations, interest groups, orbital studies) rather than fixed, permanent ability tracks.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved performance across all students, mastery of objectives by all learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Differentiated teaching ensures that all students can achieve mastery by addressing their individual learning needs and starting points.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Tomlinson, C. A. (1999). How to differentiate instruction in mixed-ability classrooms. Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development.
  • Tomlinson, C. A. (2014). The differentiated classroom: Responding to the needs of all learners (2nd ed.). Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Differentiated instruction. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Digital literacy instruction involves teaching learners how to effectively use digital technology, communication tools, and networks to locate, evaluate, use, and create information. This includes understanding computer basics and effective internet search strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers, internet connectivity, and instructors with expertise in digital literacy.

docs.title: Constraints
