docs.text: • Can be challenging for learners with limited prior experience, requires ongoing updates to keep pace with evolving technology, and may require significant time investment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly adult learners and those with limited prior experience with technology

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop digital skills, enhance information literacy, and enable learners to effectively navigate and create content in a digital environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers learners to participate fully in a digital society, enhances employability, and promotes lifelong learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction can be tailored to specific skill levels and learning goals, with options for one-on-one or group training.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to use digital tools effectively, evaluate information critically, and create digital content competently.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Digital literacy instruction improves learners' ability to find, evaluate, and use information, enhancing their employability and enabling them to participate fully in digital society.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Direct instruction on using search engines, creating email accounts, and navigating digital platforms.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Digital noise monitoring involves using apps or devices like Super Sound Box, Class Dojo, or Too Noisy to detect and signal excessive noise levels in the classroom. These tools provide auditory or visual cues when the noise exceeds a predetermined threshold, helping students self-regulate their behavior and maintain a quieter learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to digital devices or apps, setup and calibration of noise monitoring tools, clear explanation of noise level expectations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be distracting or disruptive if not implemented properly, requires technical setup and maintenance, some students may ignore the cues.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Monitor classroom noise levels, promote self-regulation, create a quieter learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time feedback on noise levels, encourages self-regulation, reduces the need for constant teacher intervention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Noise threshold can be adjusted to fit different activities and classroom environments. Visual or auditory cues can be customized to student preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track noise levels over time using monitoring tools. Observe student responses to auditory or visual cues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Digital noise monitoring can improve classroom management by providing real-time feedback and promoting self-regulation, leading to a quieter and more focused learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Digital publishing involves using online platforms and tools to share student writing and creations with a wider audience, fostering engagement and providing valuable feedback. Platforms can range from blogs and online communities to digital book creation tools and media sharing sites. Students are able to receive real-world reception and impact by writing more publicly. Publishing student writing and letting it be received and discussed by authentic audiences provides students with valuable feedback. They also get the pride of knowing that what they've produced is being enjoyed. These platforms provide a real-world outlet for student writing as well as opportunities to engage with the writing of students from all over the globe. Some sites let students participate in positive communities and discussions, others task students with sharing their stories or projects, and some even have junior reporter or media creator programs. No matter the tool, each motivates students and provides them with authentic, interest-driven opportunities to connect with real readers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to digital devices and internet connectivity. Teacher guidance on selecting appropriate platforms and managing online interactions. Understanding of copyright and fair use policies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful moderation and monitoring of online interactions. Potential for privacy concerns and exposure to inappropriate content. The need for digital literacy skills for both students and teachers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those in writing and media arts programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Elevate student voice, provide valuable feedback, motivate students, provide real-world opportunities, connect with real readers, and develop digital citizenship skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides authentic audiences for student work, enhances student motivation and engagement, develops digital citizenship skills, and fosters a sense of community among learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Choice of platform (blog, digital book, social media), topic related to students' lives, and the type of media (text, image, video).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Integration
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation in writing activities, improved quality of student work, positive feedback from online audiences, and evidence of digital citizenship skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that digital publishing can significantly enhance student motivation and engagement. It also promotes the development of writing skills and digital literacy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Digital stories are multimedia narratives that combine various elements such as photographs, video, animation, sound, music, text, and a narrative voice. Students can produce digital stories individually or collaboratively. These stories can be uploaded to the internet and made available to an international audience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers, multimedia software, recording equipment, and internet connectivity. Also requires training in digital storytelling techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires technical skills, can be time-consuming, and may require access to specialized equipment or software.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education learners across various disciplines

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Integrate subject matter with existing knowledge and skills, develop digital literacy skills, and communicate ideas effectively.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances creativity, promotes collaboration, strengthens digital literacy skills, and provides a platform for self-expression.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose topics that align with their interests, incorporate personal experiences, and experiment with different media formats.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality of the narrative, technical proficiency, effective use of multimedia, and overall impact of the story.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that digital storytelling enhances engagement, improves digital literacy skills, and promotes deeper learning. (Roland, 2006)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students create a digital story about a historical event, a personal experience, or a scientific concept. Projects from the New Media Studio at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Digital Storytelling Program managed by the Creative Industries faculty at Queensland University of Technology

docs.title: Digital Tips for Quick and Thoughtful Peer Feedback
Description
docs.text: Using digital tools to facilitate peer feedback can make the process easier and more efficient. This involves students sharing their work digitally, such as posting a link, sharing access to a document, or snapping a picture, and receiving feedback through comments or face-to-face conversations. Incorporating digital citizenship discussions can also enhance the feedback process, particularly for older learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to digital tools (e.g., Google Classroom, Padlet, Seesaw), clear guidelines for providing feedback, and a structured process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on students' digital literacy and their ability to provide constructive feedback. Requires initial training and modeling by the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners in various educational settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide quick and thoughtful peer feedback, enhance digital literacy, and promote digital citizenship.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances accessibility and efficiency of feedback, promotes digital communication skills, and fosters a sense of community.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose methods and tools that work well for their group and model expectations for students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Peer Interaction
  • Digital Tools

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of digital feedback. Observe student engagement and participation in feedback activities. Measure improvements in the quality of revised work based on feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This approach can make peer feedback more accessible and efficient, leading to improved learning outcomes and enhanced digital skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Google Classroom, Schoology, Padlet, Seesaw, and Adobe Spark to facilitate digital peer feedback.

docs.title: Digital Word Detectives: Building Vocabulary With e-Book Readers
Description
docs.text: Students read e-books and use digital tools (dictionaries and notes) to support their vocabulary development. They assume the role of "word detectives" as they look up words in digital dictionaries and use other strategies to identify the meaning of vocabulary words. This requires students to have prior knowledge of e-book reading and familiarity with the specific tools and features of their digital readers, including how to access and use the built-in digital dictionary and how to insert digital notes into an e-book. Students work in small groups to compare digital notes and discuss word meanings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Digital readers, e-books compatible with digital readers, access to digital dictionaries and note-taking tools, vocabulary pre-assessments and post-assessments, vocabulary rubric, observation form, digital reading tools assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to digital devices and reliable internet connectivity. Students need prior knowledge of e-book reading and digital tool usage.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 2-6

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase understanding of vocabulary, define and record meaning of vocabulary words in digital note form, demonstrate understanding of vocabulary words through discussion and documentation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances vocabulary acquisition through digital dictionaries, supports comprehension with digital note-taking, promotes collaboration and discussion, provides visual and interactive learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Differentiated instruction through selection of appropriate e-books, flexibility in selecting vocabulary words, and options for independent or partner reading.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Vocabulary Pre-Assessment handouts, vocabulary observation form, digital reading tools assessment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that access to digital readers allows students to use new literacy skills and strategies to envision and retrieve the potential of digital devices, extending connections between readers and text through electronic tools and features.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students read e-books and use digital tools (dictionaries and notes) to support their development of vocabulary. Students assume roles of “word detectives” as they look up words in digital dictionaries and use other strategies to identify the meaning of vocabulary words. The teacher identifies approximately 3-4 vocabulary words from each chapter of the e-book. Before reading each chapter, the teacher determines which words the students already know and which words are unfamiliar. As students read and encounter the vocabulary words, they use the digital dictionary and other strategies to figure out what each word means, inserting a digital note next to that word with an example and/or a definition in their own words. Students then meet in small groups to compare their digital notes and discuss the meaning of the vocabulary words, followed by a whole-class discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Digital readers for student use, e-books compatible with digital readers, visual presenter/document and LCD projector for demonstration, printed handouts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Access to digital readers may be limited. Students may need instruction on how to use digital dictionaries and insert digital notes into an e-book.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 2-6

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase understanding of vocabulary, define and record meaning of vocabulary words, demonstrate understanding of vocabulary words through discussion.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Electronic books extend connections between readers and text as engagement with and manipulation of text is made possible through electronic tools and features. Digital note-taking features engage students in the reading experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select multiple titles to allow for differentiated instruction, if appropriate. Number of selected vocabulary words may be adjusted depending on chapter length and student grade level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Vocabulary Pre-Assessment handouts scored according to a Vocabulary Rubric, Vocabulary Observation Form used to record misconceptions or notable examples, and Digital Reading Tools Assessment to document students’ progress.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Context clues complement semantic gradients (Greenwood). Students need instruction and practice using context clues including repeated, meaningful encounters with new words. Electronic books extend connections between readers and text as engagement with and manipulation of text is made possible through electronic tools and features. Digital note-taking features engage students in the reading experience.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using dim or natural lighting in classrooms or learning spaces to promote a calm and focused environment. This involves adjusting lighting to mimic natural light, which can have a positive impact on children’s moods and creativity. Harsh, flickering, or humming lights can be distracting or painful, especially for individuals with autism. Adjustable lighting allows for control over visual stimuli, which is beneficial for creating a calming effect.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Adjustable lighting systems (e.g., LED lights with dimming and tuning capabilities), understanding of the impact of different light settings on sensory processing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Initial investment in adjustable lighting systems may be required. Effectiveness may vary depending on individual sensitivities to light.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially beneficial for learners with autism or sensory processing disorders.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a calm and focused learning environment, reduce distractions, improve mood and creativity, support sensory needs.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports sensory regulation, reduces visual distractions, promotes a calm and focused environment conducive to learning and creativity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustable lighting can be customized to individual preferences and sensory needs. Different colors and light levels can be used to achieve the desired calming effect.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Assigned Readings
  • Lectures

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner behavior and focus levels under different lighting conditions. Collect feedback from learners on their comfort and concentration levels. Monitor the frequency of distractions or sensory-related issues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates positive associations between certain colors and mood, and adjustable lighting can help create a happy, creative environment. Calming sensory lights have been shown to benefit children with autism by meeting their sensory needs and promoting emotional well-being.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Valuelights competition showcasing creative sensory lighting such as tornadoes, bubble fish, color-changing LED lights, and rocket-shaped lava lamps. Acuity Brands Tunable White Lighting allows teachers and students to dim and tune lighting in the classroom to support increased learning and focus.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Talk with learners about the multiple dimensions of critical evaluation, including: Relevance (importance to a reading purpose), Accuracy (factual and updated details that can be verified), Bias/Perspective (author's position or slant), and Reliability (trustworthiness based on author and publishing body). Compare the terms to notice that evaluating relevance and accuracy involves considering the quality of the content itself, and judgments about perspective and reliability require an examination of details about the author and agenda. Understanding these differences provides a concrete way to remember that any judgment should be informed by a critical examination of both relevant claims and an author’s level of expertise to make those claims.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear definitions and discussion of each dimension, comparative analysis activities, and examples of sources to evaluate.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for younger learners or those unfamiliar with critical evaluation concepts. Requires ongoing reinforcement and practical application.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adolescents and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help learners understand and differentiate between the dimensions of critical evaluation: relevance, accuracy, bias/perspective, and reliability.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to evaluating sources, encourages critical thinking, and supports the development of reasoned judgments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different subjects and types of sources. Learners can explore examples relevant to their interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to define and differentiate between the dimensions of critical evaluation in discussions and written assignments. Evaluate their ability to apply these dimensions when analyzing sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners develop a more nuanced understanding of how to evaluate information. Enhanced media literacy: Learners are better equipped to assess the quality and trustworthiness of sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A media literacy class analyzes news articles using the dimensions of relevance, accuracy, bias/perspective, and reliability to determine the credibility of each source.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction of genre-specific writing strategies involves explicitly teaching the characteristics and conventions of different writing genres to enhance students' understanding and skills in both reading and writing. Teachers introduce a specific genre (e.g., argumentative writing), build on students' existing knowledge, and explain how the six traits of writing apply to that genre. This approach often includes modeling, gestures, and turn-and-talk activities to reinforce learning. Students then apply these strategies to write their own pieces within the genre.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher knowledge of various writing genres and effective teaching methods. Access to examples of different genres and materials for writing activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if students lack foundational writing skills. Requires careful planning and delivery to keep students engaged.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those in middle and high school, who need explicit instruction in writing genres

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of writing genres, improve writing skills, apply knowledge of genre conventions, reinforce key concepts through modeling and practice

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to understanding and applying genre conventions. Enhances writing skills through direct instruction, modeling, and practice. Reinforces learning through varied teaching methods such as gestures and discussions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The teacher can adjust the level of instruction and complexity of the writing tasks based on students' needs and abilities. Students can also have some choice in the topics they write about within the assigned genre.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assessment can include student writing samples, participation in discussions, and completion of genre-specific writing tasks. Success is measured by students' ability to effectively apply genre conventions in their writing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicit genre instruction has been shown to improve students' writing skills and understanding of literary elements. This approach helps students become more confident and effective writers by providing them with a clear framework and specific strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A sixth-grade teacher introduces argumentative writing by building on students' understanding of the six traits of writing and explaining what the traits look like in this genre. The teacher integrates gestures and turn-and-talk activities to reinforce learning before encouraging students to write their own argumentative pieces.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit instruction in keyword search strategies involves teaching learners how to effectively select and combine keywords to refine search queries and retrieve relevant information from the internet. This includes understanding the use of synonyms, precise descriptions, search operators (quotation marks, plus/minus signs), and Boolean logic. Learners also evaluate the credibility of online sources by checking domain extensions (.edu, .org, .gov, .com), identifying the author and their perspective, and verifying information across multiple sources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Internet access, search engines (e.g., Google, Bing), examples of reliable and unreliable websites, and instructional materials on keyword search techniques and source evaluation criteria

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require ongoing practice and reinforcement to maintain proficiency. Learners may struggle with identifying and evaluating biased or misleading information. Requires continuous updates to reflect changes in search engine algorithms and online information landscape.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, higher education students, and adult learners seeking to improve their online research skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' ability to formulate effective search queries, evaluate the credibility of online sources, and find relevant information efficiently

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances digital literacy, improves information retrieval efficiency, promotes critical evaluation of online content, and supports academic and professional research

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to specific subjects and research questions, providing targeted practice in keyword selection and source evaluation. Learners can be assigned different search tasks based on their skill level and prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the effectiveness of search queries by measuring the relevance and accuracy of search results. Evaluate learner's ability to identify credible and unreliable sources based on established criteria (CRAAP test, checklist). Assess learner's ability to verify information across multiple sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that explicit instruction in online search skills improves learners' ability to find credible and relevant information, promotes critical thinking, and supports digital literacy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction of patterning skills involves teaching learners to identify and create patterns using various mediums such as colors, sizes, shapes, sounds, and numbers. This includes copying and extending patterns, abstracting patterns by creating the same pattern with different objects, and identifying the pattern's rule (the repeating part). Explicit instruction with alphabet labels (e.g., 'ABB pattern') helps learners generalize pattern rules.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials such as colored blocks, shapes, sounds, or numbers. Explicit instruction time to introduce pattern concepts, practice activities, and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Without proper guidance, learners might focus on surface-level characteristics of patterns rather than understanding underlying rules. May not be as effective if learners are not engaged in creating patterns themselves.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily young learners (preschool to elementary school) but adaptable to all ages as a foundation for mathematical and logical thinking.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop skills in identifying, copying, extending, and abstracting patterns. Enhance understanding of pattern rules and regularity, fostering mathematical reasoning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances mathematical reasoning, supports development of problem-solving skills, and improves general math knowledge by identifying rules and regularities. Early pattern knowledge can predict later math achievement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by using different types of patterns (color, shape, number) and adjusting complexity based on learner level. Scaffolding can include alphabet labels to explain pattern rules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to extend, abstract, and identify pattern rules. Assess general math knowledge gains after patterning interventions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates early pattern knowledge supports later mathematics achievement across number, algebra, and geometry. Special attention to patterning in preschool and first grade leads to better general math knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A preschool teacher uses colored blocks to create an 'ABB pattern' and asks learners to recreate the same pattern using different objects like sounds or movements. A game such as Brainquake's Wuzzit Trouble Math can be used to build numerical patterning skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct Phonics instruction connects letters to sounds to decode and comprehend text. It includes explicit teaching of letter-sound relationships and sufficient practice to ensure retention of skills for transfer into long-term memory. Multisensory approaches, such as the Orton-Gillingham approach, can be incorporated to engage multiple senses (hearing and touch) in exploring letters and sounds.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires explicit instruction, practice materials (e.g., letter cards, word lists), and a structured approach to teaching letter-sound relationships. Multisensory materials can enhance engagement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners who already have a strong foundation in phonics. Requires consistent and structured instruction to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners who struggle with foundational reading skills, including decoding and phonemic awareness; also applicable to K-12 learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve decoding skills, enhance phonemic awareness, strengthen reading comprehension

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to learning letter-sound relationships, improves decoding skills, and builds confidence in reading. Multisensory approaches can enhance engagement and retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different learner needs by adjusting the pace of instruction and providing targeted practice on specific letter-sound relationships. Multisensory approaches can be tailored to individual learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess improvements in decoding skills, phonemic awareness, and reading comprehension through regular assessments. Monitor progress and adjust instruction as needed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of explicit phonics instruction in improving reading skills, particularly for learners who struggle with decoding. Early reading instruction assists adult literacy learning, particularly as adult readers may need to unlearn ineffective reading and writing habits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Orton-Gillingham approach uses a highly multisensory method to explore letters and their sounds. Simplex Spelling Phonics 2 app uses reverse phonics with a focus on syllables to foster phonological awareness through spelling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors teach and model various strategies for tackling problems, then give learners the opportunity to choose which strategies they use and reflect on the outcomes of their choices. Example strategies include choosing the operation, finding a pattern, creating visual images, guesstimating, creating a table, using manipulatives, working backward, creating a systematic list, etc.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors need to be knowledgeable about various problem-solving strategies and be able to model them effectively. Learners need access to a problem-solving notebook.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners who prefer a more structured, step-by-step approach. Requires learners to actively engage in reflection and self-assessment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, enhance mathematical flexibility, improve conceptual understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds mathematical flexibility and conceptual math understanding by explicitly promoting problem-solving with different strategies. Encourages learners to become responsible for their own learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose strategies that best suit their learning style and the specific problem.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the strategies learners choose and the outcomes of those choices. Analyze the quality of learners' reflections on their problem-solving processes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes a deeper understanding of mathematical concepts and enhances problem-solving abilities by encouraging learners to use and reflect on different strategies. Supports the development of a Learner Mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • DreamBox Learning allows learners to solve problems in multiple ways. Learners keep a problem solving notebook with important information that they can refer to.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction in spelling involves explicitly teaching spelling patterns, high-frequency words, and strategies for addressing frequently misspelled words. It emphasizes a structured approach where learners are directly taught the relationships between letters and sounds, memorization techniques, and the application of spelling knowledge in context.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured spelling program, word lists (high-frequency words, commonly misspelled words), multi-sensory materials, colored pencils, pretests, and ongoing monitoring.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as rote memorization if not integrated with meaningful context. Requires consistent and systematic implementation. May not address underlying issues related to language processing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beginning and developing spellers and readers of all ages, including students with learning disabilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance phonological processing skills, develop morphological knowledge, and increase reading and writing proficiency.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured and systematic approach to learning spelling, improves memory and retention of words, and enhances reading and writing skills by strengthening word recognition and usage.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction can be tailored to learners' developmental levels, focusing on appropriate word lists and spelling patterns. Teachers can differentiate instruction based on individual needs, providing extra support for struggling learners and enrichment for advanced learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Pretests and posttests to measure spelling accuracy, observation of student application of spelling rules in writing, and analysis of student errors to inform instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that explicit and systematic spelling instruction improves learners’ spelling accuracy and positively affects reading and writing abilities. Ongoing review and recycling of frequently misspelled words are crucial for mastery.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Read Naturally’s Signs for Sounds program, which provides systematic phonics instruction and strategies for learning high-frequency words with irregular spelling patterns.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Research shows that, along with traditional reading comprehension strategies, students use unique strategies to read the non-linear, hyperlinked structure of online texts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to internet, explicit instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming, requires careful planning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve online reading skills, enhance comprehension, navigate online texts effectively.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves online reading skills, enhances comprehension, effective navigation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide varied strategies, allow students to choose their methods.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reading comprehension, navigation skills, strategy use.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced online reading skills, improved comprehension, better navigation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teaching students how to identify credible sources online, showing them how to use search engines effectively, or explaining how to navigate hyperlinks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction in online learning involves pre-developed presentations, assessing student work and providing instructive feedback, diagnosing misconceptions, clarifying concepts, and referring students to additional resources or practice opportunities. It is a key component of teaching presence, ensuring students receive guidance and support to achieve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pre-developed presentations or materials, assessment tools, and timely feedback mechanisms (e.g., Speed Grader in Canvas).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not fully address individual student needs without personalized feedback. Requires careful planning and preparation to ensure clarity and relevance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Online learners of all levels, particularly those needing structured guidance and clear explanations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Clarify concepts, diagnose misconceptions, assess student understanding, provide resources for further practice

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear, structured content, immediate feedback on performance, and resources for addressing misconceptions. Allows instructors to actively guide student learning in a virtual environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized through tailored feedback, differentiated resources, and varied presentation formats to accommodate diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student performance on assessments, reduction in common misconceptions, and positive feedback on the clarity and helpfulness of the instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that effective online learning relies on careful instructional design and planning, with direct instruction playing a vital role in student success (Hodges et al.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Discipline-specific literacy involves teaching reading, writing, speaking, and thinking skills unique to each subject area. It recognizes that literacy practices vary across disciplines and that students benefit from explicit instruction in the specific ways texts are constructed, interpreted, and used in different fields. This approach reduces student anxiety by fostering deep engagement with content through interactive activities, enabling them to work through the material collaboratively. This strategy can be implemented using a read-write-think-discuss model to deeply engage students with course content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to discipline-specific mentor texts, graphic organizers, checklists, and vocabulary. Implementation involves interactive activities and opportunities for students to write for authentic audiences and purposes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Instructors may need training to understand and teach discipline-specific literacy practices effectively. Availability of appropriate mentor texts and resources may vary across disciplines.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners across all subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension of subject-specific content, improve discipline-specific communication skills, reduce anxiety around reading and writing in specific subjects, and foster deeper engagement with course content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves literacy skills by grounding them in content area knowledge, increases learner motivation and confidence, and supports effective communication within specific disciplines. It clarifies expectations for discipline-specific writing and promotes self-monitoring during the composition process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The types of mentor texts, graphic organizers, checklists, and vocabulary can be tailored to the specific discipline and level of the learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student improvement in discipline-specific writing assignments. Monitor student engagement in interactive activities and the quality of their contributions to discussions. Evaluate student self-monitoring skills using checklists and rubrics.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show discipline-specific literacy enhances comprehension, communication, and engagement by emphasizing the unique literacy practices within each field. Using the read-write-think-discuss model in interactive activities reduces student anxiety and fosters deeper engagement with course content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers in various subject areas use the read-write-think-discuss model to deeply engage students in their disciplines. They provide mentor texts, discipline-specific graphic organizers, and checklists to scaffold student writing and self-monitoring. Students write for authentic audiences and use journals to express their thinking and emotions while learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Have students read articles from subject-specific columns and publications. When students get a feel for what writing about math can look like, they will be able to do it better themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to subject-specific columns and publications. Requires time for students to read and discuss the articles.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to find articles that are appropriate for all students. Some students may struggle to understand the articles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for students who are new to a discipline.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expose students to discipline-specific writing styles and vocabulary. Improve student understanding of discipline-specific concepts. Provide students with models for their own writing.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with models for their own writing. Improves student understanding of discipline-specific concepts. Exposes students to discipline-specific writing styles and vocabulary.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can select articles that are appropriate for student reading levels. Students can also be given the option to select their own articles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions. Review student writing to assess understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides students with models for their own writing. Improves student understanding of discipline-specific concepts. Exposes students to discipline-specific writing styles and vocabulary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Have students read articles from Math Horizons or Martin Gardner's Scientific American columns. When students get a feel for what writing about math can look like, they will be able to do it better themselves.

docs.title: Discuss the Benefits of Positive Self-Talk
Description
docs.text: Openly communicating what self-talk is and how it can help. This involves explaining the psychological benefits of positive thinking and addressing skepticism about changing one's mindset. Discussions can include reviewing psychology and self-help resources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to psychology and self-help resources. Facilitator with knowledge of the benefits of positive self-talk.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if learners are deeply entrenched in negative thinking patterns. Requires a skilled facilitator to address skepticism and promote open dialogue.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Skeptical learners who need to understand the rationale behind positive self-talk.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To educate learners about the impact of self-talk and motivate them to adopt a more positive mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a deeper understanding of the science behind positive thinking. Addresses common misconceptions and resistance to changing one's mindset. Encourages critical thinking and informed decision-making.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor the discussion to learners' specific concerns and questions. Provide examples that are relevant to their lives and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' willingness to try positive self-talk strategies. Changes in their attitudes and beliefs about the power of mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that understanding the benefits of positive self-talk can increase learners' motivation to practice it. Open discussions can help dispel skepticism and promote a more positive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Explain that practicing self-talk out loud might seem silly at times, but you have to change your words before you can really change the silent thinking in your head. Use psychology and self-help resources to support the discussion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves incorporating discussions about emotions into the learning environment through whole-class discussions and individual reflections. It encourages learners to consider, label, and express their emotions to optimize their learning experiences. Apps and ed tech products can support this by including features for tracking and managing emotions, setting goals, and accessing resources for emotional support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom time for discussions and reflection; materials such as emotion charts, puppets, or art supplies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may be hesitant to share personal emotions; discussions may be superficial if not facilitated effectively

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school students; adaptable for various age groups and learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help learners identify, label, and express their emotions; promote emotional awareness; develop coping strategies for managing emotions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates emotional literacy, supports self-regulation, and enhances social-emotional development. Learners gain self-awareness and learn to manage emotions constructively.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting the emotion discussions to individual needs and experiences; allowing learners to express emotions in various ways (verbal, written, artistic)

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and express emotions, track their use of coping strategies, and monitor their engagement in emotional discussions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced emotional literacy, improved self-regulation, and positive social-emotional development (as suggested by incorporating discussions about emotions into the learning environment)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves creating a classroom environment conducive to complex conversations about race through activities that help students notice and celebrate similarities and differences. It emphasizes designing products in partnership with educators and racially diverse communities to facilitate these conversations, using multimedia tools to share diverse stories, and providing discussion guides developed with experts of color. Additionally, it suggests incorporating inclusive icons and creating feedback loops for continuous improvement, ensuring edtech solutions center learners of color.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a commitment to creating inclusive and equitable learning environments. Access to multimedia tools, diverse stories, and expert-developed discussion guides. A willingness to address and mitigate personal biases.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure respectful and productive conversations. May require additional training and support for educators and facilitators. Potential for discomfort or resistance from individuals with differing perspectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, parents, and product developers across all levels, particularly those working with diverse student populations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create environments conducive to complex conversations about race, foster understanding of diverse perspectives, promote positive racial identity formation, address inequities, and center learners of color in design.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tools and resources for meaningful conversations about race, promotes empathy and understanding, addresses inequities, and centers learners of color in design and development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Content and activities can be adapted to different age groups and cultural contexts. Discussion guides can be tailored to specific topics and learning objectives. Feedback mechanisms allow for continuous improvement based on learner input.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and quality of student discussions, assess changes in attitudes and behaviors related to race and equity, and evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to promote positive racial identity formation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of discussing race in educational settings to promote understanding, empathy, and positive racial identity formation. Culturally responsive teaching practices have been shown to improve student engagement and academic outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A classroom activity where students share stories about their cultural backgrounds and experiences. A product that uses short videos of people of color sharing their stories, accompanied by discussion guides for educators and parents. The Black Genius Profile captures Black learners’ genius using the language of the elements. Parents typically complete a Black Genius profile for their child(ren) for a number of reasons, including but not limited to: 1. as an advocacy tool when a child is being treated unfairly or being deprived of opportunities at school, 2. as a cultural tool to help the teacher learn how to be more responsive to the child’s culture when teaching 3. as a personal learning tool for the parent to learn more about the child’s interests, skills, expectations, strengths, and growth areas in order to support the child’s healthy development.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Homework is assigned in the form of video lectures and external video resources. Discussions happen in the classroom time where topics are explored further. Having studied the basics, students can add value to discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires curation of high-quality video lectures and external resources, facilitation skills to guide discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Dependent on learners' willingness to participate in discussions, may require careful moderation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners who thrive in discussion-based environments and can critically analyze information.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking, enhance communication skills, deepen understanding through peer interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages pre-class material to enable richer, more informed class discussions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussions can be tailored to explore specific areas of interest or challenge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of participation in discussions, depth of analysis, peer interaction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can foster critical thinking and improve learners' ability to articulate and defend their viewpoints.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In this pre-reading activity, the instructor prepares several sentences expressing different opinions about the reading topic and places them around the room. Learners then choose the opinion they agree with the most and stand near it. The group of learners agreeing with each opinion prepares reasons for their choice. Finally, learners interact with those from other groups, sharing their opinions and reasons, fostering critical thinking and discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a clear space for learners to move around, pre-prepared sentences with various opinions, and facilitation to guide discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful facilitation to ensure respectful and productive discussions. Some learners may be hesitant to share opinions publicly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of various ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for diverse topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage critical thinking, activate prior knowledge, and facilitate discussion about the reading topic.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes engagement through physical movement and group interaction. Encourages learners to articulate and defend their opinions, fostering critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentences can be tailored to different proficiency levels. Group sizes can be adjusted based on class size and dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Argument Construction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth of discussion, the quality of reasons provided, and the level of engagement. Collect feedback on how the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters critical thinking and active engagement with the topic, enhances communication skills, and helps learners explore multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about renewable energy, sentences like 'Renewable energy is the only solution to climate change' or 'Renewable energy is too expensive' can be used to spark discussion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A discussion web is a graphic organizer that enables students to examine both sides of an issue before agreeing on a conclusion, promoting deeper processing of texts through meaningful conversational discussion. This strategy involves students thinking of individual ideas based on their knowledge of the text, then working as a pair to record, discuss, and resolve their perspectives before meeting with another pair of partners to share these ideas. The foursome then nominates a speaker to present this information to the entire class. The discussion web promotes active engagement, allowing students to examine various points of view within a social setting, encouraging argumentation of an open-ended question, and developing critical thinking abilities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to texts, a discussion web graphic organizer (paper or digital), structured activity guidelines, and facilitation to introduce the approach and guide initial discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit instruction and modeling. May be time-consuming. May not be suitable for students who struggle with collaboration or have difficulty expressing their ideas verbally.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for students from elementary to adult learners, adaptable for a variety of grade levels and content areas, such as mathematics, science, social studies, and literature.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking, promote collaborative discussions of texts, allow for examination of various points of view within a social setting, encourage argumentation of an open-ended question, and develop listening, talking, reading, writing, viewing, and visually representing abilities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Stimulates and extends students’ thinking, builds and supports social learning communities, enables collaborative sharing of ideas, alternative perspectives, and problem solving, allows students to revisit, question, and clarify text ideas, and promotes higher cognitive abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to meet the developmental level of different age groups. Can be modified for different forms of writing, such as persuasive arguments and discussion pointers. Can be used to brainstorm and prepare students for debates about a variety of topics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Argument Construction
  • Assigned Positions

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the quality and depth of student responses in the discussion web. Evaluate the level of critical thinking demonstrated in the responses. Assess the effectiveness of group collaboration through observation and participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Meaningful conversational discussion has enormous value to the learning process, as it stimulates and extends students’ thinking (Cramer, 2004) while building and supporting social learning communities (Fish, 1980). Discussion enables collaborative sharing of ideas, alternative perspectives, and problem solving during learning (Almasi, 1996).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage learners in text-based discussions where they discuss what they read with each other, and teachers set expectations and routines for productive discussions. Activating background knowledge, checking for understanding, and fostering student-to-student conversations are key components.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Text for discussion, teacher facilitation skills, and established routines and expectations for productive discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure discussions are productive and respectful. Facilitation skills are necessary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially English language learners, can benefit from structured discussions.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop reading and writing skills, especially vocabulary development, and promote comprehension through oral language and interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports vocabulary development, encourages critical thinking, promotes active engagement with the text, and builds communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussions can be tailored to the specific text, learners' backgrounds, and learning goals. Sentence starters can be provided for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Participation in discussions, demonstrated understanding of the text, and ability to articulate ideas and respond to others.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research and practice evidence show that discussions result in measurable outcomes in literacy achievement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Invite students to think about their thinking. Conduct discussions about students' problem-solving processes. Invite students to share their metacognition, reveal their intentions, detail their strategies for solving a problem, describe their mental maps for monitoring their problem-solving process, and reflect on the strategy to determine its adequacy. During these kinds of rich discussions, students learn how to listen to and explore the implications of each other's metacognitive strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom culture that recognizes individual paths of improvement, electronic tools for easy sharing, and a commitment to collective support

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Discussions must be respectful in order for learners to be open and honest in their discussion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective in classrooms where a strong sense of community and trust has been established

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster metacognition, enhance problem-solving skills, and build habits of empathy, flexibility, and persistence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds a sense of community, provides diverse perspectives, and encourages mutual support and learning. It also reduces individual competition and promotes collaborative problem-solving.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The level of personalization is limited in that the discussion takes place with an entire group; students should have opportunity to discuss problems that are related to their individual learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • peer discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency and quality of peer interactions, noting instances of mutual support and advice-giving. Observe the level of comfort and openness in sharing weaknesses and challenges.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that learning in social contexts significantly enhances comprehension and retention of new information. Improves disciplinary literacy and strengthens understanding of new information

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Distributed practice involves practicing content in short sessions spaced out over time, contrasting with massed practice (cramming) where content is practiced in one long session. It leverages the principle that “Forgetting helps Remembering.” Time between practice sessions leads to some forgetting, requiring learners to actively reconstruct and fix what they struggled with, thus improving retention and understanding. The process starts after initial learning with pretty good accuracy, followed by spaced practice sessions with intervals depending on the time until assessment. For example, some suggest the length of time between sessions should be about 20% of the time between initial learning and when you will be assessed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires scheduling and adherence to spaced practice sessions. May initially require a mass practice session to achieve pretty good accuracy.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may initially perceive it as less effective than easier techniques like re-reading, as it involves struggling to recreate information. The 'harder' activity feels like you are not learning more. The opposite is true.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable to learners of all ages and skill levels. Especially beneficial for those preparing for exams, quizzes, or aiming for long-term retention of skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance long-term memory and understanding of studied material. Improve accuracy and fluency in skill performance over extended periods.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leads to more accurate and longer-lasting retention, helps the brain work hard to recreate 'lost' information. Results in better understanding and memory compared to easier techniques like re-reading or highlighting.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The number and length of distributed practice sessions can be adjusted based on the length of time until assessment and individual learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare long-term retention rates between learners using distributed practice and massed practice. Track decreasing errors in successive distributed practice sessions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows distributed practice is twice as effective as massed practice for long-term memory, sometimes up to several years. It helps learners better remember and understand studied content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After learning a new guitar chord, practice it in short sessions over several weeks instead of one long session. For an upcoming exam, schedule short review sessions every few days instead of cramming the night before.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Distributed practice, also known as spaced learning, involves reviewing information or practicing skills across multiple sessions spread out over time, rather than in one continuous session (massed practice). It leverages the spacing effect, where spaced reviews lead to superior long-term retention and learning compared to cramming. The gaps between occurrences of an item make retrieval more effortful, strengthening memory. Distributed practice enhances memory and higher-order learning by leveraging contextual variability.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured review materials and tools to track spacing intervals. Computer programs can deliver assignments in a distributed fashion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires advance planning to schedule review sessions. Learners may not immediately perceive the benefits compared to massed practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all learners, particularly effective when learning factual information, vocabulary, or skills that require long-term retention. Applicable across K-12, higher education, and adult learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance long-term retention, improve memory recall, support application of learned concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases the durability of learning by making retrieval more effortful, encodes information with varied contextual cues, reduces habituation, and enhances retention of complex skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Timing of review sessions can be adjusted based on individual learning needs and progress. Technology can facilitate spaced repetition schedules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Continuous Review
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare retention rates between spaced and massed practice groups. Monitor learner recall and application of knowledge over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research consistently demonstrates that distributed practice leads to better long-term retention compared to massed practice. Studies support its utility for memory, problem-solving, and generalization of learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reviewing vocabulary words at increasing intervals. Re-solving math problems from previous lessons. Utilizing spaced repetition software.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Distributed practice, also known as the spacing effect, is a learning technique where reviews of information or practice of a task are spaced out over time rather than massed together. This method promotes long-term retention because it forces the brain to actively retrieve the information from memory during each review session, making the memory more durable. Distributed practice contrasts with massed practice (cramming), where study sessions occur immediately following the initial learning event.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Scheduled review sessions, awareness of optimal spacing gaps, technology to sequence assignments effectively

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires planning and discipline, may be inconvenient to implement in traditional linear instruction settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those preparing for exams or seeking to retain information over extended periods

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.text: Learning from multiple and varying perspectives involves incorporating diverse voices, experiences, and viewpoints into the curriculum. docs.text: • Observe learner engagement in discussions and activities. Assess learner understanding of diverse perspectives through written assignments or presentations. Track improvements in empathy and cultural awareness through surveys or reflections.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The "Document outline" tool in Google Docs can be an easy and effective way to ask students to pick out evidence that supports the main ideas they’ve found. When this tool is turned on, students can write a heading for the paragraph or group of paragraphs and select “Heading 1” from the drop-down menu. When they come across a sentence or phrase that represents evidence supporting that main idea, they summarize it and label it “Heading 2.” Meanwhile, along the side of the Google Doc an outline will automatically populate with main ideas in Heading 1 and supporting evidence nested below in Heading 2. At the end, the whole essay is outlined and can be “exported to table of contents,” which will put it at the top of the document, where it can be used as a jumping-off point for writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to Google Docs. Instruction on how to use the document outline tool.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Relies on Google Docs technology. May require initial instruction to use effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students, particularly for essay writing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Organize main ideas and supporting evidence, enhance writing skills, simplify the outlining process

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simplifies outlining, aids comprehension, enhances writing readiness, saves work in an easy-to-review manner

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different writing tasks and text types. Can be used individually or in groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the clarity and accuracy of the outlines. Review the quality of supporting evidence selected.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Technology didn’t do any of the thinking for students, but in this case the software helped build an outline as students discuss and winnow down their evidence, and their work has been conveniently saved in an easy-to-review manner. That makes initiating writing -- often hard for students -- much easier.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students outline an essay using headings and subheadings in Google Docs to organize their main points and supporting evidence.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using the “Document outline” tool in Google Docs, students pick out evidence that supports the main ideas they've found. When this tool is turned on, students can write a heading for the paragraph or group of paragraphs and select “Heading 1” from the drop-down menu. When they come across a sentence or phrase that represents evidence supporting that main idea, they summarize it and label it “Heading 2.” At the end, the whole essay is outlined and can be “exported to table of contents,” which will put it at the top of the document, where it can be used as a jumping-off point for writing. The headings in the outline are links that automatically skip to the part of the text where students inserted that heading.

docs.title: Instructions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and outlining strategies have been shown to improve reading comprehension and writing skills. Summarization promotes retention and deeper understanding.

Resources include lists organized alphabetically by grade, by frequency by grade, and by frequency combined, with activities free to copy and distribute.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: Resist the urge to immediately find solutions. Sometimes, it’s more useful to just listen and understand what’s wrong. Students might not even want you to fix the problem. docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners match dot cards with equal quantities but different arrangements, or match dot cards to corresponding numeral cards. Advanced learners play 'Make 10' match, where they find pairs that total 10. Matching equal quantities with different representations helps reinforce the concept that numbers can be represented in multiple ways. Matching dot cards with numerals solidifies the connection between visual representations and symbolic numbers. 'Make 10' match supports the learning and recognition of number pairs that add up to 10, an important skill for developing number sense and mental math strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dot cards, numeral cards (optional), counters (optional).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful preparation of card sets to ensure clear matches. Some learners may need guidance to understand the matching criteria.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-K to 1st Grade learners who are developing number sense and subitizing skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Match equal quantities, match numerals to quantities, learn number combinations that make ten

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a versatile approach to learning and reinforcing number sense. Adapts to different levels of learners. Enhances understanding of numerical equivalence and composition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the matching criteria based on learner's skill level. Provide visual aids or counters for learners who need additional support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, vocabulary, and retention of content; foster a connection between reading and writing; encourage active involvement with text; promote collaborative learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves comprehension by encouraging active engagement with text. Builds vocabulary through contextual analysis and personal responses. Enhances retention by linking text with personal thoughts and reactions. Fosters a connection between reading and writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scaffolded with pre-filled entries for struggling learners; gradually released responsibility as learners improve. Can be adapted for various types of written texts, read-alouds, or listenings.

docs.title: Instructions

docs.title: Assessment Evidence

docs.text: • Shown to improve learners’ comprehension, vocabulary, and retention of content. By allowing learners to choose what they react to within a text, choice is given and perspectives honored. An interactive way to activate prior knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dramatic play, also known as pretend play, is a learning strategy where learners actively experiment with social and emotional roles through imagination. Learners reenact stories, organize play scenarios, and explore different characters, fostering empathy and understanding of diverse perspectives. This type of play encourages turn-taking, shared responsibility, and creative problem-solving. Prop boxes or themed corners filled with objects such as old clothes, cooking utensils, and writing materials can support and enrich dramatic play experiences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a designated space or prop box filled with diverse materials such as clothing, utensils, and writing supplies. Facilitation involves setting up scenarios and encouraging learners to take on different roles and responsibilities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require guidance to ensure cooperative play and prevent conflicts. Learners need to understand the purpose and expectations of the play to engage meaningfully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preschool and early elementary learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social awareness, enhance emotional skills, foster creative problem-solving, build empathy, and improve language skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe space for learners to explore social and emotional roles, encourages empathy by acting out different characters, promotes creative problem-solving skills, and builds self-esteem through imaginative expression. Supports the development of language skills by encouraging communication and reenactment of stories.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various themes and scenarios based on learner interests and curriculum goals. Prop boxes can be customized with specific materials to reflect cultural or topical relevance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' social interactions, problem-solving approaches, and emotional expressions during play. Assess their ability to take turns, share responsibilities, and resolve conflicts creatively.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research in early brain development suggests that dramatic play helps develop the frontal lobe, which regulates behavior and promotes self-regulation. Studies show that pretend play enhances social skills, emotional intelligence, and cognitive flexibility in young learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A preschool classroom uses a designated corner with costumes and props to allow learners to act out different scenarios such as a grocery store, doctor's office, or construction site. An educational game like Dr. Panda Town allows learners to roleplay daily interactions in an imaginative town, practicing social awareness and relationship skills.
