docs.title: Description
docs.text: Drawing is a powerful technique to enhance memory and recall by engaging learners in multiple cognitive processes. It requires learners to process information visually, kinesthetically, and semantically. Unlike passive activities like reading or listening, drawing forces the individual to elaborate on the meaning of a concept and translate the definition into a new form (a picture). This active process of grappling with and reconstructing information results in stronger encoding in memory, leading to nearly double the recall compared to other methods.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, drawing utensils, concepts or information to be learned.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time than passive learning activities. Some learners may initially feel uncomfortable with drawing if they perceive themselves as lacking artistic talent.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, including K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory retention, enhance recall of information, engage multiple modalities of learning, actively process and reconstruct information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Activates multiple modalities (visual, kinesthetic, semantic), promotes active processing and reconstruction of information, enhances memory encoding, increases recall by nearly double

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different skill levels; not dependent on artistic talent. Learners can choose concepts and information that are personally relevant. Can be used in a variety of contexts (note-taking, creating learning aids, data visualization, etc.).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure recall of information through quizzes or tests. Compare recall rates between learners who use drawing and those who use other methods. Observe the depth and complexity of learners' drawings to assess understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that drawing is a reliable, replicable means of boosting performance by significantly improving students' ability to remember what they are learning. It requires elaboration on the meaning of the term and translating the definition to a new form (a picture).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Understanding the developmental stages of drawing and writing can help educators tailor activities to match a child's current abilities. These stages include random scribbling, controlled scribbling, lines and patterns, pictures of objects or people, and letter and word practice. By understanding these stages, educators can provide age-appropriate materials, expectations, and encouragement to foster a child's growth in both drawing and writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the developmental stages of drawing and writing. A variety of art materials (crayons, markers, paper, etc.). A supportive and encouraging environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The timetables are approximate and do not apply to all. Sensory information may be too much for some children in this stage.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Toddlers and young children (15 months to 5 years).

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support creative growth and development in drawing and writing, ensure age-appropriate materials and expectations, and encourage independence and self-expression.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for understanding a child's drawing and writing development. Helps educators provide appropriate support and encouragement. Recognizes that art and early writing skills are interconnected.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to match a child's developmental stage. Educators can provide a variety of art materials to suit different sensory preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Drawing for Early Writing and Reading Development
Description
docs.text: Drawing is a strategy to foster creativity, planning, and the development of foundational literacy skills in young learners. By engaging in unstructured drawing time, children can unleash their imagination and develop new ideas, effectively telling a story through pictures. This "picture writing" serves as a pre-writing activity that allows children to express ideas through illustrations, which later serve as a plan for their writing. The process involves drawing a picture, talking about it, "writing" about it to the best of their ability, and then "reading" what they have written, with the instructor modeling correct writing underneath. This helps children understand that pictures represent ideas that can be turned into words, thus connecting writing and reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, crayons, or other drawing materials; time for drawing and discussion (approximately 10 minutes); instructor guidance and encouragement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires instructor to be accepting of children's drawings, regardless of artistic quality. May be challenging for children with sensory sensitivities. Requires instructor to steer children's stories back towards what is drawn to reinforce the connection between pictures and words.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-K to early elementary students (ages 2-7)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Unleash imagination, build confidence, develop foundational early literacy skills, understand the connection between pictures and words, improve planning and brainstorming skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances creativity and imagination; supports planning and brainstorming; builds confidence in writing; develops foundational reading and writing skills; helps children understand that pictures represent ideas that can be turned into words

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different skill levels, allowing children to express themselves through drawing and writing at their own pace. Can be adapted for children with sensory sensitivities by incrementally introducing art activities. Prompts and questions can be tailored to the individual child to keep them moving forward.

docs.title: Description

Drawing a picture enables children to tell a story and express ideas through illustrations, which later serve as a plan for writing. Teachers can then have students 'write' about their picture to the extent of their abilities, read their words (with the teacher writing the correct forms), and celebrate their work to reinforce that pictures represent words and ideas, and that they are writers.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Inviting learners to express their understanding through drawings provides insights into their comprehension and any misconceptions. Drawing allows learners to capture concepts, images, events, or objects, freeing up cognitive space for critical thinking. This process requires abstract and metaphorical thinking, which helps retain and understand information. By making decisions on how to represent relationships, size, shape, and placement of parts, learners reveal their preconceptions, depth of understanding, and engagement with the content. Teachers can then use these drawings to inform instruction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Drawing materials (paper, pencils, colors), structured prompts (e.g., line-color-symbol, draw an image, use simple shapes, create a comic), and time for students to create and explain their drawings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may have anxiety about drawing, so it is important to dispel myths about visual work. Verbal communication may still be needed to fully grasp a student's understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate visual feedback, encourages abstract and metaphorical thinking, reveals misconceptions, and helps retain and understand information.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Drawing involves visually, kinesthetically, and semantically processing information, which forces learners to grapple with what they’re learning and reconstruct it in a way that makes sense to them. It is an active learning strategy, not passive. Drawing encodes memory by layering together the visual memory of the image, the kinesthetic memory of drawing, and the semantic memory invoked during meaning-making. It increases the likelihood that the concept being drawn will later be recalled.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires drawing materials such as paper, crayons, pencils, or digital drawing tools. Requires time for students to create drawings and reflect on their meaning.

docs.title: Constraints

Fosters creativity and expression through interactive notebooks. Aids data visualization by helping students collect, analyze, and present data in visual form.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Behavioral scientists identify three levers a teacher controls when presenting instructional material to minimize errors and bring correct responses under reliable stimulus control (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 1987; Englemann, 1991):

Specific directions. Directions should focus only on the response the teacher wants the learner to make, discarding extraneous information that can distract from the target response. For example, teaching a sight word with "This is the word 'rabbit.' Say 'rabbit' and point to the word" is more effective than adding unrelated facts about rabbits, which risks becoming what the learner actually attends to.

Active over passive responding. Research on "opportunity to respond" (Delguardi, Greenwood, & Hall, 1979; Hall, Delguardi, Greenwood, & Thurston, 1982; Lindsley, 1992) distinguishes active responding (writing, calculating, focusing a microscope, recording observations — the learner does something) from passive responding (listening to lectures, watching, waiting for assistance). Greenwood, Delguardi, and Hall (1984) found that nearly half of a typical learner's school day involves passive responding, despite research showing a strong relationship between active responding and achievement; behavioral scientists recommend planning lessons so learners spend at least 75% of class time in active responding. Practice materials (worksheets, seatwork, homework) should also be designed to elicit correct responses 70-90% of the time (Borich, 1996; Stephens, 1976) — deliberately making practice materials difficult enough to produce frequent errors slows acquisition of basic facts and skills rather than accelerating it.

Rapid pacing. Counterintuitively, faster-paced presentation of basic academic material tends to produce fewer errors, not more, for fact and simple-sequence learning. Carnine's studies on reading-instruction pace found that rapid teacher presentations produced greater achievement, fewer errors, and more sustained learner attention during letter and word identification than slower presentations (Carnine, 1976; Carnine & Fink, 1978).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clearly defined target response, so directions can be pared down to only what supports that response
  • Instructional material and practice sets calibrated to a 70-90% success rate rather than deliberately made "challenging" to the point of frequent error

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• This cluster of techniques targets fact and basic-skill acquisition specifically; the research base does not claim rapid pacing benefits complex reasoning or open-ended problem solving in the same way
  • Designing practice for 70-90% success requires knowing where a learner currently stands — material calibrated for one learner's success rate may be miscalibrated for another

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners acquiring basic facts, letter/word identification, or other well-defined procedural skills where errors slow the learning process and provoke frustration or avoidance

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Fast, reliable acquisition of foundational facts and skills, minimizing the frustration and avoidance behavior that high error rates tend to produce

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Write directions that name only the target response; remove explanatory or contextual material that does not directly support making that response.
  2. Plan lesson activities so learners are actively responding (writing, calculating, manipulating, recording) for the large majority of instructional time, rather than passively listening or watching.
  3. Design practice materials so learners produce correct answers roughly 70-90% of the time; avoid deliberately difficult practice sets intended to "stretch" learners into frequent error.
  4. Where the content is basic facts or simple sequences, favor a brisk response pace over a slower, more deliberative one.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Least-to-Most Prompting Hierarchy — prompts are a complementary lever for minimizing errors, used alongside effective presentation
  • Behavioral Feedback for Correct and Incorrect Responses — the consequence side of the same errorless-learning approach

docs.title: Key Sources

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Feedback is any response from a teacher regarding a student's performance or behavior. It can be verbal, written, or gestural. The purpose of feedback in the learning process is to improve a student’s performance. Effective feedback determines a learner's level of understanding and skill development in order to plan the next steps towards achieving the learning intentions or goals. It should assist the learner to reflect on their learning and their learning strategies so they can make adjustments to make better progress in their learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for observation, assessment, and communication with the student. May require tools such as rubrics, notebooks, digital portfolios, or communication platforms.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not delivered sensitively, feedback can discourage learners. Requires time and effort from the instructor. May be perceived as too corrective if not balanced with positive reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learner performance, encourage self-reflection, guide future learning, provide timely and specific information on progress

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves learner confidence and self-esteem, reinforces learning, builds motivation, reduces negative feelings about learning, helps both student and teacher understand progress

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs, preferences, and learning styles. Consider diverse learners when crafting feedback, balancing proper encouragement with avoiding hurt feelings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance and attitude towards learning. Track learner progress towards goals. Analyze learner self-assessments and reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows feedback has an effect size of 1.13 on learning achievement. Effective feedback can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides written comments on a student's essay, highlighting strengths and areas for improvement, and suggesting specific steps for revision. A mentor provides verbal feedback to a mentee on their presentation skills, offering constructive criticism and encouragement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Praising learners' efforts and strategies—as opposed to their intelligence—cultivates a growth mindset and enhances motivation and performance. Focusing praise on the learning process helps learners view intelligence as malleable, encouraging them to embrace challenges and persist through setbacks. In contrast, praising intelligence can undermine motivation and performance, as learners praised for intelligence may view intelligence as a fixed trait and become less resilient in the face of failure. Effort-based praise highlights the value of hard work, effective strategies, and perseverance, reinforcing the idea that learning is a process of continuous improvement. Instructors should provide specific feedback that acknowledges the learner's effort, strategies used, and progress made, rather than making general statements about their intelligence or talent.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Observation of learner efforts and strategies. Ability to provide specific and meaningful feedback. A focus on the learning process rather than just the end result.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If praise is not genuine or specific, it may be ineffective. Overuse of praise can diminish its impact. Learners may become overly reliant on praise for motivation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who may view intelligence as a fixed trait or who struggle with setbacks

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, enhance motivation, encourage persistence, and improve performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces the value of effort and perseverance. Encourages learners to embrace challenges and see mistakes as opportunities for growth. Promotes a positive self-image and reduces fear of failure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual learner efforts and strategies. Praise can be specific to the task and the learner's approach to it. Instructors can provide individualized encouragement to help learners persist through challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in learner motivation and persistence. Measure performance improvements following effort-based praise. Assess the extent to which learners adopt a growth mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Research demonstrates that effort-based praise enhances motivation and performance, while intelligence-based praise can undermine it (reference Dweck's research on mindset). Learners who receive effort-based praise are more likely to embrace challenges and persist through setbacks (reference research on resilience).
  • The specific mechanism: telling a student they are smart when they produce a good result implicitly commits them to that same explanation when they later do poorly — if a good result means "you're smart," a poor result on the very same logic means "you're not smart" (Dweck, 2000). Effort-based praise avoids setting up this trap because it never ties the outcome to a fixed personal trait in the first place.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference — a further consideration when feedback (effort-based or otherwise) crosses a racial or ethnic difference between teacher and student

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of saying 'You're so smart!' say 'I can see you worked really hard on this, and it paid off!' Instead of saying 'You're a natural at this!' say 'I like the way you tried different strategies until you found one that worked!'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Electricity and circuit tasks involve investigating how electricity flows in simple circuits using tools like electric testers and puzzle boards. Learners identify complete circuits and determine the flow of electricity between different points. These activities enhance understanding of basic electrical concepts and build problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Electric tester, circuit boards, wires, bulbs, batteries

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to specialized materials. Safety precautions are necessary when working with electricity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand basic electrical concepts, identify complete circuits, predict and test electrical flow, develop problem-solving skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on learning enhances understanding of electrical concepts. Encourages problem-solving through practical application.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Puzzles and circuits can be modified to increase complexity. Tasks can be adapted for learners with varying levels of understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in identifying complete circuits, correct prediction of electrical flow, successful problem-solving

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of electrical concepts, enhanced problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Mystery Card (NYSED): Learners use an electric tester to determine where electricity flows between circles on a mystery card. Pathfinder (KDE): Learners identify complete circuits with puzzle boards.

docs.text: Eliminate the inclusion of homework and extra credit in final grades. Homework grades often lead to copying and reflect privilege. Emphasize practice and mastery to foster intrinsic motivation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Becoming aware of your negative thoughts and actively working to eliminate them. It involves identifying negative thoughts, challenging their validity, and consciously replacing them with more positive or neutral thoughts. Using techniques like thought-stopping (e.g., saying 'Cancel Cancel') to interrupt negative thought patterns can be effective. Over time, this practice helps to reduce the frequency and intensity of negative self-talk, fostering a more positive and constructive inner dialogue.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires consistent self-monitoring and willingness to challenge negative thoughts. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying issues. Access to resources such as thought logs, cognitive restructuring worksheets, or mindfulness apps can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel difficult or overwhelming at first, particularly for individuals with deeply ingrained negative thought patterns. May not be effective for individuals with severe mental health conditions without professional support. Can be challenging to maintain in the face of significant stress or adversity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals prone to negative thinking, self-criticism, or rumination.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase awareness of negative thoughts, reduce frequency of negative self-talk, challenge validity of negative thoughts, replace negative thoughts with positive or neutral ones.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by encouraging learners to monitor their thoughts. Reduces anxiety and stress by interrupting negative thought patterns. Fosters a growth mindset by challenging limiting beliefs. Enhances self-esteem by promoting a more positive self-perception.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized techniques for thought-stopping (e.g., visualization, affirmations). Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through journaling, mindfulness exercises, or cognitive restructuring. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as thought logs or guided reflections.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in frequency and intensity of negative thoughts using thought logs or journals. Observe improvements in mood, self-esteem, and coping strategies. Analyze ability to identify and challenge negative thoughts in real-time situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that reducing negative self-talk can improve overall well-being and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression (e.g., PositivePsychology.com). Cognitive restructuring techniques have been shown to be effective in challenging and changing negative thought patterns. Mindfulness practices can increase awareness of thoughts and promote emotional regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual prone to self-criticism uses thought-stopping techniques (e.g., saying 'Stop!' or visualizing a stop sign) to interrupt negative thoughts and replace them with positive affirmations. A student facing exam anxiety challenges negative thoughts (e.g., 'I'm going to fail') with more realistic and positive ones (e.g., 'I've studied hard, and I'm prepared'). Resource: Beck Institute for Cognitive Behavior Therapy – Cognitive Restructuring.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a classroom culture where errors become learning opportunities involves changing the assumption that math ability is binary—either you're good at it or not. Instead of moving on quickly from a wrong answer, teachers can show excitement about the student's thinking process. By identifying what is correct about the student’s approach, even when the answer is wrong, the teacher can show that the student was on the right track. This provides an opportunity for the student to uncover their own mistake or misconception and promotes a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in classroom culture and teacher mindset. Teachers need to be prepared to facilitate discussions around errors and provide constructive feedback. Worked examples with incorrect solutions can be presented.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May initially be uncomfortable for students accustomed to traditional math instruction. Requires careful facilitation to ensure that discussions remain positive and constructive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners who struggle with math confidence

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a growth mindset, improve problem-solving skills, reduce math anxiety, encourage participation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to take risks, values effort over correct answers, and supports deeper understanding of mathematical concepts. It allows students to see errors as a natural part of the learning process and reduces anxiety associated with making mistakes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different grade levels by adjusting the complexity of the problems and the depth of the discussion. For students who are particularly anxious about making mistakes, teachers can provide more explicit support and positive reinforcement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Eliciting Student Thinking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in student participation, willingness to take risks, and attitudes toward errors. Collect feedback from students on their perceptions of the classroom environment and their feelings about math. Analyze student work to identify common errors and misconceptions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that embracing errors can lead to increased student engagement, improved problem-solving skills, and a more positive attitude toward math. Research indicates that a growth mindset can help students overcome math anxiety and improve their performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers can use worked examples with wrong answers and have students find the error. Or they can rethink how they use class participation. Teachers can first say, “I don’t want to hear the answer just yet. I want to hear about the first thing you thought about.” Different students will share different ideas, which can help them all see that there can be multiple ways to solve a problem.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves creating a classroom culture where errors are seen as opportunities for learning rather than indicators of failure. When a student makes a mistake, instructors should focus on what is correct in the student's thinking, find out what is right about that student’s thinking and provide an opportunity for the student to uncover their misconception. When a student voices a wrong answer, teachers can get excited about that.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in instructor mindset and classroom culture. Instructors should be trained to facilitate error-based learning and provide constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time investment to change established beliefs and behaviors. Some learners may initially resist a focus on errors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with math and have developed a negative self-perception.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Shift learner perceptions of math ability from fixed to growth-oriented. Encourage risk-taking, resilience, and persistence in problem-solving.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe environment for learners to experiment and learn from mistakes. Boosts confidence by focusing on what learners understand rather than what they do not. Reinforces reasoning skills over rote memorization.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adjust feedback to address individual learning styles and needs. Activities can be tailored to build on learner strengths and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe shifts in learner attitudes and behaviors related to errors. Assess improvements in reasoning skills and persistence on challenging tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that a growth mindset (belief in the ability to learn and improve) enhances resilience and academic performance. Improved performance through learning from errors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting worked examples with errors and asking learners to identify them. De-emphasize answers and spend more time on reasoning. Rethink the way they use class participation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Emotion-based story discussions involve reading stories and having learners identify and discuss the characters' feelings. This activity helps learners connect emotions to specific events and understand different perspectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to age-appropriate stories. A facilitator to guide the discussion and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the chosen stories. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, including early childhood, elementary, middle school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, improve perspective-taking skills, promote empathetic understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Uses stories as a relatable medium to explore emotions. Encourages critical thinking and empathetic responses.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Stories can be selected to reflect diverse cultural backgrounds and experiences. Discussion prompts can be adapted to suit different age groups and learning levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately identify and discuss characters' emotions. Assess the depth and complexity of their responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of literature to promote emotional intelligence and social-emotional learning. (Source: Using Literature to Teach Social and Emotional Learning - https://www.edutopia.org/article/using-literature-teach-social-and-emotional-learning/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Emotion Charades involves a student acting out a scenario that makes them feel a certain way, while the rest of the group guesses the emotion being portrayed. This activity promotes emotional literacy and recognition of emotional triggers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a set of pre-written scenarios or a whiteboard to generate ideas. A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may feel uncomfortable acting out emotions. Requires a supportive and inclusive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, recognize emotional triggers, promote nonverbal communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances emotional vocabulary, promotes empathy, and offers a creative outlet for emotional expression. Supports social awareness by encouraging students to consider different perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different scenarios or focusing on specific emotions. Learners can choose scenarios relevant to their experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to accurately portray emotions and interpret others' portrayals. Assess the depth and complexity of the emotions explored.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of role-playing and dramatic activities to enhance emotional understanding and social skills. (Source: Spontaneous Drama Improves Communication Skills - https://www.livestrong.com/article/198645-spontaneous-drama-improves-communication-skills/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Emotion cue cards are portable visual or auditory prompts designed to remind students of strategies for managing emotions, such as using a fidget or taking a mindfulness break. Students can carry them on a keyring or access them digitally, selecting strategies that work best for them. Consistent use of these cards aims to integrate self-regulation techniques into long-term memory.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Cards (physical or digital), time to introduce and practice strategies, support from educators and caregivers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness may vary depending on the severity of emotional distress. Requires consistent use and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students, students with emotional regulation challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support self-regulation, promote emotional awareness, provide strategies for managing emotions, reinforce coping mechanisms

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides on-the-spot reminders, promotes self-awareness, supports the development of coping strategies, helps integrate self-regulation techniques into long-term memory.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose strategies that work best for them. Digital formats allow for audio, visuals, and animations. Blank cards can be customized with additional strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and effectiveness of strategy use. Monitor improvements in self-regulation and emotional control.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of self-regulation skills. Provides concrete strategies for managing emotions. Can be integrated into personalized learning plans.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student uses emotion cue cards on a keyring to remind themselves to take deep breaths or squeeze a fidget when feeling anxious during a test. A digital product provides a repository of prompt cards with audio, visuals, and animations for students to access when their emotions are heightened.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students express how they are feeling by drawing or sharing an emoji. Volunteers then share their emoji and explain how it reflects their current feelings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emojis (drawn or printed), time for individual reflection and whole-class sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may not be familiar with emojis or may not feel comfortable expressing their feelings through them. It is important to provide a variety of emojis to choose from and to create a safe and supportive environment where students feel comfortable sharing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially K–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Express feelings in a non-verbal way, encourage self-awareness, promote sharing and empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a fun and engaging way for students to express their feelings, especially for those who may have difficulty articulating their emotions verbally. Normalizes talking about feelings and empowers students to view their emotions as assets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose to draw their own emojis or select from a pre-made sheet. Instructors can provide a variety of emojis to choose from, representing different emotions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in the activity. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The simple act of acknowledging our emotions helps calm the amygdala and reduce the intensity of the emotions we feel. By naming our emotions, we feel more in control. We are less likely to experience an emotional hijack when we name our feelings, and students can create space to make intentional choices about how to move forward.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students express their current feelings by drawing or sharing an emoji that represents their emotional state. Volunteers then share their emoji and explain how it reflects their current feelings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to emojis (either drawn or digital), time for individual reflection (2-3 minutes), and a willingness to share in a whole-class setting.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to find an emoji that accurately represents their emotions. The effectiveness of the activity depends on creating a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for pre-K through college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Express feelings creatively, increase emotional awareness, build comfort in sharing emotions, foster a positive classroom environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a non-verbal way for students to express their emotions. Can be a fun and engaging way to check-in. Allows for individual expression and creativity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose from a range of emojis or create their own. The level of sharing can be adjusted based on individual comfort levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in creating and sharing emojis. Assess the thoughtfulness and specificity of students' explanations of their emojis.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Acknowledging emotions calms the amygdala and reduces the intensity of felt emotions, helping individuals feel more in control. Promotes emotional literacy and awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary school teachers use emotion emojis as a daily check-in to gauge how students are feeling and to create a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An emotion guessing game involves an instructor or student making an emotion face, and the others guess the emotion being expressed. After guessing, the group discusses situations that might evoke that emotion, enhancing emotional vocabulary and social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires minimal materials (e.g., paper or blanket to cover face). A facilitator to guide the game and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel uncomfortable making facial expressions in front of others. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, including early childhood, elementary, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional vocabulary, improve nonverbal communication, promote empathy and social awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging and interactive, encourages active participation, and promotes understanding of the connection between facial expressions and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by using pictures or written prompts instead of facial expressions. Learners can take turns being the 'emotion actor.'

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately identify emotions and connect them with appropriate situations. Assess the depth and complexity of the emotions discussed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that activities involving facial expression recognition can improve emotional intelligence and social skills. (Source: Facial Expression Recognition and Emotional Intelligence - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6225237/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Emotion Hello Song involves singing a greeting song with different emotional expressions. This helps learners start the day by identifying and expressing their emotions, fostering emotional awareness and connection with peers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires basic musical skills or access to a pre-made Emotion Hello Song. A facilitator to lead the singing and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These activities focus on helping learners identify and express emotions through various means, enhancing their emotional literacy and self-awareness. Examples include making emotion faces and having children guess the emotion, labeling their own emotions, and guessing the emotions of characters in stories. Puppets, emotion walking games, emotion hello songs, and emotion guessing games are used to engage learners. Learners are asked to look at each other's faces and think about how they are feeling and asked to share their own emotions. Learners also play emotion guessing games by revealing faces showing an emotion and having others guess what the emotion being shown is. Other activities involve changing familiar songs by singing them with a different emotion and modelling the silliest face you can make and have the children participate as well.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires puppets, emotion cards, stories, music, and space for movement. The instructor must facilitate discussion and model emotional expressions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may struggle to express emotions, activities must be culturally sensitive, and the instructor must be skilled in facilitating emotional discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children and early childhood learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional literacy, promote self-awareness, and foster empathy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances emotional expression, provides visual and kinesthetic engagement, and builds social interaction skills. Enhances self-regulation, empathy, and emotional expression.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptations include varying complexity of emotions, using visual aids, and adjusting activities based on learner needs and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners identify, label, and match facial expressions and feelings. Categorizing feeling words by type, analyzing characters’ feelings in literature, and connecting actions with emotions help build emotional literacy.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May oversimplify complex emotions. Requires careful facilitation to ensure learners feel safe and supported in expressing feelings. Might be challenging for learners with cognitive or communication difficulties.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted using diverse materials (pictures, books, real-life scenarios). Learners can select from a range of activities aligned with their interests and skill levels.

Such games make learning about emotions interactive and engaging.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners reflect on experiences, tracking patterns in their emotions and behaviors to enhance self-understanding and goal-setting. Journaling increases metacognitive awareness, promoting self-regulation skills. Reflections can be written or recorded, and should be facilitated through the use of supportive prompts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires journals (physical or digital) and facilitator guidance. Learners need structured prompts and supportive feedback to identify patterns and set goals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be comfortable with self-reflection and expression. Time-consuming and may require significant commitment. May be emotionally challenging for some learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students, adult learners, learners with self-regulation skill deficits

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-awareness, develop self-regulation, improve goal setting

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way for learners to explore and understand their emotions, behaviors, and patterns. Enhances self-regulation and metacognitive awareness. Supports goal setting and personal growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by offering journal prompts or allowing learners to self-select prompts that align with their needs. Flexible recording methods (written, audio, video) enable individual expression.

docs.text: • Track the depth and consistency of journal entries. Monitor the learner's ability to identify patterns in their emotions and behaviors. Assess the clarity and achievability of learner-set goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-awareness: Research indicates journaling enhances understanding of one's thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Enhanced self-regulation: Studies show that regular reflection supports better emotional and behavioral control.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An emotional thermometer is a visual tool used to help children recognize and gauge the intensity of their emotions. The thermometer typically ranges from 'calm' (green) to 'very angry' (red), allowing children to assess their emotional state and implement coping strategies early in the process. It helps children learn to differentiate between varying emotions and their intensities, providing an opportunity to prevent escalation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emotional thermometer graphic, time to introduce and discuss emotions, consistent use in various situations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective during a full-blown tantrum. Requires consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Young children, especially those learning to manage anger and other intense emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional awareness, promote self-assessment, facilitate early intervention, teach emotion regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete, visual representation of emotional intensity, supports self-monitoring, enables early intervention to prevent emotional escalation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The scale can be adjusted to include other emotions beyond anger. Different visual representations (e.g., colors, images) can be used to cater to individual preferences.

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A child uses an emotional thermometer to identify that they are feeling 'irritated' and chooses to take a break before their anger escalates. Teachers use the thermometer as a classroom tool to prompt discussions about different emotions and their intensity.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: • Enhances emotional literacy, supports understanding of nuances in feelings, and improves communication. Helps learners connect actions and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Emotional Walking Game involves learners walking around while embodying different emotions upon hearing a signal. This activity combines physical activity with emotional expression, helping learners connect emotions with physical movements.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage in actions to build an empathic mindset. Read stories from the perspective of characters similar to your students. Follow a student schedule for a day. Survey students frequently using low-tech or high-tech tools. Ask, “What’s one thing teachers should know about students?” or “What’s the most important thing I should know about you?” Use survey data to drive instruction with an empathic mindset. Remember that students watch teachers constantly, and actions can unintentionally model unempathetic behavior. Offer solutions-based perspectives and model citizenship.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, access to diverse literature, opportunities for student interaction, data collection tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires commitment from educators, may be challenging in environments with high stress or limited resources

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces bias, fosters inclusivity, strengthens student-teacher relationships, promotes effective communication

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to the specific demographics and challenges of a school or district.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: De-emphasizing answers and spending more time on reasoning can build confidence. Teachers can put a worked example with a wrong answer up on the board and have students find the error. Or they can rethink the way they use class participation, first asking learners to share their initial thoughts rather than the answer itself. These discussions and practices make mathematics class more discursive and less about a single answer, which can help students feel confident when they don’t know the answer right away, or get the wrong answer at first.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Deliberate design of learning activities and assessments that value the reasoning process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a significant shift in mindset for both learners and instructors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who are answer-focused or who have a fear of being incorrect.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, enhance self-reflection, and improve learning outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to take risks and experiment. Promotes a deeper understanding of the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Differentiation in the type of feedback provided based on individual learner needs and styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality of learner reasoning and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing reasoning enhances motivation, persistence, and overall learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The teacher could say, 'I don’t want to hear the answer just yet. I want to hear about the first thing you thought about.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Helping learners focus on and value the process of learning, rather than just the grades they receive, promotes a growth mindset. Without this emphasis, learners may base their self-perceptions of intelligence and worth on grades alone, which promotes a fixed mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Regular opportunities for reflection, ability to facilitate discussions about the learning process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are highly grade-driven. Requires a shift in mindset from evaluation to development.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for learners who are grade-focused or have a fixed mindset

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Value learning over grades, foster a growth mindset, promote self-reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to value the journey of learning, promotes intrinsic motivation, and fosters a growth mindset by focusing on improvement rather than innate ability.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Reflective prompts can be tailored to individual learner's experiences and challenges, encouraging them to focus on their personal growth.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
