docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor changes in learner attitudes towards learning, observe increased engagement in the learning process, and assess the depth of self-reflection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing the learning process increases intrinsic motivation, fosters a growth mindset, and leads to greater academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Facilitate discussions about what was learned, not just the grade received. Use reflective prompts such as, 'What did you find most challenging about this task?' and 'How did you overcome those challenges?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: De-emphasizing correct answers and spending more time on reasoning involves shifting the focus from finding the right solution to understanding the problem-solving process. This can be achieved by presenting worked examples with wrong answers and having students identify the errors. Teachers can also change how they facilitate class participation by asking students to share their initial thoughts and approaches before revealing the answer, encouraging diverse problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to shift their focus from assessing answers to assessing reasoning. They should be prepared to facilitate discussions, provide feedback on students’ thinking processes, and create a classroom culture where reasoning is valued over correct answers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in classrooms where traditional assessment methods are heavily emphasized. Requires a significant shift in teacher mindset and instructional practices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners in math classes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote deeper understanding, develop critical thinking skills, encourage diverse problem-solving strategies, reduce emphasis on memorization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports the development of critical thinking skills and problem-solving abilities. By focusing on reasoning, students are encouraged to explore different approaches, understand the underlying concepts, and learn from their mistakes. It can also make math class more inclusive and less intimidating for students who struggle with finding the right answer quickly.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to different grade levels by adjusting the complexity of the problems and the level of support provided. Teachers can also differentiate instruction by providing students with different types of worked examples and problem-solving tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students’ reasoning skills through written explanations, verbal discussions, and problem-solving tasks. Look for evidence of critical thinking, logical reasoning, and the ability to explain and justify their approaches. Provide feedback that focuses on the quality of their reasoning, not just the correctness of their answers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing reasoning over answers can lead to deeper understanding, improved problem-solving skills, and increased student engagement. Students are more likely to retain information and apply it to new situations when they understand the underlying concepts and reasoning behind the procedures.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers can present worked examples with wrong answers and have students find the error. Teachers can first say, “I don’t want to hear the answer just yet. I want to hear about the first thing you thought about.”

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Help learners focus on and value the process of learning rather than solely on grades. Without this emphasis, learners may base their self-perceptions of intelligence and worth on grades received, promoting a fixed mindset. While grades are important, the value of learning should be prioritized to foster a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to design learning activities that are engaging and meaningful. Instructors need to communicate the value of learning and provide feedback that focuses on growth and improvement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may still be motivated by grades, even when the value of learning is emphasized. Instructors need to consistently reinforce the importance of learning and provide opportunities for learners to reflect on their growth.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who are grade-oriented or tend to equate grades with intelligence

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, shift focus from grades to learning, increase intrinsic motivation, and improve self-perception of intelligence and worth

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to see learning as valuable in itself, rather than just a means to an end (i.e., a good grade). Helps learners develop a growth mindset by focusing on the process of learning and improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can provide different types of learning activities and assessments that cater to individual learner interests and needs. Learners can be given choices in how they demonstrate their learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement in learning activities, monitor their self-perception of intelligence and worth, and track their grades. Compare the effectiveness of emphasizing learning versus emphasizing grades.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that emphasizing the value of learning promotes a growth mindset and increases intrinsic motivation, leading to improved self-perception and academic performance. Without this emphasis on learning, students will often base self perceptions of intelligence and worth to grades received, promoting a fixed mindset.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Time plus energy equals learning. There is no substitute for time on task. Learning to use one’s time well is critical for all learners. Tutees need help in learning effective time management. Allocating realistic amounts of time means effective learning. How the tutor uses the tutoring session time helps to define time expectations for the tutee and can help them establish the basis for high performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured tutoring sessions, tutor guidance on time management.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires structured sessions, may not accommodate individual learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve time management skills, enhance focus and productivity, establish realistic expectations for learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves time management, enhances productivity, establishes realistic expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Communicate to tutees the amount of time they should spend preparing for class. Expect tutees to complete their assignments promptly. Underscore the importance of regular work, steady application, self-pacing, scheduling. Divide tutor sessions into timed segments so as to keep on task. Don’t hesitate to refer students to Learning Strategist to help them with their learning skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved assignment completion rates, better time management skills, positive feedback from tutees about session structure.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research emphasizes the importance of time on task for effective learning. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor communicates the amount of time tutees should spend preparing for class. The tutor divides tutor sessions into timed segments to stay on task.

docs.title: Employ Common Language and Strategies Across Disciplines
Description
docs.text: Employing common language and strategies across disciplines involves aligning writing expectations and terminology across different subject areas. This approach reduces cognitive load for students by creating consistency in how writing is taught and assessed, allowing them to focus on skill development rather than adapting to different teacher expectations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires collaboration among teachers from different disciplines to align writing expectations and terminology.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant coordination and communication among teachers. Requires flexibility to adapt common strategies to different subject areas.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 9-12 who benefit from consistent expectations and terminology across different subject areas.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students' writing skills by creating consistency in writing instruction across disciplines, improve transfer of writing skills, and reduce cognitive load.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load, promotes transfer of writing skills, and enhances consistency in writing instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Common language and strategies can be adapted to fit different content areas while maintaining consistency in core principles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased consistency in student writing across disciplines. Improved transfer of writing skills. Reduced cognitive load for students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances writing skills by creating consistency in writing instruction across disciplines, allowing students to focus on skill development rather than adapting to different expectations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identify students with challenging behaviors who exhibit leadership qualities. Assign these students leadership roles within learning groups, such as group facilitator, timekeeper, or outcome checker. Pair these student leaders with others who struggle academically. This strategy leverages the leadership potential of disruptive students while providing academic support to those who need it, fostering on-task behavior and improving test scores.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires identification of student leaders, careful pairing of students, clear role definitions, and monitoring of group dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure all learners are engaged and supported. Needs clear expectations to prevent misuse of power or off-task behavior.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially effective for those with behavioral challenges and those needing academic support.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Harness leadership potential, improve on-task behavior, enhance academic performance, foster collaboration, provide peer support.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages students with challenging behaviors in a positive way. Provides academic support to struggling learners. Improves classroom dynamics. Develops leadership and communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying leadership roles, pairing students with different needs, and providing specific tasks aligned to individual goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Role Reversal
  • Peer Teaching
  • Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Provide Guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners’ engagement, participation, and leadership skills within groups. Collect data from formative assessments, group projects, and peer evaluations. Track changes in behavior and academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students with challenging behaviors become engaged and improve academically when given leadership roles. Struggling learners receive targeted support from peers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Empowering students to advocate for themselves involves teaching them about their rights and needs, and providing them with opportunities to communicate and act on that understanding. This approach promotes student agency, allowing them to become more engaged and effective in their education. Strategies include developing self-advocacy and self-determination skills, which have been shown to improve educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in self-advocacy and self-determination skills, opportunities for students to practice these skills in real-world settings, and a supportive environment where students feel comfortable communicating their needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort from both students and educators to cultivate self-awareness and effective communication skills. Students may initially resist taking responsibility for their learning or feel uncomfortable sharing their needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities and other learners who may benefit from increased self-advocacy skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-awareness, foster self-confidence, improve communication skills, encourage problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances students' ability to recognize their strengths and needs, encourages them to take responsibility for their learning, and prepares them for success in various environments by promoting independence and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • IEPs and transition meetings can become more student-centered, and students can be supported in participating in real-world learning opportunities where they can practice self-advocacy skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' willingness to participate in discussions, request help when needed, and articulate their learning preferences. Measure students' ability to set goals, solve problems, and advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that self-advocacy skills lead to improved academic outcomes and success in post-secondary education, the workforce, and civic life. Students who self-advocate are better equipped to navigate challenges and make informed decisions about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students can become more involved participants—and eventually, leaders—in their IEP and transition meetings. Educators can provide more explicit instruction for students to develop the skills associated with self-advocacy and self-determination.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: EQUIP is a customizable observation tool designed to track patterns in student participation, empowering teachers to build more equitable classrooms. It can be used in real-time or with videos of classroom teaching. After completing an observation, EQUIP generates instant analytics that teachers can use to improve their practice by tracking social markers (race, gender, etc.) and aspects of classroom discourse (type of teacher question, quality of student talk, etc.).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to EQUIP tool, time for observation and analysis, willingness to reflect on and improve practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires training to use effectively, relies on accurate observation and data entry.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators aiming to create equitable classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote equitable classroom practices, track student participation, improve teacher practice, analyze trends in data

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides instant analytics, customizable observation criteria, tracks patterns in student participation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can customize the social markers and aspects of classroom discourse they want to track.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in teacher practice, improvements in student participation, data-driven insights.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that tools like EQUIP can help teachers recognize and address their own biases in the classroom, leading to more equitable and inclusive learning environments. Empowering teachers to reflect on their practices can improve student engagement and achievement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning is not a spectator sport. No one learns much just sitting in classes listening to teachers, memorizing prepackaged assignments, and spitting out answers. They must talk about what they are learning, write about it, relate it to past experiences, and apply it to what they feel is important. They must make what they learn a part of themselves. Equally important is the need to make explicit the learning processes that are occurring in the learning environment and why particular strategies are being used.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for discussion and application, tutor modeling of active learning strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant preparation and active facilitation by the tutor, may be challenging for passive learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active engagement with learning material, encourage reflection and application of knowledge, integrate learning into personal experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding and retention, promotes critical thinking and problem-solving skills, fosters personal relevance and engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Give tutees concrete, real-life situations to analyze. Ask tutees to summarize similarities and differences among research findings, artistic works or laboratory results. Model asking questions, listening behaviors, and feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Inquiry-Based Exploration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased participation in discussions, improved quality of written assignments, positive feedback from tutees about engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that active learning strategies enhance knowledge retention and critical thinking. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor gives tutees real-life situations to analyze. The tutor models active listening behaviors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning is enhanced when it is more like a team effort than a solo race. Good learning, like good work, is collaborative and social, not competitive and isolated. Working with others significantly expands the potential of learning and the ownership of their learning responsibilities. Articulating and sharing ideas and responding to others’ reactions improves thinking and deepens understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for group work, tutor facilitation skills.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful structuring of group activities, potential for unequal participation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance collaboration and social learning, expand the potential of learning, improve thinking and deepen understanding through shared articulation of ideas.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Expands learning potential, promotes ownership of learning, enhances critical thinking and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Create study groups within the Learning Centre. Encourage tutees to work together and use small group discussions, collaborative tutoring assignments, and case study analysis. Encourage tutees to discuss key concepts with other students whose backgrounds and viewpoints are different from their own.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased participation in group activities, improved quality of collaborative work, positive feedback from tutees about teamwork.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that collaborative learning environments foster deeper understanding and improved academic performance. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor forms study groups within the learning center. Tutees work together on collaborative assignments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encouraging learners to share their work with peers and online fosters a collaborative writing environment and broadens the audience for their work. Providing guidance on appropriate and high-quality content, instructors help learners feel comfortable and confident about sharing their writing for the world to see. The act of sharing and receiving feedback supports continuous improvement and metacognitive reflection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for peer sharing, access to online platforms, guidelines for providing and receiving feedback. Requires a classroom culture that values collaboration and constructive criticism.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for negative or unhelpful feedback. Concerns about privacy and online safety. Requires careful moderation and guidance from the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for developing digital literacy and communication skills in a digital age

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, enhance critical thinking, build confidence, improve writing quality

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Broadens the audience for learner writing, fosters peer learning and collaboration, enhances critical thinking through feedback, builds confidence by sharing work publicly

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose their audience and platform for sharing their work. The level of feedback sought can be tailored to the learners' needs and goals. Instructors can provide guidance on appropriate content and online etiquette.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Feedback/Peer Review
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner participation in peer feedback activities. Improvements in writing quality as evidenced by feedback received and revisions made.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners improve by sharing their work and receiving feedback, recognizing the value of others' opinions. Developing comfort and confidence in sharing work is essential in a digital age.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners share their writing in class, online forums, or public platforms, receiving feedback from peers and the instructor. Instructors facilitate discussions about the feedback and provide guidance on revisions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners read diverse texts and then think and talk about different genres to acquire academic language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may need guidance in selecting appropriate texts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase vocabulary and comprehension, improve Disciplinary Literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds vocabulary, increases comprehension, enhances understanding of genres

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose texts based on their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation in discussions, assess learner summaries of texts, review learner application of vocabulary

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reading and then thinking and talking about different genres is a robust sequence for learning academic language.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Empowering students to become self-advocates involves helping them understand their strengths and challenges, and providing them with a voice in their learning. By understanding what works best for them, students can confidently advocate for the support they need. Strategies include creating a classroom culture where students can comfortably ask for help, even anonymously. Self-advocacy equips learners to effectively communicate their needs and find solutions to problems they encounter.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to resources for students to explore their strengths and challenges, a supportive classroom environment, and strategies to help students articulate their needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort from both students and educators to cultivate self-awareness and effective communication skills. Students may initially resist taking responsibility for their learning or feel uncomfortable sharing their needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and learning levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-awareness, foster self-confidence, improve communication skills, encourage problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances students' ability to recognize their strengths and needs, encourages them to take responsibility for their learning, and prepares them for success in various environments by promoting independence and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adjust the complexity of self-advocacy strategies based on students' developmental stages and learning needs. Anonymity options can be provided to students who may be uncomfortable asking for help in public.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' willingness to participate in discussions, request help when needed, and articulate their learning preferences. Measure students' ability to set goals, solve problems, and advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that self-advocacy skills lead to improved academic outcomes and success in post-secondary education, the workforce, and civic life. Students who self-advocate are better equipped to navigate challenges and make informed decisions about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher implements regular check-ins to allow students to share their strengths and challenges. Students use digital tools with anonymity features to ask questions and seek assistance. Videos model self-advocacy in action.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a classroom environment where students feel comfortable asking for help. Some students may find it difficult to ask for assistance, so it's important to foster a supportive atmosphere. Research suggests that students' varied responses to academic challenges highlight the need for educators to encourage help-seeking behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A supportive classroom environment, explicit encouragement of help-seeking behavior, and accessible resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in classroom culture. Students may need explicit encouragement and support to feel comfortable asking for help.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, K-12 and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a supportive environment where students feel comfortable asking for help to overcome academic challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters a sense of community, reduces fear of judgment, and encourages students to seek assistance when needed.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailoring support to individual student needs, such as providing private or anonymous ways to ask questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation in discussions, proactive seeking of support, and positive attitudes towards asking for help.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduces academic struggles and fosters a growth mindset by encouraging students to seek assistance when needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating anonymous question boxes, providing one-on-one support, and encouraging peer tutoring.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-advocacy involves understanding one's needs, knowing what support might help, and communicating those needs to others to promote independence and problem-solving. This can involve direct instruction, models, and practice opportunities. Anonymity can help overcome barriers to asking for help. Educators can foster self-advocacy by teaching students about their racial identity and privilege, and by confronting their own biases. The goal is to empower students to disrupt systems of oppression for themselves. Specific strategies include establishing goals, and recognizing available resources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for self-reflection, opportunities for communication, willingness to address personal biases.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners to identify their needs or communicate them effectively. Requires educator to be aware of and address their own biases.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who learn and think differently

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Communicate needs, develop independence, solve problems, increase confidence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers learners to seek support, enhances self-esteem, promotes independence, increases problem-solving skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various needs by identifying specific challenges and supports. Focus on individual racial identity and privilege.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Discussion Sections
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased communication of needs, improved problem-solving skills, greater confidence in learning and working, active participation in IEP meetings

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved educational and life outcomes for students who practice self-advocacy skills and self-determination.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The 'I'm Determined' project provides direct instruction and practice opportunities. GoSoapBox uses anonymity to help students feel comfortable asking questions. Self-advocacy sentence starters are resources for students who learn and think differently.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Empowering learners to communicate their needs, understand their rights, and actively seek support. This involves fostering self-awareness, providing accessible resources, and creating a supportive learning environment where student voices are valued. Strategies include reflection on academic standing, utilizing tools effectively, and building a community where students' voices are valued.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection activities, access to educational tools, and a classroom environment that values student voice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in classroom culture to prioritize student voice and self-advocacy. Students may need explicit instruction and support to develop self-awareness and communication skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 3-8, students with disabilities, and adult learners in any setting

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop learners' ability to articulate their needs, seek appropriate support, and take ownership of their learning journey.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters independence, self-awareness, and confidence. Creates a more inclusive and equitable learning environment where students feel empowered to express their needs and contribute to their learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting tools and strategies to meet individual student needs, such as providing varied methods for self-assessment and making resources readily available.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation in discussions, improved self-assessment skills, and proactive seeking of support when needed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved educational and life outcomes for students who practice self-advocacy and self-determination. Creates a more equitable and inclusive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing learning interest inventories, exit tickets, progress monitoring, and peer/self-assessment activities. Providing easy access to manipulatives, graphic organizers, audio recordings, highlighters, choice boards, learning menus, and timers.

docs.title: Encouraging Students to Ask for Help
Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on creating a classroom environment where students feel comfortable asking for help when they are struggling. It involves normalizing trouble, teaching problem-solving strategies, and giving students the language to articulate their needs. The goal is to empower students to become self-directed learners who are not afraid to seek assistance when needed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction on the importance of asking for help, a supportive classroom environment, opportunities for students to practice articulating their needs, and coaching from the teacher.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant shift in classroom culture. Some students may still struggle with the concept of asking for help. Consistent reinforcement and modeling are essential.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly students who are hesitant to ask for help or who struggle with self-advocacy

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, reduce fear of asking for help, develop problem-solving skills, improve communication skills, and foster a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students overcome the stigma of asking for help, encourages them to embrace challenges, promotes a positive attitude towards learning, and fosters a culture of collaboration and support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adjust their approach based on individual student needs. They can provide different levels of support and scaffolding, and they can tailor the language and strategies used to the specific struggles that students are facing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' willingness to ask for help, track their usage of problem-solving strategies, analyze their ability to articulate their needs, and monitor their participation in collaborative activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students who are comfortable asking for help are more likely to persist through challenges and achieve their learning goals. Creating a classroom environment where asking for help is normalized promotes a growth mindset and fosters a culture of collaboration and support.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Sharing personal stories of seeking help, providing students with sentence stems to articulate their needs, and creating opportunities for peer support and collaboration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Involving families and community members in classroom and school activities. Integrating them into curriculum activities, assemblies, committees, after-school events, and homework support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Recruitment and coordination of family and community volunteers, clear communication of expectations and roles, opportunities for meaningful involvement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to coordinate, some families and community members may not be able to participate due to time constraints or other factors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators seeking to involve families and community members in education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student learning, provide diverse perspectives, strengthen community connections, and foster a sense of belonging

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with diverse perspectives, strengthens community connections, and fosters a sense of belonging

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor family and community involvement opportunities to align with student interests and needs. Offer a variety of ways for families and community members to participate.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Expert Groups

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Gather feedback from students, families, and community members. Observe student engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engaging positive role models can enhance student learning, provide diverse perspectives, and strengthen community connections.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher invites a local business owner to speak to students about their career and provide real-world examples of how math is used in their field.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage in effective online communication with empathy by taking the time to read and understand the original post, exchanging ideas with one or more users, tagging and mentioning community members, carefully crafting your message, presenting evidence and personal experiences, upholding the digital community’s agreed-upon norms, and consuming as much as you contribute.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Basic understanding of online communication, access to online platforms, a commitment to respectful and thoughtful interactions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires conscious effort, may be challenging for those unfamiliar with digital norms, depends on community norms and moderation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students, educators, and anyone engaging in online communities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote understanding, empathy, and effective communication in digital interactions, support ethical digital citizenship

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages thoughtful online interactions, reduces misunderstandings and conflicts, promotes respectful communication, supports inclusive online communities

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting communication styles to match audience and context; using diverse examples and experiences; adjusting sentence frames to different communication styles

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe online interactions, gather feedback from community members, assess quality of online contributions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates more positive and supportive online communities, reduces digital conflict, promotes responsible and ethical digital citizenship.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When presenting a new idea, use the sentence frame: 'According to _, we should think about __ in this way: _.' When disagreeing, say: 'I appreciate the experience shared by _, but in my experience ____.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating schools that buffer external noise from classrooms can improve student outcomes. Noise levels greatly affect teacher and student performance. In fact, excessive noise causes dis-satisfaction and stress in both teachers and students.

docs.text: • Physical Design

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Cost

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make classrooms with less external noise

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Decreases stress in both teachers and students

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustable by physical location

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teacher surveys, and student surveys

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced stress, higher test scores

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a brain-friendly and enriched classroom environment involves optimizing the learning space by considering layout, furniture choices, color selections, lighting, nature, environmental print, and organization of materials. It aims to reduce distractions, promote a sense of calm, and encourage learner agency. Specific strategies include using muted color schemes, incorporating natural light and plants, minimizing clutter, and organizing materials in accessible ways. When creating this environment, learners are given agency in their learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Thoughtful consideration of layout, furniture, color, lighting, and materials. Willingness to declutter and organize the space. Collaboration with learners to solicit their input and ideas.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial investment in furniture and materials. Requires ongoing effort to maintain organization and minimize clutter. Not all strategies may be feasible in every classroom setting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learning environments, particularly K–12 classrooms and spaces for adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance focus and reduce distractions, promote a sense of calm and well-being, encourage learner agency and self-regulation, support diverse learning styles and needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports attentional focus by minimizing distractions. Promotes a sense of calm and well-being, reducing stress. Encourages learner agency and self-regulation by providing choices and control over the learning environment. Addresses diversity by adapting to student specific needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can contribute to the design and organization of the space. Furniture and seating options can be varied to accommodate different preferences. Environmental print and visual aids can be tailored to specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner focus and engagement. Collect feedback from learners on their perceptions of the learning environment. Measure academic outcomes in enriched vs. traditional classrooms.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More room for movement and collaboration. Creation of a space that encourages reflection, relaxation, and engagement (Erin Klein). Improved emotional feel of the classroom, making it warm and welcoming.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Erin Klein’s second-grade classroom transformation: Students and teacher collaborated to redesign the learning space, resulting in increased engagement and improved learning outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers integrate art and music from diverse cultures into their lessons to enrich learning, engage students, and promote cultural understanding. Students are encouraged to share their own cultural art and music, fostering a sense of inclusion and connection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to diverse art and music resources, willingness to incorporate student input, and time for preparation and presentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to avoid cultural appropriation or misrepresentation. May need additional resources to support diverse artistic expressions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers seeking to make their lessons more engaging and culturally relevant.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learning through diverse media, promote cultural appreciation, increase student engagement, connect content to student experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Brings content to life, provides diverse perspectives, affirms students’ daily lives, and promotes discussion about cultural similarities and differences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to share their own cultural art, music, and traditions. Offers flexible ways to engage with the material, such as discussions, comparisons, and presentations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, enhanced understanding of content, improved cultural awareness, positive feedback from students and families.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, culturally responsive teaching, deeper content understanding, stronger community connections.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These activities explore the relationships between people and their environments by examining environments, inhabitants, and the tracks they leave behind. Activities prompt learners to write stories about predatory events based on tracks or to consider the role of environmental components like rocks, soil, and water in terrariums.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Terrariums, animal tracks, writing materials

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require access to specific environments and materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying life science and earth science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore characteristics of environments and inhabitants, analyze relationships between species and environments, understand the role of environmental components

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides concrete understanding of ecosystems. Encourages creative thinking and writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Terrarium and animal selection can be varied. Writing prompts can be tailored to different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in describing environmental characteristics, correctness in analyzing relationships, creativity in writing

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of ecosystems, enhanced analytical and creative skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • People Interacting with the Environment (KDE): Explore the characteristics of environments and inhabitants. Run For Your Life (NYSED): Read a story about a predatory event and draw a picture of resulting animal tracks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pair students and check-in with each other using an EQ Feeling Chart. Facilitate discussion by providing questions to explore feelings and their origins. Students then share their observations with the whole class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart (downloadable resource), time for pair discussions and whole-class sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may be hesitant to share their feelings with others, especially in a large group. It is important to create a safe and supportive environment where students feel comfortable sharing. Some students may not be able to identify their feelings or articulate them clearly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially K–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Communicate feelings, identify the source of emotions, promote sharing and empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way for students to explore and express their feelings, fostering emotional awareness and empathy. Normalizes talking about feelings and empowers students to view their emotions as assets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The EQ Feeling Chart can be adapted to different age groups and developmental levels. Students can create their own feeling charts or use pre-made ones. Instructors can modify the discussion questions to suit the needs of their students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in discussions. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The simple act of acknowledging our emotions helps calm the amygdala and reduce the intensity of the emotions we feel. By naming our emotions, we feel more in control. We are less likely to experience an emotional hijack when we name our feelings, and students can create space to make intentional choices about how to move forward.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use a provided EQ Feeling Chart to identify and communicate their current emotions. In pairs, they discuss their feelings, where those feelings are coming from, and any other emotions they may be experiencing. The class then reconvenes to share what they noticed during their discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart, time for paired discussions (5-10 minutes), and a willingness to share in a whole-class setting.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may be hesitant to share their feelings, even in pairs. The effectiveness of the activity depends on creating a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable from pre-K through college

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Communicate feelings, practice emotional awareness, build relationships, normalize discussions about emotions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for identifying and discussing emotions. Offers a visual aid (EQ Feeling Chart) to support emotional literacy. Encourages empathy and understanding through paired discussions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The EQ Feeling Chart can be adapted to include a wider range of emotions or to focus on specific emotional categories. The depth of discussion can be adjusted based on the age and maturity of the students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in paired discussions and whole-class sharing. Assess the depth and specificity of students' reflections on their emotions. Gather feedback from students on the usefulness of the EQ Feeling Chart.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Acknowledging emotions calms the amygdala and reduces the intensity of felt emotions, helping individuals feel more in control. Promotes emotional literacy and awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A college course on social emotional learning uses the EQ Feeling Chart as a regular check-in activity to help students identify and manage their emotions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use the EQ Feeling Chart to identify and communicate their feelings with a partner. They discuss their feelings and their origins, then share observations with the whole class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart, discussion questions, time for partner and whole-class sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to the EQ Feeling Chart or a similar resource. Some learners may be hesitant to share feelings openly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Communicate feelings, identify sources of emotions, share observations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way to explore and communicate feelings, enhances emotional literacy, fosters empathy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart can be adapted or modified for different age groups and cultural contexts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and honesty of learners' sharing. Assess learners' ability to identify and articulate their feelings.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional awareness and communication skills, fostering self-empathy and social empathy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rubrics aligned to learning standards, objectives, and activities that illuminate student learning and mastery, with meaningful comments for formative assessment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Standard-based rubric, meaningful comments

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time-consuming to create

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess student learning and mastery, provide meaningful comments, ensure rubrics are aligned with standards

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Aligns with learning standards, promotes clarity, supports formative assessment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and grade levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding, equitable grading

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Such a rubric allows students to understand that formative assessment checks for understanding and progress and allows mistakes and revisions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating standard-based rubrics for grades 3-5 aligned with ISTE standards

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ensure all learners get response opportunities, not just high achievers. Monitor who you call on during discussions to avoid favoring certain learners. Individual learners may 'tune out' when they are not being called on, so it's important to call on all the learners in the classroom so that they know that their participation is important.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Monitor interactions to call on all learners equitably. Keep a clipboard to record who you call on during class discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • This practice can be time-consuming in a class setting with lots of learners. Some learners may not wish to be called on at all.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote inclusion by creating a learning environment in which all learners feel valued.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts learner self-confidence, encourages engagement, and reduces off-task behavior. Helps learners believe in their own abilities and strive for success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Call on all learners, especially those who don't perform well. Monitor which learners get more chances to speak than others.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increase in learner participation, improved academic performance, and reduced behavioral issues. Observation of equitable participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on teacher expectations and learner achievement demonstrates that expectations have a dramatic impact on learner academic performance and behavior. This bolsters student self-confidence and encourages them to remain on task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: EQUIP is a customizable observation tool for tracking patterns in student participation, aiming to empower teachers in building more equitable classrooms. It can be used in real-time or with videos of classroom teaching. After completing an observation, EQUIP generates instant analytics that teachers can use to improve their practice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the EQUIP tool, training in its use, and a commitment to equitable classroom practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to use the tool effectively. Some teachers may be resistant to using data to inform their practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower teachers, track student participation, and promote equitable classroom practices.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time data on classroom dynamics. Helps teachers identify and address patterns of inequity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Observation tool can be customized to track specific social markers and aspects of classroom discourse.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased awareness of classroom dynamics, improved student participation, and more equitable classroom practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment where all students have equal opportunities to participate and succeed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Equitable grading focuses on fair and consistent grading practices to address biases. It involves collaborative grading practices and ongoing training for educators to recognize implicit biases and confront limiting beliefs about students' abilities. Successful implementation requires time for collaboration, creation of equitable processes, and support through professional learning opportunities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for collaboration among educators, professional development resources, support from school/district leadership

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant shift in mindset and established grading practices. Resistance from educators accustomed to traditional grading methods. May require substantial resources for training and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, schools, and districts aiming to create more equitable grading systems

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce inconsistencies in grading criteria, address implicit biases, promote consistent grading processes, support fair assessment of student learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Mitigates bias in grading, promotes consistency, focuses on mastery rather than compliance, creates transparency for students

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various subjects and grade levels. Can be personalized to address specific biases prevalent in different educational contexts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track consistency in grading across classrooms, measure the reduction of biased grading incidents, survey students on their perception of fairness

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that grades are a powerful predictor of whether students are on track for success, but there is significant variance in grading both within and across schools.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Collaborative grading practices, use of rubrics and portfolios, opportunities for constructive feedback, information sharing with families

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a classroom culture where errors become learning opportunities shifts the perception of mistakes as failures to opportunities for growth and understanding. When a student provides an incorrect answer, instructors should explore what aspects of the student's thinking were correct, providing a chance for the student to identify their error or misconception. For example, instead of immediately correcting a wrong answer or moving to a student with the right answer, the teacher can ask, "What is right about that student’s thinking?" This reinforces the idea that learning involves a process of discovery and refinement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom environment that values mistakes as learning opportunities. Time to explore student thinking and provide feedback. Willingness to shift from error correction to error exploration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a significant shift in classroom culture. Some students may still feel uncomfortable with making mistakes in front of others. Requires careful facilitation to ensure the focus remains on learning rather than judgment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those struggling with math or who have a fixed mindset about their abilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage self-correction, improve understanding of mathematical concepts, reduce anxiety around making mistakes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety about being wrong, encourages students to see mistakes as part of the learning process, provides insights into student thinking, allows for targeted instruction

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the types of errors addressed to the specific needs and levels of learners. Provide structured support for identifying errors, such as checklists or guided questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in error analysis discussions, track student self-corrections, monitor student attitudes toward making mistakes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing mistakes as opportunities for learning can improve student motivation, reduce math anxiety, and increase achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A math teacher uses incorrect worked examples and asks students to identify the errors. A science teacher encourages students to share their incorrect hypotheses and discuss why they were wrong. A history teacher analyzes common misconceptions in historical interpretations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Use consistent routines and methods of giving instructions to help students know what is expected of them.

A routine is a set of rules organized around a particular time (e.g., beginning of the day), context (e.g., group work), or place (e.g., library or playground) that guides students through recurring classroom demands — materials checked in and out, activities begun and ended, students needing the bathroom or forgetting supplies. The amount of time learners spend actually thinking about, acting on, or working on a learning task is called engaged learning time (Savage, 1991), and it is often much less than the time allocated to an activity — a 35-minute activity might produce only 15 minutes of real engagement, the rest lost to passing out materials, announcements, and handling requests. Teachers who taught routines to students during the first few weeks of school were the most successful at maximizing engaged learning time (Emmer et al., 1994), and engaged learning time is significantly related to achievement — arguably the strongest single argument for investing in well-established routines.

Effectively teaching a classroom routine has five elements (Institute of Educational Sciences [IES], 2022): (1) define the behavioral expectations for the routine — developmentally appropriate, culturally responsive, positively stated, specific, and observable; (2) explicitly teach the routine to students and review it often, rather than assuming it will be picked up implicitly; (3) practice the routine; (4) provide positive reinforcement when students demonstrate it correctly; and (5) provide visual prompts of the routine, keeping it to as few steps as possible. Routines are especially valuable for time-consuming noninstructional activities, which can consume up to 50 percent of the time initially allocated to a topic or lesson if left unmanaged (Jones & Jones, 1990) — and should be taught with as much planning and thoroughness as the learning objectives themselves, then followed up with monitoring of how well they're actually working (Jones & Jones, 1990; Pasch, Sparks-Langer, Gardner, Starko, & Moody, 1991).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent implementation of routines.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become monotonous if not varied periodically.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create predictability and reduce cognitive load.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and improves efficiency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt routines based on learner needs and classroom environment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow routines independently.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased efficiency and reduced anxiety.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Classroom Space and Procedural Design — the broader principle distinguishing procedures (which routines implement) from rules

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher always begins instructions by saying, 'Okay, everyone, listen up,' followed by numbered steps.

docs.title: Establish Ground Rules for Peer Critique
Description
docs.text: Establishing ground rules for peer critique ensures that the process is productive, respectful, and beneficial for all learners. These ground rules typically include: picking work that matters, being kind, being helpful, being specific, keeping it moving, and holding everyone accountable. These rules are designed to promote effective communication and provide objective feedback that supports the presenter's goals for the work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear communication of the ground rules, consistent reinforcement of the rules, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort to ensure that learners adhere to the ground rules. May be challenging to address situations where learners violate the rules.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including elementary, middle, high school, and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a positive and supportive environment for peer critique, promote effective communication, and enhance learners' ability to provide and receive feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes a respectful and constructive environment for peer critique, helping learners feel safe and supported. Provides clear guidelines for effective communication and ensures that feedback is focused on the presenter's goals.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The ground rules can be adapted to fit the specific needs of the learners and the classroom environment. Teachers can involve learners in creating the ground rules to promote ownership and buy-in.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of group interactions to assess learners' adherence to the ground rules. Analysis of feedback provided by learners to assess the quality and effectiveness of their critique.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When learners aren’t used to the process, a teacher presents it to them as though she’s offering them a code to effective adult communication. At first, following the rules starts out as a performance, but over time kids internalize it and it becomes part of them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher establishes ground rules for peer feedback, emphasizing kindness, helpfulness, and specificity to create a positive and supportive environment. Resource: Developing Students' Ability to Give and Take Effective Feedback.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establish guidelines or agreements for group members to make when having discussions of race to ensure respectful and productive dialogue. These agreements may include staying engaged, experiencing discomfort, speaking your truth, accepting non-closure, being physically considerate, being verbally considerate, respecting classmates' feelings and space, and being willing to try new things. It also involves introducing a "pause of respect" after a student has spoken something especially honest or hard, and never asking students to speak for anyone else but themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitator, a safe and comfortable space, guidelines or agreements, and a commitment to respectful dialogue.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for individuals who are uncomfortable discussing race or sharing their personal experiences. Requires ongoing commitment to creating a safe and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages, educators, and community members

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a safe and respectful environment for discussing race, promote open and honest communication, encourage active listening, and facilitate understanding of diverse perspectives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Minimizes tension in race-sensitive content, promotes psychological safety, encourages active listening and respect for diverse perspectives, and fosters a deeper understanding of racial issues.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Guidelines can be adapted to fit the specific needs and context of the group. Facilitators can adjust the level of structure and guidance based on the group's experience and comfort level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Assigned Positions

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of engagement in discussions, track the use of respectful language and behaviors, gather feedback from participants, and analyze the depth of understanding and empathy demonstrated.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Establishing guidelines promotes a more respectful and productive dialogue about race, which can lead to increased understanding, empathy, and a commitment to social justice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using the Courageous Conversations About Race framework to establish agreements for group members to stay engaged, experience discomfort, speak their truth, and accept non-closure.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establish clear guidelines for group discussions, emphasizing engagement, comfort with discomfort, speaking one's truth, and accepting non-closure. Examples include: Staying morally, intellectually, and socially engaged; acknowledging and expressing discomfort; being honest about thoughts and feelings; and accepting the lack of immediate solutions, emphasizing the continuous nature of understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitator to introduce and reinforce the guidelines, willingness of participants to adhere to the guidelines, and a safe space for open dialogue.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if participants are unwilling to engage in good faith. Requires ongoing reinforcement and adaptation to address emerging challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and backgrounds engaging in discussions about sensitive or controversial topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a safe and respectful environment for discussing sensitive topics, promote active listening and engagement, encourage honest expression of thoughts and feelings, and manage expectations for resolution.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for productive dialogue, encourages empathy and understanding, minimizes conflict, and promotes a sense of safety and inclusion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Guidelines can be adapted to suit the specific needs and context of the group. Flexibility in implementing the 'pause of respect' or check-ins allows for individualized responses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Argument Construction
  • Role Reversal
  • Consensus Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality of interactions, the level of engagement, and the degree of respect shown among participants. Collect feedback on the effectiveness of the guidelines in promoting productive dialogue.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that clear guidelines and norms can promote more effective and respectful communication in diverse groups. Creating a psychologically safe environment can improve learning and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using the four agreements from 'Courageous Conversations About Race': stay engaged, experience discomfort, speak your truth, and accept non-closure. Implementing a 'pause of respect' after someone shares something honest or difficult. Conducting a check-in to gauge participants' moods and concerns.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establishing pre-arranged talk partners helps to streamline pair talk activities. These partners should be carefully selected to ensure equitable exchange of ideas, avoiding situations where one student dominates the conversation. This minimizes set-up time and fosters a comfortable and routine environment for pair discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires initial planning to establish appropriate pairings and ongoing monitoring to ensure pairings remain effective. Adaptations may be needed if students are absent or if pairings are not working well.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Fixed pairings may limit students' exposure to diverse perspectives. Requires careful consideration to avoid creating imbalanced or ineffective partnerships.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful in classrooms where pair talk is a frequent instructional strategy.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate efficient and equitable pair discussions, promote a comfortable and routine environment for pair talk, ensure that all students have a designated partner for collaborative activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces classroom management issues during pair activities, ensures that all students have a partner, and allows for intentional pairing to support diverse learning needs. Fosters routine and comfort.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Partners can be strategically assigned based on academic level, confidence, or communication style. Pairings can be changed periodically to allow students to work with different peers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the dynamics of established pairs during discussions. Assess whether both partners are actively participating and contributing ideas. Gather feedback from students about their experiences with their talk partners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-established talk partners can lead to more productive and equitable pair discussions, enhancing student engagement and learning outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use estimation and prediction skills by asking how they might do on an upcoming project or how long it might take them to complete a task or assignment. They can record their estimates and then reflect on the accuracy of their predictions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tasks or projects for estimation, a method for recording estimates and actual outcomes, and time for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent effort and may not be effective if students are not motivated to reflect honestly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who need to improve their ability to estimate their performance and time management skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-awareness, improve accuracy in self-assessment, and develop realistic expectations about task completion.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured method for self-assessment and reflection. Helps students develop realistic expectations about their abilities and task completion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different tasks and subject areas. The level of detail in the estimates and reflections can be adjusted to suit the student’s needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare estimated performance with actual outcomes. Review student reflections for insights gained and adjustments made.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students improve their ability to estimate their performance, develop realistic expectations, and enhance their self-awareness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Asking students to use estimation and prediction skills. Asking them how they might do on an upcoming project or how long it might take them to complete a task or assignment. Recording estimates and reflecting on the accuracy of their predictions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Projects or assignments, recording sheets, and class time for estimation and reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to accurately estimate their performance or time required. Some learners may find it challenging to reflect on their predictions. Estimation and prediction can be influenced by factors beyond the learners’ control.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-awareness, improve estimation skills, promote goal-setting, encourage self-monitoring, and foster accuracy in predictions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities to practice estimation and prediction, encourages self-monitoring and reflection, promotes goal-setting and self-regulation, and supports personal growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Projects and assignments can be chosen to align with different age groups, interests, or real-world situations. Learners can be given options for how to record their estimates and reflections. Support can be provided for learners who struggle with estimation or self-monitoring.
