docs.title: Explicate, Validate, and Address Negative Emotions
Description
docs.text: When learners come into a course with negative emotions and expectations, it can affect not only their learning but also their capacity to learn. If you’re teaching a course which you know learners may have negative emotions about, make it part of your opening course routine to explicate, validate, and address those concerns. Explicate that you empathize with the students that for many of them, there is the perception that the subject is difficult and draining. Professors should be honest with students about what people find hard about the course and recognize that it’s okay, fair, and normal to feel that way. Validate that it may not feel particularly valuable to be studying texts from a time that may not relate to our current events. Address the reason we study ancient works isn’t because those stories happened but because they happen. Make the content relevant. Show that the class will provide opportunities to put on critical lenses that will allow us to better see and understand the events of today.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be empathetic and open-minded, as well as knowledgeable about common learner concerns. It is necessary to create a safe space for learners to express their feelings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Addressing negative emotions may take up valuable class time. Some learners may be resistant to sharing their feelings or may not respond to the strategies used by the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • College and university students, particularly those in courses known for high levels of anxiety or perceived irrelevance, adult learners with prior negative experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learner engagement and academic performance by acknowledging and addressing negative emotions, creating a supportive learning environment, and increasing the relevance of course content

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and resistance by openly addressing negative emotions, validates learners' feelings and experiences, increases motivation and engagement by making content relevant, and fosters a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to share their specific concerns and feelings about the course. Tailor examples and applications to address their individual interests and needs. Offer resources and support for managing anxiety and building confidence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner engagement and participation in class. Collect feedback on learners' attitudes and feelings about the course. Track learner performance on assignments and exams.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that addressing negative emotions can improve learner engagement and academic performance. Creating a supportive classroom environment can also reduce anxiety and increase motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A chemistry professor begins a course by acknowledging that many students feel anxious about organic chemistry, then shares strategies for succeeding in the course and emphasizes that it's okay to ask for help. A literature professor connects ancient texts to current events, showing students how these works can provide insight into modern issues. Resource: Topics on Potential.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Some students — particularly those with a history of behavior disorders — have had little real opportunity to learn basic social skills. Simple courtesies (remembering to say please or thank you) and body language (eye contact, sitting attentively rather than slouching and looking away) may not be entirely unknown to the student, but unpracticed and treated as unimportant. The core design challenge is teaching these skills in a way that doesn't become part of the student's punishment, doesn't come across as "preachy," and doesn't shame the student in front of classmates.

Several concrete vehicles accomplish this. Modeling through literature or story: reading or assigning books and stories whose characters model good social skills, calibrated to the class's age or grade level. Modeling through games: structured games that require courteous language to succeed (e.g., "Mother, May I?", Sullivan & Strang, 2002) turn skill practice into play rather than instruction. Mentoring relationships: pairing an at-risk student with an older student or community adult, as formalized in programs like Big Brothers Big Sisters of America (Tierney, Grossman, & Resch, 1995; Newburn & Shiner, 2006), gives the student a lower-stakes relationship in which to practice social behavior. Behaviorist practice techniques: positive reinforcement, extinction, and generalization are especially effective once a student has recently learned a skill but still feels awkward or self-conscious using it (Algozzine & Ysseldyke, 2006); contingency contracts — explicit agreements between teacher and student specifying exactly what work will be done, how it will be rewarded, and what happens if the agreement isn't met (Wilkinson, 2003) — add precision and clarity that reduces both misunderstanding and the teacher's own need to respond with frustration when infractions occur.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A vehicle (story, game, mentoring relationship, or behaviorist practice structure) that lets the student rehearse the target skill without it reading as correction or punishment
  • Enough consistency in expectations (especially under a contingency contract) that consequences are predictable and unsurprising to the student

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Framing skill instruction as an extension of punishment, or delivering it in a way that shames the student in front of peers, undermines the entire approach — the vehicle matters as much as the content
  • Behaviorist practice techniques work best once a skill has been recently learned and the student needs low-stakes rehearsal, not as the initial teaching method for a skill the student has never been shown

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with a history of behavior disorders or limited social-skill practice opportunity, for whom basic courtesies and attentive body language are genuinely underdeveloped rather than willfully withheld

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Functional social skills (courtesy, eye contact, attentive posture) practiced enough to feel natural rather than self-conscious
  • Reduced disruptive behavior stemming specifically from social-skill gaps rather than from other triggers

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify the specific social skill gap (e.g., interrupting, avoiding eye contact) rather than treating the student's behavior as a general character problem.
  2. Choose a low-pressure vehicle matched to the student's age and context: modeling literature, a skill-requiring game, or a mentoring relationship.
  3. Where the skill has already been introduced but remains unpracticed, add behaviorist reinforcement (praise, extinction of the competing behavior) to build fluency.
  4. For students needing more structure, establish an explicit contingency contract specifying expected behavior, reward, and consequence, agreed to in advance.
  5. Deliver all of the above in a way that keeps the interaction from reading as punishment — the same tactic delivered punitively will undermine the skill-building goal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit and systematic teaching of strategies, skills, and knowledge needed to be a proficient writer. Instruction should include modeling writing strategies and teaching learners how to regulate their use, such as how to monitor, evaluate, and adjust strategies as needed for particular tasks and goals. Explicit instruction is combined with extended writing practice for different purposes like recording, communicating, persuading, self-expression, and reflection. Foundational writing skills such as spelling, handwriting, and keyboarding are taught to automaticity. Skilled writing requires planning and revising, with more accomplished writers spending about 50 percent of their writing time planning and revising text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured curriculum, modeling of writing strategies, time for extended writing practice, explicit feedback on progress

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant instructional time, may be less effective without motivation or engagement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers, from beginners to college students, including those with learning difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop proficient writing skills, improve planning and revision, automate foundational skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear instruction and practice, improves planning and revision skills, automates foundational skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction is tailored to the writer’s developmental level, skills needed for specific purposes, and the writing task.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction

  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This instructional strategy involves directly teaching learners how to construct arguments and support claims with evidence, particularly in online settings. This includes providing direct links to evidence and critically evaluating sources to form well-reasoned arguments. The approach emphasizes the importance of understanding and considering opposing viewpoints to build a comprehensive and persuasive case.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to online resources, familiarity with social media platforms, and direct instruction in argumentation techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time investment to teach and practice argumentation skills. Some learners may struggle with critically evaluating sources or understanding opposing viewpoints.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and college students, as well as adult learners in professional development programs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop skills in constructing evidence-based arguments, enhance critical evaluation of sources, promote understanding of diverse viewpoints, and improve online communication.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking, improves digital literacy, and enhances communication skills. By requiring evidence-based arguments, it reduces reliance on personal biases and encourages rational discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different subject areas and learning styles. Scaffolds can be provided to support learners with varying levels of argumentation skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and relevance of evidence used to support claims, assess the ability to understand and address opposing viewpoints, and track participation in online discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that supporting online arguments with evidence is crucial for healthy argumentation and helps learners avoid retreating to echo chambers. Enhanced critical thinking and improved online communication skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit instruction in decoding involves providing direct and systematic teaching of phonics and word recognition skills. This includes teaching learners to sound out words, recognize common letter patterns, and use morphological awareness to decode unfamiliar words. Explicit decoding instruction is particularly beneficial for early readers and learners with reading difficulties.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires systematic phonics instruction, trained educators, and appropriate instructional materials (e.g., phonics workbooks, flashcards).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be sufficient for all learners with reading difficulties. Requires ongoing assessment and adjustment to meet individual needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early readers, learners with reading difficulties, and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop phonics skills, improve word recognition, enhance reading fluency, and promote overall reading comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides foundational skills for reading, enhances word recognition and fluency, supports overall reading comprehension, and builds confidence in reading abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction can be tailored to different reading levels and learner needs. Scaffolding can be provided through visual aids, manipulatives, and guided practice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess phonics skills through decoding assessments, track word recognition accuracy and fluency, and monitor overall reading comprehension.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research consistently shows that explicit phonics instruction improves reading outcomes, particularly for early readers and learners with reading difficulties.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • MeeGenius highlights words as they are read, aiding early readers in decoding, phonological awareness, morphological awareness, and sight recognition.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct teaching approach to handwriting, breaking down essential components like letter formation, size, and spacing. A multisensory approach enhances the learning experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires explicit teaching, multisensory materials (e.g., tactile tools), and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address underlying issues such as fine motor weakness or visual perception difficulties. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-3rd grade learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve letter formation, size consistency, and spacing in handwriting

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances fine motor skills, supports reading and language acquisition, and improves neurological development. Direct instruction ensures learners understand the fundamentals of handwriting.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapts to individual needs by focusing on specific components of handwriting, such as letter formation or spacing. Multisensory approach engages different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in letter formation, size consistency, and spacing. Assess legibility and fluency of handwritten work.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved handwriting skills through explicit instruction and multisensory engagement. Better written communication and academic performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit spelling instruction involves directly teaching spelling rules, patterns, and strategies rather than relying solely on incidental learning or discovery. This approach prioritizes structured lessons, clear explanations, and systematic practice. Effective explicit instruction includes teaching regular spelling patterns, high-frequency words (both regular and irregular), and frequently misspelled words. It utilizes techniques like test-study-test, where students correct their own errors immediately after a pretest, and emphasizes the connection between phonemes (sounds) and graphemes (letters). For irregular words, a ‘spell-out’ method is employed, where students say, spell, and say the word again. Emphasis is put on recurring review and recycling of frequently misspelled words, ensuring accountability and mastery.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured lessons, spelling lists, and assessment tools (e.g., pretests, posttests). Resources such as phonics charts, word lists, and spelling rules are beneficial. Implementation can be facilitated with spelling programs or apps like SpellingCity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more direct instructional time compared to other methods. Some students might find the structured approach less engaging. The effectiveness depends on the teacher's ability to deliver clear explanations and provide targeted practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students, as well as adult learners needing to improve basic literacy skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance reading skills, and build word recognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to spelling, improves encoding and decoding skills, and enhances long-term retention of spelling patterns and words. By teaching spelling in conjunction with phonics and vocabulary, it strengthens overall literacy skills. Explicit instruction is particularly beneficial for learners who struggle with implicit learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Content can be adapted to the learner's developmental level, focusing on appropriate word lists and spelling patterns. Tailor instruction to target specific spelling errors and patterns based on individual needs and performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track spelling accuracy on weekly tests, monitor the reduction of frequently misspelled words, and assess the application of spelling rules in writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that explicit spelling instruction leads to improved spelling accuracy and enhanced reading skills. Studies show that students who receive direct spelling instruction are better able to apply spelling patterns and rules in their writing. Emphasizing phoneme-grapheme correspondences and regular review reinforces learning and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Signs for Sounds program, which provides systematic, explicit phonics instruction. SpellingCity, an app that helps users practice spelling through games and activities where they see and hear words in context.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit instruction in writing strategies involves directly teaching students specific methods for planning, drafting, revising, and editing their work. This approach emphasizes breaking down the writing process into manageable steps and providing clear guidance on how to execute each one. Strategies like Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) can deepen understanding by systematically building background knowledge, discussing the strategy, modeling its use, memorizing key steps, providing ongoing support, and fostering independent practice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires explicit instruction, modeling, guided practice, and opportunities for independent practice. May also require tools for planning, drafting, revising, and editing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as overly structured by some students. Requires consistent implementation and ongoing support to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students who need structured support in developing their writing skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students' writing skills, improve their ability to apply specific writing strategies, and promote self-regulation in the writing process.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for learning and applying writing strategies, enhances self-regulation through goal setting and self-monitoring, and supports mastery through scaffolded practice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be adapted to fit different genres and writing tasks. Scaffolding can be adjusted based on individual student needs, with more support provided initially and gradually reduced as students gain proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in the quality, length, and structure of students' writing. Increased use of specific writing strategies. Enhanced self-regulation skills, such as goal setting and self-monitoring.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that explicit instruction in writing strategies, particularly through SRSD, leads to significant improvements in students' writing quality, self-regulation, and confidence as writers.

docs.title: Explicit Instruction in Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination
Description
docs.text: Providing explicit instruction for students to develop the skills associated with self-advocacy and self-determination involves teaching and encouraging them to empower themselves by understanding their needs and rights, communicating them, solving problems, setting goals, and engaging in active reflection. Engaging students in meetings where decisions about their learning and lives are made is also a key component.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for instruction, supportive classroom environment, opportunities for practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires training and resources. May be challenging for some students to understand their needs and rights.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities, particularly those in secondary and postsecondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-advocacy skills, promote self-determination, empower students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-awareness, promotes independence, improves educational and life outcomes

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and age groups. Strategies can be tailored to specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased self-advocacy skills, improved self-determination, positive educational and life outcomes

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students are more empowered to make active choices about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Incorporating goal setting and problem-solving into IEP meetings. Engaging students in service learning and work-based learning opportunities.

docs.title: Explicit Instruction on Book Selection and Care
Description
docs.text: Teach learners how to select appropriate independent reading books, care for them, understand expectations for their reading work, and follow library maintenance procedures. Model, teach, practice, and revisit all procedures related to independent reading, including selecting new books, managing browsing boxes, deciding to abandon a book, documenting reading, following bathroom procedures, accessing reading logs and printed materials, volunteering to share reading experiences, and preparing for and responding to sharing sessions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom library with labeled books, instructional time for mini-lessons, materials for modeling procedures, and tools for student practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant instructional time initially. Requires ongoing reinforcement and revisiting of procedures. Some students may need individualized support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Equip students with the skills to select appropriate books, manage reading materials, document reading progress, and engage in sharing sessions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures students select books that match their reading level and interests, fosters responsible book handling, clarifies expectations for independent reading, and promotes engagement and sharing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer mini-lessons on various topics related to independent reading procedures and allow students to practice and revisit these procedures as needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to select appropriate books and follow library procedures. Review students' reading logs and documentation. Monitor student participation in sharing sessions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Ensures students can independently manage their reading, select appropriate books, and engage in meaningful reading practices.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit instruction is a structured teaching approach where instructors make goals, objectives, expectations, and instructional content explicit. They clearly communicate the purpose of each learning activity and explain how it relates to broader learning goals. Instructors address all aspects of the learning task, including how to think about it, how and when to perform the task or use the information, and how to evaluate the task. This involves explaining and modeling the skill or concept, guiding learners as they practice, and providing opportunities for application to ensure they can transfer their learning to other contexts and situations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to plan lessons carefully, articulate learning goals clearly, and provide detailed explanations and models. Requires allocation of time for guided practice and application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as overly structured or rigid by some learners. Requires significant planning and preparation time for instructors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in basic skills programs, individuals with reading disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure learners understand the goals and objectives of each task; facilitate transfer of learning to new contexts; model effective problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clarity and structure, reduces ambiguity, and ensures learners understand the purpose and application of skills and concepts. Clearly demonstrates expectations and models effective strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs by adjusting the level of explicitness and providing varied examples and practice opportunities. Scaffolding can be tailored to support learners with different levels of prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner performance on application tasks; learner articulation of task goals and objectives; reduction in errors during practice activities

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research synthesis has identified explicit instruction as a principle of effective teaching, particularly for students with learning disabilities. Directly addressing learning goals improves comprehension and skill transfer.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Beginning a lesson by clearly stating the objective and explaining how it relates to overall reading comprehension goals. Modeling a decoding strategy by thinking aloud and demonstrating each step.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly teaching strategies involves providing learners with specific tools and techniques to solve problems and improve their learning. It includes identifying the strategies, demonstrating how to use them, and providing opportunities for practice and feedback. It goes beyond just knowing the strategies and ensures that learners understand how, when, and why to use them effectively. This approach can help learners become more self-directed and better equipped to handle complex tasks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires explicit instruction, modeling, and opportunities for practice and feedback. Educators need to be knowledgeable about effective strategies and able to guide learners in their use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming and require significant planning. Some learners may struggle to apply strategies in new contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who may struggle with complex tasks or lack effective learning strategies.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Equip learners with specific strategies for problem-solving and learning, improve their ability to apply strategies effectively, and foster self-directed learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with concrete tools and techniques, improves their ability to monitor and regulate their learning, and increases their confidence in tackling challenges.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different content areas and learning styles. Strategies can be tailored to individual learner needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' use of strategies, track their progress in applying them effectively, and gather feedback on their experiences with different strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that explicit strategy instruction can lead to improved problem-solving skills, increased self-efficacy, and greater academic success. (Research on metacognitive skills and self-directed learning)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An educator gives students a math problem that will make many of them feel stuck, and then guides them through the process of getting unstuck, helping them name their process and adding to a list of strategies. For instance, if a student says he wrote the information from the math problem down and points to a chart, the teacher will say: “Oh that’s interesting. You pulled the important information from the problem out and organized it into a chart.”

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit teacher modeling involves the teacher both describing and modeling a skill or concept. The teacher clearly describes the features of the concept or the steps in performing a skill, breaking it down into learnable parts and using multi-sensory techniques to engage students. The teacher demonstrates enthusiasm, maintains a lively pace, questions students periodically, and checks for student understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a teacher who is knowledgeable and skilled in the concept being taught. Requires a well-structured lesson plan that breaks down the skill into learnable parts. Multi-sensory materials and techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if students lack prerequisite skills. Requires significant teacher preparation and planning. Can be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages, particularly those who have learning problems, attention deficits, processing problems, memory retrieval problems, and metacognitive difficulties.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To provide students with a clear, multi-sensory model of a skill or concept; to enhance student understanding and ability to perform the skill independently.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes the concept/skill clear and learnable. Provides high levels of teacher support and direction, enabling students to make meaningful cognitive connections. Offers multiple modes to process information through multi-sensory cueing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The strategy can be adapted to different skill levels by adjusting the complexity of the concept/skill. It can also be tailored to meet individual student needs by providing varied multi-sensory experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student performance during guided practice and independent work. Check for student understanding through questioning and discussion. Monitor student progress on related tasks and assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that explicit instruction is highly effective for students with learning disabilities and those who struggle with attention, processing, memory retrieval, and metacognition. It provides a clear learning map and reduces confusion and misunderstanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A math teacher models how to solve a complex equation by breaking down each step and thinking aloud. A reading teacher models how to identify the main idea of a passage by highlighting key information and summarizing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When teachers adopt explicit teaching practices they clearly show students what to do and how to do it. The teacher decides on the learning intentions and success criteria and makes them transparent to students, demonstrating them by modelling. The teacher checks for understanding, and at the end of each lesson revisits what was covered and ties it all together.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to clearly define and communicate learning intentions and model desired outcomes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if it doesn't incorporate active learning strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure students understand the learning intentions and success criteria through clear instruction and modeling.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clarity and reduces ambiguity, supports understanding through modeling and demonstration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the level of support and modeling based on student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of learning intentions, ability to explain concepts, and successful completion of tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicit teaching helps students understand what is expected of them and how to achieve success, supported by teacher modeling and clear communication.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The approach involves specifically identifying student strengths and challenges related to social awareness and then employing aligned strategies to leverage those strengths to support learning. Social awareness, which includes understanding social norms and empathizing with others, is an essential element of emotional intelligence and social-emotional learning (SEL). Teachers model empathy, facilitate discussions about diverse perspectives, explicitly address emotions and social issues, and utilize current events and fictional characters to enhance understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Educators need to identify student strengths and challenges, implement targeted strategies, and provide ongoing support. Professional development or training in social-emotional learning may be beneficial.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a deep understanding of individual students and their social contexts, which can be time-consuming. Some students may be resistant to discussing social issues or emotions openly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators across all grade levels aiming to enhance social awareness among their students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students' understanding of social norms, improve empathy, foster constructive communication, and promote social awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop higher academic achievement, reduce disciplinary problems, improve coping skills, and reduce destructive behaviors. Enhances students' ability to understand social norms and empathize with diverse backgrounds.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be tailored to meet the specific strengths and challenges of individual students. Adaptations may include modifying activities, providing additional support, or using different types of materials.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Provide Guidance
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student interactions and communication skills to gauge their level of empathy and understanding. Collect student reflections on their experiences and growth in social awareness. Use formative assessments to track student progress and adjust strategies as needed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that early social-emotional functioning is linked to future wellness and that social-emotional learning interventions improve academic outcomes, coping skills, and behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers model empathy and explain their thought processes. Classrooms use current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness. Articles and resources from EdWeek and Edutopia provide additional guidance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage learners in structured discussions that explore diverse viewpoints and consider the experiences of others. This includes examining cultural, social, and personal perspectives to foster understanding and empathy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a safe and respectful learning environment where learners feel comfortable sharing their thoughts and opinions. Requires instructors to be skilled facilitators who can guide discussions and ensure that all voices are heard.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Discussions can become heated or unproductive if not facilitated effectively. Some learners may be hesitant to share their perspectives in a group setting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who need to broaden their understanding of diverse perspectives, K-12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of diverse viewpoints, foster empathy and tolerance, develop critical thinking skills, promote open dialogue

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured environment for exploring different perspectives, encourages critical thinking, and promotes empathy and tolerance. Helps learners develop communication and collaboration skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to specific topics or issues, allowing learners to explore perspectives relevant to their interests or concerns. Use case studies, role-playing exercises, and guest speakers to bring diverse perspectives into the classroom.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and contributions to discussions. Assess learner understanding of diverse perspectives through written assignments or presentations. Collect learner reflections on their learning and growth.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that discussing different perspectives can increase empathy, reduce prejudice, and promote more inclusive attitudes and behaviors. Studies also suggest students who understand multiple perspectives are more well rounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor might lead a discussion about a current event from different cultural perspectives. In a history class, students might analyze primary source documents from various viewpoints to understand historical events more comprehensively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establishing a dedicated computer as a station for exploration allows learners to discover their preferred composition pathway. Learners may utilize modes linearly (linguistic to audio to visual), begin by browsing digital images and audio files before writing, or use a recursive process, moving back and forth between drafts in digital, audio, and linguistic forms. Providing space for exploration creates ownership and values innovation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a dedicated computer with access to digital tools and resources. Needs a supportive environment that values exploration and experimentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who prefer structured guidance. Learners may need support in managing their time and staying focused.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners involved in multimodal composition, particularly those who benefit from hands-on exploration and self-directed learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable learners to discover their preferred composition pathway. Foster ownership and innovation in multimodal design. Encourage exploration of different modes and their combinations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-discovery and autonomy. Encourages experimentation with different modes and pathways. Values innovation and personal expression.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing a variety of digital tools and resources. Learners can choose the modes and pathways they want to explore.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how learners use the exploration station to discover their preferred composition pathways. Assess the extent to which learners incorporate their discoveries into their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that providing space for exploration creates ownership and values innovation, leading to more creative and personalized multimodal compositions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Setting up a computer with access to various digital tools and resources for multimodal composition. Encouraging learners to experiment with different modes and pathways.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a designated computer station where students can explore their preferred composition pathway. Students can utilize modes linearly (linguistic to audio to visual), start with digital images and audio files, or use a recursive process (moving back and forth between drafts in digital, audio, and linguistic forms). Providing space for exploration aims to create ownership and value innovation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated computer station, access to digital images and audio files, time for exploration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant resources to set up and maintain the station. Relies on student self-direction and exploration. Some students may need additional guidance to navigate the station effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students learning multimodal composition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster ownership and innovation in multimodal composition, encourage exploration of different composition pathways, support self-discovery of preferred modes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes student ownership and innovation, supports self-discovery of preferred composition pathways, and encourages experimentation with different modes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different learning styles and preferences. Students can explore different modes and pathways based on their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' engagement and experimentation at the station. Analyze the variety of composition pathways explored. Assess the extent to which students demonstrate ownership and innovation in their compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student ownership and innovation in multimodal composition, enhanced exploration of different composition pathways, and improved self-discovery of preferred modes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Expository advance organizers give students a broad idea of the lesson’s purpose before it begins by clearly stating the goals of the lesson. Teachers often state goals and write them on the board.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly defined learning goals and a means to communicate them to students (e.g., verbally, in writing).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if goals are too broad or not clearly connected to lesson activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly helpful for introducing new topics and units of study.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a preview of the lesson, set expectations, and guide students’ thinking by explicitly stating learning goals.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear purpose for the lesson and focuses attention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to any subject and tailored to the specific learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of lesson goals, participation in activities aligned with those goals, and ability to articulate what they have learned.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicitly stating the purpose of the lesson prepares students to think critically and purposefully about the content to be learned.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Another way to communicate positive expectations is by directly telling the learners that they have the ability to do well. Express your belief in their capabilities to handle difficult assignments or improve their behavior. This can empower the learners to work hard and behave appropriately to prove that the instructor's confidence in them is justified.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must be sincere when expressing confidence in their learners' abilities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may not believe the instructor, especially if they are struggling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' self-confidence and performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts learner self-confidence, encourages engagement, and helps learners believe they can be successful.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can provide personalized encouragement to learners who struggle the most in class.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increase in learner participation, improved academic performance, and reduced behavioral issues. Observation of learners' confidence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students often work hard to prove that teachers' confidence in them is justified.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers demonstrate genuine care for students' cultural needs by encouraging them to research and share their ethnic backgrounds, fostering a trusting classroom environment. Analyzing and celebrating differences in traditions, beliefs, and social behaviors helps students realize their beliefs and traditions constitute a culture, promoting cultural responsiveness. This strategy also involves learning the proper pronunciation of student names and showing interest in their etymology.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for students to research and share information about their ethnic backgrounds. Teacher willingness to learn about and respect diverse cultural traditions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may be uncomfortable sharing personal information. Requires careful facilitation to avoid stereotyping or cultural appropriation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in multicultural classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a trusting classroom environment, increase cultural awareness, analyze and celebrate cultural differences, improve pronunciation of names

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances cultural awareness and appreciation among students, builds trust between teacher and students, recognizes the cultural backgrounds of all students, including those of European-American descent.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can research and share aspects of their ethnic backgrounds that are most meaningful to them. Teachers can adapt the depth and breadth of the research based on students' age and abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student presentations and research papers, classroom discussions, teacher observations of student interactions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of culturally responsive teaching in fostering student engagement and achievement. Creating a culturally inclusive classroom helps students feel valued and respected, which can lead to improved academic outcomes and social-emotional well-being.

docs.title: Expressing Interest in Students' Ethnic Backgrounds
Description
docs.text: Teachers can actively demonstrate genuine care for students' cultural, emotional, and intellectual needs by encouraging students to research and share information about their ethnic backgrounds. This involves analyzing and celebrating differences in traditions, beliefs, and social behaviors. For European-American students, this helps them realize that their beliefs and traditions constitute a culture as well, which is a necessary breakthrough in the development of a truly culturally responsive classroom. Also, it is essential to take the time to learn the proper pronunciation of student names and express interest in the etymology of interesting and diverse names.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for research and sharing, a supportive and inclusive classroom environment, and a willingness to learn from students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional research and preparation for teachers. Students may feel uncomfortable sharing personal information if the classroom climate is not supportive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in culturally diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a trusting classroom environment, celebrate cultural diversity, and increase students' self-awareness and cultural pride.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes understanding and respect among students. Helps students connect with their heritage and identity. Builds trust and rapport between students and teachers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to the specific cultural backgrounds of students in the classroom. Students can choose how they share information about their culture.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation in cultural sharing activities, improved classroom climate, and greater cultural understanding among students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and culturally responsive classroom environment where all students feel valued and respected.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy encourages learners to express their emotions through journaling, drawing, or talking out loud. By externalizing their thoughts and feelings, learners can gain perspective, separate facts from emotions, and reflect on how to handle problems effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journal, art supplies, or private space; facilitator (optional)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be hesitant to express emotions; requires a safe and supportive environment; effectiveness depends on learner's willingness to engage

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children, adolescents, and adults in various settings (school, home, therapy)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote emotional expression; facilitate self-reflection; reduce anxiety and stress; enhance problem-solving skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe and private outlet for emotions; encourages self-reflection; helps clarify thoughts and feelings; supports emotional regulation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred expressive medium; provide prompts for reflection; encourage creative expression

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review journal entries or artwork for emotional content; track frequency of expressive activities; observe changes in emotional regulation

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased emotional expression; enhanced self-reflection; reduced stress and anxiety; improved problem-solving skills (as suggested by the use of expressive activities)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Expressive writing involves putting thoughts and feelings into words, often focusing on emotionally charged or stressful experiences. Learners write about their deepest thoughts and emotions regarding a looming test or stressful situation. Anonymity is key to encourage openness. The process helps learners offload suppressed thoughts and emotions, decreasing stress and improving health and academic outcomes. Writing interventions can also focus on values that are important to an individual and making meaning of life circumstances in the context of those values or writing about one’s “best possible future self” to improve emotional regulation and promote health and happiness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a short writing activity (15-30 minutes) before a test or when facing stressful academic situations. Requires anonymity to encourage openness.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May temporarily increase negative feelings immediately after the activity if focusing on stressful experiences. Not effective for every outcome. Eliciting negative emotions in the classroom could potentially backfire depending on an individual student’s prior experiences; thus, it is important to strike a balance between personal relevance and potentially counter-productive emotional elicitation. May not benefit those with low anxiety levels.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners experiencing test anxiety, stereotype threat, or general stress related to academic performance

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce stress, improve emotional regulation, free up working memory, enhance academic performance, reduce math anxiety and mitigate stereotype threat

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners manage emotions, promotes self-regulation, frees up cognitive resources, and enhances academic performance by addressing underlying anxieties and stress. Can also improve overall well-being.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to focus on different aspects of learner experience (stressful experiences, values, or aspirations). The best future self prompt may be useful in an educational context. Prompts should be personally meaningful to students to be effective.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved test scores, reduced math anxiety, enhanced emotional regulation, decreased stress levels, improved working memory capacity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show expressive writing boosts exam performance, reduces achievement gaps, and mitigates math anxiety. Benefits are often most significant for those with high anxiety levels. It is an inexpensive and time-efficient intervention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before a math test, students write for 15 minutes about their deepest thoughts and emotions regarding the upcoming test. The expressive writing group performed significantly better on graduate entrance tests (50th vs 41st percentile, respectively).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Extended writing opportunities involve providing learners with regular practice in writing to enhance their skills. This can be implemented through daily writing exercises focusing on specific skills such as sentence fluency, or by integrating chat features in digital products that allow for written communication with authentic audiences in real time or asynchronously. Such activities aim to improve processing speed, genre knowledge, and provide primary language support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for writing practice, access to digital tools with chat features (for digital implementation), clear prompts and skill-focused tasks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time allocation, learners may need scaffolding to engage effectively in extended writing tasks, some learners may find open-ended writing tasks challenging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Upper elementary students, learners of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance writing skills, improve sentence fluency, increase processing speed, expand genre knowledge, support primary language development

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides regular writing practice, enhances communication skills, increases speed of processing, builds genre knowledge, supports primary language learners, offers opportunities for authentic communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Writing prompts and chat features can be tailored to individual skill levels and interests. Language support can be provided based on the learner's needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor improvement in writing fluency, assess the complexity and accuracy of sentence construction, track engagement in digital chat features, analyze genre knowledge demonstrated in writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Regular writing practice can enhance writing skills, improve sentence fluency, increase processing speed, expand genre knowledge, and support primary language development. Authentic communication opportunities can further motivate and engage learners in the writing process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An upper elementary teacher implementing daily writing practice with a focus on sentence fluency. Developers incorporating chat features in digital products to facilitate communication with authentic audiences. Keys to Literacy offers resources on quick writes for content writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Challenge advanced learners with real-world extension projects that apply their knowledge in meaningful ways. Pool select learners from different classes to complete these projects. Provide opportunities for learners to collaborate in teams, analyze data, and develop creative solutions. This approach allows advanced learners to deepen their understanding, develop problem-solving skills, and engage in higher-order thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires identification of advanced learners, access to real-world projects, and resources aligned to project topics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure all learners are engaged and supported. Needs clear expectations to prevent off-task behavior. Requires ongoing feedback and guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Advanced learners who have mastered core concepts and standards.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Challenge advanced learners, deepen understanding, develop problem-solving skills, foster collaboration, increase engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows advanced learners to extend their knowledge and skills. Provides opportunities for collaboration and problem-solving. Increases engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying project topics, team sizes, and task complexity. Learners can also self-select project topics and tasks aligned to their interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving
  • Application of Knowledge
  • Research
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners’ engagement, participation, and problem-solving skills within projects. Collect data from project deliverables, presentations, and peer evaluations. Track changes in performance following implementation of extension projects.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Advanced learners are challenged and deepen their understanding, while also motivating other learners to work harder to qualify for future projects.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Facilitating discourse in online learning involves more than simply requiring students to post in a discussion forum. It includes regularly reading and providing feedback on student postings, encouraging participation, moving the discussion forward when it stalls or gets off track, identifying and drawing out areas of agreement and disagreement, pointing out linkages, and helping students articulate shared understandings. Immediacy behaviors, such as referring to students by name and sharing personal examples, enhance both social and teaching presence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a discussion forum or platform, active instructor participation, and clear guidelines for participation and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to manage and moderate, requires active instructor involvement, and may be difficult to ensure equitable participation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Online learners of all levels, particularly those seeking social interaction and collaborative learning experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage student participation, promote deeper understanding through discussion, identify areas of agreement and disagreement, foster a sense of community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, enhances social interaction, promotes deeper understanding through peer learning, and fosters a sense of community. Allows instructors to guide discussions and ensure relevance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by allowing students to choose discussion topics, providing tailored feedback, and using diverse formats (e.g., text, audio, video).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, improved quality of discussion postings, and positive feedback on the instructor's facilitation skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that synchronous technology increases teacher presence in the online classroom, enhancing student engagement and satisfaction (Velasquez et al., 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers should redirect their role in the classroom from instructor to facilitator to reduce the power differential between the instructor and students. Students in an authoritarian classroom may sometimes display negative behaviors as a result of a perceived sense of social injustice; in the culturally diverse classroom, the teacher thus acts more like a facilitator than an instructor. Providing students with questionnaires about what they find to be interesting or important provides them with a measure of power over what they get to learn and provides them with greater intrinsic motivation and connectedness to the material. Allowing students to bring in their own reading material and present it to the class provides them with an opportunity to both interact with and share stories, thoughts, and ideas that are important to their cultural and social perspective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A shift in teaching philosophy and classroom management techniques. Willingness to relinquish control and empower students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to plan and implement. Some students may struggle with the increased responsibility and autonomy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, increase motivation, and foster a sense of community in the classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement and ownership of learning. Creates a more equitable and inclusive classroom environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose topics and materials that are relevant to their interests and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Instructions

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and participation, improved classroom climate, and greater student ownership of learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more student-centered and culturally responsive classroom environment where all students feel valued and empowered.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Displaying anchor charts outlining fair communication protocols for class discussions and/or projects requiring teamwork involves creating visual aids that articulate the rules and expectations for respectful and inclusive communication. These charts serve as constant reminders of the agreed-upon protocols, promoting active listening, equitable participation, and constructive feedback. Fair communication protocols may include guidelines for taking turns speaking, respecting diverse perspectives, avoiding interruptions, and providing specific and actionable feedback. By making these protocols visible and accessible, educators can create a classroom environment where all learners feel safe, valued, and empowered to express their ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Development of clear and concise communication protocols that are aligned with the classroom's values and learning objectives. Creation and display of anchor charts that visually represent the protocols. Regular reminders and reinforcement of the protocols throughout classroom discussions and activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of this strategy depends on the learners' willingness to adhere to the communication protocols. There is a risk that some learners may not fully understand or internalize the protocols or that conflicts may arise despite the best efforts of the educator.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and backgrounds, particularly those who may struggle with communication or conflict resolution

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote respectful and inclusive communication, encourage active listening and equitable participation, and create a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear guidelines for respectful and inclusive communication, promotes active listening and equitable participation, and creates a safe and supportive classroom environment. This can lead to improved communication skills, stronger relationships, and increased engagement in learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The communication protocols can be tailored to the specific needs and dynamics of the classroom, ensuring that they are relevant and meaningful to the learners. Learners can also be involved in the development of the protocols, fostering a sense of ownership and accountability.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Discussion Sections
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learners' communication behaviors during class discussions and activities. Gather feedback from the learners about their experiences and perceptions of the classroom environment. Assess the extent to which the learners adhere to the communication protocols and demonstrate respectful and inclusive behaviors.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that clear communication protocols and expectations can effectively promote respectful and inclusive interactions in the classroom. When learners understand and adhere to these protocols, they are more likely to engage in meaningful discussions, build strong relationships, and achieve academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An anchor chart displaying the following communication protocols: 'Listen actively,' 'Respect different perspectives,' 'Avoid interrupting,' and 'Provide specific feedback.' The educator refers to the chart during class discussions and reminds learners to follow the protocols. Over time, the learners become more mindful of their communication behaviors and create a classroom environment where all voices are heard and valued.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using familiar, quiet, and repetitive fine motor and visual tasks can be a calming experience for many children. Completing one or two quiet, independent activities can be the perfect start to the day for children who become overwhelmed easily. These tasks can include stringing beads, simple put-in tasks, fine motor sorting tasks, and file folder tasks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Beads and string, pom poms, sorting materials, file folder tasks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Tasks should be age-appropriate and engaging. Supervision may be necessary to ensure safety.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those who are easily overwhelmed or anxious

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote relaxation, reduce overstimulation, provide a calming start to the day

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way to focus attention and engage in a calming activity, helping to reduce overstimulation and promote emotional regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The tasks can be tailored to individual interests and abilities. Some children may prefer stringing beads, while others may prefer sorting tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and emotional state before, during, and after engaging in the task. Monitor the child's ability to focus and remain calm.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Anecdotal evidence suggests that familiar, quiet, and repetitive tasks can promote relaxation and reduce overstimulation in children.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing learners with familiar, quiet, and repetitive fine motor and visual tasks to complete at the beginning of the day or during transition times to promote calmness and focus. These tasks can include stringing beads, simple put-in tasks, sorting activities, and file folder tasks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A collection of familiar, repetitive tasks and materials. A designated space for completing these tasks. Clear guidelines for participation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find these tasks boring or unchallenging. Requires careful planning to integrate these tasks into the learning schedule. May require ongoing support and monitoring to ensure engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who experience anxiety, sensory overload, or difficulty transitioning between activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote calmness, improve focus, provide a sense of predictability

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a sense of predictability and routine. Allows learners to focus on a simple, familiar task. Can be integrated into various learning activities and settings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of familiar, repetitive tasks to meet the diverse needs and preferences of learners. Allow learners to choose the type and duration of tasks that work best for them. Provide options for individual or group activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in these tasks. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of different tasks. Track changes in learners' behavior, attention, and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that familiar, repetitive tasks can reduce anxiety and promote calmness. Studies have shown that routine and predictability can improve attention and behavior in learners with autism spectrum disorder.

docs.text: Choose a book that is representative of your students and in their home language if possible. Record a video of you reading a portion of the book aloud each week until the book is complete. Post discussion questions that families can talk about with their children. Post a few questions for families in their home languages as well if possible.

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Family Engagement: Supporting Children with Disabilities
Description
docs.text: Family engagement is a practice in which families and school personnel collaborate to support and improve the learning and development of children, including those with disabilities. It involves behaviors and practices in the school environment, such as parent/guardian-child and parent/guardian-teacher communication, roles, and responsibilities at home and school. Effective engagement requires thoughtful planning, open communication, and sensitivity to the unique challenges faced by families of children with disabilities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment from school personnel, active participation from families, effective communication channels, and sensitivity to the unique needs of families and students with disabilities

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time, effort, and resources to develop and maintain. May be challenging to engage all families, especially those facing significant stressors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, educators, and families of students with disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student achievement, behavior, and social-emotional skills; support families facing unique challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increased collaboration, improved communication, shared understanding of student needs, tailored support for families

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailored to the specific needs and circumstances of individual families and students with disabilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student achievement, behavior, and social-emotional skills. Gather feedback from families and educators. Monitor IEP goal attainment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Family engagement can lead to increased student achievement, improved behavior, and enhanced social-emotional skills for students with disabilities, as well as providing much-needed support to their families.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is a specific model targeting young learners. The aim is to replace the homework with instructional lecture-videos and other resources. When students come back to the classroom, one-to-one guidance and support are provided by the teacher.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creation of engaging video lectures and resources, sufficient teacher time for individualized support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more teacher resources, dependent on learners' engagement with pre-class material.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Specifically designed for young learners who may benefit from reduced homework and increased teacher support.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Replace traditional homework, provide individualized support, reinforce understanding through one-to-one interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces homework burden, provides personalized attention and support.

docs.title: Personalization
