docs.title: Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward Model
Description
docs.text: The Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward Model is a structured approach to providing effective feedback. It involves guiding the learner through three key questions: 1. Feed Up: Where am I going (what are my learning intentions?) 2. Feed Back: How am I going (what does the evidence tell me?) 3. Feed Forward: Where to next (what learning activities should I do to make better progress?) This model encourages reflection and helps learners understand their progress towards learning goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear learning intentions and success criteria, time for discussion and reflection, tools for evidence gathering

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a well-defined learning environment, may be time-consuming, depends on the learner's ability to self-reflect

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-reflection, improve understanding of learning goals, guide future learning activities, facilitate progress monitoring

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear structure for feedback, promotes metacognition, fosters learner agency, facilitates communication between teacher and student

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The questions can be tailored to specific learning goals and individual learner needs. Learners can set their learning intentions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner progress towards goals. Analyze learner self-assessments and reflections. Monitor the effectiveness of learning activities based on feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that this model can enable students to become more self-directed and internally motivated, and what the evidence suggests about how best to implement feedback in the classroom.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses the model during a one-on-one conference with a student to discuss their writing progress. The student identifies their learning intentions, analyzes evidence of their progress, and plans future learning activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Feedback can be delivered in various formats, including written, verbal, or video. Instructors can provide written feedback directly in learning management systems (LMS) or on assignment submissions. Verbal feedback can be provided through audio podcasts or screen recordings, while video feedback can include virtual sessions or video recordings combining screen capture and verbal explanations. The format should suit the content and learner needs to enhance engagement and understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to tools and platforms for providing written, verbal, or video feedback (e.g., LMS, Vocaroo, Jing, Zoom), and clear guidelines for effective feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some formats may require more time or resources. Accessibility concerns may arise for learners with disabilities, such as hearing or visual impairments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where varied feedback formats are beneficial.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement and understanding through diverse feedback formats, provide personalized and meaningful feedback, and improve student motivation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers diverse ways to receive and understand feedback, enhances engagement through personalized and multimedia formats, and promotes a sense of connection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose the format that best suits their content and learner needs, addressing specific strengths and weaknesses in their work.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Technology Integration
  • Individual Response

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner engagement and preference for different feedback formats. Measure improvements in the quality of revised work based on different feedback formats. Evaluate the clarity and usefulness of feedback provided in various formats.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Diverse feedback formats can enhance engagement and understanding, leading to improved learning outcomes and student satisfaction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Vocaroo for audio feedback, Jing for screen capture and verbal feedback, and Zoom for virtual feedback sessions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The feedback sandwich technique involves delivering feedback in three parts: compliment, correct, compliment. This approach begins with a positive comment, followed by constructive criticism, and ends with another positive remark. The goal is to soften the impact of the negative feedback and encourage the learner to improve.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful consideration of positive and negative aspects of the learner's work

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as insincere if the compliments are not genuine. The negative feedback may still overshadow the positive comments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Soften the impact of negative feedback, encourage learners to improve, maintain a positive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces defensiveness, promotes a positive attitude, reinforces positive behaviors

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The compliments and corrections can be tailored to the individual learner's strengths and weaknesses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner attitude and behavior. Monitor the effectiveness of the feedback in promoting improvement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Discourage student effort and achievement can be avoided when feedback is predominately negative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides feedback on a student's presentation: 'I really liked your enthusiasm and energy (compliment). Consider adding more data to support your claims (correction). Overall, a great job engaging the audience (compliment).'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Delivering feedback through various media, such as video, allows for a more encouraging tone of voice and relaxed body language compared to impersonal email feedback. This approach ensures learners understand that feedback is constructive and well-meant, especially when in-person feedback is not possible.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Video recording equipment and software. LMS or platform for sharing feedback. Clear guidelines on providing constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources. Potential for technical issues. Relies on the quality of the feedback and the ability of the instructor to communicate effectively through different media.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for remote teams, offsite learners, and situations where in-person feedback is not feasible.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve the clarity and impact of feedback. Ensure learners understand the constructive intent of feedback. Enhance learner engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances clarity and reduces misinterpretation. Allows for a more personal and encouraging tone. Provides a richer and more engaging feedback experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize feedback based on individual learner progress and needs. Offer options for video, audio, or written feedback. Encourage learners to provide self-reflection as part of the feedback process.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner engagement with feedback. Assess the quality and impact of feedback on learner performance. Gather feedback from learners on their experiences with feedback through different media.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves the clarity and impact of feedback. Reduces misinterpretation. Enhances learner engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Recording a short video and posting it to an LMS. Providing feedback through audio recordings. Sharing annotated documents or slides with written comments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners pull a 'feeling face' card and eat their snack while showing the matching emotion. This playful activity connects emotions with physical actions and can facilitate conversations about how different emotions look and feel.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to snacks and 'feeling face' cards. A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be comfortable expressing emotions publicly. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood and elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve emotional awareness, promote positive associations with emotional expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects emotional expression with a familiar routine (snack time). Promotes a positive and playful approach to learning about emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Emotions can be tailored to suit the group's needs and interests. Different snacks can be used.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately portray emotions while eating their snack. Assess their participation and engagement in the activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Connecting emotions with sensory experiences can enhance emotional learning and regulation. (Source: Sensory Integration and Emotional Regulation - https://www.spdstar.org/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: During recess, learners play 'Ring Around the Rosie' while acting out different emotions. This combines play with emotional expression, helping learners connect emotions with physical movements and social interactions.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires physical mobility. Some learners may be uncomfortable expressing emotions through movement or social interaction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood and elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve physical coordination, promote emotional awareness and social interaction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines play with emotional learning. Encourages kinesthetic learners and promotes emotional awareness through movement and social interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Emotions and end actions can be tailored to suit the group's needs and interests. Different variations of the song can be used.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately portray emotions through movement. Assess their participation and engagement in the activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combining play with emotional learning can enhance emotional regulation and social skills. (Source: The Power of Play in Social-Emotional Learning - https://www.scholastic.com/teachers/articles/teaching-content/power-play-social-emotional-learning/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fidget contracts are agreements between a learner and an educator or caregiver that outline specific rules and guidelines for using fidget tools. These contracts define when, where, and how fidgets can be used to support focus, attention, and self-regulation rather than as toys. By setting clear expectations and promoting mindful use, fidget contracts help prevent misuse and distractions while maximizing the benefits of sensory tools for learners who struggle with attention or sensory processing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires open communication and collaboration between the learner and educator/caregiver. A printed or digital contract that both parties agree to and sign is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the learner does not understand or agree with the contract. Requires consistent enforcement and follow-up to ensure compliance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with ADHD, sensory processing issues, or difficulty focusing; useful for K–12 students and adults

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote mindful fidget use, improve focus and attention, prevent misuse and distractions, support self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structure and accountability for fidget use, helps learners understand the purpose of fidgets as tools rather than toys, and promotes self-awareness of their own needs and behaviors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Contracts can be customized to fit individual needs, preferences, and contexts. Rules can be tailored to specific environments, such as classrooms, homes, or workplaces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in fidget use behaviors, such as frequency, purpose, and compliance with contract rules. Monitor learner focus and attention levels during activities where fidgets are used.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved focus and attention: Fidget contracts help learners use sensory tools more effectively, leading to increased focus and attention during tasks. Reduced distractions: By setting clear expectations, contracts minimize the potential for fidgets to distract others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Understood.org provides a sample fidget contract that outlines rules for when, where, and how fidgets can be used.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fidgets are tools to aid focus and self-regulation, not toys. This strategy involves setting rules for using fidgets at home or in the classroom. Rules include being mindful of when a fidget is needed, using it only to focus or calm down, not distracting others, and returning it to a designated place after use. Experimentation helps find the right fidget.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Fidgets, clear rules, designated storage place, open communication, and a signed contract.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires commitment from both the learner and instructor to follow the rules. May not be effective if fidgets are misused as toys.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with attention, focus, or sensory processing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus and attention, calm overwhelm, promote self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to using fidgets as tools for self-regulation and focus. Promotes mindful use of fidgets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for experimenting with different types of fidgets to find what works best for the individual.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of improved focus, reduced fidgeting, and adherence to rules. Monitoring of self-regulation skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Evidence suggests that structured use of fidgets can help learners with ADHD improve focus and attention. Fidget contracts can set rules on when and how a child can use fidgets.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Families setting up a fidget basket with rules visible. Teachers implementing a fidget contract in the classroom. Download: Sample fidget contract

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Field trips are educational excursions that take learners outside of the classroom to experience real-world environments and engage with content in a multisensory, interactive manner. Field trips activate learners' background knowledge, extend classroom learning, and provide access to resources and experiences not available in the classroom. Whether physical or virtual, field trips create lasting memories and enhance understanding through direct engagement with art, history, science, and culture.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Planning, transportation, permission slips, funding (can be offset with fundraising). For virtual trips: devices and internet access.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Physical field trips can be costly and logistically challenging, potentially excluding disadvantaged learners. Overly structured trips may limit exploration and discovery. Virtual trips may lack the sensory richness and social interaction of physical trips.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly K–12 students, but also applicable to adult learners in various educational and professional settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, connect classroom learning to real-world experiences, promote socio-emotional growth, enhance critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-world context for learning, increases motivation and engagement, supports multisensory learning, builds social-emotional skills, enhances long-term memory through memorable experiences, levels the playing field for disadvantaged learners by providing equal opportunities for enriching experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Field trips can be personalized by allowing learners to choose destinations, involving them in planning, and providing options for reflection and follow-up activities. Virtual field trips can further personalize the experience by allowing learners to explore at their own pace and focus on areas of interest. Pre- and post-trip activities can also be tailored to individual learning needs and styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased test scores, improved engagement in follow-up activities, enhanced critical thinking skills, positive changes in empathy and tolerance, learner-generated artifacts (e.g., reflections, presentations) that demonstrate learning and connection to real-world experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that learners who participate in field trips have better grades, higher graduation rates, and greater income. Field trips enhance engagement, intellectual curiosity, and interest in learning both in and out of school. Additionally, field trips promote empathy, tolerance, and critical thinking skills (Whitesell, 2016). Virtual field trips, such as Google Expeditions, can increase learner motivation and provide access to inaccessible locations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Visiting a local grocery store to learn about nutrition and budgeting. Taking a trip to an art museum to foster empathy and critical thinking. Using Google Expeditions to explore faraway locations and cultures. Research: Whitesell, E. R. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Similar to 'Find the Total', but learners subtract to find the difference between two dot cards. They begin by identifying the card with the greater number of dots and then determine how many more dots are on that card than the other, reinforcing subtraction skills. This activity reinforces subtraction skills in a visual and concrete way. Encourages learners to compare quantities and understand the concept of difference. Supports the development of mental math skills and promotes fluency in subtraction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dot cards.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may need initial guidance on subtraction strategies. The activity's effectiveness relies on clear dot arrangements that are easy to count and compare.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-K to 1st Grade learners who are developing subtraction skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice subtraction, enhance mental math, promote understanding of subtraction strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete and visual representation of subtraction. Promotes number sense and understanding of comparative quantities. Enhances mental math skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the number range to suit different levels. Encourage the use of different subtraction strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the accuracy of the difference found. Observe the strategies used to find the difference.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of visual aids in early math education to enhance subtraction skills and number sense.

This activity encourages learners to practice addition in a visual and concrete way. Engaging in number talks enhances mathematical language skills and promotes the development of flexible problem-solving strategies. Supports the development of mental math skills and promotes fluency in addition.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Instructions

  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of visual aids in early math education to enhance addition skills and number sense.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating arts like fiction writing, dance, drama, graphic design, music, drawing, painting, or ceramics into all subjects helps learners learn and find their talents and interests. Arts integration fosters creativity, imagination, and deeper engagement with the curriculum. This approach is more common in elementary schools, but high school teachers can also use it to provide creative outlets and encourage learners to explore their strengths.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that arts integration enhances creativity, engagement, and academic achievement. Studies also show that creative outlets promote well-being.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school history class creates a dramatic reenactment of historical events. A college science class designs visual representations of scientific concepts. A community center offers art workshops for learners to explore different art forms.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two learners sit facing each other in the center of the room; the remaining learners sit in a circle around them. The two central learners have a conversation based on a pre-determined topic and often using specific skills the class is practicing (such as asking follow-up questions, paraphrasing, or elaborating on another person’s point). Learners on the outside observe, take notes, or perform some other discussion-related task assigned by the teacher. One variation of this strategy allows learners in the outer circle to trade places with those in the fishbowl, doing kind of a relay-style discussion, or they may periodically “coach” the fishbowl talkers from the sidelines. Teachers may also opt to have learners in the outside circle grade the participants’ conversation with a rubric, then give feedback on what they saw in a debriefing afterward.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where learners can form a circle around a central area, a topic of discussion, and clear instructions for learners. Rubrics or observation guides may be used.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are shy or reluctant to speak in front of a group, requires careful facilitation to ensure respectful communication and avoid dominance by a few learners, can be time-consuming to implement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for practicing communication skills and observing group dynamics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active listening and observation skills, enhance communication skills, provide opportunities for peer feedback and coaching, foster metacognitive awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active listening and observation, promotes communication skills, provides opportunities for peer feedback and coaching, fosters metacognitive awareness, supports modeling of effective communication strategies

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The topic of discussion and the skills being practiced can be tailored to learners' needs and interests. Learners can choose whether to participate in the fishbowl or observe.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Modeling
  • Coaching
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the activity, review learner notes and feedback, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances communication skills, promotes active listening and observation, fosters metacognitive awareness

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fishbowl is a strategy for facilitating group discussions. In a Fishbowl discussion, students inside the 'fishbowl' actively discuss a topic. Students outside the fishbowl listen carefully to the conversation. They take turns in these roles to practice being both contributors and listeners in a group discussion. A Fishbowl activity is especially useful when you want to make sure all students participate in a discussion, when you want to help students reflect on what a good discussion looks like, and when you need a structure for discussing controversial or difficult topics. A Fishbowl discussion makes for an excellent pre-writing activity, often unearthing questions or ideas that students can explore more deeply in an independent assignment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A circle of chairs ('the fishbowl') and enough room around the circle for the remaining students to observe. Effective prompts that allow for multiple perspectives and opinions. Prior preparation for the discussion. Established norms and rules for participation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful setup and clear explanation of rules to ensure all students understand the process. Some students may feel uncomfortable in the 'fishbowl' or struggle to actively listen when observing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for students in grades 6–12, advisory, civics and citizenship, English and language arts, history, and social studies. Useful in diverse educational settings to ensure all students participate and reflect on effective discussion.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage active participation, improve listening skills, promote reflection on discussion dynamics, and provide a structure for discussing controversial topics.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structure for discussions that encourages both contribution and active listening. Allows students to practice being both speakers and observers. Facilitates the discussion of complex and controversial topics. Serves as an excellent pre-writing activity, stimulating ideas and questions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Variations include a Fishbowl Debate for opposing positions, allowing each group to discuss while the other observes, and a Fishbowl Exercise for multiple perspectives, assigning different viewpoints to groups for discussion.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Question Formulation
  • Knowledge-Building Discourse

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of student participation and engagement. Evaluate the quality of contributions and active listening. Assess the ability to follow norms and rules. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of the discussion and individual performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, careful listening, and meaningful reflection. Helps students practice being both contributors and listeners in a group conversation. Promotes deeper understanding and empathy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Social studies teacher Jenna Forton uses the Fishbowl teaching strategy to structure a class discussion about primary documents related to the Plessy vs. Ferguson case.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fist tapping and arm tapping are multisensory spelling strategies that involve tapping out the syllables and sounds of words. In fist tapping, learners tap each syllable of the word using the side of their fists, then tap each sound within the syllable as they spell it. In arm tapping, they use two fingers of one hand to tap on the forearm of the other hand, following the same procedure. These strategies enhance memory by engaging muscle memory and promoting systematic processing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for physical movement, list of words to be spelled, and understanding of the connection between tapping and spelling

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners with physical limitations, requires coordination of hand movements and phonemic awareness, may be disruptive in some classroom settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, particularly those who struggle with spelling or have auditory processing difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling skills, enhance phonemic awareness, strengthen memory encoding, promote systematic processing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages muscle memory, enhances phonemic awareness, promotes systematic processing, increases engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adapt the speed and force of their tapping to suit their individual needs. They can also use different hand positions or tap on different body parts to add variety and enhance engagement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to spell words correctly after practicing fist tapping or arm tapping, assess their phonemic awareness, evaluate performance on spelling tests

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fist tapping and arm tapping have been shown to improve spelling skills, enhance phonemic awareness, and strengthen memory encoding. They engage muscle memory and promote systematic processing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student spells the word "butterfly" by first tapping out the syllables (but-ter-fly) using the side of their fists, then tapping each sound within each syllable as they spell it aloud. A student spells the word "friend" by tapping out the sounds on their forearm using two fingers, saying each sound as they tap it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A five-stage model to help learners understand, identify, and resolve issues. This involves understanding the problem by framing it in their own words, describing any barriers preventing them from achieving their goal, identifying various solutions, trying out a solution while keeping accurate records of their thoughts and procedures, and evaluating the results.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learners need to understand the five stages of the model and be willing to engage in self-reflection and evaluation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be too rigid for some learners. Requires learners to actively engage in self-assessment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance problem-solving skills, improve understanding of problem parameters, promote systematic approaches to problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to problem-solving that can be applied across various domains. Encourages learners to take responsibility for their own learning and decision-making.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The model can be adapted to different types of problems and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to apply the five-stage model to different problems. Evaluate the quality of learners' self-assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of problem-solving skills by providing a structured approach to identifying and resolving issues. Promotes self-reflection and evaluation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using drawings to help learners look at a problem from many different perspectives; listing all related relevant facts; making a list of all the given information; restating the problem in their own words; listing the conditions that surround a problem; describing related known problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students try to give a high-five to five different classmates. When they’ve gotten their five high-fives done, they sit down. This game is part mystery: sometimes it will be possible for everyone to get a high-five; sometimes not. The difference (which the teacher knows but the students don’t) is that it is only possible if there are an even number of people giving high-fives. Try this game at different times and let students guess whether they think everyone will get a high-five or not. Why does it only work sometimes, not always? If you make it four or six high-fives instead of five, then everyone will be able to get their high-fives every time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Open space where students can move freely.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may find it difficult to get their high-fives due to social dynamics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote social interaction, encourage teamwork, provide kinesthetic learning, enhance pattern recognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Quick and fun activity that reinforces social skills and cooperation. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the number of high-fives based on the size of the class. Allow students to analyze the patterns for when everyone can or can't get their high-fives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' interactions and teamwork. Assess their ability to recognize and explain the patterns.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can promote social skills and encourage pattern recognition. Supports active participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The teacher says 'go!' and the students try to give a high-five to five different classmates, trying to figure out whether everyone can complete the task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Flashcards are a study tool used for memorization and reinforcement of knowledge. They present a question, concept, or term on one side and the corresponding answer or explanation on the other, providing a quick, accessible method for self-testing and review. Using Anki, flashcards become powerful and intelligent, adapting to the learner's pace and knowledge level. Anki's system is based on spaced repetition, which helps users focus on challenging material and review less frequently on what they already know.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creation of flashcard decks with questions and answers. Anki software or similar tool is needed for digital flashcards with spaced repetition features.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Relies on rote memorization, which may not promote deeper understanding or critical thinking. Effectiveness depends on the quality of flashcard content and consistent use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and levels across various subjects. Especially useful for memorizing facts, vocabulary, definitions, and concepts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory, reinforce knowledge, facilitate efficient study habits, and optimize learning outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates efficient learning by targeting difficult material and reducing time spent on known information. Anki guarantees memory with minimal effort and makes memory a choice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable through customization options for flashcard layouts and review timing. Users can create and share decks tailored to their learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • continuous review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track progress through Anki's review scheduling and performance ratings. Monitor recall accuracy and adjust review intervals based on user performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The spaced repetition algorithm in Anki ensures that material is reviewed at optimal intervals to maximize retention. The program personalizes learning to address individual needs efficiently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use Anki to create flashcards for vocabulary in a foreign language, historical dates, scientific formulas, or medical terminology. Utilize shared decks to collaborate and learn from others.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Flexible seating involves providing learners with a variety of seating options and allowing them to choose where they sit based on their individual needs and preferences. This approach fosters collaboration, empowers learners to think about how they work best, and creates a more engaging learning environment. Options may include couches, chairs, bunk beds, canoes, five-gallon buckets, crate seating, and pillows on the floor. By giving learners a choice in their learning space, instructors can help them become more strategic about their choices and create a space that supports their individual learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of seating options (couches, chairs, buckets, pillows), flexible bookshelves, large round or rectangular tables, willingness to throw out traditional schooling equipment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial investment in alternative seating options. Requires careful management to avoid distractions or disruptions. May not be suitable for all learning environments or tasks.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various educational settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, promote collaboration, support individual learning preferences, improve learner outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports learner autonomy, promotes collaboration, enhances engagement, improves learning outcomes, caters to diverse learning preferences

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Vary seating options to accommodate different needs and preferences. Allow learners to choose seating based on task, learning style, or personal preference. Regularly assess and adjust seating arrangements based on learner feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved grades, increased engagement, more participation in discussions, learner articulation of preferred learning environments

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that flexible classrooms can improve grades, increase engagement, and promote more invigorating conversations. Learners become more strategic about their choices and articulate their preferred learning environments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing a variety of different furniture that allows students to work in different areas, depending on the project or time of day. This adapts learning space for varied learning needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of seating options such as tables and chairs, couches, and bean bag chairs. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing seating arrangements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase collaboration, reduce stress, promote flexible thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes collaboration and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred seating arrangement. Provide a variety of seating options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that flexible seating can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Flipped learning is a pedagogical approach that reverses the traditional learning environment by delivering instructional content, often via pre-recorded videos or other materials, outside of class, and using class time for active learning activities such as discussions, problem-solving, and group projects. Learners gain initial exposure to new concepts individually before class, enabling the classroom to become a dynamic, interactive environment where the instructor guides students as they apply concepts and engage creatively with the subject matter. This approach shifts students from passive recipients to active constructors of knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires the creation or curation of pre-class learning materials (e.g., videos, readings, podcasts). Class time must be structured to facilitate active learning and interaction. Instructor must be prepared to guide and facilitate student activities rather than lecture.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to set up initially due to the creation of pre-class materials. Requires students to engage with pre-class materials, which may not always happen. May not be suitable for all subjects or learners without careful planning and implementation. Reliance on pre-class quizzes may shift learner focus from understanding to test performance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Secondary and higher education learners across various disciplines, adaptable for skills-based courses (language, technology, health sciences) and potentially less effective in math and engineering courses without careful design.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, deepen understanding of content, promote active participation, improve interpersonal skills, develop metacognitive abilities, foster collaboration and communication skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to learn at their own pace and revisit material as needed. Frees up class time for interactive activities and personalized guidance. Encourages deeper understanding and application of knowledge through active learning. Increases student engagement and satisfaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to different learning styles and needs by providing a variety of pre-class materials (videos, readings, audio). In-class activities can be designed to cater to different levels of understanding and learning preferences. Instructors can offer personalized support and feedback during class time.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Pre-Class Video/Lecture
  • In-Class Activities
  • Formative Assessment
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Decision-Making
  • Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved performance on exams and assignments measuring foundational knowledge, higher-order thinking, and applied skills. Enhanced student engagement and identification with the course or discipline. Development of metacognitive skills (time management, learning strategies). Increased student satisfaction with the course and instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Meta-analysis of 317 studies (51,437 participants) shows that flipped classrooms can lead to better academic performance, improved interpersonal skills, increased student engagement, and enhanced metacognitive abilities, especially in language, technology, and health-science courses. The impact varies based on discipline and geographic location.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Michigan's Clintondale High School transformed its curriculum with flipped learning, leading to a 33% drop in failure rates. MEF University in Istanbul adopted the flipped learning model university-wide. Robert Talbert uses screencasting to teach math concepts on YouTube, providing resources for students before class.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy entails consciously choosing to fill one's mind with positive images and thoughts, making it a habit to bring the mind back every time it goes astray. It encourages gratitude for what one has presently, aligning self-talk with joy and fostering a state of gratitude that benefits the psyche. By emphasizing the good times and recognizing life's ups and downs, individuals can maintain a more positive attitude and better manage challenges.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness and a willingness to shift focus from negative to positive thoughts. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying negativity. Access to resources such as gratitude journals, mindfulness apps, or positive affirmation lists can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement for individuals with severe depression or persistent negative emotions without professional support. Requires consistent effort to maintain a positive focus and avoid getting caught up in negative thoughts. May not be effective if not accompanied by genuine appreciation and engagement with enjoyable moments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals prone to negativity, stress, or a focus on challenges rather than joys.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote positive attitude, foster gratitude, enhance joy, manage challenges, improve mental well-being, align self-talk with positive emotions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes positive emotions by focusing on enjoyable moments. Increases resilience by recognizing life's ups and downs. Fosters gratitude by encouraging appreciation for what one has presently. Enhances self-esteem by promoting a more positive self-perception.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized lists of enjoyable moments and gratitude practices tailored to individual preferences. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through journaling, mindfulness exercises, or verbal affirmations. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as gratitude prompts or guided reflections.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported mood and gratitude levels using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in positive emotions, resilience, and coping strategies. Analyze ability to identify and focus on enjoyable moments in real-life situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that focusing on positive moments and practicing gratitude can improve mental well-being and reduce stress (e.g., Greater Good Science Center). Studies show that gratitude interventions can enhance happiness and promote prosocial behavior. Regularly engaging in positive activities can foster a sense of purpose and improve overall quality of life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual starts a daily gratitude journal, writing down three things they are grateful for each day. A student feeling stressed about exams takes a few minutes each day to focus on enjoyable hobbies or activities that bring them joy. Resource: Greater Good Science Center – How to Cultivate Gratitude.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Authentic projects that focus on issues of justice engage students by having them work on something that matters, impacting their lives, their community, and the lives of those they care about. These projects go beyond teaching the standards by providing opportunities for students to become better people and act as change agents to make the world a better place.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitation by instructors to guide ethical inquiry and respectful dialogue, access to resources for research and action, a classroom culture that values social justice and equity

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful consideration of potentially sensitive or controversial topics, demands thoughtful facilitation to ensure respectful and inclusive discussions, may require collaboration with community partners

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and higher education students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote social justice awareness, develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills, foster empathy and compassion, empower students to be change agents

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Aligns learning with students' values and concerns, fosters a sense of purpose and agency, promotes critical thinking about social issues, encourages students to take action and make a difference

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to choose issues of personal significance, provides opportunities for students to connect with their community, can be adapted to different cultural contexts and perspectives

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Application of Knowledge

  • Research

  • Argumentation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth of research and understanding of social justice issues, effectiveness of proposed solutions, engagement and participation in project activities, demonstration of empathy and compassion

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Projects focused on issues of justice lead to higher student engagement and a deeper understanding of social issues. This approach empowers students to become change agents and fosters a commitment to making the world a better place. (Chaffee, 2017)

docs.title: Focus on the Question They Answered Correctly
Description
docs.text: Instead of focusing on a student’s mistake, instructors identify the question a student answered correctly, even if it’s different than the one asked. This approach assumes all student ideas are interesting and aims to value the student’s thinking. By identifying what the student understood, instructors can then connect that correct understanding to the question the student didn’t answer correctly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Skilled teachers who can ask effective questions and facilitate meaningful discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be skilled in questioning techniques. May be time-consuming, especially in large classes. This strategy is not useful for students with no prior knowledge of the topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who struggle with math or who have anxiety around making mistakes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students feel valued, promote positive student-teacher interactions, reveal potential gaps in understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning, promotes metacognition, helps students feel more valued and more connected to the classroom community, fosters a growth mindset

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be aware of their student's individual needs, and to be flexible and willing to ask open ended questions rather than simply looking for the right answer

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student confidence, increased class participation, higher test scores

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that focusing on what students did well and building from there leads to greater long term student confidence and learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of focusing on a student's error, a teacher could begin by asking them: “How are you thinking about the question right now?”

docs.title: Focus Projects on Issues of Justice
Description
docs.text: Projects center on authentic issues that matter to students and their communities, impacting their lives and the lives of those they care about. This promotes engagement and emphasizes the role of education in addressing social justice issues.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creating a classroom environment that supports open and honest discussions about social justice. Demands resources and materials that reflect diverse perspectives and experiences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May raise sensitive topics that require careful facilitation. Can be challenging to balance curriculum goals with student-driven social justice issues.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly effective for engaging students in discussions about social justice and equity.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote awareness of social justice issues, empower students to act as change agents, connect learning to real-world impact.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects learning to real-world issues, making it more relevant and meaningful. Empowers students to see themselves as agents of change in their communities. Fosters a sense of purpose and responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Projects can be tailored to address specific issues relevant to students' local communities. Allows students to explore topics related to their cultural backgrounds and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate student understanding of social justice issues. Assess student proposals and actions aimed at addressing these issues. Review student reflections on their role as change agents.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Authentic projects lead to higher student engagement by addressing issues that matter, promoting civic engagement, and empowering students to create positive change.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students developing projects to address food insecurity in their community. Learners creating awareness campaigns to combat discrimination and promote inclusion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Focused-attention practice is a brain exercise for quieting the thousands of thoughts that distract and frustrate us each day. When the mind is quiet and focused, learners are able to be present with a specific sound, sight, or taste. Quieting our minds ignites the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing heart rate and blood pressure while enhancing coping strategies to effectively handle the day-to-day challenges. Thinking improves and emotions begin to regulate so learners can approach an experience with variable options.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space and brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use guided audio, videos, or instructor-led exercises.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Calm the mind, improve focus, reduce stress, enhance coping strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, supports emotional regulation, improves attention, enhances self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various durations and settings. Start with short durations (60-90 seconds) and build to five minutes. Use different techniques to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Breathing: Use the breath as a focus point. Have students place one hand close to but not touching their nose and the other on their belly. Colors: Visualize colors while focusing on the breath. Inhale a deep green, and exhale a smoky gray. Movement: Direct students to stand and, as they inhale, lift an arm or leg and wiggle it, exhaling it back to its original position. The Deep-Dive Breath: Have students inhale for four counts, hold for four, and exhale for four counts. Energizing Breath: Have students pant like a dog with their mouths open and their tongues out for 30 seconds, and then continue for another 30 seconds with their mouths closed, taking short breaths with one hand on the belly. Sound: The use of sound is very powerful for engaging a calm response. Rise and Fall: Learners can lie on the floor and place an object on their stomachs, enhancing their focus by watching the rising and falling of their bellies.

docs.title: Focusing Projects on Issues of Justice
Description
docs.text: Focusing project-based learning (PBL) projects on issues of justice involves designing projects that allow students to work on topics that matter to their community, their lives, and the lives of those they care about. By addressing social justice in the classroom, educators can provide students with opportunities to become better people and act as change agents to make the world a better place.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Projects that are authentic and relevant to students' lives, and instructional strategies that support students in addressing complex social issues.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and sensitivity to ensure that projects are respectful and inclusive, and may necessitate additional resources or support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those from marginalized communities who may benefit from addressing issues of justice in the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To promote student engagement and create opportunities for students to become better people and act as change agents in their communities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, promotes social responsibility, and provides students with opportunities to make a positive impact on their communities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to choose topics that are personally relevant and meaningful to them, making the learning experience more personalized and engaging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, positive impact on the community, and evidence of students acting as change agents.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that focusing projects on issues of justice increases student engagement and promotes social responsibility, leading to more meaningful learning experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Designing a project where students advocate for improvements to a local park or address issues of environmental justice in their community.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After disciplining a learner, the instructor should do the following: touch base with the learner, acknowledge post-disciplinary successes, and don't give up too quickly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors should be willing to put in the effort to follow up with learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may negatively respond to positive attention, but the instructor should keep trying and not give up.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support learners' growth and change after disciplinary action has been taken.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Demonstrates that the instructor cares about the learners, even after they have made mistakes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Follow-up shows the learner that the instructor hasn't given up on them, and will support them going forward.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners will demonstrate improved behavior and respect for the instructor.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When learners are used to getting into trouble and having negative attention, it takes a while to break this cycle.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers encourage students to take actions to address inequities revealed during the discussion, such as writing letters to the editor or meeting with the principal. They offer support to students feeling ashamed or guilty, emphasizing that these feelings can be a catalyst for action.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for follow-up activities, resources for taking action (e.g., writing materials, meeting space), and a supportive teacher who can guide and mentor students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may feel overwhelmed or discouraged if their efforts do not produce immediate results. Requires careful planning and support to ensure that actions are meaningful and impactful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and backgrounds engaging in discussions about social justice or equity issues.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a sense of agency and empowerment, translate discussions into concrete actions, provide support and resources for students processing emotions, and foster a sense of community and collective responsibility.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for students to apply their learning, promotes self-reflection and emotional processing, and creates a sense of collective action.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of action options to suit students' interests and skills. Provide individualized support and resources based on students' needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in follow-up activities, assess the impact of their actions on the school or community, and gather feedback on their experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that taking action on social issues can promote a sense of agency and empowerment, improve civic engagement, and foster positive social change.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students write letters to the editor expressing their views on a local issue. A group of students meets with the principal to discuss ways to improve school climate. Students organize a fundraising event to support a local charity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Treat others the way they want and need to be treated. Focus on understanding what students need from you instead of what you think they need.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Openness to understanding others, active listening skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort and self-awareness

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, mentors, counselors, leaders

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote empathy, enhance interpersonal understanding, improve relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters better connections, improves communication, builds trust

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt interactions to meet individual needs and preferences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Perspective-Taking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe interactions, gather feedback from others

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates more supportive and inclusive environments

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask students what they need, actively listen, and adjust approaches

docs.title: Follow Up After Discussions About Race
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves taking actions that might change inequities revealed during a discussion and giving learners time to do something that will change the learning environment. This may include encouraging students to begin taking actions that might change inequities, giving kids time to do something, like write a letter to the editor of their city newspaper, or offering to go with a representative group of students to talk with the principal about the way students are being treated.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, opportunities for action, teacher support, and access to resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to find appropriate and meaningful opportunities for action. Requires ongoing commitment and support from teachers and administrators

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote action-oriented learning, address inequities, and empower students to become change agents

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students to take action on issues they care about, promotes a sense of agency, reinforces learning through practical application, and can lead to positive change in the school or community

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Opportunities for action can be tailored to student interests and skills and the specific context of the school or community. Teachers can provide different levels of support based on student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in action-oriented activities, track changes in student attitudes and behaviors, and document the impact of student actions on the school or community

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Taking action after discussions about race can empower students, promote social justice, and lead to positive change in the school or community.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students writing letters to the editor of their city newspaper to address inequities revealed during a discussion. A teacher offering to go with a representative group of students to talk with the principal about the way students are being treated.

docs.title: Formative Assessment to Gauge Student Progress and Guide Instruction
Description
docs.text: Assessing student work on a regular basis provides both the teacher and the student with a sense of the student’s progress, indicates strengths and areas for improvement, and helps the teacher plan appropriately to meet the student’s needs. This formative assessment is part of the process of a learning sequence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Regularly scheduled formative assessments, tools for data collection and feedback (e.g., Flip, Padlet, Google Sites, weekly surveys).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time for data collection and feedback, may require adaptation to different learning environments and student needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All adult learners in online or blended learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide diagnostic feedback, help educators set standards, evaluate progress, relate to a student’s progress, support student self-evaluation, and support teacher self-evaluation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides regular feedback, identifies strengths and weaknesses, helps students gauge their progress, and supports instructional planning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Uses rubrics, quizzes, observation protocols, quick comprehension check questions, or exit tickets to structure the assessment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student work samples, reflection videos, photos/screenshots of progress, weekly surveys, and progress trackers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a clear sense of student progress, identifies areas for improvement, and supports instructional planning to meet the student’s needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teacher performance management processes can be viewed as part of a growth mindset by making it formative, rather than summative, and inviting participation of the teacher in the process. The feedback can be more meaningful and applicable to the teacher’s daily practice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a clear and transparent performance management system. Teachers need to feel safe receiving feedback and have opportunities to implement changes in their practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some teachers may resist feedback or find it challenging to implement changes in their practice. Requires a long-term commitment to fostering a culture of feedback and continuous improvement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators at all levels, particularly those seeking to improve their teaching practices or develop new skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve teaching practices, promote professional growth, and create a culture of continuous improvement in schools by providing timely, actionable, and supportive feedback to teachers

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides teachers with specific and constructive feedback on their teaching practices, helps them identify their strengths and weaknesses, and supports them in developing strategies for improving their performance. Promotes a collaborative approach to professional development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor feedback to individual teacher needs and goals. Provide opportunities for teachers to reflect on their own performance and identify areas for improvement. Offer personalized coaching and mentoring to support teacher growth.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track teacher participation in feedback activities. Collect teacher reflections on their teaching practices and professional growth. Evaluate the impact of feedback on student learning outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that teachers who receive regular formative feedback are more effective and more satisfied with their jobs. Implementing formative feedback fosters a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school implements a peer observation program, where teachers observe each other's teaching practices and provide feedback using a structured framework. Resource: Gerstein, Jackie. "The Educator with a Growth Mindset: A Staff Workshop."
