docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy emphasizes the importance of developing self-advocacy and self-determination skills in students, particularly those with disabilities. It involves teaching students to understand their needs and rights, communicate them effectively, solve problems, set goals, and engage in active reflection. The goal is to empower students to become the primary agents in their learning and lives, improving their educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction on self-advocacy and self-determination skills, opportunities to practice these skills in real-world settings, a supportive and inclusive environment, and a commitment to empowering students to make choices about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset towards valuing student agency and empowerment. Some students may need significant support and encouragement to develop these skills. Success depends on consistent reinforcement and a commitment to creating a learning environment where students feel valued and respected.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities, students preparing for postsecondary education and the workforce, and learners who benefit from self-directed learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of individual needs and rights, improve communication and problem-solving skills, promote goal setting and monitoring, foster self-reflection, and empower students to take control of their learning and lives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers learners to understand their needs and rights, promotes effective communication and problem-solving, fosters self-reflection and goal setting, enhances self-determination, and improves educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific skills and strategies taught can be tailored to the individual needs and goals of the students. Educators can provide differentiated support and scaffolding to ensure that all students can participate effectively.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in self-advocacy activities, analyze their ability to articulate their needs and rights, monitor their progress in achieving established goals, and observe their engagement in problem-solving and reflection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students who practice self-advocacy skills and self-determination have improved educational and life outcomes. These skills are essential for success in postsecondary education, the workforce, and civic life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Incorporating goal setting, problem solving, and self-advocacy into student IEPs, providing hands-on learning opportunities such as service learning and work-based learning, and engaging students in meetings where decisions about their learning and lives are made.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-awareness is the ability to correctly identify your own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they impact behavior. This strategy involves helping students develop a greater understanding of themselves by leveraging their strengths to address challenges. Strategies include: Identify Feelings, Journal Reflections, Use Estimation and Prediction, and Develop Your Understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires an understanding of self-awareness principles, knowledge of specific techniques (e.g., journaling, literature analysis), and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing practice and reflection. Effectiveness depends on student engagement and willingness to explore their emotions and thoughts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with strengths and challenges related to self-awareness, including elementary, secondary, and higher education learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop student ability to identify their own emotions, thoughts, and values, promote self-understanding, and enhance self-efficacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes emotional intelligence, enhances self-confidence, and fosters a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual student strengths, emotional profiles, and learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student ability to identify and express emotions. Observe student self-confidence and growth mindset. Collect student feedback on the effectiveness of the strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that self-awareness is essential for personal and academic success. (Kalaiyarasan & Solomon, 2016; Fritz, 2011; Flavian, 2016)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using literature to have students analyze characters’ feelings. Ask students to use estimation and prediction skills. Ask them how they might do on an upcoming project or how long it might take them to complete a task or assignment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This involves prioritizing self-advocacy and self-determination skills in education systems to improve educational and life outcomes for students with disabilities. It includes making these skills critical priorities by incorporating them into teacher preparation, assessments of learning, and measures of school performance. Additionally, it focuses on ensuring that personalized learning opportunities are designed to maximize the engagement of all students, regardless of disability status, through flexible and accessible learning choices and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). Tangible opportunities and experiences are provided for students to practice self-advocacy skills and self-determination in their education by empowering themselves through understanding their needs and rights, communicating them, solving problems, setting goals, and engaging in active reflection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment to prioritizing self-advocacy and self-determination. Flexible and accessible learning opportunities. Support and resources for students to develop these skills.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires investment of time, resources, and training. May involve difficult conversations and a shift in mindset.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities, educators, families, and policy makers.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-advocacy skills and self-determination, improve educational and life outcomes, and ensure engagement for all students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves educational and life outcomes. Ensures engagement for all students, regardless of disability status. Empowers students to take ownership of their learning and lives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) that prioritize self-advocacy skills. Personalized learning opportunities that are flexible and accessible. Tangible opportunities and experiences for students to practice self-advocacy skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure self-advocacy skills and self-determination. Track educational and life outcomes. Assess student engagement and satisfaction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students who practice self-advocacy skills have improved educational and life outcomes. Prioritizing self-advocacy and self-determination is essential to aligning the education provided for students with disabilities and the demands of the world they will enter after school.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • States may choose to take up more rigorous or longer duration capstone requirements. Educators and families may decide to make skills like goal setting, problem solving, and self-advocacy explicit goals in student IEPs. Hands-on learning opportunities, such as service learning and work-based learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Fostering student self-knowledge involves implementing measures that help students understand themselves as learners. By reflecting on their strengths, areas for growth, and learning preferences, students can become more effective self-advocates. Strategies include using learning interest inventories, exit tickets, progress monitoring, and peer/self-assessments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to self-assessment tools, a supportive classroom environment, and strategies to help students articulate their needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort from both students and educators to cultivate self-awareness and effective communication skills. Students may initially resist taking responsibility for their learning or feel uncomfortable sharing their needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 3 to 8

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-awareness, foster self-confidence, improve learning strategies, encourage goal-setting

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances students' ability to recognize their strengths and needs, encourages them to take responsibility for their learning, and prepares them for success in various environments by promoting independence and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • IEPs and transition meetings can become more student-centered, and students can be supported in participating in real-world learning opportunities where they can practice self-advocacy skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' willingness to participate in discussions, request help when needed, and articulate their learning preferences. Measure students' ability to set goals, solve problems, and advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that self-knowledge leads to improved academic outcomes and success in post-secondary education, the workforce, and civic life. Students who self-advocate are better equipped to navigate challenges and make informed decisions about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learning interest inventories can identify areas of interest and ways of finding joy in learning. Exit tickets can help students identify whether they met the daily learning objective(s). Progress monitoring can identify the skills that students have mastered and which concepts need additional attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: If you have time to scroll Facebook or watch the news, you probably have a moment to decide if a news story seems credible. Ask some quick questions: Is the story so outrageous you can't believe it? Maybe you shouldn't. Is the story so outrageous you do believe it? That's also a warning sign. Many stories play on your existing beliefs. If the story perfectly confirms your worst suspicions, look for more information. Does the headline match the article? Many compelling headlines don't. Does the article match the news story it's lifted from? Many sites rewrite other news articles to fit the political slant of their presumed audience. Look for links to original sources and click through and see what the original says. Are quotes in context? Look for the sentences before and after the quote that makes your blood boil. If the article fails to give them, that's a warning sign. Is the story set in the future? It's hard to get firsthand reporting from there. Any story that tells you what will happen should be marked down 50 percent for this reason alone. Does the story attack a generic enemy? Vague denunciations of "Washington" or "the media" or "Trump supporters" or "the left" should be marked down 99 percent. Are you asked to rely on one killer factoid? Not a good idea.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of questions to evaluate news stories and examples.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires critical thinking skills and attention to detail.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation

  • Criteria Development

docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to apply the questions to evaluate news stories and identify red flags.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: Learners become more discerning consumers of news. Enhanced information literacy: Learners are better equipped to assess the credibility of news sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Evaluate a news story by checking if the headline matches the article or if the quotes are in context.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing learners with choice in activities promotes engagement, responsibility, and independence. Allowing learners to choose their reading material, writing topics, and project formats increases motivation and investment in learning tasks. When learners perceive tasks as meaningful and content as valuable to their future lives, they are more likely to engage deeply and learn effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom or learning environment where learners can make choices. A variety of reading materials, writing prompts, and project ideas. Instructor willingness to allow learner autonomy.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it challenging to make choices. Instructors need to manage the variety of activities to ensure alignment with learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12, higher education, adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, foster responsibility, promote independence, deepen learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation and investment in learning tasks. Promotes responsibility and independence. Encourages deeper engagement and learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose activities based on their interests and learning preferences. Instructors can offer a range of options to cater to diverse needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner engagement and participation. Quality of completed tasks. Learner feedback on their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that autonomy support in education increases learner motivation, engagement, and achievement. Studies also show that choice can lead to more meaningful learning experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school English teacher allows learners to choose the novel they want to read from a list of options. A college professor lets learners select the topic for their research paper. A professional development workshop offers participants a choice of sessions to attend based on their interests.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide learners with the autonomy to select their learning activities, mirroring the self-directed learning seen in preschool environments. This strategy fosters intrinsic motivation, deep engagement, and a sense of ownership over the learning process. By connecting tasks to personal interests and future goals, learners are more likely to invest in their education and retain information effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires flexibility in curriculum and assessment design. Instructors must be willing to relinquish some control over the learning process and provide support for learners' self-directed activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more planning and resources to support diverse learning choices. Learners may struggle with decision-making if they are not accustomed to having autonomy in their learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, adaptable for K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, develop independence and responsibility, enhance retention of learning, connect tasks to personal interests and future goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes intrinsic motivation, allows for deep engagement with content, and fosters a sense of ownership over learning. Learners are more likely to see the value in their work when they have a choice in what and how they learn.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of choices that cater to different interests and learning styles. Provide support and resources to help learners make informed decisions about their learning paths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and motivation during free choice activities. Assess the depth of understanding and quality of work produced by learners. Gather feedback from learners about their experiences with free choice time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that choice-based learning increases learner motivation, engagement, and retention of information. Giving learners autonomy over their learning fosters a growth mindset and prepares them for lifelong learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Allow students to choose the topic for a research paper, the format for a presentation, or the project they want to complete to demonstrate their understanding of a concept. A professor allows students to select the case study they will analyze in a business ethics course, leading to increased engagement and critical thinking.

docs.text: Free math worksheets provide accessible and structured practice materials to support math learning. These worksheets cover a range of topics and skill levels, from basic arithmetic to more advanced concepts. They offer opportunities for learners to reinforce their understanding, build fluency, and identify areas where they need additional support. Worksheets can be used for homework, in-class activities, or supplemental practice, making them a versatile tool for educators, parents, and learners alike.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to a collection of free math worksheets, either online or in print. Learners need time and motivation to complete the worksheets.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address conceptual understanding if used in isolation. Can become repetitive if not supplemented with other instructional methods.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and skill levels, from elementary students learning basic math facts to adults seeking to improve their numeracy skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce understanding, build fluency, identify learning gaps, provide structured practice, support independent learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured practice opportunities. Allows for self-paced learning and targeted skill development. Offers immediate feedback through answer keys.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Worksheets can be selected based on individual learner needs and skill levels. Learners can focus on specific areas where they need additional practice.

  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Consistent practice with math worksheets can improve fluency, accuracy, and confidence in math skills. Worksheets provide structured opportunities for learners to apply and reinforce their knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Free play is a child-led activity where learners explore and develop skills through self-directed interactions with their environment and peers. It is an essential and complex experience through which children learn and develop physical, social, cognitive, and creative skills. Free play increases their knowledge and understanding of the world around them. Teachers can facilitate quality free play by providing suitable environments, resources, and equipment, while also being responsive to individual needs. The teacher's role can be both active and passive, involving observation, support, and occasional engagement to extend learning without interrupting the flow of play. Free play allows learners to have agency in how they play, they participate in authentic social interactions and develop their motivation for exploration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a safe and stimulating environment with a variety of accessible materials and resources. Teachers need time for observation and reflection. Flexible routines that accommodate free play throughout the day.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and setup to ensure safety and accessibility. Teachers must strike a balance between providing support and allowing children to lead their own play. May be challenging to manage in large classes without adequate space or resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood learners (preschool, kindergarten, early primary grades)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop physical, social, cognitive, and creative skills; foster independence and self-regulation; enhance understanding of the world; promote motivation and engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports holistic development (physical, social, cognitive, creative). Fosters learner autonomy, motivation, and social interaction skills. Teachers gain insights into children’s interests and social dynamics through observation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a range of materials with varied characteristics (color, shape, texture) to cater to different sensory and developmental needs. Incorporate materials relevant to diverse cultures and holidays. Adapt storage and presentation of materials for accessibility.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's engagement, interactions, and skill development during free play. Document patterns of play, social dynamics, and individual interests. Discuss experiences with children to validate observations and guide resource selection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of play for child development, highlighting its role in cognitive, social, emotional, and physical growth. Free play has been shown to enhance problem-solving skills, creativity, and social competence.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Administering frequent quizzes with minimal impact on grades to reinforce learning and identify gaps in understanding. These quizzes should be short, simple, and focused on key concepts, emphasizing learning and practice over high-stakes assessment. Technology tools can streamline quiz administration and feedback. Low-stakes activities reduce student stress and increase engagement. The goal is to offer frequent feedback and reinforce concepts to cement learning for adults, increasing disciplinary literacy and strengthening understanding of new information, including numeracy skills.

Testing-and-learning research going back over 20 years found that tests promote learning, and that more frequent tests are more effective than less frequent ones (Dempster & Perkins, 1993). The mechanism is straightforward: frequent smaller tests encourage continuous effort instead of last-minute cramming, and reduce test anxiety because the consequence of any single error is smaller. College students themselves report preferring more frequent testing to infrequent testing (Bangert-Downs, Kulik, & Kulik, 1991). More broadly, a teacher's assessment purposes and beliefs, the type of assessment chosen, and the feedback given together shape the classroom's overall "assessment climate," which in turn affects student confidence and motivation — frequent low-stakes quizzing is one concrete lever on that climate, not just a test-frequency choice in isolation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires the creation of frequent quizzes and a system for providing feedback. Technology tools can assist with quiz administration and grading.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time-consuming to create and grade frequent quizzes. May not accurately reflect overall mastery of material if quizzes are too simplistic. Students may not take quizzes seriously if stakes are too low.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially beneficial for students who may struggle with high-stakes testing environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, identify gaps in understanding, reduce test anxiety, provide frequent feedback, encourage practice

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety associated with testing. Provides frequent opportunities for feedback and self-assessment. Reinforces concepts and promotes long-term retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can tailor quiz content and difficulty to individual student needs. Adaptive quiz platforms can adjust questions based on student performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Quizzes

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track quiz scores over time to measure learning progress. Compare quiz performance to overall course grades. Monitor student engagement and participation in quizzes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Frequent, low-stakes quizzes can improve retention, reduce test anxiety, and promote a growth mindset. Peer grading quizzes can ease teacher workloads and encourage collaboration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Assigning a half-page text answering four comprehension questions. Matching the audio to the sentence. Five-minute, multiple-choice, or single-sentence quizzes.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Dempster, F. N., & Perkins, P. G. (1993). Revitalizing classroom assessment: Using tests to promote learning. Journal of Instructional Psychology, 20(3), 197-203.
  • Bangert-Downs, R. L., Kulik, J. A., & Kulik, C. C. (1991). Effects of frequent classroom testing. Journal of Educational Research, 85(2), 89-99.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher-made assessments. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves prompting learners to reflect on their learning more often, allowing them to better understand their strengths and weaknesses, make connections between topics and disciplines, and grow as they self-assess their knowledge and understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Reflection prompts, a method for collecting reflections, and time for learners to respond.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time to adjust classroom routine to make time for reflections, learners must act on their reflection advice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who need to improve their self-assessment and metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-assessment skills, enhance understanding of strengths and weaknesses, foster connections between topics and disciplines, and promote a growth mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables learners to identify gaps in their knowledge, make time to determine if they understand before it is too late to seek help, and practice growth mindset comments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Collecting student reflections through various mediums (e.g., GrokSpot, OneNote, online forms). Asking students to reflect at the beginning/end of the year, during learning, and after assessments.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Honesty and detail in learners’ responses, evidence of growth in self-assessment skills, and connections made with other classes or in the community.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners to realize when they don’t fully understand a topic or idea, provides a chance to practice growth mindset comments, and enables learners to find connections they may not have noticed otherwise.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators should practice techniques to prevent/reduce their stress and frustration. Techniques include playing soft, relaxing music, displaying posters throughout the classroom of attractive destinations, modifying lesson plans and teaching a lesson that you enjoy, taking a short walk around the school, and asking a neighboring teacher to take a difficult learner for a short time. Some may find help by assigning independent reading time, or taking time to organize your work area.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must have a pre-planned list of stress/frustration reduction techniques to use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Each instructor has unique needs, and it is important that the right strategies are employed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve instructor's ability to maintain their temper and to be patient with their learners.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a classroom environment of patience and calm.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adopt techniques that suit their individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • A classroom environment that is positive, calm, and orderly.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A reduced-stress instructor is better able to support their learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Fry word list contains 1,000 high-frequency words divided into ten levels, further split into groups of twenty-five words based on frequency and difficulty. These instant words aim to build reading fluency. Students are encouraged to recognize these words by sight, practice them in context through phrase and sentence reading, and write short sentences including Fry words.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Fry word lists, reading materials, writing materials

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Focus on memorization may not suit all learners; contextual understanding of words is also needed

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early readers, struggling readers, ESL learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading fluency and comprehension by mastering high-frequency words, enhance sight word recognition, build vocabulary

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focuses on the most commonly used words, provides structured practice, promotes reading and writing skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Words can be taught explicitly and practiced through various activities such as reading and writing. Teachers can meet individually with students and identify difficult words.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess fluency in reading Fry words in context. Track progress in sight word recognition over time. Observe student engagement and confidence in reading tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mastering Fry words can significantly improve reading fluency and comprehension, reducing cognitive load during reading.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using walls for bulletin boards displaying student work and curricular supports, such as a word wall or math posters, makes resources easily accessible during instruction. Position displayed items strategically where they can be readily seen when needed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Wall space, bulletin boards, posters, student work, and an organizational system for ensuring content is current and relevant.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not managed well, wall displays can become cluttered and overwhelming, leading to distraction rather than support. Displays need to be periodically updated to stay relevant.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly visual learners and those who benefit from constant reminders of key concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To make learning materials readily accessible, promote student work, enhance classroom aesthetics, and support visual learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Maximizes use of space, creates a visually stimulating environment, serves as a continuous learning aid, fosters a sense of student ownership and pride.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Involve students in creating and updating displays. Allow students to select which pieces of their work to showcase. Make displays relevant to current learning topics and student interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how frequently students use the wall displays as resources. Gather feedback on the usefulness and clarity of displays. Monitor student engagement and behavior near the displays.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes active learning and visual reinforcement of concepts. Increases student engagement and a sense of ownership within the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use techniques such as clapping or knocking to signal students to stop, look, and listen before giving instructions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent implementation of the chosen signal.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Signal may become ineffective if overused.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly in group settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure learners are focused and ready to receive instructions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Establishes a clear signal for attention, reducing distractions and improving focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use different attention-getting signals based on learner preferences and cultural norms.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student responsiveness to the attention signal.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved attention and reduced distractions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher claps hands in a rhythmic pattern to signal students to stop talking and focus on the instructions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students pick a quote that expresses how they feel in the moment. Display quotes around the classroom to create stations. After reading all quotes, each student stands by the quote that reflects how they are feeling. Volunteers then share their quotes and how that reflects their current feelings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Quotes (printed and displayed), time for individual reflection and whole-class sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may not be drawn to written language or may not feel comfortable expressing their feelings through quotes. It is important to provide a variety of quotes to choose from and to create a safe and supportive environment where students feel comfortable sharing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially middle and high school

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Connect feelings with written expressions, encourage self-awareness, promote sharing and empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a creative and engaging way for students to explore and express their feelings, especially for those who may be drawn to written language. Normalizes talking about feelings and empowers students to view their emotions as assets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can create or pick their own quotes if there is not one that resonates with them. Instructors can provide a variety of quotes to choose from, representing different emotions and perspectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in the activity. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • All learning has an emotional base – Plato. Do you agree? Try these short activities to help grow students’ emotional intelligence skills

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students read displayed quotes and choose one that reflects their current feelings. Students gather by the quote they chose, and volunteers share why that quote resonates with them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A selection of quotes, space to display the quotes, time for individual reflection (3-5 minutes), and a willingness to share in a whole-class setting.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to find a quote that accurately represents their emotions. The effectiveness of the activity depends on creating a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for elementary through college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Express feelings through quotes, increase emotional awareness, build comfort in sharing emotions, foster a sense of connection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way for students to connect with their emotions through literature. Encourages students to share their feelings in a safe and supportive environment. Promotes a sense of community through shared reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose from a range of quotes or create their own. The level of sharing can be adjusted based on individual comfort levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in selecting and sharing quotes. Assess the thoughtfulness and specificity of students' explanations of their quotes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Acknowledging emotions calms the amygdala and reduces the intensity of felt emotions, helping individuals feel more in control. Promotes emotional literacy and awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • High school teachers use the gallery quote walk as a check-in activity to help students connect with their emotions and build a sense of community in the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Stations or posters are set up around the classroom, on the walls, or on tables. Small groups of learners travel from station to station together, performing a task or responding to a prompt, either of which will result in a conversation. Variations include groups creating informative posters and acting as tour guides, or using video tutorials created by learners themselves. The teacher prepares discussion prompts or content-related tasks and sets them up around the room for learners to visit in small groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires physical space to set up stations or posters, preparation of tasks and prompts, and clear instructions for learners. Post-it notes and markers for learners to record ideas.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging in small or crowded classrooms. Requires careful planning and monitoring to ensure all learners are engaged and on task. Can become chaotic if not well-managed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for visual and kinesthetic learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage active learning, promote collaboration, facilitate peer teaching, provide diverse perspectives

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active engagement, allows learners to move around, fosters collaboration and peer teaching, provides diverse perspectives, supports visual learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks and prompts can be differentiated to meet diverse learning needs. Learners can choose the order in which they visit stations based on interest or learning style.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner interactions and discussions at each station, review written responses or tasks completed at each station, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances active learning, promotes collaboration and peer teaching, provides diverse perspectives, supports visual learning

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implementing a game-based incentive, such as "Silent 20," where students are given 20 seconds to return to their seats and be completely quiet. If successful, the class advances on a game board (e.g., a giant facsimile of Game of Life), with a reward (e.g., a popcorn party) given upon reaching the last square.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a game board, a method for tracking progress, and a reward system. Implementation requires clear communication of rules and expectations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the reward is not motivating for all students. Could lead to competition and potential frustration among students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage students to quickly and quietly transition back to their seats after an activity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Motivates students through a fun, competitive element. Provides a clear, time-bound expectation and a tangible reward.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The game and reward can be tailored to student interests and preferences. Adjust the time limit based on student abilities and classroom dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the speed and consistency with which students comply with the “Silent 20” rule. Monitor student engagement and participation in the game.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Motivates students through a fun and competitive game. Provides clear expectations and tangible rewards for quiet transitions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Game-based learning involves designing learning activities so that game characteristics and game principles inhere within the learning activities themselves. It utilizes games to reach specific learning objectives, whether they belong to knowledge, skills, or attitudes. This includes board games, real-life games, and digital games.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful design of game activities to align with learning objectives. Selection or creation of games that support specific skills and knowledge. Facilitation to guide students through the game and debrief afterward.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to design and implement effectively. Requires careful alignment of game mechanics with learning objectives. May not be suitable for all learners or subject areas.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, adaptable to various subjects and contexts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote engagement, facilitate retention, improve collaboration, encourage experimentation, practice real-world behaviors

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging and motivating due to game-like structure. Allows for experimentation and application of knowledge in a safe environment. Fosters critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different learning styles and needs through varied game types (board, real-life, digital). Activities can be customized to align with specific learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student performance within the game environment. Observe collaboration and problem-solving skills during gameplay. Gather student feedback on engagement and learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that game-based learning can enhance motivation, engagement, complex problem-solving, and social-emotional skills such as self-regulation. Studies have found that students in game-based courses exhibit more positive working relationships and entrepreneurial skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Virtual stock-trading competition in Economics. Role-playing mock negotiations in Political Science. Creating Jeopardy-style games for chapter reviews. Using Minecraft to build virtual worlds.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Gaming involves using games as a way to help learners learn by doing. Games can be organized in a way that individuals and groups play with each other, by either collaborating or competing, like in the real world. Motivation tools such as points, badges and certificates can be awarded to make the game more engaging for participants.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A game or simulation, facilitator to guide the learning process, motivation tools such as points, badges and certificates

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Games can be seen as frivolous by some, and outcomes need to be well-defined to ensure learning is effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All employee levels in corporate training settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, promote collaboration and competition, teach valuable lessons about how to deal with on-the-job situations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides an engaging way to learn by doing, promotes teamwork and competition, teaches how to handle on-the-job situations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Games can be designed to reflect the learner's own working environment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track participation and measure game outcomes to assess the learning of valuable lessons about how to deal with on-the-job situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Games can be organized in a way that individuals and groups play with each other, by either collaborating or competing, like in the real world. This process can teach them valuable lessons about how to deal with on-the-job situations. As part of this experiential training approach, motivation tools such as points, badges and certificates can be awarded to make the game more engaging for participants.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students engage with educational games designed to introduce or reinforce specific concepts. These games are combined with a structured activity to ensure active learning and application of the concepts. Games can make learning fun and engaging, while the structured activity helps to consolidate understanding and promote application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires selection or creation of educational games, design of structured activities, and access to technology (e.g., computers, tablets).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of content or learners. Requires careful alignment of games and learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from gamified learning and interactive activities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, promote active learning, facilitate understanding and application of concepts through gamification.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a fun and engaging approach to learning, promotes active participation, and can improve motivation and retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Games can be selected or designed to match learner interests and skill levels. Structured activities can be tailored to reinforce specific concepts or skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Engagement with games, completion of structured activities, performance on related assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective when combined with well-designed structured activities that reinforce learning and promote application of the game concepts. Can improve learner outcomes and engagement by making learning more fun and interactive.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Gamification is the integration of game elements like point systems, leaderboards, badges, or other elements related to games into “conventional” learning activities in order to increase engagement and motivation. Examples include awarding badges for participation in online discussion forums or earning points for completing tasks, which can be tracked via digital gradebooks or shared online.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Integration of digital tools (e.g., learning management systems, Google Drive). Design of a point or badge system aligned with course objectives. Ongoing tracking of student progress.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be demotivating for students at the bottom of leaderboards. May not lead to improved learning outcomes if not thoughtfully integrated. Over-emphasis on extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially those familiar with digital games (e.g., Gen Z)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase engagement, sustain motivation, reward task completion, track progress, foster comradery or competition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages learners' familiarity with game mechanics. Provides immediate feedback through points and badges. Fosters motivation through competition and reward systems.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual learning preferences by offering choices in how to earn points. Point systems can be supplemented by academic rewards to suit different needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation and engagement with gamified activities. Compare learning outcomes between gamified and non-gamified courses. Monitor student feedback regarding motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows gamification can increase student engagement and motivation. Studies indicate that leaderboards can increase time-on-task and academic performance, although caution is needed to avoid discouraging low-performing students.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Online discussion forums with badge systems (e.g., earning badges for number of posts). Point systems for completing various tasks or assessments, tracked via digital gradebooks. Purdue University Global integrating gamification features into its career services network.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves readers asking themselves questions throughout the reading process. The ability to ask relevant questions helps readers integrate information, identify main ideas, and summarize effectively. Asking the right questions allows readers to focus on the most important information and address any comprehension problems they encounter. By posing questions, readers actively engage with the text and monitor their understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learners need to be prompted to ask questions before, during, and after reading. Instructors should provide models of effective questioning and facilitate discussions based on learner-generated questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to generate relevant or insightful questions if they lack background knowledge or critical thinking skills. Poorly formulated questions may lead to superficial comprehension.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those in upper elementary, middle, and high school, as well as adult learners looking to improve reading comprehension and critical thinking

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension by integrating information, identifying main ideas, summarizing content, and focusing on key details through self-questioning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances active reading by encouraging learners to pose questions and seek answers, promotes critical thinking by focusing on important information and potential comprehension issues, and improves self-monitoring skills through metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can generate questions based on their individual interests and knowledge levels. Instructors can provide question stems or examples to guide learners in generating effective questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Question Formulation
  • Inquiry-Based Exploration
  • Pre-reading Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and relevance of questions generated by learners. Assess comprehension through discussions, summaries, or written responses that demonstrate the ability to answer self-generated questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that generating and asking questions enhances reading comprehension by promoting active engagement with the text. It helps learners focus on important information and address comprehension problems effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a chapter on climate change, learners create a list of questions they want to answer. During reading, they pause to ask themselves additional questions. After reading, they review their questions and summarize the key points, addressing any unanswered questions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Genre study is an approach to teaching literature that involves exploring the characteristics and conventions of different literary genres. It typically involves students reading a variety of texts within a specific genre, discussing the elements that define that genre, and often writing their own pieces in that style. This method promotes a deeper understanding and appreciation of literature by helping students recognize the unique features of various genres and how they shape the reader's experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of books representing different genres. Printable bookmarks, genre characteristics handouts, book review handouts, website access

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and resources to gather materials. Can be challenging if students lack foundational reading skills. May need to address misconceptions about genre categories.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 3-12, adaptable for various age and ability levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify literary elements of common genres, experience and develop interest in literature, improve comprehension by interpreting, analyzing, synthesizing, and evaluating written text to categorize text into literary genres

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances reading comprehension and analytical skills. Develops an appreciation for diverse literary forms. Improves writing skills through genre-specific practice. Connects in-school literacies to out-of-school experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can select genres relevant to students' interests and cultural backgrounds. Students can choose books within a genre that appeal to them. Assignments can be adapted to suit different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation in discussions, completion of book reviews and bookmarks, ability to identify genre characteristics in texts, quality of contributions to group charts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that students who engage in genre studies have a better understanding of literary elements and are more successful in writing across different genres. Genre studies also promote cognitive development by allowing students to apply similar skills and strategies across various types of literature.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are assigned a genre to explore, use printable bookmarks to record evidence that their book fits the assigned genre, complete a book review, and share summaries of the books they read with their classmates. Conducting studies of multiple genres can help students achieve a better understanding of their characteristics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Gestures are physical movements, typically of the hands or arms, used to communicate meaning or support learning. Teachers and learners can use hand signals to communicate or support their learning. Research shows that students are more accurate in counting when they point to each item. Visual gestures that complement spoken language allow for the processing of information in multiple ways, supporting greater retention of information in Working and Short-term Memory. Providing a visualization or animation in addition to audio or text activates visual Working Memory and supports deeper comprehension. Developers can also use these visualizations or enactments to capture and maintain Attention on key content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • No specific materials required, but effective implementation depends on clear, intentional use of gestures and visualizations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overuse of gestures can be distracting. Some learners may not benefit from or understand certain gestures.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for visual learners and those needing support with counting or memory

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support counting accuracy, capture attention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports multiple modes of processing information, enhances working memory, provides a non-verbal communication tool

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different content areas and learner needs. Visualizations can be tailored to specific concepts or age groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner accuracy in tasks involving counting or memory recall. Measure comprehension through formative assessments following instruction with and without gestures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that gesturing can significantly improve learning outcomes, particularly in math. Gestures can help students transfer learning to new contexts, such as transferring knowledge learned in an addition-based equation to a multiplication-based equation.

docs.title: Give Hints and Clues to Help Students Answer Questions
Description
docs.text: Teachers should do more delving and rephrasing for learners for whom they have high expectations. When a learner is struggling, provide appropriate hints and clues. Give sufficient clues to low-performing learners to build their self-esteem and encourage them to do better in the future. Be careful to not give so many hints that you are basically giving the learner the answer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must be able to provide the right scaffolding to support learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Teachers may give too many hints, which makes it obvious to the learners that they are struggling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' academic success by giving them appropriate scaffolding.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts learner self-confidence, encourages engagement, and helps learners understand concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can make sure to give individualized attention to the low-performing learners in their classes to build their self-esteem.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increase in learner participation, improved academic performance, and reduced behavioral issues. Observation of learners' confidence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that appropriate scaffolding has a positive effect on academic success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Knowing what you know and don’t know focuses learning. Feedback is an integral part of learning. Tutees need appropriate feedback on performance to benefit from tutoring. In getting started, they will need help in assessing existing knowledge and competence. In tutoring sessions, tutees need frequent opportunities to perform and receive suggestions for improvement. At various points everyone needs chances to reflect on what they have learned, and what they still need to know.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Regular assessments, tutor expertise in providing constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time investment from the tutor, feedback must be relevant and specific.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learning through timely and relevant feedback, improve self-awareness, promote continuous improvement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focuses learning, improves performance, enhances self-awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Acknowledge successes and refocus on the next steps. Prepare problems or exercises that give tutees immediate feedback on how well they are doing. Give follow-up assignments to help tutees monitor their own progress.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved tutee performance, increased self-awareness, positive feedback from tutees about feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research emphasizes the importance of feedback for learning and improvement. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor acknowledges tutees' successes. The tutor gives follow-up assignments to help tutees monitor their own progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Setting clear goals for writing, encouraging peer support, self-assessment, and providing feedback on progress. Clear goals for writing are specific to the purpose and type of writing task. Learners set explicit goals to guide their writing, and work with them to track progress. Specific goals (e.g., “to persuade a voter”) are more effective than general goals (e.g., “write a 200-word essay”). Discuss writing quality with learners and identify areas for improvement. This supports motivation and improves writing quality.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear understanding of writing purposes, feedback mechanisms, self-assessment tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Goals must be specific and achievable, requires consistent monitoring

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing quality, enhance motivation, encourage self-assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation, improves clarity and focus, promotes self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Goals are tailored to individual learner needs and writing tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased writing quality, improved self-assessment accuracy, greater goal attainment

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Experiments show practices improve the quality of writing and affect motivation. These practices include setting clear goals for writing; encouraging students to help each other plan, draft, or revise; using self-assessment; and providing feedback on progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: GoNoodle offers videos and activities to encourage physical activity and movement breaks through gestures and movement. Incorporating movement can support attention, deepen understanding of key concepts, and enhance mathematical learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to the GoNoodle platform and appropriate technology.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reliance on digital resources may pose barriers for learners with limited access to technology or the internet.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote physical activity, enhance attention, deepen understanding of concepts, support kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a range of videos and activities to choose from, making it easy to incorporate movement into the classroom or workplace.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be selected to align with specific learning objectives or themes.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' engagement and participation in the activities. Assess their understanding of the concepts being taught.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Movement from engaging videos and activities may enhance attention, deepen understanding of geometry concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A geometry class incorporates movement to test students' understanding of math terms such as line and ray, with students mimicking gestures and movement from memorable, engaging videos.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: GoNoodle provides interactive videos that encourage learners to engage in movement and play, supporting attention and learning. It offers diverse activities that combine movement with educational content, including dance parties, breathing exercises, and ASL coloring sheets. It can be used in the classroom or designed into products using videos, prompts, and augmented reality.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to GoNoodle videos and digital platforms. Classroom space or integration into product design.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on regular implementation and alignment with curriculum goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance attention, improve focus, promote physical activity, and support emotional regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides engaging and interactive content that integrates movement with learning, making it fun and effective.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be chosen based on learner needs and preferences. Integration with digital tools allows for augmented reality experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Gain attention
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement, participation, and focus during and after GoNoodle activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combines physical activity with educational content to enhance focus and learning. Research indicates that physical activity and mindfulness exercises can improve cognitive function and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Various GoNoodle videos and activities, such as "Release Your Warrior", "Nimble Nostrils", "Pop 'N' Bop", and "Breathing Exercises For Focusing And Settling".

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Regular contact between tutees and tutors is part of the tutoring process, increasing tutee motivation and involvement. Tutor interest helps tutees keep on working and get through rough times. Getting to know your tutee enhances their intellectual and emotional commitment to learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Regularly scheduled tutoring sessions, tutor willingness to engage with tutees personally.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming for tutors, requires strong interpersonal skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase tutee motivation, foster a supportive learning environment, enhance intellectual and emotional commitment to learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation and involvement, fosters a sense of connection and support, promotes emotional commitment to learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tutors can share past experiences, values, and attitudes to connect with tutees. They can also get to know tutees by name and treat them as individuals with real lives, asking about their well-being.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased tutee attendance, improved engagement during sessions, positive feedback from tutees.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that increased contact and support enhance learner motivation and academic success. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor shares their own experiences in the subject matter to build rapport with the tutee. A tutor asks the tutee how they are doing before starting the session to show care and interest.

docs.title: Grade Students Based on Demonstrated Learning
Description
docs.text: Instead of averaging scores over time, emphasize grading students on their ultimate level of mastery at the end of a unit. This mitigates rewarding students who begin with a higher level of mastery and encourages perseverance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Assessment methods that capture mastery, flexible grading policies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant restructuring of curriculum and assessments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage perseverance, reward mastery over time, fairly assess students regardless of initial skill level

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Rewards growth, encourages persistence, fairly assesses mastery

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for individualized learning paths, focuses on final demonstration of knowledge

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student mastery levels, growth over time

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mitigates rewarding students who begin with a higher level of mastery and encourages students to persevere, even if they struggle initially with a new topic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Emphasizing final project grades over early assignments

docs.title: Gradual Increase of Independent Reading Time
Description
docs.text: Start with short independent reading sessions and gradually increase the amount of time as students build reading stamina. Begin with sessions as short as five minutes for young children and gradually increase the time as students become more focused and engaged.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for independent reading, a timer to monitor reading sessions, and a plan for gradually increasing reading time.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent implementation and monitoring. Some students may still struggle to focus even with gradual increases in time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build reading stamina, increase focus and engagement, and establish a consistent independent reading routine.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Prevents distraction and disengagement, builds reading stamina gradually, and establishes a positive association with independent reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the pace of increasing reading time based on individual student needs and progress. Provide support and encouragement for students who struggle to focus.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor students' ability to focus during reading sessions. Track the amount of time students can read independently. Collect feedback from students on their reading experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases reading stamina, improves focus and engagement, and promotes a consistent independent reading routine.

docs.title: Gradual Release of Responsibility in Multimodal Composition
Description
docs.text: Using the gradual release of responsibility model to support students in multimodal composition. This involves direct instruction on selecting and analyzing multimodal resources (e.g., websites, book trailers, blogs), followed by facilitated discussions in pairs or small groups, and then independent analysis of multimodal examples. This scaffolding approach aims to strengthen students’ interest in multimodal composition and develop recursive design skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Examples of multimodal resources, time for direct instruction and discussion, opportunities for independent analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant preparation to identify appropriate multimodal resources. Relies on active participation in direct instruction and discussions. Some students may need additional support to develop independence.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students learning multimodal composition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop independence in multimodal composition, strengthen interest in multimodal design, enhance recursive design skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured support for students to develop independence, fosters collaboration and peer learning, and promotes recursive design skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different skill levels and interests. The complexity of the resources and analysis can be adjusted based on student needs. Students can choose their favorite multimodal examples for independent analysis.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to select and analyze multimodal resources independently. Analyze the quality and depth of their independent analysis. Assess the extent to which students apply recursive design skills in their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased independence in multimodal composition, strengthened interest in multimodal design, and enhanced recursive design skills.

docs.title: Graphic Organizers / Guided Notes (for Processing Speed)
Description
docs.text: During lecture, learners are provided with graphic organizers or guided notes to help pull out the important points. These tools structure the information being presented, making it easier to process and retain. Guided notes prompt learners to fill in key information, promoting active engagement during the lecture.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Prepared graphic organizers or guided notes, writing utensils or digital input tools, and instructor guidance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires preparation time for the instructor. Some learners may find the structure too rigid if not tailored to their needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with processing speed, those who have difficulty taking effective notes, and students who benefit from structured learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support information processing, improve note-taking skills, enhance comprehension of key concepts, and increase engagement during lectures.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework, reduces cognitive load Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+M], promotes active engagement, and supports information retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize graphic organizers and guided notes to match individual learning styles and content. Provide options for filling in information (e.g., writing, drawing, digital input).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to fill in key information accurately and effectively. Review the completed graphic organizers or guided notes to assess comprehension.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and guided notes support faster processing, improve note-taking skills, and enhance comprehension during lectures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: During lecture provide students with graphic organizers or guided notes to help pull out the important points.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Visual aids, such as graphics, diagrams, and gestures

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be accessible to all learners due to visual impairments. Note-taking can be a challenging skill for some.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides reinforcement of concepts through an additional sense, graphic notes are permanent so allow the students to revisit the information whenever necessary, students can take notes that best support their learning needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow different types of graphic organizers. Some learners might prefer a mind-map while others need a timeline.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Note-taking
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how learners use graphic organizers. Provide feedback on the organizational techniques. Track test grades or other assessment results to determine if this tool is helpful.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that graphic organizers can help support learning by reinforcing learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of graphic organizers in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Provide charts that help students see connections between people and events, mind-maps that allow for creativity while taking notes. Resource: Speed of Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use visual cues in note-taking to help learners organize the information you are sharing with them orally. This allows them to keep track of the lesson as you present, and the notes can be revisited for studying.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Visual aids, such as graphics, diagrams, and gestures

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be accessible to all learners due to visual impairments. Note-taking can be a challenging skill for some.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face auditory processing challenges
