docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides reinforcement of concepts through an additional sense, graphic notes are permanent so allow the students to revisit the information whenever necessary, students can take notes that best support their learning needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow different types of graphic organizers. Some learners might prefer a mind-map while others need a timeline.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Note-taking
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how learners use graphic organizers. Provide feedback on the organizational techniques. Track test grades or other assessment results to determine if this tool is helpful.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that graphic organizers can help support learning by reinforcing learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of graphic organizers in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are taught to create mind-maps, charts, or timelines when taking notes. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Graphic organizers break down math problems into steps, which helps students figure out what’s being asked in a word problem or which operation to use. Can also be used to learn new math concepts. There are many types of math-specific graphic organizers that work for students of all ages. Types include: the Frayer model, Step-by-step, Line it up, Graph it out, Break it down, Blank Pictographs, Blank Bar Graph, Version 2, Horizontal Bar Graph, Vertical Bar Graph, Double Venn Diagram, Version 1, Triple Venn Diagram, Tens and Ones Mat, Hundreds, Tens, and Ones Mat, 2-Group Sorting Mat, 3-Group Sorting Mat, Number Lines, Blank 100 Grid, 10 x 10 Grids, Tenths Grids, Hundredths Grids, 2 x 10 Graphing Grid, Coordinate Grids: Blank Printable Template, Graphing Grid (4 rows), 4-Digit Place-Value Charts, 9-Digit Place-Value Charts, 12-Digit Place-Value Charts, 26-Digit Place-Value Charts

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizer templates, writing utensils or digital tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for all students or all types of math problems. Requires instructor guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages who need support with math, including students with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Visualize and solve math problems, understand number relationships, identify similarities and differences, learn new concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual framework for organizing information, simplifies complex problems, supports working memory, can be adapted to different learner needs

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adjusted depending on individual learner’s needs and the specific math problem or topic. Students can fill them in by hand or digitally. If a student struggles with writing, the instructor can write in the problem and let the student do the rest.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to break down problems into steps, identify key information, and choose appropriate operations. Review completed graphic organizers for accuracy and completeness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can improve problem-solving skills, comprehension, and retention of math concepts.

docs.title: Graphic Organizers and Guided Notes (Processing Speed)
Description
docs.text: Providing students with graphic organizers or guided notes during lectures to help them pull out the important points. This strategy involves offering structured note-taking templates that highlight key information and relationships.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizer templates, guided notes, and instructor guidance on their effective use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful design to ensure alignment with lecture content, may not be suitable for all types of content, and some students may prefer unstructured note-taking

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who struggle with processing speed and need support in extracting key information from lectures

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support information processing, reduce cognitive load, and improve note-taking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces the amount of information needed to be processed in real-time, highlights essential content, supports active listening, and enhances note-taking efficiency

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Templates can be customized based on subject matter and student needs, with options for visual cues, color-coding, and pre-filled sections.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student's completed graphic organizers and guided notes for accuracy and completeness. Assess their ability to recall and apply information from the lecture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that guided notes improve information retention and enhance note-taking skills, particularly for students with processing speed challenges.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tools that help students identify and focus on the most important information by presenting it in a structured and visual format. These aids support the organization of thoughts, the prioritization of key concepts, and the reduction of cognitive load, making it easier for students to filter out irrelevant stimuli and concentrate on pertinent details.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the content and key concepts, creation or selection of appropriate graphic organizers or visual aids, and explicit instruction on how to use them effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the graphic organizer or visual aid is too complex or poorly designed. Some students may become overly reliant on these tools and struggle to process information without them.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who struggle with organization, attention, or processing information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus and attention, enhance information retention, reduce cognitive load, support organization and prioritization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and structured framework for organizing information. Reduces cognitive load by externalizing key concepts and relationships. Helps students visualize connections and prioritize information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and visual aids can be customized to match individual student needs and learning preferences. Examples include concept maps, Venn diagrams, timelines, and flowcharts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior (e.g., improved focus, enhanced organization). Collect feedback from students on the helpfulness of the tools.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and visual aids can help students identify the most important information and focus in on it, supporting the development of key literacy skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using concept maps to organize thoughts, Venn diagrams to compare and contrast concepts, timelines to track events, and flowcharts to understand processes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using graphic organizers and visual aids to help students identify the most important information and focus on it. This involves tools like mind maps, charts, and diagrams that present information in a structured, visual format.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizer templates, visual aids, and instructor guidance on how to use them effectively

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of content, requires careful design to avoid overwhelming students, and may not address underlying attentional challenges

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who need help focusing on key information and filtering out distractions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Highlight essential information, improve focus, and support selective attention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Presents information in a clear, structured format, reduces cognitive load, supports visual learners, and aids in comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized based on student needs and subject matter, with options for color-coding, labeling, and adding visual cues.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student's ability to extract key information using graphic organizers. Review completed graphic organizers for accuracy and completeness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that graphic organizers improve information retention, enhance comprehension, and support attentional focus.

docs.title: Graphic Organizers and Visual Aids (for Attention)
Description
docs.text: These tools help learners identify the most important information and focus on it. Graphic organizers structure content visually, making it easier to discern key points and relationships. Visual aids, such as diagrams and color-coded notes, also support attention by presenting information in an accessible and engaging manner. This strategy is particularly effective for learners who benefit from visual supports.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizer templates, visual aids (e.g., diagrams, color-coded notes), digital tools (optional), and instructor guidance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires initial instruction on how to use the tools effectively. Some learners may find the visual structure too rigid or overwhelming if not tailored to their needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with attention, visual learners, students with learning disabilities, and those who benefit from structured learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus on key information, enhance comprehension of complex topics, support information retention, engage visual learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides visual structure, enhances comprehension, supports focused attention, improves information retention and recall.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize graphic organizers and visual aids to suit individual learning styles and content. Use color-coding, diagrams, and mind maps to match learner preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in learner's ability to identify and recall key information. Review the effectiveness of graphic organizers and visual aids through student feedback and performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and visual aids enhance focus, improve comprehension, and support effective learning strategies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students add a graphic organizer to a finished expository or argumentative writing piece to illustrate a key concept or process. The organizer is a diagram to aid in the reader's comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates and writing pieces.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be applicable to all writing topics or genres. Requires additional time and effort to create a meaningful diagram.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly useful for complex or abstract topics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reader comprehension, illustrate complex processes, reinforce learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of the text, enhancing understanding and retention for the reader.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the type of organizer and content to illustrate based on their writing topic.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Clarity and effectiveness of the illustration in supporting the written content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Diagrams in texts promote reader understanding and visual literacy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student writing about photosynthesis includes a diagram showing the process from sunlight to energy. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students interact with content by organizing chunks of it into graphic organizers in groups, pairs, or individually, then comparing their results. This helps learners grapple with content, work with similarities and differences, and engage in critical thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates and content.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to structure content into organizers effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking, enhance interaction with content, develop analytical skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way to interact with content, promotes discussion and collaboration, enhances understanding of similarities and differences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can provide different organizers for different content or allow learners to choose their preferred organizer.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of interactions and analyses of content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking and engagement with content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A foreign language class uses a hierarchical organizer to classify food vocabulary words into categories like meats, fruits, and vegetables. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students complete a graphic organizer that shows relationships between terms or concepts instead of taking a quiz, or as part of a quiz, to evaluate understanding of a body of content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates, content knowledge.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all content areas or assessment objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially beneficial for assessing holistic understanding

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess understanding, evaluate relationships between concepts, provide a visual representation of knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of understanding, identifies gaps in knowledge, allows for creative expression of knowledge.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose how to represent the relationships between concepts in their organizers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy and completeness of the relationships depicted in the organizer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enables assessment of holistic understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students complete a concept map to show how different events led to World War I. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Put the most important classroom policies, procedures, and expectations into graphic form to increase the likelihood that students will follow them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates and clear classroom rules.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all rules and procedures.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve classroom behavior, enhance understanding of rules, create a visual reminder of expectations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances clarity and adherence to rules and procedures.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adapt the organizer to fit the specific classroom rules and expectations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved classroom behavior and adherence to rules.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual reminders increase adherence to classroom policies and procedures.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher creates a visual flowchart outlining the steps for lining up for recess. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors deliver lectures using a graphic organizer to visually connect concepts, rather than using PowerPoint or a standard outline. This approach provides students with a clear way to see how concepts relate to each other.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates, lecture content organized visually.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant preparation by the instructor to translate lecture content into a visual format.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from visual learning aids

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, illustrate relationships between concepts, provide a visual framework for learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and structured way to understand complex information. Aids in visual memory and information retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adapt the graphic organizer to fit the specific content and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Ability to explain the relationships between concepts, quality of notes taken during the lecture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual presentation of content enhances retention and understanding of relationships between concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A science teacher uses a concept map to explain the classification of living organisms, showing how different species are related.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Graphic organizers help learners break down math problems into steps to understand what’s being asked or which operation to use. They can also be used to learn new math concepts. Types include: The Frayer model, Step-by-step organizers, Line it up, Graph it out, and Break it down. They can be adapted depending on learner needs and the math problem or topic.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Printed or digital graphic organizer templates, writing utensils or digital input tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial instruction on how to use effectively. Some students may find the structure too rigid if not adapted appropriately. Effectiveness depends on the design and appropriateness of the organizer for the given task.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages who need support with math, particularly those with math-related learning difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Break down complex math problems, identify relevant information, choose appropriate operations, learn new math concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides visual support, reduces cognitive load by organizing information, supports step-by-step problem-solving, enhances understanding of mathematical concepts and operations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various ages, math topics, and learner needs. The design can be customized, and additional sections can be added as needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to accurately complete steps, identify key information, select appropriate operations, and solve problems using the organizer. Assess the depth of understanding demonstrated through the completed organizer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Graphic organizers improve problem-solving skills, comprehension, and the ability to apply mathematical concepts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use graphic organizers to structure notes from readings, research, films, or podcasts. The instructor may select a specific graphic organizer to promote learning efficiency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates, materials for note-taking (paper, digital tools), and instructor guidance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May over-simplify complex material if not carefully designed. Ineffective if students are not properly trained on their use.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly beneficial for visual learners and those who benefit from structured learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Organize information, identify relationships between concepts, improve comprehension and retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual structure aids comprehension and retention. Pre-selected organizers save time and effort. Note-taking during information consumption aids engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can customize organizers based on content and learner needs. Learners can use different organizers based on their preferred style.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of notes, accuracy of information presented, and learner ability to synthesize information.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that graphic organizers incorporated into instruction improve student learning. Author-created graphic organizers can lead to deeper learning more quickly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students use a Venn diagram to compare and contrast two historical figures while reading a biography. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students identify the text structure (compare/contrast, cause/effect, etc.) before reading and complete a graphic organizer that supports that structure as they read. KWL charts help activate prior knowledge and set a purpose for reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates and reading materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires training to identify text structure. May oversimplify complex texts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Older students and challenging texts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, activate prior knowledge, identify text structure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts comprehension, activates prior knowledge, and facilitates identification of text structure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose the appropriate graphic organizer to match the text structure or allow learners to select their preferred organizer.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and ability to identify text structures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates improved reading comprehension through identifying text structures and using graphic organizers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students use a cause-and-effect diagram while reading about the American Revolution. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use graphic organizers to plan and structure their ideas before drafting a written piece, jotting down notes rather than writing complete sentences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates, writing prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be seen as an extra step and could be ineffective if students are not shown how to use them properly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from visual planning tools

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Organize thoughts, structure writing, develop ideas

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear framework for writing, enhances organization, and reduces writing anxiety.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select the type of organizer that best suits their writing task (e.g., mind map, outline).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved organization and clarity of written pieces.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps students organize their thoughts and ideas before writing, leading to better structured and more coherent writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students use a tree diagram to plan the arguments for an argumentative essay. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students recall as much as they can about a topic (Brain Dump) and then sort their dumped information into a graphic organizer. After, they check texts to confirm, correct, or add to the information they retrieved, solidifying the benefit of the retrieval and helping them get very clear on where they have gaps in their knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates, supporting texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance recall, identify knowledge gaps, improve organization of information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens learning and helps identify gaps in knowledge.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the type of organizer and organize their dumped information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completeness of recalled information and quality of organization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Solidifies learning and identifies knowledge gaps.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After reading a chapter on the Civil War, students complete a brain dump, then organize their information into a timeline. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Present students with a graphic organizer to show how the parts of a unit fit together, providing a sense of where they are in the unit and why they are learning the individual parts. This exercise helps instructors decide what concepts are most important.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizer templates and unit content.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant preparation by the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide context, explain the purpose of learning, create a sense of direction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides context, helps understand the overall unit structure, clarifies learning objectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adapt the organizer to fit the unit's specific content and objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of the unit's structure and objectives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Aids comprehension and gives a sense of purpose for learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher shows a flowchart outlining the steps in a scientific investigation at the beginning of a unit on the scientific method. Resource: Cult of Pedagogy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Because scholars have drawn from the Greek language to name scientific concepts and discoveries since the Renaissance, middle school students will encounter hundreds of words derived from Greek in math, science, and philosophy texts. Greek word parts work more like compounds than roots. Their spellings are very consistent.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, morphological charts, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6-7 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance vocabulary, develop understanding of word structure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand scientific and academic vocabulary, improves spelling accuracy, builds vocabulary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific Greek combining forms. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in spelling words with Greek combining forms. Monitor progress in spelling and vocabulary skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The study of Greek combining forms improves spelling and comprehension for middle school students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The group-based model focuses on group learning. After the students have studied the material provided, they work together on assignments during the classroom time. The students learn by explaining concepts to each other, which improves retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear instructions for group assignments, facilitation skills to manage group dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Dependent on learners' willingness to collaborate, may require careful group management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners who thrive in collaborative environments and can learn effectively from peers.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster collaboration, improve communication skills, enhance retention through peer teaching.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages peer interaction to reinforce understanding and improve retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Groups can be formed based on complementary skills or common interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Peer Teaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Group performance on assignments, quality of peer explanations, individual contribution.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can improve learners' communication skills and enhance retention through collaborative learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Business school classes using videos to introduce case studies followed by group analysis.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The teacher calls out a number (e.g., 3), and the students have 10 seconds to get themselves into groups of that size. It might be impossible for everyone to get in a group every time, but each new number gives everyone another chance. In the basic game, just call out single numbers. Once students get the gist, the teacher can call out addition or subtraction problems (i.e., “get into groups of 7-4.”). Calling out a group of 1 and a group of however many students are in the entire class at some point in the game is beneficial.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An open space where students can move freely. The teacher needs to be able to call out numbers and sums or differences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for students with physical limitations. Can be challenging for students with social anxiety or difficulty with group work.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce number recognition, encourage quick mental math, promote social interaction, support kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Quick, fun, and adaptable activity. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts. Incorporates collaborative learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the math problems based on the students' skill levels. Allow students to create their own variations to the activity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to quickly form groups based on the given number. Assess students' ability to solve the math problems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • May help students refresh while applying the concepts of group formation. Encourages active participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher calls out '4' during a transition and the students move to form groups of four, which they can then continue working in for the next exercise.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Growth mindset development involves cultivating the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through dedication, effort, and learning from mistakes. This mindset encourages individuals to embrace challenges, persist through obstacles, and view failure as an opportunity for growth. Strategies include providing praise for effort and progress, reframing mistakes as learning experiences, and teaching the concept of neuroplasticity—the brain's ability to change and grow.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from both instructors and learners to value effort and learning over innate ability. Consistent reinforcement of growth mindset principles through feedback, modeling, and explicit instruction. Activities should be designed to promote challenge and encourage persistence.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some individuals may initially resist the idea of a growth mindset due to prior experiences or ingrained beliefs. Requires consistent reinforcement and modeling from instructors to maintain a growth-oriented environment. May be challenging to implement in competitive or high-stakes situations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate belief in the ability to improve, encourage persistence, reduce fear of failure, foster a love of learning, enhance resilience

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation and persistence by fostering a belief in the ability to improve. Reduces anxiety and fear of failure, promoting greater engagement and willingness to take risks. Enhances resilience by reframing challenges as opportunities for growth. Supports deeper learning by encouraging reflection and analysis of mistakes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning contexts and individual learner needs. Praise and feedback can be tailored to specific efforts and progress. Activities can be designed to accommodate different levels of experience and prior knowledge. Focus can vary depending on the specific skills needing development.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner behavior, such as increased persistence, willingness to take risks, and positive self-talk. Track learner responses to challenges and setbacks. Analyze learner reflections on their growth and learning experiences. Measure the impact of growth mindset interventions on learner performance and achievement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that a growth mindset leads to greater academic achievement, increased motivation, and enhanced resilience. A growth mindset has been linked to improved performance in math, science, and other subjects. Individuals with a growth mindset are more likely to pursue challenging goals and persist in the face of adversity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners who fail in writing essays but don’t dwell too much on the failure, work harder to make the necessary amendments, leading to a growth mindset. When faced with a difficult math problem, learners with a growth mindset say that they made a mistake despite the problem’s difficulty because they were not yet familiar with the problem, and are ready to try a different approach to get it right on the next attempt.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Growth mindset feedback focuses on praising effort, strategies, and persistence rather than innate abilities. This approach encourages learners to view intelligence as malleable and cultivates a belief that skills can be developed through dedication and hard work. Providing respectful and specific feedback, highlighting 'good mistakes' as learning opportunities, and valuing the learning process over grades are key elements.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires intentional language and feedback practices from instructors and peers. Classroom activities should emphasize cooperative work and the value of learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Praise for intelligence can undermine motivation. Without a focus on the learning process, learners may base self-perceptions on grades alone. Competitive environments may hinder the development of a growth mindset.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a growth mindset, increase motivation, promote resilience, improve academic performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to embrace challenges and persist through setbacks. Helps learners see effort as a natural path to mastery. Enhances motivation, productivity, and confidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual learners' efforts and strategies. Different activities can be designed to match varying learner needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in learners' attitudes toward challenges and effort. Measure improvements in academic performance and persistence. Observe learners' responses to feedback and their willingness to take on difficult tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that growth mindset interventions can lead to higher academic achievement, increased motivation, and greater resilience in the face of setbacks. Students with a growth mindset are more likely to embrace challenges and see effort as a path to mastery.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers use many strategies to guide students through a period of reflection. These include discussions, interviews, questioning, and logs and journals. Discussions are about problem-solving processes. Invite students to share their metacognition, reveal their intentions, detail their strategies for solving a problem, describe their mental maps for monitoring their problem-solving process, and reflect on the strategy to determine its adequacy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, strategies to guide student reflection, and journal prompts or logs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to guide student reflection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Guide student reflection, improve problem-solving abilities, develop metacognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides teachers with strategies to guide students through a period of reflection, improves student problem-solving abilities, and develops student metacognition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of strategies to guide students through a period of reflection. They can also use a variety of journal prompts or logs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student problem-solving abilities and greater metacognition.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of guiding student reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher guides students through a period of reflection by using discussions and journal prompts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use guided discovery with word sorting and teacher questioning to help students understand spellings that depend on the position of a sound in a word or established conventions (like –ve). For example, the –ge and –dge pattern for the phoneme /j/ lends itself to word sorting and guided discovery.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, sorting materials, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction, may not be effective for learners with severe cognitive deficits

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grade 2 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop understanding of spelling patterns, improve spelling skills, enhance critical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active engagement with the material, helps learners discover patterns and rules for themselves, develops critical thinking skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific patterns or rules. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in sorting words according to spelling patterns. Monitor progress in spelling skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners discover spelling patterns and rules for themselves, promoting a deeper understanding of the spelling system.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided inquiry is an educational approach that blends inquiry activities with direct instruction. Inquiry activities let students explore and search for answers, guided to maintain a 'just right' level of difficulty similar to a mystery story. Direct instruction provides clear explanations and structures. The goal is to combine both to effectively achieve different learning objectives, such as learning ideas and skills in varied contexts like labs, lectures, and discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate lab setting, well-designed activities, skilled teachers, and tools for guidance and assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If a lab is too difficult, it can cause frustration. Requires careful design to ensure appropriate challenge. Differences in 'amount of help' raise questions of fairness if labwork is graded.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and undergraduate students, applicable in science labs and other learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach thinking skills, promote conceptual understanding, improve motivation, develop problem-solving abilities, enhance analytical skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes thinking and motivation when labs are well-designed with appropriate difficulty. Short-term frustration can motivate students to improve skills. Skillful teaching can minimize permanent frustration and build confidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Difficulty can be adjusted by modifying what students do in the lab (intrinsic difficulty) and providing guidance to support their ability to cope. Teachers can offer personally customized assistance during lab by observing students and adjusting difficulty level for individuals or groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, problem-solving skills, analytical abilities, motivation, and confidence. Assess learning outcomes based on conceptual understanding and skill development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Inquiry experiences promote thinking and motivation when labs are well designed. It combines active reception of knowledge with discovery learning, promoting effective and efficient learning experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Science labs using integrative analysis of instruction for effective planning in a course. Cognitive Apprenticeship uses modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration. (Source: Craig Rusbult, PhD)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided peer response using Turnitin PeerMark™ involves instructors pre-setting specific questions for learners to answer when providing feedback to their peers. This method provides structured prompts that guide the feedback process, making it easier to supervise and collate learner responses. It focuses on assessment by ensuring feedback addresses specific criteria.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to Turnitin PeerMark™ and clear instructions for learners on how to provide guided feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May limit the spontaneity and creativity of feedback due to structured prompts. Requires instructors to invest time in creating effective questions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where structured feedback processes are beneficial.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide structured peer feedback, ensure feedback addresses specific criteria, and facilitate easy supervision and collation of learner responses.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for learners to give feedback, ensuring that important criteria are addressed. Simplifies the supervision and collation of feedback by instructors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can customize the questions to align with specific learning objectives and assessment criteria.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Peer Interaction
  • Formative Assessment
  • Structured Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of guided peer feedback. Measure engagement and participation in the feedback process. Evaluate the impact of feedback on the quality of revised work.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This approach can enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of peer feedback, ensuring that important criteria are addressed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Turnitin PeerMark™ is a platform that supports guided peer response by allowing instructors to pre-set specific questions for learners to answer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Guided play combines the child-directed aspects of free play with intentional learning goals through light adult scaffolding. It involves exploration within a context designed to foster specific learning outcomes while maintaining child agency and gentle adult guidance to progress towards those goals. Adults can create educational settings for children to explore freely or engage in children's natural play, interjecting questions, comments, and explanations to enhance learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Play materials relevant to the learning goals, a space conducive to play, and an adult facilitator who can observe, ask guiding questions, and provide explanations without taking over the play activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The success of guided play depends on the adult's ability to strike a balance between providing guidance and allowing child-led exploration. Overly directive adults may stifle creativity and motivation. Requires preparation and thoughtful integration of learning goals into play scenarios.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preschool and elementary-aged children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster language development, enhance mathematics and spatial skills, promote cognitive development, encourage social and emotional growth

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Guided play leverages children's intrinsic motivation by allowing them to lead the activity while subtly incorporating educational elements. It is a flexible and engaging method that promotes active participation, discovery, and experimentation. The approach supports both academic and social-emotional growth through playful interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Guided play can be adapted to various settings and content areas by adjusting the learning opportunities within the play environment. Adults can tailor their level of involvement and the types of questions or prompts they provide based on individual learner needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's engagement and interactions during play to assess understanding of concepts. Evaluate their ability to apply new vocabulary, solve problems, and demonstrate spatial skills within the play context. Track the connections children make between play and real-world applications.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that guided play is an effective method for enhancing learning across various domains, including language, mathematics, and spatial skills. It supports the development of executive functions, social skills, and proactive control mechanisms. It has been shown to be more effective than direct instruction in some contexts, fostering creativity, emotional well-being, and social development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a 'restaurant' scenario, encourage creating menus, writing orders, and calculating bills to reinforce numeracy and literacy skills. During block play, ask questions about shapes and sizes to promote geometric understanding. While climbing a tree, discuss different tree characteristics and their role in the ecosystem to integrate science concepts.

docs.title: Have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice
Description
docs.text: Integrate direct instruction on understanding and managing emotions, as well as discussing relevant social issues, including social justice, to promote social awareness and emotional intelligence. Create a structured environment for safe and respectful dialogue.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a safe and supportive learning environment where learners feel comfortable sharing their thoughts and feelings. Requires instructors to be skilled facilitators who can guide discussions and manage conflict.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Discussions can be emotionally charged and potentially triggering for some learners. Instructors must be prepared to provide support and resources to learners who are struggling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who need to develop emotional intelligence and social awareness, K-12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, enhance social awareness, promote understanding of social justice issues, foster empathy and respect

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides direct instruction on emotional literacy and social issues, encourages open dialogue, and promotes empathy and respect. Helps learners develop communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to specific age groups and developmental levels. Use age-appropriate materials and activities to teach emotional literacy and discuss social issues. Topics can include bullying, discrimination, and inequality.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and contributions to discussions. Assess learner understanding of emotional literacy and social issues through written assignments or presentations. Collect learner reflections on their learning and growth.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that explicit instruction on emotions and social issues can improve emotional literacy, increase social awareness, and promote positive social and emotional outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor might teach learners how to identify and express their emotions. In a social studies class, students might discuss the history of civil rights and the ongoing struggle for social justice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students read an excerpt of a difficult article in Google Docs. First, they highlight words they don't know. Then, in pairs, they read a paragraph together and highlight key ideas, discussing why those parts are important. Next, they individually devise a four-word heading for that portion of the text based on the main ideas they've highlighted and compare headings. If they came up with something different, they have to justify why theirs is better. The teacher can then ask for all the agreed-upon headings and pair different groups together so that four students have to discuss their headings and come to consensus on the single best representation of the main ideas. At the end, the teacher might have groups present or even have the whole class vote on their favorite heading. And individually students can reflect on the process they went through, how the heading helps them understand the reading, and how it helps them answer the driving question of the unit.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to Google Docs, time for reading, discussion, and reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant instructional time. Requires learners to actively engage with the text and each other.

docs.title: Implementation Variability
docs.text: • Some implementations run this as a general reading-comprehension technique across subjects; others narrow it to a specific content area (e.g., social studies) where the highlight-then-heading routine doubles as close reading of dense, information-heavy text. The core steps are the same either way — only the text selection and framing change.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to improve their reading comprehension and analysis skills — e.g., social studies or other content-heavy subject classrooms, where the technique supports close reading of dense text.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, identify key ideas, justify thinking, improve collaboration skills, encourage active engagement with text

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active reading, promotes collaborative learning, makes thinking visible, and provides opportunities for reflection and justification.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the difficulty of the text based on the learner's reading level. Provide different levels of support for highlighting and creating headings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate students' headings and highlights for accuracy and relevance. Track their ability to justify their thinking. Collect student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The only real affordance of the technology is the ability to change the heading multiple times in a clean way. But it does help teachers see how to bring dialogue and discussion into the classroom, even when students are reading on the computer, and it has achieved the goal of slowing down reading.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tasks involve studying the food pyramid, learning about daily requirements, and planning food for one day. They promote an understanding of health and dietary needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Food pyramid chart, dietary information, planning materials

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require access to dietary information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying science and social perspectives

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the food pyramid, learn about daily requirements, plan a balanced diet

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes understanding of healthy eating habits. Enhances planning and decision-making skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Food selection can be varied. Dietary plans can be tailored to different needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in understanding the food pyramid, correctness in meeting daily requirements, appropriateness of dietary plans

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of health and diet, enhanced planning skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Food We Eat (CCSSO): Study the food pyramid, learn about daily requirements, and plan food for one day.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Heat transfer investigations involve exploring how different materials and environments affect the transfer of heat. Learners conduct experiments to determine which materials are best for keeping drinks cool or observing how temperature changes in different environments. These tasks improve understanding of heat transfer principles and their real-world applications.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Containers made of different materials, thermometers, cold/hot drinks, controlled environments

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires precise measurement and control of variables. May need access to specialized equipment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand heat transfer principles, investigate the effect of materials on heat transfer, relate cooling and warming to environmental temperature, develop experimental skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical application of heat transfer concepts. Enhances experimental skills and observation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Materials and environments can be varied for different experiments. Tasks can be modified to match the learner's skill level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in temperature measurements, correct identification of best materials for insulation, logical reasoning in explaining observations

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of heat transfer, enhanced experimental skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Containers (TIMSS): Learners investigate the effect of container materials on heat transfer. Keep Cool (CCSSO): Learners determine which type of container would be best to use to keep drinks cool on a hot day.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Hexagonal thinking is a mixed retrieval and elaboration strategy that uses hexagonal cards, paper, or programs to investigate how ideas and concepts are connected. Learners write historical events and forces on hexagons and arrange them in cause and effect relationships. The proposed connections are explained using arrows and a written document and shared with the whole class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires hexagonal cards, paper, or a program like PowerPoint or Google Slides.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to have a foundational understanding of the concepts being connected.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Secondary and higher education learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Investigate how ideas and concepts are connected.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners see connections between different concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various subjects and topics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Argument Construction
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the accuracy and depth of the connections proposed by learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy helps learners investigate how ideas and concepts are connected.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: High-frequency word lists (e.g., Dolch and Fry) are collections of the most commonly used words in reading and writing. They are designed to help learners quickly recognize these words by sight to improve reading fluency and writing skills. These lists often contain words that are difficult to sound out or illustrate, making memorization essential for early reading development. Activities for using these lists include word walls, digital spelling charts, flashcards, word searches, cloze passages, and word shape worksheets. Regularly reviewing and practicing these words in meaningful contexts, such as sentence writing, can significantly enhance reading and writing proficiency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to high-frequency word lists (Dolch, Fry), printable worksheets, flashcards, digital tools (e.g., digital spelling chart), and class time for explicit instruction and practice. Teachers need to monitor student progress and provide targeted feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reliance on memorization without contextual understanding can limit deeper comprehension. Some learners may find rote memorization tedious. Requires consistent practice and reinforcement to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily K–5 learners, but also beneficial for older students who need to improve foundational reading and writing skills, including English language learners and learners with disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading fluency, enhance writing skills, increase sight word recognition, build vocabulary, and develop spelling accuracy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports automaticity in word recognition, reduces cognitive load during reading, enhances reading comprehension, improves spelling accuracy, and provides a foundation for advanced literacy skills. Digital spelling charts can be customized for individual student needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning styles through different activities such as visual (word shape worksheets), kinesthetic (flashcards), and contextual (cloze passages). Digital versions can be tailored to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student performance on sight word recognition tests, monitor improvements in reading fluency, assess spelling accuracy in writing assignments, and analyze student engagement in various activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that sight word recognition is crucial for early reading development, enhancing fluency and comprehension. Explicit instruction and practice with high-frequency words have been shown to improve overall literacy skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A first-grade teacher uses Dolch word flashcards daily to help students quickly recognize sight words. A fourth-grade teacher incorporates Fry words into weekly spelling tests and writing assignments to reinforce learning.

docs.title: Highlight and Explore Patterns, Critical Features, Big Ideas, and Relationships
Description
docs.text: Accentuating important information and how it relates to the learning goal helps learners focus their attention and understand the key concepts. This includes highlighting critical features and big ideas. It also involves exploring patterns and relationships between concepts. The goal is to help learners make sense of complex information and develop a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be skilled in identifying key concepts and designing effective visual aids. Instructors need to be able to guide learners in exploring patterns and relationships.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and effort. Some learners may find too much highlighting distracting. It's essential to strike a balance between clarity and simplicity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance focus, improve comprehension, support knowledge organization, promote critical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports focus by highlighting critical features and big ideas, improves comprehension by helping learners understand key concepts, supports knowledge organization by exploring patterns and relationships, and promotes critical thinking by encouraging learners to analyze and evaluate information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide visual aids and graphic organizers to highlight key concepts. Use color-coding and highlighting to draw attention to critical features. Encourage learners to identify patterns and relationships in the information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of key concepts through discussions or written assignments. Track improvements in comprehension and knowledge organization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that highlighting and exploring patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships can enhance focus, improve comprehension, support knowledge organization, and promote critical thinking. Studies show that visual aids and graphic organizers can improve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using visual aids and graphic organizers to highlight key concepts. Using color-coding and highlighting to draw attention to critical features. Encouraging learners to identify patterns and relationships in the information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Model how to highlight or circle mathematical words in word problems that prompt multiplication or division. Brainstorm potential words indicating multiplication or division with learners. Display words as class word walls or graphic organizers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Highlighters or colored pencils, word wall space, time for brainstorming

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if learners lack conceptual understanding of math operations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with math vocabulary or word problems

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop math communication, support working memory

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners identify key information in word problems, reduces cognitive load

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different grade levels and math concepts. Word walls can be customized with learner-generated vocabulary.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether learners are accurately highlighting key words in word problems. Assess the completeness and accuracy of the word wall or graphic organizer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Word walls and graphic organizers have been shown to improve vocabulary acquisition and retention. Highlighting helps learners focus on important information.

docs.title: Highlighting and Exploration of Patterns, Critical Features, Big Ideas, and Relationships
Description
docs.text: Accentuation of important information and its relationship to the learning goal. This involves emphasizing key patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships within the content. Highlighting and exploring these elements helps learners focus on the most important information and understand how it relates to the overall learning objectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Visual aids, graphic organizers, concept maps, and simplified explanations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of information to highlight. Some learners may become overly reliant on highlighted information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who struggle with attention or have difficulty identifying key information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding, improve retention, focus attention, clarify learning goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focuses attention on the most important information. Enhances understanding of key concepts and relationships. Clarifies the learning goals.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use highlighting, underlining, and other visual cues to emphasize important information. Provide graphic organizers and concept maps to illustrate relationships. Break down complex concepts into simpler components.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner understanding of key patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships. Monitor learner use of visual aids and graphic organizers. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of strategies for highlighting and exploring key information.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learning outcomes: Research suggests that highlighting and exploring key information can significantly improve understanding and retention, particularly for learners who struggle with attention or have difficulty identifying key information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The highlighting strategy is a digital approach to enhance text engagement, using tools to create individualized highlighters with different colors in digital documents. For example, Argument #1 might be in red, while Argument #2 might be in green. The highlights can be exported by color, creating a table with ideas that can be summarized. This supports deeper analysis and organization of information. Highlighting strategy is made much easier and more effective because it is digital. The various colors are labeled so the student doesn’t need a key to decipher highlights and all the information can be exported in one table, rather than having to sift back through the entire article.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • It helps them discern between different things, and secondly, you’ve asked them to summarize what they’ve done

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Since some kids have difficulty prioritizing what to highlight, a teacher could limit the number of items for each color.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Discern between different ideas, summarize what they’ve done

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Consolidation of information, labeled so the student doesn’t need a key to decipher highlights and all the information can be exported in one table, rather than having to sift back through the entire article.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The various colors are labeled so the student doesn’t need a key to decipher highlights and all the information can be exported in one table, rather than having to sift back through the entire article.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • That provides good reflection and consolidation of the information they just picked out. Since some kids have difficulty prioritizing what to highlight, a teacher could limit the number of items for each color.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • In this case, the highlighting strategy is made much easier and more effective because it is digital. The various colors are labeled so the student doesn’t need a key to decipher highlights and all the information can be exported in one table, rather than having to sift back through the entire article.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher could limit the number of items for each color.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use a Google Doc add-on tool to create individualized highlighters in different colors. For example, all the text that supports “Argument #1” might be in red, while the evidence in “Argument #2” might be in green, and so on. The highlights can be exported by color, which creates a table with all the ideas. Students can then add another column to the highlighter table, where they can write summaries of everything in that highlighted category.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to Google Docs and the highlighting add-on tool, time for reading, highlighting, and summarizing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to actively engage with the text and identify relevant information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to improve their reading comprehension and analysis skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, categorize information, summarize ideas, improve analytical skills, facilitate reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual approach to organizing and categorizing information, supports the development of analytical skills, and facilitates reflection on the learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the text based on the learner's reading level. Provide different levels of support for highlighting and summarizing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate students' highlighted sections and summaries for accuracy and completeness. Track their ability to categorize information. Collect student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual organizers and summarization strategies have been shown to improve reading comprehension and analytical skills. Reflection promotes retention and deeper understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Historically Responsive Literacy (HRL) is a framework that seeks to cultivate literacy, intellect, and self-efficacy by connecting learning deeply to who we are and what agency we have in the world. It draws inspiration from 1830s-era literary societies and centers around the goals of identity development, skill development, intellectual development, criticality, and joy. HRL helps teachers reframe curriculum, objectives, goals, and standards around these elements, drawing upon Black history as a model for a more complete and comprehensive education.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A commitment to culturally responsive teaching, knowledge of Black history and literature, and a willingness to challenge traditional educational practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant curriculum redesign and professional development. Some educators may resist changes to traditional practices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators working with diverse student populations, particularly Black and Brown students (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop literacy skills, foster intellectual growth, promote self-efficacy, and cultivate critical thinking skills while recognizing and celebrating students' identities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and relevant learning experience. Empowers students to connect with their heritage and identity. Develops critical thinking skills and promotes social justice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Curriculum and activities can be tailored to reflect the cultural backgrounds and experiences of students. Students can choose texts and topics that are relevant to their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Discussion Sections
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and participation, improved literacy skills, and greater understanding of Black history and culture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more equitable and empowering learning environment for all students, particularly those from historically marginalized groups.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners examine famous website hoaxes to identify clues that suggest the site is not genuine. They look for inconsistencies, lack of corroboration, and other red flags.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to examples of famous website hoaxes and a framework for guiding the analysis (e.g., a checklist or rubric).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The activity may be less effective if learners are not familiar with the context or background of the hoax.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical evaluation skills and awareness of deceptive online information.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Sharpens critical thinking and digital literacy by engaging learners in detecting deceptive tactics and misinformation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The complexity of the hoax websites and the evaluation criteria can be adjusted based on the learners' skill level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to identify clues and justify their conclusions about the authenticity of hoax websites.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Exposure to website hoaxes can increase awareness of online deception and improve critical evaluation skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Home-based literacy support involves schools providing families with resources and guidance to support students’ learning at home. This includes strategies for having discussions about school, creating organized learning spaces, completing interactive assignments, and communicating high expectations. By equipping families with practical tools and knowledge, schools can extend learning beyond the classroom, fostering a collaborative partnership that enhances student outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Schools need to develop and distribute relevant resources, provide training for staff on how to effectively engage families, and establish clear communication channels.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on the active participation of families. Logistical barriers such as demanding work schedules, transportation difficulties, and lack of childcare can hinder engagement. Some families may require additional support to overcome these challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools aiming to improve family engagement and extend learning beyond the classroom, particularly for low-income families and families of color.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student academic achievement and positive behaviors, improve student motivation and self-efficacy, and empower families with the skills and resources to support learning at home.

docs.title: Affordances
