docs.text: • This approach has a stronger positive effect than school-based involvement alone. It supports active engagement by giving families specific tasks and knowledge. It also enhances motivation by showing families that their efforts directly contribute to their child's success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Resources can be tailored to the specific needs of different families, such as non-native English speakers, families with different cultural backgrounds, and those with students in special education. Guidance can be adapted to align with the student’s grade level and individual learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student academic progress and behavior outcomes. Track family participation in provided activities and feedback on the usefulness of resources. Assess changes in family members' sense of empowerment and well-being.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that home-based family engagement practices are often more powerful than school-based practices, leading to improved student outcomes (Thompson, K M, Gillis, T J, Fairman, J, Mason, C A. 2014). Schools that provide specific resources and guidance see greater positive effects.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school provides a guide for families on how to discuss school topics at home. They also offer training sessions for parents on creating an organized learning space and assisting with interactive assignments. Mobile communication is used to provide learning tips to parents.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When new students come to the classroom, ask them to read books in their home language to show you what they know about reading. By using the collective skills and knowledge of all students (both ELL and English-L1 students) in the classroom, even a monolingual teacher can tap into these valuable language resources that ELLs have and do so with the confidence that these methods will promote their language development — in English as well as the home language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to books in students' home languages.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to find books in all of the languages spoken by students in the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Newcomer English Language Learners (ELLs)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess students' reading skills in their home language, build confidence, and create a classroom environment that values multilingualism.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way for teachers to assess students' literacy skills even if they don't speak the students' home language. Affirms the value of students' home languages and cultures.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose books that are appropriate for their reading level and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' reading fluency, comprehension, and expression in their home language.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students with strong reading skills in the home language also have strong reading skills in their second language.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This checklist is a tool designed to help parents assess and enhance the literacy-richness of their home environment. It contains statements about resources and activities, categorized into what the child has at home, what an adult does, and what the child observes. Parents check whether each statement is true or false for their household, then tally the results to gauge the overall level of literacy support in the home. The checklist provides guidance on steps parents can take to further enrich their child's exposure to books and reading, fostering early literacy development.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to the checklist (either in print or digital format) and a few minutes for parents to reflect on and complete the assessment. Requires parent to reflect and check off items in checklist.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The checklist provides a general overview and may not capture the nuances of individual family literacy practices. The effectiveness relies on honest self-reporting and may be influenced by social desirability bias. It may not fully address the complexities of diverse family structures and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Parents and caregivers of preschool and early elementary-aged children.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate the presence of literacy-promoting resources and activities in the home environment, identify areas for improvement, and encourage parental involvement in early literacy development.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way for parents to reflect on their home literacy practices. It supports active engagement by encouraging self-assessment and goal-setting. The checklist is designed to be easily accessible and actionable, fostering a sense of empowerment and motivation for parents to enhance their child's literacy environment. Immediate feedback is provided through the scoring guide.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The checklist can be adapted to different cultural contexts and family circumstances by modifying statements to reflect available resources and culturally relevant activities. Checklists are available in both English and Spanish.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The number of statements checked as 'true' provides a quantitative measure of the home literacy environment. Qualitative insights can be gained through follow-up discussions with parents about their responses and planned actions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that a literacy-rich home environment is positively correlated with children's early literacy skills and academic achievement. This checklist aims to promote such environments by raising awareness and guiding parental actions. (See references to parent involvement and literacy success).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A parent uses the checklist to identify that their child has few rhyme books and resolves to purchase more. A school provides the checklist during parent-teacher conferences and discusses strategies for improvement based on the results.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners visit the home living center to role play different characters and relate these characters to different emotions. Help them to make their characters even more real by giving them emotions and acting those out.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator to create the context and provide guidance during the activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be willing to perform in front of others. May not be effective with learners who are naturally introverted.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, including early childhood, elementary, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve perspective-taking skills, promote empathetic understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides authentic scenario to explore emotions through role playing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select specific emotions they wish to explore. Prompts and character suggestions can also be provided.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The facilitator can observe how the learner uses vocabulary to create their story. Ask learners to do an individual reflection of how they used emotions and what they learned in the role playing exercise.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of role-playing and dramatic activities to enhance emotional understanding and social skills. (Source: Spontaneous Drama Improves Communication Skills - https://www.livestrong.com/article/198645-spontaneous-drama-improves-communication-skills/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sending weekly, biweekly, or monthly surveys home can provide ongoing data and insight into students and their families. Short surveys with one or two questions at a time have been found to be more receptive and responsive to families. Surveys can inquire about art at home, music, visual art, movies, and television shows, family traditions, favorite recipes, and student supports needed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Survey creation skills, communication channels to distribute surveys

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to analyze data, may be difficult to get high response rates

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, educators, and families

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gather data about students and families, build connections, identify needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides ongoing data, builds connections, identifies needs

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Surveys can be tailored to address specific needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Response
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track response rates, analyze survey data

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Home surveys can provide valuable insights into students and families.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One learner assumes the role of a book character, significant figure in history, or concept (such as a tornado, an animal, or the Titanic). Sitting in front of the rest of the class, the learner responds to classmates’ questions while staying in character in that role. Give more learners the opportunity to be in the hot seat while increasing everyone’s participation by having learners do hot seat discussions in small groups, where one person per group acts as the “character” and three or four others ask them questions. In another variation, several learners could form a panel of different characters, taking questions from the class all together and interacting with one another like guests on a TV talk show.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where one learner can sit in front of the rest of the class, a topic or character to role-play, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are shy or reluctant to speak in front of a group or who struggle with role-playing, requires careful facilitation to ensure respectful communication and avoid stereotyping.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for engaging learners with historical figures, literary characters, and scientific concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active recall and application of knowledge, enhance communication skills, encourage perspective-taking, foster creativity and imagination

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active recall and application of knowledge, promotes communication skills, provides opportunities for perspective-taking, fosters creativity and imagination, supports learner engagement

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the role they want to play and the questions they want to ask. Teachers can provide scaffolding for learners who struggle with role-playing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the activity, review the quality of their responses to questions, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances active recall and application of knowledge, promotes communication skills, fosters creativity and imagination

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A game played in partners where children roll two dice to determine the dimensions of an array to draw on a 100 grid, aiming to fill the grid as much as possible. They write the number sentence that describes the grid.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dice and 100 grids

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to multiplication facts within 100

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop multiplication fact fluency, understand area models

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activity, promotes strategic thinking, reinforces multiplication facts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can adjust the size of the grid or the number of dice

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's ability to strategically place arrays and accurately write number sentences

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of multiplication fact fluency and understanding of area models

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Partner rolls a 4 and a 6 to make a 4x6 array on the grid, then writes 4 x 6 = 24.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An activity where children have cubes and a cup. They hide some cubes in the cup, show the leftovers, and the other children work out how many are hiding and state the full number combination.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Cubes and cups

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to addition facts

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop addition fact fluency

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activity, promotes problem-solving, reinforces addition facts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Number of cubes can be adjusted to match skill level

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's ability to quickly and accurately determine the number of hidden cubes

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of addition fact fluency

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Child has 10 cubes, hides 4 in the cup, and shows 6. Group says that the child is hiding 4 cubes and that 6 and 4 make 10.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instruction on the relationship between spelling and reading. Research shows that learning to spell and learning to read rely on much of the same underlying knowledge, such as the relationships between letters and sounds, and that spelling instruction can be designed to help children better understand that key knowledge, resulting in better reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured spelling instruction, materials for phoneme-grapheme mapping, activities for exploring morphology, access to lists and word walls.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if spelling instruction is not integrated with reading instruction. Also, it is critical to focus on individual learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, teachers, reading specialists

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To improve reading fluency and comprehension by enhancing spelling skills and understanding of phoneme-grapheme relationships.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances reading skills by strengthening spelling proficiency, improves writing by reducing cognitive load, and builds overall literacy skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Spelling instruction can be tailored to individual student needs by focusing on specific phoneme-grapheme correspondences or morphology. Explicit, systematic instruction is provided.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assessments include spelling tests, writing samples, and reading comprehension measures to show a correlation in performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Solid research shows a strong relationship between spelling and reading. Learning to spell enhances children’s reading and writing, improving overall literacy skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Perkins and Salomon's research on transfer of learning identified two complementary teacher strategies for promoting positive transfer (Souza, 2016). Hugging encourages transfer by incorporating similarities between the learning situation and the future situations in which the learning might be used — the learning experience "hugs" its eventual application closely. Bridging encourages transfer by helping students find connections between what they already know and new concepts, and by abstracting existing knowledge so it generalizes — building a "bridge" across situations that are not superficially similar. Transfer itself is less a deliberate act by the learner than a product of the learning environment, which makes the teacher, as part of that environment, a direct instrument of transfer — for better or worse (Souza, 2016).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clear sense of the target future situation(s) the learning is meant to transfer to, so hugging techniques can be built around genuine similarity rather than superficial resemblance
  • Time for students to engage in abstraction (analogy-building, principle-seeking) rather than only practicing the surface task

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Hugging without bridging risks producing only near transfer (performance limited to closely similar situations); bridging without any grounded, concrete practice risks abstraction with nothing for students to anchor it to

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners preparing to apply a skill or concept in a substantially different context from the one in which they learned it (far transfer), where hugging and bridging are both especially load-bearing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Positive transfer of knowledge or skill to new tasks, situations, or problems, as covered generally in Transfer of Learning

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Hugging — Build the learning experience to resemble its eventual use context as closely as possible. Methods include simulation games, mental practice (rehearsing performance in the target context), and contingency learning (practicing under conditions that vary the way the target situation will vary).
  2. Bridging — Help students find connections between what they are learning and what they already know, and support them in abstracting general principles from specific instances. Methods include brainstorming connections, developing analogies and metaphors, and prompting metacognitive reflection on what makes the current problem similar to others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After learning to solve a certain class of algebra problems, a teacher has students brainstorm (bridging) other domains where the same underlying structure appears, while also practicing the skill under conditions that mimic a real assessment's time pressure and format (hugging).

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Perkins, D. N., & Salomon, G. (1992). Transfer of learning. International Encyclopedia of Education.
  • Souza, D. A. (2016). How the brain learns (5th ed.). Corwin Press.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher's perspectives on learning. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Hyperlinked teaching provides students with direct avenues for further inquiry and exploration. Students are not stifled in their learning tract but are able to choose what to learn more about within a topic, and what they already know and can move beyond. Additionally, students are encouraged to reference their connections with evidence from multiple sources. Provide pockets of opportunities for your students to explore a topic in more detail, learn about the topic from a different perspective, or to create a solution using multiple sources and products.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of learning resources (e.g., articles, videos, websites). Instructional time for exploration, discussion, and project development.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant planning to curate relevant and high-quality resources. Some learners may struggle with the open-ended nature of inquiry and require more structure.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education learners interested in pursuing self-directed inquiry and connecting learning to personal interests.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster learner autonomy, promote deeper inquiry, encourage exploration of multiple perspectives, develop research skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner motivation and engagement by allowing choice and control. Supports the development of research skills and the ability to synthesize information from multiple sources. Encourages critical thinking and problem-solving.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable by providing a range of topics, resources, and project options aligned to learner interests and skill levels. Teachers can scaffold inquiry with targeted questions and guidance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate student projects, presentations, or reports for evidence of research, synthesis, and critical thinking. Assess learner engagement and motivation through observation and self-reflection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that inquiry-based learning can lead to deeper understanding, greater retention, and increased motivation. Learner choice and control are associated with positive academic outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: At Crellin Elementary School in Oakland, Maryland, teachers encouraged students to ask “I wonder” questions to push their learning beyond the classroom. After visiting a local barn and garden, for example, Dave Miller realized his fifth-grade students had more questions about animals and plants than he had time to answer, so he had them write down anything they were confused or curious about, which helped him plan future lessons and experiments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires journals or notebooks for students to write in. Requires time for students to write in their journals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to ask questions. Teachers need to find time to review student journals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for elementary school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster curiosity and inquiry. Encourage critical thinking. Help teachers understand student questions and interests.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to ask questions and explore their interests. Provides teachers with valuable information about student understanding and interests. Can be used to plan future lessons and experiments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can write about whatever they are curious about.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Question Formulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student journals to assess understanding and identify areas of curiosity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters curiosity and inquiry. Encourages critical thinking. Helps teachers understand student questions and interests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After visiting a local barn and garden, have students write down anything they were confused or curious about. Use these questions to plan future lessons and experiments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
IDEAL (Bransford & Steen, 1984) is a general problem-solving system usable across curriculum areas and problem types, named for its five stages:

  1. Identify the problem — Learners confirm they know what the problem actually is and whether they have stated it clearly, before attempting a solution.
  2. Define terms — Learners check that they understand what each word in the problem statement actually means.
  3. Explore strategies — Learners compile relevant information and try out candidate strategies — drawing diagrams, working backward, or breaking a complex problem into manageable units.
  4. Act on the strategy — Learners select one of the explored strategies and actually apply it.
  5. Look at the effects — Learners ask themselves whether the result is an acceptable solution, closing the loop back to Identify if it is not.

Many other systems for teaching problem-solving exist for specific domains — general problem solving (Burkell, Schneider, & Pressley, 1990; Mayer, 1987; Sternberg, 1988), scientific thinking (Kuhn, 1989), mathematical problem solving (Schoenfeld, 1989), and writing at both the elementary (Harris & Graham, 1992) and adolescent (Applebee, 1984; Langer & Applebee, 1987) levels — but IDEAL's value is its explicit generality: unlike a domain-specific heuristic, it can be taught once and applied across curriculum areas (Pressley, 1995).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A problem complex enough that jumping directly to a solution attempt is likely to fail or waste effort
  • Willingness to have learners pause at each explicit stage rather than moving straight from reading a problem to attempting an answer

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The model's five stages are a general scaffold, not a domain-specific technique — for a specific problem type, a more specialized system (e.g., a mathematical problem-solving heuristic) may add value IDEAL alone does not

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners across a wide range of curriculum areas who need an explicit, transferable structure for approaching complex problems, rather than a domain-specific technique

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Applying a general, teachable problem-solving process to well- or ill-structured problems, per Well-Structured vs. Ill-Structured Problems

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify — Confirm the problem is correctly and clearly understood before proceeding.
  2. Define — Check the meaning of each term in the problem statement.
  3. Explore — Gather relevant information and generate candidate strategies (diagrams, working backward, decomposition into subproblems).
  4. Act — Choose one strategy from those explored and apply it.
  5. Look — Evaluate whether the outcome is an acceptable solution; if not, cycle back to Identify with the new information gained.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Task Analysis — both decompose a complex task, though task analysis targets prerequisite-skill sequencing rather than in-the-moment problem-solving

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bransford, J. D., & Stein, B. S. (1984). The IDEAL problem solver: A guide for improving thinking, learning, and creativity. W. H. Freeman.
  • Pressley, M. (1995). More about the development of self-regulation: Complex, long-term, and thoroughly social. Educational Psychologist.
  • Burkell, J., Schneider, B., & Pressley, M. (1990). Mathematics. In M. Pressley & Associates (Eds.), Cognitive strategy instruction that really improves children's academic performance. Brookline Books.
  • Mayer, R. E. (1987). Educational psychology: A cognitive approach. Little, Brown.
  • Sternberg, R. J. (1988). The triarchic mind: A new theory of human intelligence. Viking Penguin.
  • Kuhn, D. (1989). Children and adults as intuitive scientists. Psychological Review, 96(4), 674-689.
  • Schoenfeld, A. H. (1989). Teaching mathematical thinking and problem solving. In L. B. Resnick & L. E. Klopfer (Eds.), Toward the thinking curriculum: Current cognitive research (pp. 83-103). ASCD.
  • Harris, K. R., & Graham, S. (1992). Self-regulated strategy development: A part of the writing process. In M. Pressley, K. R. Harris, & J. T. Guthrie (Eds.), Promoting academic competence and literacy in school. Academic Press.
  • Applebee, A. N. (1984). Contexts for learning to write: Studies of secondary school instruction. Ablex.
  • Langer, J. A., & Applebee, A. N. (1987). How writing shapes thinking: A study of teaching and learning. NCTE.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Problem-solving. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings. Students categorize feeling words by the type of feeling. Literature is used to have students analyze characters’ feelings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emotion charts, picture cards, literature selections, and class time for discussion and activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may have difficulty connecting with abstract concepts of emotions, especially if they have limited experience or trauma. It's important to create a safe and supportive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, especially those who struggle with identifying their own and others' emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify emotions, categorize feelings, analyze characters' feelings in literature

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way for students to recognize and name feelings, which is a foundational step in emotional regulation. Using literature helps students connect emotions with real-life situations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different levels of support, such as matching simple emotions for younger learners or analyzing complex emotions for older learners. Literature choices can be tailored to students' interests and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to accurately identify and label emotions in themselves and others. Track their participation in discussions and activities related to analyzing characters' feelings.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students who can identify and label their emotions are better able to manage them, which can lead to improved academic performance, social relationships, and overall well-being. Research supports the connection between emotional intelligence and positive outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses picture cards of different facial expressions and asks students to match them with corresponding feeling words. A class reads a story and discusses how the characters' emotions influenced their actions.

docs.title: Identify Key Background Knowledge in Math Problems
Description
docs.text: Identify what kinds of background knowledge learners need to understand a math problem. Brainstorm potential questions learners might have, some relevant and some not. Examples: a math problem about a coupon and sales tax at a dog groomer requires knowing what a dog groomer, sales tax, coupon, deluxe, estimate, and discount are. This area is powerful for collaboration between math teachers and ELL teachers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Collaborative planning, activities to brainstorm potential questions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and collaboration, may be challenging to implement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify necessary background knowledge, enhance collaboration between math and ELL teachers

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators anticipate learner questions, improves understanding of math problems

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor instruction based on background knowledge

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner's understanding, assess the impact of the instruction

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learner understanding of math problems

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a math problem about a fishing pole on sale: What is 'percent off'? What is a sale? What is 'regularly priced'? What steps have to be followed to solve this problem?

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Have students record messages from their inner voice over a week in a journal or notebook. Remind them that self-talk is incessant and ongoing, and that they should aim to record at least 5 inner voice messages per day to capture this.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journal or notebook, writing utensil, consistent daily practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult for some learners to consistently record their self-talk. Requires time and effort to observe internal thoughts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify personal self-talk messages in various situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners become more aware of their constant internal dialogue.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by adjusting the frequency and depth of journaling prompts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review journal entries for frequency, patterns, and content of self-talk messages.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased awareness of personal self-talk patterns (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Identifying and Addressing Self-Regulation Strengths and Challenges
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves educators identifying students' strengths and challenges related to self-regulation, and then using strategies to leverage strengths to support learning. Self-regulation is the ability to alter and regulate emotional and behavioral responses. All students have varying degrees of strengths and challenges related to self-regulation, which can be addressed by focusing on strengths.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Educator awareness of self-regulation concepts and strategies. Time for observation and interaction with students. Resources for scaffolding, journaling, and mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation and understanding of individual student needs. Success depends on the educator's ability to connect with and support students. It is not something that your students will either 'have' or 'not have'.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with particular attention to those struggling with self-regulation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' self-regulation skills by leveraging their strengths, enhance emotional and behavioral control, and promote positive engagement in classroom activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop metacognitive awareness, manage emotional impulses, and react positively to challenging situations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to individual student strengths and challenges. Scaffolding, journaling, and mindfulness techniques can be adapted.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in student behavior and emotional responses. Review student journal entries for metacognitive awareness. Collect student reflections on the effectiveness of strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of self-regulation for academic performance and emotional well-being. Strategies like scaffolding, journaling, and mindfulness have been shown to improve self-regulation skills.

docs.title: Identifying and Supporting Learners with Relationship Skills
Description
docs.text: Identifying and supporting learners who have learning strengths or challenges related to relationship skills helps them improve and succeed. Relationship skills involve the ability to form and maintain healthy connections with others by communicating, cooperating, and managing conflict effectively. Relationship skills also require the capability to resist inappropriate social pressure and offer or seek help when appropriate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor must identify each learners' strengths and support them effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • This can be difficult for learners who have serious relationship challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' relationship skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focusing on learners' strengths helps them build relationship skills and succeed socially and academically.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies include pairing learners with others who model strong relationship skills, providing group assignments where learners can find common ground, display anchor charts outlining fair communication protocols for class discussions, and use literature or social stories to explicitly teach relationship skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of improved interactions between learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A classroom of learners with good relationship skills will be more harmonious and perform better academically.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings. This can include categorizing feeling words or analyzing characters' feelings in literature.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Resources for identifying and labeling feelings, such as facial expression cards, lists of feeling words, or literary texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require sensitivity to learners' emotional states and cultural backgrounds. Some learners may need additional support in recognizing and labeling emotions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners and adult learners in emotional intelligence programs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance the ability to recognize and understand emotions in oneself and others.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases emotional literacy and promotes understanding of emotional expressions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted based on age, cultural relevance, and learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately identify and label feelings in themselves and others. Review written or verbal responses for depth of emotional understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Identifying and labeling feelings fosters self-awareness and emotional intelligence. Understanding one's own emotions is a foundational skill for social and emotional learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Kaitlin Robbs’ wheel diagram to identify basic feelings and make them more specific and nuanced.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identifying obstacles involves recognizing potential challenges that could impede progress toward a goal. This includes assessing gaps in knowledge, skills, resources, or other constraints. Recognizing these obstacles allows for proactive planning and problem-solving.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness, critical thinking, and the ability to anticipate potential roadblocks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overemphasis on potential obstacles can lead to paralysis by analysis. Some challenges may be unforeseen and require adaptive responses.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Useful for anyone setting goals, particularly those involving significant changes or new ventures.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Proactively address potential challenges, improve problem-solving skills, and increase the likelihood of achieving goals.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables proactive planning and mitigation of potential issues. By anticipating challenges, learners can develop strategies to overcome them, increasing their resilience and adaptability.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can identify obstacles specific to their circumstances and goals. Tailoring strategies to address these specific challenges enhances the likelihood of success.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Individual Reflection
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Effectiveness is measured by the ability to anticipate and mitigate obstacles, as evidenced by progress towards goals despite challenges.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that proactive problem-solving increases the likelihood of achieving goals by minimizing disruptions and maintaining momentum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Identifying a lack of funding for a project and developing a fundraising plan. Recognizing a skills gap and enrolling in a training course.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students record the messages from their inner voice over the course of a week in a journal or notebook. Reminding students that self-talk is incessant and happens all the time, encouraging them to record a minimum of five inner voice messages per day.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journals or notebooks for recording self-talk. Time for students to reflect and write down their thoughts. A reminder system to ensure students record their thoughts regularly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may forget to record their thoughts. Some students may find it difficult to articulate their inner voice. The accuracy of the recordings depends on students' honesty and self-awareness.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those who are learning to become more aware of their thoughts and feelings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To enable students to recognize and document their internal dialogue over a period of time.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by encouraging learners to pay attention to their thoughts. Supports self-reflection by providing a structured way to document and review their inner voice. Helps students recognize patterns and themes in their self-talk.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and learning styles. Can be modified to focus on specific situations or emotions. Educators can provide different types of journals or notebooks to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' journals or notebooks for patterns and themes in their self-talk. Assess students' ability to accurately identify and document their inner voice. Observe students' engagement and participation in discussions about self-talk.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the benefit of self-monitoring strategies, especially when those strategies include journaling. Identifying self-talk can give students insights into their own beliefs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students keep a daily log of their inner voice messages, recording at least five messages per day. Students use a structured journal with prompts to guide their self-reflection. Students share examples of their self-talk with the class, focusing on patterns and themes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This activity enhances empathy and emotional regulation by presenting students with scenarios from YA novels or short stories, stripped of character names and page numbers, and asking them to discuss how they would approach the situation from their own perspectives. They can prepare skits, short stories, poems, or presentations to share their ideas and justify their choices. Afterwards, they read the original scene and discuss the character's approach versus their own, focusing on the motivations behind their decisions and how emotions affect behaviors. This fosters introspection, dialogue, and empathy, while also revealing personal biases and perspectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of appropriate YA novel or short story. Preparation of 'skeleton scenarios' without character names or page numbers. Facilitation of group discussions and presentations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of scenarios to ensure relevance and sensitivity. Success depends on the instructor's ability to facilitate meaningful discussions and create a safe space for sharing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle level learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote empathy, emotional regulation, self-awareness, and understanding of personal biases.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to relate to others’ experiences, see themselves in new lights, and consider the impact of their decisions on others. It also promotes dialogue and self-reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios can be tailored to address specific issues relevant to the students. Presentation formats can be chosen by students to match their strengths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student participation in group discussions, quality of presentations, and depth of reflection on personal biases and emotions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes empathy, emotional regulation, and self-awareness by connecting literature to personal experiences. Increases understanding of how emotions affect decisions and behaviors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using scenes from 'The Perks of Being a Wallflower' to discuss topics like mental health, sexual orientation, and domestic abuse.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Many misbehaviors don't deserve any response at all. A behavior that is infrequent and unlikely to spread — an otherwise-quiet student whispering to a neighbor once in a while — is often more effectively left alone than responded to, since it is likely to disappear on its own (or "extinguish," in behaviorist terms) and interrupting the activity to address it risks causing more disruption than the misbehavior itself. Some misbehaviors are worth ignoring even if frequent, as long as they don't bother other students (a student who is chronically out of her seat sharpening her pencil, unnoticed by classmates, may not actually be "a problem" despite being unnecessary or ill-timed). The genuinely difficult cases are the ambiguous ones in between — whispering that happens more than "rarely" but less than "often," or a habit that bothers a few classmates but not most — where there's no clean threshold for when ignoring stops being the right call and a more active response becomes necessary.

When misbehavior is a bit too serious or frequent to ignore, but not serious enough to warrant taking the time to actually speak to the student, nonverbal cues — gestures, eye contact, or other "body language" involving little or no speech — are often enough. A glance in the direction of two students chatting off-task, a frown, or simply moving physically closer to them can be enough of a reminder to bring them back on task, and even if it isn't fully sufficient, it can still keep the off-task behavior from spreading to others (see the ripple effect in Kounin's Classroom Management Research). The main risk of relying on nonverbal cues is that some students may not notice them (if engrossed in conversation) or may fail to correctly interpret their meaning — a risk that is higher for young children still learning the subtleties of adult nonverbal "language" (Guerrero & Floyd, 2005; Heimann et al., 2006), and higher still for students with limited English proficiency or a cultural background whose nonverbal conventions differ from the teacher's own (Marsh, Elfenbein, & Ambady, 2003).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Accurate judgment of whether a misbehavior is actually minor, infrequent, or unnoticed by others — the strategy depends on getting this classification right
  • For nonverbal redirection specifically, a shared nonverbal "vocabulary" between teacher and student

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• No sharp threshold separates "ignorable" from "needs a response" — frequency and disruptiveness exist on a continuum, and judgment calls will sometimes be wrong in either direction
  • Nonverbal cues can be missed or misread, especially by young children or students whose cultural background uses different nonverbal conventions than the teacher's — see Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms
  • Ignoring behavior that is actually escalating (rather than genuinely minor) risks letting it spread via the ripple effect before a more active response is used

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students engaged in minor, low-frequency, or unnoticed surface behaviors — not students whose behavior is already disrupting others or escalating

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Minimizing disruption to lesson flow from minor misbehavior while avoiding the greater disruption a spoken intervention would itself cause

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Judge whether the misbehavior is minor, infrequent, and unnoticed by others; if so, ignore it rather than responding.
  2. If it is a bit too serious or frequent to ignore but not serious enough to merit speaking to the student, use a nonverbal cue instead — a glance, a frown, or moving closer.
  3. Watch for whether the student notices and responds to the cue; if the behavior continues or the cue seems to go unnoticed or misunderstood, escalate to a verbal response (see Low-Profile Classroom Control).

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Low-Profile Classroom Control — the next tier up when ignoring or a nonverbal cue isn't enough
  • Teacher Effectiveness Training / Conflict Resolution — for misbehavior persistent enough that ignoring and nonverbal redirection have already failed

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Guerrero, L. K., & Floyd, K. (2005). Nonverbal communication in close relationships. Erlbaum.
  • Heimann, M., et al. (2006). Children's understanding of nonverbal communication. [cited via secondary source]
  • Marsh, A. A., Elfenbein, H. A., & Ambady, N. (2003). Nonverbal "accents": Cultural differences in facial expressions of emotion. Psychological Science, 14(4), 373-376.
