docs.title: Description
docs.text: The IKEA VR kitchen visualizer uses VR technology to give customers a better understanding of what to think about when planning and designing their kitchens and reassure them in their decisions by allowing them to walk around in a virtual version of their planned kitchen. It aims to transfer knowledge to customers, teaching them about useful issues such as the best-practice work triangle, waste sorting and corner storage. It also lets them make batter and fry pancakes in this virtual kitchen, with the option of multi-tasking by frying pancakes in four separate pans simultaneously.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • HTC Vive or Oculus Rift VR headsets, a VR-ready computer, and access to the IKEA VR Kitchen Visualizer application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited immersion due to the lack of haptic feedback, users who are not tech-literate may have difficulty setting it up, requires time and effort to plan the space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • IKEA customers who are planning or designing a new kitchen.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help customers design and plan kitchens, reduce buying mistakes, reassure customers in their decisions by allowing them to walk around in a virtual version of their planned kitchen, teach about useful issues such as the best-practice work triangle, waste sorting and corner storage.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Customers can better visualize their kitchens, try out different designs and see if they will like them before purchasing. Users may discover potential layout mistakes before purchasing materials.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different kitchen configurations, adjustable color palettes, and object placements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application
  • Whole-task performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Customer satisfaction levels, increased product knowledge, reduce purchasing mistakes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enables customers to plan their kitchens and visualize the layout. Increases sales and reduces purchase mistakes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making learning come alive with simulations, graphics, activities, and videos engages learners in a variety of ways and enhances comprehension. This includes using multimedia to present information, demonstrate concepts, and provide opportunities for active learning. The goal is to create a dynamic and engaging learning environment that caters to diverse learning preferences and promotes deep understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to multimedia resources, such as simulations, graphics, activities, and videos. Instructors need to be trained in effective multimedia design and integration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources. Some learners may find too much multimedia overwhelming. It's essential to ensure that multimedia enhances rather than distracts from learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from visual or kinesthetic learning styles; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, improve comprehension, support diverse learning preferences, promote active learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports diverse learning preferences by providing multiple modes of representation, enhances engagement by creating a dynamic and interactive learning environment, improves comprehension by reinforcing concepts through multiple modalities, and promotes active learning by providing opportunities for hands-on activities and simulations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a variety of multimedia options to suit different learning preferences. Allow learners to choose activities that align with their learning style. Use adaptive technologies to adjust the presentation of information based on individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of key concepts through discussions, written assignments, or multimedia presentations. Track improvements in comprehension and application of knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that multimedia instruction can enhance engagement, improve comprehension, and support diverse learning preferences. Studies show that multimedia presentations can improve memory and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using simulations to demonstrate scientific concepts. Using graphics to illustrate complex data. Using activities to reinforce learning. Using videos to present real-world examples.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making learning come alive with simulations, graphics, activities, and videos. This involves using a variety of media to illustrate concepts and engage learners. Multiple media formats can enhance understanding, retention, and engagement by catering to diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Diverse media resources, software for creating and delivering multimedia content, and awareness of learner preferences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of media to ensure relevance and appropriateness. Some learners may be overwhelmed by too many media options.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with diverse learning styles and preferences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding, improve retention, increase engagement, cater to diverse learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding of concepts. Improves retention of information. Increases learner engagement. Caters to diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use simulations, graphics, activities, and videos to illustrate concepts. Allow learners to choose the media formats that best suit their learning styles. Provide opportunities for learners to create their own media to demonstrate understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner engagement with different media formats. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of each format in supporting learning. Assess learner performance across different media formats.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced learning outcomes: Studies indicate that using multiple media formats can improve comprehension, retention, and engagement, particularly for learners with diverse learning styles and preferences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implementing measures for student self-knowledge involves using various tools and strategies to help students understand their strengths, interests, and areas for growth. This includes learning interest inventories, exit tickets, progress monitoring, and peer/self-assessments. By understanding themselves as learners, students can better advocate for their needs and take ownership of their learning journey.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to incorporate regular reflection activities, provide feedback on student performance, and create a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time for implementation and may require additional resources for certain assessment tools.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 3 to 8, but adaptable for other age groups.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students' self-awareness, improve their ability to identify their learning needs, and promote self-advocacy and ownership of their learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness, improves communication skills, increases student independence, and creates a more personalized learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning styles and needs through different assessment methods and reflection activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in reflection activities, monitor their ability to articulate their needs, and observe their confidence in seeking support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that self-knowledge is a key component of self-advocacy and can lead to improved academic performance and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using learning interest inventories to identify student interests. Implementing exit tickets to assess daily learning objectives. Conducting peer and self-assessments using rubrics and checklists.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implicit vocabulary instruction involves teaching vocabulary “in the moment” by providing quick explanations and leveraging heavy context, usually with Tier III words. This natural, contextual approach integrates new words into the lesson without separate, formal instruction. Teachers consciously identify words beforehand and plan brief definitions to support student understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Content-rich texts, pre-planned short definitions for potential Tier III words, and ability to identify opportunities to address vocabulary needs during instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not provide as deep an understanding as explicit instruction. Dependent on the availability of context clues. Relies heavily on teacher preparedness to anticipate vocabulary challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially beneficial during content-specific instruction

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase understanding of domain-specific (Tier III) vocabulary, enhance comprehension through contextual learning, and promote incidental vocabulary acquisition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Integrates vocabulary seamlessly into content instruction, leverages context to enhance understanding, and provides immediate clarification for unfamiliar terms.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust definitions and explanations based on students’ prior knowledge and backgrounds. Use real-world examples to illustrate word meanings. Provide visual aids to support comprehension.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Informal observation of students' use of new vocabulary in discussions and written work, improved comprehension of content-specific texts, and anecdotal evidence of students' ability to explain new terms

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that implicit vocabulary instruction, combined with explicit methods, leads to more robust vocabulary acquisition and improved reading comprehension. This approach ensures vocabulary is relevant and immediately applicable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • While teaching a science lesson about photosynthesis, the teacher briefly explains the meaning of 'chlorophyll' when it first appears in the text, providing a quick definition and visual aid without interrupting the flow of the lesson.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implicit vocabulary instruction involves teaching words 'in the moment' using heavy context, often with Tier III words. These words are taught naturally without separate instruction; teachers plan short definitions to scaffold understanding. Implicit instruction leverages context to aid comprehension without formal vocabulary lessons.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of potential vocabulary challenges in texts. Preparation of short definitions and contextual cues.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not provide deep or lasting vocabulary acquisition. Relies heavily on contextual understanding, which may not be sufficient for all learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly when encountering domain-specific texts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of domain-specific vocabulary, improve in-the-moment comprehension, build vocabulary contextually

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides natural and contextual vocabulary support, improves comprehension of complex texts, and avoids separate, formal instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust explanations based on students' existing knowledge and comprehension. Tailor context to the specific needs of the learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Assigned Readings
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to use context to understand new words. Monitor comprehension of texts containing implicitly taught vocabulary.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension of complex texts by leveraging contextual clues. Enhanced understanding of domain-specific terminology.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before diving into specifics, encourage students to share their initial impressions of the mentor text. This helps them connect with the text on a personal level and develop their own critical thinking skills. Reading to learn is something that they ultimately will do on their own.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material. Time for individual reflection and group discussion. A classroom environment where students feel comfortable sharing their thoughts and feelings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to articulate their impressions. Requires careful facilitation to ensure that all voices are heard. May be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for promoting student agency and critical thinking

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking skills, promote independent reading, encourage personal connections with text, develop the ability to analyze text based on initial reactions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to trust their own instincts. Validates diverse perspectives and interpretations. Creates a more engaging and interactive learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students are given the freedom to express their own unique impressions. The teacher can facilitate discussion without imposing their own interpretation. Students can reflect on how their impressions change over time.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation in discussions. Student reflections on their impressions. Analysis of student writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that encouraging personal connections with text improves reading comprehension and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are asked to write down their initial impressions of a poem before discussing it as a class. Students share their favorite and least favorite sentences from a short story, explaining why they feel that way. Students reflect on how their impressions of a text change after reading it multiple times.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Poor indoor air quality is a major contributor to absenteeism. This strategy involves ensuring adequate ventilation systems, regular maintenance to prevent 'sick building syndrome', and mitigating indoor pollutants. Implementing measures such as upgrading ventilation systems, using air purifiers, and choosing low-emission materials for flooring, paints, and adhesives can positively affect children and reduce student absenteeism.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Air quality monitoring equipment, ventilation systems, physical structure of the building. Consider costs related to equipment and operation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Achieving optimal air quality can be challenging due to environmental constraints and individual preferences. Resource constraints (e.g., lack of air purifiers) can limit the ability to adjust.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce absenteeism, improve overall health, create a more healty environment, limit indoor pollutants.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves overall health by reducing absenteeism. Minimizes the impact of unhealthy physical conditions on learning, creates a more conducive environment for student health

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The need for air quality systems and improvement can vary, so allowing the use of personal air purifiers can cater to different needs. Monitoring and adjusting throughout the day can accommodate fluctuating conditions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement levels, observe student health levels, measure productivity (e.g., task completion rates). Compare academic outcomes in classrooms with and without air quality adjustment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research also indicates that many schools suffer from “sick building syndrome” which affects the absenteeism and performance of all students (Jones, S. E., Axelrad, R., & Wattigney, W. A. (2007)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing measures such as upgrading ventilation systems, using air purifiers, and choosing low-emission materials for flooring, paints, and adhesives can positively affect children and reduce student absenteeism.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Poor indoor air quality in schools is a major contributor to absenteeism, especially for students with asthma. Many schools suffer from “sick building syndrome,” which affects the absenteeism and performance of all students. Indoor pollutants from office equipment, flooring materials, paints, cleaning products, and poor ventilation systems negatively affect children. Improving ventilation systems and reducing indoor pollutants can improve attendance and performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Improved ventilation systems, air purifiers, low-emission materials, regular HVAC inspections and cleaning

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly. Effectiveness may vary based on the source and type of pollutants.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, teachers, administrators, and school staff

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce absenteeism, improve student performance, and create a healthier learning environment by enhancing indoor air quality

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces health issues, improves attendance, enhances cognitive function, and promotes a healthier learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Improve ventilation systems, use air purifiers, and regularly inspect and clean HVAC systems. Use low-emission materials, paints, and cleaning products.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student and teacher absenteeism, measure indoor air quality, collect feedback from teachers and students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that improved indoor air quality reduces absenteeism and enhances student performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Schools upgrade ventilation systems, use low-VOC paints and cleaning products, and implement regular HVAC maintenance schedules.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Indoor air quality is also a concern because poor air quality is a major contributor to absenteeism for students with asthma. Research also indicates that many schools suffer from “sick building syndrome” which affects the absenteeism and performance of all students. Moreover, bacteria, viruses, and allergens that contribute to childhood disease are commonly found in schools with poor ventilation systems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Air quality management

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Upkeep cost

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve air quality in indoor settings

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Decrease absenteeis, increased attendance

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustable based on students needs

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • School absentee

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased Student Acheivement

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using improvisation and acting exercises to enhance mathematical understanding and creativity. It encourages students to think creatively, take risks, and step outside their comfort zones. Improvisation can be used to review concepts, move forward with lessons, and foster a sense of community within the classroom. By connecting mathematics with the art of acting, students can develop a deeper appreciation for both disciplines while strengthening their problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a classroom or open space for movement and activities; instructor needs to be familiar with both mathematical concepts and basic improv techniques; planning time to create relevant improv scenarios

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all learners, particularly those who are uncomfortable with public speaking or acting; requires careful facilitation to ensure that improv activities remain focused on mathematical concepts; may be perceived as a less serious learning activity if not integrated thoughtfully

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who may struggle with traditional math instruction or those who excel in creative expression.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance creativity in problem-solving, promote risk-taking in learning, foster a sense of community, deepen understanding of mathematical concepts, improve communication and collaboration skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages creative thinking and problem-solving; fosters a supportive learning environment where mistakes are seen as opportunities for growth; helps learners connect mathematical concepts to real-world scenarios; improves communication and collaboration skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various mathematical topics and skill levels; can be scaffolded with simpler improv exercises for beginners or expanded into complex scenarios for advanced learners; allows for learner choice in improv themes and characters to reflect personal interests

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in improv activities; assess learner understanding of mathematical concepts through performance and verbal explanations; use reflections or journals to assess learner's ability to connect improv to concepts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that integrating arts and creative activities into math education can enhance student engagement and improve understanding. Improvisation can help learners develop cognitive flexibility and problem-solving skills, while also fostering a more positive attitude towards mathematics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using improv exercises to explore geometric shapes or algebraic equations; creating scenarios where students act out mathematical problems and solutions; incorporating improv games to review and reinforce key concepts (Young, 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using a stimulus like a photo or item, learners create a character different from themselves, developing details about the character’s life. They then take turns in a 'hot seat,' answering questions from classmates as the character they've created. This activity encourages perspective-taking, creativity, and the ability to think from a different point of view.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A stimulus (photo, item), a form for character development, a 'hot seat' or designated space for role-playing, and time for questions and answers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may be hesitant to engage in role-playing or may rely on stereotypes when creating characters. It requires a supportive and non-judgmental environment to encourage participation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who are interested in exploring different identities and perspectives

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop creativity, promote perspective-taking, encourage role-playing, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Stimulates creativity by creating characters and backstories. Enhances perspective-taking by answering questions from the character's point of view. Improves communication skills through role-playing and discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The stimulus used to create characters can be tailored to the learners' interests and cultural backgrounds. The level of detail and complexity can be adjusted to their abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the creativity and depth of character development, the ability to answer questions from the character's perspective, and the level of engagement in role-playing. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards different identities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Role-playing has been shown to improve perspective-taking, empathy, and communication skills. Creating characters also stimulates creativity and imagination.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students pick a handbag and create a character based on the items inside. Students pick a photo of a person from a different culture and create a character based on their appearance and presumed lifestyle.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Brief breaks for active play can help children who struggle with attention. This may include bouncing on an exercise ball, breaking up learning into chunks with outdoor play times, or providing a quick stretching or jumping jacks break in the classroom. Starting with 15 minutes of active play before a challenging task can also help a child stay more engaged.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for physical activity, appropriate activities (e.g., exercise ball, stretching routines, outdoor play), and time allocated for breaks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be disruptive if not managed effectively. Some learners may be self-conscious or unable to participate in certain activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners struggling with attention, especially children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve attention span, increase engagement, reduce restlessness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a physical outlet for energy, reduces restlessness, improves focus, enhances engagement in learning activities

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual preferences and abilities. The duration and intensity of breaks can be adjusted to meet specific needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to stay on task after physical activity breaks. Track the frequency and duration of attention spans. Monitor the reduction of restless behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Physical activity breaks can significantly improve attention and engagement, particularly for learners who struggle with sustained focus. They provide a necessary outlet for energy and reduce restlessness, thereby enhancing overall learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher incorporates brief stretching breaks between segments of a lesson to help students maintain focus. A parent allows a child to play outdoors for 15 minutes before starting homework to increase concentration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Inclusive Cultural Response involves addressing gaps in cultural learning and representation by adding and including texts and making changes in units of study. This cultural response addresses historical omissions by including authors, perspectives, and experiences traditionally marginalized to make content more relevant and engaging.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Diverse and representative materials, willingness to revise curriculum, ability to facilitate inclusive discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be seen as tokenism if not implemented thoughtfully, requires ongoing effort to stay current with diverse voices and perspectives, may be challenging to address all cultural gaps within a single course.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those from underrepresented backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address historical omissions, increase cultural representation, promote inclusivity, create more relevant and engaging content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides diverse perspectives, enhances engagement by connecting with learners' lived experiences, promotes a more inclusive and equitable classroom.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Reading lists can be tailored to address the specific gaps and deficiencies in representation within a given context.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Discussion Sections
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Diversity of authors and perspectives represented in curriculum, student engagement with diverse materials, participation in inclusive discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment by addressing historical omissions and providing diverse perspectives (Wood, 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Inclusive Innovation Process is a framework that facilitates growth with equity through a student, community, and educator-led research and design process. It involves five phases: Connect and Commit, Inquire and Investigate, Design and Develop, Implement and Iterate, and Sustain and Scale. The process emphasizes intentional inclusion, collaboration, and reflection to create solutions for equity-related problems in the community.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A diverse team including students, educators, administrators, and community members, time for each phase of the process, and resources for data collection and analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The process can be time-consuming and requires a strong commitment from all participants. Success depends on the ability to foster open communication and collaboration among diverse stakeholders.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, students, community members, and district administrators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster inclusion, promote equity, develop community-led solutions, amplify student voices, enhance collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures diverse perspectives are considered, empowers students to take leadership roles, promotes collaborative problem-solving, and leads to the development of solutions that are supported by the community.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The framework can be adapted to address various equity-related problems and tailored to the specific context of the community.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Application
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Discussion Sections
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the diversity of participants, the level of student involvement, the implementation of solutions, and the impact on equity-related outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Student-led professional development on racialized experiences has been praised by educators as impactful. Intentional collaboration and inclusion can lead to improved community relations and educational outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school district created a team consisting of students, district administration, teachers, community organizations, and the Center for Inclusive Innovation team members to address an equity-related problem.

docs.title: Incorporate Crafts to Remember Positive Self-Talk
Description
docs.text: Using creative activities to reinforce positive self-talk, such as making crafts with positive affirmations written on them. These crafts serve as visual reminders and provide learners with a tangible tool to use when they need extra support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Craft supplies and instructions. Time for creative activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all learners. Effectiveness depends on learners' engagement with the craft and the meaning they attach to it.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from visual aids and hands-on activities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To use creative expression as a way for learners to develop personalized mementos of positive self-talk.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a creative outlet for self-expression. Creates a personalized tool for self-support. Makes positive self-talk more memorable and accessible.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose crafts and affirmations that resonate with them. Crafts can be tailored to specific challenges or goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' use of the craft as a tool for self-support. Self-reported changes in mindset and behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that combining creative activities with positive affirmations can enhance their impact. Visual reminders can help learners stay focused on their goals and maintain a positive mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Create a Positive Self-Talk Flower Craft that is easy to make and small enough to bring anywhere. Include positive affirmations inside the flower.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Quiet place to perform.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistency from student.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and post-secondary students, especially those with learning disabilities or other challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Manage emotional regulation and build self-awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop a deeper understanding of themselves and build emotional regulation through self-awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Change intensity of mindful activity

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in behavior and self-awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students learn to self-regulate.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students learn how to ground themselves through sensory exercises.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves integrating students' cultural backgrounds and experiences into lesson design and classroom activities. The goal is to create a supportive and inclusive classroom community where learners feel valued and the learning content is more accessible and relevant. Teachers can start by researching students’ native countries, cultures, and educational systems. Students can contribute their own cultural experience, such as bringing music or art from their culture and describing its significance and meaning to their classmates. Student choice can be incorporated with multiple settings and character representations for learners to choose from, allowing them to connect with the work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor must research and understand students' cultural backgrounds. Resources such as multicultural literature, art, and music are needed. A classroom environment that encourages sharing and respect is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort from the instructor to learn about different cultures. Risk of tokenism if not implemented thoughtfully. Students may feel uncomfortable sharing personal experiences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 and higher education learners from diverse cultural backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, make learning more accessible and relevant, build a supportive classroom community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation and engagement by connecting learning to students' lives. Fosters a sense of belonging and validation of cultural identity. Enhances comprehension by leveraging students' background knowledge.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for different age groups and subject areas. Students can share aspects of their culture they are comfortable with. Curriculum can be tailored to specific cultural backgrounds represented in the classroom.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe increased student participation and engagement. Analyze student work for connections to their cultural backgrounds. Gather feedback from students on their sense of belonging and cultural validation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that culturally responsive teaching enhances student achievement, motivation, and engagement. It also fosters positive relationships and a sense of belonging in the classroom. (e.g., Bridging Cultures Project)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A kindergarten teacher allows students to explore their own families while learning about each others', building a supportive and inclusive classroom community. Teachers can use the CREATE model in urban classrooms to incorporate relatable aspects of students' daily lives, including language, prior knowledge, and extracurricular interests.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves leveraging students' familiarity with technology to create more engaging and interactive reflection opportunities. Teachers can use microblogging, collaborative reflection tools, digital reflection prompts, and multimedia feedback tools to encourage students to reflect on their mathematical learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to technology, a variety of technology tools, and a willingness to allow students to choose the tools that they find most engaging.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology and may not be appropriate for all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, foster deeper learning, promote metacognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to use technology to reflect on their learning in a way that is engaging and interactive.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of technology tools to create reflection opportunities. Students can choose the tools that they find most engaging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, deeper understanding of math concepts, and improved metacognition.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of incorporating technology into reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses an online platform that allows students to post short reflections or respond to prompts with text, images, or short videos.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A potent method for helping students become active participants in learning is to reframe the concept of testing. While testing is usually associated with grades (and therefore stress) in traditional classrooms, in a culturally responsive classroom frequent non-graded tests can be used to provide progress checks and ensure that students don’t fall behind on required material. Teaching students to self-test while learning new information will help them better remember and use what they’ve learned in class and will help them realize on their own when they need to study a topic in greater depth.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A shift in perspective on testing, frequent low-stakes assessments, and instruction in self-testing techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may not take self-testing seriously. Teachers need to provide clear guidance and feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, promote self-regulation, and reduce test anxiety.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to take ownership of their learning. Provides opportunities for self-assessment and reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Self-testing methods can be adapted to different learning styles and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Quizzes
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student self-awareness, improved test performance, and reduced test anxiety.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more empowering and supportive learning environment where students are actively involved in their own learning.

docs.title: Incorporating Physical Activity Into Classroom Learning
Description
docs.text: Incorporate movement into classroom instruction by having science classes explore natural settings, using physical movements to teach math, or acting out stories in language arts. Connecting learning to physical movement helps cement concepts in children’s brains and increase learning speed for some students. Requires teacher buy-in, supportive policies, and classrooms designed to accommodate physical activity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher willingness and training, supportive school policies, classroom space and equipment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires teacher buy-in and creativity. May be challenging to implement in some subjects or classrooms with limited space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, enhance memory retention, improve learning outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Cements concepts in children’s brains by connecting them to movement, increases learning speed for some students, makes learning more engaging and enjoyable.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to fit different subjects and learning objectives. Movement intensity and type can be modified to suit student abilities and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement levels, assess knowledge retention through tests and quizzes, observe student behavior and participation in class

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced memory and learning: Research supports that movement can enhance memory and learning for students. Improved engagement: Active learning strategies like this can make class more fun and engaging.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reframing the concept of testing involves using frequent, non-graded tests as progress checks to ensure students don’t fall behind. Teaching students to self-test while learning new information helps them remember and use what they've learned, realizing when they need to study a topic in greater depth. This approach shifts the focus from grades to learning, reducing stress and promoting active participation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Resources for self-testing (e.g., quizzes, practice problems), time for self-testing during class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from grades to learning, may not be suitable for all learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active learning, reduce test anxiety, enhance retention, provide progress checks

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, reduces stress, provides timely feedback, promotes self-regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can self-test on topics where they feel less confident, focusing on areas needing more attention.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Frequency of self-testing, student participation in review sessions, student progress on graded assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on formative assessment and self-testing shows that these practices can significantly improve learning outcomes. Regular, low-stakes testing helps students identify areas of weakness and focus their efforts effectively.

docs.title: Increase Classroom Space and Reduce Overcrowding
Description
docs.text: Provide ample classroom space to support student engagement and learning. Overcrowded classrooms are linked to increased levels of aggression in students and decreased levels of student engagement. Ensure classrooms are large enough to accommodate flexible seating arrangements, teamwork, problem-solving, and effective communication. Create private study areas as well as smaller learning centers to reduce visual and auditory interruptions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sufficient classroom space, flexible seating arrangements, private study areas

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be costly to expand classroom sizes or build new schools. Requires careful planning to maximize the use of available space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce aggression, increase student engagement, enhance academic performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces stress and anxiety, promotes collaboration and teamwork, supports diverse learning styles, creates a more comfortable and flexible learning environment. Improves teacher effectiveness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer flexible seating arrangements that allow learners to choose their preferred learning environment. Provide private study areas for individual work.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track levels of aggression and student engagement in classrooms with different sizes. Monitor academic achievement and collaboration skills in classrooms with ample space.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Overcrowded classrooms are also associated with decreased levels of student engagement and, therefore, decreased levels of learning. Classrooms with adequate space to reconfigure seating arrangements facilitate the use of different teaching methods that are aligned to 21st century skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Remove unnecessary furniture to open up space.

docs.title: Increase Latency Periods When Questioning Students
Description
docs.text: Increasing latency (wait time) for low-achieving learners will help them improve. Give learners adequate time to answer questions to communicate that you have positive expectations for them. The instructor could ask a teaching peer to observe the instruction and chart the length of the latency periods given to each learner.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors should ensure they are not cutting off low-achieving learners too quickly. Monitor which learners are getting more time than others.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • This can be difficult to implement without practice and thought. Some learners may not need the time and may feel they are being singled out for not knowing the answer.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learners' academic success by giving them adequate time to answer questions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts learner self-confidence, encourages engagement, and reduces off-task behavior. Helps learners believe in their own abilities and strive for success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners who may struggle with answering questions will have the time they need to come up with the right answer.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increase in learner participation, improved academic performance, and reduced behavioral issues. Observation of equitable participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Giving learners adequate time to answer questions has a positive effect on their academic performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Increase student-to-student interaction with academic language. Have students translate symbols into words and write the sentence out to check comprehension. Create a 'sentence frame' and post it on the board. Have students share problem-solving strategies and discuss how they are thinking about math. Incorporate writing activities, such as entrance/exit tickets or math journals. Challenge students to create their own math problems and exchange them with a partner. Teach students how to read, interpret, and summarize data. Model the kinds of writing expected and use AI tools to rewrite math problems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured activities for language production, sentence frames, writing prompts

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning, may be challenging to implement in large classes

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student's use of academic language in math, increase student-to-student interaction, improve comprehension of math concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities to practice using academic language, enhances student comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting activities based on learner language proficiency levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student participation in discussions, review writing samples

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learner use of academic language, increased participation in math activities

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Writing out 3x + 4 = 16 as 'Three times X plus four equals sixteen.' This helps learners process the operations involved in the question and gives them an opportunity to think through how to solve it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teacher presence in synchronous sessions helps to reduce feelings of isolation in students enrolled in online courses and increase student engagement and agency, and ways to reduce distractions and cognitive overload.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers should research, study, and experiment with synchronous sessions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to manage distractions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Online learners of all levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help teachers personalize their classroom to increase their unique personal teaching presence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Students are given a chance to interact with a teacher live in the synchronous session and can reduce feelings of isolation. Research shows synchronous sessions affect how satisfied students are with online learning and how useful the classes are.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can use video chat to reveal body language and tone of voice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement.
