docs.title: Description
docs.text: Independent practice is when learners practice skills and concepts on their own, after guided practice. It is crucial for moving knowledge into long-term memory and developing fluency with foundational skills and concepts. Interweaving reviews of older content and providing feedback can support retention of accurate material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured learning materials, opportunities for practice, and mechanisms for feedback. Adaptive platforms can automate content delivery and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if learners lack foundational understanding or are not motivated to practice independently. Requires careful selection of practice materials to ensure relevance and alignment with learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for solidifying foundational skills in K–12, higher education, and adult learning contexts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Move knowledge into long-term memory, develop fluency, reinforce accurate understanding, promote retention.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens memory through retrieval practice, promotes automaticity of skills, and allows learners to apply knowledge independently. Regular review prevents forgetting.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by varying the type and difficulty of practice problems based on individual learner needs and progress. Adaptive learning technologies can adjust the pace and content of practice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance on practice activities and monitor progress toward fluency goals. Use formative assessments to identify areas where learners need additional support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that independent practice, particularly when spaced and interleaved with review, enhances long-term retention and transfer of skills. Studies support the benefits of distributed practice for diverse tasks such as spelling, phonics, grammar, math problem-solving, and recall of text.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reflex integrates personalized math fact practice in a game environment, engaging learners in mastering targeted operations skills. Cepeda et al. (2012) demonstrated the effectiveness of spacing on diverse learning forms.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Independent reading involves students selecting and reading books on their own, within their reading level and interests. It provides opportunities to practice reading strategies, develop reading interests, and improve fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary. Effective implementation includes a classroom library with a diverse collection of books, explicit instruction on selecting and caring for books, regular dedicated reading time, and conferences to support individual guidance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom or school library with a diverse collection of books, designated reading time, and teacher support for book selection and reading strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not improve skills if students are consistently challenged by difficult texts. Requires teachers to provide guidance and support to ensure students choose appropriate texts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading fluency, comprehension, vocabulary, and foster a lifelong love of reading

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to practice reading skills, build confidence, and develop a lifelong love of reading by choosing books that match their interests and reading levels. Provides access to a wide variety of books, increasing exposure to different genres and topics.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students select books based on their interests and reading levels, allowing for personalized learning experiences. Teachers can provide guidance and support to ensure students choose appropriate texts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased reading achievement, engagement, and motivation. Reduced summer reading loss and prevention of diminished reading habits at the secondary level.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies have shown a correlation between time spent reading and reading achievement. Independent reading programs with guided choice and teacher conferences yield positive results (Kuhn et al., 2006; Moss & Young, 2010).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Deliberate practice is a structured approach to skill development that focuses on intentional, effective, and consistent effort to improve performance. It involves breaking down skills into manageable parts, focusing on specific areas for improvement, setting goals, and receiving timely, descriptive feedback. This type of practice requires sustained, repeated actions to develop automaticity, which reduces mental load and facilitates the learning of more complex tasks. Key elements include goal setting, perseverance, and feedback in the moment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured training, expert feedback, and opportunities for repeated practice. Needs goal setting to give focus to practice. Requires short, sharp bursts of practice at regular intervals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement without expert guidance or feedback. Can be time-consuming and require significant effort. Overwhelming feedback can cause confusion and dishearten learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, from elementary students to adults, in various domains such as sports, driving, reading, and mathematics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop automaticity in skills, improve expert performance, enhance focus, support long-term storage of information, encourage continuous improvement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances skill development through structured training and expert feedback. Promotes automaticity, which frees up cognitive resources for more demanding tasks. Improves motivation through goal setting and seeing progress.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different skill levels and learning goals. Can be tailored to focus on specific areas of weakness. Feedback can be personalized to address individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Part-task practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the number of hours spent practicing, improvements in specific skills, and the level of automaticity achieved. Observe changes in performance and the ability to take on more challenging tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows deliberate practice leads to expertise and improved performance (Ericsson, 2007). Consistent practice with feedback promotes skill development and automaticity, improving performance in various domains (Lemov). Spaced practice has been shown to improve long-term learning and retention (Carpenter et al., 2012).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating designated areas within the classroom to serve specific functions, such as independent work, collaborative projects, or mini-lessons, can promote student engagement. By strategically arranging seating to match the learning activity, instructors can maximize student focus and participation. Different seating configurations support different types of instruction. For instance, independent work areas encourage focus, collaborative setups promote communication, and large-group arrangements facilitate discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom space, adaptable furniture (desks, tables, chairs), planning for space allocation, clear communication with students

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires physical space, may need adjustments based on specific classroom constraints, success depends on clear expectations and routines

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels and subjects, adaptable for elementary, secondary, and higher education settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, optimize classroom activities, promote focus and participation, facilitate different types of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured environments for different tasks, maximizes engagement, supports diverse learning activities, fosters a sense of community

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize configurations to suit different learning needs, provide visual and auditory cues to define each space

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Supportive information
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement levels in different spaces, collect feedback through surveys or discussions, monitor task completion rates in each zone

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that flexible seating arrangements can enhance student engagement and learning outcomes. Studies indicate that different classroom setups impact student-student and instructor-student interactions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Summit Prep School uses different seating configurations for independent work, collaborative work, mini lessons, and large-group discussions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use an individualized "highlighter tool" (e.g., a Google Doc add-on) to create custom highlighters in different colors. They label the colors (e.g., "Argument #1" in red) and use them to highlight relevant text. The highlights can be exported by color to create a table, where students summarize each highlighted category.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a digital highlighter tool, documents for highlighting, and a means of exporting and summarizing the highlights.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Depends on the usability of the highlighter tool and requires careful planning and organization.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and college students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Categorize information, enhance text analysis, promote active engagement, and facilitate reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes organized highlighting, facilitates categorization, encourages reflection and summarization, and enhances analytical skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The number of colors and the complexity of the categories can be adjusted based on students' skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Application of Knowledge
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Effectiveness of the color-coding scheme, quality of the summaries, and depth of analysis.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured highlighting can improve text analysis, facilitate categorization, and enhance overall comprehension.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Improving indoor air quality reduces absenteeism, particularly for students with asthma, and addresses “sick building syndrome.” Proper ventilation systems and pollutant reduction create a healthier learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Improved ventilation systems, air purifiers, pollutant reduction strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly and may require significant facility upgrades.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners and educators in K-12 or higher education settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce student absenteeism, improve student health, create a healthier learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces exposure to allergens and pollutants, improves respiratory health, enhances focus and concentration

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Ensure adequate ventilation and air filtration for learners with respiratory conditions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student attendance, monitor air quality, assess student health outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that improved air quality reduces absenteeism and enhances student health.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Upgrading ventilation systems, using air purifiers, reducing indoor pollutants from cleaning products and materials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Inflectional endings instruction focuses on teaching the rules for adding suffixes (e.g., -ed, -s, -es, -ing, -er, -est) to base words. These suffixes change the number, person, or tense of a word without changing its part of speech. The instruction involves making learners aware of the different sounds the suffixes make, sorting words based on the sound of the past tense ending, and explicitly teaching the rules for adding endings, such as the doubling rule, the drop -e rule, and the change y to i rule. This type of instruction improves spelling accuracy and understanding of grammar.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of words and suffixes, direct instruction from a teacher or tutor, and consistent practice with word decomposition and combination

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging for learners with significant language processing deficits. Requires explicit and systematic instruction. May be perceived as rote learning if not connected to meaningful contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily for learners in grades 2–4, but also beneficial for older students who struggle with spelling or grammar, including English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy of inflectional endings, enhance understanding of grammatical rules, and develop skills in decomposing and combining words

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances spelling skills, improves understanding of grammar, supports word building, and provides a structured approach to learning and applying morphological rules

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of the words and suffixes used in the instruction. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, while more advanced learners can tackle more complex word transformations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor spelling accuracy on regular spelling tests, track progress in writing assignments, and assess the learners' ability to apply inflectional ending rules correctly.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that explicit instruction in inflectional endings improves spelling and grammar skills. It is particularly effective for learners who struggle with morphological awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A third-grade teacher decomposes words with inflections, such as 'hoping = hope + ing,' and then guides students to combine base words and endings, like 'commit + ed = committed,' to illustrate the doubling rule.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encourage participation in informal games and jam sessions to foster creativity, collaboration, and enjoyment without the pressure of competition. This approach promotes social interaction, teamwork, and self-expression, allowing learners to explore their interests and talents in a relaxed environment. Informal games and jam sessions can enhance motivation and create a sense of community among learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a space where learners can gather and engage in activities. Instructors need to create a relaxed and supportive environment and provide materials and resources as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure inclusivity and prevent cliques from forming. Some learners may be hesitant to participate if they are not confident in their skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for middle and high school students, as well as adult learners in recreational and social settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster creativity and self-expression, promote collaboration and social interaction, enhance motivation and enjoyment, reduce the pressure of competition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for social interaction, fosters creativity and self-expression, and enhances motivation and enjoyment. Informal games and jam sessions allow learners to explore their interests and talents without the pressure of competition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of games and activities to cater to different interests and skill levels. Provide a supportive and inclusive environment where learners feel comfortable expressing themselves.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in activities. Assess their creativity and self-expression through their contributions. Gather feedback from learners about their experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that informal games and jam sessions enhance social interaction, creativity, and motivation among learners. These activities promote a sense of community and allow learners to explore their interests in a relaxed environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Organize pickup sports games during recess or after school. Create a space where learners can play music together just for fun. Host a regular improv session where learners can express themselves creatively. A group of adult learners forms a garage band and jams together, fostering social connections and musical skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These are strategies used to leverage student strengths in order to address challenges with inhibition, such as the ability to suppress attention to irrelevant input and to focus on pertinent stimuli or information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Educator must understand the principles of inhibition and have knowledge of each student’s individual strengths and challenges.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort to implement effectively. May not be effective for all learners in all situations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, enhance planning and response skills, build metacognitive skills, reduce impulsivity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens the ability to plan, focus, and control impulses. Supports effective communication and collaboration skills. Encourages self-regulation and metacognition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various classroom and workplace settings. Can be tailored to individual needs and strengths. Scaffolded support can be provided as needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved ability to focus on tasks and ignore distractions. Enhanced self-regulation and metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Let students know what order they will be called on to allow students to plan their response and wait until their turn. Graphic organizers and visual aids help students identify the most important information and focus in on it. Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help students develop their metacognitive skills and control their impulses.

docs.title: Initiating a Conversation with Learners to Correct Name Pronunciation
Description
docs.text: The instructor initiates a conversation with the learner by following the steps outlined below. Make sure not to laugh at a name or express frustration with having to learn it. Start with soul-searching to see if the name is only hard because it is coming from your perspective. Be explicit by stating that it is your limitation, not the learner's fault.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors should take the time to ask each learner their name, and make a good-faith effort to pronounce it correctly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some languages have different phonemes than the instructor is used to, which makes it difficult to achieve proper pronunciation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a positive classroom environment through proper name pronunciation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • When names are pronounced correctly, this promotes trust and respect, and eliminates negative emotional reactions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The instructor will make sure to respect the learner's identity by pronouncing their name correctly.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner engagement, decreased feelings of shame or anxiety, and improved classroom culture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • It is important that the classroom shows it will not consistently mispronounce a name because they are too afraid to ask, or too afraid to correct themselves.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage in focused investigation with “immediate and concrete data” that learners gather and analyze, as a springboard to higher quality writing. Assign authentic activities and materials as inquiry writing, either inquiry in the community or online as a web quest.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Research materials, inquiry techniques, analytical skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires research skills, may be time-consuming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing quality, enhance research skills, promote critical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances research skills, promotes critical thinking, improves writing quality

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to different topics and research questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased research skills, greater critical thinking

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners engage in a focused investigation with “immediate and concrete data” that they gather and analyze, which serves as a springboard to higher quality writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Helping students understand that positive actions lead to positive feelings about themselves. Involves teaching students a three-step process: thought, action, and feeling. Students learn to change negative thoughts into positive ones, leading to positive actions and feelings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instruction on the thought-action-feeling process, classroom activities to practice identifying and changing negative thoughts, opportunities for reflection and feedback

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires patience and consistency, some students may need additional support to change negative thought patterns.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators seeking to enhance student motivation and positive behavior

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop intrinsic motivation, improve self-esteem, enhance positive behavior, and cultivate a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances intrinsic motivation, promotes positive self-concept, improves behavior, and fosters a growth mindset

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Encourage students to identify their own positive actions and feelings. Provide individualized feedback and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and attitudes, gather student feedback through surveys or discussions, track student progress in changing negative thoughts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students who understand the connection between positive actions and positive feelings are more likely to be intrinsically motivated and exhibit positive behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher guides students through an exercise to identify negative thoughts and replace them with positive ones.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Combining instructor feedback with peer feedback enhances the learning process. While instructor feedback is essential for progress, peer feedback allows learners to synthesize and re-teach content to each other, sparking innovative thoughts and increasing content mastery. Tools like VoiceThread can be used to provide written, verbal, and/or video feedback in a presentation format. Peer feedback also heightens social presence in online environments by creating an inclusive atmosphere where learners openly share and support one another.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to tools and platforms for providing feedback (e.g., VoiceThread), clear guidelines for effective peer feedback, and a structured process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on learners' ability to provide constructive feedback and engage in supportive interactions. Requires initial training and modeling by the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where collaborative learning and peer support are valued.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance content mastery, promote collaborative learning, increase social presence in online environments, and foster a supportive learning community.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides diverse perspectives on learner work, fosters deeper understanding through re-teaching, and creates a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose tools and platforms that best support both instructor and peer feedback, and tailor activities to promote meaningful interactions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Peer Interaction
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of both instructor and peer feedback. Measure improvements in the quality of revised work based on combined feedback. Observe the level of engagement and support within the learning community.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combining instructor and peer feedback enhances learning, improves engagement, and promotes a supportive and collaborative learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using VoiceThread to provide written, verbal, and/or video feedback in a presentation format. Facilitating peer review sessions where learners provide constructive feedback to each other.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reducing the power differential between instructor and students by acting more as a facilitator than an instructor fosters a nurturing environment. Providing questionnaires about interests empowers students, enhancing intrinsic motivation. Allowing students to bring in their own reading material and present it provides them with an opportunity to interact with and share culturally relevant stories, thoughts, and ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Willingness of the instructor to relinquish some control, time for student-led presentations and activities, questionnaires or surveys.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant adjustments to traditional teaching methods, can be challenging to manage if students are unprepared or unengaged.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, increase intrinsic motivation, create a nurturing environment, share culturally relevant material

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student autonomy, fosters a sense of social justice, supports intrinsic motivation, promotes culturally relevant learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students choose topics and materials that are personally and culturally relevant. Questionnaires and activities are tailored to individual interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation in activities, quality of student-led presentations, student feedback on questionnaires and activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on learner-centered instruction shows that empowering students and increasing their autonomy can lead to greater engagement, motivation, and achievement. Providing culturally relevant content can enhance students' sense of belonging and identity.

docs.title: Integrate Emotions into Daily Schedule and Routine
Description
docs.text: Integrate the teaching of emotions into daily schedules and routines. When reviewing the daily schedule with students, ask them to predict the emotions they might experience. Explore if Math makes them anxious, tired, or bored. Ask if Recess makes them nervous because they don't always have someone to play with. Spend a few minutes anticipating what emotions might emerge, and help students think about how they will manage those emotions. Write them down so that you can remind them to use those strategies in the moment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Daily schedule, time for discussion, tools for strategy recording

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent implementation, may not cover unexpected emotions, can be time-consuming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Anticipate emotional states, practice emotion management, integrate emotional awareness into daily activities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Proactive planning for emotions, enhances emotional awareness and self-regulation, integrates SEL into academic activities

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customizable to students' individual needs and interests

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track students' ability to anticipate emotions, use coping strategies, and manage behaviors

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved emotional regulation, better academic focus, and increased self-awareness

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher reviews daily schedule and asks students how they might feel during each activity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy combines art activities with science concepts to teach specific scientific principles through artistic expression. It involves hands-on projects that encourage experimentation, observation, and creative problem-solving. Examples include creating rainbow paper to understand color science, making leaf rubbings to study trees, and exploring absorption with watercolors on texture boards.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Art supplies (e.g., paper, watercolors, glue, liquid watercolor), science materials (e.g., leaves, clear nail polish, texture boards), and instructions for specific projects.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure scientific concepts are accurately represented. May need additional resources for specialized projects.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially K-12 students, can benefit from this interdisciplinary approach.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach science concepts, encourage experimentation, enhance observation skills, promote creative problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement by connecting art and science. Promotes deeper understanding through hands-on experimentation. Develops creative thinking and problem-solving skills. Strengthens memory by connecting art and science.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Projects can be adapted to suit different learning styles and interests. Learners can choose materials and techniques that resonate with them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the scientific accuracy of the art projects. Evaluate the learners' ability to explain the science concepts. Observe engagement and participation during hands-on activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show interdisciplinary approaches like integrating art and science can increase engagement, comprehension, and retention. Hands-on projects foster deeper learning and critical thinking.

docs.title: Integrating Math with Music and Dance
Description
docs.text: Integrating math with music and dance is a strategy in which rhythm, pattern, movement, and structure are used to explore mathematical relationships.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A genuine connection between the artistic activity and the math idea.
  • Reflection that names the pattern, ratio, timing, or spatial relationship involved.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The artistic activity can become decorative unless the mathematical connection is made explicit.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support engagement, pattern recognition, and embodied understanding of mathematical structure.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Introduce a math idea through rhythm, sequencing, repetition, symmetry, or coordinated movement.
  • Ask learners to perform or compose a pattern.
  • Debrief the mathematical structure they enacted.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Real-World Math
  • Representational Drawing

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • An, S., Kulm, G., & Ma, T. (2008). The effects of music composition as a classroom teaching approach on children's mathematics achievement. Journal of Instructional Psychology, 35(3), 244-260.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating movement into daily activities involves incorporating physical activity into routines and tasks that are typically sedentary. This approach aims to increase overall physical activity levels without requiring dedicated workout sessions. It includes simple changes such as taking the stairs, walking during breaks, and engaging in active household chores.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Minimal to no equipment needed. Requires awareness and intention to incorporate movement into daily routines.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial effort to identify opportunities for integrating movement. Some individuals may need to adapt activities to accommodate physical limitations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All individuals, particularly those who find it challenging to dedicate time to structured exercise routines

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase daily physical activity, improve health outcomes, enhance energy levels, and make exercise more accessible and sustainable

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases overall physical activity levels, enhances energy levels, and makes exercise more accessible and sustainable by integrating it into existing routines.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual preferences, schedules, and physical abilities, including options for walking, stretching, and active household chores.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased daily step count, improved energy levels, enhanced mood, better health outcomes, and self-reported increases in physical activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that even small increases in daily physical activity can have significant health benefits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Taking the stairs instead of the elevator, walking during lunch breaks, standing while working, doing household chores actively, and dancing while listening to music.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Intensive instruction involves active learner engagement and plenty of time on task. Students learn more when they are active, that is, not just listening or watching, but applying "focused, sustained effort on the content or task. Intensive instruction requires a high degree of learner attention and response and frequent instructional sessions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to design engaging activities and provide frequent opportunities for practice. Requires allocation of sufficient time for active engagement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to maintain high levels of engagement over extended periods. Some learners may require additional support to stay focused.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Struggling learners, adult learners in basic skills programs, individuals with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement and time-on-task; enhance retention of information; promote active learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with increased opportunities for practice and application. Keeps learners actively involved in the learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs by providing varied activities and allowing learners to choose activities that engage them most effectively. Activities can be tailored to different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased time-on-task; active participation in learning activities; improved performance on application tasks

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows active learner engagement and time-on-task enhance learning. Provides learners with increased opportunities for practice and application.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a decoding strategy on an unfamiliar word, practicing sight words with flash cards, participating in a discussion about a text, working to solve a comprehension problem, or creating a "map" or other graphic organizer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating natural elements (views of nature, plants) into the learning environment can improve focus, well-being, and academic performance. Strategies include providing unrestricted views of nature from classrooms and introducing leafy plants into the classroom. Interaction with nature can be particularly helpful for kids with ADD and ADHD.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to views of nature or leafy plants. Integration of natural elements into the learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited availability of natural views or plants in some environments. Requires maintenance of plants.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with ADD and ADHD.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, enhance well-being, reduce attention deficit symptoms, and improve academic performance.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a cognitive reset that improves the ability to focus. Reduces attention deficit symptoms. Enhances well-being and behavior.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Varying the type and amount of natural elements based on individual preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure focus levels, behavior, and academic performance. Track instances of sick leave and disciplinary events.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students in schools with unrestricted views of nature tested higher in reading, math, and language arts (Uncapher, 2016). Introducing leafy plants into the classroom has a positive impact on students’ well-being and behavior (Uncapher, 2016).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage students through interactive discussions driven by questions and answers. Focus on personal interaction and immediate feedback, especially for struggling students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Strong questioning skills, knowledge of student needs, and willingness to provide frequent feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful management to ensure all students are engaged. May require additional resources to support individualized feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in all subjects and grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, provide immediate feedback, identify and address learning gaps, and improve overall learning outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active learning, provides immediate feedback, allows for individualized support, and enhances student self-esteem.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailors questions to individual student needs and knowledge levels, providing personalized feedback and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, improved understanding of concepts, higher test scores, and positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved student engagement, better learning outcomes, and a more supportive classroom atmosphere.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interactive Modeling is an instructional practice where the educator provides instruction for self-checking and provides an example. For example, in a second grade classroom this might look like a student leading a meditation, where the educator provides instructions and background to the student or a video of him leading the class in the meditation itself.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None noted.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Building self-efficacy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to see a clear example.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Educators provide the learning environment that is needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Successful demonstration.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interactive read-alouds involve stopping during the reading process to engage learners in discussions and activities that promote deeper understanding of the text. These interactions include asking questions, making predictions, connecting the text to personal experiences, and encouraging learners to share their thoughts and interpretations. Interactive read-alouds enhance comprehension, critical thinking, and engagement with the text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to appropriate reading materials, time for reading and discussion, facilitation skills to guide discussions, and materials for interactive activities (e.g., sticky notes, graphic organizers).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure questions and activities are aligned with learning objectives. May be challenging to implement with large groups or learners with significant attention difficulties.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, English language learners, and adult learners in literacy programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote deeper comprehension, enhance critical thinking skills, encourage personal connections to the text, and foster active engagement with the material.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comprehension through active engagement, develops critical thinking skills by encouraging analysis and interpretation, promotes personal connections to the text, and fosters a collaborative learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions and activities can be tailored to different reading levels and learner interests. Scaffolding can be provided through sentence starters and guided prompts, especially beneficial for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation in discussions, analyze learner responses to questions and activities, and track comprehension through formative assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that interactive read-alouds improve comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, and overall literacy development. The interactive elements enhance critical thinking skills and promote deeper engagement with the text.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher pauses during a read-aloud of Patricia Polacco's Thank You, Mr. Falker to ask questions that promote personal connections and discussions of character and theme, thereby deepening comprehension.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use simulated environments or situations that mirror real-world challenges. Engage learners by placing them in realistic decision-making roles where they must apply the concepts they are learning directly to solve problems or make decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Software or tools for creating interactive scenarios. A clear understanding of the learning objectives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Scenarios can be time-consuming to develop. Poorly designed scenarios can be confusing or ineffective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from hands-on learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, apply knowledge to real-world situations, promote decision-making skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Mirrors real-world challenges and places learners in realistic decision-making roles where they must apply the concepts they are learning directly to solve problems or make decisions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Create scenarios that are relevant to learners' roles and responsibilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Scenario
  • Role Reversal
  • Case Study

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' decision-making skills within the scenario. Evaluate their ability to apply concepts to solve problems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Interactive scenarios are an exceptionally powerful tool in eLearning, especially when it comes to conveying theoretical, dense, or complex concepts effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Decision-making screens, image exploration, case study screens, and role-play screens.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interactive storytelling involves creating narratives where the reader or user can make choices that affect the story's direction and outcome. This is often achieved through tools like inklewriter, which allows writers to create branching narratives with ease. Interactive storytelling enhances engagement, critical thinking, and reader agency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to interactive storytelling software or platforms like inklewriter, and a basic understanding of narrative structure.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to create, requires careful planning of multiple narrative paths, and may be technically challenging for beginners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners interested in creative writing and game design

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop creative writing skills, enhance understanding of narrative structure, and promote critical thinking through decision-making.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases reader engagement, promotes active participation, and strengthens critical thinking skills through decision-making.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Readers can explore different paths and outcomes, allowing for a customized and personalized experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Demonstration
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the creativity and coherence of the narrative, the effectiveness of the interactive elements, and the overall impact of the story.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Interactive storytelling enhances reader engagement, promotes active participation, and strengthens critical thinking skills through decision-making.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a choose-your-own-adventure story, designing an interactive game narrative.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interdisciplinary activities present issues, themes, and problems that require skills and knowledge from more than one subject to address or answer. These activities encourage learners to make connections between academic disciplines, building a more complete understanding of the topics they're studying. The interdisciplinary approach can be implemented through entire units, class-long exercises, or short activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors need to have a strong understanding of multiple disciplines. Access to varied resources such as news clips, textbooks, and multimedia. The ability to create relevant and engaging problems.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require coordination with other teachers or departments. Requires careful planning to ensure activities align with learning objectives. Can be time-consuming to prepare.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels; adaptable based on the complexity of the subject matter and required skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve critical thinking, enhance bias recognition, prepare learners for future problems, build informed understandings, make connections between academic disciplines

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves analysis abilities by using approaches from different disciplines. Challenges pre-existing ideas to help identify bias. Provides practice for solving problems outside school walls. Builds informed and complete understandings of topics.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored based on learner interests, learning styles, and the specific context of the subjects being studied. Adaptable for various class sizes and schedules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Application
  • Integration
  • Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in critical thinking, enhanced bias recognition, ability to solve complex problems, development of informed understandings, increased engagement

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to positive results across classes, helping learners appreciate subjects they disliked by connecting them to disciplines they enjoy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • News Analysis: Using a news clip about a local store closing, learners determine an ideal new location, applying skills from different subjects. Historical Pen Pals: Learners take on the role of historical figures and write to each other about relevant events, building knowledge of history and creative writing skills. Math Gym: Combining math, science, and physical education, learners estimate and measure distances during long jumps, delving into physics and body mechanics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interest-Based Negotiation involves establishing different perspectives, backgrounds, interests, and options for resolution, creating a single team out of the interested parties. It centers around people of different positions working together instead of against each other. It fosters a collaborative manner of argumentation and provides a healthier model for conflict resolution.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training in Interest-Based Negotiation, facilitator to guide the process, willingness to engage in collaborative problem-solving.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires a commitment to collaboration, may be challenging to overcome entrenched positions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in diverse classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, improve conflict resolution skills, foster empathy and understanding, create a more positive and productive classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages teamwork and empathy, enhances communication skills, provides a structured approach to conflict resolution, promotes a more positive and productive environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows learners to represent diverse perspectives and interests, provides a framework for addressing individual needs and concerns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Positions
  • Argument Construction
  • Role Reversal
  • Consensus Building
  • Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of collaborative behavior, participation in negotiation activities, quality of solutions developed, feedback from learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves collaboration, communication, and conflict resolution skills by promoting a structured and collaborative approach to problem-solving (Wood, 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Interest inventories are surveys used to assess students' areas of interest. These can be open-ended, where students generate their own topics, or closed, where students select from a predetermined list. The inventories are used to form learning clubs based on shared interests. This motivates students by allowing them to explore topics they are passionate about and connects learning to their background knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Interest inventory forms (open or closed), class time for students to complete the inventories, and a system for organizing students into groups based on their interests.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful structuring to ensure alignment with learning objectives. Some students may struggle to identify their interests or may choose topics that are not conducive to learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, adaptable for various content areas and learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify student interests, create interest-based groups, increase motivation, connect learning to personal interests

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student motivation by allowing them to choose topics of interest. Supports personalized learning and differentiation. Helps teachers understand students' backgrounds and interests.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Inventories can be tailored to specific content areas and learning objectives. Open-ended inventories allow for greater student choice and exploration.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze the range and variety of student responses, observe student engagement in interest-based groups, track student progress on interest-driven projects.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that students are more motivated to read when given the opportunity to choose materials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners pick a current news item and explore it from different points of view, examining whether the news is reported objectively and what other interpretations might exist. If the same news event is covered across different media, they compare and contrast the reporting styles, deducing the assumptions and beliefs of the reporters. This activity promotes critical thinking, media literacy, and the ability to analyze information from multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to different news sources, a space for discussions and reflections, and facilitation by an instructor to guide analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may lack the knowledge or skills to analyze news critically, or they may be resistant to considering alternative perspectives. It requires careful guidance from the instructor to ensure thoughtful and respectful analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.text: • Develops critical thinking skills by analyzing news reports from different perspectives. Enhances media literacy by examining how news is framed and presented. Improves communication skills through discussions and analysis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose news items that resonate with their interests and cultural backgrounds. The level of analysis and discussion can be adjusted to their abilities.

docs.text:

docs.text: • Assess the depth of analysis, the ability to identify bias and assumptions, and the level of critical thinking demonstrated in the analysis. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards media and current affairs.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Media literacy has been shown to promote critical thinking, awareness of bias, and responsible media consumption. Analyzing news from different perspectives also fosters tolerance, understanding, and informed citizenship.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students analyze news reports on climate change from different media outlets, examining how the issue is framed and what perspectives are emphasized. Students analyze news reports on immigration from different political perspectives, examining how language and framing shape public opinion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers must step in when abusive language occurs. This involves addressing the student using offensive language, discussing the impact of their words, and fostering empathy for those who are hurt. Techniques such as restorative justice and involving parents can be helpful.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A teacher who is aware of the language being used in the classroom, who is willing to intervene when necessary, and who has the skills and resources to address the situation effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to address in the moment, may require additional support from administrators or parents, and may not always be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those who use or are affected by abusive language.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a safe and respectful classroom environment, prevent and address abusive language, promote empathy and understanding, and teach students about the impact of their words.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students understand the impact of their words, promotes empathy and respect, and creates a safer learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The response to abusive language should depend on the situation and the students involved. Teachers should be willing to include students and their solutions in responses to these situations.

docs.text: • Observe the frequency and severity of abusive language in the classroom, assess student understanding of the impact of their words, and gather feedback from students about the safety and respectfulness of the learning environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that addressing abusive language in schools can create a safer and more respectful learning environment, promote positive social-emotional development, and improve academic outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher hears a student use a homophobic slur and immediately says, 'I don't allow that term in my classroom. I need to talk with you after class about that.' The teacher then meets with the student to discuss the impact of their words and to foster empathy for those who are hurt.

docs.text: Set aside time at the end of a learning sequence—a lesson, a unit, a school day, or a school year—to question each other about what has been learned. Guide students to look for ways they can apply their learnings to future settings. Interviews also provide teachers and students with opportunities to model and practice a variety of habits: listening with understanding and empathy, thinking and communicating with clarity and precision, and questioning and posing problems.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: Introduce concepts like “relevance, accuracy, bias, and reliability” and using these terms regularly as a part of classroom discourse can help students get used to questioning sources and the motivations authors may have.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit teaching of the terms, integration into classroom discussions, and examples of sources to analyze.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may initially struggle to apply these concepts effectively. Requires ongoing reinforcement and practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Familiarize learners with key concepts for evaluating sources, encourage critical questioning of sources, and understand author motivations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a foundational understanding of source evaluation, encourages critical thinking, and helps learners recognize potential biases in information.

docs.title: Personalization

• Direct instruction

docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to define and apply the concepts in discussions and source analyses. Assess their ability to identify relevance, accuracy, bias, and reliability in various sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved critical thinking: By understanding these concepts, learners become more discerning consumers of information. Enhanced media literacy: Learners are better equipped to evaluate the credibility and reliability of sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A history teacher introduces the concepts of relevance, accuracy, bias, and reliability when discussing primary and secondary sources related to a historical event.

docs.text: Learners read a section of text to themselves before verbally summarizing the passage to a partner or completing sentence frames. Examples of sentence frames: "_ wanted , but , so .” for problem/solution; "__ happens because ______.” for cause/effect.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Involving learners in classroom design means actively soliciting their input and ideas when creating or modifying the physical learning environment. This can include asking learners about their preferred seating arrangements, color schemes, and use of space. By incorporating learner feedback, educators can create a classroom that is more student-centered, engaging, and conducive to learning. Involving learners in the design process can also foster a sense of ownership and responsibility for the learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to solicit and incorporate learner feedback. May require adjustments to classroom management strategies to accommodate different design preferences. Instructors must be willing to relinquish some control over the physical learning environment and trust learners to make responsible choices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to solicit and incorporate learner feedback. Can be challenging to balance diverse design preferences. May not be feasible to implement all learner suggestions due to budget constraints or other limitations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower learners, foster a sense of ownership, create a more engaging learning environment, accommodate diverse learning styles, promote collaboration and communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner motivation by giving them a voice in the design of their learning environment. Supports collaboration and communication by creating spaces that are conducive to group work. Can improve focus and productivity by accommodating different learning styles and preferences. Fosters a sense of ownership and responsibility for the learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can contribute their individual ideas and preferences to the design process. Instructors can offer a variety of design options and allow learners to choose what works best for them. Involving learners in classroom design can be combined with other personalization strategies, such as flexible pacing and flexible grouping.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in class activities. Collect learner feedback on the impact of the classroom design on their learning. Measure learner achievement and compare outcomes in classrooms designed with learner input versus those designed without learner input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved engagement and motivation: Research suggests that involving learners in classroom design can increase their engagement and motivation by giving them a sense of ownership and control. Enhanced collaboration: Learner-designed classrooms can promote collaboration by creating spaces that are conducive to group work and discussion. Increased achievement: Some studies have shown that learner-designed classrooms can lead to improved learner achievement, although more research is needed to confirm these findings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher surveys learners about their preferred seating arrangements and incorporates their feedback into the classroom layout. A principal invites learners to participate in a design charrette to brainstorm ideas for renovating the school library. A professor asks learners to create a vision board for their ideal learning environment and uses these boards to inform the design of the course.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Involving learners in the process of designing and transforming their learning environment can create a space that better meets their needs and preferences. This includes soliciting their input on layout, furniture choices, color selections, and organization of materials. By presenting research on how the brain works and the impact of the physical environment on learning, educators can empower learners to make informed decisions about their learning landscape. This approach recognizes that learners are active participants in their education and that their voices should be heard when creating a supportive and engaging classroom environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Willingness to solicit student input, knowledge of brain-based learning principles, flexible approach to classroom design, resources for implementing student ideas

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort, potential for conflicting opinions among students, requires careful facilitation to ensure all voices are heard, may not be feasible in all classroom settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, higher education, adult learners in various educational and training settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower learners, enhance engagement, improve classroom environment, promote ownership of learning, support brain-based learning practices

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation and engagement, fosters a sense of ownership and responsibility, creates a more supportive and personalized learning environment, promotes critical thinking and problem-solving skills, supports brain-based learning practices

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The classroom design can be tailored to the specific needs and preferences of the learners. Learners can choose furniture, colors, and layouts that best support their learning styles. This approach allows for a more inclusive and responsive learning environment.

docs.title: Instructions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that involving students in classroom redesign can create a more supportive and engaging learning environment. This approach can lead to increased motivation, improved learning outcomes, and a stronger sense of ownership among learners.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teaching methods for irregular words include: grouping words with some memorable similarity, calling attention to the odd part of the word that must be learned by heart, using a multisensory memory strategy that gives the students many ways to repeatedly practice spelling the word, using mnemonics, and asking the learner to pay very close attention to the letter sequence by visualizing it and recalling it backwards as well as forwards.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: Exploring Islamic geometry with students centers on exploration, joy, and solidarity. Art lends itself in exploring geometry standards such as symmetry, tessellation, congruency, similarity, and composition. Students are invited to go on a virtual field trip to the Mosque of Sultan Barquq in Cairo to identify patterns and geometries. Questions are facilitated during this exploration to pique curiosity and connect art to mathematics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure students make meaningful connections between art and mathematics.

docs.text: • K-12 students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore geometry concepts, promote cultural awareness, and connect mathematics to art.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects mathematics to art, promotes cultural awareness, and invites exploration and curiosity.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, their ability to identify patterns and geometries, and their connections between art and mathematics.

docs.text: • Connecting mathematics with art can make the subject more engaging and accessible, while also promoting cultural awareness and understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In the Jigsaw method, learners are divided into 'expert groups' to master a specific portion of the material and then regroup to teach that material to their peers. This approach enhances collaboration, encourages engagement, and results in better learning as learners take on the role of both teacher and learner.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation of materials. Learners need to be divided into groups, and each group needs access to the relevant content.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time than traditional instruction. Some learners may feel uncomfortable teaching their peers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various training and educational settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, foster collaboration, improve communication, and promote active learning through peer teaching.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases math talk, strengthens math communication skills and mathematical flexibility. Supports learners' varying speeds of processing by allowing independent review before small group discussions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different subjects and content areas. The complexity of the material can be adjusted to suit different learner levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Expert Groups
  • Peer Teaching
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality of peer teaching and the depth of understanding demonstrated in group discussions. Assess individual comprehension through quizzes or written assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Cooperative learning strategies like Jigsaw increase student engagement, encourage collaboration, and result in better learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers can increase math talk in their classrooms, and in turn strengthen students' Math Communication skills and Mathematical Flexibility, by having students tackle new material in a jigsaw activity. Also, by having students first review new material independently before moving into small groups, teachers can support learners' varying Speeds of Processing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students think back on their experiences and outcomes to gain a greater understanding of themselves. Students think and write about their experiences throughout a day or class period and look for patterns, as well as create and manage goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journals or notebooks, prompts for reflection, and class time for writing and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may be resistant to journaling or struggle with self-reflection. It's important to create a safe and supportive environment and provide guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students, as well as adult learners, who want to develop self-awareness and improve their ability to manage their emotions and behaviors.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-awareness, identify patterns in behavior, improve goal-setting skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes metacognition by encouraging students to reflect on their experiences and identify patterns in their behavior. Supports goal-setting and self-management skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different prompts and structures for reflection, such as focusing on specific events or emotions. Students can also choose different formats for recording their reflections, such as writing, drawing, or audio recording.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' journal entries for evidence of self-awareness, reflection, and goal-setting. Track their progress toward meeting their goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Journaling has been shown to improve self-awareness, reduce stress, and promote emotional well-being. It can also help students develop self-management skills and improve their academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student writes in their journal about a conflict they had with a friend and reflects on their role in the situation. A student sets a goal to improve their study habits and tracks their progress in their journal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves having students think back on their experiences and outcomes and then record them in a journal. Students can think and write about their experiences throughout a day or class period and look for patterns, as well as create and manage goals. It can provide them with a greater understanding of themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires journals or notebooks and dedicated time for writing and reflection. Can be integrated into any subject area or advisory period.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on students' willingness to engage in self-reflection. Some students may struggle with writing or expressing their thoughts and feelings.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-understanding, promote metacognition, improve goal-setting skills, foster self-regulation and self-assessment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-reflection, enhances metacognition, fosters self-regulation and self-assessment, provides a personal record of learning and growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Journal prompts can be tailored to students' age, interests, and learning goals. Teachers can provide sentence starters or graphic organizers to support students who struggle with writing or self-reflection.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student journal entries to assess their level of self-awareness, metacognition, and goal-setting skills. Look for evidence of reflection on experiences, identification of patterns, and articulation of learning goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of self-awareness and metacognitive skills, fostering self-regulation, self-assessment, and lifelong learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Journaling involves writing or recording thoughts and feelings to develop metacognitive awareness and build self-regulation skills. Learners can use journals to reflect on their reactions to new or challenging situations, identify patterns in their behavior, and develop strategies for managing their emotions. Journaling can take various forms, including written entries, audio recordings, or video logs. Prompts can be used to guide reflection, such as asking learners to describe what they did in class, why, and how it helped them process emotions. The goal is to help learners become more aware of their internal processes and develop the ability to self-regulate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journals (physical or digital), prompts to guide reflection, and a safe and supportive environment for sharing thoughts and feelings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may be hesitant to share their thoughts and feelings if they do not feel safe or supported. It requires time and effort to engage in meaningful reflection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with self-regulation, particularly those who need to develop greater awareness of their internal processes, including students in K-12 and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop metacognitive awareness, improve self-regulation skills, enhance emotional intelligence, foster self-reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-reflection, helps learners identify patterns in their behavior, builds metacognitive awareness, and provides a safe space for exploring emotions. It also allows educators to gain insight into the learner’s thought processes and provide targeted support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Journaling can be adapted to individual needs by using different formats (written, audio, video) and providing prompts that are tailored to the learner’s specific challenges and strengths. For learners who struggle with writing, audio or video journals may be more effective.
