docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that journaling can effectively support the development of metacognitive awareness and self-regulation skills. Studies have shown that learners who engage in regular journaling are more likely to develop insight into their behavior and develop strategies for managing their emotions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student uses a journal to reflect on their reactions to frustrating situations in class, identifying triggers and developing strategies for managing their emotions.

docs.text: Implement Kagan Cooperative Learning Strategies to encourage active participation and engagement in learning. These strategies include: Gallery Walk (learners examine and discuss various items or prompts displayed around the room), Two Stray, One Stay (small groups discuss a topic, then two members 'stray' to other groups to share their findings while one member 'stays' to explain to new visitors), Round Robin (each member of a group takes turns sharing their ideas or responses), and Simultaneous Round Table (each group member writes their response to a prompt on a shared paper, passing it around until everyone has contributed). These small changes can easily be implemented in any learning environment to promote collaboration and active learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear instructions and prompts for each activity. Space for learners to move and interact. Willingness to facilitate cooperative learning activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure activities align with learning objectives. May be challenging to manage in large classrooms or with learners who struggle with collaboration.

docs.text: • A teacher being willing to laugh at their own faux pas to help students understand that it is okay to make mistakes and continue to grow.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Create flash cards for the four mathematical operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division). On one side of each card, write the operation and its symbol. On the reverse side, list the key words associated with that operation, providing a reference tool for students to identify the correct operation to use in word problems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Index cards, markers, list of mathematical operations and their associated key words.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reliance on key words alone may not be sufficient for solving complex word problems. Students need to understand the context of the problem in addition to identifying key words.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school learners (Grades 3-8)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of mathematical operations, enhance problem-solving skills, develop vocabulary related to math, reinforce memory of key math concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual and tactile tool to help students remember key words for mathematical operations. Promotes active recall and association between operations and key words.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to personalize their flash cards with colors, images, or additional notes. Provide different levels of flash cards based on student abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' use of flash cards to identify key words and operations. Assess students' accuracy in solving word problems using the flash cards as a guide.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased problem-solving accuracy: Visual aids like flash cards can improve students' ability to identify the correct operation for solving word problems. Enhanced memory: Active recall and association of key words with operations promote memory and retention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The keyword strategy is a mnemonic technique that enhances memory by linking new information to keywords already encoded in memory. This involves identifying a keyword that sounds similar to the new word and is easily represented by a picture or drawing. The teacher then creates a picture that connects the word to be learned with its definition. This strategy is particularly effective when the information is new to students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of relevant keywords, creation of visual aids (pictures or drawings), teaching students the association process, and regular review.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for abstract concepts or words that lack easily identifiable keywords. Effectiveness relies on the quality and relevance of the selected keywords and associated imagery.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education learners, especially beneficial for those with learning disabilities or difficulty memorizing new vocabulary.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve vocabulary retention, link new information to existing memory, enhance visual association with new concepts, facilitate recall of definitions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances encoding of new vocabulary by associating it with familiar keywords and visual imagery. Improves memory recall by providing a concrete link between the word and its definition. Makes learning new words more engaging and memorable.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor keywords and pictures to the interests and backgrounds of their students, making the learning experience more relevant and engaging. Students can also participate in generating their own keywords and images to enhance personalization.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved vocabulary test scores, increased ability to recall definitions, enhanced application of new vocabulary in context, and positive student feedback on the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies have shown that the keyword strategy significantly improves vocabulary acquisition and retention among students with and without learning disabilities. Research supports its effectiveness in helping students link new information to existing knowledge for better recall.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • To teach 'carline' (witch), use the keyword 'car' and show a picture of a witch in a car. To remember the definition, think of the keyword (car), the picture (a car), and what was happening in the picture (a witch was in the car), leading to the definition (witch).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Perform an online image search for the words “school lunch,” and project the results or create handouts with the images from the search results. Have students focus their attention on one image at a time. Ask them to make a face or display thumbs up, down or in the middle to convey their emotional reaction to the image. Chart their reactions. As a class, discuss the assumptions they might have been making when reacting to these images. Have kids write in their notebooks or journals about some of the assumptions a person might find themselves making based on a simple online image search.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Online images, chart, and notebooks or journals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation. Some students may need additional support to identify their assumptions and biases.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help learners identify their emotional reactions and assumptions when evaluating online images.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness and critical thinking and helps learners recognize their biases.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can reflect on their own assumptions and biases.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' written reflections and assess their ability to identify assumptions and biases.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased self-awareness: Students become more aware of their emotional reactions and assumptions. Enhanced critical thinking: Students are better able to evaluate information critically and recognize their biases.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples of assumptions are: All school lunches are disgusting; All school lunches are nutritious; Kids are usually smiling when they eat school lunch; Kids only like junk food; Schools are always racially diverse; American kids are less healthy than kids in other countries.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflect deeply on your own attitudes and beliefs and how they may impact your opinions and actions. Understand how your views affect the way you interpret what students say and do. Cultural background influences how we interpret situations and communicate, as well as the choices we make. An important element of culturally responsive communication is understanding how your views affect the way you interpret what students say and do.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for self-reflection, possibly guided reflection prompts or discussion questions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires honesty and willingness to confront personal biases. May be challenging for individuals resistant to self-reflection

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and instructors across all levels (K-12, higher education, professional training)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness, improve culturally responsive communication, mitigate implicit bias

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-reflection, increases awareness of personal biases, enhances culturally responsive practices

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored through reflection prompts that cater to different cultural backgrounds and experiences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in communication patterns, increased awareness of personal biases, improvements in culturally responsive teaching practices

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Better understanding of student perspectives, more inclusive and equitable classroom environments, improved student-teacher relationships

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use reflective journaling, participate in cultural awareness workshops, engage in peer discussions about biases

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A KWL chart is a graphic organizer used to structure a lesson by tapping into what students already Know (K), what they Want to know (W), and what they have Learned (L) about a topic. Before the lesson, students fill out the 'K' and 'W' columns; after the lesson, they complete the 'L' column. This makes students think about what they already know, increasing interest and focus, and helps organize new information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A pre-designed KWL chart (paper or digital); pens or pencils; access to learning materials (e.g., readings, videos, lectures)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of students' initial knowledge and questions; can be superficial if not followed up with deeper exploration

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels; useful for introducing a new topic or unit

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activate prior knowledge, set learning goals, summarize learning, and increase engagement and focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages students by connecting new material to existing knowledge; promotes active learning and reflection; easy to implement and adapt; increases interest and focus

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be used individually, in pairs, or as a whole class; adaptable for any subject or topic

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completeness and accuracy of entries in each column; ability to summarize what was learned; presentation of findings

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows KWL charts help students connect new information with existing knowledge, improving understanding and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before a lesson on rainforests, students fill out the 'K' column with what they know and the 'W' column with what they want to know. After the lesson, they complete the 'L' column with what they've learned. Resource: Understood.org - Common advance organizers and why they work

docs.title: Description
docs.text: KWL (Know, Want to know, Learned) charts are advance organizers that help students activate prior knowledge, identify learning goals, and reflect on what they have learned. Before a lesson, students fill in what they think they know (K) and what they want to know (W). After the lesson, they write what they have learned (L). This process encourages students to connect new information to existing knowledge, increasing interest and focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A chart divided into three columns (Know, Want to Know, Learned), reading materials, and class discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require teacher guidance to ensure students accurately reflect on their prior knowledge and learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly effective for introducing new topics and units.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activate prior knowledge, set learning goals, monitor comprehension, and promote reflection on learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases engagement by connecting to prior knowledge, provides a clear structure for learning, and supports metacognition by prompting reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to any subject. Students can work individually or in groups. The chart can be used for single texts or entire units.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • State objectives
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completed KWL charts, student participation in discussions, and summaries of learning based on the chart.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that KWL charts make students think about what they already know, which makes them feel more comfortable with the new material they’re learning. As a result, their interest and focus may increase.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Labeling emotions involves intentionally naming and describing one's own emotions and helping others label theirs throughout the day. This practice promotes emotional literacy and self-awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires intentionality and consistency from instructors and caregivers. Access to resources such as emotion charts can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a supportive and non-judgmental environment. Some learners may be uncomfortable expressing their emotions publicly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, including early childhood, elementary, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, improve self-awareness, enhance empathetic communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases emotional vocabulary, promotes self-reflection, and fosters a culture of emotional understanding and acceptance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by introducing more complex emotion words as learners progress. Can be integrated into various activities and routines.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Modeling
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and accuracy of emotion labeling. Track the use of emotion words and the ability to connect emotions with experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that consistent emotion labeling can improve emotional regulation and social competence. (Source: The Benefits of Emotional Labeling - https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/the_benefits_of_emotional_labeling)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Ladder of Feedback is a structured protocol to guide peer feedback that includes a sequential framework with specific questions, sentence stems, and success criteria. This process provides clear expectations for what elements to focus feedback on and scaffolds the process of giving positive but constructive feedback. The steps in the ladder typically include clarifying questions, valuing positives, addressing concerns, and making suggestions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A clear rubric or set of success criteria, structured group time, and guided prompts for each step of the ladder.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial training to ensure learners understand and follow the protocol. Some learners may find the structure restrictive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school learners and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide structured and constructive feedback, enhance critical thinking, and improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured and sequential approach to feedback, promoting a balanced and constructive critique. Helps learners focus on specific aspects of the work and offer targeted suggestions for improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific questions, sentence stems, and success criteria can be tailored to the subject matter and the learners' needs. The ladder can be adapted to include additional steps or focus on different areas.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review of feedback provided by learners to assess the depth and quality of their critique. Observation of group interactions to assess learners' ability to follow the protocol and provide constructive feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured feedback protocols help learners provide more specific and actionable feedback, leading to improved revisions and a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher introduces the Ladder of Feedback to guide learners in providing feedback on a complex project, aligning their feedback to the project's rubric.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The language experience approach is a whole language method that integrates the development of reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through the use of learners' experiences. Learners share their experiences, and the instructor records them verbatim. The recorded experience is then used as the basis for reading and writing activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learners' experiences. Instructor to record and transcribe the experiences. Materials for reading and writing activities (e.g., paper, pencils, books).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Relies on the instructor's ability to record and transcribe accurately. The quality of the experience shared can impact the effectiveness of the approach.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for young learners and English language learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills. Connect learning to learners' experiences. Build confidence and motivation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects learning to learners' experiences. Uses accessible vocabulary and syntax. Integrates multiple language skills. Builds confidence and motivation. Supports cultural and life experiences connections.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Experiences shared can be personalized to the learners' backgrounds and interests. Activities can be adapted to learners' language proficiency levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner's ability to read and write about their experiences. Participation in discussions and activities. Growth in language skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When fiction and nonfiction books are integrated into the teaching of a content area such as science, graphic organizers are useful for organizing information and enabling students to classify observations and facts, comprehend the relationships among phenomenon, draw conclusions, develop explanations, and generalize scientific concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A kindergarten teacher records students' responses to the sentence frame 'On (day of the week) (name of child) ate (number) (food)' on a language experience chart after reading 'The Very Hungry Caterpillar'.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using songs to teach language involves engaging learners through music and rhythm to enhance vocabulary development, phonological awareness, and overall literacy skills. Learners sing songs repeatedly, reinforcing vocabulary through multisensory experiences such as matching rhyming words to pictures or creating their own verses and melodies. Digital tools can be incorporated to record, play back, and share these creations, fostering interactive and creative engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to songs (audio or lyrics), musical instruments or digital recording tools (optional), and materials for illustration or game creation. Classroom or digital environment for sharing and performing songs and games.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all learners due to differing musical preferences. Some learners may struggle with the musical or rhythmic aspects, potentially hindering language learning. Requires thoughtful selection of songs to ensure relevance and cultural sensitivity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood education, primary grades (K-2), and learners who benefit from multisensory instruction and are at a variety of literacy levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary, improve phonological awareness, reinforce literacy skills, promote creative expression, improve confidence and motivation, increase cultural awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves memory and retention through rhythmic repetition and multisensory engagement. Encourages creative expression through songwriting and game creation. Supports diverse learning styles and provides a fun, engaging approach to language learning. Facilitates cultural connection by helping learners build empathy, while engaging with a new learning tool.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Songs can be adapted to include diverse content relevant to learners' cultural backgrounds and interests. Varying levels of complexity can be accommodated by having advanced learners create their own songs and games, while beginners focus on recognizing and matching sounds.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to sing lyrics, identify rhyming words, and create new verses or games. Assess their vocabulary usage in songs and related activities. Evaluate engagement and participation during musical sessions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that music activities are strongly associated with academic performance, content learning, and social skills. Singing and songwriting support early literacy instruction. Multisensory approaches enhance memory and retention, while creative expression boosts engagement and confidence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The resource references multiple lesson plans and strategies including Reading Vocabulary Down By the Bay, Using Songwriting to Build Awareness of Beginning Letter Sounds, and Rhyming Games.

docs.title: Last Lesson, Last Week, Last Month
Description
docs.text: This activity involves looking back to the most important information presented yesterday, last week, and last month. Choose three questions from each and ask students to answer (retrieval practice) the questions with no assistance. This helps students realize that the importance of studying a particular topic doesn’t end with the summative assessment and that knowledge builds knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to identify key information from each time period.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent tracking of content covered.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective in secondary and higher education.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote spaced retrieval practice and reinforce prior learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages spaced retrieval practice, reinforces learning, and demonstrates the importance of long-term retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The questions can be tailored to the specific content covered in each time period.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Quizzes

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' understanding through their answers to the questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This activity helps learners realize the importance of spaced retrieval practice and reinforces the idea that knowledge builds knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Lateral reading is a digital literacy strategy that involves evaluating the trustworthiness of online information by leaving the original site and consulting other digital sources to see what they say about it. This method contrasts with vertical reading, which involves staying on a single webpage and trusting the source's self-description. Lateral reading utilizes resources like Wikipedia, news stories, and fact-checking websites to assess the credibility and reliability of a source.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the internet and digital devices. Structured activities and guidance from instructors or product developers. Examples of online sources to evaluate.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to consult multiple sources. May be overwhelming for beginners without proper guidance. The reliability of the sources used for lateral reading also needs to be considered.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages, especially those in secondary and higher education, as well as adult learners in professional development programs focused on digital literacy and media literacy

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate the trustworthiness of online information, improve digital literacy skills, contrast lateral reading with vertical reading, identify reliable resources for fact-checking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to evaluating online sources, enhances critical thinking and reasoning skills, promotes awareness of bias and misinformation, and builds confidence in navigating digital information

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be scaffolded with guidance on which sources to consult and what to look for. The complexity of the sources and topics can be adjusted to suit different skill levels. Learners can choose topics and sources relevant to their interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Research
  • Resource Evaluation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the types of sources consulted and the criteria used for evaluation. Compare learners' assessments of source credibility before and after lateral reading. Analyze the quality of arguments and evidence used to support conclusions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that lateral reading is a more effective strategy for evaluating online information than vertical reading. Fact-checkers and experienced online readers rely on lateral reading to quickly assess the trustworthiness of sources.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher demonstrates lateral reading in a lesson on civic online reasoning. Product developers can simulate opportunities for students to analyze digital sources and practice lateral reading skills in a safe environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct teaching about the meaningful parts of words begins with the most common inflections, but then extends to prefixes, suffixes, and roots of Latin origin. This is especially helpful in grades four through eight to help students develop a larger vocabulary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, morphological charts, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grade 4 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance vocabulary, develop understanding of word structure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand how word parts contribute to meaning, improves spelling accuracy, builds vocabulary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific Latin prefixes, suffixes, and roots. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in spelling words with Latin prefixes, suffixes, and roots. Monitor progress in spelling and vocabulary skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students develop a larger vocabulary as well as more accurate spelling through an understanding of Latin roots, prefixes, and suffixes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Leaderboards showcase the distribution of point totals that learners have accumulated through various learning activities. Competition can motivate learners and can be leveraged by leaderboards. To avoid discouraging students who are performing poorly, instructors can consider using a system in which learners see only the two students who are directly above them and below them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Use of digital tools to track and display scores. Clear criteria for earning points. Careful monitoring to ensure fair competition.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be demotivating for learners at the bottom. May lead to a focus on competition rather than learning. Requires careful management to avoid creating a negative classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, with caution for those sensitive to competition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Motivate learners through competition. Provide visual representation of progress. Encourage engagement with learning activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages competitive spirit to drive engagement. Provides a clear visual representation of learner progress. Encourages learners to strive for higher achievement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can choose to display only a limited range of scores. Learners can focus on improving their own performance rather than comparing themselves to others.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner participation and engagement with leaderboard activities. Compare leaderboard rankings with learning outcomes. Gather feedback on the impact of the leaderboard.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Displaying all learners in order of point totals can be a disincentive for learners at the bottom.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Displaying a leaderboard showing the top scores in a quiz. Creating a leaderboard showing the most active participants in a discussion forum. Using a system where learners only see the scores of those directly above and below them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Understanding learners' math backgrounds is important. Some may have strong skills from consistent schooling, while others may have limited formal education but practical skills. Connect instruction to their interests and responsibilities, such as sports or family finances. Be aware of different numeric and measurement systems learners may use. Look for leadership opportunities for all learners in math class, allowing them to teach others and demonstrate what they know in multiple ways. Group learners intentionally and with sensitivity. Veteran educators stress the importance of getting to know learners as a key part of supporting their success.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Assess learner's prior math instruction and skills, integrate learner interests into instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time to gather information about each learner's background, educators must be sensitive to learners' cultural and educational differences

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All math learners, especially English language learners (ELLs)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the varying levels of math backgrounds among learners, connect instruction to learner interests and responsibilities, provide leadership opportunities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators tailor instruction to meet the specific needs and backgrounds of learners, enhances learner motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting teaching strategies based on individual math backgrounds and practical skills

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner's math background, monitor engagement in math activities

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learner understanding, increased participation in math activities

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Visiting learners' neighborhoods provided valuable insights on their experiences and familiar topics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A learning approach where the problem is presented as an open-ended one, so there are several ways to solve it, with each solution leading to a different set of outcomes. Learners must understand the problem and try to find the best solution. In the process, they develop a strong learning foundation, develop, build, and apply newly-acquired skills, experience both success and failure, learn to think in more ways than one, and find innovative ways to counteract existing problems

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An open-ended problem, access to resources, and a supportive environment that encourages exploration and risk-taking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources compared to traditional methods. Requires careful facilitation to ensure learners stay on track and achieve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners, corporate training, and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster independent thinking, problem-solving skills, and adaptability in learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding, critical thinking, and real-world application of knowledge. Increases engagement and motivation by allowing learners to explore different solutions and learn from both success and failure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The open-ended nature of the problem allows learners to tailor their approach and solutions based on their unique skills, knowledge, and interests. This can also be adapted based on the learners' skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the diversity and quality of solutions generated by learners, assess their ability to apply newly-acquired skills, and observe their problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that learner-centric approaches improve knowledge retention, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Corporate training programs using real-world case studies, higher education courses using problem-based projects, and self-directed learning initiatives where learners choose their own learning paths.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide opportunities for learners to generate their own examples of a concept. Promoting reflection and response in this way will reinforce well-formed concepts and correct misunderstandings. It may also clarify fuzzy areas, as not all concepts are neatly defined.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires an interactive learning environment where learners can share and discuss examples.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful facilitation to ensure that all examples are accurate and relevant.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially in interactive learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, correct misconceptions, promote deeper understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning and reflection. Provides opportunities for peer feedback and clarification.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to generate examples that are relevant to their own experiences and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the accuracy and relevance of learners' generated examples. Observe their ability to explain and justify their choices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Generating examples promotes learner reflection and response, reinforces well-formed concepts, and corrects misunderstandings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a sexual harassment course, asking learners to generate their own examples to clarify the boundaries of acceptable behavior.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learner-to-learner (peer) feedback involves having learners provide constructive feedback on each other's work. This approach encourages learners to reflect on their own understanding, learn to give relevant suggestions, receive specific ways to improve, and engage in metacognition. It requires modeling appropriate feedback techniques and providing guidelines for constructive criticism. Train students to give each other constructive feedback in a way that is positive and helpful. Encourage students to use post-it notes to record the given feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear guidelines for providing feedback, modeling appropriate techniques, a supportive classroom environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners to provide constructive criticism, requires time and effort

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical thinking skills, enhance self-reflection, improve communication skills, foster collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides multiple perspectives, promotes a supportive learning environment, enhances metacognition

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The feedback can be tailored to the individual learner's needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance and communication skills. Analyze the quality of feedback provided.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners provide input while reflecting on their own understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students in a writing class exchange papers and provide feedback on each other's essays. Students in a science class review each other's lab reports.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learner choice involves transitioning from teacher-led content delivery to learner-driven purpose discovery. It includes a spectrum of roles from providing a menu of options to empowering learners as designers, advocates, and entrepreneurs who self-regulate learning based on their passions and purposes. The teacher moves from providing options to inviting input from learners, while the learner identifies challenges and strategies, expanding their purpose through business creation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be open to learner input and willing to relinquish some control over content and process. Requires a flexible curriculum that allows for adaptation based on learner interests.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to make choices if they lack experience or confidence. Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure choices align with learning objectives. Some learners may choose options that are not challenging enough or that reinforce existing knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner motivation, foster self-direction, promote deeper engagement, enhance ownership of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation by allowing learners to pursue areas of interest. Encourages self-direction and responsibility for learning. Fosters a sense of ownership and agency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learner choice can be adapted to different levels by starting with a menu of options and gradually increasing the level of autonomy. Options can be structured based on learner readiness or interests. Can be tailored to different subjects and learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Learner Choice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner engagement and motivation can be measured through observation and self-report surveys. The quality of learner work can be assessed using criteria aligned with learning objectives. Reflective writing can provide insights into learner experiences and perceptions of ownership.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that learner choice increases motivation and engagement, leading to improved learning outcomes. Studies show that self-directed learning fosters a learner mindset and prepares students for lifelong learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Allowing students to choose topics for research projects, select formats for presentations, or design their own assessments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Behavioral science attributes almost all learning failure to either a lack of prerequisite skills or poorly designed instructional sequencing — not to a lack of general ability, aptitude, or intelligence. The idea of breaking a complex behavior into smaller component behaviors originates with Skinner's (1954) shaping research; Gagné (1970) demonstrated its importance for classroom learning specifically.

Task analysis is the process of analyzing the internal conditions (prerequisite skills) necessary for a target performance. Its output is a learning hierarchy: an arrangement of prerequisite skills from most foundational to most complex. The process starts by identifying the task learners should be able to perform at the end of a lesson or unit, then asking, "In order to perform this task, what prerequisite skills must my learners already have mastered?" — repeating that question recursively for each identified prerequisite until the hierarchy bottoms out at genuinely foundational skills. If the logical questioning process is difficult to apply directly, an alternative is to perform the task oneself (or observe someone else performing it) and write down each step actually used; some published curricula also provide a ready-made task analysis.

Sequencing the resulting hierarchy correctly matters as much as identifying it: teaching subtraction-with-regrouping before place value, for instance, guarantees errors regardless of how well each individual skill is taught. Published curricula are not guaranteed to sequence skills well (Englemann, 1991), so it is worth examining and, if necessary, adjusting a curriculum's built-in sequence. Complex tasks — solving multi-step math problems, writing compositions, interpreting difficult text — all require learners to perform their prerequisite skills automatically and effortlessly (Mayer, 1987); learners who cannot perform prerequisites with minimal errors find it difficult to transfer new learning to unfamiliar contexts, making prerequisite mastery one of the key ingredients for transfer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clearly specified target task or performance to work backward from
  • Willingness to verify prerequisite mastery before introducing a dependent skill, rather than assuming it based on grade level or curriculum sequence alone

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• An incorrectly sequenced hierarchy produces errors, frustration, and inefficiency even when every individual skill is taught well
  • Published curriculum sequences should not be assumed correct without inspection

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners struggling with a complex skill, where the actual bottleneck is often an unmastered prerequisite rather than a deficit in the target skill itself

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reliable acquisition of complex, multi-step skills by ensuring every prerequisite is mastered and correctly sequenced beforehand

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify the target task learners should be able to perform at the end of the lesson or unit.
  2. Ask what prerequisite skills must already be mastered to perform that task; identify the most complex, highest-level prerequisites first.
  3. For each identified prerequisite, repeat the question to find its own prerequisites, continuing until reaching genuinely foundational skills.
  4. Arrange the resulting skills into a sequenced learning hierarchy, checking that no skill is scheduled before its own prerequisites.
  5. Before teaching the target task, verify learners have mastered the hierarchy's prerequisites — treat an unexpected difficulty with the target task as a cue to check for a missing prerequisite rather than assuming a lack of ability.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Task Analysis — a narrower application of task analysis focused specifically on breaking down a writing assignment for struggling writers; this strategy addresses the more general prerequisite-sequencing process behind any complex skill

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher whose student cannot master long division asks whether the student has learned to subtract; if not, whether they can regroup; if not, whether they can identify which of two numbers is larger — tracing the difficulty back to its actual prerequisite gap rather than concluding the student lacks mathematical ability.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Skinner, B. F. (1954). The science of learning and the art of teaching. Harvard Educational Review, 24, 86-97.
  • Gagné, R. M. (1970). The conditions of learning (2nd ed.). Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
  • Englemann, S. (1991). Direct instruction. Educational Technology Publications.
  • Mayer, R. E. (1987). Educational psychology: A cognitive approach. Little, Brown.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behaviorism in the classroom. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning clubs are a grouping system used to organize active learning events based on student-selected areas of interest. Guided by the teacher, students select content area topics and draw on multiple texts—including websites, printed material, video, and music—to investigate their topics. Students then have the opportunity to share their learning using similar media, such as learning blogs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of multimedia resources. Class time for research and discussion. Facilitation by the instructor to guide research and provide support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure meaningful discussions and prevent off-topic conversations. Some students may be unprepared or dominate discussions, requiring instructor intervention. Assessment can be challenging due to varied learning materials and group dynamics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve research skills, develop digital literacy, foster collaborative discussions, increase student engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages student ownership and motivation through choice. Provides a social context for learning and discussing texts. Promotes deeper engagement with reading material and critical thinking skills. Enhances vocabulary and communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer diverse topic choices catering to different interests. Allow learners to set their research pace and discussion topics. Provide options for final projects to accommodate different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Research
  • Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor participation and engagement in discussions. Review learning logs, blog posts, and project submissions for evidence of research skills and comprehension. Assess group dynamics and collaboration through observation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of literature circles and book clubs to support learning across topics. Students are motivated to read when given the opportunity to choose materials.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Middle school students chose a topic and investigated it using various texts. They engaged in sharing that learning in a blog, which can include text, images, links and other multimedia.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves defining clear objectives prior to engaging in a learning experience, such as shadowing. By articulating specific questions and challenges to explore, learners can maximize the impact of their experience. This includes writing down assumptions, selecting a student with specific qualities, and identifying personal motivations for the learning goal. It focuses learners to observe without bias, challenging existing beliefs and facilitating more meaningful insights.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for reflection, a willingness to challenge existing assumptions, and a structured approach to defining and documenting learning goals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness and honesty. If learning goals are too broad or vague, the experience may lack focus. Resistance to challenging personal biases may limit the insights gained.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Anyone engaging in learning activities, including educators, administrators, and learners of all levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To set clear learning targets, encourage unbiased observation, maximize learning outcomes, and facilitate meaningful experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes focused attention, minimizes biases, enhances self-awareness, and increases the likelihood of achieving desired learning outcomes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The learning goals are tailored to the individual's interests and questions, ensuring that the experience is relevant and engaging. This includes selecting a student with specific qualities to shadow.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Success is measured by the extent to which the learning goals are achieved, the insights gained, and the changes made as a result of the experience. This can be documented through reflections, action plans, and feedback from participants.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that setting learning goals before an experience can increase engagement and improve outcomes. By focusing observations and challenging biases, this strategy fosters more meaningful and impactful learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning interest inventories help instructors and learners identify areas of interest and ways of finding joy in learning and demonstrating that learning. These inventories support increased participation. The instructor can incorporate those interests into teaching methods, encouraging enthusiastic participation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learning interest inventory tool, time for students to complete the inventory, willingness to incorporate student interests into teaching

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not cover all possible interests. Requires effort to align curriculum with student interests.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly in elementary and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify learning interests, increase motivation, encourage participation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, personalizes learning, promotes self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and age groups. Tailored to specific learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, improved engagement, positive feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students are more motivated and engaged in learning when their interests are incorporated into instruction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a survey to identify student interests and incorporating those interests into lesson plans. Allowing students to choose projects that align with their interests.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning logs are short, reflective writing activities completed at the beginning or end of a class to review previously learned material or focus on new concepts. Learners respond to a prompt in writing for a few minutes, focusing on mathematics. Prompts can include definitions, examples, personal connections, or summaries of key concepts. The activity encourages active engagement with the material and the construction of meaning from facts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a few minutes at the beginning or end of a lesson, a specific prompt, and a way for students to record their thoughts (e.g., notebooks, digital documents).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Quality depends on the clarity of the prompt and learners' willingness to engage thoughtfully. Requires time to review and respond to entries to be most effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Review material, encourage reflection, foster mathematical understanding, engage learners in constructing meaning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves the quality of student discussion, encourages personal connections to the material, aids in transforming information from facts to constructed meaning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be tailored to review specific concepts or address individual learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review the content and depth of student responses to assess their understanding and ability to make connections. Track improvements in discussion quality following the implementation of learning logs.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves student engagement and discussion quality, and promotes construction of meaning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fifth-grade teacher used learning logs to review mean, median, and mode, with students providing definitions and examples. Another example involves defining and illustrating probability using shapes and colored cards.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A 'Learning Strategy & Tool Fair' allows learners to explore a variety of learning strategies and tools in a hands-on, exploratory environment. Inspired by instrument petting zoos, this approach provides opportunities for learners to experiment with different strategies and tools, discovering their own interests and challenges. Product developers can design resources within their products that suggest potential strategies based on learners' needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A collection of various learning strategies and tools. Time allocated for exploration and experimentation. Adaptive product capabilities (for digital implementation).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant preparation to gather a diverse collection of strategies and tools. Learners may feel overwhelmed by too many options.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for learners who are unsure of which strategies work best for them.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage exploration of different learning strategies and tools, support personalized learning, foster learner autonomy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a low-pressure environment for experimentation. Allows learners to discover new strategies and tools that align with their individual needs and preferences. Encourages self-reflection on learning processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose which strategies and tools to explore based on their interests. Adaptive products can suggest strategies based on learner needs and performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement with different strategies and tools. Collect feedback on which strategies learners found most helpful. Track the adoption of new strategies in learner workflows.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased learner awareness of available strategies and tools. Greater self-awareness of effective learning approaches. Higher engagement and motivation in learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Link and construct meaning from experiences. Reflection has many facets. For example, reflecting on work enhances its meaning. Reflecting on experiences encourages insight and complex learning. We foster our own growth when we control our learning, so some reflection is best done alone. Reflection is also enhanced, however, when we ponder our learning with others. Reflection involves linking a current experience to previous learnings (called scaffolding). Reflection also involves drawing forth cognitive and emotional information from several sources: visual, auditory, kinesthetic, and tactile.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A process for constructive decision-making, a way to display the process in the classroom, and a willingness to help students develop constructive decision-making skills.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to brainstorm and display the process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop constructive decision-making skills, improve problem-solving abilities, promote ethical responsibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with a structured process for making good choices, improves problem-solving abilities, and promotes ethical responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can brainstorm with students to create a process for constructive decision-making. They can also display the process in the classroom as a visual reminder.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student decision-making skills, increased student problem-solving abilities, and greater ethical responsibility.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of a process for constructive decision-making.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher brainstorms with students to create a process for constructive decision-making. The teacher displays the process in the classroom as a visual reminder.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors present lecture content using graphic organizers rather than standard PowerPoints or outlines, visualizing how concepts are related to each other.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Pre-designed graphic organizers and lecture content adapted for visual presentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure all key information is included in the organizer. May not be suitable for all types of content.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from visual aids and structured presentations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students visualize how concepts are related, improving comprehension and retention during lectures.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear visual structure, enhances comprehension by showing relationships, and makes it easier to follow and retain information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Organizers can be adapted to different content areas and levels of complexity. Students can also use organizers to present their own information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Provide guidance
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of relationships between concepts, participation in discussions, and performance on related assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Presenting content in a graphic organizer instantly gives students a way to visualize how the concepts are related to each other.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Lesson plans are visual aids used by educators to stay organized and inspire their creativity. By incorporating visuals into lesson plans, it becomes easier to scan for information and present the material in an engaging way. Simple design elements such as icons, colorful headers, and thematic footers can breathe life into a mundane lesson plan. This makes lesson plans more effective and easier to share with other teachers, enhancing their teaching resources and overall impact.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to design software and planning tools. Implementation involves regular updates and use. May require training in instructional design.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overly complex designs can be distracting. Ineffective use of visuals can hinder understanding. Requires attention to detail and planning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, teachers, instructors, and educational institutions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance organization, inspire creativity, make lesson plans engaging, share resources, improve teaching effectiveness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances organization and ease of use. Inspires creativity and engagement. Makes lesson plans more effective and appealing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different subjects, grade levels, and teaching styles. Design elements can be adjusted based on the content and audience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the organization and clarity of the lesson plan. Assess the effectiveness of visual elements. Track student engagement and outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-designed lesson plans have been shown to improve teaching effectiveness and student engagement. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include lesson plans with icons, colorful headers, and thematic footers. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating lesson plans.

docs.title: Let students know what order they will be called on
Description
docs.text: This strategy allows students who are prone to challenges with inhibition to plan their response and wait until their turn. Knowing the order in advance reduces anxiety and impulsivity, providing a structured environment for participation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of student needs and potential challenges with inhibition. Flexibility in classroom management to accommodate different needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for all students with inhibition challenges. Requires ongoing assessment and adjustments based on student feedback and performance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with inhibition challenges, students who struggle with impulsivity

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, reduce impulsivity, increase participation, enhance focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a predictable structure for participation. Reduces anxiety and allows students to prepare their responses thoughtfully.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The order can be adjusted based on individual student needs. Students can be given advance notice of when they will be called on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation and self-regulation. Monitor frequency of impulsive responses. Gather student feedback on the effectiveness of the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This can allow students who are prone to challenges with inhibition to plan their response and wait until their turn.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Announcing the order of participation at the beginning of a class discussion. Using a visual aid to show the order of student presentations. Allowing students to volunteer to be called on at a specific time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities focused on teaching and practicing correct letter formation, including directionality, sequencing, and motor planning. These activities aim to establish a strong motor plan for letter formation, enabling automaticity and legibility.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Handwriting worksheets, letter formation guides, multisensory materials (e.g., sandpaper, playdough), and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address underlying issues such as fine motor weakness or visual perception difficulties. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grades, particularly useful for students who struggle with correct letter formation or have letter reversal issues.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve letter formation skills, including directionality, sequencing, and motor planning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Establishes a strong motor plan for letter formation, enabling automaticity and legibility. Addresses specific errors in letter formation through focused practice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual letter formation errors or learning styles. Multisensory approaches engage different sensory modalities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in letter formation, including correct directionality and sequencing. Track reduction in letter reversals or other common errors.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved letter formation skills, leading to more legible and fluent handwriting. Enhanced confidence in writing tasks.

docs.title: Letter Names and Letter Sounds Instruction
Description
docs.text: Explicit and direct instruction of letter names and letter sounds, which is critical for early literacy development. Children need to learn the letter names and the letter sounds in kindergarten. Letters should be taught directly and systematically. Older poor spellers should be asked to write the alphabet in order,accurately, and quickly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Alphabet charts, letter cards, phonics materials, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction, may not be effective for learners with severe cognitive deficits

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Kindergarten students, struggling readers, ESL learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop letter recognition, improve phoneme-grapheme correspondence, enhance spelling and reading skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds foundational skills for literacy, provides a structured approach to learning letter names and sounds, can be adapted for different learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction. Focus on specific letters or sounds that the learner is struggling with

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess letter recognition and sound production. Monitor progress in spelling and reading skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Letter names and letter sounds instruction is a foundational skill for literacy, improving both reading and spelling abilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The letter strategy is a mnemonic technique that involves using acronyms and acrostics to aid memory. Acronyms are words whose individual letters represent elements in lists of information (e.g., HOMES for the Great Lakes). Acrostics are sentences whose first letters represent to-be-remembered information (e.g., 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nine Pizzas' for the planets).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the information to be memorized, ability to create relevant acronyms or sentences, teaching students the association process, and regular review.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the relevance and memorability of the acronyms or sentences created. May not be suitable for all types of information or learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners, particularly useful for subjects involving lists or sequences of information. Beneficial for students with learning disabilities or memory challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory of lists and sequences, enhance encoding of information through verbal cues, facilitate recall of facts and concepts, reinforce association of letters with specific elements

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory by creating memorable acronyms or sentences. Simplifies complex lists of information into manageable forms. Can be applied across various subjects to memorize lists, steps, or key concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can involve students in creating their own acronyms and acrostics to match their learning styles and interests. Students can create personalized mnemonics that are more meaningful and memorable to them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved test scores on list-based questions, increased ability to recall sequences, enhanced retention of factual information, and positive student feedback on the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Letter strategies have been shown to be effective in helping students remember lists of information. The mnemonic 'IT FITS' provides steps to create mnemonics for vocabulary words, while 'LINCS' aids in remembering medieval history vocabulary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The mnemonic 'IT FITS' (Identify the term, Tell the definition, Find a keyword, Think about the definition, Study) provides steps for creating mnemonics for vocabulary words. LINCS (List the parts, Imagine the picture, Note a reminding word, Construct a LINCing story, Self-Test) aids in remembering vocabulary like 'catapult'.

docs.title: Letting students know what order they will be called on
Description
docs.text: Informing students of the order in which they will be called upon to respond can help reduce challenges related to inhibition. This proactive approach allows students time to mentally prepare their responses and manage their impulse to speak out of turn, thereby improving focus and participation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of individual student needs and potential challenges, planning and preparation for calling on students, and consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the sequence is not followed consistently. Some students may become overly focused on the sequence rather than the content.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with challenges related to inhibition, impulsivity, or difficulty waiting their turn

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce impulsivity, improve focus and attention, enhance student participation, support self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides predictability and reduces anxiety by clarifying expectations. Allows students to plan and organize their thoughts, improving the quality of their responses. Fosters a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment where all students have an opportunity to participate.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by using a variety of methods for calling on students, such as randomly selecting names, following a seating chart, or using a digital tool to generate a sequence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior (e.g., reduced impulsivity, increased participation). Collect feedback from students on their comfort level and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • By letting students know what order they will be called on, teachers can provide them with the opportunity to plan their response and wait until their turn, thereby improving focus and participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Informing a student who is prone to challenges with inhibition that they will be called on third allows them to plan their response and wait until their turn.

docs.title: Leverage Strengths to Address Self-Awareness Challenges
Description
docs.text: Educator identifies specific student strengths and/or challenges related to self- awareness, and uses/justifies aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Knowledge of students' strengths and challenges

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to identify students' strengths

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Leveraging Strengths to Address Attention Challenges
Description
docs.text: Identify specific student strengths and/or challenges related to attention then use strategies to leverage student strengths to support a student’s attention during learning. Key strategies include preferential seating, graphic organizers and visual aids, and chunking directions into smaller sections.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with attention challenges or varying degrees of attention strengths.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Leveraging Strengths to Improve Relationship Skills
Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on identifying and supporting students' relationship skills by leveraging their existing strengths. Relationship skills encompass the ability to form and maintain healthy connections through effective communication, cooperation, and conflict management. By recognizing and harnessing a student's strengths in these areas, educators can more effectively address their challenges. This approach emphasizes that all students have varying degrees of strengths and challenges related to relationship skills, and that focusing on strengths can be particularly beneficial. Strategies include pairing students with strong role models, providing group assignments that highlight common interests, using visual aids to outline fair communication protocols, and incorporating literature or social stories to teach relationship skills explicitly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to have a deep understanding of their students' individual strengths and challenges, as well as a willingness to provide personalized support. Clear communication and consistent reinforcement are also essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to identify and leverage students' strengths effectively. Some students may struggle to recognize their own strengths, requiring guidance and encouragement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for students across various grade levels and subjects, especially those who need support in developing positive social skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students' ability to form and maintain healthy relationships, improve communication and cooperation skills, and develop effective conflict management strategies.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • By leveraging existing strengths, this strategy boosts confidence, promotes a positive self-image, and fosters a supportive learning environment. It also encourages students to recognize and value their own and others' abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • This approach can be tailored to meet the unique needs and strengths of each student. Educators can select strategies that align with a student’s specific skills and challenges, ensuring that the support is targeted and effective.
