docs.title: Leveraging Strengths to Support Processing Speed
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves identifying a student’s strengths and using them to address challenges related to processing speed. Processing speed is the pace at which one takes in information, makes sense of it, and begins to respond. It is crucial to understand that processing speed varies among individuals and even within the same person depending on the context. Strategies include providing graphic organizers, repeating key points, using manipulatives, and allowing think-time and re-reading. Educators need to know their students well to leverage their strengths effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of processing speed and its impact on learning, knowledge of individual student strengths and challenges, access to appropriate support materials (e.g., graphic organizers, manipulatives).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to identify student strengths and tailor strategies, may not be effective if strengths are not appropriately leveraged.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with varying processing speeds, including those with diagnosed processing disorders or learning deficits

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address processing speed challenges, leverage student strengths, improve learning outcomes, enhance self-regulation, provide targeted support

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides personalized support by leveraging individual strengths, enhances comprehension and retention, addresses specific processing challenges, and fosters a sense of competence and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different learning styles and contexts, can be tailored to individual strengths and challenges, flexible implementation based on student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.text: • Student reflection on the effectiveness of the strategy, educator observation of student engagement and performance, analysis of student work samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the connection between processing speed, working memory, and fluid intelligence. Providing accommodations for processing speed challenges can improve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student strong in visual processing might use graphic organizers during lectures, while a student strong in auditory processing might benefit from repeated key points and verbal summaries.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Liberation literature involves exposing learners to literature that places out-group identities at the center of the curriculum to counter common negative stereotypes or omissions. This ensures that texts used in the classroom are mirrors for all learners. The strategy involves selecting texts that embody a variety of voices and perspectives, exploring the texts' authors, authenticity, and characters, and filling out a group representation chart for each text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to liberation literature texts, graphic organizers, and manipulatives.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Minimizing background noise, such as television, conversations, or lyrical music, enhances concentration and learning. Reading with irrelevant background speech requires more effort as the brain tries to process the meaning of the speech, reducing reading efficiency. Similarly, listening to lyrical music can be as detrimental to text comprehension as listening to speech due to the language processing demands. Instrumental music without lyrics has little to no negative effect on comprehension. By reducing noise, learners can concentrate more effectively, improving comprehension and overall performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Quiet environment, noise-canceling headphones (optional), instrumental music (optional)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in noisy environments. Success depends on learner awareness and commitment to minimizing auditory distractions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by eliminating extraneous auditory stimuli, supports deeper focus and concentration, enhances memory and retention

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Listen to the Voices of Students
Description
docs.text: Providing students authorship and allowing them to share their stories empowers them, fostering agency and leadership. This approach seeks to disrupt traditional power dynamics in the classroom by emphasizing youth voice and promoting equitable inclusion.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, foster agency and leadership, create an equitable learning environment, value student perspectives, disrupt traditional power dynamics.

docs.title: Affordances

docs.text: • Evaluate student contributions to class discussions and projects. Assess student leadership and agency in learning activities. Review student reflections on their learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Elevating student voice promotes agency and leadership, fostering a more equitable and engaging learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students leading class discussions on topics of interest. Learners designing projects that reflect their cultural backgrounds and experiences.

docs.title: Listening and reading for specific information
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves actively seeking particular details or information within a text or audio material to understand the overall message. It requires learners to listen selectively for specific words, phrases, or key ideas, monitor their comprehension, and infer meaning using linguistic, metalinguistic, and contextual clues. It is valuable in academic and workplace preparation, where adults may need to listen to lectures or prepare for exams.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading and listening materials, explicit instruction, guided practice, modeling of strategies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with limited vocabulary or background knowledge. Requires explicit instruction and practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult ESL learners, particularly those transitioning to academic study or workplace training

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve information retention, develop active listening and reading skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves focus and attention, strengthens comprehension, builds vocabulary, facilitates inference skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of the material and the specificity of the information sought. Scaffolding can include providing lists of key words or phrases.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner performance on comprehension tasks, ability to extract specific information, accuracy of inferences

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that skilled readers and listeners determine the importance of specific statements, monitor their comprehension, make predictions, and ask questions while reading and listening.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Activities such as filling in schedules while reading a story, completing mind maps based on interviews, and filling in cause-effect charts while listening to lectures.

docs.title: Listening to the Voices of Students in PBL
Description
docs.text: Listening to the voices of students involves giving them authorship in sharing and telling their own stories, creating agency and leadership. Student voice is essential in PBL, as it creates agency and leadership and helps build the culture for PBL. This approach contrasts with traditional teaching methodologies where students are not given importance in processing, challenging, and questioning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom environment that values student input and storytelling, and instructional strategies that support student voice and choice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a shift in traditional teaching roles and practices, and necessitates creating a safe and inclusive space for students to share their stories.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with a particular focus on those whose stories are often marginalized or overlooked in traditional educational settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To foster student agency, leadership, and ownership in learning by prioritizing student voices and perspectives in PBL activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students, promotes a sense of belonging, and encourages active participation in the learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to share their unique perspectives and experiences, making the learning experience more personalized and relevant.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Moderation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, more meaningful contributions to discussions, and evidence of students taking ownership of their learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that prioritizing student voice increases engagement, promotes a sense of belonging, and fosters a more equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing opportunities for students to share their personal experiences and perspectives in project work, and valuing their input in the design and implementation of PBL activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Literacy centers are designated areas in the classroom where students work independently or collaboratively on meaningful literacy tasks to explore and expand their learning. These centers provide opportunities for students to practice and extend literacy skills and standards they are learning during core instruction. Teachers can use literacy centers to provide reading instruction to small groups of students without interruption, allowing for greater instructional scaffolds and strategic coaching. Literacy centers capitalize on different learning styles by providing opportunities for multisensory learning that combines auditory, visual, and tactile elements. Effective literacy center tasks are scaffolded and provide models of exemplary work. Clear expectations and a system of accountability increase the accuracy and completeness of student work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated areas in the classroom with appropriate instructional materials. Clear expectations and procedures for using materials. Modeling and guided practice to ensure students understand the tasks. Monitoring of student progress and corrective feedback as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation to ensure tasks are developmentally appropriate and aligned with core instruction. Students need to be taught to be independent and adhere to classroom guidelines. May not be effective if tasks are not scaffolded or expectations are unclear.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, adaptable for older grades.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance and develop literacy skills, provide differentiated instruction, promote independent learning, foster intrinsic motivation, and reinforce skills and concepts in a variety of ways.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to provide targeted instruction to small groups while other students practice literacy skills independently or collaboratively. Capitalizes on different learning styles, providing opportunities for multisensory learning. Promotes intrinsic motivation and engagement by providing choices and making learning relevant and personal.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted to suit different learning styles, needs, and levels. Small group instruction allows for targeted support. Materials at varying complexity levels allow for choice and skill development.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Small Group Instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, accuracy, and completeness of work at literacy centers. Monitor student progress during small group instruction. Collect student work samples to assess skill development. Track student adherence to classroom guidelines and procedures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that providing choices and making learning relevant, personal, and engaging increases students' intrinsic motivation and attention. Small-group instruction and strategic coaching are key elements that distinguish high-achieving classrooms from those with moderate or low performances. Engaging multiple intelligences facilitates a deeper understanding of material.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using literature or social stories to explicitly teach relationship skills involves selecting or creating narratives that model positive social interactions, communication strategies, and conflict resolution techniques. These stories provide learners with vicarious experiences, allowing them to observe and analyze characters' behaviors and outcomes. By engaging with these narratives, learners can develop empathy, perspective-taking skills, and a deeper understanding of social dynamics. Social stories, in particular, are designed to provide clear and concise information about social situations, helping learners to navigate complex social interactions and develop appropriate responses.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection or creation of literature or social stories that model positive social interactions and communication strategies. Facilitation and guidance to support learners' understanding and analysis of the stories. Opportunities for learners to discuss the stories and share their own experiences and perspectives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of this strategy depends on the quality of the selected literature or social stories and the learners' willingness to engage with the narratives. There is a risk that some learners may not fully understand or internalize the lessons from the stories or that the stories may not accurately reflect their own experiences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and backgrounds, particularly those who may struggle with social interactions, communication, or conflict resolution

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop empathy and perspective-taking skills, provide models of positive social interactions and communication strategies, and increase understanding of social dynamics.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with vicarious experiences that model positive social interactions and communication strategies, fosters empathy and perspective-taking skills, and increases understanding of social dynamics. This can lead to improved social skills, stronger relationships, and increased participation in social activities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The selected literature or social stories can be tailored to the specific needs, interests, and cultural backgrounds of the learners, ensuring that they are relevant and meaningful. Learners can also be given opportunities to discuss the stories and share their own experiences and perspectives, fostering a deeper understanding and connection.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Case Study
  • Perspective-Taking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learners' responses to the literature or social stories, including their discussions, reflections, and analyses. Gather feedback from the learners about their experiences and perceptions of the stories. Assess the extent to which the learners demonstrate improved social skills, empathy, and perspective-taking abilities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that engaging with literature and social stories can effectively promote social-emotional learning and improve social skills. By providing learners with models of positive social interactions and communication strategies, these narratives can help them develop empathy, perspective-taking skills, and a deeper understanding of social dynamics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A class reads a story about a group of friends who disagree on a project but work together to find a solution that satisfies everyone. The educator facilitates a discussion about the characters' behaviors, communication styles, and conflict resolution techniques. The learners reflect on their own experiences with disagreements and identify strategies they can use to resolve conflicts in a positive and constructive manner.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Literature circles involve small groups of students who choose a book, meet to discuss it, and complete projects to demonstrate understanding. The approach emphasizes simplicity, adaptability, and student-led discussion. Teachers provide book choices, observe discussions, and offer feedback, while students use notes and marked passages to prepare for discussions. Activities include reflection, project-based expression, and awareness of common pitfalls like unpreparedness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of books suitable for group reading. Class time for discussions and project work. Teacher facilitation to guide and support students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to manage discussions and ensure student preparation. May be challenging to assess student learning consistently due to variations in book difficulty and group dynamics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school to high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, promote thoughtful discussion, encourage creative expression, foster student-led learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides student choice and vested interest in the material. Creates a fun, engaging environment for discussing books. Supports the development of critical thinking and communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer choices in books, themes, and projects to cater to individual interests and learning styles. Adapt reflection activities and project requirements based on student needs and abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe discussions for evidence of thoughtful engagement and comprehension. Review projects and reflections for understanding and creative expression. Provide feedback on discussions and projects to guide student learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The approach is different in every classroom, giving students agency while still supporting literacy. The keys to success are simplicity and adaptability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A sixth-grade teacher lets students pick a book, a theme, and a project. Students did maps, acrostic poems, and timelines. First-grade teachers have their students do puppet shows, dioramas, and a story quilt.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors demonstrate the writing process in real-time, in front of learners, to make the thinking and decision-making involved in writing visible. Using a projector or similar tool, the instructor composes a piece of writing while verbalizing their thought process, revisions, and considerations. Learners observe, critique, and provide input, turning the writing process into a collaborative and transparent activity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Projector or similar display tool, pre-planned writing task, instructor preparedness to verbalize their thought process. Requires a classroom environment that encourages participation and critique.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant instructor preparation and real-time adaptability. May be challenging for instructors who are uncomfortable writing in front of others. Learners may become passive observers if not actively engaged.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for secondary and higher education students learning specific writing skills or genres

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Demystify the writing process, enhance understanding of writing strategies, improve learners' writing skills, promote collaborative learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and immediate view of the writing process, allows learners to see revisions and decision-making in action, promotes active engagement and collaboration, builds confidence by demystifying writing

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The writing task can be tailored to the learners' current needs and interests. The level of instructor support and guidance can be adjusted based on learner skill levels. Learners can focus on different aspects of the writing process based on their individual challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Modeling
  • Articulation
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in learner writing quality as evidenced by better structure, clarity, and use of techniques observed in the demonstration. Increased learner participation in writing activities and peer feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Live writing demonstrations help learners understand how to approach writing tasks, revise their work, and prioritize concision. By seeing the instructor's weaknesses and struggles, learners become less defensive about their own work and more open to criticism.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A history teacher composes an introductory paragraph in front of the class, sharing their thought process and revisions while students critique their work. Students think of a worthy historical question for the teacher to tackle.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Logic puzzles are challenges designed to exercise the brain and improve memory, hand-eye coordination, and spatial and cognitive skills. Puzzles help to build logical reasoning with the rules of computer coding, spatial reasoning skills, and deduce how to make arrangements.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to logic puzzles and a quiet space to concentrate.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some puzzles may be too difficult for certain age groups or skill levels, leading to frustration.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Varies depending on the puzzle, but generally suitable for children and adults who enjoy mental challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory, hand-eye coordination, spatial reasoning, and cognitive skills; develop logical reasoning; enhance problem-solving abilities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Exercises the brain and improves cognitive skills. Develops logical reasoning and problem-solving abilities. Offers the joy of conquering challenges.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Puzzles can be selected based on difficulty level and specific skills to target.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe successful completion of puzzles. Track improvement in spatial reasoning and cognitive skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Puzzles help us exercise our brains, improving memory, hand-eye coordination, spatial and cognitive skills.

docs.title: Logs and Journals to Guide Reflection
Description
docs.text: Periodically ask students to reread their journals, comparing what they knew at the beginning of a learning sequence with what they know now. Ask them to select significant learnings, envision how they could apply these learnings to future situations, and commit to an action plan to consciously modify their behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Students must have journals and be aware that they may be checked on.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Student writing ability must be up to par.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective in classrooms where a strong sense of community and trust has been established

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster metacognition, enhance problem-solving skills, and build habits of empathy, flexibility, and persistence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Students gain a deeper understanding of their learning and are forced to actively engage in remembering important learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Student are able to discuss what they think are important.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • individual reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Check for journal quality and depth. Observe improvements in performance on subsequent tasks based on insights from previous reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that reflection in a variety of forms is effective.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Rinne (1982) coined low-profile classroom control for coping strategies effective teachers use to stop misbehavior without disrupting a lesson's flow. It targets surface behaviors (Levin & Nolan, 1991) — laughing, talking out of turn, passing notes, daydreaming, not following directions, combing hair, doodling, humming, tapping — the ordinary, non-pathological behaviors of children confined to a small space with many peers, which nonetheless disrupt lesson flow and other students' work engagement if left unchecked. Low-profile control has three components:

  • Anticipation — sensing changes in student motivation, attentiveness, or excitability as they happen, or even just before they happen, including knowing that certain times of year, week, or day (before/after holidays, before a major event, right after an assembly or PE class) predict lower readiness for work. Anticipation means scanning the room to size up a potential problem and head it off before it grows — picking up the class's pace to counter post-weekend lethargy, or removing distracting objects before a long holiday.
  • Deflection — noticing the verbal and nonverbal cues that have preceded disruption in the past (a glance at a friend, an abruptly closed textbook, squirming, a frustrated sigh) and redirecting before the disruption actually occurs. Moving physically nearer to a student who may be about to misbehave, making eye contact, or a raised eyebrow are nonverbal deflection techniques; verbal prompting or name-dropping are verbal ones. As the risk of escalation grows, effective managers shift from nonverbal to verbal deflection to match the seriousness of what's brewing.
  • Reaction — when disruption cannot be anticipated or unobtrusively deflected, ending the episode as quickly as possible with a warning followed by a consequence (Glasser, 1990, notes that temporary removal from the classroom is an effective consequence for rule-breaking, provided the classroom is a place the student actually wants to be — see Glasser's Choice Theory; other options include loss of privileges, detention, or loss of recess). A typical reaction sequence: (1) acknowledge a nearby student modeling the expected behavior ("Carlos, I appreciate how hard you are working on the spelling words") and wait about 15 seconds for the disruptive student to self-correct; (2) if disruption continues, issue a specific warning naming the expected behavior ("Michael, this is a warning. Complete the spelling assignment and leave Carrie alone.") and wait again; (3) if the warning isn't heeded, follow through with the stated consequence.

Anticipation and deflection are generally preferable when they work, since they let students correct themselves and so build self-control, while reaction is a fallback for behavior too fast-moving or too demanding of the teacher's divided attention to catch earlier. If low-profile techniques consistently fail for a particular student or group despite reasonable, sustained effort, that failure is itself a signal — often that an underlying need (e.g. for belonging) isn't being met — worth consulting a school counselor or psychologist about, rather than simply escalating the same techniques further.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Sustained, divided attention across the whole room (this strategy assumes something like Kounin's withitness as a prerequisite skill)
  • A consequence, decided in advance, that the reaction phase can escalate to if warnings go unheeded

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Targets only minor "surface" behaviors, not serious disruption or behavior stemming from an emotional or personality issue
  • Repeated failure of anticipation/deflection/reaction for a specific student suggests an unmet underlying need rather than a technique to apply more forcefully
  • Effectiveness depends on the teacher's own attentiveness and practice — anticipation and deflection are skills that improve with experience, not fixed abilities

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students engaging in ordinary, low-level, developmentally typical off-task behavior rather than behavior driven by an unmet emotional need or disability-related trigger

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Minimizing disruption to lesson flow and peer work engagement while preserving opportunities for student self-correction

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Anticipate. Watch for signs — in the calendar, the time of day, or individual students entering the room — that predict lower readiness for work, and adjust pace or remove distractions preemptively.
  2. Deflect. Notice pre-disruption cues (a glance, a sigh, closing a book) and redirect nonverbally first (proximity, eye contact, a facial expression), escalating to a verbal prompt only if needed.
  3. React, if needed. Acknowledge a nearby student doing the right thing and pause; if disruption continues, give one clear, specific warning naming the expected behavior; if still unresolved, follow through with the stated consequence.
  4. Escalate outside the classroom if the pattern persists despite consistent anticipation, deflection, and reaction — consult a school counselor or psychologist rather than repeating the same techniques indefinitely.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Ignoring and Nonverbal Redirection — a lighter-touch complementary technique for misbehavior too minor to warrant even deflection
  • Teacher Effectiveness Training / Conflict Resolution — the next tier of response, for conflict too persistent for low-profile control alone

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Carlos/Michael reaction-sequence script above, illustrating acknowledge-warn-consequence in three steps.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Rinne, C. H. (1982). Low-profile classroom controls. The Phi Delta Kappan, 64(1), 53. https://www.jstor.org/stable/20386554
  • Levin, J., & Nolan, J. F. (1991). Principles of classroom management: A hierarchical approach. Allyn & Bacon.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Systems of classroom management. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Low-stakes quizzes are brief assessments designed to help learners gauge their understanding without the pressure of high grades. These quizzes reduce test anxiety, prompt honest reflection, and improve focus and performance. Timing is important, with quizzes given right after a lesson and revisited throughout the school year.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to assessment tools and minimal grading effort. Should be low-impact on overall grades.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful design to avoid increasing anxiety. Needs to be integrated with other learning activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, effective for K–12 and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gauge understanding, identify strengths and weaknesses, and reduce test anxiety.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces reliance on superficial learning strategies like rereading, promotes honest self-reflection, and improves focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be delivered on paper, in Google Forms, with clickers, or using apps like Kahoot! or Quizziz.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Quizzes
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track quiz scores over time to measure improvement. Analyze common incorrect answers to identify areas for reteaching.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows low-stakes quizzes improve student focus and performance by closing the gap between perceived and actual knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers at University Park Campus School used daily low-stakes writing activities to foster student voice, self-confidence, and critical thinking skills—a school-wide strategy used in every subject.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires short writing prompts or activities. Requires time for students to write.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to generate ideas for writing. Teachers need to provide guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels and subjects.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster student voice, self-confidence, and critical thinking skills. Provide frequent opportunities for writing practice. Reduce anxiety around writing.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a low-pressure environment for writing. Encourages student voice and self-expression. Promotes critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose the topics they want to write about. Teachers can provide different prompts based on student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student writing to assess voice, self-confidence, and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters student voice, self-confidence, and critical thinking skills. Provides frequent opportunities for writing practice. Reduces anxiety around writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When learning about the conservation of mass, show students a picture and ask, “What do you notice about the atoms on both sides? How can you explain that?” Students wrote down their observations, and the entire class came up with a definition.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Magnetism investigations involve exploring how magnets interact with different objects and mapping the effects of magnets on compasses. Learners observe and predict which objects magnets attract and investigate how compasses are affected by nearby magnetic fields. These activities improve understanding of magnetic properties and their applications.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Magnets, compasses, various objects (e.g., metal, plastic, wood), controlled environments

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to magnets and compasses. Safety precautions may be needed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand basic magnetic properties, observe and predict magnetic attraction, investigate how compasses are affected by magnetic fields

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activities make abstract concepts more concrete. Encourages prediction and observation skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Variety of objects for testing magnetic attraction. Compass and magnet experiments can be adapted for varying difficulty.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in predicting magnetic attraction, correct mapping of compass deviations, logical explanations of magnetic effects

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of magnetic properties, enhanced observation and prediction skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Magnetic Testing (ILS): Learners observe and predict which objects a magnet will attract. Magnetic Mapping (CCSSO): Learners investigate how a compass can be affected by placing it near different objects.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The temperature in a workspace affects engagement levels and overall productivity. The ideal temperature range for effective learning in reading and mathematics is between 68º and 74º. Teachers need to be able to control the temperature in their own classrooms, or at least small blocks of classrooms, to maintain a comfortable learning environment. Ensuring appropriate temperature levels enhances student engagement and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Temperature controls, training for teachers on temperature management

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly. Individual preferences for temperature may vary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, teachers, and administrators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student engagement and enhance academic performance by maintaining optimal classroom temperatures

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comfort, improves focus and concentration, and boosts academic performance

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Install individual temperature controls in classrooms or small blocks of classrooms and provide training for teachers on effective temperature management.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement, measure test scores, and collect feedback from teachers and students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that maintaining optimal classroom temperatures enhances student engagement and academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Schools install individual temperature controls in classrooms, provide training for teachers, and regularly monitor classroom temperatures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers should make themselves available for short talks with students before and after school or between classes. Teachers needs to show that they are doing this tough work with the students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A teacher who is aware of the language being used in the classroom, who is willing to intervene when necessary, and who has the skills and resources to address the situation effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to address in the moment, may require additional support from administrators or parents, and may not always be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create safe environments to have open dialogues.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides safe opportunities for students to ask questions and express emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers must be willing to be available for students to come to them and express emotions and ask questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Coaching
  • Individual Reflection
  • Perspective-Taking
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and severity of abusive language in the classroom, assess student understanding of the impact of their words, and gather feedback from students about the safety and respectfulness of the learning environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that addressing abusive language in schools can create a safer and more respectful learning environment, promote positive social-emotional development, and improve academic outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher hears a student use a homophobic slur and immediately says, 'I don't allow that term in my classroom. I need to talk with you after class about that.' The teacher then meets with the student to discuss the impact of their words and to foster empathy for those who are hurt.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A culturally responsive curriculum is both inclusive in that it ensures that all students are included within all aspects of the school, and it acknowledges the unique differences students may possess. A culturally responsive curriculum also encourages teachers’ understanding and recognition of each student’s non-school cultural life and background and provides a means for them to incorporate this information into the curriculum, thus promoting inclusion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A commitment to diversity and inclusion, willingness to learn about students' cultures, and creativity in curriculum design.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to develop culturally responsive curriculum. Some students may resist changes to the traditional curriculum.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote inclusion, celebrate diversity, and connect learning to students' lives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students feel valued and respected. Makes learning more relevant and engaging.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Curriculum can be adapted to reflect the cultural backgrounds and experiences of students in the classroom.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Case Study
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, improved classroom climate, and greater understanding of cultural diversity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and equitable learning environment where all students feel valued and connected to the curriculum.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In culturally responsive instruction, achievement expectations are determined individually. Students receive praise in proportion to their accomplishments, not lavish praise for simple tasks. When a student struggles, the instructor helps guide the student positively toward explaining how to complete the initial steps, fostering self-efficacy and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Individualized assessment, clear communication, supportive guidance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to understand individual student needs, may be challenging to manage in large classes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those at risk of underperforming

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-efficacy, set individual expectations, provide proportional praise, guide students toward problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages self-efficacy, fosters a growth mindset, provides realistic feedback, promotes problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Setting expectations based on individual student needs and abilities, tailoring feedback to individual progress.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student progress toward individual goals, student self-assessments, teacher observations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on growth mindset and self-efficacy shows that these factors are critical for student success. Setting high expectations and providing supportive guidance can help students overcome challenges and achieve their full potential.

docs.title: Maintaining High Expectations for Student Performance
Description
docs.text: Given that culturally responsive instruction is a student-centered philosophy, it should come as no surprise that expectations for achievement are determined and assigned individually for each student. Students don’t receive lavish praise for simple tasks but do receive praise in proportion to their accomplishments. If a student is not completing her work, then one should engage the student positively and help guide the student toward explaining how to complete the initial steps that need to be done to complete a given assignment or task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A student-centered approach to teaching and learning, clear learning goals, and ongoing formative assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort to differentiate instruction. Some students may be resistant to high expectations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers in diverse classrooms (K-12, higher education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote high achievement, provide individualized support, and foster a growth mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to strive for excellence. Provides targeted support to help students overcome challenges.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Expectations and support are tailored to each student's individual needs and abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student achievement, improved student motivation, and a stronger growth mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a classroom environment where all students are challenged and supported to reach their full potential.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In traditional classrooms, students who are not native English speakers often feel marginalized, lost, and pressured into discarding their original language in favor of English. In a culturally responsive classroom, diversity of language is celebrated, and the level of instructional materials provided to non-native speakers are tailored to their level of English fluency. Accompanying materials should be provided in the student’s primary language, and the student should be encouraged to master English.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to resources in multiple languages, training in second language acquisition, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources to implement. Some students may be reluctant to use their primary language in the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers with English language learners in their classrooms (K-12, adult education)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support language acquisition, promote linguistic diversity, and create an inclusive classroom environment for non-native English speakers.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces feelings of marginalization and isolation. Supports language development in both English and the student's primary language.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructional materials and support can be tailored to the student's level of English fluency and language background.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation and engagement, improved language proficiency, and greater confidence in using both English and their primary language.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more linguistically diverse and inclusive classroom environment where all students feel valued and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing learners with real-world experiences and problems, and allowing them to work alongside experts, fosters engagement and prepares them for real-world challenges. Educators can give learners complex, open-ended problems that they can address collaboratively, mirroring real-world tasks and engaging learners in roles from the real world. When real-world play is incorporated into the classroom, learners are more motivated when projects are expansive and ideas are big. This approach involves thinking critically about the big ideas and finding where they live in the real world, creating situations and problems for learners to grapple with.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Real-world problems and scenarios. Expert guidance and support. Collaboration opportunities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant resources to develop and implement. Some learners may struggle with open-ended problems.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance motivation, develop real-world problem-solving skills, promote critical thinking, foster collaboration, prepare learners for real-world challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation and engagement. Develops real-world problem-solving skills. Promotes critical thinking and collaboration. Prepares learners for real-world challenges.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose projects based on their interests and skill levels. Instructors can provide different levels of scaffolding and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner projects and solutions. Participation in problem-solving activities. Critical thinking and collaboration skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that problem-based learning enhances motivation, engagement, and problem-solving skills. Studies also show that real-world experiences improve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school class designs a restaurant, including budget, menu, and brand. Learners come into class and get news that their teacher has been kidnapped, and they have to collect fingerprints and look for clues. High school learners are asked to come up with solutions for big problems like global warming.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers can boost student engagement and knowledge retention by connecting learning to students' interests, talents, learning styles, and sense of ownership in the education process. Teachers can give students a say in how the classroom operates, thus increasing students' sense of ownership in the education process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding students' talents, interests, and learning styles. Willingness to adjust teaching methods and strategies. Classroom discussions to allow students to provide input.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to understand individual student needs. May be challenging to accommodate all interests and preferences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators looking to improve student motivation and engagement

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, improve knowledge retention, foster a sense of ownership, cater to diverse learning styles and interests

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement and motivation, improves knowledge retention, fosters a sense of ownership, addresses diverse learning styles and interests

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor teaching methods to suit diverse talents and learning styles. Provide students with a choice in classroom activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement levels, monitor knowledge retention through assessments, gather student feedback through surveys or discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students are more engaged in learning and retain knowledge better when they see that it is relevant and vital to their own success and happiness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher surveys students about their hobbies and interests and then incorporates those topics into math word problems or reading assignments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This principle focuses on bringing power dynamics to the forefront and acknowledging their presence in the design process. It involves naming the dynamics, rather than ignoring them, and understanding who has decision-making authority. It highlights different approaches to design, from user-centered design (where designers consult users) to co-design (where stakeholders become part of the design team) to user-created design (where students are entrusted with power). The principle also emphasizes the use of observation tools to assess how schools either affirm and support students in their personal identities or alienate and minimize who they are. The overall goal is to promote equitable design by challenging assumptions about power and belonging.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to challenge existing power structures, as well as resources for conducting observations and facilitating discussions about power dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to implement if stakeholders are resistant to addressing power dynamics. Requires careful facilitation to ensure that discussions are productive and respectful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and school teams seeking to create more equitable and inclusive learning environments and challenge existing power structures.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify and address power dynamics, promote equitable design practices, affirm student identities, and foster a sense of belonging.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes greater awareness of power dynamics, leads to more equitable and inclusive solutions, and fosters a stronger sense of belonging for all learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific observation tools and activities can be tailored to the context and needs of the school and students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Criteria Development
  • Consensus Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure student perceptions of power and belonging in the school environment, track the implementation of more equitable policies and practices, and assess the impact of interventions on student identity development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A more equitable and inclusive school environment, a stronger sense of belonging for all learners, and improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In CityBridge’s School Design Fellowship program, they use a set of observation tools focused on student identity development and affirmation. They also draw upon Transcend’s comprehensive “Designing for Learning Primer” on learning science and a simple set of cards that summarize research findings from psychology and cognitive science, with insights about how identity intersects with learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Establish physical spaces where learners can invent, design, and build things using a variety of materials and tools, from wood scraps to technology. These spaces foster exploration, imagination, and collaboration, allowing learners to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world problems. Maker spaces encourage hands-on learning and creativity, enabling learners to see the practical applications of their knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a dedicated physical space with a variety of materials, tools, and equipment. Instructors need to be knowledgeable about different technologies and techniques and be able to provide guidance and support to learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be expensive to set up and maintain. Requires careful planning and supervision to ensure safety and prevent misuse of equipment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for middle and high school students, as well as adult learners in technical and vocational programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster creativity and innovation, promote hands-on learning, encourage collaboration, apply theoretical knowledge to real-world problems

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for experiential learning, promotes creativity and problem-solving skills, and encourages collaboration among learners. Maker spaces allow learners to see the practical applications of their knowledge and develop a deeper understanding of concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of projects and materials to cater to different interests and skill levels. Provide support and guidance to help learners overcome challenges and develop their skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate learner creativity and innovation in their projects. Assess their ability to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world problems. Observe their collaboration and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that maker spaces and fab labs enhance creativity, problem-solving skills, and collaboration among learners. Hands-on learning experiences lead to deeper understanding and retention of knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students design and build robots in a physics class, sew their own clothes in a fashion design class, or create jewelry using 3D printers in a maker space. A group of adult learners builds a functional guitar out of cigar boxes, applying principles of physics and engineering in a creative and engaging way.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves forming educated guesses or anticipations about the content or outcome of a text or audio material and then verifying these predictions as one engages with the material. It encourages active engagement, critical thinking, and monitoring of comprehension by comparing existing knowledge to new information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading and listening materials, explicit instruction, guided practice, opportunities for discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with limited vocabulary or background knowledge. Requires explicit instruction and practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult ESL learners, particularly those transitioning to academic study or workplace training

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active engagement, enhance comprehension, develop critical thinking skills, connect prior knowledge to new information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances focus and attention, strengthens comprehension, builds background knowledge, encourages active participation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of the material and the specificity of the predictions. Scaffolding can include providing sentence stems or guided questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Eliciting Student Thinking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner accuracy in predicting content, ability to confirm or revise predictions, depth of engagement with the material

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that skilled readers and listeners make predictions while engaging with texts and audio materials, which enhances comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Activities such as predicting the content of a story based on pictures, making predictions about the beliefs associated with a holiday before listening to an interview, and comparing class predictions to information from the interview.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making connections involves linking new information to existing knowledge and experiences to enhance understanding and retention. This can be done by relating the text to personal experiences (text-to-self), comparing it to other texts (text-to-text), or relating it to real-world events and knowledge (text-to-world). Proficient readers actively relate what they are reading or listening to with something in their schema to construct meaning. Modeling the process, especially text-to-self connections initially, is crucial, using strategy-related language to verbalize the connections and providing opportunities for students to share their connections.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to texts, modeling by an instructor or facilitator, chart paper or digital tools for recording connections, and structured activities for practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Superficial connections may not enhance understanding. Requires explicit instruction and modeling. Some students may struggle to make meaningful connections if they lack relevant background knowledge or experience.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, adult learners, and anyone who wants to improve their reading comprehension and ability to connect with texts on a deeper level.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, build connections between new information and prior knowledge, improve retention, and develop critical thinking skills by relating text to personal experiences, other texts, and the world.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves comprehension by linking new information to existing knowledge, increases engagement by making the material personally relevant, and fosters deeper understanding and retention of information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scaffolded prompts and sentence starters can be used for beginners. Learners can choose the type of connection (text-to-self, text-to-text, text-to-world) that resonates most with them. Can be adapted to various text types, including narrative, informational, and multimedia.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the depth and relevance of student connections through discussions, written reflections, or graphic organizers. Evaluate how well students can articulate the link between the text and their own experiences, other texts, or the world. Track improvements in comprehension scores and engagement levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that making connections enhances comprehension and engagement with text. Studies have shown that thought-provoking questions and peer discussions can force students to link newly acquired information to material outside of the current lesson. (King et al., 1997; Morrison, 2005)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making Connections is a comprehension strategy that helps learners relate a text to their own lives (text-to-self), to other texts they have read (text-to-text), or to events in the real world (text-to-world). By making these connections, learners can better understand and engage with the material. It involves modeling the different types of connections, providing guiding questions, and encouraging learners to share their connections through discussion and writing. This strategy draws on prior knowledge and experiences to connect with the text and make them more engaged in the reading experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Text to be read, guiding questions for each type of connection (text-to-self, text-to-text, text-to-world), materials for recording connections (e.g., double-entry journal, connection web).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Superficial connections may not enhance understanding. Learners may need explicit instruction and modeling to make meaningful connections.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, enhance engagement, activate prior knowledge, make personal connections to text, relate text to other texts and the world.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters deeper understanding, promotes engagement, helps learners relate to the material on a personal level, supports critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose which type of connection to focus on, and teachers can adapt the guiding questions to suit the specific text and learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and relevance of connections made by learners, participation in discussions, quality of written reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, increased engagement, and a stronger connection to the material.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy requires readers to evaluate or draw conclusions from information in a text, even when the author does not explicitly state it. Readers combine information from the text with their own background knowledge to 'read between the lines' and infer meanings. This is crucial because authors often provide clues rather than complete descriptions. Teaching readers to make inferences improves their ability to construct meaning from texts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learners need to be able to identify clues and implicit information in the text and connect it to their background knowledge. Instructors should model inference-making and provide opportunities for practice and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If learners lack sufficient background knowledge, they may struggle to make accurate inferences. Inaccurate or biased background knowledge can lead to incorrect inferences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in upper elementary, middle, and high school, as well as adult learners looking to improve reading comprehension and critical thinking skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension by drawing conclusions from implicit information, combining text details with background knowledge, and constructing deeper meaning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves critical thinking by requiring readers to analyze and synthesize information, connects new information with existing knowledge, and promotes deeper comprehension of texts where information is not explicitly stated.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can focus on making inferences about topics that align with their interests and knowledge levels. Instructors can provide prompts or graphic organizers to support inference-making.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Reassessment
  • Case Study

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to make accurate inferences through discussions, written responses, or graphic organizers that demonstrate their reasoning and connection of ideas.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research confirms that teaching readers to make inferences significantly improves their ability to construct meaning from texts, enhancing comprehension and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When reading a story about a character who is always late and unprepared, learners infer that the character is irresponsible or disorganized based on the provided details and their own experiences with similar behaviors.

docs.title: Making Self-Advocacy and Self-Determination Critical Priorities
Description
docs.text: Integrating self-advocacy and self-determination into education systems to empower students with disabilities. Incorporate self-advocacy and self-determination throughout education by including them into teacher preparation, assessments of learning, and measures of school performance such as chronic absenteeism. Provide tangible opportunities for students to practice self-advocacy skills and self-determination in their education.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time, resources, training, and intentional actions to foster self-advocacy and self-determination.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Require an investment of time, resources, and training; intentional actions; difficult conversations; and most of all, a mindset that all students can make active choices about their learning and lives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities, educators, families, and policymakers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To improve educational and life outcomes for students with disabilities by fostering self-advocacy and self-determination skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students to become active participants in their education and civic life, fostering independence and improved life outcomes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Goal setting, problem solving, and self-advocacy become explicit goals in student IEPs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Response
  • Research
  • Problem Presentation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in student participation in IEP meetings, increased self-advocacy skills, and improved life outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students who practice self-advocacy skills have improved educational and life outcomes compared to those who do not.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using physical or digital manipulatives to combine simple sentences, thereby reducing working memory load and improving syntax knowledge. This involves providing a bank of movable sentences and clauses, potentially color-coded by parts of speech, to support learners of all different needs and serve as a bridge in understanding sentence structure.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to physical or digital manipulatives representing sentences and clauses. Color-coding materials can be useful but not required.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if learners lack basic vocabulary or grammatical understanding. Reliance on manipulatives may hinder the development of abstract understanding if not faded appropriately.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for learners who struggle with sentence structure and syntax.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve syntax knowledge, reduce working memory load, support sentence construction skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by providing manageable sentence components. Supports kinesthetic learning through physical manipulation. Color-coding provides visual cues to enhance understanding of sentence structure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of sentences and clauses. Digital versions can offer adjustable levels of scaffolding and automated feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to combine sentences correctly using manipulatives. Track improvement in sentence complexity and accuracy in writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that manipulatives can improve reading comprehension and writing skills. Providing sentence components reduces cognitive load, which supports learners' working memory capacity. Color-coding parts of speech enhances syntax knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using physical objects to represent parts of speech in sentences. Learners write a sentence and then use color-coded blocks or magnetic word tiles to represent each word or phrase. This provides a hands-on way to visualize sentence structure and grammar, reinforcing syntax and vocabulary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires color-coded blocks or magnetic word tiles, along with materials for learners to write sentences (paper and pencil, or a whiteboard).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to prepare materials. Some learners may find the physical manipulation distracting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school learners who are learning to write sentences and understand parts of speech.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce understanding of sentence structure and grammar, improve vocabulary, and provide a hands-on way to practice syntax.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a tactile and visual representation of abstract concepts, making it easier for learners to grasp sentence structure. Encourages active participation and engagement, which can increase motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by customizing the words used in the magnetic tiles to match the learner's spelling words or vocabulary list. Color-coding of blocks can also be adjusted to learner preferences or specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to correctly represent sentences with manipulatives. Assess the complexity and accuracy of the sentences they construct.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a multi-sensory approach to learning sentence construction, which can improve comprehension and retention. Hands-on activities have been shown to increase engagement and motivation in learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The description references using color-coded blocks to represent parts of speech. The description also provides directions for making magnetic sentence tiles.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete. Abstract concepts can be tough to understand, but tangible objects make them easier to manage.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Readily available manipulatives and a teacher that supports their use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students might not have the cognitive awareness to benefit from manipulatives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Tangible objects help students better understand key concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to find manipulatives that work for them. Use manipulatives for every content, not just numeracy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether students make connections between the manipulatives and concepts. Use assessment results to see if they are learning from the manipulatives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that manipulatives can help support learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of manipulatives in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use blocks when teaching math, use physical items to teach about abstract concepts like history, let the kids handle maps and globes for geography. Resource: Speed of Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before a trip, children map the route, calculate mileage, estimate travel time, and track progress along the way. This promotes map reading, measurement, and problem-solving skills, enhancing their understanding of distance, time, and direction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Map, ruler, and calculator.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to a map and reliable information about distances and routes. May require assistance with calculations for younger learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve map reading skills, enhance measurement and estimation abilities, and promote problem-solving skills related to distance, time, and direction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves map reading skills and enhances understanding of distance, time, and direction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the map and calculations based on the learner's skill level. Provide pre-calculated distances and times as a scaffold.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to read and interpret the map accurately. Evaluate the accuracy of calculated distances and travel times.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Help your children become more engaged in your family adventures and help them discover all the math around them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners create visual maps to track the links and sites they visit while reading online texts. They start with a general research question and document each step and detour they take to find the answer, either by drawing or taking screenshots. Students share their maps and reflect on their decision-making process at each point.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to online reading materials and tools for creating visual maps (e.g., drawing software, mind-mapping tools, or simply paper and pencils).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it challenging to accurately recall and document their online reading behavior. The activity may also be time-consuming, especially if learners are easily distracted or tend to wander off-topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance metacognitive awareness of online reading habits, promote self-regulation, and foster critical evaluation of information sources.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports metacognition by making learners aware of their online reading processes, promotes self-regulation by encouraging them to monitor and adjust their strategies, and fosters critical evaluation of information sources by requiring them to reflect on the reliability and relevance of the content they encounter.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The complexity of the research question and the level of detail required in the maps can be adjusted to meet the needs of diverse learners. Learners can also be given the option to use different mapping tools or formats based on their preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review the maps created by learners to assess their awareness of their own online reading processes and their ability to make informed decisions about which sources to trust and which links to follow. Observe the quality of their reflections on their decision-making processes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that metacognitive reflection on online reading behavior can improve learners' comprehension, critical thinking, and self-regulation skills in digital environments.

docs.title: Description
