docs.text: Mass, density, and buoyancy experiments involve exploring how the mass and density of objects affect their buoyancy in different liquids. Learners compare the buoyancy of a pencil in freshwater versus saltwater and correlate the weight and water displacement of various balls. These experiments enhance understanding of mass, density, and buoyancy principles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Freshwater, saltwater, pencil, various balls, measuring cups, balance scale

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires precise measurement. May need access to specialized materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the principles of mass, density, and buoyancy, compare buoyancy in different liquids, correlate weight and water displacement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activities make abstract concepts more understandable. Encourages quantitative measurement and analysis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Variety of liquids and objects can be used for buoyancy experiments. Weight and water displacement tasks can be adapted for varying complexity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in measuring buoyancy, correct correlation of weight and water displacement, logical explanations of buoyancy effects

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of mass, density, and buoyancy, enhanced measurement and analytical skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Floating Pencil (NAEP): Learners compare the buoyancy of a pencil in freshwater vs. saltwater. Rising Waters (KDE): Learners correlate the weight and water displacement of various balls.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Present matched examples and nonexamples for concepts with related attributes. Nonexamples are an instance that is specifically not an example of the concept being learned. Nonexamples should vary in one attribute from the example with which it is paired. Matched examples and nonexamples should be present in working memory simultaneously.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of examples and non-examples that differ by only one attribute.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to identify appropriate non-examples. Requires careful presentation to avoid confusion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially for concepts with closely related attributes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote accurate concept formation, avoid overgeneralization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Sharpens discrimination skills by highlighting what a concept is and is not. Reduces the risk of overgeneralization.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select examples and non-examples that are relevant to learners' experiences and prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to distinguish between examples and non-examples and explain the key differences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Presenting matched examples and nonexamples helps learners form an accurate concept and to avoid overgeneralization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When defining the concept of 'comics,' pair an example of a comic book page with a Roy Lichtenstein painting that uses comic-style imagery but is intended as fine art.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math Talks, also known as Number Talks, are short, daily classroom routines where students solve math problems mentally and share their strategies. The instructor presents a problem, and students work individually to find a solution without using paper or pencil. Then, students share their answers and explain their thinking, while the instructor encourages discussion and clarifies strategies. The goal is to build students' mental math skills, flexibility in thinking about numbers, and communication skills. Math Talks can be adapted for various grade levels, from early elementary to upper grades, and can be used to explore different mathematical concepts, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, and decimals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A clean desktop, a problem to present, and a safe and respectful classroom environment. Instructor should be prepared with questions to clarify and extend student thinking, and be familiar with different math strategies to suggest them if they do not come up in conversation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require some preparation and familiarity with different math strategies on the part of the instructor. Some students may be hesitant to share their thinking or may struggle to articulate their strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, from early elementary to upper grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build mental math skills, develop flexibility in thinking about numbers and operations, enhance mathematical communication skills, encourage reasoning and critical thinking, build a community of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages flexible thinking and problem-solving skills. Promotes communication and discussion about math strategies. Supports mental math skills and numeracy. Provides opportunities for students to learn from each other's approaches.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for various grade levels and mathematical concepts. The instructor can choose problems and visuals appropriate for the students' skill levels. Students can use different strategies to solve the problems, allowing for individual approaches.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Eliciting Student Thinking
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in discussions and the variety of strategies they use. Observe student explanations and reasoning to assess their understanding of mathematical concepts. Collect student reflections on their learning and progress.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that Number Talks help students develop mathematical reasoning, critical thinking, language, and communication skills. They also build a mental storehouse of strategic tools and promote a community of learning in the classroom.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Greg Tang's The Grapes of Math to find quick ways to count objects on the page. Breaking down a multiplication problem into smaller parts (e.g., 24 x 8 = (20 x 8) + (4 x 8)). Using rekenreks or dot cards to reinforce students' understanding of number relationships.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math Art involves creating drawings and designs that explore mathematical concepts and patterns. This strategy can involve using stencils to create geometric shapes, identifying patterns and relationships within the artwork, and exploring numerical relationships through visual representation. By visually representing mathematical concepts, learners can enhance their understanding and make math more engaging.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Drawing supplies (paper, stencils, colored pencils, etc.). Mathematical concepts to be explored.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require teacher guidance to connect the art to specific mathematical concepts. Can be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary students, specifically first graders.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore mathematical concepts, enhance pattern recognition, and make math more engaging through visual representation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual representation of mathematical concepts makes abstract ideas more concrete. Engaging and fun way to explore math. Can be used across a range of math topics including geometry, number relationships, and patterns.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can use their own interests and preferences to create unique math art. Activities can be adjusted based on the students' abilities and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student's understanding of mathematical concepts through their artwork and explanations. Observe student's ability to identify and explain mathematical patterns in their art.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engaging way to learn math by using patterns and shapes and recognizing math in art.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An activity that uses cards with different representations of the same numerical answer (area model, dominoes, number sentence) to encourage number sense and understanding of multiplication, as opposed to memorization and time pressure.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A set of math cards with different representations of numbers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires preparation of the math cards

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop multiplication fact fluency, understand different representations of numbers

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual and hands-on activity, promotes understanding of multiplication, reinforces math facts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different number ranges and representations

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's ability to match cards with equivalent answers and explain how the different cards are equivalent

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of multiplication fact fluency and understanding of different number representations

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Matching a card with 9 x 4 with a card showing an area model, sets of dominoes, and the number sentence.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math centers involve setting up various stations in the classroom where learners can practice and apply mathematical concepts through activities like games and tablets. These centers can be used collaboratively or independently, offering opportunities for discovery and exploration. Products used in centers can be designed for open-ended problems and interaction to promote engagement. Guided practice of skills can also be provided for learners who need extra support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires physical space for multiple stations and access to varied materials such as games, tablets, and manipulatives. Instructor preparation is needed to design and organize the stations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Management of multiple stations can be challenging. Learners may need guidance to stay on task and use materials effectively. Ensuring all activities are aligned with learning objectives requires careful planning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide hands-on practice, encourage collaboration, and differentiate instruction in math.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging stations encourage active learning and discovery. Collaborative activities strengthen peer interaction and communication. The variety of materials caters to different learning styles and needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Math centers can be tailored to specific skills or content areas, and can accommodate individual learning styles through varied activities. Guided practice can be provided for struggling learners, while advanced learners can engage in more challenging tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in activities. Collect and review work produced at each station to assess understanding. Monitor collaborative interactions to gauge peer learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Math centers can increase learner engagement and provide differentiated instruction in math. Active, hands-on practice solidifies concepts and builds confidence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A first-grade teacher uses math centers with games and tablets to engage students in counting and operations practice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Organize students into small groups where they take turns acting as "math coaches." One student reads a word problem aloud, and the other students (the math coaches) advise the reader on which mathematical operation to use in solving the problem. Math coaches listen closely, underline key words in the problem, and use flash cards to "flash" the mathematical operation they decide to use.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word problems, key word flash cards, and small groups of students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure all students participate and benefit from the activity. Some students may be hesitant to take on the role of "math coach."

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school learners (Grades 3-8)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve problem-solving skills, enhance communication skills, develop critical thinking, promote active learning, reinforce math concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a collaborative and engaging approach to problem-solving. Encourages active listening, critical thinking, and communication skills. Reinforces math concepts through peer teaching and feedback.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose roles within the group. Provide different levels of word problems based on student abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to provide accurate advice and feedback as math coaches. Assess students' accuracy in solving word problems during role-playing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced problem-solving skills: Collaborative problem-solving promotes deeper understanding and retention of math concepts. Improved communication skills: Explaining their thinking and providing feedback enhances students' communication skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Small groups of learners work together to solve word problems. One learner reads a word problem aloud while the other learners act as 'math coaches' and advise them on which mathematical operation to use in solving the problem. They underline key words in the problem, and follow the flash card mathematical operation that they decide to 'flash.'

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word problems, flashcards.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful grouping of learners to ensure that all members of the group participate and benefit from the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in grades 3-8

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply math skills to real-world problems, reinforce understanding of key words and mathematical operations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for peer learning and collaboration, promotes active listening and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether learners are actively participating in the math coaching process. Check whether groups accurately solve each of the ten word problems and underline appropriate key words.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Peer learning has been shown to improve comprehension and retention of new information. Promotes communication and collaboration skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math games are structured activities designed to stimulate enthusiasm for math learning by providing opportunities to explore fundamental number concepts, engage in strategic mathematical thinking, and deepen understanding of numbers. These games encourage exploration of number combinations, place value, patterns, and computational strategies, deepening mathematical understanding and reasoning. They also allow teachers to observe or assess students and work with individuals or small groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to mathematical games and activities, time for repeated play, and teacher guidance to facilitate mathematical discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Games used solely to practice number facts may not engage children for long. May lead to negative feelings if recall speed determines success.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, adaptable for various age groups with modifications

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage strategic mathematical thinking, deepen understanding of numbers, develop computational fluency, explore number combinations and patterns

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages strategic thinking and problem-solving. Supports computational fluency through repeated practice. Provides opportunities for observation and assessment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Games can be varied or modified to meet the needs of different learners, encouraging the use of the Common Core's Standards for Mathematical Practice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student strategies during gameplay. Review recorded equations or representations. Analyze student reflections on skills, strategies, and potential improvements.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages strategic mathematical thinking as students find different strategies for solving problems and deepen their understanding of numbers. Supports students’ development of computational fluency when played repeatedly.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating quick, fun, physical math games for when learners get antsy. Breaks refresh students while giving them another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • No materials are needed, just quick and fun physical math games.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Student-pair games need an even number of students. The teacher's enthusiasm is critical in these games.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4th grade

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Refresh students, reinforce math concepts, energize the brain, active participation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Movement refreshes students while giving them another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • There are teacher-led games and student-pair games. Some game examples are groups, stand up/sit down, and finger speed-sums. The games are flexible and can be adapted by the teacher or student.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement and enjoyment during math games. Track student progress on math concepts following activity breaks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Win-win for students and teachers. Movement refreshes your students while giving them another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In their math journals, students can write about things they are having trouble with or things that they've figured out. Putting these thoughts into words can help students get a more concrete handle on the logic of their ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Math journals or notebooks, prompts for reflection (optional).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires regular time for journaling and may require encouragement for learners to express their thoughts openly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help learners reflect on their understanding, clarify their thinking, and develop a more concrete handle on mathematical concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a space for learners to explore their struggles and successes, promoting deeper understanding and self-reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can write about topics that are most relevant to their own learning and understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review journal entries to assess learners' understanding and identify areas of struggle. Look for evidence of self-reflection and improved clarity of thinking.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding, self-reflection, and the ability to articulate mathematical ideas.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Have students write about concepts they are struggling with or explaining solutions they have discovered.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math journals are a way to gauge a student’s understanding of particular math concepts. Students use their math journals to communicate their conceived strengths and personal concerns and reflect on their learning experiences through various journal prompts. Teachers can check the journals periodically and provide feedback to individual students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Math journals, journal prompts, and a way for teachers to check the journals and provide feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to check the journals and provide feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gauge student understanding, communicate strengths and concerns, reflect on learning experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to gauge student understanding, provides students with a way to communicate their strengths and concerns, and encourages reflection on learning experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of journal prompts to encourage reflection. They can also provide feedback to individual students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding, increased student communication, and deeper reflection on learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of math journals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher asks students to write about what they learned in a math lesson. The teacher checks the journals and provides feedback to individual students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners create flashcards for each of the four mathematical operations. On one side, they write the operation and symbol (+, -, x, /). On the other side, they list key words associated with that operation. Students use their flashcards as visual aids in math coaching.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Index cards, markers or colored pencils

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to create flashcards.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-8

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Memorize key words associated with math operations, improve problem-solving skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides visual cues to help learners identify the correct operation to use in a word problem.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can add their own key words to the flashcards.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether learners are using flashcards correctly to identify the correct operation to use in a word problem. Check for accuracy on homework.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves memory and recall of key words associated with math operations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math songs are musical compositions designed to teach and reinforce math concepts and skills. They utilize rhyme, rhythm, and repetition to make math more engaging and memorable for learners. Math songs can be used to introduce new concepts, reinforce existing knowledge, or as a regular part of classroom routines.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to audio equipment, math songs (either pre-made or created by the instructor/learners), and a space where learners can sing and move around

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all learners, especially those with limited auditory processing skills. It may not provide the depth of understanding that traditional methods offer if used as the sole teaching strategy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, particularly those who benefit from auditory and kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance retention of math facts, improve understanding of math concepts, increase engagement with math, reinforce number sense and operations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory through rhyme and rhythm, makes learning more enjoyable, caters to different learning styles, can be used in various classroom settings

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Songs can be adapted to different skill levels and concepts. Learners can create their own songs or modify existing ones to suit their needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recall math facts and concepts after listening to and singing the songs. Assess their engagement and participation in singing and related activities. Use quizzes or tests to measure knowledge retention.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that music can improve memory and engagement, making it a useful tool for teaching math concepts. Math songs promote multisensory learning and cater to various learning preferences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include songs about counting, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, and geometry. Many educational websites and apps offer math songs for various grade levels.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Math talks are structured conversations focused on mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies. These discussions promote a deeper understanding of concepts, encourage learners to share their thinking, and provide opportunities for instructors to assess comprehension. Math talks support the development of communication skills and mathematical precision by being asked to make sure everyone understands a viewpoint. It comes from the use of specific mathematical terms, from labeling answers, and from using representations as tools to support communication about mathematics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured mathematical problems or scenarios. A facilitator to guide the conversation. A classroom culture that supports open discussion and sharing of ideas.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful planning and preparation by the instructor to ensure discussions are productive. Requires a classroom culture that values discussion and the exchange of ideas.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 teachers, school and district leaders, and math coaches

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote mathematical reasoning, share problem-solving strategies, assess learner comprehension, develop communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates a deeper understanding of mathematical concepts. Encourages learners to share their thinking and reasoning. Supports the development of communication skills and mathematical precision.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Math talks can be tailored to different learner levels by adjusting the complexity of the problems discussed. Allows learners to share various approaches to problem-solving.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Eliciting Student Thinking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of engagement and participation in math talks. Evaluate learners’ ability to explain their thinking and reasoning. Assess the depth of understanding demonstrated during discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Math talks support deeper understanding of mathematical concepts, encourage learners to share their thinking, and develop communication skills. These discussions promote a deeper understanding of concepts, encourage learners to share their thinking, and provide opportunities for instructors to assess comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners engage in a math talk to discuss different strategies for solving a complex word problem. The instructor guides the discussion by asking probing questions and encouraging learners to explain their reasoning. (See original document for example.)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Create a class word wall displaying mathematical terms and vocabulary to support working memory and develop language skills. Model how to identify and highlight key mathematical words in word problems that prompt addition or subtraction. Brainstorm with students all the potential words that signal addition or subtraction, emphasizing conceptual understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Math word problems, markers or highlighters, space for a word wall in the classroom, and posters or cards for creating the word wall.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if students lack foundational mathematical knowledge. Requires ongoing maintenance and updating of the word wall.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school learners (Grades 3-8)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop math vocabulary, improve problem-solving skills, enhance language skills, aid working memory

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports learners in identifying key information in word problems. Visual aids support working memory and vocabulary development. Promotes active engagement in problem-solving.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the complexity of the word problems based on student level. Allow students to contribute to the word wall with terms relevant to their learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to identify key words in word problems. Assess students' use of math vocabulary in explanations and problem-solving.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved math problem-solving: Research suggests that explicit instruction in math vocabulary enhances comprehension and problem-solving skills. Increased working memory: Visual aids like word walls support memory and understanding of mathematical concepts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mathematical dance involves using movement to illustrate mathematical concepts. This approach can demonstrate links between different shapes and illustrate complex ideas. For instance, a dance can be created to show how two consecutive triangular numbers make a square number. It combines mathematics and performance to teach an audience complex concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Mathematical concept, choreography, performers, and an audience

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires expertise in both mathematics and dance, may be time-consuming to choreograph

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages, particularly those interested in mathematics and dance

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Illustrate mathematical concepts, demonstrate links between shapes, teach complex ideas through performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines mathematics and performance, enhances understanding through visual and kinesthetic learning, engages an audience in complex concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Dances can be adapted to suit different mathematical concepts and skill levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Peer Teaching
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate understanding of mathematical concepts through performance, assess audience comprehension

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances understanding and engagement through a creative combination of mathematics and performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Supporting the application of learning to new contexts. This involves providing opportunities for learners to practice and apply their knowledge in different situations. Maximizing transfer and generalization enhances the relevance and durability of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Case studies, real-world examples, and opportunities for practice and application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of examples and activities to ensure relevance and appropriateness. Some learners may struggle to transfer their learning to new contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who need to apply their knowledge in real-world situations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance application of knowledge, improve transfer of learning, increase relevance of learning, promote durability of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances application of knowledge to new contexts. Improves transfer of learning to different situations. Increases the relevance of learning. Promotes durability of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide opportunities for learners to practice and apply their knowledge in different situations. Offer case studies and real-world examples. Encourage learners to reflect on how their learning can be applied in their own lives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner ability to apply their knowledge in different situations. Monitor the transfer of learning to new contexts. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of strategies for maximizing transfer and generalization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learning outcomes: Research suggests that maximizing transfer and generalization can significantly improve the long-term impact of learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Applying learning to new contexts helps learners develop the ability to use what they have learned in real-world situations. This includes providing opportunities for learners to practice applying their knowledge in new and different settings. It also involves encouraging learners to reflect on their learning and identify connections between different concepts and contexts. The goal is to help learners become lifelong learners who can adapt to new challenges and opportunities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to design learning activities that provide opportunities for application and transfer of knowledge. Instructors need to be able to guide learners in reflecting on their learning and identifying connections between different concepts and contexts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources. Some learners may struggle to apply what they have learned in new contexts. It's essential to provide additional support and scaffolding as needed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote application of knowledge, improve problem-solving skills, support lifelong learning, foster adaptability

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports application of knowledge by providing opportunities to practice in new contexts, improves problem-solving skills by encouraging learners to apply what they have learned to real-world situations, supports lifelong learning by helping learners develop the ability to adapt to new challenges, and fosters adaptability by encouraging learners to reflect on their learning and identify connections between different concepts and contexts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a variety of application activities and assessment options to suit different learning styles. Encourage learners to identify real-world applications of what they have learned. Allow learners to reflect on their learning and identify connections between different concepts and contexts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in activities. Assess learner understanding of key concepts through discussions, written assignments, or problem-solving tasks. Track improvements in problem-solving skills and application of knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that maximizing transfer and generalization can promote application of knowledge, improve problem-solving skills, support lifelong learning, and foster adaptability. Studies show that learners who are able to transfer their knowledge to new contexts are more successful in school and in life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing opportunities for learners to practice applying their knowledge in new and different settings. Encouraging learners to reflect on their learning and identify connections between different concepts and contexts. Using problem-based learning activities that require learners to apply what they have learned to real-world situations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Grades should represent multiple opportunities for students to demonstrate learning based on descriptive, concrete, and actionable feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear grading policies, descriptive feedback, opportunities for students to demonstrate learning

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant effort from teachers to provide detailed feedback

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure grades reflect demonstrated learning, provide actionable feedback, promote transparency for students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides transparency for students, encourages active learning, promotes growth

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different subjects and grade levels. Feedback can be tailored to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of grading criteria, quality of feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Grading serves as an evaluative marker of assessment and grading must be transparent for students.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Multilingual learners assign themselves a grade based on drafts, preset criteria, and feedback

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Measurement tasks involve using measurement tools and techniques to quantify physical properties such as length, volume, and temperature. Learners devise techniques to measure the number of marbles that can be made out of a set volume of material and perform routine laboratory procedures using a balance. These tasks improve measurement skills and their application in scientific contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Rulers, balances, thermometers, various objects, materials for making marbles

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to measurement tools. Precise measurements are essential for accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying science and mathematics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop proficiency in measurement techniques, use tools such as rulers and balances, perform routine laboratory procedures

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances measurement skills and their application in scientific experiments. Promotes precise observation and recording of data.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various objects and measurement tools. Procedures can be modified for varying complexity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in measurements, correct use of measurement tools, clear reporting of results

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved measurement skills, enhanced precision in scientific experiments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Making Marbles (KDE): Learners devise a technique to determine how many marbles can be made out of a set volume of material. Measurement: Length, Volume, and Temperature (ILS): Learners perform routine laboratory procedures and report results.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A memory game where learners match pairs of word cards to reinforce vocabulary and memory skills. Learners turn over cards, say the words aloud, and try to find matching pairs. Successfully matched words must be used in a sentence from a familiar context, like a song, to further reinforce understanding and application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word cards (two sets of each), small group setting, and writing materials. Teachers must prepare the word cards by printing and cutting them apart. Printing on cardstock is recommended to prevent see-through.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Preparation and setup can be time-consuming. Implementation requires careful monitoring to ensure engagement. Effectiveness depends on clear instructions and appropriate vocabulary selection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary grades (K-5), learners who need vocabulary and memory reinforcement, and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve vocabulary retention, enhance memory skills, reinforce contextual understanding, promote active recall

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Active recall and memory skills are reinforced through engaging gameplay. Vocabulary is contextualized through sentence creation. Collaboration and peer support are encouraged.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can adapt the content (e.g., simpler or more complex vocabulary). Provide sentence frames for extra support. Implement in small groups for personalized learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the number of matches achieved. Observe learners' ability to use words in sentences. Collect anecdotal notes on participation and peer support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Games and memory activities enhance retention and recall. Contextual use of vocabulary improves understanding and application. Active participation increases engagement and learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The strategy should be implemented using a familiar learning activity, like a song. If students get a match, they need to use the word in a sentence from the song.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mentor texts are examples of high-quality writing used to teach students how to improve their own writing skills. Teachers and students return to these texts for various purposes, studying and imitating the techniques employed by the authors. Mentor texts can be multimodal (books, stories, poems, essays) and encompass various forms such as newspaper articles, song lyrics, comic strips, or manuals. They help students take risks, explore new strategies and formats, and develop their unique voice and confidence. The use of mentor texts involves deconstructing the writing to identify effective 'writer's moves' and then emulating those moves in student work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to high-quality writing samples (student or professional). Time for reading, analysis, and discussion in class. Structured activities for imitation and practice. A classroom environment where students can work together and share.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may mimic mentor texts without developing their unique voice, may feel overwhelmed by exemplary models, or may struggle to transfer learned techniques to their own writing. Requires careful selection of appropriate mentor texts and thoughtful scaffolding of activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students learning writing and literacy skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop students' writing abilities, enhance disciplinary literacy, foster confidence in writing, expose students to various writing techniques and genres, improve critical thinking and analytical skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides concrete examples of effective writing, allows students to see real-world applications of writing techniques, promotes active learning and critical analysis, enhances understanding of different writing styles and structures, allows students to see different authorial voices and potentially emulate/find their own voice through the process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Mentor texts can be selected based on student interests and skill levels. Questions and annotations can be adapted to meet individual student needs. Exercises can be scaffolded for struggling learners, and advanced students can be challenged to explore more complex techniques.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating the application of techniques learned from mentor texts. Student participation in discussions and analyses of mentor texts. Student reflections on their writing process and the impact of mentor texts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that using mentor texts can enhance writing skills, promote critical thinking, and increase student engagement in writing. It supports the development of disciplinary literacy by exposing students to diverse writing styles and techniques. Improved ability to notice and implement specific writing techniques, increased confidence in writing, better understanding of how different authorial choices impact the reader.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a New York Times article as a mentor text to teach narrative writing, focusing on elements like crafting a narrative arc or using details to 'show' rather than 'tell'. Analyzing published essays or short stories to understand sentence structure, diction, and overall organization. Examining successful college application essays to inspire creativity and bravery in student writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Accountable talk stems are phrases and sentence starters that facilitate structured, text-based discussions and promote higher-order thinking and metacognition. They guide students to clearly and accurately examine and convey complex ideas, effectively select and organize content, and analyze information while referring back to textual evidence and building on each other’s contributions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a set of accountable talk stems, a text or topic for discussion, and a facilitator to guide the discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel restrictive if not used flexibly. Requires careful facilitation to ensure students engage meaningfully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6-12 English Language Arts, adaptable for other subjects and learner levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build higher-order thinking skills, enhance metacognition, and foster structured text-based discussions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structure for discussions, promotes critical thinking, enhances metacognition, and fosters collaborative learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Stems can be tailored to different content areas and learning objectives. Students can create their own stems to guide discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Reciprocal Teaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the extent to which students use accountable talk stems. Evaluate the depth and quality of student responses and interactions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of higher-order thinking skills. Enhances metacognitive awareness and promotes effective communication.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers use accountable talk stems during literature circles, Socratic seminars, and other discussion-based activities. A document of metacognitive stems was developed to help build higher-order thinking skills and metacognition into structured text-based discussions in classrooms.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Journaling (or recording in an alternative form) can help students develop their metacognitive awareness to build self-regulation skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journal and questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires comfort from student.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and post-secondary students, especially those with learning disabilities or other challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop metacognitive awareness, create journaling skills, and develop self-regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps improve self-regulation by reflecting on behavior and identifying patterns.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Change format of student responses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in journaling.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved metacognition and regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Allow students to use an audio recording to record thoughts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Metacognitive journaling involves writing about one's own thinking, including tendencies, changes in thinking over time, biases, or blind spots. This can be driven by instructor prompts or self-initiation. Using approaches like the 'Muddiest point reflection' is also useful, helping learners recognize areas where their understanding is unclear, thereby positioning them to direct their learning to expand their knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a journal (physical or digital), writing utensils, and dedicated time for journaling. Instructors or facilitators need to provide prompts and feedback to guide reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be willing to engage in honest self-reflection. May be challenging for learners who are not accustomed to thinking about their own thinking.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in professional development programs, higher education, or any context where self-reflection is valued

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote metacognition, enhance self-awareness, improve understanding of thinking processes, develop the ability to direct one's own learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-awareness of one's own thinking processes, biases, and tendencies. Supports the development of self-directed learning skills. Helps learners identify areas where their understanding is unclear.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a variety of prompts to guide reflection on different aspects of thinking. Allow learners to focus on areas of thinking that are most relevant to their personal and professional goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze journal entries to assess the depth of reflection on thinking processes, the identification of biases and blind spots, and the development of self-directed learning skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of metacognitive skills, which are essential for lifelong learning. Helps learners become more aware of their own thinking and better able to direct their own learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A learner might use a metacognitive journal to reflect on their tendencies to procrastinate, analyze the reasons behind their procrastination, and develop strategies to overcome it. They might also use the journal to identify biases that influence their decision-making and develop strategies to mitigate those biases.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on learners' awareness of their thought processes as they complete tasks, emphasizing self-improvement rather than assessment. It involves reflecting on how to improve future work and developing resilience by viewing frustration as a signal to pause and think through the situation. The aim is to help learners monitor their progress, construct meaning from the content, and apply their learnings to new contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured time for reflection; prompts to guide thinking; documentation methods (e.g., logs, journals).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Danger of the reflection turning into a feedback loop. Learners need to focus on how the reflection will help them in the future.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those needing to develop problem-solving skills and resilience.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-improvement skills, enhance resilience, foster metacognitive awareness, promote application of learning to future work.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness and self-regulation. Encourages resilience in the face of challenges. Supports the application of learning to future tasks.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use of digital tools to log tasks and habits, creating a rich source of data for reflection. Setting goals and using productivity apps to create regular reflection times.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evidence of learners' ability to identify areas for improvement. Learners' application of reflection to future work. Growth in self-awareness and self-regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of resilience in the face of challenges. Encourages students to pause and think through situations instead of giving up. Helps students improve their work and understand how their past performance will influence their future work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Metacognitive strategies teach students to think about their thinking. When students become aware of the learning process, they gain control over their learning. Metacognition extends to self-regulation or managing one's own motivation toward learning. Metacognitive activities can include planning how to approach learning tasks, evaluating progress, and monitoring comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to facilitate activities that promote reflection and self-assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires students to be actively engaged in reflecting on their own thinking.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-awareness and control over the learning process by teaching students to think about their thinking.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-regulation, planning, evaluation, and monitoring of comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to different learning styles and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student self-awareness, ability to plan and evaluate learning, and improved self-regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Metacognitive strategies improve learning by helping students gain control over their learning process and manage their motivation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The method of loci involves creating a mental 'memory palace' by associating items to be remembered with specific locations in a familiar place. This technique leverages spatial memory to enhance recall. The more vivid and unusual the associations, the more effective the method.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ability to visualize locations and create vivid associations. A clear understanding of the items to be remembered.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to set up the memory palace and create associations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with strong visual and spatial skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory recall by associating information with familiar locations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages spatial memory to create a structured way to remember lists or sequences. Turns abstract information into concrete, location-based memories.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can use their own familiar locations and create personalized associations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the number of items recalled correctly using the method of loci. Monitor the ease with which learners can create and navigate their memory palaces.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that the method of loci can improve memory recall and may lead to structural changes in the brain (Engvig et al., 2010).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Remembering a grocery list by associating each item with a different location in your home. Using a virtual environment as a memory palace (Legge et al., 2012).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Setting achievable micro-goals encourages consistent, incremental learner progress. Repeated small wins can lead to a growth mindset and increased confidence. Micro-goals break down large tasks into smaller, manageable steps, making the overall goal less daunting and more attainable. This approach enables learners to experience frequent success, reinforcing positive beliefs about their ability to improve and master new skills. By focusing on incremental progress, learners can track their development, maintain motivation, and build self-efficacy. Instructors can support this strategy by helping learners define specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) micro-goals that align with their overall learning objectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly defined overall learning objectives. Ability to break down large tasks into smaller, manageable steps. Regular monitoring and feedback to track progress.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If micro-goals are too easy, learners may not experience a sense of accomplishment. If micro-goals are too difficult, learners may become discouraged. Requires careful planning and monitoring to ensure that micro-goals align with overall learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who struggle with large, complex tasks or who have low confidence in their abilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance motivation, promote a growth mindset, increase confidence, track progress, and develop self-efficacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a sense of accomplishment and motivates continued effort. Allows learners to track their progress and see tangible results of their efforts. Reduces anxiety associated with large tasks by breaking them into manageable steps.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Goals can be tailored to individual learner needs and abilities. Learners can choose the pace at which they progress through the micro-goals. Instructors can provide individualized support and feedback to help learners achieve their micro-goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the completion rate of micro-goals. Measure changes in learner confidence and motivation. Assess overall achievement of learning objectives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that setting and achieving micro-goals increases motivation, self-efficacy, and overall achievement (reference goal-setting literature). Consistent progress fosters a growth mindset and reduces fear of failure (reference growth mindset research).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student learning a new language sets micro-goals to learn five new words each day. A learner working on a research paper breaks the task into micro-goals such as outlining, researching, drafting, and editing each section separately. A professional development participant sets micro-goals to implement one new teaching strategy each week.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Short video lectures are distributed as study material along with short assignments. The rest of the lecture and assignments are conducted during the classroom time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creation of concise video lectures and targeted assignments.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for complex topics requiring more in-depth pre-class preparation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners who benefit from focused, bite-sized content and immediate application.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Introduce key concepts succinctly, reinforce learning through short assignments, facilitate in-class application and discussion.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Keeps pre-class material manageable and focused, allows for immediate reinforcement in class.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Short assignments can be tailored to different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Engagement with pre-class material, performance on in-class assignments and discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can improve learners' grasp of fundamental concepts and ability to apply them in class.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Mathematics courses using short videos to explain formulas followed by practice problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mind mapping is a visual thinking tool used to capture information and ideas. It helps learners capture and organize ideas and thoughts in a structured form. By connecting ideas via structures and branches, learners uncover new connections and discover new ideas and lines of reasoning. They can also help students learn visually and creatively by visualizing information in formats that are compatible with their favorite learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • One of the many digital or analog mind mapping tools that are available, a pen and paper, or the ability to drag and drop.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None noted

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To capture and organize information and ideas in a structured form and boost memory, creativity, and productivity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners focus on what is important, cutting through the clutter and making space for more ideas. Connects ideas via structures and branches.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use can add various types of multimedia materials to their mind maps (e.g, images, web links, icons, stickers, etc), collaborative brainstorming in real time, pre-made editable mind mapping templates, multiple third party integrations, and various export formats (e.g., PDF, plain text, image, rtf, and more.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learners progress

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can boost memory, creativity, and productivity. Help students learn visually and creatively by visualizing information in formats that are compatible with their favorite learning styles.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A mindful break involves students ringing a bell when they feel the class needs a break, stopping the lesson, standing up and stretching in silence, and then sitting down for mindful breathing. Students then think of something they are grateful for.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space and brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use guided audio, videos, or instructor-led exercises.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, reduce stress, enhance self-regulation, improve cognitive function

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, supports emotional regulation, improves attention, enhances self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various durations and settings. Can be integrated into existing lessons or used as standalone activities. Use different mindfulness techniques to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • At the beginning of each class, one student would get a bell. During that day’s lesson, the student would ring the bell when he or she felt the class needed a break (the teacher set the bell-ringing limit at twice during at 50-minute class). When the student rang the bell, even if the teacher was mid-sentence, class would stop. In silence, everyone would stand up and stretch, and then sit down for 30 seconds or so of mindful breathing. Then the student who rang the bell would prompt students to silently think of something they were grateful for.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mindful listening is a practice of focusing on sound to introduce mindfulness. It is often easier to focus on something more concrete like sound; the instruction to “notice your breath” can be a bit abstract, especially for elementary students.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A mindful moment involves pausing, settling the nervous system, and refocusing attention and energy on a new task. It entails inviting learners to close their eyes (if they’re comfortable) and take a few deep breaths, paying attention to the sensation of breathing or noticing their thoughts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space and brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use guided audio, videos, or instructor-led exercises.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, reduce stress, enhance self-regulation, improve cognitive function

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, supports emotional regulation, improves attention, enhances self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various durations and settings. Can be integrated into existing lessons or used as standalone activities. Use different mindfulness techniques to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • At the beginning of class, or after a transition, invite kids to close their eyes (if they’re comfortable doing so), and take a few deep breaths. They can pay attention to breathing — what does it feel like when they breathe in and out? Or they can notice their thoughts — is their mind really busy or quiet right now? Use a short video as a guide.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating mindfulness with movement involves combining physical activity with practices that promote awareness, focus, and presence. This approach aims to enhance both physical and mental well-being by engaging mind and body simultaneously. It includes activities such as mindful walking, yoga, and Tai Chi.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Minimal equipment needed for most activities. Requires awareness and intention to integrate mindfulness practices with physical movement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial training in mindfulness techniques. Some individuals may need to adapt activities to accommodate physical limitations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All individuals, particularly those seeking to reduce stress, improve mental clarity, and enhance physical fitness simultaneously

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance physical fitness, reduce stress, improve focus and attention, increase self-awareness, and promote overall well-being

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances physical fitness, reduces stress, improves focus and attention, increases self-awareness, and promotes overall well-being by integrating mindfulness and movement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual preferences, fitness levels, and mindfulness practices, including options for yoga, Tai Chi, and mindful walking.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduced stress levels, improved focus and attention, increased self-awareness, better mood, and enhanced physical fitness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that mindfulness practices can reduce stress and improve attention. Studies indicate that combining mindfulness with movement enhances both physical and mental health.
