docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mindfulness breaks are short, structured activities designed to create internal balance and a sense of being present in the moment. They are used in educational settings to help adults develop their awareness and ability to focus attention, which can mitigate negative effects of heavy media-multitasking and general cognitive decline. Frequent mindfulness activities enhance academic performance, support adults' physical well-being and mental health, and improve sleep. Self-regulation and inhibition can be strengthened by practicing mindfulness techniques.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space and brief periods of time (e.g., 1-5 minutes). May use guided audio, videos, or instructor-led exercises.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find it difficult to focus or may be skeptical of the practice. Requires consistent implementation to see benefits.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, reduce stress, enhance self-regulation, improve cognitive function

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, supports emotional regulation, improves attention, enhances self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various durations and settings. Can be integrated into existing lessons or used as standalone activities. Use different mindfulness techniques to suit individual preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in focus, behavior, and self-reported stress levels. Observe engagement and participation during mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates mindfulness can enhance motivation, engagement, and self-regulation. Studies show improvements in focus and cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher leads the class through several different mindfulness and movement exercises, also allowing the students to lead some of them. Use Headspace's bite-sized mindfulness exercises as breaks during class. Audio and video exercises guide students through quick meditations to destress and regulate their emotion. Edutopia also provides examples of quick mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating mindfulness practices such as yoga, breathing exercises, and meditation into the learning environment to calm the nervous system and promote self-regulation. These practices can be used throughout the school day to help learners manage stress and improve focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated space for mindfulness activities. Training for educators in mindfulness practices. Clear guidelines for participation in mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be resistant to participating in mindfulness activities. Requires careful planning to integrate mindfulness practices into the learning schedule. May require ongoing support and training for educators.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages and abilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce stress, improve focus, promote self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a way for learners to manage stress and improve focus. Can be integrated into various learning activities and settings. Is a low-cost and easily accessible strategy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of mindfulness practices to meet the diverse needs and preferences of learners. Allow learners to choose the type and duration of mindfulness activities that work best for them. Provide options for individual or group mindfulness activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and participation in mindfulness activities. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of different mindfulness practices. Track changes in learners' behavior, attention, and emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that mindfulness practices can reduce stress, improve focus, and promote self-regulation. Studies have shown that mindfulness can improve academic performance and emotional well-being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity. These techniques involve focusing on the present moment with awareness and acceptance. Examples include deep breathing exercises, body scan meditations, and mindful observation of thoughts and feelings without judgment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a quiet space, willingness to practice mindfulness, guidance from a trained instructor or audio resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find mindfulness techniques challenging or uncomfortable at first. Requires regular practice to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who are highly reactive to stimuli or have difficulty managing their emotions.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Manage emotional impulses, reduce reactivity, increase self-awareness, promote relaxation and focus.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a tool for managing immediate emotional responses, promotes self-awareness and acceptance, reduces stress and anxiety.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Mindfulness techniques can be adapted to individual learner preferences and needs. Some learners may prefer guided meditations, while others may benefit from simple breathing exercises.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in emotional reactivity, track the frequency and intensity of emotional outbursts, assess the learner's ability to use mindfulness techniques to manage emotions in real-time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that mindfulness techniques can effectively reduce emotional reactivity, improve self-regulation, and promote overall well-being in learners. Resource: Pause, Refocus, Assess: Meditation in the Classroom | Adam Kuranishi, Edutopia

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher leads a class in a short mindfulness exercise before a test to help students manage anxiety and focus their attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating mindfulness techniques helps students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity. This involves practices such as meditation, deep breathing, and body scans to promote calmness and self-awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires regular time for mindfulness practice and a quiet environment. Training in mindfulness techniques for both students and educators.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for students with attention difficulties, and requires consistent practice to achieve noticeable results.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who are highly reactive to stimuli and need to improve their emotional control.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students manage emotional impulses, reduce reactivity, and promote calmness and self-awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces emotional reactivity, promotes calmness and self-awareness, and provides tools for managing impulses.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different age levels and individual needs, offering a variety of mindfulness exercises and techniques.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in emotional reactivity and impulsivity. Track student's use of mindfulness techniques in challenging situations. Monitor self-reported levels of calmness and self-awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mindfulness techniques enhance emotional regulation by reducing reactivity and promoting self-awareness, leading to improved impulse control and emotional balance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher might lead a short mindfulness exercise at the start of each class to help students focus and manage their emotions. Example: Practicing deep breathing techniques during stressful situations.

docs.title: Mindfulness Techniques for Managing Emotional Impulses
Description
docs.text: Incorporating mindfulness techniques helps students manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity, resulting in improved self-regulation skills. It aids in developing the ability to monitor their reactions to new or challenging situations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Educator awareness of self-regulation concepts and strategies. Time for mindfulness and guided practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with mindfulness techniques, limiting its effectiveness.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with particular attention to those struggling with self-regulation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Manage students' initial emotional impulses and reactivity, improve self-regulation skills, and enhance emotional and behavioral control.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop metacognitive awareness, manage emotional impulses, and react positively to challenging situations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The techniques can be adjusted based on individual student strengths and challenges and can be adapted to their specific needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in student behavior and emotional responses. Review student reflection on the effect of their mindfulness. Collect student reflections on the effectiveness of mindfulness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research has shown that journaling is effective in improving self-regulation skills, building learner mindsets, and helping students feel supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Create mini-lessons for each writing feature you want students to emulate (organization, title, sentence variety, imagery, evidence, introduction).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Preparation of focused mini-lessons. Time for instruction and practice in class. A classroom environment that supports focused learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Some students may prefer a more holistic approach to writing. Requires careful planning to ensure that mini-lessons are relevant and engaging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for developing specific writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop specific writing skills, enhance understanding of writing features, provide focused instruction, improve overall writing quality

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides targeted instruction on key writing features. Allows students to focus on one skill at a time. Creates a more manageable and less overwhelming learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Mini-lessons can be tailored to student needs and learning goals. Students can be given opportunities to choose which features to focus on. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating improved writing features. Participation in mini-lessons and activities. Student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that focused instruction on specific writing features improves overall writing quality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A mini-lesson on how to write a strong introduction. A mini-lesson on how to use imagery effectively. A mini-lesson on how to cite evidence properly.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implement short exercise sessions throughout the school day, such as encouraging jumping jacks in the morning or scheduling five-minute movement breaks between classes where students can do activities like push-ups, dancing, or running in place. These breaks revitalize students and provide a chance to move, improving focus and attention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Scheduled breaks, teacher implementation, classroom space

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent scheduling and teacher involvement. May disrupt class flow if not managed effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase physical activity, improve student focus and attention, revitalize students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Revitalizes students by providing short bursts of physical activity, improves focus and attention, makes physical activity a regular part of the school day.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Exercises can be tailored to suit different student abilities and preferences. Intensity and duration can be adjusted based on class needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and attention levels, track student participation in exercise breaks, gather feedback from students and teachers

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved attention and behavior: Research suggests that short breaks can improve attention and behavior in students. Increased physical activity: Contributes to students meeting daily physical activity recommendations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using a minimally invasive hand gesture to secure student attention. This technique involves a simple, non-disruptive hand signal that prompts students to quiet down and focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear communication and practice to ensure students understand the meaning of the hand gesture. Consistency in using the gesture is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if students are not properly trained on the meaning of the gesture. Some students may not respond to subtle cues.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Quickly and efficiently gain the attention of students with minimal disruption.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a silent and subtle method for gaining attention, reducing classroom disruptions. Can be used discreetly without interrupting the flow of instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific hand gesture can be chosen by the teacher and students together to create a shared understanding and sense of ownership.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor how quickly and effectively students respond to the hand gesture. Observe the reduction in classroom disruptions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a silent and efficient way to gain student attention. Minimizes disruptions and supports a calm classroom environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners pair up, and one makes an emotional face while the other mirrors it, promoting recognition and understanding of facial expressions associated with different emotions. This activity enhances empathy and nonverbal communication skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires learners to be paired up. A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel uncomfortable making facial expressions in front of others. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, including early childhood, elementary, middle school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve recognition of facial expressions, enhance empathy, promote nonverbal communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging and interactive, promotes active participation, and enhances understanding of the connection between facial expressions and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose emotions to portray or be assigned specific emotions. Can be adapted by using pictures or written prompts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately mirror facial expressions. Assess their ability to identify and discuss the emotions displayed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that activities involving facial expression recognition can improve emotional intelligence and social skills. (Source: Facial Expression Recognition and Emotional Intelligence - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6225237/)

docs.title: Mirrors, Windows, and Sliding Glass Doors
Description
docs.text: Using the concept of mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors helps students engage with diverse stories and experiences. Mirrors reflect a student's own culture and identity, fostering belonging. Windows offer a view into someone else's experience, promoting understanding of the wider world. Sliding glass doors allow readers to enter a story and become part of the world, encouraging reflection and action. By diversifying classroom materials and promoting reflection, educators can help students develop empathy, understanding, and a sense of global citizenship.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to diverse resources. Time for reflection and discussion. A willingness to promote empathy and understanding.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may be resistant to engaging with diverse perspectives. Requires ongoing effort and commitment. May require additional support to address biases and stereotypes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students and educators who aim to engage with diverse stories and experiences, promoting empathy, understanding, and global citizenship.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster empathy and understanding. Promote reflection and action. Develop a sense of global citizenship.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances empathy and understanding. Encourages reflection and action. Fosters a sense of global citizenship.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to choose resources that resonate with their own interests and needs. Offers opportunities for reflection and discussion. Adapts to the specific needs and interests of the students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement with diverse resources. Improved ability to express empathy and understanding. Evidence of reflection and action.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced empathy and understanding: Engaging with mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors enhances empathy and understanding of diverse perspectives. Global citizenship: By promoting reflection and action, students develop a sense of global citizenship and a commitment to creating a more just and equitable world.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reading books that reflect diverse cultures and experiences. Discussing the perspectives of different characters in a story. Reflecting on how a story relates to one's own life and experiences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a mistake-friendly classroom involves fostering an environment where mistakes are seen as a fundamental part of learning, rather than a source of embarrassment or failure. This approach encourages students to take risks, ask questions, and engage deeply with the material without fear of negative consequences. Key strategies include acknowledging the reality of fear, working within the zone of proximal development, tapping into passion and curiosity, actively modeling mistakes, encouraging 'rough-draft thinking,' and grading fewer things.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from instructors to view mistakes as valuable learning opportunities. Implementation of specific strategies to promote a mistake-friendly environment. Ongoing modeling and reinforcement of positive attitudes toward mistakes. Creation of a supportive and collaborative classroom culture.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may initially resist the idea of embracing mistakes due to prior experiences or ingrained beliefs. Requires consistent effort and reinforcement from instructors to maintain a mistake-friendly environment. May be challenging to implement in high-stakes testing situations or highly competitive environments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce fear of failure, encourage risk-taking, foster deeper learning, promote a growth mindset, enhance creativity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety and stress associated with making mistakes. Encourages students to take risks and explore new ideas. Promotes deeper learning by fostering curiosity and engagement. Enhances creativity by allowing students to experiment without fear of judgment. Supports the development of a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various subjects and learning contexts. Strategies can be tailored to individual student needs and learning styles. Activities can be designed to accommodate different levels of experience and prior knowledge. Instructors can provide personalized feedback to support student growth.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Provide Feedback
  • Create a low-stress environment
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in student behavior, such as increased participation, willingness to ask questions, and positive self-talk. Track student responses to mistakes and challenges. Analyze student reflections on their learning experiences. Measure the impact of a mistake-friendly classroom on student performance and achievement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that creating a mistake-friendly classroom leads to increased student engagement, deeper learning, and a more positive attitude toward challenges. A mistake-friendly environment fosters creativity, innovation, and resilience. Students are more likely to take risks and persist in the face of adversity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers actively model mistakes by writing in front of their class, showing the confusion, messiness, stopping and starting, and hesitation that comes with composing. The teacher is the best writer in the room and therefore it is critical that the best writer in the room models the confusion, the messiness, the stopping and starting, the hesitation that comes with trying to compose.

docs.title: Mitigating Racial Bias in Edtech Products
Description
docs.text: The AI in Education Toolkit for Racial Equity provides guidance on how to mitigate racial bias in the design and development of edtech products. It encourages edtech companies to design for Black and Brown students, understand their needs, and champion their success. The toolkit details actions to take at every stage of product design and development, including examining data, assumptions, and algorithmic design.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A commitment to racial equity, willingness to learn about the experiences of Black and Brown students, and a commitment to data privacy and accessibility.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and commitment. May require significant changes to product design and development processes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Edtech developers and designers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Mitigate racial bias, create equitable edtech products, and promote the success of Black and Brown students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for addressing racial bias in edtech products. Encourages a focus on the needs of Black and Brown students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Toolkit can be adapted to different types of edtech products and contexts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduced racial bias in edtech products, improved outcomes for Black and Brown students, and a more equitable educational experience for all.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates more equitable and inclusive edtech products that support the success of all students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The "Mix It Up" strategy involves intentionally creating opportunities for individuals to interact with people outside of their normal social circles to foster understanding and break down social barriers. It typically involves structured activities that encourage dialogue and interaction between diverse groups, such as sitting with someone new at lunch and using conversation starters. The goal is to promote awareness, empathy, and inclusion by encouraging individuals to step outside their comfort zones and engage with others from different backgrounds or social groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated time and space for interaction, conversation starters, voluntary participation, greeters to encourage participation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May initially feel awkward or uncomfortable for participants, requires intentional effort and facilitation, success depends on participant willingness to engage openly

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, workplaces, or community programs aiming to promote inclusivity and understanding among diverse groups

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote dialogue, encourage interaction with diverse individuals, foster comfort in engaging with others, raise awareness and understanding of different backgrounds

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Breaks down social barriers, promotes empathy and understanding, encourages dialogue, fosters inclusivity, adapts to various settings

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Conversation starters can be tailored to address specific topics relevant to the group's interests or concerns, allowing for flexibility and relevance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Discussion Sections
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased interaction among diverse groups, positive feedback from participants, observed reduction in social barriers, enhanced awareness and understanding of different perspectives

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mix It Up events have been shown to help students engage in dialogue with someone new, interact with people outside of their normal social circles, encourage people to be more comfortable in interacting with others, and to promote awareness and understanding between students from different backgrounds.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mnemonic devices are memory aids that use patterns, rhymes, acronyms, or other techniques to help learners recall information. They serve as triggers that bring up information, making it easier to remember and apply. It is critical that learners understand and know the information prior to using mnemonics, as their purpose is to serve as a memory trigger, not to teach new content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learning material to be memorized, understanding of the key concepts and relationships, and creativity to develop memorable mnemonics

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time and effort to create effective mnemonics, effectiveness depends on the relevance and memorability of the mnemonics, may not be suitable for learners who prefer to understand the underlying concepts rather than memorize facts

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for learners who struggle with rote memorization or have memory difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory recall, improve retention of information, facilitate memorization of lists and sequences, increase engagement with learning material

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simplifies complex information, enhances memory through association and pattern, facilitates memorization of lists and sequences, increases engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create their own mnemonic devices that resonate with their personal interests and experiences. They can also adapt existing mnemonics to suit their individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recall information using mnemonic devices, assess their understanding of the underlying concepts, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes that require memorization

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mnemonic devices have been shown to enhance memory recall, improve retention of information, and facilitate memorization of lists and sequences. They provide a simple and effective way to organize and remember complex information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming Planets" to remember the order of the planets, using "Roy G. Biv" to remember the colors of the rainbow, using "Never Eat Shredded Wheat" to remember the sequence of directions (North, East, South, West).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Utilizing text messages to inform families about their student’s progress, as well as general tips for supporting children’s learning. Schools experiment to find out which messages are effective for their population. Technology must be adapted to reach family members who do not speak English or have limited reading skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A mobile communication platform, updated contact information for families, cultural sensitivity and translation services as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on tailoring messages to the specific needs and demographics of the family. Some families may not have access to mobile devices or may be uncomfortable receiving texts from schools.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, teachers, families (including low-income families and families of color)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student outcomes by informing and supporting families in their children's education.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Mobile communication can be particularly effective for engaging families who may face barriers to traditional forms of communication. Texts are convenient and can provide timely information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Messages should be tailored for different populations, such as non-native English speakers, families with different cultural backgrounds, and those with students in special education. Focus on the individual student’s progress or contain steps families can take to support their child.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student outcomes and correlate them with the use of mobile communication. Collect feedback from families to assess the relevance and effectiveness of the messages.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that texting families with information about their student's progress and tips for supporting learning can lead to improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Model-eliciting activities (MEAs) are activities that encourage learners to invent and test models. They are posed as open-ended problems that are designed to challenge learners to build models in order to solve complex, real-world problems. The learner products provide windows into the thinking processes they used to develop the solutions. MEAs look like authentic, real-world statistical problems and require learners to work in teams to generate solutions via written descriptions, explanations, and constructions. In this way, MEAs are thought-revealing as the learners' products provide windows into the thinking processes they used to develop the solutions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation, access to resources and materials, and a supportive learning environment. Instructors need to facilitate and guide learners through the activity, providing support and feedback as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. May require significant upfront planning and preparation. Learners may struggle with self-direction and time management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop model-building skills, enhance problem-solving abilities, foster teamwork, promote critical thinking, and encourage self-assessment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a way to build models to solve complex, real-world problems. Learners see the relevance of the learning, as MEAs help them develop skills for living in a knowledge-based, highly technological society.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • MEAs can be designed to align with learners' individual interests, needs, and learning styles. Flexible project topics and assessment methods allow for personalized learning experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Collaborative Learning
  • Application of Knowledge
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Problem Scenario
  • Eliciting Student Thinking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality of their final product, and evaluate their ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems. Measure gains in content knowledge, self-confidence, collaboration, and engagement through pre- and post-assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to increased learner engagement, improved understanding of math concepts, enhanced confidence in math skills, and promotion of transfer of learning to real-world situations. Increased learner outcomes and increased motivation. Increased ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A MEA can require an explicit construction, description, explanation, or justified prediction. The activity should foster self-reflection in order to get learners to think about their thinking (metacognition).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This approach involves communicating with learners the purpose for an assessment and/or student feedback. Demonstrate to students what you are looking for by giving them an example of what an A+ paper looks like. Provide a contrast of what a C- paper looks like. This is especially important at the upper learning levels.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • High-quality models and examples, clear explanations

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of models and examples, may be challenging for learners to transfer knowledge to new situations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Clarify expectations, provide concrete examples, enhance understanding, guide improvement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear benchmarks, reduces ambiguity, facilitates self-assessment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The models and examples can be tailored to the specific learning goals and individual learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance. Track learner progress. Analyze the effectiveness of the models and examples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Student performance increases after setting goals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides a model essay to students before they begin writing their own essays. A coach provides a video of a professional athlete demonstrating a skill before having the athletes practice the skill.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Modeling a skill or assignment by verbalizing thought processes while working through it. This allows learners to become aware of the strategies they can use to master a skill and monitor their understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a skilled practitioner or instructor who can articulate their thought processes clearly. Access to resources such as videos, examples, or demonstrations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the learner does not have the necessary background knowledge to understand the modeled task. Over-reliance on modeling without independent practice may hinder the development of problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for learners needing support with metacognition and strategy application

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner awareness of problem-solving strategies, improve self-monitoring skills, support conceptual development

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear, step-by-step example of how to approach a task. Makes internal thought processes visible, promoting self-awareness and metacognition. Can be revisited and re-analyzed for deeper understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different skill levels by varying the complexity of the modeled task. Models can be provided in various formats, such as video, live demonstration, or written examples.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's application of modeled strategies in independent practice. Assess the learner's ability to articulate their own thought processes when solving similar problems. Track the learner's progress in mastering the modeled skill.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Modeling supports conceptual development and strategy acquisition. Research suggests that explicit modeling combined with think-alouds enhances learner's problem-solving abilities and metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher models a math problem by verbalizing each step and explaining their reasoning. A video demonstrates effective communication strategies in a customer service scenario. Khan Academy videos provide models for various academic concepts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teaching fraction and percentage word problems using a model-drawing strategy. This cognitive strategy places emphasis on explicitly teaching students how to draw a schematic diagram to represent the qualitative relations described in the problem, and how to formulate the solution based on the schematic diagram.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Pencil and paper, or whiteboard and marker, along with explicit instruction of the model-drawing strategy

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners must have foundational drawing skills

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school students with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To teach fraction and percentage word problems using a visual model-drawing strategy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visually organizes qualitative relations of the word problem and allows learners to better formulate solutions. Cognitive offloading of quantitative information

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the model drawing and word problems based on learner ability

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Success in solving fraction and percentage word problems using a model-drawing strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Aids high school students with learning disabilities in understanding and solving fraction and percentage word problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly model empathy by demonstrating understanding and sharing in the feelings of others, then explain the thought process behind showing empathy. It involves expressing genuine concern, actively listening to others, and reflecting on their experiences to create a supportive and understanding learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be empathetic and demonstrate genuine concern for learners' feelings. Requires creating a safe and supportive learning environment where learners feel comfortable sharing their experiences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for some learners to understand or internalize empathy. Requires ongoing effort and reinforcement to become a natural behavior.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who struggle with social awareness and empathy, K-12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional intelligence, enhance interpersonal relationships, promote empathy and understanding, create inclusive environments

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports social and emotional development, builds stronger relationships, creates a more inclusive learning environment. Enhances communication and collaboration skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to specific situations or contexts, allowing learners to practice empathy in scenarios relevant to their lives. Can use role-playing exercises, group discussions, and real-life examples.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner interactions and participation in group activities. Assess learner responses to scenarios requiring empathy. Collect learner reflections on their understanding and demonstration of empathy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that modeling empathy can improve interpersonal relationships, reduce conflict, and enhance social-emotional development. Modeling empathy in a classroom is an extremely powerful tool because learners learn by watching and taking the lead of their instructors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor might share a personal story about a time when they showed empathy for someone and explain the positive impact it had. In a group activity, the instructor might model active listening and ask clarifying questions to understand others' perspectives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers share their own positive experiences with reading and writing to foster a positive literacy environment. This can involve sharing favorite books and encouraging students to add their own favorites to a classroom list. Developers can incorporate ways for teachers to share what they read or write with students in both physical and virtual classrooms.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A list of favorite books or examples of the teacher's writing to share. A space (physical or virtual) to display the list and encourage student contributions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The teacher's personal preferences may not align with all students' interests. It is important to create an inclusive environment where all types of literacy are valued.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a positive association with literacy, build a sense of community around reading and writing, increase motivation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages positive attitudes toward literacy by demonstrating the teacher's enthusiasm and personal connection to reading and writing. Creates a shared space where students can explore and express their own interests.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can contribute their own favorite books or writings to the classroom list, personalizing the experience and making it more relevant to their interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' engagement with the shared list of books and their willingness to contribute. Monitor their participation in discussions about reading and writing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that teacher modeling and creating a positive literacy environment can improve students' attitudes toward reading and writing and increase their motivation to engage in literacy activities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher creates a display of their favorite books and invites students to add their own recommendations, creating a dynamic and personalized reading list.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Model positive connections to math is a strategy in which educators explicitly demonstrate curiosity, usefulness, and positive affect toward mathematical thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Consistent teacher language that frames math as meaningful and learnable.
  • Examples that connect math to authentic situations and identities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Surface positivity without support for success can feel inauthentic.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learner confidence, belonging, and willingness to engage with mathematics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Narrate positive mathematical habits, such as persistence and sensemaking.
  • Connect tasks to real uses and learner interests.
  • Respond to mistakes as part of learning rather than as failure.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Real-World Math
  • Create a Low-Stress Environment

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Boaler, J. (2016). Mathematical mindsets. Jossey-Bass.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students need to encounter reflective role models. Modeling reflection can involve reflecting on a workshop session. Teachers can share journal excerpts. The journal excerpts can model evidence of good listening skills, probe for clarity and understanding, ask thoughtful questions, and share metacognitive thinking. Through experience and continuous modeling, the class begins to learn how to use the habits of mind in reflective conversations, which strengthens the transfer to the internal voice of reflection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection and a willingness to share experiences and insights.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to be vulnerable and share personal experiences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Model reflection, share insights, and promote continuous growth.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides teachers with an opportunity to model reflection, share insights, and promote continuous growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use their own experiences to model reflection. They can also share journal excerpts with students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding of reflection and increased use of reflection strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of modeling reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher reflects on a workshop session and shares journal excerpts with students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers demonstrate how to perform a task or skill by verbalizing their thought processes while completing it. This helps learners understand the strategies involved and supports auditory processing. For example, a teacher might model annotating a text or writing a paragraph, sharing their internal dialogue and decision-making process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a teacher or experienced learner to demonstrate the task while verbalizing their thoughts. Edtech tools can enhance this strategy by providing interactive models and recording features.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may passively observe the model without actively engaging in the thinking process. Models need to be clear and well-articulated to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable to all learner levels, especially beneficial for those who benefit from auditory learning and explicit demonstrations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Demonstrate effective strategies, increase awareness of thought processes, support auditory processing, and provide a model for learners to follow.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear, step-by-step example of how to approach a task, making it easier for learners to understand and replicate the process. Supports metacognition by making thinking visible. Allows learners to revisit the model as needed.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Models can be tailored to different skill levels and tasks. Teachers can create models with varying complexity. Edtech tools can allow learners to create and share their own models, fostering personalized learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners as they attempt the task, noting whether they apply the strategies modeled. Review learner-created models to assess their understanding of the process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of modeling to improve learner performance and understanding. Modeling makes abstract processes concrete and accessible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher models how to annotate a complex text by highlighting key points, asking questions, and summarizing sections aloud. Resource: https://www.readingrockets.org/strategies/think-alouds

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers, like the students they teach, can learn to develop a growth mindset, but this requires careful planning by school management. The most obvious way of applying a growth mindset to teacher professional development is through modeling. The key principle is encouraging teachers to see themselves as learners, and, just like students, they are all capable of learning and improving.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires school management to actively plan and support teacher professional development. Essential for creating a safe and supportive environment where teachers feel comfortable taking risks and making mistakes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some educators may resist the idea of a growth mindset due to deeply ingrained beliefs about fixed abilities. Requires consistent reinforcement and a supportive school culture to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators at all levels, especially those undergoing professional development or facing new challenges in their teaching practice

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote professional growth among educators by encouraging them to see themselves as continuous learners, enhance their resilience, and foster a positive attitude towards professional development

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators embrace challenges and view mistakes as learning opportunities, which can lead to greater innovation and more effective teaching strategies. Encourages a culture of continuous improvement and collaboration among staff.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide individualized support and mentorship for teachers who struggle with the concept of a growth mindset. Offer opportunities for teachers to share their own learning experiences and challenges with their peers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track participation and engagement in professional development activities. Observe changes in teacher attitudes toward challenges and new teaching methods. Collect feedback from teachers on their learning experiences and professional growth.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Teachers who model a growth mindset are more likely to create a classroom environment that supports student learning and resilience. Studies show that educators with a growth mindset are more effective in promoting student achievement and motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school principal shares their personal experiences of overcoming challenges in their career, emphasizing the importance of continuous learning and adaptation. Resource: Gerstein, Jackie. "The Educator with a Growth Mindset: A Staff Workshop."

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly model how to evaluate each dimension of source evaluation, and provide repeated opportunities for learners to practice and apply these strategies to information they encounter during the research process. Demonstration lessons can focus on how to: Verify and refute online information, investigate author credentials, detect bias and stance, and negotiate multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit modeling of evaluation strategies, repeated practice opportunities, and curriculum-based scenarios.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and resources. Learners may need ongoing support to develop proficiency.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adolescents and adults

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable learners to verify and refute online information, investigate author credentials, detect bias and stance, and negotiate multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical skills for evaluating online information, enhances critical thinking, and supports informed decision-making.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different subjects and types of sources. Learners can focus on areas of particular interest or need.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to apply evaluation strategies in research projects and assignments. Evaluate their ability to verify information, investigate credentials, detect bias, and negotiate perspectives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced critical thinking: Learners become more skilled at evaluating online information. Improved research skills: Learners can conduct more thorough and reliable research.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher demonstrates how to use fact-checking websites to verify information found online, and then asks students to practice with different sources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers' behaviors and actions create the culture in the classroom. Treat students as respected co-learners to model how all people should be treated. Reaffirm a positive, empathic response for all students by remaining consistent in pro-actions and reactions. When a student seems upset, demonstrate empathy by making eye contact, speaking privately, and maintaining respect. In emotional situations, remember that students may lack coping mechanisms and experience. The empathic response does not seek to embarrass, belittle, or punish the student but protects the learning environment and addresses the disruption with attention to the context and emotions of individual students. Own mistakes publicly to show it’s OK for students to take risks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of emotional intelligence, commitment to respectful communication, time to engage with students individually.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent effort, can be challenging in situations with significant classroom disruptions, may be difficult to implement with very large class sizes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors, mentors, counselors.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a respectful and inclusive classroom environment, build trust and rapport with students, enhance student emotional intelligence, promote positive behavior.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces student anxiety, promotes a sense of safety and belonging, encourages open communication, fosters positive relationships.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor their responses to the specific needs and emotional states of individual students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior, monitor classroom climate, gather student feedback on their sense of safety and respect.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more supportive and inclusive classroom environment, reduces behavioral issues, and promotes student well-being.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Make eye contact with upset students, speak to them privately, validate their feelings, and share personal mistakes to normalize risk-taking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Demonstrating positive thinking skills aloud when talking about oneself and others. This includes highlighting the positive aspects of situations, giving genuine compliments, and encouraging optimism, even in difficult circumstances.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires conscious effort to use positive language and reframe situations. May involve self-reflection to identify and change negative thought patterns.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be perceived as insincere if not genuine. May not be effective if learners are resistant to positive thinking or feel it is unrealistic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, parents, mentors, and leaders in any setting who wish to promote positive thinking and resilience.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To influence learners' internal dialogue through observable examples.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners internalize positive thinking patterns by seeing them in action. Creates a supportive and encouraging environment. Fosters a sense of optimism and resilience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor the modeling to specific situations or challenges that learners face. Adjust the complexity of the language and concepts to suit the audience's age and understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learners' language and behavior, such as increased use of positive statements or a more optimistic outlook. Gather feedback from learners about the impact of the modeling on their thinking and attitudes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that modeling positive behaviors can significantly influence others' attitudes and actions. Seeing positive self-talk in action can inspire learners to adopt similar strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After a bad grade on a test, say, “It’s one bad grade, and you’ll be okay. You can learn from this and get better next time. The most important thing is that you try your best.” Give genuine compliments to others freely and encourage seeing the bright side of things.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Share parts of the reflection brought them to another level of understanding as they worked together in a learning community. Reflection can bring the same spirit of community to your classroom, too.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers must be willing to share their learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Teachers who are not engaged in learning and reflection will find this challenging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Demonstrate the importance of reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • When teachers model what reflection looks like, learners become more comfortable reflecting on their own.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Personalize by sharing parts of your own learning experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• individual reflection
  • demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner ability to reflect.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • When teachers model what reflection looks like, learners become more comfortable reflecting on their own.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Modeling involves demonstrating the skills you expect from your students, both in terms of interaction and analysis. This can be done through providing examples of high-quality work, demonstrating effective communication strategies, and modeling appropriate contributions to discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be skilled communicators and analysts, and to provide clear and relevant examples.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not fully address individual student needs without personalized feedback. Requires careful planning and preparation to ensure clarity and relevance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from clear examples and demonstrations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Demonstrate expected skills, provide examples of high-quality work, model effective communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear expectations, offers practical examples, and supports the development of essential skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by providing varied examples, offering different perspectives, and allowing students to choose which skills to focus on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student performance on assessments, increased quality of student work, and positive feedback on the clarity of the instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Demonstrating the skills expected from students helps them understand what is required and how to achieve success (Cormier & Siemans, 2010).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shift away from the 0-100 scale, which punishes students severely for missing work, and use a more compressed scale like 0-4 to diminish the impact of a single missed assignment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Adjusted grading systems

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Change in mindset

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All Levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce the impact of missed assignments, make it easier to recover from setbacks, create psychological safety

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces stress

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Number of failing grades

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Feldman hates this scale for many reasons, but the biggest one is the destructive power of a “zero” for missing work

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Adopting a 0-4 scale

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The jigsaw strategy involves dividing a task into subtopics, assigning one to each group member. Students then work to become subtopic experts, sharing new knowledge with their groups. For peer teaching, you can group students together as you normally would, but give each tutor-tutee pair the same subtopic to master. Working side-by-side, they can discuss and finish activities, presenting new knowledge to their team together.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear division of tasks into subtopics, structured activities, and teacher guidance. Students need to be trained on how to give effective feedback and provide constructive criticism.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional planning and coordination to schedule activities. Requires careful planning and monitoring to ensure both students are actively engaged and benefiting from the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote collaboration, enhance understanding of concepts, and reinforce learning through teaching.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to engage students in active learning, promotes critical thinking and collaboration, and enhances understanding of concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various subjects and topics, allowing students to focus on areas where they need the most support. Flexible structure accommodates different learning styles and paces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Expert Groups
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student interactions and collaboration skills, assess individual understanding of the material through quizzes or assignments, and gather feedback from students about their experience with jigsaw activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that jigsaw activities can lead to improved academic outcomes, enhanced social skills, and increased student engagement. Students reinforce their learning by teaching, while also benefiting from personalized support.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using jigsaw activities in science or history classes to allow students to become experts on specific topics and share their knowledge with others.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Maintaining an optimal temperature range (68º and 74º Fahrenheit) in classrooms can significantly affect student engagement and productivity. This involves actively monitoring classroom temperatures and adjusting them as needed, potentially through individual teacher control over temperature settings or controlling small blocks of classrooms with similar sunlight exposure. Creating a comfortable thermal environment supports concentration and minimizes distractions related to discomfort.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Temperature monitoring equipment, temperature control systems (e.g., thermostats, HVAC), ability for teachers or administrators to adjust settings. Consider costs related to equipment and operation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Achieving optimal temperature can be challenging due to varying sunlight exposure, building insulation, and individual preferences. Resource constraints (e.g., lack of air conditioning or heating) can limit the ability to adjust.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, improve concentration, reduce distractions, optimize learning conditions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves focus and reduces distractibility, mitigates the impact of uncomfortable physical conditions on learning, creates a more conducive environment for concentration and cognitive tasks.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Temperature preferences can vary, so allowing individual or small group control can cater to different needs. Monitoring and adjusting throughout the day can accommodate fluctuating conditions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement levels, observe concentration and focus, measure productivity (e.g., task completion rates). Compare academic outcomes in classrooms with and without temperature control.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that maintaining optimal temperature ranges enhances student achievement in reading and mathematics. Comfortable temperatures support concentration, minimize distractions, and create better learning environments (Wargocki & Wyon, 2007).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary school with no air conditioning tried to cope during a heat wave by dimming the lights, opening the windows, and blowing fans in each classroom. (Lyons, 2001).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Monitoring progress involves regularly assessing advancement towards goals. This includes evaluating whether you are on schedule, identifying any deviations from the action plan, and making necessary adjustments. Regular monitoring helps maintain focus and ensures timely corrective action.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for regular review and assessment. Access to tools for tracking progress, such as calendars, spreadsheets, or project management software.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Over-monitoring can lead to stress and micromanagement. Infrequent monitoring can result in missed opportunities for corrective action.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Essential for anyone pursuing goals, particularly long-term or complex ones.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure goals stay on track, identify areas needing adjustment, and maintain motivation by visualizing progress.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides timely feedback on progress, allowing for adjustments to strategy and effort. Helps maintain focus and motivation by visualizing advancement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose monitoring methods that suit their preferences, such as progress journals, digital dashboards, or regular check-ins with mentors.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Success is measured by the ability to identify and address deviations from the plan, leading to the timely achievement of goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Regular monitoring has been shown to increase the likelihood of achieving goals by ensuring consistent effort and timely corrective action.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Tracking weekly sales figures against a quarterly target. Reviewing progress on a research project to ensure deadlines are met.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A game app made of funny characters, referred to as the Dust Funnies. These characters, at various stages, will help kids master the various types of math problems. When you come out victorious at one stage, another opens with a different set of problems. The app touches almost every basic mathematical problem in a fun way that quickly engages the learner.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Moose Math app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for older students or advanced math topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Learn addition, counting, subtraction, geometry, and sorting in a funny and engaging way.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners with funny characters and progressive levels of difficulty.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offers various types of math problems with progressive levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor progress through different stages and problem sets.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Makes learning basic mathematical problems fun and engaging for kids.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Children using the app to master math problems with funny characters, such as the Dust Funnies.

docs.title: Morphological Analysis of Latin and Greek Roots
Description
docs.text: Morphological analysis of Latin and Greek roots involves teaching learners about the meaningful parts of words, including prefixes, suffixes, and roots of Latin and Greek origin. This approach emphasizes that many words are constructed from stable and meaningful word parts. For example, learning that the Latin root 'nat' means 'to be born' can help learners understand words like 'natal,' 'native,' and 'nation.' This strategy enhances vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and spelling accuracy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of Latin and Greek roots, prefixes, and suffixes, direct instruction from a teacher or tutor, and consistent practice with word analysis

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging for learners with limited background knowledge of Latin and Greek. Requires explicit and systematic instruction. May be difficult to apply if learners lack foundational phonics skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily for learners in grades 4 and up, including middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to expand their vocabulary and improve reading comprehension

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve vocabulary, enhance reading comprehension, strengthen spelling skills, and develop an understanding of word origins and structures

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances vocabulary, improves reading comprehension, supports spelling, and provides a structured approach to learning and understanding word meanings

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by selecting roots, prefixes, and suffixes relevant to the curriculum or learners' interests. Beginners can start with common roots, while advanced learners can explore more complex morphological relationships.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor vocabulary growth, track progress in reading comprehension, and assess the learners' ability to identify and explain the meanings of morphological components.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that morphological analysis improves vocabulary and reading comprehension. It is particularly effective for learners who struggle with decoding and understanding complex academic texts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fifth-grade teacher organizes word study around a common Latin root, such as 'dict' (to speak), to teach words like 'dictum,' 'dictionary,' and 'edict.' A high school teacher uses Greek combining forms to teach scientific concepts and discoveries, such as 'thermodynamics' and 'isotherm.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instruction that makes students aware of inflections (–ed, –s, –es, –ing, –er, –est, which are also called grammatical suffixes), morphemes that change the number, person, or tense of the word to which they are added, but they do not change its part of speech.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, morphological charts, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 2-6 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance understanding of word structure, build vocabulary

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand how word parts contribute to meaning, improves spelling accuracy, builds vocabulary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction. Focus on specific morphemes that the learner is struggling with.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in spelling words with inflections and other morphemes. Monitor progress in spelling and vocabulary skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Instruction that focuses on inflections and prefixes and suffixes enhances understanding of word structure

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Motion and forces experiments involve exploring how forces affect the motion of objects. Learners demonstrate the transfer of energy by measuring the distances different balls move a cup and investigate variables that affect the movement of a pendulum. These experiments enhance understanding of energy transfer, motion, and forces.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Balls, ramps, cups, pendulums, strings, weights

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful control of variables. Precise measurements are essential for accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the relationship between forces and motion, investigate energy transfer, explore variables affecting pendulum movement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activities make abstract concepts more understandable. Encourages observation and measurement of motion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Variety of balls and ramps can be used. Pendulum experiments can be adapted for different variables.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in measuring distances and angles, correct identification of variables affecting motion, logical explanations of energy transfer

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of motion and forces, enhanced experimental skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Balls and Ramp (NYSED): Learners demonstrate transfer of energy by measuring the distances different balls move a cup. Swingers (KDE): Learners experiment with a pendulum to find out why it might swing at different speeds at different times.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Motor images, also known as muscle memory, involve using physical movements and actions to enhance learning and recall. These strategies capitalize on the brain's ability to remember procedures and information that have been practiced repeatedly. Multisensory strategies that combine seeing, hearing, touching, and moving with the information are particularly effective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for physical movement, learning material to be practiced, and understanding of the connection between movement and recall

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners with physical limitations, requires careful supervision to ensure safety, may be disruptive in some classroom settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for kinesthetic learners and those who struggle with rote memorization

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory recall, improve retention of procedures and information, increase engagement through physical activity, cater to kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages muscle memory, enhances retention through physical activity, caters to kinesthetic learning styles, increases engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific motor activities can be adapted to suit individual needs and preferences. The content being practiced can be tailored to different subjects and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
