docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recall information while performing motor activities, assess their engagement and participation, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using motor image strategies

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Motor image strategies have been shown to enhance memory recall and improve retention of procedures and information. They engage muscle memory and cater to kinesthetic learning styles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using "Fonzie fists" to remember the direction of the letters b and d, air writing letters or spelling words, fist tapping and arm tapping to spell words syllable by syllable, using finger calculation strategies in math.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Movement breaks are brief, structured activities incorporated into classroom settings to energize learners, improve focus, and enhance learning. These breaks typically last from 1–5 minutes and involve physical activity, such as stretching, dancing, or simple exercises. Movement breaks can be used after periods of sedentary activity, such as after lunch or before a test, to increase blood flow to the brain and stimulate cognitive function. They also provide an opportunity for learners to manage stress and improve self-regulation. Empowering students to suggest and lead movement breaks fosters inclusivity, motivation, and engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires 1–5 minutes of class time, 2-3 times per day. Minimal equipment, such as music, beanbags, or spot markers, may be used. Involves teacher participation and facilitation to ensure inclusivity and engagement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May disrupt classroom flow if not managed effectively. Some learners may be resistant to physical activity. Requires teacher planning and facilitation to ensure inclusivity and appropriateness.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly K–12, but also applicable in higher education and professional development settings where sedentary behavior is common.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner energy and focus, improve blood flow to the brain, stimulate cognitive function, manage stress, and enhance self-regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances attention and focus by increasing blood flow to the brain. Improves self-regulation by providing structured opportunities to manage stress and release energy. Fosters inclusivity and motivation by empowering students to suggest and lead activities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted to suit various abilities, interests, and limitations. Modifications can include seated activities for mobility-challenged learners, adjustments to game rules, and variations in intensity. Students can also choose activities they find enjoyable and accessible.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation levels. Track changes in student focus and attention after implementing movement breaks. Gather feedback from students on their preferences and perceived benefits.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that movement breaks improve cognitive function, enhance attention, and reduce stress. Studies show that integrating physical activity into the classroom can lead to improved academic outcomes and increased learner motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary teacher incorporates spelling into a movement break, having students move and stretch while spelling words. GoNoodle provides energetic brain break videos that can be used in the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Response to Intervention (RTI) is an approach to academic intervention that provides early, systematic, and appropriately intensive assistance to students at risk for or already underperforming relative to peers, through universal screening, early intervention, frequent progress monitoring, and increasingly intensive research-based instruction for students who continue to struggle. It was originally proposed as an alternative to the older ability-achievement discrepancy model, which identified a specific learning disability by requiring a significant gap between a student's ability (often IQ) and their achievement (grades, standardized test scores) — a method long criticized for over-diagnosing low-performing students as disabled. RTI instead bases decisions on how a student actually responds to targeted intervention over time, rather than on a one-time discrepancy between two test scores. As the framework broadened beyond identifying learning disabilities specifically into a general educational decision-making process, the field increasingly labels it Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS).

Service delivery is organized into three tiers of increasing intensity:

  • Tier 1 — core curriculum instruction targeting all students. Roughly 80-85% of the general student body should meet grade-level norms through Tier 1 alone, with no additional support needed.
  • Tier 2 — supplementary intervention, typically in small groups, for students who consistently underperform despite Tier 1 instruction. Roughly 3-6% of students continue to struggle even after Tier 2.
  • Tier 3 — the most intensive level, typically individualized (often one-on-one) intervention delivered within the regular education environment for students who have not responded sufficiently to Tiers 1 and 2.

Because RTI/MTSS generates ongoing, evidence-based progress data at every tier, it lets educators rule out inadequate instruction as an explanation for poor performance — supporting the claim that it identifies genuine learning disabilities (or other support needs) more defensibly than a single ability-achievement discrepancy score ever could.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Universal screening and frequent, systematic progress monitoring at every tier, not just at intervention entry/exit points
  • A genuinely tiered response capacity: core instruction reliable enough that ~80-85% of students succeed without extra support, small-group capacity for the next tier, and individualized capacity for the smallest, most intensive tier

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • MTSS/RTI requires sustained data collection and cross-tier coordination — a school adopting the label without the underlying screening and progress-monitoring infrastructure is not actually implementing the framework

docs.title: Implementation Variability
docs.text: • The specific screening instruments, intervention programs, and tier-advancement thresholds used within each tier vary considerably across schools and districts, even though the three-tier structure itself is consistent

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• All students at Tier 1, since the framework begins with universal core instruction rather than only targeting identified students
  • Students who continue to underperform despite adequate core instruction, who move through Tiers 2 and 3 based on documented response to intervention rather than a single test-score discrepancy

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Grade-level academic performance achieved through the least intensive tier sufficient for a given student
  • Defensible identification of genuine learning disabilities or other support needs, based on documented non-response to intervention rather than an ability-achievement gap alone

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Deliver strong Tier 1 core instruction to all students, ideally informed by Universal Design for Learning (UDL), so as few students as possible need to escalate further.
  2. Screen and monitor progress universally and frequently, using assessment methods sensitive enough to flag underperformance early.
  3. Move consistently underperforming students into Tier 2 small-group supplementary intervention, with feedback and progress monitoring frequent enough to judge response.
  4. Escalate students who do not respond sufficiently to Tier 2 into Tier 3 individualized, often one-on-one, intensive intervention.
  5. Use the resulting documented response-to-intervention history, not a single ability-achievement discrepancy score, to inform decisions about learning disability identification or other support needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tier assignment itself is the personalization mechanism: intensity of support scales with documented student need rather than being fixed in advance

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching students with disabilities. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
  • Response to Intervention. (n.d.). In Wikipedia. Retrieved from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Response_to_intervention

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning logs or blogs are used for groups to reflect on their learning, document the content of each session, and share what supported or interfered with their learning. They serve as tools for inquiry and for sharing their learning with others. The logs/blogs include text, visuals, video clips, and links to other resources to describe their learning. Students can embed links within their text to video clips, additional websites, and photos that describe their learning for others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers with internet access, blogging platform or learning log software, class time for reflection and documentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require technical support for students who are unfamiliar with blogging platforms. Requires careful monitoring to ensure appropriate content and respectful communication.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school students (Grades 6-8), but adaptable for other grade levels and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote reflection, document learning process, facilitate knowledge sharing, synthesize multimodal resources, enhance communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a platform for students to express their learning in various formats. Supports collaboration and peer learning. Enhances digital literacy skills. Encourages students to reflect on their learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose the format and content of their learning logs/blogs. Flexible grouping allows for diverse perspectives. Can be adapted to fit various content areas and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze student reflections, review content of learning logs/blogs, assess student engagement in peer feedback and discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances reflection, facilitates knowledge sharing, supports digital literacy skills, and promotes deeper understanding of content.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multimodal assignments involve a variety of assessment methods that challenge learners to create video or audio projects, write personal essays, or complete quizzes. These assignments encourage learners to use different parts of their brain, promoting active involvement in their own learning and improving retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to tools for creating video and audio projects. LMS or platform for uploading and sharing assignments. Clear instructions and assessment criteria.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources and technical support. Requires clear instructions and assessment criteria. Potential for inequitable access to resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for diverse learners, adaptable for various subjects and educational levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active learning, encourage creativity, improve retention, assess understanding through diverse methods.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages different parts of the brain, promoting active learning and improving retention. Allows learners to demonstrate their understanding in creative ways. Encourages learners to use different parts of their brain and think outside the box.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose assignment types based on their strengths and interests. Provide options for individual or group projects. Offer flexible deadlines and personalized feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Procedural information
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the creativity, depth of understanding, and quality of the projects. Assess performance on quizzes and essays. Gather feedback from learners on their experiences with multimodal assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases learner engagement and creativity. Encourages learners to use different parts of their brain. Improves retention through active involvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Challenging learners to create a video or audio project and upload it to an LMS. Giving instructions on a personal essay to write and post. Setting up a quiz for learners to take.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multimodal composition involves creating texts using various modes of communication such as images, words, sound, and movement. Writers compose slide shows, videos, audio documentaries, brochures, Tweets, Web sites, and much more. Digital literacy is the ability to use digital technology, communication tools or networks to locate, evaluate, use and create information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers, multimedia software, and internet connectivity. Training in various composition techniques is also beneficial.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires technical proficiency, can be time-intensive, and may require access to specific platforms or software.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly higher education and professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop digital literacy skills, express ideas through multiple media, and understand the affordances and constraints of different platforms.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances creativity, promotes critical thinking, strengthens digital literacy skills, and provides diverse ways to communicate ideas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose media formats that align with their strengths, explore different topics, and tailor their compositions to specific audiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-task performance
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the effective use of multiple modes, clarity of communication, technical skill, and overall impact of the composition.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective multimodal composers in our complex, global world, learn how to compose using different platforms, and understand what such forms allow, disallow, and require. We need both technical skill and critical understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a video essay, designing an interactive website, producing an audio documentary.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multimodal composition involves learners combining different modes of communication (linguistic, visual, audio, gestural, spatial) to enhance the message they want to convey. Learners use digital tools to combine images, audio, and video to represent their thoughts on different topics and share their perspectives. This can include creating web-based interactive stories with multiple endings and various genres to enhance comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to digital tools for creating and editing multimedia content. Needs instructor guidance on effective multimodal combinations and design principles.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires technical skills and access to technology, which may create barriers for some learners. Ineffective mode combinations can distract from the intended meaning if not carefully analyzed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially those interested in digital storytelling and creative expression

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner expression, foster digital literacy, develop composition skills, improve understanding of genres

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables creative expression, integrates digital literacy skills, provides opportunities for authentic communication, supports diverse learning preferences

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to choose their topic, modes of expression, and digital tools. Scaffolded support can be provided for learners new to multimodal composition.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the effectiveness of mode combinations in conveying the intended message. Assess the depth of learner reflection on their design decisions and the feedback they incorporate.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests multimodal composition can enhance engagement and creativity when learners understand how different modes work together. Critical analysis of mode affordances improves communication effectiveness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Stonybrook University's digital storytelling site showcases student digital compositions. Inklewriter allows learners to create web-based interactive stories.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using multiple surfaces or screens for instruction and collaboration. This strategy involves using multiple display boards or screens to enhance learning and collaboration in educational and work settings. It includes physical surfaces like smart wall paint for collaborative writing and digital setups with conjoined screens for seamless sharing and visualization of work. The approach aims to increase engagement and make information more accessible to learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires multiple screens or surfaces (e.g., smart wall paint, projectors, iPads). May require software for syncing screens (e.g., Reflector, AirServer).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be costly to implement, especially if requiring new technology. Requires setup and technical knowledge to sync screens effectively. Attention can be a factor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and professional settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, improve accessibility, facilitate collaboration, visualize work seamlessly

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement by providing visual aids and interactive surfaces. Supports collaborative group work and seamless sharing of information. Improves accessibility for learners who benefit from visual learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different classroom sizes and technological resources. Allows for flexibility in how students present and interact with information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation in collaborative activities. Assess the quality and quantity of work produced on shared screens. Monitor student understanding and retention of information through formative assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Collaborative work and increased engagement. Improved accessibility for visual learners. Enhanced sharing and visualization of group work.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary schools using smart wall paint for students to write on walls and tables with dry erase markers. Work settings using multi-boarding from SMART Board to promote collaborative group work with conjoined screens. Classrooms projecting iPads onto larger screens using software like Reflector to enhance engagement and focus.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When teaching a new technique, providing multiple examples helps students understand and apply the technique in their own writing. Definition alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Preparation of multiple examples of the technique. Time for analysis and practice in class. A supportive environment where students feel comfortable experimenting with new techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Students may become overwhelmed by too many examples. Requires careful selection of examples that are relevant and accessible to students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for struggling writers and those new to a specific technique

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of writing techniques, enhance ability to apply techniques in writing, develop fluency in using new techniques, increase confidence in writing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a range of models for imitation. Supports understanding by illustrating the technique in different contexts. Increases confidence by showing that the technique can be applied in multiple ways.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Examples can be tailored to student interests and writing goals. Students can be given opportunities to generate their own examples. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating the application of the technique. Participation in discussions and analyses of examples. Student reflections on their writing process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing multiple examples improves understanding and application of new concepts and techniques.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • If teaching figurative language, provide multiple examples of metaphors, similes, and personification. If teaching essay organization, provide examples of different ways to structure an introduction, body paragraph, or conclusion. If teaching real-world applications, provide examples of the skill used in varied situations and careers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multiple exposures provide students with multiple opportunities to encounter, engage with, and elaborate on new knowledge and skills. Research demonstrates deep learning develops over time via multiple, spaced interactions with new knowledge and concepts. This may require spacing practice over several days, and using different activities to vary the interactions learners have with new knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure spaced repetition and varied interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to implement effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning through repeated and varied interactions with new content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances retention and transfer of knowledge through spaced and varied practice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be varied to suit different learning preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Retention over time, ability to apply knowledge in different contexts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Multiple exposures facilitate deep learning by reinforcing concepts and skills through repeated and varied interactions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sharing information through various modalities beyond text and images, such as audio, video, simulations, or interactive models. This approach ensures that learners with different sensory preferences and abilities can access the content effectively. It involves presenting information in multiple formats to cater to diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Diverse multimedia resources, software for creating and delivering content in multiple formats, and awareness of learner preferences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful design to ensure coherence across modalities. Some learners may be overwhelmed by too many options.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with sensory disabilities (e.g., blindness or deafness), learning disabilities, and diverse cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, support diverse learning styles, improve engagement, accommodate sensory preferences and abilities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Caters to various learning styles. Improves accessibility for learners with sensory impairments. Enhances understanding through multiple representations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer content in text, audio, video, and interactive formats. Allow learners to choose the modalities that best suit their needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure learner engagement with different modalities. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of each modality in supporting learning. Assess learner performance across different modalities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced learning outcomes: Studies indicate that using multiple modalities can improve comprehension and retention, particularly for learners with diverse learning styles and abilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The number line is used as a visual representation of numerical relationships. Students can integrate it into game boards and activities to develop their number sense and understanding of linearity. An interactive number line can be used to teach place value, allowing learners to manipulate space and quantity to develop their understanding of place value and magnitude.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Number line (physical or digital). Integration into a game or activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may need initial guidance on how to use and interpret the number line. May not be suitable for all mathematical concepts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop number sense, understand linearity, teach place value, and develop an understanding of magnitude

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual aid to understanding numerical relationships. Allows for hands-on interaction and manipulation of quantities, making abstract concepts more concrete. Promotes deeper understanding of place value and magnitude through game-based learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be integrated into various activities and games to suit different learning styles. The complexity of the number line can be adjusted to match the learner's level of understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to use the number line to solve problems. Track their understanding of place value and magnitude through game-based activities. Assess their number sense development over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using a number line as a visual aid can improve learners' understanding of numerical relationships and place value. Interactive number lines can enhance engagement and make learning more enjoyable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Motion Math Zoom uses an interactive number line to teach place value through a fun game. An elementary teacher integrates a number line into a game board to promote the development of student number sense and linearity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using visual representations can lead to clearer delivery of content and greater retention of key concepts in long-term memory. Visuals also serve an important role in maintaining learner attention and are a touchpoint for learners to refer back to on their own as external memory aids and for individual practice. Visuals can include videos, images, graphics, and other forms of media.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to visual materials, such as videos, images, and graphics. Technology for displaying visuals, such as projectors or computers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for all learners, especially those with visual impairments. Visuals must be carefully chosen and aligned with content to avoid confusion or distraction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for visual learners and those who benefit from multimodal instruction

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding, improve retention, maintain attention, facilitate communication, foster creativity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Activates visual processing areas of the brain, supports working memory, enhances long-term retention, facilitates communication and creativity

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose different types of visual representations that best suit their learning styles and preferences. Instructors can also differentiate visuals to address a variety of learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer
  • Demonstration
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner engagement with visual materials, assess learner understanding through visual representations, compare learner performance with and without visual aids.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that visual cues help learners better retrieve and remember information, decreasing learning time, improving comprehension, enhancing retrieval, and increasing retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using DragonBox Algebra 5+ to teach algebraic concepts with visuals. Showing a short clip from The Bone Collector and having students analyze the last frame (a dollar bill next to a footprint) for mathematical significance. Creating visual curricular materials tailored to specific content areas.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reading multiple texts on the same topic expands learners' understanding, encourages critical thinking, and fosters synthesis skills. This strategy involves establishing a clear purpose for reading, selecting short texts from various sources (news articles, video clips, trade books, diagrams), modeling connections between texts using tools like Inquiry Charts, facilitating discussions to combine information from different sources, and integrating sketching and writing to deepen understanding. By engaging with multiple texts, learners develop a sense of agency and can more effectively answer their own questions, while also building more knowledge of the subject matter.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of multiple short texts related to a topic, clear research questions or purpose for reading, Inquiry Charts or other tools for recording information, time for reading, discussion, and writing or sketching.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be overwhelming for some learners if not properly scaffolded. Requires careful selection of texts to ensure relevance and accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expand understanding of a topic, improve critical thinking skills, develop synthesis skills, enhance engagement with texts, promote agency and self-directed learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages critical thinking, promotes deeper understanding, fosters synthesis skills, allows for exploration of multiple perspectives, develops research skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Choice of texts can be tailored to learner interests and reading levels. Inquiry Charts can be adapted to suit different research questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of notes and summaries recorded in Inquiry Charts, participation in discussions, depth and accuracy of written or sketched responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Deeper understanding, improved critical thinking skills, enhanced engagement, and increased agency in learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Presenting information in more ways than images and text alone enhances comprehension and caters to diverse learning preferences. This includes using audio descriptions, tactile representations, and interactive simulations to convey concepts. Multiple modalities engage different sensory pathways, making learning more accessible and inclusive. Learners can connect information in various ways.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to varied media and materials, such as audio recordings, tactile models, and interactive simulations. Instructors need to design activities that integrate multiple sensory modalities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more preparation time and resources. Some learners may find too much sensory input overwhelming. It's essential to ensure that multiple modes enhance rather than distract from learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with sensory disabilities, learning disabilities, or diverse learning preferences; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance accessibility, accommodate diverse learning preferences, improve comprehension, support engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports accessibility by providing alternative formats for learners with sensory impairments, enhances engagement by offering varied sensory experiences, improves comprehension by reinforcing concepts through multiple modalities, and aids retention by activating different cognitive processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a range of modalities to suit different needs and preferences. Provide options for learners to choose their preferred mode of learning. Use adaptive technologies to adjust the presentation of information based on individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in multimodal activities. Assess comprehension through varied formats like written, visual, or oral presentations. Track improvements in retention and application of knowledge in diverse contexts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that multimodal instruction can enhance learning outcomes by accommodating diverse learning preferences and improving engagement. Studies show that combining visual and auditory information can improve memory and comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An audio description of a visual image for learners with visual impairments. A tactile model of a molecule for learners with kinesthetic preferences. An interactive simulation that allows learners to manipulate variables and observe the effects.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multiple writing surfaces involve providing learners with a variety of spaces where they can write and express their ideas, such as walls, tables, or portable whiteboards. This strategy aims to promote active engagement, collaboration, and creative thinking by making writing more accessible and flexible. Learners can use these surfaces to brainstorm, solve problems, take notes, or share ideas with peers. This approach can enhance motivation and cater to different learning styles by offering diverse ways to interact with the material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires writable surfaces (e.g., whiteboards, painted walls, tables) and writing tools (e.g., dry erase markers, chalk). May need classroom redesign or additional materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to manage space and resources. May be disruptive if not implemented with clear guidelines. Potential for misuse or defacement of surfaces.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active learning, encourage collaboration, foster creative thinking, increase accessibility to writing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement by providing diverse and accessible writing spaces. Supports collaboration by allowing learners to work together on shared surfaces. Fosters creative thinking by encouraging free-form expression. Improves memory retention through visual and kinesthetic learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various subject areas and learning environments. Surfaces can be customized with prompts, templates, or graphic organizers. Can be integrated with digital tools for blended learning experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and collaboration on writing surfaces. Collect and analyze written work for understanding and creativity. Gather feedback from learners on their experience with multiple writing surfaces.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows active learning environments promote deeper understanding and engagement. Flexible learning spaces can accommodate diverse learning styles and enhance collaboration. Studies indicate increased motivation and creativity with accessible writing surfaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary school used smart wall paint to allow students to write on the walls and tables with dry erase markers. Schools equip new classrooms with Apple TV and multiple writing surfaces to give students and teachers the flexibility to move around the room and write anywhere on the walls. Post-it Super Sticky Dry Erase Surface allows students and teachers to quickly transform any surface into a whiteboard.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multiplicative double counting involves tracking all three units (groups, unit rate, and total) to solve a multiplication problem. For instance, with 'seven towers with three cubes each,' learners track the towers, cubes per tower, and total cubes. It contrasts with repeated addition, where only the unit rate and total are tracked. A student using multiplicative double counting would solve the above problem by tracking the amount of towers they had counted, either with their fingers, a drawing, or another form. They would also track the unit rate and total amount of singletons.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires manipulatives (e.g., cubes, towers), finger counting, or drawings to track units. Instructors should engage students in activities that encourage multiplicative double counting.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional instructional time and practice for students accustomed to repeated addition. Some learners may find tracking three units challenging initially.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students transitioning from repeated addition to multiplicative thinking, particularly those struggling with conceptual understanding of multiplication.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop a deeper conceptual understanding of multiplication, division, fractions, ratios, proportions, and algebra by tracking all three units in multiplication problems.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Establishes a stronger conceptual grounding for multiplication by enabling learners to track three units instead of two. Improves readiness for advanced math concepts, like division, fractions, ratio, proportion, and algebra.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The concrete materials (cubes), then moves students towards figural representations of the concrete materials, and ultimately ends with moving students toward an abstract way of thinking using symbols and equations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Application
  • Simple-to-complex sequencing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to track all three units (groups, unit rate, and total) by stopping them during their counting sequence and asking about each unit. Check for improved performance in related math concepts (division, fractions, etc.).

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters a deeper conceptual understanding of multiplication compared to traditional repeated addition methods.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using manipulatives to represent towers and cubes, counting on fingers to track the number of towers counted while also tracking cubes per tower and total cubes. 'Please Go Bring for Me (PGBM)' is an activity that begins with concrete materials (cubes), then moves students towards figural representations of the concrete materials, and ultimately ends with moving students toward an abstract way of thinking using symbols and equations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Designing spaces that lend themselves to a variety of learning styles and activities are best. For instance, there might be an area for presentations, performances, or cooperative groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of seating options such as tables and chairs, couches, and bean bag chairs. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing seating arrangements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase collaboration, improve communication skills, promote flexible thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes collaboration and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred seating arrangement. Provide a variety of seating options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that flexible seating can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multisensory instruction uses a combination of visual, auditory, and tactile-kinesthetic techniques to enhance memory and learning. This approach is effective for adult students with learning disabilities. Many programs are based on the Orton-Gillingham-Stillman Approach, which is considered a foundation for successful multisensory reading programs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Trained instructors, specialized materials, and structured activities. Requires instructors to integrate visual, auditory, and tactile-kinesthetic elements into instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be resource-intensive. Requires specialized training for instructors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adults with learning disabilities, struggling readers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory and learning; engage multiple senses to reinforce understanding; improve reading skills for learners with learning disabilities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages multiple cognitive pathways, making learning more accessible and memorable. Provides a structured and systematic approach to reading instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to individual learner needs by emphasizing different sensory modalities. Activities can be modified to suit specific learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved reading accuracy, fluency, and comprehension. Increased engagement and participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Proven effectiveness for adult students with learning disabilities. Engages multiple senses to reinforce understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Alphabetic Phonics, Barton Reading and Spelling System, Multisensory Teaching Approach (MTA), The Herman Method, Landmark Methodology, Lindamood-Bell, Orton-Gillingham Method, Project Read, Slingerland Approach, Wilson Reading System, and Dyslexia Training Program.

docs.title: Multisensory Memory Strategies for Irregular Words
Description
docs.text: Multisensory memory strategies for irregular words involve using multiple senses (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, and tactile) to enhance memory and retention of irregularly spelled words. These strategies include grouping words with memorable similarities, calling attention to the odd parts of words, repeated practice through copying and saying letters, discussing irregularities, and using mnemonics. This approach is beneficial because irregular words do not follow typical phoneme-grapheme correspondences, making them difficult to spell using standard phonics rules.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of irregular words, multisensory materials (e.g., letter tiles, sand tray), direct instruction from a teacher or tutor, and consistent practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, especially for learners with numerous irregular words to learn. Requires explicit and systematic instruction. May not be suitable for learners who prefer a more traditional, rule-based approach to spelling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily for learners in grades 1-3, but also effective for older students and adults who struggle with spelling irregular words

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy of irregular words, enhance memory and retention of irregularly spelled words, and develop strategies for learning and recalling non-phonetic words

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory through multiple sensory inputs, makes learning fun and engaging, provides a structured approach to learning difficult words, and caters to different learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic)

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning styles by emphasizing different sensory modalities (visual learners may focus on visualizing the word, auditory learners on saying the letters aloud, kinesthetic learners on writing the word)

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor spelling accuracy on regular spelling tests, track progress in writing assignments, and assess the effective use of mnemonic devices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that multisensory strategies improve memory and retention of information. Explicit instruction and practice with multisensory techniques enhance overall spelling skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A second-grade teacher uses letter tiles to help students spell the word 'friend,' emphasizing the irregular 'ie' spelling. A fifth-grade teacher teaches the mnemonic 'there is a rat in separate' to help students remember the spelling of 'separate.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Multisyllable word instruction focuses on teaching learners how to break words into syllables to improve spelling and reading skills. This involves learning the six basic syllable types (closed, open, vowel-consonant-e, r-controlled, vowel team, and consonant-le) and how they affect spelling. It also includes understanding compound words, recognizing the schwa sound in unaccented syllables, and learning common prefixes and suffixes. Instruction emphasizes breaking words into manageable parts to facilitate decoding and encoding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of multisyllable words, direct instruction from a teacher or tutor, and consistent practice with word decomposition and syllable identification

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging for learners with significant language processing deficits. Requires explicit and systematic instruction. May be difficult to apply if learners lack foundational phonics skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily for learners in grades 3 and up, including older students and adults who need to improve their spelling and reading skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy of multisyllable words, enhance decoding skills, increase understanding of syllable types, and develop skills in recognizing and applying prefixes and suffixes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances spelling skills, improves decoding, supports word building, and provides a structured approach to learning and applying syllabication rules

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of the words and syllable types used in the instruction. Beginning learners can start with simple compound words, while advanced learners can tackle more complex multisyllable words with multiple affixes.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor spelling accuracy on regular spelling tests, track progress in reading assessments, and assess the learners' ability to identify and apply syllabication rules correctly.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that explicit instruction in multisyllable words improves spelling and reading skills. It is particularly effective for learners who struggle with decoding and encoding complex words.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher teaches the six syllable types and then guides students to break words like 'cable,' 'bugle,' and 'dabble' into syllables to demonstrate the rules for doubling consonants in consonant-le syllables.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporate music and dance into the learning environment to engage verbal, visual, and kinesthetic senses. This strategy involves connecting content with movement and rhythm to enhance memorization and understanding. Examples include creating dances to memorize concepts, using songs to practice skills (e.g., alphabet knowledge), or allowing learners to create instrumental songs and choreograph dance moves. This approach increases learner engagement and retention by activating multiple parts of the brain.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom space for movement, access to music or instruments (optional), and willingness to integrate physical activity into lessons. Digital tools like Toca Dance Free can be used for creating music and choreography.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with physical limitations or those uncomfortable with movement. Requires careful planning to ensure activities align with learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for elementary students and kinesthetic learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memorization, improve understanding through multiple senses, increase learner engagement, activate different parts of the brain involved with various senses

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves learning by connecting verbal and visual content with movement. Activates sight, sound, touch, and emotions. Enhances memory and retention through multi-sensory engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for various subjects and age groups. Movements and songs can be tailored to specific learning needs and preferences. Learners can create their own dances and songs, promoting creativity and ownership.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation in movement activities. Assess retention of content taught through music and dance. Collect feedback from learners on their experience and understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that engaging multiple senses through movement enhances learning and retention. Brain-based learning strategies improve learning by activating different parts of the brain during the teaching process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary students performing a song and dance to practice alphabet knowledge. Using Toca Dance Free to create instrumental songs and choreograph dance moves. High school English teacher using a dance to help students memorize helping verbs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy uses movement, rhythm, and music to enhance learning and understanding of various concepts, particularly in mathematics. It involves integrating dance, drama, and music into lessons to make them more interactive and engaging. Activities can range from simple songs and dances to explore counting and operations, to more complex choreographies that illustrate mathematical concepts like triangular numbers and square numbers. Different approaches include using movement to teach mathematical concepts, learning math from different types of dances, or performing dances to teach an audience a concept.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to music and open space for movement; may require props or costumes depending on the complexity of the activity; instructor needs to have some familiarity with both the mathematical concept and the dance style; planning time to integrate the two effectively

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all learners, particularly those who are not comfortable with physical activity or creative expression; requires careful planning to ensure the dance accurately represents the mathematical concept; may be perceived as a less serious learning activity if not integrated thoughtfully

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners; particularly effective for visual and kinesthetic learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of mathematical concepts, promote kinesthetic learning, increase engagement and motivation, foster creativity and expression, improve memory and retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement and motivation through active participation; connects abstract concepts to physical movement, improving comprehension; supports different learning styles, making content more accessible; promotes creativity and self-expression; strengthens memory through multimodal learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different mathematical concepts and dance styles; can be scaffolded with simpler movements for beginners or expanded into complex choreographies for advanced learners; allows for learner choice in music and dance styles to reflect cultural backgrounds and personal interests

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the dance activities; assess learner understanding of mathematical concepts through performance and verbal explanations; use reflections or journals to assess learner's ability to connect movement to concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that integrating arts into mathematics education can enhance student engagement, improve understanding of abstract concepts, and promote a more positive attitude towards math. Studies also show that movement-based learning can improve memory and retention. Real-world examples include using dance to illustrate geometric concepts or musical rhythms to understand fractions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Erik Stern and Karl Schaffer using dance to teach counting combinations in their TEDx talk; Corinne Wolfe's mathematical dance illustrating how two consecutive triangular numbers make a square number; lesson plans that use dance, drama, music, and visual arts to teach various math concepts (KET).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners listen to different types of music and discuss how it makes them feel, fostering emotional awareness and providing a creative outlet for emotional expression. This activity can also highlight connections between music and emotions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a music player. A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be respectful of musical tastes. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve emotional awareness, promote positive associations with emotional expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects emotional expression with music. Promotes a auditory-based approach to learning about emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Music can be selected to reflect diverse cultural backgrounds and musical styles. Learners can also create their own music.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to connect specific music types with corresponding emotions. Assess their participation and engagement in the activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that listening to music helps in connecting with emotions. (Source: Music in Social and Emotional Learning - https://www.nafme.org/2023/10/music-as-a-medium-for-sel/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are challenged to guess the emotion the instructor is acting out in order to solve the mystery of what it is.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emotion prompts and a facilitator for instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners must be comfortable performing or may feel embarrassed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve self-assessment, promote empathetic understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners to recognize the faces and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Requires learners to be willing to perform in front of others. May not be effective with learners who are naturally introverted.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The facilitator can observe how the learners perform. Ask learners to do an individual reflection of how they used emotions and what they learned from the activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of role-playing and dramatic activities to enhance emotional understanding and social skills. (Source: Spontaneous Drama Improves Communication Skills - https://www.livestrong.com/article/198645-spontaneous-drama-improves-communication-skills/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pronouncing learners' names correctly can help develop trust and rapport. Mispronouncing a name can cause feelings of anxiety, invisibility, shame, resentment, and humiliation, all of which can lead to social and educational disengagement. When getting to know learners, make sure that you get their name pronunciation right from the start.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors should take the time to ask each learner their name, and make a good-faith effort to pronounce it correctly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some languages have different phonemes than the instructor is used to, which makes it difficult to achieve proper pronunciation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a positive classroom environment through proper name pronunciation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • When names are pronounced correctly, this promotes trust and respect, and eliminates negative emotional reactions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The instructor must determine each learner's individual name pronunciation and record it.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner engagement, decreased feelings of shame or anxiety, and improved classroom culture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students will take the cue of fearing or celebrating difference from the climate set up by instructors. Those who show that they can take an important step toward making all students feel seen and respected, necessary prerequisites for an engaging social and academic experience.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Have students name their negative inner voice (e.g., Adverse Antoine, Ruthless Ralph, Cranky Kirsten). This allows students to step outside themselves and understand that they are not defined by that voice and can treat it like a separate entity, thereby taking back power and control.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Creativity, understanding of negative self-talk patterns.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May seem silly or ineffective to some learners. Requires a playful and open-minded approach.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create psychological distance from negative self-talk.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners disassociate from negative thoughts and see them as external influences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose names that resonate with their experience of negative self-talk.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how students refer to and interact with their named negative voice.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased sense of control over negative thoughts and feelings (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students give their negative inner voice a name to externalize it, allowing them to treat it as a separate entity. This helps students understand that they are not defined by their negative thoughts and can take back control.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for students to brainstorm and choose names. A supportive environment for sharing names and descriptions. Encouragement from the educator to embrace the activity with enthusiasm.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may find the activity silly or uncomfortable. It may be difficult for some students to separate themselves from their negative thoughts. The activity's success depends on students' willingness to engage in the process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those who struggle with negative self-perception and fixed mindsets.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To help students externalize their negative thoughts and understand that they are not defined by them.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by distinguishing between the self and negative thoughts. Supports emotional regulation by creating distance from negative emotions. Fosters a growth mindset by understanding that negative thoughts are not fixed.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and learning styles. Students can choose names that resonate with their personal experiences. Educators can provide examples of names and descriptions to inspire students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' engagement and enthusiasm during the naming activity. Assess students' ability to articulate the difference between themselves and their negative voice. Review students' reflections on how naming the voice has impacted their self-perception.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that externalizing problems is an effective tool for promoting growth mindset. By distancing themselves from their negative thoughts, students can take back control and view those thoughts as separate.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students name their negative inner voice 'Adverse Antoine,' 'Ruthless Ralph,' or 'Cranky Kirsten.' Students share how naming their negative voice has changed their perception of their thoughts. Students use the name of their negative voice when practicing reframing negative self-talk.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Narrative advance organizers involve storytelling at the beginning of a lesson to engage students and relate to important concepts. Teachers tell an interesting story that relates to important concepts in the lesson.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Stories that relate to the learning material.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if story does not connect clearly to the lesson or if it is distracting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly effective for making connections to students' cultural & life experiences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before the advent of cheap electricity, schools often relied on natural lighting. As electric power costs declined, the amount of artificial light used in schools increased. Research has shown that artificial lighting has negative impacts on those in schools while natural lighting has positive impacts. In fact, research has shown that not only does classroom lighting boost the morale of teachers and students, appropriate amounts of natural lighting also reduces off-task behavior and improves test scores.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pair struggling learners ('tourists') with learners who have mastered the content ('navigators'). Empower navigators to teach a lesson or skill to tourists. Navigators ensure tourists understand directions, clarify confusion, and encourage them to stay on task. Tourists ask clarifying questions and collaborate with navigators to answer problems. This model fosters peer learning, strengthens communication skills, and supports academic mastery.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires identification of learners with mastery, careful pairing of learners, clear role definitions, and monitoring of group dynamics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure all learners are engaged and supported. Needs clear expectations to prevent misuse of power or off-task behavior. Requires ongoing feedback and guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for learners needing academic support and those who benefit from teaching others.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide peer support, strengthen communication skills, enhance academic mastery, foster collaboration, increase engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides academic support to struggling learners. Strengthens communication and leadership skills of advanced learners. Fosters peer learning and collaboration. Increases engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying roles, pairing learners with different needs, and providing specific tasks aligned to individual goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Peer Discussion
  • Articulation
  • Perspective-Taking
  • Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners’ engagement, participation, and teaching/learning skills within groups. Collect data from formative assessments, group projects, and peer evaluations. Track changes in performance following implementation of navigator-tourist learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Struggling learners receive targeted support, while advanced learners strengthen their understanding and develop communication skills.

docs.title: Needs and Wants Assessment with Likert Scales
Description
docs.text: Using Likert scales and fill-in questions to gauge student interest and understanding allows educators to inform their planning based on student needs. This allows students to see that they are being listened to and that the educators care about their opinions, as well as tailoring the educator's lesson plan to things that will be useful for the student.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful design of assessment questions. Educators must be willing to adapt instruction based on student feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Likert scales may not provide in-depth information about student interests and understanding. Requires careful analysis of student responses to identify patterns and trends.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify student interests and understanding, inform instructional planning, increase student engagement, provide personalized learning experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a quick and easy way to gather student feedback. Helps educators tailor instruction to meet student needs. Increases student engagement by making learning more relevant and personalized.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Assessments can be tailored to specific topics or units of study. Learners can express their unique interests and needs through the fill-in questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze student responses to identify areas of interest and understanding. Track student engagement and motivation levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that personalized learning can increase student achievement and engagement (Bray & McClaskey, 2013). When students feel that their needs are being met, they are more likely to be motivated to learn (Deci & Ryan, 2000).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses a Likert scale to assess student interest in different topics related to a unit of study. A teacher uses fill-in questions to gauge student understanding of key concepts. Resource: Edutopia - 5 Ways to Give Your Students More Voice and Choice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reducing exposure to blue light from digital screens before bed can improve sleep quality and quantity, which enhances learning by preventing disruptions to sleep patterns and storage processes. Strategies include limiting screen time before bed. American teens spend an average of nine hours per day using digital media, leading to concerns about sleep disruptions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of screen time habits and their impact on sleep. Commitment to reducing screen time before bed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential difficulty in reducing screen time due to dependence or necessity. May require alternative activities before bed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially adolescents and those who spend significant time using digital screens before bed.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve sleep quality and quantity, enhance learning, and prevent disruptions to sleep patterns.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Maximizes sleep’s benefit on learning by reducing sleep disruptions. Improves alertness and ability to learn the next day.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Varying screen time reduction based on individual needs and habits.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track sleep patterns, alertness levels, and academic outcomes. Monitor screen time habits before bed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reducing pre-bed screen time can effectively maximize sleep’s benefit on learning by improving sleep quality and quantity (Uncapher, 2016).
