docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using electronic tools to monitor classroom noise levels and provide auditory or visual signals when the noise becomes too loud. Examples include Super Sound Box, Class Dojo, and Too Noisy. These tools detect the noise level and produce a signal, such as a sound or visual indicator, when the threshold is exceeded. They provide real-time feedback on noise levels, helping students self-regulate their behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Electronic device (e.g., computer, tablet, smartphone), noise level monitoring software or app (e.g., Super Sound Box, Class Dojo, Too Noisy), and clear explanation of the tool and its purpose to students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become a distraction if not managed properly. Requires reliable technology and may not be accessible to all classrooms. Some students may become overly focused on the noise level, leading to anxiety or stress.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Monitor and manage classroom noise levels, provide real-time feedback to students, promote self-regulation of behavior, and create a quieter learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides objective, real-time feedback on noise levels, helping students become more aware of their behavior. Promotes self-regulation and encourages students to take responsibility for maintaining a quiet classroom.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Noise level thresholds can be adjusted to suit the specific needs and expectations of the classroom. Different types of auditory or visual signals can be used to provide feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency and duration of noise level alerts. Monitor the overall noise level in the classroom. Gather student feedback on the effectiveness of the tool.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-regulation: Real-time feedback on noise levels helps students become more aware of their behavior and take responsibility for maintaining a quiet classroom. Reduced noise levels: Monitoring tools can effectively reduce classroom noise, creating a more focused learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A middle school teacher uses Too Noisy to monitor the noise level during group work, providing students with immediate feedback when they become too loud. An elementary teacher uses Class Dojo to track and reward students for maintaining a quiet classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Noise monitoring tools are technological aids used to visually or audibly signal when noise levels in the classroom exceed an acceptable threshold. These tools, such as Super Sound Box, Class Dojo, or Too Noisy, provide real-time feedback on classroom noise, helping students self-regulate their volume. These tools can use visual displays (like a meter) or auditory signals to alert students when the noise level is too high. This approach encourages a sense of shared responsibility for maintaining an appropriate learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a noise monitoring tool (app or device) and a clear explanation of how it works. Consistency in using the tool and reinforcing appropriate noise levels is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be distracting if the feedback is too frequent or intrusive. Some students may become desensitized to the signals over time. Requires ongoing reinforcement and reminders.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early elementary to middle school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student awareness of noise levels, promote self-regulation of volume, create a quieter learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback, fosters self-awareness and self-regulation, encourages collective responsibility for classroom environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the sensitivity of the tool based on classroom needs and student abilities. Use different types of visual or auditory feedback to suit student preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency of alerts from the noise monitoring tool. Observe the overall noise level in the classroom before and after implementing the tool. Collect student feedback on their awareness of and ability to manage noise levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved classroom management: Reduces noise levels and promotes a calmer learning environment. Increased student self-regulation: Helps students develop the ability to monitor and manage their volume. Fosters shared responsibility: Encourages students to work together to maintain an appropriate learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A second-grade teacher uses the 'Too Noisy' app on a tablet. The app displays a visual meter that indicates the noise level in the classroom. When the meter reaches a certain threshold, the app emits a gentle chime, signaling students to lower their voices.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encourage pre-teens and teenagers who dislike organized sports to explore non-competitive physical activities. This could include activities like skipping, swimming, going to the gym, online workouts, or community activities like youth clubs, Scouts, or Girl Guides. Emphasize skill-building and confidence to encourage sustained participation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of non-competitive activities, resources and facilities, support from family and friends.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require exploration to find suitable activities. Needs encouragement and support to overcome initial hesitation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-teens and teenagers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase physical activity, build confidence, promote enjoyment of exercise

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides alternative options for physical activity, builds confidence and skills, promotes a positive attitude towards exercise.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be chosen based on individual interests and preferences. Progress can be tracked at an individual pace.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Tracking of participation rates, self-reported enjoyment and confidence, observation of skill development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased physical activity: Provides accessible and enjoyable alternatives to organized sports. Improved attitudes: Promotes a positive attitude towards exercise and physical activity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Non-confrontational check-ins involve engaging students in informal, positive interactions before they enter the classroom to socialize them into productive behaviors. This can be done by using "nonconfrontational statements" and "informal chitchat" at the door to address potential issues proactively. This approach helps to set a positive tone for the lesson and prevent disruptive behaviors before they start. By connecting with students individually and addressing any concerns or issues before they enter the classroom, teachers can create a more positive and focused learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be proactive and engaged at the classroom door. Teachers need to be able to build rapport with students and address issues in a non-confrontational manner.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming, especially with larger classes. Requires teachers to be skilled in building relationships and addressing issues proactively. Some students may be resistant to this approach.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school students and above

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student behavior, create a positive classroom environment, build relationships with students, proactively address potential issues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Sets a positive tone for the lesson, prevents disruptive behaviors before they start, builds relationships with students, addresses potential issues proactively

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor the check-in to the individual student, addressing their specific needs and concerns. Use different conversation starters to suit different students and situations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student behavior and engagement in the classroom. Track the number of disruptions and disciplinary actions. Collect student feedback on their relationships with teachers and the classroom environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced classroom management: Prevents disruptive behaviors and creates a more positive learning environment. Improved student-teacher relationships: Builds rapport and trust between students and teachers. Increased student engagement: Sets a positive tone for the lesson and encourages student participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • As students enter the classroom, a middle school teacher greets each one by name and asks a simple question, such as 'How was your lunch?' or 'Are you ready for today's lesson?' If a student seems upset, the teacher might say, 'Is everything okay? You seem a little down today.' This approach helps to build a connection with students and address any potential issues before they disrupt the class.

docs.title: Non-intensive Home Numeracy Environment (HNE) Intervention Program
Description
docs.text: Teachers can provide families information and suggestions for providing students more math exploration and play in their homes. They can also facilitate access to math games and manipulatives by allowing students to take home classroom materials. The goal is to encourage more frequent, personalized practice of math skills at home.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to math games and manipulatives, information about math exploration and play, communication between teachers and families

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires family participation and support. May not be effective if families are not able to provide a supportive home numeracy environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages, families, teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement with math, improve arithmetic fact retrieval, strengthen home-school connection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical support to families. Supports personalized learning and arithmetic fact retrieval at home. Increases access to math games and manipulatives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Recommendations and resources can be tailored to the student's grade level and the family's needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement with math at school and at home. Monitor improvements in arithmetic fact retrieval skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that parent involvement in math education can lead to increased student achievement. Provides an additional avenue to strengthen math skills outside of the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Catching students at the door before they enter the classroom and using “nonconfrontational statements” and “informal chitchat” to socialize them into productive behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be present at the door and actively engage with students. Training on effective communication and behavior management techniques is beneficial.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming and require a significant commitment from the teacher. Some students may resist or be uncomfortable with this approach.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote positive behaviors and a calm transition into the classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a positive and welcoming environment. Allows for early intervention and correction of potential behavior issues before they escalate. Fosters a sense of community and belonging.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor their conversations to individual student needs and interests. Focus on building relationships and addressing specific concerns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior upon entering the classroom. Track the frequency of positive interactions and the reduction of disruptive behaviors.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a positive and welcoming classroom environment. Allows for early behavior intervention and fosters a sense of community.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Normalizing struggle involves creating a classroom culture where challenges and failures are viewed as opportunities for growth. This approach helps students accept difficulties as a natural part of the learning process, encouraging them to persevere and develop resilience. Teachers share personal problem-solving experiences and highlight how students worked through challenges to promote independence and productivity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A supportive classroom environment, opportunities for students to encounter and work through challenges, and strategies to help students reflect on their problem-solving processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset for both students and teachers to view struggles positively. Students may initially resist embracing challenges or feel discouraged by failures.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and learning levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote resilience, encourage perseverance, foster a growth mindset, reduce fear of failure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop a positive attitude toward challenges, encourages them to view failures as learning opportunities, and builds a supportive classroom environment where students feel safe taking risks.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adjust the complexity of problems and challenges based on students' skill levels and learning needs. They can also provide personalized coaching and support to help students navigate difficulties.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' responses to challenges, their willingness to try new strategies, and their ability to articulate their problem-solving processes. Measure students' resilience and perseverance in the face of difficulties.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that normalizing struggle leads to increased resilience, perseverance, and a growth mindset among students. It also fosters a more supportive and collaborative classroom environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher shares a video of a broken escalator to illustrate how people often give up when faced with a challenge. Students work on a math problem that will make them feel 'stuck' and then reflect on how they got 'unstuck.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Normalizing struggle involves acknowledging that challenges and failures are a natural part of the learning process and a sign of growth. It shifts the mindset from viewing difficulties as negative to recognizing them as opportunities for improvement. The goal is for learners to accept challenges and failures as a chance to grow and do better. This approach encourages a Learner Mindset by reducing the fear of making mistakes and promoting resilience in the face of setbacks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a supportive classroom environment, explicit communication about the value of struggle, and opportunities for learners to reflect on their learning process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a significant shift in mindset for both learners and educators. Requires ongoing effort to reinforce the message that mistakes are a natural part of learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who may be discouraged by setbacks or have a fixed mindset about their abilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a growth mindset, reduce fear of failure, promote resilience, and encourage learners to view challenges as opportunities for growth.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe and supportive learning environment, reduces anxiety and stress, promotes risk-taking and experimentation, and fosters a positive attitude towards learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different learning contexts and content areas. Can be tailored to individual learner needs by providing personalized feedback and encouragement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' responses to challenges and setbacks, track their progress in overcoming difficulties, and gather feedback on their attitudes towards learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that normalizing struggle can lead to increased motivation, improved academic performance, and greater resilience in the face of adversity. (Peter H. Johnston's work on normalizing struggle)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An educator shares personal struggles and highlights how students worked through problems, emphasizing that teachers are there to support, not solve, problems for learners. Showing the broken escalator video to illustrate how people often give up instead of trying new ways to work through problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a classroom culture where challenges and failures are seen as opportunities for growth and learning. This involves acknowledging struggles, encouraging students to embrace challenges, and emphasizing that problem-solving skills are explicitly taught and transferable across settings. Reframing mistakes and struggles as essential parts of the learning process helps students develop resilience and a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom environment that values effort and growth, explicit instruction in problem-solving strategies, and opportunities for students to reflect on their processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset for both teachers and students. May take time to establish a classroom culture where students feel safe sharing their struggles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, K-12 and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote resilience, develop problem-solving skills, and foster a growth mindset by normalizing challenges and failures.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to embrace challenges, reduces fear of failure, and supports the development of metacognitive skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Providing individualized coaching and support as students work through problems. Adjusting language and activities to normalize trouble and encourage students to persevere.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student persistence in the face of challenges, improved problem-solving skills, and positive attitudes towards failure.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that metacognitive skills help students become better problem solvers. Normalizing struggle helps students accept challenges and view failure as a chance to grow.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Sharing problems and highlighting how students worked through them, showing videos of people getting 'stuck' and encouraging students to find ways to get 'unstuck,' and using language prompts to help students name their problem-solving processes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Note-taking/note-making involves students taking notes on key points from a lesson and then making notes by writing their own reflections, reactions, and personal connections to the material. This strategy encourages active engagement with the content and helps learners integrate new concepts with existing knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured guidance for note-taking, time for reflection and note-making, and a format for recording both types of notes (e.g., divided paper, digital document).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires clear guidance on note-taking and sufficient time for thoughtful reflection. Effectiveness depends on learners' ability to make meaningful connections.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Extend understanding of concepts, encourage reflection, foster connections between new and previously learned material, and promote personal engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages connections between new and previously learned material, promotes personal engagement, and supports deeper understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can focus on aspects of the lesson that resonate with them, making personal connections and reflecting on their own understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Note-taking
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review both the notes taken and the reflections made to assess understanding and personal connections. Look for evidence of critical thinking and integration of concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages meaningful connections, promotes deeper understanding, and fosters personal engagement with the material.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fifth-grade teacher asked students to define integers and construct number lines on one side of their paper, and then write their reactions and observations on the other side. One student noted the inverse relationship of negative numbers, connecting it to a piano scale.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use graphic organizers to take notes on their reading, research, films, or podcasts, visually structuring information and relationships between concepts to enhance comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizers, learning materials (e.g., readings, videos), and instructor modeling.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require explicit instruction on how to use different types of organizers effectively. Avoid complete sentences to maximize efficiency.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for complex or dense material.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension and retention by visually organizing information and showing relationships between concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves focus and organization, supports dual coding by combining visual and verbal information, and facilitates review and recall.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can provide pre-designed organizers or allow students to create their own. Adaptable for different content areas and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality and completeness of notes, ability to summarize and synthesize information, and performance on related assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Decades of research show that incorporating graphic organizers into instruction improves student learning. Teacher-created organizers can be more effective than student-generated ones.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Novelty attention-getters use unique and unexpected stimuli to capture young students' attention and quiet the classroom. Examples include using wind chimes, rain sticks, imaginary actions like "popping a marshmallow," or creating a "quiet spray" with a Windex bottle filled with lavender mineral oil. The use of unusual or imaginative tools can interrupt disruptive behavior and regain focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Availability of novelty items, clear explanation of expectations, consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lose effectiveness if overused, some students may be overstimulated by novelty items, requires creativity and adaptability.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early elementary educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Capture students' attention, reduce classroom noise, encourage imaginative thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Quickly captures attention, engages students' imagination, provides a break from traditional classroom routines.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Novelty items can be tailored to specific themes, subject areas, or student interests. Visual or tactile elements can be added for additional engagement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly students respond to the novelty item. Monitor classroom noise levels before and after using the attention-getter.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using novelty attention-getters can effectively capture young students' attention and reduce disruptions by providing an engaging and unexpected stimulus.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using novel sounds such as wind chimes or rain sticks captures young students’ attention. Puffing up cheeks and having students follow suit as if they are popping a marshmallow in their mouths can also quiet a class. Filling an empty Windex bottle with lavender mineral oil and labeling it "Quiet Spray,” or blowing magic “hush-bubbles” for a similar impact, can also be effective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to novelty items such as wind chimes, rain sticks, empty spray bottles, lavender mineral oil, and bubble solution. Minimal preparation time is needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The novelty may wear off over time, requiring teachers to introduce new sounds or methods periodically. This technique may not be as effective with older students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Capture students' attention and quickly quiet a classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a quick and engaging way to quiet young students using imaginative and auditory stimuli. This approach is non-intrusive and can be easily implemented with readily available materials.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The types of sounds and novelty items can be tailored to student interests and classroom themes. Teachers can rotate the novelty sounds to maintain effectiveness.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how quickly and effectively students respond to the novelty sounds. Note any resistance or waning interest over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Quick and engaging method to capture young students' attention and quiet a classroom. Easy to implement and requires minimal resources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Helps kids learn to use numbers and master them in a visual way, offering moveable, colored beads. Encourages learners to group and sort and, in the process, learn addition and subtraction. An engaging math app ideal for kids at the elementary level, offering learning modules for different skill levels and comes packed with text tools for writing equations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Number Rack app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to addition and subtraction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Kids at the elementary level.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Learn to use numbers and master them visually, focusing on addition and subtraction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual representation with colored beads and learning modules for different skill levels.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learning modules for different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor performance in visual grouping and sorting exercises.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Offers a visual way to learn addition and subtraction using interactive colored beads.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Grouping and sorting colored beads to learn addition and subtraction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Basic facts should be taught using number relationships and reasoning strategies, not memorization. Learners who learn fact strategies outperform learners who learn through other approaches. Basic fact strategies use number relationships and benchmarks and thus support learners, emerging conceptual understanding and flexibility. Strategies such as Making 10 build a foundation for strategies beyond basic facts, such as Make-a-Whole with fractions and decimals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Demands thorough preparation, creative instructional strategies, and access to resources that effectively illustrate number relationships and reasoning strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Instruction can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. May not be suitable for topics with limited real-world applications.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develops conceptual understanding, improves numerical reasoning, promotes strategic thinking, minimizes reliance on memorization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding, aids retention, and promotes flexible application of knowledge. Learners are better equipped to solve complex problems and adapt to new situations when they grasp the underlying concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt by using familiar analogies and real-world examples to suit individual Background Knowledge. Vary examples to include diverse cultural contexts and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluates learners’ ability to articulate number relationships and reasoning strategies through explanations, applications, and problem-solving tasks. Assesses learners’ strategic flexibility and conceptual understanding using multiple-choice questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances understanding, aids retention, minimizes rote memorization, and promotes flexible application of knowledge. Learners are better equipped to solve complex problems and adapt to new situations when they grasp the underlying concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Strategies such as Making 10 build a foundation for strategies beyond basic facts, such as Make-a-Whole with fractions and decimals.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Number Talks are short, daily classroom routines that provide students with opportunities to mentally solve and discuss numerical problems. The teacher poses a problem, and students share their different strategies, promoting mental math skills, number sense, and conceptual understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher preparation of appropriate problems, facilitation of discussions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require some initial training for teachers to implement effectively

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop mental math skills, promote number sense, enhance conceptual understanding, improve communication of mathematical thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances mental math skills, promotes conceptual understanding, encourages flexible thinking, improves communication skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Problems can be tailored to different skill levels, and students can choose which strategies to use

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the variety and sophistication of student strategies, assess student explanations of their thinking

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of number talks for developing number sense and mathematical understanding (Humphreys & Parker, in press; Parish, 2014)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher poses 18 x 5 and students solve the problem in these different ways (10 x 5 + 8 x 5, 20 x 5 - 2 x 5, 9 x 10).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A game where learners find numbers in sequential order on road signs, license plates, and maps to reinforce number recognition and ordering skills. Adjusting the target range (e.g., 1 to 20 or 1 to 200) adapts the difficulty to suit different age groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Road signs, license plates, maps, or other real-world number displays.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on availability of numbers in the environment. May become repetitive if played for too long without variation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students, adaptable for younger and older children by adjusting the number range

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce number recognition, sequencing, and ordering skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces number recognition and ordering in a real-world context. Adaptable to various skill levels by adjusting the number range.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the number range to suit different age groups and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to identify numbers in sequence. Track the number of correct identifications made within a given time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reinforces children’s understanding of basic math concepts and is a good way to prevent the summer slide.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Monitoring student learning through observations and conversations helps determine understanding of concepts and problem-solving abilities. Instructors can ask key questions to gauge understanding, observe student interactions, and document progress through anecdotal notes. Listening in on student dialogue allows the instructor to hear how learners are engaging with one another and what their problem-solving process is like.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires skilled instructors who can effectively observe and question students. Instructors must be able to take detailed notes and synthesize information quickly to inform instruction. Time is needed for observation and reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be subjective and influenced by instructor bias. May not provide a comprehensive measure of all learning outcomes. Time-consuming to implement effectively, especially in large classes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners. Particularly useful in hands-on, exploratory learning environments such as STEM and STEAM.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Measure student growth, assess conceptual understanding, evaluate problem-solving processes, gather qualitative data

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time insights into student learning, allows for immediate feedback and instructional adjustments, and captures qualitative data on student thinking and collaboration. Enables instructors to assess skills not easily measured by traditional tests.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Observations and conversations can be tailored to individual learners by focusing on their specific strengths, weaknesses, and learning styles. Open-ended questions can be adapted to different levels of understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Collect anecdotal notes on student understanding and problem-solving processes. Analyze responses to key questions to assess conceptual understanding. Track changes in student performance based on observational data.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced learning: Frequent observation and conversation helps learners to retain information and instructors make timely instructional adjustments. Increased engagement: Studies indicate regular monitoring of student engagement improves learners’ self-regulation strategies.

docs.title: Offer Services and Events to Bring Parents into the School
Description
docs.text: Offer free classes and workshops that focus on topics of interest to parents, such as family nutrition, child development, or homework help. Welcoming families with resources and support can help break down negative preconceived notions about school and build a community of hope and trust.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space, resources, and speakers for workshops and classes

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to find topics that appeal to all parents, requires effort to organize and promote events

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, educators, and community partners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase parent involvement, provide resources, build community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides valuable resources, builds community, breaks down barriers to participation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Workshops and classes can be tailored to meet the specific needs and interests of the community.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track attendance at events, gather feedback from parents

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing services and events can create a welcoming environment and increase parent involvement.

docs.title: Offering Multiple Options for Family Engagement
Description
docs.text: Providing a variety of options will improve overall participation, particularly for families with significant barriers to engagement. This includes school-based involvement options, home visits, materials to guide families in supporting children’s learning at home, and technology. Connect family members for peer-to-peer support and partner with local organizations to offer family members ways to learn skills needed to become leaders in schools and the local community.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Multiple engagement options, resources for home visits, technology, and partnerships with local organizations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and coordination to manage multiple engagement options. Success depends on family participation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, teachers, families

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase family engagement by providing diverse and accessible opportunities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses barriers to engagement by offering flexible options. Fosters peer-to-peer support among families and leadership development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Options can be tailored to the specific needs and preferences of families within the school community.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track family participation rates, evaluate the effectiveness of different engagement options, and monitor family-school partnerships.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that offering diverse engagement options improves overall participation and outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: On-the-job training (OJT) involves designing experiential activities for groups of trainees, based at the actual location where they will be working. OJT exposes staff to 'business as usual' situations - real customers, peers, supervisors, real products, and services - that they will continue to deal with once training is completed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A real work environment, real customers, peers, supervisors, real products, and services, facilitator to guide the learning process

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on the availability of real-world opportunities and the quality of the facilitator.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • New employees or employees transitioning to new roles

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expose staff to 'business as usual' situations, teach how to deal with real customers, peers, supervisors, real products, and services.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-world experience, teaches how to deal with real customers, peers, supervisors, real products, and services.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to reflect the learner's own working environment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Observation/Shadowing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner performance in real-world situations, provide feedback on learner performance, and assess learner understanding of the situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Exposes staff to 'business as usual' situations that they will continue to deal with once training is completed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One-on-one conferences involve providing individualized feedback to a learner in a private setting. This approach allows for personalized attention, facilitates open communication, and provides an opportunity for the learner to ask questions. One-on-one conferences should be generally optimistic, as this will encourage the student to look forward to the next meeting.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time and space for private meetings, strong communication skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires good time management

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide personalized feedback, foster open communication, encourage self-reflection, build positive relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for individualized attention, promotes a safe and supportive environment, facilitates in-depth discussion

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The conference can be tailored to the individual learner's needs, preferences, and learning style.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance and attitude. Track learner progress. Analyze the effectiveness of the conference.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students benefit from the attention and allows the opportunity to ask necessary questions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher holds a one-on-one conference with a student to discuss their progress in math. A mentor holds a one-on-one meeting with a mentee to discuss their career goals.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When instructors ask a question, rather than having students raise hands, every learner writes a sentence to answer the question. This ensures that all learners actively engage with the question and encourages writing about math. The sentences allow learners to articulate their ideas in a clear and succinct manner, fostering active participation and engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A specific question, time for writing, and a method for collecting responses (e.g., paper, digital platform).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not allow for in-depth exploration of concepts, requires clear and focused questions, and may require additional discussion to address misconceptions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage active participation, provide practice in writing about math, and promote clarity in articulating ideas.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures all learners are active, provides a low-pressure writing activity, and promotes succinct communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can respond based on their individual understanding and perspectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Response
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the clarity and accuracy of the sentences. Look for evidence of understanding and critical thinking.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages active engagement and provides practice in writing about mathematical ideas.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When asking about a mathematical concept, have every student write a one-sentence response rather than just calling on volunteers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ongoing feedback involves providing feedback at various stages of the writing process rather than only on final products. This can be achieved by focusing feedback on specific sections or stages of writing. Students can also proactively seek feedback using digital tools like Google Docs or Kaizena. Stations with self-guiding questions can help students progress at their own pace while teachers address small groups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to allocate time for feedback at multiple points during the writing process. Digital tools and self-guiding stations can help manage time.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time constraints can be a significant challenge. Requires careful planning to ensure feedback is manageable and effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students at all levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student writing by providing continuous guidance and support throughout the writing process.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for iterative improvement and prevents students from making the same mistakes throughout the writing process. Facilitates a deeper understanding of writing concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can focus on different aspects of writing at different stages, tailoring feedback to the specific needs of the assignment or student.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the frequency and timeliness of feedback provided. Monitor student progress at different stages of the writing process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Ongoing feedback helps students improve their writing skills iteratively, building a deeper understanding of writing concepts and leading to better final products.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning management systems (LMS) such as Google Classroom, Canvas, and Schoology allow teachers to conduct formative and summative assessments during PBL. Using tools like Google Slides and Adobe Spark to share work or Microsoft’s Flipgrid to engage students in weekly reflections encourages students to give each other constructive feedback and share their wins, challenges, and next steps.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to LMS and assessment tools, commitment to providing regular feedback, guidance on constructive criticism, reliable means to create a safe space for discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming for both teachers and students, potential for negative feedback, requires effective facilitation and clear protocols.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels engaging in remote or hybrid learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learning through timely assessment, foster self-reflection, encourage constructive feedback, promote student engagement.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables regular formative assessment, promotes self-reflection and metacognition, encourages constructive feedback from peers, provides diverse formats for sharing work.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored for specific needs and learning styles, various tools offer diverse modes of reflection and sharing, assignments can be adapted according to a particular group's knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Formative Assessment
  • Summative Assessment
  • Peer Feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Video-Based Reflection
  • Learning Management Systems

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of student reflection and feedback, improvement in student performance, engagement in assessment activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Ongoing feedback and reflection improve learning, promote self-awareness, and foster a positive learning environment (Castelo, 2020).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using online videos to make it easier for families with different language needs to explore and learn together. Hispanic-Latino families have reported using YouTube to learn everything from recipes and hairstyles to English lessons, and some used it to follow up on academic topics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to internet and devices to watch videos. Selection of relevant, high-quality videos.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require digital literacy skills. Not all families have access to reliable internet or devices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Families with diverse language needs, Hispanic-Latino families

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate family learning, accommodate language differences, provide accessible resources

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual learning, language accessibility, wide range of topics, flexibility in learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Families can choose videos that align with their interests and language preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track video views and engagement. Gather feedback from families on the usefulness of the videos.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Families report using online videos for a variety of learning purposes, from practical skills to academic support.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An open classroom climate is a learning environment where students feel safe to discuss social and political issues and express their opinions freely without judgment. Teachers play a crucial role in fostering this environment by encouraging students to develop and express their own opinions, and by presenting different views on topics. This approach focuses on fostering critical thinking skills, including analysis, evaluation, and reasoning, while teaching students to consider multiple perspectives and engage in respectful dialogue.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a classroom setting, a willingness from the teacher to facilitate open discussions, and the establishment of clear ground rules for respectful communication. May also require access to resources that present diverse perspectives on social and political issues.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for sensitive or controversial topics to create discomfort or conflict. Requires careful facilitation to prevent discussions from becoming unproductive or disrespectful. Teachers must be prepared to address misinformation and bias.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school students, but adaptable to higher education and adult learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance civic knowledge, promote interest in social issues, encourage critical thinking, foster respectful dialogue, and develop a sense of civic responsibility.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves civic engagement, promotes critical consciousness, and enhances understanding of diverse perspectives. It creates a space where students feel heard and respected, fostering a sense of community and shared learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various topics and age groups. Strategies can be tailored to meet specific classroom dynamics and student needs. Teachers can adjust the level of structure and guidance based on student maturity and comfort levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student participation and engagement in discussions, assess the quality of their arguments and reasoning, and evaluate their ability to consider diverse perspectives. Journal entries and written reflections can provide insights into student learning and attitude shifts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research from the International Civic and Citizenship Study (ICCS) 2016 shows that students' perceptions of classroom openness in classroom discussion are positively associated with their civic knowledge and interest in issues. Open classroom climate enables students to improve «a sense of themselves as members of a political community and as effective civic actors in that community, developing a sense of efficacy because proximate authorities listen and pay attention to them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Friendly message from teacher to foster open, comfortable communication systems and mutual respect, and when helping students succeed becomes a group effort, academics and attitudes improve.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Easy and convenient means to communicate with students and families

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Parent must respond to teacher and family to have open communication

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teacher

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a positive feedback loop between school and home

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improved student outcomes and better relationships between families and schools

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teacher can tailor messages to individual students and families

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track response rates

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Early communication can set the stage for a positive and collaborative relationship between school and home.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provides a very easy way to learn and practice math with a very easy-to-understand user interface, with everything clearly explained and accessible. The app also comes with a very user-friendly in-app support for the learners. Operation Math is unique because it creates an engaging game-like interface with 105 timed missions allowing kids to learn and practice all mathematical actions including addition, subtraction, division and multiplication. Ideally targeted for ages 9-11, it offers a fun-filled way of engaging with numbers and calculations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Operation Math app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Timed missions may stress some students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Ages 9-11.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Learn and practice all mathematical actions including addition, subtraction, division and multiplication.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging game-like interface with 105 timed missions, user-friendly support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Timed missions that pace the mathematical abilities of the student.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess proficiency in completing mathematical missions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engages with numbers and calculations in a fun and easy way.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Practicing addition, subtraction, division, and multiplication through timed missions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Organizing the classroom layout to match the flow of the day, such as moving from reading to math centers, can enhance efficiency. Clearly organized centers for math, reading, and writing, with good line of sight, support effective learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly defined learning centers, organized materials, good line of sight.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and organization. May require adjustments to adapt to changing student needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly primary students and those who benefit from structured routines.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance classroom efficiency, support student transitions, improve organization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Streamlines transitions between activities, promotes organization, improves classroom efficiency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Organize centers based on student needs and learning goals. Provide clear visual cues to guide student movement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student transitions and behavior in different learning centers. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of the classroom layout.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can enhance classroom efficiency, support student transitions, and improve overall organization through optimal student flow.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reducing noise levels in classrooms can greatly affect teacher and student performance. Schools should be designed to buffer external noise from classrooms. The use of noise-dampening materials can mitigate internal sounds. Building classrooms with less external noise is positively associated with greater student engagement and achievement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Noise-dampening materials, building design considerations, noise monitoring equipment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be costly to implement noise reduction measures in existing buildings. Some level of background noise may be necessary for social interaction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners and educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student engagement, reduce stress, increase academic performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, enhances concentration, supports effective communication, creates a more comfortable and conducive learning environment. Improves teacher satisfaction and reduces stress.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow teachers to choose from a variety of noise-canceling options. Use personalized sound systems for individuals who are hard of hearing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track noise levels in classrooms and correlate with student engagement and achievement. Monitor teacher satisfaction and stress levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that schools with classrooms that have less external noise are positively associated with greater student engagement and achievement compared to schools with classrooms that have noisier environments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A study has shown that excessive noise causes dis-satisfaction and stress in both teachers and students.

docs.title: Optimize Classroom Acoustics and Noise Levels
Description
docs.text: Classroom noise levels significantly impact teacher and student performance. Excessive noise leads to dissatisfaction and stress. Schools with classrooms that have less external noise are positively associated with greater student engagement and achievement. Building schools or modifying classrooms to buffer external noise can improve student outcomes. Minimizing noise creates a more conducive learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Acoustic materials, soundproofing, strategic classroom layout, noise-canceling headphones (optional)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly. Effectiveness may vary based on the type and source of noise.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, teachers, and administrators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student engagement, reduce stress, and enhance academic achievement by minimizing classroom noise

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, improves focus and concentration, decreases stress levels, and enhances overall learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use soundproofing materials, rearrange classroom layout to minimize noise, provide noise-canceling headphones for students who need them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.text: Pairing learners with peers who demonstrate strong relationship skills involves intentionally matching learners who may face challenges in social interactions with those who exhibit positive behaviors such as effective communication, empathy, and conflict resolution. This strategy allows the learner to observe and learn from their peer's behavior in real-time, fostering their own skills in building and maintaining positive relationships. Positive role models can demonstrate appropriate social cues, model effective problem-solving during conflicts, and encourage inclusive behavior, thereby influencing the learner's social development.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection of role models who exhibit positive social skills and are willing to provide support. Structured activities or projects that encourage interaction and collaboration between the pair. Regular monitoring and feedback to ensure the pairing is beneficial and effective.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness of the pairing depends on the compatibility of the learners and the willingness of the role model to provide support. There is a risk that the learner may become overly reliant on the role model or that the pairing may not address underlying issues contributing to social challenges.

docs.title: Personalization

Over time, the learner becomes more confident in initiating conversations and building relationships with others.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Partner reading is a cooperative learning strategy in which two learners work together to read an assigned text. Learners take turns reading and provide each other with feedback in order to monitor comprehension. This strategy is often used as part of Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS). PALS is a class-wide peer tutoring program in which teachers carefully partner a learner with a classmate. The partner reading strategy allows learners to take turns reading and provide each other with feedback as a way to monitor comprehension. When either partner makes an error while reading, the other will say, “The word is ___. What’s the word?” The reader will repeat back the correct word. Then, the partner will say, “Now reread.” and the reader will go back to the beginning of the sentence, this time reading without error.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Mixed-ability partner pairs, assigned reading texts, and an understanding of partner reading procedures. Ensure Partner A is the stronger reader and Partner B is the one more in need of the practice, but do not tell students this logic behind the pairings. Students need only to know whether they are Partner A or B.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The feedback can discourage effort and achievement if mostly negative. So, it is important to ensure the tools and protocols used promote feedback that is actionable, timely, focused, proactive, clear, and personalized to promote a growth mindset.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers may include story retelling, summarization, or writing activities for varying skill levels. English Learners can be paired with fluent students for language development. Partner reading can be done with cross age/grade partners.

Put Reading First: The Research Building Blocks for Teaching Children to Read.

docs.text: Pattern recognition is a cognitive process where the brain identifies recurring structures, relationships, or sequences to assign meaning and enhance memory. By organizing information into contextual, event-oriented situations that include motor learning, location changes, music, rhythm, and novelty, learners can maximize their ability to remember and apply new knowledge.
