docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recognize and apply patterns in new situations, assess their understanding of the underlying concepts, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes that require pattern recognition

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Pattern recognition has been shown to enhance memory recall, improve understanding of complex concepts, and promote critical thinking skills. It leverages the brain's natural tendency to seek patterns and make connections.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using music and rhyming to create a pattern for remembering information, creating a mnemonic to aid in memory, associating new concepts with familiar locations or events.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The pause procedure is one of the simplest supplements to an otherwise unchanged lecture: pause for about two minutes every 12-18 minutes and have students discuss and rework their notes in pairs. The pause gives students a moment to consider their actual understanding of the material just covered, including how it's organized, and creates a natural opportunity for questions and clarification before the lecture continues. Despite requiring no redesign of the lecture content itself, this simple interruption has been shown to significantly increase learning compared to an uninterrupted lecture covering the same material (Bonwell & Eison, 1991; Rowe, 1980, 1986; Ruhl, Hughes, & Schloss, 1980).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A lecture segment long enough (12-18 minutes) to warrant a natural break
  • Willingness to pause mid-lecture on a schedule, rather than only at natural topic boundaries

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The pause needs to be long enough (about two minutes) for genuine pair discussion and note-reworking, not just a token break

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in any lecture-format course, since the strategy requires no change to lecture content and can be layered onto an existing course with minimal preparation

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Improved retention and organization of lecture content
  • Early surfacing of confusion or questions, before they compound across a long uninterrupted lecture

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Plan lecture segments of roughly 12-18 minutes.
  2. At the end of each segment, pause for about two minutes.
  3. Have students discuss the material just covered in pairs and rework or clarify their notes.
  4. Invite questions arising from the pair discussion before resuming the lecture.
  5. Repeat for each subsequent segment.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Think-Pair-Share (Turn & Talk)

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bonwell, C. C., & Eison, J. A. (1991). Active learning: Creating excitement in the classroom (ASHE-ERIC Higher Education Report No. 1). George Washington University, School of Education and Human Development.
  • Rowe, M. B. (1980). Pausing principles and their effects on reasoning in science. New Directions for Community Colleges, 1980(31), 27-34.
  • Rowe, M. B. (1986). Wait time: Slowing down may be a way of speeding up! Journal of Teacher Education, 37(1), 43-50.
  • Ruhl, K. L., Hughes, C. A., & Schloss, P. J. (1980). Using the pause procedure to enhance lecture recall. Teacher Education and Special Education, 10(3), 14-18.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Active learning. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pay Attention, Pause, Paraphrase is a structured conversation strategy for small groups or pairs to promote active listening. Learners are assigned numbers, and only one learner speaks at a time. Others listen without formulating a response, focusing solely on understanding. After the speaker finishes, the listener pauses to paraphrase what was said before offering their own thoughts. Discussion sentence starters can support learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Small group settings, clear instructions, discussion sentence starters

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure equal participation, may feel unnatural at first

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially useful for developing communication skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate active listening, encourage thoughtful responses, promote clear communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances listening skills, promotes thoughtful responses, encourages clear communication

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt discussion sentence starters to match learners' language skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately paraphrase their peers' statements, track the quality of their responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of structured conversation in promoting active listening and thoughtful communication. Practitioner experience shows that Pay Attention, Pause, Paraphrase fosters a deeper understanding of peers' perspectives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor modeling the strategy with a learner, use of adult visitors to partner with the instructor. Resource: Rebecca Alber, Edutopia

docs.title: Description
docs.text: PALS is a structured peer tutoring approach that involves pairing learners to work together on academic activities. In PALS, learners take turns being the reader and coach, and as the reader reads a text aloud, the coach records errors and prompts any miscues during reading. After reading, learners retell information to one another using structured prompts to promote comprehension. PALS often incorporates activities such as partner reading, paragraph shrinking, and prediction relays. The instructor monitors learner interactions and provides feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriately leveled texts, structured prompts, teacher training, classroom time (approximately 35 minutes per session), and monitoring by the instructor.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the instructor's ability to pair learners appropriately and provide adequate training and support. Some learners may dominate the activity while others may be passive. Requires careful monitoring to ensure that learners are providing accurate feedback and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 2–6

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase reading fluency, improve reading comprehension, build summarizing skills, develop peer support, enhance social skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured peer interaction, promotes active learning, allows for immediate feedback from peers, encourages learners to take responsibility for their own and their partner's learning, and increases Motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Texts can be leveled to match learner reading abilities. Activity roles can be assigned based on individual needs. Structured prompts can be modified to target specific comprehension skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Teaching
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reading fluency (words correct per minute), comprehension scores, quality of summaries and retellings, observation of learner interactions, and feedback from learners on their experience with PALS.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of PALS in improving reading fluency and comprehension for learners in grades 2–6. Studies have shown that PALS can be particularly beneficial for learners with learning disabilities and English language learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Partner Reading with Retell: Learners take turns reading aloud and summarizing the text. Paragraph Shrinking: Learners identify the main idea of each paragraph. Prediction Relay: Learners make predictions about what will happen next in the text.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer review involves students providing feedback on each other's work to foster a collaborative learning environment, increase motivation, and develop a growth mindset. It allows students to give and receive constructive criticism, enhancing their understanding of writing concepts and improving their ability to evaluate and revise their own work. Specific action-oriented writing suggestions can help move writers forward.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear guidelines for providing constructive feedback, structured activities, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and facilitation to ensure feedback is constructive and not discouraging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students learning writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical thinking skills, improve writing skills, foster collaboration, and promote a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances understanding of writing concepts, improves evaluation and revision skills, fosters collaboration, and increases motivation through social interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to focus on specific writing skills or elements, allowing students to provide targeted feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved quality of student writing, increased student engagement, and positive changes in student attitudes towards writing and feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates peer feedback can significantly improve writing skills by providing multiple perspectives and reinforcing learning through teaching.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer and self-assessment give students the opportunity to review their work against a set of criteria. Students can engage in discussion about mastery of skills. These assessments are tools for student self-advocacy because they aren’t reliant on the instructor and allow students to evaluate themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Rubric, checklist, or success criteria; time for assessment and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for some students to provide constructive feedback. Requires clear criteria and guidelines.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly in elementary and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-evaluation skills, promote self-advocacy, encourage discussion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-awareness, promotes independence, encourages peer interaction

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and age groups. Criteria can be tailored to specific learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved self-awareness, increased self-advocacy, positive peer interactions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students develop self-evaluation skills and become more independent learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Having students use a rubric to evaluate their own writing. Engaging students in peer review activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer coaching is a reciprocal helping relationship between equals who support each other's learning through mutual trust and open discussion. Participants alternate between coach and client roles, sharing experiences, offering feedback, and holding each other accountable. Peer coaching fosters a strong support system, strengthens cross-functional networks, enhances leadership skills, and helps broaden understanding of organizational issues.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Trusting environment, commitment to open discussion, willingness to support peers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires skilled facilitation, potential for personality conflicts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Professionals, managers, and executives in organizations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance leadership development, strengthen support systems, improve communication and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a supportive environment, strengthens professional networks, develops leadership capabilities, broadens perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Groups can be formed based on common challenges or goals, rotating roles to maximize individual growth.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Peer Teaching
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved communication, increased collaboration, positive feedback from participants.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Peer coaching has been shown to enhance leadership development, build stronger teams, and improve organizational performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Small groups of leaders from different departments meet monthly to discuss challenges and share strategies. Participants take turns coaching each other on specific skills or projects.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peer observation is a collaborative process where teachers observe each other's classroom practices to improve teaching and learning. It is designed to be non-judgmental and supportive, focusing on providing constructive feedback and encouraging reflection. The process typically involves a pre-observation meeting to discuss goals, the observation itself, and a post-observation meeting for feedback and reflection. The goal is to foster a culture of shared inquiry and continuous improvement among educators.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires commitment from teachers and school leadership, dedicated time for observations and feedback sessions, and a culture of trust and respect.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to implement due to time constraints, resistance to being observed, and the need for careful pairing of colleagues. Success depends on creating a safe and supportive environment for honest feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers at all levels and disciplines

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve teaching practices, encourage honest conversation, provide new approaches to problems, boost confidence, and encourage reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for teachers to learn from each other, share good practices, and identify areas for development in a supportive environment. Helps to break down the isolation often experienced by teachers and promote a culture of collaboration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to focus on specific areas of interest or need, and can be adapted to fit different school contexts and schedules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in teaching practices, increased collaboration among teachers, and a more open and sharing school culture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that peer observation can lead to increased teacher effectiveness, improved student outcomes, and a stronger sense of collective teacher efficacy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers in a department observe each other to improve their use of questioning techniques. A team of teachers uses lesson study to refine a particular lesson based on detailed observation and feedback.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Peergrade is a platform that allows learners to give and receive feedback effectively. Learners anonymously offer different types of feedback using a rubric set by the teacher, which allows for some objective and some open feedback questions. The feedback receivers can then go through the feedback and react to it, rating the feedback itself and offering tips for improvement. In the case of disagreement, learners can flag responses so that teachers can intervene and respond to the feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Peergrade platform, a clear rubric or set of success criteria, and structured time for learners to provide and respond to feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology and internet connectivity. Some learners may be hesitant to provide honest feedback due to the fear of being identified.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide structured and objective feedback, promote self-reflection, and enhance critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured and anonymous platform for peer feedback, promoting honest and objective critique. The rubric-based feedback ensures that learners focus on specific aspects of the work and provide targeted suggestions for improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can customize the rubric to fit different content areas and learning objectives. Learners can provide both objective and open-ended feedback, allowing for personalized critique.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review of feedback provided by learners to assess the depth and quality of their critique. Analysis of learner ratings and responses to feedback to assess their engagement with the process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Peergrade and similar platforms can enhance the effectiveness of peer feedback, leading to improved revisions and a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher uses Peergrade to facilitate peer feedback on writing assignments, allowing learners to provide anonymous and rubric-based critique.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The pegword strategy is a mnemonic technique that uses rhyming words to represent numbers or order. These rhyming words, or “pegwords,” provide visual images that can be associated with facts or events. This strategy is particularly useful in helping students remember ordered or numbered information by associating events with numbers that rhyme with the pegwords.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Establishment of pegwords for numbers (e.g., one = bun, two = shoe, three = tree), creation of visual aids (pictures or drawings), teaching students the association process, and regular review.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant initial effort to memorize pegwords. Effectiveness depends on the clarity and memorability of the chosen pegwords and visual associations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education learners, especially those needing to memorize sequences, dates, or numbered lists. Particularly effective for students with learning disabilities or memory challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory of ordered information, enhance association of events with numbers, facilitate recall of sequences and lists, reinforce visual imagery for memory retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory encoding by associating numbers with memorable rhyming words and visual images. Facilitates recall of ordered information by providing a structured framework. Can be used across various subjects to memorize dates, events, and steps in a process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can customize the pegwords and associated images to match student interests and backgrounds, making the learning experience more relevant and engaging. Students can also create their own pegwords and images to further personalize the strategy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Demonstration
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved scores on tests involving ordered information, increased ability to recall sequences, enhanced retention of numerical data, and positive student feedback on the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research has shown that the pegword strategy is effective in helping students remember ordered information. Its use has proven useful in teaching students to remember historical facts and other numbered sequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • To help students remember the Sugar Act of 1764 (first Act), create a picture of sugar being poured on a hamburger bun (bun is the pegword for one). For the Stamp Act (second Act), picture a pair of shoes (shoe is the pegword for two) with a stamp on it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities aimed at promoting a functional pencil grasp, which is essential for comfortable and efficient handwriting. These activities focus on improving fine motor skills, hand strength, and thumb opposition to support a proper pencil grasp.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Various writing tools (e.g., small pencils, golf pencils), fine motor materials (e.g., beads, clothespins), and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address underlying issues such as sensory sensitivities or postural control. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grades, particularly useful for students with inefficient or awkward pencil grasps that impede handwriting.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a functional pencil grasp by improving fine motor skills, hand strength, and thumb opposition.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves comfort and efficiency in handwriting by establishing a functional pencil grasp. Supports fine motor development and hand strength.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual grasp patterns and hand strength. Varied tools and materials engage different motor skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in pencil grasp, including thumb opposition and open web space. Assess comfort and efficiency in handwriting.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved pencil grasp, leading to more comfortable and efficient handwriting. Enhanced fine motor control and hand strength.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A game where children roll a dice twice. The first roll tells them how many pizzas to draw, and the second roll tells them how many pepperonis to put on each pizza. They then write the number sentence that will help them answer the question, 'How many pepperonis in all?'

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dice and paper for drawing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to multiplication facts within the range of the dice used

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop multiplication fact fluency

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visual and engaging activity, promotes problem-solving, reinforces multiplication facts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can use different dice or create their own spinners for different numbers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's ability to accurately draw pizzas and pepperonis and write the correct number sentence

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of multiplication fact fluency

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Roll a 4, so draw 4 pizzas. Roll a 3, so put three pepperonis on each pizza. Write 4 x 3 = 12, indicating there are 12 pepperonis in all.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Effective math instruction connects to real-life and culturally relevant contexts, engaging students and making concepts more accessible. Incorporating hip-hop, sports, or other student interests makes learning more relevant and sincere.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of student interests, ability to create relatable examples, and willingness to adapt instructional methods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful consideration to ensure sincerity and avoid appearing insincere. May require additional resources to support culturally relevant examples.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Math teachers in diverse classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make math concepts relatable, improve student engagement, foster understanding, and connect math to student interests.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, makes math concepts relatable, fosters understanding, and reduces math anxiety.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows teachers to tailor examples and analogies to students' specific interests and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, improved understanding of concepts, enhanced engagement during lessons, and positive feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved math performance, greater student interest, and a more inclusive classroom environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Take the time to consider each student’s perspective and the challenges they may be facing. Show genuine interest in your students, ask about their opinions, interests, and background, and listen as if you might be wrong. Use nonjudgmental, solution-focused problem-solving. Use and model perspective-taking and empathy to recognize each student’s strengths and understand their daily challenges. Avoid misunderstandings that harm relationships.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training or guidance on effective communication techniques, commitment to active listening and non-judgmental interaction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort, may be challenging to implement consistently, can be difficult in environments with high stress or limited resources

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors, trainers, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase understanding of student experiences, improve communication, foster positive relationships, enhance problem-solving skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes empathy, reduces misunderstandings, builds rapport, encourages respectful communication, supports student well-being

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different age groups and learning environments, allowing for flexible integration into daily interactions

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe interactions, monitor communication patterns, gather feedback from students and colleagues

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to deeper understanding of student needs, improved classroom climate, and stronger student-teacher relationships

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask students about their interests and backgrounds, listen attentively to their responses, and use nonjudgmental language when addressing issues.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A statement that has two possible responses—agree or disagree—is read out loud. Depending on whether they agree or disagree with this statement, learners move to one side of the room or the other. From that spot, learners take turns defending their positions. A Philosophical Chairs debate is often based around a text or group of texts learners have read ahead of time; learners are required to cite textual evidence to support their claims and usually hold the texts in their hands during the discussion. Some teachers set up one hot seat to represent each side, and learners must take turns in the seat. Teachers may also opt to offer a continuum of choices, ranging from “Strongly Agree” on one side of the room, all the way to “Strongly Disagree” on the other, and have learners place themselves along that continuum based on the strength of their convictions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where learners can move freely, a provocative statement or question, and clear instructions for learners. Texts or resources for learners to cite as evidence.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are shy or reluctant to express their opinions. Requires careful facilitation to ensure respectful communication and avoid conflict. Can reinforce binary thinking if not carefully structured.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Appropriate for secondary and higher education learners, particularly those studying humanities, social sciences, and ethics

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical thinking skills, encourage perspective-taking, promote argumentation and debate, enhance understanding of complex issues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes critical thinking and argumentation, provides opportunities for perspective-taking, enhances communication skills, supports kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Statements can be tailored to learners' interests and backgrounds. Learners can choose the strength of their agreement or disagreement. Scaffolding can be provided for learners who struggle with argumentation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Positions
  • Argument Construction
  • Role Reversal
  • Consensus Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the debate, review the quality of their arguments and evidence, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking, promotes perspective-taking, improves communication skills, deepens understanding of complex issues

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Phoneme-grapheme mapping is a strategy used to match the letters or letter combinations (graphemes) in a word to the speech sounds (phonemes) they represent. This involves using a grid where each box represents a phoneme, enabling learners to segment words into their constituent sounds and write the corresponding grapheme in each box. This technique helps fix phoneme-grapheme correspondences, supporting spelling, reading, and writing development. It is particularly useful for learners who missed the fundamentals in earlier grades or struggle with explicit sound-to-print mapping.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A phoneme-grapheme grid, list of words for mapping, direct instruction from a teacher or tutor, and practice activities. Regular monitoring and feedback are essential to ensure correct application of the technique.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with significant phonological processing deficits. Requires explicit and systematic instruction to be effective. Can be time-consuming, especially for complex words.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily for learners in grades 1–3, but also beneficial for older students and adults who need to improve their foundational spelling and reading skills, including those with dyslexia

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance phonological awareness, strengthen reading skills, and develop an understanding of sound-symbol relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens the connection between sounds and letters, improves decoding and encoding skills, supports memory for whole words, and enhances reading and writing fluency. Provides a structured approach to learning and applying phonics.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by adjusting the complexity of the words used in mapping exercises. Beginners can start with simple CVC (consonant-vowel-consonant) words, while advanced learners can map more complex words with consonant blends and digraphs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student performance on spelling assessments, monitor improvements in reading accuracy, and analyze the correctness of phoneme-grapheme mapping exercises.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping improves spelling, reading, and writing skills. It is particularly effective for learners who struggle with phonological awareness and decoding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A first-grade teacher uses phoneme-grapheme mapping to help students spell words like ‘straight’ and ‘crash,’ demonstrating how letter combinations represent individual sounds. A special education teacher uses the technique with a struggling reader to improve decoding skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct instruction in phoneme awareness helps children in the early stages of learning to spell and helps remediate the problems of poor spellers at any age. A typical activity for developing this skill is direct teaching of all consonant and vowel sounds. Strengthen phonemic awareness by identifying, segmenting, and manipulating speech sounds in words. Examples include a 'sound workout' where learners use manipulatives to represent each sound.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for phoneme manipulation (e.g., chips, blocks), word lists, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction, may not be effective for learners with severe phonological deficits

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Kindergarten and early elementary students, struggling readers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop phonemic awareness, improve spelling skills, enhance reading fluency

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens foundational skills for reading and spelling, helps learners understand the sound structure of words, adaptable to different learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to target specific phonemes or skills. Can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in identifying and segmenting phonemes. Monitor progress in spelling and reading skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that phoneme awareness training improves reading and spelling skills in young children and struggling readers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encourages learners to apply their phonics skills to spell new words by segmenting phonemes (sound units) and connecting them with corresponding letters. This method builds on the understanding of the relationship between letters and sounds, making educated guesses about spelling. Encourages segmentation to spell and builds skills that can be applied when writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Knowledge of phonics, word lists that align with learners' phonics skills, and materials for segmenting and representing sounds with letters.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Not effective for all English words due to irregular spellings. Relies heavily on learners' existing phonics knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Young children learning to spell and read, particularly those who are developing phonics skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learners' ability to use phonics skills for spelling, reinforce connections between letters and sounds, and improve segmentation skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces phonics skills, builds a foundation for spelling new words, and encourages active engagement with the sounds and letters of words.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted based on learners' current phonics knowledge, focusing on specific letter-sound relationships.

docs.title: Instructions

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of learners' ability to segment and spell words using phonics skills, analysis of spelling errors to identify gaps in phonics knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of reading and spelling skills by strengthening the connection between phonemes and graphemes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Guiding a child to spell "hat" by reminding them of the letters that make the sounds /h/, /a/, and /t/.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Facilitate reading acquisition by asking students to say words that start with the same sound(s) in English or the L1. Ask how words are changed and formed in the home language (singular and plural forms, present tense and past tense forms of verbs) to enhance their word knowledge

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to have some knowledge of the phonology and morphology of students' home languages.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for monolingual teachers to implement effectively without additional training and resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • English Language Learners (ELLs) of all ages who are learning to read.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance phonological and metalinguistic awareness, facilitate reading acquisition, and improve word knowledge.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds on students' existing knowledge of their home language to support the development of English literacy skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Exercises can be tailored to the specific needs of students with different language backgrounds and reading levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor students' ability to identify sounds and manipulate words in both English and their home language.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that strong reading skills in the home language can facilitate the acquisition of reading skills in a second language.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using rhyming as a literacy tool to develop phonological awareness. During a read-aloud, students identify rhyming words in the text to enhance their understanding of sound patterns in language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Age-appropriate texts with clear rhyming patterns, interactive read-aloud sessions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for students with significant phonological processing difficulties or limited exposure to rhyming patterns.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop phonological awareness, improve literacy skills, enhance understanding of sound patterns in language

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances literacy skills through active engagement with rhyming words, supports phonological awareness, and improves reading comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for different literacy levels by selecting texts with varying degrees of complexity in rhyming patterns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student's ability to identify rhyming words in texts, monitor their participation and engagement during read-aloud sessions, and observe their use of rhyming in writing and speaking.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of phonological awareness activities, such as identifying rhyming words, to improve reading skills and literacy development in young learners. (Source: National Reading Panel)

docs.text: Design school environments that encourage physical activity by including playground equipment, walking trails, and bike racks. Classrooms can be arranged to promote movement between activities. Scheduling classes in different rooms encourages students to walk between them.

docs.text: • Increased activity levels: Provides accessible opportunities for physical activity throughout the school day. Improved health and well-being: Promotes a healthier lifestyle for students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating physical activity, such as games, walking, or jogging, with learning activities can improve students' health, focus, and social skills. For example, students can discuss assignments while walking or engage in active games before returning to class for writing tasks. Developers can create activities and games that encourage movement and play through videos, prompts, or augmented reality.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Integration of movement activities into lesson plans. Access to space for physical activity. Development of prompts, videos, or augmented reality for active learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to integrate physical activity seamlessly with academic content. May be challenging for students with certain physical limitations or disabilities. Requires additional resources and creativity from the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, adaptable for various age groups and educational settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus and attention, enhance social awareness and relationship skills, promote physical well-being, reinforce learning through movement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases physical health and well-being, improves focus and attention during learning, enhances social skills through collaborative activities, strengthens memory through active learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be adapted to various physical abilities and learning styles. Prompts and questions can be tailored to suit different subjects and grade levels.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvements in student focus and attention. Measure increases in physical activity during the school day. Assess gains in social skills and teamwork through observation and feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show integrating physical activity can enhance cognitive function, improve student engagement, and reduce disciplinary issues. Playworks’ TeamUp program demonstrates improved recess organization, increased student activity and cooperation, and declines in bullying and disciplinary referrals.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Physical activity breaks are short periods of movement integrated into daily routines to improve focus, energy levels, and physical well-being. They counteract the negative effects of prolonged sitting, reduce fatigue, and boost cognitive function. These breaks can include simple exercises, stretching, or brief walks, and they enhance both physical and mental health.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Minimal to no equipment needed. Requires only a few minutes of time integrated throughout the day.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial planning and encouragement to establish as a routine. Some individuals may need to adapt exercises to accommodate physical limitations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All individuals, including students, faculty, and staff in educational and work settings; adaptable for various fitness levels and schedules

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, prevent fatigue, relieve body stiffness, enhance mood, and increase energy levels

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Counteracts the negative effects of prolonged sitting, reduces fatigue, boosts cognitive function, and enhances overall well-being. Accessible and easily integrated into daily routines.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Breaks can be personalized based on individual preferences and physical abilities, including options for breathing exercises, stretching, standing breaks, or short walks. Customizable to fit different work environments and schedules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved focus, reduced fatigue, increased productivity, enhanced mood, and self-reported improvements in physical well-being.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that short bouts of physical activity can keep individuals on-task and focused. Studies show brain waves indicative of mental fatigue decrease during breaks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Breathing and relaxation breaks, instant recess activity breaks, standing breaks, stretch breaks, walking or power breaks, and short exercises during meetings.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Key words from the text are selected, and the class is divided into two or three groups. A learner from each group comes to the whiteboard and draws the word without using letters or numbers. Their teammates try to guess the word. This activity makes learning fun, reinforces vocabulary, and activates prior knowledge through visual representation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a whiteboard, markers, and pre-selected key words from the text.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be hesitant to draw. Effectiveness depends on the relevance and difficulty of the words.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce vocabulary, make learning fun, and activate prior knowledge through visual representation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages visual learners, promotes active participation, and enhances vocabulary retention through drawing and guessing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Words can be selected to match different proficiency levels. Group sizes can be adjusted based on class size and dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the engagement and accuracy of the drawings. Collect feedback on how well the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances vocabulary, promotes visual learning, and creates an engaging and lively learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about ecosystems, words like 'habitat,' 'species,' and 'biodiversity' can be drawn and guessed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Picture dictionaries are reference tools that use illustrations to define words and concepts, making them accessible to language learners of all ages. Each entry pairs a word with a corresponding image, aiding comprehension and vocabulary retention. Picture dictionaries cover a wide range of topics and are particularly useful for visual learners, ESL students, and young children building their language skills. They serve as effective resources in both educational and personal settings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Physical or digital picture dictionary, visual aids (images or illustrations), and relevant vocabulary.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness relies on the quality and clarity of images. Abstract concepts may be challenging to represent visually. Limited context may affect deep understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, including language learners, visual learners, young children, ESL students, and individuals with learning disabilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To support visual learning by making connections between words and images. To improve understanding and comprehension of terminology for language learners and beginning readers. To expand vocabulary and develop language proficiency. To increase engagement with texts through visual support.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comprehension and vocabulary retention through visual association. Supports self-directed learning and language acquisition. Bridges cultural and linguistic gaps by illustrating meaning. Increases motivation by visually engaging learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create their own picture dictionaries using personal drawings or images. Instructors can adapt picture dictionaries to incorporate vocabulary and concepts relevant to learners' lives and backgrounds. Digital picture dictionaries enable customization and translation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess vocabulary acquisition through tests, quizzes, and writing samples. Observe engagement and participation during reading activities. Gather feedback from learners on the usefulness of picture dictionaries.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that picture dictionaries enhance vocabulary acquisition and comprehension for language learners. Visual aids improve memory and recall, facilitating long-term retention. Picture dictionaries are effective tools for scaffolding learning and promoting language proficiency.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Oxford Picture Dictionary, Merriam-Webster's Visual Dictionary, and customized picture dictionaries for specific subjects or language groups.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Picture schedules or visual planners use images to lay out the steps to do a task. For example, a morning routine might have pictures of getting out of bed, brushing teeth, getting dressed, and eating breakfast. These kinds of visual checklists can reduce the stress of reading and look a bit like comic strips. They can also be small enough to be posted discreetly in the right location.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Images or drawings representing the steps of a task, printer (optional), laminator (optional), a place to display the schedule

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for complex tasks with many steps. Requires regular updating as routines change. Relies on the availability of appropriate and clear images.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with organization, visual learners, young learners, learners with reading difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support task completion, reduce stress associated with reading, improve routine adherence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear, visual breakdown of tasks, reduces reliance on reading skills, promotes independence and routine adherence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Images can be customized to reflect the learner's specific routines and needs. Schedules can be digital or physical.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to follow the schedule independently. Track the completion rate of tasks on the schedule. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the schedule.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual supports have been shown to enhance learning and independence for individuals with cognitive challenges. Picture schedules can improve task completion and reduce anxiety related to daily routines.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Downloadable picture schedules and visual planners are readily available online. Teachers and parents can create customized schedules using software or by hand.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Picture writing unlocks the imagination, builds confidence, and develops foundational early literacy skills. Drawing pictures allows children to unleash their imagination on paper. A writer is born the first time a child puts crayon to paper. When pre-writers use picture writing, they are expressing ideas through illustrations. As their literacy skills develop over time, the picture will serve as a plan for their writing. A picture sparks ideas, provides details, and serves as a framework for a piece of writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires paper and crayons or other drawing materials. Requires time for children to draw, talk about their pictures, and write about their pictures.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Children may need guidance to stay focused on the picture and connect it to their writing. The picture is a writing tool, not an entry into an art contest.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-writers, children ages 2-7

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Unlock imagination, build confidence, develop foundational early literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a pre-writing opportunity to plan, brainstorm, and develop new ideas. Sparks ideas, provides details, and serves as a framework for a piece of writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Children can choose their own topics and ideas to express through illustrations. Teachers can provide prompts or questions to guide hesitant pre-writers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess children's ability to match their words to their pictures. Evaluate the development of their writing skills over time. Observe their engagement and enthusiasm during picture writing activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Picture writing helps children understand that illustrations represent ideas and that ideas can be represented in print. It is a huge concept in early writing and early reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A child draws a beach scene and then writes about their picture. The child then reads their words and the teacher writes their words underneath their form of writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves the use of images, videos, and other visual aids to enhance learning and memory. Visuals summarize content, aid in understanding, and make learning more impactful and memorable. Visuals are more concrete and easily remembered than abstract words, and are processed more efficiently by the brain. Effective visuals can decrease learning time, improve comprehension, enhance retrieval, and increase retention. However, visuals can also negatively impact learning if used inappropriately, such as off-topic or poor-quality images.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to visual resources such as picture books, images, videos, and graphic organizers. Teachers need to integrate visuals purposefully into lesson plans and ensure they align with learning objectives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Inappropriate or poorly selected visuals can distract learners and hinder understanding. Overuse of visuals without clear learning objectives can also be ineffective. Stock photographs and generic graphics may lack engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary development, improve comprehension, increase retention in long-term memory, make abstract concepts more tangible, decrease learning time

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Visuals help learners make sense of content, direct attention, and facilitate emotional connections, leading to better engagement and retention. They simplify complex ideas and bridge learned materials with the unfamiliar.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Visuals can be tailored to suit different learning styles and preferences. The level of complexity and detail can be adjusted based on the learner's existing knowledge and abilities. Visuals can be presented in various formats, such as photos, illustrations, videos, and graphic organizers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure improvement in comprehension and retention through quizzes and tests. Observe learner engagement and participation in discussions. Analyze learner-created visuals and graphic organizers for understanding and application of concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies confirm that visual information is retained more effectively than written or spoken information. Visuals can improve learning by up to 400 percent. Visuals summarize content into smaller, and easier to process chunks, and when you select the right visuals, they offer more comprehensibility than text-based explanations or only audios.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses picture books with strong illustrations to support vocabulary development and comprehension. InferCabulary uses visuals to teach vocabulary by presenting related images and prompting learners to infer meaning. A math teacher uses visuals from everyday life to promote classroom conversation about math concepts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The instructor selects three or four pictures related to the reading topic and provides them to small groups of learners. The groups work together to connect the pictures and guess what the reading will be about. Each group then presents their ideas to the class. This visual-based activity stimulates curiosity and encourages predictive thinking before reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires carefully selected pictures related to the reading topic, copies for each group, and facilitation for group presentations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the pictures. Some learners may struggle with visual interpretation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate curiosity, encourage predictive thinking, and connect visual cues with the reading topic.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages visual learners, promotes collaborative problem-solving, and activates prior knowledge through visual associations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Pictures can be tailored to different proficiency levels and cultural contexts. Group sizes can be adjusted based on class size and dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the connections learners make between the pictures and the reading topic. Collect feedback on how well the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances visual literacy, promotes active engagement with the topic, and fosters a collaborative learning environment.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are divided into 4 groups. Three of these groups are assigned to represent specific points of view. Members of the fourth group are designated as “provocateurs,” tasked with making sure the discussion keeps going and stays challenging. One person from each group (the “speaker”) sits in a desk facing speakers from the other groups, so they form a square in the center of the room. Behind each speaker, the remaining group members are seated: two right behind the speaker, then three behind them, and so on, forming a kind of triangle. From above, this would look like a pinwheel. The four speakers introduce and discuss questions they prepared ahead of time (this preparation is done with their groups). After some time passes, new learners rotate from the seats behind the speaker into the center seats and continue the conversation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space that can be arranged in a pinwheel formation, preparation of discussion questions, and clear instructions for learners. Pre-reading materials may be necessary for discussions based on texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging in small or crowded classrooms. Requires careful facilitation to ensure all learners are engaged and on task. Can be time-consuming to prepare and implement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for secondary and higher education learners, particularly those studying literature, history, and social sciences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking, foster perspective-taking, encourage collaboration and peer teaching, deepen understanding of complex topics

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes critical thinking and perspective-taking, provides opportunities for peer teaching and collaboration, enhances communication skills, supports deeper understanding of complex topics

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Group roles and perspectives can be assigned based on learners' interests and strengths. Learners can choose the questions they want to discuss.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pizza box portfolios are a great space-saving solution. They stack right on top of each other. Ask your local pizza place for some clean, large pizza boxes. Kids can decorate and label them. Then start putting graded spelling homework in one box, art projects in another, and so on. Since there’s limited space, make sure the papers are flat and stacked instead of crumpled into a ball.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clean pizza boxes, markers or other decorating supplies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to clean pizza boxes. May not be suitable for large quantities of materials. Dependent on the learner maintaining the organization system.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages, learners with limited storage space

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a space-saving solution for storing learning materials, promote organization of completed work, encourage student decoration and ownership

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a designated place for storing completed work, reduces clutter, promotes organization and responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can decorate and label their pizza box portfolios. Portfolios can be organized by subject, task, or type.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the organization of materials in the pizza box portfolios. Track the learner's ability to locate specific items in the portfolios. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the portfolios.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Portfolios provide a tangible record of learning progress and can promote reflection and self-assessment. Creative projects like decorating can increase student engagement and ownership.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use pizza boxes to store graded homework, art projects, and other completed work. Decorate the boxes with colorful markers and labels.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Planning for physical activity is essential for pre-teens and teenagers to ensure they meet daily requirements. The planning process involves considering available spaces, low-cost options, active friends, and activities that the family can do together. Planning helps balance physical activity with homework, casual work, and social activities.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The PLaNS approach supports writing skills through guided play and includes practical resources to help with lesson planning. It focuses on building stories together to inspire young writers. PLaNS involves building stories together to inspire young writers through structured play and guided narrative activities.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text:

docs.title: Description

docs.text: • Research suggests that playful spaces can increase engagement, improve creativity, and enhance collaboration. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Playground: Pickup Sports and Jam Sessions
Description
docs.text: Encouraging informal games and activities without emphasizing competition provides opportunities for play and creativity. Teens can engage in pickup sports or jam sessions to foster collaboration and enjoyment. This approach contrasts with competitive extracurricular activities and allows learners to play without the pressure of winning or performing professionally. Informal play promotes social interaction, creativity, and intrinsic motivation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space and equipment for informal games and activities. Instructor encouragement and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may prefer structured activities. May require careful management to ensure inclusivity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote collaboration, foster creativity, encourage social interaction, enhance intrinsic motivation, reduce performance pressure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters social interaction and collaboration. Encourages creativity and innovation. Enhances intrinsic motivation. Reduces performance pressure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose activities based on their interests and skill levels. Instructors can provide different types of equipment and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner participation and engagement. Social interaction and collaboration. Creativity and innovation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that informal play promotes social skills, creativity, and well-being. Studies also show that intrinsic motivation leads to deeper learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school organizes informal sports games during lunch breaks. A college music program hosts jam sessions for learners to play together without performance expectations. A community center offers recreational activities for teens to socialize and engage in informal play.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide low-pressure exercises for students to experiment with the writing techniques they have analyzed. This helps them internalize the lessons and explore the possibilities of writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate writing prompts and exercises. Time for experimentation in class. A classroom environment that values creativity and self-expression.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with open-ended exercises. Requires careful planning to ensure that exercises are relevant and engaging. May be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for developing writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote experimentation and creativity, enhance understanding of writing techniques, develop fluency in using new techniques, encourage self-expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe space for students to experiment with new ideas. Encourages them to take risks and stretch their writing muscles. Promotes a playful and engaging learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Exercises can be tailored to student interests and writing goals. Students can be given the freedom to choose which techniques to experiment with. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating experimentation with new techniques. Participation in exercises and activities. Student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing opportunities for experimentation improves writing skills and promotes a more positive attitude towards writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are given a sentence from a mentor text and asked to rewrite it using different techniques. Students are asked to write a short story using a specific type of figurative language. Students are asked to create a parody of a mentor text.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Playworks TeamUp program aims to make recess more organized, safe, and healthy by fostering improvements in recess organization, enhancing students’ familiarity with a variety of games, and increasing their access to playground equipment. The program promotes increased student activity, cooperation, and conflict resolution skills while reducing bullying, disciplinary referrals, and classroom disruptions. School leaders should treat recess plans like lesson plans.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • The Playworks TeamUp program requires commitment and resources from the school.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires external support and resources, which may not be accessible to all schools.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary schools

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve school climate, enhance social-emotional development, promote physical activity, reduce behavioral issues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to improving recess and creating a more positive school climate.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Implementation can be tailored to the specific needs and context of the school.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Integration
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in recess organization, student behavior, conflict resolution skills, and disciplinary referrals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Participating schools reported improvements in recess organization, students’ familiarity with a variety of games, and their access to playground equipment. The majority of TeamUp schools said that after they started using the program, students were more active, more cooperative, and more likely to use strong conflict resolution when needed. Most schools reported declines in bullying, disciplinary referrals, the number of conflicts spilling back into class, and the amount of class time spent resolving those conflicts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school implements the Playworks TeamUp program to improve recess and the overall school climate. Recess plans are created in a way similar to how teachers create lesson plans.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using digital libraries with audio and visual components to engage learners with a variety of poems. Learners can browse poems based on category or age, enhancing their appreciation and understanding of poetry.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to digital libraries with a diverse collection of poems, devices for learners to access the library (e.g., tablets, computers).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology and digital resources, may be less effective for learners who prefer traditional print materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All ages, adaptable for elementary students through adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance appreciation for poetry, develop literacy skills, improve understanding of poetic devices and themes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides access to a wide range of poems, supports differentiated learning through varied categories and age levels, and enhances engagement through audio and visual elements.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows learners to choose poems based on their interests and reading levels, providing a tailored and engaging learning experience.

• Demonstration
  • Application

docs.text: • Assess student's engagement with the digital library, their ability to select and analyze poems, and their understanding of poetic devices and themes. Monitor participation in discussions and written reflections on the poems.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that integrating digital resources and multimedia can enhance learner engagement and understanding in literacy education. (Source: International Literacy Association)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Point systems or experience (XP) systems reward learners for completing various tasks, assignments, or assessments. They offer limitless points, flexible goals, and learner choice, where learners can accumulate points by focusing on reflection activities, tests, or other relevant activities. Points can be tracked using gradebook features or shared using online tools.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Integration with learning management systems or digital gradebooks. Design of a point system aligned with course objectives. Clear communication of point values and rewards.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lead to a focus on points rather than learning. Can be demotivating if points are not distributed equitably. Requires careful planning to ensure meaningful activities are rewarded.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially effective in online learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reward task completion, provide feedback, track progress, offer flexible goals, support learner choice

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback through point accumulation. Offers flexible goals and learner choice, increasing motivation. Allows learners to track their progress and see their accomplishments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose activities that align with their interests and learning preferences. Instructors can tailor point values and rewards to meet individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner participation in point-earning activities. Compare point accumulation with learning outcomes. Gather feedback on motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Experience points can introduce useful affordances to learning environments, including limitless points, flexible goals, and student choice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Awarding points for completing assignments, participating in discussions, or attending events. Allowing learners to use points to gain extra time on assignments or bypass certain tasks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Political education involves developing a comprehensive understanding of the historical, social, and political contexts that shape a problem. It is crucial for understanding root causes and systemic issues before engaging in empirical research or action. This process includes examining power dynamics and positionality within dominant structures to foster critical consciousness and informed action.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to relevant resources, skilled facilitators to guide discussions, and a safe space for open and honest dialogue.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be emotionally challenging and may require addressing sensitive or controversial topics. Requires a significant time commitment to develop a comprehensive understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students, educators, and community members involved in social justice work

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical consciousness, understand systemic issues, analyze power dynamics, inform action, foster empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a foundation for informed decision-making, promotes deeper understanding of complex issues, empowers individuals to challenge unjust systems, and fosters empathy and solidarity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The content and focus of political education can be tailored to the specific issues and contexts being addressed.

docs.text: • Observe the depth of understanding and critical thinking demonstrated in discussions and written work. Track the extent to which participants apply their learning to inform their actions and advocacy.

docs.title: Examples
