docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Learners regularly select work samples, reflect on their choices, and organize their work into a portfolio. Sticky notes are used to explain why each work sample was chosen. Portfolios can be digital or physical and used to showcase strengths, progress, and areas for improvement.

A portfolio is "a meaningful collection of student work that tells the story of student achievement or growth" (Arter, Spandel, & Culham, 1995, p. 2) — a purposeful selection, not simply a folder of everything a student produced. Because portfolio systems can become confusing without a clear purpose, it helps to be explicit about where a given portfolio sits along four independent dimensions (Linn & Miller, 2005): assessment for learning ↔ assessment of learning (self-reflection and student ownership vs. certifying an accomplishment for a grade or requirement, with more student choice of contents in the former); current accomplishments ↔ progress (only recent work vs. multiple versions of the same piece — draft, feedback, revision, final — showing growth over time); best-work showcase ↔ documentation (student-identified strongest work vs. an inclusive record of everything produced); and finished ↔ working (a polished portfolio built for a specific external audience, like a job application, vs. an evolving day-to-day collection where mistakes and rough drafts are expected and useful). A finished portfolio is typically drawn selectively from a working portfolio rather than built from scratch, and — since a working portfolio's purpose is developing ideas, not certifying achievement — it should never be treated as an assessment-of-learning instrument in its own right.

Portfolios have real advantages over selected-response testing: they document growth with more nuance, integrate naturally into ongoing instruction, and encourage student self-evaluation, reflection, and ownership (Popham, 2005). But they carry two serious costs. First, they take an enormous amount of teacher time — for one-to-one conferences, guiding student selection and reflection, and out-of-class review — that has to be weighed against the benefit. Second, portfolio reliability is genuinely harder to establish than for constructed-response assessment, precisely because the work samples are more varied. Vermont's statewide use of portfolios for writing and math assessment in fourth and eighth grade is a sobering case study: even with a shared analytic scoring rubric and an external panel of raters, inter-rater agreement was poor for both subjects in the first year of implementation, improved for math (but not reading) in the second year, and even that improved math reliability remained too low to support individual student accountability decisions (Koretz, Stecher, Klein, & McCaffrey, 1994). When reliability is this low, validity is compromised as well, since an unstable score can't support a defensible interpretation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires regular class time for students to select and reflect on their work. Teachers need to provide guidance and feedback on portfolio development. Storage space or digital platforms are necessary.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time investment from students and teachers. Some students may struggle to select representative work samples or articulate their reflections. The assessment of portfolios can be subjective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and professional development contexts. Adaptable for various subjects and learning goals.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote student reflection and self-assessment, showcase learning progress, encourage ownership of work, and provide concrete examples for discussions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates self-reflection and metacognition. Provides a tangible record of learning over time. Empowers learners to take ownership of their work. Supports personalized learning by allowing students to showcase their unique strengths and progress.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects, grade levels, and learning goals. Students can choose which work samples to include and how to organize their portfolios. Digital portfolios allow for multimedia integration and personalization.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Talk with students about the portfolio's purpose and the variety of possible work samples — where possible, involve them in deciding what kind of portfolio to build.
  2. Decide the purpose along the four dimensions above (growth vs. current accomplishments; showcase vs. documentation; and so on) — a portfolio can serve multiple purposes, but teacher and students both need to be clear on which.
  3. Decide what work samples to collect (every assignment, or a selection; drafts as well as final products, or final products only).
  4. Collect and store the samples (a physical folder, a digital platform).
  5. Select or co-develop scoring criteria — rubrics may need to vary across different kinds of work samples, and existing rubrics may need revision after their first use.
  6. Teach and require students to self-evaluate their own work against the agreed criteria — simply (strengths/weaknesses/next steps) for younger students, more analytically (using the same rubric the teacher will use) for older ones.
  7. Schedule and conduct portfolio conferences — time-consuming, but the step most responsible for the process actually enhancing learning rather than just accumulating work.
  8. Involve parents — explain the portfolio process, encourage them to review work samples, and consider parent-teacher-student conferences where students present their own work.

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review portfolio content for evidence of student learning and reflection. Assess the depth and quality of student reflections. Gather feedback from students and teachers regarding the value of portfolio development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Portfolio development has been shown to increase student engagement, promote self-reflection, and provide a more holistic assessment of learning than traditional methods. Digital portfolios can enhance student creativity and digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Related Elements
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Wildwood IB World Magnet School in Chicago, Illinois, uses a student portfolio manual to guide the structure and collection of materials.
  • Kentucky's required fourth- and seventh-grade writing portfolios, which must include a self-reflective statement and three specific pieces (reflective, personal experience/literary, and transactive), with students choosing which piece to submit in each category.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Arter, J., Spandel, V., & Culham, R. (1995). Portfolios for assessment and instruction. ERIC Digest.
  • Linn, R. L., & Miller, M. D. (2005). Measurement and assessment in teaching (9th ed.). Pearson.
  • Popham, W. J. (2005). Classroom assessment: What teachers need to know (4th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Koretz, D., Stecher, B., Klein, S., & McCaffrey, D. (1994). The Vermont Portfolio Assessment Program: Findings and implications. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 13(3), 5-16.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher-made assessments. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using positive affirmations involves creating and repeating positive statements about oneself to build inroads into the subconscious mind, opening up the possibility of a new state of thoughts. These statements should be short, believable, focused, and delivered with feeling to influence the subconscious mind. Regular practice of repeating affirmations helps internalize these positive beliefs, leading to enhanced self-esteem, confidence, and a more optimistic outlook.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires consistent practice and willingness to believe in the positive statements. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to identify and address underlying beliefs. Access to resources such as affirmation lists, guided meditations, or visualization exercises can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel unnatural or insincere at first, particularly for individuals with deeply ingrained negative self-perceptions. May not be effective if not accompanied by genuine belief and emotional engagement. Can be challenging to maintain consistency in the face of significant stress or adversity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals seeking to improve self-perception and overcome limiting beliefs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build self-confidence, enhance self-esteem, promote positive thinking, influence subconscious mind, develop a more optimistic outlook.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-esteem by promoting positive self-perception. Influences subconscious mind by repeatedly reinforcing positive beliefs. Fosters a growth mindset by encouraging learners to focus on their potential. Increases motivation by instilling a sense of self-efficacy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized affirmations tailored to individual needs and goals. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through verbal repetition, journaling, or visualization. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as lists of common affirmations or guided scripts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported self-esteem and confidence using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in mood, motivation, and goal achievement. Analyze ability to articulate and embody positive beliefs in real-life situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that positive affirmations can improve self-esteem, reduce stress, and promote goal achievement (e.g., PositivePsychology.com). Studies show that repeating affirmations can activate brain regions associated with self-related processing and reward. Regular practice has been linked to improved psychological well-being and resilience.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual struggling with self-doubt repeats affirmations such as 'I am capable and worthy of success' to build confidence and overcome limiting beliefs. A student preparing for an exam uses affirmations such as 'I am prepared and I will do my best' to reduce anxiety and enhance performance. Resource: Psychology Today – How Affirmations Can Improve Your Life.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: PBIS is a proactive approach schools use to improve school safety and promote positive behavior. It focuses on prevention, not punishment. With PBIS, schools teach students positive behavior strategies, just as they would teach about any other subject. All students learn about positive behavior, including kids with IEPs and 504 plans. PBIS recognizes that students can only meet behavior expectations if they know what the expectations are. Everyone learns what’s considered appropriate behavior, using a common language to talk about it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear behavior expectations, consistent implementation, and ongoing evaluation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires school-wide commitment and may not be effective if not implemented consistently.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, including those with IEPs and 504 plans.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve school safety, promote positive behavior, and teach students positive behavior strategies.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leads to better student behavior, fewer detentions and suspensions, better grades, and may lead to less bullying.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • PBIS is implemented at the school-wide level, but can be adapted to meet the needs of individual students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student behavior, detentions, suspensions, grades, and bullying incidents.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that PBIS leads to better student behavior. In many schools that use PBIS, students get fewer detentions and suspensions. They also earn better grades. And there’s some evidence that PBIS may lead to less bullying.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Schools teach students positive behavior strategies throughout the school day — in class, at lunch, and on the bus — so students understand what’s expected of them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The "Positive Intention & Generosity in Networking" strategy emphasizes focusing on how one's interests and goals align with those of the people they meet and offering valuable resources beyond the obvious. It encourages individuals to think broadly about what they can offer others, such as gratitude, recognition, inclusion, unique insights, or knowledge. Framing networking in terms of collective benefits instead of personal gains fosters authenticity and increases the likelihood of successful relationship-building.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A shift in mindset to focus on providing value, active listening, empathetic engagement, recognition of others’ contributions, and willingness to offer support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a genuine commitment to helping others, may not yield immediate personal gains, challenges traditional self-promotional networking approaches.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Professionals seeking to build genuine connections, leaders aiming to foster a supportive environment, individuals hesitant about traditional networking methods.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage authentic networking, promote generosity and mutual support, foster inclusivity, enhance relationship-building, focus on collective benefits.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces feelings of inauthenticity, increases willingness to network, enhances relationships through mutual support, promotes a selfless approach to networking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Individuals can tailor their approach to offer unique resources, insights, or support based on their strengths, accommodating diverse networking goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Positive feedback from contacts, increased opportunities for collaboration, stronger relationships, enhanced reputation, a sense of fulfillment from helping others.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that attorneys who focused on the collective benefits of making connections felt more authentic and were more likely to network, resulting in more billable hours. Framing networking in terms of supporting the firm or clients leads to increased success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating positive scripts involves regularly constructing and narrating uplifting stories with a positive outline, visualizing goals as already achieved to internalize them. This exercise aims to replace negative thought patterns with a drama that is trapping and limiting the individual. It supports the internalization of goals and dreams as if they have already been achieved, fostering a sense of accomplishment and enhancing motivation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires consistent practice and willingness to engage in positive visualization. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying beliefs. Access to resources such as script templates, visualization exercises, or guided meditations can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel unnatural or unrealistic at first, particularly for individuals with deeply ingrained negative self-perceptions. May not be effective if not accompanied by genuine belief and emotional engagement. Can be challenging to maintain consistency in the face of significant stress or adversity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals prone to negative thought patterns, self-doubt, or lack of motivation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Replace negative thoughts with positive narratives, internalize goals and dreams, enhance motivation, foster a sense of accomplishment, promote positive visualization.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation by visualizing goals as already achieved. Influences subconscious mind by repeatedly reinforcing positive outcomes. Fosters a growth mindset by encouraging learners to focus on their potential. Increases self-esteem by promoting a more positive self-perception.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized scripts tailored to individual goals and aspirations. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through journaling, visualization exercises, or verbal storytelling. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as guided prompts or script templates.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported motivation and optimism using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in mood, goal-setting, and goal-achievement. Analyze the level of detail and emotional engagement in the created scripts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that positive visualization can enhance motivation, improve performance, and promote goal achievement (e.g., Psychology Today). Studies show that mental imagery can activate brain regions associated with planning and action. Regular practice has been linked to increased confidence and a more positive outlook.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual preparing for a job interview creates a positive script in which they confidently answer questions, impress the interviewer, and receive a job offer. A student facing academic challenges visualizes themselves successfully completing assignments, achieving good grades, and excelling in their studies. Resource: Psychology Today – The Power of Visualization.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After reading, instructors facilitate discussions to explore learners' favorite parts of a narrative text or to confirm information learned in an informational text. These discussions promote student-to-student interaction and deeper engagement with the material. Revisiting opening questions helps learners reflect on their understanding and connections made throughout the reading process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires facilitation skills and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be hesitant to participate. Discussions may veer off-topic without proper guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially effective after reading activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Deepen engagement, promote student interaction, reinforce key takeaways

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages deeper engagement with the text. Reinforces understanding through peer interaction. Provides opportunities for reflection and synthesis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose topics for discussion. Use varied discussion formats, such as small groups or think-pair-share.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and analyze the depth of discussion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances understanding and fosters a sense of community.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The PQP (Praise-Question-Polish) technique guides learners to provide specific and constructive feedback on each other's work. In PQP, group members take turns reading their drafts aloud as the other students follow along with copies. The responders then react to the piece by writing specific comments guided by questions on the PQP form, which require specific examples of praiseworthy elements, questions the responders have about the draft, and specific suggestions for improvement. This form gives structure, objectivity, and positivity to peer feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • PQP forms for each learner, copies of drafts for all group members, and structured group time

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial training to ensure learners provide specific and constructive feedback. Learners may need guidance to maintain a positive attitude toward the peer-review process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in grades 6-12 and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide specific and constructive feedback, improve self-editing skills, and enhance listening skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured feedback, fosters a positive attitude toward critique, and enhances learners' ability to self-edit and listen effectively. Helps learners identify specific areas for improvement and recognize praiseworthy elements.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The PQP form can be adapted to include specific criteria relevant to the task or subject matter. Sentence stems may be used for learners who need additional support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review of PQP forms to assess the specificity and constructiveness of feedback. Observation of group interactions to assess learners' listening skills and positive attitude.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that when learners receive concrete suggestions for revisions, they do revise with the suggestions in mind.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a writing classroom, learners exchange drafts and use the PQP form to provide feedback on each other's narratives. Resource: ReadWriteThink - Peer Review: Narrative.

docs.title: Practice Changing Negative Thoughts into Positive Ones
Description
docs.text: Challenging learners to reframe negative thoughts into positive affirmations. This involves providing examples of negative statements and asking learners to transform them into more positive ones. Can be done with made-up examples or real-life situations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Examples of negative statements. Facilitator to guide the activity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are deeply entrenched in negative thinking patterns. Requires a supportive and non-judgmental environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with negative self-talk and want to develop a more positive mindset.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop learners' ability to identify and reframe negative thoughts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops critical thinking skills. Increases self-awareness. Empowers learners to actively manage their thoughts and emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use examples that are relevant to learners' lives and experiences. Tailor the activity to specific challenges or goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to reframe negative thoughts in various situations. Self-reported changes in mindset and behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that cognitive reframing can reduce stress and improve mental well-being. Practicing this skill can help learners develop a more resilient mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use an example like, “I only did well on this test due to luck,” and challenge learners to turn the statement into a more positive one. Use positive thinking task cards to reinforce positive self-talk.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Give students opportunities to practice responsible decision-making by using pairs or small groups to analyze problem scenarios (e.g., cheating, bullying) that connect to their everyday lives at school, in order to make decisions about, including analyzing the situation and possible consequences. Have them share their decisions with the whole class and reflect on how they arrived at them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Problem scenarios, time for students to analyze the scenarios, and a way for students to share their decisions and reflect on how they arrived at them.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to create and facilitate the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve decision-making skills, analyze situations and consequences, promote ethical responsibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with opportunities to practice responsible decision-making, improves analysis of situations and consequences, and promotes ethical responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of problem scenarios that connect to students' everyday lives at school. They can also have students share their decisions with the whole class and reflect on how they arrived at them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Case Study
  • Class Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student decision-making skills, increased student analysis of situations and consequences, and greater ethical responsibility.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of practicing responsible decision-making.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher gives students problem scenarios to analyze in pairs. The students share their decisions with the whole class and reflect on how they arrived at them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Give students time to practice what they just learned in a low-stakes environment, without grading or evaluation. Provide feedback from near neighbors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate writing prompts and exercises. Time for practice in class. A classroom environment that values creativity and self-expression.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with open-ended exercises. Requires careful planning to ensure that exercises are relevant and engaging. May be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for developing writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote experimentation and risk-taking, enhance understanding of writing techniques, develop fluency in using new techniques, reduce anxiety and pressure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe space for students to experiment with new ideas. Encourages them to take risks and stretch their writing muscles. Promotes a playful and engaging learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Practice activities can be tailored to student interests and writing goals. Students can be given the freedom to choose which techniques to experiment with. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating experimentation with new techniques. Participation in exercises and activities. Student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing opportunities for experimentation improves writing skills and promotes a more positive attitude towards writing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are given a writing prompt and asked to write for 10 minutes without stopping. Students are asked to rewrite a sentence using a different technique. Students are asked to create a parody of a mentor text.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When learners succeed, praise their efforts and strategies rather than their intelligence. Praising intelligence can undermine motivation and performance, as learners may view intelligence as a fixed trait. In the face of failure, they may display less task persistence, less task enjoyment, and overall worse performance. Focus on the process and the strategies used to achieve success to foster a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to observe learners' processes and strategies carefully. Instructors need to provide specific and meaningful feedback that focuses on effort and strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Generic praise can be ineffective and may not promote a growth mindset. Praise must be specific and focused on the process to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially those who are sensitive to failure or tend to attribute success to innate ability rather than effort

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, increase task persistence, improve task enjoyment, and enhance overall performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to focus on the process of learning and the strategies they use, rather than on their perceived intelligence. Helps learners see that effort and effective strategies lead to success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual learner strengths and areas for improvement. Instructors can provide specific examples of effective strategies that learners used.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner persistence in the face of challenges, monitor their task enjoyment, and track their overall performance. Compare the effectiveness of praising effort and strategies versus praising intelligence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that praising effort and strategies promotes a growth mindset and increases task persistence and enjoyment, leading to improved performance. Praise for intelligence can actually undermine motivation and performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Praising effort and strategies focuses on acknowledging the process and hard work learners invest in their tasks, rather than praising innate intelligence. By highlighting specific actions, effective strategies, and persistence, instructors can reinforce the idea that effort leads to success and that intelligence is not a fixed trait.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be mindful of their language and focus on specific actions. Requires a shift from praising intelligence to praising effort.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Praise that is not genuine or specific can be ineffective. Over-praising can lead to complacency.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially children and adolescents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a growth mindset, encourage effort, promote effective strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to value effort and hard work. Reinforces the idea that skills can be developed through practice. Helps learners see mistakes as opportunities for learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual learners' specific efforts and strategies. Instructors can provide different types of praise based on individual needs and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' responses to challenges and setbacks. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward effort. Measure the effectiveness of different praise strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that praising effort and strategies can lead to increased motivation, improved performance, and a greater willingness to take on challenges. Learners who are praised for their effort are more likely to persist in the face of difficulty.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-entry socialization involves engaging students in brief, positive interactions before they enter the classroom to set a productive tone. Behavior management expert Rob Plevin recommends using "nonconfrontational statements" and "informal chitchat" at the door to socialize students into productive behaviors. This proactive approach helps mitigate potential disruptions and create a positive classroom atmosphere.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher presence at the door, conversational skills, consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort, may not be effective for all students, relies on teacher-student rapport.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Establish a positive classroom atmosphere, reduce disruptions, build rapport with students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Proactive approach prevents disruptions, builds rapport with students, sets a positive tone for learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Conversations can be tailored to individual student interests and needs. Nonconfrontational statements can address specific behavior concerns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and mood upon entering the classroom. Track the frequency and severity of disruptions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Pre-entry socialization can improve classroom management by proactively setting a positive tone and building rapport with students, reducing disruptions and promoting a more productive learning environment.

docs.title: Pre-reading: 4 Ps (Preview, Predict, Prior Knowledge, Purpose)
Description
docs.text: The 4 Ps of pre-reading include previewing the text, predicting the content, activating prior knowledge, and defining the purpose for reading. Previewing involves taking a quick look at the text. Predicting means using clues to figure out what information the reading will provide. Activating prior knowledge involves recalling what one already knows about the subject. Defining the purpose involves understanding the author's intent, which helps in comprehending the text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the text and a few minutes to engage in the 4 Ps of pre-reading.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require guidance for learners who are new to the 4 Ps approach. Effectiveness depends on active engagement with the text.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages who want to improve their reading comprehension skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension by previewing, predicting, activating prior knowledge, and defining the purpose for reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to pre-reading, improves comprehension, and enhances engagement with the text.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can tailor their pre-reading activities based on their individual needs and learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the learner's ability to summarize the main points of the text after applying the 4 Ps.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances reading comprehension by providing a structured and comprehensive approach to pre-reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a historical text, previewing the chapter titles, predicting the main events, recalling prior knowledge about the period, and defining the purpose for reading (e.g., understanding the causes of a specific event).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Generating a list of pre-reading questions that will help learners achieve their purpose for reading. Leading students in creating questions that will help them to achieve their purpose.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A text and some time to formulate questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The questions must be relatable to the learner.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and all learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activating learner's interest by posing questions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Build learner's interest and encourage active learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can ask different questions about the same reading materials.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Question Formulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners are active and engaged in learning and have questions about the reading materials.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Build student's interest and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking students what they know about dinosaurs before starting a reading about them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Skimming or pre-reading a book involves a systematic approach to discover whether the book requires a more careful reading. This includes looking at the title page, preface, table of contents, and index to obtain a general sense of the book's structure and range of topics. Additionally, one should read the publisher's blurb and skim pivotal chapters for summary statements, dipping in and out to read paragraphs or pages.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the book and time to systematically skim through its key sections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for books with dense or complex content that require immediate, detailed attention. Effectiveness depends on the structure and clarity of the book.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for students and adult learners who need to assess the relevance and depth of a book before committing to a full read.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Determine whether a book requires more careful reading, obtain a general sense of its structure, and estimate the range of topics covered.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners efficiently decide whether a book is worth reading in detail, improves time management, and enhances comprehension by providing a preliminary overview.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adjust the depth of their skimming based on their familiarity with the topic and their reading goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Advance Organizers
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the learner's ability to summarize the book's main topics and structure after skimming.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves reading efficiency by allowing learners to quickly assess the value and relevance of a book before a full reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a non-fiction book for a research project, systematically skimming the title page, table of contents, index, and pivotal chapters to determine its relevance and usefulness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-reading involves skimming a text to identify key ideas before reading from start to finish. It typically includes reviewing titles, introductions, summaries, headings, subheadings, study questions, and conclusions to create an overview that increases reading speed and efficiency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the text and a few minutes to skim through key sections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for texts that require careful, detailed analysis. Effectiveness depends on the clarity and structure of the text.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for adult learners and students in higher education who need to quickly grasp the main points of a text.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase reading speed and efficiency, locate key ideas, and provide an overview of the text before detailed reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners quickly grasp the main ideas of a text, improves comprehension, and supports efficient reading strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adjust the depth of their skimming based on their prior knowledge and the complexity of the text.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Advance Organizers
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the learner's ability to identify key ideas and summarize the text after skimming.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves reading comprehension and efficiency by providing a framework before detailed reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a chapter in a textbook, skimming the introduction, headings, and conclusion to understand the main topics and structure.

docs.title: Pre-reading: Understand the Purpose of the Reading
Description
docs.text: Understanding the purpose of pre-reading is to increase the capacity to comprehend material before starting to read. By building a conceptual framework, learners can better integrate new details and evidence they encounter in the text. This involves thinking about what one already knows about a given topic, predicting what will be read, and increasing interest in the text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the text and a few minutes to engage in pre-reading activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require guidance for learners who are new to pre-reading strategies. Effectiveness depends on active engagement with the text.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners who want to enhance their reading comprehension and retention skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase reading comprehension and retention by establishing a conceptual framework before detailed reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners build a big picture before starting to read, improves comprehension, and increases interest in the text.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can tailor their pre-reading activities based on their prior knowledge and learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the learner's ability to summarize the main points of the text after pre-reading and detailed reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances reading comprehension and retention by providing a conceptual framework before detailed reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading a scientific article, thinking about what you already know about the topic, predicting the main findings, and setting a purpose for reading (e.g., understanding a specific concept).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students identify the text structure prior to reading (e.g., compare and contrast, description, problem-solution, cause and effect, sequence of events) and complete a supporting graphic organizer while reading to fill in the components.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Supporting graphic organizer and texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Identification of text structure and students may need teacher modeling and guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Older students, particularly those facing more challenging texts in content areas outside of English language arts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension by identifying text structure before reading and actively filling in components in a graphic organizer.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts comprehension by preparing students for the structure of the text and actively engaging them during reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can model how to use the organizers and provide a KWL chart.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Activation
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accurate completion of graphic organizer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students gain a considerable boost in their comprehension.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-recording instructional videos in advance is a versatile teaching strategy. The production of video content can range from quick-and-easy to in-depth. There are many ways instructors can benefit from delivering course content in video format, including: students can access and rewatch videos freely, frees up synchronous class time for more interactive learning activities and instructors can reuse and re-edit recorded videos

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Recording equipment, editing software, and a platform for hosting and sharing videos (e.g., Canvas, YouTube).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time investment in video creation, technical skills required, and potential lack of real-time interaction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in online or blended learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance the learning experience by providing accessible, reusable, and versatile video content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Flexibility in accessing and reviewing content, more interactive synchronous sessions, and reusable content for instructors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be tailored to different learning styles and levels of detail.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student engagement (views, comments), performance on related tasks, and feedback on the video content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves content accessibility, enhances synchronous interactions, and provides reusable teaching materials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-recording instructional videos in advance is a versatile teaching strategy. Instructors can deliver course content in video format, which can be accessed and rewatched freely by students. It frees up synchronous class time for more interactive learning activities, and instructors can reuse and re-edit recorded videos. Types of videos may include a welcome video, weekly video messages, supplemental instruction, and lecture recordings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires video recording equipment (camera, microphone), editing software, and a platform for hosting and sharing videos (e.g., Canvas, YouTube).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to produce high-quality videos. Requires technical skills for recording and editing. May not be suitable for all types of content or instructors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in online or blended learning environments, and those who benefit from flexible access to content.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate flexible learning, improve accessibility, enhance engagement, and optimize class time for interactive activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with the ability to review content at their own pace. Increases accessibility for learners with different learning styles and needs. Allows for efficient use of synchronous class time for more engaging activities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can create videos addressing specific learner needs or challenging concepts. Videos can be tailored to different levels of understanding and learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Demonstration
  • Provide Guidance
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Video views, completion rates, learner feedback, performance on related assignments, and engagement in synchronous class activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies and anecdotal evidence suggest that pre-recorded videos can improve learner outcomes by providing flexible access to content and enhancing engagement in class. (Stanford Teaching Commons)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-shadowing preparation involves several activities to set up a meaningful shadowing experience. These activities include: (1) creating learning goals for the Shadow Day to focus observations; (2) choosing a student who can help meet those learning goals; (3) coordinating with the student, parents, and staff; (4) questioning assumptions to approach the shadowing day with beginner's eyes. Examples of learning goals include understanding student engagement, college and career readiness, or experiences of English Learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time to dedicate to preparation activities (approximately 1 hour), templates or worksheets for goal setting and assumption questioning, and coordination with the student, parents, and staff.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort, potential for logistical challenges in coordinating with students and staff, and dependence on the willingness of students and parents to participate.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and school leaders participating in student shadowing to gain insights into student experiences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prepare educators for meaningful shadowing experiences, promote open-minded observation, and ensure ethical and logistical considerations are addressed.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps educators focus their observations, reduce bias, and ensure a productive shadowing experience. Encourages reflection on assumptions and learning goals.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learning goals can be tailored to specific interests or areas of concern. The student selection process allows for focusing on particular student populations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Individual Reflection
  • Practice
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Written learning goals, list of assumptions, coordination notes, and feedback from students, parents, and staff.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced focus and purpose during shadowing, reduced bias in observations, and improved coordination with stakeholders. Increases the likelihood of actionable insights and meaningful change.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pre-teaching vocabulary involves introducing new words before encountering them in a text or lesson. This strategy helps learners activate prior knowledge, increase motivation, and assess what they already know about a topic. By addressing any misconceptions or gaps in background knowledge, instructors can ensure learners are better prepared to understand the material. Pre-teaching vocabulary can also help learners understand the purpose for reading or engaging with a text, ultimately leading to increased comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of key vocabulary words from the text or lesson. Development of engaging activities to introduce and reinforce the new words.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and planning to prepare vocabulary activities. Can be challenging to select the most relevant and impactful words for pre-teaching.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those in upper elementary through high school, who need additional support in building vocabulary and improving comprehension.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary acquisition, improve reading comprehension, and activate background knowledge by introducing new words before engaging with a text.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Activates prior knowledge and reduces cognitive load during reading. Ensures learners understand key terms and concepts, promoting deeper engagement with the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can select vocabulary words based on the specific needs of their learners and the content they are studying. Activities can be tailored to address individual learning styles and prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Assigned Readings
  • Question Formulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance on pre- and post-tests, participation in vocabulary activities, and demonstration of understanding during discussions. Monitor improvement in reading comprehension.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners demonstrate improved vocabulary, enhanced reading comprehension, and a greater ability to engage with complex texts. Pre-teaching vocabulary provides a solid foundation for learning and ensures that learners are prepared to succeed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities focused on building foundational skills necessary before formal handwriting instruction begins, such as line awareness, spatial awareness, and pencil grasp. These skills are crucial for developing legible and efficient handwriting.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Basic art supplies (paper, crayons, markers), various pre-writing templates, and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address specific letter formation issues. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • PreK-1st grade learners or those with underdeveloped pre-writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve line awareness, spatial awareness, and pencil grasp in preparation for handwriting.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops essential fine motor and visual perceptual skills. Builds a strong foundation for legible handwriting.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be modified based on skill level, focusing on specific areas such as line tracking or shape formation. Can also be adapted to sensory needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in line tracking, shape formation, and pencil control. Assess readiness for formal handwriting instruction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Builds essential pre-writing skills, leading to improved handwriting readiness and legibility. Stronger fine motor and visual perceptual abilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use graphic organizers to plan and structure their ideas before writing drafts, aiding in idea generation and organization.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Graphic organizers and writing prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Organizers should be used for note-taking, not as a replacement for the writing piece itself. Most writing time should be spent drafting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who struggle with organizing their thoughts before writing.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate brainstorming, organization, and structuring of ideas before writing, improving the coherence and quality of written work.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual framework for organizing ideas, reduces cognitive load during the writing process, and promotes structured thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • A variety of organizers can be used, depending on the writing task (e.g., outlining, clustering, concept mapping).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Argument Construction
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved organization and coherence of written work, demonstrated ability to structure ideas, and effective use of evidence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Adding graphic organizers into the writing process can support writing quality.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating consistent interfaces and repetitive structures or frameworks in learning environments to facilitate predictability. This helps learners know what to expect, allowing them to focus their attention on learning content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Establishing and maintaining consistent routines, procedures, and interfaces. Regular communication about expectations and schedules.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Over-reliance on predictability may reduce adaptability in novel situations. Must be balanced with flexibility to accommodate unexpected changes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from structured environments and clear expectations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce uncertainty, enhance focus, create a sense of safety, improve learner attention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by providing a stable and predictable environment. Allows learners to focus on content rather than adapting to changing structures.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various environments by establishing routines and procedures that are consistently followed. Structures can be adjusted based on learner feedback and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior (e.g., reduced anxiety, increased focus). Gather feedback on the clarity and effectiveness of routines and structures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Classroom routines and procedures help make classrooms more predictable and, subsequently, help students feel safe. When students can confidently predict classroom structure and teacher behavior, they are free to immerse themselves in their curiosities, freely take risks and safely negotiate their social interactions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A kindergarten class transitions from desks to a line using a repetitive rhythm to establish expectations and routine.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Predicting involves anticipating what will happen next in a text or problem. This engages learners' interest and helps them assess what they already know about a given topic. In math, it involves asking what type of question is being asked, what type of operations might be used, and what the answer might look like.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A clear understanding of the topic and the ability to formulate relevant questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to have some prior knowledge of the topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from structured approaches to learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase motivation, engage interest, activate prior knowledge, and improve comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners, activates prior knowledge, and increases motivation to learn.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different levels of scaffolding and support based on learners' needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Direct instruction
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased engagement, improved comprehension, and better problem-solving accuracy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners connect new information to what they already know, leading to increased comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking students to predict what the next step in a math problem might be.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A PALS activity that emphasizes making predictions while reading. Students each read a paragraph and then predict what will happen next, which helps develop reading comprehension and expand their Vocabulary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material, trained students, timer

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires clear instructions, effectiveness depends on active peer support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 2–6, students who need to improve prediction skills and reading comprehension

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop prediction skills, improve reading comprehension, expand vocabulary, practice summarizing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging activity that encourages active reading and critical thinking, peer support for generating predictions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Texts can be adjusted to reading levels; prompts can be varied to encourage different types of predictions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Modeling
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess prediction accuracy, evaluate reading comprehension, collect student feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on PALS shows improved reading comprehension and prediction skills.

docs.text: • PALS program at Vanderbilt University: http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners anticipate emotions linked to upcoming activities. Identifying potential feelings (anxiety, boredom, excitement) allows pre-planning of coping strategies. This builds the emotional regulation process, improving focus and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a schedule of daily activities and facilitator guidance. Learners need to reflect on their feelings and develop coping plans.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not fully prepare learners for unexpected emotional challenges. Requires ongoing practice to become effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to high school students, learners with anxiety or attention difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, develop coping strategies, enhance emotional awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Proactively addresses potential emotional challenges, enhances self-regulation, and improves focus. Provides a framework for managing emotional responses.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to self-select activities and strategies. Flexible formats can include written plans, checklists, or discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the use of coping strategies in real-time scenarios. Monitor changes in emotional responses over time. Assess the clarity and relevance of learner-developed plans.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-regulation: Planning enhances the ability to manage emotions proactively. Enhanced focus: Better emotional management supports improved attention and learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Review the daily schedule and ask learners to identify potential emotions. Write down coping strategies for each activity. Source: KidConnect Ready2Learn Curriculum.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Place students who have trouble hearing, seeing, focusing on, or paying attention to instruction happening in seats where they will be best able to focus.

docs.text: • Flexibility in classroom seating arrangements.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with attentional or sensory processing challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Minimize distractions and improve ability to focus on instructions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces distractions, promotes focus and attention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Consider the specific needs of the learner when determining seating arrangements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' focus and engagement in different seating locations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved focus and attention for learners with attentional or sensory processing challenges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher seats a student with attention challenges near the front of the classroom, away from windows and other distractions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Preliminary data collection involves gathering contextual data to gain a deeper understanding of the local settings where a problem exists. This includes collecting both quantitative and qualitative data to paint a comprehensive picture of the issue. Quantitative data can provide statistics and hard numbers, while qualitative data offers insights into the lived experiences and perspectives of individuals affected by the problem.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to data sources, tools for data collection (e.g., surveys, observation protocols), and skills for data analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Data collection can be time-consuming and may require navigating gatekeepers or obtaining permission to access data. Ensuring the quality and reliability of data is crucial.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Researchers, students, and community members

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand local contexts, gather quantitative data, collect qualitative data, identify patterns, inform research questions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a comprehensive understanding of the problem, informs the development of research questions, and helps to contextualize findings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The types of data collected and the methods used can be tailored to the specific problem and context.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Research
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Data Analysis
  • Individual Reflection
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the comprehensiveness and quality of the data collected. Assess the extent to which the data informs the development of research questions and actions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps to understand the culture of schools and identify policies and practices that reinforce disproportionality. Essential for contextualizing and humanizing data by directly asking youth and school adults about their experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reviewing quantitative achievement and behavioral data disaggregated by race. Conducting walkthroughs and observations to assess school culture.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This involves creating learning goals for the shadowing day, choosing a student to shadow, and coordinating with the student, their parents, and school staff to ensure a smooth and meaningful experience. It also includes questioning one's own assumptions about students and the school environment to approach the shadowing experience with an open mind.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for planning and coordination, a clear shadowing protocol, and willingness to question one's own assumptions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort to coordinate with students, parents, and staff. May be challenging to set aside preconceived notions and approach the experience with a truly open mind.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, school leaders, and product designers who are planning to shadow a student and want to maximize the value of the experience.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prepare educators for a meaningful shadowing experience, set learning goals, choose an appropriate student to shadow, coordinate logistics, and foster an open mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures the shadowing experience is focused and purposeful. Helps educators identify their learning goals and select a student who can provide valuable insights. Facilitates communication and coordination with key stakeholders. Encourages an open and unbiased approach to observation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Educators can tailor their learning goals, student selection criteria, and coordination efforts to align with their specific needs and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learning goals are clearly defined and aligned with the shadowing experience. Student selection criteria are well-considered. Coordination efforts are thorough and effective. Reflections demonstrate an open and unbiased approach to observation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More focused and impactful shadowing experiences, improved communication and coordination, and a deeper understanding of student experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Educators use a toolkit to define learning goals such as understanding student engagement or college and career readiness. They use a matrix to identify students who meet specific criteria (e.g., year in school, gender, socioeconomic status) and coordinate with the selected student, their parents, and relevant staff members.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: To do this work, a teacher must be confident in her belief that such discussions are essential for students' development, that they are part of her curriculum, that they're important for helping students understand their world and giving them hope that they can change this world. Teachers need administrators to back them up, and they need their colleagues' support, too. Most teachers make sure that their plans and activities tied to addressing racism reflect state standards, and send a letter to students' parents or guardians, outlining what students will be doing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Administrative and collegial support, a clear curriculum plan, and effective communication skills.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to address parental concerns or align activities with state standards.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, administrators, and parents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure administrative and collegial support for discussions about race, communicate plans to parents and guardians, and align activities with state standards

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds support for discussions about race, promotes transparency, and ensures alignment with educational standards.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Communications with parents can be tailored to their specific concerns and questions. Teachers can provide different levels of detail based on parent preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection
  • Argument Construction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track parental feedback and support, review curriculum plans for alignment with state standards, and gather feedback from administrators and colleagues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Preparing for parental reactions can build support for discussions about race, promote transparency, and ensure alignment with educational standards.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher sending a letter to students' parents or guardians, outlining what students will be doing related to discussions about race.

docs.text: Plan and organize instructions beforehand, grouping similar tasks together to streamline the instruction-giving process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Thorough planning and organization.

docs.title: Constraints
