docs.title: Description
docs.text: Building a trusting community is crucial for honest talks about race. Giving students time to reflect and share about their lives creates connections that lay the foundation for fruitful discussions. Highlighting student voices and bringing in diverse experts helps create a safe and inclusive environment. Additionally, recognizing and addressing inequities within the school environment, such as disparities in class placement or disciplinary actions, helps to foster a sense of justice and trust.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection and sharing. Access to diverse experts. A willingness to address inequities within the school environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may be hesitant to share their stories. Requires ongoing effort and commitment. May require additional support to address systemic inequities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students and educators who aim to create a trusting and inclusive community where honest talks about race can take place.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build a trusting community. Create a safe and inclusive learning environment. Foster a sense of justice and equity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances trust and rapport. Fosters inclusivity and equity. Creates a safe space for open dialogue.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to share their own stories and experiences. Offers opportunities for diverse experts to share their perspectives. Adapts to the specific needs and interests of the students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation and engagement. Improved classroom climate. Evidence of a more equitable and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced trust and safety: Building a trusting community creates a safer and more inclusive learning environment, fostering open and honest dialogue. Equitable participation: Addressing inequities within the school environment promotes a sense of justice and encourages equitable participation in discussions about race.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Giving students time to reflect and write about their lives. Bringing in diverse experts to speak to the class. Addressing inequities within the school environment, such as disparities in class placement or disciplinary actions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves shifting the focus of internal dialogue from future anxieties to actionable steps in the present to manage overwhelming feelings. It encourages individuals to concentrate on what they can do right now rather than getting caught up in endless streams of worry about the future. By changing internal talk to focus on the manageable present, individuals can take necessary steps to build a better tomorrow, focusing thoughts and inner dialogue on the present moment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness and a willingness to shift focus from future worries to present actions. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying anxiety. Access to resources such as to-do lists, goal-setting templates, or mindfulness apps can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement for individuals with severe anxiety or panic disorders without professional support. Requires consistent effort to maintain focus on the present moment and avoid getting caught up in future worries. May not be effective if not accompanied by a willingness to take action in the present.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals prone to anxiety, procrastination, or feeling overwhelmed by future challenges.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce anxiety about the future, shift focus to actionable steps in the present, promote a sense of control, manage overwhelming feelings, encourage proactive behavior.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety by shifting focus from future worries to present actions. Increases motivation by breaking down overwhelming tasks into manageable steps. Fosters a sense of control by empowering learners to take action in the present. Enhances self-esteem by promoting a sense of accomplishment and progress.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with customized questions tailored to individual anxieties and goals. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through journaling, mindfulness exercises, or goal-setting activities. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as lists of present-focused actions or guided prompts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported anxiety levels using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in productivity, task completion, and proactive behavior. Analyze ability to identify and shift focus from future worries to present actions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that focusing on the present moment can reduce anxiety and improve well-being (e.g., American Psychological Association). Studies show that mindfulness practices can enhance attention and promote emotional regulation. Regularly engaging in present-focused activities can foster a sense of control and reduce stress.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual feeling anxious about an upcoming deadline breaks down the task into smaller, present-focused steps, such as 'I will spend the next hour outlining the report.' A student feeling overwhelmed by a challenging course focuses on completing one assignment at a time, rather than worrying about the entire course. Resource: American Psychological Association – Mindfulness Can Help Improve Mental Well-Being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pretend play, also known as dramatic play or make-believe, involves learners exploring imagined situations and roles. It fosters communication, social awareness, relationship skills, and can integrate math skills through activities like shopping lists, measuring in a play kitchen, or creating a cash register. It allows children to explore and develop their Social Awareness and Relationship Skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom or play area. Props such as shopping lists, plastic measuring cups, or paper money. Integration with math activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on the learners' engagement and willingness to participate. May not be effective if the learner does not understand the scenario or lacks interest.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Toddlers (1-3), Preschoolers (3-5), Kindergartners (5-6)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance communication skills, develop social and emotional skills, integrate mathematical concepts, foster imagination and creativity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops social skills by interacting with peers in various simulated scenarios. Supports the development of emotional skills by allowing learners to explore and express their feelings in a safe environment. Strengthens mathematical skills through integration with counting, measuring, and problem-solving activities within play scenarios.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable based on learners' interests and cultural backgrounds. Different themes and scenarios can be introduced to cater to various preferences. Tools and props used can be selected based on the learner's developmental level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' communication skills, interaction with peers, and integration of math concepts during play. Track the level of engagement and creativity displayed during the play scenarios.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports development of language, social-emotional, and math skills. Enhances creativity and problem-solving abilities through engagement in imagined scenarios. Builds Social Awareness and Relationship Skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A preschool classroom uses dramatic and pretend play to support student learning, focusing on communication and Social Awareness and Relationship Skills. The Supermarket - Game for Kids allows learners to pretend play with interactions at a supermarket.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Prepare learners for upcoming tasks or materials. Previewing is one of the simplest and most flexible strategies. This can be used for all students, especially those with trouble staying organized, impulse control problems, or difficulties paying attention. Tailor what you preview and when according to the students’ needs - then follow through.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ability to plan ahead and anticipate learner needs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with anxiety, attention challenges, or difficulty with organization.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Set expectations, reduce anxiety, and improve focus.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety, improves focus, and promotes proactive learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor content of preview based on individual learner needs and challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' preparedness and engagement with upcoming tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced anxiety, improved focus, and increased engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before a reading assignment, the teacher provides a brief summary of the main points and key vocabulary.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage in brainstorming before beginning to draft a composition. Has a positive impact on the final written product. Prewriting activities can be done individually or as a collaborative process. Prewriting activities may be particularly important to low-achieving writers for compensating and overcoming documented weak prior knowledge and vocabulary. Engaging learners and supporting vocabulary development and background knowledge through prereading strategies can support writing about the topic, too. Generate lists, word webs, and personal glossaries that can help writers demonstrate what they know.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Brainstorming techniques, graphic organizers, vocabulary lists

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort, effectiveness depends on activity engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates idea generation, supports vocabulary development, improves writing quality

docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to different topics and writing tasks.

docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased idea generation, greater vocabulary use

docs.text: • Prewriting activities help low-achieving writers to compensate and overcome documented weak prior knowledge and vocabulary

docs.title: Primary Language Support with Bilingual Texts
Description
docs.text: Using bilingual picture books and resources in a learner's primary language to support their comprehension and engagement with new content. This strategy leverages the learner's existing linguistic knowledge to scaffold understanding and facilitate exposure to English or other target languages. It can be implemented by incorporating bilingual texts in classroom libraries, using websites like the International Digital Children's Library, and providing access to digital books in multiple languages. This approach not only aids in language acquisition but also validates the learner's cultural and linguistic background.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to bilingual books, digital libraries, or online resources. Educators need to be aware of and value the linguistic diversity of their learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Availability of bilingual resources may be limited for certain languages. Educators need to ensure that the materials are high-quality and culturally appropriate.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Bi- and multilingual learners, especially those who are developing proficiency in a new language.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support comprehension in bi- and multilingual learners, provide exposure to English, validate cultural and linguistic backgrounds.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comprehension by leveraging existing linguistic knowledge, increases engagement through culturally relevant materials, and supports language acquisition by providing exposure to the target language.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of bilingual books and resources to cater to different languages and reading levels. Allow learners to choose texts that align with their interests and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and comprehension when using bilingual texts. Assess their ability to make connections between their primary language and the target language.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that using learners' primary language as a bridge to learning new languages enhances comprehension and promotes positive attitudes towards learning.

docs.title: Prioritizing Agency for Students With Disabilities
Description
docs.text: Prioritizing agency for students with disabilities involves fostering self-advocacy and self-determination skills to enable them to engage more effectively in their education. This includes understanding their rights and needs, communicating them effectively, solving problems, setting goals, and reflecting actively. Engaging students in their IEP meetings and providing hands-on learning opportunities are key components of this approach.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to prioritize self-advocacy and self-determination, provide tangible opportunities for practice, and fully engage students in decision-making processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset and a significant investment of time, resources, and training.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-advocacy and self-determination skills, improve educational and life outcomes, and empower students to take an active role in their learning and lives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness, improves communication skills, increases student independence, and enhances their ability to navigate challenges in education and beyond.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Involves individualized instruction and support tailored to the specific needs and goals of each student.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Modeling
  • Articulation
  • Consensus-Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student participation in decision-making meetings, monitor their ability to articulate their needs, and observe improvements in their educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students who practice self-advocacy and self-determination skills have improved educational and life outcomes compared to those who don't.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Involving students in their IEP meetings, providing hands-on learning opportunities such as service learning and work-based learning, and teaching explicit skills like goal setting and problem solving.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making self-advocacy and self-determination critical priorities in education systems involves prioritizing them throughout, such as by incorporating them into teacher preparation and assessments of learning and through associated measures of school performance such as chronic absenteeism. This can be done by setting explicit goals in student IEPs and assessing them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Policy changes, training for educators, assessment tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant changes in education systems. May be challenging to implement and sustain.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Education systems, policymakers, educators, and students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prioritize self-advocacy, improve educational systems, enhance school performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances educational quality, improves student outcomes, promotes a culture of self-advocacy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different educational contexts. Goals can be tailored to specific needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved teacher preparation, enhanced assessments, reduced chronic absenteeism

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Education systems prioritize self-advocacy and self-determination, leading to improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Incorporating self-advocacy into teacher preparation programs. Assessing self-advocacy skills as part of student assessments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Probing questions are used to encourage deeper reflection and critical thinking by challenging assumptions, exploring reasons and evidence, considering different viewpoints, examining implications, and questioning the basis of the inquiry itself. R.W. Paul's six types of Socratic questions include: Questions for clarification, Questions that probe assumptions, Questions that probe reasons and evidence, Questions about Viewpoints and Perspectives, Questions that probe implications and consequences, and Questions about the question. Probing questions help learners to explore material more deeply by making connections, summarizing, and assessing understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator to guide the discussion. May require learners to have some background knowledge on the topic.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are not comfortable with open-ended questioning. Effectiveness depends on the facilitator's ability to guide discussion.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for higher education and professional development.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking skills, promote deeper understanding, and encourage self-reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages critical analysis, promotes deeper engagement with content, provides immediate feedback, supports self-reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Question types can be adapted to different learner needs and content areas. Learners can generate their own questions to guide inquiry.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment
  • Inquiry-Based Exploration
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze the depth and specificity of learner responses. Track the types of questions learners generate themselves.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking and deeper understanding. Enhances self-reflection and metacognition. Research shows that frequent questioning helps learners retain information and make instructional adjustments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses probing questions to encourage students to analyze evidence from multiple texts in a Socratic seminar. ThinkCerca uses prompts and questions to encourage students to reflect on what they have learned and to engage with a digital text during a mini-lesson.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing students with real-life problem scenarios (e.g., cheating, bullying) and having them analyze the situation, consider possible consequences, share their decisions, and reflect on their reasoning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Prepared problem scenarios, class time for analysis and discussion, and materials for recording decisions and reflections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Scenarios may not always reflect the specific experiences or cultural backgrounds of all learners. Some learners may dominate discussions. Students may struggle to apply the skills to real-life situations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance problem-solving skills, promote ethical decision-making, develop empathy, improve communication skills, and encourage reflection on decision-making processes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical application of decision-making skills, encourages collaborative problem-solving, promotes understanding of different perspectives, and fosters self-reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios can be tailored to align with specific age groups, interests, or real-world situations. Learners can be given options for how to present their decisions and reflections. Support can be provided for analyzing situations and evaluating consequences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Case Study

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions. Review student-generated analyses of scenarios. Evaluate student reflections on their decision-making processes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Case-based learning has been shown to increase student engagement, develop critical thinking skills, and enhance problem-solving abilities. Real-world scenarios make learning more relevant and meaningful.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Present a scenario where a student is caught cheating and have students analyze the situation, consider possible consequences, share their decisions, and reflect on their reasoning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The 'draw a picture' strategy is a problem-solving technique in which learners make a visual representation of the problem. This intermediate step between language-as-text and the symbolic language of mathematics allows students to begin to think about the problem mathematically. Pictures and diagrams are also good ways of describing solutions to problems; therefore, they are an important part of mathematical communication.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Emphasizing and valuing the process of learning, rather than solely focusing on grades, promotes a growth mindset and encourages learners to embrace challenges. When learners prioritize the learning process, they are more likely to view intelligence as malleable and see effort as a path to mastery. In contrast, focusing on grades can lead learners to equate their self-worth with their academic performance, fostering a fixed mindset. Instructors should design learning experiences that highlight the importance of exploration, experimentation, and reflection. Providing opportunities for learners to make mistakes, learn from them, and revise their work can reinforce the value of the learning process. Encouraging learners to set goals, track their progress, and reflect on their learning strategies can further enhance their focus on the process of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A shift in focus from grades to learning. Design of engaging and meaningful learning activities. Opportunities for exploration, experimentation, and reflection. Supportive feedback that emphasizes the learning process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require a significant shift in mindset for both learners and instructors. Some learners may initially resist a focus on the process rather than the outcome. Requires careful planning to ensure that learning activities are both engaging and aligned with learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who are grade-focused or who have a fear of failure

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage exploration, enhance self-reflection, and improve learning outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to take risks and experiment. Promotes a deeper understanding of the material. Reduces anxiety associated with grades and performance. Fosters a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learning activities can be tailored to individual learner interests and needs. Learners can choose the pace at which they progress through the material. Instructors can provide individualized feedback that focuses on the learning process.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in learner attitudes towards learning. Measure the depth of learner understanding. Assess the quality of learner reflections. Observe changes in learner engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that emphasizing the learning process enhances motivation, persistence, and overall learning outcomes (reference Dweck's research on mindset and learning). A focus on the process promotes a growth mindset and reduces fear of failure (reference research on resilience).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Encouraging learners to keep a learning journal to reflect on their progress and challenges. Providing opportunities for learners to revise their work based on feedback. Designing project-based learning activities that require learners to explore, experiment, and solve problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Brainstorm with students a process for constructive decision-making and display it in the classroom as a visual reminder of how to make good choices. The process involves steps such as staying calm, observing and identifying the problem, stopping to think and analyze the situation, capturing thoughts as you consider choices and consequences, making a choice to solve the problem, and evaluating and reflecting on the outcome.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A process for constructive decision-making, a way to display the process in the classroom, and a willingness to help students develop constructive decision-making skills.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Process writing uses journals to encourage writing skills from the beginning levels of English proficiency. Learners write frequently, focusing on communication rather than perfect grammar. Mistakes are addressed gradually, based on material covered in class. Journal entries are written on one side of the page, with teacher feedback on the back. Topics can include hobbies, work, or observations. It eases learners’ fears about producing subpar written work, encouraging them to improve their writing abilities. Only mistakes made in grammar and vocabulary that has been covered up to the current point in time should be corrected.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Notebooks, regular writing prompts, teacher feedback, class time for writing and review

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent teacher feedback, may not suit learners who need immediate error correction

docs.text: • Beginning to advanced ESL/EFL learners, particularly adults

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing skills, encourage communication despite errors, reinforce classroom learning

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: • Encourages writing from early stages, promotes gradual skill development, aligns instruction with learner progress. Addresses the reality that adults are often hesitant to produce written or spoken work that is not up to the same level as their native language skills.

docs.text: Includes many related activities, including a greatly increased quantity of writing (only some of which is completed to publication) and a focus on writing throughout the course, along with mini-lessons on embedded skills. Modeling of writing by instructors. It is a professional development model as well, and results seen in students’ writing are correlated to teachers’ training in the approach. Instructional activities of sentence combining and inquiry are part of the approach.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When learners are flagged for rapid guessing during assessments, proctors should approach them, pause their test, and engage them in a low-pressure conversation about what’s going on. Students might be rushing through the test for any number of personal reasons, including confusion and anxiety. Proctors can take this opportunity to see what’s going on for the student and address the issue sensitively before encouraging them to resume the test. The goal is to help students understand the importance of assessment, not to pressure them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Real-time monitoring of assessment data, trained proctors who can engage in supportive conversations with learners, a non-judgmental approach.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources for proctor training, effectiveness depends on proctor’s ability to build rapport with learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who show signs of rapid guessing during assessments, particularly those who may be experiencing confusion or anxiety.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce instances of rapid guessing, improve engagement and focus, address underlying reasons for disengagement, increase validity of assessment data.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses disengagement in real-time, helps learners understand the importance of assessment, provides a supportive environment to address underlying issues.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Producing counter-texts involves crafting alternative versions of existing texts to highlight missing perspectives, challenge stereotypes, and address biases. Learners rewrite texts from different points of view, recognizing power structures and critically evaluating messages. Formats include rewritten fairy tales, historical accounts from marginalized perspectives, or responses to biased media.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to have a solid understanding of the original text. May be challenging for learners with limited writing or creative skills.

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical literacy, enhance composition skills, challenge stereotypes, empower learners to critically evaluate messages and voice their views

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking, develops empathy, enhances understanding of power dynamics, encourages self-expression

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Project-based learning (PBL) is an instructional approach that engages learners in real-world, complex problems or challenges. Learners research, plan, and create solutions, developing skills in collaboration, communication, critical thinking, and creativity. PBL involves inquiry, student choice, multimodal tools, collaboration, and reflection. Effective implementation includes managing groups, monitoring progress, and providing ongoing feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful and intentional planning, access to technology and resources, and a supportive learning environment. Project management tools and regular feedback mechanisms are essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to implement in online or hybrid learning environments if not carefully planned. Requires significant time for planning, execution, and assessment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12, higher education, and professional development settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop skills in collaboration, communication, critical thinking, and creativity. Connect learning to real-world issues and contexts. Promote deeper understanding through inquiry and problem-solving.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement and motivation by connecting learning to real-world issues. Develops 21st-century skills, fosters agency, and promotes authentic assessment. Encourages metacognition and self-evaluation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for student choice in project topics and methods of presentation. Can be adapted to different learning styles through multimodal tools and flexible group structures.

docs.text: • Improved outcomes in elementary science and social studies: Research indicates increased engagement and achievement through hands-on, inquiry-based projects. Enhanced equity: Benefits learners regardless of geography, socio-economics, race, ethnicity, or special needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Project Based Learning is a teaching method in which learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to investigate and respond to an engaging and complex question, problem, or challenge. Learners tackle authentic problems in the world and accomplish tangible change while learning. Research indicates positive gains in achievement and content knowledge, self-confidence, collaboration, and engagement. PBL helps learners develop skills for living in a knowledge-based, highly technological society, brings new relevance to the learning at hand, lends itself to authentic assessment, promotes lifelong learning, and accommodates learners with varying learning styles and differences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation, access to resources and materials, and a supportive learning environment. Instructors need to facilitate and guide learners through the project, providing support and feedback as needed.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. May require significant upfront planning and preparation. Learners may struggle with self-direction and time management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, increase content knowledge, enhance self-confidence, foster collaboration, promote engagement, and encourage lifelong learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a way to tackle authentic problems in the world and accomplish tangible change while learning. Learners see the relevance of the learning, as PBL helps them develop skills for living in a knowledge-based, highly technological society.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Projects can be designed to align with learners' individual interests, needs, and learning styles. Flexible project topics and assessment methods allow for personalized learning experiences.

docs.text: • Track learner progress on project milestones, assess the quality of their final product, and evaluate their ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems. Measure gains in content knowledge, self-confidence, collaboration, and engagement through pre- and post-assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates positive gains in achievement and content knowledge, self-confidence, collaboration, and engagement. Improved learner outcomes and increased motivation. Increased ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • My Restaurant Project: Students remedy a food desert situation in their neighborhood by planning out a healthy restaurant, including nutritional facts for all the dishes, food costs, grant proposals, and cash flow models. Geodesic Greenhouses: Learners design a geodesic greenhouse, to allow people to grow fresh vegetables, flowers, fruit and herbs year-round, with minimal extra heating or cooling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Project-Based Learning (PBL) is a teaching method where learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period to investigate and respond to an engaging and complex question, problem, or challenge. In math, PBL involves tackling authentic, real-world problems, allowing learners to apply mathematical concepts in practical ways. Key components include real-world problems with no single solution, learners working in groups and being self-directed, and instructors serving as facilitators.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes learning more engaging and relevant. Improves learning outcomes and retention. Builds essential skills for college, career, and life. Provides opportunities to use technology. Connects learners with communities and the real world.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This instructional strategy involves students working in small groups to identify and propose solutions to crucial problems in their society. Students are tasked with transforming the United States by coming up with 15 crucial problems and 15 laws to address those problems. They then must decide how to enforce each law, such as by fines, rewards, prison sentences, reliance on propaganda, and economic stimuli. This involves identifying issues, developing potential solutions, and considering the practical and ethical implications of their proposals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sufficient time for group work, access to resources for researching societal issues, and clear guidelines for ethical and respectful communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for students to propose inappropriate or offensive solutions. Requires careful facilitation to ensure ethical considerations and prevent the reinforcement of harmful stereotypes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school students, particularly those in advanced English or social studies classes, but adaptable to college and adult learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance problem-solving skills, promote critical thinking about societal issues, foster collaboration and compromise, and encourage consideration of diverse perspectives.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes engagement and ownership of learning, encourages real-world problem-solving, and enhances understanding of complex social issues. It also fosters collaboration and communication skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different societal contexts and student interests. Teachers can adjust the scope and complexity of the project based on student abilities and available resources.

docs.text: • Experience shows that students appreciate how hard it is to compromise and solve national problems to everyone's satisfaction. A few students begin to question simplistic solutions. Some students are shocked to discover how many of their classmates think differently from them, which is not surprising, considering that many have not been allowed to talk about controversial subjects at school.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Promoting a growth mindset involves giving feedback that values effort and encourages persistence. In mathematics, students often think that intelligence is fixed. By valuing effort and encouraging persistence, teachers can show students that there is always room for them to improve their skills. This helps students develop a more positive attitude toward learning and encourages them to persevere through challenges.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to shift their focus from assessing innate ability to assessing effort and progress. They should be prepared to provide specific, actionable feedback that focuses on students’ strategies and approaches.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in classrooms where traditional assessment methods are heavily emphasized. Requires a significant shift in teacher mindset and instructional practices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners in all subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a growth mindset, encourage persistence, improve attitudes toward learning, increase self-efficacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports the development of a growth mindset and encourages students to persevere through challenges. It helps students see learning as a process of continuous improvement and encourages them to take risks and embrace new challenges. It can also lead to increased self-efficacy and a more positive attitude toward learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor feedback to individual students, focusing on their effort, strategies, and progress. They can also provide opportunities for students to reflect on their own learning and identify areas for improvement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students’ attitudes toward learning through observation and participation. Collect feedback from students on their perceptions of the classroom environment and their feelings about their own learning. Analyze student work to identify evidence of effort, persistence, and a growth mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that promoting a growth mindset can lead to increased motivation, improved performance, and a more positive attitude toward learning. Students are more likely to persevere through challenges and achieve their goals when they believe that their abilities can be developed through effort and practice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Giving feedback in ways that values effort and encourages persistence, which can show students that there is always room for them to improve their skills.

docs.title: Promote a Growth Mindset in Math
Description
docs.text: Promote a growth mindset by giving feedback that values effort and encourages persistence, showing learners that there is always room to improve their skills. In mathematics in particular, learners often think that intelligence is fixed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent feedback, a focus on effort and strategies, and a classroom culture that values growth and improvement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset for both learners and teachers, may be challenging to implement in traditional, performance-focused classrooms.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with math or have a fixed mindset about their math abilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage effort and persistence, foster a growth mindset, promote continuous improvement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages persistence, promotes a growth mindset, and helps learners see themselves as capable of improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide specific and meaningful feedback on individual learner efforts and strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner persistence, monitor increased effort and engagement, and assess the development of a growth mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that promoting a growth mindset increases persistence, improves problem-solving skills, and leads to greater academic success in math.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of saying, 'You're good at math,' say, 'I can see you worked really hard on this, and it paid off!' or 'I like the way you kept trying different strategies until you found one that worked.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Promoting a growth mindset, particularly in mathematics, encourages learners to believe that intelligence is not fixed. Feedback that values effort and encourages persistence, rather than focusing solely on innate ability, can show students that there is always room for them to improve their skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A focus on the learning process rather than just the end result.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If praise is not genuine or specific, it may be ineffective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who may view intelligence as a fixed trait.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage persistence, and improve learning outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces the value of effort and perseverance. Encourages learners to embrace challenges and see mistakes as opportunities for growth. Promotes a positive self-image and reduces fear of failure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Feedback can be tailored to individual learner efforts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure the depth of learner understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that effort-based praise enhances motivation and performance, while intelligence-based praise can undermine it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Say 'I can see you worked really hard on this, and it paid off!' instead of saying 'You're so smart!'

docs.title: Promoting Belonging Through Cues and Representations
Description
docs.text: Promoting belonging involves using small, but powerful cues in the environment to foster a sense of connection and recognition. This includes incorporating representations of all students in the classroom to validate their identities and experiences. Strategies include using simple cues and inclusive representations to create a welcoming and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of student diversity, intentional design of classroom environment, commitment to inclusion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort to maintain an inclusive environment, potential challenges in addressing sensitive topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and educators in diverse classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a sense of belonging, create a welcoming environment, validate student identities, foster inclusion

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances student motivation, improves engagement, fosters a sense of community, and supports overall well-being.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor cues and representations to reflect the specific backgrounds and experiences of their students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation, classroom climate, student feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that when students feel they belong, they are more motivated, engaged, and ultimately show higher performance. Inclusive classrooms can improve academic outcomes and overall well-being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers promote belonging in the math classroom through instructional choices and practices that address equity and opportunity. Developing healthy mindsets and using equity-based teaching practices help create a sense of belonging.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training on promoting belonging, understanding of diverse learners, and commitment to creating an inclusive classroom.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and sensitivity. May require additional resources to support students who have experienced marginalization or discrimination.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • PreK-12 and higher education teachers and school and district leaders.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a sense of belonging, improve academic motivation, enhance achievement, and promote mental and physical health.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student motivation, fosters a positive classroom environment, and supports academic success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows teachers to tailor strategies to meet the specific needs of individual students and address different types of barriers to belonging.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student engagement, higher academic performance, increased self-esteem, and positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced academic success, greater sense of belonging, and a more equitable learning environment.

docs.title: Promoting Self-Determination and Self-Advocacy in Students with Disabilities
Description
docs.text: Fostering self-determination and self-advocacy involves empowering students with disabilities to understand their needs, rights, and goals, and to actively participate in decisions about their education and lives. This includes teaching skills such as goal setting, problem-solving, communication, and reflection. By prioritizing these skills, educators help students develop agency and improve their educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to prioritize self-determination and self-advocacy. Needs a supportive environment where students feel safe to express their needs and make choices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may initially lack the skills and confidence to advocate for themselves. Requires ongoing support and reinforcement to build self-determination skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities, their families, and educators.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students with disabilities to actively participate in their education, develop agency, and improve their life outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement and investment in learning. Fosters a sense of agency and control. Improves educational and life outcomes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide individualized support and instruction based on students' specific needs and abilities. Offer diverse opportunities for students to practice self-advocacy skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in IEP meetings and other decision-making processes. Track changes in students' self-confidence, self-advocacy skills, and academic outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that students who practice self-advocacy skills and self-determination have improved educational and life outcomes. These skills are essential for success in postsecondary education, the workforce, and civic life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students participate in their IEP meetings, setting goals and discussing their needs. Students engage in hands-on learning opportunities, such as service learning and work-based learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Promoting self-directed learning involves explicitly teaching students strategies for problem-solving, metacognition, and self-reflection to become independent learners. This approach includes providing opportunities to practice these strategies and reflect on their effectiveness. Teachers help students name their processes and give them the language to match what they did, providing them with strategies they can use in future struggles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in problem-solving, metacognitive, and self-reflection strategies; opportunities for practice and feedback; and resources to support students in reflecting on their learning processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort from both students and teachers to develop and implement effective strategies. Students may initially resist taking responsibility for their learning or struggle to articulate their thought processes.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and learning levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, enhance metacognitive awareness, improve self-reflection abilities, foster independence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students to take control of their learning, provides them with tools and strategies to overcome challenges, and promotes a deeper understanding of their learning processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor the strategies to meet individual student needs and provide personalized feedback to help students refine their approaches. Language prompts and strategy lists can be co-authored with students to ensure relevance and engagement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to apply strategies to solve problems, their level of metacognitive awareness, and their capacity for self-reflection. Measure students' independence and self-direction in their learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that self-directed learning strategies lead to improved problem-solving skills, metacognitive awareness, and academic outcomes. Students become more engaged, motivated, and successful in their learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers provide math problems to make students feel 'stuck', then prompt them to name their processes and strategies for getting 'unstuck'. Lists of strategies and language prompts are co-authored with students to support their self-talk and communication with partners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Prompt cards, particularly emotion cue cards, offer accessible reminders of self-regulation strategies. Students can keep these cards on hand and reference them when emotions escalate or they feel a loss of control. Consistent use of these cards can help internalize strategies, supporting emotional self-regulation and moving coping mechanisms into long-term memory. The cards can include a range of strategies, such as squeezing a fidget toy or taking a mindfulness break. The cards prompt the user to identify their own emotions, teach calming strategies, and encourage practice of those strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires the creation or purchase of prompt cards. The cards should be readily accessible to the learner. Regular practice and reinforcement of the strategies are necessary for long-term effectiveness.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective in cases of severe emotional dysregulation or mental health conditions. The cards are most effective when used proactively, before emotions escalate to an unmanageable level.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages, especially those who struggle with emotional regulation, including children, adolescents, and adults.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support emotional regulation, teach coping strategies, promote self-awareness, and facilitate the internalization of calming techniques.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate reminders of coping strategies, supports self-reflection on emotional states, and promotes the development of self-regulation skills. The visual cues on the cards can be especially helpful for learners who benefit from visual aids.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The content of the cards can be tailored to individual needs and preferences, including specific coping strategies that are most effective for each learner. The cards can be customized with personal images or phrases.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and effectiveness of card use during moments of emotional distress. Track the learner's ability to independently apply the strategies over time. Gather feedback from learners on the usefulness of the cards and specific strategies.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional regulation and self-awareness: Regular use of prompt cards can help learners develop a greater awareness of their emotions and effective coping strategies. Promotes internalization of calming techniques: Consistent use of the cards can lead to the internalization of strategies, making them more readily available in moments of need.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Liz's Early Learning Spot provides free calming strategy cards in multiple languages. TestingMom offers social-emotional flashcards to help students identify and express emotions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Pair strategy instruction with written prompts to guide students toward independence. Prompts can ask students to systematically look for evidence that supports and refutes key claims. To examine relevance and accuracy, have students consider the quality of the content. To determine reliability and perspective, they should consider the author and his or her agenda in relation to his or her affiliations. Cross-checking claims between multiple sources can help adolescents recognize ideas they might otherwise ignore, weigh the usefulness (and reliability) of these ideas against what they previously believed to be true, and consider that new ideas may actually be more accurate than their original thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Written prompts, examples of sources, and a framework for cross-checking claims.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort. Some students may need additional support to understand and apply the prompts effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adolescents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Guide students to systematically evaluate sources, recognize and weigh evidence, and consider new ideas against existing beliefs.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages thorough and unbiased evaluation of sources. Helps learners recognize and weigh evidence, and supports critical thinking and reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be tailored to different subjects, types of sources, and learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review written responses to prompts to assess ability to evaluate sources and weigh evidence. Evaluate ability to recognize and consider new ideas against existing beliefs.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More thorough source evaluation: Students are guided to systematically evaluate sources and weigh evidence. Enhanced critical thinking: Students are better able to recognize and consider new ideas against existing beliefs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use a planning guide to evaluate sources and prompt learners to systematically look for evidence that supports and refutes key claims.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A prompt is a hint or supplementary instructional stimulus that helps a learner make a correct response. Behavioral-science practice identifies three categories of prompt, ordered from least to most intrusive:

  • Verbal prompts — cues, reminders, or instructions delivered verbally (e.g., "Leave a space between words"; "First adjust the object lens").
  • Gestural prompts — a demonstration or gesture that models the step for the learner (e.g., pointing to a microscope's fine adjustment knob and making a turning gesture).
  • Physical prompts — hand-over-hand guidance for learners who lack the fine motor control to follow a verbal or gestural prompt alone (e.g., guiding a child's hand while forming a letter).

Least-to-most prompting is the practice of starting with the least intrusive prompt that might work (verbal) and escalating to gestural or physical only if needed, rather than defaulting to a more intrusive prompt. The rationale is fading: verbal prompts are far easier to withdraw than physical ones, so a learner who becomes dependent on physical prompts will find it harder to demonstrate the skill independently of the teacher.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A clearly defined target skill or response, so the teacher can judge whether a given prompt level is sufficient
  • Willingness to attempt the least intrusive prompt first, even when a more intrusive one might feel faster in the moment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Starting with (or over-relying on) physical prompts risks creating prompt-dependence that is difficult to fade later
  • Prompts are a support for acquiring stimulus control over a correct response, not a permanent substitute for independent performance — the whole rationale for ordering prompts from least to most intrusive is to make eventual fading easier

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners acquiring a new procedural or motor skill who are prone to errors without support
  • Learners with fine-motor-control limitations that make gestural or verbal prompting alone insufficient, for whom physical prompting may be necessary at first

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Errorless or near-errorless initial skill acquisition, followed by independent performance once prompts are faded

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify the target response and anticipate where the learner is likely to need support.
  2. Attempt a verbal prompt first (a cue, reminder, or instruction).
  3. If the verbal prompt is insufficient, escalate to a gestural prompt (demonstration or gesture).
  4. If the gestural prompt is insufficient, escalate to a physical prompt (hand-over-hand guidance).
  5. As the learner succeeds at a given level, drop back to a less intrusive prompt level on subsequent attempts, working toward no prompt at all.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Behavioral Feedback for Correct and Incorrect Responses — prompts precede the learner's response; feedback follows it

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher first says "Don't forget the fine adjustment!" while a student uses a microscope (verbal), only pointing and gesturing at the knob (gestural) if the verbal reminder alone doesn't produce the correct response, and only physically guiding the student's hand (physical) as a last resort.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (1987). Applied behavior analysis. Merrill.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behaviorism in the classroom. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing guiding prompts and questions for students to use when reading or participating in discussions deepens their understanding of texts and gives them space to question and grapple with issues of power, justice, and equity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Thought-provoking questions, supportive discussion environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time, some students may struggle to articulate their thoughts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Deepen understanding, encourage critical thinking, promote reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking, enhances understanding, encourages reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use open-ended questions to allow for varied responses, provide different sets of questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of discussions, depth of understanding, thoughtfulness of responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Deeper student understanding, increased critical thinking, enhanced reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking guiding questions during a class discussion about a novel, providing prompts for a research paper, or using reflective prompts after a group activity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are taught about propaganda techniques and then asked to identify the use of these techniques in online advertising. They reflect on how the interactive medium of online reading can increase or decrease the power of a particular technique.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Examples of online advertisements and instructional materials on propaganda techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness depends on the learners' prior knowledge of propaganda techniques, and they may require guidance in identifying and analyzing them.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase awareness of propaganda techniques and their use in online advertising, and to understand how the interactive nature of online media affects their impact.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking and media literacy skills by enabling learners to recognize and analyze persuasive techniques used in advertising.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The complexity of the propaganda techniques and the advertisements selected for analysis can be adjusted based on the learners' skill level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to accurately identify propaganda techniques and explain their effects in online advertising.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learning about propaganda techniques can increase awareness of manipulative tactics and improve critical media literacy skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Bandura's observational-learning research showed that model consequences shape imitation in both directions: children who watched a model punished for aggressive behavior decreased their own aggression, while children who watched the same behavior praised or simply ignored (not punished) imitated it, including specific words and actions (Bandura, Ross, & Ross, 1961) — see Social Learning Theory. Bandura concluded this dynamic has both prosocial (positive) and antisocial effects: children observe and learn from models' behavior, including parents' own conduct, and tend to copy what a model actually does rather than what the model merely says to do. Research on abuse cycles illustrates the antisocial side: children who grow up witnessing parents manage anger through violence often learn to behave the same way, and roughly 30% of abused children go on to become abusive parents themselves (Murrell, Christoff, & Henning, 2007; U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, 2013).

Prosocial modeling deliberately uses this same mechanism for socially desirable ends: parents, teachers, and public figures (Martin Luther King Jr. and Mahatma Gandhi are commonly cited examples) can function as models who inspire imitation of reading habits, healthy behavior, kindness, courtesy, and honesty — but only if the model's actual behavior, not just their stated expectations, consistently demonstrates the target behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Consistency between what the model says and what the model actually does, since observers copy the latter
  • Live, verbal, or symbolic models (see Social Learning Theory) that are visible and credible to the observer

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Inconsistent modeling ("do as I say, not as I do") undermines the strategy, since the behavior actually observed — not the verbal instruction — is what tends to be copied
  • The same mechanism transmits antisocial as well as prosocial behavior, so an adult modeling aggression, dishonesty, or disengagement risks that behavior being imitated just as readily

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Children and adolescents forming behavioral norms from observed adult and peer behavior
  • Learners at risk of imitating antisocial behavior modeled at home, where deliberately introducing consistent prosocial models (teachers, mentors, public figures) may help counteract it

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Adoption of socially desirable behaviors and values (reading habits, health behaviors, kindness, honesty) through consistent observed example rather than instruction alone

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify the specific prosocial behavior to be modeled (e.g., reading, exercise, honesty).
  2. Ensure the model (teacher, parent, or featured public figure) is consistently seen actually performing the behavior, not only describing or requesting it.
  3. Make the model's engagement visible and discussable (e.g., talking about favorite books while visibly reading them) rather than private or assumed.
  4. Where possible, pair modeling with the natural or social consequences the model experiences, since observers are more motivated to imitate a model they see reinforced rather than punished.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Conditioning Natural Reinforcers — both rely on the target behavior eventually carrying its own reinforcing consequence, whether observed vicariously (modeling) or experienced directly (natural reinforcement)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A parent who wants a child to read keeps books visibly present at home, is seen reading regularly, and talks about favorite books, rather than only telling the child to read.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Bandura, A., Ross, D., & Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575-582.
  • Murrell, A. R., Christoff, K. A., & Henning, K. R. (2007). Characteristics of domestic violence offenders: Associations with childhood exposure to violence. Journal of Family Violence, 22(7), 523-532.
  • U.S. Department of Health & Human Services. (2013). Child maltreatment 2012. Administration for Children and Families.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Social cognitive learning theory. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing easy-access educational tools involves making a variety of resources readily available to students to support their learning. This includes manipulatives, graphic organizers, audio recordings, magnifying paper, highlighters, choice boards, learning menus, and timers. By having these tools easily accessible, students can independently manage their learning and advocate for their needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to gather and organize a variety of learning tools, make them easily accessible to students, and provide instruction on how and when to use each tool.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires resources for acquiring and maintaining the tools. Some students may need additional support to learn how to use the tools effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those with disabilities or diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student independence, improve access to learning materials, and promote self-advocacy and self-regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student independence, promotes self-regulation, and provides accommodations for diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning styles and needs through a variety of tool options.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Resource Evaluation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student use of the tools, track their ability to independently manage their learning, and monitor improvements in academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that providing easy-access educational tools can lead to increased student independence, improved self-regulation, and greater academic success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Storing manipulatives and graphic organizers in hanging file folders or on a bookcase. Making audio recordings and highlighters available for students with disabilities. Providing choice boards and learning menus to diversify learning options.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ensure instructions are given before learners begin their tasks to avoid confusion and errors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful timing and delivery of instructions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time for clarification.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent errors and ensure learners understand the task requirements.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces confusion and ensures learners understand expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to ask clarifying questions before beginning the task.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe task completion rates and accuracy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced errors and improved task completion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher clearly explains the steps for a science experiment before students begin handling materials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are provided with manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete. These tangible aids enable learners to physically interact with the material, making abstract ideas more accessible and understandable. Manipulatives can be especially helpful in math and science, where visualization and hands-on exploration are crucial.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate manipulatives, clear instructions on how to use them, and a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires preparation time for gathering and distributing manipulatives. Some learners may become distracted by the manipulatives if not used effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with abstract concepts, tactile learners, and students who benefit from hands-on activities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make abstract concepts concrete, enhance understanding through hands-on exploration, improve problem-solving skills, and support tactile learners.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tactile experiences, enhances visualization, improves problem-solving skills, and makes learning more engaging.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use a variety of manipulatives to suit different learning styles and content areas. Offer options for using manipulatives individually or in small groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to use manipulatives to solve problems and demonstrate understanding. Assess comprehension through hands-on activities and discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Manipulatives make abstract concepts concrete, enhance understanding, and improve problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete and support processing speed. This strategy involves using physical objects and hands-on materials to illustrate abstract ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Availability of manipulatives, careful planning of activities, and instructor guidance on their effective use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure alignment with learning objectives, may not be suitable for all types of content, and some students may find manipulatives distracting

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who struggle with abstract concepts and benefit from tactile experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make abstract concepts concrete, improve comprehension, and support hands-on learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages multiple senses, reduces cognitive load, provides a physical representation of abstract ideas, and supports active learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Manipulatives can be selected based on subject matter and student needs, with options for different materials and interactive activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student's engagement and understanding through the use of manipulatives. Assess their ability to apply concepts to problem-solving tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that manipulatives improve comprehension, enhance problem-solving skills, and support concrete learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Setting reasonable and realistic expectations, changing modifications for every student, and insisting on high-quality and excellent work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding student needs, setting appropriate expectations

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires awareness of students' backgrounds and needs

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Set realistic expectations, provide modifications, promote high-quality work

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures inclusivity, promotes high standards, supports diverse needs

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailored teaching and curricular materials

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student achievement, meeting high-quality standards

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Teachers who understand that knowing their students well, respecting students' cultural values, and tailoring their teaching and curricular materials to meet diverse needs are able to provide opportunities for student success

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Tailoring teaching and curricular materials to meet diverse needs

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing writing models involves sharing exemplary pieces of writing with learners to illustrate effective writing techniques and structures. Learners analyze these models to identify strengths and areas for improvement, applying these insights to their own writing. This strategy can include teacher-created models, peer writing, or published works. Effective implementation involves guiding learners to observe and critique specific elements, such as structure, transitions, terminology, and use of sources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to well-written models, structured analysis activities, feedback mechanisms. Requires instructor guidance to ensure learners focus on relevant aspects of the models.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may blindly imitate models without critical thinking. Models might not align with all writing contexts or learner needs. Over-reliance on models can stifle creativity and originality.

docs.title: Target Learners
