docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for K–12 and higher education students learning composition and rhetoric

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Illustrate effective writing techniques, develop critical analysis skills, improve writing quality, promote self-reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear examples of effective writing, supports understanding of writing conventions, enhances analytical skills, promotes self-improvement through observation and critique

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Models can be tailored to different genres, skill levels, and individual learner needs. Learners can select models based on their specific writing challenges or interests. Flexible analysis methods accommodate varied learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in learner writing quality as evidenced by better structure, clarity, and use of techniques observed in the models. Increased self-awareness and critical analysis skills demonstrated through reflective writing and peer feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing models enhances writing skills by making effective writing strategies visible and accessible. Observing and analyzing models helps learners internalize effective writing practices, leading to improved writing outcomes. (See Write Alouds Strategy Guide from ReadWriteThink)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school English teacher shares a draft of an education feature article, including detailed feedback from an editor, and asks students for advice on how to address the edits. A publishing platform allows teachers and learners to find different genres of writing that can be used as models.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing easy access to a variety of educational tools empowers students to take control of their learning. This approach involves making resources readily available in the classroom and teaching students how and when to use each tool. Tools include manipulatives, graphic organizers, audio recordings, magnifying paper, highlighters, choice boards, learning menus, and timers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A variety of educational tools, a well-organized classroom environment, and explicit instruction in how and when to use each tool.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires an investment in educational tools and a well-organized classroom environment. Students may initially struggle to use the tools effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with disabilities and other learners who may benefit from increased access to educational tools

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student independence, promote self-directed learning, enhance accessibility, provide accommodations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students to take control of their learning, provides them with tools and strategies to overcome challenges, and promotes a deeper understanding of their learning processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tools can be chosen based on students’ interests and needs to accommodate individual learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' use of educational tools, their engagement in learning, and their ability to overcome challenges. Measure students' independence and self-direction in their learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that access to educational tools leads to improved academic outcomes, increased engagement, and a more supportive learning environment. Students become more confident, capable, and successful in their learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Place value mats can be used in math, and story planners can be used for English language arts. Audio recordings, magnifying paper, and highlighters can provide accommodations for students with disabilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Mature learners decide what to learn when they discover there’s something they need to know or something about which they need to know more. Choosing what to learn involves skill. The content must be identified, questions about it framed, and content boundaries set.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires learners to have sufficient background knowledge and self-regulation skills. Requires teachers to provide a range of content options and resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who lack experience in making decisions about their learning. Requires careful planning to ensure learners have access to high-quality content and resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable to higher education and adult learners, particularly in self-directed learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote independent learning, develop decision-making skills, and increase motivation by allowing learners to pursue areas of interest.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops independent learning skills and self-directedness. Increases motivation by allowing learners to pursue areas of interest. Fosters a sense of ownership over the learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the level of structure and guidance provided. Scaffolds can be used to support learners in identifying content, framing questions, and setting boundaries.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assessment of independent learning skills and self-directedness. Evaluation of content selected and questions framed by learners. Student reflections and self-evaluations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that self-directed learning increases motivation and engagement. Studies indicate that independent learning fosters lifelong learning skills and self-regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students choosing topics for research papers. Learners selecting readings from a collection on a particular topic.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Making educational tools readily available to learners promotes independence and self-directed learning. By storing materials in accessible locations, learners can quickly and independently access the resources they need to support their learning. This approach is particularly helpful for learners who require accommodations or have specific learning preferences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires organizing materials in accessible locations, providing clear instructions on how to use the tools, and encouraging learners to use them independently.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and organization. Some learners may need additional support in learning how to use the tools effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who may struggle to access materials or require accommodations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote learner independence, facilitate self-directed learning, and ensure that all learners have access to the tools they need to succeed.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner autonomy, promotes self-reliance, and reduces reliance on the educator for support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different types of tools and resources based on individual learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' use of tools, track their progress in applying them effectively, and gather feedback on their experiences with different resources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Making tools readily available can lead to increased learner engagement, improved self-efficacy, and greater academic success. (Edutopia article on Getting Students on the Road to Self-Advocacy)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Storing manipulatives and graphic organizers in hanging file folders or digital folders, making audio recordings and highlighters available for learners with disabilities, and providing choice boards and learning menus to showcase learning in various ways.

docs.title: Providing Graphic Organizers or Guided Notes
Description
docs.text: During lectures, providing students with graphic organizers or guided notes helps them pull out the important points and follow the structure of the lecture. This supports students with challenges related to processing speed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Preparation of structured graphic organizers or guided notes aligned with the lecture content.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time to prepare. Effectiveness depends on the relevance and clarity of the provided materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with challenges related to processing speed or note-taking skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve note-taking, enhance information processing, and facilitate comprehension during lectures.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by providing a structured framework for note-taking. Helps learners focus on key information and relationships.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Customize the graphic organizers or guided notes based on individual learning preferences and content complexity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Provide Guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student notes for completeness and accuracy. Gather feedback on whether the materials helped them follow and understand the lecture.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing graphic organizers or guided notes enhances note-taking and information processing, facilitating comprehension during lectures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing manipulatives to help make complex concepts concrete supports understanding and processing, particularly in subjects like math or science. Manipulatives provide a hands-on way to visualize and interact with abstract ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Availability of suitable manipulatives. Integration of manipulatives into instructional activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional preparation and resources. Can be less effective if not integrated thoughtfully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with abstract concepts or benefit from hands-on learning experiences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, and support learners who need a concrete way to understand abstract concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete way to visualize and interact with abstract ideas. Enhances comprehension and retention through active engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select manipulatives that are appropriate for the content and individual learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Concrete modeling
  • Representational drawing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student understanding through manipulation and interaction. Assess improvement in comprehension through problem-solving tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing manipulatives enhances comprehension and improves retention by providing a concrete way to visualize and interact with abstract ideas.

docs.title: Publicize Volunteer Opportunities and Student Involvement
Description
docs.text: Schools outline specific ways for parents to help in the classroom and at school, from inviting parents to watch group presentations to asking them to chaperone field trips. A direct call for volunteers is less daunting than a general statement about the importance of parental involvement. Showcasing student work, such as artwork on display or pep assemblies, also guides parents to students’ successful efforts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly defined volunteer roles, communication channels to recruit volunteers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to find enough volunteers, requires effort to organize and manage volunteer activities

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, educators, and parent volunteers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase parent involvement, showcase student work, build community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear opportunities for involvement, showcases student achievements, builds community

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Volunteer roles can be tailored to match parent skills and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track volunteer hours, gather feedback from parents and educators

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing specific volunteer opportunities and showcasing student achievements can increase parent involvement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners create their own word problems to enhance awareness and sharpen basic math skills, fostering comfort in solving a variety of math problems. This active creation process helps learners become more attuned to the structure and components of word problems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to math resources, tools for writing and solving problems (e.g., paper, pencils), and structured time for learners to create, share, and solve problems.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle with creating problems that are appropriately challenging and aligned with learning objectives. Some learners may be hesitant to share their problems or may be less motivated to solve problems created by their peers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and middle school learners, particularly those studying math and related subjects.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, enhance awareness of math concepts in real-world contexts, promote critical thinking, and foster creativity and confidence in solving math problems.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding of math concepts, enhances problem-solving skills, fosters creativity, and builds confidence in solving a variety of math problems. Learners become more aware of the structure and components of word problems, which aids in comprehension and application.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Problems can be tailored to different skill levels, math operations, and real-world contexts. Learners can choose the type of problem they want to create, the complexity of the problem, and the settings in which the problem is situated.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Problem Presentation
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and complexity of problems created by learners. Assess the accuracy and completeness of solutions provided by learners. Observe learner engagement and participation in the problem-solving process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Word problem creation helps pupils encounter and solve basic math problems and become more aware of these problems, sharpening their skills of basic maths.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learners create their own word problems, which can then be used in class activities or assessments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Puppet shows can be used to act out different scenarios and explore the emotions of the characters involved. After the show, learners discuss the emotions displayed and how the puppets coped with them, promoting emotional understanding and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires puppets and a stage or performance area. A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the chosen scenarios. Some learners may be shy about performing or using puppets.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood and elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, improve problem-solving skills, promote empathetic understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe and engaging way to explore complex emotions. Encourages creativity and imaginative play.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios and puppet characters can be adapted to reflect diverse cultural backgrounds and experiences. Learners can create their own puppet shows.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' participation and engagement in the puppet show and discussion. Assess their ability to identify and discuss the emotions displayed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that dramatic play and puppet shows can enhance emotional development and social skills. (Source: The Benefits of Dramatic Play and Puppet Shows - https://www.earlychildhoodaustralia.org.au/our-publications/every-child-magazine/every-child-index/benefits-dramatic-play-puppet-shows/)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are given a specific purpose for reading, typically in the form of discussion questions about the content prepared by the teacher. They review these questions before reading and prepare answers while reading the text. Afterward, they discuss the questions with a partner. This strategy focuses attention, activates prior knowledge, and enhances comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pre-prepared discussion questions related to the reading content.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the questions. Some learners may focus too narrowly on finding answers rather than engaging deeply with the text.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Focus attention, activate prior knowledge, and enhance comprehension by providing a clear purpose for reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear focus, encourages active reading, and promotes collaborative discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to match different proficiency levels and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality of discussions and the answers provided. Collect feedback on how well the questions guided their reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances reading comprehension, promotes active engagement with the text, and improves the ability to extract relevant information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about the American Civil War, learners might be asked, 'What were the main causes of the Civil War?' or 'How did the Civil War impact American society?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors can allocate class time specifically for getting to know learners through various activities. Sitting with learners during group work facilitates learning more about them. One-on-one conferences allow learners to share information, fostering connections. Before and after class, instructors can engage with learners, uncovering their interests and building rapport. This strategy makes content personal and relevant by integrating learners' experiences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated class time, incorporation of individual or small-group activities, and willingness of the instructor to share personal anecdotes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Time constraints, curriculum demands, and careful planning are needed to balance content delivery and relationship-building activities. Relevance of the activity to learners’ lives must be considered to foster authentic engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve relationships by scheduling purposeful activities with the learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Integrates relationship-building into the curriculum, making content personal and relevant. Facilitates learning more about the learners while they learn the content. Enhances motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The instructor can tailor content-related activities and discussions to the learners' interests and personal experiences, making the learning more relevant and meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe increased learner participation, positive feedback, and reduced behavioral issues. The instructor can gather insights into learner interests and experiences through class discussions and individual responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that personalizing content and curriculum can enhance motivation and engagement in learners, fostering a sense of relevance and connection to the material. This can increase Motivation in adult learners as it incorporates relevant real-world application and enhances learner autonomy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encourage students to go beyond surface-level analysis and consider how sentence structure and other elements create meaning. Give them time to reread and think.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material. Time for reflection and analysis. A classroom environment that values critical thinking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with deeper analysis. Requires careful scaffolding and support. May be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for promoting critical thinking and analytical skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking skills, promote deeper understanding of text, develop the ability to analyze complex relationships between elements of writing, encourage thoughtful reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Challenges students to think beyond the obvious. Encourages them to consider multiple layers of meaning. Creates a more engaging and intellectually stimulating learning experience.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students are given the freedom to explore their own interpretations. The teacher can provide prompts and questions to guide their analysis. Students can work independently or in groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation in discussions. Student reflections on their analysis. Analysis of student writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that encouraging deeper analysis improves critical thinking skills and promotes a more nuanced understanding of text.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students are asked to analyze how sentence structure contributes to the overall tone of a poem. Students work in groups to identify patterns and relationships between different elements of a short story. Students reflect on how their understanding of a text changes after analyzing it in detail.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly discuss empathy with students and integrate it into existing lessons. Define empathy as a class. Identify characters in stories, novels, or plays that demonstrate empathy. Use the design-thinking model for empathizing with the user by identifying their thoughts, feelings, values, and worries. When requiring a presentation, ask students to empathize with their audience. When introducing behavioral expectations, role-play different scenarios and brainstorm how empathy could change or shape those scenarios.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Integration into lesson plans, access to relevant resources (stories, design-thinking models), time for role-playing and discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and integration, may be challenging in overly structured curricula, and depends on student engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators across all subjects, higher education instructors, curriculum developers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance students’ understanding of empathy, integrate empathy into various subjects, promote empathetic problem-solving, create a culture of caring and respect

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens social and emotional learning, promotes critical thinking, fosters positive classroom dynamics, encourages real-world application of empathy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor activities to suit different age groups, subject areas, and classroom contexts; use diverse literature and scenarios that reflect student experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Role Reversal

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student understanding of empathy through written assignments, class discussions, and role-playing activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases social awareness, improves classroom climate, enhances students' abilities to understand and relate to others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Discuss empathic characters in literature, use design thinking to empathize with users, role-play scenarios with empathetic responses.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Assigning homework that reinforces learning, encourages real-world application, and offers enriching experiences. These assignments should be designed to be meaningful, low-stakes, and aligned with learning goals. Encouraging learners to use the language they are learning in real-life situations, such as conversations with native speakers or writing emails or messages, can reinforce the material and provide opportunities for spacing out learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires thoughtful design of homework assignments. Access to resources and tools for completing assignments. Clear instructions and expectations for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to create meaningful homework assignments for all topics. Requires time for learners to complete and instructors to review and provide feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially effective for adults and those in language learning programs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, encourage real-world application, enhance engagement, provide meaningful practice, promote long-term retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities to apply learning in real-world contexts. Reinforces concepts and promotes long-term retention. Encourages engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can tailor homework assignments to individual student interests and skill levels. Students can choose from a variety of assignment options.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review homework submissions to assess learning progress. Monitor student engagement and participation in homework assignments. Gather feedback from learners on the relevance and value of assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Quality homework assignments can improve retention, enhance engagement, and promote real-world application of learning. Using collaborative tools like Flip can encourage peer-to-peer discussions and presentation skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking an elder in their family about how the students themselves were as babies (conducted in their home language). Use the target language in class by talking to a partner about their childhood, using imperfect vs. preterite—if you’re a Spanish teacher—in an engaging and real-life focused way.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Question-based eLearning design is an instructional approach that replaces the traditional expository method with a more inquiry-based one. Instead of presenting information as statements, learners are posed with questions and invited to gather information to answer them, promoting active exploration and critical thinking. This can be achieved by presenting realistic scenarios, examples for concept identification, or complex problems that guide learners through a solution using questions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Well-designed questions, relevant content, and guidance to support learners in finding answers. Requires careful consideration of the audience's abilities and knowledge.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more development time and resources. Needs careful design to ensure questions are relevant and engaging. May not be suitable for all learners or topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners, professionals seeking self-paced or collaborative learning experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate curiosity, encourage active engagement, promote independent thinking, facilitate knowledge construction, enhance problem-solving skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Arouses curiosity through relevant questions, makes learning active and engaging, aligns with natural learning processes, promotes independent thinking and knowledge construction, works in self-paced and collaborative settings, motivates adults through varied approaches, encourages creative learning design.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the level of assistance and structure based on the audience's abilities and knowledge. Provide more guidance for novices and decrease it for experts to avoid the expertise reversal effect.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how learners engage with the questions, their ability to gather and use information to answer them, and their overall performance in problem-solving scenarios.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Posing questions that learners must answer has benefits over expository approaches as it stimulates attention and curiosity, makes learning active and engaging, and promotes independent thinking and knowledge construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Scenario-based learning, concept identification, interactive case studies, reflective question wrap-ups, problem-solving exercises (Source: Connie Malamed, The eLearning Coach)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Question Formulation Technique (QFT) is a structured method for generating and improving questions to develop critical thinking skills, increase self-efficacy, and encourage participation in civic life. It involves divergent, convergent, and metacognitive thinking. Participants are presented with a Question Focus (QFocus), which can be a statement, phrase, image, video, or other stimulus. They then follow four rules: Ask as many questions as possible, do not discuss or judge the questions, write down every question exactly as stated, and change statements into questions. Participants categorize questions as open- or closed-ended, discuss the value of each type, and change questions from one type to another. They prioritize questions based on specific instructions related to the central objective, such as identifying the most important questions or those that will aid research. The process concludes with a discussion of next steps and a reflection on what was learned and how it can be applied. The facilitator guides participants through the steps, validating contributions equally and avoiding examples that might impede independent thinking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A facilitator, a Question Focus (QFocus), writing materials, and a structured environment following the rules of the technique. Time is needed for each step of the QFT process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a structured environment and adherence to specific rules, which may feel restrictive to some learners. The effectiveness depends on the facilitator's ability to guide the process without influencing the content of the questions. Some participants may struggle with generating questions or prioritizing them effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, adult learners, and professionals in various fields

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical thinking, enhance questioning skills, promote self-efficacy, encourage active participation, clarify program goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes divergent and convergent thinking, develops metacognitive skills, enhances problem-solving abilities, increases motivation, fosters active participation, supports self-directed learning, allows for personalized learning goals

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The QFocus can be tailored to the individual's or group's specific interests or needs. Individual question generation allows for personalized exploration, and prioritization can be aligned with personal goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The quality and quantity of questions generated, the ability to categorize and prioritize questions, and the depth of reflection on the learning process can be assessed. Participants' feedback on the usefulness of the technique and their plans for applying what they learned can also be evaluated.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The QFT has been shown to be transformative for both students and professionals, helping them identify key goals, clarify objectives, and develop a mindset of inquiry. It enhances motivation, promotes self-directed learning, and fosters active solution-seeking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using the QFT with educators to create actionable questions and clarify program goals. Having participants develop their own QFocus during a session or choose from a list of options. Applying the QFT to personal professional growth by creating statements of fact after reviewing data. (Source: Right Question Institute)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Questioning is a powerful tool and effective teachers regularly use it for a range of purposes. Effective questioning yields immediate feedback on student understanding, it supports informal and formative assessment and helps capture feedback on the effectiveness of teaching strategies. Questioning opens up opportunities for students to discuss, argue, and express opinions and alternative points of view. It engages students, stimulates interest and curiosity in learning, and can create links to students’ lives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to prepare and deliver effective questions and facilitate discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be intimidating for some students if not implemented carefully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess understanding, stimulate critical thinking, and promote engagement through effective questioning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback, encourages discussion, and links learning to students' lives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to different levels of understanding and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Eliciting Student Thinking
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation, quality of responses, and level of engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective questioning supports formative assessment, stimulates curiosity, and enhances engagement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Strategic questioning is used to guide students to recognize their errors and correct their thinking, emphasizing conceptual understanding over rote memorization. Questions should focus on the student's reasoning, the reasonableness of the answer, and the underlying concepts. The teacher acts as a facilitator, guiding the student through the process of self-discovery and correction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Skilled teachers who can ask effective questions and facilitate meaningful discussions. Base-10 blocks or play money (for math interventions).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be skilled in questioning techniques. May be time-consuming, especially in large classes. Students need to feel safe to respond honestly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who benefit from guided inquiry and self-discovery

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-reflection, guide students to identify their own errors, deepen conceptual understanding, develop critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning, promotes metacognition, helps students internalize concepts, fosters a growth mindset

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The types of questions and level of scaffolding can be adapted to meet individual learner needs. Some students may require more direct guidance, while others may benefit from more open-ended questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in student thinking and reasoning, accuracy in correcting errors, ability to explain concepts in their own words, improved performance on subsequent assessments

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that strategic questioning can promote deeper understanding and long-term retention. Students are more likely to internalize concepts when they discover them for themselves through guided inquiry.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of telling a student that they cannot subtract a larger number from a smaller number, ask: “Do we have enough ones to take 7 ones from 3 ones?” Instead of directly correcting an incorrectly renamed minuend, ask: “Does 8 tens and 13 tens = 83?”

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using short, focused prompts at the end of a class period or learning experience to encourage learners to articulate their ideas and deepen their understanding. These prompts can be jotted down and shared out loud or used for larger writing assignments. The goal is to allow quiet thinkers to articulate their ideas and for entire groups to share ideas and make meaning of content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time at the end of a class period or learning experience; specific reflection prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require clear instructions and a supportive classroom environment to ensure honest and thoughtful responses. Some learners may need more time to process their thoughts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those in environments that require quick and meaningful closings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Deepen learning, encourage articulation of ideas, provide multiple avenues for engaging with complex ideas, help teachers understand and adapt to learners' intellectual processes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for quick and easy integration into classroom practice. Provides a structured way for learners to engage with complex ideas. Helps teachers adapt to learners' intellectual processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be adapted based on the content, type of learning experience, and needs of learners. Can be used for individual or group reflections.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality and depth of learner responses; participation in sharing activities; evidence of deeper understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes deeper learning and allows more learners to find broader meaning in their work. Helps teachers understand and adapt to the intellectual processes of their learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Quick Writes are short, focused informational writing tasks completed in under ten minutes, aimed at helping students process, organize, and remember information and ideas. This strategy is designed to improve content writing skills by providing regular, brief opportunities for students to articulate their understanding of a topic. Quick Writes are intended to encourage students to think critically and express their thoughts concisely, enhancing both comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires brief dedicated time for writing, clear and concise prompts, and potential access to writing tools (paper, digital devices).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for in-depth exploration of complex topics, students may need scaffolding to write effectively within the time constraint.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 4-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance content writing skills, improve information processing, organize ideas, enhance memory of information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a quick and efficient way to process and retain information, encourages concise and focused writing, promotes critical thinking and organization of ideas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Topics and prompts can be tailored to individual student interests and learning levels. The format can be adapted to suit different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Assess Performance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the clarity, organization, and accuracy of information in student responses. Track improvement in writing fluency and conciseness over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies and educator reports indicate quick writes can improve comprehension, retention, and writing skills by providing frequent, low-stakes opportunities to process and articulate understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Joan Sedita from Keys to Literacy discusses Quick Writes as a strategy to teach content writing. Teachers use Quick Writes in various subjects to help students process and remember information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a quiet classroom by reducing background noise to support increased Attention towards learning. Designing small areas as quiet spaces can also be beneficial for students who need to be away from excess noise, leading to greater Self-regulation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated space and efforts to reduce background noise. May involve tools to monitor and control noise levels.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in noisy environments or crowded classrooms. Requires clear guidelines for when and how to use quiet spaces.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those sensitive to noise or with attention difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student attention and self-regulation by reducing noise and providing quiet spaces

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances focus and reduces stress by minimizing auditory distractions. Provides a safe space for learners who need to self-regulate.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be personalized by allowing students to choose when and how to use quiet spaces. Different types of quiet spaces can be created to meet different needs (e.g., individual quiet zones, small group quiet areas).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' use of quiet spaces and self-reporting on focus and stress levels. Monitor classroom noise levels and their impact on student engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that reducing noise and providing quiet spaces can improve attention and reduce stress, leading to better learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using noise-canceling headphones, creating a designated quiet corner, implementing a noise level monitoring system like Too Noisy Pro.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reducing background noise in classrooms supports increased learner attention. This can be achieved by creating quiet classrooms, designating small quiet areas, or providing noise-blocking devices. These spaces or devices help learners self-regulate by providing an environment away from excess noise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated quiet space or noise-blocking devices. Instructor must establish clear expectations for use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be feasible in all environments. Requires consistent enforcement and may isolate learners if not implemented thoughtfully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners who struggle with focus due to environmental distractions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner attention, foster self-regulation, reduce distractions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a space for focused work, reduces sensory overload, supports self-regulation skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer various options for creating quiet: designated spaces, noise-canceling devices, or flexible seating arrangements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student focus and engagement in quiet spaces. Collect feedback from students on the effectiveness of quiet spaces. Measure noise levels in classroom.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that reducing background noise can improve focus and reduce stress in learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Too Noisy Pro is a tool that allows learners to self-monitor the noise level in the classroom, adjusting accordingly. Teachers can designate a 'calm-down spot' where students can safely go to regain control over their emotions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Quiet signals are predetermined cues or actions used by teachers to quickly and effectively quiet a noisy classroom. They include methods like flicking the lights, ringing a call bell, raising fingers, or using call-and-response techniques. When consistently implemented, these signals help establish a predictable routine for managing classroom noise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Consistent implementation, clear explanation of the signal to students, practice and reinforcement of expected behaviors.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lose effectiveness if overused, some signals may not work for all students, requires initial training and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Regain student attention, reduce classroom noise, establish classroom management routines

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Quickly and effectively quiets a noisy classroom, establishes clear expectations, reduces the need for verbal commands.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Signals can be adapted for different age groups and classroom contexts. Call-and-response cues can be customized to student interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the speed and effectiveness with which students respond to the quiet signal. Track the reduction in classroom noise levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research and practice demonstrate that consistent use of quiet signals can improve classroom management and reduce disruptions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating a designated quiet space in the classroom allows children to self-regulate and reduce sensory overload by limiting auditory, visual, and other sensory input. These spaces can range from a corner with a bean bag chair to a desk with a partition, providing privacy and a refuge for regrouping. A clear communication system, like a sign-up sheet or laminated card, enables children to easily request time in the space when needed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated area in the classroom, furniture like a bean bag chair, and a system for children to request time in the space.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The space must be respected by other students to ensure it remains a safe and calming area. The effectiveness may vary based on individual preferences and needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in school settings, particularly those with sensory sensitivities or who are easily overwhelmed

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce sensory overload, promote self-regulation, provide a calming environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a physical and mental break from classroom stimuli, helping children to manage their sensory experiences and emotions. Reduces sensory overload, aiding in self-regulation and emotional well-being.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The quiet space can be customized with items that provide additional comfort, such as pillows or blankets. The method of requesting the space can also be tailored to individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and duration of use, as well as the child's behavior before and after using the space. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage sensory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that designated quiet spaces can improve children's ability to manage their emotions and sensory input, leading to increased focus and participation in classroom activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Designating a quiet space in the learning environment where learners can take breaks to regroup and calm themselves. This area limits auditory, visual, and other sensory input, allowing learners to self-regulate when feeling overwhelmed. The space can be a corner with a comfortable seat or a small tent or canopy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated quiet space in the learning environment. Calming sensory tools and activities (e.g., pillows, bean bag chair, tactile bin, sensory bottles). A clear system for learners to request time in the quiet space (e.g., sign-up sheet, laminated card).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be accessible to all learners due to space constraints or logistical challenges. Some learners may be reluctant to use the quiet space due to stigma or social pressures. Requires clear expectations and guidelines for appropriate use of the space.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who experience sensory overload, anxiety, or difficulty managing their emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-regulation, reduce overstimulation, provide a safe space for learners to calm down

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe and private space for learners to de-escalate and regain control. Reduces sensory input and promotes relaxation. Supports self-awareness and emotional regulation skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to personalize the quiet space with calming objects or activities that suit their individual needs. Offer choices in the type of space (e.g., tent, corner, desk with partition) and the sensory tools available (e.g., weighted blanket, fidget toys).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' use of the quiet space and their ability to self-regulate. Collect feedback from learners on the effectiveness of the quiet space in helping them calm down and refocus. Track the frequency and duration of learners' visits to the quiet space.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing quiet spaces in learning environments can reduce stress, improve attention, and promote self-regulation. Studies have shown that mindfulness and relaxation techniques can improve learners' emotional well-being and academic performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Quiet time is a structured period of 10–15 minutes where students engage in calming activities like reading, writing, drawing, puzzles, or meditation to transition back into the classroom in a purposeful and relaxed manner. It helps students take a physical, mental, and emotional breather, reducing energy spills and disputes, and preparing them for afternoon learning. Teachers may participate or use the time for preparation, but not to engage with students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • 10–15 minutes of class time, a variety of quiet activities, and consistent implementation. Teachers should model and enforce quiet time rules.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement with students who have difficulty with self-regulation. Requires clear routines and consistent enforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to middle school students, adaptable for various age groups.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote relaxation, reduce classroom disruptions, enhance focus, and improve emotional regulation for students and teachers.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a peaceful transition, reduces conflict, and supports emotional regulation. Students gain a sense of control through activity choices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adjust activity choices based on student needs and classroom goals, ranging from academic tasks to relaxation techniques.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior before and after quiet time for changes in energy levels, focus, and conflict resolution. Collect student feedback on the helpfulness of quiet time activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved classroom atmosphere, reduced disruptions, and enhanced student focus. Some teachers find it saves time by preempting disputes and worries.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary school teachers implement daily quiet time with choices like reading, writing, or drawing to help students transition smoothly after lunch and recess.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Build Community Through Peer Feedback
Description
docs.text: When students are given the opportunity during projects to frequently share feedback and revise their work, it creates moments to witness growth and progress. Providing meaningful feedback to each other allows students to contribute to a strong, supportive classroom culture, building the relationships and connection they need.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom environment that values feedback; facilitator who is skilled in facilitating peer feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time for feedback and revision; facilitator must be prepared to address potential conflicts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster a supportive classroom culture; build relationships and connections among students; provide opportunities for growth and progress through feedback and revision.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters a supportive classroom culture, builds relationships and connections, provides opportunities for growth and progress, improves critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose how they give and receive feedback; provide different formats for feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Interaction
  • Feedback
  • Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of feedback provided, demonstration of growth and progress, improved relationships and connections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More supportive classroom culture; stronger relationships and connections among students; improved critical thinking skills; increased growth and progress.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Create Beautiful Spaces
Description
docs.text: For so many of our students, their communities and homes are not always beautiful places... Imagine the power then for these same students to be able to walk into a building made beautiful by displaying student work from projects... It’s transformative and brings back life and energy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for display; resources for creating a beautiful environment; commitment to valuing student work.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires resources and effort to maintain; facilitator must be intentional about creating a welcoming space for all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students from underserved communities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a welcoming and inspiring learning environment; showcase student work and accomplishments; foster a sense of pride and belonging.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a welcoming and inspiring learning environment, showcases student work, fosters a sense of pride and belonging, transforms the learning space.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to contribute to the creation of the space; showcase diverse perspectives and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Public Display

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student engagement, sense of pride and belonging, transformation of the learning space.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More welcoming and inspiring learning environment; increased student engagement; improved sense of pride and belonging; transformation of the learning space.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Create Space for Students to Reflect
Description
docs.text: Reflection is rare in traditional classrooms, where the emphasis is on urgency and doing assignments quickly. Sadly, this makes many schools unsafe places that can activate trauma and drain the energy out of our students. PBL flips this script by allowing these students to pause now and then, to stop and think about themselves, their ideas and questions, and how they feel about the project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection; facilitator who is skilled in creating a safe and supportive environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift away from traditional instruction; facilitator must be comfortable addressing sensitive topics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students who have experienced trauma.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a safe and reflective learning environment; allow students to pause, think, and process their experiences; promote socio-emotional learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe learning environment, allows for processing of experiences, promotes socio-emotional learning, reduces stress and anxiety.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose how they reflect; provide different formats for reflection.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth of reflection, demonstration of socio-emotional learning, improved well-being.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Safer and more reflective learning environment; reduced stress and anxiety; improved socio-emotional learning; increased student well-being.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Expect Excellence
Description
docs.text: A belief in excellence, demonstrated by setting high expectations, is the fuel that runs a successful PBL culture. Dispel the myth that PBL does not work for "those kids". The challenge lives in ensuring the proper scaffolding, knowing their current reality, to get your students towards the excellence they are capable of without lowering your expectations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitator who believes in the potential of all students; understanding of students' current realities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset; facilitator must be willing to challenge their own assumptions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students who are traditionally underserved.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a culture of excellence; set high expectations for all students; provide proper scaffolding to support student success.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters a culture of excellence, sets high expectations, provides scaffolding to support student success, dispels myths about who can succeed in PBL.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide differentiated scaffolding to meet individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Coaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student achievement, demonstration of growth, meeting of high expectations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Culture of excellence; increased student achievement; dispelling of myths about who can succeed; improved student self-efficacy.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Focus Projects on Issues of Justice
Description
docs.text: Authentic projects that address issues of justice lead to higher student engagement because students are doing work that matters, work that impacts their community, their lives, the lives of those they love and deeply care about.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Curriculum that allows for exploration of issues of justice; facilitator who is comfortable discussing these topics.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more preparation to address sensitive topics; facilitator must be prepared to handle differing perspectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for students from marginalized communities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement; make learning more relevant and meaningful; empower students to act as change agents; address issues of justice.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances student engagement, makes learning more relevant and meaningful, empowers students to act as change agents, addresses issues of justice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose issues of justice that are personally relevant to them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation, depth of engagement with the issue, quality of proposed solutions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and motivation; improved sense of purpose; deeper learning through real-world application; positive impact on the community.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students research and advocate for policy changes related to racial justice, environmental justice, or economic justice; students design and implement a community project to address a local issue of injustice.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Listen to the Voices of Students
Description
docs.text: Give students authorship in sharing and telling their own stories, which a good project allows them to do. Student voice matters. It creates agency and leadership that will help build the culture for PBL. Advancing youth voice is directly connected to advancing youth equity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom environment that values student voice; facilitator who is willing to listen and learn from students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in power dynamics; facilitator must be comfortable relinquishing some control.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for Black and Latinx students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students by giving them a voice in their learning; create agency and leadership skills; foster a more equitable classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students, creates agency, develops leadership skills, fosters an equitable classroom environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose how they share their stories; provide different formats for student voice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Interaction
  • Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation, confidence in sharing, leadership skills demonstrated.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and motivation; improved sense of agency; development of leadership skills; more equitable classroom environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students create podcasts, videos, or presentations to share their experiences and perspectives; students lead discussions about issues that are important to them; students serve as mentors to younger students.

docs.title: Racial Equity in PBL - Spark Engagement with Student-Generated Questions
Description
docs.text: Projects driven by student-generated questions result in increased engagement and investment. Instead of spoon-feeding information, ask students what they care about, want to learn more about, or need to know the answer to. Black and Latinx students, in particular, can experience traditional instruction as disempowering and another example of systemic oppression.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitator who is open to student-driven inquiry, classroom environment that supports questioning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift away from traditional instruction; may require more planning to align with curriculum standards.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for Black and Latinx students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement and investment; promote a sense of empowerment; encourage student-driven inquiry.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement, fosters a sense of empowerment, encourages student-driven inquiry, mitigates feelings of oppression.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose their project topics and research questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Question Formulation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation, investment in project, quality of student-generated questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and motivation; improved sense of empowerment; deeper learning through student-driven inquiry.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A history class asks students to generate questions about historical events that are relevant to their lives. A science class asks students to identify environmental problems in their community and formulate research questions to address them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Racial identity work involves examining one's own racial identity, confronting personal biases, and understanding how privilege and misinformation can affect work as an educator. This includes recognizing and addressing one's own privilege, learning about the racial identities of learners, and actively working against biases. By modeling this work for learners, educators show them how to advocate for themselves and disrupt systems of oppression.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to be willing to examine their own racial identity, confront their biases, and take responsibility for their own education around race in America.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort and commitment. Some educators may be hesitant to address issues of race and privilege.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators who want to become better advocates for their learners, particularly those from marginalized racial groups.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-awareness, challenge biases, and empower learners to advocate for themselves and disrupt systems of oppression.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a more equitable and inclusive learning environment, promotes learner engagement, and supports the development of self-awareness and cultural competence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by using different types of resources, engaging in challenging conversations, and tailoring activities to individual learners and cultural backgrounds.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Case Study

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learners' engagement and participation in learning activities, track their progress in developing self-awareness and cultural competence, and gather feedback on their experiences in the classroom.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Racial identity work can lead to a more equitable and inclusive learning environment, increased learner engagement, and improved academic outcomes for learners from marginalized racial groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Taking responsibility for one's own education around race in America, creating space in peer groups to have challenging conversations, and learning about the racial identity of learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Racial identity work for educators involves understanding one's own racial identity, privilege, and biases to create a more inclusive and equitable learning environment. This includes confronting personal biases, seeking information about different racial groups, and disrupting systems of oppression in the classroom. By modeling this work, educators empower students to advocate for themselves and others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Willingness to engage in self-reflection, access to resources about race and racism, and a commitment to disrupting systems of oppression.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be emotionally challenging and time-consuming. Educators may encounter resistance or discomfort from themselves or others.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators of all backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness, reduce bias, promote equity, foster inclusivity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment, reduces barriers to learning for students from marginalized groups, and empowers students to advocate for themselves and others.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Educators can tailor their racial identity work to their own backgrounds and experiences, focusing on areas where they have the most privilege or misinformation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe educators' behavior in the classroom, their interactions with students, and their responses to issues of race and equity. Measure students' sense of belonging and their perceptions of fairness and inclusion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that racial identity work for educators leads to improved student outcomes, reduced bias, and a more equitable learning environment. Students feel more valued, respected, and empowered to succeed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Educators take responsibility for their own education around race in America, create space for challenging conversations, and learn about the racial identity of their students. They also disrupt systems of oppression in their classrooms and provide students with the language of self-advocacy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Raise awareness by helping students understand the concept of self-talk: what it is, how it affects self-esteem and confidence. Then, ask students to identify the judgements they have about their abilities in different areas (sports, the arts, school subjects). Identify areas of struggle and strength. Discuss what their inner voice says when faced with a manageable task vs. a difficult one, and how confidence and past experiences impact their inner voice. A KWL chart can serve as a pre- and post-activity reflection tool.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Journal, notebook, or KWL chart.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners to initially identify their self-talk. Requires a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness, identify the impact of self-talk on confidence and self-esteem.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand how their internal dialogue affects their self-perception and motivation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the level of discussion and complexity of self-reflection questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student journals or notebooks reflecting identified patterns in self-talk.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased self-awareness and understanding of the connection between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Present instances of a concept in rapid sequence or allow all instances to be viewed simultaneously. This enables them to be active in working memory all at once, facilitating the process of generalization. If there is a time gap between the presentation of examples, the learner might not generalize from them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a format that allows for simultaneous or rapid sequential presentation of examples.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May overwhelm learners if the pace is too fast. Requires careful design to ensure examples are clear and distinct.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly with abstract concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate generalization and concept formation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by keeping examples active in working memory. Enhances pattern recognition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the pace of presentation based on learner processing speed. Provide optional review materials.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify common features and accurately classify new examples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Presenting examples close together in time helps learners to generalize from them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting several different examples of Impressionist paintings in quick succession to highlight common characteristics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ask learners to rate the level of challenge in an activity on a scale of 1 to 10. If the activity is rated an eight or higher, ask what could be done to make the task a two or three. This provides insight into how to help the learner decrease frustration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A rating scale, structured tasks, and the ability to adjust tasks based on feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may not always provide accurate ratings. Some adjustments may not be feasible.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who avoid work or appear distracted

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce frustration, increase engagement, adjust task difficulty

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learner input, reduces frustration, increases engagement, allows for task adjustment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks can be tailored based on learner feedback. Strategies can be adjusted to meet individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the learner's ratings of task difficulty. Monitor changes in engagement and frustration levels. Collect feedback on the effectiveness of task adjustments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Rating and changing tasks can significantly reduce frustration and increase engagement by ensuring tasks are appropriately challenging. This approach promotes a positive learning environment and supports individualized instruction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher asks a student to rate the difficulty of a math problem and then simplifies it based on the student's feedback. A parent adjusts a homework assignment based on a child's assessment of the challenge level.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reaction observations involve observing and describing the properties of liquids and their mixtures. Learners examine the bleeding of colored inks in water and the properties of two liquids and their mixture. These activities improve observational skills and understanding of basic chemical reactions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Colored inks, water, various liquids, containers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation. May need safety precautions when working with chemicals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying physical science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop observational skills, describe properties of liquids and mixtures, understand basic chemical reactions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simple experiments make chemical concepts accessible. Enhances observational and descriptive skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Variety of colored inks and liquids can be used. Tasks can be adapted for different observation skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in describing observations, correct identification of properties, logical explanations of reactions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved observational skills, enhanced understanding of chemical reactions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Colored Dots (NYSED): Learners observe bleeding of colored inks with water. Colored Drops (NYSED): Learners examine the properties of two liquids and their mixture.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reactive Cultural Response is the ability to change the structure, activities, and focus of a class within the school year as you see the personality of a given group of kids emerge. This dynamic process is dependent on a classroom's day-to-day operations and the personalities and challenges that crop up throughout the year.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Observation skills, flexibility, ability to adapt activities quickly, willingness to adjust classroom norms.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires strong classroom management skills, may be challenging to balance diverse needs within a single class.
