docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in diverse classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address immediate challenges, foster a positive classroom culture, adjust activities to match student personalities, increase collaboration and inclusivity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Flexibility, adaptability, and responsiveness to student needs, promotes a positive and inclusive classroom culture, enhances student engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjustments are made in real-time based on the specific needs and dynamics of a given group of students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Discussion Sections
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Assigned Positions
  • Role Reversal
  • Consensus Building

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of student engagement and behavior, participation in class discussions, feedback from students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters a positive and inclusive classroom culture by addressing immediate challenges and adapting activities to student needs (Wood, 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Read-alouds involve an educator reading a text aloud to learners, often pausing to model effective reading and thinking strategies such as questioning, inferencing, and using context cues. This approach enhances narrative skills, connects text elements to background knowledge, builds vocabulary, develops understandings of story structures, supports developing connections between print elements, encourages high levels of understanding, teaches the reading process in a meaningful context, models fluency, and motivates learners to read. Discussions are supportive and engaging, allowing learners to extend their worldview and develop critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to appropriate reading materials, time for reading and discussion (15-20 minutes per session), and facilitation skills to guide discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may have varying levels of interest in the selected texts. Effective implementation requires skilled facilitation to guide discussions and ensure engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beginning readers and writers, including K-12 learners and potentially adult learners with emerging literacy skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance narrative skills, connect text elements to background knowledge, build vocabulary, develop understandings of story structures, support developing connections between print elements, encourage high levels of understanding, teach the reading process in a meaningful context, model fluency, motivate learners to read, extend worldview and develop critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Models effective reading strategies, supports comprehension, enhances vocabulary, promotes critical thinking, connects learning to personal experiences, and motivates learners to engage with literature.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Texts can be chosen based on learner interests and experiences. Discussions can be tailored to different levels of understanding. Scaffolding can be provided through prompts and sentence starters, especially beneficial for English language learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation in discussions, track comprehension through questioning and predictions, and analyze learner responses to open-ended questions about the text.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that read-alouds significantly contribute to vocabulary acquisition, comprehension, and overall literacy development. Engaging discussions enhance critical thinking skills and extend learners’ worldview.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A first-grade teacher uses a read-aloud to model questioning, inferencing, and using context cues, enabling students to practice these strategies and connect elements of the text with their background knowledge. MeeGenius highlights words as they are read, aiding early readers in decoding, phonological awareness, morphological awareness, and sight recognition.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers strategically select and read aloud stories that incorporate social-emotional learning (SEL) themes to foster self-reflection, promote social awareness, and strengthen relationship skills among students. By guiding discussions centered around the characters' experiences and challenges, instructors facilitate deeper understanding and provide concrete examples of SEL skills in relatable contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a curated collection of books with relevant SEL themes, time allocated for read-aloud sessions and guided discussions, facilitation skills to promote meaningful reflection and sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of books to align with the needs and interests of the students. Facilitation skills are necessary to guide discussions effectively and ensure all voices are heard. Success depends on creating a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, educators seeking to integrate social-emotional learning into their curriculum

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance social awareness, build empathy, promote self-reflection, develop relationship skills, provide concrete examples of SEL skills in relatable contexts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates emotional engagement through relatable stories, develops social awareness and empathy by exploring diverse characters and scenarios, reinforces key SEL concepts through guided discussions and reflection.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Selection of books can be tailored to specific age groups, cultural backgrounds, and social-emotional needs of the students. Discussion prompts can be differentiated to accommodate varying levels of understanding and reflection.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, analyze their reflections and insights shared during and after the read-aloud sessions, assess their ability to apply SEL concepts to real-life situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that read-alouds with deliberate topics can enhance students' emotional intelligence, improve social skills, and promote positive relationships. By connecting literature to real-world scenarios, educators can foster empathy and responsible decision-making.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Utilizing digital libraries like Epic! to curate text collections based on specific SEL topics and skills. Examples include picture books that deal with emotions, friendships, and navigating social situations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers read aloud stories about social and emotional learning and facilitate discussions that prompt student self-reflection. These read-alouds provide concrete examples of social awareness and relationship skills in a relatable context, deepening understanding through shared experiences and reflection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to age-appropriate books focused on social and emotional learning. Time for read-alouds and facilitated discussions. Teacher facilitation skills.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the selected literature and the teacher's ability to facilitate meaningful discussions. Students may not connect with all texts or scenarios.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-8 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance social awareness, develop relationship skills, foster self-reflection, provide concrete examples of SEL concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides relatable examples of social and emotional skills, encourages self-reflection, enhances understanding of complex social situations, promotes empathy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Selection of texts can be tailored to student interests and relevant social-emotional themes. Discussion prompts can be differentiated to meet individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Class Discussion
  • Modeling
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions, analyze student reflections, and assess their ability to apply SEL skills in real-life situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that read-alouds combined with discussion can promote social-emotional development and enhance students' understanding of complex social issues. Enhanced self-regulation: Studies indicate regular metacognitive reflection improves learners’ ability to monitor and adjust their learning strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using books from the Social Emotional Learning Diverse Book List for Grades PreK-8 to discuss empathy, positive relationships, and problem-solving. Video series by Peg Sawyer demonstrating how to use children's literature to support social and emotional learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encouraging learners to read questions and their own writing aloud helps leverage auditory processing strengths. Reading aloud allows learners to discern what good writing "sounds like," improving their comprehension and composition skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for learners to read aloud

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are uncomfortable reading in front of others

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with strengths in auditory processing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve writing skills, support learners with auditory strengths

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages auditory strengths, provides auditory feedback on writing quality, enhances comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide structured prompts for reading aloud, offer feedback on pronunciation and intonation

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess reading fluency, track improvements in writing quality, gather learner feedback on the effectiveness of reading aloud.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that reading aloud can improve reading comprehension and writing skills. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of reading aloud in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reading test questions aloud, reading written assignments aloud during the revision process. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Read aloud features, often combined with word and sentence highlighting, provide auditory support while reading digital text. This can help with decoding, visual impairments, and second language acquisition. Highlighting helps learners focus their attention on the text as it is being read.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A digital device (computer, smartphone, tablet) with read aloud software or apps installed. Digital text content in a compatible format. Headphones or speakers for audio output.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The quality of speech synthesis can vary. Effectiveness depends on the clarity and accuracy of the highlighting. May not be suitable for all types of content.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with decoding difficulties, visual impairments, English language learners, or those who benefit from multisensory learning. Useful across all age groups and educational levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve decoding skills, enhance focus, support visual impairments, aid second language acquisition, promote multisensory learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides auditory reinforcement of written text. Improves reading fluency and comprehension. Enhances focus and reduces distractions. Supports phonological awareness and vocabulary development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can select from different voices, adjust the reading speed, and customize the highlighting style. Some tools offer options for sentence and word highlighting.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in reading fluency, accuracy, and comprehension. Collect user feedback on the usefulness of highlighting. Measure the time it takes to complete reading tasks with and without read aloud and highlighting.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that read aloud with highlighting can significantly improve reading outcomes for students with decoding difficulties, visual impairments, and English language learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • iPad Spoken Content features, Chromebook Select-to-speak, Read and Write for Google extension, Android Select to Speak, Microsoft Edge Immersive Reader.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Read and reflect involves students engaging in discussions or summarizing activities after reading independently. Students can do a turn and talk about their favorite part of a book, if they would recommend the book to a friend, or whether or not they would have ended the book differently. For a challenge, students can try to summarize the book in fewer than 280 characters.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for reflection and discussion after independent reading. Clear prompts or questions to guide reflection and summarization.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require scaffolding for students who struggle with reflection or summarization. Success depends on students engaging thoughtfully in the reflection and discussion process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, promote critical thinking, and encourage reflection on reading material

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding of the text through reflection and discussion. Encourages critical thinking and the ability to summarize information concisely.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose to reflect on aspects of the book that are most meaningful to them. Activities can be adapted to suit different reading levels and learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, critical thinking, and summarization skills. Increased student engagement and participation in discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reflection and discussion have been shown to enhance comprehension and retention of information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reader's Theater is a strategy that combines reading practice and performing by having learners read scripts created from books or stories aloud. Students perform by reading scripts without the use of costumes or props. Reader's theater can be used to involve students in reading aloud, enhance reading skills, increase confidence, improve fluency, and motivate reluctant readers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Scripts that are fun to do with lots of good dialogue. Students do not memorize their parts; they always read from their scripts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Boring scripts are no better than boring stories. It is important that students feel comfortable in the performance mode.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading skills, increase confidence, improve fluency, motivate reluctant readers, explore genre and characterization.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reader's theater offers an entertaining and engaging means of improving fluency and enhancing comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scripts can be purchased or created out of an existing book or chapter. Scripts can be adapted to fit the reading levels of individual students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Argument Construction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students' abilities to read aloud with comprehension, expression, and fluency.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The value of reader’s theater is increased tenfold when used as a strategy for increasing understanding of what is being read (Susan Finney). Reader’s theater is a wonderful technique for helping readers learn to read aloud with expression (Dr. Peggy Sharp).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encouraging students to read questions and their own writing aloud leverages strengths in auditory processing. Students with strengths in auditory processing can often discern what good writing "sounds like," which can improve their composition skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom environment that supports reading aloud without distractions or self-consciousness. Guidance on how to provide and receive constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may feel self-conscious about reading aloud in front of others. Requires explicit instruction on what to listen for when reading aloud.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with strengths in auditory processing, students who need to improve their writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve composition skills, enhance auditory processing, promote self-correction, build self-awareness of writing quality

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reading aloud allows students to identify errors and areas for improvement in their writing through auditory feedback. It can also help them internalize the rhythm and structure of effective writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose to read aloud to themselves, to a partner, or to the whole class. Feedback can be provided by the teacher or by peers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor improvements in writing quality through student work samples. Observe student engagement and participation in reading aloud activities. Gather student feedback on the effectiveness of reading aloud.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students with strengths in auditory processing can often discern what good writing “sounds like,” which can improve their composition skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Having students read their essays aloud during the revision process. Encouraging students to read questions aloud to themselves before answering them. Using read-alouds as a model for effective writing style.

docs.title: Reading and Understanding Written Math Problems
Description
docs.text: Word problems can be challenging. Use background knowledge of math as a stepping stone for other language learning by accelerating math instruction at the beginning of the school year and building on what students have learned. Read math word problems and demonstrate the logical thinking process while translating words into pictures and number sentences. Have students explain their thinking and correct each other. Capitalize on enthusiasm to teach them how to extract information from texts and move them toward oral and reading fluency. Provide explicit instruction of key vocabulary, daily practice of problem-solving, repeated readings, and hands-on activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured activities, explicit instruction, and hands-on materials

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires planning and resources, may be challenging to implement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of word problems, enhance critical thinking, and language skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to solving word problems, enhances language and problem-solving skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt activities to meet the specific needs of the learners

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner's comprehension of word problems, assess problem-solving skills

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved ability to solve word problems, enhanced language proficiency

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Demonstrate the logical thinking process while translating words into pictures and, finally, into number sentences.

docs.title: Reading and Writing for Real-World Math Applications
Description
docs.text: Learners select and summarize published articles that highlight the ways math is present in different facets of the real world. They post summaries on an online magazine and include a visual to aid comprehension and cite sources. The assignment connects math concepts to everyday experiences, fostering a quantitative understanding of the world around them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to articles highlighting math applications, online magazine platform, and assessment rubric.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to relevant articles and a platform for creating the magazine. May be time-consuming and require technical support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Illustrate the relevance of mathematics, develop comprehension and summarization skills, enhance critical thinking, and provide a deeper appreciation for the usefulness of mathematics.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to choose articles according to their interests, and appreciate that the end product, the magazine, can be easily shared with family and friends and stored in their own e-portfolios.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select articles that pique their interest, allowing for a personalized exploration of math applications.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Research
  • Summarization and Synthesis
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess content understanding, clarity of communication, editing, critical thinking, initiative, and creativity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages students who enjoy reading and writing more than the computational side of math and gives all a deeper understanding and stronger appreciation of the usefulness and effectiveness of mathematics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students create a magazine of excerpts of articles about various applications of mathematics in real life, from the probability of soccer teams in the World Cup to fractals in Jackson Pollock’s paintings.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reading conferences involve one-on-one interactions between an instructor and a learner during independent reading time. The instructor asks questions, provides targeted feedback, and guides the learner in practicing comprehension strategies tailored to improve their genre knowledge and overall reading skills. These conferences allow for individual support, identifying strengths and learning gaps, and providing opportunities for practice in authentic contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for one-on-one conferences during independent reading. Instructor needs to be trained in conducting effective reading conferences, asking targeted questions, and providing appropriate feedback. Digital tools or reading materials suitable for independent reading at various levels.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming for the instructor, especially in large classes. Requires careful planning and organization to ensure all learners receive adequate support. May not be suitable for learners who are uncomfortable with one-on-one interactions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, especially those who need individualized support in reading comprehension

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, provide individualized feedback, identify learning gaps, enhance genre knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides personalized learning experiences, allows for immediate feedback, and supports the development of comprehension strategies. Instructors can adapt their instruction based on individual learner needs and progress. It supports the development of learner independence and self-regulation in reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different reading levels and learning needs by adjusting the complexity of questions and comprehension strategies used. Can also be delivered using different modalities (e.g., in-person, video conferencing) to accommodate different learner preferences and access.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in reading comprehension skills, track progress in genre knowledge, monitor the application of comprehension strategies, and analyze learner responses during conferences to gauge understanding and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Personalized reading support: Research shows that one-on-one reading conferences can lead to significant improvements in reading comprehension and motivation, particularly for struggling readers. Targeted feedback: Studies indicate that providing specific and actionable feedback during reading conferences helps learners develop effective comprehension strategies and build confidence in their reading abilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher conducts one-on-one reading conferences with students during independent reading time to provide personalized feedback and support their comprehension skills. A digital reading app uses open-ended questions to simulate reading conferences, providing insights into student thinking and learning gaps, and offering exercises for remediation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Have students record details about their reading such as book titles, number of pages read, and new vocabulary. This process encourages reflection on their reading and can increase accountability. However, this should not be overly burdensome and should align with the goals of fostering a love of reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tools for recording reading details, such as journals, logs, or digital apps, and time for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become a chore if not implemented thoughtfully. Some students may find it burdensome or demotivating. Requires clear expectations and guidelines.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote reflection on reading, increase accountability, and build vocabulary.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages students to think about their reading, provides a record of reading progress, and supports vocabulary development.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose what they record based on their interests and needs. Provide a variety of recording methods, such as journals, reading logs, or digital tools.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' reading records to assess their reflection and progress. Monitor vocabulary development based on recorded words.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages reflection, increases accountability, and builds vocabulary.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Have students read articles from sources such as Math Horizons or Martin Gardner's Scientific American columns. When students get a feel for what writing about math can look like, they will be able to do it better themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to articles from relevant sources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to suitable reading materials and may require guidance in selecting appropriate articles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for middle and high school levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expose learners to effective writing about math and improve their own writing skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides models of effective writing and exposes learners to diverse perspectives on math topics.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose articles that interest them, allowing for a more engaging and relevant reading experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to summarize and analyze the articles they read. Look for improvements in their own writing about math.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides models of effective writing and exposes learners to diverse perspectives on math topics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Have students read and discuss articles from Math Horizons or Martin Gardner's Scientific American columns.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reading Laterally is the practice of verifying information by consulting multiple external sources to evaluate the credibility of a source before engaging deeply with it. Rather than examining a website's 'About Us' page or internal links (vertical reading), lateral reading involves opening multiple browser tabs to investigate what other reputable sources say about the original source's expertise, reputation, and potential biases. This approach helps readers quickly assess trustworthiness and distinguish reliable information from misinformation or propaganda. Good fact-checkers read “laterally,” across many connected sites instead of digging deep into the site at hand.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a computer or mobile device with internet access. Proficiency in using search engines and navigating websites. Awareness of reliable fact-checking resources and reputable sources of information.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to consult multiple sources. May be challenging for individuals with limited digital literacy skills. Relies on the availability of credible external sources to provide accurate assessments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who frequently encounter online information and need to assess its reliability, including students, researchers, and general consumers of news and social media

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate the credibility of online sources, identify bias and misinformation, improve critical thinking skills, enhance information literacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a rapid and effective method for assessing the trustworthiness of online sources. Encourages a more objective and informed approach to information consumption. Reduces susceptibility to misinformation and propaganda.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different types of sources and claims, ranging from news articles to scientific studies. The level of scrutiny can be adjusted based on the potential impact of the information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Research
  • Resource Evaluation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify unreliable sources and misinformation. Assess the quality of their source evaluations based on external evidence. Measure improvements in their critical thinking and information literacy skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research from Stanford indicates that professional fact-checkers using lateral reading techniques arrive at more warranted conclusions in a fraction of the time compared to those who read vertically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When encountering a statistic on a website, a lateral reader would open a new tab and search for that statistic from other reputable sources, such as government agencies or academic studies, before accepting the original website's claim.

docs.title: Reading Online Strategy: Evaluating Online Information
Description
docs.text: Students learn to analyze and evaluate the information they encounter online by assessing the reliability of websites. This includes mini-lessons on the differences between .com, .gov, .org, and .edu domains. Students examine selected websites (both reliable and unreliable sources) and check for the following elements: can the information presented be corroborated elsewhere, is the writer of the information reliable, is the information current, is the information documented, is the website advocating for something and therefore potentially challenged as a neutral source, and is there a conflict of interest present? Students also examine famous website hoaxes and search for clues that suggest it is a hoax, as well as mini-lessons on propaganda techniques and identifying the use of the same techniques in online advertising.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of websites, time for explicit instruction, and guided practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant instructional time for learners to develop evaluation skills. Requires ongoing practice and application of the strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to improve their digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance critical thinking skills, develop evaluation strategies for online information, identify reliable sources, recognize propaganda techniques, understand website domains

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear set of criteria for evaluating online information, supports critical thinking and reasoning skills, and enhances digital literacy.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the complexity of the websites examined based on the learner's level. Provide different levels of support for identifying and evaluating information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate students' ability to identify reliable sources. Track their use of evaluation strategies. Collect student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in evaluating online information has been shown to improve critical thinking skills and digital literacy. Identifying reliable sources promotes effective learning and decision-making.

docs.title: Reading Online Strategy: Formulating Effective Search Queries
Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on teaching students how to formulate effective search queries to locate reliable information online. For younger students, this involves using appropriate search terms and quotation marks instead of full questions. For older students, it includes teaching Boolean Operators (and, or, not, near, parentheses, asterisk) to refine searches. By reflecting on their online behavior, students can engage in metacognitive reflection about their information-seeking and what skills they need to develop.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to search engines, time for explicit instruction, and guided practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant instructional time for learners to master advanced search techniques. Requires ongoing practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to improve their digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve search skills, develop effective search queries, learn Boolean operators, increase metacognitive reflection on information seeking behavior

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides specific skills and strategies, promotes metacognitive reflection, and enables students to find more reliable information online.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the search tasks and the explicitness of the instruction based on the learner's level. Start with basic search terms and gradually introduce more advanced operators.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate students' ability to formulate effective search queries. Track the reliability and relevance of the information students find. Collect student reflections on their information-seeking process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in search strategies has been shown to improve online reading comprehension and information literacy. Metacognitive reflection enhances self-regulation and strategic learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Connecting math concepts to real-world applications is a strategy that can be used to enhance understanding, relevance, and engagement. Instructors provide context and connect math concepts to an adult learner's world, so math can be seen as relevant and applicable to their daily lives and work. Real-world connections are also great ways to integrate math with other disciplines to create cross-curricular connections, supporting Disciplinary Literacy, and fostering confidence and Motivation by helping adults see the relevance of all they are learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation, access to relevant resources and materials, and a supportive learning environment. Instructors need to be knowledgeable about real-world applications of math and able to make connections to learners' lives.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. May require significant upfront planning and preparation. Learners may struggle with self-direction and time management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in basic education programs, particularly those who struggle to see the relevance of math to their lives.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner engagement, improve understanding of math concepts, enhance confidence in math skills, and promote transfer of learning to real-world situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners see the relevance of math to their daily lives, increasing motivation and engagement. Provides concrete examples and applications that make abstract concepts more understandable. Strengthens retention by connecting new information to existing knowledge and experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor real-world examples to learners' individual interests, experiences, and cultural backgrounds. Allow learners to choose projects or activities that are relevant to their lives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Integration
  • Problem Scenario

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner progress on project milestones, assess the quality of their final product, and evaluate their ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems. Measure gains in content knowledge, self-confidence, collaboration, and engagement through pre- and post-assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to increased learner engagement, improved understanding of math concepts, enhanced confidence in math skills, and promotion of transfer of learning to real-world situations. Increased learner outcomes and increased motivation. Increased ability to apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Shopping and consumer awareness (understanding percentages as used in sales and taxes), financial literacy (basic operations for budgeting), and home and appliance use and maintenance (reading gauges, understanding measurement systems).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When a student expresses frustration or negativity (e.g., 'I can’t do this stuff!'), reflect their feelings and then prompt them to take action. For example, 'You sound really frustrated Jackson. I wonder what strategy or first step you might be able to take?' Suggest actions like: checking the inner voice and reframing the message, taking deep breaths, checking with a friend, rereading instructions, or asking for help.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Active listening skills, empathy, list of reframing strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires presence of mind and quick thinking. May not be effective if student is highly emotional.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply reframing techniques in real-time situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical strategies for managing negative emotions and promoting problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor suggestions to individual needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student responses to challenging situations and their use of reframing techniques.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved emotional regulation and problem-solving skills in real-world contexts (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reasonable feedback involves providing feedback that is manageable and not overwhelming for the student. This can be achieved by selecting a focus for feedback with each assignment, such as transitions or evidence. Another strategy is to provide a 'Glow and a Grow' comment, highlighting one area the student did well on and one area that needs improvement. Students can then refer back to these comments and goals before writing future assignments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to carefully select the focus of their feedback and provide balanced comments. Students need to reflect on and apply the feedback to future assignments.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require teachers to limit the scope of their feedback. Students must be willing to engage with feedback and use it to improve.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students at all levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent students from becoming overwhelmed by feedback and encourage them to take meaningful steps for revision and growth as writers.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes feedback more manageable and less discouraging for students. Helps them focus on specific areas for improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can select feedback focuses based on the assignment and the individual needs of the student. Glow and Grow comments allow for personalized praise and constructive criticism.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the focus and balance of feedback provided. Monitor student's ability to identify strengths and areas for improvement in their writing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reasonable feedback ensures that students are not overwhelmed by feedback, helping them to set learning goals and take charge of their own writing and learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: De-emphasizing correct answers and focusing on the reasoning process can build student confidence and provide insight into problem-solving strategies. Teachers can present worked examples with incorrect solutions and ask students to identify the error. Another technique involves restructuring class participation: instead of immediately seeking the right answer, instructors ask students to share their initial thoughts or approaches to the problem. This emphasizes the variety of ways a problem can be tackled and values the process of thinking over simply finding the answer. Making math class more discursive and less about a single correct answer can help students feel more confident when they don’t know the answer right away, or get the wrong answer at first.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Prepared examples of worked problems with errors. Facilitation skills to guide discussions and manage diverse perspectives. A classroom environment that values exploration and reasoning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure all students are engaged and contributing. May be time-consuming to explore multiple solution paths. Some students may feel frustrated by not focusing on the "right" answer.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and levels, particularly those who are intimidated by math or believe there is only one way to solve a problem.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage diverse approaches to problem-solving, build confidence in reasoning abilities, shift focus from answers to processes, enhance collaborative learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages exploration of multiple perspectives, reduces pressure to find the correct answer immediately, enhances understanding of problem-solving strategies, fosters a more inclusive learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the complexity of problems to suit different skill levels. Provide sentence starters or prompts to guide student explanations of their reasoning. Allow students to choose the method they use to solve problems.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the depth and clarity of students' explanations of their reasoning. Assess student engagement in discussions and their ability to identify errors in worked examples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that emphasizing reasoning over answers can improve student understanding of mathematical concepts, increase confidence, and promote a more positive attitude toward math.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting a worked example with an error on the board and having students find the mistake. Asking students to explain their thought process before revealing the answer. Facilitating discussions on multiple methods to solve a single problem.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Offer daily recess to allow students to be active, which can improve memory, conflict resolution skills, and creativity. Structure recess with activity zones to provide options for different games and sports. A 20-30 minute recess can help students minimize disruptive classroom behavior and provide a much-needed daily break.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated time, space, and supervision. Structured activity zones

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time allocation. Needs effective supervision to ensure safety and fair play.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase physical activity, improve memory and cognitive skills, reduce disruptive behavior

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to burn off energy and be active, improves memory and cognitive skills, reduces disruptive behavior.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activity zones can cater to different interests and abilities. Students can choose activities they enjoy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor behavior and engagement in class, track recess participation rates, assess improvements in memory and cognitive skills

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved academic performance: Research suggests that recess can enhance academic performance and cognitive skills. Reduced behavioral issues: Active recess can lead to better behavior in the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reciprocal peer tutoring (RPT) involves pairing students of similar abilities to work together, alternating the roles of tutor and tutee. Students take turns teaching each other, offering praise and feedback as opportunities arise. This approach eliminates the need to designate fixed tutor and tutee roles, allowing for a more collaborative learning environment where both students engage in teaching and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful pairing of students, clear learning objectives, and structured activities. Teachers need to provide guidance and monitor progress to ensure effective collaboration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all students, particularly those who struggle with collaboration or prefer individual work. Requires careful planning and monitoring to ensure both students are actively engaged and benefiting from the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for elementary and secondary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of content, improve communication skills, promote collaboration, and foster a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active participation, encourages collaborative problem-solving, and supports the development of communication skills. Both students benefit from teaching and learning from each other, reinforcing their understanding of the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various subjects and topics, allowing students to focus on areas where they need the most support. Flexible structure accommodates different learning styles and paces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student interactions and collaboration skills, assess individual understanding of the material through quizzes or assignments, and gather feedback from students about their experience with reciprocal peer tutoring.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research has shown that reciprocal peer tutoring can lead to improved academic outcomes, enhanced social skills, and increased student engagement. Students benefit from teaching and learning from each other, reinforcing their understanding of the material.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ohio University study where students who read and discussed story passages with their peers recalled more content and scored higher on assessments.

docs.title: Reciprocal Teaching: Peer Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS)
Description
docs.text: PALS is a peer tutoring strategy designed to improve reading comprehension and fluency among students, primarily in grades 2–6. In PALS, students are paired, and each member of the pair takes turns being the 'Coach' and 'Player.' The PALS structure includes three main activities: Partner Reading with Retell, Paragraph Shrinking, and Prediction Relay. During each activity, the lower-performing reader serves as the Coach, while the higher-performing reader performs the role of Reader, modeling good reading skills. After five minutes, the students switch roles. The pairs proceed through each of the three activities in the same manner. The teacher selects appropriate text for each student pair based on the reading level of the weaker reader. It is essential that while the students are engaged in peer tutoring activities, the teacher moves about the room and monitors their work. Doing so also provides a great opportunity for the teacher to offer feedback to students about how well they are reading, implementing the PALS activities and working with their partners. Each PALS session lasts for approximately 35 minutes, with about 10 minutes devoted to each of the activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading materials at varying reading levels, training for students on the PALS activities, classroom time of approximately 35 minutes per session.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful pairing of students to ensure effective tutoring. Requires initial training and ongoing monitoring by the teacher to ensure proper implementation. Effectiveness may vary based on student dynamics and reading skill levels.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily designed for students in grades 2–6, but adaptable for older students with reading difficulties.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, improve reading fluency, practice summarizing, improve vocabulary, develop social awareness and relationship skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Peer support can increase motivation and engagement. The structure allows for targeted practice of specific reading skills. Peer interactions also provide opportunities to practice social awareness and relationship skills. Facilitating conversations between learners about texts increases retention of content in Long-term Memory and also develops Speed of Processing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adapt the complexity of the texts and the roles within the pairs to suit individual student needs. Flexible pairing allows for students to work with different partners, providing diverse perspectives and learning opportunities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Peer Teaching
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student progress in reading fluency and comprehension through observation and assessment. Collect feedback from students regarding their experience with the PALS activities. Assess student ability to summarize and identify main ideas effectively.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that PALS is an evidence-based practice to promote reading achievement. It has been shown to improve reading skills for students with and without learning disabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Numerous schools and districts have implemented PALS as part of their reading intervention programs. For example, Vanderbilt University has developed and researched PALS extensively.

docs.title: Recognizing the Value of Learning from Mistakes
Description
docs.text: This strategy changes perceptions about mistakes, viewing them as learning opportunities. Students are encouraged to take more risks, think in new ways, cheat less, and solve mysteries that had previously eluded them. Key actions include stopping the practice of marking errors without explaining why they're wrong, providing a chance to correct mistakes, making improvement a significant factor in evaluation, and responding constructively to mistakes made in class discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A willingness from teachers to change their approach to mistakes, a classroom environment that supports risk-taking, and clear communication about the value of learning from errors.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant shift in mindset from both teachers and students. May face resistance from those who are accustomed to traditional evaluation methods.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and teachers, particularly those in environments where mistakes are heavily stigmatized.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Shift the perception of mistakes from negative to positive, encouraging risk-taking, exploration, and independent thinking.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages a growth mindset, reduces fear of failure, promotes risk-taking and creativity, and increases student engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and grade levels. Focus can be tailored to specific types of mistakes or learning goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation, willingness to take risks, improved problem-solving skills, and positive attitudes toward mistakes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced learning outcomes, greater creativity, and a more resilient learner mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Conducting a class discussion about famous mistakes that led to breakthroughs, creating a 'mistake-friendly' zone in the classroom, or implementing a revision policy that allows students to improve their grades based on corrections.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Allowing students to record lessons so they can play them back and go over anything that might be confusing. Encourage them to write down timestamps of when they got lost in their notes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to recording devices or software

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who struggle with self-monitoring or note-taking

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for revisiting content, provides auditory feedback on writing quality, enhances comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Encourage students to play back the recordings as many times as needed. Allow them to adjust playback speed for a comfortable listening experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe if learners revisit recordings and use them during study sessions. Encourage learners to self-assess if they feel supported by the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that recording devices can help support learning by reinforcing learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of recording devices in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Recording lectures, recording explanations of complex processes, recording peer teaching sessions. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Redirecting language is a classroom management tool that uses clear, non-negotiable instructions to redirect student behavior. It involves firm words in the form of statements or commands that are clear and respectful. This strategy emphasizes what students should do rather than what they shouldn't, using 'do' statements instead of 'don't' statements. Redirecting Language is direct and specific, names the desired behavior, is kept brief, and uses statements rather than questions to maintain a firm and non-negotiable tone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A clear understanding of classroom expectations and the ability to communicate these expectations in a firm and respectful manner.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for students with severe behavioral issues that require more intensive interventions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who are off-task or exhibiting inappropriate behavior in the classroom.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To redirect student behavior in a firm, direct, and respectful way, promoting a safe and respectful classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a direct and clear method to correct student behavior, reducing ambiguity and potential for negotiation. This helps to maintain a safe and respectful classroom environment by clearly defining expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptations may include visuals of redirected behavior.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and the effectiveness of the redirection, track instances of off-task behavior, and monitor the overall classroom environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Redirecting language, when used effectively, can positively impact student behavior and create a more structured and respectful learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of asking 'Why is Jerome not focusing on his work?', the teacher directs, 'Jerome, start your work now.' Instead of asking 'Why do I hear chatter?', the teacher directs, 'All eyes should be on me and every mouth closed.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reducing visual clutter involves minimizing the amount of unnecessary or distracting visual stimuli in the learning environment. This can include removing posters, decorations, and other items that are not directly related to the learning objectives. By reducing visual clutter, educators can create a more focused and calming environment that supports learner attention and concentration. A less cluttered environment is thought to reduce cognitive overload and improve the brain’s ability to process information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to remove unnecessary items from the learning environment. May require adjustments to classroom management strategies to address learner attention and concentration. Instructors must be mindful of the impact of visual clutter on learner focus and concentration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find a minimalist environment to be sterile or uninviting. It may be challenging to balance the need for visual stimulation with the need to reduce distractions. Reducing visual clutter may not be sufficient to address learner attention and concentration problems.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve learner focus, reduce distractions, create a calming learning environment, promote learner attention and concentration, reduce cognitive overload

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner focus by minimizing distractions. Supports attention and concentration by creating a more calming environment. Reduces cognitive overload by simplifying the visual landscape. Can improve learner performance by making it easier to process information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can work with learners to identify and remove items that are particularly distracting for them. The level of visual clutter can be adjusted to meet the needs of different learners. Reducing visual clutter can be combined with other personalization strategies, such as flexible seating and flexible pacing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner focus and attention in class activities. Collect learner feedback on the impact of visual clutter on their learning. Measure learner achievement and compare outcomes in less cluttered environments versus more cluttered environments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved focus and attention: Research suggests that reducing visual clutter can improve learner focus and attention by minimizing distractions. Reduced cognitive overload: A less cluttered environment can reduce cognitive overload, making it easier for learners to process information. Increased achievement: Some studies have shown that reducing visual clutter can lead to improved learner achievement, although more research is needed to confirm these findings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher removes all posters and decorations from the classroom walls except for a few essential anchor charts. A professor uses a minimalist design for their online course website to reduce visual distractions. A trainer eliminates unnecessary graphics and animations from their presentation slides to improve learner focus.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student reflection on learning, particularly when done collaboratively, is critical for moving knowledge of content and strategies into Long-term Memory.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured reflection time, prompts for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel tedious, requires careful facilitation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance long-term memory, promote metacognition, encourage self-assessment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory, promotes metacognition, encourages self-assessment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide varied reflection methods, allow students to choose how they reflect.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth of reflection, self-assessment accuracy, long-term retention.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced long-term memory, improved metacognition, better self-assessment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Journaling about learning experiences, discussing reflections in groups, or sharing reflections with the class.

docs.title: Reflecting on Student Strengths and Challenges
Description
docs.text: Educators identify specific student strengths and/or challenges related to learning, social-emotional learning or other domains, and uses aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning and address challenges. This involves a deep understanding of each student's individual profile and tailoring instruction to meet their unique needs. The educator uses student data and evidence to inform instruction and identify student strengths and challenges.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Student data (e.g., assessment results, observations), knowledge of student strengths and challenges, and a repertoire of instructional strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time and effort to understand each student's individual profile. May be challenging to implement in large classes or with limited resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, special education teachers, and instructional coaches

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify and leverage student strengths, address learning differences, promote student self-awareness, tailor instruction to meet individual needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses individual student needs, fosters a positive learning environment, promotes self-awareness and metacognition. Allows instructors to leverage existing strengths of learners to address areas of need.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be tailored to specific learning domains (e.g., literacy, numeracy, social-emotional learning). Interventions can be adapted based on student age, grade level, and specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observations of student engagement, analysis of student work, and student self-reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of strengths-based approaches in promoting student motivation, engagement, and academic achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher identifies that a student struggles with reading comprehension but excels in visual learning. The teacher uses graphic organizers and visual aids to support the student's comprehension of texts. (See Apply Student-centered Strategies to Support Learning Differences Micro-credential)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection involves pausing after completing a writing assignment to consider how the assignment went. Students are encouraged to identify roadblocks, discuss which strategies worked, and brainstorm changes for the future.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Writing assignment; facilitator; reflection questions or prompts

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for some students to reflect; requires consistent practice; effectiveness depends on student engagement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students struggling with writing assignments, particularly those with learning and thinking differences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing strategies; enhance self-awareness; promote continuous improvement; develop critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves writing strategies; enhances self-awareness; promotes continuous improvement

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt reflection questions to suit different types of writing assignments; provide additional support for learners who struggle to reflect on their work

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student's ability to reflect on their writing; track improvements in writing strategies; monitor student self-awareness and critical thinking skills

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved writing strategies; enhanced self-awareness; promoted continuous improvement; developed critical thinking skills (as suggested by reflection practice)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection exercises are activities designed to promote emotional self-awareness and regulation by encouraging learners to think about their feelings and behaviors. Examples include: Journal Reflections: Students think back on their experiences and outcomes helps provide them with a greater understanding of themselves. Students can think and write about their experiences throughout a day or class period and look for patterns, as well as create and manage goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, pencils, journaling apps.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may not know how to be introspective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To help learners reflect on their own feelings and behaviors.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to be introspective.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be personalized.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner participation

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Unknown

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Not applicable.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection on learning involves linking a current experience to previous learnings (called scaffolding). It also means drawing forth cognitive and emotional information from several sources (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, tactile). It also means applying what is learned to contexts beyond the original situations in which something was learned. Reflection can be enhanced when we ponder our learning with others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection during or after learning. Various strategies to guide students through a period of reflection (discussions, interviews, questioning, logs and journals).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may be caught in a dilemma: 'What am I supposed to do? How do I ‘reflect’? I've already completed this assignment! Why do I have to think about it anymore?'

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Link current experiences to previous learnings, draw forth cognitive and emotional information from several sources, and apply learnings to new situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances the meaning of work, encourages insight and complex learning, and fosters personal growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Reflection can be done alone or with others. Various strategies to guide students through a period of reflection (discussions, interviews, questioning, logs and journals).

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evidence of linking current experiences to previous learnings in student work. Documentation of reflection in student writing or discussion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Teachers who promote reflective classrooms ensure that students are fully engaged in the process of making meaning. They organize instruction so that students are the producers, not just the consumers, of knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Conduct discussions about students' problem-solving processes. Guide students to look for ways they can apply their learnings to future settings.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves teachers reflecting on each lesson before and after teaching. Record what worked well and what could be improved. Keep these reflections organized alongside your lesson plans, whether digitally or in a journal, and revisit them to make necessary adjustments for future lessons.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection, a way to record reflections, and a willingness to make adjustments for future lessons.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to reflect on each lesson.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve teaching practice, identify areas for improvement, make necessary adjustments for future lessons

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to improve their teaching practice by reflecting on what worked well and what could be improved.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use digital tools or a journal to record their reflections. They can also revisit their reflections to make necessary adjustments for future lessons.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved teaching practice, identification of areas for improvement, and necessary adjustments made for future lessons.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of reflection on teaching practice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher reflects on a lesson and identifies that the students struggled with a particular concept. The teacher revises the lesson to provide more support for that concept.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves teachers assessing and reflecting on each student's comprehension and engagement by using critical thinking questions that encourage deep thinking about math concepts. Teachers should observe their responses to gauge understanding. Look for clarity in explanations, their ability to apply concepts to real-world scenarios, and evidence of critical and flexible thinking and problem-solving. Embrace productive struggle to help students engage with challenging material, fostering deeper learning and a growth mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Critical thinking questions, a way to assess student responses, and a willingness to embrace productive struggle.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to assess each student's comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess student comprehension, gauge student engagement, foster deeper learning, promote a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to assess student comprehension, gauge student engagement, foster deeper learning, and promote a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of critical thinking questions to assess student comprehension. They can also observe student responses to gauge understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student comprehension, increased student engagement, and a growth mindset.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of reflection on student learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher asks students to explain a math concept in their own words. The teacher observes the students' responses to gauge understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection prompts are specific questions or statements used to guide learners in thinking deeply about their learning process, content understanding, and personal growth. They encourage metacognition, self-assessment, and the application of knowledge to new contexts. Effective reflection prompts facilitate deeper engagement with complex ideas and allow students to find broader meaning in their work. Teachers can use various closing and reflective activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for reflection during or after learning. Prompts can be delivered orally or in writing. Recording medium (paper, digital, etc.)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require explicit instruction on how to reflect effectively. Students may need support to move beyond superficial responses.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-assessment, deepen understanding, and enable application of knowledge to new situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports metacognition, self-assessment, and critical thinking. Provides avenues for engaging with complex ideas and finding broader meaning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be adapted to suit the lesson, subject, and learners' needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and insightfulness of student responses. Evidence of metacognition and application of knowledge. Changes in attitude and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Strategic integration of meaningful closings and reflection into classroom practice gives students multiple avenues for engaging with complex ideas and allows more students to find broader meaning in their work. Activities also help teachers to more deeply understand and adapt to the intellectual processes of our students.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A classroom example of a world history class discussing an excerpt from The Power of Myth, asking everyone to jot down a one-sentence final thought.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves teachers reflecting on their teaching practice by engaging in peer collaboration and seeking feedback from colleagues who teach similar math concepts. Schedule informal meetings or visits to discuss what's working well in your classroom and identify areas for improvement. Invite colleagues to observe a lesson and provide non-evaluative feedback, focusing on specific strategies, techniques, and best practices that you can incorporate into your own teaching.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for peer collaboration, a willingness to seek feedback, and a focus on specific strategies, techniques, and best practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to engage in peer collaboration.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
