docs.text: • Improve teaching practice, identify areas for improvement, incorporate best practices

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to improve their teaching practice by engaging in peer collaboration and seeking feedback from colleagues.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can schedule informal meetings or visits to discuss what's working well in their classroom. They can also invite colleagues to observe a lesson and provide non-evaluative feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved teaching practice, identification of areas for improvement, and incorporation of best practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of reflection with others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher invites a colleague to observe a lesson and provide non-evaluative feedback. The teacher incorporates the feedback into their teaching practice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Grades should reflect learning over time rather than be an end in and of itself. Learning through multiple modalities that leverage learners' languages and cultural insights.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Flexible assessment methods, emphasis on learning over evaluation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from traditional grading

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Shift focus from punitive grading to learning, promote continuous improvement, recognize diverse learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages continuous improvement, values diverse learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for assessment of learning through multiple modalities

docs.title: Instructions

• Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student progress over time, recognition of diverse learning styles

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Grades should reveal what students can do, not serve a punitive purpose, and multilingual learners’ accomplishments should represent learning through multiple modalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Evaluating student progress using visual, auditory, and kinesthetic methods

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflective journaling is a technique used to encourage reflective learning by highlighting students’ thoughts and perceptions about course content. It's a learning exercise where students express their understanding, reflections, response, or analysis of an event, experience, or concept in writing, encompassing all aspects of their thoughts and emotions. This form of writing increases attention and concentration during class time and plays a major role in the transformative learning process by allowing students to critically reflect on their beliefs and consciously make and implement plans that bring about improved ways of redefining those beliefs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a journal (physical or digital), writing utensils, and dedicated time for journaling. Instructors need to provide prompts and feedback, and create a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reflective journals should not be a simple summary of course material or a learning log. Focus should be on reactions to what has been read and reflections and thoughts about the material.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for students in higher education and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster critical thinking skills, develop reflective practices, increase student interest, encourage further investigation, enhance understanding of course content, facilitate transformative learning, promote self-discovery

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a channel of inner communication that connects beliefs, feelings, and actions. Creates effective learning conditions that result in self-discovery. Helps students develop their knowledge and understanding of course content.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a range of prompts to address diverse interests and experiences. Allow learners to focus on aspects of the course content that are most relevant to their personal and professional goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze journal entries to assess learners' understanding of concepts, critical thinking skills, and personal reflections. Track changes in learners' thinking over time. Evaluate the depth and quality of learners' responses to prompts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes transformative learning by helping individuals make meaning of their own experiences in order to develop as learners and leaders. Through this practice, they develop into reflective practitioners, understanding more about why things are done rather than how.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Possible questions for a reflective journal include: What was the most interesting thing I read for this lesson? What were three main things I learned from this lesson? What did I previously think was true, but now know to be wrong? What did we not cover that I expected we should?

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reflection prompts encourage learners to think deeply about their learning experiences. These prompts can be used at the end of a class period or when a large piece of work is submitted. Prompts include sharing one thing learned, posing a question for future investigation, responding with a single word, analyzing what worked and what didn’t, identifying a point of pride in their work, and suggesting how they would approach the task differently next time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time allocated at the end of a lesson or upon submission of a major assignment. A list of reflection prompts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel repetitive if used too frequently without variation. Requires a classroom culture that values reflection and self-assessment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from structured reflection activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote deeper engagement with complex ideas, allow more students to find broader meaning in their work, help teachers to more deeply understand and adapt to the intellectual processes of our students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured opportunities for reflection, promotes metacognition, helps students connect learning to personal experiences, and gives teachers insights into student thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Prompts can be chosen based on individual student needs or learning goals. Adaptations can be made for verbal, written, or digital formats. Sentence stems may be provided to scaffold responses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and thoughtfulness of student responses, ability to connect learning to personal experiences, and evidence of metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that reflection is an essential part of learning. Intentional reflection can increase retention of learning and transfer of skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • At the end of a history lesson, students are asked to share one thing they learned. Before submitting a science project, students respond to the prompt: 'What is one part of your work that you are proud of?'

docs.text: Among all the math fluency apps listed here, Reflex stands out with a research-based system of learning math for students ages 2-8. It offers an adaptive learning environment creating scopes of learning math for students with different ability levels. It is thoroughly intuitive to offer learners problems in line with their skill levels.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Reflex math app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be expensive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students ages 2-8.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Learn math with an adaptive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Adaptive learning environment and problems in line with skill levels.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offers adaptive learning environments for students with different ability levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice

  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track progress in math fact fluency and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This technique involves changing one’s mindset from anxiety to excitement, leveraging the similar physiological responses (faster heartbeats and cortisol surges) associated with both emotions. Excitement puts people in an opportunity mindset (“I can do something about this”), whereas anxiety can put people in a threat mindset. By reframing anxiety as excitement, learners may experience better math performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Simple prompt or message before starting a task. Requires some awareness of one's emotional state.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not work for everyone; some may find it difficult to shift from anxiety to excitement. The Atlantic published a video about this strategy, and some find this difficult to do.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages experiencing math anxiety or performance anxiety

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance math performance, shift mindset from threat to opportunity, improve problem-solving focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners approach challenges with a positive mindset, improves focus and problem-solving abilities, avoids the need for significant physiological shifts required to achieve calmness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The reframing technique can be personalized with different encouragement messages and opportunities mindset prompts. The written message, “Try to get excited,” before completing a task.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved math performance, increased problem-solving focus, positive mindset

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that showing participants the written message, “Try to get excited,” on their computer screens before giving them difficult math problems to do resulted in better math performance than showing the message, “Try to remain calm,” or the neutral message, “Please wait a few moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before starting a math exam, students are encouraged to reframe their anxiety as excitement, focusing on the opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Practice reframing negative thoughts, statements, or situations into more positive alternatives. Use the self-talk journal or notes. Start with examples of negative self-talk (e.g., 'Everyone knows I can’t win this challenge'). Ask students to restate the fixed mindset phrase into a positive message using the name they chose for their negative voice (e.g., 'Good try, Ruthless Ralph. Even if I don’t win, I will learn something from this challenge!').

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of negative self-talk statements, positive reframing strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel forced or inauthentic at first. Requires consistent practice to become a habit.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary to adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop the ability to reframe negative self-talk into positive messages.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Cultivates a more optimistic and growth-oriented mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor reframing exercises to individual negative self-talk patterns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and frequency of positive reframing in journal entries or discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Shift from fixed to growth mindset; improved self-perception and motivation (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reframing involves rephrasing negative thoughts, statements, or situations into more positive alternatives. Students use their self-talk logs or notes to identify negative messages and restate them into positive messages, often using the name they chose for their negative voice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Self-talk logs or notes containing negative messages. Examples of negative self-talk to reframe. A supportive environment for practicing and sharing reframes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may struggle to identify positive alternatives. Some reframes may feel forced or insincere. The activity's success depends on students' willingness to practice and apply reframing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students who are learning to manage negative thoughts and develop a more positive self-perception.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To help students transform negative thoughts into positive alternatives, promoting a growth mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by identifying negative thoughts. Supports emotional regulation by changing negative thoughts into positive ones. Fosters a growth mindset by seeing challenges as opportunities for growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and learning styles. Students can use their own self-talk logs or pre-made examples. Educators can provide varying levels of support and scaffolding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review students' reframes for accuracy and positivity. Assess students' ability to articulate the impact of reframing on their emotions. Observe students' use of reframing in real-life situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that cognitive reframing has a positive impact on mindset. Reframing can foster stress resilience and promote problem solving when facing adversity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Restating the fixed mindset phrase 'Everyone knows I can’t win this challenge' into a positive message like 'Good try, Ruthless Ralph. Even if I don’t win, I will learn something from this challenge!' Practicing with a variety of negative messages and reframing them into positive alternatives. Using a journal to track and reframe negative self-talk over time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implement consistent PE classes to help students burn off energy and be active, improving their ability to focus in class. Guidelines recommend 150 minutes of PE weekly for elementary school students and 225 minutes for middle and high school students. Provide multiple activity choices and cycle through different sports and activities to encourage participation and exploration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Scheduled class time, trained PE teachers, appropriate facilities and equipment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires dedicated resources and facilities. May not appeal to all students if activities are not varied and engaging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase physical activity, enhance focus and concentration, improve overall health

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students burn off energy and be active, improves focus and concentration, provides structured physical activity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer multiple choices for activities to cater to different interests and abilities. Cycle through different sports and activities to keep students engaged.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track participation rates in PE classes, assess improvements in physical fitness, monitor student behavior and engagement in other classes

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved health and fitness: Regular PE classes can improve students' physical health and fitness levels. Enhanced academic performance: Increased physical activity can lead to better focus and academic outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Regularly referring back to mentor texts in teacher conferences, whole-class lessons, or discussions reinforces learning and helps students internalize new techniques. Remind students that this can be applied in the future.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to previously used mentor texts. Time for review and discussion in class. A classroom environment where students feel comfortable revisiting and reflecting on past learning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be repetitive if not implemented thoughtfully. Students may become bored or disengaged. Requires careful planning to ensure that referencing is relevant and meaningful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for reinforcing previously taught concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning of writing techniques, promote internalization of new concepts, enhance transfer of learning to new contexts, increase retention of information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides ongoing support and reinforcement. Helps students connect new learning to prior knowledge. Promotes long-term retention of information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Frequency and type of referencing can be tailored to student needs. Students can be given opportunities to choose which mentor texts to revisit. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating the application of previously learned techniques. Participation in discussions and analyses of mentor texts. Student reflections on their learning process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that regular review and referencing improves retention and transfer of learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a writing conference, the teacher refers back to a mentor text to illustrate a specific technique. In a whole-class lesson, students revisit a mentor text to identify examples of strong voice. Students are asked to reflect on how they have applied techniques from mentor texts in their own writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognizing and positively reinforcing positive actions when they are observed. This involves recognizing positive behavior, asking how it made the student feel, and connecting extrinsic rewards to positive feelings to enhance intrinsic motivation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Recognition activities and items, such as tokens, stickers, and certificates. Teacher awareness of positive behaviors.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent implementation, some students may become overly reliant on extrinsic rewards.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators aiming to reinforce positive behaviors in students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Strengthen intrinsic motivation, reinforce positive behaviors, increase student engagement, and foster a positive classroom environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages positive behavior, enhances student engagement, and promotes a positive classroom environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of recognition activities and items to appeal to diverse student preferences. Provide individualized feedback and praise.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior, track the frequency of positive behaviors, gather student feedback through surveys or discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Recognizing and positively reinforcing positive actions strengthens intrinsic motivation and encourages positive behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher gives a student a certificate for helping a classmate and asks how it made them feel, connecting the reward to the positive feeling of helping others.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Help learners understand how math gets used in the world in ways that relate to their personal strengths. By connecting math concepts to learners' interests and expertise, teachers can empower students as math learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors need to get to know their learners and their interests and be creative in finding ways to connect math to those interests.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be flexible and adaptable. May be challenging to implement in large classes with diverse interests.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels of learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase motivation, enhance confidence, promote a deeper understanding of math concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner motivation and confidence by connecting math to their interests and expertise. Makes math more relevant and engaging.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can tailor their examples and activities to individual learners' interests and strengths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learners' engagement and motivation in math activities. Evaluate their ability to apply math concepts to real-world situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that connecting math to learners' interests and experiences can significantly increase their motivation, confidence, and understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Relating percentages to basketball statistics for learners who love playing basketball; connecting geometry to architecture for learners interested in design.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Connecting math to students' personal strengths involves helping students understand how math is used in the real world in ways that align with their interests and expertise. For example, if students enjoy basketball, teachers can relate percentages to basketball statistics. This allows students to feel more confident with the content because they can bring something to the table that is valued, important, and relevant to them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers need to be aware of students’ interests and strengths. They should be prepared to find or create examples and activities that connect math to these areas. This may require some creativity and flexibility.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to find examples that resonate with all students. Requires a deep understanding of students’ interests and strengths.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners struggling with math

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student confidence, make math more relevant, activate student expertise, improve engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student motivation and engagement by making math more relevant and meaningful. It allows students to see the value of math in their own lives and to connect it to their personal strengths and interests. It can also help students develop a more positive attitude toward math and increase their confidence in their abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor examples and activities to match students’ specific interests and strengths. They can also encourage students to share their own examples of how math is used in their lives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Analogies and prior knowledge activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students’ engagement and motivation through observation and participation. Collect feedback from students on their perceptions of the relevance of math to their lives. Analyze student work to identify connections to their personal interests and strengths.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that connecting math to students’ interests and strengths can lead to increased engagement, improved performance, and a more positive attitude toward math. Students are more likely to retain information and apply it to new situations when they see the relevance and value of the content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Relating percentages to the basketball statistics students often look at. Students might not be experts on how to calculate percents, but they could be experts on which NBA players have the highest shooting percentages. When students make that connection, their positionality changes. They’re the ones bringing something to the table that’s valued and important and relevant.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy leverages learners’ existing strengths and interests to make math more relatable and engaging. By connecting math concepts to learners’ passions, instructors can increase confidence and motivation. For example, if some students love playing basketball. Teachers can relate percentages to the basketball statistics students often look at, which allows students to feel more confident with the content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors need to be aware of learners’ interests and be able to make meaningful math connections. May require additional time and effort to identify and create relevant examples.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may not have clearly defined interests or strengths. Connections may seem forced if not carefully aligned with content and learner needs.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who struggle with math or have negative attitudes toward the subject.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner motivation, engagement, and confidence in math. Demonstrate the relevance of math to learners’ lives and interests.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner engagement by tapping into intrinsic motivation. Builds confidence by leveraging learners’ expertise in other areas. Provides opportunities for learners to see themselves as capable math learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailored to individual learner interests and strengths. Instructors should gather information about learners’ passions and find relevant math connections.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Integration
  • Whole-task performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe increases in learner engagement and participation. Assess improvements in confidence and attitudes toward math.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases learner confidence by activating students’ expertise in math contexts. Positionality changes as learners bringing something to the table that’s valued and important and relevant.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Connecting percentages to basketball statistics for learners who love basketball. Applying geometry concepts to art or design projects for creative learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves educators identifying students with strengths or challenges in relationship skills and implementing targeted supports. Relationship skills encompass effective communication, cooperation, conflict management, and resisting inappropriate social pressure. The strategy focuses on leveraging students’ existing strengths to address their challenges. Educators observe student behavior to identify relationship skills strengths and challenges. Strategies include pairing students with positive role models, providing group assignments that foster common interests, displaying communication protocols, and using literature to explicitly teach relationship skills. Student reflection on the strategies used is essential to determine effectiveness and guide adjustments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Observation skills, understanding of relationship skills, targeted strategies, student reflection, assessment rubrics

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation and accurate identification of strengths and challenges. Effectiveness depends on the specific strategies chosen and student engagement. May require additional resources for implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those with identified strengths or challenges in relationship skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, cooperation, and conflict management skills; foster positive relationships; leverage student strengths; develop social awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengths-based approach enhances self-esteem and motivation. Targeted supports address specific challenges. Promotes a positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Supports can be tailored to individual strengths and challenges, learning styles, and cultural backgrounds. Choice of strategies can involve student input.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Coaching
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student reflection, observation of behavior, educator reflection, work examples, assessment rubrics

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that strong relationship skills predict academic performance and social development. Parent involvement is also linked to children's academic and social development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learner Variability Project (Digital Promise Global), Responsive Classroom, Edutopia, KQED MindShift

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors should present vocabulary that is useful and/or necessary for learners, based on their learning goals. One way to do this is to ask learners to identify vocabulary topics they want to learn in class, then compile the most common suggestions. For students who need to learn vocabulary topics not of general interest (e.g., writing a CV/resume), instructors can assign individual homework assignments and suggest online resources. After instructors teach a new word, learners should use it in their own words, such as in a conversation, role play, or original sentence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pre-planning to determine most useful vocabulary topics, access to relevant resources, time for practice and conversation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires instructor to tailor instruction to meet diverse needs, may be time-consuming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve English vocabulary, increase understanding and memory, promote Disciplinary Literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear purpose for learning vocabulary, increases student engagement, promotes deeper understanding and memory

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can teach vocabulary relevant to the majority of students, while providing tailored assignments and resources to individuals with unique interests or needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners use new vocabulary in conversation or role play, write original sentences

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • In my opinion happier and more productive adult English classes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: AR apps allow technicians and users to communicate with experts in real time. The tech support highlights objects in the user's field of view so they can assist in repair without ever having to leave their seats. AR headsets connect to Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and other diagnostic information to help technicians assess repair needs more quickly and reduce downtime.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • AR hardware (smartphones or tablets), high-speed and reliable internet connection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires expertise to operate properly and the risk of poor signal hampering communication.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Technicians, experts, and remote workers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication between experts and users, assist repair of technical systems more quickly, enhance field communication skills, troubleshoot equipment more efficiently.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Support for the troubleshooting of complex problems more quickly, reduced downtime, better expert and technician communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tech support specialists highlight objects in the user's field of vision and tailor their suggestions to better help the user.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Time to troubleshoot and repair an issue, feedback from user and expert.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Faster repair times, improved satisfaction with technical solutions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When learners are struggling with a difficult task, clutter in the classroom or on the desk can make it impossible to keep the brain focused. Remove unnecessary clutter and visual stimuli from the workspace to help the learner focus on the task at hand.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clean workspace, minimal visual stimuli, designated quiet space.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in shared spaces. Some learners may find the lack of stimulation demotivating.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners struggling with attention, especially those with sensory sensitivities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus, reduce distractions, enhance attention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces sensory overload, minimizes distractions, promotes focus, enhances attention, creates a calm environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The level of reduction can be adjusted based on individual needs and sensitivities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to stay on task. Track the frequency of distractions. Collect feedback on the learner's sense of focus.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Removing visual distractions can significantly improve focus and attention, especially for learners who are sensitive to sensory overload. It creates a calm and supportive environment that enhances concentration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides a designated quiet corner with minimal decorations for students who need a distraction-free space. A parent removes toys and clutter from a child's desk during homework time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Repairing harm is a restorative practice where, instead of simply being sent off to a punishment, a student who has misbehaved is tasked with figuring out how to repair whatever damage was caused by their behavior, and then to actually carry out that repair with everyone who was impacted by their actions. First, the student meets with an adult to identify the harm caused and all the stakeholders impacted. Next, the student considers how the behavior affected others, developing empathy. Finally, the student creates and carries out a plan to repair the harm with every stakeholder, which may involve an apology or more extensive actions. This process is an alternative to traditional punishment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An administrator or responsible adult to facilitate the process, a private conference space, and a willingness from the student to engage in self-reflection and take responsibility for their actions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May take more time than traditional punishment and requires a genuine effort from the student to understand and repair the harm caused. Some students may deny the behavior, requiring careful handling by the adult facilitator.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who have misbehaved or caused harm to others in the classroom or school environment.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address and correct the source of misbehavior, fix any damage caused, and develop empathy and responsibility in students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students understand the ripple effect of their actions, develop empathy skills, and take responsibility for their behavior. It is more effective in opening up a child's eyes to how their behavior made others feel and offers a less traumatic approach compared to traditional punishment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptations can be made based on the severity of the harm and the needs of the stakeholders involved.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the student's engagement in the process, the quality of the repair plan, and the impact of the repair on the stakeholders involved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Restorative justice practices like repairing harm can lead to deeper and longer-lasting regret in students, stemming from a place of empathy. It is a more effective way to open up a child's eyes to how their behavior made others feel, and it is less traumatic than traditional punishment.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Teacher Effectiveness Training / Conflict Resolution — a complementary process for the persistent conflicts or misbehavior that repairing harm alone may not fully resolve
  • Natural and Logical Consequences — the principle distinguishing repair-focused consequences like this one from punishment

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • If a student throws food across the cafeteria and spills milk all over the floor, they might clean all of the tables, mop the floor, and work with the custodian to help clean, as they caused harm to the environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Repeat the key points for students several times and in several different ways. Multiple representations of the key ideas can provide learners the opportunity to absorb all concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful lesson planning to identify key concepts. Thoughtful language choices so students can follow along.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Repetition can be boring, so use sparingly. Students need to be self-aware to identify if they aren't processing information and ask for repetition.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides multiple exposures to key concepts, uses plain language that provides comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to repeat concepts for other students. Encourage self-monitoring so that students can realize what they didn't understand.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether students take advantage of the repetition and can respond accurately. Encourage learners to self-assess if they feel supported by the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that repetition can help support learning by reinforcing learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of repetition in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • During lessons, teachers emphasize key points. Students explain the key points to another student. Resource: Speed of Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Repeating key points for students several times and in several different ways to support processing speed. This strategy involves reinforcing essential information through varied repetition and rephrasing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Conscious effort to repeat and rephrase key points, use of diverse instructional methods, and awareness of student's processing needs

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May become redundant if not varied effectively, requires careful planning to avoid overwhelming students, and some students may find repetition tedious

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who need extra time to process information and benefit from repetition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce key concepts, improve retention, and support students with slower processing speeds

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory, provides multiple exposures to key content, supports diverse learning styles, and reinforces understanding

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Repetition can be tailored to individual needs, using different modalities (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) and varying levels of complexity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student's recall of key points through quizzes, discussions, and assignments. Observe for improved comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that repetition and varied instructional methods improve information retention and benefit students with processing speed challenges.

docs.title: Repeating Key Points in Different Ways
Description
docs.text: Repeating the key points for students several times and in several different ways helps reinforce understanding and supports learners who need more time to process information. This can involve rephrasing, providing examples, or using visual aids.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Conscious effort to repeat key points in different ways during instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time during instruction. Needs to be done thoughtfully to avoid being repetitive or boring.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who need additional time to process information or struggle with grasping key concepts.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, and support learners with processing speed challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces learning through repetition and multiple modalities. Provides additional processing time for learners with slower processing speeds.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Vary the repetition and modalities based on individual learner needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student understanding through questioning and feedback. Assess improvement in retention through quizzes or summaries.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Repeating key points in different ways enhances comprehension and improves retention, particularly for learners with processing speed challenges.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Procedural fluency requires having a repertoire of strategies. Before learners can flexibly choose an appropriate strategy, they must have strategies from which to choose. Strategies are flexible ways to solve a problem; algorithms are step-by-step procedures. Students should be able to flexibly use and adapt strategies and switch to a different strategy when their first choice is not working well. Every student must have the opportunity to learn more than one method. Limiting students to only one method puts them at a disadvantage, denying them access to more intuitive methods and the opportunity to flexibly choose a method that fits the problem at hand.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to provide varied methods, promote strategy comparisons, and cultivate a learning environment that values exploration and adaptation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant preparation, may overwhelm learners with too many options, and can be time-consuming to teach multiple strategies effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develops flexible problem-solving, improves strategic thinking, promotes adaptive learning, minimizes dependency on single methods

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers learners with multiple tools, enables adaptation to diverse problem types, and reduces reliance on rote memorization. Encourages adaptive and intuitive problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Cater by introducing strategies based on learner preferences, offering options for algorithm selection, and supporting exploration of diverse solution paths.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assesses learners' strategic flexibility through problem-solving tasks, evaluating their ability to select and adapt appropriate methods based on problem context. Examines learners' reasoning behind strategy choice and evaluates their efficiency in applying chosen methods.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Empowers learners with multiple tools, enables adaptation to diverse problem types, and reduces reliance on rote memorization. Encourages adaptive and intuitive problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Every student must have the opportunity to learn more than one method. Limiting students to only one method puts them at a disadvantage, denying them access to more intuitive methods and the opportunity to flexibly choose a method that fits the problem at hand.
