docs.title: Replace Negative Influences with Positive Ones
Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on intentionally minimizing exposure to negative external factors and actively seeking out positive influences to support a more constructive mindset. It involves identifying negative influences, such as toxic relationships or unsupportive environments, and limiting contact with them. Simultaneously, it emphasizes surrounding oneself with positive influences, such as supportive friends, uplifting content, and empowering communities, to foster a more optimistic and growth-oriented mindset.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires self-awareness and a willingness to evaluate and manage social and environmental influences. May benefit from external support such as therapy or coaching to address underlying issues. Access to resources such as support groups, positive media outlets, or mentorship programs can be helpful.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in situations where negative influences are unavoidable (e.g., family relationships, work environments). Requires ongoing effort and vigilance to maintain positive influences and minimize negative ones. May not be effective for individuals with severe mental health conditions without professional support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for individuals seeking to improve their mindset and overall well-being by managing their social and environmental influences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Minimize exposure to negative external factors, identify and limit contact with negative influences, surround oneself with positive and supportive people, foster a more optimistic and growth-oriented mindset.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes positive emotions by reducing exposure to negativity. Increases motivation by surrounding learners with supportive and empowering influences. Fosters a growth mindset by encouraging learners to seek out environments that support their goals. Enhances self-esteem by promoting a more positive self-perception.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by identifying and prioritizing individual sources of negativity or positivity. Flexible practice allows for integration into daily routines through social media curation, community involvement, or relationship management. Scaffolding can be provided for beginners, such as checklists of negative influences or templates for building positive relationships.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Coaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in self-reported mood and optimism using questionnaires or journals. Observe improvements in social interactions, relationship quality, and sense of belonging. Analyze the frequency and type of social and environmental influences experienced.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that social support and positive relationships are associated with improved mental health and overall well-being (e.g., Harvard Study of Adult Development). Studies show that exposure to positive media can enhance mood and promote prosocial behavior. Regularly engaging with supportive communities can foster a sense of belonging and purpose.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An individual prone to negative social media feeds unfollows accounts that promote negativity and follows accounts that promote positivity and inspiration. A student struggling with a challenging academic environment joins a study group with supportive and encouraging peers. Resource: Harvard Medical School – In It Together: The Science of Social Bonds.

docs.title: Representation of Diverse Perspectives and Identities
Description
docs.text: Incorporating multiple and varying perspectives within learning content to honor and value diverse approaches to learning. This involves presenting content that reflects different cultures, identities, and ways of knowing. The approach supports learners in making connections within and between concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Diverse learning materials, awareness of cultural differences, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of materials to avoid stereotypes and misrepresentations. Some learners may feel uncomfortable sharing personal experiences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those from diverse or non-dominant cultures and/or languages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote inclusivity, enhance cultural awareness, improve understanding of diverse perspectives, foster empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters inclusivity and respect for diverse perspectives. Enhances cultural awareness. Supports learners in making connections between concepts and their own experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer content that reflects different cultural backgrounds, identities, and perspectives. Encourage learners to share their own experiences and perspectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner engagement with diverse content. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of diverse perspectives in promoting understanding. Assess learner understanding of different cultural contexts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved cultural competence: Research shows that exposure to diverse perspectives can enhance cultural competence and foster empathy among learners.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Allowing or requiring retakes emphasizes a growth mindset and reinforces perseverance. It provides opportunities to learn from mistakes and successfully demonstrate learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Flexible testing schedules, resources for remediation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires resources for additional testing and remediation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote growth mindset, reinforce perseverance, encourage learning from mistakes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports growth mindset, encourages continuous learning, provides additional practice

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offers individualized remediation, supports learning at individual pace

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Number of retakes, improvement in scores over time

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • If struggle is part of the learning process, students should have the opportunity to learn from mistakes, engage in additional practice of targeted skills, and ultimately successfully demonstrate what they have learned.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Mandatory test retakes for scores below a certain level

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rereading is a literacy strategy where a reader revisits a sentence, paragraph, or entire text to improve accuracy, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. Teachers can model rereading during read-alouds, and learners can practice independently or in pairs. Rereading encourages closer attention to words and meanings and builds confidence in reading skills. Repeated readings, focusing on short chunks of text, support both fluency and comprehension, leading to better initial readings of new texts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to reading materials. Class time for read-alouds, shared reading, guided reading, or independent reading. Opportunities for modeling and practice. Can be integrated into various instructional contexts, such as shared reading, guided reading, Readers Theater, and close reading.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the initial text is too challenging for the learner. Requires careful selection of texts that are both engaging and appropriate for the learner's reading level. Rereading can become monotonous if not implemented with variety and purpose.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, struggling readers, and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading accuracy, enhance fluency, build vocabulary, and increase comprehension

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances decoding and sight recognition, promoting fluent reading. Supports deeper understanding through multiple exposures to the text. Improves prosody (reading with expression) and inferential understanding. Provides an opportunity for learners to self-correct and clarify misunderstandings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to individual learner needs and reading levels. Short texts or specific passages can be selected for focused rereading. Teachers can provide specific prompts or questions to guide rereading.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's fluency and expression during oral reading. Assess comprehension through questioning or summarizing after rereading. Monitor decoding accuracy and sight word recognition. Track improvement in reading speed and accuracy over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that rereading improves decoding, fluency, and comprehension. It helps learners develop a deeper understanding of the text, read with greater accuracy, and allocate more attention to making sense of what they have read. Fluency built through rereading one passage often transfers to new readings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a One Minute Reader iPad App, learners reread a text at least three times (cold read, read along, read alone) to develop more fluent reading and a deeper understanding of the text. Shared reading: A teacher and students share the responsibility for reading and comprehending the text, rereading the story or poem to continue the development of fluency. Guided reading: Students reread the text if they finish before others have finished or are prompted to reread a passage to gain better fluency and understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A research map is a visual representation of research topics and their interconnections, allowing users to explore academic literature in a structured and intuitive way. It displays clusters of related articles and topics, with connections indicating shared references or themes. This tool supports learners in navigating complex research landscapes, identifying key areas of study, and understanding the relationships between different concepts. It can enhance research skills, promote interdisciplinary thinking, and facilitate the discovery of relevant resources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a research map tool or platform. Basic understanding of research concepts and terminology.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The map may not be exhaustive or completely up-to-date. Requires users to critically evaluate the sources and connections presented.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beneficial for higher education students, researchers, and professionals seeking to understand and explore academic literature.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Navigate complex research, identify key study areas, understand concept relationships, enhance research skills, promote interdisciplinary thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual overview of research topics. Facilitates the discovery of relevant articles and connections. Supports interdisciplinary thinking and exploration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can customize their exploration by focusing on specific topics or connections of interest. The map can be filtered to show relevant information.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Research

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track user engagement with the research map. Monitor the number of articles and connections explored. Assess the quality of research questions and investigations informed by the map.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research maps can enhance research skills and promote interdisciplinary thinking. By providing a structured overview of the research landscape, these tools can facilitate the discovery of relevant resources and connections.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Digital Promise's Research Map is a visual representation of education and learning sciences research. Users can explore common topics and connections between topics, and save articles of interest.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is a visual representation of education and learning sciences research published in peer-reviewed journals from 2009-2018. Data from over 110,000 articles published between 2009 and 2018, found in 191 academic journals from the Web of Science database, was used to analyze the bibliographic record (title, keywords, author, cited references, and abstract) for each article and create a bibliographic coupling network, to link articles sharing at least two common references. An algorithm was used to detect groups of articles with densely shared links and gathered into nodes/circles called topics. Circle size indicates article numbers and line thickness shows connection strength. The analysis and visualization was completed using BiblioTools and D3.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Web access, visualization tool (BiblioTools and D3).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Does not subscribe to a particular point of view about teaching and learning. More like an interactive encyclopedia than a literature review.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, researchers, and practitioners in the field of education and learning sciences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore common topics in education and learning sciences research, identify connections between topics, and facilitate saving articles of interest. Act as an interactive encyclopedia of research.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables users to visually explore research topics and their interconnections. Provides access to a wide breadth of information arranged by subject. Facilitates the discovery of relevant articles and resources.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can explore the map based on their specific interests and research needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Hypertext Navigation
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Usage patterns, frequency of article downloads, and feedback from users on the utility of the map.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a comprehensive overview of research trends in education and learning sciences. Supports informed decision-making by educators and researchers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Digital Promise’s Research Map, which includes data from over 110,000 articles published between 2009 and 2018

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Research reports are visual aids designed to present data and insights in an engaging and accessible format. These reports use visuals to emphasize important information and inspire readers to understand and act on research findings. Effective research reports employ elements such as circle icons to highlight key findings and bar graphs to present achievements. By making research visually appealing, it becomes easier to share findings with students, staff, and the broader community.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to design software and data. Implementation involves careful integration of visuals and text. May require training in research communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Poorly designed reports can be confusing or misleading. Inaccurate data can undermine credibility. Requires attention to detail and accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Researchers, students, educators, and community members across all disciplines

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Share research findings, engage readers, emphasize key information, inspire action, promote understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes research more engaging and accessible. Enhances understanding and retention of information. Provides a clear and organized format for presenting data.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different research topics, audiences, and presentation styles. Design elements can be adjusted based on the message and context.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the clarity and effectiveness of communication. Assess reader comprehension and engagement. Track the impact of research findings.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual research reports have been shown to improve engagement and understanding. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include research reports using circle icons to highlight main findings and bar graphs to showcase achievements. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating research reports.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Resistance reading and writing counter-narratives are strategies to develop learners' abilities to critique a text (or an image or other media) and to respond in writing, sharing their concerns and critiques. Resistance reading requires learners to analyze a book, song lyrics, a commercial, or a poem by first thinking about the context and purpose that informed the text. Counter-narratives involve crafting a response to the text, either as a rebuttal or as a rewriting of the original from a different perspective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to texts or media. Writing materials or digital tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to have strong reading comprehension skills. May be challenging for learners to critique texts or media that they agree with.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • 6-12 grade learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop the skill to critique a text, image, or other media. Enable students to respond in writing, sharing concerns and critiques. Encourage questioning and pushing back on information or stories.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports learners in questioning and critiquing messages in texts and other media. Helps learners develop their ability to voice their views beyond the classroom walls.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose to write a rebuttal as a letter to the author, as an essay, or in the style of an op-ed article. They can also rewrite the original from a different perspective.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Assigned Positions
  • Argument Construction
  • Role Reversal

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student-created rebuttals and rewritten texts. Assess the ability to identify biases and power structures in original texts. Evaluate the clarity and persuasiveness of alternative perspectives presented.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages critical thinking: Research shows counter-narratives can reveal hidden assumptions in texts. Enhances empathy: Understanding multiple perspectives develops learners’ social awareness. Improves writing skills: Composition tasks develop voice and argumentation.

docs.title: Respect Diverse Talents and Ways of Learning
Description
docs.text: There are many roads to learning. People bring different talents and styles of learning to college. Brilliant learners in the classroom may be all thumbs in the lab or design studio. Learners with much hands-on experience may not do so well in theory or creative problem-solving. Learners need the opportunities to show their talents and learn in ways that work for them. Then they can be pushed to learning in new ways that do not come so easily. As a tutor you can vary your tutoring style.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tutor flexibility and adaptability, diverse tutoring materials and strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant tutor preparation, can be challenging to accommodate all learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Tutees in higher education or adult learning programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance inclusivity and engagement, promote individualized learning, support diverse learning styles and talents.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances inclusivity, promotes individualized learning, supports diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use a range of tutoring activities to address a broad spectrum of tutees. Identify extra material or exercises when there is a lack of background knowledge or skills. Give tutees real-world problems to solve that have multiple solutions. Provide examples and questions to guide them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased tutee engagement, improved performance in diverse activities, positive feedback about tutor adaptability.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the importance of accommodating diverse learning styles for enhanced learning outcomes. Chickering and Gamson, 1987, p. 1

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A tutor uses a range of tutoring activities to address a broad spectrum of tutees. The tutor provides examples and questions to guide tutees.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Respectful redirection is a quick, in-the-moment strategy to give corrective feedback to students using a calm tone, neutral body language, and clear, concise wording. The instructor tells students exactly what they’re doing incorrectly and what they should be doing instead with as few words as possible, reducing confusion. It provides brief, consistent, systematic correction with feedback, which has a positive effect on student behavior. Tone, word choice, and brevity affect how students respond.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Classroom expectations must be set and regularly reviewed. The instructor must be able to assess behavior in the moment and intervene with a calm and neutral tone.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may look off-task when they are using strategies that actually keep them on-task.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students, especially those who learn and think differently, including students with ADHD and those who have experienced trauma.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Correct student behavior, communicate expectations, and foster a safe and respectful classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students recognize cause and effect, enforces rules consistently for all students, and provides a predictable framework that builds trust and allows students to feel safe. When done successfully, it can remove the need for further intervention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptations may include visual aids to classroom expectations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student behavior and the effectiveness of the redirections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that this type of brief, consistent, systematic correction with feedback has a positive effect on student behavior. Immediate redirection helps students with ADHD recognize cause and effect. As a predictable framework, respectful redirection can be comforting to students, especially those who have experienced trauma.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • If a student is struggling to have their ideas recognized during group work and keeps interrupting another student, the instructor walks to the student and says quietly and calmly, 'Josh, I can tell you really want to share your ideas, but you were talking while Laurel was talking.' Point to a visual of classroom expectations and say, 'In this class, we take turns speaking during discussions. Next time you have an idea to share with the group, wait until the person who is speaking stops, and then share your idea.' Explain why the alternate behavior is a better option: 'It’s easier for people to listen when one person is talking at a time.' Ask the student to demonstrate understanding. When the student follows the redirection, provide feedback and reinforcement: 'Josh, the way you waited to speak until after Laurel was finished talking allowed everyone in your group to listen and share their ideas. Well done.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Adding the word "yet" to responses when learners express frustration or inability (e.g., "I can't do this") introduces the idea of a growth mindset, fostering the belief that abilities can improve over time. This simple addition signals that current limitations are not permanent and encourages persistence by implying that success is still attainable with continued effort and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset from instructors and learners to view limitations as temporary. Consistent use of "yet" in responses to learner frustrations and challenges. Provides support and encouragement to help learners overcome obstacles.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may initially dismiss the use of "yet" as empty encouragement if not accompanied by concrete support and guidance. Requires consistent reinforcement to maintain a positive effect. May be challenging to implement in situations where there are genuine limitations or barriers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage persistence, reduce frustration, foster a sense of hope, enhance self-efficacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Shifts focus from current inability to future potential. Reduces frustration and feelings of inadequacy. Reinforces the idea that learning is a process and that improvement is possible. Encourages persistence and a willingness to continue trying.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning contexts and individual learner needs. Can be used in response to a wide range of challenges and difficulties. Can be combined with other strategies, such as providing support and breaking down tasks into smaller steps.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Modeling
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner behavior, such as increased persistence, positive self-talk, and willingness to seek help. Track learner responses to challenges after the introduction of "yet". Analyze learner reflections on their growth and learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of "yet" to promote a growth mindset and encourage persistence. Adding "yet" can shift learners' perspectives and increase their motivation to continue learning. Encouragement helps learners make progress more smoothly and climb the ladder faster.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When learners express frustration (e.g., "I can't do this"), instructors respond with "You can't do this yet." When learners feel overwhelmed by a task, instructors say, "You haven't mastered this skill yet."

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Response devices allow learners to anonymously share answers with the whole class. They provide a way to encourage whole-group participation and collect formative data. Instructors can present a problem, have learners work on it individually (e.g., on whiteboards), and then share their answers using a response system. The instructor and class then view the responses to assess overall comprehension and inform next steps.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Response system (e.g., clickers, mobile app, whiteboards), structured prompts, time for individual work and sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a reliable response system, potential for technical issues, may be perceived as superficial if not integrated into meaningful discussion

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and professional development; beneficial for learners of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage active participation, collect formative data on learner understanding, provide immediate feedback, promote self-reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured format for engagement, creates a safe space for sharing answers, supports formative assessment, gives immediate feedback to the instructor, can be gamified to increase motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different question types and content areas, can be used in a variety of settings (in-person, online, hybrid), may allow for open-ended responses or predetermined options.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track participation rates, monitor answer accuracy, assess the depth of learner engagement, analyze the feedback provided by learners

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased engagement, improved formative assessment, and a better understanding of learner comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A kindergarten teacher uses student response systems to encourage whole-group math participation and collect formative data on student learning. Socrative allows for a variety of student interactions and for teachers to assess student learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners engage in problem-solving scenarios in pairs or small groups, connecting to their everyday lives (e.g., cheating, bullying), to make decisions, analyze situations, and consider possible consequences. They then share their decisions with the whole class and reflect on how they arrived at them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Relevant problem scenarios, facilitation to guide discussions, and time for group work and class sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Scenarios must be carefully selected to be relevant and inclusive. Facilitation is needed to ensure respectful and productive discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners and adult learners in social skills development programs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply responsible decision-making skills in real-life scenarios, enhance collaborative problem-solving, and promote self-reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides practical application of decision-making skills, promotes peer learning and collaboration, and encourages reflection on reasoning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios can be tailored to match the age, interests, and experiences of learners. Support and scaffolding can be provided to learners who struggle with analysis or reflection.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Peer Discussion
  • Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality of group discussions, the depth of scenario analysis, and the level of self-reflection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engaging in real-world problem scenarios improves decision-making skills and fosters ethical reasoning. Participative decision-making can help students develop skills for responsible citizenship (Ross & Bondy, 1993).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ethical Dilemmas for Classroom Discussion offer age-appropriate, real-life dilemmas for practicing responsible decision-making.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Restating the question encourages critical reading skills and provides clarity around instructions. The culture of “right answer” is filled with shame and shaming, and students will try repeatedly to just give the “correct” answer to the original question. To avoid missed opportunities for developing understanding, instructors must insist students restate the question/problem in their own words.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Skilled teachers who can ask effective questions and facilitate meaningful discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be skilled in questioning techniques. May be time-consuming, especially in large classes. This strategy is not useful for students with no prior knowledge of the topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who struggle with math or who have anxiety around making mistakes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students to slow down, avoid rote recall, understand underlying concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning, promotes metacognition, helps students feel more confident, fosters a growth mindset

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be aware of their student's individual needs, and to be flexible and willing to ask open ended questions rather than simply looking for the right answer

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student confidence, increased class participation, higher test scores

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that focusing on clarity and conceptual understanding leads to greater long term student confidence and learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of focusing on a student's error, a teacher could ask them to state what the verb is in the prompt/question, circle it in red, and ask what the verb means.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Recognize that students did not choose the current situation and should not be unjustly penalized for its challenges. Balance generosity and high standards in grading practices. Offer empathy and flexibility in grading decisions. Modify assignments, adjust expectations, and conduct alternative assessments based on each situation. Prioritize keeping connected with students and cultivating hope. Place yourself in students’ shoes in all instructional decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Open communication with students, flexibility in grading policies, access to alternative assessment methods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time and effort, may be challenging to balance with institutional grading requirements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote student well-being, reduce stress, maintain engagement, ensure fair assessment, foster a sense of hope

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages flexibility, compassion, and understanding; reduces student anxiety; promotes a supportive learning environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Assignments and assessments are tailored to individual student needs and circumstances.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement, well-being, and academic progress; gather feedback from students on assessment fairness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduces student stress, promotes a more supportive and equitable learning environment, and improves overall student outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Offer extensions, allow for retakes, provide alternative assignment options, and communicate regularly with students about their progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Retrieval practice involves actively recalling information from memory without having it in front of you. This strategy strengthens long-term retention and promotes deeper learning by encouraging learners to actively use and recall information rather than passively re-reading or re-studying. Effective retrieval practice includes spacing (practicing at intervals), feedback (providing the correct answer if the learner struggles), and aligning practice with assessment (using similar question types).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured activities such as quizzes, discussions, or flashcard exercises. Immediate feedback mechanisms and spaced repetition schedules enhance effectiveness. Low-stakes environment encourages participation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lead to rote learning if not combined with deeper understanding activities. Requires careful design to align with assessment goals. Learners need clear instructions to avoid ineffective strategies (e.g., superficial re-reading).

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve long-term retention, foster deeper understanding, enhance metacognition, and identify gaps in knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens memory through active recall, improves self-assessment skills, identifies knowledge gaps, and facilitates better transfer of learning to new contexts. Teachers can use it formatively to adjust instruction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with different formats such as quizzes, brain dumps, flashcards, or discussions. Difficulty can be adjusted by providing cues or scaffolding. Learners can choose topics or questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure improvement in test scores, quality of participation in discussions, and self-assessment accuracy. Track the type of questions answered correctly or incorrectly to identify areas of strength and weakness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that retrieval practice leads to better retention compared to restudying. It also fosters deeper learning by improving transfer to new forms of questions and enhances metacognition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Implementing no-stakes quizzes in middle school social studies led to a full grade level improvement on unit exams. A university professor integrated brief quizzes at the end of class to encourage students to attend class and pay attention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After students do a Brain Dump, where they try to recall as much as they can about a given topic, without the aid of any supporting texts, they sort their dumped information into some kind of graphic organizer, and possibly working in pairs to do so.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to graphic organizers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may need to check their texts to confirm, correct, or add to the information they retrieved.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Solidify the benefit of the retrieval and help them get very clear on where they have gaps in their knowledge.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Aids in memorization through repetition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be paired or individualized.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student feedback on gaps in their knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Solidify the benefit of the retrieval and help them get very clear on where they have gaps in their knowledge.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rhyming games involve activities that focus on identifying and creating rhyming words to enhance phonological awareness. These games often include matching rhyming words, drawing rhyming pictures, and creating word family charts. Direct instruction on rhyme recognition, paired with engaging activities, helps children develop essential reading and spelling skills. Games can be adapted for individual, small group, or whole-class settings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials vary by game but may include rhyming books, picture cards, markers, chart paper, and printable activities. Preparation involves gathering materials and setting up game stations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness relies on clear instructions and targeted activities. Some games may require significant preparation time. Ensure diversity in activities to maintain learner engagement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood education (Pre-K to 2nd grade), learners who need phonological awareness support, and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve phonological awareness, enhance reading skills, develop spelling skills, promote word recognition, and reinforce letter-sound correspondence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners actively in recognizing and generating rhymes. Reinforces phonological awareness and letter-sound correspondence. Adaptable to diverse skill levels and learning environments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Picture-based rhyming for younger and struggling learners. Writing and creating activities for advanced learners. Diagrams and templates for scaffolding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track participation and engagement in rhyming activities. Assess learners’ ability to identify and generate rhymes. Collect and review completed activities and word charts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Direct instruction on rhyming improves phonological awareness and reading skills. Active participation and engagement enhance learning outcomes. Games and activities promote a fun and effective learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples provided include rhyming body parts game, space-themed rhyming game, word family charts, and using picture prompts to identify rhyming words.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The teacher claps/counts out a rhythm. Students imitate the rhythm of the clap and the count.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may have difficulty with auditory processing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance auditory discrimination, improve coordination, reinforce rhythm, build pattern recognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simple and engaging activity to reinforce rhythm and coordination. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of the rhythm based on students' abilities. Students can create their own rhythms.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess students' ability to accurately imitate the rhythm. Observe their coordination and timing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • May help students improve their auditory processing skills and coordination in a fun way. Encourages active engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher claps a pattern like 'clap-clap-pause, clap-clap-clap' and students mimic the rhythm.

docs.title: Rice Tables and Sandboxes: Science Through Inquiry
Description
docs.text: Engaging learners in hands-on exploration and inquiry-based science education allows them to discover and test new understandings. Students follow the same processes real scientists use, asking questions, making discoveries, and testing those discoveries in the search for new understanding. It's less about understanding the basics of science, and more about creativity and innovation to design an exciting experiment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials and tools for scientific exploration. Instructor training and support.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant resources and planning. Some learners may struggle with open-ended inquiry.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop scientific inquiry skills, foster creativity and innovation, encourage hands-on exploration, promote discovery and testing, enhance understanding of scientific concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops scientific inquiry skills. Fosters creativity and innovation. Encourages hands-on exploration. Promotes discovery and testing. Enhances understanding of scientific concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose topics and projects based on their interests. Instructors can provide different materials and tools to accommodate various needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Inquiry and Research
  • Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner projects and experiments. Participation in inquiry-based activities. Scientific inquiry skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that inquiry-based learning enhances scientific understanding and critical thinking. Studies also show that hands-on exploration promotes engagement and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Exploratorium's Institute of Inquiry offers workshops and online curriculum ideas for teachers to incorporate inquiry into their science classrooms. The Inquiry Approach to Learning Science.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using audiobooks and Braille texts to reinforce and inspire literacy skills. This includes providing access to literature and other reading selections in audio form for all students, including emerging readers and ESL/ELL learners. Some resources provide accompanying text to follow along, while others include options to interact with the book through clicking, responding, and watching animations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to audiobooks and Braille texts, digital devices or players, and internet access for online resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of resources to ensure quality and alignment with curriculum goals. May not be suitable for all types of content or learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, including emerging readers, ESL/ELL learners, and students with visual impairments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce literacy skills, improve English skills, study literature in new ways, cater to diverse learning needs, and enhance comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides auditory learning experiences, supports learners with visual difficulties, reinforces literacy skills through multiple modalities, and allows for personalized learning experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adjust settings like speaker voice and speed to suit their needs. Resources vary in format, offering audio-only, text-to-follow, and interactive options.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student engagement with audiobooks, assess comprehension through quizzes and discussions, and evaluate improvements in literacy skills over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that audiobooks can improve comprehension, vocabulary, and reading fluency, especially for struggling readers and English language learners. Braille texts support literacy development for visually impaired students. Interactive resources can enhance engagement and motivation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • NaturalReader uses text-to-speech software to support learners with visual difficulties, allowing them to adjust the speaker voice and speed. TeachersFirst offers educator-reviewed audiobooks and interactive audiobooks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing access to a diverse collection of reading materials that vary in academic vocabulary and syntax complexity supports literacy and reading fluency. This includes different types of materials such as nonfiction news articles and fictional stories to facilitate understanding of disciplinary literacy for reading and writing. Allowing learners to choose texts they want to read improves their motivation to read, in turn supporting their growth in background knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The RIP Toolbox is a memory-enhancing strategy that utilizes three key elements: Repetition, Imagery, and Patterns. It helps learners organize and rehearse information in a memorable format, enhancing the transfer of information from short-term to long-term memory. Pediatrician Dr. Mel Levine suggests that before a test, learners should submit a memory plan detailing how they will use the RIP Toolbox.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the core concepts to be remembered, access to materials for creating images and patterns (e.g., paper, markers), and dedicated time for rehearsal and repetition

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort, can be overwhelming if too many strategies are introduced at once, may not be effective for learners who struggle with abstract thinking

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for learners who need structured approaches to memorization

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory recall, enhance information retention, facilitate organization of information, encourage purposeful learning

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using flashcards (Repetition), creating visual mnemonics (Imagery), organizing information using graphic organizers (Patterns). For instance, using the mnemonic "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles" to remember the order of planets.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: RSOWV (Relax, Slowdown, Organize, Write, Visualize) and TRAP (Translate, Repeat, A Picture, Practice) are mnemonic strategies designed to enhance memory and learning. RSOWV focuses on creating a conducive learning environment, while TRAP emphasizes active processing and rehearsal of information. These mnemonics provide learners with a structured approach to encoding and retrieving information effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the core concepts to be remembered, access to materials for note-taking and visualization, and dedicated time for practicing the mnemonic strategies

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: • Improve memory recall, enhance focus and concentration, facilitate effective information processing, encourage active learning strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to memory and learning, promotes active engagement with the material, caters to different learning styles through diverse strategies (visual, auditory, kinesthetic), enhances self-regulation and metacognition

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can adapt the specific strategies within each mnemonic to suit their learning style and preferences. Adaptations can be made based on individual strengths and needs.

docs.text: • Monitor learners' ability to recall information using the strategies, assess the effectiveness of the chosen strategies through self-reflection and feedback, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using the mnemonics

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using RSOWV/TRAP mnemonics has been shown to enhance memory recall, improve focus and concentration, and promote active learning. The use of structured strategies supports self-regulation and metacognition, leading to improved academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before a test, a learner uses RSOWV by relaxing and concentrating, slowing down to carefully read each question, organizing their notes, writing down key information, and visualizing the concepts. To study vocabulary, a learner uses TRAP by translating definitions into their own words, repeating the definitions aloud, drawing a picture to represent each word, and practicing using the words in sentences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Rubrics are evaluation tools consisting of a set of criteria, a fixed scale, and descriptors that distinguish the differences in the levels of the scale. They are used to judge the degree of understanding, proficiency levels of skills, the quality of products or performances, and learner growth from one level to the next. Three types of rubrics are commonly used in schools: holistic (provides an overall impression), analytic (divides performance into distinct elements and judges each independently), and developmental (describes growth along a proficiency continuum).

Holistic rubrics use a short narrative of characteristics tied to each numeric score, based on an overall impression of performance; because the same score-description applies across multiple components of the assignment at once, the descriptions tend to be fairly vague and don't identify specific strengths or weaknesses component by component — a real cost in directive feedback, but one that's often worth it when assignments vary too much to score component-by-component consistently (e.g., independent capstone projects), or when practicality demands faster scoring across a large volume of work. Analytic rubrics divide the assignment into its component parts and describe acceptable/unacceptable performance separately for each — more time-consuming to build and apply, but far more diagnostic, since a student can see exactly which component needs work rather than only an overall impression. Before either, a basic rating scale (a checklist plus a numeric quality score, but without narrative descriptors) is a common intermediate step — it's more informative than a bare checklist, but the numbers alone are genuinely ambiguous: one rater's "3" might mean "good" while another's "3" means "marginal," and a student may not read the number the same way the teacher intended it either. Adding narrative descriptors to a rating scale is precisely what turns it into a holistic rubric.

Rubrics pay off across the whole assessment cycle, not just at scoring time: they force the teacher to plan assignment expectations carefully in advance, reduce the time spent clarifying requirements to students during the assignment (since expectations are already explicit), tend to improve the quality of student work once students know precisely what's expected, reduce time spent grading while still supporting constructive feedback, and reduce student complaints and questions about grades because the basis for a score is already visible. The upfront time cost of building a rubric is real, but is paid once per assignment type rather than repeatedly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear learning objectives, well-defined criteria aligned to standards, and a rating scale with detailed descriptors. Time is needed for teachers to create or select appropriate rubrics, teach students how to use them, and provide feedback based on rubric scores.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not constructed carefully, rubrics may be too generic and not provide specific enough feedback. Holistic rubrics may not offer enough detail for learners to understand areas for improvement. Students need explicit instruction on how to interpret and use rubrics effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly K–12 and higher education. Adaptable for use in various subjects and skill-based areas.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess student learning, provide specific feedback, guide self-assessment, track progress, promote self-regulation, set learning goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear expectations, supports self-assessment, offers specific feedback, and aids in monitoring progress. Benefits teachers by specifying qualities of successful performance and offering insights into instructional adjustments. Supports a shared understanding of learning targets between educators and students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Rubrics can be customized with different scales (e.g., 4-point, 7-point), criteria, and descriptors to align with specific learning objectives and standards. For younger learners, symbols, charts, or faces can be incorporated for easier comprehension.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track alignment between self-assessments and teacher evaluations. Monitor improvements in performance over time. Analyze depth and specificity of feedback provided based on rubric results. Measure student engagement with self-assessment and goal-setting activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learning outcomes: Research demonstrates rubrics enhance assessment, feedback, and self-regulation skills. Increased student engagement: Studies show clear learning targets and criteria improve learner understanding and motivation. Effective instruction: Rubrics inform targeted instructional adjustments.

docs.text: • Checklists — the least complex form of scoring rubric, indicating presence/absence of a component without judging its quality

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Repeating instructions can lead to lazy listening habits in learners. By establishing a practice of providing instructions only once, instructors can encourage learners to actively listen the first time. For learners who may have missed the instruction, instructors can suggest they, "ask three, then ask me."

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor consistency in providing instructions only once, establishment of 'ask three, then ask me' protocol

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel left behind if they miss the initial instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve active listening skills, reduce dependency on repeated instructions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to pay attention and retain information, promotes independence and peer support

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners who struggle can be supported by peers

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow instructions after they are given once, track instances of learners seeking clarification from peers before the instructor

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that clear expectations and reduced repetition can improve learner engagement and attention spans. Practitioner experience suggests that consistent application of this strategy leads to improved listening habits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher implementing this strategy found that students were more attentive during instruction and relied less on the teacher for repeated explanations. Resource: Rebecca Alber, Edutopia

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolded instruction involves supporting learners in various ways as they learn and gradually withdrawing supports as they become capable of independent performance of a task or skill. Supports include clues, clarifying questions, reminders, encouragement, breaking the problem down into steps, or anything else that allows the student to grow in independence. This interactive process bases instruction on learners' prior knowledge, provides needed support, and gradually removes the support as it becomes less necessary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be attentive to learner needs and provide tailored support. Requires allocation of time for monitoring learner progress and adjusting support accordingly.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to implement effectively. Some learners may become overly reliant on support if not gradually withdrawn.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in basic skills programs, individuals with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support learners in achieving independent performance; build confidence; adapt instruction to learner needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides individualized support tailored to the learner's current level of skill. Allows learners to gradually take ownership of their learning process.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs by varying the types and levels of support provided. Support can be adjusted dynamically based on learner performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner progress toward independent performance; reduction in reliance on support; increased confidence and self-efficacy

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows scaffolded instruction supports learners in achieving independent performance. Gradually removing support encourages self-reliance and skill development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Breaking a complex task into smaller steps. Providing clues and reminders during initial attempts at a task, then gradually fading these prompts as the learner becomes more proficient.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolded peer review involves providing learners with structured support and guidance to improve the quality and effectiveness of their feedback. This can include using student-produced samples as exemplars, limiting the scope of feedback to one specific area, and fostering a culture of constructive criticism. This technique is especially helpful when learners feel uncomfortable or unconfident providing feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Exemplars of high-quality work, structured prompts and questions, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and preparation to ensure the scaffolding is effective. May be time-consuming, especially in the initial stages.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve the quality and effectiveness of peer feedback, build confidence in providing critique, and foster a culture of constructive criticism

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured support and guidance, helping learners overcome their fears of inadequacy and providing unhelpful feedback. Fosters a classroom environment where criticism is embraced and learners are comfortable providing and receiving critique.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The level of scaffolding can be adjusted based on the learners' needs and abilities. The specific focus of feedback can be tailored to the subject matter and learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review of feedback provided by learners to assess the depth and quality of their critique. Observation of group interactions to assess learners' confidence and engagement in the process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Scaffolding matters: Using more student-produced samples to look at as a class and giving the students models to compare their own writing to can improve the level of peer review.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher uses student-produced samples to model constructive feedback and limits the scope of feedback to one specific area to reduce learners' anxiety. Resource: Peer Review Done Right.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding is a support technique to help learners manage their responses in an emotionally safe context. It involves providing temporary support tailored to the learner's needs and gradually removing it as they become more competent. Scaffolding in self-regulation might involve providing structured prompts, modeling self-regulation strategies, or breaking down tasks into smaller, more manageable steps.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires awareness of individual learner needs and emotional triggers, ability to provide tailored support and guidance, a safe and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If scaffolds are not gradually removed, learners may become dependent on them. Requires careful observation and adaptation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners struggling with self-regulation, particularly those who are highly reactive to new or challenging situations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help learners manage emotional responses, build self-regulation skills, foster a sense of emotional safety

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides emotional safety, reduces overwhelm, promotes gradual independence in self-regulation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scaffolds can be tailored to individual learner needs and strengths. The level of support can be adjusted as learners progress.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to manage emotional responses with decreasing levels of scaffolding, track their progress in using self-regulation strategies independently.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that scaffolding can effectively support learners in developing self-regulation skills by providing temporary support and gradually promoting independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides sentence stems to help a student articulate their feelings in a journal. As the student becomes more comfortable, the teacher gradually removes the sentence stems. Resource: Learner Variability Project | Digital Promise Global

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding involves providing temporary support to learners to help them manage their emotional and behavioral responses in new or challenging situations. This support is gradually reduced as learners develop their self-regulation skills. For example, in emotionally safe contexts, educators can help students learn how to manage their reactions by providing structured activities, clear expectations, and immediate feedback. The goal is to provide enough support initially so that learners can succeed, then gradually reduce the level of assistance as they become more confident and capable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A supportive and emotionally safe learning environment, clear expectations, structured activities, immediate feedback, and an understanding of the learner’s strengths and challenges related to self-regulation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If scaffolding is not gradually reduced, learners may become overly reliant on external support. It requires careful observation and assessment of the learner’s progress to ensure that the level of support is appropriate.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with self-regulation, particularly those who are highly reactive to new or challenging situations, including students in K-12 and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional self-regulation, improve behavioral control, build confidence in challenging situations, enhance emotional intelligence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe and supportive learning environment, helps learners manage emotional impulses, builds self-awareness, and promotes gradual independence in self-regulation. It also allows educators to tailor support to individual needs, ensuring that learners are not overwhelmed by the task.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scaffolding can be adapted to individual needs by adjusting the level of support based on the learner’s progress. For learners with significant challenges, more structured activities and frequent feedback may be necessary. For those who are more advanced, the level of support can be reduced to promote independence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in emotional reactivity and behavioral control. Monitor the learner’s ability to use self-regulation strategies independently. Collect self-reports from learners regarding their confidence and ability to manage challenging situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that scaffolding can effectively support the development of self-regulation skills by providing a safe and structured environment for learning. Studies have shown that learners who receive appropriate scaffolding are more likely to succeed in challenging situations and develop confidence in their abilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An educator provides structured activities and clear expectations for a student who struggles with emotional outbursts in class. The educator gradually reduces the level of support as the student becomes more confident in managing their emotions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding can help students learn how to manage their responses in an emotionally safe context.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Knowledge of student skill.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Difficult to find skill level of student.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and post-secondary students, especially those with learning disabilities or other challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Manage emotional responses, create emotionally safe learning, provide scaffolding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Breaks learning into achievable steps while providing a safe and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust tasks to suit student abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in student behavior and skill development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improves confidence and mastery.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Model behavior or assignments.

docs.title: Scaffolding Structure and Function in PBL
Description
docs.text: Scaffolding structure and function in project-based learning (PBL) involves providing students with the necessary tools to demonstrate their understanding of content by giving them specific functions and structures of the language. This includes offering sentence starters, stems, and creating lessons that scaffold how to justify answers or use specific language structures (e.g., "If __, then ____").

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful analysis of project requirements, creation of appropriate sentence starters and stems, and explicit instruction on language structures.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional preparation time and careful monitoring to ensure students are using the scaffolds effectively and not becoming overly reliant on them.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with a particular focus on English Language Learners (ELLs) in project-based learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To support students, especially English Language Learners (ELLs), in effectively communicating their knowledge and understanding within project-based learning activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework that helps students express complex ideas, enhances language skills, and promotes confidence in communication.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different project types and proficiency levels, allowing educators to tailor sentence starters and stems to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student communication, enhanced use of specific language structures in project work, and positive feedback from students and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that scaffolding language structure and function enhances student understanding and performance, particularly for ELLs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing sentence starters for students to justify answers in a science project, such as "I believe this because..." or "The evidence shows that...".

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Schema-based instruction involves teaching learners to recognize and understand the underlying structure (schema) of problems, particularly word problems in mathematics. By identifying the problem structure, learners can better understand the relationships between the problem's elements and select appropriate strategies to solve it. This strategy emphasizes identifying key words associated with different operations and modeling the problem structure.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructional materials with various word problems, explicit teaching of problem structures and associated keywords, modeling of problem-solving strategies, and opportunities for practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of mathematical problems, and the over-reliance on keywords can sometimes lead to misinterpretation of problems. Requires explicit instruction and practice to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school learners, particularly those struggling with mathematical word problems

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve problem-solving skills, enhance comprehension of word problems, facilitate the translation of word problems into mathematical equations, develop strategic thinking in problem-solving.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to problem-solving, enhances understanding of mathematical concepts, promotes active engagement with word problems, and can improve confidence in solving mathematical problems.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The strategy can be adapted to different types of word problems and mathematical operations. Scaffolding can be provided for learners who struggle with identifying problem structures, and more challenging problems can be presented to advanced learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner accuracy in identifying problem structures, monitor the correct application of problem-solving strategies, and assess improvements in overall problem-solving performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that schema-based instruction can improve learners' ability to solve mathematical word problems, particularly when combined with explicit instruction and practice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using videos to demonstrate how to identify and model problem structures for addition and subtraction word problems. Providing general problem structures to support converting word problems into mathematical equations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: School newsletters are visual aids designed to keep staff, students, and parents informed and engaged with school events and activities. By adding school spirit to the design and using newsletter templates, it's easy to customize the text and visuals for each week or month. Incorporating school colors, fonts, icons, and images of school events helps to create a sense of community and excitement. These newsletters help ensure that everyone stays on the same page and feels connected to the school.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to design software and information. Implementation involves regular updates and distribution. May require training in design and communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Poorly designed newsletters can be overlooked. Inaccurate or outdated information can cause confusion. Requires attention to detail and consistency.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, teachers, students, parents, and community members

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Inform staff, students, and parents, engage community, promote school spirit, customize design, keep everyone on the same page

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Keeps everyone informed and engaged. Promotes school spirit and community. Enhances communication and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different schools, events, and audiences. Design elements can be adjusted based on the school's branding and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track readership and engagement. Evaluate the clarity and effectiveness of communication. Collect feedback on content and design.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-designed school newsletters have been shown to improve communication and engagement. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include newsletters using school colors, fonts, icons, and images of school events. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating school newsletters.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teach children about schwa (/ ə/), the unaccented vowel sound that has been emptied of its identity and can be described as a lazy vowel. Explain that some vowel sounds have the stuffing taken out of them when they are unaccented. After students spell a word such as prob-lem, a-dept, or com-mit, they can say the word naturally and mark the syllable that has a schwa.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grade 3 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance phonological awareness, develop understanding of schwa sounds

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners understand why some words do not sound the way they are spelled, improves spelling accuracy, enhances phonological awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific words with schwa sounds. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in identifying and marking schwa sounds. Monitor progress in spelling skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Understanding the shwa allows students to better grasp multisyllabic spelling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Engage learners in hands-on, exploratory science activities that encourage questioning, discovery, and testing to develop new understandings. This methodology mirrors the processes used by real scientists, fostering creativity and innovation.
