Inquiry-based science education promotes a deeper understanding of scientific concepts through direct experience and investigation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to provide materials and resources for hands-on activities. Need time for learners to conduct experiments and investigations. Instructors should be knowledgeable about scientific concepts and processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming and require significant planning. May be challenging to assess learning outcomes. Some learners may struggle with the open-ended nature of inquiry-based learning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for elementary and middle school students, as well as adult learners in science-based programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop scientific inquiry skills, foster creativity and innovation, enhance understanding of scientific concepts, promote hands-on learning and exploration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides hands-on learning experiences, fosters creativity and innovation, and enhances understanding of scientific concepts. Inquiry-based science education allows learners to follow the same processes used by real scientists.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of inquiry-based activities that cater to different interests and skill levels. Provide support and guidance to help learners develop their scientific skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Evidence-Based Reasoning
  • Model Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate learner scientific inquiry skills and critical thinking. Assess their ability to design and conduct experiments. Observe their collaboration and communication skills. Assess the quality of their proposed solutions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that inquiry-based science education enhances scientific inquiry skills, creativity, and understanding of scientific concepts. Hands-on learning experiences make science more engaging and meaningful.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students design and conduct an experiment to test a hypothesis, investigate a local environmental issue, or build a model to explain a scientific phenomenon. Adult learners participate in a citizen science project, collecting and analyzing data to contribute to scientific research.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Screen readers convert text into spoken audio, enabling learners to listen to written material. This strategy benefits learners with strengths in auditory processing by allowing them to access information through their preferred modality.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to screen reader software, training on its use

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of text, some learners may prefer visual reading

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with strengths in auditory processing who struggle with reading

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve access to written materials, support learners with auditory strengths

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages auditory strengths, provides an alternative to traditional reading, enhances comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer training on screen reader software, allow learners to adjust reading speed and voice preferences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess comprehension through quizzes, discussions, or written assignments, compare performance with traditional reading tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that screen readers can improve reading comprehension and access to information for learners with auditory processing strengths. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of screen readers in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using screen readers to access textbooks, articles, or online resources. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A classroom management system where a student's name is secretly selected each day, and the teacher observes whether the "Secret Student" exhibits good listening and learning behaviors. At the end of the day, the Secret Student is revealed and rewarded if they met expectations. This system encourages all students to behave well, as anyone could be the Secret Student.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sticky notes, 'Secret Student' sign, small prizes or rewards. Regular observation and assessment of student behavior.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if students realize the selection is random. Some students may become overly focused on the reward rather than intrinsic motivation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those who need reminders of classroom behavior expectations

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve classroom behavior, encourage listening, reward good choices, create a positive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages attentive listening and good behavior. Provides positive reinforcement for students meeting expectations. Creates a classroom environment focused on responsible behavior.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Rewards can be adjusted to suit student interests. Frequency of rewards can be modified to maintain effectiveness.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in classroom behavior, track the frequency of rewards given, and gather feedback from students on their motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Overall energy of class calmed significantly and that students were working hard to be responsible for their own behaviors. It turned a very energetic, rowdy group of kids into focused listeners and learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A second-grade teacher introduced the Secret Student system after winter break to remind students of behavior expectations, resulting in a significant improvement in classroom behavior.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A thinking routine developed by Project Zero to stimulate curiosity, normalize error, increase critical thinking skills, and ensure that every learner starts from a place of success. It involves students observing a stimulating image, then recording what they see, what they think about it, and what it makes them wonder.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A three-column organizer (See, Think, Wonder), stimulating images, time for individual brainstorming and sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful selection of images to ensure they are engaging and appropriate; some students may need prompting to move beyond surface-level observations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, from elementary to higher education, as it promotes critical thinking and curiosity; adaptable to diverse subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate curiosity, increase critical thinking skills, normalize error, activate background knowledge, facilitate inquiry

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking, encourages curiosity, makes thinking visible, lowers the stakes for participation, allows for diverse interpretations

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Image complexity can be tailored to student skill levels; response formats can be varied; students choose which question to share with a peer

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain Attention
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and breadth of student responses, evidence of critical thinking, number and quality of questions asked, level of engagement in discussions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Facilitates a more inquisitive and thoughtful classroom environment, encourages deeper engagement with content, builds critical thinking skills

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a science class, students observe a microscopic image of a cell. In a history class, students observe a primary source photograph from a historical event.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves curating digital libraries to include a section of books dedicated to Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) topics. This allows teachers and students to easily search for and find titles that are relevant to them or focused on specific SEL skills, facilitating integration of SEL into literacy and reading activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a digital library platform, curated collection of SEL-focused books, and awareness among teachers and students about the availability and purpose of the collection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and diversity of the book collection and the extent to which teachers integrate the resources into their instruction. Digital access may be a barrier for some students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and students, especially in K-12 settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate easy access to SEL resources, integrate SEL into literacy, promote SEL skill development, enhance relevance of reading materials

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides easy access to SEL-related content, integrates SEL into reading activities, supports targeted instruction in specific SEL skills, enhances the relevance of reading materials to students' lives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Libraries can be customized to include books relevant to the specific needs and interests of the student population, cultural backgrounds, and specific SEL goals of the school or district.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Hypertext Navigation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track usage of SEL-focused books, survey teachers about their use of the digital library, and assess students' SEL skills before and after implementation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports systemic integration of SEL into literacy instruction, enhancing students' social-emotional development and academic performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using age-appropriate, real-life ethical dilemmas as discussion starters to help students practice responsible decision-making. It encourages students to identify problems, analyze situations, solve problems, and evaluate solutions while considering the well-being of themselves and others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a collection of age-appropriate ethical dilemmas and a teacher to facilitate discussion. Can be integrated into social studies, language arts, or advisory periods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the selected dilemmas and the teacher's ability to guide discussion. Some students may struggle with ethical reasoning or expressing their opinions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop responsible decision-making skills, enhance ethical reasoning, improve problem-solving abilities, foster empathy and social awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes ethical reasoning, enhances problem-solving skills, fosters empathy and social awareness, provides a safe context to explore complex ethical issues.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Dilemmas can be selected to match students' age, interests, and cultural backgrounds. Teachers can provide scaffolds to support students who struggle with ethical reasoning or problem-solving.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Decision-Making

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, analyze their reasoning and problem-solving approaches, and assess their ability to consider multiple perspectives and ethical principles.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of responsible decision-making skills and promotes ethical reasoning, fostering responsible citizenship and social awareness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students read and discuss social and emotional learning (SEL) topics through the lens of characters in literature. This involves selecting texts with strong characters who solve problems and address significant issues, analyzing character relationships, outlining plots, and exploring character change as a result of conflict and resolution. Discussions are structured to teach talking and listening skills using verbal prompts, clarifying questions, and confirmations. This approach connects students' emotions and backgrounds to the material, fostering community building, empathy, and problem-solving skills. The goal is to provide students with strategies applicable to their own lives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to appropriate literature, structured discussion prompts, and a supportive classroom environment. Teachers need to facilitate discussions and provide guidance on analyzing character relationships and themes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful selection of texts to avoid triggering or alienating students. Discussions need to be managed to ensure respectful communication and avoid dominating voices. Some students may find it challenging to connect personal experiences to fictional characters.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in grades 4–12, adaptable for various age groups and learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social values, improve communication skills, encourage empathy, foster problem-solving abilities, and connect personal experiences to literature.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances emotional intelligence, provides a safe space for discussing sensitive topics, builds community, promotes active listening, and strengthens comprehension skills through character analysis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Texts can be selected based on student interests and reading levels. Discussion prompts can be modified to suit different developmental stages and cultural contexts. Students can choose characters or themes that resonate with their own experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions, analyze written reflections on character relationships and themes, and assess the application of SEL skills in real-life scenarios. Track changes in student attitudes and behaviors related to empathy, communication, and problem-solving.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that integrating SEL into literacy instruction improves academic performance, enhances emotional well-being, and reduces behavioral problems. Students develop greater empathy, improved communication skills, and enhanced problem-solving abilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Lois Lowry’s 'The Giver' to discuss themes of community and responsibility, or exploring conflict resolution in 'From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler.' The Morningside Center for Teaching Social Responsibility uses 'The Librarian of Basra' to help students connect to real-world issues and their own lives.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating social and emotional learning (SEL) into language arts curricula involves using literature to explore emotions, build community, handle conflict, and counter bias. Books with strong characters solving problems can help students connect to stories and learn problem-solving strategies. Discussions prompted by the literature enable students to access their own backgrounds, emotions, and relationships. It also emphasizes distinguishing conflict from violence and prompts reflection on character feelings and conflict resolution. Furthermore, integrating SEL lessons into reading curriculum can connect learners to the universality of literature, its power to transport them to different experiences, and connect with others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to appropriate literature, structured lesson plans, and facilitated discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of literature to ensure relevance and appropriateness. Success depends on the instructor's ability to facilitate meaningful discussions and create a safe space for sharing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly middle and high school learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social values, understand underlying themes, analyze character relationships, connect stories to personal lives, and promote empathy and emotional intelligence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to connect to characters, understand diverse perspectives, and reflect on their own experiences and emotions. Enhances social awareness, relationship skills, and self-awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Choice of literature can be tailored to different age groups and cultural backgrounds. Discussion questions can be adapted to suit specific classroom needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions, analyze written reflections, and assess understanding of character motivations and themes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies suggest that integrating SEL can positively impact classroom productivity and academic performance by addressing the emotional needs of students. Research shows improved coping skills, academic achievement, and social-emotional functioning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using Lois Lowry's 'The Giver' to explore themes of utopia, truth, and individuality; Tom Roderick's curriculum based on 'The Librarian of Basra' to discuss conflict, responsibility, and making a difference. The Perks of Being a Wallflower (1999) by Stephen Chbosky; Tears of a Tiger (1994) by Sharon Draper's novel; The Outsiders (1967) by S.E. Hinton.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers can implement simple SEL questions focused on kindess, metaphors, challenges, and support to grow students’ emotional intelligence skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of SEL questions, time for individual reflection and class discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may not feel comfortable sharing their feelings in a group setting. It is important to create a safe and supportive environment where students feel comfortable sharing. Some students may not be able to answer the questions fully or accurately.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially K–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate feelings of empathy and support, facilitate self-reflection, promote emotional awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with opportunities to reflect on their own experiences and feelings, as well as those of others. Promotes a sense of community and connection in the classroom. Normalizes talking about feelings and empowers students to view their emotions as assets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adapt the questions to suit the needs of their students and the topics being studied in class. Students can also be encouraged to create their own questions to explore their feelings and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in the discussions. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness. Monitor student behavior and academic performance to assess the impact of the activity on their social and emotional learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • All learning has an emotional base – Plato. Do you agree? Try these short activities to help grow students’ emotional intelligence skills

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves showing short video clips on Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) topics, followed by discussions or related activities. By connecting the video content to learners' background knowledge and personal lives, the strategy aims to make SEL topics more relevant and meaningful.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to videos on SEL topics, playback device, class time for viewing, discussion, and activities. Instructor needs to create or select discussion prompts and related activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Videos may not always reflect the specific experiences or cultural backgrounds of all learners. Discussions can be dominated by a few learners. Activities may not engage all learners equally.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote relevance and meaningful connection of SEL topics, connect SEL topics to students' background knowledge and personal lives, develop a better understanding of emotions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-world examples, facilitates discussion, strengthens connection between SEL concepts and learners' lived experiences, promotes critical thinking through discussions, enhances emotional intelligence and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be selected to align with specific age groups or learner interests. Discussion prompts can be scaffolded to meet varying learner needs. Activities can be chosen based on student preference.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Discussion Sections
  • Application
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation in discussions. Review responses in related activities to assess comprehension and application of SEL concepts. Collect learner feedback on relevance and meaningfulness of the videos and activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that incorporating social and emotional learning (SEL) into educational settings leads to improved academic outcomes, enhanced social skills, and increased emotional well-being. Video-based instruction, combined with discussion, can make abstract concepts more relatable, fostering deeper understanding and application of SEL principles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • iLearn with Poko: Emotions and Colors! uses videos to teach about emotions. After viewing a short animated story, learners identify the emotions experienced by the characters and, with this practice, develop a better understanding of emotions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves selecting and incorporating culturally responsive texts into the curriculum and classroom libraries. It focuses on providing learners with a diverse range of books that reflect different cultures and experiences, enabling them to develop a stronger sense of identity and broader perspectives. Educators can conduct audits of their classroom libraries to ensure representation and diversity. Digital tools and interactive quizzes can also be used to help learners discover books that celebrate diverse experiences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to diverse book collections and digital resources. Time for educators to conduct library audits and curate culturally responsive texts. Integration of chosen texts into instructional practices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Selecting texts requires careful consideration to avoid surface-level diversity, stereotypes, and token representation. It is important to avoid a singular focus on suffering and to include authentic #OwnVoices authors and narratives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 educators and learners, curriculum developers, and anyone seeking to create more inclusive and representative learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop learners' sense of identity, broaden perspectives, foster empathy, promote cultural awareness, ensure representation in curriculum

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with mirrors and windows into other cultures, supporting self-reflection and empathy. Enhances engagement by making learning materials relevant and relatable. Connects learning to real-world applications, increasing motivation and cultural awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Text selections can be tailored to specific learner interests, cultural backgrounds, and reading levels. Formats include physical books, digital resources, interactive quizzes, and multimedia projects.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze representation and diversity in classroom and library collections. Observe learners' engagement, discussions, and reflections on diverse texts. Assess the inclusion of multiple perspectives and voices in learning activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Culturally responsive texts promote a sense of belonging, enhance engagement, and foster critical thinking. Diverse representation in literature supports identity development and broadens cultural awareness, contributing to more equitable and inclusive learning environments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Educators conduct library audits to create diverse text collections. Learners use interactive quizzes (e.g., OurStory) to find books celebrating diverse experiences. Resources: 1000 Black Girl Books Resource Guide, Loyola University Chicago Libraries Multicultural/Culturally-Responsive Books, MindShift – Diversifying Your Classroom Book Collections.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Categorize vocabulary words into three tiers to prioritize instruction: Tier 1 (basic words, rarely require instruction), Tier 2 (high-frequency academic words, crucial for mature language), and Tier 3 (low-frequency, content-specific words). Focus primarily on Tier 2 words for broader academic benefit, but also include relevant Tier 3 words specific to the current topic or text. Let students select words, rate their knowledge, and guess meanings to inform instruction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Knowledge of tiered vocabulary system, ability to analyze text for relevant words, and time for learners to select and rate words.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection to avoid overwhelming learners. Tier criteria can be subjective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly middle and high school learners, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prioritize vocabulary instruction, focus on high-impact words, tailor instruction to learner needs, promote independent word selection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focuses on the most useful vocabulary for academic success, makes vocabulary learning relevant, and promotes self-assessment and metacognition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners select their own words for review. Instructors choose words based on formative assessment data.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner self-ratings, pre-reading vocabulary charts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that focusing on Tier 2 words improves academic language and comprehension. (Reference: Isabel Beck's "Bringing Words to Life")

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading Lord of the Flies, have students skim chapter one and select words they 'know it,' 'sort of know it,' or 'don't know it at all.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self- and peer-editing are collaborative processes where learners evaluate their own writing and provide feedback to peers. The self-edit step encourages students to evaluate specific features of their writing, increasing self-awareness of writing conventions. The peer-edit step helps build a learning community in which peers work collaboratively and heightens the awareness of various print and grammatical conventions for the peer editor and the author.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a structured checklist or rubric and a supportive classroom environment for collaborative work. Effective modeling of the process is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit instruction and modeling to be effective. Some learners may be uncomfortable providing or receiving feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-5

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness of writing conventions, build a learning community, enhance collaboration, improve print and grammatical conventions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-evaluation and peer interaction, reinforcing learning and improving writing skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can focus on specific areas of writing based on their individual needs. Peer-editing allows for varied perspectives and feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback
  • Revision
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor students' self- and peer-assessment skills through observation and feedback analysis.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances writing skills and fosters a collaborative learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a checklist, students self-edit their work and then meet with a partner to engage in peer editing. The teacher models the use of the checklist with sample text, and students work in groups to edit one piece of writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves having learners identify, label, or match facial expressions and feelings. You can also ask learners to categorize feeling words by the type of feeling. Using literature to have learners analyze characters’ feelings is also helpful. Self-awareness is the ability to correctly identify your own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they impact behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator and a set of expressions and emotions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be more extroverted and find categorizing emotions difficult.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-awareness, identify facial expressions and emotions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • This strategy focuses on self-awareness and identifying one's feelings through various methods such as matching expressions, labeling, and analyzing literature.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can utilize a variety of mediums to suit their students' needs. Students who are introverted may find analyzing literature to be a better option.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teachers can listen and observe students' conversations to evaluate whether or not the goal was achieved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy relies on building empathy to establish self-awareness (Jones, Damon E., Mark Greenberg, and Max Crowley. "Early Social-Emotional Functioning and Public Health: The Relationship Between Kindergarten Social Competence and Future Wellness." American Journal of Public Health, 105, no. 11, 2015, 2283-2290.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This activity involves having learners think back on their experiences and outcomes, which helps provide them with a greater understanding of themselves. Learners can think and write about their experiences throughout a day or class period and look for patterns, as well as create and manage goals. Self-awareness is the ability to correctly identify your own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they impact behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator and writing materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find annotating to be challenging and overwhelming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-awareness, promote annotations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • This strategy helps learners improve self-awareness through annotations during journal writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can utilize a variety of prompts to suit their students' needs. Students who are introverted may find this activity to be a better option.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teachers can read and observe students' journal writing to evaluate whether or not the goal was achieved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy relies on reflection to establish self-awareness (Flavian, Heidi. “Towards Teaching and Beyond: Strengthening Education by Understanding Students’ Self-Awareness Development.” Power and Education, vol. 8, no. 1, Jan. 2016, pp. 88–100.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-evaluation involves teaching students how to review their writing to decide if changes are needed. By modeling when to stop and evaluate writing and providing specific questions to ask about each paragraph, students can learn to identify areas for improvement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Writing assignment; facilitator; self-evaluation checklist or questions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for some students to self-assess; requires consistent practice and feedback; effectiveness depends on student engagement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students struggling with writing assignments, particularly those with learning and thinking differences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing quality; enhance self-awareness; develop self-assessment skills; promote independent learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves writing quality; enhances self-awareness; promotes independent learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt self-evaluation questions to suit different types of writing assignments; provide additional support for learners who struggle to assess their own writing

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student's ability to evaluate their own writing; track improvements in writing quality; monitor student self-awareness and assessment skills

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved writing quality; enhanced self-awareness; developed self-assessment skills; promoted independent learning (as suggested by explicit self-evaluation instruction)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-instruction, also known as self-talk or self-statements, is a strategy where learners talk themselves through a task or activity to self-regulate their behavior. It involves using self-induced statements to direct or control actions, such as defining the problem, focusing attention, explaining strategies, self-evaluating, coping with difficulties, and self-reinforcing accomplishments. The goal is to progress from overt self-statements to covert, internalized speech.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • The learner must be capable of performing the designated academic or behavioral skill. Self-statements should be developmentally appropriate and meaningful to the learner.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Self-instruction alone is useless if the learner cannot perform the designated academic or behavioral skill. Self-statements must be meaningful to the learner for successful implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for learners with learning difficulties or those needing support with task initiation and completion

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-regulation, improve task focus, promote error detection and correction, develop coping strategies, reinforce positive behavior

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides an element of control over learning, efficient use of teacher's time, minimal maintenance once developed, promotes metacognitive awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Self-statements can be tailored to individual needs and learning styles. Learners can choose from different types of self-instruction (problem definition, focusing attention, strategy, self-evaluation, coping, self-reinforcement) based on the task or situation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to articulate and use self-statements during tasks. Monitor improvements in task completion, accuracy, and self-regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Self-instruction interventions have been shown to improve self-regulation, task completion, and accuracy, especially among learners with learning difficulties.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A young child talks themselves through the shoe-tying process. A medical student mentally rehearses the procedural steps while engaged in an injury evaluation. A student uses self-statements to calm themselves down and remain motivated to complete a frustrating task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers model articulating how they solve a problem and prompt students to explain their own thinking. This allows students to become aware of how they think while also providing teachers insight on how students are understanding the concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for teachers to model problem-solving and prompt students to explain their thinking. Requires careful listening and observation to understand student thought processes.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for students who struggle to articulate their thoughts or have difficulty with metacognition. Requires a supportive classroom environment where students feel comfortable sharing their thinking.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote metacognition, improve self-awareness, provide insights into student understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases metacognitive awareness by prompting students to articulate their thought processes. Provides teachers with insights into student understanding and potential misconceptions. Fosters self-reflection and awareness of problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing structured prompts or scaffolding to guide students in explaining their thinking. Teachers can tailor their modeling to address specific learning needs or challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Articulation
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student explanations to identify strengths and areas for improvement in their understanding. Collect data on the frequency and quality of student self-explanations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of metacognitive skills, enhances self-awareness, and provides teachers with valuable insights into student understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-monitoring of attention is a strategy where learners self-assess their behavior and record the results. This can increase or decrease the frequency, intensity, or duration of existing behaviors, such as students who are easily distracted, get up from their seats, bother other students, or fidget with objects. The student monitors either the frequency or duration of these behaviors. SMA usually uses cues to remind students to self-assess.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a defined behavior to monitor, a method for recording behavior (e.g., a tally sheet), and cues to prompt self-assessment (e.g., beep tape).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not create new skills or knowledge, but rather modifies existing behaviors. Requires willing participation from the learner for successful implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who exhibit attention difficulties, including elementary, secondary, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase awareness of behavior, improve attention, and reduce distractions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback to learners, facilitates communication between learners and parents, increases awareness of one's behavior, promotes self-regulation. Saves instructors time by shifting monitoring responsibility to the learner.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with personalized self-monitoring forms to reflect the learner's age, developmental level, and individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency and duration of targeted behaviors. Compare data before and after implementation to gauge effectiveness. Monitor consistency of self-monitoring procedures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows positive changes in social behaviors, completion of written work, ability to follow directions, and on-task behavior. (Gumpel & Shlomit, 2000; Hughes et al., 2002; McDougall & Brady, 1998; Rock, 2005; Wehmeyer et al., 2003)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses an audio tape with tones at fixed intervals to cue a student to self-assess their on-task behavior every 5 minutes. A student monitors how often they talk to a neighbor during instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-monitoring is a strategy where learners self-assess their behavior and record the results, increasing or decreasing the frequency, intensity, or duration of existing behavior. It involves students keeping track of whether they are on-task, compliant, and following rules and routines, essentially evaluating their own behavior. This can be applied to various aspects, such as attention (SMA) or academic performance (SMP). Self-monitoring saves instructors time monitoring learner behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a self-monitoring form or tally sheet, a method for signaling time intervals (e.g., timer, beep tape), and instructor guidance and support. Clear definitions of the behavior to be monitored are essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may be tempted to rate their behavior more positively than is accurate, necessitating monitoring by the instructor. Requires initial training and ongoing support to ensure accurate and consistent implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners, particularly those needing support in attention, task completion, and social skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase learner awareness of their own behavior, improve specific behaviors (e.g., attention, task completion, social interactions), and promote self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback, engages learners actively, facilitates communication between learners and instructors, and promotes self-awareness. It also fosters a sense of responsibility and independence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to various behaviors and settings. The self-monitoring form can be personalized to reflect the learner's age, developmental level, and individual needs. Cues and prompts can be tailored to the specific behavior being monitored.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in the frequency, intensity, or duration of the target behavior. Compare baseline data with post-implementation data to assess effectiveness. Monitor the agreement between learner self-assessments and instructor observations to ensure accuracy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies have shown positive changes in social behaviors, completion of written work, ability to follow directions, and academic engagement. Improves on-task behavior, reduces disruptive behavior, and enhances listening skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher implements SMA (self-monitoring of attention) with a student who has difficulty paying attention during instruction, using an audio tape with tones to signal time intervals. SMP (self-monitoring of performance) is used with a student who needs to monitor the rate at which they correctly complete class work or the overall accuracy of their performance.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-monitoring of performance is a strategy where learners monitor an aspect of their academic performance, such as the rate at which they correctly complete class work or the overall accuracy of their performance. It is useful for building fluency and encourages learners to self-assess their behavior and record the results. It increases or decreases the frequency, intensity, or duration of existing behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a defined academic behavior to monitor, a method for recording performance (e.g., a tally sheet), and a clear understanding of performance expectations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not create new academic skills, but rather improves the application of existing skills. Requires willing participation from the learner for successful implementation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners needing to improve academic performance, including elementary, secondary, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve academic performance, build fluency, and increase accuracy of completed work

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback to learners, facilitates self-regulation, and promotes learner engagement. Saves instructors time by shifting monitoring responsibility to the learner.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with personalized self-monitoring forms to reflect the learner's age, developmental level, and individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track rate of work completion and accuracy of performance. Compare data before and after implementation to gauge effectiveness. Monitor consistency of self-monitoring procedures.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies demonstrate positive changes in completion of written classroom work, academic engagement, and math fluency. (Gumpel & Shlomit, 2000; Hughes et al., 2002; McDougall & Brady, 1998; Rock, 2005; Wehmeyer et al., 2003)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student counts the number of math problems completed during independent work. A learner tracks the number of pages of text read during study periods.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learning cohorts can be formed for employees to learn from each other on topics like improving Scrum processes or new skills such as technical tools or programming languages. These groups provide a structured way for employees to share knowledge and support each other's professional development, fostering a culture of continuous learning within the organization. Key elements include a commitment from leadership, dedicated time for learning, a platform for employees to find colleagues with shared learning objectives, facilitation support, and a designated physical or online space for meet-ups.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires commitment from leadership, dedicated time for learning, a platform for employees to find colleagues with shared learning objectives, facilitation support, and a designated physical or online space for meet-ups.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on employee engagement, commitment to learning, and support from leadership to allocate time and resources.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Employees in organizations looking to upskill and learn from each other, with a focus on continuous improvement and collaboration.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To foster continuous learning, skill development, and knowledge sharing among employees within an organization.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates knowledge sharing, supports skill development through peer interaction, and promotes a culture of continuous learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learning groups can focus on diverse topics and skill areas based on employee interests and organizational needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Teaching
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Peer Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Success can be measured by tracking employee participation in learning groups, skill development, and knowledge sharing within the organization.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved employee skills, enhanced collaboration, and a culture of continuous learning within the organization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples of concepts for self-organizing learning groups include Working Out Loud, Social Learning, Communities of Practice, and Liberating Structures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: SRSD is an instructional approach designed to enhance students' writing skills by addressing their affective, behavioral, and cognitive characteristics. It integrates findings from cognitive development, behavior, and affect research. The model supports students in developing writing knowledge, monitoring their writing, and fostering positive attitudes towards writing and themselves as writers. Teachers provide scaffolding to develop skillful strategy use, self-regulation, and understanding of strategy limitations. The core goals are to assist students in developing knowledge about writing, support their ability to monitor and manage their own writing, and promote positive attitudes about writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction, scaffolding, collaborative learning, assessment of student needs, flexible curriculum integration, support network for teachers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant teacher training and effort. May not be uniformly effective for all students without adaptation. Can be time-intensive to implement fully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students facing difficulties in writing, including those with learning disabilities, across elementary, middle, and high school levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop writing skills, improve self-regulation, foster positive attitudes towards writing, enhance strategic performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves writing quality, knowledge, and approach, and enhances self-efficacy. Promotes active collaboration, individualized instruction, and criterion-based progression. Addresses affective, behavioral, and cognitive aspects of writing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction is individualized based on students’ characteristics and skills. Strategies and instructional components are selected and modified to fit individual needs, with differentiated self-instructions, goals, and feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in writing quality (length, structure, content), changes in attitudes toward writing, and increased use of self-regulation strategies. Observation of strategy use and student self-assessment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show significant improvements in the quality, length, and structure of students’ compositions. Students show improved planning, revising, and substantive content. Gains are maintained over time and generalize across settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • SRSD has been used to teach planning and revising strategies, including brainstorming, self-monitoring, and organizing writing content. Examples include the SPACE strategy (Setting, Purpose, Action, Conclusion, Emotions) for story writing and the TREE strategy (Topic sentence, Reasons, Examine reasons, Ending) for opinion essays.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporate mindfulness techniques to help learners manage their initial emotional impulses and reactivity. Self-regulation is the ability to alter and regulate our emotional and behavioral responses.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find this activity to be limiting or not helpful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, promote focus, and improve emotional awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • This strategy focuses on mindfulness and regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor the techniques that are most helpful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teachers can listen and observe students' emotions to evaluate whether or not the goal was achieved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy relies on providing opportunities to practice meditation. (Zumbrunn S, Tadlock J, Roberts ED (2011) Encouraging Self-Regulated Learning in the Classroom: A Review of the Literature. Metropolitan Educational Research Consortium (MERC), Virginia Commonwealth University.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding can help learners learn how to manage their responses in an emotionally safe context. Self-regulation is the ability to alter and regulate our emotional and behavioral responses.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find this activity to be limiting or not helpful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, promote safe environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • This strategy focuses on scaffolding and building a safe environment for expression.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor guidance and scaffold efforts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teachers can listen and observe students' emotions to evaluate whether or not the goal was achieved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy relies on a safe environment to develop self-regulation skills (Bridgett, D. J., Burt, N. M., Edwards, E. S., & Deater-Deckard, K. (2015). Intergenerational transmission of self-regulation: A multidisciplinary review and integrative conceptual framework. Psychological Bulletin, 141(3), 602-654.).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Scaffolding provides learners with a safe and emotionally supportive context to learn how to manage their responses to challenging or stimulating situations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A safe learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The instructor needs to be skilled at building a supportive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Creating a learning environment where learners are able to safely explore their reactions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to explore self-regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be personalized.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner participation

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Unknown

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Not applicable.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-reinforcement involves individuals selecting a reinforcer and rewarding themselves for reaching or exceeding a set criterion. This strategy actively involves students in their learning environment, teaching a beneficial skill for independent adult living and often creating greater changes than teacher-imposed rewards.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher and students must set a clear and objective goal. Students must select a reinforcer. Procedures for evaluation must be determined. Student must administer the reinforcer.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • What is reinforcing for students will vary according to factors such as age, personality, culture, and gender.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who need help staying on task and being motivated to learn.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve performance, actively involve students in their learning environment, teach a skill beneficial to independent adult living, and create greater changes than teacher-imposed rewards.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Substantial improvement in performance, active involvement in the learning environment, teaching a skill beneficial to independent adult living, and creating greater changes than teacher-imposed rewards.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can involve the student in the process of choosing a reinforcer by asking the student to suggest possible reinforcers or by providing a reinforcement menu for the student to choose from or rank order.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure the substantial improvement in the student's performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Self-reinforcement produces substantial improvement in performance. The strategy actively involves students in their learning environment. It serves to teach a skill beneficial to independent adult living. Self-reinforcement creates greater changes than teacher-imposed rewards.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Step 1: Set a Goal for Receiving Rewards Step 2: Select a Reinforcer Step 3: Determine Student Evaluation Procedures Step 4: Administer the Reinforcer

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Self-reinforcement involves using effort-based and behavior-specific praise to encourage students during the writing process. Praising students for their hard work, focus, and adherence to timing can help them feel more comfortable with their writing skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Writing assignment; facilitator; positive and encouraging language

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Praise must be genuine and specific; may not be effective for all learners; effectiveness depends on the facilitator's approach

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students struggling with writing assignments, particularly those with learning and thinking differences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase motivation and engagement; improve comfort with writing skills; reduce negative thoughts; promote a positive mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation and engagement; improves comfort with writing skills; promotes a positive mindset

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor praise to individual strengths and challenges; provide specific feedback; use a variety of praise methods

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student motivation and engagement levels; track improvements in comfort with writing skills; observe changes in mindset

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased motivation and engagement; improved comfort with writing skills; promoted a positive mindset (as suggested by positive reinforcement during writing)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Provide learners with scenarios of challenging situations and have them brainstorm possible neutral or positive self-talk responses. Examples include: being excluded from a lunch table, a teacher not having time for your question, being blamed for something you didn't do, and failing a test. For each scenario, provide examples of negative self-talk and prompt learners to generate more positive or neutral alternatives.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of challenging scenarios, brainstorming techniques.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be creative and open-minded.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop learners' ability to generate positive self-talk responses in challenging situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners build a repertoire of positive self-talk phrases and strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use scenarios that are relevant and meaningful to the learners' lives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and variety of positive self-talk responses generated by learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased confidence in using positive self-talk to cope with challenging situations (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Celebrating diversity of language and tailoring instructional materials to non-native English speakers are essential for a culturally responsive classroom. This involves providing materials in the student's primary language while encouraging mastery of English. Students who are not native English speakers feel less marginalized when their original language is valued and supported.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Bilingual instructional materials, resources for language support, teacher awareness of students' language backgrounds.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Availability of resources in multiple languages, potential for logistical challenges in providing individualized support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Multilingual learners of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Value linguistic diversity, reduce marginalization, improve English fluency, provide tailored instructional materials

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces feelings of marginalization, supports the maintenance of native languages, enhances English language acquisition, promotes inclusivity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Providing materials in each student's primary language, tailoring instruction to individual fluency levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student progress in English language acquisition, student participation in class, student feedback on instructional materials.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research on bilingual education shows that valuing and supporting students' native languages can improve their academic achievement and overall well-being. Tailoring instruction to meet the needs of multilingual learners enhances their engagement and success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities that incorporate sensory experiences to enhance handwriting skills. These activities engage different senses (e.g., tactile, proprioceptive, visual) to improve letter formation, pencil pressure, and motor planning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Multisensory materials (e.g., playdough, shaving cream, sandpaper), writing tools, and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for students with significant sensory aversions. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grades, particularly useful for students with sensory sensitivities or motor planning difficulties.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance handwriting skills by engaging different senses (tactile, proprioceptive, visual).

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves sensory integration and motor planning, leading to better letter formation and pencil control. Engages different learning styles through multisensory experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual sensory preferences and needs. Varied materials and techniques engage different sensory modalities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in letter formation, pencil pressure, and motor planning. Assess engagement and sensory comfort during writing tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved handwriting skills through multisensory engagement. Enhanced sensory integration and motor planning abilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sensory stimulation involves providing experiences that engage a person's senses to improve regulation, attention, and focus. This is achieved by introducing tactile toys, fidgets, and activities that awaken sensory receptors, helping individuals manage sensory defensiveness and seek tactile experiences as needed. Addressing sensory needs can reduce fidgeting, attention issues, and behavior problems, promoting calmness and focus for higher learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to sensory toys, fidgets, or activities. Implementation benefits from clear rules and guidelines for use, as well as ongoing conversations about their effectiveness.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be misused as toys if not properly managed, potentially distracting others. Effectiveness varies based on individual sensory needs and preferences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with sensory processing needs, including children with sensory sensitivities, sensory seekers, and those with attention deficits; applicable across K–12 and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-regulation, enhance attention and focus, reduce fidgeting and behavior problems, integrate sensory experiences

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate sensory input, promotes self-regulation, and supports emotional and behavioral stability. Helps learners calm their bodies and minds for better concentration and learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to individual sensory preferences, with options for tactile, visual, auditory, and proprioceptive fidgets and activities. Rules and guidelines can be customized to fit specific contexts and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in attention, focus, fidgeting, and behavior. Monitor the frequency and purpose of fidget use, as well as feedback from learners about the effectiveness of different sensory tools.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved focus and attention: Research suggests that sensory stimulation can help individuals regulate their emotions and behavior, leading to increased attention and focus. Enhanced self-regulation: Studies indicate that addressing sensory needs can improve self-regulation skills, reducing fidgeting and behavior problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary schools integrating fidgets into classrooms to support student attention and sensory integration. Tactile cubes like Skoog provide immediate sensory input and acoustic feedback to promote exploration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Practice how to combine two simple sentences into a compound or complex sentence. Use this technique in conjunction with other effective writing techniques, such as encouraging peer discussion as part of collaborative writing, to help reinforce the practice. Has a positive impact on overall writing quality and can boost learners’ reading comprehension skills as well.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction, sentence combining exercises, feedback on practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires grammar knowledge, may not suit all learners

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing quality, enhance reading comprehension, promote sentence variety

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances sentence variety, improves writing quality, reinforces reading comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Exercises can be tailored to different sentence structures and writing tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased sentence variety, greater reading comprehension

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Sentence combining has a positive impact on overall writing quality and can boost learners’ reading comprehension skills as well.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use sentence frames to help structure respectful responses in debate or disagreement situations online. Provides examples of how digital citizens can present new ideas, agree with viewpoints, respectfully disagree, seek more information, or acknowledge new learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of respectful communication, ability to use online platforms, willingness to engage in thoughtful dialogue

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel artificial at first, requires practice, depends on community norms and moderation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students, educators, digital citizens

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve online communication, foster respectful dialogue, reduce conflict, promote empathy, enhance clarity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structure for respectful communication, promotes thoughtful responses, enhances online interactions

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt sentence frames to suit different situations, communication styles, and individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe online interactions, gather feedback from participants, assess clarity and respectfulness of communications

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Leads to more positive and productive online interactions, reduces conflict, promotes understanding and empathy

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • “I realize my views on __ are limited. _, would you mind expanding on your idea a bit more?” or “Thank you, _, for presenting your viewpoint. I agree because ___.”

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When you ask a question, rather than just having students raise hands and you picking one volunteer, have every student in the class write a sentence. This way, students can be active and can get the feel of writing about math.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a question or prompt that can be answered in a sentence. Requires time for students to write and share their sentences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of questions. Some students may struggle to write a sentence if they do not understand the concept.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for students who are hesitant to speak up in class.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student participation, encourage active learning, and provide opportunities for students to practice writing about math.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active participation from all students, not just those who volunteer. Provides a low-stakes way for students to practice writing about math. Allows the teacher to quickly assess student understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can provide different sentence stems or prompts based on student needs and abilities. Students can also be given the option to write more than one sentence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement. Review student sentences to assess understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases student participation and provides opportunities for students to practice writing about math.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When asking a question about a math problem, have every student write a sentence explaining their answer. This way, students can be active and can get the feel of writing about math.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers can use sentence stems to stimulate reflection and make it more accessible to learners. Use sentence stems in conferences (where reflection can be modeled), or put them on a sheet for students who choose writing to jump-start their reflections. Examples of possible sentence stems: 'I selected this piece of writing because...', 'What really surprised me about this piece of writing was...', 'When I look at my other pieces of writing, this piece is different because...', 'What makes this piece of writing strong is my use of...', 'Here is one example from my writing to show you what I mean', and 'What I want to really work on to make my writing better for a reader is...'

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sentence stems and a way for students to record their reflections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Sentence stems may limit students' creativity and ability to reflect in their own way.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate reflection, encourage self-assessment, facilitate writing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with a starting point for reflection and makes it more accessible. Reduces cognitive load by providing structure.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use sentence stems that are relevant to the specific task or learning experience. They can also allow students to choose the sentence stems that they find most helpful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Deeper and more thoughtful reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of sentence stems in promoting reflection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides students with a sheet of sentence stems and asks them to choose one to start their reflection on a recent writing assignment.

docs.title: Separate Product, Process, and Progress Criteria
Description
docs.text: Instead of eliminating grades for behavior and participation, differentiate between grades for product, process, and progress criteria. This ensures grades for mastery are clearly delineated from more subjective factors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Detailed rubrics, clear grading guidelines

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant effort to differentiate grading criteria

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Clearly delineate between mastery, behavior, and participation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides comprehensive feedback, separates objective and subjective measures

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for targeted feedback on specific areas

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of grading, effectiveness of feedback

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Ensures that grades for mastery are clearly delineated from grades for more subjective factors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Assigning separate grades for a research paper (product), participation in discussions (process), and improvement over time (progress)

docs.title: Set a High Bar for Each Student
Description
docs.text: Hold high expectations for all students. Convince students that they can learn and succeed through social-psychological interventions that focus on changing students’ thoughts, feelings, and beliefs in and about school. Focus on fostering a Learner Mindset, and building self-efficacy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training or guidance on effective communication and motivation techniques, a supportive and encouraging classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires consistent effort, may be challenging with students who have deeply ingrained negative beliefs about their abilities

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, higher education instructors, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student achievement, foster a growth mindset, increase self-efficacy, create a positive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts student confidence, motivates learning, enhances resilience, promotes positive self-perception

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different learning styles and individual needs through targeted feedback and support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvements in student performance, monitor changes in self-efficacy and mindset, observe student engagement and participation

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Small social-psychological interventions can lead to large gains in student achievement for each and every student.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use growth mindset language, provide specific and actionable feedback, celebrate effort and progress, and highlight student strengths.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Responding with empathy means letting students’ reactions come first. You don’t have to bury your own feelings or agree with or accept their behavior. But try to keep your focus on hearing students out and seeing the situation through their eyes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Self-awareness, emotional regulation skills, active listening abilities

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort and practice, may be challenging in emotionally charged situations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, counselors, parents, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of student perspectives, reduce conflict, promote empathy, build trust

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters better communication, reduces misunderstandings, creates a more supportive environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust approach based on individual student needs and circumstances

docs.title: Instructions
