docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor communication patterns, observe interactions, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances relationships, promotes a more inclusive and understanding environment, improves conflict resolution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Listen attentively, validate student feelings, and postpone judgment until after understanding their perspective.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Objectives aligned with standards, activities, and assessments, providing students with a clear understanding of the knowledge and skills they will demonstrate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly written objectives, aligned activities and assessments

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and alignment

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, Higher Education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide clarity on learning expectations, align activities and assessments, promote student understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances student understanding, ensures alignment, promotes clear goals

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different subjects and grade levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of objectives, alignment of assessments

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students should have a clear understanding of what knowledge and skills they will demonstrate upon completing the lesson/unit/course activities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Clear science objectives for 3rd graders classifying organisms

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Micro-goals involve breaking down larger objectives into smaller, manageable steps. This strategy supports consistent, incremental progress, which can foster a growth mindset and increase confidence. Achieving small wins repeatedly over time helps learners build momentum and develop a positive attitude toward learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and breaking down of larger goals into smaller, achievable steps. Requires regular monitoring and feedback to track progress.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of tasks. Learners may need guidance in setting appropriate micro-goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with large or complex tasks

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage consistent progress, build confidence, foster a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a sense of accomplishment and builds momentum. Makes large tasks seem less daunting. Increases motivation through repeated success.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Micro-goals can be tailored to individual learners' skill levels and learning styles. The pace of progress can be adjusted to meet individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the completion of micro-goals. Measure learners' confidence and motivation levels. Observe learners' ability to tackle larger tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that setting achievable micro-goals can lead to increased motivation, improved performance, and a greater sense of self-efficacy. Small wins repeated over time can significantly impact a learner's overall growth and mindset.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Lessons have clear learning intentions with goals that clarify what success looks like. Lesson goals always explain what students need to understand, and what they must be able to do. Having clear learning goals helps the teacher to plan learning activities and it helps students understand what is required.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to define clear learning intentions and success criteria before the lesson.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Goals must be communicated effectively to students to be beneficial.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Clarify learning intentions and success criteria for students

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a framework for teachers to plan learning activities and helps students understand expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Goals can be tailored to different subjects and student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of lesson objectives, alignment of activities with goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Clear learning goals help students understand what is required of them and help teachers plan learning activities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners hear the story 'Seven Blind Mice,' stopping after each mouse’s perspective to take notes or engage in jigsaw reading. They then discuss and speculate on what the object might be based on the different perspectives, exploring how different viewpoints contribute to a fuller understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • The story 'Seven Blind Mice' or a similar narrative, a space for discussions and reflections, and facilitation by an instructor to guide analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to understand the characters' perspectives or may impose their own biases on the interpretation. It requires careful guidance from the instructor to ensure thoughtful and respectful analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who are learning about perspective-taking and collaboration

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote perspective-taking, enhance comprehension of storytelling, encourage collaborative problem-solving, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Illustrates the importance of considering multiple perspectives to understand a situation fully. Encourages collaborative problem-solving through discussion and speculation. Improves communication skills through sharing ideas and perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The level of analysis and discussion can be adjusted to the learners' abilities. The activity can be adapted for different age groups by using more complex stories or films.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the ability to understand and articulate different perspectives, the quality of collaborative problem-solving, and the level of critical thinking demonstrated in the analysis. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards different viewpoints.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Collaborative problem-solving has been shown to improve critical thinking, communication skills, and perspective-taking abilities. Exploring different viewpoints also promotes tolerance and understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students read the story 'Seven Blind Mice' and discuss how each mouse's perspective contributes to the overall understanding of the object. Students watch the film 'Twelve Angry Men' and analyze how each juror's perspective shapes the verdict.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shadowing involves following a student throughout their school day to gain insights into their experiences, challenges, and needs. By observing without assumptions, educators can question their preconceived ideas and learn how to better support their students. It encourages them to create learning goals, coordinate with students and staff, and prepare for a meaningful shadowing experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Coordination with students and staff, commitment to observation without judgment, reflective practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, may be disruptive to student routine, requires careful planning to avoid biases

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, school administrators, counselors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gain insights into student experiences, question assumptions, improve educator understanding, enhance student support

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides firsthand perspective, reduces biases, enhances empathy, promotes student-centered approaches

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select students based on specific learning goals, tailor observation to individual needs

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess changes in teacher behavior, improvements in student support strategies, gather feedback from students and educators

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creates a more supportive classroom environment, improves student engagement, enhances educator effectiveness, and promotes better student-teacher relationships

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Create learning goals, select a student, coordinate with parents, and shadow the student throughout the day to observe their experiences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An adult follows a child closely, within arm's reach, to provide constant direct supervision and prevent unwanted behaviors (e.g., biting) before they occur. The adult remains unobtrusive, ideally ensuring the child doesn't feel singled out or that their play is being adjusted. The goal is to keep the class safe while the child develops alternative, more appropriate behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated adult (preferably the same one), close proximity to the child, and consistency in shadowing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant adult effort and dedication. Could be perceived negatively if not implemented carefully (child feels singled out).

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children with behavioral issues (biting, hitting)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Adjust behavior problems, ensure classroom safety, teach new behavior strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Keeps the class safe while adjusting behavior, helps break behavior cycles, provides protection while the child learns new strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • This strategy is specifically tailored to a child's behavior problems, such as biting or hitting. The adult can adjust their proximity based on the child's behavior patterns and intensity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Decrease in targeted behavior incidents over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a safe environment for all children while the child with the behavior problem is taught new strategies and coping mechanisms.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An adult follows a child everywhere they go, staying within arm's reach to prevent unwanted behavior before it happens. The child should not feel singled out or punished, and the other children should not be aware of the shadowing. It is used to keep the class safe while teaching the child new strategies or waiting for them to outgrow the behavior. Shadowing continues until the child is two weeks incident-free.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated adult, close proximity to the child, awareness of the child's typical behavior patterns

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a dedicated adult resource, can be labor-intensive, may not address the underlying cause of the behavior

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children exhibiting behaviors that can hurt themselves or others

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Adjust behavior problems, maintain class safety, teach new coping strategies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides constant supervision to prevent unwanted behavior, keeps the class safe while addressing the underlying issue, breaks the cycle of negative behavior

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The adult can be the same person each time to build trust and consistency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduction in behavior incidents, improved social interactions, development of new coping strategies

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a safe classroom environment while the child learns new strategies. May also break the cycle of negative behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Used in preschool settings to address biting or hitting. Can also be used in other settings where behavior modification is needed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shadowing is a direct observation technique where an adult follows a student throughout their school day to gain real-time qualitative evidence of the student's experiences. The goal is to observe and note facts about the student’s learning, interactions, and daily experiences without interpretation, opinion, or judgment. This practice allows educators to uncover insights into a student's lived experiences, identify areas that need to be addressed, and understand the school environment from the student’s perspective.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated adult (educator, administrator, or other staff member), a student willing to be shadowed, a shadowing template for note-taking, and a scheduled school day for the observation. Requires staying objective and making low-inference observations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time commitment. Can be intrusive if not done sensitively. May be influenced by the observer's biases, despite efforts to remain objective. Effectiveness depends on the observer's ability to accurately record and interpret observations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, school leaders, product designers, and anyone seeking to understand student experiences and improve school environments, particularly focusing on diverse student populations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Gain insights into student experiences, identify areas needing improvement, uncover truths about the school environment, understand the impact of race on teaching and learning, and inform actions to support students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time, qualitative data about student experiences. Allows for direct observation of student interactions, relationships, and learning. Uncovers hidden biases and disparities. Facilitates empathy and understanding of diverse student needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The focus of shadowing can be personalized based on specific learning goals, such as understanding the experiences of English learners, students of color, or students with specific needs. Educators can choose students with different profiles to broaden their understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Notes and observations recorded during the shadowing experience, summaries of findings, reflections on insights gained, and plans for action based on the shadowing data. Analysis of student interactions, teacher practices, and school environment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased understanding of student experiences, identification of disparities and biases, improved instructional practices, and enhanced support for diverse student populations. Improved school culture and climate through data-driven decision-making.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A principal shadows a seventh-grade ESL student and discovers the student has limited opportunities to speak during the school day, leading to changes in instructional practices. A teacher shadows a quiet student to better understand their engagement and learning needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shadowing is a strategy used to address harmful behaviors in children, such as biting or hitting. An adult closely follows the child at all times, maintaining an arm's reach distance, to prevent the behavior before it occurs. The goal is to provide constant supervision without drawing special attention to the child or making them feel punished. This approach is typically used after a couple of incidents and continues until the child is incident-free for two weeks, aiming to break the cycle of negative behavior and protect classmates.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated adult to shadow the child, clear understanding of the behavior goals, and consistency in implementation. The adult must maintain close proximity and be ready to intervene immediately.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant adult resources and attention. The shadowed child must not feel singled out or punished. Success depends on consistent application and the child's ability to learn new strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily used for young children exhibiting aggressive behaviors, such as biting or hitting, in classroom settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent harmful behaviors, maintain class safety, teach alternative strategies, and support the child's development of appropriate social skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures immediate safety for all children, interrupts negative behavior patterns, and allows for the teaching of new, appropriate behaviors. It provides a structured environment for behavior modification.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific techniques used in conjunction with shadowing can be tailored to the individual child's needs, such as growing vocabulary or teaching new social strategies.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The primary measure of effectiveness is the reduction or elimination of the targeted behavior. Progress is tracked by monitoring incidents and noting the child's development of alternative social skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Proven to be effective in breaking negative behavior cycles, particularly in young children. By preventing harmful behaviors, it allows children to develop more appropriate social interactions and protects their classmates.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shadowing can be used as a direct intervention to address behavior problems in the classroom. An adult shadow closely follows a child exhibiting harmful behaviors (e.g., biting) to prevent incidents before they occur. The adult stays within arm's reach, providing constant direct supervision without drawing special attention to the child. This approach aims to break the cycle of negative behavior and keep the classroom safe while teaching the child alternative strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A trained adult shadow, administrative and parental support, and clear protocols for intervention.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires dedicated resources and staffing, can be labor-intensive, and may not address the root causes of the behavior.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and aides working with elementary students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent harmful behaviors, keep the classroom safe, teach alternative strategies, and break the cycle of negative behavior.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides direct, immediate intervention, protects other students, and allows for teaching new behavior strategies in real time.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The adult shadow can be the same individual each time to create consistency, and the approach can be tailored to the specific behavior issue.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Reduction in the frequency of negative behaviors, increased use of alternative strategies by the child, and positive changes in classroom safety and dynamics.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Safer classroom environment, improved behavior management, and enhanced learning experiences for all students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is a behavior management technique where an adult closely follows a child, acting as their "shadow," to prevent harmful behaviors like biting or hitting. The adult stays within arm's reach to intervene immediately if the child attempts the behavior. The goal is to provide constant, direct supervision without making the child feel singled out or punished, allowing them to play and interact freely while ensuring the safety of themselves and others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A designated adult, such as a teacher, aide, or trained volunteer. Consistent application of the shadowing technique. A clear understanding of the target behavior and intervention strategies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be labor-intensive, requiring dedicated adult supervision. May not be suitable for all behaviors or children. Requires careful implementation to avoid making the child feel singled out or punished.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily used with young children (e.g., preschool or early elementary) who exhibit behaviors that can harm themselves or others, such as biting or hitting.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prevent harmful behaviors, ensure safety, break negative behavior cycles, support positive behavior development, and teach alternative communication strategies.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate intervention to prevent harm. Breaks negative behavior cycles. Allows the child to continue playing and interacting with peers. Offers an opportunity to teach alternative communication strategies.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The intensity and duration of shadowing can be adjusted based on the child's specific needs and behavior patterns. Techniques can be combined with other strategies to support the child's development.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Frequency of target behavior incidents before and during shadowing. Duration of shadowing required to eliminate the behavior. Observations of the child's interactions and behavior during and after shadowing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced incidents of harmful behaviors, improved safety in the classroom, development of alternative communication strategies, and positive behavior changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A preschool teacher shadows a child who bites classmates, intervening immediately to prevent biting and teaching alternative ways to express frustration. A classroom aide shadows a child who hits others, helping them develop non-aggressive responses.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners identify two- and three-dimensional shapes in their surroundings, promoting geometric awareness and real-world application of geometric concepts. Starting with simple shapes and progressing to more complex ones increases the challenge.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on availability of shapes in the environment. May become repetitive if played for too long without variation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve shape recognition, enhance geometric awareness, and connect geometric concepts to real-world objects

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves shape recognition and connects geometric concepts to real-world objects.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of shapes based on learner's skill level. Provide a list of shapes to search for as a scaffold.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to identify and name shapes accurately. Track the number of shapes correctly identified within a given time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engages children to put down their gadgets and explore the world around them and playing games and activities will help your children become more engaged in your family adventures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors share their written work with learners, soliciting feedback and criticism to model the value of continuous improvement. This approach fosters a culture of openness and demonstrates that everyone, including the teacher, benefits from constructive feedback. The shared work can include current drafts, polished pieces, or even writing from the instructor's earlier education.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor willingness to share their work, structured opportunities for feedback, guidelines for providing constructive criticism. Requires a classroom culture that values openness and collaboration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Instructor vulnerability can be challenging. Learners may be hesitant to provide critical feedback to the instructor. Potential for superficial or insincere feedback if not managed carefully.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful in secondary and higher education to foster a collaborative learning environment

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Model continuous improvement, encourage feedback seeking, promote a growth mindset, build confidence in learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds trust and rapport between instructor and learners, demonstrates the value of feedback, enhances learners' critical analysis skills, promotes a growth mindset by showing that even experts seek improvement

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can share different types of writing based on the course content and learner interests. The level of detail and complexity of the feedback sought can be tailored to the learners' skill levels. Learners can provide feedback through various channels, such as written comments, verbal discussions, or online forums.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Feedback/Peer Review
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner participation in feedback activities, improved quality of learner feedback, changes in learners' attitudes towards receiving feedback on their own work.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Sharing instructor work and soliciting feedback helps learners feel more comfortable receiving criticism, viewing it as an opportunity for growth rather than an affront. This approach enhances learners' writing by encouraging them to take the time and care to consider and respond to reader insight.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher shares a draft of an education feature article with students, including detailed feedback from an editor, and asks students for advice on how to address the edits. A teacher shares high school, college, and graduate school essays with students, who analyze what was improved upon over time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shared reading is an interactive reading experience where an adult reads aloud while children follow along. The adult models fluent reading, uses engaging intonation, and encourages prediction and picture clue usage. Taking turns reading aloud is beneficial for older readers. It helps children connect print to story, builds tracking skills, and fosters an excitement for reading. Key components include making predictions, using picture walks, modeling fluency, asking comprehension questions, and connecting reading and writing through journaling and illustration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to age-appropriate books, a trained adult reader, and time for interactive reading sessions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective if the adult reader is not engaging or lacks strong reading fluency. Some children may require additional, individualized support to fully benefit from the activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Beginning and seasoned readers in preschool through early elementary school, including children who benefit from modeling and explicit instruction.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, build print awareness, model fluent reading, enhance prediction skills, and foster a love of reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a structured, engaging way to develop literacy skills. It is especially beneficial for building confidence, expanding vocabulary, and improving comprehension. This approach allows for immediate feedback and correction, making it easier for children to learn and retain new information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by selecting books that match the child's interests and reading level. Scaffolding can be provided through targeted questioning and support with picture walks and predictions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess through observation of child's engagement and participation. Monitor comprehension through questioning and analysis of predictions. Evaluate improvement in fluency through oral reading assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that shared reading enhances literacy skills and comprehension. Studies show the importance of parent involvement and specific literacy-building strategies for pre-literacy development. (See Roberts, Jurgens, & Burchinal, M., 2005, and Phillips et al., 2008).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A parent points to each word while reading a picture book with their child. A teacher models fluency and asks comprehension questions after reading aloud to the class. A child dictates a sentence related to the story, which the parent writes down, connecting reading and writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shared reflection involves creating a classroom culture where each student is recognized as being on an individual path of improvement—and, no student has reached the end of the path, because there is no end. It involves students sharing their reflections on their academic work, and collectively supporting each other. By sharing their achievements, students help those who struggled with that particular task, and by sharing their weak spots they troubleshoot as they work through a problem set or have a peer edit a rough draft.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom culture of trust and support, structured opportunities for sharing reflections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure that students feel comfortable sharing their weaknesses.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who are hesitant to share their weaknesses or ask for help

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a supportive learning environment, promote peer learning, build empathy, encourage collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a culture of collective support, allows students to advise and seek help from their peers, promotes empathy and understanding. Electronic tools make reflections easy to access and share.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can index, search, and organize material by theme. Anonymous posting allows them to receive guidance and support without embarrassment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Teaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student participation in discussions, evidence of peer support, and a positive classroom climate.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that peer learning improves student understanding and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher facilitates a class discussion where students share their reflections on a recent project, offering advice and support to one another.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shared writing involves a teacher and students collaboratively composing a text, with the teacher acting as a scribe. The teacher records student-generated ideas and then guides them to revise and refine the writing. This process helps learners internalize concepts and improve their communication skills through group interaction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Chart paper, pens (different colors for revisions), a student-generated word bank, and a teacher to guide and scribe the writing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires strong facilitation skills to manage diverse contributions and guide revisions effectively. May be time-consuming and require multiple sessions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for elementary and middle school levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Internalize concepts, improve communication skills, extend mathematical thinking, and promote group interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students internalize concepts, promotes communication skills, extends mathematical thinking, and fosters group interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows for varied contributions and perspectives from all students, making the writing reflective of the collective understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Revision

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality of the final shared writing, looking for accurate and detailed explanations of concepts. Observe student engagement and participation during the collaborative process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances internalization of concepts, improves communication skills, and promotes collaborative learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A third-grade teacher used shared writing to review a geometry unit. Students generated a word bank, composed sentences, and then revised them to improve word choice and include attributes of 3-D shapes.

docs.title: Sharing and Discussion of Independent Reading
Description
docs.text: After independent reading, gather students to talk about their books through various activities such as book clubs or creating commercials to interest others. These activities foster engagement and allow students to share their reading experiences. When possible, allow students to take books home to encourage reading outside of class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time for sharing sessions, materials for creating commercials or other activities, and permission for students to take books home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires structured activities to be effective. Some students may be hesitant to share their reading experiences. Requires careful planning and management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Foster engagement, encourage sharing, and promote a love of reading.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities for students to share their reading experiences, fosters a sense of community, and encourages reading outside of class.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of sharing activities to cater to different learning styles and preferences. Allow students to choose the books they want to share.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in sharing sessions. Collect feedback from students on their reading experiences. Monitor the number of books students take home and read.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fosters engagement, encourages sharing, promotes a love of reading, and supports reading outside of class.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Creating shoeless learning spaces where children often learn with shoes off, perhaps because it reminds them of home and creates a relaxed learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Comfortable seating options such as bean bag chairs, cushions, and rugs. A designated space for reading and relaxation. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may find it difficult to focus in a relaxed environment. Requires clear expectations and guidelines for appropriate behavior.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase comfort, reduce stress, promote relaxation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes relaxation and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred seating arrangement. Provide a variety of comfortable seating options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Create a relaxed learning environment
  • Promote a sense of home

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that creating comfortable learning environments can reduce stress and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are given a sentence from the reading and engage in a conversation with a partner about the sentence. A rule is set that they cannot use more than three words each time it is their turn to speak. This activity encourages concise communication, critical thinking, and collaborative engagement with the text's content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pre-selected sentences from the reading and clear explanation of the three-word limit rule.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find the word limit restrictive. The effectiveness depends on the relevance and clarity of the chosen sentence.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage concise communication, critical thinking, and collaborative engagement with the text’s content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active participation, encourages concise expression, and activates prior knowledge through focused discussion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentences can be selected to match different proficiency levels. The three-word limit can be adjusted based on the challenge level desired.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the creativity and depth of the conversations. Collect feedback on how well the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances engagement, promotes concise communication skills, and activates prior knowledge in a focused way.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about artificial intelligence, the sentence 'AI is transformative' is given to pairs to discuss, each using a maximum of three words per turn.

docs.title: Show and Tell for Multimodal Composition
Description
docs.text: Devoting a few minutes each week for learners to show the effects of different multimodal combinations or tell about their multimodal composition process creates a space akin to an author’s chair in writing workshops. Learners explain their design decisions and receive constructive feedback from their peers. These learner-led discussions generate concrete examples of the various processes that can be used for multimodal composition.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for show and tell sessions. Needs a structured format for learners to present their work and receive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are hesitant to share their work or provide feedback. Learners may need support in providing constructive feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners involved in multimodal composition, particularly those who benefit from peer interaction and feedback.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage learners to reflect on and articulate their design decisions. Provide constructive feedback to peers. Generate concrete examples of multimodal composition processes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes metacognition and self-reflection. Enhances peer learning and collaboration. Provides opportunities for authentic communication and feedback.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by allowing learners to choose the multimodal combinations they want to showcase. Feedback protocols can be customized to meet the needs of different learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and specificity of learner reflections on their design decisions. Assess the quality and relevance of peer feedback. Evaluate the extent to which learners incorporate feedback into their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that learner-led discussions generate concrete examples of the various processes that can be used for multimodal composition, leading to more informed design choices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Setting aside time each week for learners to present their multimodal combinations and explain their design decisions. Providing structured feedback protocols for peer review.

docs.title: Show and Tell for Multimodal Design
Description
docs.text: Devoting time each week for students to show the effects of different multimodal combinations or tell about their multimodal composition process. Similar to an author’s chair in writing workshop, students explain their design decisions and receive constructive feedback from their peers. These student-led discussions generate concrete examples of the various processes used for multimodal composition.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated time for show and tell, opportunities for peer feedback, a structured format for sharing and discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful facilitation to ensure constructive feedback. Relies on active participation and engagement from all students. Some students may need additional support to articulate their design decisions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students learning multimodal composition

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance communication skills, generate concrete examples of multimodal processes, provide constructive feedback, promote metacognitive awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters communication skills, provides concrete examples of multimodal processes, promotes peer learning, and encourages metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different grade levels and skill levels. Students can share examples and processes based on their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the quality of student explanations and feedback. Analyze the depth of metacognitive reflection. Assess the extent to which students apply the feedback in their own compositions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved communication skills, enhanced understanding of multimodal processes, and increased metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use slides or the board to provide another way for learners to get the information or directions. This provides reinforcement, but also allows time for students to catch up if they missed something in the spoken lecture.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers should be able to create slides or write clearly on the board to enhance comprehension and avoid cognitive overload.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Visuals need to be high quality. This also depends on whether students are self-aware enough to notice that they missed something in the spoken lecture.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides multiple exposures to key concepts through the permanent visual. Students can take their time to grasp information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide graphics that are as clear as possible and match the learning goals. Also allow students to provide input into the types of visuals that best support their learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe how frequently students rely on this strategy to fill in learning gaps. Talk to students and see if they feel supported.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that clear presentation can help support learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of presenting visually in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Presenting lectures, providing written instructions for tasks. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Small details, such as wall displays are important. For example, signage in the classroom should try to stay away from the negative. Lists of rules with DO NOT drink, eat or talk, can send a bad message. Instead, signs might include positive reinforcement. In addition, student displays can include a description of the thought process behind the work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of signage options such as posters, banners, and bulletin boards. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the signage.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, increase motivation, enhance self-worth

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes communication and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred signage options. Provide a variety of signage options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more fun.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that positive signage and displays can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Silent Countdown is a technique where the teacher uses a visual countdown (e.g., with fingers) to signal the students to become quiet and attentive. This method often involves a minimally invasive hand gesture, such as raising fingers to indicate the number of seconds remaining until silence is expected. The countdown provides a clear, non-verbal cue that helps students understand the expectation for quiet behavior and allows them time to comply.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be consistent and clear in their expectations. Students need to understand the meaning of the countdown signal.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lose its effectiveness if overused or if students become desensitized to the signal. Some students may require additional support or reminders.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Quickly gain student attention, promote a calm and focused environment, improve student compliance, provide a clear non-verbal cue

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and non-verbal cue, allows students time to comply, minimizes disruption, can be used discreetly

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the countdown time based on the needs of the class. Use different hand gestures or visual aids to suit different students and situations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the time it takes for students to become quiet after the countdown begins. Observe student compliance and engagement in the classroom.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced classroom management: Quickly gains student attention and promotes a calm environment. Improved student compliance: Provides a clear and non-verbal cue that students can easily follow. Increased student engagement: Allows the teacher to quickly regain focus and continue with the lesson.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A middle school teacher raises five fingers, then lowers one finger at a time, silently counting down from five to one. As the fingers are lowered, students are expected to become progressively quieter and more attentive. By the time the teacher reaches one finger, the classroom should be completely silent.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A silent game incentive uses a gamified approach to encourage students to quiet down after an activity. For instance, students are given a short time frame (e.g., "Silent 20") to return to their seats and be completely quiet. If they succeed within the time limit, they advance on a game board, such as a facsimile of "Game of Life," and earn a reward (e.g., a popcorn party) upon reaching the end. This technique leverages competition and reward to motivate quiet behavior.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Game board or tracking system, clear explanation of rules and rewards, consistent implementation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not appeal to all students, can create competition or anxiety, requires consistent tracking and reward delivery.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Late elementary and middle school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote quiet transitions, encourage teamwork, provide positive reinforcement for desired behaviors

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Gamified approach increases motivation, encourages teamwork, provides clear goals and rewards.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Game themes and rewards can be tailored to student interests. Time limits can be adjusted based on student capabilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the speed and effectiveness of students returning to quiet. Track progress on the game board and reward distribution.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Silent game incentives can improve classroom management by leveraging competition and reward to encourage quiet transitions and positive behavior.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Start with simple examples when introducing a concept, then progress to more complex ones later. If a learner only sees simple instances of a concept, they will be less likely to classify the more difficult instances, causing under-generalization.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful sequencing of examples from simple to complex. Requires an understanding of the concept's varying levels of complexity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant planning to sequence examples effectively. Can be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly when concepts have varying levels of complexity

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote comprehensive understanding of a concept, avoid under-generalization

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds confidence by starting with easier examples. Gradually increases cognitive load, leading to a more nuanced understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the difficulty level of examples based on learner progress and prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to classify both simple and complex instances of the concept correctly.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that progressing from simple to complex examples allows learners to classify instances of concepts at varying difficulty levels.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A radiologist learning to identify bone fractures starts with obvious cases where fragments are completely separated before moving to fractures where fragments are partially joined.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Ensure formulations are short, easy to understand, and precise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful consideration of language and phrasing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Over-simplification may omit necessary details.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those with low English proficiency or learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance clarity and understanding of instructions for learners.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load, improves comprehension, and minimizes confusion.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt language complexity and sentence structure based on learners' proficiency levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner comprehension and task completion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and reduced frustration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of saying, 'Please retrieve your textbooks and turn to page 57,' say, 'Get your books. Open to page 57.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Eliminate the 0 to 100 scale as it disproportionately punishes missed assignments. Simpler scales, such as a 0-4 scale, allow for a clear delineation between levels of performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Adoption of simpler grading scales

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires changing existing grading systems

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce punishment for missed assignments, simplify grading process, ensure clear performance delineation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces impact of missed assignments, simplifies grading

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Easier for students to understand performance levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Distribution of grades, student understanding

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Simpler scales allow for a clear delineation between levels of performance without overly dramatic consequences for a single missed assignment or instance of poor performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Adopting a 0-4 grading scale

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Simulation learning engages learners in active learning experiences where they learn from each other, not just from the instructor. Simulations are simplified versions of reality that allow learners to evaluate actions and carry them out consistently, mirroring real-life situations without the same consequences. This fosters autonomy, social interaction, and problem-solving skills. Effective simulations include preparation, active student participation, and post-simulation debriefing to connect the experience to course goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires intensive pre-simulation lesson preparation, including aligning the simulation with course goals, reviewing supporting materials, and conducting a trial run. Active student participation is crucial, with each student assuming a role. Sufficient time must be allocated for post-simulation debriefing to ensure students reflect on and discuss what they learned.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Simulations can be resource-intensive to prepare. Students may get carried away or not be adequately prepared, requiring instructors to redirect them. Some students may not prefer experiential learning. Simulations may not always align perfectly with course goals if not carefully designed.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12, higher education, and professional development programs across various disciplines, including business, social sciences, healthcare, and education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Challenge misconceptions, promote critical thinking, encourage self-directed learning, foster deeper understanding of subject matter, develop empathy, and emphasize abstract concepts over factual information

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances higher-order learning and problem-solving skills by providing hands-on experience. Allows for safe exploration of consequences without real-world risks. Promotes engagement and motivation through active participation. Fosters empathy and understanding of complex systems. Increases long-term retention of information by connecting theory to practice.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Simulations can be adapted to suit different learning objectives, subject areas, and learner levels. Complexity and roles can be adjusted. Simulations can be designed for face-to-face or online environments. Can be integrated with other pedagogies, such as cooperative learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Scenario
  • Application of Knowledge
  • Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and participation during the simulation. Assess the depth of reflection and discussion during the debriefing. Evaluate student understanding of course goals and alignment with the simulation. Gather feedback on the simulation's effectiveness from students.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows simulations promote critical thinking, self-directed learning, and deeper understanding of subject matter. Effective at emphasizing abstract concepts and engendering empathy. Experiential learning enhances competence as practitioners. (References: McClintock, 2000; Kreber, 2001; Hakeem, 2001; Rocha, 2000; Jessup, 2001).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Simulations use electronic or software-based activities to simulate a real-world situation to which a learner must react. Learners have the opportunity to practice certain skills and make mistakes in a safe environment. Simulation-based training is popular in the healthcare and aviation industries, however, with the advancement of technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Virtual Reality (VR), simulation-based training is being adopted across all types of industries.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A computer or other device to run the simulation, software to create the simulation, facilitator to guide the learning process

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Simulations can be expensive to create and run, and success depends on the realism of the simulation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All employee levels in corporate training settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice certain skills, make mistakes in a safe environment, understand the consequences of different decisions.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides an opportunity to practice certain skills and make mistakes in a safe environment, allows learners to understand the consequences of different decisions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Simulations can be tailored to reflect the learner's own working environment.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Problem Scenario
  • Decision-Making

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner decisions in the simulation, provide feedback on learner decisions, and assess learner understanding of the consequences of different decisions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides an opportunity to practice certain skills and make mistakes in a safe environment, allows learners to understand the consequences of different decisions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students engage with simulations designed to provide hands-on experience with real-world scenarios or abstract concepts. These simulations are combined with a structured activity to ensure active learning and application of the concepts. Simulations allow students to experiment and learn from their mistakes in a safe and controlled environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to simulations (physical or virtual), design of structured activities, and facilitation of simulation experiences.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of content or learners. Requires careful alignment of simulations and learning objectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from hands-on learning and real-world applications.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide authentic learning experiences, promote active learning, facilitate understanding and application of complex concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a hands-on and interactive approach to learning, promotes critical thinking and problem-solving skills, enhances engagement and retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Simulations can be tailored to match learner interests and skill levels. Structured activities can be designed to address specific learning objectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Engagement with simulations, completion of structured activities, performance on related assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective when combined with well-designed structured activities that promote reflection and application of the simulation experiences. Can improve learner outcomes and engagement by providing authentic and interactive learning opportunities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A set of six questions designed to help evaluate the trustworthiness of a news story. These include asking who made the story, how it was made, why it was made, when it was made, what is missing, and where to go from here.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to news stories

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires critical thinking skills and attention to detail

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • General audience

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate news stories for credibility

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to evaluating news stories

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different age groups and levels of expertise

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Ability to answer questions about the credibility of a news story

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps readers evaluate news stories for trustworthiness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Used by the Newseum to help teachers and students evaluate news stories

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Six Thinking Hats technique is a parallel thinking process that separates thinking into six clear functions and roles, each identified with a colored symbolic 'thinking hat.' By mentally wearing and switching 'hats,' participants can easily focus or redirect thoughts, the conversation, or the meeting.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Training on the Six Thinking Hats technique, a space for group discussions, and a facilitator to guide the process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort to learn and implement effectively, and may not be suitable for all types of teams or organizations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teams and organizations seeking to enhance their collaboration, communication, and problem-solving skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Maximize productive collaboration, improve communication, stimulate innovation, enhance problem-solving

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for thinking, encourages consideration of multiple perspectives, reduces conflict, and stimulates innovation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The technique can be applied to a wide range of issues, problems, decisions, and opportunities, and can be used in both individual and group settings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Team-Based Inquiry
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving
  • Decision-Making
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track changes in team productivity, communication, and problem-solving effectiveness. Measure the number of ideas generated and the quality of decisions made.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies have shown that the Six Thinking Hats technique can improve team collaboration, communication, and problem-solving skills, leading to increased productivity and innovation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A product development team uses the Six Thinking Hats technique to generate new ideas for a product. A management team uses the technique to evaluate a potential investment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Skimming involves reviewing a text quickly, focusing on headings, captions, and highlighted information, to gain familiarity with the material before reading it thoroughly. Younger students might take a "picture walk" through the reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Reading materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if the skimming is not focused or if the student does not have the background knowledge necessary to understand the material.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly students who struggle with reading comprehension.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To make students familiar with the material before they read it more thoroughly, to improve reading comprehension.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a preview of the text and highlights key points, making it easier for students to understand the material when they read it more thoroughly.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The teacher can select the headings, captions, and highlighted information that are most relevant to the lesson.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved reading comprehension, demonstrated understanding of the key points in the text.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Skimming can make students familiar with the material before they read it more thoroughly, which can improve reading comprehension.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Make up a movement that comes in 2, 3, or more parts. Whisper the first parts, and call out the final move loudly. Example: Windmills. Whisper “1” and touch your right hand to your left foot. Whisper “2” and touch your left hand to your right foot. Call out “3” and do a jumping jack! Continue counting like this up to 30, calling out the multiples of 3 and whispering the numbers in between.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Open space where students can move freely.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for students with physical limitations. Can be difficult for students who struggle with skip counting.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce skip counting, enhance kinesthetic learning, improve rhythm and coordination, build pattern recognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging way to practice skip counting and combine math with movement. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust complexity of skip counting pattern based on student skill level. Allow students to create their own patterns.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to coordinate the movement with the skip counting pattern. Assess the accurate of the count.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can help reinforce skip counting skills through active engagement and kinesthetic learning. Supports active participation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Skip counting by 5s, students tap their shoulders four times whispering each time, and then do a jumping jack and call out the multiple of 5.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Small group instruction involves a teacher working with a small number of students on a specific skill or concept. It allows for targeted support and individualized attention, helping to address the unique needs of each learner. This approach enables teachers to provide instructional scaffolds, engage learners more effectively, and offer strategic coaching.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Small group of students, focused instructional materials, and a teacher or facilitator with expertise in the target skill or concept.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to ensure alignment with overall learning objectives. May be challenging to manage if students have significantly different skill levels.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for students needing additional support or those with diverse learning needs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide targeted support, address individual needs, scaffold learning, and improve skill mastery.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for personalized attention, enables targeted intervention, provides opportunities for immediate feedback, and facilitates deeper engagement with the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Content, pace, and instructional strategies can be tailored to meet the specific needs of the students in the group. Scaffolding can be adjusted based on individual progress.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation, monitor progress on targeted skills, and collect work samples to assess mastery.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that strategic coaching and small group instruction are key elements that distinguish high-achieving classrooms from those with moderate or low performances.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: SMART goal setting ensures goals are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-Specific. This involves setting clear, well-defined goals with measurable elements like dates and amounts, ensuring they align with resources and skills, and setting realistic deadlines to create urgency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires understanding of the SMART criteria and the ability to critically evaluate goals against these criteria.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overemphasis on structure can sometimes stifle creativity. Ensuring goals are truly relevant and aligned with broader objectives requires careful consideration.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable to anyone seeking structured, effective goal setting, including students, professionals, and teams.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure goals are clear, achievable, and aligned with overall objectives, and improve motivation and accountability.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for goal setting, ensuring each goal is well-defined, achievable, and relevant. This clarity boosts motivation and commitment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can use SMART criteria to tailor goals to their specific contexts and needs, adjusting timelines and relevance to fit their circumstances.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Progress can be measured by tracking the completion of specific, measurable components of each goal within the set timeframe.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • SMART goals have been shown to increase productivity and achievement by providing a clear roadmap and fostering accountability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Setting a goal to increase sales by 10% (Specific, Measurable) within the next quarter (Time-Specific), based on available resources (Attainable) and aligned with the company's growth strategy (Relevant).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A game where children make a train of connecting cubes, snap the train into two parts, hide one part behind their back, and show the remaining cubes. The other children work out the full number combination.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Connecting cubes

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to addition facts

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primary school children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop addition fact fluency

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Hands-on activity, promotes collaboration, reinforces addition facts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Number of cubes can be adjusted to match skill level

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's ability to quickly and accurately determine the missing number

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of addition fact fluency

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Child has 8 cubes, snaps it, puts 3 behind their back, and shows 5. Group says that three are missing and that 5 and 3 make 8.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners begin in pairs, responding to a discussion question only with a single partner. After each person has had a chance to share their ideas, the pair joins another pair, creating a group of four. Pairs share their ideas with the pair they just joined. Next, groups of four join together to form groups of eight, and so on, until the whole class is joined up in one large discussion. This structure could simply be used to share ideas on a topic, or learners could be required to reach consensus every time they join up with a new group.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a physical space where learners can form pairs and small groups, a discussion question, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming, requires careful facilitation to ensure all learners are engaged and on task, may be difficult for learners who struggle with social interaction or working in large groups.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for brainstorming, problem-solving, and decision-making activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active participation, encourage peer learning and collaboration, enhance communication skills, build consensus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation, promotes peer learning and collaboration, enhances communication skills, builds consensus, supports gradual increase in group size

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussion questions can be tailored to learners' interests and backgrounds. Learners can choose the partners they want to work with.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Consensus Discussion
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and engagement in the activity, review the quality of their responses to the discussion question, collect feedback from learners about their experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances communication skills, promotes collaboration and peer learning, builds consensus

docs.title: Description
docs.text: SOAP is an acronym that serves as a guide for teachers when selecting behaviors for students to self-monitor. Each letter represents a criterion to ensure the behavior is well-defined and suitable for the student.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the SOAP criteria and the student's behavior and abilities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The criteria require careful consideration and may not always be easy to apply, particularly for complex behaviors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers or instructors who are implementing self-monitoring strategies with students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure the selection of effective and manageable behaviors for self-monitoring.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and structured way to select appropriate behaviors, leading to more effective self-monitoring interventions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The criteria ensure that the behavior is tailored to the individual student’s needs and abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The selected behaviors should be easily observable and measurable, allowing for clear assessment of progress.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • By following the SOAP criteria, teachers can select behaviors that are more likely to lead to positive outcomes and student engagement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The SOAR method helps maximize the impact of feedback on student writing by ensuring it is Specific, Ongoing, Action-Oriented, and Reasonable. Specific feedback ties comments to particular elements of the writing (words, phrases, sentences, paragraphs) and addresses both the content (what) and the writing itself (how). Ongoing feedback is provided throughout the writing process, not just on the final product. Action-oriented feedback helps students take specific steps to improve their writing and build a growth mindset. Reasonable feedback is focused and avoids overwhelming students by selecting a specific area for feedback with each assignment and using 'Glow and Grow' comments to highlight strengths and areas for improvement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to be trained in the SOAR method, allocate time for ongoing feedback, and have access to tools for providing feedback (e.g., Google Docs, Kaizena).

docs.title: Constraints
