docs.text: • Requires significant time and effort from the teacher to provide specific and ongoing feedback. Students may become overwhelmed if feedback is not reasonable or focused.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students learning writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student writing skills, promote a growth mindset, provide actionable feedback, and enhance self-regulated learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear, actionable steps for students to improve their writing, encourages self-reflection, and fosters a growth mindset by focusing on progress and improvement rather than just error correction. It allows instructors to provide targeted feedback that is more likely to be understood and acted upon by students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adapt the focus of the feedback to meet the specific needs of students or the learning objectives of the assignment. Students can choose which area of their writing they want feedback on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvement in student writing quality over time, increased student engagement with the writing process, and positive changes in student attitudes towards writing and feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • High-quality feedback enhances student learning and engagement. Specificity ensures comments connect directly to the work. Ongoing feedback supports iterative development. Action-oriented suggestions empower students to make improvements. Reasonableness prevents overwhelming students with too much information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Social annotation is a collaborative method where learners add notes, comments, and multimedia to texts, images, and other digital content, fostering conversation and deeper understanding. Unlike traditional individual annotation, it transforms reading into a social activity where learners interact directly within the text, creating an anchored context for conversation. This approach allows students to enhance texts by sharing personal connections, asking questions, and integrating multimedia elements like images, GIFs, and videos.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to digital annotation tools such as Hypothesis, NowComment, or Diigo. A stable internet connection and devices for learners to access and annotate content. A clear understanding of the platform's features and guidelines for respectful interaction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful moderation to ensure respectful and productive discussions. May be challenging for learners unfamiliar with digital annotation tools. Dependent on reliable internet access and device availability.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for middle and high school students, as well as adult learners in higher education, who seek to improve their collaborative reading and analytical skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote deeper engagement with texts, foster collaborative learning, enhance critical thinking, facilitate peer interaction, encourage multimedia integration, develop digital literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active participation and discussion by anchoring conversations directly in the text. Facilitates the sharing of diverse perspectives and knowledge. Enhances engagement by allowing multimedia integration. Promotes critical thinking by requiring analysis and interpretation. Supports learners in developing digital literacy skills through the use of online tools.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by creating private online rooms for smaller groups, assigning specific annotation tasks, or allowing learners to choose texts that align with their interests. Teachers can also seed the text with conversation starters to guide learners' interactions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and depth of annotations to determine comprehension and critical thinking. Monitor the level of peer interaction and the diversity of perspectives shared. Assess the ability to integrate multimedia elements effectively.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced engagement: Social annotation tools promote active reading, analysis, and discussions, helping learners to engage more deeply with course materials. Knowledge construction: Supports learners in making connections between concepts, and helps them to build new knowledge together.

docs.title: Social Awareness - Model Empathy and Explain
Description
docs.text: Model empathy and explain explicitly discuss different perspectives have explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, including issues of social justice. Use current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a facilitator and a class to teach to.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may find this activity to be triggering.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve social awareness, promote expression, and improve perspective-taking skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • This strategy focuses on social awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor the conversations and lessons.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Teachers can listen and observe learners' conversations to evaluate whether or not the goal was achieved.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • This strategy relies on a building empathy with others to create social awareness. (Jones, Damon E., Mark Greenberg, and Max Crowley. "Early Social-Emotional Functioning and Public Health: The Relationship Between Kindergarten Social Competence and Future Wellness." American Journal of Public Health, 105, no. 11, 2015, 2283-2290.).

docs.title: Social Awareness Instruction with Current Events
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using current events and fictional characters to explicitly teach social awareness. Students learn to understand different perspectives, empathize with others, and discuss social issues, including social justice. This activity directly connects learning to real-world applications and enhances learner autonomy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to current events news and a teacher to facilitate discussion. Can be integrated into social studies, language arts, or advisory periods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the selected news articles and the teacher's ability to guide discussion. Some students may be sensitive to certain social issues.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social awareness, enhance empathy, improve perspective-taking skills, promote understanding of social issues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects learning to real-world events, promotes understanding of diverse perspectives, enhances empathy and social awareness, fosters critical thinking about social issues.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Current events can be selected to match students' age, interests, and cultural backgrounds. Teachers can provide background information and scaffolding to support students who are unfamiliar with social issues.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' participation in discussions, analyze their responses to questions about current events, and assess their ability to understand different perspectives and empathize with others.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports the development of social awareness, enhances empathy, and promotes understanding of social issues, fostering responsible citizenship and social justice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Socratic seminars are formal discussions based on a text, where the leader asks open-ended questions. Students listen closely to others' comments, think critically, and articulate their own thoughts and responses. Participants learn to work cooperatively and question intelligently and civilly. These seminars emphasize inquiry over information and discussion over debate, acknowledging the social nature of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a carefully selected text that invites inquiry. Requires preparation time for students to read and annotate the text. Requires a facilitator to guide the discussion with open-ended questions. A classroom environment conducive to respectful dialogue is essential.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on careful text selection and thorough preparation. Some students may struggle with open-ended questioning and discussion. Requires a skilled facilitator to maintain focus and encourage participation. May not be suitable for learners who prefer direct instruction or structured activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6-12, higher education, and adult learners who need to engage in deep textual analysis and discussion.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote critical thinking, cooperative learning, and respectful inquiry. Encourage students to listen actively, articulate their thoughts, and respond thoughtfully to others' ideas.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters critical thinking and civil discourse. Encourages active listening and collaborative learning. Connects learning to real-world experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Text selection can be tailored to learner interests and reading levels. Question prompts can be adjusted to accommodate varying levels of comprehension and analytical skills. Student roles can be differentiated to support diverse learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Question Formulation
  • Knowledge-Building Discourse
  • Peer Interaction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the extent to which students engage in text-centered talk. Collect reflective writing where students describe their participation and set goals for future seminars. Evaluate the depth and thoughtfulness of student responses and interactions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Socratic seminars enhance critical thinking, communication, and collaboration skills. They promote a deeper understanding of texts and foster a communal spirit of inquiry. Research supports the effectiveness of Socratic seminars in promoting student engagement and intellectual growth.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In an English class, students use a Socratic seminar to explore themes in a novel. In a social studies class, students analyze contrasting primary documents. In a science class, students discuss a controversial approach to an ongoing scientific problem. Source: ReadWriteThink Strategy Guide.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors should encourage learners to provide feedback on their teaching. By actively soliciting student feedback, instructors can gain insights into their teaching effectiveness, identify areas for improvement, and create a more engaging and supportive learning environment. If we are open to it, we will quickly learn a few things about ourselves as educators. Remember that feedback goes both ways and as teachers it is wise to never stop improving and honing our skills as teachers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A supportive environment, clear channels for providing feedback, willingness to listen and act on feedback

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to receive negative feedback, requires a commitment to continuous improvement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All instructors, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve teaching effectiveness, create a more engaging learning environment, foster collaboration, build positive relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides valuable insights, promotes reflection, enhances communication, builds trust

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The feedback can be tailored to the individual instructor and their specific teaching context.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze student feedback. Observe changes in teaching practices. Monitor the effectiveness of the changes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Insights into the learning environement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor provides an anonymous survey for students to provide feedback on the course. A professor holds a focus group with students to discuss their experiences in the class.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using songs and rhymes to memorize information is a mnemonic technique that leverages rhythm and melody to enhance recall. Information is set to a familiar tune or rhyme, making it easier to remember and recall. This method is effective for all ages.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ability to create or adapt songs and rhymes. A clear understanding of the information to be remembered.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of information. The song or rhyme must be easily remembered itself.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for auditory learners and young children.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory recall by associating information with music and rhythm.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes learning fun and engaging. Leverages the brain's natural affinity for music and rhythm to enhance memory.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create their own songs or rhymes based on their favorite tunes or rhythms.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the number of items recalled correctly after learning a song or rhyme. Monitor the ease with which learners can generate and remember their own songs and rhymes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that songs and rhymes can improve memory and well-being, especially in people with dementia (Thompson et al., 2021).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Learning the alphabet using the alphabet song. Memorizing a foreign language vocabulary by setting it to a tune (Ludke et al., 2013).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Songwriting involves students creating their own verses or entire songs to enhance language development, phonemic awareness, and vocabulary. This method engages students in identifying letter sounds, brainstorming words, and structuring verses that integrate new language concepts. The activity culminates in illustrating the song verses, reinforcing learning through multisensory engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Chart paper, drawing materials, markers, paper, and pencils. Preparation involves ensuring access to materials and pre-teaching any needed technological skills for illustration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming to implement fully. Effectiveness depends on clear instructions and active participation. May require technological support for digital illustration.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary grades (K-2), English language learners, and learners who benefit from creative and multisensory activities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary skills, improve phonemic awareness, develop songwriting abilities, promote creative expression, and reinforce language concepts through multisensory engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances learning through a combination of auditory, visual, and kinesthetic activities. Increases motivation and engagement by allowing students to express creativity. Reinforces letter-sound correspondence and vocabulary in a meaningful context.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose different letters or topics for their verses, providing choice and relevance. Varying complexity can be accommodated by having younger students focus on identifying sounds, while older students create complete verses.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate student illustrations and verses for accuracy and creativity. Track letter sounds and vocabulary words used correctly. Observe engagement and participation during songwriting and illustration activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combining songwriting with art enhances memory retention and creative expression. Multisensory activities are effective for diverse learners. Creative integration boosts engagement and improves learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Multiple examples are provided using different base songs. For example, one example provides new verses to the tune of, Mary Had a Little Lamb.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sound-blocking devices, such as noise-reducing headphones or earmuffs, can help children with auditory sensitivities manage sensory input by reducing background noise. These devices lower the overall decibel rate of background noise, allowing children to focus and process information more effectively. They can be used in various settings, including school cafeterias, malls, concerts, and noisy streets.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Noise-reducing headphones or earmuffs.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some children may find headphones uncomfortable or may resist wearing them. The effectiveness of noise reduction may vary depending on the device and the environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children with auditory sensitivities, autism, or auditory processing disorder

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce auditory overstimulation, improve focus and concentration, promote self-regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces background noise, allowing children to better process information and focus on tasks. Provides a sense of control over the auditory environment, reducing anxiety and promoting self-regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different types of headphones and earmuffs are available to suit individual preferences and needs. Some offer adjustable levels of noise reduction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child's behavior and focus levels when using sound-blocking devices in noisy environments. Monitor the child's self-regulation and ability to manage auditory input.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research and anecdotal evidence suggest that sound-blocking devices can improve focus and reduce anxiety in children with auditory sensitivities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sound walls help educators reinforce the importance of explicitly teaching the skills of letter-sound correspondence and support key aspects of learning to read that are backed by the science of reading, including phonemic awareness (the ability to isolate and manipulate the smallest units of sounds within spoken language) and phonics (the ability to make the connection between the sounds of spoken language and the printed letters and words on a page).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Space for a sound wall, materials for creating the wall, and activities for reinforcing letter-sound correspondence.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and implementation. May be challenging to create and maintain. Requires explicit instruction to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-5 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce letter-sound correspondence, support phonemic awareness and phonics skills, and improve reading accuracy and fluency.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual and auditory reference for letter-sound relationships, supports explicit phonics instruction, and enhances reading accuracy and fluency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Create sound walls that cater to different learning styles and needs, such as visual, auditory, and kinesthetic. Use a variety of activities to reinforce letter-sound correspondence.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student use of the sound wall. Track student progress in phonemic awareness and phonics skills. Monitor reading accuracy and fluency improvements.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reinforces letter-sound correspondence, supports phonemic awareness and phonics skills, and improves reading accuracy and fluency.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Breaking up learning or work into short chunks of time interspersed with activity breaks leverages the 'spacing effect,' a well-replicated phenomenon in psychology. This method enhances memory retention by giving the brain time to process information and retrieve it later. Activity breaks during these intervals can include physical movement or other engaging tasks, optimizing cognitive function and creativity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A structured schedule that incorporates short intervals of focused learning or work interspersed with brief activity breaks. Minimal to no equipment needed for most breaks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning to balance learning intervals and break times effectively. Individuals may need initial guidance to understand the benefits and adapt to this method.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, including students and professionals, who need to retain complex information and maintain focus over extended periods

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memory retention, enhance cognitive processing, boost creativity, and prevent mental fatigue

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Optimizes cognitive function by allowing time for information processing and retrieval. Enhances memory retention and prevents mental fatigue through strategic breaks.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Breaks can be tailored to individual preferences, including physical activities, mindfulness exercises, or creative tasks. Learning intervals can be adjusted based on cognitive load and subject matter.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved recall and retention of information, enhanced focus and attention, increased creativity, and reduced mental fatigue.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows the 'spacing effect' enhances memory retention. Studies indicate that breaks can improve creative insight and problem-solving.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Toddlers recalling names of novel objects better with 30-second breaks, adults finding shortcuts to math problems with 10-minute breaks, and increased focus and productivity when incorporating activity breaks into work routines.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Spaced practice involves distributing learning sessions over time, contrasting with massed practice (cramming). This technique enhances long-term retention by requiring the brain to actively recall information, creating stronger neural connections. Educators can implement this by breaking large lessons into smaller sessions spread out over several days and use retrieval practice, beginning each session with opportunities for learners to recall prior lessons. Online tools can support spaced practice by allowing personalized study schedules, sending reminders, and incorporating online flashcards with mixed content. To optimize spaced practice, there can be a maximum time allowed for learners to spend in one session, timing them out and only allowing learners to re-engage once the desired time interval has passed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires planning and scheduling of learning sessions. Access to study materials and tools. Implementation can be facilitated by online platforms that automate spacing and reminders.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial effort to set up schedules. Learners may resist the method due to its distributed nature. Requires consistent adherence to the schedule for optimal results.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs, but particularly effective for world language learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance long-term retention, improve recall, promote efficient learning, prevent overload, reinforce understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves long-term memory and retention of information. Encourages active recall and strengthens neural connections. Prevents information overload and ensures learners keep up with the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can set personalized study schedules and receive reminders. Instructors can adjust the spacing and content based on learners' skill levels and needs. Online tools can offer varied formats and difficulty levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance over time to measure retention. Compare results of spaced practice versus massed practice. Monitor learner engagement and adherence to study schedules.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research consistently shows spaced practice is superior to massed practice for long-term retention. Retrieval practice paired with spaced practice further enhances memory. Savings in relearning can occur with spaced review sessions—i.e., individuals may not be able to recall every item correctly at the start of a review session (because of forgetting), but are quicker at relearning the information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A language teacher spaces out vocabulary review over several weeks, using short, frequent quizzes to reinforce learning. An online learning platform times users out of learning content after a set time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Traditional spaces designed in the industrial revolution were designed to maximize efficiency. For the 21st century, employers tend to look for teams that work organically in collaborative groups to solve problems. It would make sense to structure classrooms to reflect the needs of our global economy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of activity options such as art supplies, games, and toys. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the playful spaces.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve creativity, improve problem solving skills, enhance collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes creativity and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred activities. Provide a variety of playful activity options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more fun.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that playful spaces can increase engagement, improve creativity, and enhance collaboration. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Activities designed to improve spacing between letters and words, which is crucial for overall legibility. These activities involve using spacing tools, visual cues, and puzzles to promote consistent and appropriate spacing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Spacing tools (e.g., craft sticks, clothespins), visual cues, spacing puzzles, and structured practice sessions. Can be implemented in classrooms or at home.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not address underlying issues such as visual perception difficulties or fine motor weakness. Relies on consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grades, particularly useful for students who struggle with inconsistent or inadequate spacing.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spacing between letters and words, enhancing overall legibility.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes legibility by improving spacing consistency. Addresses visual perceptual skills related to spatial awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be tailored to individual spacing difficulties or learning styles. Spacing tools and visual cues support consistent spacing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in spacing consistency and legibility. Assess spatial awareness during writing tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved spacing skills, leading to more legible and organized handwriting. Enhanced visual perceptual skills and spatial awareness.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students formulate questions and investigate topics they are curious about or consider important. This method encourages inquiry and investment in the learning process by allowing students to drive their own learning, and it contrasts with traditional, teacher-directed instruction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creating a classroom environment that values student questions and exploration. Demands flexibility in curriculum planning to accommodate student interests.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and resources to support diverse student interests. Can be challenging to manage if student questions are misaligned with curriculum goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners, particularly beneficial for students of color who may experience disempowerment in traditional educational settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement and motivation, foster ownership of learning, encourage critical thinking, address student interests and needs.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students by valuing their curiosity and questions. Liberates students by allowing them to determine their own learning paths. Fosters engagement by addressing topics that are personally meaningful to students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to choose topics and questions that align with their interests and cultural backgrounds. Adaptable to various subjects and learning levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Inquiry and Research

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the depth and quality of student-generated questions. Assess student engagement and participation in inquiry-based activities. Review student projects and presentations for evidence of learning and understanding.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Projects driven by student-generated questions lead to increased engagement and investment in the inquiry process, helping to create more equitable learning environments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students identifying questions they want to answer related to social justice issues in their community. Learners formulating research questions about environmental sustainability to guide their project-based learning activities.

docs.title: Speak the Future, Design the Future (Changing the Discourse)
Description
docs.text: This principle emphasizes that the language used to discuss education shapes the limits of our imagination. It encourages critiquing and changing the way we talk and write about learning to create more equitable schools. It contrasts 'Discourse I' (DI), which maintains the status quo, with 'Discourse II' (DII), which is about liberation and transformation. For example, it highlights the difference between the term 'dropout' (DI), which blames students for failing, and 'pushout' (DII), which shifts the problem to school structures that alienate students. The principle involves using this framework to check the language and ideas generated during the design process, ensuring that they promote equity and challenge oppressive systems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to challenge existing norms and assumptions, as well as resources for facilitating discussions about language and power.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be challenging to implement if stakeholders are resistant to changing their language or beliefs. Requires careful facilitation to ensure that discussions are productive and respectful.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators and school teams seeking to create more equitable and transformative learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Transform the language used in education, challenge existing power structures, promote equity, and foster liberation and transformation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes critical thinking about language and its impact, challenges existing power structures, and fosters a more equitable and transformative learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific examples of DI and DII language can be tailored to the context and needs of the school and students.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Question Formulation
  • Discussion Prompt

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze the language used in school policies, communications, and curriculum materials, track changes in the use of DI and DII language, and assess the impact of these changes on student outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A more equitable and transformative learning environment, increased student engagement, and improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • CityBridge School Design Fellows use this discourse framework to talk about what they see and what sort of language they hear from school leaders. They also use it to check the language and ideas that educators generate during the design process. For example, at a gathering of Fellows in January 2020, the lens of DI and DII was used to facilitate an “equity pause” during a brainstorming session, challenging teams to sort their ideas along a spectrum of DI to DII.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves providing targeted feedback on student writing that is directly tied to specific words, phrases, sentences, or paragraphs. It focuses on both the 'what' (content such as evidence, claims, and analysis) and the 'how' (writing elements such as organization, rhetorical strategies, style, voice, and conventions). Teachers can focus on the content if they are less comfortable assessing writing mechanics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to read student writing closely and provide specific comments. Digital tools like Kaizena can facilitate voice note feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time if not focused. Vague feedback can be ineffective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education students at all levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student writing by guiding them to enhance content, organization, and writing mechanics.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students understand exactly what needs improvement in their writing, guiding them in content and mechanics. Allows teachers to focus on areas they are most comfortable assessing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adapt the focus of the feedback based on the assignment or the student's individual needs. Students can also ask for specific feedback on areas they are working on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the specificity of feedback provided and monitor improvements in student writing over time. Observe student's ability to apply feedback to future writing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Specific feedback is critical to student learning by guiding them to improve both the content and mechanics of their writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Design questions with a specific goal in mind, such as identifying grabbers or understanding essay structure. This helps students pinpoint why a passage made them feel a certain way. Ask "why?"

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material. Preparation of targeted questions. Time for analysis and discussion in class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be overly directive. Students may miss other important elements of the text. Requires careful planning to ensure that questions are relevant and engaging.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for developing specific writing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of writing techniques, enhance ability to analyze and interpret text, develop targeted questioning skills, focus attention on specific elements of the text

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to analyzing mentor texts. Helps students connect specific techniques to their overall effect. Increases efficiency by focusing attention on key elements.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to specific student needs and learning goals. Students can be given opportunities to generate their own questions. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student responses to questions. Participation in discussions. Analysis of student writing samples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that targeted questioning improves understanding and application of specific writing techniques.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher asks students to identify the 'grabber' in a mentor text and explain why it is effective. Students work in groups to analyze the structure of an essay, identifying the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Students generate their own questions about a mentor text, focusing on a specific writing technique.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing specific guidance on what to look for in a text, naming sentences or words whenever possible, helps students learn from the text. The teacher should point out specific examples and explain their significance, rather than leaving students to learn on their own. Questions with quotes or line numbers can be more accessible.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Appropriate reading material. Preparation of specific examples and explanations. Time for analysis and discussion in class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be overly directive. Students may become too reliant on teacher guidance. Requires careful planning and implementation to avoid spoon-feeding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for struggling learners and those new to literary analysis

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of writing techniques, enhance ability to analyze and interpret text, develop close reading skills, reduce cognitive load for struggling learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear and direct guidance. Reduces cognitive load by focusing attention on specific elements of the text. Increases confidence in analyzing complex texts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Specific techniques can be tailored to student needs and interests. Examples can be chosen from a variety of texts and genres. Scaffolding can be provided for struggling learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student participation in discussions. Analysis of student writing samples. Reading comprehension quizzes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that explicit instruction in specific techniques improves reading comprehension and analytical skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher points out an example of metaphor in a poem and explains its effect. Students work in groups to identify examples of alliteration in a passage. Teacher provides sentence stems to help students analyze the author's use of imagery.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Speech-to-text technology converts spoken language into written text, benefiting individuals with dyslexia, dysgraphia, or physical disabilities by enabling them to express themselves in writing without the barriers of spelling, handwriting, or typing. This technology has evolved significantly since its inception in 1936. The workflow involves speaking into a device (computer, tablet, or smartphone) equipped with speech recognition software, which then transcribes the spoken words into text. Users may need to correct errors and add punctuation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A device (computer, tablet, or smartphone) with a microphone and speech recognition software or app. A quiet environment is recommended to minimize background noise and improve accuracy. Training may be required to familiarize users with the software and optimize performance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Accuracy can be affected by background noise, accents, and unclear speech. Some speech recognition software may struggle with complex vocabulary or grammatical structures. Editing and proofreading are often necessary to correct errors and add punctuation. There may be a learning curve associated with mastering the software and speaking clearly.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students and adults with dyslexia, dysgraphia, physical disabilities, or anyone who struggles with typing or handwriting

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable students with dyslexia and dysgraphia to express themselves in writing, improve writing speed and fluency, enhance access to digital content, support searching the internet

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces the cognitive load associated with writing, allowing individuals to focus on content and ideas rather than the mechanics of writing. Provides an alternative means of written expression for those with physical limitations. Builds confidence and independence by enabling individuals to create written content more easily.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can choose from various speech recognition software options and adjust settings like language, accent, and speed. They can also train the software to recognize their voice patterns for improved accuracy. The technology supports diverse devices and platforms, including computers, tablets, and smartphones.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure writing speed and fluency with and without speech recognition software. Evaluate the accuracy of transcriptions produced by the software. Gather feedback from users on their experience and perceived benefits. Track improvements in writing quality and confidence over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show speech recognition software improves writing skills for students with learning disabilities by reducing the cognitive demands of spelling and handwriting. Accuracy has increased dramatically in recent years, making this a valuable tool for improving written communication and academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Dragon Speech Recognition (Nuance), Google Docs Voice Typing, Windows Speech Recognition, Apple Dictation. Example usage includes students using speech-to-text to write essays, complete assignments, search the internet, and communicate with others.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Speed chatting is a pre-reading activity where learners form two rows facing each other and ask simple questions related to the reading topic. They have a limited time (e.g., 60 seconds) to discuss each question with their partner before one row rotates, creating new pairs. This process is repeated several times to encourage quick, engaging interactions and activate prior knowledge about the topic.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a clear space for learners to form rows and pre-prepared simple questions related to the reading topic.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners who are shy or have difficulty speaking under time pressure. The effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the questions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activate prior knowledge, encourage quick and engaging interactions, prepare learners for the reading activity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active participation, encourages quick thinking, and activates prior knowledge efficiently. It helps learners feel more prepared and engaged with the reading material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to different proficiency levels, making it accessible for diverse learners. The number of rotations can be adjusted based on time and engagement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of engagement and participation. Collect feedback on how well the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Encourages active recall of background knowledge, enhances motivation through social interaction, and can make learners more comfortable with the topic before reading.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading an article about climate change, learners might discuss 'What are the main causes of climate change?' or 'How does climate change affect our daily lives?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing a squeeze ball or Theraputty offers a tactile outlet for students to manage frustration and agitation. These tools can help students redirect their physical energy, reducing emotional intensity and promoting self-regulation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Accessibility to squeeze balls or Theraputty, explicit instruction on their purpose and use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be distracting if not used properly. Requires clear expectations and guidance to prevent misuse.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly useful for students with ADHD or those who benefit from sensory tools.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide a physical outlet for frustration and agitation, redirect physical energy, and promote emotional self-regulation.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a discrete and accessible way to manage frustration and agitation, helping students stay focused and emotionally regulated.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer different types of sensory tools (e.g., squeeze balls with different textures or resistance) to meet individual student preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Provide Guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior for signs of reduced frustration and improved focus. Collect student feedback on the helpfulness of the sensory tools.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports emotional self-regulation, reduces physical tension, and helps students stay focused and emotionally regulated.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher provides students with Theraputty to use during independent work to help them manage frustration when encountering challenging tasks.

docs.title: Stages of Drawing and Writing Development
Description
docs.text: Children progress through stages of drawing and writing development, from random scribbling to controlled scribbling, lines and patterns, pictures of objects or people, and letter and word practice. Art and early writing skills are one and the same. Children discover the link between their hand holding the crayon and the line they made on the page, experiencing the power of cause-and-effect. As children develop better control over the muscles in their hands and fingers, their scribbles become more controlled.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires art and writing materials such as crayons, markers, and paper. Requires time for children to experiment and explore.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The timetables for each stage are approximate, and children may master these skills faster or slower.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Very young children, toddlers from 15 months to 5 years old

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand the stages of drawing and writing development. Encourage children's artistic and writing skills through experimentation and exploration.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Children learn that their movements result in lines and scribbles on the page. They develop better control over the muscles in their hands and fingers. They understand that writing is made up of lines, curves, and repeated patterns. They realize that their drawing conveys meaning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Children can progress through the stages at their own pace. Teachers can offer repeated fun experiences with a variety of art and writing materials.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe children's progress through the stages of drawing and writing development. Evaluate the complexity and control in their drawings and writings. Notice their ability to represent objects and people and use letters and words.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Art experiences help children develop independence within limits, and gives them the opportunity to represent their ideas on paper or in other formats. Creative expression lets children tap into the magic of their own imaginations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Children experiment with scribbling, make repeated marks on the page, imitate lines and curves, draw pictures of objects or people, and practice using letters and words.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The rules are simple: if the teacher gives the number 10, students stand up. Any other number, they sit down. The trick is, the teacher will say things like '7+3' and '14 -5' (pick appropriate sums and differences for your students to solve mentally). This is a great game to try to 'trick' the students by standing up or sitting down on when they should be doing the opposite. There are endless variations, for example: stand when the number is larger than 5; sit if it is 5 or below, stand when the number is even; sit when it is odd, stand if the digit 1 appears on the number; sit otherwise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An open space where students can move freely. Teacher needs to be able to call out math problems.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may get confused by the 'trick' component. Not suitable for students with mobility issues or difficulty following instructions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-4, adaptable to other grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce math skills, increase response time, promote active engagement, encourage kinesthetic learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simple rules and variations make it easy to adapt to various learning needs. Incorporates active recall of math facts. Movement refreshes students and provides another take on math concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt math problems to match the skill levels of the students. Allow students to come up with their own rules.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the speed and accuracy with which students stand up or sit down. Assess students' mental math skills through the responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • May help students refresh while applying their mental math. Encourages active participation and critical thinking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When the teacher says '6+4' the students stand up, but when the teacher says '9' the students sit down.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Form homogeneous groups based on learners' mastery of specific standards. Assess learners formatively through pre-assessments, warm-up questions, and exit tickets to identify standard deficits. Pool learners from different classes into groups focused on mastering specific standards. This method allows instructors to address gaps efficiently and ensures that learners who have already mastered a standard are not held back.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires formative assessments to identify standard deficits, flexible scheduling to pool learners from different classes, and resources aligned to specific standards.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful management to ensure all learners are engaged and supported. Needs clear expectations to prevent off-task behavior. Requires ongoing data collection and analysis to ensure appropriate group placement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective in classrooms with diverse skill levels and standards-based curricula.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Address specific standard deficits, improve efficiency of instruction, provide targeted support, challenge advanced learners.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows instructors to focus on specific skills and standards. Provides targeted support for struggling learners. Ensures that advanced learners are not held back. Efficient use of instructional time.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying group sizes, providing differentiated tasks aligned to specific standards, and allowing learners to self-select standards to focus on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction
  • Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners’ engagement, participation, and mastery of standards within groups. Collect data from formative assessments, exit tickets, and group projects. Track changes in performance following implementation of standard-based regrouping.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mastery of multiple standards can be achieved in a single class period, improving learning outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are asked to go through lecture videos and other study material that are prerequisites for the next class. Usually, all the aspects of a topic are converted into video lectures. The class time is reserved for practicing the concepts studied at home and to improve the students’ understanding in various ways like a one-to-one interaction with the teacher.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires creation of comprehensive video lectures and study materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Dependent on learner compliance with pre-class work, may not suit all learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners who can self-regulate and engage with online materials independently.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Prepare learners for in-class practice, reinforce understanding of key concepts, facilitate one-on-one teacher interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to review material at their own pace, provides dedicated class time for clarification and application.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose when and where to engage with pre-class materials.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Lectures
  • Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Pre-class material completion rates, in-class engagement, performance on application-based tasks.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can improve learners' understanding and application of concepts if pre-class material is effectively designed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • High school chemistry classes using video lectures for content delivery.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shift from arbitrary points and percentages to evaluating students on mastery of specific learning standards, making expectations clear and grades meaningful.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clearly defined standards

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant training

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle & High School

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure grading is an accurate measure of mastery, set clear standards, promote focus on learning rather than points

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear expectations, promotes mastery, creates transparency

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Focuses on individual mastery, not compliance

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Correlation with standardized tests

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The rates of D's and F's went down, but the number of A's also went down

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • High School Physics Grading

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Standards-/Mastery-Based Grading emphasizes grading based on the level of mastery of learning objectives. Explicit criteria are developed and made transparent to students, ensuring grades reflect learning rather than gaming the system.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear learning objectives, transparent grading criteria, systems for tracking mastery levels

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant restructuring of curriculum and assessments. Requires thorough development of learning objectives and criteria.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for higher education and professional training

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Ensure grades reflect mastery of learning objectives, provide clear grading criteria to students, reduce focus on accumulating 'points' rather than learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Ensures clear criteria for grades, promotes student understanding of learning goals, encourages mastery of content

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by setting personalized mastery goals for individual learners. Flexible assessments can accommodate different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track alignment of grades with mastery levels, measure student understanding of grading criteria, compare outcomes to traditional grading methods

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Clear learning objectives ensures that the criteria for grades are clear to students and that grades meaningfully reflect learning as opposed to a student’s ability to game the system by earning “points”.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Developing explicit criteria based on grade level standards. Making the grading criteria transparent to learners

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This principle encourages educators to reflect on their own intersectional identities and how these identities shape their perceptions and relationships with others. It involves activities like identity mapping exercises and constructivist listening dyads to explore personal identity markers (race, gender, income, citizenship status, etc.) and their impact on one's work as an educator. This practice is crucial for empathy work, as it helps educators become aware of their biases and assumptions, leading to more equitable interactions with students and families. The goal is to foster self-awareness and create a more inclusive and understanding learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a safe and supportive environment for self-reflection and sharing, as well as trained facilitators to guide the activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be emotionally challenging and may require significant time for reflection and processing. The benefits depend on the participants' willingness to be open and honest.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators at all levels who seek to understand and address their own biases and create more inclusive learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase self-awareness, identify personal biases, improve relationships with students, and promote equity in educational practices.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances self-reflection, fosters empathy, improves communication, and promotes equitable practices in education.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific identity markers and prompts can be tailored to the individual's background and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in educator behavior and interactions with students, gather feedback from students about the inclusiveness of the classroom environment, and track the implementation of more equitable practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved educator-student relationships, increased student engagement, and more equitable outcomes for all learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • CityBridge Education uses an identity mapping exercise, modeled on a National School Reform Faculty protocol called “The Paseo,” in their Breakthrough Design Fellowship. Participants map key identifiers of their identity and discuss how these markers have shaped their experiences as educators.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Stations strategy involves small groups of learners rotating through different stations to interact with a variety of resources (informational texts, poetry, art, photography, maps, videos, audio clips) related to a specific event, theme, or question. At each station, learners engage with the material and either answer questions or complete a reflective activity. This approach allows learners to engage with the topic using multiple modalities, promoting deeper understanding and multiple perspectives. The stations activity works well to launch a new unit or to explore in more depth something learners have already studied.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of diverse resources (texts, videos, images, etc.), materials for each station (folders, copies of resources, instructions), space for multiple stations, time for learners to rotate through stations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant preparation to gather and organize resources. May be challenging to manage time and ensure all learners are engaged at each station.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore a topic from multiple perspectives, develop deeper understanding, engage with material using multiple modalities, promote collaborative learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners through diverse media, promotes collaborative learning, allows for exploration of multiple perspectives, accommodates different learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Groups can be heterogeneous, leveled, or self-selected. Activities at each station can be tailored to different skill levels or interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections
  • Peer Discussion
  • Knowledge Synthesis
  • Collaborative Learning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of student responses to station activities, participation in debriefing discussions, ability to synthesize information from multiple sources.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding, enhances engagement, and fosters collaborative learning through exploration of multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Step In When Abusive Language Occurs
Description
docs.text: Addressing offensive language promptly and consistently is crucial for creating a safe and respectful classroom environment. This involves immediately stopping the use of offensive terms and addressing the student privately to discuss the impact of their words. Consistency in these responses is vital, as students watch teachers to see if they follow through and can be trusted. Addressing offensive language demonstrates to students that the classroom is a safe space where all members are respected and protected from harm.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A teacher who is willing to address offensive language consistently and impartially. Time for private discussions with students. A willingness to involve students in finding solutions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may resist being corrected or may not understand the impact of their words. Requires ongoing monitoring and reinforcement. May require additional support from administrators or parents.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students and educators in classrooms where offensive language may occur, aiming to create a more inclusive and respectful learning environment.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create a safe and respectful classroom environment where all students feel protected from harm. Promote understanding of the impact of offensive language and encourage empathy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces the importance of respectful communication. Provides a clear message that offensive language will not be tolerated. Encourages empathy and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Responses can be tailored to the specific situation and the students involved. Teachers can include students in developing solutions to address offensive language. Offers the option for students to write about their feelings or discuss them privately with the teacher.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Decreased use of offensive language in the classroom. Increased student understanding of the impact of their words. Improved classroom climate and sense of safety.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced safety and respect: Promptly addressing offensive language creates a safer and more respectful classroom environment, where all students feel valued and protected. Increased empathy and understanding: Encouraging students to reflect on the impact of their words promotes empathy and understanding, fostering a more inclusive and compassionate learning community.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Responding to offensive language by saying, 'I don't allow that term in my classroom. I need to talk with you after class about that.' Following up with a private conversation about the impact of their words and asking them to reflect on how it feels to be hurt.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students work in small groups to collaboratively solve math problems. Each student initially works individually on a sticky note, then the group combines their ideas to create the best possible answer on a common page, defending their thinking and building on each other's work. Variations include projecting the problem and grouping students based on completion time, chosen criteria, or randomly. The activity emphasizes accountability, participation, and developing the best possible group response.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Sticky notes, problem-solving pages (one per student or group), time for individual work and group discussion, whiteboard or projector for sharing results.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful facilitation to ensure all students participate equally. Some students may dominate discussions, while others may be passive. Requires well-designed problems aligned to learning goals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3–6, adaptable for higher grades with appropriate content. Beneficial for learners who benefit from collaborative work and peer interaction.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance collaboration, promote accountability, foster teamwork skills, review math concepts, improve problem-solving abilities, and develop communication skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active participation, encourages critical thinking through discussion and justification, builds teamwork and communication skills, reinforces math concepts through peer teaching, and offers administrative appeal due to accountability.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be varied by grouping strategies (completion time, teacher choice, random), different problem types, or modifying the problem difficulty. Individual contributions can be weighted differently based on learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation, assess the quality of collaborative answers, analyze the reasoning and justification presented by groups, and review individual contributions on sticky notes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Practitioner evidence suggests improved student engagement and comprehension, enhanced teamwork skills, and positive administrative feedback. Collaboration and peer interaction in problem-solving boost knowledge retention and comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A 5th-grade math teacher uses Stick-It Together to review fraction concepts. Students solve individually, discuss their approaches in groups, and present their collaborative solution to the class, explaining their reasoning. Variations include grouping students by prior performance to promote peer teaching.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Stop and Jot is a processing activity that provides structured opportunities for learners to pause and respond in writing to key questions during a lesson. This technique involves designating a “stop box” on learners' notes where they jot down their thoughts, summaries, or answers to instructor-posed questions. It promotes retention, comprehension, and active engagement by giving learners time to process and make sense of the material before moving forward. The strategy serves as both a check for understanding and a study tool, highlighting essential information for future review.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires minimal materials: paper, pens/pencils, and prepared questions or prompts. Effective implementation requires instructors to provide sufficient processing time and facilitate sharing of responses.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be less effective for learners who struggle with writing or prefer alternative processing methods. Some learners may require additional support to formulate clear and concise responses.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable across all learner levels and subject areas, particularly useful for learners who benefit from structured processing activities and note-taking assistance

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active engagement, increase retention and comprehension, provide processing time, assess understanding, facilitate summarization, encourage personal relevance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports active recall and critical thinking by prompting learners to reflect on key concepts. Enhances note-taking skills by providing a structured format. Allows instructors to quickly assess understanding and address misunderstandings. Encourages personal relevance by allowing learners to make connections to previously learned material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various learning styles through variations like Jot-Pair-Share, Quick Jot, and Stop and Fill. Templates and prompts can be customized to fit the topic of study. Digital versions can be implemented using collaborative documents or online note-taking tools.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review the content and depth of student jots to assess comprehension and critical thinking. Observe the level of engagement during sharing and discussion. Analyze the connections made between new and previously learned material.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased retention: Research shows that activities like Stop and Jot, which encourage learners to pause and reflect, aid in memory and retention of new information. Enhanced comprehension: By providing structured processing time, learners are better able to make sense of the material and identify key ideas.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Organization is a key component of successful learning environments. A de-cluttered learning environment is free from distractions and allows the focus to be on learning. Students can move quickly through the space and easily access resources needed for various learning purposes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of storage options such as shelves, bins, and cubbies. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing storage arrangements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve organization, reduce stress, promote focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes organization and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred storage options. Provide a variety of storage options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Activation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that organization can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Story and concept maps are visual representations used to organize information and enhance comprehension, particularly of narratives and complex relationships. Story maps focus on key story elements like characters, setting, problem, and solution. Concept maps show relationships between words and phrases. These maps support prewriting and postreading activities, summarizing main ideas, and identifying key details in both fiction and nonfiction texts. Learners create, write, draw, and organize information from a text into meaning with a dynamic graphic organizer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Story or informational text, blank story or concept map templates (paper or digital), colored pencils/markers (optional)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming, requires explicit instruction and modeling, can be overwhelming for learners if not properly scaffolded, effectiveness depends on the quality of teacher guidance and support

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, organize information, summarize main ideas, identify key details, visualize relationships between concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports visual learning, enhances memory through organization, aids in summarizing and identifying key elements, provides a structured approach to comprehension, fosters critical thinking through analysis of relationships

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different text types (fiction, nonfiction), allows for individual or group work, can be tailored to specific learning objectives, supports diverse learning preferences with visual and textual components

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the completeness and accuracy of the story or concept map, assess the depth of understanding demonstrated by the connections made between elements, track learner progress in identifying key details and summarizing main ideas

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that story maps improve comprehension by helping learners organize story elements and summarize main ideas. (Reutzel, 1985). Graphic organizers, in general, support cognition and literacy skills by helping learners visualize how ideas fit together.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using story maps to analyze character development in a novel, creating concept maps to understand relationships between vocabulary words, using graphic organizers to summarize key events in history.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Story maps are graphic organizers that help learners visually represent and understand the key elements of a narrative, such as characters, setting, plot, conflict, and resolution. They can be used before, during, or after reading to improve comprehension, provide a framework for identifying story elements, and help learners organize information and ideas. Story maps can range from simple formats focusing on the beginning, middle, and end of a story to more complex organizers focusing on plot, character development, or theme.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Blank story map organizers or digital tools for creating story maps, familiar stories or texts to use as examples, chart paper for whole-class story map construction
