docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who struggle with graphic organizers or visual representations. Effectiveness depends on the quality of the story map template and the instructor's guidance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including elementary, middle, and high school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension of narrative text, provide a framework for identifying story elements, help learners organize information and ideas, develop a deeper understanding of how stories work

docs.title: Affordances

docs.text: • Improved text comprehension: Research indicates that story mapping enhances comprehension of narrative text by helping learners focus on key elements of a story. Enhanced organization and recall: Visual representation of story elements helps learners organize information and improves recall.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary teacher uses a story map during a read-aloud with a small group. A digital product, such as Kidspiration, can allow learners to create complex story maps to visualize and enhance their learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The instructor prepares a short, personalized narrative related to the reading topic. The story should be creative, engaging, and told enthusiastically, ideally including elements of suspense and humor. Sharing this personal narrative helps create interest, activate prior knowledge, and set the stage for the reading material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a well-crafted, engaging personal narrative and effective storytelling skills from the instructor.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the story and the instructor's storytelling ability. Some learners may not connect with the personal narrative.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Create interest, activate prior knowledge, and set the stage for the reading material.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners through storytelling, activates prior knowledge through personal connections, and enhances motivation through suspense and humor.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Stories can be tailored to be relevant to different proficiency levels and cultural contexts. The length and complexity of the narrative can be adjusted based on the audience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learners' engagement and interest during the storytelling. Collect feedback on how well the story prepared them for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances engagement, activates prior knowledge in a memorable way, and creates a positive association with the reading topic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about environmental conservation, the instructor might share a personal story about a time they witnessed the impact of pollution on a local ecosystem.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using storybooks to explore and discuss the emotions of characters. Learners guess how characters are feeling based on the narrative and visual cues, then discuss the reasons behind these emotions. This activity promotes empathy and helps learners understand the connection between events, feelings, and expressions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of storybooks; facilitator to guide discussion; classroom setting or reading space

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful book selection to ensure emotional content is appropriate; discussions may be superficial without skilled facilitation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Children in early childhood and primary school settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional recognition; promote understanding of emotions in context; develop empathy and perspective-taking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging and accessible learning; encourages empathy; helps connect emotions to real-life situations; supports literacy development

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select books relevant to learners' backgrounds and experiences; adjust discussion prompts to match developmental levels; provide visual aids for diverse learners

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and discuss emotions accurately; track participation and engagement in discussions; monitor ability to connect emotions to narrative events

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved emotional recognition; increased empathy; and enhanced understanding of emotional connections (as suggested by the use of storybooks)

docs.title: Storytelling in Explainer Animations and Videos
Description
docs.text: Combining visual elements with engaging narratives to capture the learners' attention and facilitate long-term information retention. The video or animation should start by presenting a common problem or a realistic situation that your audience might face in their daily lives. This introduction creates a familiar context and piques the persons' interest.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tools for creating animations or videos. A compelling story that illustrates the concept.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Animations and videos can be time-consuming to produce. Poorly designed stories can be confusing or ineffective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from visual and auditory learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance engagement, connect learning to real-world experiences, improve information retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates long-term information retention and allows for creating an emotional connection with the audience by featuring characters or situations they can identify with.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use stories that are relevant to learners' backgrounds and interests.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to recall and explain the concept after watching the animation or video. Evaluate their ability to apply the concept in new situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using animations and explainer videos with storytelling is one of the most effective ways to teach concepts, especially in eLearning courses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a character who experiences stressful situations at work and, through storytelling, show how the concept of "stress management" helps them effectively overcome their challenges, animating the story of a character who faces and overcomes various obstacles to illustrate resilience.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Arranging desks strategically can support different learning activities. Small group work benefits from tables, while rows can focus attention on the board. Consider the needs of students with vision impairments when arranging seating.

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time to adjust seating arrangements. Requires careful consideration of student needs and learning activities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with specific learning needs or preferences.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support varied instructional activities, enhance student focus, accommodate individual needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports different instructional strategies, improves student focus, and accommodates individual needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow students to choose their seating arrangement based on the activity. Provide accommodations for students with specific needs (e.g., vision impairments).

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can enhance student focus, support different learning activities, and accommodate individual needs through strategic desk arrangement.

docs.title: Strategies to Develop Positive Classroom Pride
Description
docs.text: Use these strategies to develop positive classroom pride: display learner work, positively reinforce learners verbally on a regular basis, publicly ask other staff members to enter the classroom so that they can see a specific accomplishment of your class, recognize accomplishments in areas such as kindness, citizenship, test scores, or athletics, and extend the pride taken in the class by developing parental pride in learner accomplishments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructors must be sincere in their proclamations of pride in learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Pride does not always have to involve only excellence. Pride in improvement is an important type of pride to nurture.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve classroom dynamics by creating a positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • A positive classroom culture can improve learners' pride in their accomplishments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can recognize and acknowledge learners' accomplishments through parent conferences, school newsletters, and back-to-school events.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of positive classroom environment, respectful learners, and increased participation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Positive classroom pride helps learners build positive behaviors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use time-honored tricks to remember name pronunciation, like word association, writing down each syllable in English phonetics, and rhyming, as well as new-fangled ones like name pronunciation websites.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor should take the time to use the above techniques to help them memorize learners' names.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • This can be time consuming and may not be possible in a large class.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve memorization of learners' names

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • If the instructor makes an effort to learn and properly pronounce the learners' names, this demonstrates respect and care.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use word association to match learners' names with other well-known words. Use websites to find out how to pronounce names from other cultures.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • If the instructor properly pronounces the learners' names.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • It is important that the classroom shows it will not consistently mispronounce a name because they are too afraid to ask, or too afraid to correct themselves.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves having students actively identify and reflect on the strategies they use to overcome challenges. The instructor checks in with learners to help them name their process, and then add to a list of strategies that students are using and, if they are struggling, help students name a specific process. By providing language to match what learners do, they have a strategy they could use in other times of struggle.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor must provide prompts and check-ins to help students name their process. Requires a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort from the instructor. Some students may struggle to articulate their strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly in elementary and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-awareness, enhance problem-solving skills, increase metacognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances metacognition, promotes self-directed learning, provides a resource for students to use when struggling

docs.title: Personalization

docs.text: • Increased self-awareness, improved problem-solving skills, enhanced metacognition

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students become more aware of their learning processes and can apply strategies more effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing language prompts for students to use for self-talk or when talking with a partner. Creating charts of strategies that students can refer to when they are stuck or struggling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves explicitly teaching problem-solving strategies and providing opportunities for students to practice using them when they feel 'stuck.' Students are encouraged to be mindful of how they are getting themselves unstuck and to name their process. This helps them develop self-directed learning skills. The teacher checks in to help students name their process by asking questions like, 'How did you get yourself unstuck?' or 'What was your first step? What are you doing now? What might you try next?' As students talk about their process, the teacher adds to a list of strategies that students are using, giving them the language to match what they did so that they now have a strategy they could use in other times of struggle.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction on problem-solving strategies. Opportunities for learners to practice using these strategies. A supportive environment where learners feel comfortable making mistakes and reflecting on their process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort to develop a repertoire of problem-solving strategies. Some learners may struggle to identify and apply appropriate strategies. Requires consistent reinforcement and modeling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who need support in developing effective problem-solving strategies.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-directed learning skills, promote metacognition, and increase problem-solving abilities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a repertoire of problem-solving strategies. Encourages metacognitive thinking and self-monitoring. Supports the development of self-directed learning skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide a variety of problem-solving strategies to accommodate different learning styles. Offer individualized support and guidance. Tailor problems to align with learner interests and abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and apply appropriate problem-solving strategies. Track changes in learners' metacognitive skills. Measure learners' problem-solving abilities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that explicitly teaching problem-solving strategies can lead to increased problem-solving abilities and improved metacognition. Supports the development of self-directed learning skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides a list of problem-solving strategies, such as breaking down the problem into smaller steps, drawing a diagram, or trying a different approach. Students work on a problem and reflect on the strategies they used to solve it. A class discusses different problem-solving strategies and when to use them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Strategy instruction teaches learners how to learn effectively by applying principles, rules, or multi-step processes to solve problems or accomplish learning tasks. Examples of strategies include phonics rules, ways to monitor comprehension, procedures for decoding multi-syllabic words, tips for using context clues to define words, and test-taking strategies. Instructors model their thought processes, demonstrating when and how to use the strategy, and then prompting or cueing learners as needed when it is appropriate for them to use a strategy that has been taught.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be knowledgeable about a range of learning strategies. Requires allocation of time for modeling, guided practice, and application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be overwhelming if too many strategies are introduced at once. Some learners may struggle to generalize strategies to new contexts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in basic skills programs, individuals with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Equip learners with tools to approach learning tasks effectively; enhance problem-solving skills; improve self-regulation and metacognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with adaptable tools for independent learning. Improves their ability to monitor and manage their own learning processes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs by providing varied strategies and allowing learners to choose the strategies that work best for them. Strategies can be scaffolded to support learners with different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner application of strategies in new contexts; learner articulation of when and how to use specific strategies; improved performance on problem-solving tasks

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows strategy instruction improves learners' ability to solve problems and accomplish learning tasks. Modeling thought processes helps learners internalize effective strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Demonstrating how to use context clues to define unknown words. Modeling how to monitor comprehension by asking self-questions while reading.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit teaching of writing strategies, especially self-regulated strategy development (SRSD). Writers are explicitly taught strategies that are reinforced in class over time, helping them internalize and draw on them for support when writing. Strategies replace negative self-talk with positive self-instructions to help learners overcome frustration and past failure. Requires professional development and practice leading to instruction that is consistent and explicit. Strategy instruction is introduced to adult education through the professional development programs, Bridges to Practice and Learning to Achieve, developed by the National Institute for Literacy to address the needs of students with learning disabilities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Professional development for instructors, consistent reinforcement, positive learning environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant training, may not be effective without motivation or engagement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Low-achieving writers, students with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing skills, promote self-regulation, overcome negative self-talk

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tools to manage writing process, promotes positive self-talk, builds confidence

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to individual needs and writing tasks.

docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased self-regulation, reduced negative self-talk

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This approach involves identifying and leveraging a student’s strengths to address challenges in responsible decision-making. Educators identify specific student strengths and/or challenges related to responsible decision-making and uses aligned strategies to leverage student strengths to support student learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Educator understanding of student strengths and challenges. Access to tailored strategies and activities. Supportive and positive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful assessment of student strengths and challenges. May be difficult to identify and leverage strengths for all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who have challenges with responsible decision-making

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve responsible decision-making skills, leverage existing strengths, enhance self-awareness, promote ethical reasoning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds confidence by focusing on strengths, promotes positive self-image, enhances motivation, fosters ethical reasoning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to individual student strengths and challenges. Activities and scenarios are designed to be personally relevant.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback
  • Problem Scenario
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student progress in decision-making, analyze their reflections, and assess their ability to apply strengths to overcome challenges.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies indicate that strength-based approaches can enhance self-esteem and improve student outcomes. Classroom Management for Responsible Citizenship: Practical Strategies for Teachers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Having students create if/then decision trees or using sticky notes to create an option wall. Reading current events, discussing if the decisions made are ethical, and evaluating those decisions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This method involves identifying a student's strengths related to self-awareness and using those strengths to address their challenges. Self-awareness is the ability to correctly identify one's own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they impact behavior. Strategies include having students identify and label feelings, engaging in journal reflections to understand patterns and manage goals, and using estimation and prediction skills to reflect on accuracy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of student's strengths and challenges. Journal materials and prompts. Activities for estimation and prediction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires accurate identification of student's strengths and challenges. May need to provide additional support for students with significant challenges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, with a focus on students struggling with self-awareness.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' ability to identify their own emotions, thoughts, and values, and how they impact behavior.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages individual strengths to address challenges, promotes self-reflection, and provides practical activities for understanding emotions and behaviors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to the student's specific strengths and challenges. Journal prompts and estimation activities can be customized to individual interests.

docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.text: • Student's ability to identify emotions, reflect on experiences, and make accurate predictions. Quality of journal reflections and participation in activities.

docs.title: Impact

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This method involves identifying a student's strengths related to social awareness and using those strengths to address their challenges. Social awareness is the understanding of social norms for behavior and the ability to understand the perspectives of others. Strategies include modeling empathy, discussing different perspectives explicitly, having conversations about emotions and social issues, and using current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of student's strengths and challenges. Current events and fictional stories. Facilitation of discussions.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' ability to understand social norms, empathize with others, and communicate constructively.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Leverages individual strengths to address challenges, promotes empathy, and provides practical activities for understanding social norms and perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators identify students' strengths related to responsible decision-making and leverage these strengths to address challenges. Responsible decision-making involves making constructive and ethical choices, analyzing situations, evaluating consequences, and reflecting on outcomes. Strategies include brainstorming a decision-making process, practicing with problem scenarios, defining ethical responsibility using graphic organizers, reading current events, and developing the educator's understanding of responsible decision-making through resources like the Learner Variability Navigator. The focus is on helping students use their inherent abilities to improve their decision-making skills and overall well-being.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires understanding of students' strengths, access to problem scenarios, graphic organizers, current events, and resources like the Learner Variability Navigator. Educators need to facilitate discussions and provide guidance on ethical decision-making.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time to identify individual student strengths and tailor strategies accordingly. Some students may struggle to reflect on their decisions. Ethical dilemmas need to be carefully chosen to avoid triggering or alienating students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages who need support in developing responsible decision-making skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' responsible decision-making skills by leveraging their strengths, promote ethical behavior, enhance problem-solving abilities, and foster self-reflection.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances ethical development, promotes problem-solving skills, encourages self-reflection, and leverages students' strengths to address challenges, fostering a positive learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be tailored to individual student strengths and challenges. Scenarios can be made relevant to students' lives and cultural backgrounds. Graphic organizers and decision-making tools can be adapted to different age levels and learning styles.

Strategies involve identifying feelings, using journal reflections, estimating and predicting outcomes, and leveraging resources like the Learner Variability Navigator. The goal is to enhance students' understanding of themselves, their emotions, and their capabilities, fostering a growth mindset and improving academic and social outcomes.

docs.text: • Enhance students' self-awareness, improve emotional identification, promote self-reflection, foster a growth mindset, and improve academic and social outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances

Strategies include modeling empathy, discussing different perspectives, having explicit conversations about emotions and social issues, and using current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness. This approach helps students develop empathy, improve communication skills, and foster positive relationships, leading to higher academic achievement and fewer disciplinary problems.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A shift in mindset where the Individualized Education Program (IEP) focuses as much on the learner’s strengths as it does on their weaknesses, leveraging abilities to help address needs. This approach involves identifying the learner's strengths, interests, and preferences, and using those insights to develop strategies for success. It promotes self-awareness and self-advocacy and requires IEP teams to gather more information, often from the learners themselves. By reframing the way strengths are discussed and weaving them into IEP goals, IEPs become more positive and actionable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to strength finder tools, a commitment from the IEP team to shift mindset, and the inclusion of learners in the IEP process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Not yet widely used. May require teacher training in strengths-based IEPs and may require districts to rewrite their IEP templates.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with IEPs, special education staff

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help adults and learners see more than just weaknesses, promote self-awareness and self-advocacy, chart a path to progress using strengths

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages a positive tone, helps educators understand how to help learners move forward, and develops self-awareness

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strength tests and self-assessments can help deepen the discussion about strengths. Learners can participate in parts of the IEP meetings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Whether IEP goals are written in a strengths-based manner, the level of learner involvement in IEP meetings, and the inclusion of the learner's strengths, interests, and preferences in IEP goals.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • More positive and actionable IEPs with SMART goals built around what the learner can do and how the team can use that ability to work on an area of weakness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • By May 15, Elana will use her skills with a times table to help transition to knowing from memory all products of two one-digit numbers with 90% accuracy in four out of five tries. Sam will use his creativity and interpersonal skills to develop and lead his peers in a class vocabulary game with 90% accuracy in three out of four weekly opportunities. Resource: Understood.org - Strengths-based IEPs: What you need to know

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A teaching approach that focuses on identifying and leveraging learners’ strengths to improve overall learning and engagement. By acknowledging and creating opportunities for learners to let their skills shine, instructors can redefine learners’ perspectives on their education and capabilities. Instead of focusing on deficits, this model harnesses strengths to create more engaged, confident learners. Key components include measuring strengths, noticing and acknowledging strengths daily, creating opportunities for success, providing options for demonstrating knowledge, and teaching collaboration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Strengths assessment tools, opportunities for learners to demonstrate their talents, a positive and supportive classroom environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a shift in mindset and a willingness to focus on learners’ strengths rather than deficits. Can be challenging to implement in a classroom with diverse abilities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with ADHD or learning disorders

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Boost learner confidence, increase engagement, promote self-awareness, foster a positive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to redefine themselves and their education in terms of their strengths. Increases engagement and creates a more independent, self-advocating learner. Fosters a positive atmosphere and promotes collaboration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor activities and assessments to allow learners to showcase their unique skills and talents. Provide options for demonstrating knowledge to accommodate different learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Learner Choice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased learner engagement, improved academic performance, greater self-confidence, positive feedback from learners

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners taught in a strengths-based model earned higher GPAs and were absent from school less often. Helps learners develop the confidence to be learners and the courage to overcome weaknesses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher begins the year by having learners share their strengths. A teacher challenges themselves to compliment each learner daily, identifying what they did well and acknowledging their effort. Resource: ADDitude - How I Bring Out My Students’ Unique Skills

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Structured instruction involves systematically teaching information that has been chunked into manageable pieces. Complex skills or large bodies of information are broken into parts, which are taught systematically according to a planned sequence. Each task is analyzed and broken into its component parts, and then after teaching the parts systematically, bring them back together so learners are aware of the process or concept as a whole.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to analyze tasks and break them into component parts. Requires careful planning and sequencing of instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as overly structured or rigid by some learners. Requires significant planning and preparation time for instructors.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in basic skills programs, individuals with learning disabilities

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate comprehension of complex skills and information; improve retention; provide a clear, organized framework for learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by breaking information into smaller, more manageable chunks Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+M], consistent with part-task practice for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [+M]. Provides a clear and organized framework for learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to individual learner needs by adjusting the size of the chunks and providing varied examples and practice opportunities. Sequencing can be tailored to support learners with different levels of prior knowledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learner performance on component parts; learner comprehension of the overall process or concept; improved retention of information

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Breaking complex skills into manageable parts facilitates comprehension. Clear and organized framework supports learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Breaking a decoding strategy into a series of steps, teaching each step individually, and then bringing the steps together to decode a word. Teaching prefixes and suffixes separately before combining them to analyze word meanings.

docs.title: Structured and Sustained Family Engagement Programs
Description
docs.text: Creating engagement programs that are embedded throughout a school’s structure and are sustainable. These programs involve families participating in activities that are central to students’ academic learning, and evaluate programs to determine which offerings are effective. Led by a school principal who values family involvement and is willing to share power, and has high expectations for all students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured programs, school leadership support, family participation, evaluation metrics, and resources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant investment of resources and time. Success depends on the commitment of school staff, families, and the school leadership.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, teachers, and families

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve family involvement in education, leading to positive outcomes for students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • By embedding engagement programs within the school's structure, it ensures that families are actively involved in their children's academic learning. Principals with high expectations for all students promote a positive school culture.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Programs can be adapted to meet the unique needs and demographics of the school community.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Application
  • Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate family participation rates, student academic outcomes, and overall school culture to assess program effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that sustainable and well-structured family engagement programs can lead to improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Facilitating productive discussions requires clear expectations, modeling, sentence starters (particularly for English language learners), and routines. These techniques ensure that effective discussions can occur among learners even without direct instructor supervision. Structured discussions promote engagement, respect, and deeper understanding of the material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires training in facilitation techniques and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel constrained by structured techniques. Requires ongoing monitoring and adjustment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote engagement, foster respect, deepen understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structure and support for meaningful discussions. Encourages active participation and respect among learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust sentence starters to suit learner needs. Provide varied roles within discussions to engage diverse learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Peer Collaboration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and analyze the depth and quality of discussion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances engagement, promotes respect, and deepens understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Structured music and dance activities involve incorporating movement and rhythm into educational content, particularly for preschoolers. Activities are designed to be done indoors in small spaces, and incorporate healthy messaging related to physical activity and healthy eating. These activities integrate math, science, music, creativity, and fundamental motor skills to promote brain development and social interaction.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Music, dance resources, small indoor space, and facilitation by a teacher or caregiver

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires planning to align with educational content, some children may have physical limitations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Preschoolers and young children

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote physical activity, enhance motor skills, integrate multiple subjects (math, science, music), foster brain development, encourage social interaction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages children in physical activity, enhances motor skills, integrates multiple subjects, fosters brain development, and encourages social interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be modified to suit various skill levels and cultural backgrounds

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Integration
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe participation, assess motor skill development, monitor engagement with educational content

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured music and dance activities enhance physical activity, cognitive development, and social interaction in young children.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A structured observation protocol involves using a template or guide to record factual details about a student's experiences without interpretation, opinion, or judgment. For instance, note the student's body language, facial expressions, and interactions with teachers and peers. The protocol also encourages gathering perceptions of the school from teachers, staff, students, parents, and community members. After shadowing, summarize and organize notes to pinpoint areas needing attention and reflect on the insights gained.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Student Shadowing Template from racialquityleadership.com, a willing student, time to shadow the student for a significant portion of the school day, time for reflection and analysis of observations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Potential for observer bias, may not capture the full complexity of a student's experience, and requires a high degree of self-awareness for the observer. Requires a trusting environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, school leaders, and administrators seeking to gather objective data and insights into student experiences and school environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Record factual details without bias, identify areas needing attention, reflect on insights gained, and gather perceptions from various stakeholders.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to gathering objective data, helps uncover hidden challenges and inequities, and informs instructional practices. Promotes self-reflection, perspective-taking, and critical analysis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The protocol can be adapted to focus on specific areas of interest or concern, such as student engagement, interactions with teachers, or access to resources.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Detailed notes and observations, summaries of findings, reflections on insights gained, and action plans for addressing identified issues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased awareness of student experiences, improved instructional practices, promotion of equity and inclusion, and enhanced empathy and cultural awareness among educators. Can influence shifts in policy and improved resource allocation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using structured questions with clear goals and timeframes provides focus and scaffolding for pair talk activities. These questions should be designed to elicit specific types of responses, such as identifying key factors, comparing advantages and disadvantages, or explaining processes. Announcing the timeframe in advance helps students manage their time and stay on task.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful planning of questions that align with learning objectives. A visible timer can be useful for managing time.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overly structured questions may limit creativity and exploration. Questions must be clear and easily understood by all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly helpful for students who struggle with open-ended discussions or time management.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Focus pair discussions, provide structure and scaffolding for students, encourage in-depth exploration of topics, and improve time management during collaborative activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces aimless discussions, promotes focused thinking, helps students structure their responses, and improves their ability to stay on task. Acts as a scaffold.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be differentiated to match students' readiness levels. Timeframes can be adjusted based on the complexity of the question and students' needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe whether students stay on task and address the key components of the question. Assess the quality and depth of their responses. Monitor how well they manage their time during the discussion.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured questioning can improve the focus and effectiveness of pair talk activities, leading to deeper understanding and better learning outcomes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A lesson structure maps the teaching and learning that occurs in class. Sound lesson structures reinforce routines, scaffold learning via specific steps/activities, optimise time on task and classroom climate by using smooth transitions, and stimulate and maintain engagement by linking lesson and unit learning through planned sequencing of teaching and learning activities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to plan the sequence of activities and transitions within a lesson.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Overly rigid structures may limit flexibility and student autonomy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Optimize learning through structured and scaffolded activities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a predictable and supportive learning environment, enhances time management, and promotes engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Lesson structures can be adapted to fit different learning styles and subject matter.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Simple-to-complex sequencing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Effective time management, smooth transitions, and student engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-structured lessons improve classroom climate, optimize time on task, and scaffold learning effectively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In Alessandra King’s algebra class, students created a magazine with dozens of articles about real world applications of math. For each article, they selected a primary source—an article from Scientific American, for example—read it closely, and then wrote a summary. Students wrote about a range of topics, from gerrymandering to fractals in Jackson Pollock’s paintings to invisibility cloaks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to primary sources. Requires time for research, writing, and collaboration.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle with research or writing. Teachers need to provide guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Secondary school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Explore real-world applications of math. Develop research and writing skills. Foster collaboration and creativity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects math to real-world contexts. Develops research and writing skills. Fosters collaboration and creativity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose the topics they want to write about.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Research
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student magazines to assess research, writing, and understanding of math concepts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Explores real-world applications of math. Develops research and writing skills. Fosters collaboration and creativity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students create a magazine with articles about real world applications of math, such as gerrymandering, fractals in Jackson Pollock’s paintings, or invisibility cloaks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Involving students in the design and transformation of their learning environment to promote ownership, engagement, and a sense of community. This approach leverages student input to create a brain-friendly enriched classroom environment by considering factors such as layout, furniture choices, color selections, lighting, nature, environmental print, and organization of materials. By actively participating in the transformation, students are empowered to shape their learning space in a way that best suits their needs and preferences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A teacher willing to share control over the classroom environment. Open communication and collaboration between teacher and students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time and effort. Some students may be hesitant to participate. Requires careful facilitation to ensure all voices are heard and valued.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Empower students, increase ownership, promote a brain-friendly environment, enhance engagement, and foster a sense of community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Capitalizes on student creativity and insights. Aligns the learning environment with students’ needs and preferences. Can improve student motivation and engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The transformation process can be tailored to the specific needs and interests of the students. Students can contribute ideas, make design choices, and participate in the physical transformation of the space.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Cognitive Conflict
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, collect student feedback, and assess the overall impact on teaching and learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creating a space that makes it more natural to take our time, relax, and be reflective as we work towards mastery and understanding. The physical landscape of our room took on a different emotional feel upon entering. Our space was inspiring. It was warm. And most of all, it was an invitation for learning where all felt welcomed and valued. After all, students knew their voice mattered—they helped created their space.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners create their own problems based on concepts they're learning, share them with peers, and solve each other's problems. This encourages deeper engagement with the material, promotes problem-solving skills, and fosters motivation. Problems can be shared on digital platforms, allowing for dynamic visualizations and peer learning. For geometric reasoning, technology can be used to create dynamic visualizations of the problems. Seeing and solving problems written by peers fosters motivation and excitement for learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to relevant subject matter content, tools for creating and sharing problems (e.g., paper, pencils, digital platforms), and time for learners to create, share, and solve problems.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle with creating problems that are appropriately challenging and aligned with learning objectives. Some learners may be hesitant to share their problems or may be less motivated to solve problems created by their peers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners in various subject areas, particularly mathematics, science, and engineering.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, promote deeper understanding of mathematical concepts, foster motivation and engagement, build critical thinking, and improve communication skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances problem-solving skills, promotes critical thinking, fosters motivation, encourages peer learning, and reinforces understanding of mathematical concepts. Learners apply their knowledge in a creative and meaningful way, which aids in retention and transfer of skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Problems can be tailored to different skill levels, subject areas, and individual interests. Learners can choose the type of problem they want to create, the complexity of the problem, and the context in which the problem is situated.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Solution Development
  • Peer Teaching
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and complexity of problems created by learners. Assess the accuracy and completeness of solutions provided by learners. Observe learner engagement and participation in the problem-solving process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Active learning: Creating and solving problems enhances learner engagement and deeper understanding of mathematical concepts. Peer learning: Sharing and solving problems with peers promotes collaboration, communication, and critical thinking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a 3rd-grade math class, students create and solve division word problems, which are then used in subsequent lessons. In a geometry class, students create dynamic visualizations of geometric problems using technology, fostering motivation and excitement for learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Projects driven by student-generated questions allow learners to investigate topics they are curious about or think are important. This approach engages and invests students in the inquiry process, promoting ownership of learning. Instead of being spoon-fed information, learners identify the questions they need or want to answer, fostering a sense of empowerment and relevance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitation by instructors to guide inquiry and reflection, access to resources for research and investigation, a classroom culture that values student voice and questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires flexibility and adaptability on the part of the instructor, may be challenging to manage diverse interests and questions, demands thoughtful curation of resources to support student inquiry

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, foster curiosity and ownership of learning, promote inquiry-based thinking, encourage critical questioning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases motivation by aligning learning with student interests, promotes deeper engagement with content, develops inquiry and critical thinking skills, fosters a sense of ownership and agency

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to explore topics relevant to their lives and interests, provides opportunities for students to pursue individual lines of inquiry, can be tailored to different learning styles and preferences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Conceptual Questioning
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of student-generated questions, depth of inquiry and research, evidence of critical thinking and problem-solving, engagement and participation in project activities

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Student-generated questions lead to higher engagement and deeper learning, creating a sense of ownership and investment in the inquiry process. This strategy empowers students to take control of their learning and fosters a curiosity-driven approach to education. (Becton-Consuegra, 2019)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sparking engagement with student-generated questions involves encouraging students to investigate topics they care about and identify questions they want to answer. This approach fosters investment in the inquiry process and empowers students to take ownership of their learning. In contrast to traditional instruction where information is spoon-fed, PBL allows students to explore what matters to them, making learning more meaningful and relevant.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom environment that values student input and curiosity, and instructional strategies that support student-generated questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and flexibility in the curriculum, and may necessitate additional support for students who are not used to generating their own questions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, particularly those who may feel disempowered by traditional instructional methods. This approach can be especially beneficial for students of color.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To increase student engagement and investment in learning by allowing them to explore topics and questions that are meaningful to them.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students, fosters curiosity, promotes ownership of learning, and makes the inquiry process more engaging and relevant.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allows students to tailor their learning to their interests and concerns, making the learning experience more personalized and meaningful.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement, higher levels of participation in discussions, and more meaningful and relevant project outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that student-generated questions increase motivation and engagement in learning, leading to deeper understanding and more meaningful learning experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking students, "What do you care about? What do you want to learn more about? What questions do you need to know the answer to?" to guide their inquiry.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student-led conferences (SLCs) are meetings where students take the lead in discussions with parents about their progress and learning, supported by the teacher. Unlike traditional parent-teacher conferences, SLCs involve students in preparing, reflecting on, and discussing evidence of their learning and growth, often through student portfolios. This approach empowers students to take responsibility for their learning, encourages goal-setting and assessment, and engages families in richer conversations about student progress.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated preparation time for students to select work samples, reflect on their progress, and practice presentations. Teachers need to provide guidance and structure to support student-led discussions. A student-led conference form can be used to guide questioning.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant preparation time for students and teachers, especially when implementing for the first time. Some students may feel anxious or unprepared to lead discussions. Parents may initially be hesitant to shift from traditional conferences.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, adaptable for various grade levels and subject areas.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage student responsibility, engage families, promote reflection, set goals, demonstrate progress, and empower student voice.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes student ownership and accountability, enhances family engagement, fosters self-reflection, and improves communication skills. Reduces teacher workload by focusing on student-led discussions and insights.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for different grade levels by adjusting the complexity of reflection prompts and portfolio requirements. Flexible formats allow for student-selected work samples and individualized goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased student engagement and ownership, improved communication skills, richer family-teacher interactions, and more student-driven goal setting.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Schools implementing SLCs report increased student responsibility, enhanced family engagement, and deeper understanding of student progress. Higher parent turnout has been observed due to increased student investment in the process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Delaware Ridge Elementary School (Kindergarten), Washington Heights Expeditionary Learning School (WHEELS) (Middle and High School). University Park Campus School in Worcester, Massachusetts. Wildwood IB World Magnet School in Chicago, Illinois.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Pair-based games facilitate active learning through friendly competition, requiring students to recall and apply math skills in a dynamic setting. Examples include:

  • Finger Speed-Sums: Students show fingers, and the first to call out the sum wins.
  • Finger Speed-Differences: Students show fingers, and the first to call out the difference wins.
  • Five High Fives: Students give high-fives to five different classmates; the game is only possible if there are an even number of people.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pairs of students and a space for movement.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Uneven numbers of participants may cause issues in some games (e.g., 'Five High Fives').

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary grades, adaptable to older learners with adjustments in complexity

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance mathematical skills, encourage social interaction, and promote quick mental calculations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes quick mental calculations and social interaction in a fun, engaging manner.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the complexity of mathematical tasks (addition, subtraction, etc.) to meet different skill levels. Tweak competitive games to make them collaborative.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Interaction
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the accuracy and speed of mathematical responses, as well as participation and engagement levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Peer interaction and physical activity combine to enhance math skills. Social contexts in learning have been shown to improve comprehension and retention of new information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Math for Love offers several student-pair games for quick and fun mathematical practice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A teacher or coach shadows a student to gain insights into their experiences and identify areas for improvement in teaching practices. This involves observing the student's behavior, engagement, and interactions throughout the school day, then reflecting on the observations to inform instructional adjustments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for shadowing, willingness to observe and reflect on student experiences, and a commitment to making instructional adjustments based on observations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming, requires careful observation and reflection, and may not capture the full picture of a student's experience.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers and coaches seeking to improve their understanding of student needs and adjust their instructional practices

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand student experiences, improve teaching practices, increase student engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a firsthand view of student experiences, helps identify areas for improvement in teaching, and promotes student engagement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Shadowing can be tailored to specific students or groups of students to address particular learning needs or challenges.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in teaching practices based on shadowing observations, increased student engagement and participation, and improved student outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Offers valuable insights into student experiences, can lead to improved teaching practices, and promotes student engagement and success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student-Teams Achievement Divisions (STAD; Slavin, 1994) is a cooperative-learning technique built around teams of 4-5 students. The teacher presents a lesson or unit to the whole class and later tests students on it individually, but grades are based partly on each student's own improvement and the team's collective improvement, not solely on absolute test performance. Team members work together during the lesson to help each other improve as much as possible, then take the actual test as individuals — combining team-based preparation with individual accountability at assessment time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A whole-class lesson or unit content that all teams study together before individual testing
  • An improvement-based scoring scheme (baseline vs. current performance) rather than only absolute score, so that both stronger and weaker students can contribute meaningfully to their team's result

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Without an improvement-based scoring component, STAD collapses into ordinary group study with no distinct accountability structure

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Mixed-ability teams, since improvement-based scoring gives lower-performing students a genuine stake in contributing to team success rather than being outscored regardless of effort

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Content mastery verified individually, combined with a team incentive to help every member improve

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Present the lesson or unit to the whole class.
  2. Assign students to teams of 4-5.
  3. Have teams study and prepare together, with team members helping each other toward individual improvement.
  4. Test all students individually on the material.
  5. Score individuals partly on their own improvement relative to their own baseline, and partly on the team's collective improvement — not solely on absolute performance level.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Jigsaw Method — another 4-6-student cooperative structure, but organized around expert specialization on subtopics rather than shared study of the same whole-class content

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Slavin, R. E. (1994). Cooperative learning: Theory, research, and practice (2nd ed.). Allyn & Bacon.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Cooperative learning. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student assessment reports are visual aids used to track and communicate student progress in an engaging and approachable manner. By incorporating creative designs, playful color palettes, and star pictograms, these reports can reduce stress and make assessments less intimidating, especially for younger students. Charts are also included to summarize student progress in a clear and understandable format. These reports can highlight main educational areas and facilitate better communication between teachers, students, and parents.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to design software or templates. Implementation involves careful integration of data and visuals. May require training in design and communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Poorly designed reports can be confusing or misleading. Subjective interpretations of progress can create bias. Requires attention to detail and accuracy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, students, and parents in preschool, elementary, and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Track student progress, communicate assessment results, reduce stress, make assessments approachable, facilitate communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes assessments more approachable and less intimidating. Enhances communication and understanding of student progress. Provides a clear and organized format for tracking performance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to different grade levels, subjects, and assessment criteria. Design elements can be adjusted based on the audience and student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track improvements in student engagement and motivation. Evaluate the clarity and effectiveness of communication. Assess understanding of assessment results.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Engaging assessment reports have been shown to improve communication and reduce stress. Visual aids, in general, have been found to enhance learning and engagement in educational settings.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include progress reports using rainbow color palettes and star pictograms, and charts summarizing progress in main educational areas. Venngage and other design platforms offer templates for creating student assessment reports.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student blogs allow time to reflect on their mathematical process. Students can blog about how they solved a particular problem and what steps were needed. Blog explanations are especially useful when explaining solutions to problem-based learning activities. It’s also a stellar documentation tool. Keep in mind that the blogs may be public and not all students want to wave their mistakes in the air.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to blogs, time for blogging, and a way for students to share their thinking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to blogs and may not be appropriate for all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reflect on mathematical processes, explain problem-solving steps, document learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to reflect on their mathematical process, provides a way for students to explain problem-solving steps, and encourages students to document their learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can have students blog about how they solved a particular problem and what steps were needed. They can also have students blog about solutions to problem-based learning activities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding, increased student communication, and deeper reflection on learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of student blogging.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student blogs about how they solved a particular math problem. The student explains the steps they needed to take to solve the problem.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating student choice involves allowing learners to make decisions about their learning experiences, such as selecting which strategy to use in problem-solving, choosing how to demonstrate their knowledge, or deciding the sequence of their activities. This empowers students to take responsibility for their learning, develop independence, and become self-directed learners. It fosters engagement, deeper thinking, and a sense of autonomy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers must be willing to relinquish some control and trust students to make appropriate choices. Requires careful planning to ensure choices are aligned with learning objectives. Requires resources and materials to support a variety of choices.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not implemented thoughtfully, student choice can lead to disengagement or a lack of focus. Some students may struggle to make choices effectively. Requires careful monitoring and support from the teacher.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, foster independence, promote deeper thinking, develop self-directed learning skills, increase motivation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation by giving students a sense of control over their learning. Allows students to connect learning to their interests. Supports self-regulation and self-directed learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of choices to cater to different learning styles and interests. Provide support and guidance to help students make informed choices. Allow students to reflect on their choices and their impact on learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement and motivation levels. Collect student feedback on their choices. Assess student learning outcomes to determine the impact of choice on academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that student choice can increase motivation, engagement, and achievement. When students feel a sense of ownership over their learning, they are more likely to invest time and effort. A meta-analysis of research on choice in the classroom found a positive effect on student achievement (Patall et al., 2008).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A math teacher allows students to choose which strategy to use to solve a problem. A writing teacher allows students to choose their topic and writing style.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student demonstrations involve learners showcasing their understanding of a topic or skill through a performance, presentation, or hands-on activity. These demonstrations are incorporated as components of an assessment plan to evaluate what learners have learned.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires clear learning objectives, well-defined assessment criteria, and sufficient time for learners to prepare and present. Instructors must provide constructive feedback and create a supportive environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Assessment can be subjective and influenced by presentation skills. May not comprehensively assess all aspects of learning. Requires careful planning and scaffolding to ensure all learners can participate effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, adaptable for K–12, higher education, and professional training. Particularly useful in subjects involving practical skills, performance, and creative expression.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assess knowledge application, evaluate practical skills, promote active learning, encourage self-reflection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables learners to actively apply knowledge, promotes deeper understanding, provides instructors with direct evidence of learning, fosters confidence and communication skills. Showcases practical skills and creativity, and offers an opportunity for self-reflection and feedback.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Demonstrations can be tailored to learner interests, learning styles, and skill levels. Flexible formats allow learners to choose presentation methods, topics, and assessment criteria.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance against predefined criteria. Analyze depth and accuracy of presented content. Measure audience engagement and understanding of the demonstration.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increased engagement: Research indicates active learning and demonstrations enhance student interest and motivation. Enhanced comprehension: Studies show learners retain information more effectively through application and demonstration. Improved communication skills: Practicing presentations bolsters learners’ communication abilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves asking for student feedback to inform your teaching practice and improve engagement. Regularly solicit feedback from students to understand what works and what doesn't, especially when starting a new grading period or introducing new content. Be mindful of how you ask questions to encourage honest and constructive criticism and consider providing sentence starters or multiple-choice options to make it easier for students to provide feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A way to solicit feedback from students, a willingness to listen to student feedback, and a willingness to make changes based on student feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a willingness to be open to criticism.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve teaching practice, increase student engagement, foster a positive classroom environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows teachers to improve their teaching practice by soliciting feedback from students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use a variety of methods to solicit feedback from students. They can also provide sentence starters or multiple-choice options to make it easier for students to provide feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student engagement, a more positive classroom environment, and improved teaching practice.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of student feedback.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher sets up an anonymous feedback box or online platform to allow students to share their thoughts without fear of retribution.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In this approach, learners build their own game around a specific course topic or principle. Learners identify learning objectives, design game mechanics, and create rules, fostering creativity and critical thinking while reinforcing content knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Instructor guidance and resources. Time for game design and development. Opportunities for testing and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be time-consuming. Requires instructor expertise in game design. May be challenging for learners with limited technical skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective in technical and design-focused classes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of course topics. Develop creativity and problem-solving skills. Promote learner engagement and ownership.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes deeper understanding through active design. Fosters creativity and critical thinking. Increases engagement and motivation through ownership.

docs.title: Personalization
