docs.text: • Learners can choose topics and design games that align with their interests. Instructors can provide guidance and support to meet individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality and accuracy of the game's content. Assess the creativity and effectiveness of the game mechanics. Gather learner feedback on the learning experience.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • By creating a game learners are actively engaging with the content in a deeper way that encourages retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Engineering students designing a game to teach middle schoolers about engineering. History students creating a board game based on a historical event.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student Hand Signals is a strategy where learners use non-verbal cues to indicate their understanding or opinion after listening to a statement. Instructors present information, such as a statement, and learners respond using pre-defined hand signals (e.g., one finger for agree, two fingers for disagree, three fingers for undecided or question). This allows whole-class participation and provides a "voice" for learners who may be shy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear explanation of hand signals, appropriate content for discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not capture the nuances of learners' opinions, some learners may feel pressured to conform

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially useful for shy learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage active listening, facilitate whole-class participation, provide a non-verbal means of expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows for quick assessment of understanding, encourages participation from all learners, provides a discreet way to express opinions

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can use different hand signals to represent varying levels of understanding or agreement

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the distribution of hand signals to gauge overall understanding, track participation rates of shy learners.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that non-verbal cues can enhance communication and participation in the classroom. Practitioner experience shows that Student Hand Signals encourages active listening and provides a voice for all learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fifth-grade classroom using hand signals to respond to a former president's statement about war. Resource: Rebecca Alber, Edutopia

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Throughout the year, teachers can have personal math conferences with the students. Students bring their formative assessments to the conference and reflect on their progress. The teachers and students work together to find areas that need strengthening and write a personal goal related to specific academic concepts. Students may decide to bring their math journal to their math conference.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Formative assessments, time for personal math conferences, and a way for teachers and students to work together to find areas that need strengthening and write personal goals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to have personal math conferences with each student.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reflect on progress, identify areas for strengthening, write personal goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows students to reflect on their progress, provides a way for teachers and students to work together to find areas that need strengthening, and encourages students to write personal goals.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can have personal math conferences with the students. They can also work with the students to write personal goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student understanding, increased student communication, and deeper reflection on learning experiences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of student led math conferences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher has a personal math conference with a student. The student brings their formative assessments to the conference and reflects on their progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student models are examples of writing produced by other students, typically curated by instructors and made available for learners to reference. They provide concrete illustrations of effective writing strategies, structures, and techniques within a specific context, such as a particular genre or assignment. Student models help learners understand expectations, develop critical analysis skills, and improve their own writing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Collection of well-written student models, structured analysis activities, instructor guidance to ensure learners focus on relevant aspects of the models.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may blindly imitate models without critical thinking. Models might not align with all writing contexts or learner needs. Over-reliance on models can stifle creativity and originality.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for K–12 and higher education students learning composition and rhetoric

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide concrete examples of effective writing, enhance understanding of expectations, foster critical analysis skills, improve writing quality

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear and relatable examples of effective writing. Supports understanding of assignment expectations. Enhances analytical skills through comparison and critique. Promotes self-improvement through observation and imitation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Models can be tailored to different genres, skill levels, and individual learner needs. Learners can select models based on their specific writing challenges or interests. Flexible analysis methods accommodate varied learning styles.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Teaching
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in learner writing quality as evidenced by better structure, clarity, and use of techniques observed in the models. Increased self-awareness and critical analysis skills demonstrated through reflective writing and peer feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing student models helps learners understand expectations and see what effective writing looks like in practice. Observing and analyzing models helps learners internalize effective writing practices, leading to improved writing outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An online platform provides a collection of student models organized by grade level and genre, such as explanatory, persuasive, and narrative writing. Students can scroll through the list or search for a specific type of writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student portfolio creation involves students selecting and organizing their best work samples to demonstrate their progress, reflect on their learning, and set goals. Portfolios can include a variety of artifacts, such as written assignments, projects, artwork, and reflections. The process of creating a portfolio encourages students to take ownership of their learning, identify strengths and weaknesses, and communicate their growth to others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires dedicated time for students to select work samples, reflect on their learning, and organize their portfolios. Teachers need to provide guidance and feedback to support the portfolio creation process. Various portfolio formats can be used (e.g., hanging files, file folders, digital platforms).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort for both students and teachers. Some students may struggle with self-assessment or portfolio organization. Portfolios can become overwhelming if not managed effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, adaptable for various subject areas and learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-reflection, encourage student ownership, demonstrate progress, showcase strengths, and support goal setting.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters self-assessment skills, enhances metacognition, provides a comprehensive view of student learning, and supports meaningful communication with parents and teachers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable for different grade levels by adjusting the complexity of portfolio requirements. Flexible formats allow for diverse work samples and individualized reflection prompts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Practice
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and quality of student reflections, variety of work samples, evidence of progress over time, and engagement in portfolio creation process.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Student portfolios enhance self-reflection, promote ownership of learning, and improve communication with parents and teachers. They provide a comprehensive view of student growth and achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Wildwood IB World Magnet School uses a student portfolio manual to structure portfolio collection and reflection. Encouraging learners to create digital portfolios to showcase strengths and progress.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After completing a collaborative problem-solving task, groups project their work and present their final responses to the class. Learners take turns explaining how they arrived at their answers and why they believe they accomplished the task of building the best answer they could. This practice enhances communication skills, reinforces learning, and builds confidence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Projector or whiteboard, collaborative work samples, time for presentations

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be hesitant to present in front of the class. Requires a supportive classroom environment to encourage participation and constructive feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 3-6, adaptable for other grade levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance communication skills, reinforce learning, build confidence, encourage reflection on problem-solving process

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities to practice oral communication, reinforces understanding of concepts through explanation, builds confidence by sharing work with peers, encourages reflection on the problem-solving process

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Presentation format can be adapted to suit different learning styles and abilities. Learners can choose which aspects of their work to highlight and how they want to present it.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe presentations and assess the clarity and accuracy of explanations, evaluate student reflections on their problem-solving process, track student participation and engagement

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners improve their communication skills and reinforce their understanding of the concepts. Presenting their work to the class builds confidence and encourages reflection on the problem-solving process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A 6th-grade class completes a collaborative science project and then presents their findings to the class. They explain the steps they took, the challenges they faced, and how they arrived at their conclusions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors begin the year having the learners do an 'All About Me' presentation, which involves sharing facts about themselves and including pictures or video. The instructor should also present first, in order to model what they're looking for. This also allows the learners to get to know the instructor on a more personal level. This can be modified to suit any age range or subject.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time needed to prep the presentation, access to presentation tools. This strategy will also require presentation time during class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may be hesitant to share too much about themselves for privacy reasons. Requires time and thought, and can be difficult to execute effectively without proper planning.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance instructor-learner relationships through sharing and connection

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows instructors and learners to get to know one another. Helps the learners understand the instructor on a more personal level. Can be modified to suit any age range or subject.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can showcase their own interests, experiences, and culture through the presentation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved instructor-learner relationships, increased class engagement, and enhanced understanding of learners' interests.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that personalizing content and curriculum can enhance motivation and engagement in learners, fostering a sense of relevance and connection to the material. This can increase Motivation in adult learners as it incorporates relevant real-world application and enhances learner autonomy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on using student reflection to leverage strengths and address challenges related to responsible decision-making, which is the ability to make constructive choices about one’s behavior and social interactions in an ethically responsible way.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of student strengths and challenges, targeted strategies, and student reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a supportive classroom environment and careful facilitation to ensure students engage thoughtfully with the reflection prompts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who may have strengths and/or challenges in responsible decision-making.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop students' ability to make responsible and ethical decisions by leveraging their strengths and addressing their challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students become more aware of their decision-making processes, consider the consequences of their actions, and make more ethical choices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies are tailored to the individual student's strengths and challenges, using graphic organizers, visual representations, and real-life scenarios.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • individual reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the use of ethical tools to assess growth and reflect on whether the decisions made were ethical.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports ethical competencies alongside social and emotional learning and part of providing an education for the whole child.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Student self-knowledge involves helping learners understand their strengths, interests, and areas for growth as learners. It is a foundational element of self-advocacy, as individuals cannot effectively advocate for themselves if they do not understand their own needs and preferences. This practice helps to intentionally incorporate voice and choice into learning experiences, which is critical for making learning meaningful and relevant.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires the use of self-assessment tools, opportunities for reflection, and a supportive classroom environment that values learner voice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may struggle with self-assessment or may be hesitant to share their thoughts and feelings. Educators need to create a safe and supportive environment to encourage honest reflection.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in grades 3-8, but applicable to all ages, who need to take more responsibility for their learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate learners' understanding of their strengths, interests, and areas for growth, and support the development of self-awareness and self-advocacy skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases learner motivation and engagement, empowers learners to make informed choices about their learning, and promotes a sense of ownership and agency.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by using different types of self-assessment tools, providing a variety of learning options, and tailoring instruction to individual learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learners' self-assessment skills, track their use of self-advocacy strategies, and gather feedback on their experiences with different learning options.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that self-awareness and self-advocacy are linked to improved academic outcomes, increased self-esteem, and greater success in post-secondary education and employment. (Edutopia article on Getting Students on the Road to Self-Advocacy)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using learning interest inventories to identify areas of interest and ways of finding joy in learning, exit tickets to identify whether learners met the daily learning objective(s), progress monitoring to identify skills mastered and concepts needing additional attention, and peer and self-assessment to review work against a set of criteria.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An adult (educator, administrator, or school leader) follows a student throughout their school day to observe their experiences, interactions, and environment firsthand. The goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the student's perspective, identify challenges, and inform strategies to increase engagement, motivation, and learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A willing student and their parent/guardian, a shadowing protocol or template, a scheduled day for observation, and a commitment to objective note-taking and reflection. Access to digital platforms for recording observations can enhance efficiency.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time commitment, relies on the observer's ability to remain objective and avoid influencing the student's behavior, and may not capture the full complexity of a student's experience if conducted only once.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, administrators, school leaders, and product designers seeking to understand student experiences and improve learning environments, particularly for students of color, English learners, or those who may be overlooked.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand students’ lived experiences, identify areas for improvement in teaching practices and school environment, gather qualitative data to inform equity initiatives, increase educator empathy and awareness of student needs.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time qualitative data, uncovers hidden challenges and disparities, promotes empathy and perspective-taking, informs targeted interventions and support, and can reveal biases or unintended consequences of existing practices.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by focusing on specific student populations or learning goals. Protocols and templates can be modified to address particular areas of concern, such as academic needs, social interactions, or access to resources.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection
  • Problem Presentation
  • Inquiry and Research
  • Solution Development
  • Question Formulation
  • Knowledge Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observations of student engagement, interactions, and access to resources; educator reflections on insights gained; changes in teaching practices or school policies; student feedback on implemented changes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that student shadowing can uncover disparities in access to learning opportunities, promote more equitable practices, and improve student outcomes. It also enhances educator awareness of student needs and challenges, fostering a more supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A principal shadows a seventh-grade ESL student and discovers they are only given two opportunities to speak the entire day, despite Title III language programs in place. A teacher shadows a quiet student and finds they are disengaged due to excessive sitting and passive listening in class. Resources: Shadow a Student Challenge Toolkit.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Educators spend the majority of a school day shadowing a student to gain real-time qualitative data about their experiences. The key is to stay objective, making low-inference observations without interpretation or judgment. Notes are taken on body language, facial expressions, and interactions with teachers and fellow students. This raw data is then analyzed to pinpoint areas that need to be addressed, such as instructional practices or biases.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Student Shadowing Template, dedicated school day, objective observation skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires significant time commitment, may be subject to observer bias, may not be representative of all students' experiences

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • School leaders and educators seeking to improve their understanding of student experiences and address equity issues

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand students' lived experiences, identify areas for improvement in teaching practices and school climate, address racial equity issues

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides direct observation of student experiences, uncovers surprising data, reveals hidden biases, pinpoints areas that need to be addressed

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The choice of student to shadow can be based on specific learning goals or areas of interest.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in instructional practices, addressing of biases, improved student engagement and outcomes

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps educators understand students' lived experiences, identify areas for improvement in teaching practices and school climate, and address racial equity issues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A school principal shadowed a seventh-grade ESL student and discovered that she only had two opportunities to speak the entire day, despite Title III language programs in place.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A veteran teacher or coach shadows one or two students for a couple of days to gain insights into their experiences. Key takeaways often include recognizing that students sit all day, listen passively for 90% of the time, and may not be held accountable for participating in class. The goal is to understand the students' perspective and adjust teaching practices accordingly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time to shadow students, awareness of key areas to observe (sitting time, passive listening, participation)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be representative of all students' experiences, requires willingness to adjust teaching practices

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school teachers and coaches

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand students' experiences, improve teaching practices, increase student engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides direct observation of student experiences, reveals areas where teaching practices can be improved, increases awareness of student needs

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The choice of students to shadow can be based on specific learning goals or areas of interest.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in teaching practices, increased student engagement, improved student outcomes

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps teachers understand students' experiences, improve teaching practices, and increase student engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A veteran teacher shadowed two students and realized that they were sitting all day and listening passively for 90% of the time. This led the teacher to incorporate more collaborative activities and movement into the classroom.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A school leader spends time shadowing a student to gather qualitative data about their lived experiences in the school. This involves objective observation and note-taking on facts (body language, interactions, behaviors) without interpretation or judgment. The goal is to uncover truths about the school environment from the student's perspective and identify areas needing improvement (e.g., instructional practices, biases).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Shadowing template, dedicated time to shadow the student, and willingness to objectively observe and reflect.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful note-taking to avoid bias, may not capture the full picture of a student's experience, and can be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • School leaders seeking to improve equity and school climate for students, especially students of color or multilingual learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand student lived experiences, uncover inequities, inform changes in instructional practices

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-time qualitative data about student experiences, helps identify areas of inequity, and informs targeted interventions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • School leaders choose a student based on specific criteria (e.g., race, language) to align with their learning goals and improvement efforts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Observation/Shadowing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Identification of areas needing improvement in instructional practices and school climate. Changes in school policies and practices based on shadowing data.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides valuable qualitative data that can inform equity work, helps uncover surprising data about student experiences, and promotes targeted interventions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Direct, guided practice was found to be an effective instructional strategy, especially for students with low skills. Many adult education students are not familiar with different types of written genres; the explicit study of formats, styles, tones, vocabularies, sentence structures, etc., can provide new frames and words for their own work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Written models, guided practice, feedback on imitation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of models, may limit creativity

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers, especially students with low skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing skills, enhance genre awareness, promote effective writing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides models for writing, enhances genre awareness, promotes effective writing

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Models can be tailored to different genres and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased genre awareness, greater writing effectiveness

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • The explicit study of formats, styles, tones, vocabularies, sentence structures, etc., can provide new frames and words for their own work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reinforce and clarify concepts, making sure information is both understood and remembered. Break content into smaller pieces, explain a part of the concept, then do a quick recap using different words, images, or examples. Include interactive activities lets students apply what they’ve learned in practical ways.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tools for creating summaries and recaps. A clear understanding of the key concepts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Summaries and recaps can be ineffective if not well-designed. Overuse of summaries and recaps can become repetitive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who need extra support

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding and retention, reinforce key concepts

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Clarifies concepts and helps learners see the information from different perspectives.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor summaries and recaps to learners' individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Continuous Review
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to recall and explain the key concepts after the summary or recap. Evaluate their ability to apply the concepts in new situations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using summaries and recaps can make teaching concepts a more dynamic and effective experience, ensuring that students really understand each idea and can use it in the future.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Splitting concepts into smaller, simpler sections, recapping using different words, images, or examples, and adding questions, reflective exercises, or small challenges.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicit teaching of the elements of a summary of a text leads to improved ability and increased confidence in writing summaries. Having learners write summaries about what they read is a key recommendation from Writing to Read. In addition, summarization is an increasingly common expectation as students advance in their education and are assigned more complex texts to read and comprehend. Connect this instruction and practice with increasingly complex texts to reinforce learners’ comprehension as well as writing skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in summarization, complex texts for practice, feedback on summaries

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant time and effort, effectiveness depends on text complexity and instruction quality

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers, especially those needing to summarize complex texts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve summarization skills, enhance reading comprehension, build confidence

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves ability to identify key information, enhances reading comprehension, reinforces writing skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Summarization tasks can be tailored to different text types and reading levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved summarization quality, increased reading comprehension, greater confidence

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners improve in the ability and confidence in writing summaries

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Summarizing involves integrating important information from a text or problem to create a concise overview. In math, this means justifying the answer and evaluating the success of the plan for solving the problem. It also includes explaining the problem-solving strategies used.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A clear understanding of the topic and the ability to identify key information.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional support for learners who struggle with identifying key information.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who benefit from structured approaches to learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, consolidate information, and improve retention.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners consolidate information and improve retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different levels of scaffolding and support for summarizing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, better retention, and the ability to create concise summaries.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners consolidate information and improve retention, leading to better understanding of the material.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Asking learners to summarize the main points of a text or the steps taken to solve a problem.

docs.title: Summative Assessment to Measure Learning Over Time
Description
docs.text: Interim and summative assessments both measure learning over time. Interim assessments show individual student progress toward a set of standards. Summative assessments compare a student or group of students against a set of standards.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Summative assessments, performance assessments, clear standards, and consideration of technology access.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be limited by what can be assessed in the available time, and may not account for varying access to technology.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in online or blended learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Measure learning over time, show individual student progress, compare student performance against standards, evaluate the efficacy of instruction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Measures learning over time, provides a comprehensive understanding of student progress, and allows for comparison among students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Determining what to prioritize based on the R.E.A.L guide, making use of performance assessment, taking into account differing access to technology.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Test scores, performance assessment results, and demonstrated skills in real-life contexts.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Provides a measure of student learning over time, individual progress, and the efficacy of instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instead of having supplies scattered all over the place, keep them all in a shower caddy or cleaning supply caddy. Help kids organize supplies by function (like pencils and markers, and scissors and glue). Get a supply caddy that has a handle so it can be stored when not in use and carried to a homework spot when needed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Shower caddy or cleaning supply caddy, learning supplies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires initial setup and organization. May not be suitable for large quantities of supplies. Dependent on the learner maintaining the organization system.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with organization, learners of all ages

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve organization of learning materials, reduce clutter, enhance efficiency in accessing supplies

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a designated place for supplies, reduces time spent searching for materials, promotes independence and responsibility.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Caddy can be customized to fit the learner's specific supplies and needs. Supplies can be organized by subject, task, or type.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner's ability to quickly access supplies. Track the cleanliness and organization of the learning space. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the caddy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Organized learning environments have been shown to improve focus and reduce distractions. A designated supply caddy can promote efficiency and independence in learning tasks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use a shower caddy to organize pencils, markers, scissors, and glue. Store the caddy in a designated spot when not in use.

docs.title: Support Decoding of Text, Mathematical Notation, and Symbols
Description
docs.text: Ensuring that text and symbols do not impede the learning goal involves providing strategies and tools to help learners decode and understand written and symbolic information. This includes explicit instruction in phonics, decoding strategies, and mathematical notation. It also involves providing assistive technologies, such as screen readers and text-to-speech software, to support learners with reading difficulties. The aim is to remove barriers to learning by making information more accessible.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to appropriate instructional materials and assistive technologies. Instructors need to be trained in effective decoding strategies and assistive technology.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time and resources. Some learners may be resistant to using assistive technology. It's essential to provide support and encouragement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those with reading disabilities, English language learners, or those new to mathematics; suitable for K–12, higher education, and adult learning environments

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading fluency, improve comprehension, support mathematical literacy, promote accessible learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports reading fluency by providing explicit instruction in decoding strategies, improves comprehension by helping learners understand written information, supports mathematical literacy by clarifying mathematical notation, and promotes accessible learning by catering to diverse reading and learning needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide individualized instruction in phonics and decoding strategies. Offer assistive technologies, such as screen readers and text-to-speech software. Use visual aids and graphic organizers to clarify complex concepts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner reading fluency and comprehension. Assess learner understanding of mathematical notation and symbols. Track improvements in reading and mathematical skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that explicit instruction in decoding strategies and assistive technology can improve reading and mathematical skills. Studies show that assistive technology can improve academic outcomes for learners with disabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing explicit instruction in phonics and decoding strategies. Using screen readers and text-to-speech software. Using visual aids to clarify mathematical notation.

docs.title: Support for Decoding Text, Mathematical Notation, and Symbols
Description
docs.text: Ensuring that text and symbols do not impede the learning goal by providing necessary support for decoding. This involves offering tools and strategies to help learners interpret and understand text, mathematical notation, and other symbolic representations. It also ensures that symbols and text do not distract from learning goals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Decoding tools, visual aids, mnemonics, and simplified explanations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of tools and strategies to ensure they are appropriate for the learner's needs. Some learners may become overly reliant on decoding tools.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with reading disabilities (e.g., dyslexia), math difficulties, and those encountering unfamiliar symbols or notations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve decoding skills, enhance comprehension, reduce cognitive load, ensure symbols and text support learning goals

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by providing support for decoding. Enhances comprehension by improving understanding of symbols and notations. Supports learners with reading and math difficulties.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide decoding tools (e.g., phonics instruction, calculators). Offer visual aids and mnemonics to support memory. Break down complex symbols into simpler components.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner decoding skills through reading and math assessments. Monitor learner use of decoding tools and strategies. Gather feedback on the effectiveness of decoding support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved decoding skills: Studies show that providing support for decoding can significantly improve reading and math skills, particularly for learners with disabilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Independent reading involves students selecting and reading texts at their independent reading level or texts easy enough to decode and understand without much effort. This practice allows students to apply reading strategies learned in more structured instructional contexts and fosters a love of reading. Effective independent reading includes guided choices, teaching students how to select books at an appropriate reading level, and providing time for teachers to confer with students. To maximize impact, balance student choice with appropriate text demands and align independent reading activities with skills practiced during read-aloud, shared reading, and guided reading sessions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A classroom library with a diverse collection of books, dedicated time for independent reading (15-30 minutes), explicit instruction on book selection and reading procedures, tools for conferencing with students, and activities to engage students with their books.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be ineffective if there is little or no structure. Students may not make optimal book choices without guidance. Struggling readers may not improve if challenged with difficult texts. Requires careful planning and implementation to balance student choice and text demands.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Practice reading skills, develop reading fluency and comprehension, exercise choice in reading material, cultivate reading interests, build background knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides opportunities to practice reading strategies independently, fosters a love of reading through choice, increases reading fluency and comprehension, builds background knowledge across various topics, and encourages self-regulation in reading habits.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer a variety of reading options including multicultural books of various genres and reading levels. Guide students in selecting appropriate books based on their reading level and interests. Offer a read-aloud option for non-fluent readers. Implement book talks and sharing sessions to maintain accountability and engagement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application
  • Integration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the quantity and quality of books read. Observe student engagement and participation in book-related activities. Track reading fluency and comprehension improvements over time. Collect feedback from students on their reading experiences and interests.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show a correlation between time spent reading and reading achievement. Provides ready access to books, allows for autonomy, increases engagement and motivation, reduces summer reading loss, and prevents diminished reading habits at the secondary level.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identifying and supporting students who have learning strengths or challenges related to self-regulation. Self-regulation involves the ability to alter and regulate emotional and behavioral responses. It addresses how to leverage student strengths to support learning, rather than focusing solely on deficits. Strategies include scaffolding, journaling, and mindfulness techniques to help students manage their responses in emotionally safe contexts and build metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of student strengths and challenges, implementation of strategies like scaffolding, journaling, and mindfulness techniques, and assessment of student reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful observation and understanding of individual student needs. Strategies may not be effective for all students. Requires time and effort to implement and monitor effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students with varying degrees of strengths and challenges related to self-regulation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop self-regulation skills, enhance emotional and behavioral control, and improve metacognitive awareness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides strategies for managing emotional responses, develops metacognitive awareness, and creates an emotionally safe learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Strategies can be adapted based on individual student strengths and needs. Journaling can be tailored to different age levels and learning styles. Scaffolding can be adjusted to provide appropriate levels of support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and emotional responses, assess student reflection through journal entries, and evaluate the effectiveness of strategies used.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that self-regulation skills are crucial for academic performance and emotional well-being. Strategies like mindfulness and journaling have been shown to improve self-regulation skills in students.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using journaling to develop metacognitive awareness, incorporating mindfulness techniques to manage emotional impulses, and scaffolding to help students manage responses in emotionally safe contexts. Resources: Learner Variability Project | Digital Promise Global, Pause, Refocus, Assess: Meditation in the Classroom | Adam Kuranishi, Edutopia.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A free math app with a playful interface and characters to help kids expand their math skills and knowledge. The app offers 12 different levels of play including 7 levels for addition and 5 different levels for multiplication. Plates of sushi with their respective numbers are placed by a chef on the counter. The player makes the right combination of the numbers on the plates, and tries to achieve a target number which is carried by a sushi monster. In case the combination of the numbers is right, the sushi is gobbled up by the monster. Each round, consisting of 14 target numbers, creates an engaging way to deal with numbers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to the Sushi Monster app on a compatible device.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Limited to addition and multiplication.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expand math skills, especially in addition and multiplication.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engaging and fun interface, immediate feedback, playful characters.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • 12 different levels of play, including 7 for addition and 5 for multiplication.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track progress and completion rates in the app.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Offers a fun way for kids to engage with numbers and calculations, increasing math skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Kids expanding their addition and multiplication skills using the app's playful interface and characters.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teach children the six basic syllable types and how they affect spelling. For example, once children learn about the open, closed, and consonant –le syllable types, they can reliably predict when they should double consonants in words that end with a consonant –le syllable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Word lists, syllable charts, direct instruction

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires explicit and systematic instruction

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grade 3 students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance reading fluency, develop understanding of syllable structure

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners decode multisyllable words, improves spelling accuracy, supports reading fluency

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word lists can be adapted to target specific syllable types. Instruction can be adapted for one-on-one or group instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess accuracy in dividing words into syllables. Monitor progress in spelling and reading skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • If children learn the six basic syllable types and how they affect spelling, children’s spelling is greatly improved

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A T-chart is a graphic organizer shaped like the letter T, with a horizontal line at the top to signify a broad category and a vertical line that allows learners to compare attributes of a concept, organism, or phenomenon. With a topic as the title on the horizontal line, learners compare two aspects of the topic on each side of the vertical line. These can be mutually exclusive, such as comparing mammals and non-mammals or insects and spiders, or they can compare two types of spiders with different characteristics.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • T-chart template (either pre-made or self-drawn). Materials for recording information (e.g., paper, pencils, markers). Topic for comparison.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be too simplistic for complex topics with multiple variables. Requires learners to be able to identify relevant attributes for comparison.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those needing support in comparing and contrasting information or ideas.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Compare and contrast concepts, organisms, or phenomena. Identify similarities and differences. Organize and analyze information.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured way to compare two aspects of a topic. Helps learners organize and analyze information. Facilitates identification of similarities and differences. Supports visual learners.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be used with a wide range of topics and subject areas. Can be adapted for individual, paired, or group work. The complexity of the information can be adjusted based on the learner's needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy and completeness of the information recorded on the T-chart. Ability to identify key similarities and differences between the two aspects being compared. Clarity and organization of the information presented.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Charts and other graphic organizers have been found to be effective with students who are struggling with learning content at their grade level or who have difficulty learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a T-chart to compare mammals and non-mammals. Using a T-chart to compare two types of spiders with different characteristics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tactile toys and fidgets are self-regulation tools that promote movement and tactile input to help with attention, focus, and sensory processing. They can decrease fidgeting, attention issues, and behavior problems by meeting sensory needs and developing self-regulation skills. Examples include squeeze balls, key chains, spinning toys, pop-its, and squishies. They are used to calm down when overwhelmed or to focus and are not just toys.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of appropriate tactile toys or fidgets. Clear understanding of their purpose as a self-regulation tool, not just a toy. Establishment of rules for when and how to use them. A designated spot for storage.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be misused as toys, distracting the user or others. May not be suitable for all environments or activities. Requires proper guidance and rules to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals who struggle with attention, focus, and sensory processing challenges, including those with tactile defensiveness or sensory-seeking behaviors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve focus and attention, calm down when overwhelmed, develop self-regulation skills, enhance sensory processing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides tactile and movement input to help regulate emotions, behavior, and attention. Can be used in various settings, such as classrooms, homes, or movie theaters. Offers a discreet way to manage sensory needs.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different types of fidgets cater to various sensory preferences (visual, auditory, tactile). Users can choose fidgets based on their individual needs and the context of use. Rules can be adapted based on individual and environmental needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in focus, attention, and behavior when using fidgets. Track frequency of use and effectiveness in different situations. Monitor feedback from the user regarding their experience and preferences.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies and anecdotal evidence suggest that fidgets can improve focus and attention in individuals with ADHD and sensory processing issues. By providing tactile and movement input, fidgets can help regulate emotions and behavior, leading to better learning and performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An elementary school integrates fidgets into classrooms to support student attention and sensory integration. A tactile cube (Skoog) allows learners to create music through touch, providing immediate sensory input and acoustic feedback.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing tactile toys can help awaken sensory receptors, which may decrease fidgeting, attention issues, and behavior problems. Tactile stimulation is important for helping learners regulate their emotions, behavior, and focus. Tactile toys can be introduced into a learner's routine for calming and focus.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tactile toys and a routine for their use. Understanding of individual sensory needs to select appropriate toys.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective for all learners, and some toys may be distracting if not used as intended. It's important to differentiate between using a tactile toy as a tool versus using it as a toy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with sensory processing challenges, including those who are hypersensitive to textures or sensory seekers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve sensory integration, regulate emotions, behavior, attention, and focus

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a means for learners to calm their bodies and brains for better learning. Helps learners who are hypersensitive or sensory seekers to regulate their needs and improve concentration.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tactile toys can be chosen based on individual sensory preferences, either providing calming input for hypersensitive learners or stimulating input for sensory seekers.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observation of reduced fidgeting, improved attention span, and fewer behavior problems. Monitoring of learner's emotional regulation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Anecdotal evidence suggests that tactile toys can support sensory integration, leading to improved emotional regulation and focus.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include toys with tactile elements, such as those found in the Integrated Movement Center membership. Watch how this elementary school has integrated fidgets into their classrooms to support student Attention and Sensory Integration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A designated space in the classroom where children can take a moment to decompress, reset, and self-regulate their emotions and behaviors. It's not a consequence (unlike a 'Time Out'), but a chance for students to recognize their emotions, understand the impact of their behavior on others, and learn self-management skills. The station includes a basket of materials (stress balls, timers, notebooks, etc.) and a comfortable place to sit and reflect.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Designated space in the classroom, basket of calming materials (stress balls, notebooks, etc.), reflection prompts (written or visual), and consistent implementation. Teachers need to introduce the station and model its use.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If overused, may indicate deeper needs that require a different intervention. Requires consistent teaching and modeling to ensure students understand its purpose and use it effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Primarily K–5 students, but adaptable for older students with social-emotional needs.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students recognize and manage their emotions, self-regulate their behavior, and understand the impact of their actions on others.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Empowers students to self-regulate without constant adult intervention, reduces classroom disruptions, and promotes emotional intelligence. Provides a safe space for students to calm down and refocus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The station can be personalized with different materials based on student needs (e.g., visual prompts for non-readers). The reflection process can be guided by an adult until the student can work independently.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior before and after using the station for changes in emotional state and behavior. Collect student reflections on their experience at the station. Track frequency of use to identify students who may need additional support.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduces repeat behaviors and classroom disruptions. Empowers students to take responsibility for their emotions and actions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A first-grade teacher creates a Take A Break station with stress balls, drawing materials, and picture prompts. Students can go to the station when they feel overwhelmed, work through the reflection process, and return to class when ready.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Create an atmosphere that enables teachers to meet the needs of all students. Know students to reach them and remember that when a student comes in hungry or tired from a challenging environment, he or she may not be in the best position to succeed. How we act and react will determine whether we reach that student and their peers. Create the environment and personify the culture, and reduce the empathic mindset gap between teachers and students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment to building relationships, awareness of student backgrounds, supportive school policies

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort, may be challenging in large classes or with limited resources

docs.title: Target Learners

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Personalization

docs.title: Talk About Real-Life Challenges and Situations
Description
docs.text: Facilitating discussions about the challenges learners are facing and how they feel about those situations. This involves asking questions that encourage reflection and focusing on the positive aspects of the situation, what went right, and what can be learned.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Facilitator to guide the discussion. Safe and supportive environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are not comfortable sharing their feelings. Requires a skilled facilitator to manage the discussion and ensure that it remains positive and constructive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who need support in navigating difficult situations and developing resilience.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop learners' ability to process challenges in a positive and constructive manner.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe space for learners to share their experiences and feelings. Encourages reflection and learning from setbacks. Fosters a sense of community and support.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor the discussion to learners' specific challenges and concerns. Provide opportunities for individual reflection and group sharing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to articulate their feelings and identify positive aspects of challenging situations. Self-reported changes in mindset and behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that social support and positive reframing can help individuals cope with stress and build resilience. Open discussions can foster a sense of community and promote mental well-being.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Ask questions like, “What can you learn from that situation?”, “What could the positive to that be?”, “What did you do right?”, and “How could that help you for the future?” Focus on the positive, what went right, and what can be learned instead of dwelling on the negative.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Talk moves are sentence frames we supply to our learners that help them express ideas and interact with one another in respectful, academically appropriate ways. From kindergarten all the way through college, learners can benefit from explicit instruction in the skills of summarizing another person’s argument before presenting an alternate view, asking clarifying questions, and expressing agreement or partial agreement with the stance of another participant. Talk moves can be incorporated into any of the other discussion formats listed here.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a set of sentence frames or talk moves, a discussion topic, and clear instructions for learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel artificial or restrictive to some learners, requires careful modeling and practice to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all ages and subject areas, particularly effective for promoting respectful communication and enhancing critical thinking

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote respectful and academically appropriate communication, enhance critical thinking skills, encourage active listening and perspective-taking, build a positive classroom culture

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides explicit instruction in communication skills, promotes respectful and academically appropriate communication, enhances critical thinking skills, encourages active listening and perspective-taking, builds a positive classroom culture

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Sentence frames can be tailored to learners' needs and the specific content being discussed. Teachers can provide scaffolding and support for learners who struggle with communication skills.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion

  • Argumentation

docs.title: Assessment Evidence

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances communication skills, promotes respectful and academically appropriate communication, improves critical thinking skills

docs.title: Talking to Young Children About Race and Racism
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves parents and caregivers initiating conversations with young children about race, racism, and anti-racism. It emphasizes the importance of being honest, specific, and trustworthy in these discussions to raise the next generation to confront racial injustice. It utilizes resources such as watch and play guides, discussion guides, and commitment activities to facilitate meaningful conversations. It includes using media, stories, and books to talk about race and racism.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Watch and play guides, discussion guides, commitment activities, media resources, books, and a safe and supportive environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for parents and caregivers who are uncomfortable or lack experience in discussing race and racism. Requires ongoing commitment to anti-racist education and advocacy.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Young children (3 months to 8 years), parents, caregivers, and educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Introduce children to the many cultures and people of our world, address racial identity and sense of belonging, develop positive feelings about themselves, effectively manage and heal when treated unfairly, and promote anti-racist behavior.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Addresses race and racism in an age-appropriate way, promotes understanding and empathy, encourages positive racial identity, fosters a sense of belonging, and equips children with the tools to stand up for themselves and others.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Resources can be adapted based on the child's age, understanding, and cultural background. Parents and caregivers can select resources that align with their values and beliefs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of engagement in conversations, analyze children's questions and comments, track changes in attitudes and behaviors, and gather feedback from parents and caregivers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Early conversations about race and racism can reduce prejudice, increase empathy, and promote social justice. Children who are taught to understand and confront racial injustice are more likely to become anti-racist advocates and allies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Parents using the PBS KIDS Talk About Race & Racism program to have conversations with their children about race and racial justice. Families brainstorming a list of ideas for standing up against racism as a family. Reading children's books with strong Black characters to encourage conversations about race and diversity.

docs.text: Tailoring message content for different populations, such as non-native English speakers, families with different cultural backgrounds, and those with students in special education. Schools should also offer modes of two-way communication between educators and families.

docs.title: Affordances

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The "Targeted Networking" strategy involves focusing on specific activities, groups, or individuals who align with one's interests and goals in order to build meaningful relationships and connections. It includes doing substantive research on prospective contacts and identifying shared interests or purposes to facilitate more authentic and mutually beneficial interactions. This approach emphasizes quality over quantity, aiming to develop potent networks through high-stakes activities that connect individuals with diverse backgrounds.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.text: A peer teaching strategy that begins with the teacher spending a few minutes introducing a concept to the class. Next, the teacher says Teach!, the class responds with Okay!, and pairs of learners take turns re-teaching the concept to each other. It’s a bit like think-pair-share, but it’s faster-paced, it focuses more on re-teaching than general sharing, and learners are encouraged to use gestures to animate their discussion. I have also used Teach-OK with college learners, and most of my learners said they were happy for a change from the sit-and-listen they were used to in college classrooms.

docs.title: Teach Kids to Choose Their Self-Talk
Description
docs.text: 1) Share a definition of self-talk. 2) Explain that we all experience silent self-talk within our minds, unconsciously, during our everyday lives. 3) Set a timer and tell students that for the next minute, we’ll sit in silent meditation, with eyes closed, and observe our silent self-talk. 4) After the minute has passed, ask students to open their eyes and share the self-talk that they observed inside their own minds, and chart the students’ answers. 5) Categorize those answers as positive/neutral or negative. 6) Help students realize that when thoughts are focused on a real mistake or problem that needs to be addressed, negative self-talk might include berating ourselves over and over. Positive self-talk could include thinking about how we can address the problem and reminding ourselves that making mistakes is part of life and doesn’t make us “bad.”

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When a student misbehaves persistently and disruptively, strategies more active than ignoring, nonverbal redirection, or a single consequence become necessary — strategies aimed at conflict resolution, the reduction of disagreements that persist over time. Most conflict-resolution approaches educators use combine two moves: precisely identifying what "the" problem actually is, and reminding the student of classroom expectations with clarity and assertiveness, but without apology or harshness (Jones, 2004). Thomas Gordon's widely cited Teacher Effectiveness Training develops this into a four-step model.

Step 1: Clarifying and focusing — problem ownership. Classrooms are emotional places even though their stated purpose is to promote thinking, and when a student misbehaves, negative feelings (annoyance, anger, discomfort) can interfere with figuring out exactly what's wrong. Gordon (2003) frames this as an issue of problem ownership — deciding whose problem the behavior or conflict really is. The "owner" is whoever is actually troubled by it, and might be the misbehaving student, the teacher, or another student who merely witnesses it; since the owner needs to take primary responsibility for solving the problem, correctly identifying ownership changes how to deal with it effectively. If a student privately makes an offensive remark to a teacher and is unlikely to repeat it, the problem may be mainly the teacher's; if the student is likely to repeat it to others, it becomes more the student's own problem. A problem can also come to be shared — a student who offends a classmate may find that other classmates start avoiding him too, at which point the whole class begins sharing some part of "the" problem.

Step 2: Active, empathetic listening. Diagnosing who really owns a problem is helped by active listening — attending carefully to everything a student says and trying to understand or empathize fully, even without agreeing (Cooper & Simonds, 2003). This means asking questions to check understanding, encouraging the student to elaborate, and paraphrasing or summarizing what they've said to confirm the teacher's own perception is accurate. Moving too quickly toward advice, instructions, or scolding — even responses a teacher might feel obligated to give — can shut down communication prematurely and leave the teacher with an inaccurate picture of the problem's actual source.

Step 3: Assertive discipline and "I-messages." Once the student's point of view has actually been heard, responses should be framed around how the behavior affects the teacher specifically, with three features: assertive, neither passively apologetic nor unnecessarily hostile (Cantor, 1996) — "Joe, you are talking while I'm explaining something," not "Joe, do you think you could be quiet now?" nor "Joe, be quiet!"; framed as I-messages (Gordon, 1981) — focused on how the behavior affects the teacher's ability to teach and how it makes the teacher feel, distinct from accusatory "you-messages" that evaluate the student's mistake ("Your talking is making it hard for me to remember what I'm trying to say," not "Your talking is rude"); and phrased to encourage the student to consider effects on others (Gibbs, 2003) — "How do you think the other kids feel when you cut in line ahead of them?" rather than simply asserting "that was not fair to them."

Step 4: Negotiation. The first three steps work well for conflicts that are fairly bounded, but persistent problems — chronic lateness, repeated rudeness between two students, habitually incomplete homework — can become stressful enough for everyone involved that a teacher is tempted to simply dictate a resolution, which tends to leave everyone, including the teacher, feeling defeated. Negotiating a solution instead — systematically discussing options and compromising where possible — usually costs less time and effort than continuing to cope with the original problem (Davidson & Wood, 2004), and typically combines: deciding as accurately as possible what the problem is (drawing heavily on active listening); brainstorming possible solutions with the student's own input, rather than simply imposing one; choosing a solution by consensus where possible (a vote can work when feelings aren't running high, but can otherwise just let a majority impose its will while leaving the underlying conflict unresolved); and monitoring how well the chosen solution actually works once underway, renegotiating if it doesn't.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Genuine, unhurried listening before responding — the model explicitly warns against moving to advice or discipline before the problem is accurately understood
  • A teacher willing to frame feedback around their own experience of the behavior (I-messages) rather than around judgments of the student

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Not a fast technique — active listening and negotiation both take real time, which is worthwhile mainly for conflicts that are persistent or complex enough to justify it
  • Negotiation that excludes genuine student input, or that resorts to a vote when feelings are running high, can function as imposition dressed up as negotiation and leave the underlying conflict unresolved
  • Best suited to conflict a teacher and student can work through together — not a substitute for Functional Behavior Assessment when the behavior is actually driven by an identifiable environmental trigger rather than an interpersonal conflict

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students engaged in persistent, recurring misbehavior or conflict that lighter-touch responses (ignoring, nonverbal cues, a single consequence) have not resolved

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Durable resolution of a recurring behavior or conflict, achieved through the student's own understanding and buy-in rather than through a solution simply imposed by the teacher
  • Modeling a conflict-resolution process other students can also learn to use with their own disagreements

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Clarify problem ownership — determine who is actually troubled by the behavior (the student, the teacher, a bystanding classmate, or some combination) before deciding how to respond.
  2. Listen actively and empathetically — ask questions, encourage elaboration, and paraphrase back what the student says, resisting the urge to jump straight to a solution.
  3. State the problem assertively as an I-message — describe how the behavior affects you specifically, and invite the student to consider its effects on others, without blame or hostility.
  4. Negotiate if the conflict persists — decide the problem together, brainstorm solutions with the student's input, choose one by consensus if possible, and monitor and renegotiate as needed.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Low-Profile Classroom Control — the appropriate response tier for misbehavior less persistent than what this strategy addresses
  • Repairing Harm — a restorative process that overlaps with this strategy's emphasis on repair over blame, particularly relevant once a specific harm has occurred

docs.text: • Negotiation
