docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Teacher-led physical activities integrate movement and mathematical practice in an abbreviated time frame, suitable for station breaks and transitions, and are adaptable to different grade levels. Examples include:

  • Groups: Students form groups of a size called out by the teacher.
  • Stand Up/Sit Down: Students stand or sit based on whether the teacher's number meets a certain condition.
  • Bigger/Smaller/Equal: Students expand or shrink their bodies based on the size of a number called out by the teacher.
  • Rhythmic Clapping/Counting: Students imitate a rhythm clapped or counted out by the teacher.
  • Skip Counting with Movement: Students create a movement with parts, whispering the first parts and calling out the final move loudly as they skip count.
  • Circle Count: Students stand in a circle and count off as quickly as possible, then count by twos, fives, tens, or threes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a classroom space, teacher instruction, and enthusiastic participation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may feel ashamed if they don't already know the right answer, so avoid shaming and tweak competitive games to make them collaborative.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Especially suitable for K–4, but adaptable to older and younger grades

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Integrate physical activity with mathematical concepts, enhance student engagement, reinforce learning, and improve focus.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Movement refreshes students while reinforcing math concepts. The games are quick and fun.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptations include modifying the numbers, conditions, or movements to suit different grade levels or skill levels. Tweak competitive games to make them collaborative.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Guidance
  • Part-task practice
  • Direct instruction

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement, participation, and mathematical accuracy during the activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combines physical activity with learning to enhance focus and retention. Research has shown that physical activity can improve cognitive function and academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Math for Love provides various teacher-led games with Common Core tagging.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Schedule regular conferences with students to get a sense of their independent reading and provide instructional support. Develop a plan for meeting with all students regularly, using a combination of scheduled and spontaneous conferences. Use these conferences to understand students' reading habits, offer individual guidance, and make notes about how students solve problems while reading.

docs.title: Constraints

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Monitor student progress in independent reading, provide personalized feedback, offer instructional support, and identify reading challenges.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides individualized attention and support, allows teachers to monitor student reading habits, identifies reading challenges, and offers personalized guidance.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt conferences to meet individual student needs, focusing on reading level, interests, and challenges. Use a variety of forms and tools to support conferencing.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances student engagement in independent reading, provides personalized feedback and support, and improves reading skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A good teacher evaluates their own practice and reflects on how to improve — analyzing data, assessing student work, talking to students about what they found difficult, or asking a colleague to observe a lesson. This kind of evaluation shapes future planning, but it doesn't automatically count as research. Research is "systematic investigation towards increasing the sum of knowledge," and a piece of inquiry or evaluation work becomes research specifically when: the work involves capturing data (recording conversations or lessons, collecting student work as evidence) so it can be used outside the moment it happened; participants are asked to do something out of their ordinary routine (a focus group, a disruptive interview); and the output is public, which means the knowledge behind it needs to be defensible — based on reliable evidence, valid conclusions, and properly conducted work — before it can contribute anything to the wider field.

The advantage of treating an inquiry as research rather than only as reflection is that its knowledge is evidence-based, can be defended and explained, and is more likely to be taken seriously than an account of personal experience alone; conducted over a meaningful stretch of time, it can reveal not just what works but why. This has further implications: the work should take account of other studies in the field (which also gives ideas for how to tackle the issue), and it should be systematic and purposeful, underpinned by a clear set of beliefs, specific research questions, and an ethical design likely to produce results others will consider valid.

For a teacher investigating their own classroom, this is most often small-scale and short-term, and action research is the strategy best suited to it — best understood as a strategy rather than a single specific method (McNiff & Whitehead, 2011; Wilson, 2013), involving practitioners systematically investigating their own practice with a view to improving it. Action research is inherently cyclical, moving through repeated intervention and analysis until the practitioner genuinely understands the issue and has done something about it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A specific problem the teacher wants to solve in their own classroom — something as narrow as why certain students avoid answering questions, or as broad as how to organize group work effectively
  • Willingness to consult existing literature on the issue before designing an intervention, rather than intervening on intuition alone

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Reflection and good practice alone (without captured data, an out-of-the-ordinary element, and a public, defensible output) don't rise to the level of research, even when genuinely valuable
  • A small-scale, single-classroom study cannot claim the same generalizability as larger, publicly-scrutinized educational research

docs.title: Implementation Variability
docs.text: • Case studies are the other methodology well-suited to small-scale, single-classroom teacher research, alongside action research

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Practicing teachers investigating and improving their own classroom practice, distinct from student-led inquiry (see Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR))

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • A specific, evidence-grounded understanding of one classroom problem, and a defensible account of what did or didn't help

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify a specific problem to solve in your own classroom.
  2. Define the purpose and clarify what the intervention might look like, consulting the existing literature on the issue.
  3. Plan an intervention designed to tackle the issue.
  4. Collect empirical data and analyze it.
  5. Plan another intervention based on what you found, to further understand the issue.
  6. Repeat the cycle — action research is cyclical, not a single pass.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) — a related but distinct methodology: student-led inquiry into their own communities, rather than teacher-led inquiry into their own classroom practice
  • Peer Observation — one data-collection method commonly used within an action research cycle
  • Build Time for Self-Reflection — the reflective habit action research systematizes into a research cycle

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher noticing that certain students rarely volunteer answers, reviewing the literature on classroom participation, trying a cold-call-with-think-time intervention, collecting participation data, and refining the approach for the next cycle

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• McNiff, J., & Whitehead, J. (2011). All you need to know about action research (2nd ed.). Sage.
  • Wilson, E. (Ed.). (2013). School-based research: A guide for education students (2nd ed.). Sage.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teachers as researchers. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: To understand the writing process, teachers have to write also. Start by writing about your family or yourself. Get "uncomfortable" as you try to make your writing efficient and interesting. Just as students are uncomfortable doing unfamiliar math, teachers should experience that same feeling of being out of their comfort zone, and writing is a good way to do that.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires time for teachers to write. Requires a willingness to be vulnerable and share their writing with others.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some teachers may be resistant to writing. May be difficult to find time for teachers to write.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers of all subjects.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help teachers understand the writing process from the student's perspective. Encourage teachers to improve their own writing skills. Build empathy between teachers and students.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides teachers with a better understanding of the challenges students face when writing. Improves teacher writing skills. Builds empathy between teachers and students.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can write about whatever they are interested in.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Modeling
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe teacher attitudes and behaviors towards student writing. Review teacher writing to assess improvement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps teachers understand the writing process from the student's perspective. Encourages teachers to improve their own writing skills. Builds empathy between teachers and students.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Start by writing about your family or yourself. Get "uncomfortable" as you try to make your writing efficient and interesting. Just as students are uncomfortable doing unfamiliar math, teachers should experience that same feeling of being out of their comfort zone, and writing is a good way to do that.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Demonstrating writing strategies and techniques by showing students how you use them yourself. Students will be more willing to try new strategies if they see their instructor applying them. The teacher's own struggle with writing is important for students to see.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher willingness to share their own writing process. Time for modeling in class. A supportive and encouraging classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Some students may be intimidated by the teacher's writing skills. Requires careful planning to ensure that modeling is relevant and accessible to students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for struggling writers and those who lack confidence

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student confidence in writing, promote risk-taking and experimentation, model effective writing strategies, demonstrate the writing process, encourage a growth mindset

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear and relatable model for students to follow. Reduces anxiety by showing that even experienced writers struggle. Encourages experimentation by demonstrating that writing is a process of trial and error.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The teacher can model strategies that are relevant to specific student needs. The teacher can share their own personal struggles and successes with writing. Students can be invited to participate in the modeling process.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Modeling

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student writing samples demonstrating increased risk-taking and experimentation. Student reflections on their writing process. Observation of student engagement during writing activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that teacher modeling improves student confidence, promotes risk-taking, and enhances writing skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher shares a draft of their own writing, highlighting the strategies they used and the challenges they faced. Teacher models how to brainstorm ideas, outline an essay, or revise a draft. Teacher invites students to provide feedback on their writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teacher racial identity work involves educators examining their own racial identity, biases, and privilege to create a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment. This includes taking responsibility for one's own education around race, creating space for challenging conversations, and learning about the racial identities of students. By modeling this self-awareness, teachers can empower students to advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires educators to commit to ongoing self-reflection, engage in challenging conversations, and seek out resources to learn about race and cultural identity.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be emotionally challenging and time-consuming. Requires a willingness to confront personal biases and privileges.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All educators, particularly those who work with diverse student populations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase educators' self-awareness, reduce bias, promote equity, and empower students to advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a more inclusive and equitable classroom environment, enhances educators' ability to understand and support students from diverse backgrounds, and empowers students to advocate for themselves.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Involves individualized self-reflection and ongoing learning based on personal experiences and biases.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Assigned Readings
  • Conceptual Questioning

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor changes in educators' attitudes and behaviors, track their engagement in equity-focused activities, and observe the impact on student experiences and outcomes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that teacher racial identity work can lead to more equitable classroom practices and improved outcomes for students from marginalized groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Taking responsibility for one's own education around race in America. Creating space in peer groups to have challenging conversations. Learning about the racial identity of students.

docs.title: Teacher Read-Aloud That Models Reading for Deep Understanding
Description
docs.text: A teacher read-aloud involves a teacher fluently reading a text aloud to learners, intentionally modeling strategies of understanding that can be reinforced in shared, guided, and independent reading. The teacher engages learners at the edge of their speaking vocabulary, selecting texts a grade or two above their grade level. Read alouds should include think-aloud or interactive elements and focus intentionally on the meaning within the text, about the text, and beyond the text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A teacher-selected text, open-ended questions, and a plan for introducing vocabulary. The read-aloud requires preparation and practice, including selecting relevant texts and planning for discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can become a passive activity if learners are not actively engaged. Requires careful planning and selection of appropriate texts. If the discussion is not properly guided, it may not lead to deeper understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Build vocabulary, develop understandings of story structures, support developing connections between print elements, encourage high levels of understanding, teach the reading process in a meaningful context, model fluency, motivate learners to read.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a model of fluent reading, helps learners practice reading with expression, supports comprehension monitoring, offers opportunities for individualized instruction, improves reading accuracy, and encourages peer feedback and correction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select books and discussion topics that meet the learners' needs, cultural backgrounds, and experiences. Ask guiding questions tailored to the learners' needs, cultural backgrounds, and experiences. Practice reading aloud to build fluency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation during read-aloud sessions. Collect evidence of deeper conversation and connections to the big idea through student discussions and responses.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Teachers model the ways that involvement with text engages us, and we give them energy for learning how reading works. By showing them how to search for meaning, we introduce strategies of understanding we can reinforce in shared, guided, and independent reading. Research: Clay (1991) writes that when teachers read aloud to students “meanings can be negotiated in discussion before, during, and after the story reading.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly teach mathematical academic vocabulary, including math-specific terms and the difference between mathematical and common definitions of words. Introduce vocabulary within the context of the content. Use scaffolds such as visuals, real objects, graphic organizers, and anchor charts. Offer opportunities to work with objects and images. Ask learners which strategies support their learning. Demonstrate that vocabulary can have multiple meanings and help learners understand how to use them correctly in a mathematical context. Draw on learners' home languages and use cognates, translated words, and encourage the use of their languages in group work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of key vocabulary, scaffolds for vocabulary instruction, resources in learners' home languages

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires planning and resources, may be challenging to find translated materials for all languages

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of math concepts through vocabulary instruction, improve ability to use math vocabulary in context, leverage learners' home languages to support learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Improves comprehension of math concepts, supports language acquisition, leverages home languages as a resource

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapting vocabulary instruction based on learners' needs and home languages

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learner's use of math vocabulary in context, monitor learner's comprehension of mathematical concepts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved learner understanding of math, increased learner participation in math activities

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Creating a Math Word Wall that has three parts: key vocabulary, 'in your own words' definitions, and a variety of ways to portray a function.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: In project-based learning (PBL), teaching academic vocabulary involves identifying specialized or technical words that students will encounter during a project and planning instruction to teach these words. This ensures that all students, particularly English Language Learners (ELLs), have the necessary vocabulary to succeed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection of academic vocabulary relevant to the project, explicit instruction strategies, and opportunities for practice and application.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires additional planning and instructional time, and may necessitate ongoing adjustments based on student progress and assessment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, with a particular focus on English Language Learners (ELLs) in project-based learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To equip students with the academic vocabulary necessary for successful participation and comprehension in project-based learning activities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to vocabulary acquisition, ensuring that students understand and can use academic language in meaningful contexts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different project topics and proficiency levels, allowing educators to tailor vocabulary instruction to individual student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved student comprehension, accurate use of academic vocabulary in project work, and positive feedback from students and educators.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports that explicit vocabulary instruction enhances student understanding and performance in content areas, particularly for ELLs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Identifying specialized vocabulary in a science project and providing targeted instruction and practice activities.

docs.title: Teaching Social Awareness Through Current Events and Fictional Characters
Description
docs.text: Model empathy and explain different perspectives in current events and fictional characters.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Stories.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may not know how to be introspective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To help learners reflect on their own feelings and behaviors.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners to be introspective.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be personalized.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor learner participation

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Unknown

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Not applicable.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using problem-based learning in multi-cultural groups helps learners get used to working in a multi-cultural environment. Though diversity in the group may hamper coming to a quick solution, one is eventually reached. In the process, the group will also learn to put aside their differences, understand the way other cultures work, and find a way to work together as a team and come up with a solution

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A diverse group of learners, a facilitator to guide the process, and a problem that requires collaborative problem-solving.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to manage conflicts and ensure equal participation from all members. Requires careful facilitation and attention to group dynamics.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Corporate teams, multicultural groups, and educational settings with diverse learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote teamwork, cross-cultural understanding, and effective communication in diverse groups

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances collaboration, empathy, and adaptability in diverse environments. Learners develop skills in resolving conflicts, appreciating different perspectives, and working towards a common goal.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teams can be formed based on diverse backgrounds and skill sets. Problems can be tailored to reflect real-world multicultural challenges. Ground rules can be tailored to accommodate different opinions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving
  • Consensus Building
  • Perspective-Taking

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe team dynamics, assess the quality of collaborative solutions, and evaluate individual contributions to the team effort.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that team-based learning enhances communication, collaboration, and problem-solving skills. It also promotes empathy and cross-cultural understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Corporate training programs using diverse teams to solve real-world business problems, educational settings using project-based learning to promote teamwork, and community initiatives using collaborative problem-solving to address local issues.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classrooms that have a variety of media allow for different learning activities and might include a projector, a white board, digital cameras, laptops, satellite TV, video production, and even Ipad accessibility.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of technology options such as computers, tablets, and projectors. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the technology.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve engagement, improve digital skills, enhance collaboration

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes engagement and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred technology. Provide a variety of technology options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more fun.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that technology can increase engagement, improve learning outcomes, and enhance collaboration. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Taking short, scheduled breaks from technology during study periods reduces the negative effects of media multitasking. Engaging with devices and social media during study time distracts from the material and reduces comprehension. Implementing short 'technology breaks' allows learners to access the internet, but then restrict its use for the rest of the study period. Alternative strategies include avoiding smartphones and other devices before studying or keeping technology away from the study space. These breaks help to maintain focus, improve learning, and enhance overall performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Scheduled breaks from technology, self-regulation strategies for managing technology use, a designated study space free from digital distractions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Success depends on self-regulation and commitment to limiting technology use during study periods. Some learners may find it challenging to disengage from technology completely.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who tend to multitask with technology during study or work periods

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce distractions, improve focus, and enhance cognitive performance during learning activities

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by minimizing distractions, supports deeper focus and concentration, enhances memory and retention

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can set specific times for technology breaks, choose which activities to engage in during those breaks, or use apps to block distracting websites.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Self-monitoring

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track study time and frequency of technology breaks, measure task completion rates, conduct self-reports on focus and concentration.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that multitasking with technology reduces learning and comprehension. Technology breaks can help to maintain focus and improve cognitive performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student schedules 10-minute technology breaks every hour during study sessions. A professional blocks distracting websites during work periods. A learner uses an app to track and limit their technology use during study time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Encourage teens to engage in regular exercise as a way to manage stress, improve focus, and enhance overall well-being. Exercise helps regulate stress hormones, pumps the body with endorphins, and balances stress levels. Different intensities and types of exercise, such as walks, bike rides, dance classes, or yoga, can cater to different stress levels and preferences.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to various exercise options, awareness of the benefits of exercise, support and encouragement from parents and peers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require initial effort to establish a routine. Some teens may have health concerns that limit their ability to exercise.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teenagers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Manage stress levels, improve focus and concentration, enhance overall well-being

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps regulate stress hormones, pumps the body with endorphins, and balances stress levels. Provides an outlet for managing stress and improving mental health.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teens can choose their preferred form of exercise, tailoring the intensity and type to their individual needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Self-reported stress levels, observation of mood and behavior, tracking of exercise frequency and intensity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Reduced stress levels: Regular exercise helps manage stress and improves mental health. Improved focus and concentration: Exercise enhances cognitive function and clears the mind.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Maintaining an optimal temperature range in classrooms affects student engagement and productivity. The ideal range for effective learning in reading and mathematics is between 68°F and 74°F. Teachers need the ability to control the temperature to ensure a comfortable learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Temperature control systems, thermostats, proper insulation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementation can be costly and may require significant facility upgrades.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners and educators in K-12 or higher education settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student engagement and achievement, enhance comfort, create a more conducive learning environment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces discomfort and distraction, improves focus and concentration

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow teachers to control the temperature in their classrooms or blocks of classrooms.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement and achievement, monitor classroom temperature, survey teacher and student satisfaction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that maintaining an optimal temperature range improves student learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Installing individual thermostats in classrooms, providing temperature control systems for blocks of classrooms, improving insulation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Monitoring the temperature of a learning environment and making adjustments to maintain an optimal temperature range can improve learner focus and reduce distractions. Being in an environment that is too cold can lead to distractibility and decreased Attention, while an environment that is too warm can cause decreased concentration due to discomfort and drowsiness. The ideal temperature range for effective learning in reading and mathematics is between 68º and 74º.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Temperature monitoring tools (thermometers, sensors), HVAC systems with sufficient control, understanding of optimal temperature ranges for learning, ability to adjust temperature based on feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Achieving ideal temperature for all learners in a shared space can be challenging due to individual preferences; older buildings may have limited temperature control capabilities; reliance on technology for monitoring and adjustment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in environments with variable temperature control.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Optimize learning environments by maintaining comfortable temperatures, improve focus and reduce distractibility.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances cognitive performance by reducing thermal discomfort and distractions, supporting attention and focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Temperature can be adjusted based on individual preferences within certain group constraints (e.g., small blocks of classrooms), and the provision of individual fans or heaters.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure learner focus and engagement levels under different temperature conditions, track performance metrics (e.g., test scores) in relation to temperature, survey learners about their comfort levels and perceived impact on learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that maintaining an optimal temperature range (68º-74º) enhances engagement levels and overall productivity, including student achievement. Studies show a correlation between comfortable temperatures and improved test scores and reduced off-task behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary schools dimming lights, opening windows, and using fans during heat waves. Implementing smart HVAC systems that automatically adjust temperatures based on real-time feedback and occupancy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves monitoring the temperature of a learning environment and making adjustments to maintain optimal conditions for learners. Research suggests that environments that are too cold can lead to distractibility and decreased attention, while environments that are too warm can result in decreased concentration due to discomfort and drowsiness. This strategy can be implemented through product design or direct intervention, such as adjusting thermostats, opening windows, using fans, or dimming lights.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires monitoring devices (thermometers, sensors) and adjustable environmental controls (thermostats, fans, air conditioning). Regular monitoring and adjustment are needed to respond to changing conditions and learner feedback. Implementation might involve policy changes regarding temperature control in learning spaces.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Individual preferences for temperature can vary, making it challenging to satisfy everyone. Energy costs associated with maintaining optimal temperatures may be a limiting factor. Overemphasis on temperature control may distract from other important aspects of the learning environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in various learning environments, including classrooms, offices, and training facilities.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Maintain an optimal temperature range to maximize learner attention, engagement, and productivity; mitigate the negative impacts of uncomfortable temperatures on learning outcomes.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Optimizing temperature supports cognitive function by minimizing distractions and discomfort, thereby enhancing focus and concentration. Creating a comfortable learning environment fosters positive attitudes and improves motivation. This approach addresses the physical well-being of learners, leading to increased engagement and productivity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different individuals may have different temperature preferences. The strategy can be personalized by allowing learners some control over their immediate environment, such as adjusting individual thermostats or using personal fans or heaters. Consider factors such as clothing, activity level, and individual differences in thermal sensitivity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner performance metrics (e.g., test scores, task completion rates) in relation to temperature levels. Monitor learner feedback regarding thermal comfort and its impact on concentration. Observe changes in learner behavior (e.g., fidgeting, drowsiness) as indicators of temperature-related discomfort.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that maintaining an optimal temperature range (68º-74ºF) can significantly improve engagement levels and overall productivity, including student achievement. Air conditioning in schools can mitigate the adverse effects of high temperatures on test scores. Studies have found that temperature effects account for a notable percentage of the U.S. racial achievement gap due to differences in environmental conditions and school resources. The article in the INPUT references Lyons, J. B. (2001). Do school facilities really impact a child's education? Scottsdale, AZ: Council of Educational Facility Planners, International.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Temperature regulation is an important finding across individuals of all ages is that the temperature in which a person works affects engagement levels and overall productivity—including student achievement. Anyone that has worked in a classroom or office that is too hot or too cold knows how difficult it can be when trying to work when the temperature is uncomfortable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Physical Design

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Cost

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, teachers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • The ideal temperature range for effective learning in reading and mathematics is between 68º and 74º.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Maintaining such a temperature in every classroom within a school, teachers typically need to be able to control the temperature in their own classroom.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Temperature

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Test scores

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Greater levels of student achievement

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The test-study-test technique is a spelling instruction strategy where students take a pretest, correct their errors under teacher guidance, and then study the corrected words before taking a final test. This method involves immediate correction of errors after the pretest, where the teacher spells each word, emphasizing each letter as the student points to it. Students use a colored pencil to mark the incorrect part of the word and then write the correct spelling. This process allows students to identify difficult words, locate the specific parts causing trouble, and correct errors immediately. The technique allows focused study on trouble areas, improving retention and spelling accuracy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires pretests, colored pencils, and teacher guidance. The teacher must be prepared to spell out words and emphasize each letter during the correction process. It is beneficial to provide a quiet study environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require more time than traditional study methods. Some students may find the correction process tedious. The effectiveness depends on the teacher's ability to provide clear guidance during the correction phase.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, as well as adult learners needing to improve spelling skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling accuracy, enhance error recognition, and focus study efforts on problem areas

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides immediate feedback and error correction, focuses study efforts on specific problem areas, and improves retention through active engagement with the material. This technique enhances metacognitive awareness by making students aware of their spelling errors.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Technique can be applied to any spelling list or curriculum. Students can self-correct and study at their own pace.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track spelling accuracy from pretest to final test. Monitor the reduction in specific errors and assess overall improvement in spelling proficiency.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research demonstrates that the test-study-test technique is highly effective in improving spelling skills. It allows students to focus on their specific errors and actively engage with the material, leading to better retention and accuracy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Having students take a spelling pretest, correct their errors immediately with teacher guidance, and then study the corrected words before taking a final test. Using a colored pencil to mark and correct the specific parts of the word that are misspelled.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Text-based discussions involve engaging learners in discussions about what they read, with a focus on using evidence from the text to support their responses. Teachers set expectations and routines for productive discussions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Text or material to be read. Clear expectations and routines for discussions. Facilitation skills from the teacher.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure productive and respectful discussions. May be challenging for learners who are hesitant to speak in class.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for developing literacy skills and vocabulary.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop oral language skills. Improve comprehension. Support vocabulary development. Engage with the text critically.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Develops oral language skills. Improves comprehension. Supports vocabulary development. Promotes critical thinking. Encourages student-to-student interaction.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Discussions can be tailored to the learners' interests and language proficiency levels. Sentence starters can be provided to support participation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Discussion Sections
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Participation in discussions. Use of evidence from the text to support responses. Clarity and organization of ideas. Respectful interaction with peers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • There is both research and practice evidence showing that discussions result in measurable outcomes in literacy achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • After reading a book, the teacher engages learners in discussing their favorite parts of the text or the information that they learned. Sentence starters are provided to support participation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Text-to-speech (TTS) technology converts written text into spoken words, enhancing accessibility and comprehension for individuals with dyslexia, visual impairments, or other learning differences. It involves highlighting text on a digital device, and then using software or an app to read the text aloud. Users can adjust the voice, speed, and pitch to suit their preferences. Devices include computers, tablets, and smartphones with TTS capabilities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A device (computer, tablet, or smartphone) with text-to-speech software or app. Digital text that can be highlighted and read aloud. Headphones or speakers for audio output.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Comprehension may be reduced if the synthesized voice is difficult to understand. May not accurately convey tone or emotion. Not all digital content is compatible with TTS technology. Reliance on TTS may hinder the development of decoding skills for some individuals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students and adults with dyslexia, visual impairments, or anyone who struggles with reading.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading comprehension, support independent learning, enhance access to digital content, and increase vocabulary development.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces the cognitive load associated with decoding and reading, allowing individuals to focus on comprehension. Provides an alternative means of accessing written information for those with visual impairments. Improves vocabulary development by exposing individuals to new words in context.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can select different voices, adjust the speaking rate, and choose whether to highlight words as they are read aloud. The technology supports diverse devices and platforms, including computers, tablets, and smartphones. Languages and accents can be selected based on learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure reading comprehension with and without TTS. Evaluate the speed and accuracy of reading aloud. Gather feedback from users on their experience and perceived benefits. Track improvements in reading skills and vocabulary development over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that TTS technology improves reading comprehension and reduces reading fatigue for individuals with dyslexia and visual impairments. Enhances access to digital content and supports independent learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • NaturalReader, Read&Write, ClaroRead, voice dictation function in Mac and Android devices. Use cases include students listening to textbooks, completing assignments, and conducting research; professionals accessing documents and emails; and individuals with visual impairments reading digital content.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Text-to-speech (TTS) software allows written text to be read aloud. It can convert files like Word documents and PDFs into spoken words, read emails and web pages, and convert text to audio files (MP3, WAV) for portable devices. TTS software often includes a toolbar for reading within applications and can integrate with OCR software to convert printed text into voice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Computer or device with TTS software installed, compatible operating system, and necessary file formats (PDF, DOCX, PPT, TXT, HTML). Headphones may be required depending on the environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness may vary based on voice quality and customization options. Some TTS may not read system information like screen readers. Compatibility issues may arise with certain applications or file formats.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals who prefer or need to hear text, including students with reading difficulties, individuals with visual impairments, and those who benefit from auditory learning.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assist with proofreading, enhance time management and productivity, provide accessible formats for diverse learners

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances auditory processing, provides multisensory support by activating verbal and visual working memory, strengthens visual processing through tracking (highlighting the spoken word), offers alternative formats for communication, and increases accessibility to digital content.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Users can customize voices (speech, pitch, volume), adjust reading chunks (paragraph, sentence), and select compatible applications and file formats. Some TTS offer multiple installations per license, online or built-in options.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved reading comprehension, increased fluency, enhanced productivity, and positive user feedback. Assess user's ability to proofread, manage time, and engage with digital content more effectively.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of TTS in improving reading comprehension, enhancing learning outcomes for students with dyslexia, and increasing accessibility to educational materials. Read&Write has been used to support all learners, promoting accessibility and deeper learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Read&Write by Texthelp, NaturalReader, ClaroRead, Snap&Read. Examples of TTS software implementation in classrooms and for personal use can be found on vendor websites.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Text-to-speech (TTS) software converts written text into spoken words, aiding individuals who benefit from auditory learning or have reading difficulties. It can convert various file formats (Word, PDF) into spoken words, read emails and web pages, and create audio files (MP3, WAV) for portable devices. TTS often includes a toolbar for reading text within applications and can be integrated with OCR software to convert printed text to voice. Features include customizable voice settings, visual supports like highlighting, and compatibility with screen magnification software. It is used to proofread, enhance productivity, and improve time management.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires installation of text-to-speech software on a computer or device, compatible operating system, and access to digital text. Headphones may be needed to minimize distractions. Ensure the software is compatible with the user's existing technology (e.g., screen magnification).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not accurately pronounce all words or convey nuanced meaning. Over-reliance on TTS can hinder development of independent reading skills. Some software can be expensive, and compatibility issues can arise.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Individuals with reading difficulties, auditory learners, students with learning disabilities, anyone seeking to improve productivity

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Assist with reading comprehension, support proofreading and editing, enhance productivity, provide alternative format for accessing written materials

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides auditory reinforcement of written text, supports multisensory learning, improves accessibility of digital content, enhances comprehension, and facilitates independent learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offers customizable voice settings (speed, pitch, volume), visual supports (highlighting, masking), and compatibility with various file formats and applications. Users can select voices and languages to suit their preferences and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Application
  • Demonstration
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track usage patterns and student feedback to assess engagement. Compare reading comprehension scores with and without TTS. Monitor the quality of spoken output and customization options used.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates TTS enhances reading comprehension, particularly for students with dyslexia. It improves proofreading accuracy and increases efficiency in processing written information. Studies show increased student engagement and motivation when using TTS.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Read&Write, NaturalReader, ClaroRead are examples of text-to-speech software used in educational settings and workplaces. Many devices have built-in TTS features, such as Microsoft Narrator and Apple VoiceOver. Digital Promise describes Read&Write in the classroom to help students who struggle with reading.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Text-to-Text, Text-to-Self, Text-to-World is a strategy that helps learners connect ideas in a text to their own experiences and beliefs (text-to-self), events happening in the world (text-to-world), and other texts they have encountered (text-to-text). This approach encourages deeper engagement with the material and promotes meaningful connections that enhance understanding. This strategy can be used at the beginning, middle, or end of the reading process to get learners engaged with a text, to help learners understand the text more deeply, or to evaluate learners’ understanding of the text.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Text to be read, guiding questions for each type of connection (text-to-self, text-to-text, text-to-world), materials for recording connections (e.g., handout, journal).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Superficial connections may not enhance understanding. Learners may need explicit instruction and modeling to make meaningful connections.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Grades 6-12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reading comprehension, promote meaningful connections, encourage self-reflection, relate text to personal experiences, connect text to other texts and the world.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters deeper understanding, promotes self-reflection, connects learning to real-world events and personal experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose which type of connection to focus on, and questions can be tailored to suit the specific text and learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Depth and relevance of connections made by learners, participation in discussions, quality of written reflections.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, increased engagement, and a stronger connection to the material.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students engage with text resources, typically online versions, that are equipped with social annotation tools. These tools allow students to mark up the text, leave notes, and engage in discussions with each other, all visible to all the students. This is combined with a structured activity to ensure active learning and application of the concepts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires online text resources with social annotation tools (e.g., Perusall, hypothes.is), design of structured activities, and facilitation of online discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology and online resources, may require moderation to ensure productive discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from collaborative learning and online discussions.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active learning, enhance collaboration and communication, facilitate deeper understanding of text material.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a collaborative and interactive approach to text-based learning, promotes critical thinking and communication skills, enhances engagement with the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can annotate and discuss specific aspects of the text that are relevant to their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality and quantity of annotations, engagement in discussions, completion of structured activities, performance on related assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective when combined with well-designed structured activities and effective facilitation of online discussions. Can improve learner outcomes and engagement by promoting active learning and collaboration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students engage with text resources (physical or digital) accompanied by a structured activity designed to ensure active learning and engagement with the material. This combination provides instruction even in the pre-class phase. The text serves to convey information, while the structured activity facilitates understanding and application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful selection or creation of text resources and design of structured activities. Instructor must provide clear instructions and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all types of content or learners. Requires careful planning to ensure active engagement and understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who prefer text-based learning and those with limited access to technology or bandwidth.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide accessible and flexible content, promote active learning, facilitate understanding and application of concepts.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a low-tech alternative to video, provides flexibility and accessibility, promotes active engagement with the material.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Structured activities can be tailored to different learning styles and needs. Text resources can be selected based on learner interests and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completion and quality of structured activities, learner feedback, performance on related assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Effective when paired with well-designed structured activities that promote active engagement and application of the text material. Can improve learner outcomes and engagement in the absence of video technology.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Integrating text chats into instruction involves using real-time messaging platforms to facilitate communication and collaboration among learners. This strategy allows for immediate feedback, quick Q&A sessions, and collaborative brainstorming. Text chats can be used during lectures, group projects, or online discussions to promote active participation and engagement. It also provides a space for shy learners to voice their ideas without the pressure of speaking up in person.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to a text chat platform (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat), devices for learners to participate, and clear guidelines for respectful communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can be distracting if not moderated effectively. May exclude learners with limited access to technology or digital literacy skills. Requires careful monitoring to prevent misuse and ensure inclusivity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Effective for all grade levels and learning environments, particularly useful in online and blended learning settings.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance communication skills, encourage active participation, facilitate real-time feedback, promote collaborative learning, and support diverse communication styles.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a low-stakes environment for learners to express ideas, supports asynchronous communication, and allows for easy documentation of discussions. Promotes digital literacy and collaboration skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can use text chats to ask clarifying questions, share resources, and provide peer support. Teachers can monitor chats to identify misconceptions and provide targeted feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Analyze chat logs to assess participation, comprehension, and collaboration skills. Monitor the quality of feedback and support provided by learners. Track the use of text chats to improve communication practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that integrating text chats into instruction can increase student engagement and improve learning outcomes. Studies show that real-time feedback and collaborative discussions can enhance comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses a text chat platform to facilitate Q&A during a virtual lecture. A project team uses a text chat to coordinate tasks and share resources. Resource: Educause, ISTE.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners add graphic organizers to finished expository or argumentative writing to illustrate a concept, providing a supportive diagram that aids reader comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Finished writing piece and relevant graphic organizer templates.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all topics. Students should pay attention to diagrams in the texts they read.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly useful for explaining complex or abstract topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance reader comprehension by visually illustrating concepts within expository or argumentative writing.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Clarifies concepts through visual representation, aids reader comprehension, and encourages deeper engagement with the text.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Organizers can be tailored to the specific content of the writing piece. Students can create diagrams to support their own texts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Enhance retention and transfer
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved reader comprehension, clarity of explanations, and ability to connect visual aids with textual content.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Adding a graphic organizer to a finished product aids in the reader's comprehension.

docs.title: The Best Part of Me Book
Description
docs.text: Have the class create a book in which each student tells one thing they like about themselves. Each student chooses one part of their body that they love and then photographs it. Students write the name of the body part and the reason they love it, promoting self-esteem and positive body image.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for creating the book, camera for taking photos

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be uncomfortable for some students, requires sensitivity to body image issues

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early grade students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-esteem, encourage positive body image, build community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters self-acceptance, promotes positive body image, encourages self-expression

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students choose their own body part and reason.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Whole-Class Sharing
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and self-expression, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Creating a "best part of me" book can promote self-esteem and positive body image.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Follow these steps when disciplining learners: review what happened, identify and accept the learner's feelings, review alternative actions, explain the building policy as it applies to the situation, let the learner know that all learners are treated the same, invoke an immediate and meaningful consequence, let the learner know that you are disappointed that you have to invoke a consequence to their action, communicate an expectation that the learner will do better in the future.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • The instructor should be trained and familiar with the disciplinary process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Following this process can be time-consuming, and may not be possible in all situations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Follow a specific process to improve learners' behavior and demonstrate fairness.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Learners will understand the disciplinary process and will hopefully be more receptive to changing their behavior.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The process takes into consideration each individual's background and circumstances, but fairness and equality are paramount.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners will demonstrate improved behavior and respect for the instructor.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A consistent disciplinary process gives learners the opportunity to grow and change their behavior.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A tool for teaching a concept, not isolated facts. Includes four pieces: Definition, Essential Characteristics, Examples, and Non-Examples.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Definition, essential characteristics, examples and non-examples of the topic.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require some teachers to clarify what the concept really means.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Fully understand a concept

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers essential characteristics, examples, and non-examples to clarify what the concept really means.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt the concept to individual learners

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Cognitive Conflict

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare a complete Frayer Model to a mere definition and see how powerful it is to offer essential characteristics, examples, and non-examples.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Deepens understanding of concept.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Hero, lake and prime number.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Pencil Pledge is a classroom management technique that helps create a positive learning environment by promoting respect for materials and self-regulation. It involves having students commit to using pencils responsibly, taking care of classroom supplies, and maintaining a respectful attitude towards learning. This approach encourages students to be mindful of their behavior and to take ownership of their learning environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a clear and concise pledge. Regular reinforcement and reminders of the pledge. Consistent implementation by the teacher.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be effective if not consistently enforced. Some students may not take the pledge seriously. Requires ongoing effort from the teacher to maintain.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for all grade levels, particularly elementary and middle school students. Can be adapted for use in any classroom setting.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote responsible behavior, foster self-regulation, create a positive learning environment, encourage respect for materials, instill a sense of ownership

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-regulation and responsible behavior. Creates a positive and respectful classroom environment. Encourages students to take ownership of their learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The pledge can be customized to fit the specific needs and expectations of the classroom. Students can participate in creating the pledge.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • State objectives

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and respect for materials. Monitor classroom environment and student interactions. Track instances of responsible behavior.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A positive classroom environment fosters self-regulation, respect, and a growth mindset. Consistent implementation of the Pencil Pledge can contribute to improved student behavior and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • At the beginning of the school year, a teacher leads students in reciting the Pencil Pledge. The pledge includes promises to use pencils responsibly, take care of classroom supplies, and respect the learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When it comes to background knowledge, learners may have relevant experiences that just need to be drawn out. Otherwise, students may not have needed background knowledge. Identify connections to students' experiences, modify linguistic complexity, and rephrase math problems. Guide students to cross out unnecessary vocabulary and build knowledge from real-world examples. Use manipulatives purposefully. These cubes and the terms 'hot' and 'cold' numbers can be used when teaching with the concept of negative numbers. A teacher was trying to teach points on a grid and vertical/horizontal axis to her ESL students, three boys from Vietnam. She tried many approaches, including visuals, games, simulations, and manipulatives, and was just about to give up after very little progress. Suddenly, a student said, 'Oh, I know — same same you drive a boat!' ('The same as you drive a boat!') It turns out the child had helped his uncle use the stars to navigate a raft when they were fleeing Vietnam and trying to reach refugee camps in Thailand. He explained the concept to the other boys in Vietnamese with gestures and drawings on the board, who knew exactly what he was talking about. The teacher reflected, 'I felt so humble. These boys knew a lot more about math than I had given them credit for. I had failed to activate their prior knowledge, and in the process had almost given up.'

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Acknowledge and find out the background knowledge of each student

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Hard to accommodate each student's background individually

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Connect to experiences, modify linguistic complexity, use manipulatives to clarify concept, build on background knowledge

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Better understanding of concept due to connecting to learner's experience

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instruction is modified to meet the background understanding of each student

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Recall prior knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • How well students understand the concept using the different methods

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Greatly improve understanding when instruction is tailored to each student

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students using the red cubes as 'hot' or positive numbers and the blue cubes as 'cold' or negative numbers.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are given the title of the reading and asked to form small groups to pool their knowledge about the topic. After the group discussion, each group shares their ideas with the rest of the class. This activity activates prior knowledge, encourages collaborative thinking, and prepares learners for the content they are about to read.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires only the title of the reading and facilitation for group sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the clarity and relevance of the title. Some learners may have limited prior knowledge about the topic.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Activate prior knowledge, encourage collaborative thinking, and prepare learners for the reading content.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active recall of background knowledge, fosters collaborative learning, and helps learners approach the reading with a prepared mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Titles can be selected based on different proficiency levels and cultural contexts. Group sizes can be adjusted based on class size and dynamics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the range and depth of knowledge shared by each group. Collect feedback on how well the activity prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances active engagement with the topic, fosters a collaborative learning environment, and improves reading comprehension by activating relevant prior knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading an article titled 'The History of Jazz Music,' learners brainstorm what they already know about jazz, its origins, and its impact on culture.

docs.title: Things to Consider as a Healthy Skeptic
Description
docs.text: Provide adolescents with opportunities to see the value of a healthy skepticism toward information they encounter in both online and offline contexts. Use curriculum as a springboard for introducing students to multiple perspectives and new ways of thinking about content. Use thinking prompts that move beyond the typical checklist and ask for evidence that supports their thinking. Adolescents also like working in small groups as they grapple with these issues, and then meeting with the whole class to exchange strategies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Curriculum that introduces multiple perspectives, thinking prompts, small group activities, and whole-class discussion.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation. Some students may need support to express their thinking and perspectives effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adolescents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote healthy skepticism, encourage multiple perspectives, and foster critical thinking through discussion and collaboration.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages critical evaluation, promotes multiple perspectives, and supports collaborative learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt prompts to fit student needs. Encourage small group work to facilitate diverse perspectives.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation in discussions and small group activities. Evaluate their ability to apply critical thinking skills and consider multiple perspectives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhanced critical thinking: Students develop a healthy skepticism and are more likely to evaluate information critically. Improved collaboration: Students learn to work together and exchange strategies.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Introduce multiple perspectives and thinking prompts to move beyond the typical checklist and ask for evidence that supports thinking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Think-aloud modeling is a strategy in which an instructor performs a task while verbalizing the reasoning, checks, and decisions normally kept internal. It helps learners see not just what to do, but how an expert monitors and adapts during performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task with meaningful decisions to narrate
  • Clear verbalization of why steps are taken, not just what steps occur

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Can overload learners if narration is too dense or too fast

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Novices learning a new process, strategy, or text interpretation routine

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Make expert reasoning visible and support later independent use

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Think-Aloud
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners can articulate the reasoning behind a modeled process and apply it in a similar task.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Stronger transfer than silent modeling when the explanation reveals strategic thinking and self-monitoring moves.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• An instructor solves a math problem aloud, naming why a particular representation is chosen.
  • A teacher reads a text and verbalizes how they infer meaning, notice confusion, and reread.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: <ul> <li>Chi, M. T. H. (1996). Constructing self-explanations and scaffolded explanations in tutoring. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 10(7), S33-S49. https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1099-0720(199612)10:73.0.CO;2-2

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Model learning by reading aloud an article on a current event or topic of study, pausing to ask questions and make comments and connections to prior knowledge. Have students do the same with a partner, then in groups of three or four.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires teachers to select articles that are relevant and engaging. Facilitation to ensure all students have an opportunity to participate and contribute.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who struggle with reading or who prefer more individual work. Requires careful planning to ensure the activity stays focused and productive.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable across all learner levels, including K-12, higher education, and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Model effective reading strategies, promote critical thinking, build prior knowledge, and develop collaborative learning skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a model for effective reading and learning strategies. Encourages active engagement with the material. Builds prior knowledge and makes connections to real-world events.

docs.title: Personalization
