docs.text: • Can be adapted by varying the complexity of the articles used. Students can be allowed to choose articles that are of interest to them. Group sizes can be adjusted to suit different learning preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct Instruction
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observations of student participation and engagement. Assessment of critical thinking and reflection skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that think-alouds increase student comprehension and critical thinking. Studies indicate that collaborative learning fosters deeper engagement and learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teachers modeling their thinking while reading a news article. Students practicing think-alouds with a partner or in small groups.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Teachers model their online reading strategies through think-alouds. This involves verbalizing the thought processes behind finding relevant information and choosing which links to click. By explicitly modeling these processes, teachers support students' self-regulation and inhibition while building their background knowledge for effectively navigating non-linear texts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to online reading materials, a platform for modeling (e.g., projector, interactive whiteboard), and time for explicit instruction and guided practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant preparation time for the teacher to identify appropriate online resources and plan the think-alouds. Students may need additional support to internalize and apply the modeled strategies independently.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners who need to improve their digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance self-regulation, build background knowledge, improve online reading comprehension, develop information literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear model of expert thinking, reduces cognitive load by demonstrating effective strategies, and promotes metacognition by making thinking visible. Supports learners in developing self-regulation skills for online reading.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different reading levels and content areas. Teachers can adjust the complexity of the online reading tasks and the explicitness of the think-alouds based on learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Modeling
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' online reading behaviors and strategies. Collect student reflections on their own information-seeking processes. Compare pre- and post-intervention scores on online reading comprehension assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of think-alouds for improving reading comprehension. Explicit modeling and metacognitive reflection have been shown to enhance self-regulation and strategic learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Think-Pair-Share is a cooperative learning strategy designed to encourage individual participation and articulate communication. It involves three distinct steps: Think (students think independently about a question or topic), Pair (students discuss their thoughts in pairs), and Share (pairs share their ideas with a larger group). This technique promotes critical thinking, active listening, and the development of well-formed responses.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a well-defined question or topic, clear instructions for each step, and a designated time frame for individual thinking, pair discussion, and whole-class sharing. Requires instructor to actively monitor and facilitate discussions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If not carefully structured, dominant students may overshadow quieter peers. Time constraints can limit the depth of discussion. Questions must be designed to promote meaningful sharing and avoid simple, single-answer responses.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable across all grade levels and class sizes, from elementary to adult learners. Adaptable for various subject areas and learning environments.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active participation, critical thinking, and articulate communication; enhance understanding through peer interaction; provide a safe space for students to develop and refine their ideas before sharing with the whole class.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases student engagement and participation, provides structured thinking time, allows for peer support and collaboration, and boosts confidence in sharing ideas with the whole class. Encourages students to take ownership of their learning and negotiate meanings.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different types of questions or prompts, varying the time allotted for each step, and modifying the sharing format. Pairings can be strategically assigned based on learners' needs and communication preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of student participation and engagement during each step. Assess the quality and depth of student responses during pair and whole-class discussions. Monitor the types of questions students ask and the connections they make between ideas.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that Think-Pair-Share enhances learning by providing opportunities for students to elaborate on ideas through talk. It increases personal communication necessary for internal processing and retention. Students take ownership of learning and negotiate meanings, leading to positive changes in self-esteem and higher-level thinking skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sufficient time is allowed for learners to process information and re-read materials if needed. This provides opportunities for deeper processing, reflection, and clarification. Allowing extra think-time supports learners who need more time to internalize and formulate responses.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Flexible scheduling, willingness to provide extra time, and a supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require adjustments to lesson pacing. Some learners may become disengaged if given too much unstructured time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who struggle with processing speed, those who benefit from extra time, and students who need support with reflection.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve comprehension, support deeper processing, enhance reflection, reduce anxiety, and promote successful learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports deeper processing, reduces anxiety, promotes reflection, and enhances comprehension.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Offer flexible deadlines, provide extended time on assessments, and encourage learners to re-read materials as needed.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to provide thoughtful responses. Assess comprehension through detailed assignments and discussions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Think-time and re-reading promote deeper processing, enhance comprehension, and reduce anxiety.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Think-Write-Pair-Share is a collaborative learning strategy where students first think individually about a topic or question, then write down their thoughts, pair with a partner to discuss their responses, and finally share their ideas with the larger group. This method encourages individual reflection and active participation before engaging in group discussion. It can be used as an introduction to a topic, a formative assessment, or a way to generate ideas.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A topic or question, writing materials, and time for individual thinking, pair sharing, and whole-class sharing.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful facilitation to ensure all students participate actively. Some students may be hesitant to share their ideas with the larger group. Effectiveness depends on the quality of the topic or question.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K-12, higher education, and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote individual reflection, enhance collaborative discussion, improve communication skills, and generate diverse ideas.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured opportunities for individual and group thinking, encourages active participation, and supports the development of communication skills. Creates a safe environment for sharing ideas.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The topic or question can be tailored to the learners' interests and abilities. The time allocated for each stage can be adjusted based on the task and the learners' needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement during pair and whole-class discussions, assess the quality and diversity of ideas generated, and collect written responses for formative assessment.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Think-Write-Pair-Share promotes active learning, encourages collaboration, and supports the development of critical thinking and communication skills. It can be used effectively in various subject areas and with diverse learner populations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A university professor uses Think-Write-Pair-Share to introduce a new concept in a lecture. Students first think individually about their understanding of the concept, then write down their thoughts, pair with a partner to discuss their responses, and finally share their ideas with the class.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Think-Write-Share is a strategy that involves learners thinking about a question, writing down their responses, and then sharing their thoughts with the class. This allows every learner to engage with the material and encourages active participation. The written component ensures accountability, while the sharing component promotes discussion and revision based on feedback.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A specific question, time for thinking and writing, and a method for sharing responses (e.g., document camera, whiteboard).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality of the question and learners' willingness to share their thoughts. May require strategic selection of students to share to address misconceptions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Appropriate for all grade levels.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student engagement, promote individual accountability, address misconceptions, and foster deeper mathematical understanding.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Heightens engagement, ensures accountability, reveals misconceptions, and encourages revision based on increased understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to address specific concepts or challenges. The sharing component allows for differentiated responses and peer learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the initial responses to identify common misconceptions. Assess the quality of revisions following the sharing and discussion phase. Track overall participation and engagement levels.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Heightens student engagement, ensures accountability, and addresses misconceptions effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A fourth-grade teacher asked 'What is an equivalent fraction?' Students wrote their responses, shared, and then revised their work after a class discussion to reflect a better understanding of the concept.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Allow plenty of think-time and time for re-reading for students who might need more time to process. Thinking takes time. Avoid penalizing learners who need more time to process.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Readily available think time and an instructor that reinforces it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may not be self-aware enough to ask for more think time. It is on the instructor to encourage it.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face speed of processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners the opportunity to grasp concepts at their own pace.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide differentiated assessments so that learners who need more think time have more opportunity for it.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Provide assessments where think time can be observed. Use assessment results to see if they are learning from the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that think time can help support learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of think time in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Provide think time during lecture, and test taking. Resource: Speed of Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Begin the school day by asking your students a question to find out how they are feeling or what might be bothering them. Writing the question on the whiteboard and having students write their answers on sticky notes is an easy way to implement it into your routine. Discuss any event that likely elicited a feeling and have everyone share. This sets the tone for the day, giving you the heads up on who might have a tough day and why.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Whiteboard, sticky notes, and time for discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may be hesitant to share. Requires sensitive and supportive facilitation by the teacher.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective in elementary and middle school classrooms to establish a supportive environment

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify emotional states, promote empathy, build classroom community

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Early identification of students' emotional states, promotes a sense of community, encourages empathy and understanding among peers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can tailor questions to suit the age and experiences of students. Students can express feelings through writing, drawing, or speaking.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Activation
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student willingness to share and demonstrate understanding of emotions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps students feel seen and understood, promotes a positive classroom climate, and enhances emotional intelligence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher asks: "How are you feeling today?" or "Is anything bothering you?" Students write responses on sticky notes and share.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy encompasses questioning, reflection, and evaluation to understand, solve problems, and make informed decisions. Critical thinking skills are essential for adults in their communities, education, and workplaces. It includes identifying assumptions, organizing, categorizing, interpreting, inquiring, analyzing, evaluating, summarizing, synthesizing, and making decisions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Explicit instruction in critical thinking skills, opportunities for discussion and reflection, tasks that require analysis and evaluation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners from educational systems that do not focus on critical thinking. Requires intentional integration into instruction.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners in all contexts, particularly those in ESL programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop problem-solving skills, enhance decision-making abilities, promote independent thinking, foster a deeper understanding of content

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active engagement, strengthens analytical skills, builds confidence, promotes lifelong learning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted through differentiated questioning, varied problem-solving tasks, and flexible grouping.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Conceptual Questioning
  • Individual Response
  • Reassessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Quality of responses to open-ended questions, ability to analyze and evaluate information, problem-solving skills

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Critical thinking is essential for adults to thrive in their communities, postsecondary education, and at work. Students may have had limited experience with formal schooling or have come from an educational system that does not focus on critical thinking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Activities such as placing vocabulary words on a continuum to reflect contrasting values, preparing questionnaires to conduct studies, and discussing the origins of beliefs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When teachers deliver content through lectures, readings, or video, they can have students interact with the content by completing a graphic organizer in groups, pairs, or even on their own.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Ability to interact with students.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Need to ensure students interact with each other.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Give students a chance to grapple with the content through a class activity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Gives students a chance to interact with the content by organizing chunks of the content into graphic organizers, and then compare their results to other groups.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be completed with class discussions, lab work, or project-based learning.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student comparisons of their results to other groups.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Gives students more interaction with the terms and helps them work with similarities and differences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Three-Tiered Writing Conference approach provides a structured format for brief, effective writing conferences between teachers and students. It involves three distinct layers of feedback: first, a personal response to the writing to connect emotionally; second, feedback as a member of a writing community offering suggestions; and third, a teacherly response providing direct instruction or strategies. The conference concludes with the student reflecting on the feedback and planning next steps, reinforcing their role as an author. This method ensures conferences are predictable, brief, and useful by disciplining the feedback to focus on one aspect in each tier.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of the three-tier structure, preparation with prompts and questions, time management (5-7 minutes per student), active listening and documentation skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires discipline to maintain structure, may feel unnatural initially, students need to be prepared for the conference format

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, higher education, and adult learners in writing programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide structured feedback, connect emotionally with students, offer actionable suggestions, reinforce student's role as an author

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers a structured approach to feedback, provides emotional connection, integrates community and teacherly perspectives, empowers students through self-reflection and planning

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various writing needs, allows for customized strategies and feedback, enables teachers to address unique challenges of individual students

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Articulation
  • Modeling
  • Coaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased student engagement, enhanced self-reflection skills, positive conference experiences

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured conferences enhance feedback effectiveness, encourage students to take ownership of their writing, and support focused and personalized instruction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses the personal response tier to connect with a student's story about skiing, then suggests clarifying a confusing element as a community member, and finally offers direct instruction on sentence length. Another teacher models a recorded conference to prepare students for the process.

docs.title: Through the Eyes of the People in a Story
Description
docs.text: Learners pick a character from a short story or book and relive the main events from that character’s point of view. This encourages consideration of the character’s emotions and thoughts about others and the events around them, promoting a deeper understanding of the story and perspective-taking.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A short story or book, a space for individual reflection and group discussion, and time for role-playing or presentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may struggle to understand the characters' motivations or may impose their own biases on the interpretation. It requires careful guidance from the instructor to ensure accurate and thoughtful analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who are studying literature and want to deepen their understanding of characters and themes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote perspective-taking, enhance comprehension of literature, encourage emotional intelligence, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances comprehension of literature by exploring different characters' perspectives. Promotes emotional intelligence by considering characters' emotions and motivations. Improves communication skills through discussion and role-playing.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose characters that resonate with their interests and values. The level of analysis and interpretation can be adjusted to their abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Role Reversal

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the depth of analysis, the accuracy of interpretation, and the level of empathy demonstrated in the analysis. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards different characters and themes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Literature has been shown to promote empathy, perspective-taking, and emotional intelligence. Exploring characters' perspectives also enhances comprehension and critical thinking skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students read 'The Great Gatsby' and explore the events from the perspective of Nick Carraway, Jay Gatsby, or Daisy Buchanan. Students read 'To Kill a Mockingbird' and explore the events from the perspective of Scout Finch, Atticus Finch, or Tom Robinson.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Focuses on teaching high-frequency words used by mature language users that can add significantly to language ability. This involves identifying Tier Two words in texts, selecting a manageable number of words to teach, and ensuring that learners understand the concepts represented by these words. Instruction includes helping learners express ideas using more precise and mature vocabulary.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Texts suitable for the target grade level, teacher knowledge of Tier Two vocabulary, and instructional time for vocabulary activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of words to avoid overwhelming learners, and instruction must be engaging and meaningful to ensure retention.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Intermediate to upper-grade students (Grades 3-12) and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary, improve comprehension, and develop precise language skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Expands vocabulary repertoire, enhances communication skills, and facilitates deeper understanding of texts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word selection can be tailored to specific texts and learner needs, with varying levels of attention given to different words based on their importance and utility.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Vocabulary quizzes, use of new words in writing and speaking, and comprehension of texts containing Tier Two words.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved vocabulary knowledge, enhanced reading comprehension, and increased ability to express ideas precisely and effectively.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teaching words like 'benevolent,' 'merchant,' and 'fortunes' from texts, followed by activities to reinforce their understanding and use.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tiered areas allow for groups to convene to discuss ideas and communicate procedures. These areas are especially helpful in classrooms that employ groups regularly. They allow for a space for group instruction or presentations. The speaker can maintain eye contact and a steady volume, rather than projecting their voice. Tiered seating creates an intimate, small group discussion format. Similarly, “cozy” carpet would work well for younger children.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Variety of seating options such as tables and chairs, couches, and bean bag chairs. A designated space for group work and discussion. A welcoming and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional resources. Some learners may be distracted by the changing seating arrangements.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication skills, increase collaboration, enhance eye contact

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes communication and reduces stress. Creates a more welcoming and inviting learning environment. Encourages a love of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to choose their preferred seating arrangement. Provide a variety of seating options. Allow learners to bring personal items from home to make the space more comfortable.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the comfort and appeal of the learning environment. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that flexible seating can increase engagement, reduce stress, and improve academic performance. Studies have shown that learners are more likely to engage in activities when they feel comfortable and supported.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tiered vocabulary instruction categorizes words into three tiers based on their frequency and utility. Tier One words are basic and commonly known, rarely requiring instruction. Tier Two words are high-frequency words for mature language users and are ideal for direct instruction. Tier Three words are low-frequency and domain-specific, best learned within specific content areas. Selecting Tier Two words for explicit teaching enhances learners' overall language ability by providing more precise and mature ways of expressing ideas they already understand.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Careful selection of Tier Two words from texts and content areas. Direct instruction and activities that promote active use and understanding of these words.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires instructors to be knowledgeable about vocabulary tiers and able to identify appropriate words for instruction. May need to adapt instruction to account for learners with varying levels of prior knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those in upper elementary through high school, who need to develop a more sophisticated vocabulary.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Expand vocabulary, improve language proficiency, and enhance comprehension by focusing on high-utility words.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Focuses instruction on the most useful words, allowing learners to express ideas with greater precision and maturity. Helps build a robust vocabulary that supports reading comprehension across different subjects.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can select words based on the specific needs and interests of their learners, as well as the content they are studying. The depth of instruction can be tailored based on learner proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track learner use of Tier Two words in writing and speaking. Assess comprehension of texts containing Tier Two words. Monitor engagement and participation in activities focused on vocabulary development.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Learners show improved vocabulary, enhanced reading comprehension, and greater confidence in expressing themselves using precise language. Direct teaching of Tier Two words provides learners with a strong foundation for academic success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Time-out operates on the principle of negative punishment: removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease a behavior. When a child displays an undesirable behavior, the child is removed from the desirable activity at hand and placed somewhere less desirable for a brief period, then returned to ordinary activity. Time-out is one instance of a broader category of negative consequences called exclusion — removing a learner from one setting and placing them in another.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• The activity the child is removed from must actually be desirable to the child — removing a child from an undesirable activity will backfire, since being removed becomes rewarding rather than punishing
  • A timer or other clear duration signal, so the child knows how long the time-out lasts

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Time-out is a negative consequence, not automatically an effective punisher — under behavioral-science convention, something only counts as a punisher if it demonstrably reduces the frequency of the target behavior; if records don't show the target behavior decreasing, the technique is not functioning as a punisher and should be reassessed rather than simply repeated
  • Caregiver attention during time-out can itself reinforce the very misbehavior the time-out is meant to reduce, since attention-seeking is a common reason learners persist in mistakes or misbehavior

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Young children (the "one minute per year of age" duration guideline is aimed at early-childhood contexts)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reducing a specific undesirable behavior (e.g., hitting, throwing objects) without relying on verbal reprimand, overcorrection, or response cost

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Warn the child once, naming the specific behavior and consequence, before applying time-out for a first instance.
  2. When the behavior recurs, remove the child calmly from the desirable activity and place them in a designated, less desirable location.
  3. Set the duration to roughly one minute per year of the child's age (e.g., five minutes for a five-year-old), using a visible timer.
  4. Remain calm while directing the child to time-out; ignore the child during the time-out itself, since attention may reinforce the misbehavior.
  5. When time-out ends, return the child to the activity with a brief hug or kind word rather than a lecture or continued discussion of the incident.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Token Economies — token loss is a milder negative-punishment technique (removing an earned token rather than access to an entire activity) that can be used alongside or instead of time-out

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Two children are playing with building blocks; one throws blocks at the other. After a warning, a repeat instance leads to the child being removed from the room for a duration matched to their age; on return, they resume play without the incident being revisited.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behaviorism. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Timely feedback involves providing feedback as soon as possible after the learner demonstrates proof of learning. This approach helps the learner connect the feedback with the action and reinforces learning in a confident manner. When feedback is delayed, the moment is lost and the learner may not make the connections between the feedback and their work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Efficient assessment and communication processes

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to provide immediate feedback in all situations. Requires good time management.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, across grade levels and subject areas

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, promote retention, increase confidence, improve performance

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates connection between feedback and action, enhances memory, increases motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The timing of feedback can be adjusted to individual learner needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe changes in learner performance. Track learner progress. Analyze the effectiveness of timely feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Hattie’s research shows feedback has an effect size of 1.13 on learning achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher provides immediate verbal feedback to a student after they complete a math problem on the board. A coach provides real-time feedback to an athlete during practice.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves conducting peer reviews at multiple points in the writing process, including before the assignment is due, on the day it is due, and after it has been graded. This tells learners that the writing process is ongoing and that feedback can be used to drive improvement and growth, and supports a cycle of learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured time for peer review at multiple points in the writing process, a clear understanding of the assignment goals, and a supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful planning and scheduling to ensure that peer reviews are conducted at appropriate times. May be challenging to implement in classrooms with limited time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and higher education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce the iterative nature of the writing process, promote continuous improvement, and enhance learners' ability to use feedback to drive growth

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces the idea that writing is a process and that feedback is valuable at all stages. Encourages learners to see peer and teacher feedback as a tool for continuous improvement.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The timing and frequency of peer reviews can be adjusted based on the learners' needs and the nature of the assignment. Different partners can be used for each round of review.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Assess performance
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Tracking of revisions made by learners based on peer feedback. Comparison of drafts before and after peer review to assess the impact of feedback on the quality of writing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Adding subsequent peer reviews to revisit the same assignment with the same or different partners the day the assignment is due and again after it’s been graded encourages the writing process is never over, and improving products that have been graded is an opportunity for students to see peer and teacher feedback can be used to drive their improvement and growth.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A high school teacher conducts peer reviews before the assignment is due, on the day it is due, and after it has been graded to emphasize the iterative nature of the writing process. Resource: Peer Review Done Right.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Timers, both visual and auditory, are used to help learners gauge how much time remains during an activity, supporting greater attention and task completion. Visual timers, in particular, help learners see and understand time passing, developing a conceptual understanding of time and improving their ability to maintain attention. Timers can be used to limit turn times during games, allocate time for group projects or writing assignments, or manage classroom transitions. Classroom timers with a visual representation of the time passed and time remaining also helps children to develop a sense of time and employ important time management skills. Classroom timers have nearly endless uses: use one minute timers to limit turn times during an educational game, give students a specific amount of time to complete a group project, provide a specific time for a writing assignment, give the class a time to ask the teacher questions, and much more.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Timers (physical or digital), a designated activity or task, and a structured environment to use the timer effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may become anxious or distracted by timers if not used appropriately. The timer should be relevant and meaningful to the task. Some timers may be disruptive if alarms are too loud or frequent.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who struggle with attention, including students with special needs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve attention span, develop time management skills, structure activities, manage transitions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides visual and auditory cues for time management, improves focus and task completion, helps develop a sense of time, supports structured activities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Timers can be adjusted for different time intervals and activities. Visual and auditory alerts can be customized to meet individual needs. Digital timers can be selected with varying features and interfaces.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to stay on task and complete activities within the allotted time. Track the learner's use of time management skills. Monitor the reduction of distractions or anxiety related to time constraints.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual and auditory timers can significantly improve attention and task completion, especially for learners who benefit from structured environments and clear time management cues. They support the development of time management skills and can reduce anxiety related to deadlines.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher uses a timer during group work to ensure that students stay on task and manage their time effectively. A parent uses a timer to help a child with autism transition between activities, providing a clear visual cue for the end of one activity and the start of another.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A secondary reinforcer has no inherent reinforcing value of its own and only reinforces because it has been linked to a primary reinforcer (food, water, sleep, shelter, touch, pleasure — reinforcers organisms do not lose their drive for). Praise, money, and stickers are all secondary reinforcers. A token economy is an entire behavior-management system built around token-form secondary reinforcers: learners earn tokens for target behaviors, then exchange accumulated tokens for backup rewards or privileges. Token economies have been found effective at modifying behavior across settings including schools, prisons, and mental hospitals. A sticker chart, in which children earn a sticker per target behavior and redeem accumulated stickers for a prize, is a familiar classroom-scale token economy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Clearly and consistently defined target behaviors that earn (or lose) a token
  • A meaningful, motivating backup reinforcer the learner can exchange tokens for
  • Consistent, immediate delivery of tokens contingent on the target behavior

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Tokens are secondary reinforcers — the system depends on the backup reward retaining genuine value to the learner; if the backup reward loses appeal, the tokens lose their reinforcing power
  • As with any extrinsic-reinforcement system, an unmanaged token economy risks crowding out intrinsic motivation for the target behavior if never faded — see Conditioning Natural Reinforcers for a fading strategy
  • Establishing and running a token economy well is a real time and record-keeping commitment (tracking token delivery/loss, exchange rates, and effectiveness), not merely handing out stickers

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners for whom clear, immediate, tangible feedback on specific target behaviors is more motivating than delayed or abstract consequences
  • Populations documented in research to benefit strongly from structured token systems, including autistic learners needing support reducing disruptive behaviors and increasing appropriate social behaviors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reducing specific undesirable behaviors (e.g., hitting, pinching) while increasing specific desirable replacement behaviors (e.g., "quiet hands"), and building classroom-wide behavior-management routines around clear, consistent contingencies

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Identify the specific target behavior(s) to increase (and, if applicable, the incompatible behavior to decrease).
  2. Select a token that is easy to deliver and track (physical tokens, points, stickers).
  3. Select a backup reinforcer the learner can exchange tokens for (privileges, prizes, activity time).
  4. Deliver a token immediately and consistently upon the target behavior; remove a token immediately and consistently upon the incompatible undesirable behavior, if using a loss condition.
  5. Allow exchange of accumulated tokens for the backup reinforcer at defined intervals.
  6. Monitor whether the target behavior is actually changing; if not, reassess whether the backup reinforcer still has value to the learner.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Conditioning Natural Reinforcers — a token economy is an extrinsic system; this strategy addresses how to transfer control from tokens to natural, intrinsic reinforcers over time
  • Time-Out (Negative Punishment) — token loss and time-out are both negative-punishment techniques, but token loss removes a specific earned token while time-out removes access to an entire desirable activity

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Cangi and Daly (2013) implemented a token economy with a group of autistic school children who tended toward disruptive behaviors such as hitting and pinching. Children received a "quiet hands" token for appropriate behavior and lost a token for hitting or pinching; accumulated tokens were exchanged for minutes of playtime. The intervention increased appropriate social behaviors and reduced inappropriate ones.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Cangi, A. D., & Daly, P. M. (2013). [Token economy study with autistic school children, cited via secondary source without full publication details]
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Behaviorism. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A hands-on activity that integrates movement with learning, often involving the physical act of tossing objects. This can stimulate brain/body connections, especially in areas like math, by engaging students through movement and active participation. The activity can be adapted to various subjects by customizing the object being tossed to include numbers, visuals, or other relevant content. It promotes engagement and can foster a love for the subject matter.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Physical space for tossing, objects for tossing (e.g., bean bags, balls), and materials for customization (e.g., markers, numbers, visuals).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional space and preparation. Could be challenging for learners with physical limitations without appropriate modifications. Requires active engagement from learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, adaptable for various age groups and subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Stimulate brain/body connections, build specific skills, foster engagement and enjoyment in learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active learning, integrates physical movement with cognitive processes, enhances engagement, and provides a fun and interactive way to reinforce learning concepts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to fit various subjects and age groups. Adaptations include altering the object being tossed, customizing visuals or content on the object, and adjusting the complexity of the task.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Application
  • Gain attention

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement and participation levels. Assess skill development through performance during the tossing activity. Monitor enjoyment and interest in the subject matter.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Integration of movement with learning can stimulate brain function and improve retention. Hands-on activities enhance engagement and foster a positive attitude toward learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Elementary schools integrating bean bag toss math games to stimulate brain/body connections for math learning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The TPRI (Texas Primary Reading Inventory) is a diagnostic instrument designed to identify the reading development of students in kindergarten through third grade. It's an easy-to-use, one-on-one assessment that helps teachers provide targeted instruction to improve students' reading skills. The assessment includes both a screening section (to identify students at risk for reading difficulties) and an inventory section (to gather more data and match reading instruction to specific student needs).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Administer the TPRI assessment, analyze the data, and develop targeted instruction based on the results.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires one-on-one assessment time, which can be time-consuming.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students in kindergarten through third grade

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify students at risk for reading difficulties, provide targeted instruction to improve reading skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps teachers identify specific areas where students need additional support. Allows for targeted instruction, leading to improved reading skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use the inventory section to acquire more data and tailor reading instruction to meet specific student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The TPRI assessment provides data on various reading skills, such as letter sound, blending, word reading, phonemic awareness, graphophonemic knowledge, reading accuracy, fluency, and listening/reading comprehension.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Information derived from the TPRI will assist teachers in planning targeted instruction for their students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Students mark their own confidence in a just-completed assignment or homework using a traffic-light color: red means unsure of success, orange means partially unsure, and green means confident of success (Black & Wiliam, 2006). The colors then drive differentiated grouping rather than functioning as a mere display of feeling: students who marked orange or green work together in mixed groups evaluating each other's work through peer assessment, while the teacher works directly with the students who marked red, giving them more direct support rather than expecting them to benefit as much from peer evaluation alone.

Self-assessment more generally depends on students having a clear enough sense of a learning goal, the steps to reach it, and their own progress toward it (Sadler, 1989), and effective self-assessment research finds it can genuinely enhance learning and motivation, not just provide teachers an efficiency shortcut (Black & Wiliam, 2006). Because students often find it easier to judge quality by comparing their own work against others', self-assessment in practice tends to blend into peer assessment, and having explicit criteria — such as an analytical scoring rubric, whether teacher-provided or co-developed with students — makes both far more reliable than an unstructured judgment call.

One classroom-culture precondition matters here: self and peer assessment work as intended only when the classroom atmosphere is genuinely built around incremental views of ability and learning goals (see Goal-Orientation Theory). In a classroom that instead emphasizes interpersonal competition for limited rewards, students have a real incentive to inflate their own (and their friends') self-assessments, since accuracy costs them relative standing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Explicit, shared criteria (ideally a rubric) that students can actually judge their own work against, rather than an unstructured sense of "how well did I do"
  • A classroom culture oriented toward incremental ability and learning goals rather than competitive ranking — the strategy's honesty depends on this

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• In a competitively-oriented classroom, self-assessment (traffic lights included) creates a direct incentive to over-report confidence, undermining the very information the strategy is meant to surface
  • Requires the teacher to actually have capacity to work directly with the "red" group while the rest self-organize — the strategy assumes this differentiated capacity, not just the color-coding step itself

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students; the differentiated response (teacher attention to "red," peer evaluation for "orange"/"green") specifically targets students who are least confident with the most direct support

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Accurate self-monitoring of understanding, and efficient allocation of teacher attention toward students who most need it, driven by student-reported rather than teacher-guessed confidence

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. After an assignment or homework is complete, have students mark their own confidence in their success: red (unsure), orange (partially unsure), or green (confident).
  2. Group students who marked orange or green together to evaluate each other's work using shared criteria (ideally a rubric).
  3. Work directly with students who marked red, rather than routing them into peer evaluation alone.
  4. Maintain a classroom culture oriented toward incremental ability and learning goals — without it, the color-coding will tend to inflate rather than inform.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text: • Rubrics — the explicit-criteria tool that makes both the self-assessment and the peer evaluation groups' work reliable rather than an unstructured guess

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2006). Assessment for learning in the classroom. In J. Gardner (Ed.), Assessment and learning (pp. 9-25). Sage.
  • Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18(2), 119-144.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Providing feedback. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Training handouts are supplementary materials distributed during training sessions to enhance learner engagement, structure interactions, and provide a reference for key content. They can take various forms, including outlines, worksheets, feedback forms, and action plans. Effective handouts should not merely duplicate presentation slides but should instead encourage active participation by incorporating note-taking sections, interactive exercises, and opportunities for peer collaboration. Well-designed handouts contribute to a more professional learning environment and improve learner retention by prompting learners to actively engage with the material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful instructional design to align with learning objectives. May require printing or digital distribution. Implementation involves guiding learners to actively use handouts during the session.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If poorly designed, handouts may distract from the presentation. If handouts contain all the information, learners may become passive. Effectiveness depends on active engagement by learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Trainers and educators in corporate, academic, and professional development settings

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learner engagement, structure peer interactions, provide a reference for key content, encourage active participation, improve learner retention

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active learning by encouraging note-taking and participation. Structures peer interactions and feedback. Enhances retention by providing a tangible reference. Contributes to a professional learning environment.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be tailored to different learning styles and content areas. Formats can be adapted to include fill-in-the-blanks, checklists, or open-ended questions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Discussion Sections

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner engagement with handouts during the session. Collect feedback on the usefulness of handouts. Assess retention of key content after the session.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Well-designed handouts have been shown to improve learner engagement, retention, and overall satisfaction with training sessions. Research indicates that active learning strategies, such as those facilitated by effective handouts, lead to deeper understanding and better application of knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Examples include fill-in-the-blank outlines, peer feedback forms, action planning worksheets, and BINGO cards for observation activities. Soapbox is a presentation tool that automatically generates handouts from lesson plans.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These tasks involve the study of traits, requiring learners to identify animal body parts from puzzle pieces and construct either real or mythical animals. They encourage learners to measure, observe, and justify the design of their constructions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Puzzle pieces, drawing materials, rulers, measuring tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require access to specialized materials.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying life science

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify animal traits, construct animals based on their traits, measure and analyze data

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides hands-on activity with life science concepts. Enhances observation and analytical skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Puzzle selection and animal design can be varied. Tasks can be adapted for different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in identifying animal traits, correctness in constructions, precision in measurements

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved understanding of animal traits, enhanced analytical skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Animals Piece by Piece (TEKS): Identifies body parts of animals from puzzle pieces, assembles the puzzle, and names the animal. Mythical Animals (TEKS): Create an imaginary animal by assembling pictures of body parts from pictures of real animals.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Trampoline Review is a kinesthetic learning strategy that involves learners jumping on a small trampoline or performing other motor activities while reviewing information. The combination of physical movement and mental rehearsal enhances memory consolidation and engagement. This method is particularly effective for learners who benefit from kinesthetic learning styles.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Small trampoline or other safe space for motor activities, learning material to be reviewed, and supervision to ensure safety during physical activity

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners with physical limitations, requires careful supervision to ensure safety, may be disruptive in some classroom settings

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for learners who benefit from kinesthetic and tactile learning styles

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory consolidation, increase engagement with learning material, reinforce associations through motor activity, cater to kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Combines physical movement with mental rehearsal, enhances memory through multisensory engagement, increases engagement and motivation, caters to kinesthetic learning styles

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The specific motor activities can be adapted to suit individual needs and preferences. The content being reviewed can be tailored to different subjects and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recall information while performing motor activities, assess their engagement and participation, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using the Trampoline Review

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Combining physical movement with mental rehearsal has been shown to enhance memory consolidation and engagement. Kinesthetic learning strategies cater to diverse learning styles and improve overall academic performance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A learner jumps on a trampoline while reciting multiplication facts or state capitals. Another learner plays catch while answering review questions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Translanguaging recognizes that multilingual speakers have a single linguistic repertoire that they use to understand the world. It involves leveraging students’ full linguistic repertoire, while also teaching students to suppress certain features when asked to perform overtly according to the norms of a named language, whether that language is English or another language. Teachers can invite translanguaging practices into the classroom by providing tools such as dictionaries and translation across languages, and the ability for students to reflect and share feedback in multiple formats.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in teacher mindset to value students' home languages and see them as a resource rather than a deficit. Teachers may need to incorporate new tools and strategies into their instruction.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May face resistance from school administrators or colleagues who do not understand the value of translanguaging. Teachers may need additional training and support to effectively implement translanguaging strategies.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Multilingual learners, English language learners, special education students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Tap into students’ multilingual skills, allow students to communicate and collaborate across languages and modalities, support academic and social gains

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates spaces in which non-English speaking parents can support their child’s development as well as feel welcome in the classroom, fosters cross-cultural sharing, increases student collaborations and individual self-esteem, acknowledges and celebrates linguistic diversity among students

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to students with varying levels of language proficiency and comfort. Teachers can allow flexible language use by each student based on their need and comfort level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the child carefully performing different tasks with their entire repertoire, as well as when using only certain language features. Separate the child’s ability to provide text-based evidence, make inferences, identify main ideas and recognize texts’ craft and structure from their ability to use certain language conventions in English.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Meta-analyses have shown that educational programs that systematically incorporate use of ELLs' home language result in levels of academic success, including achievement in literacy and other academic subjects, that are as high as and often better than that of ELLs in English-only programs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Model how to say something in a more academic way or how to paraphrase academic texts into more conversational language. Have teams reinterpret text using everyday language.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Select academic texts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners with limited background knowledge.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase vocabulary, improve comprehension, increase Disciplinary Literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Builds vocabulary, increases comprehension, enhances ability to communicate in different contexts

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose texts based on their interests and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student translations for accuracy and clarity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Students learn to look at and through both registers.

docs.title: Translate Report Cards Into Multiple Languages
Description
docs.text: Using communication apps to translate report cards into multiple languages (e.g., Spanish, Arabic, Vietnamese, and Mandarin Chinese) makes it easier for parents to understand their child's progress, particularly in districts with diverse populations of English language learners.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Communication apps with translation features, translated report card templates

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be difficult to ensure accuracy of translations, requires ongoing effort to update translations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools and districts with diverse student populations, parents who are English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase parent understanding of student progress, improve communication, support diverse populations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Breaks down language barriers, provides clear and accessible information, supports parent understanding

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Report cards are translated into the parent's native language.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Gather feedback from parents on the usefulness of translations, track parent understanding of student progress

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Translation features can increase parent understanding and engagement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Every student at Normal Park Museum Magnet, a K–8 school in Chattanooga, Tennessee, created a travel journal to chart their learning. These journals included not only charts, drawings, and graphic organizers, but also writing and reflection pieces that capture students’ learning about a topic.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires journals or notebooks for students to write in. Requires time for students to work on their journals.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to integrate writing, drawing, and graphic organizers. Teachers need to provide guidance and support.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-8 students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students chart their learning progress. Encourage reflection on learning experiences. Integrate writing, drawing, and graphic organizers.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual record of learning. Encourages reflection on learning experiences. Integrates writing, drawing, and graphic organizers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can select the topics they want to focus on in their journals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Review student journals to assess learning progress and reflection.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps students chart their learning progress. Encourages reflection on learning experiences. Integrates writing, drawing, and graphic organizers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When beginning a unit on earth science, ask students to imagine they were explorers looking for a new world that could sustain life. In their travel journal, they kept track of everything they were learning, from the impact of man-made disasters to their designs and calculations for a manned rocket that could reach distant planets.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Turn-and-talk involves having learners engage in short, structured discussions with a partner to review and reinforce what they have learned. This strategy promotes active recall, peer interaction, and immediate feedback. Learners take turns sharing their understanding, comparing notes, and helping each other identify gaps in their knowledge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires structured prompts and guidelines for discussion. Instructor must facilitate the activity and provide feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful management to ensure all learners participate actively. Effectiveness depends on learners' ability to articulate their understanding.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly effective for adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning, promote active recall, and enhance peer interaction.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Increases disciplinary literacy, strengthens understanding, and encourages critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted with different prompts tailored to learners' needs. Flexible formats allow for structured or open-ended discussions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Summarization and Synthesis

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and specificity of student responses to assess comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that discussions with peers cement learning and increase disciplinary literacy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Providing timely feedback is crucial for learners to reflect, correct, and extend their performance. Avoiding long delays between assignment submission and feedback delivery helps prevent content disconnection and student isolation, especially in online courses. Short turn-around times support a mentoring or coaching relationship, facilitating a more connected learning environment. Learners should be able to use feedback to influence their future work effectively.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires instructors to prioritize grading and feedback, and to set clear expectations for turn-around times. Utilizing efficient grading methods and tools can help expedite the process.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for instructors with heavy workloads or large class sizes. Requires careful planning and time management to ensure timely feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where timely feedback is essential.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enable timely reflection and improvement, prevent content disconnection, foster a connected learning environment, and facilitate a mentoring relationship.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances learning by allowing learners to apply feedback to future assignments, promotes a sense of connection with the instructor, and prevents feelings of isolation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can adjust the turn-around time based on the complexity of the assignment and the needs of the learners.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Assess Performance
  • Continuous Review

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Measure the impact of timely feedback on learner performance and engagement. Assess learner satisfaction with the turn-around time for feedback. Observe the application of feedback in subsequent assignments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Timely feedback enhances learning, improves engagement, and promotes a connected learning environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing feedback within one week of assignment submission to allow learners to apply it to future work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Turn and Talk involves learners engaging in short discussions with a partner to explain what they heard. The instructor describes a process, pauses at intervals, and directs learners to turn to a partner to explain what they understood. Learners alternate turns speaking, while the instructor observes conversations to check for understanding. This strategy reinforces learning through active discussion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Structured prompts and pauses during instruction, ability to pair learners effectively

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are uncomfortable speaking in pairs, requires careful monitoring to ensure productive conversations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote active listening, enhance understanding through verbalization, provide immediate feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages active listening, provides opportunities for learners to articulate understanding, allows instructors to gauge comprehension

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Pair learners strategically to support diverse learning needs

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the depth and accuracy of learners' explanations during partner discussions, collect feedback on the clarity of their explanations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of peer discussion in reinforcing learning and promoting deeper understanding. Practitioner experience shows that Turn and Talk enhances learner engagement and comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor using Turn and Talk in a science lesson found that students were better able to explain complex concepts after discussing them with a partner. Resource: Rebecca Alber, Edutopia; TeachLikeThis, Turn and Talk video.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A learning environment with minimal visual distractions is created by storing supplies and materials off of tables and desks and limiting decorations and other things hanging on the walls. When students are the primary users of the space, the majority of materials should be for students. A de-cluttered learning environment allows the focus to be on learning. This practice can be used for any learning environment, including classrooms, workspaces, and homes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dedicated time for decluttering and organizing the learning space. Storage solutions such as shelves, cabinets, and bins. A commitment to maintaining a clutter-free environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant effort and resources to implement initially. Some learners may find a completely minimalist environment uninspiring or sterile. Regular maintenance is required to prevent clutter from accumulating.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners who are easily distracted or overstimulated by visual clutter

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce distractions, improve focus, support attention, enhance creativity

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load and distractions, enhances focus and attention, improves visual processing, promotes a sense of calm and order

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the level of decluttering based on the individual needs and preferences of learners. Provide personalized storage solutions or visual barriers for students who need additional support.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to focus and engage in learning activities. Collect feedback from learners on the impact of the uncluttered environment on their learning experience. Compare academic performance and behavior before and after implementing the strategy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that reducing visual clutter can improve attention, reduce stress, and enhance creativity. Research suggests that well-organized and visually appealing learning environments can positively impact student achievement and well-being.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A clean, organized, and uncluttered learning environment is free from distractions and allows the focus to be on learning. Clear workspaces, limited decorations, and organized materials can positively impact student focus and engagement.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Storage solutions (shelves, cubbies), organization tools (bins, labels), and a commitment to maintaining a clutter-free space.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort to maintain organization. May require adjusting personal preferences for decoration.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those sensitive to visual clutter or with attention challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce distractions, improve focus, enhance learning outcomes

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces visual distractions, promotes a calm and organized atmosphere, supports concentration and focus.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Provide individual storage spaces to keep personal items organized. Allow for flexibility in arranging workspaces based on activity needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student behavior and focus levels. Gather feedback on the impact of the environment on learning.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can reduce distractions, improve focus, and create a more conducive learning environment.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This activity increases awareness of personal stereotypes and prejudices, helping learners recognize how their viewpoint influences their perception of others. By examining photographs or actions that trigger snap judgments, learners reflect on pre-conditioned assumptions and explore alternative interpretations. This fosters self-awareness and helps individuals see that their initial judgments may limit relationships with others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Photographs of people or actions that might trigger a response based on snap perceptions, a space for group discussion, and facilitation by an instructor to guide reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may resist acknowledging their biases, or the activity may trigger uncomfortable emotions. It requires a skilled facilitator to guide the discussion and ensure a safe and respectful environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who are unaware of their biases and stereotypes

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-awareness, identify personal biases, encourage open-mindedness, improve interpersonal relationships

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates self-reflection, promotes critical thinking about personal assumptions, encourages empathy and understanding of others. It enables learners to question their initial judgments and explore alternative viewpoints, which can lead to more inclusive attitudes.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The photographs or actions used can be tailored to the specific cultural context and interests of the learners. The level of reflection can be adjusted to suit the learners' cognitive abilities and emotional maturity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of engagement in self-reflection, the ability to identify personal biases, and the willingness to consider alternative interpretations. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes and behaviors towards others.

docs.title: Impact
