docs.text: • Studies suggest that awareness of personal biases can reduce discriminatory behavior and promote more inclusive attitudes. Increased self-awareness also enhances emotional intelligence and interpersonal skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A diversity and inclusion workshop uses photographs of people from different ethnic backgrounds and asks participants to describe them without making assumptions. Participants then reflect on how their descriptions reveal their biases. A classroom exercise asks students to analyze media representations of different social groups and identify stereotypes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When introducing a unit to students, show them how the parts of the unit fit together with a graphic organizer, providing a sense of where they are in the unit at any given time and helping them understand why they are learning the individual parts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teachers must understand the material to be taught.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • None.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide students with a sense of where they are in the unit at any given time.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students understand why they are learning the individual parts.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can decide what concepts are most important for students to learn, and identify other things that may be “nice to know,” but aren’t necessarily vital to student understanding.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• State objectives
  • Advance Organizers

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Student understanding of the information presented.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Could help teachers decide what concepts are most important for students to learn, and identify other things that may be “nice to know,” but aren’t necessarily vital to student understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Untimed tests remove the pressure of completing assessments within a set time limit, allowing learners to focus on problem-solving without time-related anxiety. This approach provides learners cognitive space to work through problems, potentially improving performance by reducing stress and allowing for deeper engagement with the material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Adjustments to testing procedures to remove time constraints. May require additional planning to accommodate extended testing periods.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be feasible in all testing situations (e.g., standardized assessments). Could potentially allow more time for cheating if not properly monitored.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who experience test anxiety or benefit from additional time to process information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce test anxiety, improve problem-solving abilities, assess true understanding without time constraints

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces anxiety, allows for deeper processing, provides a more accurate measure of knowledge

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be combined with other accommodations, such as extended time or reduced distractions, as needed. Difficulty levels can be adjusted to match learner needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare performance on timed vs. untimed tests to assess the impact of time pressure. Observe learners' problem-solving approaches and depth of engagement during untimed tests.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that timed tests can induce math anxiety, blocking working memory and hindering performance (Beilock, 2011; Ramirez, et al, 2013). Untimed conditions may improve performance and reduce anxiety.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Brainquake's Wuzzit Trouble Math promotes problem-solving and pattern recognition under untimed conditions, with a redo option allowing learners to practice more efficient strategies.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Avoid using “you” statements, which can make students defensive. Instead, use “I” statements to talk about situations without placing blame and to acknowledge your own feelings. These questions also allow you to acknowledge your own feelings, and may encourage students to consider your emotions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Awareness of communication techniques, active listening skills

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires conscious effort and practice, may feel unnatural at first

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, counselors, parents, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve communication, reduce defensiveness, promote empathy, encourage emotional awareness

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters better dialogue, reduces conflict, promotes a more supportive environment

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers use personalized “I” statements to reflect on their experiences and feelings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor communication patterns, observe interactions, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances relationships, promotes a more inclusive and understanding environment, improves conflict resolution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Instead of saying, 'You distracted other students in class today,' try 'I felt that other students were distracted by your behavior today.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Reinforce verbal instructions with body language, gestures, and demonstrations to aid comprehension.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Skillful use of non-verbal communication.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all learners or tasks.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially visual and kinesthetic learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension through visual and kinesthetic cues.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages multiple senses and learning styles, enhancing understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use different demonstration techniques based on learner preferences and task requirements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow demonstrated steps.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher models the proper way to hold a paintbrush while explaining a painting technique.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Stories are used as examples of handling emotions in a responsible way. Serve as safe and inviting ways to start the conversation about the range of feelings we have and how to handle each. By reading and talking through how the characters’ emotions connect with their actions, students can start to talk through how emotions drive behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selection of appropriate books, time for reading and discussion

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may struggle to connect with characters or themes, requiring thoughtful facilitation and adaptation.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All age groups, particularly effective in elementary and middle school classrooms to provide a safe context for exploring emotions

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop emotional literacy, connect emotions with behaviors, practice responsible handling of emotions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides vicarious learning experiences, enhances emotional literacy through character analysis, promotes empathy and understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Choice of books to match student interests and experiences, discussions and activities tailored to students’ emotional levels

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student participation in discussions, reflective writing, and other activities that demonstrate understanding of emotional concepts

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances students' emotional literacy and their ability to connect emotions with behaviors, leading to better emotional regulation and social skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Reading a story about a character dealing with anger and discussing alternative ways they could have handled the situation

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using current events and fictional characters as tools to teach social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to current events articles or fictional texts, class time for analysis and discussion, and a skilled facilitator.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some current events or fictional characters may be sensitive or controversial. Learners may struggle to relate to certain characters or events. Discussions can be dominated by a few learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, including K–12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development programs

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop social awareness, enhance empathy, improve understanding of different perspectives, promote critical thinking, and foster positive relationships.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides real-world examples and relatable characters, encourages critical thinking, promotes empathy and understanding, supports positive relationships, and fosters social awareness.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Current events and fictional characters can be chosen to align with different age groups, cultural backgrounds, or interests. Support can be provided for learners who struggle with social awareness or empathy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners’ participation in discussions. Review learners’ written or verbal reflections on current events or fictional characters. Evaluate learners’ understanding of social awareness and empathy.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using current events and fictional characters can enhance social awareness, promote empathy, and improve understanding of different perspectives. Real-world examples and relatable characters can make social awareness more engaging and meaningful.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Analyze current events related to social justice, discuss the perspectives of different characters in a novel, or conduct role-playing activities based on real-world scenarios.

docs.title: Use current events and fictional characters to teach social awareness
Description
docs.text: Utilize real-world events and fictional narratives to explore social dynamics, ethical dilemmas, and diverse perspectives. Analyze characters' actions, motivations, and relationships to promote critical thinking and empathy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to current events and fictional narratives. Requires instructors to be skilled facilitators who can guide discussions and help learners analyze characters' actions and motivations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Current events can be controversial and emotionally charged. Instructors must be prepared to manage discussions and provide support to learners who are struggling.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those who need to develop social awareness and critical thinking skills, K-12, higher education, and adult learners in professional development

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance social awareness, develop critical thinking skills, promote empathy and perspective-taking, foster understanding of social dynamics

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a relatable context for learning about social awareness. Encourages critical thinking, empathy, and perspective-taking. Helps learners develop problem-solving and decision-making skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Select current events and fictional narratives that are relevant to learners' interests and experiences. Topics can include social justice issues, ethical dilemmas, and interpersonal conflicts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Class Discussion
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learner participation and contributions to discussions. Assess learner understanding of social dynamics through written assignments or presentations. Collect learner reflections on their learning and growth.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that using current events and fictional characters can enhance social awareness, develop critical thinking skills, and promote empathy and perspective-taking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • An instructor might use a news article about a social justice issue to spark a discussion about different perspectives and ethical considerations. In a literature class, students might analyze characters' actions and motivations in a novel to understand social dynamics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students use estimation and prediction skills. Ask them how they might do on an upcoming project or how long it might take them to complete a task or assignment. They can record their estimates and then reflect on the accuracy of their predictions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tasks or assignments with clear expectations, recording tools, time for reflection

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may be inaccurate when starting, especially if lacking background knowledge. Requires support, guidance, and ongoing feedback.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who struggle with estimating their performance or time needed for tasks

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve self-awareness, develop realistic expectations, improve time management skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by encouraging students to reflect on their past performance and use that information to make predictions about future performance. Improves time management skills and helps students develop realistic expectations.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tasks can be adjusted based on student abilities. Focus can be on academic projects or general tasks.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Compare student estimates with their actual performance to assess the accuracy of their predictions. Track their ability to improve their estimation skills over time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-awareness, realistic expectations, better time management, and increased self-efficacy. Aids development of a Learner Mindset.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Student estimates grade on a project before submitting, then compares grade with estimate.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Replace negative messages from the inner voice with positive affirmations. A negative message can be replaced with a positive affirmation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • List of positive affirmations, time for daily reflection and repetition.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May feel artificial or ineffective if not genuinely believed. Requires consistent practice and reinforcement.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Cultivate a positive mindset by replacing negative self-talk with positive affirmations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Boosts self-esteem, promotes a positive outlook, reduces stress and anxiety.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can select or create affirmations that resonate with their personal values and goals.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency of positive affirmations used and reported changes in mood or self-perception.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved self-esteem, reduced stress, and increased motivation (Practitioner-based evidence).

docs.title: Use Quotations to Cite Textual Evidence
Description
docs.text: Using quotations to cite textual evidence involves teaching students to select and incorporate direct quotes from texts to support their claims. This strategy provides students with clear guidelines on how to identify and use evidence, enhancing their ability to construct well-supported arguments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to texts, explicit instruction on how to select and integrate quotations, and opportunities for practice and feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May lead to overuse of quotations if not balanced with student commentary. Requires careful instruction to avoid formulaic writing.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Freshman and sophomore students who need structured guidance in citing textual evidence.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve students' ability to support claims with textual evidence, enhance analytical skills, and develop proficiency in constructing evidence-based arguments.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete method for identifying and integrating evidence, enhances argumentative writing skills, and supports critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different content areas and writing tasks. Scaffolds can be adjusted based on student needs, with more support provided initially and gradually reduced as students gain proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased use of textual evidence in student writing. Improved ability to construct well-supported arguments. Enhanced analytical skills.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • High-impact strategy for improving students' writing with evidence, providing clear guidelines and structure for identifying and using textual evidence.

docs.title: Use Templates and Tools That Allow for Scaffolding
Description
docs.text: Using templates and tools that allow for scaffolding involves providing students with structured supports to guide their writing process. This approach includes using planning templates, graphic organizers, and post-it notes to help students organize their ideas and develop their writing skills. Scaffolding is gradually removed as students become more proficient, fostering independence and confidence.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to templates, graphic organizers, and other tools for planning and organizing ideas. Also requires explicit instruction on how to use these tools effectively.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as overly structured by some students. Requires consistent implementation and ongoing support to be effective.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, including reluctant writers, who benefit from structured supports in developing their writing skills.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Support students' writing process through structured supports, enhance organizational skills, and promote independence and confidence.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured framework for organizing ideas, enhances writing skills, and supports independence and confidence.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Templates and tools can be adapted to fit different genres and writing tasks. Scaffolding can be adjusted based on individual student needs, with more support provided initially and gradually reduced as students gain proficiency.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Whole-task performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased use of planning and organizational tools in student writing. Improved ability to construct well-organized writing. Enhanced confidence and independence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Highly effective for supporting students' writing process through structured supports, enhancing organizational skills, and promoting independence and confidence.

docs.title: Use this Toolkit: Mitigating Racial Bias in Edtech
Description
docs.text: This toolkit is designed to guide educational technology (edtech) companies in identifying and mitigating racial bias in the design and development of their products. It emphasizes that without rigorous and intentional oversight, AI and machine learning in edtech can amplify existing racial biases in school systems and introduce new ones through algorithmic design. The toolkit offers actions to take at every stage of product design and development, advocating for racial equity and a commitment to changing education for all students, especially those the system is not designed for.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Commitment to racial equity, willingness to adopt new design and development practices, and openness to feedback from Black and Brown students and teachers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Implementing the toolkit requires significant effort and resources. May not solve all problems related to racial bias in edtech. Relies on the ongoing commitment of edtech companies to prioritize equity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Edtech companies, product designers, developers, and educational institutions committed to addressing racial equity in technology.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To mitigate racial bias in edtech products, promote equitable design and development practices, and ensure that technology supports all students, particularly Black and Brown children.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides structured actions to identify and mitigate bias. Offers a framework for evaluating data, algorithms, and user experiences. Advocates for a partnership approach to address racial inequity.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Encourages the development of products that are sensitive to the specific needs of diverse student populations. Supports culturally responsive teaching and equitable instruction.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Procedural information
  • Provide guidance
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvements in product design, reduced bias in algorithms, increased user satisfaction among Black and Brown students, and alignment with culturally responsive teaching practices.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Mitigation of racial bias: Adopting the toolkit's guidance leads to a reduction in racial bias in edtech products, promoting equity and fairness. Improved learning outcomes: By designing for all students, especially those the system is not designed for, the toolkit supports improved learning outcomes for Black and Brown children.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Each section of the toolkit details actions to take at every stage of product design and development. The Edtech Equity Project encourages feedback and partnership to refine the toolkit and promote its wider adoption.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Supplement verbal instructions with visual aids to support learners' understanding, especially for low-level students.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Availability of visual aids.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all learners or tasks.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially visual learners and those with low English proficiency.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension through visual support.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages visual learning channels, improving understanding and retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use different types of visual aids based on learners' preferences and task requirements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to follow instructions with visual aids.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved comprehension and engagement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher uses a diagram to explain the steps of a scientific process.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The instructor presents a fully solved problem — showing each step and explaining the reasoning behind it — and then asks learners to solve a similar problem independently or in pairs. The cycle of study-then-solve can repeat multiple times, with the level of detail in the example gradually reduced (faded) as learners gain confidence.

docs.title: Design Implications
docs.text: By externalizing the solution process, worked examples let novices study task structure before attempting problems themselves, reducing the unproductive search that characterizes early skill acquisition Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]. The strategy works best when it is not passive: prompting learners to explain each step to themselves (self-explanation) substantially amplifies learning beyond silent study. Examples should be followed immediately by a practice problem of comparable difficulty — the example-then-problem sequence improves both cognitive load and transfer outcomes compared to problem-only practice Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S].

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A worked example that is clear, correctly solved, and annotated with reasoning — not just the steps
  • An immediate practice problem at comparable difficulty
  • Optional: self-explanation prompts ("Why did we do this step?") before moving to independent practice

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Does not substitute for practice; learners who only study examples without solving problems do not develop fluency Pairing worked examples with practice or fading supports transfer better than examples alone. [-S]
  • Less effective for open-ended or design tasks where there is no single correct approach
  • Benefits diminish as expertise grows; continuing to use worked examples past the novice stage can become redundant or counterproductive Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M]

docs.title: Implementation Variability
docs.text:
• Faded examples: Progressively remove steps from successive examples, requiring learners to complete the missing parts — bridges toward fully independent problem solving
  • Incorrect examples: Present a worked example with a deliberate error and ask learners to find and fix it — effective for building error-detection and deepening procedural understanding
  • Comparison: Present two worked examples solving the same problem by different methods and ask which is more efficient or generalizable

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices in any domain where problem-solving involves learnable steps: mathematics, programming, science, writing, clinical reasoning
  • Learners at risk of cognitive overload during unguided problem solving Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M]
  • Less beneficial once learners have sufficient prior knowledge Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M]

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Early procedural fluency: understanding the steps of a solution process
  • Schema acquisition: recognizing the structure shared by a class of problems
  • Metacognitive awareness: monitoring one's own understanding of each step

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Select or write a problem that exemplifies the target skill or procedure
  2. Solve it fully, annotating each step with a brief explanation of why, not just what — use think-aloud if delivering live
  3. Ask learners to study the example and, if time permits, prompt self-explanation: "In your own words, why does this step work?"
  4. Present a near-transfer practice problem of similar structure before providing feedback
  5. Repeat with a second example-problem pair, optionally fading detail from the example
  6. As learners gain confidence, shift to problem-only practice

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Worked Example Routine — a structured classroom routine that formalizes this cycle
  • Comparing Multiple Solution Methods — an extension that pairs two worked examples for comparison
  • Think-Aloud Modeling — the live narration technique for delivering demonstrations

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Mathematics (secondary): Teacher works through a two-step equation on the board, narrating each algebraic move ("I'm dividing both sides because I want to isolate x"). Students then solve a similar equation independently before the class discusses it. Common in direct instruction math curricula such as Saxon Math and Singapore Math.

Programming (introductory CS): An annotated code example shows how to write a function with a loop; comments explain the logic at each line. Students then write a function that solves a parallel problem. Used extensively in CS50, Codecademy, and most introductory coding textbooks.

Science (lab skills): Before students conduct a titration, the instructor performs one live with narrated reasoning. Students complete their own titrations with a checklist that mirrors the steps shown. The checklist is removed in subsequent labs as fluency develops.

Writing (argument structure): Teacher annotates a model paragraph (claim → evidence → warrant) using a think-aloud. Students then write their own paragraph on a different topic using the same structure, with the annotated model visible for reference until it is faded in later assignments.

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59–89. doi:10.1207/s1532690xci0201_3
  • van Gog, T., Kester, L., & Paas, F. (2011). Effects of worked examples, example–problem, and problem–example pairs on novices' learning. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 36(3), 212–218. doi:10.1016/j.cedpsych.2010.10.004
  • Atkinson, R. K., Derry, S. J., Renkl, A., & Wortham, D. (2000). Learning from examples: Instructional principles from the worked examples research. Review of Educational Research, 70(2), 181–214. doi:10.3102/00346543070002181
  • Renkl, A. (2014). Toward an instructionally oriented theory of example-based learning. Cognitive Science, 38(1), 1–37. doi:10.1111/cogs.12086

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy focuses on making library websites more accessible and user-friendly to encourage greater utilization of library resources by students. Key elements include having a clear vision for the website, ensuring easy access to search functionality, simplifying navigation, designing the homepage as a gateway to resources, eliminating library jargon, empowering all users by making the website accessible, and conducting usability testing to inform design decisions. Implementing these practices ensures that students can efficiently find and use library resources, regardless of their familiarity with library systems or any disabilities they may have.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Understanding of web design principles, commitment to accessibility, willingness to conduct usability testing, and ability to implement changes based on user feedback

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires ongoing effort to maintain usability and accessibility. Some recommendations may require technical expertise or resources to implement

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Library staff, website designers, students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve library website usability, increase student utilization of library resources, enhance accessibility for all users, reduce barriers to research

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Simplifies the research process, reduces frustration for students, makes resources more accessible, and ensures the library website meets user expectations

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Recommendations can be tailored to specific library contexts and user needs, ensuring the website is optimized for its unique user base

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Website analytics (e.g., page views, search usage), usability testing results, user surveys, feedback from library staff

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • A user-friendly library website can significantly increase student engagement with library resources and improve their research skills. Studies show that students often find library websites challenging to use, which can be a major barrier to their academic success

docs.title: Using a Culturally Responsive Curriculum Scorecard
Description
docs.text: The Culturally Responsive Curriculum Scorecard is a tool designed to evaluate the extent to which curricula are culturally responsive. It involves a team of individuals with diverse backgrounds (including parents, students, educators, and community members) analyzing various components of the curriculum, such as textbooks, lesson plans, and teaching materials, to assess the presence of representation, social justice themes, and culturally responsive elements in teacher materials. The tool can be adapted for English Language Arts (ELA) and STEAM subjects, and is customizable for different school contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to curriculum materials (textbooks, lesson plans, teacher manuals). A diverse evaluation team with representation from various roles (parents, students, teachers). Time for team members to review and score curriculum based on the scorecard's criteria.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a significant time investment for thorough evaluation. Subjectivity in scoring can lead to variations in results, necessitating clear scoring guidelines and team discussions.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Educators, parents, curriculum developers, and community members involved in evaluating and improving curriculum for K–12 education.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Evaluate and improve the cultural responsiveness of curriculum materials, ensuring they reflect diverse perspectives and promote equity.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured method for evaluating curriculum, ensuring a systematic approach to cultural responsiveness. Promotes inclusivity and representation by assessing materials for bias and cultural relevance. Supports collaborative evaluation through team involvement, enhancing the depth and breadth of analysis.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be customized to fit specific school or district contexts and campaigns, allowing for flexibility and relevance. Applicable to various subjects (ELA, STEAM) and grade levels, catering to different educational needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Criteria Development
  • Resource Evaluation
  • Consensus Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • The final scorecard provides a detailed assessment of various aspects of the curriculum, indicating strengths and areas for improvement. Results can be shared to drive changes in curriculum design and implementation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Culturally responsive curricula enhance student engagement, promote a sense of belonging, and foster critical thinking. Equitable education practices can mitigate the effects of stereotype threat and enhance student success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The NYC Coalition for Educational Justice and the Education Justice Research and Organizing Collaborative (EJ-ROC) used the scorecard to analyze English Language Arts curricula, revealing underrepresentation of authors of color. Toolkits are available to support educators and facilitators in implementing the scorecard effectively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use different colors to represent different emotions in art, which creates associations between emotions and visual cues, enhancing emotional expression and awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to art supplies (e.g., crayons, paint, paper). A facilitator to guide the activity and ensure respectful interactions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires learners to be comfortable expressing emotions through art. Requires a supportive and inclusive environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early childhood and elementary students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance emotional expression, improve emotional awareness, promote positive associations with emotional expression

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Connects emotional expression with a creative outlet (art). Promotes a visual and tangible approach to learning about emotions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Colors can be chosen by learners or assigned based on cultural associations. Different art mediums can be used.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to connect colors with appropriate emotions. Assess their participation and engagement in the activity.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Connecting emotions with visual cues can enhance emotional learning and regulation. (Source: Art Therapy and Emotional Regulation - https://www.arttherapy.org/)

docs.title: Using Empathy Interviews for Family Engagement
Description
docs.text: Empathy interviews involve targeted, one-on-one conversations with a small sample of people to learn from their lived experiences, such as used by organizations like Stanford d.School and The Learning Accelerator. This strategy allows educators to collect stories that ultimately drive district decisions, build trust, and strengthen relationships between families and schools. The empathetic listening starts with asking questions to create a trusting environment for open communication.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Time, thoughtfulness, and care

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Require care to make decisions that best supports students

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Holistic picture of community needs

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Holistic picture of community needs and a closer relationships between families and schools

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Questions can be tailored to specific audiences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Question Formulation
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track community responses

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Building trust and a desire to support the decisions of the district

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Manipulatives are physical objects used as teaching tools to engage students in hands-on learning, especially in mathematics. They introduce, practice, or remediate concepts across all math areas (number and operations, algebra, geometry, measurement, data analysis, probability) and grade levels. Examples include counters, base-10 blocks, fraction strips, pattern blocks, geoboards, and rulers. Effective use of manipulatives involves making their mathematical structure transparent, ensuring learners are familiar with the resource, and allowing learners to use them to support their own arguments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of physical manipulatives relevant to the mathematical concepts being taught, instructor guidance on how to use the manipulatives effectively, and time for exploration and practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • If used without proper understanding, manipulatives can become a crutch rather than a tool. Learners may focus on the manipulative itself rather than the underlying mathematical concepts. Requires careful planning and instruction to ensure effectiveness.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly elementary and middle school learners; useful for learners who benefit from visual and tactile learning experiences

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Introduce mathematical concepts, practice skills, remediate learning gaps, engage in hands-on learning, build understanding of mathematical processes and procedures

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a concrete way to understand abstract mathematical concepts, supports active learning and engagement, allows learners to build understanding and internalize math processes through manipulation of objects, and facilitates the transition from concrete to pictorial to abstract understanding.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Manipulatives can be adapted to suit different learning styles and content areas. Learners can choose from a variety of manipulatives based on their individual preferences and the specific mathematical concept being taught. Tasks can be adapted for individual students to meet their specific needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to explain mathematical concepts using manipulatives, assess their ability to solve problems using manipulatives, and evaluate their transition from using manipulatives to abstract representations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that manipulatives have a positive effect on learning, particularly in retention of mathematical concepts. Studies show manipulatives contribute to well-grounded, interconnected understandings of mathematical ideas.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Counters for teaching one-to-one correspondence, base-10 blocks for modeling number representation and regrouping, fraction strips for showing equivalent fractions, and geoboards for identifying geometric shapes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Replacing negative messages from the inner voice with positive affirmations. Positive affirmations can be specific to growth mindset or general statements of self-worth and capability.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Examples of positive affirmations. Time for students to reflect and choose affirmations. Encouragement and support from the educator.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Affirmations may feel insincere or ineffective if not genuinely believed. Some students may resist using affirmations. The activity's success depends on students' willingness to engage in the process.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those who need support in building self-confidence and resilience.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • To cultivate a positive mindset and increase self-esteem through the use of positive affirmations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes self-awareness by identifying negative messages. Supports emotional regulation by replacing negative thoughts with positive ones. Fosters a growth mindset by emphasizing potential and possibilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to different age groups and learning styles. Students can create their own affirmations or use pre-made examples. Educators can provide varying levels of support and guidance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' engagement and enthusiasm when using affirmations. Assess students' ability to articulate the impact of affirmations on their emotions. Review students' journals or reflections for evidence of positive self-talk.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that positive affirmations can support growth mindset. In order to realize the effects of positive affirmations, the learners need to engage with them regularly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Replacing a negative message with a positive affirmation. Creating personalized affirmations specific to growth mindset. Using affirmations to start the day or before facing a challenging task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy promotes reflective classrooms to ensure learners are fully engaged in making meaning. Reflection enhances the meaning of work, encourages insight, and fosters complex learning. Teachers act as facilitators of meaning-making, guiding learners to approach activities strategically, monitor individual progress, construct meaning, and apply learnings to other contexts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Reflective role models, intentional structuring of classroom activities, and facilitating teachers.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students need to be taught how to reflect to derive rich meaning from their experiences. The students must understand that the students will now look back rather than move forward.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly those needing to develop habits of reflection and meaning-making.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Engage learners in making meaning, enhance insight and learning, develop metacognitive strategies, and facilitate application of learnings to new situations.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes active engagement, enhances meaning-making, develops metacognitive skills, and facilitates application of learning.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can use discussions, interviews, questioning, and logs and journals to guide student reflection. Students also need to see adults—parents, teachers, and administrators—reflect on their practice.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Documentation of reflective conversations, examples of learners’ in-depth reflections, and evidence of habit formation.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Develops the habits of mind related to continuous growth and improvement. As students reflect on their learning, they gain important assessment information about how they perceive the efficacy of their thinking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Technology is a powerful tool in math instruction for ELLs. Look for educational resources that accompany school's technology tools and programs. Find out what's available online. If students are using a calculator or other device, ensure that they learn how to use it. Learn more about how to use AI tools in math. Look for interactive games that offer students a chance to practice their mathematical skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tools and devices and a learning approach to teaching it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students have to learn how to use the technology.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • ELLs in math classrooms

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Use technology for students to better understand math and practice with mathematical skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Technology can simplify and help better grasp difficult math instructions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Use different kind of technology that works for the student and the type of concepts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • By seeing students' improvement.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can greatly improve students' understanding and practice of mathematical concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Interactive math games.

docs.title: Utilize Text Messaging for Parent Engagement
Description
docs.text: Text messaging is used as a primary means of communication for educators and community leaders to engage parents. Studies show high rates of parent engagement and positive outcomes for middle school students and preschoolers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a texting platform, contact information for parents, and willingness to send regular updates.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some parents may not have access to or be comfortable with texting. Text messages can be easily missed or ignored.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Parents of middle school and preschool students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance parent engagement, improve student outcomes, increase communication

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Easy, accessible, and familiar communication method for most parents. Provides quick updates and reminders. Can break down language barriers.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Messages can be tailored to specific students or groups of parents. Translation features support multilingual families.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track response rates to text messages. Monitor student attendance and academic performance. Gather feedback from parents on the usefulness of text messages.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that text messaging efforts can lead to higher rates of parent engagement and positive outcomes for students.

docs.title: Utilizing Mobile Communication Apps for Parent Engagement
Description
docs.text: Mobile communication apps (e.g., ClassDojo, Spotlight, Remind, and Seesaw) offer simple ways for educators to send texts, video summaries, and alerts to parents about school activities or their child’s progress. These tools give parents a deeper look into their children’s performance and experience in the classroom, while strengthening relationships between schools and families. Advanced features include translation of report cards into multiple languages.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Mobile devices, internet access, app installation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires technology access, may be time-consuming, reliance on parent participation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Teachers, educators, and parents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance parent engagement, improve communication, provide support

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Convenient communication, instant updates, deeper insights into student progress, translation features

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Messages and updates can be tailored to individual students and families.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency of communication, gather feedback from parents and teachers

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that mobile apps can increase parent engagement and improve communication between schools and families.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tell students they have the right to feel the way they feel. Recognize that the way they’re feeling is real to them. You can say, “Your feelings aren’t right or wrong” as a way to show respect for how they’re feeling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Emotional intelligence, empathy skills, ability to create a supportive environment

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to implement in highly structured environments, requires careful wording to avoid condoning inappropriate behavior

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 educators, counselors, parents, mentors

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote emotional well-being, build trust, enhance empathy, reduce judgment

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Creates a safe and supportive environment, validates student experiences, promotes emotional literacy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Acknowledge student emotions as valid without necessarily agreeing with their behaviors or choices

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor student emotional well-being, observe interactions, gather feedback from students

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances student self-esteem, promotes emotional resilience, improves relationships, creates a more supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use phrases like 'I understand you're feeling frustrated' or 'It's okay to feel sad about this.'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Valuing the learning process involves emphasizing the importance of understanding, exploration, and growth over achieving high grades. Instructors can promote a growth mindset by focusing on the journey of learning, encouraging curiosity, and celebrating progress rather than solely focusing on outcomes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires a shift in emphasis from grades to learning. Requires instructors to create a supportive and encouraging learning environment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging in systems that heavily emphasize grades. Requires a change in mindset for both instructors and learners.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially those who are grade-focused

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote a growth mindset, encourage curiosity, foster a love of learning

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages learners to focus on understanding rather than just memorization. Promotes intrinsic motivation and a love of learning. Helps learners see mistakes as opportunities for growth.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Activities can be designed to cater to individual learners' interests and learning styles. Instructors can provide different types of support based on individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' engagement and enthusiasm for learning. Track changes in learners' attitudes toward grades. Measure learners' ability to explain concepts and apply knowledge.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that valuing the learning process can lead to increased motivation, improved understanding, and a greater love of learning. Learners who value the process are more likely to persist in the face of challenges and achieve long-term success.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When teaching concepts, use examples in which the irrelevant attributes vary widely. By varying the less relevant attributes of your examples, learners get a more refined understanding of a concept. Learners may form inaccurate concepts if the examples of the concept don’t vary widely on irrelevant attributes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of examples that illustrate the concept while varying irrelevant details.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires effort to identify and present varied examples; may be challenging for highly abstract concepts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially when introducing complex concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Refine understanding of a concept, avoid narrow generalizations

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners distinguish relevant from irrelevant information. Prevents learners from forming overly narrow or inaccurate mental models of a concept.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Vary the complexity and context of the examples to suit different learner backgrounds and needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Demonstration

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to accurately classify new instances of the concept despite variations in irrelevant attributes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows varying less relevant attributes in examples refines learners' understanding of a concept and prevents them from forming inaccurate concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In a course on sexual harassment, including examples of harassment between people of the same gender to avoid the misconception that it only occurs between opposite genders.

docs.title: Varying Levels of Choice in Assessments
Description
docs.text: Give students a choice about the areas of focus in a paper or project. For in-class or online essay questions, each student generates a designated number of questions, and the teacher selects one of those questions for the student to answer. Choice on homework problems of different difficulty.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear guidelines for project expectations and grading criteria. Resources and support for different assessment formats.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires more planning and preparation from teachers. Some students may struggle to make effective choices.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Applicable across K-12, higher education, and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase student agency, promote creativity, and provide personalized learning experiences through varied assessment options.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances motivation by allowing students to choose assessment formats that align with their strengths and interests. Fosters creativity and ownership of learning. Provides personalized learning experiences.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor project options to learner interests and skill sets. Vary levels of support and scaffolding based on individual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess Performance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluation of project outcomes, student reflections, and feedback surveys.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that providing choice increases student engagement and motivation. Studies show that project-based learning promotes deeper understanding and application of knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students choose to submit a video, a presentation, or a written report. Students create their own quiz questions for each other.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Venn diagrams are visual organizers that emphasize comparisons and contrasts between two or more items or concepts. They consist of overlapping circles, with each circle representing a different item. The overlapping sections represent the characteristics that are common to all items, while the non-overlapping sections represent the unique characteristics of each item.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, markers, or digital tools for creating Venn diagrams, learning material to be compared and contrasted, and understanding of the key characteristics of the items being analyzed

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time and effort to create effective Venn diagrams, effectiveness depends on the accuracy and completeness of the information included, may not be suitable for learners who prefer linear note-taking

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for visual learners and those who need support in comparing and contrasting information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension of similarities and differences, facilitate critical thinking and analysis, improve organization of information, strengthen recall

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a clear visual representation of similarities and differences, supports critical thinking and analysis, enhances comprehension and recall, promotes organization of information

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the items or concepts to be compared and contrasted based on their personal interests and learning goals. They can also customize the diagram with colors, images, and personal annotations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to use Venn diagrams to compare and contrast information, assess the accuracy and completeness of their diagrams, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using Venn diagrams

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Venn diagrams have been shown to enhance comprehension of similarities and differences, facilitate critical thinking and analysis, and improve organization of information. They provide a visual structure that supports understanding and recall of complex concepts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a Venn diagram to compare and contrast volcanoes and revolutions, mammals and reptiles, or two characters in a story.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Verbal feedback uses voice recording technology to provide balanced feedback and promote a growth mindset. Instead of writing comments on student papers, the teacher makes symbols or writes numbers and speaks comments into a voice recorder. The first comment should express high expectations and a growth mindset. Students listen to the feedback on devices and revise their work.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Teacher familiarity with voice recording technology, student access to devices for listening to feedback, and a rubric for the assignment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology and may be time-consuming for the teacher.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • 6th grade through postsecondary students in any subject

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve student writing skills, promote a growth mindset, provide engaging feedback, and enhance revision skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides balanced feedback, engages students more easily, and promotes a growth mindset.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Focuses on three main areas identified by the teacher, allowing for targeted feedback.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improvement in student writing quality, increased student engagement with feedback, and positive changes in student attitudes towards writing and revision.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Verbal feedback provides a more engaging way for students to receive feedback, enhancing their understanding and promoting a growth mindset.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Verbal repetition is a strategy where learners repeat information verbally to reinforce understanding and retention. This can include turn-and-talk activities, where learners explain concepts to a partner, or checking for understanding of skills through verbal explanations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Opportunities for learners to verbalize their understanding, structured prompts or questions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging for learners who are uncomfortable speaking in front of others

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial for learners with strong auditory processing skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reinforce learning through verbalization, improve retention, enhance auditory processing

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Strengthens memory through active recall, promotes deeper understanding through explanation, supports auditory processing skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adapt prompts and activities to suit learners' language skills and communication preferences

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Teaching

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the accuracy and clarity of learners' verbal explanations, track improvements in retention and comprehension.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the effectiveness of verbal repetition in reinforcing learning and improving retention. Practitioner experience shows that verbal repetition enhances understanding and supports auditory processing skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using turn-and-talk activities to explain concepts, checking for understanding of counting skills. Resource: Verbal Repetition summary from lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Sending parents a link to a personalized video that provides context about their child’s report card, such as a history of the child’s performance in core subjects, areas for growth, and recommendations to further support the child’s learning. These video report cards can be translated into a parent’s native language to improve clarity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Video recording equipment, video editing skills, translated video templates

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires time and effort to create personalized videos, may be difficult to ensure accuracy of translations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Schools, educators, and parents

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance parent understanding of student progress, improve communication, personalize feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides personalized and accessible information, offers visual and auditory learning, breaks down language barriers

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Video report cards are tailored to individual students and their performance.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide Guidance
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Gather feedback from parents on the usefulness of video report cards, track parent understanding of student progress

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Personalized video report cards can enhance parent understanding and engagement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Videoconferencing platforms with built-in collaboration features such as Microsoft Teams and Google Meet can help teachers replicate teamwork experiences online. These platforms often include digital whiteboards, screensharing capabilities, and real-time co-editing features, making it easier for students to brainstorm strategies and find resources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to videoconferencing platforms with collaboration features, reliable internet connection, familiarity with the platform's tools.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires reliable technology access for all students, potential for technical difficulties, may require additional time for students to learn the platform.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels engaging in remote or hybrid learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance teamwork and collaboration, foster communication and brainstorming, promote student engagement in online learning.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enables real-time collaboration, facilitates brainstorming and problem-solving, promotes communication and teamwork skills, provides a digital space for group work.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tools can be adapted for different group sizes and project types. Options for private and public sharing allow for tailored collaboration experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Collaboration
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving
  • Shared Documents
  • Virtual Whiteboards

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Participation in online collaboration, quality of teamwork and brainstorming, effectiveness of problem-solving, engagement and communication.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Videoconferencing enables meaningful collaboration in online environments, enhancing student engagement and teamwork skills (Castelo, 2020).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using short video clips on SEL topics followed by discussions and/or related activities promotes relevance and meaningful connection of these topics to learners' background knowledge and personal lives. Digital products can create or provide videos that simplify complex SEL topics through storytelling, making the lessons more accessible and applicable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to short video clips on SEL topics and platforms for discussion and related activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the videos. Discussions must be facilitated to ensure inclusivity and respect for diverse perspectives.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 learners and adult learners interested in social and emotional learning

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote relevance of SEL topics, connect SEL to personal lives, simplify complex topics through storytelling

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances engagement by connecting content to learners' background knowledge and personal experiences. Facilitates understanding through simplified storytelling and relatable content.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be selected based on age, cultural relevance, and specific learning needs. Discussion prompts and activities can be tailored to individual learning styles and experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Peer Discussion
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the level of learner engagement in discussions and activities. Assess the depth of connections learners make between video content and their own lives.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Relevant SEL videos support emotional development, social awareness, and academic performance. Research emphasizes the importance of connecting learning to personal lives to enhance motivation and retention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • ClassDojo offers videos on growth mindset, empathy, and more, designed to spark classroom discussions. Flocabulary provides videos on managing frustration, building empathy, and other life skills suitable for K-12.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Videos are dynamic resources for supporting curricula, engaging students through sight and sound. When enhanced with subtitles, they cater to a wider range of learning styles by allowing students to watch, listen, or read the content. Videos stimulate and maintain interest, providing an innovative and effective means for educators to deliver curriculum content. They create immersive experiences by introducing voices from the past, showcasing diverse cultures, and investigating scientific phenomena, thereby making abstract concepts more concrete and memorable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to video resources, internet connectivity (for online videos), devices for playback, and additional support tools such as interactive word glossary, dictionary, thesaurus, and online encyclopedia.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Videos should be used as an enhancement to a lesson, not as a standalone activity. The quality of content and instruction provided by the video service provider is extremely important. Free educational video-sharing websites may require teachers or parents to spend countless hours sieving through video of only a general educational nature.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–12 students, auditory and visual learners, English language learners (with subtitles)

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance student engagement, improve reading and literacy skills, cater to auditory and visual learners, provide interactive instruction

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers sensory experiences that bring concepts to life, flexible teaching medium with stop, start, and rewind capabilities, supports interactive instruction by challenging students to predict outcomes or debate historical references. The use of subtitles can improve reading and literacy skills simultaneously, and cater to the greatest range of preferred learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can isolate specific parts of videos, record their own voice-overs, and embed questions to check for student understanding. Subtitles can be adjusted for font size to cater to different visual needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track student engagement and participation during and after video viewing. Assess comprehension through embedded questions, quizzes, and discussions. Analyze improvements in reading and literacy skills through pre- and post-video assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of video in the classroom as a dynamic resource for supporting curricula, increasing student interest, and improving reading and literacy skills. Teachers can effectively use video during the course of the academic year to address and deliver the required curriculum content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • EDpuzzle allows teachers to edit, customize, and enhance existing videos to meet their classroom needs, isolating parts of videos, recording voice-overs, and embedding questions. Zane Education provides a comprehensive online video library with subtitled videos teaching curriculum-aligned topics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A short video relating to the topic of the reading is shown. Discussion questions are prepared based on the video content. After watching the video, learners discuss what they saw with a partner. This approach leverages visual media to engage learners, activate prior knowledge, and provide a context for the reading material.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to a relevant video and pre-prepared discussion questions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the video. Some learners may be distracted by the visual media.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for learners of all ages and proficiency levels, adaptable for various topics.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Engage learners with visual media, activate prior knowledge, and provide context for the reading material.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages visual learners, provides a shared experience, and activates prior knowledge in an accessible way.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be selected to match different proficiency levels and learning objectives. Discussion questions can be adapted based on the content of the video.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Pre-Class Video/Lecture
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the engagement and quality of discussions. Collect feedback on how well the video prepared learners for the reading.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances engagement, activates prior knowledge through visual stimulation, and provides a contextual framework for the reading material.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Before reading about the rainforest, a short documentary showcasing its biodiversity and environmental challenges can be shown, followed by discussions on key features and conservation efforts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Virtual embodiment is used to give people the experience of the golden rule in operation. VR can place people virtually in the body of another, such that an “ingroup” member can temporarily occupy the body and position of an “outgroup” member: a person with pale skin can temporarily have dark skin, an adult can become a child, and someone can experience a world where they are taller or shorter than their real height

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • adult and non-patient groups, headset

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not distinguish well between reality and virtual reality.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adults and non-patient groups

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Experience the golden rule in operation, temporarily occupy the body and position of an “outgroup” member

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Perspective of another person

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Tailor the embodiment experience

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Gain attention
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Application
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Changes in implicit attitudes.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can lead to emotional, cognitive, and behavioral changes

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Classroom time for tutoring is completely eliminated in this model. Educators, like university professors, share all the resources and allocate time for individual sessions during office hours. Assignments are collected online through learning management systems.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires comprehensive online resources, availability for individual sessions, learning management system.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Dependent on learners' self-motivation, may not suit all learning styles.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Suitable for independent learners who can manage their time and seek assistance when needed.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide flexibility, support self-directed learning, offer personalized assistance during office hours.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Offers maximum flexibility, allows learners to progress at their own pace.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Individual sessions can be tailored to address specific learning needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Individual Reflection
  • Provide Feedback
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Completion rates of online assignments, utilization of office hours, overall academic performance.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Can provide a flexible, personalized learning experience for self-directed learners.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Online university courses using videos, readings, and virtual office hours.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: VR is used to guide new workers through a virtual phone call with a Fidelity “customer” going through a financial crisis, training them about empathy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • VR headsets, appropriate software, and a space to practice in.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some workers may have technical difficulties with VR.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • New workers, customer service reps, customer service trainers

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve workers' empathy skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows workers to experience a customer facing crisis in a safe environment and to receive feedback

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scenarios can be tailored to different customer concerns, job functions, and worker skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved employee metrics with customer issues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Train empathy effectively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Virtual reality is used to prepare employees for the commotion when customers swarm stores on Black Friday and evaluating how workers respond to angry shoppers. Additionally, VR is being used to ascertain which employees have the skills to fill middle management positions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • VR systems with interactive customer service simulations.

docs.title: Constraints
