docs.text: • Relies on accuracy of VR and does not replicate all aspects of live customer service.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Retail employees and managers.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve hiring, employee experience, and assess skills more accurately.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides safe environments to experiment and practice managing customer service crises.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Assessments can be tailored to individual roles, responsibilities and skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assess performance
  • Provide feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Performance and response quality.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Better identification of staff skills and skill needs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Virtual Reality (VR) training is a method of using VR technology to create simulated environments where learners can engage in interactive training scenarios. VR training has proven effective in enhancing training efficiency and improving skill retention, especially in hands-on jobs. VR simulates real-world situations, allowing learners to practice and make mistakes in a safe, controlled environment, promoting experiential learning and mastery.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • VR headsets and equipment, appropriate software, realistic and well-designed virtual environments, trained facilitators.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Initial setup costs can be high, requires technical expertise, may cause motion sickness in some users, needs ongoing updates and maintenance.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Workforce training, medical professionals, aviation personnel, military, technicians, and any field benefiting from hands-on practice and realistic scenario simulation.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve skill retention, increase training efficiency, enhance safety in training, provide realistic and immersive learning experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a safe and controlled environment for practice, enables realistic scenario simulations, facilitates experiential learning, improves engagement and knowledge retention.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • VR training can be tailored to specific job roles, tasks, and skill levels, with varying difficulty levels and interactive elements.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide Feedback
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Metrics on skill improvement, error reduction, task completion time, knowledge retention, and learner engagement can be collected and analyzed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show increased efficiency, improved memory recall, reduced procedural errors, enhanced performance, and higher engagement levels in various industries.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using graphics or gestures can help learners who face auditory processing challenges. Providing visual support alongside spoken information can enhance comprehension and retention.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Visual aids, such as graphics, diagrams, and gestures

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be accessible to all learners due to visual impairments

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve retention, support learners who face auditory processing challenges

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides reinforcement of concepts through an additional sense, visual cues are permanent so allow the students to revisit the information whenever necessary

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow different types of visual cues. Some learners might like to see literal graphics while others need a few gestures.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the frequency and effectiveness of visual cue use. Review notes to see if students take advantage of the visual aids.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that visual aids can help support learning by reinforcing learning. Practitioner experience supports the effectiveness of visual cues in enhancing learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using gestures when explaining a concept, showing a graphic organizer when explaining a process. Resource: Auditory Processing micro-credential, Friday Institute at NC State

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Visual mnemonics involve creating visual images to cue a strategy or represent a concept. These images serve as memorable triggers that help learners recall information effectively. By associating abstract concepts with concrete visuals, visual mnemonics enhance memory encoding and retrieval.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, markers, or digital tools for creating visual images, learning material to be memorized, and creativity to develop memorable associations

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for learners with visual impairments, requires creativity and imagination, effectiveness depends on the memorability of the visuals

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for visual learners and those who struggle with abstract concepts

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance memory recall, facilitate understanding of abstract concepts, improve encoding and retrieval of information, cater to visual learning styles

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances memory through visual association, simplifies complex concepts, caters to visual learning styles, increases engagement and motivation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can create their own visual mnemonics that resonate with their personal interests and experiences. The complexity of the visuals can be adapted to suit different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to recall information using the visual mnemonics, assess the creativity and relevance of the visuals, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using visual mnemonics

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual mnemonics have been shown to enhance memory recall and improve understanding of complex concepts. They cater to visual learning styles and increase engagement with the material.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a sun with legs and arms singing "RAPS" to remember the freedoms of Religion, Assembly, Press, and Speech (First Amendment rights). Drawing a picture of a person saying, "Oh, hi, oh Columbus" to associate the word "Columbus" with the word "Ohio."

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Visual organizers are tools that visually represent ideas and concepts, helping learners construct meaning and strengthen recall. They mimic the brain's mental schema, supporting learners' cognition and literacy skills. Visual organizers can be used to emphasize cause-and-effect, sequence of events, or create summaries.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Paper, markers, or digital tools for creating visual organizers, learning material to be organized, and understanding of the different types of visual organizers (e.g., mind maps, Venn diagrams)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require time and effort to create effective visual organizers, effectiveness depends on the clarity and organization of the visual representation, may not be suitable for learners who prefer linear note-taking

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly useful for visual learners and those who need support in organizing information

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, strengthen recall, facilitate organization of information, improve critical thinking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of ideas, supports organization and comprehension, enhances recall through visual cues, promotes critical thinking skills

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose the type of visual organizer that best suits their learning style and the specific content being studied. They can also customize the organizer with colors, images, and personal annotations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Supportive information
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Enhance retention and transfer

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to use visual organizers to summarize and analyze information, assess the clarity and organization of their organizers, evaluate performance on tests and quizzes after using visual organizers

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual organizers have been shown to enhance comprehension, strengthen recall, and improve critical thinking skills. They provide a visual structure that supports organization and understanding of complex information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a mind map to brainstorm ideas for a writing assignment, creating a Venn diagram to compare and contrast two characters in a story, using a flowchart to outline the steps in a scientific process.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using artwork along with life lesson statements can help adolescents write essays. With an image attached, students have plenty to say about the statement. Students gaze at the photo, ask themselves what it’s about, and make up a life lesson that fits. This method involves an 11-minute essay with specific instructions for timed writing, guiding students to connect the visuals with their own experiences and beliefs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Royalty-free photos, life lesson statements, and instructions for the 11-minute essay.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all learners or writing tasks, and requires thoughtful selection of visuals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adolescents and adult learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve essay writing skills, encourage deeper thinking, and connect thoughts to personal experiences.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides visual prompts to stimulate thinking, helps students connect visuals with their own experiences, and guides the writing process through structured steps.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose photos that resonate with them and create their own life lessons.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the depth of students' thoughts, the connections they make between visuals and experiences, and the quality of their essays.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps students plunge into deeper meanings of statements, grapple with the abstract, and connect thoughts to their world, resulting in more insightful essays.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Visual reading aids, such as reading guides, colored overlays, and tracking rulers, are tools designed to make text more accessible and readable. They help learners with visual difficulties, visual tracking problems, or those who struggle to maintain focus while reading. These aids can reduce visual stress, minimize distractions, and improve reading fluency and accuracy. Examples include reading guides that highlight one line of text, colored overlays that change the background color of the page, and tracking rulers that help maintain place while reading.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Reading materials, visual reading aids (reading guides, colored overlays, tracking rulers). For colored overlays, a selection of colors should be available to determine the most effective hue for the individual. These can be implemented in both print and digital reading contexts.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Elementary-aged kids learning to read may find it difficult to use until they grasp the concept of word-by-word reading. High school students may be hesitant to use reading guides at school due to social stigma, but may adopt them for homework. The effectiveness of colored overlays depends on selecting the correct color for the individual, which may require a process of trial and error.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with visual difficulties, dyslexia, ADHD, visual processing issues, and those who struggle with reading fluency, including K-12 students and adults

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve reading fluency, reduce visual stress, enhance focus, support visual tracking skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces visual distractions, supports visual tracking, increases reading rate, improves focus, and provides a low-tech, accessible solution for reading difficulties. Colored overlays can filter out rogue wavelengths of light that cause visual stress, stabilizing the image of the text.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Visual reading aids come in various forms (reading guides, colored overlays, tracking rulers) and can be chosen based on individual preferences and needs. Colored overlays can be selected in specific hues and saturations that work best for each individual. Reading guides can be adjusted to highlight different amounts of text.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe improvements in reading speed, accuracy, and fluency. Monitor the frequency of losing place while reading. Collect self-reports from learners regarding their comfort and focus while using the aids. Track the usage and preference for different types of reading aids.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that colored overlays can significantly improve reading speed and comprehension over extended periods. Eye Level Reading Rulers are used in approximately 60% of schools in England as an intervention strategy for students with reading difficulties. Studies have shown that visual stress can be remedied with colored overlays or lenses, leading to improved reading experiences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • BeeLine Reader uses color gradients to support fluent reading. Eye Level Reading Ruler is a user-friendly alternative to colored overlays. A teenage boy's experience was transformed by reading through a colored overlay, allowing him to see text clearly for the first time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This evidence-based strategy involves using visual representations, such as schematic diagrams, to help learners understand abstract mathematics concepts and solve problems. These visual aids accurately depict a problem’s mathematical quantities and relationships, reflecting a learner's understanding of the problem and aiding in its correct solution. Visual representations can take various forms, including number lines, strip diagrams, pictures, graphs/charts, and graphic organizers.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Materials for creating visual representations, instruction on different types of visual representations, and opportunities for practice.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Students may need explicit instruction on how to create and use visual representations effectively. Some may require additional support to avoid disorganized or inaccurate visuals.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly students with mathematics learning disabilities or difficulties

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve understanding of mathematics concepts, enhance problem-solving skills, facilitate the transition from concrete to abstract thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports understanding of abstract concepts, enhances problem-solving skills, facilitates mathematical communication, flexible for various grade levels and math topics

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Students can choose the type of visual representation that works best for them.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the accuracy and clarity of the visual representations. Assess the learners' ability to use the diagrams to solve problems correctly. Analyze the explanations of the solutions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show using visual representations significantly improves problem-solving accuracy. Visuals help students with and without disabilities understand and solve math problems effectively.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Visual timers help teach the concept of time to children with special needs. It also gives them an understanding that every activity is limited to a set amount of time.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Visual timer (physical or digital), structured activities, clear expectations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May not be suitable for all learners. Some learners may become overly reliant on the timer.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners with special needs, especially children with autism and ADHD

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Teach the concept of time, provide structure, support transitions, increase understanding

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of time, supports transitions, increases understanding of time limits, reduces anxiety, promotes self-regulation

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different types of visual timers (physical, digital, apps) can be selected based on individual preferences and needs. Time intervals can be adjusted.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to transition between activities. Track compliance with time limits. Collect feedback on the effectiveness of the timer.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual timers can significantly improve understanding of time and support transitions for learners with special needs. They provide a structured and predictable environment that reduces anxiety and promotes self-regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A parent uses a visual timer to signal the end of playtime and the start of homework. A teacher uses a visual timer during classroom activities to help students stay on task.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use visuals such as infographics and mind maps to help transform abstract concepts into clear and engaging formats. By visually breaking down complex ideas, these tools make it easier for learners to grasp how different elements of a concept connect and interact within a broader business context.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Tools for creating visuals (e.g., software, whiteboards). A clear understanding of the concept to be visualized.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Visuals can be overwhelming if not designed effectively. Some concepts may be difficult to represent visually.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who benefit from visual aids

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance understanding of complex concepts, facilitate information retention, improve learner engagement

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Transforms abstract concepts into clear and engaging formats. Visually breaks down complex ideas, making it easier for learners to grasp how different elements of a concept connect and interact within a broader business context.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Allow learners to create their own mind maps or visualizations to personalize the learning experience.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Supportive information

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to explain concepts using the visuals they created or analyzed.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visuals and mind maps play a vital role in organizing information and enhancing understanding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using a flowchart to delineate a complicated concept into simpler, visually attractive components or using infographics to effectively summarize complex regulations into key, manageable points by utilizing different icons and color codes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Visualizing involves creating a mental image or representation of a problem or text to aid in understanding. This can include drawing a picture, diagram, table, or other representation to help solve the problem.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to tools or materials for creating visual representations, such as paper, pencils, or software.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional support for learners who struggle with visualizing abstract concepts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, especially visual learners and those who benefit from concrete representations.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance comprehension, improve problem-solving skills, and promote creative thinking.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps learners create mental images and representations, improving comprehension and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted by providing different tools or techniques for visualizing problems or texts.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved comprehension, better problem-solving accuracy, and the ability to create meaningful visual representations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Helps learners understand abstract concepts and improve their problem-solving skills by creating visual representations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Drawing a diagram to represent the relationships between different elements in a problem.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Explicitly teaching vocabulary words and their definitions, along with providing context, to help students understand and use new words effectively. Vocabulary instruction can include pre-teaching challenging words before reading a text, so students don't become discouraged. Activities can be incorporated into any content area.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Identification of key vocabulary words. Preparation of clear and concise definitions. Time for instruction and practice in class.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming. Students may memorize definitions without truly understanding the words in context. May not address underlying issues with decoding or reading fluency.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All grade levels, particularly beneficial for struggling learners and those with limited vocabulary

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase students' vocabulary, improve reading comprehension, enhance ability to understand challenging texts, reduce frustration when encountering unfamiliar words

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reduces cognitive load by pre-teaching difficult words. Supports reading comprehension and engagement by making text more accessible. Increases confidence in reading challenging materials.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Vocabulary words can be tailored to specific texts or topics. Definitions can be provided in multiple formats (visual, audio, written). Students can choose to focus on words that are most relevant to their needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Assigned Readings
  • Lectures

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Vocabulary quizzes. Student use of new words in writing and speaking. Observation of student engagement during reading activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Studies show that explicit vocabulary instruction improves reading comprehension and overall academic achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Providing definitions for difficult words before reading a challenging text. Using flashcards or games to practice vocabulary words. Incorporating new vocabulary words into writing assignments.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Instructors should present vocabulary in context so that learners can deduce the meaning for themselves, aiding understanding and retention. Instructors should not simply define words and phrases. If learners guess the meaning incorrectly, provide another example or let them compare examples. Use texts written specifically for vocabulary instruction. After learning new words or phrases, learners should practice using them in their own words. One way to accomplish this is to start each class with a 5–10 minute conversation on a topic that allows them to reuse what they have learned.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires texts with vocabulary presented in context, time for practice and conversation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Context does not always help in explaining meaning, may be time-consuming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve English vocabulary, increase understanding and memory, develop self-teaching skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Aids understanding and memory, provides satisfaction, teaches students how to learn on their own

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can provide additional support based on student needs, such as another example or time to work it out on their own

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners use new vocabulary in conversation or role play, write original sentences

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using context to learn meaning is an essential skill that your students need to know for the future. The students we have today won't be going to English class forever. It is part of our responsibility as English teachers (sorry to sound pompous) to make sure that they can continue improving their English by themselves and without the need for us.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Wait time is the period of silence between the time a question is asked and the time when one or more learners respond to that question. It involves pausing for a minimum of three seconds after posing a question to allow learners time to process and formulate a response. It also involves waiting after getting a response to allow other learners to process the answer as well. The specific duration of wait time depends on the complexity of the question, the ability of the learners, and the clarity with which the question was asked. Recall and lower-level questions may require 1-3 seconds, calculation questions may take 4-6 seconds, and higher-order questions may require 6-10 seconds.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires conscious effort from the instructor to pause for at least three seconds after asking a question. It may also require adjusting the pace of instruction to accommodate the additional time.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Teachers may feel uncomfortable with silence or pressured to cover content quickly, making it difficult to consistently implement wait time. Students accustomed to quick-fire questions and answers may initially resist the change.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, particularly beneficial in elementary and secondary education

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve the quality and length of student responses, involve more class members, elicit better quality answers, encourage students to ask their own questions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Allows learners time to process information, formulate thoughtful responses, and take intellectual risks. It also provides an opportunity for both the teacher and all students to complete appropriate information processing tasks, feelings, oral responses, and actions.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Teachers can adjust the wait time based on the complexity of the question, the ability of the students, and the clarity with which the question was asked. Different students may require different amounts of time to process information and formulate a response.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Increased length and correctness of student responses, decreased number of no answers or "I don't know" responses, increased number of students volunteering answers, improved academic achievement test scores

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research by Mary Budd Rowe in 1972 and Robert Stahl in the 1990s demonstrated that wait time can lead to positive changes in student and teacher behaviors and attitudes, including improved response quality, increased participation, and enhanced academic achievement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A teacher implementing wait time in a science lesson allows at least three seconds after asking a question about a scientific concept, resulting in more students volunteering thoughtful and detailed answers. A product reminds students to pause a video or activity to take time to think before they answer.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A large calendar for family appointments and events can help kids see that organization is a lifelong skill. Everyone — even young kids — can see how they fit into the bigger picture of the household. Try using a different color marker for each family member to highlight different schedules.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Large wall calendar, colored markers

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a central location for the calendar. Dependent on consistent updating and use. May not be effective for learners with visual impairments.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners of all ages, families

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote awareness of schedules and events, enhance time management skills, foster a sense of belonging within the household

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a visual representation of time and events, reduces reliance on verbal reminders, promotes communication and coordination.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Calendar can be customized with different colors, symbols, and images. Family members can add their own events and appointments.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to recall and anticipate events. Track the frequency of on-time arrival at appointments. Gather feedback from the learner on the usefulness of the calendar.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Visual calendars have been shown to improve time management and reduce stress. Family calendars promote communication and a sense of shared responsibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Use different colored markers for each family member. Add stickers or images to represent important events.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This technique involves giving high school students a clear warning that talking during the lesson will result in a consequence, such as taking time off their break. The teacher writes instructions in bold letters on the board, stating that students need to be sitting in silence by the time the title is written, and anyone still talking will be kept behind for five minutes. This approach provides adequate warning and sets clear expectations.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Clear communication of expectations, consistent enforcement of consequences, willingness to follow through on warnings.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be perceived as punitive, requires consistent follow-through, may not be effective for all students.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • High school educators

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Reduce classroom noise, establish clear expectations, enforce consequences for disruptive behavior

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides clear warning and expectations, enforces consequences for disruptive behavior, reduces the need for verbal reprimands.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The consequence can be adjusted based on school policy and student needs. The warning can be tailored to specific classroom situations.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor classroom noise levels after implementing the warning system. Track the number of students kept behind for talking.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Providing a clear warning and consequence can improve classroom management by establishing clear expectations and reducing disruptive behavior in high school classrooms.

docs.title: Related Strategies
docs.text:
• Low-Profile Classroom Control — the warn-then-follow-through reaction sequence this technique instantiates
  • Natural and Logical Consequences — worth checking this specific consequence against, since a fixed break-time deduction can read as punishment rather than a consequence proportionate to and connected with the misbehavior

docs.title: Description
docs.text: These tasks involve examining and sorting waste items in a garbage can, categorizing and charting the items, and proposing solutions to reduce the amount of solid waste. They enhance awareness of waste management and health issues.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Waste items, sorting materials, charting tools

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require access to waste items. Safety precautions are necessary.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K–4 learners studying science and social perspectives

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Examine and sort waste, categorize waste items, propose waste reduction solutions

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes environmental awareness. Enhances problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Waste selection can be varied. Solutions can be tailored to different skill levels.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy in sorting and categorizing waste, correctness in proposing solutions, logical justification of solutions

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improved awareness of waste management, enhanced problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Discovering the Problem of Solid Waste (LCESC): Examine and sort waste items in a garbage can, categorizing and charting the items on a graph, and proposing a solution to reduce the amount of solid waste in the garbage can.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Share helpful videos that explains big emotions to kids. Reinforce topic using different medium while providing simple steps to get students thinking about their own emotional regulation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to video and time for debrief.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires thought about appropriate video. Some students may need different sensory activity.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-5 Learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Understand emotional regulation process, apply steps to manage their own emotional regulation

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Reinforces emotional regulation through a different medium while providing steps for their own emotional regulation.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Videos can be adjusted to the grade level.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Demonstration
  • Provide guidance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe students' ability to apply techniques from videos.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Improve students to think about steps for emotional regulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Watching a video and then having student participate in a debrief to ask questions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Incorporating web dictionaries and thesauruses into vocabulary lessons allows learners to quickly search for and understand unfamiliar words. When learners look up challenging words while they read, they monitor their comprehension and activate cognitive processes that support increased recall and consolidation to long-term memory. Features such as voice search, audio pronunciation, and embedded quizzes are also helpful for vocabulary building and practice.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to web-based dictionary and thesaurus tools (e.g., Merriam-Webster Dictionary, Dictionary.com), electronic devices, and reading materials.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Reliance on technology and internet access. May not be suitable for learners with limited digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12, higher education, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Increase vocabulary, enhance comprehension, promote self-monitoring

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Supports active reading, enhances understanding of unfamiliar words, reinforces learning through voice search, audio pronunciation, and quizzes. Promotes self-monitoring and metacognition.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adaptable to various reading levels and learning styles through features like voice search and quizzes. Can be used independently or in group settings.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assigned Readings

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track frequency of dictionary use, assess accuracy of definitions and explanations, and monitor improvement in vocabulary knowledge through pre- and post-assessments.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research indicates that frequent use of dictionaries and thesauruses enhances vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension, supporting effective learning and long-term retention.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A web-search scavenger hunt is a fun way to help students learn how to effectively use search engines to find accurate information. Students work in teams to answer questions by researching online and awarding points for every credible website students identify to correctly answer the questions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Questions to answer.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires preparation and time.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Effectively use search engines to find accurate information.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students learn how to effectively use search engines to find accurate information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Make up your own questions for students to answer by researching online or use the worksheet included in this lesson plan.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Collaboration
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Every credible website students identify to correctly answer the questions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Fun learning experience.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students can encourage friendly competition by having your class work in teams and awarding points for every credible website students identify to correctly answer the questions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners use free web-based tools to annotate online documents, including slideshows, blog posts, or PDFs. These tools often have group chat functions, facilitating the assignment of groups for giving and receiving feedback on work in progress. This method enables direct, contextual feedback on digital content.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Requires access to web annotation tools, digital documents to annotate, and clear guidelines for providing constructive feedback.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Effectiveness depends on learners' familiarity with the tools and their ability to provide thoughtful, relevant feedback. May require initial training on tool usage.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Higher education, adult learners, and professional development programs where learners engage with digital documents.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Facilitate peer review, provide contextual feedback, enhance collaborative learning, and improve digital literacy.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a direct and contextual way for learners to give and receive feedback on digital content. Enhances collaborative learning by facilitating group discussions and annotations. Improves digital literacy through the use of online tools.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Different tools offer varying features such as group chat, assignment management, and annotation types, allowing instructors to choose the most suitable platform for their needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide Feedback
  • Peer Interaction
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Digital Tools

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the quality and relevance of annotations. Observe engagement and participation in group discussions. Measure improvements in the quality of revised documents based on feedback.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • These tools can enhance engagement and collaboration in online learning environments, leading to improved understanding and retention of content.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Hypothes.is, Diigo, Markup, Perusall, and CommentPress are examples of web annotation tools that support peer feedback on digital documents.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners are taught the differences between .com, .gov, .org, and .edu domains to assess the reliability of websites. This can be taught as a mini-lesson where students learn the typical purpose and potential biases of each domain type.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a variety of websites with different domain types and a framework for guiding the analysis (e.g., a checklist or rubric).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Domain analysis is just one factor to consider when evaluating the reliability of a website. Learners should also be taught to consider other factors, such as the author's credentials, the currency of the information, and the presence of bias.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance learners' ability to evaluate the credibility and reliability of online sources.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides learners with a simple and practical framework for assessing the trustworthiness of websites, supports the development of critical literacy skills, and promotes informed decision-making in online environments.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The depth of the analysis can be adjusted to meet the needs of diverse learners. Scaffolding can be provided to learners who are less familiar with website domains and online source evaluation.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess learners' ability to accurately identify the domain type of a website and to explain the potential implications for its reliability. Observe the quality of their source evaluations and the arguments they make to support their conclusions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research suggests that explicit instruction in website domain analysis can improve learners' ability to evaluate the credibility of online sources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners examine websites (both reliable and unreliable) using a checklist to assess various elements such as the corroboration of information, writer reliability, information currency, documentation, advocacy, and conflict of interest.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A checklist of evaluation criteria and access to a variety of websites, including both reliable and unreliable sources.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effectiveness depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the checklist, and learners may require guidance in interpreting and applying the criteria.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school, high school, and adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop critical evaluation skills for assessing the reliability of online information sources.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a structured approach to evaluating websites, encouraging critical thinking about information reliability, and enhancing digital literacy skills.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The checklist can be modified to include additional or more specific criteria based on the learners' needs and the context of the task.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide feedback
  • Assessment

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Learners' ability to accurately apply the checklist criteria and justify their evaluations of website reliability.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Structured evaluation tools can enhance critical thinking and digital literacy skills, enabling learners to make informed judgments about online sources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Students spend 10-15 minutes every week reflecting on their learning experiences by responding to prompts, enhancing dialogue, inspiring openness, and diversity.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Allocated time for reflection, structured reflection prompts, and a teacher committed to reviewing and responding to student reflections.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require careful planning and facilitation to ensure students engage meaningfully with the reflection prompts.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle school learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Provide students with regular opportunities to reflect on what they have learned, how they have learned, and their experiences in the classroom.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students recognize mastery, enhance self-awareness and character development, appreciate diversity and relationships, think about their learning process, and engage in dialogue with the teacher.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The prompts can be tailored to the specific content and activities of the week, allowing for personalized reflection based on individual learning experiences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: • individual reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student growth in content knowledge, self-awareness, metacognition, and their ability to strengthen relationships within the class.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Promotes student autonomy and self-efficacy, which contribute to enhanced learning and character development.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using an EQ Feeling Chart, students identify how they are feeling individually. Then, a student demonstrates how they are feeling through body language and facial expressions only, and the whole class tries to guess what that student is feeling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart, time for individual reflection and whole-class sharing

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some students may not feel comfortable demonstrating their feelings in front of the class. It is important to create a safe and supportive environment where students feel comfortable sharing. Some students may not be able to accurately identify or demonstrate their feelings.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels, especially K–12

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify and demonstrate feelings non-verbally, encourage self-awareness, promote sharing and empathy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides a fun and engaging way for students to explore and express their feelings, especially for those who may have difficulty articulating their emotions verbally. Normalizes talking about feelings and empowers students to view their emotions as assets.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The EQ Feeling Chart can be adapted to different age groups and developmental levels. Students can choose to demonstrate different emotions, and the class can provide feedback on their accuracy.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Individual Reflection
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student participation and engagement in the activity. Collect student feedback on the activity to assess its effectiveness.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • All learning has an emotional base – Plato. Do you agree? Try these short activities to help grow students’ emotional intelligence skills

docs.title: What Would Their Day Look Like?
Description
docs.text: Learners select a photo of a person or animal in an unfamiliar situation and imagine what their daily life might be like. They research the topic further and present their chosen character’s daily routine to the class. This activity encourages learners to step into someone else’s shoes and understand the challenges and experiences of others.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Photos of people or animals in unfamiliar situations, access to research resources, and time for presentation.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may make stereotypical assumptions if they lack sufficient knowledge. It requires careful selection of photos and guidance from the instructor to ensure accurate and respectful representations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who are interested in exploring different cultures and lifestyles

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop empathy, promote perspective-taking, encourage research skills, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Encourages perspective-taking by imagining the daily life of someone different. Develops research skills by exploring unfamiliar situations. Improves communication skills through presentations and diary entries.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose characters and situations that resonate with their interests and values. The level of research and presentation can be tailored to their abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Research
  • Demonstration
  • Individual Reflection
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the depth of research, the accuracy of representations, and the level of empathy demonstrated in presentations or diary entries. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards different groups.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that perspective-taking exercises can increase empathy and reduce prejudice. Learning about different cultures and lifestyles also promotes cultural understanding and global awareness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students choose a photo of a refugee and research what their daily life might be like, including the challenges they face and the resources they rely on. Students write a diary entry from the perspective of a battery hen, describing their living conditions and experiences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using the metaphor of an iceberg to encourage students to extend their knowledge and further develop their ideas beyond the surface level. Students start with a question related to a key event featuring an adolescent protagonist, then illustrate an iceberg with a clear waterline. Above the surface, they cite obvious scenes from the text that caused the event. Below the surface, they explore deeper nuances of the story, character traits, and facets of identity that led the characters to the event. Students then discuss how these underlying ideas help them understand more about the event and characters. This promotes self-management and responsible decision-making skills.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Selected text featuring an adolescent protagonist and key events. Illustration of an iceberg. Facilitation of discussions and reflective activities.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires careful selection of texts and questions to ensure relevance. Success depends on the instructor's ability to guide students in exploring complex character traits and motivations.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Middle and high school learners.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Encourage critical thinking, promote deeper analysis of character traits, and develop self-management and responsible decision-making skills.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students deconstruct characters and events, improving their ability to analyze and manage their own actions. Fosters introspection and critical thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Choice of text and key questions can be tailored to address specific themes or character issues. Students can choose different aspects of the iceberg to focus on.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Case Study
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess student illustrations of icebergs, quality of discussions, and depth of analysis of character motivations.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances critical thinking, self-management, and responsible decision-making by promoting deeper analysis of characters and events. Fosters a better understanding of personal actions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Using S.E. Hinton’s 'The Outsiders' to explore issues related to the adolescent experience and asking, 'Why does Johnny kill Bob?'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One learner demonstrates an emotion through body language and facial expressions, while the rest of the class guesses the emotion.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • EQ Feeling Chart (optional), space for learners to act out emotions

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Some learners may feel self-conscious acting out emotions. Requires a safe and supportive classroom environment.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learner levels

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Identify emotions, interpret body language, enhance emotional literacy

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fun and engaging way to learn about emotions, improves non-verbal communication skills, fosters empathy

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can use the EQ Feeling Chart as a reference for emotions.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Peer Interaction
  • Whole-Class Sharing

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to identify and interpret emotions. Assess learners' understanding of body language and facial expressions.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Enhances emotional literacy, improves non-verbal communication skills, fosters empathy and understanding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A guessing game where one person thinks of a number and provides clues, and others use logical reasoning and deduction to determine the number. This promotes number sense, problem-solving, and strategic thinking.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires clear and logical clues for effective gameplay. May be challenging for learners with limited number sense.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary school students

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote number sense, improve problem-solving skills, and enhance strategic thinking

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Promotes number sense, problem-solving, and strategic thinking.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the difficulty of clues based on the learner's skill level. Vary the number range to suit different age groups.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Problem Presentation
  • Application of Knowledge

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to use clues to deduce the number. Track the number of clues needed to guess the correct number.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Help children become more engaged in your family adventures.

docs.title: Where Are the People Like Me?
Description
docs.text: Learners examine media examples to consider who is represented and who is not, then explore the impact of this lack of diversity and how it might affect those who are misrepresented or not represented. This activity raises awareness of media representation and its effects, promoting critical media literacy and social awareness.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Media examples (films, TV shows, music, fashion), a space for discussions and reflections, and facilitation by an instructor to guide analysis.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Learners may be resistant to analyzing media critically or may lack awareness of the issues involved. It requires careful guidance from the instructor to ensure thoughtful and respectful analysis.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly those who want to understand the impact of media on society and culture

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote media literacy, raise awareness of representation, encourage critical thinking, improve communication skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances media literacy by analyzing representation in media. Raises awareness of the impact of misrepresentation and underrepresentation. Improves communication skills through discussions and reflections.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Learners can choose media examples that resonate with their interests and cultural backgrounds. The level of analysis and reflection can be adjusted to their abilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Class Discussion
  • Individual Reflection
  • Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Assess the depth of analysis, the ability to identify issues of representation, and the level of critical thinking demonstrated in the analysis. Monitor changes in learners' attitudes towards media and social issues.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Media literacy has been shown to promote critical thinking, awareness of bias, and responsible media consumption. Raising awareness of representation also fosters social justice and inclusion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students analyze the representation of different ethnic groups in popular films or TV shows. Students analyze the representation of LGBTQ+ individuals in the music industry or fashion magazines.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The instructor or learners place 3-4 dot cards on the table. Two or three cards represent the same quantity, while one represents a different quantity. The learner then identifies the card that doesn't belong, prompting them to analyze and compare different quantities. This activity enhances critical thinking skills as learners must analyze and compare quantities to determine which one is different. Supports the development of number sense by encouraging learners to recognize and differentiate between various numerical quantities. Allows for differentiation by adjusting the numerical range and complexity of the dot arrangements.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Dot cards.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require clear explanation and examples to ensure learners understand the game's objective. The activity's effectiveness depends on selecting appropriate cards that clearly represent different quantities.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Pre-K to 1st Grade learners who are developing number sense.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Differentiate between quantities, enhance critical thinking, develop number sense

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Enhances analytical and comparative skills. Reinforces number recognition and differentiation. Promotes critical thinking and problem-solving.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Adjust the number of cards and the complexity of arrangements. Modify the activity by including non-numerical cards.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Provide Feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe the learner's ability to accurately identify the card that doesn't belong. Assess the justification provided for their choice.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research supports the use of comparative activities to enhance critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Whole class self-monitoring involves the entire class participating in self-monitoring techniques, adapted from individual self-monitoring methods. This approach aims to increase self-control and constructive introspection in all students, rather than targeting just a few at-risk individuals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Regular, evenly spaced behavior checks; individual tracking sheets for students; an audible or visual cue; an operant response to the cue; and a plan for withdrawal from the system. A short discussion period is also needed for objective self-assessment.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires a structured classroom environment and may initially disrupt the instructional day. Requires consistent modeling and reinforcement of the language and concepts of self-monitoring. Inappropriate behavior may initially increase as students test the limits of the system.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Elementary and secondary classrooms where the teacher wants to promote self-regulation and responsible behavior in all students.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Promote self-control, introspection, and responsible behavior in the entire classroom, fostering a positive and supportive learning environment.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Prevents at-risk students from feeling singled out, provides positive role models for self-control, and creates a structured classroom environment that benefits all students. The language of self-monitoring and introspection can be taught and modeled.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted to different grade levels and classroom schedules. The specific behaviors to monitor can be chosen based on class needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Practice
  • Peer Discussion
  • Provide feedback
  • Assess performance

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Monitor the frequency and accuracy of student self-reports. Observe changes in on-task behavior, classroom interruptions, and overall classroom climate.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Increases on-task time, decreases classroom interruptions, and promotes a positive classroom climate. Students become more aware of and honest about their behavior.

docs.title: Windows, Mirrors, and Sliding Glass Doors
Description
docs.text: This strategy involves using stories and materials that act as mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors to help students identify their place in the world. A window offers a view into someone else’s experience, a sliding door allows the reader to enter the story and become a part of the world, and a mirror is a story that reflects one's own culture and helps build identity. It is critical to understand that students cannot truly learn about themselves unless they learn about others as well. Students can learn about how other people conduct themselves in the world in order to understand how they might fit in.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Diverse resources, a culturally sensitive curriculum, and time for reflection.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be challenging to find diverse resources that accurately reflect the experiences of all students. Requires ongoing commitment and support from teachers and administrators.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students of all ages and backgrounds

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Help students identify their place in the world, develop understanding about the wider world, build identity, and encourage reflection and action

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Provides students with diverse perspectives, promotes empathy and understanding, supports identity development, and encourages critical thinking and reflection

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Materials can be selected based on student interests and backgrounds. Teachers can provide different levels of support based on student needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Assigned Readings
  • Peer Discussion
  • Individual Reflection

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe student engagement with materials, track changes in student attitudes and behaviors, and gather feedback from students and staff

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Using stories and materials that act as mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors can help students identify their place in the world, develop understanding about the wider world, build identity, and encourage reflection and action.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Students reading books where they see characters like themselves who are valued in the world. Students learning about how other people conduct themselves in the world in order to understand how they might fit in.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Word building is a literacy strategy used to reinforce vocabulary and spelling skills by having learners manipulate letter tiles or squares to construct words. This hands-on activity promotes phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence, and word recognition. Learners rearrange letters to form target words, often drawn from a specific context like a song or reading material. This method enhances memory and retention through active engagement and multisensory learning.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Letter tiles or squares, word lists, chart paper (optional), writing materials. Preparation involves cutting apart letter squares and selecting target words.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May be time-consuming to prepare letter tiles. Requires sufficient space for learners to manipulate letters. Effectiveness depends on clear instructions and active facilitation by the instructor.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early learners (K-2), learners with dyslexia, English language learners, and anyone needing to reinforce basic spelling and phonics skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve spelling skills, strengthen word recognition, reinforce letter-sound correspondence, develop phonemic awareness, enhance vocabulary, build foundational literacy skills

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Engages learners actively in constructing words, improving retention and recall. Promotes phonemic awareness and understanding of letter-sound relationships. Provides immediate feedback as learners manipulate letters. Supports multisensory learning, catering to different learning styles.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Can be adapted for different skill levels by selecting appropriate words. Provides scaffolded support for struggling learners by giving hints or partially completed words. Offers a challenge for advanced learners by having them build longer or more complex words.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Observe learners' ability to rearrange letters accurately and efficiently. Collect and review the words they build to assess spelling skills. Track progress over time to measure improvement in word recognition and construction.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Hands-on activities like word building enhance phonemic awareness and letter-sound correspondence, crucial for early literacy. Direct instruction in phonics and vocabulary supports reading and spelling skills. Active engagement improves retention and comprehension.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The resource describes a particular process for implementing this strategy using the letters from the song, Down by the Bay.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners identify target vocabulary within varied contexts. Learners search for and highlight specific words in diverse reading materials like song lyrics or sentences from a familiar text. This method reinforces word recognition and contextual understanding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to various reading materials (e.g., song lyrics, sentences from texts), highlighters or markers, and target word lists. Preparation involves highlighting words in the song lyrics for educators, and distributing song lyrics without the highlighting to the learners.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Material must be appropriate for learners. Implementation requires sufficient reading resources and targeted words. Success relies on consistent reinforcement and practice.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Early elementary grades (1-3), learners who need vocabulary reinforcement, and English language learners

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Enhance vocabulary recognition, improve contextual understanding, reinforce reading skills, develop pattern recognition

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Actively engages learners in identifying vocabulary. Reinforces reading skills through contextual application. Provides repetition and pattern recognition for improved memory. Adaptable to diverse materials and skill levels.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Scaffolded support is achieved by assigning a manageable number of words. Can modify word complexity based on proficiency. Adaptable to fit various reading materials and topics.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Track the words identified within the context. Observe the ability to locate, highlight, and verbally share the vocabulary.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Direct instruction in vocabulary and context improves overall reading comprehension. Repetition supports memory and retention. Active participation increases engagement and learning outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The resource references different children's songs, and directs the educator to highlight vocabulary in one version of the document for teacher reference only. The students receive the version without highlighted words.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A word map is a visual organizer that promotes vocabulary development. Most word map organizers engage students in developing a definition, synonyms, antonyms, and a picture for a given vocabulary word or concept. Word maps can be used effectively with classroom read-alouds and word walls.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Vocabulary word, word map template, guidance on how to use the map, synonyms, antonyms, a picture to help illustrate the new target word or concept

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require additional time to teach and implement effectively.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All learners, particularly effective for second language learners and students with varying reading skills

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Develop understanding of vocabulary, think about new terms and concepts in multiple ways, build upon prior knowledge, support oral and reading comprehension

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Helps students develop their understanding of a word, encourages students to think about new terms or concepts in several ways by asking questions such as: What is it? What is it like? What are some examples? It helps students build upon prior knowledge and visually represent new information.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Instructors can give students who need extra help the chance to work with a partner, allow students to use pictures to illustrate when appropriate, adjust the number of words students need to map, or provide students with sentences each containing the target word.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Recall prior knowledge
  • Direct instruction
  • Provide guidance
  • Practice

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Accuracy and completeness of the word map, ability to use the vocabulary word correctly in context.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Supports oral and reading comprehension and reinforces vocabulary learning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A student fills out a word map for the word 'harbor,' including its definition, synonyms, antonyms, and a picture. Resource: Reading Rockets.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Learners select math operations and create multistep word problems for peers to solve, integrating math and literacy skills. This promotes careful reading, understanding of problem-solving steps, and application of math concepts in creative contexts. The strategy can be used across multiple strands in math (e.g., operations, geometry, statistics).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to math resources, tools for writing and solving problems (e.g., paper, pencils, calculators), and structured time for creating, sharing, and solving problems.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • May require significant instructional support to ensure learners create solvable and relevant problems. Some learners may struggle with the creative aspect of the task or with accurately solving problems created by peers.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Upper elementary, middle school, and high school learners, particularly those studying math and related subjects.

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Apply math operations in real-world contexts, enhance problem-solving skills, integrate math and literacy skills, promote creative thinking, and develop peer assessment abilities.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Fosters creativity and critical thinking, promotes deeper understanding of mathematical concepts, and enhances communication skills. It also allows for personalized learning experiences as learners create problems tailored to their interests and abilities.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • The complexity and type of word problems can be tailored to different skill levels. Learners can choose the math operations to use, the context of the problem, and the degree of complexity.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Application
  • Individual Response
  • Peer Discussion

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Evaluate the quality, complexity, and accuracy of the word problems created by learners. Assess the completeness and correctness of solutions provided by learners. Observe learner engagement and participation in problem-solving activities.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Word problems are seen as a concrete and fun way to link math and literacy skills together. They require reading carefully, understanding what is being solved for, and underlining the most relevant information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Following a Flocabulary math video, students create word problems that use math operations they've learned, then solve problems created by their classmates. Variations include giving students the answer and asking them to write the word problem that leads to it, or creating stories with a word problem at the center.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Use word processing and other technology tools to support writing. These tools are especially supportive for struggling writers, providing the means to move more easily from idea to composition, supporting spelling, revising, and proofreading. Technology-assisted writing also makes collaborative writing more feasible and productive.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers, word processing software, technology training

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires technology access and skills, may not suit all learners

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All writers, especially those struggling with writing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve writing skills, enhance technology literacy, support struggling writers

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Facilitates drafting, revising, and proofreading, enhances technology literacy, supports collaboration

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Technology tools can be tailored to different needs and preferences.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide guidance
  • Practice
  • Provide feedback

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved writing quality, increased technology use, greater confidence

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Technology supports spelling, revising, and proof reading, and collaborative writing

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Word processing involves using computer software to write, edit, and format text. This process enhances the quality of student composition by making the writing process more automatic and allowing for more frequent and meaningful teacher feedback. Features such as age-appropriate word suggestions, audio integration for learners to record thoughts, and text-to-speech support diverse needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Computer or tablet, word processing software, and internet access (optional, for online tools).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Requires access to technology, potential for distraction if not managed properly, and may not be suitable for all types of writing tasks.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • K-12 students, particularly those who benefit from technological support in writing

docs.title: Target Learning Goals
docs.text: • Improve composition quality, enhance student engagement in the writing process, provide accessible writing tools, facilitate frequent and meaningful feedback

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text: • Makes the writing process more efficient and accessible, provides immediate feedback, enhances engagement, and supports diverse learner needs through customizable features.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: • Word processing software can be adapted to individual learner needs through adjustable font sizes, text-to-speech features, and word suggestions. Learners can record their thoughts through audio integration.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• Provide feedback
  • Practice
  • Application

docs.title: Assessment Evidence
docs.text: • Improved composition quality, increased student engagement in writing activities, and frequency of feedback exchanged between students and teachers.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: • Research shows that using computers for writing increases the quality of student composition and immersion in the writing process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A seventh-grade teacher using technology during writing instruction to increase student performance by facilitating more frequent and meaningful feedback.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Using word processing software like Google Docs allows learners to write, share, review, and revise their work. Collaborative features enable peer review and feedback, enhancing Foundational Writing Skills and supporting Metacognition. Features such as age-appropriate word suggestions, audio integration for recording thoughts, and text-to-speech can support diverse learner needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to computers or devices with word processing software and internet connectivity.

docs.title: Constraints
