docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Attribution Theory (Weiner, 1986) holds that people try to explain the causes of their own successes and failures — attributing an outcome to ability, effort, luck, task difficulty, mood, fatigue, and so on — and that it is the perceived cause, whether or not it is the actual cause, that drives subsequent motivation and behavior (Park, 2018). Weiner (2010) classifies these attributions along three independent dimensions:

  • Locus — whether the cause is internal to the learner (ability, effort) or external (luck, task difficulty).
  • Stability — whether the cause is relatively constant over time (ability) or variable (effort, luck).
  • Controllability — whether the learner can influence the cause (effort, choice of strategy) or not (luck, innate ability, task difficulty).

Each dimension drives a different motivational consequence. Locus affects self-esteem and self-directed emotion: success attributed internally produces pride, failure attributed internally produces shame or guilt. Stability affects expectancy for future outcomes: a stable attribution (ability) implies the same outcome will likely recur, so a stable failure attribution ("I'm just not good at this") is far more damaging to future motivation than an unstable one ("I didn't study enough this time," which implies next time could go differently). Controllability interacts with the other two to shape specific emotions: failure attributed to a controllable cause (effort) tends to produce guilt and a drive to change; failure attributed to an internal, uncontrollable cause (low ability) tends to produce shame; failure attributed to an external, uncontrollable cause tends to produce helplessness and disengagement, since the learner believes nothing they do will change the outcome. Attributing success to internal, stable factors like ability is itself a mixed blessing: it can build optimism about future success, but can also breed indifference to correcting mistakes, or produce pessimism the moment performance dips below the accustomed level ("Maybe I'm not as smart as I thought") (Dweck, 2000, 2006).

The clearest instructional implication is that internal, controllable, and — ideally — unstable attributions for failure (effort, strategy choice) sustain motivation better than internal-stable ones (fixed ability) or external ones (luck, task difficulty), because they leave the learner believing a different outcome is achievable through their own action. This is why "your effort really made a difference" is better feedback than "you're smart" after success, and "let's find a better strategy" is better than "this material is just too hard for you" after failure (Seifert & Sutton, 2018) — though attributions to effort are only credible when tasks are genuinely at an appropriate difficulty level and assessment is reliable enough that effort actually does predict outcomes.

Effort-based attributions are only convincing under three conditions: tasks pitched at a genuinely appropriate difficulty with reliable assessment; teachers ready to help individuals even when a task seems easy enough not to need it, since it is often hard to predict in advance how hard a task will actually prove for a particular student; and — often forgotten — recognizing that ability, though usually treated as a relatively fixed trait, actually changes incrementally over the long term through accumulated effort (a fluent second-grade reader was, at some point in the past, unable to read at all). Because effort's results are visible almost immediately while ability changes only gradually over weeks, months, or years, it is easy to treat a current ability gap as fixed rather than as the product of effort not yet accumulated — and recognizing that mismatch explicitly is one of the more effective ways to actually help students increase their abilities (Blackwell, Trzniewski, & Dweck, 2007; Schunk, Pintrich, & Meece, 2008).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Tasks pitched at an appropriate difficulty level and assessed reliably — attribution-shaping feedback about effort or strategy is not credible if the task was actually too hard or the grading too inconsistent for effort to matter
  • Willingness from instructors to frame their own explanations of student success/failure around internal, controllable causes rather than fixed ability or external luck

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Praising ability directly ("you're smart") can be a blessing and a curse: it can build short-term optimism but also produce indifference to correcting mistakes, and can produce pessimism if the student later underperforms ("maybe I'm not as smart as I thought")
  • Attributions to stable, uncontrollable, internal causes (fixed low ability) are the most damaging combination and the hardest to intervene on directly, since they require changing a belief about a stable trait, not just a single explanation

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who have recently experienced failure or underperformance, where the attribution they form will shape whether they re-engage or disengage
  • Learners at risk of developing a fixed, stable, internal explanation for repeated struggle (closely related to learned helplessness, see Self-Efficacy Theory)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained motivation and re-engagement after failure or setbacks
  • Willingness to use and adjust learning strategies, which depends on believing that strategy/effort (not fixed ability or luck) drives outcomes

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Weiner's (1986) attribution framework draws on locus, stability, and controllability as the three dimensions organizing how causal beliefs translate into motivational and emotional consequences

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Efficacy Theory — both concern learners' beliefs about the causes of their own performance; sustained internal-stable-uncontrollable failure attributions are a direct pathway to the learned helplessness that self-efficacy theory also describes
  • Self-Determination Theory — controllable attributions support the sense of autonomy and competence SDT identifies as basic psychological needs
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — the stability dimension of an attribution directly shapes a learner's expectancy for future success, the central construct of expectancy-value theory

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Behaviorism is a learning theory that defines learning as a change in observable behavior produced by environmental stimuli and reinforcement contingencies. Associated with Watson, Thorndike, and Skinner, behaviorism holds that the internal workings of the mind are not directly accessible and therefore not the proper object of scientific study — what matters is the measurable relationship between stimulus and response ("conclusions about human development should be based on observation of overt behavior rather than speculation about subconscious motives or latent cognitive processes," Shaffer, 2000). Learning occurs when a desired behavior is reliably elicited and strengthened through reinforcement or extinguished through removal of reinforcement.

Behaviorism distinguishes two conditioning mechanisms. Classical conditioning (Pavlov) pairs a neutral stimulus with one that already produces a reflexive response — Pavlov's dogs learned to salivate (conditioned response) to a bell (conditioned stimulus) that had been repeatedly paired with food, and the conditioned reflex extinguishes if the bell reliably stops predicting food. Operant conditioning (Skinner) instead shapes voluntary behavior through its consequences: in the "Skinner box," a rat's bar-press produces either a reinforcer (a food pellet, which strengthens the behavior) or a punisher (a shock, which suppresses it). As Skinner (1972, p. 74) put it, "the things we call pleasant have an energizing or strengthening effect on our behavior."

In instructional design, behaviorist principles underlie practices such as direct reinforcement of correct responses, shaping through successive approximation, massed and distributed practice, programmed instruction, and mastery learning. Behavioral objectives (precise, observable, measurable) are a direct product of this framework. Named classroom techniques include behavioral contracts (an explicit agreement tying a specific behavior to a specific consequence); the standard reinforcement/punishment grid — positive reinforcement (adding something desirable, e.g. praise), negative reinforcement (removing something undesirable, e.g. making a high-scoring student exempt from the final exam), positive punishment (adding something undesirable, e.g. detention), and negative punishment (removing something desirable, e.g. lost recess); extinction (withdrawing reinforcement so a behavior fades, e.g. a teacher no longer accepting late work for partial credit); shaping (reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior); cueing (a verbal or non-verbal prompt delivered before the expected behavior, rather than corrective feedback after); and a named behavior modification protocol (Brewer, Campbell, & Petty, 2000): specify the desired outcome, build a positive environment, identify reinforcers, reinforce until the pattern is established, fade the reinforcement's frequency, then evaluate.

Skinner's account of consequences rests on Thorndike's earlier law of effect (Thorndike, 1911): behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to recur, while behaviors followed by unpleasant consequences are less likely to recur. Reinforcers themselves are further divided into primary reinforcers (food, water, sleep, shelter, touch, and pleasure — reinforcing without having been learned) and secondary reinforcers (praise, money, stickers, tokens — reinforcing only because they have been linked to a primary reinforcer); token-based secondary reinforcers scaled into a full classroom system are called a token economy (see Token Economies). Generalization is the incidental spread of a reinforced behavior to similar, non-reinforced behaviors (a student praised for reading library books starts reading newspapers and comics too); discrimination is learning not to overgeneralize (the same student learns to speak during discussion but not to blurt out at other times), and typically results from combining reinforcement of the target behavior with extinction of the overgeneralized version. Reinforcement scheduling also matters: intermittent (partial) schedules of reinforcement make a behavior take longer to learn, but also take longer to extinguish once learned — good news for sustaining praised behaviors that cannot be reinforced every time, but equally bad news for extinguishing misbehavior that has been intermittently reinforced by peer attention (Ferster et al., 1997; Mazur, 2005).

Rewarding a behavior the learner already finds intrinsically interesting can backfire: the overjustification effect describes measurably reduced later engagement with a task after it was extrinsically rewarded, compared to never having been rewarded at all — an important caution against reflexively applying reinforcement to activities that do not need it (see Rewarding an already-intrinsically-motivating activity can reduce future engagement with it).

Bandura's observational learning — "of the many cues that influence behavior, at any point in time, none is more common than the actions of others" (Bandura, 1986, p. 45) — extended behaviorist accounts of learning to include modeling; the wiki treats this extension as its own theory (see Social Learning Theory) rather than folding it into behaviorism itself.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Most applicable when a discrete, observable skill or behavior is the learning target (e.g., fluent recall, procedural execution)
  • Less suited to complex reasoning, conceptual understanding, or transfer — outcomes that require attending to internal cognitive processes
  • Useful for designing feedback systems, reinforcement schedules, and formative assessment criteria

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• No strong learner-characteristic boundary within the behavioral framework; all learners respond to reinforcement contingencies
  • Expertise level affects which behaviors need reinforcement and at what grain size

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Behavioral objectives: observable, measurable outcomes specified in advance
  • Best fit: procedural fluency, factual recall, conditioned responses
  • Weaker fit: conceptual transfer, metacognition, adaptive expertise

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text: Behaviorism is criticized as overly deterministic and as denying free will; by treating only observable behavior as scientifically valid, it has little to say about internal mental processes and struggles to explain behavior change that isn't traceable to an environmental input. Research by ethologists has also shown that conditioning principles are not universal across species and contexts, countering behaviorism's original claim of equipotentiality — that any stimulus could be conditioned to any response with equal ease.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Rewarding an already-intrinsically-motivating activity can reduce future engagement with it [-M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Cognitivism — arose partly in reaction to behaviorism's neglect of internal cognitive processes
  • Cognitive Load Theory — arose partly in reaction to behaviorism's neglect of internal cognitive processes
  • Constructivism — contrasts with behaviorism by centering the learner's active construction of meaning
  • Information Processing Theory — replaced behaviorist black-box assumptions with explicit models of memory and attention
  • Connectivism — positions itself against behaviorism (along with cognitivism and constructivism) as a pre-networked-era theory of individual, internal learning

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Token Economies — a classroom-scale system of secondary (token) reinforcers
  • Time-Out (Negative Punishment) — removal from a desirable activity as negative punishment
  • Least-to-Most Prompting Hierarchy — verbal, gestural, and physical prompts sequenced from least to most intrusive
  • Effective Presentation for Errorless Learning — specific directions, active responding, and pacing to minimize errors
  • Behavioral Feedback for Correct and Incorrect Responses — consequence delivery following correct and incorrect responses
  • Conditioning Natural Reinforcers — fading extrinsic reinforcers toward intrinsic ones
  • Learning Hierarchy Task Analysis — sequencing prerequisite skills into a learning hierarchy

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Urie Bronfenbrenner's bioecological model holds that human development results from proximal processes — "stimulating, regular face-to-face interactions over extended periods with people, objects, or symbols" (Bronfenbrenner, 1994) — that realize a person's biological, psychological, and social potential. A parent shaping a child through parenting behaviors, modeling, and encouragement is a proximal process. Development is transactional and bidirectional: children affect their immediate contexts as much as contexts affect children — insecurely attached children are more emotionally demanding, and language-delayed children elicit less verbal exchange from adults.

The model is explicitly interdisciplinary, drawing on biology, behavioral genetics, neurobiology, psychology, sociology, cultural anthropology, history, and economics, and was developed partly to explain how macro-level events (e.g., an economic shock) propagate down through progressively more immediate layers of a person's environment to affect development. Development spans three broad, non-hierarchical domains: physical/biological/neuroanatomical, cognitive/language/academic, and social/emotional/behavioral.

docs.title: The Nested Systems
docs.text:
• Microsystem — "a pattern of activities, social roles, and interpersonal relations experienced by the developing person in a given face-to-face setting" (Bronfenbrenner, 1994, p. 39): families, neighborhoods, day care centers, schools, playgrounds.
  • Mesosystem — "the linkages and processes taking place between two or more settings containing the developing person" (Bronfenbrenner, 1994, p. 40): the relationship between home and school, or peer-group norms that conflict with school behavioral expectations.
  • Exosystem — "linkages and processes...between two or more settings, at least one of which does not contain the developing person, but in which events occur that indirectly influence" the person's immediate setting (Bronfenbrenner, 1994, p. 40): a parent's workplace, family social networks, and neighborhood-community contexts are the three most prominent exosystems.
  • Macrosystem — "the overarching pattern of micro-, meso-, and exosystems characteristic of a given culture or subculture, with particular reference to the belief systems, bodies of knowledge, material resources, customs, lifestyles, opportunity structures, hazards, and lifecourse options embedded in each" (Bronfenbrenner, 1994, p. 40): laws, political economy, and broad cultural values, such as an American upper-middle-class emphasis on self-esteem and individualization.
  • Chronosystem — the dimension of time across which proximal processes accumulate and unfold; described more thinly than the other four systems, as a temporal frame rather than a fully worked-out fifth "system" of its own content.

The model also emphasizes experience: "the scientifically relevant features of any environment include not only its objective properties but also the way in which these properties are perceived by the persons in that environment" (Bronfenbrenner, 1979, p. 22) — the same objective context can be experienced, and therefore act, differently depending on the surrounding macrosystem. For example, authoritative parenting generally outperforms authoritarian parenting (Baumrind, 1989), but authoritarian parenting was associated with less adolescent delinquency in a sample of African American and Latino American families in dangerous inner-city neighborhoods (Florsheim, Tolan, & Gorman-Smith, 1996) — the same parenting style functions differently depending on the macrosystem-level risk context surrounding the family.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Establishing that an exosystem-level event affects development requires a two-step causal chain: a link between the external event and a process in the child's microsystem, and a link from that process to an actual developmental change
  • Criticized for weighting biological and cognitive aspects of development more heavily than socioemotional aspects; alternative frameworks put biological, cognitive, and socioemotional domains on more equal footing

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Not scoped to a single age band — the model applies across the lifespan, though its clearest classroom applications concern children and adolescents whose immediate systems (family, school, peers) are still actively shaping development

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not an instructional-objective framework — it is a lens for understanding how the systems surrounding a learner (family, school, peer group, community, culture, policy) interact to support or constrain any given learning objective, rather than a framework for writing the objectives themselves

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Sociocultural Theory — both frame development as inseparable from social context; Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development operates within what Bronfenbrenner would call the microsystem
  • Situated Learning — shares the claim that knowledge and development cannot be understood apart from the social, material, and cultural context in which they occur
  • Social Learning Theory — Bandura's observational learning (e.g., parental role modeling) operates within the microsystem this model describes

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Benjamin Bloom (1913-1999), working with his mentor Ralph W. Tyler at the University of Chicago and with collaborators Engelhart, Furst, Hill, and Krathwohl, published Taxonomy of Educational Objectives: Handbook I, The Cognitive Domain in 1956, followed by a second handbook on the affective domain in 1964 (Krathwohl, Bloom, & Masia, 1973). Bloom et al. (1956) identified three domains of educational goals — often summarized as KSA:

  • Cognitive Domain — mental skills (Knowledge)
  • Psychomotor Domain — manual or physical skills (Skills)
  • Affective Domain — growth in feelings or emotional areas (Attitudes)

Each domain is organized as a hierarchy running from the simplest behavior to the most complex, on the premise that lower levels must generally be mastered before the next level can take place — though this strict hierarchical assumption has drawn criticism (see below). Bloom et al. (1956) produced a detailed compilation for the cognitive and affective domains but explicitly omitted the psychomotor domain, citing their own lack of experience teaching manual skills at the college level; other researchers later filled this gap with at least three competing psychomotor models (Simpson, 1972; Dave, 1970; Harrow, 1972).

docs.title: The Cognitive Domain
docs.text:
The original (1956) cognitive domain has six levels, from simplest to most complex: Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis, Evaluation — each paired with characteristic key words useful for writing objectives: Knowledge (defines, lists, recalls, states), Comprehension (explains, summarizes, translates), Application (applies, computes, solves), Analysis (compares, differentiates, distinguishes), Synthesis (composes, designs, generates), Evaluation (appraises, critiques, justifies).

In the mid-1990s, Lorin Anderson (a former student of Bloom's) and David Krathwohl revised the cognitive domain (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001; Anderson et al., 2000), making three changes: renaming the levels from nouns to verbs, reordering the top two levels, and adding a Knowledge Dimension. The revised levels are Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating — swapping the original "Synthesis" and "Evaluation" so that Creating (synthesis-like) sits above Evaluating, on the reasoning that creating something new is a more demanding cognitive act than judging existing material.

Original (1956) Revised (2001) Example (Goldilocks and the Three Bears) Knowledge: recall data or information Remembering: recall or retrieve previously learned information List three things Goldilocks did in the three bears' house Comprehension: understand meaning, interpret, translate Understanding: comprehend the meaning, translation, interpretation of instructions and problems Explain why Goldilocks liked the little bear's chair best Application: use a concept in a new situation Applying: use a concept in a new situation or unprompted use of an abstraction Predict what Goldilocks might have used if she had entered your house Analysis: separate material into component parts Analyzing: separate material or concepts into component parts so the organizational structure may be understood Select the part of the story where Goldilocks seemed most comfortable Synthesis: build a structure or pattern from diverse elements (moved below Evaluating, renamed) Creating: build a structure or pattern from diverse elements Tell how the story would have been different if it had been about three fish Evaluation: judge the value of ideas or materials Evaluating: make judgments about the value of ideas or materials Decide whether Goldilocks was a bad girl, and justify your position

The revised levels pair with their own characteristic key words — e.g., Remembering: defines, identifies, lists, recalls; Understanding: explains, summarizes, paraphrases; Applying: demonstrates, solves, uses; Analyzing: compares, differentiates, distinguishes; Evaluating: critiques, defends, justifies; Creating: designs, composes, formulates (Clark, 2015a).

docs.title: Cognitive Process and Knowledge Dimension Matrix
docs.text:
The revised taxonomy also crosses the six cognitive processes with a Knowledge Dimension, adding a fourth knowledge type (metacognitive) to the three Bloom's original work had mentioned only in passing:

  • Factual — the basic elements a learner must know to be acquainted with a discipline or solve problems
  • Conceptual — the interrelationships among basic elements within a larger structure that let them function together
  • Procedural — how to do something: methods of inquiry, and criteria for using skills, algorithms, techniques, and methods
  • Metacognitive — knowledge of cognition in general, and awareness of one's own cognition (see Metacognition)

Crossing these four knowledge types against the six cognitive processes produces a 4×6 matrix (Krathwohl & Anderson, 2001) that functions as a performance-aid for writing precise objectives — e.g., a cell at Factual × Remembering might be "list," while Metacognitive × Create might be "actualize." A related five-part knowledge scheme (facts, concepts, processes, procedures, principles) is also used by some instructional designers (Clark & Chopeta, 2004; Clark & Mayer, 2007) as an alternative to the four-part matrix.

docs.title: The Psychomotor Domain
docs.text: Because Bloom et al. (1956) did not produce a psychomotor model, at least three independent hierarchies have been proposed. Simpson (1972), the model most commonly treated as primary, proposes seven levels: Perception (using sensory cues to guide motor activity), Set (mental/physical/emotional readiness to act), Guided Response (early imitation and trial-and-error), Mechanism (habitual, moderately confident performance), Complex Overt Response (skillful, quick, accurate, largely automatic performance), Adaptation (modifying well-developed skills to fit new requirements), and Origination (creating new movement patterns for a novel problem). Dave (1970) proposes five levels — Imitation, Manipulation, Precision, Articulation, Naturalization (performance becomes second-nature). Harrow (1972) proposes six — Reflex Movements, Fundamental Movements, Perceptual Abilities, Physical Abilities (fitness), Skilled Movements, and Non-discursive Communication (expressive use of gesture and body language).

docs.title: The Affective Domain
docs.text: The affective domain (Krathwohl, Bloom, & Masia, 1973) covers feelings, values, appreciation, enthusiasm, motivation, and attitude, in five levels from simplest to most complex: Receiving Phenomena (willingness to hear, selective attention) → Responding to Phenomena (active participation, e.g. participating in discussion) → Valuing (attaching worth to an object or behavior, from simple acceptance to commitment) → Organizing (building a value system by comparing, relating, and resolving conflicts among values) → Internalizing Values (a value system that consistently, predictably controls behavior — the value has become characteristic of the person).

docs.title: Uses and Matching Instructional Strategy to Taxonomy Level
docs.text: The taxonomy is most often used to write lesson objectives, learning goals, and instructional activities pitched at a target level of complexity, and to design assessment questions that match that level. An Instructional Strategy Selection Chart (Clark, 2015d) maps strategy type to the level being targeted across all three domains: passive methods (lecture, reading, demonstration) suit the lowest levels (Knowledge/Remembering, Perception/Set, Receiving Phenomena); active methods (practice with coaching, simulated settings) suit the middle levels; use in real situations and self-directed, informally-acquired learning (with mentoring/coaching to speed the process) suit the highest levels (Evaluation/Creating, Origination, Internalizing Values). The general pattern: lower levels of performance can normally be taught with more passive learning methods, while higher levels usually require some action or involvement by the learner.

docs.title: Application in the Classroom
docs.text: Bloom's taxonomy helps a teacher target a student's Zone of Proximal Development in the sense meant by Vygotsky: a student who knows few terms for a topic (stuck at Knowledge/Remembering and Comprehension/Understanding) may need support remembering and defining terms before they can make useful comparisons (Analysis/Analyzing). The teacher arranges the zone of proximal development that makes the higher-level task reachable, but the student still has to construct the comparison for themselves (Arduini-Van Hoose, 2020).

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text: As Morshead (1965) pointed out on publication of the affective-domain handbook, the classification lacked a systematic rationale of construction — a critique later acknowledged in the taxonomy's own 2001 revision, which reestablished it on more systematic lines. Some critics accept the six cognitive categories but question whether they form a genuine sequential hierarchy (Paul, 1993); educators sometimes over-read the hierarchy and mistakenly treat the lowest levels as unworthy of teaching, when in some fields (e.g., species identification in natural history) the lower levels are themselves the most important skill (Flannery, 2007; Lawler, 2016) — the lower levels enable building the higher ones, an application of Vygotskian scaffolding (Keene, Colvin, & Sissons, 2010; Vygotsky, 1978). Anderson and Krathwohl (2001) themselves argue the three lowest levels are hierarchically ordered but the three higher levels are parallel rather than strictly sequential; others argue it can be pedagogically better to move to Application before formally introducing a concept (Tomei, 2010), aligning with problem-based approaches that put real-world context before theory. More broadly, the clean separation of cognitive processes into discrete categories can be seen as artificial, since any real cognitive task typically draws on several categories at once, and any attempt to cleanly classify cognition risks understating its holistic, interconnected nature (Fadul, 2009) — a criticism applicable to taxonomies of mental process generally.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Most useful when writing precise, assessable learning objectives, and when selecting instructional strategies matched to a target level of complexity

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The apparent strict hierarchy can mislead teachers into treating lower levels as unimportant busywork, when in some domains the lower levels are the core skill
  • The clean level-by-level classification is an analytical convenience; real tasks usually draw on multiple levels/domains simultaneously

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Applicable across all ages and grade levels — the framework structures the objective, not the learner population
  • Broadly applicable across K-12, higher education, and workplace/corporate training — the taxonomy's own worked examples span classroom tasks (writing an essay) and workplace tasks (hiring the most qualified candidate, calculating vacation time)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Writing objectives at a deliberately targeted level of cognitive, psychomotor, or affective complexity, and sequencing instruction from lower to higher levels within a domain
  • Objectives classifiable by cognitive complexity (recall through creation), by domain (knowledge, skill, or attitude), and, in the revised cognitive-domain matrix, by knowledge type (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive) — this is the taxonomy's most directly actionable use

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development — Bloom's cognitive domain describes levels of instructional objective, distinct from Piaget's account of the learner's underlying developmental stage
  • Sociocultural Theory — Bloom's taxonomy helps a teacher target the zone of proximal development by pinpointing which cognitive level a student needs support at; the scaffolding logic of building lower-level skills toward higher-level ones has been explicitly connected to Vygotskian scaffolding (Keene, Colvin, & Sissons, 2010)
  • Information Processing Theory — both concern stages of increasing cognitive complexity, though IP theory models internal processing stages while Bloom's Taxonomy classifies external objectives
  • Metacognition — the revised taxonomy's Metacognitive knowledge dimension names this directly as a fourth type of knowledge alongside factual, conceptual, and procedural
  • Mastery Learning — mastery learning's step-by-step progression is often organized around Bloom's cognitive hierarchy

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Five "E" Model — a constructivist lesson pattern often used alongside Bloom's taxonomy to target progressively higher cognitive levels across a lesson's stages
  • Develop Observable Criteria — a strategy for writing measurable objectives using this taxonomy alongside Webb's Depth of Knowledge and Marzano's Dimensions of Learning
  • Problem-based Learning — Tomei's (2010) sequencing critique connects PBL's applied-before-abstract approach to a challenge against the taxonomy's strict hierarchy assumption

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Cognitive apprenticeship is the theory that complex thinking is learned through modeled expert performance, coached participation, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and gradual fading in authentic tasks.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Situated Learning
  • Cognitive Load Theory
  • Sociocultural Theory — operationalizes the Zone of Proximal Development and scaffolding via modeling, coaching, and fading

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Collins, A., Brown, J. S., & Newman, S. E. (1989). Cognitive apprenticeship. In Knowing, learning, and instruction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) proposes that learning is constrained by the limited capacity of working memory. When the total cognitive demand of a learning task exceeds that capacity, learning breaks down — not because the learner lacks ability, but because the instructional design has exhausted the resources available for processing. The theory distinguishes three sources of load and argues that effective instruction reduces unnecessary load to free capacity for the mental work that actually builds schema.

CLT was developed by John Sweller and colleagues in the 1980s–1990s, drawing on George Miller's work on working memory limits and Alan Baddeley's model of working memory components. Its central claim is that instructional design should treat working memory capacity as the binding constraint: the question is not just "what should I teach?" but "how much mental demand does this design impose, and on what?"

docs.title: Three Types of Load
docs.text:
Intrinsic load is inherent to the material itself — determined by the number of interacting elements the learner must hold in mind simultaneously. High-element-interactivity content (e.g., parsing a sentence, debugging a recursive function) cannot be simplified without distorting it; but it can be sequenced so simpler schemas are built first.

Extraneous load is imposed by poor instructional design — split-attention effects, redundant information, unnecessary navigation, irrelevant detail. Extraneous load consumes working memory capacity without contributing to learning. This is the type CLT most directly targets: the primary design goal is to eliminate it.

Germane load (in revised CLT) refers to the cognitive effort invested in schema construction and automation — the work that actually produces learning. Earlier formulations treated germane load as a third type to be increased; current CLT treats it as the portion of intrinsic load that is productively engaged, not a separate load type.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Applies wherever learning requires holding multiple interacting elements in working memory simultaneously — mathematics, programming, language acquisition, clinical reasoning, reading comprehension
  • Effect is strongest with novices; as expertise develops, previously separated elements are chunked into single schemas and cease to impose separate load demands (the basis of the expertise reversal effect)
  • Design choices that reduce extraneous load are never harmful; but scaffolding that reduces intrinsic load too aggressively can prevent the element-interactivity processing needed for schema formation
  • Additions intended to make material more interesting rather than to reduce load can themselves become an extraneous-load source — see Seductive details can distract from learning [-M]

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices with limited prior knowledge in the domain benefit most from CLT-informed design
  • Experts may find the same scaffolds redundant or distracting — what reduces load for a novice can introduce it for an expert
  • Learners with limited working memory capacity (e.g., younger children, learners under high cognitive stress) are most sensitive to extraneous load

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Procedural skill acquisition: learning to execute multi-step processes
  • Conceptual understanding of content with high element interactivity
  • Transfer: schema formation is the mechanism by which knowledge transfers to new problems

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+S] — example-based sequences reduce load compared to problem-only practice for novices; provides direct experimental evidence for the worked example effect as a CLT application
  • Worked examples reduce unnecessary search for novices. [+M] — worked examples reduce unnecessary search load, freeing working memory for schema construction
  • Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as learner expertise increases. [~M] — expertise reversal: as schemas develop, the same guidance that reduced load for novices begins to impose redundancy load on more experienced learners

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Situated Learning — CLT treats working memory as an individual cognitive limit; situated learning argues that cognition is distributed across tools, people, and environment, which can extend effective working memory capacity
  • Self-Regulated Learning — SRL requires learners to monitor and regulate their own processing; CLT explains why novices often cannot self-regulate effectively — metacognitive monitoring itself consumes working memory
  • Dual Coding Theory — Paivio's dual coding theory (separate verbal and visual channels) is a compatible model; multimedia learning theory (Mayer) applies both CLT and dual coding to instructional media design
  • Constructivism — tension point: constructivist approaches favor active discovery, which can impose high extraneous load; CLT favors explicit instruction for novices, but converges with constructivism for more expert learners (see expertise reversal)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Cognitive Apprenticeship — implements CLT by sequencing the modeling → coaching → fading arc: the modeling phase offloads element-interactivity processing onto the expert's narrated demonstration, reducing load during initial acquisition and fading support as schemas form.

Demonstration — the worked example is CLT's most direct instructional expression; by presenting a fully solved problem, demonstration eliminates the search component of problem solving, which is the primary source of extraneous load for novices.

Use Worked Examples — concrete application of CLT's worked example effect; the study-then-solve cycle is a direct implementation of the example-problem sequence shown to reduce load and improve transfer.

User-Centered Design for Learning — applies CLT's extraneous-load concept to interface design: confusing navigation and inconsistent terminology impose extraneous load exactly as an unnecessarily split-attention diagram does.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Cognitivism emerged in the late 1950s as a reaction against behaviorism's refusal to look inside the "black box" of the mind. Rather than treating learning as a change in observable stimulus-response associations, cognitivists treat it as a change in internal mental structures — the way information is received, organized, stored, and retrieved. Learning is equated with discrete changes between states of knowledge, not with changes in the probability of a response, and the learner is viewed as an active participant who attends to, codes, transforms, rehearses, and stores information rather than merely reacting to it (Ertmer & Newby, 2013).

Cognitivism shares with behaviorism an interest in environmental conditions (explanations, demonstrations, examples, practice with feedback), but interprets their role differently: a behaviorist arranges the environment to shape observable responses, while a cognitivist arranges it to support internal mental processing. Memory is central — learning succeeds when information is stored in an organized, meaningful way, and forgetting is explained as a retrieval failure (interference, decay, or missing retrieval cues) rather than the "nonuse" of a habit.

Cognitivism is the broader theoretical paradigm; Information Processing Theory is the specific mechanistic model (attention, working memory, encoding, long-term storage, retrieval) most often used to operationalize it, and Cognitive Load Theory extends it with a working-memory-capacity account of instructional design.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Instruction can name and organize its content structure explicitly (hierarchies, categories, relationships) so learners have something to encode it into
  • Best suited to content or tasks with identifiable mental structure — concepts, procedures, principles — that can be related to what the learner already knows

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Because it treats knowledge as something that can be organized and mapped onto the learner, cognitivism gives limited guidance for ill-structured, highly context-dependent problems, where Constructivism offers a better account

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who already have some relevant prior knowledge to which new information can be connected via analogy, advance organizers, or hierarchical structure
  • Novice-to-intermediate learners acquiring rule-, concept-, or procedure-based knowledge, where cognitive task analysis and explicit sequencing pay off

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Complex forms of learning that a purely behavioral account struggles to explain: reasoning, problem-solving, classification, rule and procedure application
  • Conceptual understanding and transfer that depend on how information is organized in memory rather than only on reinforcement history

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Grew directly out of dissatisfaction with behaviorism's inability to explain higher-level skills (language development, problem solving, inference, critical thinking) (Ertmer & Newby, 2013)

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Constructivism rejects cognitivism's assumption that knowledge is mind-independent and can be "mapped" onto a learner, arguing instead that learners construct their own meaning from experience

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Behaviorism – the paradigm cognitivism reacted against; both value practice and feedback, but for different reasons (shaping observable responses vs. supporting mental encoding)
  • Constructivism – shares cognitivism's view of learning as mental activity but rejects the assumption that a fixed body of knowledge can be transmitted or "mapped" onto the learner
  • Information Processing Theory + the specific memory-system model most commonly used to implement cognitivist instructional design
  • Cognitive Load Theory + a working-memory-capacity account built on cognitivist assumptions about encoding and storage
  • Dual Coding Theory + a cognitivist account of how verbal and nonverbal information are represented in memory

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Advance Organizers
  • Concept Mapping
  • Analogies and Prior-Knowledge Activation
  • Analogical Reasoning

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Ertmer, P. A., & Newby, T. J. (2013). Behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism: Comparing critical features from an instructional design perspective. Performance Improvement Quarterly, 26(2), 43–71. doi:10.1002/piq.21143

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Connectivism, proposed by George Siemens (2004/2005), argues that behaviorism, cognitivism, and constructivism were all developed before digital technology reorganized how people communicate and learn, and that the conditions underlying them have shifted too far for those theories to simply be revised. Where the earlier theories differ on how learning happens inside a person, they share the assumption that learning is knowable and occurs inside an individual. Connectivism drops that assumption: learning can reside outside the person entirely — in an organization, a database, or a network — and the central skill is not holding knowledge but forming and maintaining the connections needed to access it when needed.

Siemens frames this against the rapidly shrinking "half-life of knowledge" — much of what is known today did not exist a decade ago — and draws on chaos theory, network theory, and self-organization to argue that learning is "a process that occurs within nebulous environments of shifting core elements — not entirely under the control of the individual" (Siemens, 2004).

Principles of connectivism (Siemens, 2004):

  • Learning and knowledge rest in a diversity of opinions.
  • Learning is a process of connecting specialized nodes or information sources.
  • Learning may reside in non-human appliances (databases, tools, organizations).
  • The capacity to know more is more critical than what is currently known.
  • Nurturing and maintaining connections is needed to facilitate continual learning.
  • The ability to see connections between fields, ideas, and concepts is a core skill.
  • Currency (accurate, up-to-date knowledge) is the intent of all connectivist learning activities.
  • Decision-making is itself a learning process — the "right" choice today may be wrong tomorrow as the information landscape shifts.

Connectivism also draws on network science: nodes compete for connections, well-connected nodes ("hubs") are more likely to gain further connections, and "weak ties" — links between otherwise dissimilar networks — are disproportionately valuable for innovation and serendipitous discovery (Barabási, 2002; Granovetter's weak-ties idea as applied by Siemens). Personal knowledge is understood as a network that feeds into organizational networks and back again, so that staying current is a matter of cultivating and pruning connections rather than accumulating facts.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An information environment rich enough to make network-navigation itself a meaningful skill — online courses, professional networks, rapidly evolving fields
  • Tools or platforms that make connections visible and traversable (personal learning networks, social bookmarking, MOOCs, organizational knowledge bases)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Connectivism is a descriptive account of learning in networked environments rather than a tested, falsifiable psychological theory; it has drawn criticism for lacking the mechanism-level specificity of the theories it responds to
  • Provides little direct guidance for foundational skill acquisition (e.g., novice procedural learning), where explicit instruction and practice still dominate

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who already have enough foundational knowledge to evaluate and integrate information from a network — the theory targets continuing, professional, and self-directed learning rather than initial skill acquisition
  • Professionals in fields where the "half-life of knowledge" is short and staying current matters more than mastering a fixed curriculum

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Building and maintaining a personal or organizational knowledge network
  • Pattern recognition across disparate fields, ideas, and information sources
  • Knowing "where" to find current, accurate information rather than only "what" is currently known

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Explicitly positions itself against Behaviorism, Cognitivism, and Constructivism as theories built for a pre-networked era that cannot account for learning distributed across people, organizations, and technology

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Behaviorism – predates networked learning; treats learning as entirely internal to the individual
  • Cognitivism – also treats learning as an internal information-processing activity, which connectivism explicitly rejects as insufficient
  • Constructivism – shares connectivism's interest in learner-directed, socially situated learning, but still assumes knowledge is constructed inside the individual mind
  • Situated Learning ~ both emphasize that knowledge exists in a context beyond the individual, though situated learning centers embodied practice rather than digital networks

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) as an implementation of network-based, distributed learning
  • Personal learning networks built through social media, RSS, and professional communities

docs.text:

  • Siemens, G. (2005). Connectivism: A learning theory for the digital age. International Journal of Instructional Technology and Distance Learning, 2(1).
  • Siemens, G. (2018). Connectivism. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/connectivism

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Constructionism is Seymour Papert's extension of Piagetian constructivism, developed at the MIT AI Lab alongside Marvin Minsky and expressed through the Logo programming language Papert created with Wallace Feurzig (Lee, 2018). Where constructivism broadly holds that learners build understanding by connecting new experience to existing knowledge, constructionism adds a specific, stronger claim: learning is most effective when that building takes the form of constructing a public, shareable artifact — a program, a model, an object — that a learner can inspect, debug, show to others, and revise (Papert, 1980).

Papert saw computers as giving children unprecedented power to explore what he called "powerful ideas" — significant, generative concepts (in mathematics, in systems thinking) — through their own constructions, rather than through transmission. His research migrated from classical artificial intelligence toward epistemology and learning, eventually leading to the founding of the MIT Media Lab; the ideas and technologies from that lab spread through students who went on to positions at other institutions, making constructionism, computational thinking, and Papert's notion of "powerful ideas" enduring strands of the learning sciences (Lee, 2018). A footnote worth preserving: a strict Papert perspective would not privilege computer programming specifically so much as any rich, generative representational medium — embedded in a context that allows exploration, construction, and sharing of powerful ideas — of which programming was simply the most available example in his own era.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A medium in which learners can actually build and revise an artifact (code, a physical model, a simulation) rather than only consume or discuss content
  • A social context in which the artifact can be shared, shown, or discussed with others — the "public" aspect is not incidental; sharing and defending a construction is part of the mechanism, not just a motivational add-on

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The theory is specifically about learning through building an external, inspectable artifact — it is a stronger and narrower claim than generic "active learning" or "hands-on" activities that don't result in a shareable construction
  • Effective use requires the constructed artifact to actually embody the "powerful idea" being targeted, not just be an engaging but conceptually shallow production task

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners of any age, though Papert's own work and Logo were developed and studied primarily with children
  • Learners in domains where a concept can be embodied in a buildable, debuggable artifact (mathematical relationships, systems behavior, programmed logic)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Deep conceptual understanding of "powerful ideas" — generative concepts that extend beyond the immediate artifact being built
  • Debugging and self-correction skills that emerge naturally from iterating on a construction that either works or doesn't

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Extends Constructivism [+S] with a specific mechanism (constructing a public, shareable artifact) rather than construction of understanding in the abstract

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Constructivism — constructionism is Papert's specific extension of constructivism, adding the requirement of a concrete, shareable, inspectable artifact as the vehicle for learning
  • Stages of Cognitive Development — the chapter this page draws on identifies Piaget's stage theory as the foundation constructionism (via constructivism) ultimately builds on

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Makerspace — a direct institutional expression of constructionist learning: learners build tangible, shareable artifacts with support from more experienced makers
  • The Logo programming language and "turtle graphics," Papert's original vehicle for children to construct and debug geometric ideas through programming

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Papert, S. (1980). Mindstorms: Children, computers, and powerful ideas. Basic Books.
  • Lee, V. (2018). A short history of the learning sciences. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/history_of_learning_sciences

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Constructivism is the broad view that learners actively build understanding by connecting new experiences and information to what they already know. Rather than treating knowledge as something transmitted whole from teacher to learner, constructivist perspectives emphasize interpretation, prior knowledge, social interaction, and meaning-making.

In instruction, constructivism is less a single method than a family resemblance across approaches that value active engagement, explanation, inquiry, collaboration, and reflection. It is often contrasted with highly transmissive teaching, but in practice many effective designs mix constructivist processes with explicit modeling, sequencing, and feedback.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Especially relevant where interpretation, inquiry, discussion, and application matter
  • Supports designs that connect learning to prior knowledge, authentic tasks, and social interaction
  • Often used to justify active learning, problem-centered learning, and collaborative meaning-making

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners building new understanding on top of prior knowledge and lived experience
  • Learners in contexts where dialogue, inquiry, and interpretation matter more than rote repetition alone
  • Groups that benefit from discussion and collaborative refinement of ideas

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Conceptual understanding through active sense-making
  • Transfer through connecting ideas across contexts
  • Learner agency in explanation, interpretation, and problem solving

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-explanation improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. [+S]
  • Whole-task performance improves transfer of complex skills to real-world settings. [~S]
  • Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support. [~M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development — Piaget's stage theory is the direct historical foundation constructivism builds on
  • Self-Regulated Learning — constructivist learning often depends on learners monitoring and revising their own understanding
  • Cognitive Load Theory — constructivist tasks still have to manage working-memory limits, especially for novices
  • Information Processing Theory — active construction still depends on attention, encoding, and retrieval processes
  • Cognitivism — constructivism grew out of cognitivism but rejects the assumption that knowledge is mind-independent and can be mapped onto a learner
  • Sociocultural Theory — Vygotsky is a direct historical source for constructivism's emphasis on social interaction and meaning-making
  • Situated Learning — shares constructivism's emphasis on authentic context, but centers participation in social practice rather than individual meaning-making
  • Constructionism — Papert's extension of constructivism, adding the requirement that learning takes the form of building a public, shareable artifact

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Inquiry-based Learning
  • Problem-based Learning
  • Peer Discussion
  • Purposeful Reflection
  • Makerspace
