  • Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.
  • Bransford, J. D., Brown, A. L., & Cocking, R. R. (Eds.). (2000). How people learn. National Academy Press.
  • Ertmer, P. A., & Newby, T. J. (2013). Behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism: Comparing critical features from an instructional design perspective. Performance Improvement Quarterly, 26(2), 43–71. doi:10.1002/piq.21143

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Social reconstructionism was founded as a response to the atrocities of World War II and the Holocaust, aiming at social reform that would help prepare students to build a better world by instilling democratic values. Critical pedagogy emerged from that foundation.

Critical pedagogy is the application of critical theory to education. For critical pedagogues, teaching and learning is inherently a political act: knowledge and language are never fully neutral or objective, so issues of social, environmental, or economic justice cannot be separated from the curriculum. Its goal, following Paulo Freire, is to emancipate marginalized or oppressed groups by developing conscientização — critical consciousness — in students.

Critical pedagogy de-centers the traditional teacher-centered classroom. Curriculum and classroom practice under this stance are student-centered and aim to instill a desire to make the world a better place, focusing on controversial world issues and using current events as a springboard for thinking. Students are taught the importance of working together to bring about change, and teachers explicitly connect what is happening in the world with what is being learned in the classroom (Ganly, 2007).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Willingness to treat the curriculum itself, not just the delivery method, as carrying social, environmental, or economic-justice content
  • Current events and controversial issues as legitimate, regular curricular material rather than a departure from "the real content"

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The explicitly political framing can create real tension in contexts (or with stakeholders) that expect curriculum neutrality

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Students from marginalized or historically oppressed groups, for whom the framework's emancipatory aim is most directly targeted
  • More broadly, any student a teacher wants to prepare for active, collective participation in social change

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Critical consciousness — the capacity to analyze and act on social, environmental, or economic injustice — rather than neutral mastery of disciplinary content alone

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Pragmatism and Progressivism (Educational Philosophy) — critical pedagogy shares Progressivism's de-centering of the teacher, but adds an explicit political and emancipatory aim that Progressivism itself does not require

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A unit built around a current social-justice issue, where students research the issue, discuss competing perspectives, and plan a collective response

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ganly, S. (2007). Educational philosophies in the classroom: The categories of various teaching philosophies. Retrieved from https://archive.is/20130628165859/www.associatedcontent.com/article/352631/educational_philosophies_in_the_classroom_pg2.html
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching philosophy. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Critical thinking requires both a skill (analyzing the reliability and validity of information) and a disposition to actually apply that skill, in principle across any realm of knowledge, not only a single subject or topic (Halpern, 2003; Williams, Oliver, & Stockade, 2004). A critical thinker is not simply someone with a negative or fault-finding attitude; rather, the critical thinker asks key questions, evaluates evidence for ideas, reasons about problems logically and objectively, and expresses ideas and conclusions clearly and precisely — and can carry these habits of mind across more than one domain of life or knowledge.

What makes thinking "critical," rather than merely correct, is largely metacognition — strategies for thinking about one's own thinking, and for monitoring the success and quality of that thinking. In fostering critical thinking, a teacher is fostering a student's ability to construct and control their own thinking, rather than being controlled by ideas unreflectively.

Two studies illustrate concretely different routes to critical thinking. In one, students were taught to annotate readings — writing questions and comments in the margins rather than simply underlining passages; students who actually used annotation more heavily produced essays that were later judged better-reasoned and more critically astute than essays from students who annotated less (Liu, 2006; see Annotating). In another, students verbally described a recent, personal, disturbing incident, and classmates discussed it together to identify the precise reasons the incident was disturbing and the assumptions underlying the original student's account; one student's account of being snubbed by a store clerk led the group to surface an unstated assumption (suspected racial profiling), which the student then used as the basis for a research essay (Hawkins, 2006; see Socratic Seminar). Both studies illustrate that critical thinking can be stimulated through quite different instructional means — written annotation versus oral group discussion — while both ultimately rely on, and further build, the learner's own prior critical-thinking skill.

docs.title: How to Teach It, and to Whom
docs.text:
How best to teach critical thinking remains debated along two axes. First, whether to infuse critical-thinking skills into existing subject courses, or teach them through free-standing dedicated units. Infusion has the potential advantage of integrating critical thinking across a student's whole education, but risks diluting understanding because critical thinking takes a different form in each learning context; the free-standing approach stands a better chance of being understood clearly and coherently, at the cost of obscuring how it relates to other courses and tasks — essentially the same dilemma posed by transfer of learning. Research comparing the two approaches does not settle the matter; either can work as long as it is implemented thoroughly and the teacher is genuinely committed to critical thinking's value (Halpern, 2003).

Second, who should be taught critical thinking. Surveys have found that teachers sometimes favor teaching critical thinking primarily to already high-achieving, higher-income, or university-track students (Warburton & Torff, 2005) — presumably on the assumption that such students can better benefit from or use it. There is little research evidence supporting this assumption, and it is ethically questionable regardless: Hawkins's (2006) discussion-based study above found critical thinking fostered even among students considered low-advantage.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Thorough, sustained implementation and genuine teacher commitment — either infusion or free-standing instruction can work, but only with real follow-through

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Teaching critical thinking only to already-advantaged students is both poorly supported by evidence and ethically questionable, since research shows it can be fostered in low-advantage students as well

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students, not selectively the already high-achieving — evidence does not support restricting critical-thinking instruction to advantaged learners

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Analyzing the reliability and validity of information; asking key questions; evaluating evidence; reasoning logically and objectively; expressing conclusions clearly; applying these habits across more than one domain

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Metacognition — the self-monitoring and thinking-about-thinking mechanism that underlies what makes thinking "critical" rather than merely correct
  • Transfer of Learning — the infusion-vs-free-standing debate in teaching critical thinking is a specific instance of the general transfer problem

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Annotating — written annotation of readings as one route to critical thinking (Liu, 2006)
  • Socratic Seminar — oral group discussion of personal dilemmas as another route to critical thinking (Hawkins, 2006)

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Halpern, D. F. (2003). Thought and knowledge: An introduction to critical thinking (4th ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
  • Williams, R. L., Oliver, R., & Stockdale, S. (2004). Psychological versus generic critical thinking as predictors and outcome measures in a large undergraduate human development course. The Journal of General Education, 53(1), 37-58.
  • Liu, J. (2006). Assessing student critical thinking through annotation. [Cited via secondary source without full publication details]
  • Hawkins, K. (2006). Discussion-based critical thinking through personal-incident analysis. [Cited via secondary source without full publication details]
  • Warburton, E. C., & Torff, B. (2005). The effect of perceived learner advantages on teachers' beliefs about critical-thinking instruction. Journal of Teacher Education, 56(1), 24-33.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Critical thinking. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Gibbons (2003/2018) argues that instructional designs are not unitary objects but stacks of layers, borrowing the analogy directly from architect Stewart Brand's account of how buildings are actually structured — site, structure, skin, services, space plan, and stuff, each aging and changing at a different rate, each requiring deliberate "articulation" with the others so a change to one layer doesn't force a rebuild of the whole. Gibbons and colleagues found the same structure holds for instructional designs, identifying seven layers: model/content (subject-matter structure — concepts, rules, principles, tasks), strategy (event structures — problems, exercises, instructional periods), control (rules governing learner actions and system responses), message (main ideas, examples, feedback, explanations), representation (media selection and display structures), media-logic (the underlying program/logic implementation), and management (session control, record-keeping, evaluation planning). Each layer carries its own design goals, constructs, theoretic principles, tools, and specialized skills — which is why, over time, these skills harden into separate professional roles (a media producer, a strategy/instructional designer, a programmer).

The theory's most distinctive claim is about designer cognition: designers predictably mature through a sequence of "centrisms" — media-centrism (thinking in the vocabulary of the medium — "the page," "the hyperlink"), message-centrism (shifting focus to telling the content better — examples, analogies, emphasis), strategy-centrism (recognizing structural patterns across messages that generalize across subject matter, and governing delivery through rules — Gagné's conditions of learning fit here), and model-centrism (entering the design through the subject matter's own system and model constructs first, then adding strategy, message, and media — the stance Gibbons identifies as underlying most "new-paradigm" approaches, including problem-solving-centered and simulation-based instruction). Each phase does not discard the previous one; it adds a new primary entry point while retaining the earlier layers' constructs as secondary considerations. Which layer a designer should enter through is not universally fixed — project constraints (e.g., an assignment specifically to produce a set of videotapes) can force representation/media-logic to the front regardless of the designer's own maturity level.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Enough design-team maturity or explicit training to recognize which layer a design problem actually lives in, since a symptom that looks like a message problem (an explanation "not landing") can actually originate in a missing or incoherent strategy or model layer
  • Deliberate "articulation" between layers when a design is revised — changing a representation/media choice should not require rebuilding the model or strategy layer underneath it, and a design that doesn't allow this is architecturally brittle

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The theory describes the designer's own cognitive process and the design artifact's internal structure — it does not by itself prescribe which layer to prioritize for a given project; project constraints can override an individual designer's natural entry point
  • A design polished at the message or media layer can disguise a genuinely missing or weak strategy or model layer, producing content that reads well but doesn't hold together instructionally — the theory's main diagnostic value is spotting this mismatch, not preventing it outright

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Not learner-facing directly — this is a designer/instructional-design-team framework, in the same category as TPACK and Performance Technology: its downstream effect on learners runs through the quality and coherence of the resulting instructional artifact

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not a learning objective — a diagnostic and pedagogical framework for instructional design education and design-team practice: explaining why novice designers over-index on media, and providing a vocabulary for locating where a design's incoherence actually originates

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Directly adapted from Stewart Brand's (1994) "shearing layers" analysis of building architecture, applied to instructional design by Gibbons, Nelson, and Richards (2000)
  • Model-centrism is described as the shared thread running through most new-paradigm, problem-solving-centered instructional approaches (Gibbons & Fairweather, 2000)

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• First Principles of Instruction — Merrill's problem-centered principles reflect a model-centered design stance in Gibbons' framework, entering through subject-matter and problem structure rather than media or message
  • Cognitive Load Theory — poor articulation between the representation/media-logic layer and the message layer is one route by which extraneous cognitive load enters a design

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A course visibly built around PowerPoint slide templates and video-hosting conventions (media-centric) versus one built by first mapping the domain's own concept/rule/task structure and only then choosing media to represent it (model-centric)
  • Revising a course's video platform (a representation/media-logic change) without needing to rewrite its underlying strategy or content structure — evidence of well-articulated layers

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Gibbons, A. S. (2018). What and how do designers design? A theory of design structure and layers. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/what_and_how_do_designers_design (originally published as Gibbons, A. S. (2003). TechTrends, 47(5), 22–25.)
  • Brand, S. (1994). How buildings learn: What happens after they're built. Penguin.
  • Gibbons, A. S., Nelson, J., & Richards, R. (2000). The architecture of instructional simulation: A design for tool construction. Center for Human-System Simulation Technical Report, Idaho National Engineering and Environmental Laboratory.
  • Gibbons, A. S. (2013). An architectural approach to instructional design. Routledge.

docs.title: Developmental Research Designs — Cross-Sectional, Longitudinal, and Sequential
Description
docs.text:
Research design is the strategy or blueprint for deciding how to collect and analyze information, distinct from the specific methods used to gather it; when the goal is examining change over time, three designs are available, each with a different cost and a different vulnerability.

Cross-sectional designs examine participants of different ages tested at the same point in time, and are the most common developmental design because they are less time-consuming and less expensive than the alternatives. Their core limitation is that the results describe age differences, not change over time within the same people: if 80-year-olds score lower than 50-year-olds who score lower than 20-year-olds on some measure, the study cannot say whether any individual actually declines with age, since no one was followed as they aged — it's equally possible the 20-year-olds will keep scoring just as high decades from now. Cross-sectional comparisons are also vulnerable to cohort effects: since each age group belongs to a different generation, an observed difference may reflect that cohort's distinct life experience (education, economic conditions, technology, health and nutrition standards) rather than age itself.

Longitudinal designs begin with a single cohort — people of similar age and background — and measure them repeatedly over an extended period, so people can be compared with their own earlier selves and age-related change can actually be measured. This design carries its own two hazards. Attrition — participants who move, change contact information, die, or simply lose interest — erodes the sample over time, and is often selective: it tends to be the least healthy, least educated, and lowest-socioeconomic-status participants who drop out, which can bias what remains. Practice effects are the second hazard: repeated administration of the same or similar assessment can make participants appear to improve simply because they've practiced the task, not because they've genuinely developed.

Sequential designs combine both approaches: participants of different ages are enrolled at different points in time and then followed longitudinally, so the design supports longitudinal comparisons (within-person change), cross-sectional comparisons (age/cohort differences), and — uniquely — the ability to disentangle cohort effects from time-of-measurement effects from true age-related change. As Schaie and Baltes (1975) put it, cross-sectional and longitudinal designs can reveal a pattern of change, while sequential designs can help identify what's actually driving that pattern.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A large enough initial longitudinal sample to absorb expected attrition without leaving the remaining sample unrepresentative
  • Enough resources (time, funding, participant retention effort) for a longitudinal or sequential design when the research question genuinely requires within-person change, not just an age comparison

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A cross-sectional finding of age-group differences cannot, by itself, support a claim about individual developmental change — the design simply doesn't measure that
  • Selective attrition in a longitudinal study can make its final sample systematically healthier, more educated, or more advantaged than its starting sample, biasing later-wave findings
  • Improvement across repeated waves of a longitudinal study may reflect practice with the instrument rather than genuine development

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Researchers and consumers of developmental research choosing or evaluating a design against what the research question actually requires

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Recognizing which developmental claims a given study's design can and cannot support — age-difference versus age-change being the central distinction

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Research Design Taxonomy — Quantitative/Qualitative and Descriptive/Correlational/Experimental — the general research-design taxonomy this specializes for studying change over time

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A cross-sectional study comparing vocabulary size across 5-, 10-, and 15-year-olds, versus a longitudinal study following the same children from age 5 to 15

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Schaie, K. W., & Baltes, P. B. (1975). On sequential strategies in developmental research: Description or explanation? Human Development, 18(6), 384-390.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Developmental research designs. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Dual Coding Theory proposes that verbal and nonverbal information can be processed in partly distinct but connected representational systems. Learning can improve when instruction coordinates language with meaningful imagery or other visual representation.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text: • Concepts become easier to understand and remember when learners can encode them through both verbal and visual routes.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: • Supports diagrams, concept maps, visual examples, and multimedia design when the visual is instructionally meaningful.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Cognitive Load Theory

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Paivio, A. (1990). Mental representations: A dual coding approach. Oxford University Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Essentialism adheres to the belief that a core set of essential skills — a universal pool of knowledge needed by all students — must be taught to everyone. Essentialists favor traditional academic disciplines that develop prescribed skills and objectives across content areas and build a common culture, typically arguing for a back-to-basics approach to intellectual and moral standards; vocational classes are not seen as a necessary part of educational training. Schools should be sites of rigor where students learn to work hard and respect authority. Because of this stance, Essentialism tends to subscribe to the tenets of Realism. Essentialist classrooms tend to be teacher-centered, emphasizing lecture and teacher demonstration; assessment is predominately through testing, with few if any projects or portfolios — a stance that made it comfortable with the No Child Left Behind Act's reliance on test scores as the main form of evaluation (Ornstein & Levine, 2003).

Perennialism advocates seeking, teaching, and learning universal truths that span the ages and, Perennialists argue, have everlasting importance for solving human problems regardless of time or place. While Perennialism resembles Essentialism at first glance, it focuses on the individual development of the student rather than emphasizing skills, and supports a liberal-arts curriculum meant to produce well-rounded individuals with knowledge across the arts and sciences — English language arts, foreign languages, mathematics, natural sciences, fine arts, and philosophy. Like Essentialism, Perennialism tends toward teacher-centered instruction, but Perennialists also use student-centered activities like Socratic Seminar, which encourages students to think, rationalize, and develop their own ideas. Perennialists hold that knowledge passed through the ages — the classic works of figures like Plato and Einstein — should remain the basis of the curriculum, grounded in reason, logic, and analytical thought; only information that has stood the test of time is considered relevant, and student input is not generally elicited (Ganly, 2007).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A stable, well-defined canon of content (essential skills for Essentialism, timeless works and ideas for Perennialism) that the curriculum can be built around

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Both traditions constrain curricular breadth to a fixed core, which can leave less room for student interest, current events, or emerging content areas than Progressivism allows [~M]

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Essentialism: learners for whom a common, universal skill base is the priority (e.g., accountability-driven public schooling contexts)
  • Perennialism: learners in liberal-arts contexts aiming for well-rounded individual development through engagement with canonical ideas

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Essentialism: mastery of a prescribed, universal set of academic skills, verified through testing
  • Perennialism: reasoned, analytical engagement with timeless ideas, verified through discussion and reasoning rather than testing alone

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Realism (Educational Philosophy) — the ontology Essentialism tends to subscribe to
  • Idealism (Educational Philosophy) — Perennialism's use of Socratic dialogue and a canon of "universal truths" echoes Idealism's own commitments
  • Pragmatism and Progressivism (Educational Philosophy) — explicitly contrasts with both Essentialism and Perennialism on curriculum structure, teacher role, and assessment

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A standardized, testing-heavy curriculum built around a fixed set of core subjects (Essentialism)
  • A great-books or liberal-arts seminar sequence built around canonical texts across disciplines (Perennialism)

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ornstein, A., & Levine, D. (2003). Foundations of education (8th ed.). Houghton Mifflin.
  • Ganly, S. (2007). Educational philosophies in the classroom: The categories of various teaching philosophies. Retrieved from https://archive.is/20130628165859/www.associatedcontent.com/article/352631/educational_philosophies_in_the_classroom_pg2.html
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching philosophy. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Executive functions are the self-regulatory processes that let a person inhibit an impulsive response, flexibly shift between tasks or perspectives, hold and manipulate information in mind, and organize behavior toward a goal rather than react automatically to the immediate situation. They emerge gradually starting in early childhood and continue developing through adolescence, driven both by brain maturation — particularly of the prefrontal cortex, which matures later than most other brain regions — and by experience (Fay-Stammbach, Hawes, & Meredith, 2014).

The quality of a child's early environment measurably shapes executive function development: warm, responsive parenting, scaffolded support during challenging tasks, and cognitively stimulating environments are all associated with stronger executive function skills. Bibok, Carpendale, and Müller (2009) found that maternal scaffolding predicted cognitive flexibility in 2-year-olds and inhibitory control in 4-year-olds — showing that executive function is not simply a matter of waiting for the brain to mature, but is actively supported (or under-supported) by the responsiveness of a child's environment, in a manner directly consistent with Sociocultural Theory's account of scaffolding.

Executive function is closely tied to, but distinct from, adolescent risk-taking and self-regulation more broadly: adolescents can show competent executive function under low-stress conditions, but self-regulation reliably degrades under high stress or high emotional/social demand, a pattern tied to the same maturational mismatch between limbic and prefrontal brain systems described in Adolescent Brain Development (Luciana & Collins, 2012).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Executive function is not fixed at any single age — it develops gradually into the mid-20s, meaning instruction that assumes fully adult-level self-regulation in adolescents or even young adults will be miscalibrated for a meaningful share of learners
  • Scaffolding and cognitively stimulating environments measurably support executive function development, making this one of the more actionable levers available to caregivers and instructors, rather than a purely maturational given
  • Executive function that is intact under calm conditions can still fail under high stress or high social/emotional demand — a "test" of self-regulation given under low-stakes conditions may not predict performance under exam pressure or social conflict

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Young children, where scaffolded support during challenging tasks measurably builds early executive function
  • Adolescents, where executive function is present but less reliable under stress than in calm conditions
  • Learners of any age engaged in tasks requiring sustained inhibition, flexible task-switching, or working-memory-heavy planning

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not itself a content-objective framework — it explains a capacity (self-regulation) that many other objectives (sustained independent work, following multi-step instructions, resisting distraction) implicitly depend on

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Information Processing Theory — executive function is the control system that coordinates attention and working memory within the broader information-processing model
  • Adolescent Brain Development — the prefrontal cortex maturation underlying executive function is the same maturational process described there
  • Sociocultural Theory — scaffolding's measurable effect on executive function development is a direct, testable instance of Vygotsky's broader claim about guided interaction

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Fay-Stammbach, T., Hawes, D. J., & Meredith, P. (2014). Parenting influences on executive function in early childhood: A review. Child Development Perspectives, 8(4), 258-264.
  • Bibok, M. B., Carpendale, J. I. M., & Müller, U. (2009). Parental scaffolding and the development of executive function. New Directions for Child and Adolescent Development, 2009(123), 17-34.
  • Luciana, M., & Collins, P. F. (2012). Incentive motivation, cognitive control, and the adolescent brain: Is it time for a paradigm shift? Child Development Perspectives, 6(4), 392-399.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Information processing theories. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Existentialism grew out of continental philosophies forming in 19th- and early-20th-century Europe, most notably hermeneutic phenomenology — the examination of lived experience — and it countered the mind/body and mind/world dualisms inherent in both Idealism and Realism: the world has no meaning outside human existence within it. Jean-Paul Sartre held that "existence precedes essence" — an individual's existence comes before the nature or fact of what they are, meaning individual human beings are free to determine their own meaning for life rather than possessing any inherent identity beyond what they choose or create.

Existentialists position the individual as responsible for their own being. "Who am I? What should I do?" become central questions for a person's project of being — if one identifies as a teacher (or any other identity), one must evaluate what someone who holds that identity actually does, and after careful reflection choose to authentically enact it. Acting in accordance with one's own chosen beliefs and values despite social pressure constitutes authentic existence; acting on false values adopted because of social pressure is acting in "bad faith," an inauthentic existence, in Sartre's terms.

In educational settings, Existentialists focus on giving students personal choices where they must confront others' views to clarify and develop authentic actions as part of their own developing identity. Existentialists have real difficulty positioning students as objects to be measured, tracked, or standardized. Teachers working from this ontology create activities that guide students toward self-direction and self-actualization.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Genuine opportunities for students to make personal choices about their own learning, not just choices among options the teacher has already fully determined

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Sits in tension with standardized measurement and tracking, which the philosophy treats as objectifying students rather than respecting their self-determined identity [~M]

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners for whom identity development and self-direction are as central a goal as content mastery

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Authentic self-direction and self-actualization, achieved through personal choice and confrontation with differing views rather than through externally imposed standards

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Idealism (Educational Philosophy) — one of the dualist traditions Existentialism explicitly positions itself against
  • Realism (Educational Philosophy) — the other dualist tradition Existentialism rejects

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A classroom structure that lets students choose their own topics, evaluation criteria, or project direction as a matter of principle, not just as a motivational device

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching philosophy. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Expectancy-Value Theory (Wigfield & Eccles, 2000) proposes that achievement behavior is most immediately predicted by two beliefs: expectancy for success (whether the learner believes they will do well on an upcoming task) and task value (why the learner believes the task is worth doing). Expectancy for success is conceptually distinct from present-tense ability beliefs — expectancy is about future potential, ability belief is about current competence — though the two are closely related in practice.

Task value answers "why should I do this?" with four components (Wigfield & Eccles, 1992):

  • Intrinsic value — the pure enjoyment of doing the task itself.
  • Attainment value — the importance of doing well because the task reflects something important about one's identity.
  • Utility value — the task's perceived usefulness for a future goal (e.g., taking a language class to get a specific job).
  • Cost — what the learner has to give up (time, effort, competing opportunities) to engage in the task; high cost suppresses engagement even when expectancy and the other value components are favorable.

Expectancy and value are often described as combining multiplicatively rather than additively (Wigfield & Eccles, 2002; Wigfield, Tonks, & Eccles, 2004): motivation requires at least a modest expectancy and at least some positive value, so a learner with high expectancy for success but zero perceived value ("I could ace this, but why bother?") will be no more motivated than one with high value but zero expectancy ("this matters a lot to me, but there's no way I can do it") — either factor at zero drives the product to zero.

Numerous studies link both expectancy and task value independently to achievement outcomes, including in online learning: perceived competence and task value each significantly predicted learner satisfaction, persistence, and achievement in an online university sample (Joo, Lim, & Kim, 2013), and expectancies/task values more broadly predict achievement behaviors and outcomes across studies (Dennissen, Zarrett, & Eccles, 2007; Durik, Shechter, Noh, Rozek, & Harackiewicz, 2015; Wigfield & Eccles, 2000). Bong (2001) found that college students' perceived competence significantly predicted their performance, while perceived utility value separately predicted their intentions to enroll in future courses — evidence that expectancy and value operate as genuinely separate levers rather than one driving the other.

Because expectancy and value require different remedies, low motivation calls for diagnosing which one is missing before intervening. Raising expectancy means calibrating task difficulty so success is a realistic prospect (neither too hard nor too easy), backed by thoughtful planning, adjusted objectives, supportive materials, and help when needed; it also means addressing non-skill causes of low expectancy, such as a student's belief that fairness or favoritism — not their own effort — determines outcomes, or an external locus of control that makes effort feel disconnected from results, both of which may call for a clearer, more predictable path to success and encouraging feedback rather than more skill practice. Raising value (sometimes decomposed further into instrumentality — whether good performance is reliably rewarded — and valence — whether the available rewards are ones the student actually wants) means linking the task to students' existing interests and prior knowledge, making its utility toward future goals explicit, showing that people the student respects value it too, and — for instrumentality specifically — making sure any reward system tracks genuine performance and progress rather than being awarded meritlessly, since rewards perceived as unearned can erode the motivation of the highest performers.

The theory is explicitly integrative — it is often used as the organizing frame that ties together goal orientation, self-efficacy, interest, and self-determination theories into a single motivational-design framework, most visibly in Keller's ARCS model, where the relevance category maps closely onto task value and the confidence category maps onto expectancy for success.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• The ability to make a task's value legible to the learner along at least one of the four dimensions (why it's enjoyable, why it matters to identity, what it's useful for, or what it costs) rather than assuming value is self-evident
  • Tasks calibrated so that a learner's expectancy for success is realistic and not chronically suppressed by consistent failure

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The four value components can trade off against each other — a task can have high utility value but such high cost (time, competing demands) that overall engagement still suffers
  • Expectancy and value are both learner beliefs, not task properties; the same task can carry very different expectancy/value profiles for different learners, so this is not a one-size-fits-all task-design checklist

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who can articulate or be observed to lack a sense of either "can I succeed at this" (expectancy) or "why does this matter" (value) — the theory implies different interventions depending on which is missing
  • Learners weighing competing time/effort demands, where the cost component of task value is especially salient

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained engagement and enrollment/persistence decisions (e.g., choosing to continue in a subject area), which expectancy and task value have both been shown to predict
  • Deeper engagement that depends on genuine valuing of the task, not just extrinsic compliance

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Integrates elements of Self-Efficacy Theory, Attribution Theory (the stability dimension of an attribution shapes expectancy), and Self-Determination Theory (task value overlaps with the sense of relevance SDT-informed design also targets)

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Self-efficacy and "expectancies for success" are often used interchangeably, but conceptually self-efficacy is task-specific while expectancy for success tends to be domain-specific (Wigfield & Eccles, 2000) — see Self-Efficacy Theory

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Efficacy Theory — the expectancy component overlaps heavily with self-efficacy, differing mainly in grain (domain-specific vs. task-specific)
  • Attribution Theory — the stability dimension of a learner's attributions for past outcomes directly shapes their expectancy for future success
  • Self-Determination Theory — task value (especially attainment and utility value) overlaps with the sense of personal relevance and autonomy SDT identifies as motivating
  • ARCS Model of Motivational Design — Keller's Relevance and Confidence categories directly operationalize task value and expectancy for success

docs.text:

  • Wigfield, A., & Eccles, J. (1992). The development of achievement task values: A theoretical analysis. Developmental Review, 12, 265–310.
  • Park, S. W. (2018). Motivation theories and instructional design. In R. West (Ed.), Foundations of Learning and Instructional Design Technology. EdTech Books. https://edtechbooks.org/lidtfoundations/motivation_theories_and_instructional_design
  • Joo, Y. J., Lim, K. Y., & Kim, J. (2013). Locus of control, self-efficacy, and task value as predictors of learning outcome in an online university context. Computers & Education, 62, 149–158.
  • Wigfield, A., Tonks, S., & Eccles, J. S. (2004). Expectancy-value theory in cross-cultural perspective. In D. M. McInerney & S. Van Etten (Eds.), Big theories revisited (pp. 165-198). Information Age Publishing.
  • Bong, M. (2001). Role of self-efficacy and task-value in predicting college students' course performance and future enrollment intentions. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 26(4), 553-570.
  • Dennissen, J. J. A., Zarrett, N. R., & Eccles, J. S. (2007). I like to do it, I'm able, and I know I am: Longitudinal couplings between domain-specific achievement, self-concept, and interest. Child Development, 78(2), 430-447.
  • Durik, A. M., Shechter, O. G., Noh, M., Rozek, C. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2015). What if I can't? Success expectancies moderate the effects of utility value information on situational interest and performance. Motivation and Emotion, 39(1), 104-118.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Expectancy-value theory. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
David Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory (ELT) is "a holistic model of the learning process and a multi-linear model of adult development" (Baker, Jensen, & Kolb, 2002, p. 51), rooted explicitly in Dewey, Kurt Lewin, and Piaget. It models learning as a four-stage cycle — concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation — organized around two underlying dialectical continuums: apprehension (concrete experience) versus comprehension (abstract conceptualization), and intension (reflective observation) versus extension (active experimentation). Kolb's central theoretical claim is that learning requires actively resolving the discomfort of whichever pole of each continuum a learner is not naturally comfortable with: "perception alone is not sufficient for learning; something must be done with it," and "transformation alone cannot represent learning, for there must be something to be transformed" (Baker, Jensen, & Kolb, pp. 56–67). This dialectical-resolution requirement is the theory's core explanatory mechanism, distinguishing it from a purely descriptive account of "learning by doing."

The theory targets adult learners specifically, framed as an inclusive model of adult development within a single framework, and underlies applications such as cooperative education, internships, and continuing-professional-development e-learning.

docs.title: A Rival Account: Dewey's Reflective Experience
docs.text: Miettinen (2000) contrasts Kolb's model against Dewey's own philosophy of experience, on which Kolb draws but from which the model departs in two significant ways. First, Dewey held that non-reflective, habitual experience is the dominant mode of everyday functioning, and that reflective experience arises only when habitual experience is contradicted by something unexpected; Kolb's model, by contrast, does not address non-reflective experience at all, treating every turn of the cycle as if it begins from reflection. Second, Dewey held that observation of an external reality is the starting point of knowledge, whereas Kolb makes the learner's own subjective experience the starting point, disregarding the learner's prior objective reality.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
"Concrete experience" is under-theorized in Kolb's own writing — it is "nowhere defined or elaborated," leading some to argue the model is really about reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation rather than a genuine four-part cycle (Herron, cited in Yorks & Kasl, 2002). The very idea of "immediate and concrete" experience is itself philosophically contestable (Miettinen, 2000). Kolb's concepts are criticized as an eclectic blend of disparate theorists (Dewey, Lewin, Piaget) that does not fully cohere into a single logical account, and critics have argued the theory exists partly to justify Kolb's commercial Learning Style Inventory (Miettinen, 2000). The model has also been criticized for treating its four phases as potentially disconnected rather than truly integrated, and for having no account of the social dimension of experience or knowledge construction — the cycle is modeled as happening within a single learner, not within a group.

In response to the last two criticisms, some accounts propose a revised experiential learning cycle: starting from subjective stimuli (the learner's own prior observations and felt judgments, performed individually), through a disruptive experience (an explicitly Deweyan break from habitual experience), an emotion inventory, reflective observation, conceptualization/hypothesizing, and addressing (planning, experimentation, or cautious testing) — looping back via either expected or further disruptive experiences, situated within an encompassing environment, and explicitly able to occur either individually or within a social group.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Best suited to settings where learners can genuinely act, observe consequences, and revise understanding across repeated cycles — internships, cooperative education, service learning, simulations, and structured reflection practices
  • The model's silence on non-reflective, habitual experience means it does not, by itself, explain everyday functioning that doesn't involve active reflection

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Adult learners specifically — Kolb frames the theory as a model of adult development, and its signature applications (internships, cooperative education, professional continuing education) are adult/professional contexts

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Integration of concrete experience with abstract understanding through repeated cycles of action and reflection
  • Development toward more complete engagement with all four modes of the cycle, since the theory holds that skilled learning requires resolving discomfort with whichever pole (concrete/abstract, reflective/active) a learner is less naturally inclined toward

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Constructivism — shares an emphasis on active meaning-making from experience, though ELT specifies experience-transformation mechanics constructivism leaves more general
  • Stages of Cognitive Development — one of Kolb's own cited influences, alongside Dewey and Lewin

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Experiential Learning — the wiki's design-facing principle page for applying this theory: requirements, constraints, and worked classroom examples (field courses, role play, a step-by-step lesson-integration recipe) live there rather than here, mirroring how Constructivism and its companion principle page are split

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The expertise reversal effect is the idea that instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as learner expertise increases.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory
  • Information Processing Theory

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
First Principles of Instruction (Merrill, 2002, 2013) is M. David Merrill's answer to the question "what makes instruction effective, efficient, and engaging?" Reviewing a wide range of existing instructional design theories and models, Merrill argued that despite differing vocabularies and areas of emphasis, they converge on a small common set of principles. He deliberately avoided the term "presentation" in favor of "demonstration," on the grounds that showing (not just telling) is what most instruction is missing.

The five principles:

  • Activation — learning is promoted when learners activate a relevant mental model of prior knowledge or experience as a foundation for new skills.
  • Demonstration — learning is promoted when learners observe a demonstration of the skill to be learned (Tell–Show), not merely a presentation of information.
  • Application — learning is promoted when learners apply their newly acquired knowledge or skill (Tell–Show–Do), consistent with the type of content being taught, rather than only being asked to remember it.
  • Integration — learning is promoted when learners integrate new knowledge into their existing mental models by reflecting on, discussing, and defending their work through peer collaboration and critique.
  • Problem-centered — learning is promoted when learners are engaged in solving a progression of whole, real-world problems or tasks, rather than only assembling isolated topics at the end of a course.

Merrill frames instruction as a progression of four learning-event types: Tell (present information), Ask (have learners recall it), Show (demonstrate the skill with examples), and Do (have learners apply it — first by identifying correct instances, then by executing the skill themselves). A Tell-only or Tell–Ask sequence is the weakest strategy; adding Show produces a Tell–Show sequence; adding Do produces the more effective Tell–Show–Do sequence. Merrill considered motivation an outcome of effective, engaging instruction rather than a precondition to design for directly: "the greatest motivation comes when people learn."

The problem-centered principle further restructures the typical topic-by-topic sequence (teach each topic in isolation, then apply everything in a final project) into one where a whole instance of the target problem is demonstrated first, component skills are taught and shown as they are needed to solve successive instances of the problem, and guidance is gradually withdrawn until learners can solve a new instance independently.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A task or skill that can be organized around whole, realistic problem instances rather than only isolated topics
  • Ability to sequence instruction so demonstration and application happen close to when each component skill is introduced, not only in a final capstone project

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Adds the most value where existing instruction relies mainly on Tell–Ask (information plus recall testing); where demonstration and application are already present, the added benefit is smaller
  • Requires more up-front design effort to build a progression of realistic problem instances than a topic-by-topic outline does

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners acquiring problem-solving or complex-task skills, from novice to intermediate
  • Applies across settings — corporate training, K-12, higher education, MOOCs

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Applying knowledge or skill to solve real problems or complete real tasks, as opposed to recalling information
  • Transfer of component skills to novel instances of a problem

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Presented as a synthesis of convergent principles across many named instructional design theories and models (Merrill, 2002), rather than a wholly new theory

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Cognitive Apprenticeship + shares the modeling → coaching → fading structure with the demonstration and application principles
  • ARCS Model of Motivational Design ~ both are integrative, practitioner-facing syntheses, but Merrill treats motivation as an outcome of effective instruction rather than ARCS's separately diagnosable, designable condition
  • Cognitive Load Theory ~ whole-task, problem-centered sequencing must still be paced to avoid overwhelming novices' working memory
  • Constructivism + shares an emphasis on authentic, whole tasks and learner integration of new knowledge into existing mental models

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Problem-based Learning
  • Demonstration
  • Practice
  • Worked Examples

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Interest, distinct from effort, is a source of intrinsic motivation: when students learn from interest rather than pure effort, they devote more attention to the topic and tend to use more thoughtful learning strategies (Hidi & Renninger, 2006; Hidi, 2001). The distinction between interest and effort is often artificial in practice — the two commonly blend, as when a student works hard at a skill they also genuinely enjoy — but the useful instructional target is to draw on interest as much as possible so that required effort stays within a reasonable, sustainable range.

Interest itself splits into two kinds. Situational interest is triggered temporarily by features of the immediate environment — an unusual image, a brief piece of music, a surprising comment or fact. Personal interest is a relatively permanent, cross-situational preference (a subject, activity, or even a person) that a student carries with them, and that can conflict with, rather than support, academic engagement (e.g., preferring to be at the mall with a friend over studying a favorite subject at home). Personal interest in a topic generally correlates with achievement in it, though the causal direction runs both ways — interest plausibly drives learning (elementary students learned more from self-chosen books than from assigned ones on the same topic; Reynolds & Symons, 2001) and learning plausibly deepens interest in turn, so the two likely reinforce each other rather than one simply causing the other.

Hidi and Renninger (2006) describe how situational interest can, under the right conditions, develop into stable personal interest through four phases:

  1. Triggered situational interest — sparked by novel, incongruous, or surprising environmental features; provokes attention and arousal only in the short term (e.g., a counter-intuitive fact, a science demonstration with an unexpected result) (Guthrie, Wigfield, & Humenick, 2006).
  2. Maintained situational interest — sustained focus over a longer period, once the learner perceives the task's meaningfulness or a personal connection to it (e.g., connecting the physics of projectile motion to a sport the student already plays). Only interest that reaches this second phase can go on to develop into individual interest.
  3. Emerging individual interest — the learner begins to reengage with the material on their own initiative, generating their own curiosity-driven questions with less external support, alongside positive feelings about the topic; encouraging active response (e.g., peer discussion) can help students form these connections themselves.
  4. Well-developed individual interest — a deep-seated, durable tendency to engage with the topic, accompanied by positive feelings, sustained over an extended period.

The model is widely cited but only partially validated: it has received limited direct empirical testing, and — its clearest limitation — it does not specify a psychological mechanism explaining how a learner moves from one phase to the next.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Some initial environmental hook (novelty, surprise, incongruity) capable of triggering Phase 1 situational interest in students who lack prior personal interest in a topic
  • A believable route from the material to a personal connection or perceived meaningfulness, needed to move interest from Phase 1 (triggered) to Phase 2 (maintained) — without it, situational interest stays transient and never develops further

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The model does not specify the mechanism of transition between phases, so it functions more as a descriptive stage map than a prescriptive design algorithm
  • Stimulating features added to arouse interest can misfire into distraction if they don't genuinely connect to the material — see Seductive details can distract from learning [-M]
  • Students already struggling academically are more prone to distraction from poorly-integrated "interesting" additions than students who are already learning successfully (Sanchez & Wiley, 2006)

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners with little or no prior personal interest in a topic, where the instructional task is to spark and then sustain situational interest in hopes it develops further
  • Learners already showing early (Phase 3) engagement, where the goal shifts to supporting self-generated curiosity rather than externally driving attention

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained, self-initiated engagement with a topic beyond the immediate lesson
  • Development of durable personal interest that outlasts a single unit or course

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • ARCS Model of Motivational Design [+M] — Keller's perceptual arousal and inquiry arousal attention tactics map closely onto this model's triggered and maintained situational interest phases, respectively

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Seductive details can distract from learning [-M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• ARCS Model of Motivational Design — Keller's Attention category operationalizes the triggering and maintaining of situational interest as design tactics
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — intrinsic value in the value taxonomy overlaps with personal interest as this model defines it
  • Self-Determination Theory — both treat intrinsically-driven engagement as qualitatively different from, and generally more durable than, externally-driven effort

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:

  • Hidi, S., & Renninger, K. A. (2006). The four-phase model of interest development. Educational Psychologist, 41(2), 111-127.
  • Reynolds, R. E., & Symons, S. (2001). Text relevance and learning from text. In R. K. Sawyer (Ed.), Handbook of the learning sciences. Cambridge University Press.
