  • Sanchez, C. A., & Wiley, J. (2006). An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity. Memory & Cognition, 34(2), 344-355.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Interest as motivation. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Fuller's Concerns Theory of Teacher Development
Description
docs.text:
Fuller (1969) grew concerns theory out of analysis of recorded interview transcripts with student teachers, tracking what problems and concerns they expressed at different points in their training. The theory conceptualizes a prospective teacher's development as a natural flow from concerns for self (teacher), to task (teaching), to impact (pupil).

The survival stage is marked by concerns centered on the teacher's own well-being rather than the teaching task or the learners: will my students like me, will they listen, what will parents and the principal think of me, will I ever have time to myself (Borich, 1993; Burden, 1986; Fuller, 1969; Ryan, 1992). Bullough (1989) described it as "the fight for one's professional life" (p. 16).

The task stage (also called the mastery stage, consolidation and exploration, or trial and error by other authors) begins once survival and self-concerns start to diminish — there is no precise moment this happens, only a gradual shift. Concerns turn to how best to deliver instruction: are my materials good enough, will I have time to cover the content, how can I add variety, what's the best way to teach a given skill.

The impact stage is characterized by concerns about the effect of teaching on learners rather than management or lesson delivery: how can I increase learners' feelings of accomplishment, how do I meet their social and emotional needs, how do I challenge unmotivated learners, what do they need for the next grade.

Fuller found that during the early, middle, and late phases of student teaching, preservice teachers' concerns shifted in exactly this order — self, then task, then impact — representing a developmental growth pattern that can extend over months or years of a career, with the most effective and experienced teachers expressing student-centered (impact) concerns at a high level of commitment. The progression is not strictly one-directional, however: a teacher can return to an earlier stage of concern (for example, from concern for pupils back to concern for task) as a result of being assigned a new grade or subject, or moving to an unfamiliar school — concerns can be context-dependent as well as developmental, and the three stages are not mutually exclusive at any given time, only differing in relative intensity.

Shulman (1992) identifies four types of knowledge important to this progression: practical knowledge (from field experience and student teaching itself), case knowledge (from reading what successful and unsuccessful teachers have done), theoretical knowledge (from conceptual systems and paradigms for thinking about teaching), and empirical knowledge (from research on a subject and how to teach it). Educational psychology as a discipline focuses primarily on the latter two.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Recognition, in teacher preparation and induction programs, that self-focused concerns in a new teacher's first year are a normal developmental stage rather than a sign of inadequate commitment to students

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A new placement (different grade, subject, or school) can push an experienced teacher's concerns back toward task or even survival, so concern level is not a fixed trait of the individual teacher [~M]
  • The three stages overlap in practice — a teacher can hold impact-level concerns predominantly while still carrying lower-intensity task or self concerns

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Preservice and early-career teachers, whose predominant concerns can be expected to be self- and task-focused rather than a personal shortcoming
  • Teacher educators and mentors designing support that matches the concerns a teacher is actually likely to have at a given career stage

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Progression from self- and task-focused concerns toward sustained, high-commitment concern for student impact

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Educational Psychology as Both Art and Science — the practical/theoretical/empirical knowledge split Shulman describes is one way of cashing out the art-science relationship for teacher preparation specifically

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A mentoring program that expects a first-year teacher's questions to center on classroom control and time management rather than individual student growth, and treats that as developmentally normal rather than a deficiency

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Fuller, F. F. (1969). Concerns of teachers: A developmental conceptualization. American Educational Research Journal, 6, 207–226.
  • Bullough, R. V. (1989). First-year teacher: A case study. Teachers College Press.
  • Borich, G. (1993). Clearly outstanding: Making each day count in your classroom. Allyn & Bacon.
  • Burden, P. R. (1986). Teachers' perceptions of the characteristics and influences on their personal and professional development. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the Association of Teacher Educators.
  • Ryan, K. (1992). The roller coaster year: Essays by and for beginning teachers. HarperCollins.
  • Shulman, L. S. (1992). Toward a pedagogy of substance. AAHE Bulletin, 44, 3–7.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teacher development. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Carol Gilligan, a former student of Kohlberg's, argued that his Stages of Moral Development were built on all-male original samples and, in centering abstract justice, undervalued an equally legitimate moral orientation: an ethic of care — a system of beliefs about responsibility, interdependence, and responsiveness to the needs of others. Gilligan proposed this morality of care not as a replacement for justice reasoning but as a complementary orientation; a fully developed moral reasoner draws on both. Subsequent research has generally found no consistent gender difference in which orientation people use, which tempers Gilligan's original hypothesis that care reasoning was distinctly more common among women — but the justice-versus-care framing itself has remained a live and useful distinction in moral education independent of that empirical question.

Rather than Kohlberg's strict sequential stages, Gilligan organized care reasoning into three positions, ranked by depth and sophistication but not treated as a rigid, universal sequence everyone must pass through in order:

  1. Caring as survival — a person is primarily concerned with their own welfare; "morally good" means minimizing stress or harm to oneself. This is not simply immature selfishness — for a child in an abusive or otherwise threatening situation, prioritizing one's own safety is the healthy, appropriate response, even though it would not sustain a workable classroom norm as a general orientation.
  2. Conventional caring — a person is concerned with others' happiness and welfare, and works to reconcile the sometimes-conflicting needs of multiple people; "morally good" means pleasing others. This can produce desirable traits — cooperativeness, eagerness to please — but if it is the only orientation a learner is encouraged toward, it risks neglecting the learner's own development, goals, and identity, and can undermine autonomy.
  3. Integrated caring — a person coordinates their own needs and values with those of others; "morally good" accounts for everyone, including oneself. This is the most sophisticated and cognitively demanding position, and typically requires sustained opportunities to make real choices with real consequences to develop.

Gilligan's framework surfaces classroom dilemmas that a pure justice lens can obscure. A justice orientation asks "What is fair?" (e.g., should every student get equal time reading aloud?); a care orientation asks "What does this student, specifically, need right now?" Neither question alone is sufficient — a teacher who only asks about fairness may miss individual need, while one who only asks about care may produce inconsistency that itself feels unfair to other students.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Care reasoning develops through opportunities to actually reconcile competing needs — being told the "right" answer to a dilemma does not substitute for practicing the reconciliation itself
  • Long-term, open-ended tasks that require balancing one's own goals against a group's needs (e.g., a self-directed inquiry project with a collaborative component) are well suited to activating and developing Position 3 (integrated caring); highly structured, single-right-answer tasks give less room for it to develop
  • A teacher's own orientation matters: consistently emphasizing pleasing others (Position 2) as the classroom ideal can inadvertently discourage the more mature integration of self and others (Position 3)

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• K–12 learners across the developmental span; unlike Kohlberg's and Piaget's stage models, positions are not tightly age-bound
  • Not gender-specific — despite the theory's origin as a critique of gender bias in Kohlberg's sampling, later research does not support a consistent gender difference in which orientation people default to

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Balancing personal needs and values against the needs of others, rather than treating either as automatically overriding
  • Recognizing that "fairness" (justice) and "responsiveness to need" (care) are both legitimate, sometimes competing, considerations in a moral decision

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development — Gilligan's framework is a direct response to and complement of Kohlberg's justice-centered stage theory
  • Turiel's Social Domain Theory — both frameworks push back on treating moral reasoning as a single, unified developmental ladder
  • Self-Determination Theory — the autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs SDT identifies parallel the self/other balance Gilligan's Position 3 describes

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Brown, L., & Gilligan, C. (1992). Meeting at the crossroads: Women's psychology and girls' development. Harvard University Press.
  • Taylor, J., Gilligan, C., & Sullivan, A. (1995). Between voice and silence: Women and girls, race and relationship. Harvard University Press.
  • Kohlberg, L., Levine, C., & Hewer, A. (1983). Moral stages: A current formulation and a response to critics. S. Karger.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Moral development. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Ginott's (1972) communication skills approach — one of the two humanist traditions in classroom management, alongside Glasser's Choice Theory — rests on a cardinal principle: learners can control their own behavior if teachers allow them to. Teachers foster this self-control by letting students choose how they wish to change their own behavior and how the class will be run, and by helping students express their inner thoughts and feelings through effective communication. In this tradition, communication skills are the primary vehicle for influencing students' self-esteem, which in turn is the primary force underlying acceptable behavior — congruent communication is what promotes that self-esteem.

Teachers communicate congruently, typically during private conferences with a misbehaving student (though it can also happen during whole-class problem-solving), through several specific practices:

  • Express "sane" messages — messages that communicate a behavior is unacceptable without blaming, scolding, preaching, accusing, demanding, threatening, or humiliating, describing what should be done rather than scolding what was done. Example: "Rosalyn, we are all supposed to be in our seats before the bell rings," not "Rosalyn, you're always gossiping at the doorway and coming late to class."
  • Accept rather than deny feelings — accepting a student's feelings about their circumstances rather than arguing about them. If a student says "I have no friends," the teacher accepts and identifies with the feeling of isolation ("So, you're feeling that you don't belong to any group") rather than trying to convince the student they've misperceived the situation.
  • Avoid using labels — avoiding terms like "lazy," "sloppy," or "bad attitude" (and equally, "dedicated," "intelligent," or "perfectionist"), instead describing what the teacher likes or doesn't like about specific things a student does: "You have a lot of erasures and whiteouts on your homework," not "Your homework is sloppy"; "You form your letters correctly," not "You are a good writer."
  • Use praise cautiously — Ginott holds that many teachers use praise excessively and manipulatively to control behavior rather than to acknowledge genuinely exceptional performance: praising judgmentally ("Horace, you are a good student"), confusing correctness with goodness (calling a student who makes few mistakes a "good child"), praising minimally acceptable behavior as a way of influencing other students ("I like the way Joan is sitting in her seat"), or praising so often the statements lose all significance. Ginott urges reserving praise for exceptional performance and phrasing it to separate the deed from the doer — "That essay showed a great deal of original thought and research," not a judgment of the student as a person.
  • Elicit cooperation — once a behavioral concern is identified, offering the student alternatives for solving the problem rather than telling them what to do. Ginott's maxim: "Cooperate, don't legislate."
  • Communicate anger through "I-messages," not "you-messages" — teachers get frustrated too, and Ginott holds they should express that through "I-messages" that focus on the teacher's own feelings about the behavior ("You talked when the guest speaker was lecturing, and I feel very unhappy and embarrassed by that") rather than "you-messages" that accuse and blame ("You were rude to the guest speaker"). I-messages are for use when the teacher owns the problem — is the one who is angry or upset — a distinction Gordon's Teacher Effectiveness Training develops further as "problem ownership."

Applied concretely: taking over a disruptive class, Ginott's approach would have the teacher hold an open discussion drawing students' attention to the problem, invite their cooperation in developing mutually agreed-upon rules and consequences, and then hold individual conferences using congruent communication as further problems arise.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Congruent communication is primarily deployed in one-on-one private conferences with a student who has misbehaved, though whole-class problem-solving discussions use the same techniques
  • Depends on a teacher's willingness to describe specific behaviors rather than judge character, and to name their own feelings rather than assign blame

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students whose misbehavior is driven at least partly by low self-esteem or unmet needs to be heard and understood, rather than by a need for firm external structure alone

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Development of student self-control and self-esteem as the route to acceptable classroom behavior, rather than compliance driven by external reward or punishment

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Glasser's Choice Theory and Cooperative Learning — the other half of the humanist tradition; Glasser and Ginott "represent two sides of the same coin"
  • Kounin's Classroom Management Research — the prevention-oriented tradition that developed partly in response to the largely reactive humanist and behavior-analysis traditions
  • Teaching Styles as Warmth and Control — congruent communication is one concrete way of building the warm side of an authoritative teaching style

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Teacher Effectiveness Training / Conflict Resolution — Gordon's later "problem ownership" and "I-message" framework builds directly on the same communication-skills tradition

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:
• Ginott, H. G. (1972). Teacher and child: A book for parents and teachers. Macmillan.
  • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Systems of classroom management. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Glasser's Choice Theory and Cooperative Learning
Description
docs.text:
Glasser's (1990) cooperation-through-problem-solving approach — also called reality therapy — is the other half of the humanist tradition in classroom management, alongside Ginott's Congruent Communication; Glasser and Ginott "represent two sides of the same coin." Glasser holds that effective classroom managers create a learning environment students want to be in, develop mutually agreed-upon standards of behavior that must be followed to remain in that environment, and hold problem-solving conferences with students who violate those standards.

Glasser advocates cooperative learning as the specific instructional approach that makes a classroom a place students want to be. In his view, whole-group instruction — where students compete with one another for limited rewards — inevitably leaves roughly half the class bored, frustrated, inattentive, or disruptive. Faced with the resulting misbehavior, Glasser argues, teachers commonly fall back on boss management: using reward and coercive power to manipulate and control learners. Boss management jeopardizes the development of self-control, teaches students to value external reward over the satisfaction of doing good work, and produces disruption, frustration, and inattentiveness once those rewards fail to materialize. Glasser (1990) contrasts boss management with lead management directly:

Boss Leader Drives Leads Relies on authority Relies on cooperation Says "I" Says "We" Creates fear Creates confidence Knows how Shows how Creates resentment Breeds enthusiasm Fixes blame Fixes mistakes Makes work drudgery Makes work interesting

For Glasser, dealing with a disruptive student is straightforward once students already experience belonging, power, and freedom in the classroom — in other words, once it is genuinely a classroom the student would regret leaving. When a student persists in violating rules the group considers essential, the teacher holds a brief private conference reviewing the rules, describing the disruptive behavior, asserting the need to follow the rules, and making clear the consequence for continued noncompliance (for example, removal from the room until the student chooses to follow the rules). Glasser cautions teachers not to accept excuses — including socioeconomic or sociocultural excuses — for a student's inability to control their own behavior, on the premise that there is no excuse for disrupting an environment genuinely designed to meet learners' needs: "students will soon discover that you have given them every chance. If they want to stay in class, they have no choice but to follow the rules... And if your students are satisfied most of the time, they'll want to stay" (Glasser, 1990, p. 142) — students choose to behave, rather than needing to be forced to.

Applied concretely, Glasser's specific recommendations for taking over a disruptive class are to (1) develop workplace rules together with students, (2) get administrator support for an area to which disruptive students can be removed, (3) hold private conferences with disruptive students that stress correct choices and accept no excuses for wrong ones, and (4) follow through consistently when students must be removed, while always allowing them to return once they choose to obey the rules.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Depends on genuinely making the classroom rewarding enough that removal from it functions as a real, felt consequence — the approach does not work in a classroom students are indifferent to leaving
  • Requires administrative support for a removal space, and consistent follow-through on both removal and readmission

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Students who are bored, frustrated, or disruptive specifically because whole-group competitive instruction leaves them without a rewarding role in the classroom

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Sustained engagement and self-chosen good behavior, driven by wanting to remain in a valued environment rather than by fear of a boss-managed authority

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Boss management's reliance on reward and coercive power to control students parallels the risk documented under the overjustification effect [-M] and under the authoritarian profile in Teaching Styles as Warmth and Control

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Ginott's Congruent Communication — the other humanist-tradition approach; Glasser's private-conference protocol draws on similar communication-skills groundwork
  • Social Interdependence [+M] — the direct theoretical grounding for why cooperative learning succeeds where competitive whole-group instruction produces disengagement
  • Kounin's Classroom Management Research — the prevention-oriented tradition that, unlike Glasser's largely reactive problem-solving conferences, focuses on what effective managers do before misbehavior occurs

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Cooperative Learning — the concrete instructional strategy Glasser recommends as an alternative to competitive whole-group instruction
  • Low-Profile Classroom Control — cites Glasser's point that an effective consequence for rule-breaking is temporary removal from the classroom, provided the classroom is somewhere the student wants to be

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Goal setting is itself a key motivational process (Locke & Latham, 1984, 2006) — the goals learners choose, and how committed they are to attaining them, shape motivation to learn (Wentzel, 2000). But beyond goal content (what a learner wants to achieve), goal orientation theory argues that the reason a learner pursues a goal has its own independent effect on learning and performance, explaining differences in how individuals approach and respond to achievement situations (Ames & Archer, 1988; Meece, Anderman, & Anderman, 2006).

The two most basic goal orientations are mastery goals (a focus on mastering new skills, gaining understanding, and improving competence, defining success as improvement and learning) and performance goals (a focus on doing better than others and demonstrating competence via social comparison, seeking favorable judgment) (Ames & Archer, 1988; Dweck & Leggett, 1988). The same distinction appears under other names in the literature: learning vs. performance goals (Elliot & Dweck, 1988), task-involved vs. ego-involved goals (Nicholls, 1984), and task-focused vs. ability-focused goals (Maehr & Midgley, 1991).

Both categories further split along an approach/avoidance dimension (Elliot & Church, 1997; Elliot & Harackiewicz, 1996; Elliot & McGregor, 2001), producing a 2×2 model:

Approach focus Avoidance focus Mastery Improve knowledge/skills; errors are learning opportunities; judge performance against self-improvement standards Avoid misunderstanding or failing to master the task; errors indicate failure; judge performance against a "not being wrong" standard Performance Outperform others, demonstrate superiority; judge performance against normative "being the best" standards Avoid negative judgment or appearing inferior; errors indicate failure; judge performance against a "not being the worst" standard

Mastery-avoidance is the least-studied and most contested of the four cells — despite confirmatory factor-analytic support for the full 2×2 structure (Elliot & McGregor, 2001), it remains the least accepted construct in the field, illustrated by cases like an athlete anxious specifically about falling short of their own past performance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • An achievement context where a learner's implicit reason for pursuing a goal (mastery vs. demonstrating/protecting standing) can plausibly be shaped by classroom structure, framing, and feedback

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Goal orientations rarely occur in pure form; a single learner typically holds a blend (e.g., enjoying an activity for its own sake while also wanting to look skilled to peers and fearing embarrassment), so intervention should shift the balance among orientations rather than assume a learner has exactly one
  • Some degree of performance orientation is likely inevitable simply from the presence of classmates and social comparison, and cannot be fully eliminated by design
  • Mastery-avoidance remains a contested, under-validated construct; treat claims specific to that cell with more caution than the other three

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Any learner in an evaluated, socially comparative setting, since goal orientation concerns the reason behind engagement rather than a fixed trait tied to one population
  • Learners showing signs of failure-avoidant self-handicapping (procrastination, deliberate under-effort, unrealistically high goals) — a byproduct of excessive performance-goal emphasis (Urdan, 2004) worth diagnosing and addressing directly

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Deep, thoughtful processing and durable, transferable learning (favored by mastery-approach orientation)
  • Short-term performance metrics like grades and test scores (favored, though sometimes at the expense of deep learning, by performance orientations)
  • Reduced anxiety and self-handicapping behavior (favored by avoiding performance-avoidance and failure-avoidant orientations)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Elliot & McGregor's (2001) confirmatory factor analyses support treating the 2×2 mastery/performance × approach/avoidance grid as measuring four genuinely distinct orientations, not just two

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• The mastery-avoidance cell remains the field's least accepted construct, weakening the 2×2 model's claim to being fully validated

Empirically, the four orientations diverge sharply in outcome. Mastery-approach goals are consistently associated with high effort, task interest, and use of deep learning strategies (Greene, Miller, Crowson, Duke, & Akey, 2004; Harackiewicz, Barron, Pintrich, Elliot, & Thrash, 2002; Wolters, 2004), and — because they are a form of intrinsic motivation — sustain interest in a subject well beyond a course's official end, predicting further enrollment in the same subject area. Performance-avoidance goals are consistently linked to poor persistence, high anxiety, superficial strategy use, and low achievement (Linnenbrink, 2005; Urdan, 2004; Wolters, 2003, 2004) — the most reliably detrimental of the four. Performance-approach goals show genuinely mixed results: some studies find modest positive links to achievement (Linnenbrink-Garcia, Tyson, & Patall, 2008), others find maladaptive outcomes like poor strategy use and test anxiety (Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Keys, Conley, Duncan, & Domina, 2012; Middleton & Midgley, 1997) — taken together, performance-approach students tend to achieve well but at the cost of negative emotionality such as test anxiety, and though they often get higher grades than mastery-oriented peers (both short-term and cumulatively), they tend not to learn the material as deeply or durably (Midgley, Kaplan, & Middleton, 2001), plausibly because performance metrics reward shallow memorization and because the competitive framing of performance goals discourages the peer help-seeking and help-giving that supports deeper learning. Mastery-avoidance goals are the least-studied orientation, but existing evidence links them to increased anxiety and reduced performance (Howell & Watson, 2007; Hulleman, Schrager, Bodmann, & Harackiewicz, 2010).

Two further goal categories affect achievement indirectly rather than being achievement goals themselves. Failure-avoidant goals are often a negative byproduct of performance-goal competitiveness (Urdan, 2004): when success feels unattainable or interest in the material itself has been crowded out, a student may shift to simply avoiding failure, deliberately underachieving via self-handicapping (procrastination, minimal effort, unrealistically high goals chosen specifically to make failure unsurprising rather than shameful). Social goals — most students value relationships with teachers and peers — cut both ways: a positive teacher relationship tends to motivate hard work, though this effect is closer to performance than mastery motivation since the student is primarily concerned with pleasing someone else (Dowson & McInerney, 2003); peer relationships help achievement when the underlying motive is genuine closeness (leading to mutual help-seeking and help-giving) but can hurt it when the motive is impressing peers, which reintroduces performance-goal competitiveness and discourages collaboration. Peer effects are also context-dependent: low peer achievement/motivation affects an individual's motivation more in elementary than high school, more in math than reading, and more in classrooms with a wide ability range than a narrow one (Burke & Sass, 2006). Structured cooperative or community-connected activities (Butin, 2005) can help realize the positive side of social goals while limiting the competitive downside.

Because mastery-approach goals reliably support the more sustained, thoughtful learning teachers usually want (Darnon, Butera, & Harackiewicz, 2006), several concrete tactics can shift the classroom balance toward it: offering students choice over specific tasks where feasible, since self-chosen work more often connects to genuine prior interest; explicitly pointing out connections between current material and students' existing interests when those connections aren't obvious on their own (e.g., linking a music-loving student's interest to acoustics in physics, hearing physiology in biology, or stylistic change over time in history); focusing feedback and structure on individual improvement rather than social comparison; and arranging collaboration rather than competition on shared tasks.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Expectancy-Value Theory — task value and goal orientation both address why a learner engages, though EVT frames it as a value judgment while goal orientation frames it as the purpose behind pursuing a goal
  • Self-Determination Theory — mastery goals are intrinsically motivated in SDT's sense, while performance goals are extrinsically motivated; both theories treat this distinction as consequential for depth of learning
  • Student Orientation Toward Achievement — Covington's self-worth-protection typology (success-oriented, overstriving, failure-avoiding, failure-accepting) describes a closely parallel set of learner profiles organized around approaching success versus avoiding failure
  • Attribution Theory — a mastery orientation's tolerance for errors as learning opportunities parallels attribution theory's preference for controllable, unstable failure attributions over stable, uncontrollable ones

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
For Idealists, ideas are the only true reality; conscious reasoning is the only way to locate what is true, beautiful, and just. Plato founded Idealism and outlined its tenets in The Republic. For Plato there are two worlds: a spiritual or mental world where universal ideas and truth are permanent, reachable only through conscious reasoning, and a world of appearances and imperfection experienced through the senses. Plato dramatizes this duality in the Allegory of the Cave — people chained facing a wall mistake shadows cast by a fire for reality; only by breaking free and reaching the world outside does one discover the true source of everything previously known, the realm of pure fact and form. The everyday world is only an imperfect projection of that realm of ideas.

Roughly two centuries later, René Descartes shifted Platonic Idealism toward mind-body dualism with "Cogito, ergo sum" (I think, therefore I am) — for Descartes the only proof of his own existence is his thinking, and only rational deduction, not unreliable sense perception, could reach truth. Where Plato posited two separate worlds, Descartes grounded Idealism in a dualism privileging the thinking mind over the physical body and external world — an influence that shaped educational philosophy well into the 20th century.

For Idealists, teaching focuses on moral excellence that benefits society. Students focus on subjects of the mind — literature, history, philosophy — and demonstrate understanding through participation in lectures and Socratic dialogues meant to engage introspection and bring universal forms and concepts to consciousness.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: • An idealist classroom is organized around lecture and Socratic dialogue rather than hands-on or applied tasks, since the goal is conscious reasoning toward universal truths rather than skill in manipulating the physical world

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in curricula weighted toward the humanities (literature, history, philosophy) rather than applied or vocational subjects

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Moral excellence and insight into universal, unchanging truths, reached through introspection and reasoned dialogue rather than direct experience

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Realism (Educational Philosophy) — Aristotle's antithetical ontology, formed in direct reply to his teacher Plato's Idealism
  • Pragmatism and Progressivism (Educational Philosophy) — a later tradition explicitly rejecting both Idealism's and Realism's assumption of a fixed, unchanging reality

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Socratic Seminar — the idealist teaching method of dialogue aimed at bringing understanding to consciousness through structured questioning

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Information Processing Theory treats learning as the movement and transformation of information through attention, working memory, encoding, storage, and retrieval. In broad terms, the theory asks what learners notice, how much they can actively process at once, how they organize new information, and how it becomes retrievable later.

This theory family is especially useful for instructional design because it highlights bottlenecks: limited working-memory capacity, the need for organization, the role of prior knowledge in encoding, and the importance of retrieval and feedback. Many common design moves such as chunking, worked examples, sequencing, and review are partly justified in information-processing terms.

Attention is the entry point to the whole system, and it develops substantially across childhood and adolescence. Selective attention — filtering out irrelevant input to focus on what matters — improves sharply from around age 6 into adolescence; young children (ages 4–7) are markedly worse than teens or adults at filtering background noise specifically (Jones, Moore, & Amitay, 2015). Sustained attention grows roughly linearly with age in early-to-middle childhood (a rough rule of thumb: a 5-year-old sustains attention for about 5 minutes, gaining roughly a minute per year of age up to about 10, then plateauing around 10–20 minutes through the teen years and adulthood; Raichle, 1999). Divided attention (multitasking) also has a clear developmental trajectory — 3-to-4-year-olds perform on some divided-attention tasks at roughly the level of chimpanzees, 5-year-olds already surpass this, and capacity continues improving into adolescence (Hermann, Misch, Hernandez-Lloreda, & Tomasello, 2015) — but divided attention has real limits at any age: automaticity, task complexity, anxiety, and arousal all affect how much can genuinely be attended to at once, and the well-documented degradation of driving performance under simultaneous phone use (Strayer & Drews, 2007) illustrates that "multitasking" is often really rapid task-switching with a real performance cost, not true parallel processing.

Sensory memory is the system's entry point, holding roughly four items very briefly — visual (iconic) memory lasts roughly half a second, auditory (echoic) memory a few seconds longer (touch and smell/taste registers are much less understood) — and this duration does not appear to change developmentally from infancy onward (Siegler, 1998). Information sensory memory doesn't capture, or that isn't attended to and encoded further, is lost to decay. The classic Stroop effect (interference in naming the ink color of a color word when the word and ink color mismatch, e.g., the word "red" printed in blue ink) illustrates how automatic, overlearned processing (reading) can compete with attention for a different, task-relevant feature.

Working memory capacity itself develops with age: a 5-year-old can typically hold about 4 digits in mind, versus about 7 for an older teen or adult (a developmental gradient consistent with, though distinct from, Miller's cross-sectional 7±2 estimate below), with the growth partly explained by underlying myelination and synaptic pruning that increases processing speed and the ability to filter irrelevant information (Kail, McBride-Chang, Ferrer, Cho, & Shu, 2013). Without active rehearsal, working memory contents fade within roughly 20–30 seconds. Young children rely on simple rote rehearsal (repeating items) rather than clustering (grouping items meaningfully before rehearsing), and don't spontaneously adopt clustering until later in childhood; one longitudinal study found a majority of kindergarteners used no deliberate memory strategy at all (Schneider, Kron-Sperl, & Hunnerkopf, 2009). Working-memory limitations have direct instructional consequences: children with weaker working memory are more likely to struggle in math and reading and to lose track of multi-step directions (Alloway, 2009; Prebler, Krajewski, & Hasselhorn, 2013) — supportable through familiar vocabulary, shorter sentences, repeated instructions, and breaking tasks into smaller steps — and intensive training in chunking and related working-memory strategies has been shown to improve capacity in children who start out low (Alloway, Bibile, & Lau, 2013).

Encoding can be semantic (meaning-based), visual, or acoustic; Craik and Tulving's (1975) levels-of-processing finding is that semantic encoding — connecting new information to existing meaning — produces the strongest recall of the three, and the closely related self-reference effect (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) shows recall improves further when learners relate new material to themselves specifically. This distinction underlies a practical contrast between maintenance rehearsal (simply repeating information to keep it active in working memory, which the evidence base treats as inefficient for long-term retention on its own) and elaboration (actively relating new information to existing knowledge), which is what actually moves information into long-term memory. Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) working-memory model offers a more differentiated alternative to Atkinson and Shiffrin's original single short-term store, splitting working memory into a central executive, a phonological loop (verbal/acoustic information), a visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial information), and an episodic buffer (integrating information across the other components) — a structure consistent with Miller's (1956) classic finding that working memory holds roughly 7±2 discrete chunks at once. Information in working memory that isn't consolidated is vulnerable to interference rather than simple decay.

Long-term memory is commonly split into explicit (declarative — semantic and episodic) and implicit (procedural) memory, with three modes of retrieval: recall, recognition, and relearning. A more fine-grained taxonomy adds imagery knowledge (mental representations of sensory experience), strategic knowledge (knowing which strategy to apply and when), and conceptual knowledge (organized relationships among ideas) alongside declarative, procedural, and episodic knowledge. Long-term forgetting is generally attributed to retrieval failure — losing the pathway to stored information — rather than true loss of the information itself, distinguishing it from the decay (sensory memory) and interference (working memory) mechanisms above.

Paivio's (1986) dual coding hypothesis — that information stored as both an image and a verbal label is better retained than information stored in only one format — is closely related and is covered in its own page, Dual Coding Theory.

Autobiographical memory — the ability to recall specific, personally-experienced past events — develops notably late. Most people show infantile amnesia: an inability to recall events from roughly the first three years of life, even though other kinds of learning (skills, some semantic knowledge) from that period persist. Coherent autobiographical memory develops gradually through early-to-middle childhood, aided by brain maturation, growing language ability, adult-child conversation about shared experiences, developing theory of mind, and an emerging sense of self as a continuous entity across time (Nelson & Fivush, 2004).

Two closely related but distinct topics — executive function (the self-regulatory processes that control and coordinate attention, memory, and behavior toward a goal) and metacognition (knowledge about, and regulation of, one's own thinking, including a learner's developing understanding of their own memory, or metamemory — and the production deficiency/utilization deficiency gap between having a strategy and actually benefiting from it) — are substantial enough to warrant their own pages; see Executive Function Development and Metacognition.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text: Information processing models are often criticized as overly linear and serial, in tension with evidence that some processing is parallel rather than strictly sequential. The model's rehearsal-dependent account of encoding struggles to explain single-exposure or emotionally charged (e.g., traumatic) memories, which can be strongly encoded without repetition. The computer-processing metaphor at the theory's core is imperfect and can obscure rather than illuminate certain phenomena, and the theory has little to say about the "hardware" changes underlying cognitive development itself (e.g., the emergence of abstract, formal-operational thought — see Stages of Cognitive Development), or about how environment, culture, and individual differences shape processing. It also generally does not account for the effect of emotional state on processing and recall.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Relevant whenever instruction depends on attention, working memory, schema formation, or retrieval
  • Often used to justify sequencing, chunking, modeling, review, and explicit guidance
  • Particularly useful for novice learners who have not yet organized content into efficient schemas

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners encountering unfamiliar or cognitively dense material
  • Learners who benefit from clear structure and manageable information flow
  • Novices who need help organizing steps, concepts, or representations

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Building durable schema and conceptual organization
  • Reducing overload during initial learning
  • Improving transfer from working memory to long-term memory
  • Supporting later retrieval and application

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units. [+S]
  • Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes [+M]
  • Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition. [+M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Cognitive Load Theory — CLT sharpens the working-memory constraint central to information-processing approaches
  • Self-Regulated Learning — regulation depends partly on how learners manage attention, memory, and strategy use during processing
  • Executive Function Development — the self-regulatory processes that control attention and working-memory use as they develop across childhood and adolescence
  • Metacognition — knowledge about and regulation of one's own thinking, including the strategy deficiencies that shape how children use (or fail to use) memory strategies
  • Dual Coding Theory — Paivio's hypothesis that combined visual and verbal encoding improves retention is a specific application of information-processing encoding mechanisms
  • Stages of Cognitive Development — Piaget's schema/assimilation/accommodation mechanism is a developmental precursor to the schema and encoding concepts used here

  • Pre-reading Questioning
  • Note-Taking

docs.title: Educational Implications
docs.text: Gain students' attention; ask students to recall prior relevant learning; point out important information; organize information from simple to complex; categorize related information; have students relate new information to what they already know; teach encoding techniques for memorizing lists (mnemonics, imagery); repeat and present information in multiple ways; use overlearning — practice continued beyond initial mastery — to build durable retention; make learning multi-modal by engaging more senses (e.g., physically acting out new vocabulary, video demonstrations); and avoid cognitive overload.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
These three theories represent an early, largely biological line of thinking about motivation, each superseding the last, and each still echoed in later frameworks.

Instinct theory (William James, in the earliest years of American psychology) proposed that behavior is driven by a number of species-specific, unlearned patterns — instincts — that aid survival (e.g., a mother's protection of her infant). James and his contemporaries could never agree on a definitive list of human instincts, and the theory fell out of favor once instinctive-seeming behaviors began to be experimentally demonstrated as products of associative learning instead (Faris, 1921) — an early instance of the learned/innate debate that recurs throughout the field.

Drive theory replaced instinct with a homeostatic mechanism: deviations from a biological equilibrium (e.g., low blood sugar) create a physiological need, which produces a psychological drive state (hunger) that directs behavior toward restoring balance. Whatever behavior successfully reduces the drive is reinforced and becomes habitual — drive reduction is treated as the underlying mechanism for both activity and learning (Graham & Weiner, 1996). The theory distinguishes primary drives (biologically triggered — hunger, thirst — producing directionless activity until satisfied) from acquired drives (money, love, sport, creative work — with no direct biological basis, learned through association with a primary drive). Because it explains extrinsic reinforcers (money, grades) as incentives that activate acquired drives, drive theory is the direct historical foundation of Behaviorism's account of reinforcement, and — unlike instinct theory — still has active proponents.

Arousal theory extends drive theory by treating physiological arousal itself, not just specific need states, as something the organism works to keep at an optimal level: under-arousal produces boredom and stimulation-seeking, over-arousal produces arousal-reducing behavior (Berlyne, 1960). Yerkes and Dodson's (1908) classic finding refines "optimal" further: the ideal arousal level is not a fixed midpoint but depends on task complexity — the Yerkes-Dodson law holds that simple tasks are performed best under relatively high arousal, while complex tasks are performed best under lower arousal (e.g., high test anxiety impairs performance more on a hard exam than an easy one).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A task or activity where the physiological/arousal dimension of motivation is plausible to isolate (e.g., anxiety before an assessment, restlessness after long unbroken instruction)

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Instinct theory has essentially no direct instructional application today — it is included primarily as the historical starting point that drive and arousal theories reacted against
  • These theories describe motivational mechanism, not content — they say little about why a learner values one topic over another; cognitive theories like Expectancy-Value Theory and Self-Determination Theory fill that gap
  • The Yerkes-Dodson law's practical guidance (match arousal level to task difficulty) is easier to state than to operationalize precisely, since "arousal level" is not directly observable or easily dialed by a teacher in the moment

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners facing high-stakes or high-anxiety assessment situations, where excess arousal specifically (not lack of effort or interest) may be suppressing performance on complex tasks
  • Learners in long, low-stimulation instructional stretches, where under-arousal (boredom) is the more likely motivational problem

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Maintaining an arousal level appropriate to task complexity during assessment or complex problem-solving
  • Sustaining engagement across long spans of instruction by avoiding prolonged under- or over-stimulation

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Behaviorism [+M] — drive theory's drive-reduction-through-reinforcement mechanism is a direct historical precursor to behaviorist reinforcement theory

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Instinct theory has been broadly superseded within the wiki's other motivation theories, which treat most human motives as learned or constructed rather than innate

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Behaviorism — drive theory supplies the drive-reduction mechanism that behaviorist reinforcement builds on
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — a later, cognitive account of motivation that addresses the content (why value a task) these biological theories leave unanswered
  • Self-Determination Theory — treats motivation as involving psychological, not just physiological, needs

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Lawrence Kohlberg (1927–1987), building directly on Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development, proposed that moral reasoning — not moral behavior or the specific choice a person makes — develops through three levels and six stages. Kohlberg assessed stage using the Moral Judgment Interview, a semi-structured interview (established in his 1958 dissertation) that scores the structure of a person's justification for a moral choice, not the choice itself. His signature instrument is the Heinz dilemma: a man, Heinz, cannot afford a drug that could save his dying wife; should he steal it? The "right" answer is irrelevant to scoring — a person can justify either "steal it" or "don't steal it" from any of the six stages, and it is the form of the justification that reveals the stage.

Following Piaget's constructivist requirements for a stage model, Kohlberg held the six stages to be invariant (no skipping) and essentially non-regressive. Progression occurs when a person's current stage of reasoning proves inadequate to resolve a new dilemma, pushing them toward the next stage's more differentiated notion of justice — built from the "justice operations" of equality and reciprocity, resolving toward reversibility (a rule a person could accept regardless of which party they were).

docs.title: Levels and Stages
docs.text:
• Level 1 — Preconventional (egocentric; typical of children, possible in adults)
  • Stage 1: Obedience and punishment orientation — "How can I avoid punishment?"
  • Stage 2: Self-interest orientation — "What's in it for me?"
  • Level 2 — Conventional (typical of adolescents and most adults; judges morality against society's norms)
  • Stage 3: Interpersonal accord and conformity — "good boy/good girl" reasoning
  • Stage 4: Authority and social-order-maintaining orientation — "law and order"
  • Level 3 — Postconventional / Principled (rare — many people never reach this level)
  • Stage 5: Social contract orientation — laws are changeable social contracts serving "the greatest good for the greatest number"
  • Stage 6: Universal ethical principles — Kantian, self-chosen, categorical; Kohlberg struggled to find anyone who consistently reasoned here

A transitional Stage 4½ is sometimes noted — disaffection with arbitrary law-and-order reasoning, often seen in students entering college — along with a speculative, evidentially unsupported seventh stage ("Transcendental" or "Cosmic" morality) linking religion and moral reasoning, which Kohlberg himself treated as tentative.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text: Kohlberg's theory has drawn sustained criticism. Carol Gilligan, a former student of Kohlberg's, argued the theory is androcentric — built on all-male original samples — and undervalues an "ethic of care" alongside the theory's emphasis on abstract justice; research since has generally found no consistent gender difference in moral-reasoning stage, tempering the strongest form of Gilligan's critique while keeping the justice-vs-care framing alive as a live discussion (see Gilligan's Ethic of Care for the full framework). Turiel's Social Domain Theory raises a more structural challenge: children differentiate moral, societal, and personal domains of social knowledge from early in development, meaning a person's reasoning in one domain doesn't necessarily predict their reasoning in another — in tension with the idea of a single, unified stage of moral development (see Turiel's Social Domain Theory). A cultural-bias critique notes that while the stage order replicates across cultures, the rate of progression differs; Kohlberg's own rebuttal is that stages track a mode of reasoning, not the content of any particular culture's beliefs. Social intuitionists (notably Jonathan Haidt) argue moral judgments are often made intuitively first, with "reasoning" arriving after as post-hoc justification — a challenge to the theory's core assumption that reasoning drives judgment. Directly relevant to instructional design: moral reasoning stage does not reliably predict moral behavior. Classroom cheating research (Hartshorne & May, 1928–1930; Kline, 2017; Leming, 2008) has found that whether a student cheats is largely situation-specific, regardless of the student's measured moral-development stage — a caution against assuming that raising a class's stage of moral reasoning is sufficient to change behavior.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Stages cannot be skipped, and regression is extremely rare — instruction premised on this theory should meet a learner at their current stage rather than assume higher stages can simply be taught by explanation
  • Preconventional reasoning: mainly children (also some adults); Conventional: adolescents and most adults, who tend to remain at Stage 4; Postconventional: rare — arguably a minority of adults reach Stage 5, and Stage 6 is nearly unobserved in practice

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• K–12 learners across the developmental span, since the theory is most often applied to character/moral education in schools
  • Learners in contexts where academic integrity, ethical reasoning, or civic/social responsibility are explicit goals

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Development of more differentiated, principled moral reasoning over time
  • Distinguishing moral reasoning (what a person can articulate and justify) from moral behavior (what a person actually does), since the two do not reliably track each other

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development — Kohlberg explicitly modeled his stage requirements (invariance, non-skippability) on Piaget's own constructivist stage theory
  • Piaget's Theory of Moral Development — Kohlberg built directly on Piaget's own two-phase (heteronomous/autonomous) account of moral reasoning, elaborating it into three levels and six stages
  • Gilligan's Ethic of Care — proposes a complementary care-based orientation alongside Kohlberg's justice-centered account
  • Turiel's Social Domain Theory — challenges the assumption that moral reasoning operates as a single, unified developmental ladder
  • Self-Determination Theory — classroom-management practices this theory motivates (favoring autonomy, belonging, competence, and fairness over extrinsic reward/punishment) parallel SDT's argument that extrinsic control can undermine intrinsic motivation

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Where the humanist tradition (Ginott, Glasser) and the applied-behavior-analysis tradition are both largely reactive — emphasizing solutions to misbehavior after it occurs — the classroom-management tradition begun by Kounin (1970), and continued by the Research and Development Center for Teacher Education at the University of Texas at Austin (Emmer et al., 1994) and the Institute for Research on Teaching at Michigan State University (Brophy, 1986, 1988), reframed the question of control and warmth in terms of prevention. Its research base observed experienced and inexperienced teachers while they taught, and its major conclusion was that the distinction between more and less effective classroom managers can be made more by what they do to prevent misbehavior than by how they respond to it.

The Emmer, Evertson, and Anderson (1980) study. Twenty-seven third-grade teachers across eight elementary schools were observed for a full year. Based on average student engagement and off-task rates measured after the first three weeks, teachers were classified as more-effective or less-effective managers; the more-effective group sustained significantly higher engagement and significantly less off-task behavior for the rest of the year. Comparing the two groups' classroom-management procedures during those first three weeks — room arrangement, rules, consequences, responses to misbehavior, consistency, monitoring, and reward systems — revealed a clear pattern. More effective managers established themselves as instructional leaders early, working on rules and procedures until students had fully learned them, while also emphasizing group cohesiveness and socialization into shared classroom norms; by the end of three weeks their classes were ready for the rest of the year. Less effective managers, especially first-year teachers, lacked well-worked-out procedures in advance (one new teacher had no procedure at all for the bathroom, pencil sharpener, or water fountain, so children came and went at will); when they did have rules, the rules were often vague ("Be in the right place at the right time") or introduced casually without discussion; and they monitored their classes poorly, often because they withdrew from whole-class surveillance to work at length with one child. Consequences for behavior were also either largely absent or delivered inconsistently — general criticisms that didn't identify a specific offender, repeated unenforced warnings, or vague disciplinary messages ("You're being too noisy"). These deficiencies became recurring "windows of opportunity" for misbehavior, and within a few weeks undesirable behavior patterns and low teacher credibility had become established. Synthesizing this and related studies (Evertson, Emmer, Clements, & Worsham, 1994; Evertson & Emmer, 1982), effective classroom managers show three broad classes of behavior: they devote extensive time before and during the first weeks of school to planning and organizing the classroom; they teach rules and routines as methodically as they teach subject matter, providing clear instructions and monitoring compliance carefully early on; and they inform students of the consequences of breaking rules and enforce those consequences consistently.

Withitness and overlapping. A lot of classroom management is really about keeping activities flowing — but there is never just one thing happening at a time, even during a single planned activity. A common beginning-teacher mistake in these multi-event settings is to attend fully to one activity, student, or group at the expense of noticing and responding to everything else; finishing with a student before attending to a disruption elsewhere in the room, or interrupting yourself to handle it, both cause some disruption. Kounin (1970) named the alternative withitness: attending to multiple events at once, without necessarily giving each equal care — remaining aware of activities, behaviors, and events "in some corner of your mind" even while focused on one of them, colloquially "eyes in the back of your head." Research finds experienced teachers show withitness far more than inexperienced teachers, and that it is associated with managing classrooms successfully (Emmer & Stough, 2001). Withitness in turn makes possible overlapping — nearly simultaneous responses to multiple events that need not take equal time or even be equally noticeable to everyone (a quick glance at a chatting student may barely interrupt an ongoing conversation with someone else, and may not even be noticed by others). The result is a smoother overall flow of activity. Withitness and overlapping develop more easily during familiar routines than during unfamiliar or complex activities, but they improve with practice; merely appearing "withit" — even without actually making overlapping responses — can itself deter off-task behavior, since a student tempted to misbehave may believe the teacher will probably notice regardless.

The ripple effect. Left alone, misbehavior can spread — chatting between two students gradually becomes chatting among six; rudeness by one student becomes rudeness by several — a contagion process Kounin (1970) called the ripple effect. Because of this tendency, delaying a response to inappropriate behavior tends to make the job of getting students back on track harder than responding as immediately as possible, giving prevention-oriented management (rather than purely reactive response) much of its practical urgency.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Extensive investment in rule- and routine-teaching during the first weeks of school, methodical enough to match the effort put into teaching subject content
  • Ongoing, divided attention across multiple simultaneous classroom events rather than sustained exclusive focus on any one

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Withitness and overlapping are skills that develop with practice and are harder in unfamiliar or complex activities — a new teacher's difficulty maintaining them in a new topic is not itself a sign of poor management aptitude
  • Prevention-oriented management has comparatively little to offer once a serious disruption is already fully underway and spreading — its value is concentrated in the first weeks of a course and in responding to early, minor signs of misbehavior before the ripple effect takes hold

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students benefit from reduced classroom disruption; the tradition's evidence base (Emmer, Evertson, & Anderson, 1980) specifically concerns elementary classrooms, though its principles are widely applied more broadly

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Sustained student engagement and minimized off-task behavior across a full school year, achieved primarily through investment during the first few weeks rather than through response after problems emerge

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Ginott's Congruent Communication — a reactive, communication-focused approach that Kounin's tradition explicitly contrasts itself with by emphasizing prevention instead
  • Glasser's Choice Theory and Cooperative Learning — similarly reactive/problem-solving-focused, in contrast to Kounin's prevention emphasis
  • Teaching Styles as Warmth and Control — Kounin's tradition describes concrete teaching behaviors that help realize an authoritative (warm-and-controlled) climate regardless of a teacher's natural style

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Effective Classroom Management Plan Criteria — synthesizes prevention-oriented criteria consistent with this tradition
  • Low-Profile Classroom Control — Rinne's anticipation/deflection/reaction framework operationalizes withitness into concrete teacher techniques
  • Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence Model — the applied-behavior-analysis tradition's own account of prevention through antecedent management, developed independently but converging on similar prevention-first advice

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
How children acquire language so quickly and reliably, without formal instruction, is a long-running theoretical debate with three main competing accounts.

Learning theory (Skinner, 1957) holds that children acquire language the same way they acquire any other behavior: through reinforcement, imitation, and shaping by caregivers who respond to and correct speech attempts. This account struggles with generativity — children routinely produce novel, grammatically patterned utterances they have never heard and could not simply be imitating (e.g., over-regularized past tenses like "I swimmed," which no adult models but which follows the regular past-tense rule). It also struggles to explain cases where children invent structured language with no model to imitate at all: deaf children raised without exposure to a conventional sign language have been observed spontaneously inventing gestural systems with language-like structure (Goldin-Meadow & Mylander, 1998), and the emergence of Nicaraguan Sign Language among deaf children brought together for the first time in a school (Senghas, Senghas, & Pyers, 2005) shows a full, structured language arising from peer interaction alone, without adult teaching.

Nativism (Chomsky, 1965) holds that humans are born with an innate, biologically specified capacity for language — a "Language Acquisition Device" pre-loaded with universal grammatical structure — that environmental input merely triggers and fills in with the specifics of a particular language. This account is supported by the generativity problem above and by evidence of critical periods: language acquired early is qualitatively different from language acquired later, and severely delayed first-language exposure (as in extreme deprivation cases) produces permanent limitations no later intervention fully reverses (Lenneberg, 1967; Johnson & Newport, 1989). But strong nativist claims about universal grammatical structure have also been challenged empirically: Evans and Levinson (2009) catalog human languages that lack features (such as clear noun/verb phrase distinctions or grammatical tense) that a strict universal-grammar account predicts should be near-universal, suggesting the innate constraints are looser or more flexible than originally proposed.

Social-interactionism, most closely associated with Sociocultural Theory, holds that language develops through the child's social need and desire to communicate, accelerated by responsive interaction with more knowledgeable others rather than by exposure to input alone. On this account, the quality and responsiveness of interaction — not simply the presence of language in the environment — is what drives development; see the related claim on conversational turn-taking.

The current consensus among researchers is that no single account is sufficient on its own: language acquisition requires both a biological readiness that only humans of a certain age reliably have, and rich, responsive environmental interaction that gives that readiness something to work with (Gleitman & Newport, 1995; Stork & Widdowson, 1974).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Instructional or parenting advice that assumes language develops from either "just exposure" (a pure nativist reading) or "just correction and reinforcement" (a pure behaviorist reading) is oversimplified relative to the evidence
  • Critical-period evidence means early language exposure — including early exposure to a signed language for deaf children, and early exposure to additional languages for multilingual development — has effects that are difficult or impossible to fully replicate with later intervention

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Infants and young children during first-language acquisition
  • Older children and adults acquiring an additional language, where the theory's critical-period claims predict (and evidence generally supports) an advantage for earlier exposure, though not an absolute cutoff

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not itself an instructional-objective framework — it explains the mechanism underlying language development that principles like supporting early language development and heritage-language maintenance build on

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Sociocultural Theory — the social-interactionist account is a direct application of Vygotsky's broader framework to language specifically
  • Behaviorism — the learning-theory account of language acquisition is a direct application of behaviorist principles, and shares its central limitation (difficulty explaining generativity)
  • Constructivism — compatible with the interactionist account's emphasis on meaning-making through social interaction

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Julian Rotter (1966) proposed locus of control as a cognitive factor shaping behavior and personality, distinct from Self-Efficacy Theory: self-efficacy is a belief about one's own ability to perform a specific task, while locus of control is a broader belief about who or what controls outcomes in one's life generally. People with an internal locus of control ("internals") tend to believe their outcomes are the direct result of their own effort; people with an external locus of control ("externals") tend to believe their outcomes are controlled by other people, luck, or chance. Rotter framed the two orientations as ends of a continuum rather than a strict dichotomy.

A student who does poorly on a test after skipping study time illustrates the contrast: an internal is more likely to attribute the outcome to insufficient studying and resolve to study more next time; an external is more likely to attribute it to the test being unfairly hard and see little point in studying harder, since outcomes are seen as outside personal control. Researchers have found that people with an internal locus of control perform better academically, achieve more in their careers, are more independent, are healthier, cope better, and are less depressed than people with an external locus of control (Benassi, Sweeney, & Durfour, 1988; Lefcourt, 1982; Maltby, Day, & Macaskill, 2007; Whyte, 1977, 1978, 1980).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Best applied where a learner's persistence or disengagement after failure is the concern, not raw ability

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Locus of control is a generalized belief across situations, not task-specific — it should not be conflated with self-efficacy, which can vary sharply from one domain to another for the same person

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners who attribute poor performance to external, uncontrollable factors and consequently disengage from further effort
  • Learners for whom attribution retraining (shifting explanations toward effort, a controllable and internal factor) may improve persistence

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Building a sense that effort causally shapes outcomes, to sustain engagement after setbacks
  • Not itself an instructional-objective framework — it describes a learner disposition relevant to how feedback and attributions for success/failure should be framed

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Efficacy Theory — self-efficacy is task-specific competence belief; locus of control is a broader, more stable belief about the general controllability of outcomes
  • Attribution Theory — locus (internal vs. external) is one of attribution theory's own core dimensions, applied there to explanations for specific past outcomes rather than a generalized trait
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — internal locus of control has been linked to higher expectancy for success and task value in online learning contexts (Joo, Lim, & Kim, 2013)
  • Self-Regulated Learning — an internal locus of control is a plausible precondition for sustained self-regulatory effort, since self-regulation presumes outcomes respond to one's own strategic action

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Abraham Maslow proposed that human motivation is organized into a hierarchy of five need levels, in ascending order of "prepotency": physiological needs (food, water, sleep — "the most pre-potent of all needs"), safety (structure, order, security, freedom from danger and chaos), love/belonging (friends, family, group identification, intimate relationship), esteem (both strength/achievement/confidence and earned respect/recognition from others — Maslow is explicit that esteem "must come from earned respect and not from fame or social status"), and self-actualization (growth and self-improvement, which Maslow described as rare). Maslow also discussed a desire to know and understand as a separate cognitive drive, prepotent in itself (the desire to know precedes the desire to understand), but he treated it as distinct from, not a sixth member of, the core five-level hierarchy.

Emergence of a need is gradual rather than all-or-none: Maslow illustrated this with rough satisfaction percentages for an "average citizen" — physiological 85%, safety 70%, love 50%, esteem 40%, self-actualization 10%. Needs are largely unconscious and are claimed to be universal across cultures even though their specific expression varies. A related but distinct set of preconditions for need satisfaction — freedom to speak, freedom of expression, freedom to investigate, freedom to defend oneself, justice, fairness, honesty, orderliness — are reacted to almost as strongly as direct threats to the basic needs themselves when they are threatened.

Maslow himself catalogued several exceptions to the standard order: some people's self-esteem outranks their need for love; innately creative people may keep creating despite unmet lower needs; long-term deprivation (e.g., extended unemployment) can permanently lower a person's aspirations; early, prolonged loss of love can produce a "psychopathic personality" that permanently forgoes that need; a need satisfied for a long time can be underestimated in importance; a person's conscious desires and their actual behavior can diverge; and self-sacrifice for an ideal is explained as increased frustration-tolerance built through early gratification. Behavior is typically multi-motivated — a single act can express several needs simultaneously — and not all behavior is need-driven at all.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Contemporary research treats motivation as more pluralistic than a strict ladder: Tay and Diener (2011), analyzing Gallup data from 60,865 people across 123 countries, tested six needs analogous to Maslow's against three wellbeing measures and found the needs themselves are cross-culturally universal, but the hierarchical ordering was not supported — people can benefit from "higher" needs without first satisfying "lower" ones
  • Maslow derived the self-actualization traits from a biographical analysis of only 18 people he judged self-actualized, and his sample (Jefferson, Lincoln, Einstein, Gandhi, and a few women such as Eleanor Roosevelt) skewed heavily toward highly educated white men — a methodological limitation on the theory's claim to generalize
  • Counter-examples exist to a strict reading of the hierarchy: people in severe poverty who still achieve love and belonging, and impoverished artists (Rembrandt, Van Gogh) who appear to have reached self-actualization without their lower needs being reliably met

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners whose physiological, safety, belonging, or esteem needs are unmet or precarious — hunger, fatigue, insecurity, and low self-esteem are named as direct barriers to learning
  • Applicable across ages, though classroom applications are most often drawn from K-12 contexts

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not objective-specific; the theory is a framework for the conditions (safety, belonging, respect) that make any learning objective attainable, and for self-directed growth as an aspirational long-term outcome

docs.title: Educational Implications
docs.text: A tired and hungry student will find it difficult to focus on learning — physiological needs must be substantially met before cognitive/learning needs can be productively addressed. Students must feel emotionally and physically safe and accepted in the classroom to progress toward their potential; a teacher should visibly show students they are valued and respected. Students with low self-esteem will not progress academically at an optimal rate until their self-esteem is strengthened. Maslow (1971, p. 195) framed the goal of a humanistic educational approach as producing people who "would be stronger, healthier, and would take their own lives into their hands to a greater extent," actively shaping the society they live in rather than simply being shaped by it.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Determination Theory — SDT's autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs partially echo Maslow's esteem, self-actualization, and love/belonging tiers, but SDT treats its three needs as co-equal and simultaneously active rather than hierarchically ordered
  • Self-Efficacy Theory — task-specific capability belief maps loosely onto the confidence component of Maslow's esteem tier, but is narrower and more directly testable
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — a contrasting motivational paradigm (expectancy × value predicting engagement) rather than a need-satisfaction account
  • Behaviorism – the chapter this page draws on explicitly contrasts Maslow's holistic, needs-based view of the learner against reductionist stimulus-response accounts of motivation
