docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Metacognition is knowledge about, and the ability to regulate, one's own cognitive processes — realistically judging how difficult a task will be, monitoring whether a strategy is working, and adjusting accordingly. It is closely related to, but distinct from, Executive Function Development: executive function is the underlying capacity to control and coordinate cognition, while metacognition is specifically the learner's own knowledge about that cognition and the strategies available to direct it.

Metacognitive strategy use develops gradually. Bjorklund (2005) and Schneider, Kron-Sperl, and Hunnerkopf (2009) trace a steady increase in strategy use across elementary school, and identify three distinct ways a learner can fail to benefit from a strategy, which matter for diagnosing why a particular intervention isn't working rather than simply concluding "the strategy doesn't work":

  • Mediation deficiency — the learner doesn't understand the strategy at all, even when taught it directly.
  • Production deficiency — the learner understands and can use the strategy when prompted, but doesn't spontaneously produce it on their own without a cue.
  • Utilization deficiency — the learner spontaneously uses the strategy, but it doesn't yet actually improve performance, often because executing the strategy itself consumes so much cognitive effort that little capacity is left over for the task it's meant to support; this is common early in learning a new strategy and tends to resolve with practice.

A rough age-8 inflection point has been observed in some longitudinal work: strategies acquired before around age 8 tend to show gradual, incremental improvement with practice, while strategies acquired after age 8 show more of an "all-or-nothing" jump once the child grasps them (Sodian & Schneider, 1999) — though this pattern should be treated as a descriptive tendency from a specific line of research rather than a firm developmental law.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• A learner who fails to benefit from a taught strategy may be experiencing any of three distinct problems (not understanding it, not spontaneously using it, or using it without yet benefiting from it) — and each calls for a different instructional response: reteaching, prompting/cueing, or simply more practice
  • Utilization deficiency in particular means a newly-taught strategy may show no visible benefit, or even a temporary cost, before it becomes beneficial — a discouraging early phase that shouldn't be mistaken for the strategy being ineffective

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Elementary-age children, where strategy use (rehearsal, organization, visualization, mnemonics) develops most visibly across this age range
  • Learners of any age newly acquiring an unfamiliar cognitive strategy, where utilization deficiency is a predictable early-stage phenomenon rather than a sign the strategy has failed

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Realistic self-assessment of task difficulty and one's own current performance
  • Spontaneous, self-initiated use of previously-learned strategies without needing an external prompt
  • Efficient execution of a strategy so that it frees rather than consumes cognitive capacity

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Fluent bilingualism enhances metalinguistic awareness [+M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Executive Function Development — the underlying self-regulatory capacity that metacognitive knowledge is applied through
  • Information Processing Theory — metacognitive strategy use directly targets the working-memory and encoding bottlenecks central to information-processing accounts
  • Self-Regulated Learning — metacognitive monitoring is one of the core components of self-regulation
  • Critical Thinking — what makes thinking "critical" rather than merely correct is largely the metacognitive monitoring of one's own thinking

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Howard Gardner (1983) proposed that intelligence is not the single general factor ("g") that Charles Spearman and earlier theorists described, but a set of at least eight relatively independent intelligences — commonly listed as linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic. Gardner (1999) later proposed a ninth, existential intelligence, which he himself notes "has yet to experience full acceptance by educators in the classroom." A person typically excels in some of these and not others, which is a direct challenge to instructional designs that treat "ability" as a single scale a learner sits somewhere on.

Gardner justifies treating each intelligence as genuinely separate using eight identification criteria: isolation by brain damage, the existence of prodigies or exceptional individuals, a distinguishable set of core operations, developmental stages with an expert end state, evolutionary plausibility, susceptibility to symbolic encoding, and support from both experimental-psychology tasks and psychometric research.

Gardner's inter- and intrapersonal intelligences are often combined by other researchers into "emotional intelligence" — the ability to understand and regulate one's own and others' emotions and social relationships (Parker, Saklofske, & Stough, 2009). Daniel Goleman (1995) popularized the claim that emotional intelligence predicts life success better than traditional IQ, but this claim is contested: researchers have pointed to inconsistent definitions and measurement difficulty for the construct (Locke, 2005; Mayer, Salovey, & Caruso, 2004). Multiple Intelligences Theory itself faces a parallel and more sustained empirical challenge. Critics (Morgan, 1996) argue it largely relabels existing "cognitive styles" research as separate "intelligences." The psychometric community has pointed to the persistence of a general intelligence ("g") factor: Gottfredson (2004) reports that a test giving two items per intelligence found people scored similarly across all eight, showing no discriminant validity between them; Gardner's own response is that a g-factor exists but is itself simply a manifestation of logical-mathematical intelligence, not evidence against the broader theory. More strikingly, the theory has drawn a decades-long "no published validating studies" critique — repeated by Sternberg (1994), Allix (2000), Sternberg and Grigorenko (2004), and even by Gardner and Connell (2000, p. 292), who conceded "little hard evidence for MI theory," and by Gardner (2004, p. 214) himself, who wrote he would be "delighted were such evidence to accrue" and noted the theory "has few enthusiasts among psychometricians." Waterhouse (2006) adds a neuroscience critique: shared neural pathways and genetic factors across language, music, motor skill, and general intelligence undercut the claim that each intelligence operates via a wholly separate neural mechanism, and the theory lacks a clear evolutionary account of why nine independent intelligences would emerge. Developing valid, reliable psychometric measures for each proposed intelligence has proven difficult in general (Furnham, 2009; Gardner & Moran, 2006; Klein, 1997). The theory remains influential in justifying differentiated, multi-modal instructional design despite this unresolved empirical status.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Willingness to design multiple task/assessment formats (verbal, spatial, kinesthetic, interpersonal) rather than assuming a single format measures a learner's capability fairly

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The theory's empirical validation remains contested — standard psychometric measures for the proposed intelligences are difficult to construct, and critics argue the eight categories may simply relabel existing "cognitive style" findings rather than identify genuinely separate abilities
  • Should not be used to conclude a learner is incapable in a domain because it doesn't match their "strongest" intelligence — Gardner's own framing is about relative strengths, not fixed limits

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners assessed or taught through only one modality (typically linguistic/logical), where the theory argues for recognizing strengths a narrower assessment format would miss

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Objectives that can be demonstrated through varied task types (a project, a performance, a verbal explanation) rather than only a single test format

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text:
• Morgan (1996) argues the theory relabels existing cognitive-styles research rather than identifying genuinely independent abilities
  • Standard measurement approaches struggle to validate the eight intelligences as empirically distinct (Furnham, 2009; Klein, 1997)
  • No published studies have directly validated the theory as a whole, a gap acknowledged even by Gardner himself (Sternberg, 1994; Allix, 2000; Gardner & Connell, 2000; Gardner, 2004; Sternberg & Grigorenko, 2004)
  • Waterhouse (2006) argues shared neural pathways and genetic factors across cognitive domains, and the absence of a clear evolutionary rationale, count against treating each intelligence as a separate neural mechanism

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Triarchic Theory of Intelligence — a competing, more parsimonious (three-part) account of intelligence developed as an alternative to both single-factor ("g") and highly multi-factor models

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Before Kohlberg extended and formalized the study of moral reasoning, Piaget studied it directly — partly by observing how children negotiate and enforce the rules of their own games, and partly through structured moral dilemmas. He described a two-phase progression driven by the same cognitive maturation that underlies his broader stage theory, tied to a shift from viewing rules as fixed and externally imposed to viewing them as constructed, revisable social agreements.

In the heteronomous phase (morality of constraint), typical of younger children, rules originate from authority — parents, teachers, or a generalized "elder" — and are treated as permanent and unchangeable. Children in this phase judge wrongdoing largely by its consequences rather than the actor's intent, and believe in immanent justice: the conviction that misbehavior is automatically and proportionally punished by the world itself, independent of whether anyone witnessed or reported it. This orientation is visible in young children's play, where rules (even ones they don't fully understand) are treated as sacred and unquestionable simply because "that's how it's always been done."

In the autonomous phase, typical of older children and adults, moral judgment shifts to weigh intention over consequence — a person's reason for acting matters more than the outcome alone. Children in this phase recognize that rules are not universal or eternal but are social agreements that can be renegotiated by the people bound by them (Piaget's own example: children revising the rules of a marbles game by mutual consent). They also stop believing in immanent justice, recognizing that wrongdoing sometimes goes unpunished and that punishment sometimes falls on the innocent — a recognition with real moral weight, since it underlies principled civil disobedience (e.g., someone breaking an unjust law with the deliberate intention of prompting its revision, as in Rosa Parks's refusal to give up her seat).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• The heteronomous-to-autonomous shift parallels, and is partly explained by, the broader move from concrete to more flexible, decentered thinking described in Stages of Cognitive Development
  • Because young children in the heteronomous phase judge wrongdoing by outcome rather than intent, punishing "bad results" without regard to intention reinforces rather than challenges this stage of reasoning
  • Recognizing that rules are socially constructed and revisable is a precondition for later principled reasoning about when a rule itself is unjust

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Children broadly, with the heteronomous phase most visible in early-to-middle childhood and the autonomous phase emerging through later childhood and adolescence
  • Especially relevant wherever classroom rule-setting itself is a design choice (e.g., whether students participate in creating classroom rules, which is a concrete way to practice autonomous rather than merely obedient reasoning)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Shifting moral judgment from outcome-based to intention-based reasoning
  • Understanding rules as negotiable social agreements rather than immutable decrees from authority

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development — the heteronomous/autonomous shift is a direct application of Piaget's broader account of cognitive decentration
  • Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development — Kohlberg built directly on this two-phase account, elaborating it into three levels and six stages
  • Play and Cognitive Development — Piaget observed heteronomous moral reasoning directly in how young children treat the rules of their own games

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Play is self-directed, individually constructed, imaginative activity, distinct from product-focused work, that serves cognitive skill development, social-emotional learning, and identity exploration. Piaget identified types of play that track a child's cognitive maturation; Smilansky added an intermediate category; Vygotsky offered a complementary account of why pretend play matters developmentally, independent of Piaget's stage framework.

docs.title: Piaget's Types of Play
docs.text:
1. Functional play — repetitive motor and object manipulation, beginning in infancy (shaking, banging, mouthing); foundational for coordinated voluntary action.
  2. Constructive play — goal-directed, creative manipulation of materials (blocks, clay, art supplies); bridges functional and symbolic play; develops planning, problem-solving, fine-motor coordination, spatial reasoning, and self-esteem through visible accomplishment.
  3. Symbolic (pretend) play — using an object or action to represent something else (a broom as a horse, a block as a phone); emerges in single-object transformations and grows into elaborate multi-role scenarios with both realistic and non-realistic props.
  4. Games with rules — play structured by shared, externally imposed logic, order, and strategy (board games, sports); requires self-regulation to follow rules, cooperation, and tolerance of competition.

docs.title: Parten's Stages of Social Play
docs.text: Mildred Parten's classic scheme describes increasing social participation, moving from non-social to fully coordinated social play: unoccupied (no specific goal-directed behavior) → solitary (playing alone, no interaction with others) → onlooker (watching others play without joining) → parallel (playing alongside others without coordinating) → associative (shared activity without a common goal) → cooperative (coordinated activity with assigned roles toward a shared goal). Younger children (2–3) engage more in non-social play; by around age 5, associative and cooperative play dominate.

docs.title: Vygotsky's Account of Pretend Play
docs.text: Vygotsky treated pretend play as central to development in its own right: it lets children fulfill needs and desires imaginatively that they cannot yet fulfill in reality, provides practice in delaying gratification and following self-imposed rules (a role tacitly requires acting the way that role would act), and operates within the child's Zone of Proximal Development — a child can typically act "a head taller than himself" in pretend play compared to unstructured behavior. Smilansky's research further links play deprivation, especially symbolic play, to cognitive and emotional delays, particularly among underprivileged children, and identifies concrete facilitation strategies: imitative role play, make-believe with objects, verbal make-believe, sustained persistence in a role (10+ minutes), interaction with at least one other player, and verbal communication about the play itself.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Play types are age-linked but overlapping — prominence shifts with maturation rather than replacing earlier types outright
  • Progression depends on access to unstructured time, varied materials, and (for symbolic and cooperative play) peers or responsive adults
  • Some children develop imaginary companions (estimates range widely, roughly 6–65% depending on definition); this is a normal variant most common among highly sociable children, not a sign of poor social skills or difficult circumstances

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Early childhood through elementary-age learners (preschool through roughly grade 5), where play is a primary developmental activity
  • Applicable wherever unstructured or lightly structured time is part of the learning environment

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Cognitive: spatial reasoning, planning, exploration, flexible thinking, early metacognition (pretend play requires simultaneously tracking an imagined reality and the actual one)
  • Social-emotional: negotiation, turn-taking, perspective-taking, self-regulation, persistence, adaptability

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development — Piaget's play types map onto the broader stage sequence (e.g., symbolic play emerging alongside preoperational thought)
  • Sociocultural Theory — Vygotsky's account of pretend play as operating within the Zone of Proximal Development is a direct extension of his broader theory
  • Self-Determination Theory — play is prototypically autonomous, self-chosen activity

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Like Realism, Pragmatism requires empirical observation of the real world; unlike Realism and Idealism, however, that world is not an unchanging whole but is evolving and changing according to how thought is applied to action on a problem. Thought should not merely describe or represent reality — it should be applied practically to problems as they arise, so that the universe is always evolving according to newly applied thoughts turned into action. Pragmatism's founder, Charles Sanders Peirce, held that thought must produce action toward an ever-changing universe.

Progressivism, founded by John Dewey, follows an explicit pragmatic ontology: experience is central to explaining the world, and is itself what needs explaining. A learner needs practical experience and uses that experience to find models that fit a given problem or situation; as new experiences and explanations arise, reality evolves to new situations and problems. Educationally, Progressivism focuses on experiential learning and developing the whole child: students learn by doing rather than being lectured to, following something like the scientific method of questioning and searching for answers, working in cooperative or collaborative groups on project-based, expeditionary, problem-based, or service-learning activities, and pursuing their own interests. The teacher is a facilitator rather than the center of the educational process, sharing authority in planning and decision-making with students. Curriculum is usually integrated across content areas rather than siloed by discipline, current events are used to sustain interest in required subject matter, and evaluation relies on projects and portfolios rather than tests alone. Progressivism's stance stands in stark contrast to both Essentialism and Perennialism on nearly every one of these points.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Time and structure for extended, cooperative, project-based work, rather than a schedule built around lecture and discrete tests
  • A teacher willing to act as facilitator and share planning authority with students, rather than remaining the sole source and arbiter of content

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • Integrated, project-based curricula can be harder to align cleanly to discrete, disciplinary content standards than a subject-siloed approach

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners who benefit from hands-on, real-world problem work over lecture-based instruction

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Practical competence in applying thought to real, evolving problems, rather than mastery of a fixed body of facts or ideas

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Essentialism and Perennialism (Educational Philosophy) — the traditional, teacher-centered, fact-based curricula Progressivism explicitly positions itself against

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Idealism (Educational Philosophy)
  • Realism (Educational Philosophy) — Pragmatism shares Realism's commitment to empirical observation, but rejects its assumption of a fixed, unchanging reality
  • Critical Pedagogy — a later tradition that, like Progressivism, de-centers the teacher, but adds an explicitly political and emancipatory aim that Progressivism itself does not

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Project-Based Learning
  • Problem-Based Learning

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching philosophy. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Erik Erikson took the psychoanalytic foundation laid by Freud and extended it across the full lifespan rather than stopping at adolescence, shifting emphasis from purely biological drives toward social and cultural forces, and toward human strength and constructive potential rather than pathology. Each of Erikson's eight stages is defined by a psychosocial crisis between two opposing forces; resolving a stage in favor of its positive pole yields a corresponding virtue carried into later stages. Mastery of a stage is not required to advance — "the outcome of one stage is not permanent and can be modified by later experiences" — but unresolved crises tend to resurface as problems later. All eight crises are present from birth, but each becomes most prominent according to both a maturational schedule and a person's ecological and cultural upbringing.

docs.title: The Eight Stages
docs.text:
Stage Age Crisis Virtue Existential Question Infancy 0–2 yrs Trust vs. Mistrust Hope "Can I trust the world?" Early Childhood 2–4 yrs Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt Will "Is it okay to be me?" Preschool Age 4–5 yrs Initiative vs. Guilt Purpose "Is it okay for me to do, move, and act?" School Age 5–12 yrs Industry vs. Inferiority Competence "Can I make it in the world of people and things?" Adolescence 13–19 yrs Identity vs. Role Confusion Fidelity "Who am I? Who can I be?" Early Adulthood 20–39 yrs Intimacy vs. Isolation Love "Can I love?" Adulthood 40–64 yrs Generativity vs. Stagnation Care "Can I make my life count?" Maturity 65–death Ego Integrity vs. Despair Wisdom "Is it okay to have been me?"

Trust vs. Mistrust turns on whether caregivers consistently meet basic needs; some experience of mistrust has adaptive value, but infancy is not the stage to deliberately induce it. Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt turns on whether caregivers encourage self-sufficient behavior (self-feeding, dressing, toileting) versus demanding too much too soon. Initiative vs. Guilt covers the child's first self-directed plans; adults — parents and preschool teachers alike — who support effort while guiding realistic choices foster initiative, while those who dismiss early efforts as "silly and bothersome" foster guilt. Industry vs. Inferiority is "critical for the development of self-confidence": school provides recognition for accomplishment (drawing, solving problems, writing), building diligence and perseverance, while ridicule or unmet expectations build inferiority; this is also the stage in which children discover and pursue special talents, and being denied the chance to do so on their own timeline is linked to low motivation and low self-esteem later. Identity vs. Role Confusion is the stage Erikson is best known for — he coined the term "identity crisis" — and centers on a psychosocial moratorium, a socially sanctioned space for adolescents to experiment with roles, affiliations, and values before settling into an identity; the age boundary is explicitly fluid, and identity formation is noted to take longer in industrial/technological societies and "for persons of genius." Its virtue, fidelity, is "the ability to sustain loyalties freely pledged in spite of the inevitable contradictions and confusions of value systems." Intimacy vs. Isolation begins once identity is reasonably settled and concerns forming reciprocal, committed relationships versus distantiation — "the readiness to isolate and if necessary to destroy those forces and people whose essence seems dangerous to our own" (Erikson, 1950, p. 237). Generativity vs. Stagnation concerns concern for guiding the next generation, broadly applied across family, work, and society, not only parenting. Ego Integrity vs. Despair is retrospective: contentment if life is seen as productive, despair (often depression or hopelessness) if seen as full of disappointments; this stage can occur out of sequence when a person feels near the end of life, such as after a terminal diagnosis.

docs.title: Marcia's Identity Statuses
docs.text:
James Marcia (1966) operationalized Erikson's Identity vs. Role Confusion stage into four empirically distinguishable identity statuses, defined by two independent dimensions: whether a person has gone through a period of active exploration of identity options, and whether they have reached a commitment. Identity diffusion (no exploration, no commitment) describes a person who has neither examined identity options nor made commitments, and may show little urgency about doing so. Foreclosure (commitment without exploration) describes a person who has adopted an identity — often one handed down by parents or another authority — without ever seriously questioning alternatives. Moratorium (exploration without commitment) describes a person actively exploring options but not yet settled; this is the status Erikson's own "psychosocial moratorium" concept describes most directly. Achievement (exploration followed by commitment) describes a person who has explored options and reached their own considered commitments. Later work (Meeus et al., 2012) has proposed a fifth status, searching moratorium, for people who reopen exploration after having reached achievement — recognizing that identity commitment is often revisited rather than permanently fixed once reached in early adulthood.

Joan M. Erikson, Erik's wife and collaborator, later added a ninth stage (Erikson & Erikson, 1998), written when she was 93: in old age, all eight prior crises recur but with the negative pole ascendant as capacities decline (e.g., "Basic Mistrust vs. Trust," "Despair and Disgust vs. Integrity"), each still paired with its original virtue.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Applies across the full lifespan, but school-relevant stages are Initiative vs. Guilt (preschool), Industry vs. Inferiority (elementary), and Identity vs. Role Confusion (middle/high school)
  • Empirical support is strongest for the adolescent identity stage, notably through James Marcia's (1966) work distinguishing forms of identity status; coherent adolescent self-concept has been linked to more successful intimate attachment in early adulthood, consistent with the theory's stage-sequencing claim
  • Critics, including Erikson himself (1956), question whether the crises are strictly sequential and confined to the suggested age ranges rather than recurring throughout life at varying prominence

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Preschool, elementary, and middle/high school learners, for the stage-specific classroom guidance below
  • Learners at any life stage more broadly, since the theory's full scope runs from infancy through old age

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Not an instructional-objective framework — its "objectives" are developmental tasks (e.g., learning whether people can be trusted to meet one's needs; discovering whether one's efforts at initiative succeed) rather than content or skill objectives

docs.title: Educational Implications by School Stage
docs.text:
Preschool (Initiative vs. Guilt): build projects around students' interests; let children lead classroom projects; praise good choices; give continuous feedback; never ridicule choices openly — redirect privately; don't punish experiments that turn out differently than planned; use physical activity to teach fairness and sportsmanship.

Elementary (Industry vs. Inferiority): create a scheduled list of classroom duties with student input; post classroom rules with students included in the decision; encourage role-play to think beyond routine; teach that striving for growth matters more than avoiding mistakes; encourage peer helping and never allow mockery; build confidence by recognizing what each child does best; offer varied assignment choices; use physical activity for social development.

Middle/High School (Identity vs. Role Confusion): treat all students equally regardless of gender, race, academic ability, or socioeconomic status; bring in guest speakers and activities spanning many career paths; focus on and acknowledge student strengths; build confidence through trying different problem-solving approaches; incorporate life skills into lesson planning; use physical activity to relieve stress.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Sociocultural Theory — the theory explicitly frames each stage as a negotiation of biological and sociocultural forces, paralleling sociocultural theory's emphasis on social and cultural shaping of development
  • Self-Determination Theory — Autonomy vs. Shame/Doubt and Industry vs. Inferiority echo SDT's autonomy and competence needs; this is the wiki's own analytical connection rather than one drawn directly from the source
  • Bioecological Model of Human Development — both treat development as shaped jointly by maturation and surrounding social/cultural context
  • Adolescent Peer Group Structure — crowd and clique dynamics are a primary arena in which the Identity vs. Role Confusion crisis plays out
  • Adolescent Brain Development — the same adolescent period covered by Identity vs. Role Confusion is also when the limbic/prefrontal maturational mismatch is most pronounced

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Realism's central tenet holds that reality — the external universe — exists independent of the human mind. Aristotle, Plato's student, contradicted his teacher's Idealism and formulated a philosophy centered on determining truth through observation: reality can be truly understood by careful observation of all the data, and through logic humans can reason about the physical universe. Because of this emphasis, Aristotle is often called the Father of the Scientific Method; his logic emphasizes both induction and deduction, with the essence of a thing determinable through examination of the thing itself.

During the Enlightenment, Common Sense Realism — associated with John Locke — countered Cartesian Idealism's skepticism about the external world, arguing instead that ordinary experience directly intuits a self and a physical world without needing to doubt that world's reality. This strand of Realism went on to influence the later development of Empiricism and Pragmatism.

For Realists, teaching methods focus on basic skills, memorization, and mastery of facts, with students demonstrating content mastery through critical observation and applied experimentation.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: • A realist classroom emphasizes direct observation of the physical world and mastery of established facts, contrasting with Idealism's emphasis on introspection and dialogue about ideas

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners in subjects where mastery of observable, factual content is the primary goal (e.g., natural sciences)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Accurate understanding of an external reality, verified through observation and logical reasoning rather than introspection

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Idealism (Educational Philosophy) — the antithetical ontology Aristotle formed in reply to his teacher Plato
  • Essentialism and Perennialism (Educational Philosophy) — Essentialism in particular tends to subscribe to Realism's tenets, favoring a factual, back-to-basics curriculum

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A science curriculum centered on observation, experimentation, and mastery of established facts rather than open-ended discussion of what those facts mean

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Arduini-Van Hoose, N. (2020). Teaching philosophy. In Educational psychology. Retrieved from https://edpsych.pressbooks.sunycreate.cloud. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Research Design Taxonomy — Quantitative/Qualitative and Descriptive/Correlational/Experimental
Description
docs.text:
Quantitative research typically starts with a focused research question or hypothesis, collects a small amount of data from each of a large number of individuals, describes the resulting data with statistical techniques, and draws general conclusions about a population. It is comparatively weak at generating novel, interesting research questions or providing rich description of behavior in particular situations. Qualitative research does the reverse: it can generate new questions and hypotheses, collects large amounts of relatively unfiltered data from a relatively small number of individuals, describes that data with non-statistical techniques, and can produce rich, detailed description of behavior in the real-world contexts where it occurs — what qualitative researchers call the "lived experience" of participants. Because the two approaches have complementary strengths, some researchers combine them into mixed-methods research, either by using qualitative work to generate hypotheses that quantitative work then tests, or through triangulation — using both approaches simultaneously on the same question and comparing results. Convergent results reinforce and enrich each other; divergent results raise a genuinely useful further question: why do they diverge, and how can that be reconciled?

A separate dimension classifies research by what kind of conclusion the design can support, regardless of whether the underlying data is quantitative or qualitative. Descriptive research measures and reports a variable without testing any relationship between variables — it can answer interesting and important questions, but not questions about relationships. Correlational research goes a step further and formally tests whether a relationship exists between two or more variables, expressed as a correlation coefficient (r) from −1 to +1: the closer to 1 in either direction, the stronger and more predictable the relationship. Correlations have genuine predictive value — a university admissions committee, for instance, can use the correlation between current students' standardized test scores and their college GPA to help predict applicants' likely success. But correlation is limited in a specific way: establishing that a relationship exists tells us little about cause and effect. A correlation between two variables can arise because one variable is a confounding variable driving both — the classic textbook case is ice cream sales correlating with crime rates, where temperature drives both rather than either causing the other — or because people accept a causal story (do healthier people eat cereal, or does eating cereal make you healthier?) without checking for a confound.

People also perceive relationships between variables that don't actually exist at all — illusory correlations. The persistent belief that a full moon affects human behavior is a textbook case: a meta-analysis of nearly 40 studies found no such relationship (Rotton & Kelly, 1985), yet the belief persists because people notice and remember odd behavior during a full moon while failing to notice that odd behavior occurs at a constant rate throughout the lunar cycle — the same confirmation-bias mechanism (see Evidence-Based Teaching and Scientific Reasoning) that makes personal inquiry generally unreliable. Illusory correlations are not merely a curiosity: research suggests they are involved in forming the prejudicial attitudes toward particular groups that can escalate into discriminatory behavior (Fiedler, 2004).

Experimental research goes further still, randomly assigning participants to conditions so that hypothesis testing can support inferences about causal relationships — see Designing a Valid Experiment for the mechanics. Descriptive, correlational, and experimental research form a genuine hierarchy of what a design can conclude, not a hierarchy of rigor or value: a descriptive study of what a phenomenon even looks like is often the necessary first step before a correlational study is worth running, which in turn can motivate a specific causal hypothesis worth testing experimentally.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Matching the research question actually being asked to a design that can support the kind of conclusion it needs — a descriptive or correlational question does not need (and cannot be answered by mis-reading) an experimental design, and vice versa

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• A strong correlation, however large r is, never by itself establishes which variable (if either) causes the other, or whether a third variable causes both
  • Readers as well as researchers are vulnerable to illusory correlations — noticing confirming instances and failing to notice the (much larger) set of disconfirming ones

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Anyone reading, citing, or designing educational research — including this wiki's own claim pages, whose evidence-quality (q) ratings track exactly this design hierarchy (see CLAUDE.md's evidence-quality tiers)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Reading a correlational finding (in a study, a news article, or a claim page) without silently upgrading it to a causal one

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Illusory correlations, like the belief that a full moon affects behavior, persist through confirmation bias despite having no basis in evidence [X]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Designing a Valid Experiment — the design that actually supports causal conclusions, and the mechanics of running one properly
  • Developmental Research Designs — a further, orthogonal set of design choices specific to studying change over time

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A study reporting that students who use a particular study app have higher grades (correlational) is a different, weaker claim than a study that randomly assigns students to use the app or not and then compares outcomes (experimental)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Self-Determination Theory (SDT) explains motivation in terms of the degree to which behavior is experienced as autonomous, competent, and socially connected. Developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, the theory argues that learners are more likely to engage deeply and persist when three basic psychological needs are supported: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

In instructional design, SDT is most often used to explain why some environments invite engaged, internally endorsed effort while others produce compliance, avoidance, or disengagement. The theory does not claim that structure is bad. It claims that structure works best when it supports rather than undermines a learner's sense of agency and capability.

"Pure" self-determination is an ideal rather than a realistic classroom default: class size, curricular obligations, and students' own personal histories all limit how fully a teacher can meet every student's basic needs at all times. The practical result is that most students experience only a partial sense of self-determination, and SDT treats the "intrinsic-ness" of any given motivation as a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing state — ranging from "pure" extrinsic motivation (no intention to act regardless of pressure or incentive), through externally-controlled, introjected (acting to avoid guilt or shame, without reflection), identified (recognizing an action's value toward a goal the learner does value, e.g. grades toward college admission), and integrated regulation (an action adopted as part of the learner's own self-concept), up to "pure" intrinsic regulation (acting solely because the activity itself is enjoyable) (Koestner & Losier, 2004). This reframes the teacher's job: not to expect purely intrinsic motivation at all times, but to arrange conditions that make each of a student's motivations as intrinsic as possible by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

Concrete tactics cluster around each need. Autonomy is supported chiefly by offering students choices wherever possible — the largest gains come from choices with real consequences (e.g., choosing project partners), but even minor choices (desk organization, folder color) contribute some sense of self-control, and choices should be offered to every student, not reserved for the highest performers (Ryan & Lynch, 2003). Minimizing external rewards and social comparison, and orienting instruction around students' own expressed interests, reinforces the same need. Competence is best supported by selecting tasks that are challenging but achievable with reasonable effort and assistance, favoring activities and questions (divergent rather than single-answer) that require an active response, giving feedback as immediately as possible, and providing accessible routes to help (a teacher, aide, reading, or program) when students get stuck (Elliott, McGregor, & Thrash, 2004). Relatedness is supported by structuring cooperative work that recognizes students' diversity and minimizes competition — "rich group work" tasks that deliberately require a mix of talents so each student contributes something distinct (Cohen, 1994; Cohen, Brody, & Sapon-Shevin, 2004; see also Social Interdependence) — and by the teacher's own relationship-building, such as habitually speaking of "we" rather than "you students." The Jigsaw Method (Aronson & Patnoe, 1997) is a structured example: expert groups research a subtopic, then reform into generalist groups so each member both contributes unique expertise and depends on peers for the rest.

These tactics are not unconditionally beneficial, however. Offering choice can help or backfire depending on how many options are offered and how meaningfully they differ: too many options, or options that don't actually differ in ways the learner cares about, can increase anxiety and indecision rather than autonomy — the evidence on how much choice is "enough" is genuinely mixed (Flowerday & Schraw, 2003; Deci & Ryan, 2003), and Schwartz (2004) argues explicitly that more choice is not always better once a threshold is passed.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Relevant wherever motivation, persistence, and ownership matter
  • Particularly useful in goal setting, feedback, choice, game-based environments, and adult learning contexts
  • Helps explain why autonomy-supportive structures can improve engagement even when tasks remain demanding

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners whose motivation depends strongly on perceived relevance and agency
  • Learners rebuilding confidence or persistence after prior failure
  • Adults and adolescents balancing external demands with internal goals

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained engagement and persistence
  • Willingness to take ownership of learning goals
  • Increased confidence through supported competence
  • Stronger sense of belonging and participation

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [~S]
  • Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [~M]

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Regulated Learning — SDT helps explain why learners may or may not take up the self-regulatory behaviors SRL describes
  • Self-Efficacy Theory — both treat perceived competence as central, though SDT frames it as one of three basic needs (with autonomy and relatedness) rather than a task-specific belief
  • Attribution Theory — controllable attributions support the sense of autonomy and competence SDT identifies as basic needs
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — task value overlaps with the sense of relevance and autonomy SDT-informed design also targets
  • ARCS Model of Motivational Design — ARCS's Relevance and Confidence tactics draw directly on SDT's autonomy and competence needs

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Goal Setting & Monitoring
  • Learner Choice
  • Strengths-based Approach
  • Game-Based Learning
  • Epistemic Games
  • Digital Open Badges

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Self-efficacy is "people's beliefs in their ability to perform a course of action required to achieve a specific task" (Bandura, 1977). The theory's central claim is specificity: self-efficacy is not a general trait like self-confidence or self-concept, and it is not the same as documented ability. A learner's self-efficacy for "correctly subtracting fractions" is a distinct belief from their self-efficacy for "writing a persuasive essay," even though both might contribute to a broader (and much less predictive) sense of being "good at school" (Seifert & Sutton, 2018). Because self-efficacy beliefs are self-constructed rather than measured, they can diverge from true capability in either direction; the most functional level is at or slightly above actual capacity (Bandura, 1997).

Bandura (1977) identified four sources of self-efficacy, in order of typical strength (Pajares & Schunk, 2001, 2002): (1) prior mastery experience — the strongest source; succeeding at similar tasks raises self-efficacy, failing lowers it — but only if the success is genuine and the task actually meaningful, since success at trivial tasks, or praise for successes a student has not really had, does not raise self-efficacy (Erikson, 1968/1994); younger, elementary-age students in particular draw on a much shorter personal history when judging whether they can succeed again, so building a convincing history of success may require deliberately widening what counts as "the past" for them (Eccles et al., 1998); (2) vicarious experience/modeling — watching a similar peer succeed raises the observer's own expectation that they can succeed too, an effect that is strongest when the observer lacks direct experience of the task and when the model is respected or seen as genuinely comparable in ability (Schunk & Zimmerman, 1997) — overused without any real success of the student's own, or with a model perceived as "out of their league," vicarious mastery can backfire, since students may simply disqualify the model as irrelevant to their own potential; (3) verbal persuasion — a trusted person's encouragement can raise self-efficacy, though its effect is comparatively limited on its own, working mainly to reinforce direct or vicarious experience, and more so when persuasion comes from more than one person (Goddard, Hoy, & Hoy, 2004); and (4) physiological/emotional states — anxiety or bodily stress signals (sweating, racing heart) can be interpreted as evidence of incapability, lowering self-efficacy. Critically, these four sources don't operate directly — a learner interprets each event, and it is that interpretation, not the raw experience, that shapes the belief.

High self-efficacy for a task produces three effects, each with an upside and a downside: it makes learners more willing to choose tasks they feel confident about (which can mean avoiding valuable but unfamiliar challenges); it increases persistence at the task (which is beneficial unless it crowds out other priorities); and it improves coping with stress and recovery from failure (which generalizes to non-academic pursuits as readily as academic ones). When self-efficacy is very low and sustained, it can produce learned helplessness — the belief that effort makes no difference — a phenomenon Seligman (1995) first demonstrated behaviorally: animals repeatedly shocked with no way to escape later failed to escape even once escape became possible simply by moving to the other side of the cage. In people, learned helplessness produces a characteristic attribution pattern — attributing a problem to oneself, generalizing it across many areas of life, and seeing it as permanent ("I'm stupid; I never perform well on any schoolwork, and I never will") — contrasted with a more optimistic pattern that attributes problems to outside, specific, temporary causes ("The teacher made the test too hard this time; it doesn't prove anything about next time or other subjects"). The optimistic pattern closely resembles high self-efficacy's own framing of a setback as limited to a specific, temporary task rather than a stable trait of the self.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Opportunities for learners to actually succeed at meaningfully similar tasks (mastery experience is the strongest, most reliable lever)
  • Visible peer models roughly similar to the learner in ability, since modeling works by the observer inferring "if they can do it, so can I"

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Self-efficacy theory explains the process of motivation (how beliefs affect behavior) but says little about content — which tasks are intrinsically satisfying rather than merely achievable (Seifert & Sutton, 2018); pairing it with content-focused theories (interest, task value) fills this gap
  • Persuasion-based interventions ("I know you can do this") are the weakest of the four sources and unlikely to work alone without genuine opportunities for mastery
  • Self-efficacy beliefs can be miscalibrated (too high or too low relative to true capability), and large discrepancies create their own motivational problems

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners facing a specific, definable task or skill, since self-efficacy is inherently task-specific rather than a global trait
  • Learners at risk of learned helplessness after repeated failure, where breaking the pattern requires engineered opportunities for genuine, attributable success

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Sustained engagement, task persistence, and resilience after setbacks
  • Willingness to attempt appropriately challenging tasks rather than avoiding them

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text: • Social Learning Theory [+S] — self-efficacy is Bandura's own extension of social learning theory, and modeling (one of the four sources) is a direct application of observational learning

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Self-efficacy is often used interchangeably with "expectancies for success" in Expectancy-Value Theory, but the two are conceptually distinct: self-efficacy is task-specific, while expectancies for success are typically domain-specific (Park, 2018)

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Social Learning Theory — self-efficacy is Bandura's own theoretical extension, adding a cognitive, belief-based mediator to observational learning
  • Self-Determination Theory — both treat perceived competence as central to motivation, though SDT frames it as one of three basic psychological needs (alongside autonomy and relatedness) rather than a task-specific belief
  • Self-Regulated Learning — self-efficacy beliefs shape whether a learner persists with self-regulatory strategies after an initial setback
  • Expectancy-Value Theory — shares the "expectancy" component but frames it as domain-general rather than task-specific
  • ARCS Model of Motivational Design — the Confidence category is a direct, practitioner-facing operationalization of self-efficacy-building tactics
  • Locus of Control — a related but distinct cognitive factor: self-efficacy is belief in one's own task-specific ability, while locus of control is a broader belief about whether outcomes generally are controlled by one's own effort or by external forces

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) explains learning as a cyclical process in which learners set goals, choose strategies, monitor progress, and reflect on outcomes in order to improve later performance. Rather than treating learning as passive reception, SRL emphasizes that effective learners actively manage attention, effort, strategy use, and feedback across time.

Barry Zimmerman's work is one of the most influential formulations of SRL. In that model, learners move through forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases. Goal setting, strategy selection, self-monitoring, and self-evaluation are therefore not add-ons to learning; they are central mechanisms that shape whether learning efforts become effective.

A second, complementary formulation comes from clinical and addiction-behavior research: building on Kanfer's foundational work (Kanfer, 1970a, 1970b), Miller and Brown (1991; Brown, 1998) proposed a seven-step model in which self-regulation can falter at any of seven points: (1) receiving relevant information, (2) evaluating it against a norm, (3) triggering the decision to change, (4) searching for options, (5) formulating a plan, (6) implementing the plan, and (7) assessing the plan's effectiveness — which recycles back to steps 1-2. Unlike Zimmerman's three-phase cycle, this model is explicitly diagnostic: a scored instrument, the Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ) (Brown, Miller, & Lawendowski, 1999), lets a practitioner identify which specific step in the cycle is failing for a given person rather than treating self-regulation as a single undifferentiated capacity.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Strong fit where learners must plan, monitor, and revise over extended tasks
  • Especially relevant in independent study, writing, problem solving, exam preparation, and online learning
  • Often requires instructional supports such as explicit goals, feedback, prompts, and reflection routines before learners can regulate effectively on their own

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners developing independence and metacognitive control
  • Adults and adolescents managing long-term goals, deadlines, and self-study demands
  • Novices who need support learning how to learn, not just what to learn

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Goal setting and strategic planning
  • Monitoring understanding and performance during work
  • Adjusting strategy in response to feedback or error
  • Building persistence and more accurate self-evaluation

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
• Self-monitoring improves self-regulation and supports better learning decisions. [+M]
  • Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals. [+M]
  • Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. [+S]
  • Early ability to delay gratification predicts later academic and social outcomes, but the association is weaker and more context-dependent than originally reported. [~M] — self-control/delay of gratification is closely related to self-regulation, though the relationship to later outcomes is more context-dependent than the classic marshmallow-test framing suggests

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Determination Theory — motivation and autonomy shape whether learners engage in self-regulatory behaviors
  • Cognitive Load Theory — working-memory demands can constrain learners' ability to monitor and regulate effectively, especially when they are novices
  • Executive Function Development — self-regulation depends substantially on executive-function capacities (inhibitory control, working memory) that develop across childhood and adolescence

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Goal Setting & Monitoring
  • Self-monitoring
  • Formative Assessment
  • Immediate Feedback
  • Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ) — a scored instrument built directly on the Miller & Brown seven-step model described above

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Situated learning holds that knowledge is inseparable from the social, material, and cultural contexts in which it is used. Learning is strengthened when it happens through participation in authentic practices rather than only through abstract decontextualized instruction.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text: • Cognition is shaped by activity, tools, roles, and communities, not just by the individual mind in isolation.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
• Supports authentic tasks, apprenticeship, communities of practice, and scenario-based learning.
  • Qualifies theories that treat learning only as internal information processing.

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Constructivism
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship
  • Sociocultural Theory — shares the view that knowledge and cognition are inseparable from social and cultural context
  • Connectivism — also locates learning outside the individual mind, but in digital networks rather than embodied social practice

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Epistemic Games

docs.title: Key Sources
docs.text: • Lave, J., & Wenger, E. (1991). Situated learning: Legitimate peripheral participation. Cambridge University Press.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Social Learning Theory, developed primarily by Albert Bandura, proposes that learning occurs not only through direct reinforcement (as behaviorism holds) but also through observation of others and the cognitive processing of those observations. The core mechanism is modeling: learners observe a model performing a behavior, encode the behavioral pattern, and reproduce it — with reproduction mediated by attention, retention, motor reproduction, and motivation. Bandura's Bobo doll studies (Bandura, Ross, & Ross, 1961) are the theory's signature demonstration: children who watched an adult model act aggressively toward an inflatable doll reproduced that aggression themselves. Observational learning can occur in at least three ways (Lefrançois, 2012): a learner acquires an entirely new response; a learner decides whether to imitate a model based on what happened to the model; or a learner extracts a general rule applicable beyond the specific modeled instance. Bandura distinguished three kinds of models: a live model demonstrates the behavior in person; a verbal instructional model describes or explains the behavior without performing it (e.g., a coach describing correct kicking technique); and a symbolic model is a real or fictional figure demonstrating behavior through media (books, film, television, video games, the internet).

Bandura (1986) later renamed and substantially expanded the theory as Social Cognitive Theory, foregrounding cognition rather than simple observation-and-reproduction. Its central architecture is triadic reciprocal causation (or reciprocal determinism): behavior, personal factors (cognition, self-efficacy), and environment are "equal, interlocking determinants of each other" (Bandura, 1986). A hostile act draws an unfriendly response roughly 75% of the time (Bandura, 1973), reshaping the actor's environment, which in turn reshapes further behavior — a concrete illustration of the loop. Bandura used this to argue against pure environmental determinism: people act as agents within and upon their environment, not merely as products of it (Bandura, 1977a).

Social Cognitive Theory names four modes of human agency (Bandura, 1986, 2006; Pajares, Prestin, Chen, & Nabi, 2009) — individual (a person's own influence on their environment), proxy (another's efforts on one's behalf), and collective (a group acting for shared benefit) — built on four properties: intentionality, forethought, self-reactiveness, and self-reflectiveness. It also names four foundational human capabilities (Bandura, 2002): symbolizing capability (perceiving and constructing solutions symbolically, rather than only through trial and error), self-regulation capability, self-reflective capability, and vicarious capability (learning from consequences observed in others or media, increasingly central given modern media saturation).

Modeling itself is more differentiated than simple imitation: its effectiveness depends on characteristics of the model (status, competence, power cues such as a lab coat or expertise signals), attributes of the observer, and the consequences the model experiences. Observers can recombine cues from multiple models into new, innovative behavior rather than only copying one model rotely, and modeling can inhibit as well as produce behavior — a teacher's glare can suppress off-task talk in students who merely observe another student being corrected. Observers don't expect the model's literal reward or punishment for themselves but form outcome expectancies — an anticipation of a similar consequence if they imitate — which are themselves shaped by environment and culture (e.g., DUI penalties, and their expected consequences, vary by country). In the Bobo doll experiment specifically, children who saw a model punished for aggression toward the doll decreased their own imitation of that aggression (vicarious punishment), while children who saw the model praised or simply left unpunished imitated the behavior, including the model's specific words (vicarious reinforcement) — motivation to imitate, not just attention or retention, depends on the consequence observed. The full modeling sequence Bandura described is therefore four steps: attention, retention, (motor) reproduction, and motivation.

Bandura later extended the theory into a dedicated account of self-efficacy — a learner's belief in their capacity to perform a specific task — as a central determinant of whether observed behavior is translated into action; this extension is covered in its own page, Self-Efficacy Theory. Self-efficacy develops across the lifespan: infants build early "personal agency" through learning they can cause predictable effects (shaking a rattle); young children have unrealistic self-efficacy and need adult guidance to calibrate it (Bandura, 1986, p. 414); school-age children develop "cognitive efficacy" partly through the ranking effects of grades and peer comparison, and a child low in social self-efficacy but high in coercive or aggressive self-efficacy is at risk of becoming a bully.

Self-regulation is a related but distinct mechanism: learners engage in self-reinforcement and self-punishment as internally generated complements to external reward and punishment (Bandura, 1977b, p. 129). The standards a learner judges themselves against are often relative (e.g., a weightlifter tracking their own totals over time) and are themselves typically acquired through modeling — children tend to model moderately competent rather than highly expert standards, keeping self-set goals within reach. Cumulative self-judgment against these standards shapes overall self-concept.

The theory sits between behaviorism and cognitive constructivism: it accepts that behavior is shaped by consequences, but insists that cognitive factors (observation, expectation, self-belief, self-regulation) are essential mediators. It also distinguishes moral competence (the capacity to reason about right and wrong) from moral performance (what a person actually does), since the two do not always align (Santrock, 2008).

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text: Social Cognitive Theory is not a fully unified theory: the literature offers no established mechanistic connection between observational learning and self-efficacy, leaving the framework broad but under-integrated. It is difficult to observe or quantify all forms of social learning, and the theory largely treats observational learning as undifferentiated across the lifespan, without a strong account of developmental or maturational differences between how children and adults learn from models.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Applies wherever learners can observe expert or peer performance — particularly powerful in skill-based domains (sports, surgery, teaching, craft)
  • Social presence is not strictly required; recorded models (video demonstrations, worked examples) can be effective
  • Self-efficacy effects are strongest at the boundary of competence — when a task is challenging but not overwhelming

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Novices benefit most from watching competent models; the gap between model and observer should not be too large
  • Peer models (slightly more capable) can be more effective than expert models because they feel attainable
  • Learners with low self-efficacy may avoid modeling opportunities — design should provide early success experiences to calibrate beliefs

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Procedural skills with visible performance
  • Professional practices and norms
  • Self-regulation and strategy use (cognitive modeling)

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Cognitive Apprenticeship — operationalizes social learning via modeling, coaching, and fading in authentic contexts
  • Situated Learning — extends observational learning to communities of practice
  • Self-Regulated Learning — incorporates self-efficacy as a regulatory mechanism
  • Constructivism — shares emphasis on active sense-making; differs in granting social observation a direct instructional role
  • Sociocultural Theory — both center learning through interaction with others, but Vygotsky's account is developmental (mediated by language and culture) rather than mediated by observation, attention, and self-efficacy
  • Self-Efficacy Theory — Bandura's own extension of this theory into a dedicated account of task-specific competence beliefs
  • Locus of Control — another cognitive factor Bandura's tradition treats as shaping behavior, distinct from self-efficacy: locus of control concerns general beliefs about who or what controls outcomes, not task-specific competence

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Prosocial Modeling — deliberately applies vicarious reinforcement to encourage socially desirable behavior

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Sociocultural theory originates in the work of Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky (1924–1934) and holds that human development and higher-order thinking originate in social, historical, and cultural interaction rather than inside an isolated individual mind. Vygotsky summarized this as a developmental law: "Every function in the child's cultural development appears twice: first, on the social level, and later, on the individual level; first between people (interpsychological) and then inside the child (intrapsychological)" (Vygotsky, 1978, p. 57). Development is a transformation of participation in shared social activity, not a transmission of discrete facts or skills (Polly et al., 2018).

Three ideas anchor the theory:

  1. Social origin of thinking — cognitive development cannot be understood apart from its social and historical context; learners adopt shared strategies and knowledge through working with others (Rogoff's "guided participation"). Tomasello, Kruger, and Ratner (1993) distinguish three modes of cultural-tool transmission: imitative learning (directly copying another), instructed learning (internalizing a teacher's instructions and using them for self-regulation), and collaborative learning (peers jointly working to understand a skill).
  2. Mediation by psychological tools, especially language — social and individual functioning is mediated by signs and tools (language, counting systems, cultural artifacts); learners appropriate these tools rather than reinventing them, and language plays the dual role of enabling communication and constructing meaning. Elementary, innate mental functions (e.g., an infant responding to a mother's voice) are transformed into higher mental functions (problem-solving, logic, hypothetical thinking) through this cultural mediation.
  3. The Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) — "the distance between the actual developmental level as determined by independent problem solving and the level of potential development as determined through problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers" (Vygotsky, 1978, p. 86). Learning is most productive when instruction is aimed at this zone rather than at what a learner can already do alone. Tudge and Winterhoff (1993) note the ZPD is not a fixed, pre-existing space but is co-created in the course of the social interaction itself, and that Vygotsky specifically emphasized adults over peers as the paradigmatic more knowledgeable other, since adults are more reliably competent and less likely to cause regression rather than progression in a collaboration.

Sociocultural theory stands in explicit contrast to Piaget's view that developmental stages are biologically determined and precede learning; Vygotsky instead held that learning drives development. Piaget's own writing reflects this contrast directly: he argued that "teachers who take control of the child's learning place the child into a passive role," and that children must discover concepts largely on their own — a view Vygotsky's emphasis on guided social interaction pushes directly against. Vygotsky also held that development and the social world shape each other dialectically — the social world shapes the learner, but the learner's development in turn changes the social world around them (Tudge & Winterhoff, 1993) — and that natural (biological) and cultural development "coincide and merge" into an integrated influence on personality (Vygotsky, 1986), a more integrative position than a strict nature-vs-culture framing suggests. This has direct instructional consequences: rather than waiting for learners to be developmentally "ready," instruction can be structured to promote development by working just ahead of a learner's independent capability.

Scaffolding is the practical corollary of the ZPD: the mutual, dynamic set of tools or actions — modeling, prompting questions, highlighting critical features — that a more capable other provides to help a learner complete a task within their ZPD, gradually withdrawn as competence increases (Polly et al., 2018). Vygotsky himself never used the word "scaffolding" — the term, and its application of the ZPD to concrete teaching practice, comes from Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976), who emphasize that scaffolding should target the upper end of a learner's ZPD, not just a safe lower bound, since the goal is to sustain interest and stretch capability rather than simply guarantee success; Biggs and Moore (1993) similarly describe scaffolding as chaining together successive ZPDs to reach outcomes beyond a learner's starting potential.

A related developmental mechanism is private speech: children's habit of talking aloud to themselves to guide or regulate their own behavior, distinct from (and, per Vygotsky, misread by Piaget as merely) "egocentric speech." Vygotsky (1986) described three stages: social/external speech (up to about age 3), used to influence others' behavior; egocentric speech (roughly ages 3–7), spoken aloud to control or justify one's own actions — an intermediate, transitional form, not a developmental dead end as Piaget's original label implied; and inner speech, an internalized, silent "stream of consciousness" (James, 1890) that organizes directed, higher-order thinking. This progression is itself an instance of the broader mechanism of internalization, which Vygotsky distinguishes sharply from two superficially similar but mechanistically different processes: introjection, a passive absorption of an idea with little active participation by the learner (akin to operant conditioning or hypnosis), and socialization, conformity-driven adoption of a belief the person hasn't actually made their own. Internalization, by contrast, is the genuine transformation of a socially-mediated process into an individually-owned mental function — the same transformation the theory's developmental law describes moving from the interpsychological to the intrapsychological plane.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A more knowledgeable other (teacher, peer, or embedded digital scaffold) available to provide guidance pitched at the learner's ZPD
  • Tasks structured to allow guidance to be gradually withdrawn (faded) as the learner's independent competence grows

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The ZPD is difficult to measure precisely — there is no common metric, and it is unclear whether a learner's zone is comparable across domains or stable over time (Miller, 2011); Palinscar (1998, p. 370) calls it "one of the most used and least understood constructs...in contemporary educational literature," and Faukner, Littleton, and Woodhead (2013, p. 114) warn it is sometimes used as "little more than a fashionable alternative to Piagetian terminology or the concept of IQ"
  • Vygotsky's own work was left incomplete by his early death (age 37) and was not widely known in the West until decades later (slowed further by translation from Russian), so some of the theory's specifics — including a fully developed account of language — remain underdeveloped, and its predictions are harder to test than Piaget's more specific stage claims
  • The theory offers no built-in experimental methodology of its own — Vygotsky relied primarily on observation rather than controlled experiment — and does not specify which particular forms of social interaction are most effective
  • Some critics argue learning can occur passively or "osmotically," with some children simply developing more slowly regardless of the support offered, implicating genetic factors the theory does not directly address
  • Rogoff (1990) notes that some sociocultural techniques (e.g., verbally mediated scaffolding) may be less effective across all cultures, since their evidence base skews toward Western, middle-class populations

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Learners at any age; Vygotsky's original work focused on child development, but the theory's core mechanisms (guided participation, scaffolding, mediation through language) generalize to adult and workplace learning
  • Learners working just beyond their current independent capability — the theory has little to add when a task is already within a learner's independent reach

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Higher-order thinking skills, language and concept development, and collaborative problem-solving
  • Objectives well-suited to gradual release of responsibility from expert/teacher to learner

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Piaget's stage theory of cognitive development, which holds that development precedes and constrains learning rather than the reverse

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Stages of Cognitive Development – stands in explicit contrast: Piaget held that development is biologically determined and precedes learning, while Vygotsky held that learning (mediated by social interaction) drives development
  • Constructivism + shares the view of learning as active meaning-making, and draws directly on Vygotsky as a source
  • Cognitive Apprenticeship + operationalizes the "more capable other" and modeling/coaching/fading structure implied by the ZPD
  • Situated Learning + shares the emphasis on learning as inseparable from social and cultural context
  • Social Learning Theory ~ both treat observation of and interaction with others as central, but Bandura's account is individually mediated (attention, retention, motivation) rather than developmental

  • Collaborative Learning
  • Problem-based Learning
