docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Jean Piaget (1896–1980), a Swiss psychologist, proposed that children are not passive recipients of knowledge from parents or teachers but actively construct their own understanding of the world by progressing through four universal, sequential, and invariant stages of cognitive development. Each stage represents a qualitatively different way of reasoning; stages cannot be skipped, though the ages at which individual children pass through them vary with environment and background, and a child may show behaviors characteristic of more than one stage at a time. Piaget's work is the historical foundation on which later constructivist and constructionist theories are built.

The theory's core mechanisms are schema (an organized unit of knowledge — e.g., a child's schema for "dog"), assimilation (fitting new experience into an existing schema, as when a child sees a dog in the park and expands their existing "dog" schema), disequilibrium (the cognitive conflict created when new information doesn't fit an existing schema — a dog that barks or licks doesn't match what the schema predicted), accommodation (revising a schema, or building a new one, when assimilation fails — seeing a cat that shares traits with a dog but meows and climbs trees prompts a new "cat" schema rather than stretching the dog schema), and equilibration — the overall self-regulating process of resolving disequilibrium and returning to a stable state ("equilibrium") through assimilation and accommodation.

docs.title: The Four Stages
docs.text:
1. Sensorimotor (birth – 18/24 months). Cognition is built through motor activity and sensory experience rather than symbols. Piaget divided this stage into six substages: (1) reflexive action (0–1 month) — automatic reflexes like sucking and grasping, gradually adapted to different objects; (2) first adaptations (1–4 months) — reflexes replaced by voluntary movement, centered on the infant's own body; (3) secondary circular reactions (4–8 months) — delight in repeating actions that produce interesting effects (banging, shaking); (4) coordination of secondary circular reactions (8–12 months) — deliberate, goal-directed behavior and imitation; object permanence — understanding that an object continues to exist even when it can't be seen — is traditionally placed here, around 8–9 months; (5) tertiary circular reactions (12–18 months) — active, trial-and-error experimentation, the "little scientist" testing what happens when objects are thrown, squeezed, or poured; (6) mental representations (18–24 months) — problem-solving via mental strategies rather than physical trial-and-error, deferred imitation of things seen earlier, and the beginnings of pretend play. Modern research qualifies the timing here: Baillargeon's (1987) eye-tracking studies suggest object permanence is present by around 4 months, much earlier than Piaget's estimate, and Meltzoff (1988) found deferred imitation in 9-month-olds — almost a year earlier than Piaget's account predicts. Piaget's sequence of skills has held up better than his specific age estimates.

2. Preoperational (~2–7 years). Language, memory, and imagination develop rapidly. Reasoning is dominated by precausal thinking, not yet logical cause-and-effect: animism (belief that inanimate objects have lifelike qualities — a sidewalk is "mad" for making a child trip), artificialism (belief that natural features result from human action — the wind exists because someone is blowing), and transductive reasoning (linking two specific, unrelated events causally, e.g., "the dog barked, so the balloon popped"). Reasoning is also limited by centration — focusing on one salient dimension of a problem while ignoring others — which produces the classic conservation failure: shown two identical beakers of liquid, a preoperational child says a taller, thinner beaker has "more" after a beaker is poured, unable to mentally reverse the pouring (irreversibility) or attend to both height and width at once. The same centration limits class inclusion — shown 8 dogs and 3 cats, a child who knows both categories are "animals" will still say there are "more dogs than animals," unable to hold the subclass and superclass in mind simultaneously — and transitive inference — given "A is taller than B" and "B is taller than C," a preoperational child cannot deduce that A is taller than C.

This stage is also where theory of mind — understanding that other people (and one's own past self) can hold beliefs that are false — develops. In the classic task, a 3-year-old shown a candy box that actually contains crayons will, even after seeing the crayons, say they originally thought (and that a friend would think) the box contained crayons — unable to represent a false belief, whether someone else's or their own earlier one. By age 4, most children pass this task, recognizing that belief and reality can diverge. The Sally-Anne test (a doll moves an object while another doll, unaware, is absent) is the equivalent test used with somewhat older children; children under 4, and children with autism spectrum disorder at any age, disproportionately fail it, predicting based on what they themselves know rather than what the absent character could know. This connects Piaget's stage theory to clinical practice: autism spectrum disorder is characterized in part by persistent, marked delay in theory-of-mind development, alongside restricted/repetitive behavior patterns, with signs often noticeable by 18–24 months.

Pretend play also emerges and elaborates through this stage (see Play and Cognitive Development); dual-level engagement in pretend play — tracking both the imagined and the real situation at once — is considered an early precursor of metacognition. More recent research qualifies Piaget's account of this stage overall: when task instructions are simplified and distractions removed, children as young as 3–4 show less egocentrism, and even some conservation and class-inclusion competence, than Piaget's original tasks suggested — indicating some of the original findings reflected task difficulty and unfamiliarity with the researcher's question, not the total absence of the underlying capacity (Donaldson, 1978; Gelman, 1972).

3. Concrete Operational (7–11 years). Children manipulate symbols logically and systematically, but only in relation to concrete objects and situations — logic still needs something to be "about." Two mechanisms mature here: reversibility, the ability to mentally run a sequence of steps in either direction (enabling both correct conservation judgments and multi-step tasks a child can move back and forth through, like "find unfamiliar words, define them, then have a friend quiz you on the list"), and decentration, the ability to deliberately attend to more than one feature of a problem at once (e.g., "circle only the two-digit subtraction problems that require borrowing," which requires tracking both "two-digit" and "requires borrowing" simultaneously). Because logic here is still tied to the concrete, hands-on materials and physical examples matter for instruction at this stage in a way they matter less once formal operations is reached; a child at this stage can correctly order three dolls by height when they can see them, but the same child may struggle to order them from a purely verbal description.

4. Formal Operational (adolescence through adulthood). Reasoning extends to abstract concepts and multiple variables simultaneously. Hypothetical-deductive reasoning — forming a hypothesis about what should logically follow, then testing it systematically, rather than relying on trial and error — is the hallmark capacity; Piaget's own pendulum problem (what determines a pendulum's swing speed: string length, weight, or push force?) requires holding several variables in mind and testing them one at a time through pure reasoning, and cannot be solved by trial-and-error alone. Transitivity (if A < B and B < C, then A < C) becomes reliable. Piaget held that once formal operations is reached, no new cognitive structures are needed — further adult development is the addition of more complex schema through knowledge, not new stages.

Formal operational capacity, however, does not mean formal operational reasoning is always used. Modern dual-process research (Kuhn, 2013) distinguishes intuitive thought (automatic, fast, unconscious, emotional) from analytic thought (deliberate, conscious, effortful); adolescents and adults alike rely on intuitive thought for most everyday reasoning, and adolescents in particular may lean on it more than adults because a mismatch in developmental timing between limbic and prefrontal brain systems makes emotionally-driven, intuitive judgment relatively more available (see Adolescent Brain Development). Adolescents also develop relativistic thinking — questioning whether rules and assertions are absolute or context-dependent — which can manifest as questioning authority more broadly as teens learn to distinguish genuinely universal rules (don't touch a hot stove) from culturally relative ones (etiquette norms). A related, much-studied finding concerns risk-taking: adolescents and adults weigh potential rewards against consequences similarly, but adolescents give disproportionately more weight to social rewards specifically (peer approval, belonging) than adults do — a pattern some researchers frame as evolutionarily adaptive, since a cohort willing to take risks and try new approaches provides a population-level counterweight to older adults' more conservative, established knowledge.

Formal operational reasoning is also more situation-specific than Piaget's original account suggests: research finds 40–60% of college students fail simple formal-logic tasks (Keating, 1979), and performance is strongly tied to domain familiarity — physics majors reason more formally about physics problems, psychology majors about psychological ones, and reasoning often does not transfer well across domains a person hasn't studied (DeLisi & Staudt, 1980). Teaching strategies suited to this stage include posing genuinely hypothetical or contrary-to-fact problems ("What if oil had never been discovered?") that require holding several varying factors in mind at once, entirely mentally.

docs.title: Beyond Formal Operations: Postformal Thought
docs.text:
Later researchers have argued Piaget's four stages don't capture the most sophisticated adult reasoning. Arlin (1975, 1977) proposed a problem-finding stage, in which especially creative thinkers (she names Einstein, Freud, and Piaget himself as examples) don't just solve problems within an existing frame but reconceptualize the frame itself, discovering new problems worth solving. Sinnott (1998) described postformal thought as a shift from purely idealistic, abstract possibility-generation toward realistic, adaptive choice-making grounded in experience — recognizing that not every logically possible option is a practical one. Basseches (1984) described dialectical thought, the ability to hold and reconcile two genuinely opposing positions rather than treating problems as simple dichotomies (right/wrong, good/bad) — a shift often summarized as moving from seeing one's parents as either all-good or all-bad toward seeing them as "just people, with strengths, weaknesses, endearing qualities, and faults." Across all of these, a recurring theme is that experience and education, not age alone, drive whether and how far someone moves beyond formal operations — many adults never receive the kind of extended education or professional practice that cultivates this level of reasoning, and even people fully capable of it may not use it outside their strongest domain of interest.

Huitt and Hummel (1998) note that only about 35% of high school graduates in industrialized countries reliably attain formal operational thought, and many adults never think formally — a significant constraint for anyone designing instruction or performance support for chronologically adult learners who may still reason concretely.

Critics working in the 1960s–70s argued Piaget likely underestimated children's abilities: confusing, overly abstract task framing produced false negatives, and simplified versions of the same tasks were often solved by younger children. Empirically, children's performance is also less stage-consistent across tasks than the theory predicts — a child assessed as "preoperational" on one task doesn't reliably perform at that level on all cognitive tasks. Contrary to Piaget's prediction that teaching developmentally "advanced" concepts would fail, researchers have found children sometimes learn advanced concepts with relatively brief instruction, suggesting stage boundaries are less rigid than originally proposed.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Instructional content should be matched to the learner's current developmental/operational stage — a "readiness" model that contrasts with Vygotsky's view that learning can drive development (see Related Theories)
  • Works best where hands-on, concrete, or visually/socially scaffolded materials are available
  • A substantial share of adult learners have not reliably attained formal operational thought, which matters for designing instruction and performance support for chronologically-adult audiences

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Children and adolescents, developmentally segmented by the four stages above
  • Adults: a meaningful minority never reliably reason formally, so concrete scaffolding (visual aids, familiar examples, worked models) remains useful even for adult learners

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Concept and schema formation in general, applicable broadly across content areas
  • Classification and categorization tasks (concrete operational stage)
  • Hypothesis formation, abstract and multi-variable reasoning, systematic problem solving (formal operational stage)
  • Not well-suited on its own to specifying precise, measurable behavioral objectives — the theory is developmental/explanatory rather than prescriptive at that grain

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Constructivism — Piaget's work is the direct historical foundation constructivist theories build on: children actively construct rather than passively receive knowledge
  • Constructionism — Papert's extension of Piagetian constructivism, adding the requirement that learning takes the form of building a public, shareable artifact
  • Sociocultural Theory — stands in explicit contrast: Piaget holds that developmental stages are biologically determined and precede learning, while Vygotsky held that learning (mediated by social interaction) drives development
  • Information Processing Theory — Piaget's schema/assimilation/accommodation mechanism is a developmental precursor to the more general schema and encoding concepts used in information-processing accounts
  • Piaget's Theory of Moral Development — Piaget's account of moral reasoning applies the same cognitive-maturation logic (here, to how children treat rules) as the broader stage theory
  • Play and Cognitive Development — Piaget's types of play track the cognitive-stage sequence described here
  • Adolescent Brain Development — the formal-operational capacity for abstract reasoning does not by itself guarantee consistent application under the emotional/social pressures adolescents face

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Chart-Based Retrieval and Spaced Practice — uses a chart to outline Piaget's stage theory in an AP Psychology class

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Students' motivation can be decomposed along two independent spectrums: how strongly they are motivated to approach success, and how strongly they are motivated to avoid failure (Bohlin, 2011). Crossing these two spectrums yields four student profiles, closely paralleling the approach/avoidance distinction in Goal Orientation Theory.

Success-oriented students are highly motivated to approach success and relatively unconcerned with avoiding failure. They are intrinsically motivated, desire mastery, and — distinctively — define success as being the best they can be, regardless of how others perform, rather than as outperforming peers.

Overstrivers are, like success-oriented students, driven to achieve success — but unlike them, they also fear failure, and are motivated to prove themselves by outperforming others. To maximize their odds, overstrivers may employ several strategies (Covington, 1984; Stipek, 2002): selecting easy tasks to guarantee success with little actual learning; deliberately maintaining low expectations so that any success looks impressive relative to the (artificially lowered) bar; rehearsing responses in advance to appear more able than they feel; excessive attention to detail and effort, often accompanied by frequent check-ins and feedback requests, stemming from self-doubt about their actual ability; and, in the worst case, cheating, chosen over asking for help because asking for help feels like admitting inability.

Failure-avoiding students are highly motivated to avoid failure but, unlike overstrivers, do not hold high expectations for success — they are avoiding not just failure itself but its associated costs (anxiety, criticism), and rather than learning to feel proud of successes, they learn mainly to feel relief at having avoided failure (Covington & Müeller, 2001). To avoid appearing incompetent, they use self-handicapping strategies (Covington, 1984; Covington & Beery, 1976): minimizing, avoiding, or withdrawing from participation; making excuses for poor performance or lack of effort; procrastinating; setting unattainable goals or selecting tasks so difficult that success becomes unlikely; and deliberately appearing not to try. Low-achieving students use more of these self-handicapping strategies than students who are already doing well (Leondari & Gonida, 2007) — the underlying logic is that failing despite real effort exposes low ability, whereas failing without effort lets the student attribute the failure to lack of effort rather than lack of ability. This creates a genuine bind, however: teachers tend to value effort, so withholding it risks its own negative consequences — criticism or punishment for not trying (Urdan et al., 1998; Weiner, 1994) — leaving these students caught between the risk of trying and failing versus the risk of visibly not trying at all.

Failure-accepting students are, unlike the other three profiles, motivated toward neither success nor away from failure — they have experienced significant failure and have come to accept it. They do not take credit for successes, believing success is determined by external, uncontrollable factors, yet they do blame themselves for failures, with each failure confirming a fixed lack of ability (Covington, 1984). This combination produces learned helplessness (see Self-Efficacy Theory): because of an external locus of control regarding success but an internal one regarding failure, these students believe they lack control over outcomes either way, making them the most difficult of the four profiles to motivate — positive reinforcement for successes does not work, and convincing them of future success is difficult (Ames, 1990; Covington & Omelich, 1985).

To protect a sense of self-worth, both failure-avoiding and failure-accepting students may discount the importance of school altogether (Harter, Whitesell, & Junkin, 1998), redirecting effort toward other domains (sports, creative pursuits, trade skills) or, in some cases, toward delinquent behavior (Stipek, 2002). Because these two profiles are the hardest to reach and the least likely to signal their struggle directly, identifying which students hold a failure-avoiding or failure-accepting orientation — rather than assuming disengagement is simple laziness — is an important diagnostic step before attempting to build more positive mastery behaviors.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Enough observation of a student's actual strategies (not just outcomes) to distinguish, e.g., an overstriver's excessive rehearsal and detail-focus from a success-oriented student's genuine mastery orientation, or self-handicapping from simple low effort

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Positive reinforcement for successes is specifically documented as ineffective with failure-accepting students, since they attribute success to external causes rather than their own capability — a generic praise-based intervention will not reach this group [-M]
  • Self-handicapping strategies (procrastination, deliberate low effort, choosing unrealistically hard or easy tasks) can look identical to simple disengagement from the outside, risking misdiagnosis and mistargeted intervention

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text:
• Overstrivers, whose visible high achievement can mask fragile, fear-driven motivation and a real risk of burnout or cheating under pressure
  • Failure-avoiding and failure-accepting students specifically, since these two profiles are the ones teachers are most likely to overlook or misread as unmotivated rather than self-protecting

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Shifting failure-avoiding and failure-accepting students toward more positive mastery behaviors and an internal, controllable sense of agency over outcomes
  • Reducing self-handicapping behaviors that directly suppress learning opportunities (withdrawal, procrastination, deliberate non-effort)

docs.title: Supporting
docs.text:
• Goal Orientation Theory [+S] — this typology's approach/avoidance-of-failure axis directly parallels goal orientation theory's own approach/avoidance dimension
  • Self-Efficacy Theory [+S] — the failure-accepting profile is this typology's clearest instance of learned helplessness
  • Attribution Theory [+S] — failure-accepting students' external-success/internal-failure attribution pattern is a direct application of attribution theory's locus dimension

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Goal Orientation Theory — success-oriented students closely resemble a mastery-approach orientation; overstrivers resemble performance-approach mixed with performance-avoidance; failure-avoiding students resemble performance-avoidance and failure-avoidant goals directly
  • Self-Efficacy Theory — failure-accepting students' learned helplessness is this theory's own central failure mode
  • Attribution Theory — the typology's four profiles differ systematically in their attributions for success and failure

docs.title: Teaching Styles as Warmth and Control
Description
docs.text:
For many years, warmth and control were treated as opposite ends of a single continuum — a teacher who chose to be warm could not also be in control, and vice versa. Soar and Soar (1983) proposed instead that warmth and control are two independent dimensions that can occur in any combination and to any degree, each measured by its own set of classroom behaviors. Control runs from low (student spontaneity, risk-taking, student-initiated responses) to high (teacher talk, task orientation, teacher authority). Warmth runs from low (frequent reference to formal rules and procedures, punishment, criticism, scolding, reprimanding) to high (praise and rewards, use of student ideas, responsiveness to student requests). Crossing the two dimensions yields four teaching-style profiles:

  • Authoritarian (high control, low warmth) — a cold, controlling style that may humiliate or criticize students to control their behavior, producing a businesslike, task-oriented classroom with few teacher-student interchanges the teacher didn't initiate. Motivation to do high-level work is driven more by fear of punishment or embarrassment than by expectation of reward.
  • Authoritative (high control, high warmth) — classroom rules are mutually determined and a consistently applied system of praise and rewards motivates good behavior, so warmth and control coexist. Motivation for good behavior comes from that well-defined reward system, rather than from rules and punishment as in the authoritarian style. Soar and Soar (1983) note a specific risk here: excessive reliance on rewards can create an almost suffocating climate in which only teacher-identified behaviors are eligible for reward, leaving students little room to pursue behavior or activity independently.
  • Permissive (low control, high warmth) — the teacher praises and rewards frequently while giving students near-complete freedom to set the limits of their own behavior, which can produce confusion at the extreme. In a milder form, praise and rewards flow freely but student spontaneity and risk-taking are bounded to certain times or content areas, with the teacher acting as moderator or co-discussant rather than controller; warmth is conveyed mostly nonverbally, through rules that encourage individual initiative.
  • Neglectful (low control, low warmth) — a cold, permissive combination in which the teacher spends much of the time scolding and criticizing but has few rules actually constraining the behavior being criticized. This extreme sometimes appears when a substitute teacher takes over unannounced: unfamiliar with established rules and unable to fall back on them, and with a role limited to keeping order rather than creating rules, the substitute ends up "holding the line" mainly through criticizing, reprimanding, and punishing.

An effective classroom management plan blends warmth and control in a way that avoids the overly rigid, dictatorial form of control found in the authoritarian style — using instead a mutually agreed-upon set of rules paired with a well-defined, consistently applied system of praise and rewards, striking a genuine balance between the two dimensions rather than treating them as a single trade-off.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Applies to the ongoing, everyday climate a teacher establishes through rule-setting, response to misbehavior, and use of praise and reward — not to any single isolated classroom event
  • The four profiles describe corners of a continuous space; real teachers fall at varying points and may shift position across contexts (e.g., a normally authoritative teacher managing a lesson very strictly during a fire drill)

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • All students are affected by the ambient teaching style, though see Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms [~M] for how the same style can land differently depending on a student's cultural background (e.g. an interdependent-self student may experience a permissive, low-structure climate as unsettling rather than liberating)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Sustained work engagement and reduced disruptive behavior through a climate students want to remain part of, rather than one they comply with only under threat

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Rewarding an already-intrinsically-motivating activity can reduce future engagement with it [-M] — the authoritative style's own documented risk (a reward system so tightly managed it crowds out independent behavior) is a specific case of this broader effect

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Self-Determination Theory [~M] — SDT's caution against controlling, non-autonomy-supportive environments describes the same failure mode as the authoritarian profile and the authoritative style's reward-saturation risk
  • Ginott's Congruent Communication — a specific humanist technique set for building the communication side of an authoritative, warm-but-structured climate
  • Glasser's Choice Theory and Cooperative Learning — Glasser's "boss vs. leader" contrast maps closely onto the authoritarian/authoritative distinction
  • Kounin's Classroom Management Research — describes the specific teaching behaviors (rule-teaching, monitoring, timely consequences) that distinguish more effective managers regardless of where they fall on the warmth/control grid

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Effective Classroom Management Plan Criteria — a concrete synthesis of practices aimed at the authoritative combination of warmth and control

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Robert Sternberg's (1988) triarchic theory of intelligence proposes three distinct components of intelligence — analytical, creative, and practical — offered partly as a rebuttal to both Spearman's single-factor "g" and Cattell's fluid/crystallized split. Analytical intelligence is closely aligned with academic problem-solving: the ability to analyze, evaluate, judge, compare, and contrast, of the kind exercised in comparing literary characters or working a multi-step math problem. Creative intelligence is the ability to invent or imagine a novel solution to a problem or situation. Practical intelligence — sometimes compared to "street smarts" — is the ability to find solutions that work in everyday life by applying knowledge from one's own experience, and Sternberg's own research indicates it is empirically separable from the other two: a person can score high on practical intelligence without scoring comparably on analytical or creative measures, or vice versa.

Creativity itself, as measured against analytical intelligence, is not highly correlated with it (Furnham & Bakhtiar, 2008) — exceptionally creative scientists, artists, and mathematicians do not reliably outscore their less creative peers on intelligence tests (Simonton, 2000), and the brain areas associated with convergent thinking (finding the single correct answer) differ from those associated with divergent thinking (generating many possible answers) (Tarasova, Volf, & Razoumnikova, 2010; see Fostering Creative Thinking). Still, creativity draws on some of the same underlying abilities "g" measures, including learning from experience, remembering information, and abstract thought (Bink & Marsh, 2000). Across several researchers' work studying creative individuals (Ericsson, 1998; Weisberg, 2006; Hennessey & Amabile, 2010; Simonton, 1992), five components recur as important to creativity: expertise (creative people have studied and learned deeply about their domain), imaginative thinking (viewing problems in new ways), risk-taking (pursuing new but potentially unsuccessful approaches), intrinsic interest (working from genuine interest rather than external reward), and working in creative environments (being supported, aided, and challenged by others working on similar problems).

Practical intelligence has proven the hardest of the three components to validate as genuinely distinct from "g": although tests have been devised to measure it (Sternberg, Wagner, & Okazaki, 1993; Wagner & Sternberg, 1985), research has not found strong evidence that practical intelligence is separable from general intelligence or that it predicts success at particular tasks better than "g" does (Gottfredson, 2003) — it may capture certain job-specific abilities not strongly correlated with general intelligence, but the theory's claim that it constitutes a third, independent form of intelligence remains the triarchic model's weakest empirical leg.

The theory illustrates its analytical/creative/practical separability with a real-world case: during the 2007 Virginia Tech shootings, one student, hearing a chained-shut exit door, crawled back through a window into a room near the danger rather than questioning why the door was chained — a response reflecting some creative problem-solving but low practical judgment. Meanwhile, a pair of students who heard gunshots nearby chose to run away rather than investigate, demonstrating high practical intelligence. Neither case turns on academic or analytical ability; the decisive factor was practical judgment specifically.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Learning objectives or assessments that can distinguish which kind of intelligence a task actually exercises, rather than treating "problem-solving" as a single undifferentiated skill

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Like other multi-component intelligence theories, valid and reliable separate measurement of the three components is not straightforward
  • A learner's low performance on an analytical task does not imply low practical or creative ability, and instructional design should not conflate the three

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners whose strengths lie outside traditional academic/analytical measures (e.g., strong practical or creative problem-solvers who underperform on conventional analytical assessments)

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Real-world, applied judgment and decision-making (practical intelligence) as a target distinct from academic analysis or generating novel solutions

docs.title: Contradicting / Qualifying
docs.text: • Positioned as an alternative to Spearman's single-factor "g" model and Cattell's fluid/crystallized intelligence split, both of which treat intelligence as a smaller number of general factors rather than three functionally distinct components

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text: • Multiple Intelligences Theory — a more finely subdivided (eight-part) alternative to the same single-factor "g" model this theory also rejects, though the two frameworks propose different numbers and kinds of components

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Fostering Creative Thinking — the divergent/convergent thinking distinction this principle builds on maps directly onto the triarchic model's creative-intelligence component

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Elliot Turiel proposed that stage-based models of moral development (Piaget's and Kohlberg's) share an assumption worth questioning: that a person reasons from one unified "level" of moral development that applies uniformly across every kind of social rule. Turiel's social domain theory argues instead that children differentiate at least three distinct domains of social knowledge from early in development, and reason differently within each:

  • Moral domain — concerns fairness, equality, justice, and the welfare of others; violations in this domain (e.g., hitting another child) are treated as wrong independent of whether a rule against them exists, and independent of what an authority figure says.
  • Societal (conventional) domain — concerns social conventions, group functioning, and traditions (e.g., raising a hand before speaking, forms of address); these rules are understood to be context-dependent and changeable by group consensus rather than inherently right or wrong.
  • Personal domain — concerns matters of individual prerogative (e.g., choice of friends, personal appearance) that children come to see as not properly subject to group regulation at all.

Because these domains are differentiated rather than unified, a student's moral reasoning in one domain does not straightforwardly predict their reasoning in another — a student who reasons at a sophisticated level about fairness (moral domain) may reason quite differently about a dress code (societal domain) or a friendship choice (personal domain), and this is not a contradiction or a sign of inconsistent development. Decades of supporting research (spanning roughly 1980 onward) have found that even young children make this three-way distinction, well before they can articulate it explicitly, which challenges the assumption embedded in strict stage models that moral reasoning develops as a single, general-purpose capacity.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• A student's apparent "inconsistency" — reasoning at a high level about one kind of rule but a lower level about another — may simply reflect that the two situations belong to different domains, not a developmental contradiction requiring correction
  • Treating a societal-domain rule (a dress code, a seating chart) with the same moral weight as a moral-domain violation (harming another student) can undermine a student's ability to distinguish genuinely important ethical stakes from negotiable conventions

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • Learners across the developmental span — the domain distinction is present even in young children and persists into adulthood, unlike stage theories that describe a single trajectory of increasing sophistication

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Distinguishing moral obligations (fairness, harm) from social conventions (context-dependent norms) and from matters of personal choice
  • Recognizing that a rule's source (an authority, a group consensus, or an individual's own domain) affects whether it is properly treated as fixed or negotiable

docs.title: Related Theories
docs.text:
• Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development — Turiel's framework directly challenges the assumption that moral reasoning is a single, unified developmental ladder that Kohlberg's stage sequence depends on
  • Piaget's Theory of Moral Development — similarly complicated by domain differentiation, since Piaget's heteronomous/autonomous shift is described as a general cognitive change rather than domain-specific
  • Gilligan's Ethic of Care — both frameworks push back on collapsing moral reasoning into a single scale

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Classroom Space and Procedural Design — applies the moral/conventional distinction directly to why classroom procedures (conventional) and rules (moral) warrant different levels of student input and enforcement

docs.title: The von Restorff effect in text marking
Description
docs.text: The von Restorff effect is used to explain how underlining functions by isolating information against a background. The article suggests that if text is underlined, students "tend to study and remember that information better than nonunderlined information."

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Information must be isolated against a homogeneous background to increase recall.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: • The effect's utility depends on whether the underlined information is important or unimportant.

docs.title: Target Learners
docs.text: • College freshmen

docs.title: Target Learning Objectives
docs.text: • Text comprehension and recall
